15785-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
A weekly newspaper for boys and girls from William Beverley Harison of New York, sold at five cents. The copy held here opens with a picture of golf clubs, from wooden putter to niblick, offered as a premium for two new subscribers. News, science, and serial tales fill the rest, in plain words for young readers. The paper aimed to keep children abreast of the world week by week.

Golf notes, news items, and stories share the pages in the paper's usual lively mix. Editors explain distant events and new inventions without talking down to their readers. Serial threads and picture notes keep young eyes moving. Read today, the issue shows an 1897 childhood of clubs, premiums, and a weekly window on the wider world.
30769-the-baptist-magazine-vol-27-januar:
Held here is the 1835 annual volume of The Baptist Magazine, volume twenty-seven and volume ten of its third series, published in London by George Wightman. Its title page says profits from the sale went to the widows of Baptist ministers, at the recommendation of the contributors. Its motto, from Ephesians chapter four, verse fifteen, urges speaking the truth in love.

The editors' preface looks back on a year of anxious labor and thanks readers for candid appreciation and kind commendation. They aimed to give, in each number, religious instruction and denominational information suited to the magazine's design. For modern readers the volume offers sermons, news, and Baptist life in 1835, in the earnest, plain style of a church paper that served its readers month by month.
37583-the-baptist-magazine-vol-27-1835:
Baptist Magazine, volume twenty seven, is the eighteen thirty five year of the monthly. The March number opens with a memoir of Boswell Beddome of Weymouth. Beddome was youngest son of a Maze Pond deacon of long standing. His grandfather was Benjamin Beddome of Bourton, famed for sermons and hymns.

Relatives describe the boy as bright, generous, lively, and principled early. His maternal guardian praised his striking filial obedience in those years. All signs promised no common character in after life for the lad. The magazine served Baptist churches with memoirs, essays, and church news monthly. Bound yearly volumes gathered the numbers for chapel and home shelves.
39537-medieval-english-nunneries-c-1275-:
Eileen Power wrote this history of medieval English nunneries from about 1275 to 1535, printed at Cambridge in 1922. Power had been a fellow and lecturer at Girton College, Cambridge. The book sits in the Cambridge Studies in Medieval Life and Thought series. A plate from La Sainte Abbaye shows an abbess with her staff, nuns, and priests at the sacrament.

The general preface sets a high bar for the series. It holds that the historian must mark what is certain as certain, what is false as false, and what is doubtful as doubtful. That rule, drawn from a monk of the seventeenth century, guides the work. Readers get a careful study of how English nuns lived in the late middle ages.
40542-the-baptist-magazine-vol-27-june-1:
The June 1835 issue of The Baptist Magazine opens with a memoir of Isaac Wyke of Abergavenny. Wyke was a surgeon and a member of the Baptist church at Leominster. He was born there on July 25, 1770.

The memoir traces his youth under pious parents and a worthy pastor. At sixteen he was, in the words of the piece, renewed by grace. He was baptized and joined the church, and in time he was chosen as a deacon. His zeal and humble conduct won him the love of his fellow members. The issue preserves a full life of faith. Such memoirs were a staple of the magazine and of Baptist home reading.
53943-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger, volume one, number five, came out at Richmond in January eighteen hundred thirty five. T W White owned and printed the monthly. A year of the journal cost five dollars. Its motto says men move as they will, not as the winds will.

The lead piece is part three of sketches on Tripoli and the Barbary states. It centers on William Eaton, once a captain in the United States army. Eaton served as consul in Tunis from seventeen hundred ninety eight. His lord there, Bey Hamouda, had held his throne for years by wit and force. Frank talk and clash mark each meeting of the two men. The piece shows early United States ties in North Africa.
54451-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger was a Richmond monthly of letters and art. Volume one, number six is dated February 1835. White of Richmond owned and put out the sheet. Five dollars bought a year of its numbers then. Its motto says we rule our fate, not the winds.

The lead piece tells of the Virginia past society's year meet. It hopes that body will save the state's good name for lore. Rich stuffs for science and for the state's past lie at hand, it says. A taste for fine books must be spread through the land. Verse, tales, and grave talks fill the rest of the month. South letters had few such proud starts.
57732-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger of Richmond, Virginia, sold for five dollars a year under its owner and printer, White. Number 8 of the first volume is dated April 1835. The magazine pledged itself to every branch of letters and the fine arts, with a French motto from Crebillon at its head.

A note at the front regrets that the sixth part of Sketches of the History of Tripoli came too late for this month. The lead piece, written for the Messenger, takes up the sway of free government on the mind. Its writer calls mind the great centre that holds the thousand ties of life in order, as weight in space holds the rolling orbs.
58497-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger for July 1835 is the eleventh number of the first volume of a Richmond magazine. White published and printed the journal in that city. Its banner promises matter on every department of literature and the fine arts. The price was five dollars a year to subscribers.

A valedictory address by Professor Beverley Tucker heads this number. Tucker spoke to his class at William and Mary College on leaving them. The class sent his words to the magazine for printing. The editors give them place with pleasure, they say. They commend the counsel of the learned professor to all young gentlemen. The Messenger became a famed voice of southern letters. This early number shows it still in its first freshness.
58729-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger of Richmond, Virginia, closes its first volume with this number for August 1835. White published and printed the magazine at five dollars a year, devoted to every department of literature and the fine arts. A French motto heads the title page: as we will, and not as the winds will.

The lead piece is the seventh of a series of sketches of Tripoli and the other Barbary states. This installment turns to Algiers. That stronghold of piracy, the writer says, has been stripped of its terrors. A pasha of Algiers kept his throne only by keeping his troops busy in wars they could profit from. In 1805 the soldiery murdered their dey Mustapha for being too peaceable a man. The United States, the sketch notes, still paid its tribute. Southern readers of 1835 got the pirate coast surveyed from Richmond.
5938-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Crowded adventures fill chapters fifty-eight and fifty-nine of this Don Quixote portion, after the duke's household. Chapter fifty-eight tells how adventures came crowding on Quixote. They came in such numbers that they gave one another no breathing time. He saw himself in open country, free and relieved from Altisidora's attentions. Fresh spirits return for the pursuit of knight-errantry, with road, inns, and strangers ahead.

Chapter fifty-nine relates a strange thing, which may be regarded as adventure or omen, as the road offers new wonders. Readers get Quixote loose again, after captivity by courtesy, with the open country as his proper stage. The part suits readers following volume two toward Barcelona, since its crowded road prepares bandits, Roque, and the city's spectacles.
59383-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger, volume one, number thirteen, was printed at Richmond, Virginia, in September 1835, by White, publisher and proprietor, at five dollars per annum. The magazine is devoted to every department of literature and the fine arts. This number closes the first volume, and a title page and index go to each subscriber with it.

The leading piece continues the Sketches of the History and Present Condition of Tripoli, with some account of the other Barbary states. Number eight takes up April 1816. Admiral Lord Exmouth, commanding the British fleet in the Mediterranean, arrived at Algiers to negotiate with the Dey. He came with six sail of the line and nineteen smaller vessels, to give weight to his arguments. The terms he finally won freed thirty three Maltese and Gibraltar slaves without ransom. A treaty of peace followed for Sardinia, and ransom terms for the Two Sicilies.
59553-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger, volume I, is the first year of a Richmond literary magazine. T W White published and printed it in 1834-5. The magazine devoted itself to every department of literature and the fine arts. Its motto, from Crebillon's Electre, runs: as we will, and not as the winds will. The price was five dollars per annum.

The first number appeared in August 1834. White's notice prints letters of encouragement from eminent men. Washington Irving gives the enterprise his highest approbation. He professes a warm attachment to Virginia and the south. J K Paulding hopes the attempt will succeed. Virginia's talent, he writes, has chiefly run to politics. Directed to other literature, it should earn equal distinction. White hoped the letters would awaken the south's literary exertion from its long slumber. The volume gathers the magazine's first twelve months of essays, tales, and verse.
64767-the-southern-literary-messenger-vo:
The Southern Literary Messenger for December of eighteen thirty five is one issue of a monthly. This copy is the first number of the second volume of the run. Five dollars a year bought the Richmond sheet in that age. Its motto says it sails as we will, not as the winds will.

A front note tells that the past editor has left his chair of late. The house chief now runs the sheet with a man of high prose gifts. Rich feasts for the mind are pled in the year to come in the note. Verse, tales, and fine art notes fill the bulk of the issue in kind. The sheet was the souths chief voice in prose in its great years.
65265-the-migration-of-north-american-bi:
A government circular on bird migration by Frederick C Lincoln. The United States Department of Agriculture issued it in October 1935. It appeared as Circular Number 363 of the Bureau of Biological Survey. Lincoln led the section on distribution and migration of birds. The circular sold for ten cents through the Superintendent of Documents.

It replaced an older standard work. Wells W Cooke's Bird Migration bulletin dated from 1915. Lincoln added his own field investigations and newer records. Banding returns had begun to map the flyways by then. The circular summarises where North American birds breed and winter. It also explains the routes and timing of their travel. Wildlife managers and bird students used it as a basic reference.
6711-philip-dru-administrator-a-story-of:
Philip Dru, Administrator, subtitled A Story of Tomorrow, 1920-1935, opens with a Mazzini motto. It calls for no war of classes and no hostility to wealth. Instead it urges a steady wish to better the lot of those least favored by fortune. The book is dedicated to the unhappy many who lived and died lacking opportunity, because the world's social frame was wrongly begun.

Chapters follow Dru from graduation day and a vision in the desert to the winning of a medal, the story of the Levinskys, and the making of a president. Selwyn plots, Gloria proselytes the rich, and Dru meets his rival. Philip Dru is a curious, idealistic political novel, famous as a window on reform dreams of its day.
7106-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chap:
This part of Huckleberry Finn opens at chapter thirty one, with the raft kept from towns for days, running south into warm weather far from home. Trees draped in Spanish moss, hanging like long gray beards, strike Huck as solemn and dismal at first sight. The frauds, reckoning danger past, work the villages again, first with a temperance lecture that earns too little for both to get drunk on.

A dancing school follows, but the pair dance no better than a kangaroo, and the public prances them out of town. Elocution fails next, as the audience rises with a solid cussing and sends them skipping, and then come missionarying and mesmerizing. Chapters thirty one to thirty five close amid failed shows and southern river towns.
75571-symptoms-of-being-35:
Ring W Lardner wrote Symptoms of Being 35, a book of fun put out at Indianapolis in 1921. Helen E Jacoby drew the forms that mark the pages. Lardner had won a name with Gullible Travels and tales of war and home life. He opens by his claim that he makes no plaint on the score of age.

He says he will give the rules that brought him to 35 years. A man with a wife and four young ones, he jokes, has no call to hide his age. A friend named Legion rings him to ask him to a game of cards. Lardner begs off, since the last calls cost him dear. He claims he must write the book he owes his firm. The fun runs on tall tales, bad grammar used on purpose, and pride in plain life.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-:
Chapters 31 to 35 of Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn open with the king and duke broke and scheming worse deviltry. the blow falls on Jim: the king sells him for forty dollars and vanishes into a doggery in Pikesville. Huck, torn between the law he was taught and the friend he knows, writes to Miss Watson, tears the letter up, and decides to go to hell and free Jim.

At the Phelps farm, where Jim is held in a cabin, Huck is mistaken for Tom Sawyer, and the real Tom soon arrives under the name Sid. Tom insists that freeing a prisoner must follow the rules of adventure books, however simple the real way out would be. The stage is set for the long, absurd escape plot that closes the novel.
arxiv-2412-00035:
Marliadi Susanto, Nadihah Wahi, and Adem Kilicman modeled abalone growth with fractional calculus in twenty twenty-four. Abalone are valuable shellfish, and predicting their length growth helps farming and harvesting. The team adapted the McKendrick growth equation by giving it a fractional order, solved with the Adomian decomposition method and the Caputo fractional derivative.

Their analysis shows the model reduces to a special case of a Taylor series. Simulations across fractional orders show larger orders give larger predicted lengths. The order one half matched real growth data most closely. The authors conclude the fractional model predicts abalone growth more accurately than the classic whole-order version. The work is a small case study in how fractional models can flex to fit biological growth.
arxiv-2412-00235:
Low Earth orbit satellite fleets promise worldwide broadband, but how much data they can carry per unit of spectrum has a ceiling. Cuneyd Ozturk and co-authors compute that ceiling in a 2024 paper. They define spectral efficiency as the total data rate per unit bandwidth per unit area of Earth's surface.

To bound the value, the authors reduce the network to a single shared channel and study neat hexagonal layouts of satellites and ground terminals. Their math and simulations show this layout does cap the efficiency of multi-channel systems when each terminal connects to minimize total link distance. Smarter assignment rules do better by stopping neighboring satellites from serving the same patch at once. The paper underlines interference-aware pairing as the lever that matters.
arxiv-2412-01135:
Cashous Bortner, John Gilliana, Dev Patel, and Zaia Tamras reprove model sameness results with graph tools, in work from 2024. Different compartment models can yield identical behaviour, making data unable to pick the true one. Linear compartment models serve drug, cell, and ecology studies across many fields.

Path shaped models form the family under study, built on a directed path graph. Recent work gave first graph based rules for when such models cannot be told apart. Those proofs leaned hard on linear algebra machinery throughout their steps. Graph theory now carries the same results in a cleaner frame here. Shared structure, not matrix crunching, drives the indistinguishability verdicts.
arxiv-2412-01235:
Canqiang Weng and co-authors built a traffic system for city air taxis in a 2024 paper. Large fleets of short-hop aircraft will cluster over hot routes, such as suburb to center runs. Where routes cross, crash risk peaks, much as at road junctions, so guidance and dodging must work as one.

Their frame joins route guidance with collision avoidance in a real-time simulation. It steers each craft's path while keeping safe gaps at conflict points. Tests at city scale probe whether the frame holds as fleets grow. The work is a step toward safe skies over dense towns.
arxiv-2412-01535:
Alexandrou and co-authors compute key traits of the nucleon in a 2024 lattice study of quantum chromodynamics. The nucleon is the core building block of atomic nuclei, and its charges and sigma terms are basic numbers for nuclear physics.

The team used twisted mass fermions on three grids with like volume and three spacings, with quark masses near their true values. They computed axial, scalar, and tensor charges, plus the sigma terms, for both flavor types and with parts that are often left out. A model choice tool helped weigh errors from excited states. Their axial charge matched the measured value well, and they give sigma terms for light and strange quarks.
arxiv-2412-01935:
Manpreet Kaur, Ankur Tomar, Srijan Mishra, and Shashwat Verma work on teaching image translators to carry their skill from one data domain to another, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Deep networks are brittle: small shifts between training and target data can wreck accuracy. The team studies generator networks that translate images across domains under an adversarial setup.

They experiment with activation choices and encoder-decoder layouts, and they add a new training signal, a cyclic loss, that keeps the translator honest on round trips. The aim is a translator that stays effective when paired with the original domain's network. Motivating uses include making labeled data from synthetic inputs without hand annotation, and widening where trained models can be trusted.
arxiv-2412-02035:
Nadeen Fathallah, Steffen Staab, and Alsayed Algergawy test large language models as builders of ontologies for the life sciences. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses the NeOn-GPT pipeline, extended with sharper prompts and reuse of past ontologies. Ontologies map a field concepts and links in a form machines can reason with.

Life science ontologies are deep, with many levels and rich cross-links. Plain models run out of room and miss domain depth. The team judges output against a real water research ontology called AquaDiva. Checks cover logical soundness, coverage, and scale. Readers learn where language models can draft domain maps today and where expert hands remain vital.
arxiv-2412-02235:
Sourav Chakraborty and co-authors prove that a cheap test for a class of vast string traits buys a gap gauge for the same traits, in a paper from 2024. The traits live on strings so long that one full read is out of reach. Probes sip bits of a few strings, and cost counts probes, not time.

The traits here hold still when all strings shift their bits by one shared shuffle. A grid smooth trick bent from graph math does the lift. If a trait of this class can be probed or waved off with few probes, then its gap to the trait can also be read with few probes. Test ease and gauge ease thus stand or fall as one for this class.
arxiv-2412-02735:
Bhargava, Ghosh, and Dutta built a test set in twenty twenty-four to gauge if chat models can write hard unit tests for C++ code. Their set holds more than two thousand code and test pairs from fourteen open code bases. Those bases span nine fields, from learning tools to log and store code.

They try the set with in-text learning, light tune, and full tune of chat models. Tuned models beat their base forms in most tests by a large gap. The set's build snags and tune lessons are shared in full. Weights of the tuned models are shared for more work.
arxiv-2412-02935:
Shou and co-authors (2024) propose a network that reads emotions from conversations using text, audio, and video together. Emotion recognition in dialogue is usually built on graph networks that link utterances, but those tend to overfit and miss how a speaker's feelings evolve over time. Their model, DGODE, treats the conversation graph as a system that changes continuously.

An adaptive mixing mechanism spreads information across the graph in a way that generalizes better and resists the over-smoothing that flattens deep graph networks. A graph ordinary differential equation layer then evolves each node's state over time, capturing the temporal drift of emotion. On two public multimodal conversation datasets, the model beat a range of baselines. The authors also report that the design allows deeper graph networks than usual without the usual collapse of signal.
arxiv-2412-03935:
Sotirios Fragkos and eight co-authors create, in a 2024 preprint, a new controlled quantum state by shining twisting light on a layered crystal. The material, WSe2, has two valleys in its electron band structure that respond to opposite twists of light. That trait anchors valleytronics, which hopes to store information in valley choice. Separately, rhythmic driving can dress electrons into Floquet-Bloch states with new traits. The team merges the two ideas and names the result Floquet-Bloch valleytronics.

Using ultrafast ultraviolet microscopy plus theory, they show valley-polarized dressed states forming. The drive used below-bandgap chiral light pulses. Interference between the dressed states and free-electron-like states depended on both valley and light twist. A dichroism signal in the emitted electrons showed the orbital character of the states can be steered. The authors offer the work as a guide to building such phases with tailored light.
arxiv-2412-04135:
Jibril Ben Achour reviews exact black hole solutions inside a broad family of modified gravity theories. His manuscript, from twenty twenty-four, covers DHOST theories, which add a scalar field to gravity. The review first maps the theory space and its degeneracy rules. It then explains how field redefinitions shuffle solutions between theories.

That disformal map becomes a solution factory for hairy black holes. The disformed Kerr black hole gets a detailed walkthrough. Rotating cases found so far are surveyed, with an eye toward mimicking Kerr closely. The map also reshapes the field's algebraic type. Newer work extends the trick to radiating space-times.
arxiv-2412-04635:
Wance Wang, Sarthak Subhankar, and Joseph Britton wrote a practical guide to stabilizing lasers in a 2024 paper. A standard technique locks a laser's color to a reference by feeding back a correction signal, narrowing its spread. Getting that lock to perform well takes engineering craft that is scattered across papers and lab lore.

Older guides explain the error signal's theory but skip the feedback design. General control theory texts rarely mention this laser method at all. The authors fill the gap with a control-first walk-through: how to pick parts, measure the loop with modern instruments, and tune it step by step. They show the process on a real infrared laser used in atomic physics. Advanced tricks are left out on purpose. The target reader is a researcher building such a lock for the first time.
arxiv-2412-04835:
Ran Tian and five co-authors align robot policies with human tastes using far fewer preference judgments than earlier methods needed. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Robots pretrained on huge data still miss what each user actually wants. Asking people to rank endless robot clips to teach that taste is too costly.

Their method, RAPL, spends human feedback where it counts most: tuning the robot's visual encoder. Once the encoder sees the world more as the user does, feature matching builds a dense reward on its own. Tests in simulation covered a magic-themed bench and a real robot arm design. Hardware trials then tuned pretrained policies for three object tasks. RAPL matched rivals while using a fifth of the human data. It also carried across different robot bodies.
arxiv-2412-04935:
Eye scans called OCT show the retina's layers, and marking those layers guides care for retinal disease. Islam and co-authors present a method that outlines each layer through a signed distance function, a smooth map whose zero line traces the layer edge, instead of labeling pixels one by one. They add probability modeling so each shape estimate carries its own uncertainty.

The method beat rival approaches in both scores and visual checks. On scans spoiled by shadowing, blinking, speckle, or motion, the uncertainty maps flagged the doubtful zones. The authors see the work as a step toward judging layer integrity, a marker of how disease advances.
arxiv-2412-05035:
Tom Bachard and Thomas Maugey compress whole photo collections by meaning in a 2024 paper. Semantic compression judges loss by whether the meaning survives, not by pixel error. Most such schemes lean on the CLIP model, whose space describes images in words and pictures together.

Collections repeat themselves, and that redundancy is the target. The authors show CLIP's space supports easy semantic adding and subtracting. On that fact they build a shared dictionary codec for many images at once. It beat a leading generative codec on rate, near a hundred-thousandth of a bit per pixel per image, with fidelity kept. The learned dictionary itself reads as a semantic projector of image content.
arxiv-2412-05135:
Checking whether computer samples truly match a target distribution is a quiet headache in Bayesian statistics. Narayan Srinivasan and three co-authors note that the standard check, the kernel Stein discrepancy, costs too much for big sample sets, struggles in high dimensions, and needs fiddly tuning. Fast sampling methods that carry a small bias make the need for a good test sharper.

Their answer is a polynomial Stein discrepancy with a matching goodness-of-fit test. It is not a complete test of sameness, but they prove it catches any mismatch in the first several moments when the target is Gaussian. In experiments it proved stronger than rival tests at lower cost. It also helped users pick sampler settings more efficiently. The method appears in a 2024 paper.
arxiv-2412-05435:
Bohan Li and a large team of co-authors present UniScene, a single framework that makes training data for self-driving cars. Their work from two thousand twenty-four notes that most past methods make just one data form from a rough layout. Real driving tasks need more forms, and direct layout-to-data mapping is hard to learn.

UniScene works in two steps. First it builds semantic occupancy, a rich map of what fills space, from a set layout. Then, guided by that map, it makes video and LiDAR data with two new transfer tricks. In tests, UniScene beat prior best methods on all three data forms. The made data also helped real driving tasks downstream.
arxiv-2412-05735:
Zohair Shafi, Germans Savcisens, and Tina Eliassi-Rad present REGE in a 2024 paper on graph learning. Models that embed network data into numbers face two kinds of doubt: noisy or missing data, and the model's own unsure outputs. Attacks on the data can make both worse.

REGE attaches a radius to each embedding, a value that states how uncertain that point is. One training scheme folds in doubt about the data, and a second handles doubt about the output. In tests, the embeddings held up better under attack than leading rival methods, gaining about 1.5 percent in accuracy on average. The authors offer the radius as a built-in warning label for graph model results.
arxiv-2412-05835:
Patricio Peralta-Braz and co-authors modeled in 2024 structures that harvest vibration energy while also damping it. Metastructures are grids of identical resonators that block waves in chosen frequency bands. Adding piezoelectric patches lets them turn low-frequency shaking into electricity. The team built a multi-patch isogeometric model of such a plate, gluing patches together with a penalty method that enforces smooth bending.

The model matched published experimental and numerical data. A fresh plate design then went through a parameter sweep over resonator shapes. The sweep showed how geometry moves the blocked band and the first voltage peak. Those knobs decide whether a design favors power output or quiet. The authors offer the model as a partner for optimization routines. Bridges, machines, and vehicles supply the target vibrations.
arxiv-2412-06235:
Michael Yeung and co-authors present VariFace, a way to build fake face photo sets for training face recognition systems, in a research paper from 2024. Large sets scraped from the web raise privacy and bias concerns. Fake sets are safer, but past sets lacked variety and trained weaker systems than real photos did.

VariFace works in two stages with a diffusion model, a tool that builds images step by step. The team added three fixes: one cleans up group labels, one raises variety between people, and one balances keeping a person's look against varying their photos. At the same set size, VariFace beat older fake sets on test scores. In a larger run, it even beat a well-known real photo set across six test sets.
arxiv-2412-06335:
Jiexi Zhan and colleagues mine rider sharing graphs to group shared rides better, in work from 2024. Shared rides cut traffic jams, exhaust fumes, and per rider trip costs at once. Past matching tools skip how riders link with each other, trading speed for match quality.

Their frame builds a graph where riders join when a shared trip could serve both. A sharing loss score picks groups whose left out riders still pair well later. The core method then solves live matching fast on that graph structure. Two real data sets show big speed gains over the best prior tools. Served request counts also rose, by up to half in the best runs.
arxiv-2412-06735:
Ali Devran Kara and Serdar Yüksel review recent progress on steering systems when only part of the state can be seen, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Such problems model choices under fog, where beliefs about the hidden state guide action. The review spans math groundwork, sound shortcuts, and learning methods.

First come conditions that keep the belief model stable as data flows in. Those conditions yield proof that best plans exist and that value curves behave well. Next come finite shortcuts, by gridding or by short memory windows. Learning results close the review, with proof that methods can reach near-best plans under two cost styles.
arxiv-2412-06935:
Charo I del Genio, writing alone, extends a classic community-finding tool to networks with group interactions. The 2024 paper concerns hypergraphs, where one link can join many nodes at once, as in team authorship or group chats. Standard community detection assumes pairwise links, so it misses structure that only groups create.

The author defines a hypermodularity score that judges how well a grouping fits the higher-order links. With that score in hand, spectral methods, which use matrix eigenvalues, can search for good groupings. Tests on synthetic networks and real data show the groupings reflect how the modeled interactions actually behave. The tool helps analysts extract hidden modules from data sets where relationships come in groups rather than pairs.
arxiv-2412-07135:
Song, Zhang, and Yan defended a core security feature in this paper from twenty twenty-four. ASLR shuffles a program's memory layout so attackers cannot find targets. Tiny hardware side channels, though, can leak the shuffle secret. The authors catalogued the known leak paths across processor structures.

Their fix, Oreo, changes how memory addresses are handed to the hardware. The secret shuffled bits are stripped before address translation, so internal structures never see them. Programs need no changes to benefit. A prototype on Linux, tested in a hardware simulator, kept overhead low. The authors present the co-design as a broad shield against this class of leaks.
arxiv-2412-07335:
Wentao Qu and co-authors speed up a streaming data method in 2024 that sorts points into groups as they arrive. Such grouping must track data whose shape keeps shifting, yet older methods lean on a fixed codebook that cannot bend. Their model mixes a strict sparsity rule with a smooth penalty to get clean block-shaped groupings, a prized property.

A fast solver updates the codebook only at anchor points that mirror the stream's current shape, the team reports. That selective update keeps the method nimble and cheap. They prove the solver settles, and broad number tests back the design. Streams from cameras, sensors, and markets all drift; a grouper that drifts with them stays useful far longer than a frozen one.
arxiv-2412-07435:
Huanjian Zhou and Masashi Sugiyama cut the sequential cost of sampling from well-shaped probability distributions. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Sampling underlies machine learning and statistics, and as data grows, the number of serial steps becomes the bottleneck.

Recent parallel methods still lagged the best known limits for these log-concave distributions. Borrowing parallel simulation tricks from scientific computing, the pair devised a scheme with far fewer rounds. The depth now grows like the logarithm of the dimension, down from its square. For some cases that rate is provably optimal. The same ideas serve score-based diffusion models, the engines behind modern image generators. The authors frame the gain as closing a real gap in theory.
arxiv-2412-07835:
Ravi Joshi and co-authors study galaxies that host very strong magnesium gas clouds in a 2024 paper using deep Subaru telescope images. These clouds, seen against bright quasars, trace gas around galaxies at small distances.

From over four hundred strong systems, the team found more than a hundred host galaxies through glowing oxygen gas and light fitting. Hosts are mostly normal star-forming galaxies, with about a fifth in a starburst phase. The clouds line up with galaxy disk and wind paths. Some sight lines glow with no seen galaxy, hinting at faint hosts. The work ties these gas clouds to disks and outflows around young galaxies.
arxiv-2412-07935:
Henry Li broadens the theory of diffusion models, the systems behind much AI image making, in work from 2024. Such models learn to reverse a process that turns data into noise step by step. Textbooks assume each small step follows a bell curve shape.

Li shows that as steps shrink, the reversed process does not care about the step shape at all. That freedom was hiding in plain sight in the standard setup. Lifting the bell curve rule yields a wider family of valid models. It also frees the choice of training loss. Tests on standard image sets show that step shape changes the look of samples in clear ways.
arxiv-2412-08035:
Hanliang Zhang and four co-authors tackled whole-project code translation with large language models in twenty twenty-four. Such models write natural code in a new language, but their success drops sharply once code passes about one hundred lines. The team instead split a project into small pieces, translated each piece alone, and checked that each piece behaves the same as the source.

Two ideas made this work. Fixed rules guide the model where the two languages differ in subtle ways. Signature-level checks catch errors early, so repairs stay small. Applied to real Go projects moved to Rust, the method handled up to six thousand six hundred lines. About seventy-three percent of functions passed the behavior checks, well above prior work.
arxiv-2412-08235:
Doha Ouardi, Manel Barkallah, and Jean-Marie Jacquet introduce a software tool called B2Scala in this 2024 paper. The tool brings Bach, a small language for programs that share data through a common space, into the Scala programming language. Programs written this way pass notes by placing and reading items in the shared space rather than sending direct messages.

The authors also add a logic that limits program runs to those that meet stated rules. As a test, they model a classic security protocol with two parties and a secret exchange. Their setup found again, on its own, the well-known man-in-the-middle attack on that protocol.
arxiv-2412-08335:
A superconductor that breaks the arrow of time should not exist in peace with its own field, which makes any sighting worth a hard look. Naoki Matsubara and six co-authors report such a sighting in 2024 in a doped crystal that also hosts odd surface states. They read the crystal's face with a tunneling probe, watching how the current trace bends under a magnet.

The trace bore a lopsided mark near zero push. Flip the magnet, and the mark flipped with it, exact as a mirror. That dance fits a pair state whose own shape breaks time's arrow and grips the field hard. The team say the probe's feel for this break opens a new hunt in the family of topological stuffs.
arxiv-2412-08535:
José Carrillo, Tommaso Lorenzi, and Fiona Macfarlane model how mixed cell populations sort themselves as they invade new space. Tumors hold cell types that differ in shape and stiffness, and those traits change how each type moves. In their model, cells drift toward places where they feel less squeezed, and each type adds its own weight to the pressure. Their work appeared in 2024.

The team first writes the same process as single agents on a grid that divide, die, and wander under pressure rules. They then show the smooth model is the large-scale limit of that agent model. Wave solutions of the smooth model place the types in separate bands across the moving front. Computer runs of both models matched each other and the wave analysis closely. The results suggest that plain differences in mobility can drive the sorting.
arxiv-2412-08735:
Ares and co-authors present a physics method, published in 2024, for telling whether a quantum system's motion truly creates entanglement. Entanglement links particles so their states cannot be described apart, and it powers quantum technology. In open systems, where the surroundings interfere, apparent entanglement can be a mirage. Their method runs the usual random-path simulation of the system's waves, but bends each path away from entangled states. The bent paths carry only classical links.

Comparing the bent and free evolutions exposes how much entanglement the dynamics really build. The comparison needs no assumptions about inputs or outputs. The team also extends the matching master equations from two simple particles to many richer ones. The tool helps theorists judge whether a device or material can entangle on demand. That judgment is central to designing quantum machines.
arxiv-2412-08835:
Amirreza Shiralinasab Langari, Leila Yeganeh, and Kim Khoa Nguyen propose swapping out the neighborhood as the basic unit of graph neural networks, in a two thousand twenty-four paper. Message passing over neighborhoods caps what the network can say, at the Weisfeiler-Lehman test's power.

Their Grothendieck setup swaps in covers for neighborhoods, bringing back usual adjacency as a special case. Covers are turned, step by step, into matrices, making the idea both easy to analyze and easy to build. A flagship instance, Sieve Neural Networks, uses a cover of sieves borrowed from group theory to capture richer topology. The model records zero seen failures on hard graph isomorphism benchmarks and improves a label-spreading probe of topology awareness.
arxiv-2412-09235:
Alberto Chiarini and co-authors present a 2024 mathematics paper on entropic optimal transport. Transport with an entropy penalty is solved by Sinkhorn's algorithm, a workhorse in machine learning. How fast it converges, and how stable its plans are, matters for practice. The authors take a semiconcavity route: a curvature property of the transport potentials. For quadratic costs, stability bounds tie plan distance to marginal distance.

Those bounds yield a clean condition for exponential convergence of Sinkhorn's method. The condition needs no bounded cost, which widens its reach. Hessian control in key examples gives new fast-convergence results. Log-concave marginals with quadratic cost now converge exponentially for every penalty value. Optimization readers get guarantees where folklore once stood. Faster proven convergence means less compute burned per transport plan in real pipelines.
arxiv-2412-09335:
Lee asks if low food spoilage in cold climates fostered cultural complexity among early foragers, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Scholars have long debated how ecology freed time beyond subsistence. Cold settings with large game spoil stored food slowly. Lee builds a math framework linking spoilage, yield, skill, and cultural activity.

Within the framework, lower spoilage and adequate yields cut hunting frequency. Freed time then flows into cultural pursuits in the model. A reinforcement learning simulation trains agents across yield and spoilage settings. Agents in low-spoilage, stable niches develop the richest cultures, as predicted. The study blends humanistic questions with formal and computational rigor.
arxiv-2412-09435:
Vyacheslav Shalyapin, Luis Goicoechea, and Eleana Ruiz-Hinojosa settle, in a 2024 paper, a long argument over a lensed quasar's time delay. Gravity from a foreground galaxy splits the quasar's light into two images, and the light paths differ in length. Combining old records with seventeen years of new monitoring, the team measures the delay at 13.5 days, give or take a day and a half.

That firm number, plus other constraints, lets them weigh the lensing galaxy's structure. Its mass profile comes out close to isothermal, the standard simple shape. The mass also lines up well with the galaxy's infrared light, and the team recovers its true mass scale. The system is an odd one: outside deflectors bend the light unusually strongly while adding little shear. A simpler constant mass-to-light model also fits acceptably, they note.
arxiv-2412-09635:
Siwei Luo published this paper in 2024. It proposes a way for one AI system to hold many skills at once, modeled loosely on the hippocampus, the brain region that handles memory. The puzzle is how a system can learn task after task without each new skill wiping out the old ones.

The method stores the settings of each skill as a compact code. An autoencoder squeezes the settings of a working policy into a short skill vector, and a matching decoder rebuilds the settings from that vector when the skill is needed again. A graph network then maps how the subtasks relate and plans their order. In effect, the system swaps skills in and out the way a person recalls a learned routine.
arxiv-2412-09935:
Smart contracts guard millions of dollars on the Ethereum blockchain, and two bug families — reentrancy and unhandled exceptions — drain funds when missed. Chavhan Sujeet Yashavant and co-authors released in 2024 SCRUBD, a labeled dataset for grading the tools that hunt those bugs.

Existing datasets cover few scenarios and carry wrong labels, they note. SCRUBD mixes real contracts, labeled by crowd workers and checked by an expert, with crafted contracts spanning many reentrancy tricks. Grading six popular tools on it, they found different winners on real versus crafted data. The dataset aims to give the field a shared, trustworthy yardstick.
arxiv-2412-10335:
Joseph Brennan and Susan Morey work in 2024 on a branch of algebra that links graphs with sets of equations. Each graph gives rise to a set built from its edges, and the pair ask when sums of corner points act in a clean, regular way on that set. Their test turns on how the neighbors of an edge connect to each other.

Under a mild split condition, they show when such clean elements can be chained into a longer clean sequence. Those chains then let them work out a key counting series for the graph from a simpler count on a related graph. In one neat case, the result is the count vector of a graph with half as many corners. The work gives algebra users a graph based shortcut for counts that are hard to get by direct means.
arxiv-2412-10435:
Xin Dong, Sen Jia, and their co-authors present COEF-VQ, a 2024 system that judges short video quality with large multimodal models while saving computing power. Running such models on every video of a big platform would demand huge graphics hardware. Their design adds a cheap filter in front of the heavy model.

A light model first rates how unsure it is about each video. Only the unsure cases go on to the large model for the final call, in a cascade. This focus keeps the sorting quality of a full large model setup while cutting graphics use sharply. The team deployed the system on the video management platform of a short video service and ran detailed tests there.
arxiv-2412-10535:
April Yang and co-authors probe two kinds of toughness in language models in a 2024 paper. Models can break under crafted attacks or under odd new inputs. Whether strength on one front buys strength on the other was unknown. Fixes built for one type were cross tested on the other.

Gains barely carried across the two fronts in their benchmarks. Bigger models even showed a negative link between the two strengths. One mixture model broke the pattern with a positive link instead. Tailored, per model toughness plans are the authors' main advice.
arxiv-2412-10635:
Nick Huntington-Klein and Eleanor Murray test whether language models truly store causal knowledge. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Automating causal inference would speed up science greatly. Models would need to name the right confounders for a study. The Coronary Drug Project offers a ground truth. Expert lists of its confounders exist in several studies.

The models perform only mediocrely at the task. Expert-chosen confounders are barely likelier to be flagged than non-confounders. That is despite the truth sitting in the training text. Judgments swing widely across models and prompts. Even irrelevant wording changes flip answers. The authors warn against trusting models as causal oracles. Science automation needs stronger evidence than fluency.
arxiv-2412-10835:
Hasan Cildiroglu and Oguz Yayla built a quantum form of a light cipher called SLIM. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with how to run this code on a quantum machine. SLIM works on small blocks of data with a key of set size. It uses a Feistel structure, a common way to mix data in rounds.

Quantum machines could break some codes but block ciphers can stay safe with longer keys. The pair aimed to use as few qubits as they could. Their design keeps strength while it cuts the quantum cost. Readers who work on safe light codes get a lean path to run one on quantum hardware.
arxiv-2412-11235:
Vaibhav Pandey and Matteo Varbaro describe the hidden equations of a generic link built from the largest minors of a matrix of variables, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. In commutative algebra, linkage is a way to build new ideals from old ones, and this generic link's generators were not known.

The authors pin down the lead terms of those generators by degenerating the problem with a Gröbner basis. Their degeneration is careful: the simpler initial ideal keeps the full graded Betti table of the original, so no homological information is lost. From the initial ideal they prove that the link's symbolic and ordinary powers coincide, a strong regularity property. They also extract that an associated graded ring is Gorenstein. In positive characteristic, the blowup algebras turn out to be exceptionally well behaved as well. The paper turns an abstract link into something computable.
arxiv-2412-12135:
Aleena Thomas and two co-authors study controllability of a nonlinear networked system. Most results on this property cover networked systems with linear dynamics, while real networks are mixed and nonlinear. Their system is a controllable linear network with a nonlinear added term.

The added term is assumed to satisfy a Holder continuity condition, with the Lipschitz case included. Using a fixed point theorem, they prove the perturbed system remains controllable under those assumptions. Worked examples in numbers illustrate the result. The work extends network control theory toward the nonlinear systems met in practice.
arxiv-2412-12435:
One radio setup can both talk and sense if its receivers untangle the shared signals well. Walter Freitas, Gérard Favier, and André de Almeida build such receivers in a 2024 paper. Their scene pairs a sensing base with a talking user device.

Signals at the two ends follow two twin tensor shapes. Those shapes let the sensor read target traits from known data. The user side decodes symbols and channels with no prior channel map. Uniqueness terms spell out when the untangling holds. Tests show sharp sensing at mid noise levels. Talk quality held up alongside the sensing.
arxiv-2412-12935:
Mainak Poddar and Abhishek Sarkar put out a mathematics paper in 2024 broadening a framework in geometry. Lie algebroids over ringed spaces unite many shapes in geometry. They connect closely with certain structures of algebra used in physics. The authors push that framework one level more general.

Starting from any given Lie algebroid, they define a broader linked version. A matching broadening is built for the related Gerstenhaber algebras. The paper then checks which standard correspondences survive the move. Stretching those links shows the new meanings behave well. The work is basic, aimed at those who work in geometry and use these structures. It widens the setting where algebroid methods can be applied.
arxiv-2412-13135:
Jackson Gold and Maria Cuellar questioned fingerprint uniqueness in twenty twenty-four using the birthday paradox. Forensic practice treats fingerprints as unique identifiers, but hard evidence for that claim is thin, and recent artificial intelligence results hint that different people can share very similar prints. The authors revisit Francis Galton's eighteen ninety-two argument with modern probability.

Their calculation finds a fifty percent chance of a coincidental match in a population of fourteen million people, rising to near certainty at forty million. They introduce a Random Overlap Probability measure for given population sizes. The conclusion urges courts and examiners toward probabilistic reporting that prices in repetition risk, rather than categorical uniqueness claims, to improve reliability and fairness.
arxiv-2412-13435:
Mason Sawtell and co-authors guard chat models with a light sieve read off the model's own depths, in a study from 2024. Safety checks flag bad prompts and jail-break tries. Big guard models do it well but cost much. The team asks if a small, shrewd read can beat them.

Their way trains a plain ruled sieve on the hidden state of one mid layer of a language model. Small stock models, down to half a billion parts, gave rich traits. The sieve then beat a top paid model and tuned guards on both safety and jail-break tasks, from fewer than a hundred prime cases. Mid layers beat the last layer. One model can thus chat and guard at once, or be cut to its best layer and run as a lean guard.
arxiv-2412-13735:
Jiaqi Yang and twelve co-authors wrote this 2024 arXiv survey of three decades of 3D registration research. Registration is the task of aligning point clouds, the clouds of measured points that scanners and depth cameras produce, so separate views fuse into one model. Robots, self-driving systems, and mapping tools all depend on it.

The survey organizes the field's many solutions into families: rough pairwise alignment, fine pairwise alignment, aligning many views at once, alignment across scales, and scenes holding several copies of an object. For each it lays out data sets, scoring metrics, and the honest strengths and weaknesses of leading methods. A living project page tracks new work. The authors aim to give newcomers a map of thirty years of progress and give veterans a sober account of what remains unsolved.
arxiv-2412-13835:
Alberto Testoni, Barbara Plank, and Raquel Fernández probe ambiguous questions in image-based AI in a paper from 2024. A question about a picture can point to more than one thing in the scene. People resolve such ambiguity by asking follow-ups, but models may just guess. The team built a curated data set called RAcQUEt that targets several kinds of referential ambiguity.

Leading multimodal models often answered with misplaced confidence. A special subset showed a sharper risk, where unaddressed ambiguity led to stereotyped, biased replies. The authors argue models need honest ways to handle uncertainty. Guessing may look fluent while quietly spreading social bias. Their data set gives the field a focused test for this weakness.
arxiv-2412-13935:
Malay Pandey and colleagues forecast fine particle air pollution across cities and days in a 2024 paper. PM2.5, particles small enough to enter lungs, drifts with weather and long-range transport, so tomorrow's level at one station depends on today's levels far away as much as on local history. Their graph neural network treats monitoring stations as nodes and learns the spatial diffusion between them inside an encoder-decoder that reads the past and writes the future.

Gated recurrent units handle time, while a transformer-style graph convolution moves information across the station network. The design generalizes several earlier forecasting models as special cases. On two real datasets, including one from a new low-cost sensor network spanning hundreds of sites, the model proved effective, per the authors.
arxiv-2412-14035:
Manuel Egner, Matteo Fael, Alexander Lenz, Maria Laura Piscopo, Aleksey Rusov, Kay Schönwald, and Matthias Steinhauser wrote a 2024 paper predicting how long B mesons live. The catalog title carries a string of preprint codes, but the paper itself updates a standard theory for these short-lived particles. B mesons contain a heavy bottom quark, and their lifetimes test that theory sharply.

The team added the newest layer of quantum corrections to the decay rates of the free bottom quark. With those in place, their error bars shrank a lot, mostly because the results stopped shifting with an arbitrary scale choice. The new values for lifetimes and decay shares match lab data well. Such agreement strengthens trust in the theory used to hunt for new physics in these decays.
arxiv-2412-14135:
Zhiyuan Zeng and co-authors laid out a road map in 2024 to rebuild the reasoning skill of OpenAI's o1 from a learning-by-reward view. That model hit expert marks on hard tasks, and its maker credits reward-based learning as the core trick. Past copy work just mimics its style from a teacher, which caps how far it can go. This team breaks the skill into four parts: a start policy, reward design, search, and learning.

Each part plays its own role. The start policy gives the model a human-like way to probe. Rewards give dense guides. Search finds strong attempts in training and in use. Learning turns those attempts into a better policy. Past open projects map onto parts of this road, the team shows.
arxiv-2412-14235:
Dark matter may touch our world through a heavy go-between that pairs with known matter. Pouya Asadi and three co-authors map how a future muon collider could hunt that link in 2024. Their frame is freeze-in, where the dark stuff was never in full heat balance, so the sums set a top mass for the go-between.

Two hunt styles are worked out. Fast-decay cases call for cuts on pair masses, missing sideways push, angles, and energies to strip the known noise. Slow cases leave charged tracks or odd R-named lumps that decay late inside the machine. Each portal type gets its own signal and count. The study hands collider teams a ready playbook for a class of models that today's machines can miss.
arxiv-2412-14435:
Luis Roque, Carlos Soares, Vitor Cerqueira, and Luis Torgo expose cherry-picking in forecasting research in a 2024 paper. New forecasting methods are usually proven on a handful of chosen datasets. The team asks how much that choice bends the verdict. A broad bench of standard series lets them replay many papers' selection habits.

Picking just four friendly datasets lets nearly half of all methods claim best in class, they find. Over three quarters can reach the top three. Deep learning methods wobble most under selection, while classical ones hold steadier. Testing six datasets instead of three cuts the risk of crowning a false winner by about forty percent. Wider benches are the cure.
arxiv-2412-14635:
Bartosz Naskręcki and Piotr Pokora survey the geography of log-surfaces in a 2024 math review. A log-surface pairs a smooth surface with a rim curve drawn on it. Geography here means asking which sets of shape numbers such pairs can take, a guide to how rich or plain the pair can be.

The first half deals with the flat plane plus a set of smooth curves that cross in plain ways. The curves there are all of the simplest curved kind. The second half gives new results for pairs built on a K3 surface, a calm but deep shape in geometry. The pair give tests, in count terms, for when such a pair hits a slope value of three. Clear cases fill the text and help readers see the abstract rules at work.
arxiv-2412-14735:
Maria Chatzieleftheriou and co-authors wrote this 2024 physics paper on a layered material that superconducts in an unusual way. The compound Sr2RuO4 has puzzled physicists for decades, mixing superconductivity with strong magnetic fluctuations. Whether those fluctuations help or hinder the pairing of electrons is still argued.

The team built a theory that folds spatial magnetic fluctuations back into a realistic many-body model of the material. The fluctuations turned out to soften the correlations in the system. That softening stops the material from settling into magnetic order, matching what experiments see. Their computed spin response lines up closely with measured data, peaks and all. An odd dome in the response was traced to one flat, two-dimensional orbital, the same one thought to drive the superconductivity.
arxiv-2412-14935:
Daniil Medyakov, Gleb Molodtsov, and Aleksandr Beznosikov present, in a 2024 paper, a method for solving variational inequalities when the data are split across many machines. Such problems cover tasks from training generative models to game theory. Sharing data between machines is costly, so squeezing what is sent, called compression, is a prized trick.

Their method adapts advanced tools first built for plain minimization to the inequality setting, where each machine sends compressed updates. They give a full proof of convergence for a class of well-behaved, strongly monotone problems. Tests back the theory and show strong practical speed. The work matters for federated learning, where phones or hospitals must train together without shipping raw data.
arxiv-2412-15035:
Felix Friedrich and co-authors test language model safety across languages in a 2024 paper. A model that refuses a harmful request in English may comply in Italian, and safety work rarely checks. Their benchmark, M-ALERT, holds fifteen thousand prompts in each of five languages, tagged by harm category.

Thirty nine leading models faced the full set. Safety swung widely by language and topic: one flagship model failed often on tax crime prompts in Italian while staying safe elsewhere. A few categories, like cannabis and propaganda crime, tripped nearly every model in every language. The authors argue that multilingual safety testing must become routine, since users everywhere deserve the same guardrails.
arxiv-2412-15135:
Chunyan Mu, Nima Motamed, Natasha Alechina, and Brian Logan extend a logic for reasoning about strategy under chance and partial views. Their 2024 paper adds operators that grade how visible one agent's acts are to others. Past logics could not state such transparency claims.

Transparency matters in security, privacy, and choice design. The new frame grades observability of time-based properties for each agent. It works over stochastic systems with many agents. The authors prove that checking models against the new logic can always be settled by an algorithm. That decidability result keeps the richer language usable in practice. The work opens formal checks on who can see what, and how much.
arxiv-2412-15535:
Growing up with a father who drinks too much can scar adult life, and William Bekerman and co-authors lay out a study plan to trace those scars, in work from twenty twenty-four. Past work tracked harm in youth, but adult echoes are thinly known. Their plan uses a long Wisconsin study that follows lives over decades.

Outcomes span money success, bonds with others, and body and mind health. The same check runs on two split groups, so the team can test whether the story repeats. A new design, called data turnover, lets one team weigh proof strength across splits while mixing number work with close reading. The plan closes with notes on care points for such split-sample work.
arxiv-2412-15635:
Pyatkov and Soldatov study inverse problems for heat and mass transfer in a 2024 paper. The setting is a second-order parabolic equation, the classic model for spreading heat. Some lower-order coefficients in the equation are unknown, written as short time-varying series, and the task is to recover them from measurements.

The extra data are weighted integrals of the solution taken over the domain's boundary. The authors prove that solutions exist, are unique, and depend stably on the data. Their route reshapes the problem into an operator equation and solves it with a fixed point argument backed by prior estimates. Since the proof builds the solution step by step, it can seed new numerical methods for these recovery problems.
arxiv-2412-16135:
Seyedreza Mohseni and seven co-authors ask whether large language models can obfuscate assembly code, in work from 2024. Malware writers use obfuscation to evade detection, but current tools need source code and much manual work. Their benchmark, MetamorphASM, tests models on three techniques: dead code, register substitution and control flow change.

The linked dataset holds a very large set of obfuscated assembly samples. A range of leading code and language models were scored with information measures and human review. Results confirm that models can produce such code, which the authors frame as a risk for antivirus tools. The dataset is released so others can study defences.
arxiv-2412-16335:
Daniel Smolyak and co-authors study fairness in health models in this 2024 paper. Medical data sets often hold uneven shares of demographic groups, and models trained on them can serve the larger groups better. One proposed fix is to add made-up data. The team built a pipeline that uses GPT-4 Turbo to create extra records for each group on its own.

They tried the method on two real data sets and checked the fake records for quality first. Then they trained models with and without the added data and compared scores across groups. The added data usually beat standard baselines, though asking the model to target a named group gave little extra gain. The authors present the method as one more tool for fairer health models, and call for more work on when it helps.
arxiv-2412-16735:
Daoming Liu, Jonathan Klein, and four co-authors present FlameForge, a simulator for burning wooden structures. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, handles general shapes, not just flat boards. Wood burns in phases, forming a char layer that insulates what lies beneath. Their grid-based volume model captures that multi-phase process.

A distance field tracks surfaces so char effects price in cheaply. Non-charring glass and non-burning stone also fit the model. Memory-saving structures keep big scenes affordable. Test scenes span many shapes and materials. Coupling with a physics engine bends structures as they burn. Readings from a real burn check the numbers.
arxiv-2412-17435:
Jinhyeok Heo, Donghoon Ha, and Jeong San Kim show that extra information handed over after a quantum measurement can create or destroy nonlocality, in a 2024 paper. Which of the two happens depends on how the clues are grouped. In state discrimination, distant parties guess which state was prepared; sometimes no local strategy achieves the best possible guess, and that gap is the nonlocality.

Recent work showed that revealing which subensemble the state came from can switch the gap on or off. The new result makes the effect partition-dependent: how the original ensemble is split into subensembles decides the outcome. The authors derive sufficient conditions for each direction and build explicit two-party ensembles satisfying them. The moral is that nonlocality here is not a fixed property of the states alone. It lives partly in how the question is framed after the fact.
arxiv-2412-17535:
Gregory Adkins and Ulrich Jentschura tackle a fine correction in atomic physics in a 2024 paper. They study muonic bound systems, where a heavy muon orbits a nucleus. Tiny shifts in energy levels test how well theory matches nature. Their target is a three-loop effect from empty space itself.

They compute the part of that effect that cannot be broken into simpler pieces. The work covers light nuclei across a small range of charges. The shift turns out to be as large as other corrections that workers already take seriously. Their method also removes a source of doubt that troubled earlier calculations, making the result cleaner to use.
arxiv-2412-18035:
Palit and Sharma built a learning tool in twenty twenty-four that rewrites code in a clean form on its own, for Java code. The task pulls a block of code out into its own named step. Past tools need a coder to mark the block and give it a name.

Their tool tunes a code model, then aligns it with trial-and-score learning. Pay comes from clean builds and the pull-out being in the new code. The aligned tool beat plain tune on score tests by a clear gap. It also passed far more unit tests than the plain tool did.
arxiv-2412-18435:
Why are some particle masses enormously larger than others? Tetsutaro Higaki and co-authors build hierarchy from symmetry. In their models, a finite modular symmetry governs extra fields called moduli, and quantum corrections from heavy partner particles pin those moduli at large values. At such values an approximate shift symmetry survives, and its leftovers suppress some interactions by a tiny exponential factor, the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism long used to explain flavor patterns.

Earlier work stabilized one modulus; this paper stabilizes several at once, letting different hierarchies coexist in a single model. One modulus, settled at a modest value, can generate the quark and lepton mass patterns of the Standard Model. Another, settled far higher, leaves a flat direction that the authors identify as a candidate for the QCD axion, the hypothetical particle tied to dark matter.
arxiv-2412-18535:
Xinyu Yang, Yu Sun, Xinyang Chen, Ying Zhang, and Xiaojie Yuan fill gaps in sensor data by learning the map between stations as they go, in a 2024 paper. Spatial-temporal data often arrive with missing values. Most filling methods assume one fixed map of relations. That assumption fails when different measures relate differently across space. Air temperature and traffic, say, follow different geographies. The team's framework learns several maps at once.

One learning layer adapts the map per feature across stations. Another finds shared structure among features at each station. A prominence step weights important stations and features more. Cross-feature and cross-time learning capture the remaining patterns. Six real incomplete datasets tested the system. It beat prior methods on the filling task. The authors argue dynamic maps are the key advance. Fixed graphs, they say, belong to a simpler era of sensor networks.
arxiv-2412-19235:
Neural nets that fold physics laws into their training can solve hard equations, and a long-standing claim says two hidden layers are plenty. Vasiliy Es'kin and co-authors test that claim in work from twenty twenty-four, and push it further with nets that hold a single hidden layer. Much of the work deals with how to start and train such small nets well.

The team gives a fixed, step-by-step start rule with no random draws, plus fresh ways to weigh errors during training. A neuron-by-neuron fit method needs no outside solver at all. Tests cover one- and two-dim problems, the latter split across paired small nets. The results show small nets can still solve physics tasks with tight control over how far they stretch to new cases.
arxiv-2412-19435: Dmitry Demskoi gives the exact general solution for the finite forms of the Ferapontov-Shabat-Yamilov lattice in this 2024 paper. That lattice is a chain of coupled equations from lattice physics. His method avoids quadrature, so no integrals need solving along the way. A recurrence also builds the system's characteristic integrals. They are the conserved quantities that mark such systems as integrable. The derivation runs through the determinantal equations beneath the lattice, and a case with two parts shows the method at work in practice.
arxiv-2412-19735:
Siqiang Su, Zhenghao Li, Long Feng, and Ting Li presented in 2024 a general framework for imaging genetics, which links brain scans, genes, and traits. Both data types are high-dimensional, and brain images carry spatial structure that plain flattening wastes. Their method models all three parts jointly.

Built on canonical correlation analysis, the model can pick out significant brain regions and select important genetic variants tied to a clinical outcome at the same time. Scalable algorithms handle the double big-data load. Applied to UK Biobank data, the method tied reaction speed, a sign of cognitive function, to the caudate nucleus region and to specific genetic markers and the genes they regulate.
arxiv-2501-00235:
Daeyoung Jeong, Tongseok Lim, and Euncheol Shin design interventions that survive a hostile network. Their paper, published in 2024 per the head, casts the problem as a game: a decision maker acts while an adversary reshapes the network inside a set of plausible forms. Settings span learning, social spread, and financial contagion.

Using duality, they pin down the one best robust move and the worst-case network it guards against. That worst case has a rank-one shape, piling risk along the intervention itself. They price the cost of robustness under broad and narrow doubt, and study how deeper layers of uncertainty shift the answer. The frame suits policy and regulation where the web itself cannot be trusted.
arxiv-2501-00435:
Cutting a marked surface into pieces with d sides gives rise to an algebraic object: a quiver carrying an extra structure called a superpotential. Bo Le and Bin Zhu build that object for each such cutting of an unpunctured marked surface, generalizing earlier work on triangulations. Their head dates the work to 2024.

The main result links geometry to algebra. Flipping one piece of the cutting matches, up to a standard equivalence, a known mutation operation on the quiver's Ginzburg algebra. Working in the higher cluster categories built from these quivers, the authors also prove that certain nearly complete tilting objects have exactly d minus one complements. The results extend the dictionary between surface geometry and cluster theory to higher dimensions.
arxiv-2501-00535:
Yating Liu and Claire Donnat extend topic modeling to data with extra dimensions, in a paper whose head dates it to 2024. Topic models sort documents into themes, treating each document as a mix of topics. Fast recent methods handle plain document piles well, but they cannot easily use time, place, or other labels attached to each text.

Their method reshapes the data as a tensor, a grid with several axes, and applies a higher-order splitting method to estimate topics and clusters at once. A core grid then shows how the hidden factors interact. They prove how fast the estimates converge, in a strict entry-by-entry sense. Tests on made-up data and on research abstracts showed the method recovers patterns across dimensions better than flat approaches.
arxiv-2501-00635:
Natasha Kirova and Serguei Brazovskii model how light pulses can flip a material into a new state in this paper, recorded in the head as published in 2024. In certain organic compounds, light-made excitations tangle with the material's own ordering, which can switch between neutral and ionic forms. Both the excitation and the order grow from the same electron transfers, which complicates the picture.

Their model treats the ground state as an excitonic insulator, a phase that appears when excitation energy turns negative. After a pulse, excitations can condense into a shared quantum state, then pile up until they trigger the switch locally. The material splits into domains that change at different times, and the new pattern can outlive the excitations that caused it.
arxiv-2501-00735:
Maurya and co-authors model compact stars heavy enough to sit in the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes, in a 2025 paper. Such objects arise in star mergers and as giant pulsars, yet their sizes are hard to gauge. The team uses a gravity decoupling trick on a strange star model. Two dials, a decoupling value and a bag value, shape the star's stiffness.

Mass and radius curves from the model can cover the gap masses seen in wave events. Top mass reaches near three solar masses at the softest bag setting. Radius and spin inertia forecasts follow from the same curves. The authors offer the model as a test bed for merger leftovers.
arxiv-2501-01335:
Johan Wahreus, Ahmed Mohamed Hussain, and Panos Papadimitratos published a computing paper in 2025 on a prompt dataset for testing language model safety in cybersecurity. Jailbreak studies usually use broad, open-ended prompt sets, which blur results in a single domain. Their dataset, CySecBench, holds over twelve thousand close-ended prompts across ten attack types, all in the security domain.

They also detail how the set was generated and filtered, a recipe others can adapt. A prompt-obfuscation attack tested on it freed harmful content from two commercial models at high rates, while a third model resisted far better. The authors argue domain-specific benchmarks give cleaner measures of model safeguards.
arxiv-2501-01435:
Mario Fritz warns that general purpose AI is absorbing lessons cybersecurity learned the hard way, in a paper published in 2024. Language models have raced from chatbots toward something like an operating system for applications, gaining tool use, data access, and the power to trigger actions. Each step widens the attack surface.

Fritz surveys evaluation work his group and others have done on these systems, then maps what remains open. The core claim is that deployment practice treats models as features while they behave like privileged infrastructure. Borrowing security habits such as threat modeling and least privilege, he argues, should happen before incidents force the issue rather than after.
arxiv-2501-01735:
Jiangtao Shi and Yunfeng Tian wrote a 2025 math paper on finite groups and their large subgroups. The work looks at groups where some of the largest subgroups that stay fixed under a group action have a special size. That size is a prime number, or the square of a prime.

The authors first prove results on when such groups must be solvable, a key trait in group theory. Their results extend a known theorem by Hall and other past work. They then give a full description of groups that meet a tighter form of the condition, tied to subgroups that hold the normalizer of a Sylow subgroup. The paper is a pure math proof, aimed at readers who work on group structure.
arxiv-2501-02035:
Stella Girtsou and co-authors present a 2025 method to rebuild 3D cloud structure from satellite views. Clouds sway Earth energy balance and cloud climate models. Live 3D cloud data would sharpen forecasts. The team pairs geostationary images with space radar profiles of clouds.

Masked autoencoders first learn from unlabeled satellite images. A geospatial-aware variant adds place knowledge to that learning. Fine-tuning then matches images to radar cloud profiles. The method beat standard U-Net baselines. Geospatial encoding lifted scores further. Better cloud maps feed weather and climate models alike. They also help nowcasting for storms and aviation safety.
arxiv-2501-02135:
Sanjoy Chowdhury and co-authors build AVTrustBench to grade how much audio-visual AI models can be trusted. Benchmarks so far test sight alone, skipping half of what these models claim to do. Their set holds 600,000 samples across nine crafted tasks. Three trust angles are probed: attacks, combined reasoning, and leaning on one sense over the other.

Thirteen leading models took the full battery of tests. Most fell well short of human-like grasp of sound plus sight. The team also offers CAVPref, a training tweak that calibrates answers under tampered inputs. It lifted scores by up to about thirty percent across all nine tasks. Code and data will be released for public use.
arxiv-2501-02235: Camille Barboule, Benjamin Piwowarski, and Yoan Chabot survey in 2025 the young field of question answering over visually rich documents: forms, invoices, and scanned pages where layout carries meaning. The field is evolving fast and still lacks consensus on key parts of the processing pipeline. Their overview walks through the state of the art, weighing each approach's strengths and limits, names the main open challenges, and proposes research directions they judge most promising.
arxiv-2501-02435:
Sudarshan Vijay and co-authors speed up charged-system simulations in a 2025 paper. Density functional theory drives work on catalysts and energy materials, yet standard codes force overall charge neutrality. Charged molecules and surfaces break that rule, so special handling is needed.

Their method truncates the electric kernel to impose zero- or two-dimensional boundary rules inside a major simulation package. A padding trick strips false potentials from empty space at low cost. Tests include a charged chlorine defect on salt and long simulations of a stepped gold surface in water. The approach makes large charged supercells practical for routine study.
arxiv-2501-02535:
Alexander Kozachinskiy and Tomasz Steifer solve a neat problem about transformer models, in a 2025 paper. Parity asks whether a string of bits holds an even or odd count of ones. It is a classic hard test for simple networks. The authors build a transformer that can judge parity for strings of any length.
