Their design has three layers and a fixed size. Neither the weights nor the code for position in the string depends on string length. An earlier design needed only two layers, but its position code grew with the input. The new result trades one extra layer for full sameness across lengths. Results of this kind map the true limits of the transformer design. They show which tasks the design can handle in a strict, uniform way.
arxiv-2501-02635:
Kevin Ros, Dhyey Pandya, and ChengXiang Zhai present a 2025 arXiv paper on predicting what a searcher wants before they finish asking. The user picks a context, such as a paragraph or a single word, and may add a partial intent word like "how" or "why". Models must then guess the full information need behind the search.

The team tested generative models that state the need as a question, and retrieval models that answer it directly. Prediction worked in many cases. A partial intent word helped most when the chosen context was large and vague. The authors present the setup as ready for real search tools.
arxiv-2501-02935:
Verena Heidrich-Meisner and co-authors ask why two trusted schemes for spotting solar wind from coronal holes disagree so sharply. During a quiet sun phase in two thousand nine, one scheme called nearly all wind coronal hole wind, while the other called almost none. Their 2025 study compares the schemes on a decade of spacecraft data.

The charge-based scheme likely mislabels some slow wind as coronal hole wind during quiet times, they find. A machine learning grouping, used as a referee, splits coronal hole wind into two types that swap dominance across the sun's cycle. Few low-latitude holes existed in that quiet year, making a low count plausible. The authors urge that origin labels for wind take the sun's cycle phase into account.
arxiv-2501-03635:
Mei Wu, Yiqian Lin, Tianfan Jiang, and Wenchao Weng present a graph neural network for traffic prediction in this 2025 paper. Traffic data does not sit on a neat grid, and older models often force it into a simple graph with one kind of node and edge.

Their network, MHGNet, builds a richer graph with several node and edge types. One module splits single pattern data into several patterns using time and node embeddings. Another groups like nodes fast, and further modules mix space and time signals and reweight nodes. Wide tests and ablation studies on four benchmarks showed strong results, which the authors offer for smart transport systems.
arxiv-2501-03735:
Pawłowski and co-authors probe spin transport in Heisenberg chains through the Thouless lens of level sensitivity. The test asks how energy levels shift when boundary rules twist, a probe of how spin flows. The clean easy-axis chain is integrable, and its spin flow is diffusive, yet its sensitivity looks near ballistic.

In their 2025 paper, one ensemble lets that odd match be proved outright, while numeric work backs the other. A small integrability-breaking nudge then cuts the sensitivity hard. The dip lands where odd diffusion gives way to plain dissipation, the same point where random matrix behavior sets in. The spin conductivity seems to jump, scaled by the nudge strength.
arxiv-2501-03835:
Yindu Su and co-authors recast a core e-commerce chore, reading attribute values out of product listings, as a search problem, in a 2025 paper. Sellers write profiles in free text; platforms need tidy values for search and recommendation. Older methods stumble on values that are implied rather than stated, on values never seen before, and on messy output formats. Their method, TACLR, encodes profiles and candidate values into vectors and retrieves the closest matches.

Training uses contrastive learning with hard negative examples chosen by the product taxonomy, and inference adapts its threshold on the fly. The system scales to thousands of categories and millions of values. It already runs on the Xianyu marketplace, processing millions of listings daily against a frequently updated taxonomy. Benchmarks on public and private data back the design, and the code is public.
arxiv-2501-03935:
Motoo Tange, writing alone in 2025, studies when exotic four-dimensional surfaces admit simple handle decompositions. The surfaces arise from elliptic surfaces by knot surgery or log transformation, operations that can produce exotic copies of known spaces. A decomposition without one-handles is a strong simplicity property.

Tange gives a sufficient condition in terms of a knot's bridge number. When that number is small enough relative to the surface, the surgered surface needs no one-handles. Similar bounds hold for single and double log transformations. Such results help topologists compare the smooth structures that make four dimensions unique.
arxiv-2501-04035:
Ning Jiang and his three co-authors, publishing in 2025, settle a basic question about the thin gas layer where a flow meets a wall. This Knudsen layer sits at the scale where gas stops behaving like a fluid and starts behaving like individual molecules. Its governing equation, with particles streaming in at the boundary, was known to change character with the speed of the distant gas, and proofs covered only slices of the problem.

The team proves the equation has exactly one solution across the full range. All standard collision kernels for how molecules bounce are covered, and every far-field Mach number, from still air to supersonic. The solution also decays exponentially away from the wall, at a rate they state precisely. The trick is an added damping term and a carefully mixed weight over position and velocity. The result closes a long-standing gap in kinetic theory.
arxiv-2501-04635:
Te-Lun Yang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a question-answering system built on retrieval and generation. The system draws facts from Chinese Wikipedia and a legal database called Lawbank. A dense retriever model, BGE-M3, finds passages close in meaning to each question. A reranker then orders those passages by true relevance. The best passages feed a large language model as reference knowledge. Two question sets test the system, one general and one exam-style.

Scoring runs in two stages: fully automatic checks, and assisted scoring with human help on finance-related items. Information retrieval readers get a worked pipeline where retrieval quality visibly drives answer quality. Grounding answers in retrieved law and encyclopedia text fights the confident invention language models are known for. The legal source adds a high-stakes domain where invented answers carry real cost.
arxiv-2501-05135:
Senthamizhan and co-authors explore in 2025 the odd states that arise when swarming oscillators feel frustration, a lag in how their phases pull on each other. Such units, called swarmalators, both gather in space and fall into step in time. That pairing makes them a model for many real groups. The team studied them spread across a flat plane.

As the lag varied, the units formed still clusters and split states where only part of the group fell into step. In other states the whole crowd drifted across the plane on its own. The split states point to the lag's role in breaking the crowd into clusters. The authors sort the states by clear measures.
arxiv-2501-05235:
Lucas Moriggi and Magno Machado study gluon spread in 2025 through nonextensive statistics, with an eye on what the shift means for QCD. Gluons pack dense in fast crashes, and their cross-motion spread shapes what flies out of the hit zone. A nonextensive frame tweaks that spread at high pack grades in a set way.

Growth rules seen in crash data fall out of the tweak, the authors argue in the study. Both high and low cross-motion zones of made hadrons fit well under the frame. Crash types span proton pairs, proton on nucleus, and heavy ion hits, which gives the claim wide scope.
arxiv-2501-05335:
Magid Badaoui and Serge Dmitrieff study how branched actin networks grow under load in a 2025 paper. Actin is a protein that builds scaffolding inside cells. Its branched networks push on cell membranes and help cells move and divide. The team asked how fast such a network grows when a force resists it. They combined computer simulations with theory to trace the link between force and speed.

The network adapts to the load and shows two regimes. At low stress it grows at a steady finite speed. At higher stress its speed fades in a power law pattern. The authors explain the fade through the network's elasticity and the tangling of its filaments. Drag inside the network caps the top speed. They also find a sharp switch: once the stall force of single filaments passes a threshold set by the stress, a stalled network starts growing again.
arxiv-2501-06235:
Self-driving systems must label every point in a laser scan and keep each object's identity steady over time. Nirit Alkalay, Roy Orfaig, and Ben-Zion Bobrovsky presented a tracker for that task in 2025, called NextStop. Earlier trackers relied on short-term detection only, ignored motion estimates, and dropped small objects, which caused frequent identity switches between frames.

NextStop adds motion estimation with Kalman filters, careful matching of objects across frames, and management of how long a track should live. A tracklet state system ranks which tracks to trust. On a standard validation set, it tracked small objects such as people and cyclists better, started tracks earlier, and switched identities less often.
arxiv-2501-06435:
Mohsen Soltanifar and Chel Hee Lee present a software package for health data research, in work from 2025. Their R package, CMHSU, flags mental health status, substance use status, and both at once in large North American record banks. Doctors and policy makers have sought such joint flags for four decades, but no stand-alone tool applied the leading data-driven method.

The package counts hospital and doctor visits and weighs time spans to assign each flag. A worked case built on fake but lifelike data shows its main checks and time trends. The authors also list the tool's limits and paths to grow it. The package is free through the CRAN archive.
arxiv-2501-06935:
Gregory Gutin, Mads Anker Nielsen, Anders Yeo, and Yacong Zhou work in 2025 on one of graph theory's long-open puzzles. How many disjoint ways can a directed network's arrows be cut to break every loop? Removing a set of arcs that kills all directed cycles is called a feedback arc set. Packing the maximum number of disjoint such sets into one graph defines its decomposition number.

A 1978 conjecture by Woodall claims that for planar networks this number always equals the shortest loop's length. The authors study weighted and unweighted cases, pushing at the bounds. Progress here also informs ranking and ordering problems far beyond pure math.
arxiv-2501-07135:
Linze Li and William Ferreira present a trend-following trading method for commodity futures that looks across markets, not just at each one alone. Trends in one market can spill into a related market that follows behind. Spotting those lead-lag links may sharpen a simple trend signal.

Their method uses two ways to find such links and builds a network momentum signal from them. A portfolio driven by the new signal is compared with one using single-market signals only. On samples drawn from real price history, the new approach showed better risk-adjusted returns, better shape of returns, and softer downside results.
arxiv-2501-07435:
Ramon Amela and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on Union, a bridge that moves bitcoin between Bitcoin and a second chain with minimal trust. Bridges are a weak point in crypto, often run by federations that demand majority honesty. Union needs only one honest participant out of many.

Its core is an optimistic proving system that runs on Bitcoin itself. Packets let one safety bond back many transfers, easing capital cost. Enablers police who serves and punish cheating. A flexible light client fits many chain designs, and a stopwatch scheme trims time lock waste. The authors present Union as a practical, scalable route that keeps Bitcoin grade safety.
arxiv-2501-07735:
Dario Lucente and four co-authors find best control plans for a device that harvests energy from shakes, by varying its electrical resistance over time. Control theory tools made for set rules now serve noisy processes too. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The harvester's noise comes from shakes in its setting, and the reward is the average power drawn from them. The plan must steer the device between set states while it lifts that reward. Near the steady state, the authors work out best plans in a small shift math frame. Those plans beat any plan that holds resistance fixed, they show.
arxiv-2501-07835:
Yikai Wang and co-authors review and extend deep learning methods for the study of fluid flow in 2025. Flow fields are hard to measure in full and costly to compute. Uses range from filling gaps in data to raising image detail. The study links deep learning with sparse methods and with diffusion models.

Two new methods are put forward. One uses diffusion for tasks that raise flow detail. The other uses a sparse, low rank model to fill missing parts of a flow field. The authors say the methods lift accuracy and speed. They also adapt better to new cases. Work covers fluid and structure links, short lived flows, and flows inside pipes and parts.
arxiv-2501-08035:
Rohit Sharma, Shanu Kumar, and Avinash Kumar tackle text classification when labeled examples are scarce. Modern language models sort text well but hunger for thousands of hand-labeled samples, which cost time and money to make. Unlabeled text, by contrast, is cheap to gather. Their method, READ, squeezes value from that unlabeled pool in two ways at once.

A reinforcement learning agent generates varied synthetic text, guided by rewards rather than fixed rules. An adversarial training step then forces the classifier to stay steady when inputs are nudged, which sharpens its judgment. Together the two tricks teach the model from both real labels and manufactured practice data. Across several benchmark datasets, READ beat the strongest existing methods for low-label classification. The authors offer it as a route to good classifiers where labeling budgets are thin.
arxiv-2501-08335:
Xin Huang and seven co-authors tailor an open language model for four Asian tongues, in a report whose text is dated 2024 (the catalog says 2025). Chinese, Indonesian, Malay, and Singlish are underserved by models trained mostly on English.

Starting from Llama-3's eight-billion-parameter base, the team continued training on crafted data, then merged weights. The result, MERaLiON-TextLLM, beat the official Llama-3 models on benchmarks in all four languages. Singlish, Singapore's colloquial blend, is a rare inclusion. The catalog record mangles the author field with team and institute text; the printed byline is used here. The checkpoints are released openly. The authors offer them as a base for research on cross-lingual understanding.
arxiv-2501-08435:
Kunal Dey and Reihaneh Safavi-Naini prove that quantum-distributed keys can safely feed ordinary encryption in a 2025 paper. Quantum key distribution gives two parties a shared secret with safety guaranteed by physics. Standard proofs cover using that key with a one-time pad, an impractical scheme for long messages.

Real systems want modern ciphers instead. Borrowing hybrid encryption ideas, the pair build a quantum key encapsulation scheme from an existing proven protocol. Pairing it with a secure data wrapping step yields encryption for messages of any length. Their main theorem shows the combined system resists even quantum-equipped attackers, with no unproven assumptions. The result bridges quantum key sharing and practical encryption.
arxiv-2501-09035:
Kai-Cheng Yang and co-authors release DomainDemo, a dataset linking what gets shared on Twitter to who is sharing it, demographically, in a 2025 paper. Social media shape public discourse, especially around elections, but tying sharing behavior to age, gender, race, politics, and place has been hard. The dataset was built from a panel of over 1.5 million users matched to United States voter registration records, covering 2011 to 2022.

Aggregating those demographics onto the websites users shared yields metrics for more than 129,000 domains. Two stand out: localness, how geographically concentrated a domain's audience is, and partisan audience, its ideological lean. Both agree substantially with existing classifications, validating the approach. The authors offer the resource for studying a decade of information flow among registered voters. They note it can support research on how different groups encounter and spread different corners of the web.
arxiv-2501-09135:
Yu Shi and co-authors published a 2025 paper on using language models to fix software bugs with help from a project's past. Most AI bug-fixing tools look only at the current state of the code. Real projects, though, carry rich histories: past bugs, past fixes, and the patterns they leave. The authors asked whether that history makes a model a better fixer.

Their approach, HAFix, draws seven kinds of hints from a repository's history. Each hint guides the model in a different way. A combined version votes across all seven. They tested three code-focused language models on single-line bugs in Python and Java collections. Several single hints beat a baseline modeled on a popular coding assistant. The combined version did best of all, raising fix rates by roughly half on both collections. The paper shows history is a resource bug-fixing tools should not waste.
arxiv-2501-09235:
Ji Eun Kim and co-authors study how generosity spreads in live streaming. Their 2025 paper uses Twitch, where viewers can gift subscriptions to others in the chat, most often to random strangers through community gifting. That randomness gives the team a natural experiment.

People who received a gift were more likely to gift others later than those who did not. The effect grew when the receiver was the giver's only beneficiary, as if the gift felt personal. But gifts from very frequent gifters actually discouraged paying it forward, and anonymous gifts had no effect at all. The authors draw lessons for platforms that want kind behavior to cascade.
arxiv-2501-09335:
Ye Ming Qing and co-authors build a tunable one way heat radiator in a 2025 paper. Nonreciprocal radiation lets a surface emit and absorb unevenly by direction, breaking a textbook symmetry with magnetic materials. Their stack pairs graphene with a Weyl semimetal in a grating. Two bands show the one way effect at once.

Resonance of graphene plasmons drives the effect, and grating geometry steers it while staying sturdy across settings. Dynamic tuning means one device can serve shifting needs. One way thermal surfaces matter for energy harvesting, cooling, and infrared camouflage. A dual band, adjustable version widens each of those uses.
arxiv-2501-09435:
Zhichao Chen and Zixu Li connect cluster algebras to classical number puzzles in a 2025 paper. Cluster algebras grow from matrices that mutate by fixed rules. Some values stay unchanged under those mutations, and their whole-number points echo Diophantine equations, the ancient hunt for integer solutions.

The authors define and classify matrices that are equivalent up to signs. For rank-two algebras, they give a Diophantine account of the split between finite and affine types. They then classify the positive integer points of the Markov mutation invariant, an offshoot of the famous Markov equation, and of its variant. As a payoff, several families of Diophantine equations with cluster structure are exhibited. The paper treats the two fields as one landscape: mutation dynamics on one side, integer solutions on the other.
arxiv-2501-09635:
Arun Kunwar and Ajita Rattani merge face matching and spoof detection into a single model, in a 2025 paper. Face recognition now guards phones, payments, and secure sites. Attackers answer with printed photos, screens, and digital fakes. Most systems run separate models for matching and attack checks. That doubles cost on small devices.

Their unified model performs both tasks in one pass. Shared computation cuts the load for phones and cameras. The design also aims to keep accuracy high on both jobs. Tests cover physical and digital spoof styles. A single model simplifies deployment for makers of access systems. The work speaks to the wider fight against identity fraud.
arxiv-2501-09735:
Haibin Chen, Wenqi Zhu, and Coralia Cartis wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on computing special values for tensors. Tensors are multi-way arrays of numbers used across physics and data science. Their eigenvalues, in a generalized sense, mark extreme behaviors of the system the tensor describes. Finding the largest or smallest such value is a hard problem with uses in other tasks, such as trust-region steps in optimization.

The authors adapt a classic method for fractions, the Dinkelbach approach, to tensors. The extreme value problem becomes a linked chain of smaller problems, each a multilinear optimization under a simple round constraint. They solve those with an efficient alternating method and prove it settles to the answer from any start. A second form of the problem, without constraints, lets them pin down how fast the method converges. Early computer tests on eigenvalue problems and trust-region tasks support the theory.
arxiv-2501-09835:
Ziv Hellman and Miklós Pintér revisit in 2025 a foundation of game theory: the common prior, the idea that all players' beliefs spring from one shared probability view. A classic result ties such a prior, when it gives every type some chance, to the absence of a bet all sides would accept. That result covered only finite type spaces.

The pair extend the characterization to infinite type spaces. Their extension holds whether beliefs are built with standard countable probability or with the weaker purely additive kind. A deeper lesson follows: a real common prior, read as one distribution or even a set of them, may not always be a meaningful notion. The paper is a work of economic theory, aimed at the logic of belief itself rather than at any market data.
arxiv-2501-10035:
Victor Barbier and Eric Jeangirard map research communities at national scale in a 2025 paper. Tracing who works with whom, and on what, helps funders and policymakers steer science, but huge publication databases resist classic network tools. Their method builds on a French research portal's enriched records.

Strong links are filtered first, and names, institutions, and topics are cleaned with persistent identifiers. Search and graph tools lay out the networks and find communities, a language model labels each cluster, and open data add citation counts to spot hot topics. The web tool works for the whole country or a single lab, and the code is public.
arxiv-2501-10535:
Harrison Katz and co-authors track Airbnb booking lead times through global shocks in a 2025 study. How far ahead guests book shapes price and demand calls, yet plain averages hide shifts in the whole spread. The team built a normalized gap gauge for booking lead times from 2018 to 2022 in four big United States cities.

The gauge caught a two phase upset around COVID-19: a sharp break at the start, then a partial heal that still sat off the old pattern. That full spread view showed planning spans changing in ways medians miss. The lesson helps travel firms price through shaky markets.
arxiv-2501-10635:
Butler studies maps that act almost like linear ones in a 2025 paper. A quasi-linear map keeps the rules of linearity only on the small subalgebras built from a single function, yet it sends a space of functions into a normed space. Even with that slack, the map is bounded exactly when it is continuous. When the target is the real numbers, such maps become quasi-integrals, which match set functions that drop the usual add-up rule.

The paper ties these maps to image transformations, which push such loose measures from one space to another, much as a function pulls a measure back. Tests tell when a transformation truly comes from a continuous function. One-to-one matches link the maps, the transformations, and set functions of a special kind.
arxiv-2501-10935:
Shuai Lyu and seven co-authors built a retrieval method in two thousand twenty-five that stays strong when image-text pairs are wrongly matched. Search systems that pair photos with captions assume the pairs are clean, but real data sets carry noisy links that drag accuracy down. Past fixes used twin models that slowly grow too alike to help.

Their method, TSVC, uses three models in distinct roles: a coordinator that hands out data, a master, and an assistant that feeds the master varied views. A soft label scheme judges how noisy each new pair is. Tests on three data sets show clear gains in accuracy even as noise rises.
arxiv-2501-11335:
Checking whether a story obeys a written policy sounds simple, until the policy hides conditions inside conditions. Kyle Erwin and ten co-authors propose LDPC in 2025, a framework that makes a language model do the checking out loud. It splits policies into sub questions and assigns each a truth value from the conversation. Then it writes the logic down as explicit statements. Only a few examples are shown to the model.

On the standard ShARC benchmark the method matched systems trained for the task, without any task specific training. Because the logic is written out, errors can be traced to ambiguous benchmark items as often as to the model. Transparency, the authors argue, is a feature compliance work cannot skip.
arxiv-2501-11435:
Jeet Amrit Pattnaik and co-authors probe dark matter inside neutron stars in a 2025 paper. Neutron stars pack huge mass into a tiny sphere, so their inner gravity is extreme. The team adds dark matter and exotic quark matter to a star model. They then track how space bends at each depth inside the star.

Dark matter raised central density and lifted most measures of bending near the core. Quark matter pulled those same measures down. Stiffer matter gave smooth curves, while softer mixes shifted bending in sharp ways. Key settings for when quarks appear also shaped compact size and pressure. The results help link star shape to the unseen matter inside.
arxiv-2501-11835:
Zihan Liu, Prashant N Kambali, and C Nataraj build hybrid models that marry physics equations with neural networks fed by dynamics-based features. Their 2025 paper starts from a lifecycle problem. Physics models are sharp at design time but drift as real systems age. Pure data models hunger for data and fail when conditions change.

Their approach extracts information from nonlinear dynamics analysis, using perturbation methods, and embeds it as features for the learning side. Fresh measurements then update the model as the system runs. The aim is a model that keeps the physics model's feel for parameters while gaining the data model's fit to the present state. Such adaptive twins serve design, control, and fault diagnosis for complex machines.
arxiv-2501-12435:
Bernhard Putzer and Mathias Scheurer study an unusual pairing state in twisted graphene with Eliashberg theory, in work from 2025. In band-off-diagonal pairing, electrons pair across bands rather than within one, a state proposed to explain tunnelling results in twisted graphene. The stronger theory adds frequency dependence that the earlier mean-field picture lacked.

A symmetry argument shows no within-band part can mix into the interband state, while even- and odd-frequency pairing do mix. The computed spectrum keeps the odd excess of weight below the pairing energy. Superfluid stiffness saturates later than usual for such states, and for the chiral case the saturation scale can vanish, a possible match to new measurements.
arxiv-2501-12535:
Mirali Purohit and co-authors ask a basic question about Earth observation AI: does it matter where on the planet the training images came from? Geospatial foundation models promise help with climate, farming, and disaster response. Their builders obsessed over model design and training tasks, but not over the map of the data itself.

The team sampled varied regional mixes from a global pool, pretrained two such models on each mix, and scored them on downstream tasks. Balanced world coverage behaved differently from skewed diets. For a technology sold as planetary, proof that the training map matters could redirect how the big shared datasets get built and shared.
arxiv-2501-12835:
Viktor Moskvoretskii and co-authors test when a language model should search for facts in a 2025 paper. Search-fed answers cut made-up facts but cost time and compute. Search can also add noise when the model knows the answer. Smart search tools try to ask the model what it knows. The team put 35 such methods through one wide test.

Eight fresh methods faced 27 older doubt-score methods on six data sets. Ten scores graded answer quality, self-knowledge, and speed. Doubt scores, which grade how sure the model is, often beat the fancy pipelines. They ran faster and judged self-knowledge as well, with answer quality close behind. The work backs doubt scores as a cheap, strong base for search choices. It also sets a shared test bed for later tools.
arxiv-2501-13035:
Zhi-Min Chen studies in 2025 the stability of a still convective state in a fractional model of heated fluid outside a sphere. The fluid fills the unbounded space around a heated ball, and viscosity follows a fractional power of the Stokes operator. Heat alone sustains a purely conductive steady state.

A weak solution for the full motion problem is built first. Global stability of the steady state is then proved in the L2 sense. Disturbances of any size, within the weak class, decay back to the still state. The result extends fractional convection theory to exterior domains, where unbounded geometry complicates energy estimates.
arxiv-2501-13235:
Daniela Ballari and co-authors study open map data systems in Latin America in this 2025 paper. Open geographical data infrastructures let the public reach and reuse government map data. Such access can boost openness and sound choices in public life.

The authors review how far these systems have come in the region and where the gaps lie. Few systems in Latin America allow free use and reuse of their data. A wide digital divide shapes what gets built. The team sees early growth, with room for citizens and groups to help shape the work. They call for a shared research plan across borders.
arxiv-2501-13735:
The authors test if attention maps can plausibly explain model decisions in a 2025 paper on natural language inference. Attention weights look like explanations, since they point to words behind a verdict. Most tests of that claim use text classification, not sentence comparison, and they rest on a few examples.

The team set cross attention between two recurrent encoders against human and heuristic annotations on a large inference corpus. That route matched human judgments fairly well, which gives a cheap way to test such claims. Raw weights, though, stayed only loosely tied to plausible explanations. That tempers claims that attention alone explains these models.
arxiv-2501-13835:
Armin Nurkanović and Sven Leyffer gave an algorithm in 2025 that finds certified best points for optimization problems that contain an equilibrium inside them. Such problems show up in energy markets and engineering, and their tied constraints make standard solvers stumble.

A best point of this kind is one where no allowed first step can improve the goal. The method checks that property with a linear subproblem, then fixes the guessed pattern of the tied constraints and solves smoother subproblems. Under a standard condition, only finitely many rounds are needed. In practice one linear solve often suffices per round, a big saving. Tests beat relaxation and mixed integer rivals in speed and toughness, with a certificate included.
arxiv-2501-14035:
Nina Corvelo Benz and Manuel Gomez Rodriguez study trust in AI advice in a 2025 paper. When an AI gives a prediction plus a confidence score, people struggle to know when to rely on it. Theory says the benefit is capped by how well the AI's confidence aligns with the person's own confidence. The team tested that claim with seven hundred three people playing an online card game.

Help from a better-aligned AI proved more useful in practice. Recalibrating the AI's scores against each player's own confidence raised both alignment and usefulness. Readers get a design rule: match machine confidence to human confidence.
arxiv-2501-14135:
Daniel Bartl and four colleagues present a 2025 probability paper uniting several rival ways to say that one random process resembles another. When information flow matters, ordinary convergence of distributions is too crude, and different schools invented their own fixes: prediction-process convergence, an information topology, adapted distributions, and a topology from optimal stopping. The authors show that for continuous processes these are all the same idea.

A single adapted Wasserstein distance measures the unified notion. The space of processes with their natural information flow is not complete. Its completion is exactly the space allowing general filtrations, and that space is Polish, with martingales forming a closed subset. Even the central limit theorem survives the upgrade, the authors show.
arxiv-2501-14235:
Eleftherios Nikolidakis studies a constant tied to a tool used to bound averages in math analysis. His 2025 paper is Part B of a study of the Bellman function for a dyadic maximal operator with three integral inputs. Past papers pinned down a constant that helps fix that function, and this part looks at the constant itself.

The focus is narrow: how the constant behaves as its first input changes. Nikolidakis checks whether it rises, falls, or stays level as that input moves. Work of this kind helps analysts trust the sharp bounds that the Bellman method gives. The note is short and dense, written for readers who know the dyadic setting and the earlier parts of the argument.
arxiv-2501-14335:
Nico Schramma, Eric Weeks, and Maziyar Jalaal ask whether chloroplasts pack inside plant cells in an optimal way. Chloroplasts move with light: they spread to catch dim light and retreat to dodge excess light that can harm the cell. These disk-shaped organelles must pack densely yet stay free to rearrange. The team measured chloroplast densities and three-dimensional cell shape in the water plant Elodea densa.

A model of random close packing, matched with simulations of polydisperse hard disks in rectangular boxes, formalized the two targets. The optimal cell shape from the model closely matched the real box-like cells. The result frames light adaptation in plants as a particle packing problem.
arxiv-2501-14435:
Robin Marzucca, Andrew McLeod, and Christoph Nega worked out core integrals for Higgs boson making in a 2025 particle physics paper. Making a Higgs by fusing two gluons receives mixed fixes from the strong and electroweak forces. Precision forecasts need the two-loop master integrals behind them. Using change-based math rules, the authors work out every such integral to second order in the size regulator. They keep exact dependence on the masses of the top quark, Higgs, and the W and Z bosons.

Results are written as iterated integrals whose kernels live on elliptic curves, a sign of the problem's depth. Exact mass dependence removes a common approximation, sharpening Higgs rate forecasts for smasher checks.
arxiv-2501-14735:
Junyong Chen and co-authors present ARCEAK, a framework for automated rule checking of building designs, in a paper dated 2024 by its journal record. Checking designs against building codes by hand is slow, uneven, and prone to error. Software checks help only if the legal text can be turned into code, which has taken heavy manual work.

ARCEAK splits the job in two. First it extracts the key facts from a rule's text. Then it generates the checking code itself. Both steps lean on generative pre-trained transformer models. Tests and case studies showed the pipeline can automate compliance checks with good effect. The authors aim it at faster, more reliable construction projects.
arxiv-2501-14935:
Restrepo and three co-authors weigh whether the densest stars could be made of strange quark matter. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Quark stars are hypothetical, and telling strange from ordinary quark versions needs precise equations of state.

A resummation method called RGOPT handles the strong-force math at next-to-leading order. It produced mass-radius curves for both flavors of quark star. With sensible scale choices, maximum masses landed between two and two point six solar masses. Those curves match several freshly observed pulsars, strange or not. The strange version's matter runs softer, needing a higher scale to reach the same peak. The method's answers also wobbled less under scale changes than standard perturbation theory.
arxiv-2501-15535:
Benjamin Florentin, a solo author, studies a sound like spectrum in a 2025 math paper. For a shape with an edge, the Steklov spectrum lists the tones of a map that turns edge values into their outward slope. The hard question runs backward: can the tones alone reveal the shape's metric, apart from the usual freedoms?

For spaces of three or more dimensions, and for metrics that differ only by a scale factor field, the answer is partly yes. The setting needs a well behaved flow along the edge. Wave trace methods and an X-ray style transform do the work. The tones pin down the metric's full Taylor data at the edge.
arxiv-2501-15635:
Simone Marchesi and Rosa Miró-Roig characterize special matrix families in twenty twenty-five. They study linear spaces of matrices whose rank stays constant throughout. The matrices are built from linear forms. Such families appear in algebraic geometry through the bundles they define.

Under natural assumptions, the authors tie these matrices to syzygy bundles. The bundle fits into a resolution that is partially linear. That link turns a matrix question into a bundle question with known tools. Using it, they list all indecomposable constant rank matrices up to size seven. They also describe moduli spaces of simple bundles arising from these families. Readers get a classification grounded in geometry rather than case-by-case algebra.
arxiv-2501-15735:
Cell towers jam each other, and Madan Dahal and Mojtaba Vaezi let each tower's learning agent share only its best lessons with neighbors, in work from twenty twenty-five. Each agent hears its own users' signal quality and judges which past plays are worth passing on. Training and play stay fully local.

The picky sharing beat top rival methods that train the same local way. With three-quarters less sharing, it kept near all of the airwave yield of share-all methods. Talk overhead, the usual tax on such schemes, fell hard. The lesson for fleets of agents: a few right lessons beat a flood.
arxiv-2501-16035:
He-Liang Huang, Youwei Zhao, and Chu Guo explain how to design random quantum circuits that are hard to simulate classically, in a 2025 paper. Quantum advantage experiments race a quantum processor against the best classical computers. The circuits must run smoothly on real hardware yet crush classical simulation, which demands careful design.

The authors share the automated approach used to pick the circuit for the Zuchongzhi advantage experiment. Without it, that machine's fifty-six-qubit circuit would barely have outrun Google's smaller test in simulation cost. Applied to Google's newest seventy-qubit experiment, their method raises the estimated classical cost at least tenfold. The recipe fits generic flat chip layouts and tolerates real defects.
arxiv-2501-16135:
Madsack and co-authors evaluate a way to make one data-to-text system speak many languages without rebuilding it for each one. Their approach translates the system's grammar settings from the source language into each target language ahead of time. Machine translation does the first pass, a human reviews it once, and a cross-language model of grammar dependencies ties the setup together. At run time, the system then generates text in the target language with no human in the loop.

The test bed is a basketball data set, and the authors also propose a way to grade the translated output through human post-editing. Their system performed well, with strong grammatical correctness in the generated text. For builders of reporting tools that must serve many markets, the paper offers a route to scale: pay the translation cost once, up front, rather than on every document.
arxiv-2501-16535:
Keerthana Gurushankar, Noah Singer, and Bernardo Subercaseaux prove latency bounds for caching with delayed hits in this 2025 paper. Classic caching assumes a missed page arrives before the next request. Real systems like content delivery networks break that assumption. In the delayed hits model, retrieval takes measurable time while requests keep coming.

Two numbers describe the setting, the delay ratio and the cache size. The authors analyze Least Recently Used, the standard practical policy. They prove it is competitive within a factor tied to delay times cache size. That guarantee is the first tight one for this model. Matching lower bounds show the analysis cannot improve in general. Practice favorite LRU now has firm theory for delayed settings.
arxiv-2501-16635:
Koji Inoue and three co-authors asked why people laugh during casual text chats, in a 2025 study of Japanese conversation data. Laughter signals many things at once, from humor to warmth, and chat systems still read it poorly. The team set out to mark the chat moments that invite laughter and sort them by cause.

Human readers first labeled chat excerpts as laughable or not. A large language model then wrote short reasons for each laughable case, and the team grouped those reasons into ten classes, among them empathy and affinity, and humor and surprise. They also tested a leading model on the task of spotting the agreed labels. It scored under half on the test, which shows how much room is left for systems that handle laughter well.
arxiv-2501-16835:
Maity and co-authors study small spinning spheres that stir the fluid around them in a chiral way. Their 2025 paper defines such a rotor: the flow above it turns one way, and the flow below it turns the other. A lone rotor stays in place, but a pair can push each other along.

Two rotors linked by their flows move in straight or curved paths, based on their type and on how their spin axes point. The team then adds a chemical slope to the scene. In some setups both rotors drift away from the chemical source. In others, one rotor homes in on it. The work speaks to how tiny swimmers, both living and built, move as a group.
arxiv-2501-16935:
Suzie Grondin, Arthur Charpentier, and Philipp Ratz probe whether pricing algorithms can learn to collude on their own in a 2025 paper. Human collusion, rivals quietly holding prices high, is illegal and watched. But when pricing is handed to learning agents, collusive outcomes can emerge with no human intent and no messages passed. Critics doubt such collusion could survive in real markets, where rivals exploit any predictable pattern.

The authors give one agent a two-part strategy: exploit the market patterns the other agents create, and model the other agents' behavior directly. With both skills, the agent's collusion proves harder to exploit than earlier designs suggested. The results answer common objections about real-world viability. For regulators, the message is sharp: collusion may need no smoke-filled room, and no chat logs either.
arxiv-2501-17235:
Seval Tasdemir and Deniz Cennet Cinar analyze two star clusters that sit close together in the sky, in a 2025 astronomy paper. Open clusters are family groups of stars born together, and close pairs raise questions about shared origins. The pair studied here is named CWNU 2666 and HSC 224.

Using data from the Gaia space mission, the team picked out the likely member stars of each cluster by how they move together. Both clusters drift through space in nearly the same direction. Their distances came out almost equal too, at roughly nineteen hundred parsecs, and their ages were close, around one hundred sixty and one hundred forty million years. On that evidence the authors confirm the two groups form a genuine close pair of open clusters.
arxiv-2501-17535:
Janisch gives a probability reading of the Selberg Delange method in analytic number theory in twenty twenty-five. The method yields counts for sums of number functions with a zeta powered series. His bridge is mod Poisson convergence, a sharp form of bell curve approach. It grants fine control over spread and rare swings.

He shows method based results imply that convergence for the count of distinct prime factors. The random integer is drawn under a wide class of weights. A recent central limit theorem falls out as a side gain, under shifted conditions. The paper ties two fields' toolkits closer.
arxiv-2501-17835:
Sky Qiu, Jens Tarp, Andrew Mertens, and Mark van der Laan propose a safer way to borrow real-world patient data to sharpen randomized trials, in a 2025 paper. Adding outside data can make treatment estimates more precise, but mismatches between trial and outside patients can also bias them. Their method splits the treatment effect into a pooled part and a bias part, using the trial itself as the reference.

The paper first studies when this estimator stays trustworthy. It then adds a matching step that picks outside patients by two simple scores: how likely they were to join a trial, and their treatment propensity. The matching never looks at outcomes. In simulations, the chosen sample gave better coverage and tighter intervals than naive pooling.
arxiv-2501-18835:
Samitha Vidhanaarachchi and co-authors teach cameras to scout coconut plantations for two scourges: Weligama leaf wilt disease and caterpillar infestation. Both are still spotted by walking inspectors, slowly and late. Using image sets gathered in three Sri Lankan districts, the team trained transfer-learned convolutional networks for diagnosis and a mask network for severity.

The classifiers caught the wilt disease at about ninety percent accuracy and caterpillar damage at about ninety-five. A severity grader for the wilt hit about ninety-seven. YOLO detectors in three versions then counted individual caterpillars on leaflets at around ninety-six percent accuracy. The authors present the pipeline as an early-warning system for a crop whose losses are currently found by eye, after the fact.
arxiv-2502-00335: Tomas Lasic Latimer derives how a broad class of multiple q-orthogonal polynomials behaves as the degree grows without bound, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The result is drawn from the Riemann-Hilbert problem for these polynomials, not from term by term sums. The class is broad rather than a single family. The hosted record is thin: a one line abstract that states the aim and the method, with no further detail on the form of the limit law.
arxiv-2502-00735:
Linghan Huang, Bo Li, Huaming Chen, and Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo build a test frame that tries to jailbreak voice-based AI. Voice apps come in two builds: one turns speech to text first, and one hears raw sound end to end. Each build has its own weak spots, and past tests tended to cover one build at a time. Their 2025 frame tests both builds in one shared setup.

At its heart sits a mutation engine that breeds new attack tries from past near-hits. It works on both the words of a prompt and the sound of its delivery, which widens the spread of tries. Tests on six voice systems found both builds wide open to such attacks. The frame beat top past methods on hit rate across the set. The team offers it as a yardstick for voice AI safety.
arxiv-2502-00935:
Robot safety checks usually guard against crashes, but some dangers are hard to write down, such as spilling the contents of a bag. Kensuke Nakamura, Lasse Peters, and Andrea Bajcsy build safety filters that work from raw camera images instead of hand-written rules. Their method learns a model of the world from mixed robot data, good and bad, then marks safe and unsafe spots inside that model's inner picture of each scene.

In tests on real and simulated robots, the filters guarded other controllers, from learned policies to a human driving by hand. They kept a robot arm from spilling a bag or knocking over clutter. The approach extends a strict math framework for safety to hazards seen, not stated.
arxiv-2502-01035:
Jiuhong Xiao and Giuseppe Loianno present a 2025 arXiv paper on drone self-location when GPS fails or light is low. Thermal cameras can match a drone's view against satellite maps, but past methods give no estimate of how sure the match is. Bad matches can follow from blank or damaged thermal images, stale maps, or views that spill past the map edge.

Their method, UASTHN, gauges doubt in two ways. A crop-based test-time trick checks whether image crops agree on the alignment, which exposes data problems. Ensembles of models expose model doubt instead. Tests across several alignment models showed the pairing flags failures well under hard conditions.
arxiv-2502-01235:
Yuanhe Zhang, Fanghui Liu, and Yudong Chen study a popular cheap way to adapt large language models to new tasks. The method, called LoRA, tweaks only small add-on parts of the model instead of the whole thing. The authors ask what those add-ons learn during training. They prove that, under a standard training rule, the add-ons line up with key directions drawn from a single full training step.

That result suggests a better start: set the add-ons from that one full step at the outset, so they begin already aligned. Their method, LoRA-One, does exactly this and adds a scaling fix for poorly shaped problems. They prove it converges steadily and show it beats plain LoRA and its variants on tests of language understanding, math reasoning, and code writing. The paper also clears up links between their method and other alignment-based tricks.
arxiv-2502-01335:
Ciusdel and co-authors introduce a training framework in two thousand twenty-five that teaches image models to separate fine concepts in heart ultrasound scans. Standard self-taught methods compress a scan into one vector, which can blur distinct structures such as blood pools and chamber walls. Finding those parts without labels could improve pretraining and enable searches by anatomy.

Their framework, ConceptVAE, splits each scan into a set number of concepts, each with its own local style. A suite of loss terms and design choices keeps the split clean. Tests showed it could pick out structures like blood pools and the septum wall on its own. It beat standard methods at region search, segmentation, spotting odd cases, and object detection, and could also make fresh synthetic scans.
arxiv-2502-01435:
Chamalee Wickrama Arachchi, Iiro Kumpulainen, and Nikolaj Tatti merged two network ideas in twenty twenty-five: dense subgraph discovery and strong triadic closure. Dense subgraphs flag communities and anomalies, but real ties differ in strength. Strong triadic closure says that if a node binds strongly to two others, those two must share at least a weak tie — a rule that labels edges strong or weak.

Their score for a subgraph weighs strong edges fully and weak edges by a user parameter, per node. At one extreme the problem equals finding the densest subgraph; at the other, the largest clique, so it is hard in general. They give an exact integer programming algorithm and four fast heuristics. Experiments recover planted truth in synthetic data and run efficiently on real networks.
arxiv-2502-01535:
Duy-Cat Can and seven co-authors build VisTA, a model that reads brain images and text together to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. Scans hold rich clues, but models that use them often cannot explain their calls. Their 2025 model aligns image features with written descriptions through contrastive learning, which pulls matching pairs together and pushes others apart. The aim is a diagnosis that comes with evidence a doctor can check.

The team frames the design around three goals: accurate prediction, clear reasons, and trust. Explanations tied to image regions and known signs may help clinicians spot model errors. The paper adds to a push for medical AI that shows its work. Tests on Alzheimer's data check both the calls and the quality of the reasons given.
arxiv-2502-01635:
Stephen Casper and a large team of co-authors launched a public index in 2025 that documents AI agent systems already at work in the world. Agents that plan and act with little human help are spreading fast, yet no shared record described their parts, uses, and safety steps. The index aims to fill that gap.

For each system that qualifies, the team logs the base model, the reasoning setup, the tools it can use, its job areas, and its risk controls. The facts come from public sources and direct contact with builders. A clear pattern emerged: builders share plenty about what their agents can do and where they work. They share far less about testing and guardrails. The index is live online for anyone to browse.
arxiv-2502-02535:
Alexey Lotnikov and Anna Kotova study a branching math model in which each step sums a random number of copies, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A fixed amount is then subtracted, and negative results are cut to zero. Over many steps, the mean value either fades away or stays positive when scaled.

The scaled limit acts as the model's energy. The authors give clear conditions, based on the starting spread and the count spread, for each outcome. One outcome marks the fading, low regime. The other marks the regime where energy survives. The conditions settle when the model sits at its critical edge.
arxiv-2502-02635:
Karin Kjellgren and a large team of co-authors wrote this astrophysics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how cosmic rays push on galaxies. Cosmic rays carry real energy, and simulations in the Rhea suite let them flow, diffuse, and press on gas in a Milky Way-like galaxy.

The runs include a multi-phase gas disk and magnetic fields. With cosmic rays on, star formation slows. Weak but steady winds rise from the whole disk, not just the center, carrying off a fifth to three fifths of the injected cosmic ray energy. Disks puff up under cosmic ray support. Magnetic flux also leaks out into the halo, seeding it with fields while cooling its gas. The authors find cosmic ray pressure spread smoothly across the disk. The picture makes cosmic rays a quiet but constant hand in galaxy life.
arxiv-2502-03235:
Mohamed Ben Ayed and Khalil El Mehdi prove that a class of nonlinear partial differential equations has solutions that blow up in clusters inside the domain. Their paper came out in 2025. The equation models steady states with a reaction term pushed almost to a critical power, where standard existence theory breaks down.

As the small parameter in the exponent shrinks, their solutions concentrate into several sharp peaks, or bubbles, grouped together at an interior point. Earlier constructions placed single bubbles or bubbles at the boundary. The authors say theirs is the first result for clustered interior blow-up in general domains. The proof rests on fine estimates of the gradient of the energy function behind the equation. Such results map out exactly how solutions can degenerate at criticality.
arxiv-2502-03435:
Wu, Marion, Biau, and Boyer explained in twenty twenty-five why diffusion image models do not simply memorize their training data. Diffusion models learn by denoising, and the perfect solution to that task would copy training samples exactly. Yet real models show only moderate copying, even without explicit safeguards.

The authors credit large learning rates, the step size used in training. In the small-noise regime, the perfect score function is highly irregular. They prove a network trained with big enough steps cannot settle stably near that perfect solution. So the learned score stays safely distant, limiting memorization. Their proof uses one-dimensional data and two-layer networks for tractability. Experiments confirm the learning rate's key role beyond that simple setting.
arxiv-2502-03635:
Muhammad Raees, Vassilis-Javed Khan, and Konstantinos Papangelis report user experience lessons from a business tool in this 2025 case study. The tool helps a global manufacturer group its customers with machine learning clusters. Sales experts must make sense of those groups to act on them.

The main hurdle was the effort needed to interpret what each cluster means. A second hurdle was choosing interactions that help users probe the output in useful ways. The team built an interactive prototype and tested it with real multi-year data. Feedback from domain experts shaped their verdicts. They report which design choices worked, to guide builders of similar unsupervised learning tools.
arxiv-2502-03935:
Leon Blumrich and six co-authors tackle heat in electric motors in a 2025 paper. A squirrel cage induction machine can fail if hot spots form, so designers need heat models they can trust early on. The team tune the values in a flat model of the machine so the model matches measured heat.

They treat the tuning as an inverse problem, solving for both material values and terms that stand in for three dimensional effects. First they test the method on a simple case with made up data. Then they apply it to a real machine model, where it works well and supports safer use of the motor.
arxiv-2502-04035:
Robert Hierons and Mohammad Reza Mousavi work on complete testing for state machines in this 2025 paper. Model-based testing checks a system against a formal model, and a complete test suite misses no fault of a set kind. Their starting point is apartness, a notion from constructive math used to tell states apart.

The pair find that apartness has real flaws in quantitative models, such as hybrid and random systems. They propose a close cousin, strong separability, that fixes the flaws. They then rebuild a known complete test method, the HSI method, around the new notion and prove the rebuilt method stays complete. They claim this is the first route to complete test suites for quantitative models, a class that shows up across cyber-physical systems.
arxiv-2502-04535:
Chenyang Huang and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on summaries with a strict length cap. Many tasks need a summary that fits a set budget, not just a shortish one. Past models treat the cap as a soft wish and often miss it.

Their method builds on a transformer that lays out text pieces as a web rather than a chain. A decoder then picks a path through the web that forms the summary. A new search scores whole paths at once, weighing all ways the pieces could join. Beam search plus a reranker polish the final pick. On two news data sets, the method set the best scores for cap-respecting summaries. The authors say hard caps need search over paths, not token-by-token writing.
arxiv-2502-04635:
Matthew Lamsey and co-authors ask exercise specialists to judge a robot-led therapy system for Parkinson disease in a 2025 study. Robots could coach home exercise between clinic visits, but professionals must trust them first. Eleven specialists tried the system and rated it through questionnaires and interviews.

The reception ran broadly positive: the robot could support adherence and engagement, they judged, and extend specialist reach. Two fixes topped their list, more human-like feedback and a broader exercise repertoire. Acceptance scores and workload ratings filled out the picture. The study treats clinicians as co-designers, not bystanders, of therapy robots.
arxiv-2502-04835:
Abir Bouraffa, Yen Dieu Pham, and Walid Maalej study in 2025 how developers use code suggestions inside pull request reviews on GitHub. The feature lets reviewers propose exact code edits, making feedback concrete. Little was known about what kinds of edits get suggested or what they do to a request's fate.

Pull requests from forty-six engineered projects are coded by hand for suggestion type. Improvements lead, ahead of style tweaks, fixes, and documentation. Requests using suggestions merge more often, yet take longer to resolve and show no drop in code complexity. A survey adds the social side: trust and tone sway whether suggestions are accepted. Review tooling, the authors suggest, should ease careful reading of edits.
arxiv-2502-04935:
Ciaran O'Connor and four co-authors apply conformal prediction in 2025 to electricity price forecasts for day-ahead and balancing markets. Renewable growth makes prices jumpier and harder to call. Traders need intervals that state uncertainty in plain terms, not just point guesses.

Two such methods wrap price models in ranges with firm coverage. An ensemble blends the speed of quantile regression with the strength of that coverage. The ranges stay narrow yet still hit their coverage targets. A simulated trading run with a battery then grades the worth of the ranges in use. Better ranges show when to charge and discharge for profit. The authors argue that calibrated uncertainty is a tradable edge in volatile power markets.
arxiv-2502-05335:
Roussel Nzoyem and co-authors build a mixture-of-experts system that learns whole families of dynamical systems at once. Reconstructing dynamics from data usually means one model per system, and meta-learners falter when data are sparse and the systems form loose hierarchies. Their answer, MixER, routes each task to a specialist reconstructor.

The novelty is the gate: instead of learning routing by gradient descent, which updates slowly and fights itself, MixER updates its gate with a K-means and least squares routine. Training proved efficient, and the system scaled to ten parametric differential equations. Honest limits appear in data-rich regimes of closely related points, where classic meta-learners win. Tests on synthetic and brain time series tie performance to how hierarchical the data truly are.
arxiv-2502-05535:
Jaehyup Seong and co-authors match data rates to user demand in satellite networks, in work from 2025. Multibeam low-orbit satellites aim for world-wide reach, but demand varies a lot across their wide footprint. Their frame uses rate-splitting access to close the gap between demand and served rates while spending less power.

The frame also weighs phase errors from rough channel reads, a real flaw in such systems. A step-by-step smoothing trick turns the hard problem into a solvable one. Wide tests showed the split method flexes power between shared and private streams by beam. Shared streams proved key to handling clash within and across beams.
arxiv-2502-05735:
Danial Khatamsaz and co-authors offered a more autonomous way to design alloys in 2025. Machine-run substances find usually optimizes a fixed problem, yet the real hardness is deciding what to ask for: a turbine blade alloy must balance ductility, strength. Weight, and how cleanly it solidifies, and no exact specification exists at the start. Their method lets the system search over problem forms themselves.

Using Bayesian optimization mapped onto a multi-trait utility function that encodes a choice maker's preferences. The system tests varied design forms and steers toward the one that best matches those preferences. In a computer-only case study on a molybdenum, niobium, titanium, vanadium, and tungsten alloy for gas turbine blades, the search converged on a sweet spot meeting the key results thresholds. Future work will add human feedback into the loop.
arxiv-2502-06035:
Yun Yang studies curves that flow along a light cone, the surface where light itself travels in three-dimensional Minkowski space. Such flows bend curves by their curvature under strict rules. Solitons, the self-similar shapes that flow without changing form, reveal the flow's character.

For the heat flow on the cone, Yang proves a Harnack inequality that bounds how solutions can vary. For a third-order curvature flow, he sorts all space-periodic solitons into a neat family. The wavy members are written with the Jacobi elliptic sine function. Closed members form a family tagged by two whole numbers: a rotation index and a period count, locked in a set ratio band. The sorting also solves a linked second-order equation in closed form.
arxiv-2502-06335:
Emanuel Sommer and co-authors speed up the sampling that gives Bayesian neural networks their sense of doubt. Such networks answer with a spread of guesses rather than one, but drawing fair samples from their tangled posterior landscapes takes far too long. Samplers wander, find good regions late, and leave run times a lottery.

Their answer pairs a newer sampler, Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo, with an ensemble wrapper borrowed from optimization. Head to head with the field's standard No-U-Turn Sampler, the method ran up to ten times faster. Forecast skill and honesty of the uncertainty held or improved across tasks and data types. Predictable costs and easy parallel runs make the approach fit for daily use.
arxiv-2502-06635:
Qingshui Gu and co-authors tell the story of Steel-LLM, a Chinese-centric language model built from scratch, in a 2025 paper. Launched in March 2024, the project aimed for a quality open-source model despite limited computing power. It trained a one-billion-parameter model mostly on Chinese data, with a small share of English.

The paper gives a full, practical account of the journey: collecting data, designing the model, and the training methods and hurdles along the way. Steel-LLM scored competitively on Chinese benchmarks such as CEVAL and CMMLU, beating some early models from much larger institutions. With code and checkpoints released openly, the account serves builders who want to train their own models on a budget.
arxiv-2502-07135:
Andreas Galanis, Leslie Ann Goldberg, and Xusheng Zhang wrote a 2025 theoretical computer science paper on one shot learning for the k-SAT problem. A single satisfying assignment is sampled with a bias toward assignments that set more variables true. From that one sample and the formula, can a learner recover the bias parameter efficiently?

Recent work showed learning is possible when each variable appears few times, and impossible past a much higher count. It also left open whether the learning limit matches the satisfiability limit for bounded degree formulas. The authors answer no. They prove learning fails well below the satisfiability threshold, at degrees as low as the square of k for strong bias. A bootstrapping step extends the result to weak bias at exponential degrees.
arxiv-2502-07235:
Ilija Vego and Benjy Marks introduce the Sand Atlas, an open repository of three-dimensional sand particle models, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Sand grains carry clues about where they formed and how they traveled, but shape data are scattered and hard to compare. The atlas collects high-resolution surface meshes and level-set data for natural and synthetic particles from many regions and mineral types.

Uniform processing keeps the models comparable, and the conversion code ships as an open Python package. Researchers, educators and industry users can browse and download the shapes freely. Contributors are invited to add their own scans, growing a shared resource for granular materials science.
arxiv-2502-07435:
Timothé Taminiau, Estelle Massart, and Geovani Nunes Grapiglia let an optimizer learn from its own scratch work, in a 2025 paper. Derivative-free optimization tunes systems by trying values, never seeing a gradient. Finite-difference versions fake the gradient from nearby tries. Every run generates a rich trail: points tried, values found, approximate slopes, step sizes that worked. Their auxiliary procedure trains a surrogate model on that trail.

The method then descends the surrogate with a guarded line search until the surrogate stops predicting real improvement, falls back to the base algorithm, and retrains on the fresh data. Bolted onto a recent derivative-free method, the loop improved performance significantly in numerical tests, especially when the approximate gradients also trained the surrogate. The authors offer the wrapper as a cheap upgrade for a whole family of optimizers.
arxiv-2502-07535:
Wearable devices measure the pulse at the wrist, and the variability of that pulse is often treated as a stand-in for heart rate variability from an electrocardiogram. Runwei Lin and co-authors test whether the swap is safe during a common daily movement: standing up from lying down. They extracted fifteen features, across time, frequency, and nonlinear families, from both signal types in young adults.

Statistical tests compared the two measures while lying, while rising, and while standing. Only one feature differed significantly during lying, but the count rose to four during the transition and standing phases. Both measures did reflect the sympathetic activation that standing triggers. Still, the authors conclude the two are not interchangeable in these tests: devices that report pulse variability are not quite reporting heart variability, and the gap widens exactly when posture changes.
arxiv-2502-07635:
Guilherme Varela, Alberto Sardinha, and Francisco Melo study teams of learning agents that cannot train in one central place, in this 2025 paper. In their setting, each agent sees only part of the world and must learn by acting, while sharing notes with peers. They propose a method that splits the team's joint value score into per-agent scores.

Two versions of the method cover teams whose members differ and teams whose members match. In ten test tasks across three standard settings, both versions came close to the results of the central-training method they build on. The gap stayed small even though messages between agents lose some information.
arxiv-2502-07735:
Nikita Morozov, Ian Maksimov, Daniil Tiapkin, and Sergey Samsonov revisited the theory of GFlowNets in 2025 when their sampling graph contains cycles. These generative models learn to sample objects with a target probability by walking a directed graph. Standard theory needs that graph to have no cycles, which limits designs.

The authors present a simpler theory for the cyclic case in discrete settings. New results cover training with fixed backward policies, the nature of flow functions, and links to entropy-regularised reinforcement learning. Each result generalises its acyclic counterpart. Experiments recheck how stable training losses are without acyclicity and confirm the new findings. The work widens where these samplers can be applied.
arxiv-2502-07835:
Ahilan Ayyachamy Nadar Ponnusamy tackles a trust problem in AI-written code, in a solo 2025 paper. Language models now write code for developers, but judging that code is hard. Word-overlap scores borrowed from text work match human judgement poorly for code, and junior developers may miss invented features or wrong logic that senior staff would catch.

Ponnusamy proposes working backwards. A model first rebuilds the written requirements from the generated code, and that rebuild is compared with the original request. The resulting SBC score joins meaning similarity, word overlap, and a completeness check. Gaps in the rebuild flag missing features and invented ones. The score is designed to fit into daily development, not just research, giving developers clear points to review. Code and data sets are shared on GitHub, the author notes.
arxiv-2502-07935:
Bezuglov and colleagues present a software package for computing Lauricella functions to very high precision. These functions, kin to the hypergeometric family, appear across physics calculations. Their indexes here slide with a small parameter, which makes standard series methods slow and clumsy.

The package, built in Wolfram Mathematica, leans on analytic continuation through Frobenius power series. That one-dimensional route beats multidimensional sums and integral forms for accuracy work. Values at chosen points can be stitched back into full parameter dependence, which also suits parallel runs. The paper focuses on the design, build, and uses of the tool, building on the team's earlier theory work.
arxiv-2502-08235:
Alejandro Cuadron and a large team study overthinking in large reasoning models that act as agents on software tasks. These models can favor long internal reasoning over checking the real environment. The authors name three patterns: freezing in analysis, acting wildly after long thought, and quitting too early.

They build a framework to score overthinking and check it against human expert judgment, then apply it to thousands of task runs. Higher overthinking scores went with worse results, and reasoning models overthought more than plain ones. Picking the run with the lower score improved success greatly while cutting computing cost. The team releases its tools for further study.
arxiv-2502-08435:
Mohammed Mourabit and Nevin Weinberg study coupled vibration modes in pulsating stars in a paper from 2025. Delta Scuti stars ring with many modes, and recent data show three modes coupling together. In direct coupling, two driven modes excite a stable third. In parametric coupling, one driven mode excites two stable ones. One star shows especially strong signs of direct coupling.

Direct coupling alone cannot settle the modes into balance, the authors show. Adding parametric coupling lets small mode networks reach equilibrium. Mode values from a star model suggest both couplings act at once. Parametric coupling also preserves the amplitude and phase patterns observers found. The pair urge modelers to include both in large networks.
arxiv-2502-08735:
Prasanth Shyamsundar and Wern Yeen Yeong adapt a classic statistics trick to cut the sampling cost of quantum error cancellation, in a 2025 paper. Error cancellation methods rewrite a noisy quantum circuit as a blend of circuits, then sample from that blend. The sample count can grow fast as more errors are handled, which limits real use.

Their method, CV4Quantum, adds control variates, extra quantities with known averages, to steady the estimates. In simulations modeled on a realistic error cancellation task, more than half the estimates needed over 50 percent fewer samples for the same precision. The authors note that better control variates could cut the cost further.
arxiv-2502-08835:
Feng-Yi Liao and Yang Zheng propose a faster way in 2025 to solve constrained convex problems. These are math tasks where the goal is to find the best point inside a set of rules. The classic method for such tasks works in two nested loops, which can be slow.

Their framework runs in a single loop. It keeps a bundle of past trial points and uses them to guess the next step cheaply. The authors prove the method still homes in on a valid answer. Progress is slow at first, then fast under stronger conditions. The fast rate even holds for hard cone-shaped problems, such as semidefinite programs used in control and design.
arxiv-2502-09235:
Nicolas Ruhling wrote a 2025 paper on the logic behind a style of problem solving called answer set programming. That style is strong for puzzles of rules and choices, but many real problems also involve numbers and tight limits. Hybrid solvers bolt on special tools for those parts, yet their logic base is thin.

The paper studies a logic built to ground such hybrid systems, one that extends an older logic of here-and-there reasoning. Open questions remain about the logic's basic traits and about how it should steer solver design. A firm formal base also helps users shape real problems for these solvers. Product configuration, building a valid item from parts and options, serves as the test case. The work aims to give hybrid solving the same solid footing that the older logic gave the basic method.
arxiv-2502-09735: Michael Kemeny gives a new proof of a classic result in algebraic geometry in a 2025 note. Green's conjecture links the equations defining a curve to its geometry, and Voisin proved it for typical curves of odd genus. Kemeny reproves that odd-genus case by a route modeled on his earlier work on secant bundles and syzygies of canonical curves, avoiding the hard computations the original proof required.
arxiv-2502-09835:
Talashila and eight co-authors showed in twenty twenty-five that an atomic sensor can tell where a radio signal comes from. Rydberg sensors use highly excited atoms to detect radio fields far below antenna size limits, across wide frequency bands. Most designs need a strong reference field to read phase, which complicates use.

Their sensor places a metal plate inside the atom cell, creating a standing wave pattern. Reading only the wave's amplitude at tiny scales reveals the incoming angle, with no reference field needed and no dependence on signal strength. A robot positioned test antennas precisely at three frequencies near five gigahertz. Angular resolution reached about two degrees across a sixty-degree span. The authors present the design as a compact direction finder for radio applications.
arxiv-2502-09935:
Staniszewski and co-authors hunt down where text comes from inside image-generating diffusion models. Modern models can render words inside pictures, sometimes well and sometimes garbled. Using a probing method that swaps internal activations between runs, the team shows that less than one percent of the model's parameters shape the text in the image. All of them sit in attention layers. The rest of the model handles the picture itself.

That narrow address book opens several tricks. Tuning only those layers improved text rendering while leaving image quality and variety intact. The same layers can be steered to edit words in a finished image, or blocked to stop toxic text from appearing, at no extra cost. The authors show the approach works across several model families and text encoders. For model builders, the paper turns text quality from a whole-model problem into a small, cheap fix.
arxiv-2502-10635:
Robert Dilworth, writing alone in 2025, studies machine unlearning as a way to guard privacy in trained models. Models learn from huge data sets and adapt over time. Privacy law may demand that a person's data be removed. Unlearning removes set data without a full rebuild. Dilworth tests naive retraining and an exact method built on data shards.

He weighs cost, stability, and real world fit on a spam data set. He also probes a link to learning from partly labeled data. A forest based unlearning frame stands out for keeping model quality while meeting privacy rules. Costs can be steep, though. The study backs unlearning as a key part of ethical AI.
arxiv-2502-10735:
Shuqi Liu and three co-authors make pruning of large language models adaptive instead of one-size-fits-all. Their framework appeared in twenty twenty-five. Pruning trims a trained model's weights for speed, but models differ so much in weight patterns that fixed recipes fail across them.

Their system, OptiShear, searches for the right scoring metric for each model. A fast error measure lets it test many candidates cheaply. A multi-goal genetic algorithm tunes both the metric and how much each layer is cut.
