On LLaMA and Mistral models from seven to seventy billion parameters, the adaptive metrics beat fixed ones across benchmarks. The learned layer patterns also boosted rival methods. The authors show the gains transfer across tasks and models.
arxiv-2502-10835:
Zeping Yu, Yonatan Belinkov, and Sophia Ananiadou ask how large language models work through multi step thought in their heads. They bring in logit flow, a way to read how picks build up through layers and word spots. Used on one step prompts, it shows four steps. Those steps run from growth of traits of the main thing to pull out of the trait asked for.

When they use the same lens on multi step thought, the team finds faults often start at one late step. Clash of signals there cuts score. Their fix, back attention, lets low layers use high layer states from other spots as they weigh words. Back attention lifted scores for four language models. It did so on five sets of thought tasks.
arxiv-2502-11135:
Zhehan Li, Zhifeng Li, and Jia Tian study uneven energy landscapes in two-dimensional quantum field theories, in a 2025 paper. A conformal field theory with a Hamiltonian that varies from place to place models systems driven out of uniform conditions. Holography links such theories to gravity in one higher dimension, letting hard quantum questions be read off from curved space.

The team sort the uneven Hamiltonians by a symmetry scheme based on the Virasoro algebra. Each class pairs with a known family of curved-space solutions, and the authors add a mapping that makes those solutions easier to handle. One known case ties to a three-dimensional geometry for accelerating objects. The sorting opens new classes of driven quantum systems to study.
arxiv-2502-11235:
Sandeep Joy and Brian Skinner explain, in a 2025 paper, a puzzle from images of electrons in a flat sheet. Near the point where the electron system freezes from liquid to solid, cameras see the two phases mixed in patches of middle size. Oddly, the patches hold the same electron density, which rules out the usual stories told about such mixing.

The authors show that random bumps in a short-range disorder landscape can do the job. Their model yields mixed liquid and solid domains with no density contrast, matching the images. Disorder also props the solid, the Wigner crystal, up to higher densities than a clean system would allow, again in line with what was seen. The paper gives experimenters a cleaner frame for reading these mixed states.
arxiv-2502-11335:
Geonwoo Ko, Minseo Jeon and Jinhong Jung propose CascadingRank for multi-behavior recommendation, in work from 2025. Such systems predict purchases from actions such as viewing, adding to a cart and buying. Older methods either learn embeddings, which can over-smooth and favor frequent actions, or rank on graphs, which has mostly been tried for single behaviors.

CascadingRank models the natural order of behaviors as a cascading graph and computes personal ranking scores step by step. The method balances smoothness, fit to the query and alignment across the cascade. Tests on three real datasets beat leading methods on hit rate and ranking quality. Theory on convergence and scale is also given.
arxiv-2502-11835:
Bahmani, Kevrekidis, and Shields present a method, published in 2025, for building stand-in models of random systems. Engineers often need a fast copy of a costly simulation, one that also reports its own uncertainty. A classic approach expands the randomness into a sum of smooth terms. It works well until the system grows complex, when the sum balloons and accuracy or stability suffers. It also struggles when the random inputs lean on each other.

The team's method keeps the classic expansion's spirit but hands the work to a neural network. The network learns the expansion's structure in a form that scales to harder problems. Tests show it can match the classic method's accuracy with less fuss. It also handles tangled, dependent inputs more gracefully. The result is a practical tool for design under uncertainty, from materials to structures.
arxiv-2502-12235:
Alexander Nikolaenko and five co-authors explain a cold-atom experiment in twenty twenty-five. Fermionic lithium atoms were placed in a Lieb lattice, a pattern with flat bands. Experiments varied the Hubbard repulsion and the filling fraction. At half filling, observations matched theory at both weak and strong repulsion.

Near quarter filling with strong repulsion, something unexpected appeared. Compressibility on certain sites was large, pointing to a flat band at the Fermi level. The authors' Hartree-Fock computations find an explanation. States with canted magnetism, and related spiral states, arise there. Those states carry nearly flat bands on the same sites. Readers get a magnetic account of a surprising flat band in a designer quantum material.
arxiv-2502-12435:
Mohamed Aghzal, Erion Plaku, Gregory Stein, and Ziyu Yao survey research on large language models for automated planning in this 2025 paper. Planning means working out a chain of steps to reach a goal. Language models have drawn wide interest here, thanks to their step-by-step reasoning and their range across topics.

Views on their skill split sharply. Some researchers stress their promise on complex tasks, while others stress clear limits, above all on long chains of steps. The survey weighs both sides in detail, study by study. The authors conclude that the models are not fit to plan alone. Yet they see huge value in pairing the models with other planning tools. Their call is for a balanced method that uses the models' flexible language skills where they help most.
arxiv-2502-12635:
Training vision-language models on scraped instruction data often means training on flawed data: made-up details, wrong answers, poor text reads. Yunhao Gou and co-authors studied in 2025 how deep that damage goes, and reached a hopeful verdict.

Although flawed data drag scores down, the harm proves largely reversible. Turning off a small set of model weights almost fully restores performance. The flawed models also turn out to carry an inner sense of which samples are clean, which can guide data cleaning with no outside help. Building on these findings, the authors propose a training scheme that beats earlier fixes for learning from dirty data.
arxiv-2502-12835:
Bastian Bunzeck and Sina Zarrieß ask how language models learn single words. Most models read text in chunks of letters rather than whole words or single letters. Their 2025 study uses a word task from mind research: judge fast whether a string of letters is a real word. They compare chunk-based models with letter-based ones.

Chunk models did poorly at the task unless they were given more context. Letter models solved it with ease every time. The two kinds also grew in unlike ways. In letter models, word skill came first and sentence skill came later. In chunk models, both grew at once. The authors say letter models may be the better tool for studying how word learning works.
arxiv-2502-12935:
Olesia Dogonasheva, Anne-Lise Giraud, Denis Zakharov, and Boris Gutkin review neuro-oscillatory models of cortical speech processing in a 2025 paper. The brain hears speech as a flow of sound, and it uses rhythms of cell firing, at gamma, theta, and delta rates, to track that flow in real time.

The models they weigh use those rhythms to code phonemes, to cut speech into syllables and words, and to join the parts into meaning. The review checks how each model works, how well it fits brain facts, and where it could serve live speech tech, a skill machines still lack.
arxiv-2502-13135:
Taedong Yun and co-authors present a 2025 frame for building fake users to test health coaching agents. Real trials with people are slow, so test users shaped by real health traits can give a safer first check. The study grounds its fake users in sleep habits and diabetes care.

Fake users are built in two steps, first as structured data on health and daily life, then as full profiles. Talks between the fake users and a coach are then played out with agent models or a language model. Human experts judged the talks blind, and two real coaching agents served as test cases for the frame.
arxiv-2502-13435:
James Leung and fifteen co-authors present the radio afterglow of the most distant ultra-long gamma-ray burst yet found, GRB 220627A. Its gamma-ray light curve fired twice, with about fifteen quiet minutes between pulses, raising the exotic possibility of gravitational lensing. The burst sits at a redshift above three.

Spectra from the Fermi satellite during the two pulses differ clearly, which argues against one event being imaged twice. Radio telescopes then followed the fading afterglow from a week to well over a year after the burst. Its decay steepens then shallows in a pattern the authors explain three ways, involving extra ejecta or a stratified environment. The paper weighs each scenario against the data.
arxiv-2502-13635:
Riccardo Catena, Taylor Gray, and Thomas Jerkvall extend a dark matter hunt to new kinds of dark photon in this 2025 paper. The experiment, LDMX, fires electrons at a target and watches for missing energy that would betray invisible particles. Dark photons might couple to ordinary matter not only directly but through higher electromagnetic moments born in particle loops.

The authors study four such couplings: magnetic and electric dipoles, charge radius, and the anapole moment. Each changes the angles and energies of the recoiling electron in its own way. Simulations show the experiment's second phase should reach the favored target zone for all four models. If a signal appears, its shape can hint at the model, though mass and model partly mimic each other. Watching both the electron's energy and sideways kick breaks much of that confusion.
arxiv-2502-13935:
Zeki Doruk Erden and Boi Faltings published a paper in 2025 proposing a new design approach for learning machines. Current systems struggle to keep learning without forgetting. They also reuse knowledge poorly and act without clear deliberation. The authors borrow ideas from evolutionary developmental biology to fix this.

Their design has three main parts. One part, called the Modeller, learns without gradient methods and can adapt its structure. A planner then chooses goal-directed actions over the learned models. A third part packages complex behavior into layered units. Tests in a simple environment showed the design working in principle. A harder test used handwritten digit images for shape detection. The authors claim the approach eases several known limits.
arxiv-2502-14135:
Aniket Mishra and Mark Stamp hunt for drift in malware families in a 2025 paper. Malware evolves, and a detector trained on last year's samples quietly decays as the code's traits shift, a change called concept drift. Catching the moment of drift tells defenders when to retrain.

The pair cluster samples from a time-stamped Android malware collection into batches and watch a clustering quality score. Dips in that score flag likely drift points. They then test four standard classifiers under three policies: never retrain, retrain on a schedule, and retrain when drift is flagged. The drift-aware policy, guided by the clustering signal, is the contender the experiments judge.
arxiv-2502-14435:
Hui Tong, Serdar Elhatisari, and Ulf Meißner compute neutron star matter from first principles. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, adds strange particles called hyperons to the mix. At high density these particles should appear, but they soften the matter. Soft matter cannot hold up the heaviest neutron stars we see, a puzzle for the field.

A new simulation method lets them include many hyperons with no sign trouble. They build three versions of the matter rule with two- and three-body forces. The top star mass lands just above two suns, matching what telescopes find. Size and tidal stretch for a mid-weight star also come out. The puzzle eases without ad hoc fixes.
arxiv-2502-14835:
Noah Berthusen, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Eric Huang, and Daniel Gottesman cut the cost of quantum error correction by measuring only the checks most likely to matter, in a paper from 2025. Error correction circuits can inject as many errors as they fix, and they slow the machine down. The team's adaptive scheme watches early results and reshapes later measurements on the fly.

They demonstrate it on a small code joined to a hypergraph product code. The adaptive version reached logical error rates over ten times lower than plain setups, with fewer entangling gates and fewer physical qubits. They also show the scheme supports universal fault-tolerant computing on this code family. The savings come from skipping checks the data says are not needed.
arxiv-2502-15235:
Siddhant Manna and Shantanu Desai stack faint sky signals from galaxy clusters in a 2025 study. Each cluster alone glows too faintly in gamma rays for a firm call. Stacking many clusters can pull a shared glow out of the noise, if the glow is truly there.

The team used more than sixteen years of space scope data on clusters picked by a ground survey. For the set with the faintest lone marks, the stack gave a firm joint signal. A dimmer cut gave a weak hint in line with plain noise. The glow's shape fits a smooth fall with energy, as the paper reports.
arxiv-2502-15335:
Siyuan Wang, Enda Zhao, Zhongyu Wei and Xiang Ren sharpen step-by-step reasoning in language models, in work from 2025. Long chains of thought tend to drift: later steps forget early facts and repeat what is already known. Their stepwise informativeness search is a tree search run at inference time, steered by two heuristics.

One favours steps that attend to neglected earlier steps, and a self-grounding prompt makes the model cite its premises before each deduction. The other favours steps whose conclusions are new. On four reasoning datasets the method raised accuracy while producing shorter rationales with fewer errors and less redundancy than standard decoding.
arxiv-2502-15435:
Leyla Candogan and co-authors present a single-pass detector for jailbreak prompts in a 2025 paper. Jailbreaks trick aligned language models into harmful output. Past defenses need many requests or help from other models, which is costly and slow.

Their method reads the model's own output scores, called logits, in one forward pass. Those scores carry signs of whether the coming answer will be harmful. The detector caught attacks well on open models and rarely flagged harmless input. It also worked with partial score access on two commercial models. A light, fast guard could sit in front of many deployed systems.
arxiv-2502-15535:
Software testers chase coverage, but loops defeat them: a loop may run any number of times. Most teams settle for branch coverage, which only checks the cases of zero or one pass through the loop. Bugs that need two passes stay invisible. Li Huang, Bertrand Meyer, and Reto Weber give loop unrolling a formal definition. Unrolling means running loops up to a chosen number of times, and its properties are proved mechanically in the Isabelle proof assistant.

They then plug the strategy into an existing automated testing framework and count the payoff in extra bugs found. The results offer a first measure of whether unrolling deserves a standard place in test generation and in how coverage itself is defined. The authors argue the concept was used loosely for years because it lacked a precise specification, and they supply one.
arxiv-2502-15735:
Xian Peng and co-authors built DistrEE in 2025, a method that lets a team of modest edge devices run a deep neural network and stop early when the answer is good enough. Edge intelligence, in vehicles, factories, and homes, more and more needs server-class inference on device-class hardware. And splitting a network across devices helps until fluctuating resources and uneven input hardness spoil the plan. Early exit points inside the network offer an escape hatch, if something decides when to use them.

DistrEE is presented as the first design to fuse distributed inference with early exiting for collaborative multi-node cases. Its exit policy reads the situation and terminates inference when the deployment's quality of service targets are met, rather than always paying for the full network. Models show the method delivering lean collaborative inference with a working balance between accuracy and cost.
arxiv-2502-15935:
Joseph Jensen and co-authors noted a recalibration of the cosmic distance scale in 2025, part of a project building a distance ladder independent of the usual Cepheid stars and supernovae. Their route uses the tip of the red giant branch. A sharp cutoff in old stars' brightness, to set the scale for surface brightness swings, a texture-based distance method for elliptical galaxies. Independence matters because measured and forecast expansion rates of the universe disagree.

Using James Webb Space Telescope distances anchored on the galaxy NGC 4258, whose distance is known geometrically from orbiting masers. The team derived a new zero point for Hubble telescope swing readings, with boosted colors from ground surveys. Their updated expansion rate lands virtually equal to an earlier swing-based value, strengthening the case that the tension is not a simple calibration error.
arxiv-2502-16335:
Rikako Yamamoto and fourteen co-authors measured spin-split surface bands on the antiferromagnet NdBi, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Splitting electron spins with magnetic order, rather than with heavy atoms, is a fresh route to spintronics parts. Using laser-based photoemission that reads both angle and spin, the team watched two surface bands appear when the material turned antiferromagnetic.

The two bands carried opposite spins, and the polarization flipped sign with momentum, the mark of split degeneracy. Computer modeling with a single-wave magnetic pattern matched the picture. The authors trace the effect to the surface losing its inversion symmetry in step with the magnetic order. They pitch such surfaces as tunable spin sources.
arxiv-2502-16835:
Luo, Xu, and Xu present a study from twenty twenty-five on finding code flaws with graph neural networks. Code can be drawn as a graph of elements and their links. Uniform graphs miss the varied link types that shape flaws. Their representation spans across procedure calls in a language-neutral way. A custom network learns from several feature subgraphs separately. Global attention then merges those views for a final verdict. Accuracy tops ninety-six percent on a large C dataset.

A Java dataset scores even higher in their tests. Both beat prior leaders for flaw detection. Real projects show low false alarm rates as well. The authors pitch the method for security assurance work.
arxiv-2502-17035:
Karine Altisen and Marius Bozga give a constructive proof that a classic self-stabilizing tree algorithm settles, even under an unfair scheduler. Their paper from twenty twenty-five revisits the BFS spanning tree method of Dolev and co-authors. Self-stabilizing systems recover from any state, so proofs must cover hostile run orders. An unfair daemon is the harshest such order.

Past proofs leaned on contradiction or assumed kinder daemons. The new proof builds well-founded orders and potential functions that force progress in the general case. Each step can be pointed to, not just inferred. The full proof is formalized in PADEC, a Coq-based tool for certifying such algorithms. Machine checking backs the claim end to end. The work firms up a textbook result in distributed computing.
arxiv-2502-17135:
Herle and co-authors present a way to measure the true shapes of dark matter halos from the sprinkle of satellite galaxies around them. Halo shapes test both cosmology and the physics of galaxy formation. But a typical halo hosts only a handful of visible satellites. Shapes estimated from so few points come out biased, systematically too round or too flat. The team modeled that sampling noise directly.

Their predictions matched the bias measured in a large suite of universe simulations, and the results held up against changes in resolution and in how strongly star formation feedback was modeled. Traced by only five satellites, a halo's projected axis ratio is biased low by about 0.31 on average. Correcting for sampling removes roughly two thirds of that error. The authors say the fix opens halo shape measurement to smaller systems than before, in both simulations and future sky surveys.
arxiv-2502-17435:
Chen-Wei Chang and colleagues presented GCC in 2025, a generative approach to color constancy. That task means judging scene light so colors look right across cameras. Methods often fail on new sensors because each sensor sees color differently. GCC uses a diffusion model to paint a color checker into the image, then reads the scene light from it.

Three ideas carry the method: one-step deterministic painting of the checker, and a Laplacian split that keeps the checker's structure while its colors adapt. Mask-based training tricks handle rough checker labels. Borrowing priors from pretrained diffusion models, GCC held up well across cameras with no sensor-specific training.
arxiv-2502-17835:
Gefei Zhang and co-authors build CPVis, a visual analytics system that helps teachers judge how student teams are programming together, in a 2025 paper. Pair and group coding builds skill, but instructors cannot watch every team at once. CPVis gathers multimodal data from real classrooms and shows group and individual performance at a glance, with a flower-shaped display per student and time views that trace how collaboration evolves.

In a within-subject test with 22 users, the system beat two baseline tools: users drew more insights, found the display more intuitive, and felt surer of their judgments. The authors aim the tool at busy programming courses with many novice teams.
arxiv-2502-18335:
Oliveira, Frederico, and de Paula explore the momentum structure of the quark propagator in a 2025 paper. The propagator describes how a quark travels and interacts inside matter, and its shape encodes how quarks gain mass in quantum chromodynamics. The authors build on earlier constraints from the theory's non-perturbative dynamics for the propagator's spectral parts.

They assume the propagator's two components share a simple pole but not its strength, and they link that pole to zeros of the quark wave function. Scaling laws for the remaining structure follow. Their results agree well with lattice simulations of full quantum chromodynamics. From that link they estimate the shared pole mass, which matches the constituent quark mass used in quark models, plus related quantities for pion physics.
arxiv-2502-18635:
Matthew Barker and five co-authors tackle the tuning problem for AI systems that answer questions using retrieved documents in a 2025 paper. Such systems involve many choices at once: which language model, which embedding and ranking models, and dozens of settings. Optimizing cost, speed, safety, and alignment together is hard because the option space is huge and each test run is expensive and noisy.

The authors present the first approach aimed at all these objectives across a whole system at once. Bayesian optimization methods clearly beat baseline strategies on two new benchmark tasks, finding better trade off frontiers. A caution closes the paper: the best configuration for one task may not transfer to another, so practitioners should tune per task.
arxiv-2502-18835:
Two researchers, Srikireddy Dhanunjay Reddy and Tharun Kumar Reddy Bollu, present a 2025 study on predicting stress from brain signals during music listening. Stress is common in school and office life. Many people use music to unwind. The team asked whether brain wave patterns could show the calming effect of a specific classical mode, Raag Darbari, and sort stressed from relaxed states.

They used a public data set of brain recordings gathered during music based sessions. Their method comes from topological data analysis, which reads the shape of data. Features such as the birth and death rates of shapes, and a form of entropy, served as markers. The approach classified subjects with an average accuracy of eighty six percent. The authors say these shape based features are robust markers for closely spaced subject data.
arxiv-2502-19335:
Stephan Rabanser and seven co-authors tune model cascades in twenty twenty-five. Big models perform well but cost heavily to run. Cascades pair a small local model with a large one, deferring hard tasks upward. Existing routing often defers too much or wastes the small model's real abilities.

Their loss function, Gatekeeper, fine-tunes the small model for its role. It should handle confidently the tasks it can do correctly. It should defer the rest to the larger model. A mechanism manages the trade-off between performance and deferral accuracy. The result is a cascade whose gatekeeper knows its own limits. Readers who serve models at scale get cheaper inference without silently dropping quality on easy tasks.
arxiv-2502-19535:
Muhibullah and co-authors present a 2025 X-ray study of nine huge galaxy clusters seen as they were about eight billion years ago. Clusters still in the act of merging may stir their central black holes into feeding frenzies. The team used a space X-ray eye to map each cluster's shape and count its bright cores.

A photon lopsided score sorted the shapes. The four most lopsided clusters look like mergers in flight. Most clusters held more bright cores than the open field at the same light cut. Core crowding rose with the lopsided score, a link past two sigma. Core density also fell as cluster mass grew. The pattern casts a rough house setting as a trigger for black hole meals.
arxiv-2502-19635:
Youran Zhou, Mohamed Bouadjenek, and Sunil Aryal set out a 2025 research agenda on missing data. Missing values show up in tables, sensors, time series, and images alike. Past work leaned on the case where data are missing purely by chance. Two other cases, where missingness links to known or unknown factors, are just as common but less studied. This PhD project plan tackles all three.

The aim is methods that stay sound under each missing pattern. The plan weighs what each pattern does to results across data types. It seeks tools that let users work with incomplete data in a confident way. Industries from health to transport face the same gaps. The paper is a forum agenda, so it maps work to come rather than final results.
arxiv-2502-19835:
Jana Nickel proves, in a 2025 math paper, a sharp test for when a signed network contains a set of paths that link a chosen set of nodes without touching each other. The networks, called bidirected graphs, give each edge end a plus or minus sign. Paths of this kind extend a classic result for plain graphs due to Gallai.

The test says the paths exist exactly when a counting rule holds for every pair of node sets that agree on the chosen set. The count weighs shared nodes plus the parts left after some edges are cut by the sign rule. Nickel also draws out a packing-versus-covering property for such paths, of the kind named for Erdős and Pósa.
arxiv-2502-19935:
A single message can carry several feelings at once, and sorting them is harder than it looks. Niloofar Ranjbar and Hamed Baghbani entered a shared task on multi label emotion detection with a two model recipe. First, a large language model, Llama-3, writes a short explanation of the text, spelling out the emotional cues that a quick read might blur.

That explanation then travels with the original text into RoBERTa, a smaller classifier that assigns the final emotion labels. The added context improved scores, especially for fear, joy, and sadness, and beat systems reading the text alone. The authors argue that explanations help most exactly where emotions overlap and cues conflict, the cases that dominate real world language data.
arxiv-2502-20035:
Xuyang Wei, Chunlin Tian, and Li Li published a 2025 paper on fine-tuning multimodal language models without letting their skills fight. Training one model on many image-text datasets brings conflict: tasks pull the model in opposite directions. It also brings synergy, where tasks teach each other. Most tuning methods handle one side or the other. Their framework, AsymLoRA, handles both at once.

The method splits the tuning machinery asymmetrically. Each task gets its own low-rank projection, a private pathway that protects its distinct needs. A second projection is shared across tasks, gathering what they have in common. In evaluations, the design beat both plain tuning, which keeps only the common part, and a mixture-of-experts variant, which keeps only the separate parts. It also ran more efficiently. The lesson is architectural humility: conflicts and commonalities are both real, and a tuner should make room for each.
arxiv-2502-20935:
Philemon Urbain Mballa wrote a 2025 paper attacking three famous unsolved conjectures about unit fractions. The Erdős–Straus conjecture says 4/n always splits into three unit fractions. A Sierpiński variant makes the same claim for 5/n. Their generalization covers other numerators. None has been proved in full.

Mballa reformulates the conjectures equivalently and builds two explicit formulas. The first works whenever a divisibility condition holds. The second, broader formula needs a suitable perfect square to exist, which he conjectures always happens. Under those conditions the formulas verify the claims even for very large numbers. The approach shrinks the problem to hunting for one perfect square. The paper closes with open questions inviting the community to complete the proof.
arxiv-2502-21035:
Forecasting a building's energy use is hard because sensor readings tangle with shifting weather, and a 2025 paper by Melanie Schaller and Bodo Rosenhahn offers a leaner model for the job. Their model, S4ConvD, reshapes a deep state space design with convolution so it needs little data cleanup before use.

Built-in scaling and frequency tweaks let the model catch complex patterns in how buildings use energy over time. On a large public contest data set for energy prediction, it beat the current benchmarks. A tiling trick also cut its graphics card run time a great deal. The full code and data are public, and the authors note the method could help blend renewable power into smart grids.
arxiv-2502-21235:
Brain scans produce huge webs of links between tiny regions, and studies of autism need models that can handle that scale. Hyoshin Kim, Sujit Ghosh, and Emily Hector propose such a model in a 2025 paper. Their data come from a shared autism brain imaging collection with more than a trillion data points.

The model groups brain regions into blocks, which keeps the link web simple enough to fit for each person. It then ties those links to traits such as age, sex, and whether the eyes were open during the scan. A Bayesian setup flags regions tied to an autism diagnosis. In the shared data, the method matched known findings and pointed to new ones.
arxiv-2503-00135:
Loganayagam and Omkar Shetye extend a holography proposal to electromagnetism in a 2025 paper. Their earlier work framed static patch holography for de Sitter space, the geometry of an expanding universe. Here they ask how an observer inside that space feels the push and pull of bulk electromagnetic fields.

Using the on-shell action on a de Sitter Schwinger-Keldysh geometry, they derive the observer's influence phase. This quantity encodes radiation reaction and the matching Hawking radiation, with the self-force kept finite by holographic renormalization. In the short-time limit, the classic Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac reaction reappears, plus corrections from the cosmos. The paper also extends multipole expansions and vector spherical harmonics to these curved settings.
arxiv-2503-00735:
Toby Simonds and Akira Yoshiyama let a language model tutor itself by breaking hard problems into easier ones, recursively. Their framework, LADDER, needs no curated data set and no human feedback. The model generates progressively simpler variants of a problem, solves its way up the ladder, and learns from the climb. Mathematical integration is the proving ground.

A small open model's accuracy on undergraduate integrals leapt from one percent to eighty-two. A distilled reasoning model reached seventy-three percent on the MIT Integration Bee qualifier. The authors then move the trick to test time: reinforcement learning on variants of the very problems being attempted. That variant hit ninety percent on the same qualifier, above a famous commercial system's score. Self-directed decomposition, they argue, can substitute for scale and supervision.
arxiv-2503-00835:
Karunathilaka leads a team presenting Intuit, an augmented reality system that teaches quantum computing through everyday analogies in a 2025 paper. Quantum ideas are abstract and counterintuitive for beginners. Coins and paper cutters are not.

Expert interviews and literature shaped a framework mapping quantum concepts to daily objects. Traits such as qubit count, output duality, and probability are matched to familiar phenomena. The prototype layers these analogies onto the real world using situated analytics. Interviews with users and experts judged the approach effective and usable. Learners grasped abstract ideas more intuitively and stayed engaged. The authors offer analogy design as a route into quantum literacy. Stakeholders beyond physics are the audience.
arxiv-2503-01235:
Timothee Mickus, Aman Sinha, and Raúl Vázquez ask how we should judge whether a test example is truly hard for a language model. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Hardness can come from the example itself, when its meaning is unclear. The team compared three ways to measure it. These were disagreement among human raters, how training unfolds, and how sure the model sounds.

They ran twenty-nine models on three data sets. The three measures did line up in part, but the links were neither straight nor steady. A case that looks hard by one measure may look easy by another. The authors argue that splitting these kinds of doubt apart gives a clearer view of data complexity. That view can help researchers judge and improve their models.
arxiv-2503-01435:
Joseph Webber and Thomas Montenegro-Johnson model gels that pump when heated in a 2025 paper. Certain hydrogels flip between swollen and shrunken states past a threshold heat, changing volume tenfold. That flip could drive tiny pumps for lab-on-chip devices, but modeling it usually needs many fitted microscopic parameters. The pair present a leaner, macroscopic description of the gel's porous mechanics.

Their model reproduces the switch without the parameter thicket. It then explores shrinking, swelling, and pumping cycles for tube-shaped gel pumps. The closing discussion suggests hollowing larger gel actuators into tubes so heat reaches the core faster. Faster response would unlock shape-changing devices that now move too slowly to use.
arxiv-2503-01735:
Grace McKnight, Channyung Lee, and Elif Ertekin charted oxygen drift in a crystal in a 2025 study. The crystal, beta gallium oxide, is a prized wide-gap semiconductor for power devices. Its low-symmetry frame makes atoms drift in unlike ways by direction, which sways how devices are grown and doped.

From first-principles math joined with master diffusion equations, they built the full three-dimensional drift maps for stray oxygen atoms in two charge states. They first found every stable nook such an atom can sit in and its energy cost. Linked hops between nooks then give the drift rates. The maps guide growers who need oxygen to stay put.
arxiv-2503-01835:
Transformer networks conquered language and images, yet plain convolutional networks still win at outlining organs in 3D medical scans. Tassilo Wald and co-authors asked why. They found that many so-called transformer models lean on their convolutional parts. Removing the transformer sometimes changed nothing.

Their answer is Primus, a design that forces attention to do the work, using fine-grained tokens and updated positional schemes. A second version refines how image patches enter the network. Across nine public datasets, the first Primus matched the standard champion network. The second version surpassed it and stood level with the best convolutional designs. The authors call Primus the first truly competitive transformer-first segmenter.
arxiv-2503-01935:
Kunlun Zhu and co-authors introduce MultiAgentBench, a test suite for teams of AI agents, in a 2025 paper. Single-agent tests cannot show how agents cooperate or compete. This benchmark stages varied interactive scenes for language model teams. It scores not just task success but the quality of teamwork and rivalry, using milestone-based measures.

The team compared ways for agents to organize: star, chain, tree, and graph layouts. Group discussion and cognitive planning were also tested as strategies. One compact model earned the top average task score. Graph layout won among the structures in the research scene. Planning raised milestone success by a modest margin. Code and data are public for other labs.
arxiv-2503-02135:
Nisha Devasia, Runhua Zhao, and Jin Ha Lee ask whether story shapes how players learn from escape room games about misinformation, in a paper from 2025. False claims spread fast, and games are one proposed way to build media literacy. Most such games, though, skip the social and emotional pulls that make falsehoods stick.

The team studied 123 young adults who played two story-led escape room games built for libraries. They measured how far players were carried into the story and how far they identified with its roles. A taste for fan culture, and a habit of sharing on social media, swayed those immersion scores. The authors draw design lessons for fitting games to each falsehood setting.
arxiv-2503-02335:
Renshuang Jiang and Pan Dong lead a team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, whose text lists Duan with a variant spelling. It presents RustBrain, a language model frame that hunts undefined behaviors in Rust code that uses the unsafe tag.

Unsafe Rust buys speed and low-level reach but can break memory safety. The frame thinks in two gears: a fast gear drafts fixes from code traits, and a slow gear breaks them down, checks them, and draws broad rules. A feedback loop feeds the checks back into the drafts. On the Miri test set it clears most cases and runs most of them too. The design aims at both reach and care.
arxiv-2503-02635:
Sarif Khan and Hyun Min Lee build a dark matter model with two flavors of dark particle in a 2025 paper. Their scheme adds a new symmetry to the standard model, one tied to the difference between baryon and lepton counts. The symmetry is free of anomalies without adding right-handed neutrinos.

When the symmetry breaks, dark fermions gain mass through single scalar fields. One component interacts enough to freeze out like a classic thermal relic. The other barely interacts and builds up slowly from decays. The new force carrier grows heavy despite a tiny coupling and also feeds dark particle production. Both components can share the dark matter budget in fitting fractions. The design dodges current detection limits while explaining neutrino masses.
arxiv-2503-02835:
Afsana Ahsan Jeny, Masum Shah Junayed, Md Robel Mia, and Md Baharul Islam build an automated system to sort acne types from face photos, in this 2025 paper. The catalog creator carries extra department text, but the head gives the clean byline. Acne is common in teens and harms both skin and mood, and telling its types apart by eye is slow.

Their pipeline cleans each photo, boosts contrast, and converts color space to cut noise. A clustering step cuts out the diseased patches. Texture and statistical features are then pulled from those patches. Five standard classifiers were tried on six acne types. A random forest won, reaching 98.50 percent accuracy, ahead of published rival methods. The authors present the system as a desk aid for dermatologists, not a replacement for them.
arxiv-2503-03035:
Hoessler and a team of co-authors run high-fidelity airflow simulation over a Formula 1 front wing joined to a rolling wheel. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such combined shapes had never been tackled with higher-order methods before.

The spectral element code Nektar++ solved the flow equations at a Reynolds number of two hundred twenty thousand. The wing came from a real McLaren design, already a benchmark alone. Adding the spinning, ground-touching wheel made the setup truly industrial. Time-averaged results were checked against wind-tunnel particle imaging. Agreement judged the method's reliability for design work. The authors detail what resolution levels real racing geometries demand from this class of solver.
arxiv-2503-03235:
Len Bos and three co-authors refine the mathematics of the fastest way to ride a bicycle uphill. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Power is capped on average, above, and below, and the rider's speed profile must respect all three.

An earlier model forced a flying start at a speed the math chose. The new version allows any launch, from standing still to full sprint, by letting speed vary linearly in pieces. Whatever the start, slope, or profile, the optimal plan settles toward constant ground speed. The freedom to vary the start unlocks practical calls. In time trials mixing flats and climbs, the analysis says when swapping to a climbing bike, stop and all, actually pays.
arxiv-2503-03535:
Po-Chien Luan and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on tracking people with a single camera. Robot systems often need costly gear or hand-labeled data to locate a person and guess where they will walk next. Models trained on such clean data also falter on noisy real input. The team builds one transformer framework, MonoTransmotion, that does both jobs at once.

One module maps 2D body poses to a bird's-eye position, guided by a new loss that keeps estimates smooth over time. A second module forecasts the path from those estimates. Joint training lifted scores by about twelve percent on a curated set and held up on messy real-world data.
arxiv-2503-03735:
Adrian Crawford and co-authors conduct the first population study of a two-peaked kind of exploding star, in a 2025 paper. Type IIb supernovae come from massive stars that lost most of their hydrogen skin before exploding. Their light curves show a brief shock-cooling flash, then the main peak powered by radioactive nickel. The team gathered fourteen confirmed cases from two sky surveys, including unpublished and reclassified ones, all with public light curves from 2018 to 2022.

They fit a simple piecewise model, nicknamed the lightning bolt. The first peak lasts under five days above half brightness and rises startlingly fast, over ten times faster than the main peak and only a third as long. Those rise rates rival the fastest known cosmic transients. The authors also demonstrate an alert filter that could flag such events live in the coming Rubin Observatory stream, using their numbers as the sieve.
arxiv-2503-03835:
Shalgar and Tamborra solve neutrino quantum kinetics in three flavors inside a supernova shell, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Shifts of flavor may reshape how supernovae explode and heat up. Their equations include flow and hits, and keep the full strength of the pull neutrinos exert on each other. A shell near the zone where neutrinos break free is modeled at two times.

Early on, slow shared effects drive flavor change with no crossings in angle. Later, fast instabilities set off a near-full sharing out of flavors, close to even. Heating by neutrinos rises by up to thirty percent once flavor change is in. Small crossings in the muon and tau sectors barely matter. Late in time, what the shell gives off looks much the same across flavors.
arxiv-2503-03935:
Abdullah Mamun and co-authors predict blood sugar spikes after meals from wearable data, in work from 2025. Such spikes mark a step toward type two diabetes in people at risk. Their system, GlucoLens, fuses motion and glucose sensors with food and work logs from a five-week trial of ten working adults.

Language models help clean and frame the mixed data for the predictor. The best setup beat rival models by a wide margin on error scores. It flagged high sugar with solid exactness too. It also offers counterfactual tips, showing what habit tweaks might dodge a spike. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2503-04535: Mihai Fulger and Victor Lozovanu compute a Newton-Okounkov body for products of curves in a 2025 paper. These bodies turn divisor data into convex shapes whose volumes encode geometric truths. The infinitesimal version, zoomed at a point, is notoriously hard to pin down. For certain box-product polarizations on products of curves, the authors compute the generic infinitesimal body at any point. They present it as the first nontrivial description of such a body in arbitrary dimension, a benchmark case for a theory long short on examples.
arxiv-2503-04835:
Donghyeok Shin and four co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on shrinking huge data sets for training AI models. Big data sets teach well but cost a lot to store and process. A field called dataset distillation boils a big set down to a small fake one that still trains models well. Past fake sets are stored as fixed grids of values, which limits their shape.

The new method stores the fake data inside a neural field, a network that takes coordinates as input and gives values back. That design can make data of many shapes, from images to video, sound, and 3D blocks. The authors prove the design can express more than older ones at the same storage size. Tests across those data types beat prior methods, and the code is shared for others to try.
arxiv-2503-05135:
Suliman Khan, Sakander Hayat, and Mohammed Alenazi wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 about signed graphs, where each edge carries a plus or minus sign. Their focus is the positive inertia index, a count tied to the positive values that come from the graph's adjacency matrix. They study connected signed graphs that contain at least one cycle, and they relate the count to girth, the length of the shortest cycle.

The authors prove a lower bound for the index based on girth. They also describe the exact graphs that reach the bound and the graphs that sit one step above it. The results extend recent work on ordinary graphs into the signed setting, giving graph theorists a sharper tool for this class.
arxiv-2503-05235:
Wankai Li and five co-authors study ionization phase shifts between two laser dressed states in two thousand twenty-five. Their test bed is resonance enhanced multiphoton ionization of potassium. Strong coupling dresses the atomic states with the laser field. Photoelectron momentum images record the freed electrons.

Energy spectra reveal the dressed state energies in clear peaks. Their split, of Autler-Townes kind, grows with field strength. Angle patterns of the electrons expose phase shifts between the states. Those shifts tie to attosecond ionization time delays. Coulomb and quantum defect phases jointly drive the seen shift.
arxiv-2503-05335:
Joel Honkamaa and Pekka Marttinen craft in a 2025 paper a new similarity score for aligning medical images from unlike scanners. Warped alignment across modes is core to many care tasks and stays hard. The snag is judging overlap when each image shows tissue in its own way.

Their score rests on local functional dependence between pixel values in matched spots. Global dependence is too strict, but small patches make the idea work well. Basis functions, learned jointly with the warp itself, model that local link. Convolution math keeps the score fast to compute on graphics hardware. The tool is released for easy use and beats set baselines on three data sets.
arxiv-2503-05935:
Yasir Khan and seven co-authors summarize big tables by shrinking them first in a 2025 paper. Query-focused table summaries must answer from rows and columns. Giant tables overflow the token limits of transformers. Reasoning across them also strains standard models.

Their system, DETQUS, trims tables with a language model's help. Only columns the query needs survive the cut. A fine-tuned encoder-decoder then writes the summary. A table question-answering model aids the pipeline further. Scores beat the prior best system on the standard metric. The design scales better than heavier architectures. Accuracy gains come from the leaner input.
arxiv-2503-06435:
Adrian Chow, Evelien Riddell, Yimu Wang, Sean Sedwards, and Krzysztof Czarnecki presented OV-SCAN in twenty twenty-five, a system that lets self-driving cars spot object types they were never trained on. Open-vocabulary detection links a classic three-dimensional detector with a vision-language model, so new objects can be named from text. The weak point is pairing three-dimensional features with image features that truly mean the same thing.

OV-SCAN attacks that pairing in two ways. It finds precise three-dimensional annotations for new objects, and it filters out bad pairs caused by sloppy labels, blocked views, or low image resolution. On the nuScenes driving data set it reached top performance. The approach targets a real safety need: cars must notice the unexpected, not just the catalogued.
arxiv-2503-06635:
Zhiyuan Ning and ten co-authors present, in 2025 work, a new way to sort linked data into groups. Such data form nets, where points join by lines. New deep methods often blur the codes of close points, so groups smear and the sort fails. The team traces that flaw to how the nets pass news along their links.

Their fix skips the usual net layers. One part builds codes by a cut rule that weighs both links and traits of each point. The next part assigns groups with a transport method that stops all points from being dumped in one group. Tests against rival methods, the team reports, show strong results with a simple design. They frame the cut view as a better base for the task.
arxiv-2503-07135:
Hanzhi Chen and four co-authors teach robots household manipulation by watching ordinary human videos. Their framework, VidBot, appeared in twenty twenty-five. Training robots directly is slow and physical, while the internet already holds endless footage of hands doing tasks.

The pipeline lifts three-dimensional hand paths out of flat monocular clips. Depth estimation and structure-from-motion rebuild the paths at true scale, consistent over time. A two-stage learner first picks the coarse action, then a diffusion model drafts the fine contact trajectory, steered by test-time constraints. Across thirteen manipulation tasks, VidBot beat rivals in zero-shot tests, never having practiced the tasks. It also transferred onto real robot hardware in everyday rooms.
arxiv-2503-07335:
A Sudoku puzzle gives away just enough cells to force one full solution, and graph theorists ask the same question of colored networks. Jack Dippel, Austin Eide, Paweł Prałat, and Daniel Willhalm study that number in this 2025 paper for random graphs where every node has exactly three neighbors. Such graphs need three colors, and the question is how few precolored nodes force the rest.

They show the number stays near one third of the nodes, for large random graphs, almost surely. Their proof runs an algorithm that colors the graph so as to create many locally forced nodes, those that already see two colors next door. The analysis leans on a fresh use of a differential equations method joined with Markov chain tools.
arxiv-2503-07935:
Hossen, Gurses, Sichitiu, and Güvenç build a fast simulation framework for drone network digital twins in a 2025 paper. Drones can extend coverage in next-generation wireless networks. Testing new flight and radio ideas inside a twin is safer than field trials, but twins are slow to build.

Their Matlab framework is tuned with real measurements to mimic a full network twin. It was checked against a national testbed twin under like settings. Signal strength results matched closely between the two. That match supports swapping between the quick simulator and the full twin during design. The goal is a shorter development cycle for drone networks.
arxiv-2503-08135:
Junfu Guo and five co-authors build digital twins of jointed objects from photos, in a paper from 2025. Objects such as tools or doors move at joints, so a twin must learn each part shape and how the parts move.

Their method, ArticulatedGS, learns from two sets of views that show the object in two still poses. It needs no three dimensional ground truth, no motion cues, and no part labels. Steps split the linked unknowns so training stays steady. In tests it beat like methods on part splits, motion scores, and how true the views looked.
arxiv-2503-08335:
Long videos, like full lectures and news broadcasts, are hard for computer models to understand end to end. Soumya Shamarao Jahagirdar, Jayasree Saha, and CV Jawahar assemble a dataset of such long-form videos to study the problem. Labels for hours of footage would need expert annotators, which makes hand-made datasets costly and rare.

Speech recognition can pull the spoken words from a video, and text recognition can read words shown on screen. The authors build baseline systems on those two text streams and show where they fall short. They argue the way forward is prompt engineering: asking large language models the right questions so they can piece a whole video together. Their dataset and baselines give that idea a concrete test bed.
arxiv-2503-08535:
Denis Illesca, Andres Piatti, Matias Chiarpotti, and Roberto Butron measure star clusters toward the disturbed outskirts of the Small Magellanic Cloud, in work from twenty twenty-five. Tidal tugs from the larger neighbour galaxy warp the small galaxy's edges. Cluster ages, distances, and metal levels may trace that warping. Deep survey colour charts, cleaned of stray field stars, supply the data. Thousands of fake charts help pin each cluster's traits.

Distances are derived for many clusters for the first time here. That haul raises the count of clusters with known distances by half. Outer and inner clusters share the same broad enrichment history. Half the studied clusters sit in front of or behind the main body, though. Those clusters likely formed inside and drifted outward under tidal pull. Rich young clusters in the outskirts grew from gas dragged out the same way.
arxiv-2503-08635:
Christopher Latchford and Daniel Maser describe a low-cost optical frequency comb in this 2025 paper. A frequency comb is a laser tool whose light forms many evenly spaced lines. Such tools cost a lot in commercial form, which limits lab access.

Their design uses off-the-shelf parts based on an erbium fiber plan, with several upgrades. An undergraduate built the full device for a fraction of the commercial price. Its pulse rate sits near one hundred megahertz and can be tuned across three megahertz. A control loop held long-term drift under one hertz over days. The comb is meant for dual-comb spectroscopy work.
arxiv-2503-09035:
Stunt drivers pull off sharp moves at the edge of grip. Shawn Azdam, Pranav Doma, and Aliasghar Moj Arab ask whether a self-driving car could do the same to dodge a crash. Their twenty twenty-five work builds a control setup run by large language model agents. Tests took place in a driving simulator, with J-turns as the test move.

Three agents split the job: one adds context to the driver's command, one sets the move values, and one checks those values against physics and safety rules. The setup starts from scratch, with no fresh training of the model. J-turns worked across several car models through text prompts that adapt to each car. The authors note weak spots in fine number control and in harder scenes.
arxiv-2503-09635:
GeonU Kim, Youwang Kim, Hyoseok Lee, and Tae-Hyun Oh present FPGS, a fast way to restyle large 3D scenes in a photo-like way. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works with Gaussian Splatting, a scene format built from many soft blobs. Past style tools needed slow per-style tuning or per-scene training. They also stuck to small scenes.

FPGS skips retraining by styling a shared 3D feature field in one pass. It borrows a classic feed-forward styling step and lifts it into 3D. Users can mix several style images at once. Meaning-based matching pairs scene parts with the right style source. Local styling then adds user control area by area. Tests on large still and moving scenes show strong photo-like quality. The method keeps views in line with each other and renders in real time.
arxiv-2503-09835:
Becker, Koutentakis, and Schmelcher watch an impurity atom move through a one-line Fermi gas in two thousand twenty-five. Simple theory treats the impurity as gliding on smooth energy curves, an adiabatic picture. Strong contact with the gas can break that picture where curves nearly cross.

Those crossings stem from the pseudo Jahn-Teller effect, borrowed from molecular physics. Full quantum simulations, checked against a multi-channel form of the simple theory, track the impurity after a sudden quench. A small starting shift gives one crossing and clean hops between curves. A large shift stacks crossings, boosting hops, self-trapping, and energy spread. The setup offers a tunable stage for non-adiabatic dynamics in labs.
arxiv-2503-10135:
Jinze Li and six co-authors present Gumiho, a design that speeds up text generation by guessing ahead, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes a run of tokens and the big model checks them, accepting the ones that line up. Most designs treat every guessed token as equal, but the authors prove the early guesses matter far more, since one bad early token voids the rest.

Gumiho therefore spends its strength up front: a full transformer drafts the first tokens one by one, while light, simple heads guess the later tokens all at once. The split gives better accuracy where it counts and speed where it is safe. Tests against rival designs showed the hybrid ahead overall.
arxiv-2503-10235:
Murray Stokely, Neel Nadgir, Jack Peele, and Orestis Kostakis study how cloud customers should commit to compute capacity, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Providers offer discounts for long-term commitments, which guarantee them revenue for data center investment. Customers, though, face demand risk if expected usage never materializes. The trade-offs for large services were little reported.

The authors characterize demand using a three-year study of the Snowflake Data Cloud. That service spans data warehousing, lakes, science, and engineering workloads across multiple clouds. They quantify demand drivers from user workloads, hardware generations, and software improvements. With that data, they formulate practical optimizations. The goal is to maximize capacity availability while minimizing customer cost. Their findings give large cloud buyers an evidence base for sizing long-term commitments.
arxiv-2503-10635:
Zhaoyi Li and co-authors show a plain attack that fools top closed vision-language models in a 2025 paper. Past attacks honed on open models often fail on closed shop models. The team traces the flaw to noise that lacks clear sense, which closed models shrug off or misread.

Their fix keeps noise rich in sense and aims it at the parts of an image that hold most sense. At each step they crop and resize the image at random, then align it with a target in the model space. The trick tops nine in ten tries on the strongest closed models in their tests.
arxiv-2503-10735:
Business records that track many kinds of objects at once need a careful extraction plan, and a 2025 paper by Najmeh Miri and co-authors supplies one. Object-centric process mining studies a process from several views at once, such as students, teachers, and groups in a school path. That view needs event data that keeps links between events and objects.

Building such logs is harder than building plain logs, since links are rich. The new method extends a known mining framework with clear steps for analysts and engineers. A real school case shows the method can build a sound log in practice. Teams gain a guide that cuts repeat work when views shift.
arxiv-2503-11435:
Marianne Defresne and co-authors speed up how solvers learn user tastes in a 2025 paper. Real design tasks juggle clashing aims like price, quality, and green cost, and users rarely can state trade weights up front. Asking users to compare pairs of options can teach those weights, if each round stays cheap.

Their upgrades work on three fronts at once. Pools of near solutions make each query fast to build. A Bradley Terry model fit by likelihood sharpens what pairs teach. An ensemble pick, drawn from active learning, cuts the count of rounds. Tests on a PC build task and a routing case beat past methods on all three fronts.
arxiv-2503-11535:
Mario Scrocca and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on a shared metadata standard for mobility data in Europe. Transport data sit in many portals with varied formats, which makes them hard to find and reuse across borders. Metadata can fix that, if portals describe data in the same way.

Their standard, mobilityDCAT-AP, was built with transport experts and Semantic Web specialists. The paper reports how the model was made, the best practices in its release, and the teaching aids made to spread it. Early adopters share success stories and the snags they hit when using web-based methods. The authors argue a common metadata frame is a key step toward joined, efficient mobility across countries.
arxiv-2503-11635: Navarro-Obregón and Queiruga discuss, in a 2025 paper, sphaleron-like solutions placed on a circle. A sphaleron is a static but unstable lump of field energy, poised to decay. The authors explore how exciting the lump's own internal modes might steady it. They also watch large sphalerons collapse on the ring. On time scales set by the ring's size, that collapse looks like a kink and antikink crashing on an endless line.
arxiv-2503-11735:
Babujian and co-authors tie proton smash data to solvable models in a 2025 paper. Deep hits on protons map how their parts share push at small slices. Data from a German ring set the map across many scales.

At small slices, the map grows by a clean power law whose tilt rises with scale. A crossover form from group flow fits that tilt well. The end tilt matches the sine-Gordon class among solvable fields. That class fit the full data sheet with near prime scores. Small slice growth may thus be ruled by that shared class, a bridge from data to exact math.
arxiv-2503-11835:
Haoxin Liu and eight co-authors survey how time series study can gain from other data types, such as text, images, and sound. Time series work is old and broad, yet this data type has grown apart from richer types. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The authors call this new field by a short name and sort its gains into three kinds. Other types can lend their large pre-trained models, can extend a time task with extra detail, or can mix with time data for deeper study. Works are grouped by the added type, from text and images to sound and tables. The survey ends with gaps and next steps for each gain kind.
arxiv-2503-12135:
Wei Xie and Wei-Hua Lei describe magnetically driven jets from accretion disks in 2025. Jets erupt from many cosmic objects, yet their launch mechanism stays debated. One idea says large scale magnetic fields on the disk fling the plasma out. The pair work in full general relativity around a non spinning black hole.

Their outflow solution is traced by a Bernoulli style function passing through two critical points. Plasma conditions at the disk footpoint bound whether a jet solution exists at all. The result extends a classic 1994 treatment into the relativistic regime. It sharpens how magnetic launch models are tested against real jets.
arxiv-2503-12435:
Martino Chiarani, Swastika Roy, Christos Verikoukis, and Fabrizio Granelli propose a smarter way to pick devices for shared learning in future 6G networks. Their 2025 paper deals with network slicing, where one network is split into virtual parts for varied uses. Learning across devices avoids pooling private data in one center.

The catch is choosing which devices to trust for each round of training. Their method uses explainable AI scores to guide that choice for slice resource planning at the network edge. The setting allows devices whose data differs a lot from each other. Simulations beat the standard approach on speed of convergence and computing cost, and the method scaled well. The work also makes neural models less of a black box for network operators.
arxiv-2503-12635:
Amin Banayeeanzade and Mohammad Rostami fight machine forgetting by splitting the learner in two, in a 2025 paper. Neural networks that learn task after task tend to erase old skills. The human brain avoids this with a fast intuitive system and a slow reasoning one. Their framework copies that split: a neural network adapts quickly to the newest task, while a symbolic reasoner banks what came before.

A bridge moves knowledge from the reasoner back into the network when needed. The team also built two new continual learning benchmarks with compositional structure. On those tests, the hybrid beat purely neural methods at holding onto old tasks. The authors argue memory lives better in symbols than in weights alone.
arxiv-2503-12735:
Sam Olesker-Taylor, Lucas Teyssier, and Paul Thévenin develop sharp bounds for characters of symmetric groups. Their 2025 paper blends a hook-length formula, known character bounds, and careful diagram slicing into one flexible method. Characters set mixing behavior for random walks on these groups.

The method yields a uniform exponential bound with the best possible constant. For classes with many fixed points, the bounds sharpen further. Those gains let the authors prove cutoff behavior for random walks on the linked Cayley graphs. Cutoff means the walk snaps from unmixed to mixed in a short window. Both total variation and mean-square senses are covered.
arxiv-2503-13035:
Giuseppe Brusca, Davide Donati, and Chiara Trifone study phase transitions in a twenty twenty-five paper. Their model uses a double-well potential, perturbed by terms that involve derivatives of high order. The materials are anisotropic, meaning they behave differently by direction. The question is what the model does as a small parameter shrinks toward zero.

They use Gamma-convergence to track that limit. Some coefficients in the model may be negative, which breaks the usual bounds. The authors overcome this by proving a nonlinear interpolation inequality. With it, they gain a compactness result for the functionals. Readers in analysis get a model that allows high-order and sign-changing effects in phase change problems.
arxiv-2503-13135:
The ATLAS Collaboration hunts for partner particles of leptons in proton crashes at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 paper. Supersymmetry predicts charged sleptons and sneutrinos that could decay in cascades ending in three leptons plus invisible momentum. The target scene also ties to the muon's odd magnetic wobble and to dark matter counts.

The search used 140 inverse femtobarns of crashes at 13 TeV. No excess over standard model forecasts appeared. That null result sets firm bounds: slepton and sneutrino masses up to 450 GeV are ruled out when the lightest neutral partner weighs 100 GeV. The bounds squeeze a favored corner of supersymmetry that many models had kept open.
arxiv-2503-13335:
Sang Truong and co-authors cut the cost of testing language models without losing trust in the scores, in work from 2025. Full test suites hold huge numbers of questions, so frequent testing is pricey. Testing on a small subset can mislead, since subset hardness skews the mean.

A classic testing theory handles hardness, but rating each question is itself costly. The authors train a model that predicts question hardness from the question text alone. That trick lets the theory run cheaply on new suites. Scores then adjust for which questions were picked. Teams can test more often during building and launch. The method aims for scores that stay stable across subsets.
arxiv-2503-13635:
Giordano Paoletti and four co-authors present a 2025 study of what sparks people to post in Telegram groups. They studied about six million messages from near 30,000 users in 409 public groups. The team measured five sparks of curiosity: social pull, novelty, complexity, uncertainty, and conflict.

After grouping the messages, they labeled clusters with plain profiles of these sparks. Some users post when peers or influencers draw them in. Others react to rare media types or a mix of senders. Most users kept a stable spark profile over time, though long gaps could shift it. A network view showed socially driven users on the edges, while users with no clear spark sat near the center and often started talks. The findings may guide outreach plans.
arxiv-2503-13935:
Yuan and co-authors present a 2025 paper on SCORE, a method for shrinking training datasets without swelling storage. Dataset condensation brews tiny stand-in sets that train models nearly as well as the full data. Soft-labeled realistic images scale nicely, yet the labels can eat more space than the originals. SCORE reframes the brew as a tug-of-war among three virtues: information, separation, and squeezability.

A coding-rate formula, borrowed from information theory, runs the contest. The team prove the goal has a submodular shape, so optimizing it presses labels into tidy low-rank form. Large-scale trials on image sets close the case. Storage drops while training power holds.
arxiv-2503-14535:
Huaqiu Li, Xiaowan Hu, and Haoqian Wang present a method to clean and brighten real world low light photos in a 2025 paper. Such photos mix glare, dim regions, noise, and uneven light. Methods trained on paired examples overfit, while unsupervised methods lack reference images to learn the damage from.

Their method trains on paired crops from the same photo that differ in light and noise, guided by imaging physics. A frequency based split helps separate the mixed damage types, and a retinal style network does the repair. The authors report the method beat rivals across many tests, with code to follow.
arxiv-2503-14635:
Jianghao Zhang, writing alone in 2025, proves bounds for a class of multi-input singular operators in higher dimensions. The operators act on groups of functions, and their defining rule is well behaved away from a flat subspace. The hard part is that proof gets tougher as the size of that subspace grows relative to the whole space.

Zhang focuses on the case where that size ratio falls in a narrow, awkward band between two landmarks. In that band he establishes the norm bounds the field seeks. The paper is short, dense, and aimed at specialists in harmonic analysis. Its value lies in closing a gap in the known range of cases for these operators.
arxiv-2503-15235:
Who is the Spy is a party word game: most players share a secret word, one spy does not, and everyone bluffs by describing it. The three authors ask how large language models play such games, which mix language skill with social deduction. They propose a training-free framework that schedules the models' play with chain-of-thought reasoning, covering both inferring the role word and disguising an identity.

They score the framework by game success rates and by how accurate the agents' analysis is. Across multiple data sets the framework lifted model performance notably. The authors present word games as a sharp test bed for situational reasoning and social interaction in language models, and they publish their code.
arxiv-2503-15335: Marleau and the Euclid Consortium present a census of dwarf galaxies from the Euclid space telescope's first quick data release. The Q1 fields were picked for calibration work in cosmology and so hold few nearby galaxies. That emptiness, the team notes, is exactly what suits them to a dwarf galaxy census across a range of distances and environments. The 2025 paper appears on behalf of the whole consortium, whose member list runs to hundreds of names.
arxiv-2503-15435:
Baolu Li and six co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on cars that share what they sense. When cars and road units pool sensor views, driving can be safer. But models trained on one data set often fail on new ones. The team named this gap and tested it across four open data sets.

Their method mixes views from fake new partners to mimic unseen cases. It also keeps the mixed features close to the source features, for steady learning. Trials showed clear gains on unseen data sets. Scores on the source set stayed strong as well. The work is a first study of this shift problem for pooled car sensing.
arxiv-2503-15635:
The Euclid Collaboration and many co-authors test whether the Euclid space telescope can map the ages and makeup of stars across nearby galaxies, patch by patch. Their 2025 paper is a proof of concept built on fake images from the TNG50 simulation, which grows realistic galaxies inside a computer universe.

Working from synthetic Euclid views, the team checks how well the telescope's sharp imaging recovers local star histories. Such maps show where in a galaxy stars formed early or late. The study serves as preparation for the real survey data to come. It also sets the methods the collaboration will use to read galaxy growth from the mission's images. Findings from the test runs guide the analysis pipeline the team will apply once true observations land.
arxiv-2503-16035:
Skander Charfi stood for the eternal answers of a Hamilton-Jacobi equation in a 2025 analysis paper. For time-dependent Tonelli Hamiltonians, a answer defined for all past and future times is a rare global object. The Lax-Oleinik semigroup that usually builds answers fails to converge in this non-self-running setting, as Fathi and Mather showed. Charfi studies the semigroup's action on its non-wandering set, the states it returns to forever.

On that set the semigroup acts as an isometry, and the set equals exactly the global viscosity answers. A broad Peierls barrier and static classes inside the Mather set then yield a formula writing each global answer as an infimum over those classes. Fathi's self-running convergence theorem falls out as a corollary.
arxiv-2503-16135:
Adam Herout, Vojtech Bartl, Martin Gaens, and Oskar Tvrd'och pose a new visualization puzzle called the Malleable Glyph, in a 2025 challenge paper. The idea grew from user research on card sorting. The task is to pack as much information as possible into a fixed, flat, still shape.

A viewer comparing two glyphs must judge which shows more, or whether they are equal. The design must follow an illiteracy rule: viewers ask how much, not how many, so counting tricks are banned. Uses could span interfaces, games, and maps. The authors explain the rules and scoring protocol and invite the graphics community to enter the public challenge.
arxiv-2503-16235:
Shamisa Shoja and co-authors unify cost checks for branch and bound solvers in 2025. Such solvers tackle mixed integer tuning problems that arise in predictive control of hybrid systems. Real time use demands firm bounds on worst case computing effort. Past checks handled linear and quadratic forms apart.

The new framework certifies both forms under one roof. It covers families of problems that shift with system parameters, as control tasks do. Bounds can count iterations or relaxed sub problems, as the user needs. Unified proof of effort helps engineers trust solvers inside fast control loops.
arxiv-2503-16535:
Jinchang Zhang and Guoyu Lu estimated scene depth from a single camera in 2025 by building the camera's own physics into the learning model and letting words help. One flat image cannot by itself say how far things are, yet robots must guess depth from exactly that.

Their model computes an embodied depth from the camera's fixed properties as it moves through road scenes, with no extra sensors. That depth joins the image features for a fuller picture. Text notes about the scene, including rough depth hints, act as a prior that sharpens object sense. Two fuzzy sources, image and language, cover each other's gaps. Tests across scenes showed gains over image only methods.
arxiv-2503-16835:
Huiqiang Chen and co-authors present SAFER, a 2025 method for scrubbing unwanted concepts out of text-to-image diffusion models for good. Today's filters often fail quietly: block Van Gogh by name and his style still returns when the prompt says Starry Night. Concepts hide in the geometry of the model's text space.

SAFER first finds the low-dimensional subspace tied to the target concept. It then projects every prompt embedding onto the remaining space, erasing the concept before generation starts. Learned embeddings from a reference image sharpen the estimate when words alone are vague, and a subspace expansion step widens the net. Tests showed thorough removal where earlier methods leaked. The approach is cheap enough to apply concept by concept, a practical safety dial for image generators.
arxiv-2503-16935:
Tommaso Faraci and Roberto Lampariello present a control method that guarantees a robot can intercept a moving target even when the target's motion is uncertain. Robots that catch or dock with moving objects usually trust their best estimate of the motion. If that estimate is off, the plan can fail with no warning.

Their approach starts from reachability analysis for rigid bodies, working out every state the target could truly reach within known bounds. The control problem is then set up so that interception is guaranteed for all those possibilities, while still optimizing a cost. A tumbling object in space serves as the test case. Guaranteed interception matters when a miss is costly or dangerous.
arxiv-2503-17135:
Yuganthi Liyanage, Gerardo Chowell, Gleb Pogudin, and Necibe Tuncer checked in 2025 whether epidemic growth models can actually be pinned down by data. Simple curve models forecast outbreaks well when mechanisms are murky, but only if their parameters are identifiable, both in principle and under noise.

Six standard models were recast with extra variables so rigorous structural tests could run in software. All six proved structurally identifiable in the new form. Fitting tools then forecast monkeypox, COVID-19, and Ebola series. Monte Carlo tests under rising noise showed estimates stayed fairly robust, though sensitivity differed by model and data set. The study maps where these forecast tools can be trusted.
arxiv-2503-17235:
Janis Nötzel and Pere Munar-Vallespir study how to spot faint correlations in thermal light in this 2025 paper. The task is a decision problem: tell correlated noise from plain noise of the same energy, spread over many detectors. Standard light measurements with classical processing set the bar to beat.

The authors compare those standard methods with the best possible quantum strategy and with a simple chip using basic optics and on-off detectors. As the energy per detector fades toward zero, the simple chip reaches the best possible error fall-off, while the standard methods fall behind. The gap grows without bound, which the authors call an infinite-fold quantum advantage.
arxiv-2503-17435:
