Jieqiong Zhang, Jizu Huang, and Zihao Yang speed up atomistic simulations of metals with a randomized shortcut, in a 2025 paper. The embedded atom method is the standard way to model metallic bonding in molecular dynamics, but computing every neighbor interaction is costly. Their random batch list variant computes nearby interactions exactly, in a core zone, while sampling only a random subset in the outer shell. Two such lists handle electron density and forces separately.

The estimates stay unbiased in theory, and a symmetry of metallic systems halves the cost again. Tests on lattice constants, atomic distributions, and elastic constants matched full calculations while running several times faster. Memory needs also dropped sharply. The authors aim the method at large, long metal simulations that were previously too slow.
arxiv-2503-17535:
Owen Melia, Daniel Fortunato, Jeremy Hoskins, and Rebecca Willett move a fast equation-solving method onto graphics processors. Their paper appeared in 2025. The HPS family builds direct solvers for the elliptic equations behind heat, flow, and electrostatics by patching together local solutions. The team wrote an open framework that runs these solvers massively in parallel on GPUs, with two redesigns for the hardware.

In two dimensions, a recomputation trick cuts expensive data transfers to the card. In three, an adaptive mesh scheme slashes peak memory. Built in a modern accelerated algebra package, the solver also plugs into automatic differentiation tools, a first for this class. Tests in two and three dimensions showed speed with high-order accuracy.
arxiv-2503-17735:
Zhiqiang Yuan and co-authors train small models from scratch to animate stickers, arguing this beats borrowing a giant video model for such a narrow job. Animated stickers are odd material: few frames, abstract meanings, and wildly varied lengths. The team's framework, RDTF, is built around those quirks. A dedicated network generates frames singly in discrete steps, sized for low frame rates.

A dual-mask data strategy squeezes more training value from limited clips, and a curriculum sorting samples by difficulty, part fixed and part adaptive, teaches easy cases before hard ones. To feed training, the authors assembled a dataset of over a million stickers, still and animated, with action-focused captions. In tests the framework beat parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for large models, in both measured quality and human judgment. They present it as a case for purpose-built small models under tight budgets.
arxiv-2503-18335:
Yanna Ding, Malik Magdon-Ismail, and Jianxi Gao present a 2025 paper on inferring the rules of a networked system from a single snapshot of its resting state. Gene levels, species counts, and infection tallies often settle into steady states, and only noisy versions of those are measurable. Estimating the governing parameters the usual way means simulating coupled differential equations again and again, which is slow.

Their surrogate objective swaps the coupled system for decoupled equations that yield steady states cheaply. Fitting that surrogate also denoises the observations, landing closer to the truth than the raw data. The fitted model even predicts new equilibria if the network's wiring changes. Tests on ecological, gene regulatory, and epidemic networks confirm the gains. The authors offer the method for the many fields where time series simply do not exist.
arxiv-2503-18435:
Junteng Liu and co-authors studied why vision-language models struggle with charts in 2025. Reading a chart needs numbers, text, and visual parts at once. The authors argue the weak point is perception: how much chart detail the model actually takes in.

They split the bottleneck in two. The vision encoder may fail to store the right detail, and the language part may fail to pull detail out of what was stored. Tests showed the stored detail is far richer than simple probes suggest. Tuning helped the language part pull more out, but the encoder stayed the main limit. A contrastive training step for the encoder eased that limit and raised chart scores. Code was released.
arxiv-2503-18535:
Fabbrichesi, Floreanini, and Marzola explain how particle colliders can test Bell locality, one of the deepest checks of quantum mechanics. Their 2025 paper reviews the principles and methods behind these tests. Colliders produce systems of qubits, carried by fermions, and qutrits, carried by heavy spin one bosons, all under strong and electroweak forces.

Quantum state tomography at colliders can witness both entanglement and Bell nonlocality in these short lived systems. The authors lay out how the states are rebuilt from decay products and how the nonlocality tests are framed. The paper serves as a full guide to a young field that moves quantum foundations into the high energy lab.
arxiv-2503-18635:
Merging an infrared image with a normal photo can reveal people and objects hidden by darkness or glare. Li and five co-authors propose OCCO, a fusion method guided by a large pretrained vision model. The big model supplies meaning-level guidance, so the fusion network can focus on blending while still learning the features that matter.

A new feature-mixing network settles clashes between the two image types. Training with contrastive learning, comparing matched and mismatched samples in a hidden feature space, keeps target details intact in the merged image. The team compares OCCO with eight leading methods on four datasets. It produced high-quality fused images and also improved the visual tasks that use them, a balance earlier methods struggled to hold. The authors pitch the design for surveillance, driving, and other fields that fuse sensor views.
arxiv-2503-19435:
Johan Soderstrom and co-authors report a new X-ray effect in salt water in a 2025 paper. When an ion in water loses a deep electron, a neighbor water molecule can fill the gap and release the energy as an X-ray. This non-local decay, seen for sodium and magnesium ions, reports on the water shell hugging the ion.

That shell differs from bulk water in shape and chemistry, yet it steers how solutes behave. Theory helps the team read the signal. Readers get a fresh probe that views the shell from inside the ion itself.
arxiv-2503-19635:
Atoms arranged in tight lattices can glow together or hold light back, effects that quantum engineers hope to use. Maor Carmi, Michal Roth, and Rivka Bekenstein develop the math for such lattices in 2025, set inside thin curved waveguides rather than flat space.

Modeling how atoms trade light inside odd-shaped materials is usually very hard. The authors simplify the wave equation for a broad class of curved guides, which makes the atom-to-atom coupling tractable. For surfaces with steady positive curvature they derive an exact tool for computing the bright and dark collective states. They also show how the guide's curve and thickness shift those states, through a wavelength set by the surface itself.
arxiv-2503-19835:
Adam Kłosiński, Roman Drachynskyi, Krzysztof Wohlfeld, and Wojciech Brzezicki study magnetism in NdNiO2 in two thousand twenty five. The infinite layer nickelate self dopes through its neodymium bands. Charge escapes onto those bands in their tight binding model. Unrestricted Hartree-Fock runs map the magnetic phase diagram.

Undoped material sits just outside the antiferromagnetic region of the diagram. That matches experiments finding no long range order. Short range correlations and broad excitations still appear. Electron doping boosts the antiferromagnetic solution sharply, unlike cuprates. Stripe patterns may stabilize at smaller charge transfer energies.
arxiv-2503-19935:
Reza Rahimi Azghan and co-authors release a real-world data set on cannabis use, stress, and body signals, in work from twenty twenty-five. Coping with stress is a top reason people give for steady cannabis use. That raises a testable claim: users may show distinct body stress patterns. Those gaps may widen at the moments when cannabis is used. Few open data sets let that claim be tested in daily life.

Wrist bands tracked skin response, heart rate, and skin heat as people lived their days. The pool held dozens of adults, split between users and non-users. Surveys logged moments of cannabis use, exercise, and felt stress levels. The team now shares the full set for open study. Others can test how cannabis links to stress in body signals. The set fills a clear gap for field research on this topic.
arxiv-2503-20035:
Zheng Bian and Erik Bollt tackle a paradox where standard measures say information flow is either zero or infinite. Transfer entropy is widely used to claim causal links. When one variable is a fixed function of others, it breaks.

Under mild conditions they prove a strict dichotomy. The flow measure lands at one extreme or the other. That verdict cannot rank strong versus weak flows. A discretization strategy is proposed to restore gradations. A conjectured formula estimates the relative ambiguity instead. Numerical tests support the proxy's reliability. The result warns data scientists against naive readings. It offers a steadier way to compare information flow. It is a sharp note of care for the field.
arxiv-2503-20135:
Dongliang Gong, Junyi Yang, and a team of co-authors wrote a 2025 condensed matter paper on a large Nernst effect in a magnetic oxide. The Nernst effect turns a heat flow into a sideways voltage. Its anomalous form, driven by magnetism rather than an external field, is prized for harvesting energy in a sideways geometry.

The material is an antiferromagnetic strontium iridate with tin substituted in. Textbook reasoning links the Nernst and Hall effects by symmetry, but this material breaks that expectation. Below its magnetic ordering point, near room temperature's lower range, the spontaneous Nernst signal rose fast to a level matching top topological materials and beating other oxides. The authors trace the effect to a mix of symmetric and antisymmetric parts, a clue for designing better thermoelectrics.
arxiv-2503-20235:
Ahyun Seo and Minsu Cho improve rotation symmetry detection in images in this 2025 paper. Symmetry helps computers spot objects and read scenes, but flat image methods can fail when a viewpoint warps the shape.

Their model predicts the center and corner points of a symmetric shape in three dimensions, then projects them back to the flat image. A rebuild step enforces 3D rules, such as equal side lengths and matched angles, which keeps the shape sound. On a standard dataset the method beat past work on finding the rotation axis. Tests that removed parts of the method confirmed that the 3D rules drove the gain.
arxiv-2503-20435:
Bao-Dong Sun works out a hard problem in particle physics in this 2025 paper. When a proton turns into a heavier partner called the Delta, gravity-like probes can measure how mass and energy flow inside the particles. Sun computes the numbers that describe that change, using a theory built for low-energy strong forces.

The work runs to one loop, the first level of detail past the simplest picture. Even with small breaking effects from charge and mass gaps added in, the math stays clean, with no terms that break the counting rules. Sun used no free settings, so the values stand as firm predictions that other methods can check.
arxiv-2503-20535:
Krikova and Pereira test a little-used hydrogen line as a spyglass into the Sun's smallest explosions. Ellerman bombs, ultraviolet bursts, and miniature flares all heat the lower chromosphere, but reading their speeds and temperatures from the usual lines is tricky. The pair ran three-dimensional simulations of a restless solar atmosphere and computed how the H-epsilon line forms inside it, photon by photon.

Ellerman bombs turned out optically thick in this line, standing out as crisp structures. Ultraviolet bursts and small flares stayed partly transparent, showing as diffuse glows. The line's shift reported gas velocity faithfully, beating estimates from the wings of stronger hydrogen lines, while its brightness said little about temperature and its width was muddled by rival broadening effects.
arxiv-2503-20635: Israel Sigal and Xiaoxu Wu study how effects spread in space and time in open quantum systems whose future depends only on their present state. For a large class of the equations behind such systems, they prove that an effective light cone exists. Outside the cone the leftover effect is not zero, but it shrinks at an exponential rate with distance, giving these noisy systems a clean causal shape.
arxiv-2503-20935:
Health records are cheap and rich, but the holes in them are rarely random: sicker patients often have more missing values, which can bend results. Jungwun Lee and co-authors extend a blended analysis framework in this 2025 paper to handle data that may be missing not at random. The blended method splits how the data arose into steps, mixing weighting and imputation across them.

Their extension adds sensitivity analyses that ask how strongly the hidden missingness would have to misbehave before conclusions change. Simulations test the framework, and the authors apply it to a real dataset on long-term outcomes after weight-loss surgery. They close with practical advice on reading such sensitivity results.
arxiv-2503-21035:
Felipe Díaz-Jaramillo, Silvia Nagy, and Giorgio Pizzolo build a homotopy algebra for fields near the edge of spacetime in a 2025 paper. Null infinity is where light rays end up in an expanding universe, and physics there governs the radiation that distant observers receive. An expansion in falling powers of distance organizes that physics.

Working with self-dual Yang-Mills theory in Bondi coordinates, the authors show the algebra's rules force the correct fall-off of fields near infinity on their own. They then construct kinematic algebras systematically inside the frame. Kinematic algebras expose hidden simplicity in scattering calculations. Rooting them at null infinity ties that simplicity to gravitational wave and radiation physics.
arxiv-2503-21235:
Aryan Esmailpour and co-authors give dataset search a theory base in a 2025 paper. Hunters of data often want sets with set traits, like a share of rows in a range or a top value along a chosen line. Past search tools lean on rules of thumb with no proof behind them.

Two index tasks anchor the frame: one for percentile shares, one for preference scores. The team shows near linear stores with fast queries are out of reach when data sit in one place. Near linear stores do exist for both tasks in wider setups, with bounds spelled out. The work covers lone and federated stores alike.
arxiv-2503-21535:
Pierrick Gaudry, Julien Soumier, and Pierre-Jean Spaenlehauer give ways to compute maps between products of special elliptic curves, in a 2025 paper. A classic theorem says such maps exist for these curves over finite fields. The task here is to find them in practice, not just to know they exist. The authors assume the rings of maps for each curve are known at the start.

Their route turns the curve problem into an algebra problem with quaternions, a type of number system with four parts. The work then comes down to solving sets of equations over whole numbers. New tools handle those equations when a small subring is at hand. Put together, the steps give a fast randomized method that runs in fair time.
arxiv-2503-21935:
Andrea Valassi and nine co-authors report on a five-year push to run a major particle physics program on graphics chips and modern processors. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The program, MadGraph, simulates collisions for labs like the one behind the Large Hadron Collider. Faster runs mean more events can be simulated.

Work began in two thousand twenty and brought many new features, tests, and fixes. Early feedback from the CMS experiment helped shape the code. The first full release for the simplest class of processes came out in the autumn of the year before the paper. The authors describe the state of that release as of a major computing meeting. They also set out what remains for fuller production use. Speed matters because collider data keeps growing.
arxiv-2503-22035:
Isabella Loaiza and Roberto Rigobon wrote a 2025 essay on the limits of artificial intelligence in finance. AI excels at data-heavy tasks, they argue, but it falters with tiny data sets, judgment calls, and questions of trust and ethics. Their framework, named EPOCH, lists five human strengths machines cannot copy: empathy, presence, opinion, creativity, and hope.

In banking those traits carry client trust, inclusion, and new ideas. The authors expect AI to reshape jobs rather than erase them, much as cash machines changed the work of bank tellers. The real task, they say, is training staff to pair machine speed with human judgment. The essay speaks to managers weighing how far to automate.
arxiv-2503-22135:
Zhipeng Lu sets out a new optimization frame built on convolution with convex kernels, in work from 2025. Most global search methods lean on chance based models that give no firm promise. The aim here is a more rule bound model for finding the global best point of a general function.

A power lift step joins the convex kernel convolution at the core of the frame. Early numeric tests check how well derived algorithms work in practice. Results so far are limited and early, and the author says so plainly. The note serves as a founding sketch meant to draw more work. Readers in optimization get the core idea and first proof of concept runs.
arxiv-2503-22235:
Haoxing Du and seven co-authors present WeatherMesh-3, a machine learning system for global weather forecasts, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Classic weather models are slow and costly to run. WeatherMesh-3 uses a transformer, the same broad design as large language models, tuned for weather data.

Two ideas drive the gains. A latent rollout lets the model roll a forecast forward in its inner space, for any length, with no need to decode each step. A modular build blends many real-time weather analyses into the start state. The system makes a fourteen-day global forecast in twelve seconds on one consumer GPU, and beats standard models on error.
arxiv-2503-22335:
Niels Goedegebure and Kateryna Marynets present a numerical method for equations with a broad fractional derivative, in a 2025 paper. The Hilfer derivative blends two classic fractional forms. Solutions to such equations often spike near the start time. That spike makes accurate computing hard.

Their method uses Bernstein spline curves to trace the solution. They state clear conditions for the method to converge, with rates. The code runs in a vectorized, parallel way for speed. Tests matched the theory and beat a standard predictor method on accuracy by a wide margin. Fractional equations model memory effects in materials and fluids, so sharper solvers widen their use.
arxiv-2503-22935:
Jiangrui Zheng and five co-authors present SPFinder for tracing vulnerability patches in two thousand twenty-five. Patch hunting finds the commit that fixes a known flaw. Long diffs in patch commits stump past tools at scale. Quiet commit messages make those long diffs common in practice.

A hierarchical embedding stretches context over whole commits without decay. A three phase retrieval then scales the hunt to full repositories. Tests beat top patch tracers and a leading commercial code model. Recall and ranking gains ran large in both data sets. Dozens of patch links were merged into a public advisory base.
arxiv-2503-23135:
Ao Wang, Hui Chen, Zijia Lin, Jungong Han, and Guiguang Ding wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on LSNet, a lightweight network built on the motto see large, focus small. Vision networks have grown accurate but heavy, which hurts real time use on modest devices. Lightweight rivals lean on attention and convolutions in ways that limit both quality and speed.

The design borrows from human vision, which takes in a wide scene yet focuses sharply where it matters. Their large small convolution pairs a wide kernel that perceives broadly with a small kernel that aggregates precisely. That split aims to capture rich context and fine detail within a tight computing budget. The paper positions the network as a better balance point for practical deployment.
arxiv-2503-23235:
Konstantin Bliokh (2025) reviews how waves carry momentum and two kinds of angular momentum. Any wave's momentum follows its direction of travel. When that momentum circulates, it produces orbital angular momentum. Vector waves add a second kind, spin, from the local rotation of the field itself. These effects matter most in structured wavefields that vary from place to place. The review covers light, sound, elastic waves, plasma waves, and water surface waves in one frame.

A single field-theory approach, grounded in Noether's theorem, handles all of them. It copes with waves that push along their travel direction, across it, or both. Bliokh connects the abstract quantities to things experiments can see, such as forces and torques on small particles. The paper serves as an entry point to a fast-growing topic. Designers of optical tweezers, acoustic devices, and wave-based sensors all draw on these ideas.
arxiv-2503-23735:
I V Solovyev, S A Nikolaev, and A Tanaka study a new kind of magnet in a 2025 arXiv paper. Altermagnets act like antiferromagnets, whose tiny internal arrows cancel out, yet they split electron energy bands in a way once thought to need net magnetism. The team asks how that trait links to weak ferromagnetism and to an odd sideways voltage called the anomalous Hall effect.

They build a model based on a real copper oxide and trace each effect to one push between spins, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Parts of that push with one sign bend spins into weak magnetism. Parts that flip sign from bond to bond drive the Hall effect and net orbital magnetism instead. Strain in the crystal, they find, matters more than the band split itself.
arxiv-2504-00135:
Lais Borbolato and co-authors argue, in a 2025 astronomy paper, that the Milky Way's thin and thick disks grew up together from very early times. The two disks differ in chemistry, and many blamed a later merger for splitting them. The team combined space mission positions, two big star surveys, and age estimates for nearby stars.

They find a thin disk population older than eleven billion years. That means the galaxy began forming its low-alpha disk on its own, before the famous merger arrived. The merger still mattered: it seems to have halted star birth in the thick disk. The result softens the merger's role from creator to interrupter.
arxiv-2504-00335:
Renato Calleja, Alex Haro, and Pedro Porras presented this 2025 algorithm for finding stable tori in systems that pulse with time. KAM theory studies motions that stay orderly despite disturbance. Here the systems repeat with more than one rhythm, and the target shapes are fiber-wise Lagrangian tori. A companion work proves the method converges; this paper lays out the method itself.

The authors show the algorithm at work on two models. One comes from tokamak research, where a small tweak to magnetic fields may wall off wandering field lines in a fusion device. The other tracks swirls in a steady flow, a model born in plasma and fluid physics. Worked examples show the abstract method handling real models from both fields.
arxiv-2504-00535:
Boyuan Liu and co-authors ask how fast-spinning first stars would have changed the early universe's radio glow and reionization, in a 2025 paper. The first stars were metal-free and may have spun fast enough to mix themselves fully, staying compact, hot, and blue. The team combined detailed star atmosphere models with large simulations of cosmic dawn. They varied how efficiently the first stars formed and when normal stars took over.

Spinning stars pour out more ionizing light, so fewer of them are needed to match the observed fingerprint of reionization, about half the stellar mass. The deep radio absorption dip from that era becomes shallower by up to eleven percent. Large-scale radio patchiness also drops at the earliest times. The authors say these shifts rival the effects of the star-formation settings themselves. They urge future work to fit both puzzles together.
arxiv-2504-00735:
Sebastián Espinel-Ríos, River Walser, and Dongda Zhang propose a learning method in 2025 to steer living cells that make useful goods. Staff can tune cell parts in real time to lift yield, but the best tune plan is hard to find. Shaky, chance-driven cell acts make the task still harder.

Their plan lets a smart agent learn by trial on a stand-in model of the cells. The agent trains across many varied runs, so it learns to cope with doubt and change. In time, it could keep learning on the real setup. The method offers a fresh path past fixed models that crack when cell acts drift.
arxiv-2504-01435:
Tomoya Hirotani and Kensuke Gallock-Yoshimura study a tiny heat engine that works in curved spacetime, in a 2025 paper. Their engine follows the Otto cycle, a classic four-step loop of heating, expansion, cooling, and squeezing. The working part is a three-level atom-like detector that moves through a quantum field and feels the bending of space.

A three-level system has two energy gaps that can be tuned apart, unlike a two-level one with a single gap. That freedom allows more varied ways to draw work from the field. The pair derive a general rule for when the engine gives out more work than it takes in. The rule rests on the effective warmth each gap senses. They also flag new quirks, such as coherence terms that never appear in the simpler two-level case.
arxiv-2504-01535:
Qin Fang and co-authors fixed a gap in a stats method in a 2025 paper on curve fitting. Their tool builds trust ranges for a fitted curve without presuming its shape. It is also used in cutoff designs, where a rule splits cases at a set score and the jump at the split is the prize.

The classic form only proved sound when the curve was smoothed more than most users would pick. A bias-fixed form was known for plain cases, but its proof for curve work had stayed open. The authors give a robust form that works under more real-like picks. Their proof clears a long-standing snag for applied users of the method.
arxiv-2504-01835:
Takayuki Hosonuma and seven co-authors designed a self-guided navigation method in two thousand twenty-five for the DESTINY+ asteroid flyby mission. The craft will pass several asteroids, including Phaethon, using a rotating telescope that doubles as its navigation camera. Past missions calibrated that camera's alignment first, a step that eats mission time.

Their method lets alignment errors stay and estimates them on the fly, alongside the craft's orbit relative to the target. A filter suited to nonlinear links handles the joint estimate. Computer tests and hardware-in-the-loop runs check the scheme. Cutting calibration could free the mission plan for more science at closest approach.
arxiv-2504-01935:
Celine Lee, Alexander Rush, and Keyon Vafa ask how much reasoning a language model should do in this 2025 paper. Extra reasoning steps often help, but the best amount was a mystery. The team framed tasks as tiny state machines, whose run length and state count give clean difficulty measures.

Across tasks and models, accuracy peaked at a sweet spot of reasoning length, then fell. Longer machine runs, meaning more hidden state tracking, went with longer ideal reasoning. Surprisingly, the number of states did not matter. The team then predicted the sweet spot for new problems and kept only answers of that length, which steadily raised accuracy. The results give a practical dial for reasoning effort.
arxiv-2504-02235:
Kohtaro Kato and Tomotaka Kuwahara attack a conjecture about how fast quantum correlations fade with distance, in a 2025 paper. Conditional mutual information measures the correlations a middle region mediates between two sides of a many-body system. In thermal Gibbs states it is expected to decay quickly, but a general proof has resisted the field.

The authors recast the problem through belief propagation channels, local maps that enact small changes to the Hamiltonian. If those channels are quasi-local, information decay follows, so the conjecture becomes a statement about channels. Under conditions like rapid mixing they build such channels, proving decay at all temperatures conditionally and outright at high temperatures. A fresh look at cluster expansions rounds out the picture.
arxiv-2504-02335:
Seif Mzoughi, Mohamed Elshafei, and Foutse Khomh stress-test image segmentation models with distortions a genetic search invents. Segmentation drives medical imaging, augmented reality, and surveillance, yet small warps can break it. Their tester, SegRMT, chains spatial and spectral changes into attack sequences. A quality threshold keeps the warped images faithful to the originals.

On the Cityscapes street-scene set, the attacks cut a leading model's overlap score to about six percent. Rival attack methods only reached nine to twenty-two percent. The team then flipped the tool around and trained on its attacks. Robustness jumped: scores rose by up to seventy-three percent on attack sets, and cross-attack scores hit about fifty-four percent. Rivals managed only two to ten percent there. Realistic distortion testing, they conclude, both exposes and repairs fragility.
arxiv-2504-02435:
Jan Grebík and Konstantin Recke prove, in a 2025 math paper, a surprising fact about random cell networks in the curved spaces tied to higher-rank groups. Cells are built around random points, and the question is when a giant connected web forms. The threshold for having just one giant web behaves unlike all cases studied before.

As point density drops toward zero, that uniqueness threshold also drops to zero in these spaces. Their route builds on a recent breakthrough and gives a new proof path for a famous fixed-price problem in group theory. They also build new examples of networks that keep one giant cluster even at tiny average degree. That answers a question raised by earlier work on random networks.
arxiv-2504-02735:
Manh Pham Hung and co-authors fix a flaw in wrist based health sensing in a 2025 paper. The sensing method shines light into the skin to read the pulse, but poor contact between skin and sensor can warp the signal even when the wearer sits still.

Their framework rebuilds warped signals into clean waveforms with the right shape. It joins a custom data gathering protocol, a careful signal cleaning pipeline, and a deep adversarial model trained with a pulse aware loss. Tests on their own data, on public sets, and in daily life all showed clear gains. Signal error fell by forty percent, and heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure estimates all improved.
arxiv-2504-02835:
Dikande and Matabaro study in 2025 a leapfrog pattern in a fixed rule model of two firms that sell the same goods. Each firm invests based on its market place, so sales evolve in a linked way. In the leapfrog regime, the lead swaps back and forth over time.

They recast the model with two fresh measures, the sales gap and total sales. Fixed points were checked for stability, and charts tracked how the gap and sum shift with a key elasticity value. The leapfrog pattern held for set parameter ranges and a fairly high elasticity. Total sales stayed positive, which keeps goods on hand. The study maps when steady swapping of the lead can persist.
arxiv-2504-03035:
Issa-Mbenard Dabo and Jérémie Bigot study high-dimensional regression where data points do not share one distribution in a 2025 paper. Random feature ridge regression is a fast learning method often analyzed when all samples share the same spread. Real data break that assumption: rows can carry different variances, described by a variance profile.

The authors derive how the method performs under that profile, for both training and test data. The theory shows when the method still works and how error depends on the profile's shape. Such results matter for data pooled from many sensors or sites, where equal spread is a fiction. Practitioners get guidance on when random features remain a safe shortcut.
arxiv-2504-03735:
Erfan Shayegani and co-authors show that shuffling the structure of a prompt, not its words, can break safety training in image-language models, in work from 2025. Safety tuning mostly polices the assistant's seat. The user's seat and the fixed token layout stay untested.

Their attacks swap roles so text lands in the wrong seat, or move the image token out of place. The query itself stays untouched. Across eight settings and several models, the tricks drew out harmful output, and stacking them hit harder. Internal traces leaned toward non-refusal, as in known jailbreaks. A training fix that mixes scrambled harmful and benign prompts made models sturdier. The work flags structure as a blind spot.
arxiv-2504-03835: Hausmann and Renner present a paper from twenty twenty-five linking two famed puzzles in physics. The firewall puzzle concerns an observer falling into a black hole, and it rests on a hidden rule that lets inside and outside views merge. A newer form of the Wigner's friend puzzle shows that merging rule clashes with quantum theory alone, with no gravity needed. The authors argue the usual firewall verdict is thus undercut, and suggest both puzzles spring from one root issue.
arxiv-2504-03935:
Nicholas Newsome proves a result that classifies bounded domains in complex geometry. In several complex variables there is no uniformization theorem. So mathematicians want to classify the simply linked domains straight. Newsome extends a recent classification. He uses set compute methods and a localization method.

He treats a domain with a mildly smooth boundary on a Kobayashi hyperbolic complex manifold. If the domain holds a totally real boundary point and covers a compact manifold, he shows its universal cover must be the Euclidean ball. Results of this kind are rigidity claims. They say a domain that meets broad geometric conditions has only one shape it can take. The paper adds to the long effort to grasp which domains can arise in complex manifolds.
arxiv-2504-04035:
Ting-Tung Wang, Xiaoxue Ran, and Zi Yang Meng present a new simulation method for constrained quantum lattice models in a 2025 paper. Such models force local rules on each site, which standard tensor methods handle poorly. Their method builds the rules in as symmetries of the tensor network itself.

With that change, they can run the method on wide cylinders of any lattice shape. They map the ground state of a quantum dimer model on a triangular lattice. The map captures two ordered solid phases and the entropy signature of a liquid like phase with topological order. The authors say the method opens tensor tools to frustrated magnets and quantum simulators. It may also suit other strongly constrained systems.
arxiv-2504-04235:
Quantum machine learning promises new ways to find patterns, but today's quantum hardware is slow and its gradient math is costly. Ziqing Guo and co-authors propose a hybrid design in this 2025 paper, called QPIE, that runs classical and quantum parts side by side rather than in sequence. Trained weights from a classical network are fed into the quantum circuit to give it a head start.

A dynamic method picks how each gradient is computed, splitting work between quantum chips and graphics cards. In tests, the design reached higher accuracy on standard benchmarks and cut the extra time from randomness on time-series data by about 88 percent within one hundred steps. Checks of the model's information matrix showed a fairer spread of values across hardware types.
arxiv-2504-04335:
Yuya Ogasa and Yuki Arase spot the exact spans of text a language model made up. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tackles hallucination at the span level. Most past work flags a whole answer as false or true. Pinpointing the false stretch is more useful, and attention maps hold clues.

When a model invents, its attention often looks off in telling ways. The team builds features that view attention from three angles. They check if tokens are heeded or ignored, if focus is skewed, and how wide the context is. A transformer judge then labels each token in turn. On long tasks like summaries, their method beats strong rivals.
arxiv-2504-04435:
Tatiana Merkulova and Bharani Jayakumar present a framework for judging image segmentation methods, in work from 2025. Segmentation splits an image into parts, a base step in many vision tasks. Methods range from simple rules to deep learning, and users can also guide the process by hand.

The framework covers naive, machine learning, and deep learning approaches. Background sections explain thresholding, edge finding, region growing, and leading network designs. Three modes of user help are set out and tested. Scores include overlap with truth, compute time, and user time. The comparison lays out the strengths and trade offs of each method.
arxiv-2504-04635:
Da Silva and co-authors stress-test methods that steer a language model's behavior by nudging its inner activations. Steering is prized as a cheap stand-in for retraining. Their 2025 study tries three known steering methods on up to 36 models from 14 families, far more than the handful used in the original papers.

Results swung widely from model to model. Many models gained nothing from steering, and some got worse. The team traces the failures to weak assumptions built into the methods themselves. They argue that steering cannot yet be trusted as a general fix that scales across models. The study urges broader testing before any steering claim is believed.
arxiv-2504-04835:
Shanshan Wang and co-authors build a dataset for spotting ships on inland rivers in this 2025 paper. Smart ship perception needs rich training images, yet river fleets lack the datasets that sea work enjoys. Narrow channels, shifting weather, and city glare make river scenes hard.

Their set holds 32,478 images across sun, rain, fog, and artificial light. It covers the common vessel types of the Yangtze River Basin. Alongside the data, they present a detection approach tuned to the mix. Benchmarks on the set give later teams a yardstick. The work fills a data gap for inland navigation safety.
arxiv-2504-05035:
Joseph Chege, Arie Yeredor, and Martin Haardt use position to help millimeter-wave radios pick their best beam. Such radios send tight beams to beat heavy signal loss. Testing every beam pair is slow, and the search space is huge.

Their method learns how user positions and best beam pairs occur together, stored as a compact probability table. Bayesian fitting builds the table from training data. For a new user, the table predicts the best beam, or a short list of likely beams, from position alone. Tests used data from a high-grade ray-tracing simulator. Rivals included a neural network and a fingerprint method. Cutting the beam search saves time and battery in dense future networks.
arxiv-2504-05235:
Sneh Pandya and four co-authors present IAEmu in this 2025 paper, a neural network emulator for galaxy intrinsic alignments. Galaxy shapes tend to align with each other through tides and formation history. That alignment contaminates weak lensing, a key tool for cosmology, so it must be modeled well. Classic models break down on small scales, and full simulations are costly. IAEmu learns from mock catalogs built on a halo occupation frame. It predicts three correlation functions, for positions and orientations, with error bars.

Against simulations, its errors ran near three percent for the position correlation and five percent for the mixed one. It even fit a hydrodynamical simulation's alignment signal outside its training family. On graphics hardware it runs about ten thousand times faster than CPU simulation. The authors offer it as a surrogate for lensing surveys now being planned.
arxiv-2504-05335:
Sebastián Tinoco and co-authors test how price rise shapes tacit price fixing by learning agents. The work dates to 2025. Code-led price sets now shape many markets, and past work showed such agents can learn to fix prices in a tacit way. Big-scale price forces got less care in that work.

The team adds price rise shocks to a learn-based price model. Agents kept high gains as one, with no direct pact. Price rise cut how hard agents fought each other, the team finds. Yet the agents built no firm stick to punish price cuts. The work flags a need for watch in code-priced markets.
arxiv-2504-05635:
Zijun Wan and Xiaohua Yao settle a boundedness ask in 2025 for the wave tools of a fourth-order Schrödinger operator with a bump. The operator mixes a stiff fourth-order spread with a pull and a fading field. Its wave operators translate between the free tale and the bumped tale; the ask is whether that translation stays tame on every size scale of functions. The catalog title doubles the math type and trails a grant note; the head title is clean.

For spaces of five sizes and up, the answer is yes, as long as zero sits as a plain edge of the spectrum. Sharp spread bounds for the wave and beam flows fall out of the proof. A knob on the stiff term leaves the tale whole, which frees the method for kin models.
arxiv-2504-05835:
Alexander Ganz, Chunshan Lin, and Mian Zhu propose a fresh route to cosmic magnetic fields in this 2025 paper. Magnetic fields fill the cosmos, but their origin in the early universe is unsettled. Many birth scenarios suffer from over-strong electric fields or other flaws.

Their plan lets a charged scalar field give the light field an effective mass. That breaks a symmetry that normally forbids field growth. The action starts after electroweak symmetry breaking, in the radiation era. High conductivity then cannot flood the system with electric fields. A tachyonic phase of the light, weakly coupled scalar can seed strong fields. The setup also dodges back-reaction and strong coupling troubles.
arxiv-2504-05935:
Aleksei Volkov wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on a type of equation called a non-local continuity equation. Such an equation tracks a huge set of like particles that act on each other through a shared field. Its solution gives the spread of the particles in space at each moment.

Volkov asks how to steer that spread toward a chosen target and keep it there. He adapts a tool called a control-Lyapunov function to spaces of probability measures. From it he builds feedback rules, first for targets near the start point and then for targets anywhere. The result gives a firm base for control problems with many interacting parts.
arxiv-2504-06035:
Some quantum gravity ideas make gravity non-local, with effects smeared through infinite-derivative terms. Alexey Koshelev and Abhishek Naskar ask what that smearing does during cosmic inflation, the early universe's burst of expansion. They focus on the three-point pattern of primordial ripples, called the bispectrum, which observations constrain tightly.

The non-local terms add new ripple states with complex masses during inflation, states that stay stable in the curved background. The authors compute the bispectrum for an inflaton plus one such pair of states. Its strength reacts sharply to the complex masses: the squeezed shape can grow easily, while the equilateral shape stays tame. Planck data then bounds the masses, the 2025 paper shows.
arxiv-2504-06235:
Shahryar Zehtabi and three co-authors build a shared learning way that lets a web of peer devices train a model that works in new places, by sharing style facts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Shared learning most often takes local data to stay the same from train time to test time. In real life, the data shift. Past work on this task lacked formal math, and stuck to a star shape with one hub. The new way, StyleDDG, works peer to peer, with no hub. Devices share style facts drawn from their own data. The team gives the first step-by-step frame for the aim and proves the method settles as it runs.
arxiv-2504-06335:
Pier Bonifacio, Elisabetta Caffau, Patrick François, and Monique Spite review the most metal-poor stars. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Such stars, in our galaxy and near ones, hold near no heavy elements. Since metals grow with time, they are the most raw things we can see.

Their element shares tell of the first star breed that forged those nuclei. Since the load may come from one or a few blasts, their read is simpler than full galaxy chemistry. The price is rarity: hunts need tailor-made plans to build a fair sample. The review sums a decade of finds on these early witnesses.
arxiv-2504-06435:
Haiwen Li and Sinan Aral run a giant experiment on how much people trust AI search answers. Generative search now steers shopping, votes, and health choices, yet its grip on trust was unmeasured. The team fired about twelve thousand queries across seven countries to map real exposure.

A preregistered trial with a representative United States sample then varied the design. People trusted AI answers less than normal results on average. Citations and links raised trust sharply, even when those links were fake. Showing the model's own confidence, high or low, made people share less and trust less. Praise from others pushed trust up. Trust, in turn, predicted lazier checking.
arxiv-2504-07235:
Hunting for planets like Earth costs telescope time, so Jeanne Davoult, Romain Eltschinger, and Yann Alibert ask whether a computer can point the search at the best stars first. They trained a Random Forest, a machine learning tool, on made-up planetary systems from a well-known model of how planets form. The tool sorts systems into those likely to hold an Earth-like planet and those that are not.

On test systems the tool was right up to ninety-nine percent of the time. Run on real observed systems, it picked out forty-four as strong candidates, and checks showed an added Earth-like planet would leave those systems stable. Future missions could use such lists to spend their viewing hours where the odds are best.
arxiv-2504-07635:
Fabrizio Mangione, Claudio Savaglio, and Giancarlo Fortino survey the fast-growing union of generative AI with the Internet of Things. Generative models can create text, images, and plans, while connected devices sense and act in the physical world. Together they are reshaping health care, factories, and smart cities.

Most past research, the authors note, treats narrow single applications. A field-wide view is missing: how the two technologies interlock, what their synergy can and cannot do, and where the risks lie. Their systematic survey gathers the scattered work into one map. It sorts the uses, weighs the challenges, and marks open questions for builders of smart systems.
arxiv-2504-07735:
Julio Cesar Jaramillo Quiceno builds differential operators for a changed form of spinor variables. His 2025 paper works in q-calculus, based on a deformation parameter. Spinors are objects used to describe particles with spin. The paper adapts one such tool to these variables. It also sets out a chain rule for the new setting.

Both standard and Dirac type forms are defined in this frame. He also derives integral formulas. Worked cases then apply the ideas to changed spinor equations. The paper extends that branch to spinorial structures. It may offer insight into quantum deformations of relativistic field equations. Future work could build a q-analogue of the known algebra that joins the Dirac and Maxwell equations.
arxiv-2504-07835:
Erin Carson and Xinye Chen present pychop, a Python toolkit that emulates low-precision arithmetic for numerical work and neural networks, in a 2025 paper. Cutting number precision saves memory and time, and deep learning already thrives on it, but scientists need a safe sandbox to test where the cuts bite. The tool supports custom floating-point formats and a full shelf of rounding modes.

Interfaces cover plain arrays and tensor backends, running emulation on CPUs and graphics cards alike. Experiments on image classification and object detection show how accuracy bends under reduced precision, and what quantization-aware training can recover. The authors position pychop as groundwork for mixed-precision algorithms and for designing future low-precision hardware.
arxiv-2504-07935:
Amit Singh and co-authors find switchable electric polarization in four-layer graphene made only by how the sheets stack, in a 2025 paper. Single and few-layer graphene normally has no permanent dipole, yet the mixed ABCB stacking breaks the needed symmetries and was predicted to hold a dipole that a gate can flip. The team built dual-gated devices of this natural stack, sealed in boron nitride.

Resistance showed clear hysteresis under both gates, lasting up to room temperature, as the stack flipped between ABCB and its mirror form and the layer charges reordered. No moiré pattern was needed. The authors propose stacking order itself as a route to ferroelectric memory in carbon materials.
arxiv-2504-08035:
Jonathan Petersson and co-authors simulate why dwarf galaxies struggle to grow their central black holes. Their 2025 study runs a suite of detailed simulations of one low-mass galaxy, switching stellar feedback processes on and off to see what starves or feeds the hole.

Left alone, a seed black hole doubled its mass over eight hundred million years. Radiation from young stars alone, surprisingly, more than doubled growth: it throttled star formation while leaving gas free to flow inward. Supernova explosions did the opposite, choking accretion early and hard. Combined, the explosions still dominated, though less severely. The authors trace growth to which gas phases reach the center under each feedback mix, a caution for models of early black hole growth.
arxiv-2504-08235:
Jiarui Guan and six co-authors study how to design a smart tool that helps lawyers search past cases in Chinese law. Their short paper, from two thousand twenty-five, starts from what lawyers say they need.

Lawyers have found most smart legal tools of limited use in daily work. A key flaw is that the user can set the input and see the output, but has no grip on the steps in between. That gap raises doubt on both quality and fair use. The team held a study with five legal workers on case search. They drew out needs that can guide a tool where the user stays in charge of the search path, not just its ends.
arxiv-2504-08535:
Yankai Lin, Michelle Chong, and Carlos Murguia design backup safety controls for systems whose behavior is nonlinear within known bounds, in a paper from 2025. Many engineered systems already have a main controller that keeps them stable. The worry is an attack on sensors or actuators that could push the system out of its safe zone.

The authors first give conditions that verify a closed loop system stays safe under attack. The checks rest on invariant sets and barrier certificates, recast as matrix problems that solvers handle well. They then assume a subset of sensors stays clean. From those trusted readings they build a secondary controller that adds safety on top of the main one. Number based examples close the paper and show the method at work.
arxiv-2504-08735:
Muhammad Akram and Onur Erten wrote this 2025 physics paper on new phases that arise when a solvable spin model meets skyrmion textures. In metals, electrons feel an extra force when they couple to swirling spin patterns called skyrmions. That coupling can produce clear effects, such as the topological Hall effect.

The authors build a two-layer model. On one layer sits the Yao-Lee model, whose Majorana fermions interact with spin textures on the second layer. Unlike the Kitaev model, the Yao-Lee model stays exactly solvable, so Monte Carlo simulations can find its ground state. The results show that skyrmion crystals can give rise to vison crystals, tidy arrays of flux with odd patterns, one like a kagome lattice. The fermions also gain a large Berry phase, leading to phases with set Chern numbers.
arxiv-2504-08935:
Ivan Matić, Radoš Radoičić, and Dan Stefanica introduce derivative-like measures for first-passage percolation, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In this model, each edge of a grid carries a random travel time, and the passage time between distant points is the fastest route's total.

Their edge weights take just two values. The derivatives record how the passage time responds to flipping individual edges, a sensitivity analysis of the random medium. The authors show the variance of the passage time can be written exactly in terms of these derivatives. They then map the derivatives' structure and prove basic properties and bounds. Bounds on the low Fourier levels raise a striking possibility. In three or more dimensions, the variance might grow slower than any positive power of distance. That would overturn the common belief in a positive fluctuation exponent, a long-standing expectation in the field.
arxiv-2504-09335:
Jihoon Suh and Takashi Tanaka study how to train control rules on coded data held in the cloud, in a 2025 paper. The catalog title is garbled with journal text, but the paper itself bears the clean title given in its head. Coding the data keeps it private while the cloud does the heavy math. The hard part is that standard training steps need checks for the larger or smaller of two values, which coded data cannot do with ease.

The authors focus on a class of training problems that needs no such checks. They show that three known methods in this class can run on coded data in a direct way. A test run in a small grid world, using a standard coding scheme, learned well with only small errors. The work points to safer cloud training for control tasks.
arxiv-2504-09435:
Mao and co-authors (2025) explore how artificial intelligence could help people with aphasia communicate. Aphasia leaves people with very different language barriers, and AI tools that generate text, images, and audio in real time might be shaped to fit them. Rather than building a finished product, the team created four early prototypes and used them as design probes to learn what users actually need.

Eleven people with aphasia took part across two phases, sharing design ideas and trying the prototypes. The tools aimed to support shared understanding and a stronger voice in conversation through picture checks, help building correct sentences, error fixing, and a lighter language load. Some outputs missed what the user meant, but the work shows where AI's speed and flexibility can help, and it offers design lessons for future augmentative and alternative communication systems.
arxiv-2504-09635:
Sahil Shikalgar and Md. Noor-E-Alam present a new way to match people in health studies, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Matching pairs a treated person with a similar untreated person, so a study can mimic a trial run by chance. Their method works in two clear stages that a reader can follow step by step.

First, it seeks exact matches on all traits. For people left over, it drops the least key trait and tries again, one trait at a time. A distance rule keeps the near matches close. Tests on made-up data and on real health data showed less bias. The team used it to study high cholesterol and diabetes.
arxiv-2504-09935:
Shiguang Wu and co-authors examine a basic weakness of generative retrieval, in a 2025 information retrieval paper. Generative retrieval seeks to swap out traditional search index structures for a single large neural network. It offers better efficiency and seamless integration with generative large language models, which made the idea fashionable for a time.

As an end-to-end paradigm, it finds results by writing out document identifiers through corpus-specific constrained decoding, with the corpus built into the search itself. The authors argue that this constraint itself limits the method, above all its generalization to unfamiliar corpora that it has not seen in training. Their analysis, given at the SIGIR conference, shows when generative retrieval should give way to hybrid designs that keep a traditional index in place.
arxiv-2504-10435:
Guerra, Li, Yue, and Zepeda-Núñez ask which goal a controller should chase when calming an unstable plasma in this 2025 paper. Fusion devices fight plasma wiggles with applied electric fields, but finding the right field is hard even in a simplified kinetic model. The team treats the search as an optimization problem tied to the plasma equations.

First, the model's wave spectrum reveals where stable settings lie, giving starting points near the best answer. Then they compare several goal functions head to head. Different goals led to similar calming settings, but goals that fold in the whole time history shaped smoother search landscapes. Gradient methods therefore work better with those richer goals.
arxiv-2504-10735:
Timur Carstensen, Neeratyoy Mallik, Frank Hutter, and Martin Rapp find a cheaper way to tune deep learning models. Tuning means trying many settings, and full training runs for each try are slow and memory hungry. Cheaper short runs can rank settings, but they break down when hardware is tight. Their 2025 work uses a new shortcut: freeze part of the network and train only the rest.

Freezing more layers cuts cost and memory while keeping the rank order of settings close to full training. The team shows this on image networks and on transformer models. The trick can also pair with other shortcuts, such as smaller data or fewer passes. They argue the joint space of shortcuts can make tuning far more efficient for big models.
arxiv-2504-10835:
Kantaro Ohmori and Shutaro Shimamura build a new twin formulation of a fracton theory in this 2025 paper. Fractons are odd excitations that cannot move freely, modeled here by a gapless field theory with tensor gauge fields. The theory carries a paired subsystem symmetry with a known anomaly.

The authors construct a foliated version, sliced into layers, and prove it matches the original exotic theory. They use the anomaly's inflow from a higher-dimensional phase as the bridge. A mirror version of the theory gets the same treatment. These are the first such dualities for gapless fracton theories. Dual pictures let physicists compute in whichever frame is easier.
arxiv-2504-11235:
Yiming Fan, Dimitris Giovanis, and Fotis Kopsaftopoulos compress guided wave signals to track structure health as conditions change, in a paper from 2025. Wave-based monitoring can spot early damage in aircraft parts, but sensor arrays produce huge fast data streams. Heat and load shifts further tangle the signals.

Older compression can miss the curved patterns typical of guided waves. Shape-learning methods and neural autoencoders capture those patterns better, yet state tracking still falters when conditions vary. Their framework first squeezes signals into a compact form, then uses that form to both judge structural state and rebuild the raw signal. One pipeline thus serves two tasks under shifting conditions.
arxiv-2504-11635:
Moritz Beber argued in 2025 for total reproducibility in computational systems biology through a software method called event sourcing. Most work in that field rests on math models, either dynamic or steady-state. Models are shared in markup languages meant to standardize them, yet results still prove hard to reproduce.

Beber notes that standards demand heavy effort, tools vary, and researchers get little reward for the extra work. Event sourcing instead keeps a full, unchanging record of every change, and the current state is rebuilt from that record, much as version control does for code. Worked examples show how the approach handles model history. Readers get a practical shift in focus: rather than asking authors to polish a final file, keep the whole trail so any result can be rebuilt.
arxiv-2504-11735:
Xiaohui Hu, Ningyu He, and Haoyu Wang present WalletProbe, a 2025 testing framework for browser cryptocurrency wallet extensions. Wallets are the front door to crypto assets and a prime hacker target. Earlier studies mapped wallet flaws only coarsely, missing interaction-level and advanced-feature risks. WalletProbe mutates inputs and judges results with visual-level oracles to pinpoint component flaws.

The team cataloged 13 attack vectors and 21 concrete attack strategies. Applied to 39 widely used wallet extensions, the framework found every single one abusable to steal user assets. Findings were reported to developers promptly, and 26 issues have been patched. The authors promise to release code and data, and urge the community to treat wallet security as urgent.
arxiv-2504-11835:
Donghui Son and Liangliang Wang present a statistics method in a 2025 paper on differential equations. Such equations model dynamic systems across science, but fitting their parameters is tricky. The best-fit surface often has many peaks, so a search can get stuck on a local peak and give unstable results.

Their method, particle data cloning, copies the data set to sharpen that surface, then draws information from the sharpened result in stages. A particle sampling scheme carries the search toward the global peak. Compared with standard cloning, the method gave more reliable results and better searches in tests. The authors show a prey-predator model as a worked case and share their code in public.
arxiv-2504-11935: Sergey Krivonos and Armen Nersessian wrote a 2025 physics note on a toy model of a particle with both supersymmetry and a spin-orbit link, where spin steers motion. Their model lives in two dimensions and keeps a high degree of symmetry. It also keeps the Galilean symmetry of a free particle, which they show with care. They then build a four dimensional cousin based on quaternions. In that version the particle moves on a cone, and the spin-orbit term is forced, not optional.
arxiv-2504-12535:
Andy Dimnaku and five co-authors describe an aid for heart ultrasound scans in a 2025 paper. Getting good heart images takes a trained operator and costly gear, usually found only in hospitals. Newer systems help beginners by guiding how to turn the probe. Their system takes a different, decision-based route.

The model learns from heart scan videos to judge whether a key vein is visible in a clip. A location method then marks where that vein sits, in real time. It worked well on high-quality hospital videos, and also on cheaper handheld scans it had never been trained on. The system is now in clinical trials through a handheld device app.
arxiv-2504-12735:
Lidong Zhai and seven co-authors propose a seven-layer frame for multi-agent systems, named for the Athenian Academy. Their paper from twenty twenty-five aims at AI art creation, where agent teams stumble on coordination, role splits, scene shifts, and parallel work. The layers run from team collaboration down through one agent's many roles, scenes, and skills. Model swaps and merges of agents into one target fill the lower layers.

Art-making trials test the frame's claims. Team tasks, cross-scene travel, and model fusion all show the promised gains in their runs. Open hurdles get a frank section: coordination polish, model stability, and system security. Meta-learning and federated learning are floated as next tools. The authors offer the frame as a shared method for agent teamwork in creative fields.
arxiv-2504-13035:
A research team tackles partially relevant video retrieval in this 2025 paper. In this task a text query matches only part of a long video, and systems face a trade: richer context at many time scales improves accuracy but costs more compute and memory.

Their framework squeezes a video's varied contexts into a fixed set of prototypes, balanced units that stand for its content. Extra objectives keep the prototypes diverse and tied to the right text, and two reconstruction tasks keep them both searchable by text and faithful to the video. A video mixing trick adds weak alignment guidance. Tests on three standard benchmarks check the balance of speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2504-13135:
John Ellis, Hong-Jian He, and Rui-Qing Xiao work out how future electron-positron colliders could spot a CP-violating twist in gauge boson interactions. Neutral triple gauge couplings that break CP symmetry arise from dimension-8 operators in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. The authors give a form factor setup that respects spontaneous symmetry breaking and match it to the operators in the broken phase. Collider energies from 250 GeV to 5 TeV are studied.

Beam polarization sharpens the probes. Reach on the new physics scale runs from the TeV range at the smallest machine to about 10 TeV at the largest. Form factor sensitivity tightens by orders of magnitude with energy.
arxiv-2504-13235:
Daipeng Xiao and co-authors work on radar detection when training data are scarce. Their 2025 paper targets a source spread across several range cells, hidden in interference and noise. The interference sits in a known subspace with an unknown position, and the noise follows a bell curve with an unknown spread pattern.

With few training samples, older detectors lose their edge. The team takes a Bayesian route, treating the unknown spread pattern as drawn from an inverse Wishart prior, and builds a detector from the Rao test. Tests on both simulated and real data show the new detector beats existing ones in some settings. The result matters for radar work where clean training data are hard to gather.
arxiv-2504-13335:
Vanja Nikolić and Teresa Rauscher develop faster math methods for contrast-enhanced ultrasound in this 2025 paper. In this imaging method, tiny gas bubbles sharpen the sound picture, but the bubbles also create harmonics that are costly to compute over time. The pair model the sound pressure together with the bubble motion, using linked equations.

They first prove that steady repeating solutions exist for the system. They then build methods that split the motion into a set of harmonics and solve for them step by step. Tests show how the count of harmonics, and the presence of bubbles, change the way sound waves travel through tissue.
arxiv-2504-13735:
Six authors build a virtual reality test of functional vision in this 2025 paper. Orientation and mobility tests measure how well people use sight to move through space, a truer gauge of daily vision than eye charts, but real courses are hard to standardize.

Their seated virtual test varies lighting and course layout while players navigate a path and clear marked obstacles. Forty-two normally sighted people took the test, and the team logged completion time, missed objects, and hesitation before the first step. Behavior around missed objects carried extra signal. The paper releases the first dataset of its kind and argues the protocol can sharpen vision assessment.
arxiv-2504-13835:
Yicheng Chen and five co-authors choose instruction-tuning data by measuring what the whole set teaches. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Open instruction datasets are vast and uneven. Picking a good subset beats training on all of it. Older pickers score single examples and use rough diversity rules. Embedding distances miss the intent of complex instructions. A global view is missing.

Their method, MIG, builds a label graph over the semantic space. Diversity is scored from how labels spread across that graph. Selection then maximizes total information gain. Quality and coverage are judged together, not in turns. The subsets train models that punch above their size. Data curation gains a principled yardstick.
arxiv-2504-13935:
Théo Verhelst and co-authors present a general way to compute spacecraft collision odds without assuming tidy bell-curve errors, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Current tools lean on such guesses and can mislead when orbits bend sharply. Their method pushes starting uncertainty through the motion using high-order polynomial maps.

From the pushed moments, a semi-exact formula gives the spread of closest-approach distances. Special polynomial fits recover that spread without a bell-curve guess. Tests on short and long low-orbit encounters handled bent dynamics and odd error shapes well. The frame suits any system with uncertain starts, they add.
arxiv-2504-14335:
Zhengbo Zhang and co-authors present a way to edit a video by editing only its first frame in this 2025 paper. The user changes the opening image with any tool, and the system must carry that change through every later frame while keeping the rest true to the source. Older methods first dissolve the frames into noise, a step that blurs away detail and lets errors creep in.

Their method skips that inversion step entirely and treats the edited first frame as a visual prompt instead. Two sampling schemes guard the result. One keeps each frame faithful to its source content, and the other keeps the frames smooth against each other in time. Wide experiments showed cleaner, steadier edits than rival systems. The authors offer the approach for film touch-ups, ads, and other edits where one frame should rule the rest.
arxiv-2504-14535:
Kuanting Wu, Kei Ota, and Asako Kanezaki train video models with motion as the guide. They match the flow fields of made clips and real clips. Video diffusion models draw fine frames but move in odd ways. Smooth time flow is their weak joint. Past fixes warped frames in place of a plain flow match. FlowLoss scores the gap in a direct way.

Flow reads go bad when the input is full of noise. So the loss is weighed by noise step by step. Trust the flow cue where it earns trust. Play it down where it does not. On robot video sets, the plan made motion more sound. Training settled fast in its first phase too. The lesson fits any noise-based maker of clips or frames. Extra cues must be timed to the noise, or they mislead. With that care, motion cues hold the frames in line.
arxiv-2504-14735:
Chin-Yun Yu and co-authors present DiffVox, a model that captures how vocal effects are set in music production, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The system rebuilds equalization, compression, delay, and reverb in forms that gradient methods can tune, so a target vocal sound can be matched by optimization rather than by hand. Presets were drawn from 70 MedleyDB tracks and 365 tracks from a private set.

Studying the fitted settings, the team found tight links between controls, such as low-end filters teaming up and delay time tracking echo strength. The main axis of variation mapped to spaciousness, the next to brightness. Settings also refused to follow a neat bell curve, marking a tangled design space. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2504-15135:
Entity linking means matching a name mentioned in text to the right entry in a knowledge base, a step behind semantic search and question answering. Juyeon Kim and three co-authors note that adding images helps settle ambiguous mentions, yet most methods ignore the structured facts stored in knowledge graphs. Their framework, KGMEL, works in three stages to bring those facts in.

First, a vision-language model generates high-quality fact triples for each mention from its text and image. Next, contrastive learning builds joint representations of mentions and candidate entities from text, images, and triples, and retrieves the best candidates. Finally, the candidates' triples are refined and a large language model picks the best match. On benchmark datasets, KGMEL outperformed existing methods, and the authors release their code and data.
arxiv-2504-15235:
Kaustubh Joshi, Tianchen Liu, and Nikhil Chopra present a cascade observer for underwater robots in two thousand twenty-five. Robots below water lose outside fixes at times, or lose sensors outright. State must then be gauged from inertial reads alone. Their observer chains two nonlinear stages built on a gradient method.

The first stage reads a quaternion based model fed by inertial preintegration. Its output drives the second stage, which finds velocity and then position. Tests span a public underwater data set and a real robot run. The method beat Kalman filter rivals on accuracy and spread. It held up when outside help was gone.
arxiv-2504-15335:
Dhvanil Desai and co-authors tackle a puzzle in the light of exploding stars: what traps the fast charged particles that feed the glow? As the wreck of a star spreads and thins, particles should escape, yet late light shows they stay held in. Magnetic fields were thought to do the holding, but their source was unclear.

Computer runs that track each particle showed the particles make their own fields. Streaming particles stir the plasma, which grows fields that slow their spread and pass their energy to the gas. That self-trapping matches what watchers see in two kinds of supernova. The team also judges that the glow from such particles needs next-generation radio scopes to spot.
arxiv-2504-15735:
Kyeongbae Kim, Ho-Sik Lee, and Harsh Prasad prove that solutions of certain nonlocal diffusion equations are locally smooth in the Hölder sense. The equations model porous media flow and fast diffusion, but with jumps driven by a general kernel rather than plain local spread. Such regularity is the base for most further theory.

Working with merely bounded, measurable kernels, they build a full local theory in the spirit of De Giorgi, Nash, and Moser. The proof needs delicate handling of where the equation degenerates or blows up, in a geometry set by the solution itself, plus careful control of far-away effects. The results need the equation to hold only locally and are new even for positive solutions with constant coefficients.
arxiv-2504-15835:
Making a moving 3D head from a line of text is a prized goal for games, film, and virtual helpers. Yiqian Wu, Malte Prinzler, Xiaogang Jin, and Siyu Tang present AnimPortrait3D in this 2025 paper, a method built around a standard morphable face model. Older methods often made heads that looked off or moved in odd ways.

The authors trace those flaws to loose guidance from the text and weak alignment with the face model. They start from a pretrained text-to-3D model to set a strong base shape and rig, then refine expressions with a control network fed by maps from the face model. Tests show gains in image quality, alignment, and motion faithfulness over prior methods.
arxiv-2504-16035:
Wenjing Zhang, Wandi Ding, and Huaiping Zhu recast optimal control problems so that neural networks can solve them. Their paper appeared in 2025. Optimal control means steering a changing system toward a goal at least cost. A classic method sweeps forward and backward through time, but it can be unstable. The team noticed that the sweep mirrors how neural networks are trained.

In their setup, a network stands in for the control choices, and training replaces the backward sweep. The method still obeys the classic rule for the best control, known as the maximum principle. As a test case, they planned a mix of two cancer treatments, immune therapy and chemotherapy. The authors say the same trick could serve disease models, ecology, engineering, and finance.
arxiv-2504-16435:
Qianyu Dong and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how to map health rates for small areas from household surveys. In poor and middle income lands, such surveys are the main source of health facts. Fine maps are now made in bulk, yet plain guidance on how to make them has lagged. Model picks and how to read the maps are weak spots, above all when data is thin.

The team sets out a full workflow, from raw data to map. They stress model choice, checks, and clear reading of results at each stage. A case study maps clinic visits in pregnancy across Kenya. Shared code lets others rerun and extend the flow to many other health signs.
arxiv-2504-16735:
Henning Basold, Chase Ford, and Lulof Pirée build a logic for reasoning about cellular automata. Automata are grids of cells that update in steps by local rules. The classic setup forces the same layout and rule on each cell. Their 2025 paper drops those limits by viewing automata as coalgebras. That view also yields a notion of when two cells act alike.

On that base the authors craft a modal logic tuned to the automata. They then prove a Hennessy-Milner style theorem. It says two cells meet the same logic claims exactly when they act alike under their equivalence. The result gives a firm bridge between what a system does and what can be said about it. Such bridges help verify large grid-based systems.
arxiv-2504-17535:
Dimitri Leemans and Jessica Mulpas glue together diagrams to disprove a conjecture about symmetry. String C-groups encode highly symmetric shapes as permutations, and their representation graphs for the symmetric group have been catalogued at high ranks. A recent list by Cameron and colleagues claimed certain graphs with a fracture pattern and imperfect split were such representations.

Testing that claim produced something better: two general techniques for fusing two representation graphs into a new one. The team works out when the fusions stay valid as string C-group graphs. The fused examples break the Cameron conjecture, since some listed graphs cannot arise after all. The authors expect the gluing toolkit to serve the wider hunt for high-rank representations.
arxiv-2504-18435:
Maria Groyne and three co-authors present a method to measure how strongly molecules stick to space ice, in a 2025 paper. Such ice coats dust grains between the stars. How tightly a molecule binds shapes how it moves and reacts there. The team built a realistic model of loose, glassy water ice.

Their approach joins motion simulations with layered quantum methods. They sample many binding spots on the ice surface. They also vary how each molecule sits at each spot, since the surface is rough. Three test molecules were used, each important in icy dust mantles. Binding patterns differed by molecule, and ammonia needed the most orientations to settle. The work extends and confirms earlier reported results, the authors say.
arxiv-2504-18535:
Gwen Yidou Weng, Benjie Wang, and Guy Van den Broeck steer language model output with exact probability math in this 2025 paper. Users want text that fits set traits, like safe tone or a chosen topic. Models that write word by word struggle to honor such whole-text traits.

Older fixes retrain the model per trait or guess future trait odds by sampling, which is slow and shaky for rare traits. Their framework, TRACE, computes those odds exactly with tractable reasoning circuits. New traits can be added without retraining. Control becomes faster and more reliable. The work joins logic-based reasoning with fluent generation.
arxiv-2504-19135:
The Borexino Collaboration reports a search for high-energy axions from the Sun. Their 2025 paper uses the full data set of the Borexino detector, with 3,995 days of live measurement time. Axions are hypothetical particles that could be made in a nuclear reaction in the Sun at a set energy.

The team looked for four ways an axion could show up in the detector, from decay into light to effects on electrons and nuclei. No signal claim is made; instead, the paper sets firm limits on how strongly axions can couple to light, electrons, and nucleons. The results rule out wide new ranges of coupling values and axion masses, and they tighten bounds for two leading axion models.
arxiv-2504-19335:
