Gan and Brown set out a plan to study how interface testing inside automated pipelines affects open-source projects on GitHub, in this 2025 paper. Interface tests check that buttons and screens behave as users expect. Little is known about how often teams wire them into delivery pipelines, or what changes when they do.

The study will gather projects that use three popular testing tools in their GitHub Actions workflows. It will compare pipelines with and without interface tests inside the same projects. Measures of development activity and workflow runs will feed comparison and time-based analyses. The authors aim to learn whether this testing changes project pace or pipeline health. Results will guide teams weighing the cost of adding such tests.
arxiv-2504-19435:
Peter Todd Williams proposes in 2025 a birthplace for two famous ingredients of meteorites: round melted droplets called chondrules, and pale inclusions rich in calcium and aluminum. He places their origin in twin ring-shaped swirls of gas above and below the young Sun's disk, close to the star. The swirls act like spinning separators for dust.

In his picture, standing shock waves in the swirls heat and fuse small dust clumps. The smallest clumps boil away, and the largest are too heavy to lift. Mid-sized ones get flung outward and rain down on the outer disk, where they can end up in growing rocks. The swirls would also pile dust into cap shapes that glow in infrared light. Williams links those caps to the puffed-up inner dust rims that telescopes see around young stars.
arxiv-2504-19535:
Changshuai Lan and nine colleagues watch quantum critical behavior change its character three times across one material family, in a 2025 paper. Quantum criticality, the fingerprint of a zero-temperature phase change, is exquisitely sensitive, yet reports in the same system often disagree. Sample quirks were blamed without a systematic account.

Studying the superconductor-to-insulator transition in underdoped cuprate flakes, the team found a staged evolution with doping. First a single clean critical point appears at the edge of the antiferromagnetic phase. Then an anomalous Griffiths singularity, where rare regions dominate, takes over at middle doping. Deep in the superconducting regime, a standard Griffiths phase replaces it. A puddle model with growing magnetic correlations reproduces the sequence. The authors offer the map as a lens for re-reading past contradictions, and as a clue to how magnetism and superconductivity intertwine.
arxiv-2504-19935:
Xiem HoangVan and co-authors adapt, in a 2025 paper, an omniscient quality enhancement network to clean up videos compressed with the newest VVC standard. VVC squeezes far harder than its predecessor, but viewers still demand cleaner pictures at the decoder. Their model reads spatial, temporal, and cross-frequency clues from the decoded frames to rebuild lost detail.

Plugged into the standard VVC decoder, the enhancer lifted picture quality by about 0.74 decibels on average and up to 1.2 at best, measured in peak signal-to-noise. Looked at the other way, the same quality could be kept while saving about a fifth of the bitrate. The gains held across a rich spread of test conditions. Smarter post-processing, the authors argue, is now part of the codec itself.
arxiv-2504-20035:
Brandon Woodard and five co-authors explore using both phone cameras at once for augmented reality in a 2025 paper. Typical phone AR uses one camera, squeezing interaction into a narrow view and a small screen. Their concept, built into three prototype apps, lets interaction span the front and rear cameras together.

Thirty participants tried the apps, and a qualitative analysis produced two main lessons. First, designers must balance familiar real world gestures against the quality of the AR feedback those gestures trigger. Second, switching or combining camera feeds needs care to avoid disorienting users. Observed user habits round out the guidance. The authors frame the work as a first step toward richer phone AR.
arxiv-2504-20135:
Marco Chianese and co-authors trace the birth of matter through gravity waves in a 2025 paper. Leptogenesis makes the matter surplus of the cosmos at huge heat scales. Such scales sit far past any lab reach, so proof seemed out of grasp.

Induced gravity waves can rise in leptogenesis models with an early matter phase. Fresh software runs gauge those waves in the wild, non linear regime. Wave pitch and size then track the heat scale where matter was born. A set model shows the link in full. Sky wave hunts may thus peek at the birth of matter.
arxiv-2504-20435:
Love Panta and co-authors build an AI screening system for cervical cancer aimed at low-resource settings in a 2025 paper. The standard liquid-based test needs expert pathologists and long hours, and errors creep in. Their setup pairs cheap microscopes with automated slide reading.

A motorized scope captures slide images, which software stitches into whole-slide views. A light segmentation model, trained with a human in the loop on few outlined regions, picks out cells. A second model then sorts cells into five types, trained on a public data set. The team reports stronger accuracy and speed than prior automated methods on their checks. The frame is meant to bring reliable screening where pathologists are scarce.
arxiv-2504-20635:
Clinical machine learning models often fail when moved to a new hospital, because patient mix, disease rates, and local habits differ. Real data sets are scarce, carry hidden biases, and cannot be reshaped at will for testing. Generative models that mimic real data add little control over what drives the shift. The four authors propose a structured synthetic data framework that gives explicit control over the data-making process, including site-specific disease rates, subgroup effects, and feature links.

With that control, teams can test how a model reacts to one shift at a time, audit fairness, and spot failures in generalization. Their experiments show the framework can isolate site effects and reveal how model complexity interacts with site-specific quirks. The paper offers the tool as a reproducible, interpretable way to check robustness and fairness before a clinical model is trusted in a new setting.
arxiv-2504-20735:
Tariq Qayyum, Asadullah Tariq, Muhammad Ali, and three co-authors tune computing for connected vehicles in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Vehicles in ad-hoc networks can offload work to roadside units and edge servers for real-time processing. But the setting is harsh and live: terms shift in ways no one can call, bringing latency, wasted energy, and failed tasks. The team puts forth an AI frame to call what to offload, and where.

Supervised learning models call offloading plans from current terms. Reinforcement learning adapts the calls as the network shifts. Particle swarm optimization tunes the trade between latency and energy use. Wide runs showed cuts in latency and energy use, and task success rates and network throughput beat the ways set off against them too. The team sets the frame out as a scalable base for vehicular uses. They run from safety systems to traffic intelligence.
arxiv-2504-20935:
Sylvain Gravier, Matthieu Petiteau, and Isabelle Sivignon settle a hardness result for graph orientations in this 2025 paper. An orientation points each edge of a graph one way. A T-odd orientation demands odd in-degree exactly at a chosen vertex set.

Plain T-odd orientation can be found fast, a fact known since 1983. Adding a ban on directed cycles makes the problem far thornier. A randomized method exists, and flat graphs have a full solution in one case. The authors study a wider version where some edges come pre-pointed. They prove that version is NP-complete. The result tightens what is known about this long-open problem.
arxiv-2504-21035:
Rui Xin and co-authors show that scrubbed text data can still betray private facts about people, in a 2025 paper. Data cleaning usually strips names and other direct identifiers. Synthetic replacement data is also assumed safe. Those checks mostly measure surface leaks. Subtle clues in writing can still re-identify a person.

The team built a framework that attacks sanitized data on purpose. Even routine details, like everyday social activities, can reveal sensitive traits. Their tests quantify the risk of re-identification after release. Results challenge the comfort that simple scrubbing provides. Data stewards gain a stricter yardstick for safe sharing. Privacy methods must now prove themselves against real attacks, not checklists.
arxiv-2504-21135:
Hanjing Xu and co-authors move tuned quantum algorithm settings from small graphs to large ones with a neural network, published in 2025. The algorithm, QAOA, is a leading approach for hard combinatorial problems on quantum machines. Its settings must be tuned by solving a hard series of programs, which is costly for large problems.

The team tunes settings on small graphs, then uses a graph attention network to transfer them to larger graphs. The test problem is the maximum independent set. They also build a hybrid method that splits large problems into pieces small enough for near-term quantum hardware. Combined, the approach matched a leading classical solver on graphs with thousands of points in their tests.
arxiv-2505-00035:
Aayam Bansal, Raghav Agarwal, and Kaashvi Jain study hip-hop lyrics in a 2025 paper that spans four decades of songs. They built a set of more than three thousand songs by 146 artists. Computer tools then measured word choice, rhyme, themes, and tone in the lyrics.

Word range grew over the study years, and East Coast artists used the widest range of words. Rhyme per line rose as well, with Midwest artists at the top. Themes shifted over time, with justice themes falling and self focused themes rising. Lyrics also grew more dark in tone after times of unrest. The team found four main styles, linked to place and era.
arxiv-2505-00335:
Seungjun Shin, Suji Kim, and Dokwan Oh present a 2025 paper on a faster way to store video as a neural network. Such storage can shrink files and speed playback, but training the network is slow. A leading method uses grids of tunable values, which speeds training yet wastes values because it ignores how video changes over time.

Their method splits the video into flat grids plus flow data that tracks motion between frames. Pixels that correspond across time are processed together. The result is the fastest encoding speed among rivals at fair quality, with better use of each tunable value. The work suits real-world video tools better.
arxiv-2505-00535:
Six authors, Sandi Klavžar, Aditi Krishnakumar, Dorota Kuziak, Ethan Shallcross, James Tuite, and Ismael Yero, wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on robots moving through graphs. The setting is the mobile general position problem. A set of vertices is in general position when no three of them lie on one shortest path.

In the mobile version, a team of robots must visit every vertex of a graph. At each step, the robots' spots must stay in general position. The authors study this task on graphs built by three product rules: Cartesian products, corona products, and joins. They prove upper and lower bounds for general graphs. They also find exact values for named families, among them grids, cylinders, Hamming graphs, and prisms of trees. The work mixes graph theory with motion planning ideas.
arxiv-2505-00635:
Yifei Xiong and Nianqiao Phyllis Ju propose a new sampling algorithm for private data analysis in a 2025 statistics study. Official data are often released only in noisy, privacy-protected form. Bayesian methods can still draw conclusions by filling in the hidden true values during computation, but standard versions mix slowly and waste time.

Their sampler offers one proposal and tests it against many components at once, rather than checking each one separately. Sharing proposals in that way cuts rejections. The authors prove bounds on acceptance and convergence in a simple case. Tests on synthetic and real census data with regression models show efficiency gains.
arxiv-2505-00735:
Filling in missing parts of a photo works better when the model knows how far away things are. Jin Hyun Park, Harine Choi, and Praewa Pitiphat build an image inpainting system that reads depth maps alongside the usual color image. One encoder handles color and another handles depth, and an attention step in the decoder blends the two streams before rebuilding the picture. They test the model with thin line masks and square masks that hide different parts of a scene.

Across their measures, the depth-aware model rebuilt hidden regions more accurately than the color-only baseline, and attention improved results further. The team also used heat-map visualizations to check where the model looks while filling gaps. Those maps support their claim that depth cues guide the reconstruction toward the right structures.
arxiv-2505-00835:
Nathan Huet, Philippe Naveau, and Anne Sabourin model extreme sea surges on the French Atlantic coast in a 2025 paper. A skew surge is the gap between predicted tide and actual water at high tide, and rare big ones drive coastal flooding. Planners need to reconstruct past extremes at spots where records are short.

The team studies how extremes at nearby stations relate, using records from ports with more than 150 years of data. They propose a new way to set the line above which a surge counts as extreme. One model then generates likely extremes at one station from observed extremes at its neighbors. A second method predicts values using only the direction of the input pattern, not its size. Both feed the goal of rebuilding long histories at data-poor stations, which sharpens flood risk estimates.
arxiv-2505-01335:
Rare loud quasars are hunted among quiet ones by Ramkrishna Joshi and Vivek Shinde in a 2025 arXiv paper. Loud quasars are one in ten, which skews any sorting tool. The team uses a sky survey set and a pipeline that shrinks traits by main axes. Two shrunk traits hold near all the spread in the data. Four sorters face off on the set.

A plain forest scored best overall but caught near no loud ones. Their balanced sort caught half the loud set at lower total score. Boost and fake-fill tools sat in between. Recall for the rare class is the true test here.
arxiv-2505-01535:
Adrián Moreno-Sánchez and Ajdin Palavrić study how a symmetry rule could shape new physics for leptons, in a research paper from 2025. Leptons are light particles such as electrons and neutrinos. No direct sign of new particles has shown up at current colliders, so the team looks for indirect signs instead.

They use a framework that lists possible small effects from heavy, unseen particles. A pattern rule called A4, tied to modular forms, limits which effects can appear. The authors sort the possible heavy go-between particles by how they fit the rule. They then check what each option would mean for processes that keep or change lepton flavor.
arxiv-2505-01635:
Nafiul Islam and co-authors build computer neurons with dendrites, the branching input arms real neurons use. Chip neurons are usually bare points, far simpler than brain cells. Their 2025 design uses a multi-gate ferroelectric transistor. Each gate acts as one dendrite branch, doing local nonlinear math before the cell fires. Ferroelectric material supplies the bend. The branched build also shrinks the wiring arrays a chip needs.

A lab-tuned simulation chain tests device, circuit, and learning together. Networks with dendritic cells beat much larger plain ones. They used about seventeen times fewer trainable weights for the win. The team aims the design at edge gear that must learn on a power diet.
arxiv-2505-01735:
Eva Andres, Manuel Pegalajar Cuellar, and Gabriel Navarro design a brain-inspired quantum model for fraud detection in a 2025 paper. Credit card fraud is an anomaly detection problem with costly misses. Quantum spiking networks and quantum memory networks offer fresh machinery. The team fuses both into a two-stage architecture.

Stage one extracts low-level features like a sensory brain region. Stage two processes patterns at a higher level, like memory areas. The analogy maps hypothalamus and hippocampus roles onto the stages. Comparisons include other quantum models and classical counterparts. Pattern recognition benchmarks frame the evaluation plan. The manuscript emphasizes architecture over final scores. Brain-like staging is the conceptual contribution claimed. Quantum hardware limits shape what can run today. The authors position the design for future quantum advantage tests. Finance is the lead application, with broader anomaly uses implied.
arxiv-2505-02035:
Tianshu Yu studies how a family of generative models learns. His 2025 paper deals with GFlowNets, models that build complex objects step by step with odds set by a reward. Their uses are spreading, but the theory of how they learn has lagged behind.

Yu picks four fronts for a strict analysis: whether training settles, how many samples it needs, what hidden biases it carries, and how it holds up under noise. The results map both strengths and limits of the method. From them he draws design rules for building and fielding such models. The aim is a firmer base for a tool many teams now use.
arxiv-2505-02135:
Jincheng Yue and co-authors explain why a copper compound carries heat so poorly once its atoms start to move like a liquid. Their 2025 study deals with a crystal that is ordered when cool. Warming frees some copper atoms to wander, making it part liquid. Such materials are prized for turning heat into power, but their heat flow is hard to model. The team made samples and tracked the structure as temperature rose.

Calculations joined phonon theory with a transport equation that counts both wave like and diffuse carriers. The diffuse side, called diffusons, dominated. Predicted conductivity was an ultralow 0.34 units at 400 degrees. That matched the measurements well. Machine learned simulations reproduced both the structure and the heat flow. The wandering ions themselves added almost nothing, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2505-02335:
Knowing how much a person eats is hard to measure without asking them, and self-reports are unreliable. Kevin Tan, Fan Yang, and Yuhao Chen built a system that watches people eat on a stationary video feed. The system tracks the three-dimensional pose of their hands and spoons: where each is, and how it is rotated. From those movements, systems like this can estimate food volume and eating behavior.

The paper focuses on the segmentation step, the part that outlines hands and spoons in each frame. The authors compare two leading video object segmentation models, scoring them with numbers and by eye. They identify where the errors creep in, pointing to the weak spots that any dietary monitoring system built this way would need to fix.
arxiv-2505-02435:
Pouria Fatemi, Ehsan Sharifian, and Mohammad Hossein Yassaee present a 2025 method for explaining model calls with what-if cases that respect cause and effect. Plain what-if tools swap inputs freely and can craft cases that could never occur. Causal versions fix that flaw but cost much compute. The gap calls for a fast, causal route.

Their method, called BRACE, works backward through a causal model to build the what-if case. It claims deeper insight into why a model ruled as it did. The authors show their frame covers older methods as special cases. Tests back the speed and depth claims. The paper also lays out where older methods fall short, to frame the gain.
arxiv-2505-02535:
Abha Tripathi, writing with Tiwari, unifies several fuzzy mathematics categories in a 2025 paper. One side holds F-transforms, a tool for compressing and approximating fuzzy data. The other holds fuzzy pretopological spaces, a soft version of the spaces used to define nearness and limits.

The meeting point is a new category called Qua. Its objects are success measurements of answers, and its arrows pair measurements of how answers transform. Spaces built on fuzzy partitions, fuzzy lower transformation systems, and fuzzy pretopological spaces all turn out to relate to Qua in tidy ways. A fourth family, built on fuzzy interior operators in the style of Čech, joins the pattern. The authors present the unification as a shared language for fields that grew up apart.
arxiv-2505-04035:
Laurel Barnett and co-authors improve a classic physics demonstration with liquid nitrogen droplets, in a 2025 paper. A rotating saddle can hold a rolling ball in a stable path, a mechanical cousin of the Paul trap used for ions. Ball bearings, though, roll and rub, which hides the pure particle motion the demo should show.

Droplets of liquid nitrogen float on their own vapor, so they slide with almost no friction. Their paths match theory well and show a sharp switch from unstable to stable motion at a set spin rate. Bearings switch in a gradual way, with friction bent paths. The clearer demo cuts common misconceptions and opens paths to deeper class tests.
arxiv-2505-04135:
App store reviews carry fine-grained feelings that star ratings flatten. Vihaan Miriyala, Smrithi Bukkapatnam, and Lavanya Prahallad tested whether making a language model reason aloud improves its reading of those feelings. They ran two thousand Amazon app reviews through two setups. One asked the model for a direct label. The other asked it to think step by step first.

Human judges graded both. Plain prompting scored 84 percent accuracy. Chain-of-thought prompting reached 93 percent. The gain held across the detailed sentiment categories the team used. The authors conclude that explicit reasoning helps models sort mixed, nuanced feedback. That matters for developers mining reviews for what users actually want.
arxiv-2505-04235:
Solieri and Lund lead a long CERN team on this report from two thousand twenty-five. It tells how the two LHC beam dumps, pulled out in twenty eighteen after a decade of use, were taken apart and studied between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three.

Each dump weighs well over six tonnes and must soak up the collider's beam safely. Scope checks and beam tests on samples had raised doubts about the carbon cores. The team built a work frame, cut the thick steel shell of the hot vessel, and sequenced the cuts with care. Inside, the extruded graphite plates showed cracks and their rings had shifted. The expanded sheets held up with light wear. The isostatic blocks showed no decay at all.
arxiv-2505-04335:
Swagato Das, Arghya Pratihar, and Swagatam Das present a clustering method for data that live in curved spaces in this 2025 paper. Clustering groups like items without labels. The popular fuzzy C-means method lets items belong partly to several groups, yet it assumes flat Euclidean geometry. Real data often carry tree like or network structure that flat distance distorts. Their method, HypeFCM, moves the clustering into hyperbolic space, using the Poincaré disc model.

A weight based filtering step, seeded from a Dirichlet distribution, refines the group centers and memberships step by step. Distance is measured with the hyperbolic metric, which stretches space near the disc edge. Tests covered six synthetic and twelve real world data sets. The method beat standard fuzzy clustering in the non-Euclidean settings by clear margins. The authors present it as a sturdier tool for complex, high dimensional data whose structure is not flat.
arxiv-2505-04535:
Training a large language model on data spread across many sites, without moving the data, protects privacy but costs time in constant updates. A 2025 paper by Theologitis and co-authors proposes a smarter schedule for when those updates should happen.

Standard methods swap model updates at fixed gaps, picked in advance. The new family of methods, called FDA-Opt, watches training progress and adjusts the gaps as it goes, and it needs no extra tuning knob that is hard to set. In tests on language tasks, it beat the standard method even when that method had been tuned with care. The authors offer it as a drop-in replacement for current tools.
arxiv-2505-04835:
Shashank Agnihotri and co-authors test whether synthetic corruptions are a reliable proxy for real-world corruptions when judging how robust models are, published in 2025. Deep learning models are widely used, but they remain at risk from shifts in weather and lighting. Collecting varied real-world test data is costly, so synthetic corruptions are an attractive alternative.

The team ran a large test study on semantic segmentation models. They compared how the models did on data sets with real-world corruptions and how they did on data sets with synthetic ones. Mean scores tracked each other strongly, which supports the use of synthetic tests. They also analyzed correlations for each corruption type. That finer view shows when synthetic corruptions succeed at representing real ones, and when they fall short, guiding safer use of the cheaper proxy.
arxiv-2505-05235:
Luca Marzari, Isabella Mastroeni, and Alessandro Farinelli propose a richer way to check neural network safety in a 2025 paper. Standard checks give a yes-or-no verdict: a model is safe or it is not. That coarse split hides the fact that some bad outputs are far worse than others.

The new approach checks a ranked ladder of unsafe outputs at once, using set-based reasoning about what a network can produce. It can rank attack inputs by how badly they break the ladder. The cost is no worse than the old check, and can be lower. Tests cover a complex game-like task and standard benchmarks. Readers get a finer lens on model risk.
arxiv-2505-05335:
Yusong Wu and seven co-authors introduced FLAM in 2025, a model that links sound recordings with words at fine time scales. Audio-language models are good at matching whole clips to text, but weak at saying when a sound occurs. Older event detectors pin down timing, yet only for fixed lists of sounds. FLAM aims to keep the timing skill while accepting any sound a user names.

The model trains with a frame-wise goal that stays light on memory and corrects for skewed labels and linked events. Its training data mixes many sound types, machine-written captions, and simulated clips. In tests, FLAM found named sounds in time far better than rivals, while staying strong at whole-clip search. The authors see it serving search and editing tools that need exact sound timing.
arxiv-2505-05635:
Faizan Farooq Khan and co-authors present a system for naming bird species in photos, including species it was not trained on, in a 2025 paper. Naming a bird from the thousands of possible species is hard, because many look alike and sound alike in text. Standard systems lose more than thirty percent of their accuracy in such open settings, the authors find.

Their framework first pulls candidate species from short, sharp summaries distilled from encyclopedia articles on more than eleven thousand bird species. Unlike text-only rivals, it uses the photo itself during retrieval, so final picks must fit both the text and the image. Across five bird benchmarks and two other domains, the method raised a leading vision model score by about eighteen percent on average. The authors offer it for wildlife monitoring where new species keep appearing.
arxiv-2505-05735:
Orr Fischer and Merav Parter study fault-proof messaging when an attacker roams a network's edges in two thousand twenty-five. Classic models cap the total count of bad edges. A newer model caps instead how many bad edges touch any one node, which can allow far more faults overall.

Their results are compilers: they turn any algorithm for a fully linked chatty network into one that runs round by round under attack. The attacker may corrupt a fixed share of edges at each node in each round, and may pick fresh edges each round. Even an attacker who adapts to the run is handled. The gain, nearly a linear jump in faults borne, comes at no extra cost.
arxiv-2505-05935:
Dean Doron and co-authors study list recovery for random linear codes over small fields in a 2025 paper. Error-correcting codes let a receiver rebuild data despite noise. List recovery goes further: each position comes with a short list of candidate symbols, and the decoder must return a short list of codewords that fit. Code rate sits near the theoretical limit in their setup.

Earlier bounds on the output list size were far weaker, dating to 1981. The authors show that for prime fields with erasures, and for any field with errors, the list size grows only in direct proportion to the inverse gap from capacity. That matches the best nonlinear codes in these regimes, so linearity costs little here.
arxiv-2505-06935:
Disease modelers track how an outbreak moves through compartments like susceptible and infected, but they often see only part of the picture. Michael Whitehouse, writing alone in a 2025 paper, speeds up the math for such models. His method handles reports that swing more than chance alone would explain.

The trick treats the chance of a case being reported as a hidden variable and folds it into an approximate likelihood. In large populations, the filter recovers the true hidden states almost exactly. Simulations found honest estimates with order-of-magnitude speed gains over particle methods. He also packages the method in the Stan language and applies it to COVID-19 data from Switzerland.
arxiv-2505-07335:
Drone swarms could act as flying antenna arrays, but their shifting positions threaten the clean signal focus that arrays promise. Tiebin Mi, Miyu Feng, Ruichu Shao, Cao Zeng, and Robert Caiming Qiu study that tension in 2025, moving the math from fixed layouts to random ones.

For tidy linear layouts they prove exact conditions for when unwanted grating lobes appear, and show that two rows of antennas can safely break the classic half-wavelength spacing rule. For messy real layouts they analyze random position errors and find the shared signal gain roughly survives, with a measurable softening of the main beam. Tests back the theory. The authors argue swarm arrays can stay coherent without perfect formation flying.
arxiv-2505-07435:
Rabia Bashir, Ramoona Shehzadi, Ashraf, and Khan forecast what three simulation codes will say about oxygen nuclei smashing together at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 paper. Oxygen-oxygen runs are new, and model predictions guide the experiments that will read them. The team ran EPOS4, a string-melting transport model, and the Angantyr model inside Pythia 8, and compared their outputs for pions, kaons, and protons.

Predictions cover particle counts, momentum spectra, yields, and average masses. Ratios of kaons and protons to pions probe whether the debris flows collectively, like a fluid. EPOS4, with its full fluid dynamics, showed the strongest flow; the transport model sat in the middle; Pythia's effects were weakest. The authors offer the spread as a pre-data benchmark: the coming measurements will discipline all three codes.
arxiv-2505-07635:
Dazhuo Qiu, Haolai Che, Arijit Khan, and Yinghui Wu introduce skyline explanations for graph neural networks, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Graph neural networks answer inference queries on networks, but their outputs are hard to interpret. Earlier explanation methods usually optimize one chosen measure, such as fidelity, which biases the result.

A skyline explanation instead balances several measures at once. It is a Pareto set of subgraphs that beat all others across the chosen measures. The authors formulate the problem, prove hardness results, and design algorithms. Their onion-peeling method builds explanations incrementally, with a diversification step for variety. Parallel versions with load balancing extend the approach to large-scale inference tasks.
arxiv-2505-07735:
Nicholas Runcie, Charlotte Deane, and Fergus Imrie present a 2025 paper that tests how well language models handle chemistry. Newer reasoning models have leapt ahead in math and coding. The team asked whether they can do core chemistry tasks on their own, with no outside tools to lean on.

They built a test of 816 questions on organic chemistry, focused on grasping molecules and reasoning about reactions. Unlike older tests, theirs demands short written answers, not a choice from a list. The best reasoning models scored about half correct in their strongest modes. Plain models scored near zero, which shows how much the reasoning step adds.
arxiv-2505-08135:
Keita Teranishi and co-authors chart how artificial intelligence could reshape the writing of supercomputer software, in a 2025 paper. High-performance computing code is a niche craft: it must squeeze huge machines hard without breaking trust in the results. Language models have already changed everyday coding, yet this field's codes are rare, long, and steeped in physics and math.

The authors list where AI help snags on such code: scarce training stock, hard correctness bars, and hardware quirks no generic model knows. They then lay out research paths to make AI a productive and trustworthy partner here. Two United States energy department projects, Ellora and Durban, carry the work. The paper doubles as a field map, marking open problems for others. Its wager is that AI can speed expert coders rather than replace them.
arxiv-2505-08635:
Jiale Huang and co-authors presented this 2025 method to sharpen a workhorse of quantum simulation. The DMRG method represents quantum states as chains of small tensors. Some added circuit types, though easy to fake on classic computers alone, can enrich that representation. The authors blend two such circuit kinds, matchgates and Clifford circuits, into the chain ansatz.

The combined form can be tuned within the standard DMRG routine without heavy cost. Tests on a one-dimensional chain of hydrogen atoms showed the blend improved ground-state energy accuracy by orders of magnitude. The gain came at the same chain width as the plain method. The authors offer the ansatz as a stronger tool for many-body quantum problems, and as a clue to which quantum states classic machines can capture.
arxiv-2505-08935:
Max Alekseyev and co-authors published a mathematics paper in 2025 on values of a classic family of polynomials at a prime. The family, Legendre polynomials, shows up across physics and number theory. The team studies how many times a prime divides the polynomial's value at that prime, a measure called the p-adic valuation. They prove an exact formula for that measure.

The formula also settles and broadens an old conjecture by one of the authors. In addition, the paper solves a problem posed by Cigler in 2017. The work gives a complete answer for this prime case rather than bounds or partial cases.
arxiv-2505-09135:
Peihang Wu builds the missing edges onto Shimura varieties over the integers. His 2025 paper constructs toroidal and minimal compactifications, in the framework of Lan and Stroh, for integral models of abelian-type Shimura varieties, the arithmetic surfaces whose points encode abelian varieties.

The strategy borrows from the better-understood Hodge-type case. Wu first finds cusp labels and cone decompositions that match the Hodge-type data. Then he studies how rational points of the adjoint group act on boundary charts, extending a twisting construction of Kisin and Pappas to those charts. The abelian-type compactification emerges as a subspace of a quotient built from Hodge-type pieces. He also verifies formulas for nearby cycles under parahoric level structures at p.
arxiv-2505-09335:
Jianjun Jin and Huabing Li study a family of p-adic integral operators, in a 2025 paper. The catalog title adds a support note, so the head title governs. The operators extend a classic Hardy, Littlewood, and Pólya form into the p-adic world, with added parameters for range.

Working on weighted p-adic spaces, the authors fully settle when these operators stay bounded between every pair of exponent spaces. For special cases they compute the exact norm, not just a bound. The results both fill gaps and extend what was known for such operators. Sharp norm values matter where these tools serve harmonic analysis on p-adic fields.
arxiv-2505-10335:
Gabriele Naselli and Ion Cosma Fulga study walls between magnetic zones in a class of exotic crystals in a 2025 paper. These crystals block current in their bulk yet carry it on their faces, a trait prized for new devices. When the crystal is also magnetic, with spins set in a striped pattern, zone walls form where the stripe flips. What lives on those walls was the open question here.

The team built two model crystals that pair this trait with one of two mirror rules. In the first, the wall bulk stays gapped, but the wall end hosts one-way edge states. In the second, the wall itself is a sheet of free states, shielded by the mirror rule. A sign flip in a key count splits the two cases. Stack faults in weak crystals sparked the study.
arxiv-2505-10435:
Constance Lainé and eleven co-authors demonstrate a compact spin sensor for silicon quantum computers in this 2025 paper. Silicon spin qubits are built like transistors, which suits mass production. Reading their spins usually takes bulky sensors that crowd the layout. Their device, a single electron box, sits inside a two dot unit cell made on an industrial 300 millimeter wafer line. Independent gates tune the sensor and the dot coupling separately. The sensor read a spin correctly 99.92 percent of the time.

Speed matched accuracy: ninety-nine percent fidelity arrived in twenty microseconds. A hidden Markov model of the two electron dynamics sharpened the fidelity estimate itself. The authors stress layout economics. A small sensor leaves room for the connections a large machine needs. Faster readout also speeds the reset step every computation repeats. The work brings a manufacturing grade sensor to an architecture whose selling point is manufacturability.
arxiv-2505-10635:
Abdelghani Zeghib surveyed left-invariant semi-Riemannian metrics on compact Lie groups in twenty twenty-five. Semi-Riemannian metrics allow distances of mixed sign, unlike the purely positive Riemannian case, which changes the geometry deeply. Fixing the metric to be unchanged by the group's own multiplications makes the problem tractable and rich.

The survey poses four guiding questions. Do geodesics run for all time? Does the isometry group act properly? What is the full isometry group, beyond the group itself? And when is the conformal group genuinely larger than the isometry group? Zeghib reviews what is known for compact groups, including how larger semisimple groups can act through their maximal compact subgroups. The note maps a field where many Riemannian intuitions fail and must be rebuilt.
arxiv-2505-10735:
Hardeep Bassi, Yizhi Shen, Harish Bhat, and Roel Van Beeumen present a hybrid quantum classical method that reads ground state energies from noisy signals. The method stays robust under heavy noise and shrugs off tuning choices. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Fourier denoising first strips false noise modes from time signals. A dynamic mode method then works on many cleaned runs at once to pin the system's tones. Error bounds back the method. On molecular tests, it converged in noise levels where baselines failed, on a tight quantum budget. The gain is fully classical, so quantum cost stays flat.
arxiv-2505-11035:
Kihun Hong, Sejun Park, and Ganguk Hwang present a 2025 framework for vertical federated learning under messy real-world conditions. In vertical setups, institutions hold different features for the same users, and learning must proceed without pooling private data. Existing methods assume few parties, perfectly aligned records, or labels everywhere. The authors recast alignment gaps as missing data and build one framework that trains and predicts under any alignment and labeling pattern.

Across 168 configurations, spanning four data sets and many missingness patterns at training and test time, their method beat every baseline in 160 cases. The average margin over the next-best rival was 9.6 percentage points. The authors claim the first framework to juggle arbitrary alignment, unlabeled data, and many parties at once.
arxiv-2505-11535:
Yuhang Wang and Hao Zhou build a warn-ahead tool for lane keeping in cars, in work from 2025. Lane Keeping Assist steers a car to hold its lane, but it can fail with no clear sign. Drivers then have scant time to take over, and trust in the tool falls.

Their system, LKAlert, watches dash-cam video and car data to call a risk one to three seconds early. It also gives a short plain note on why the risk is high. To train it, the pair built a data set of clips with human notes on the risky spans. The tool called failures with fair scores and ran fast enough for live use in a car. The pair offer the method as a way to watch over other opaque machine aids as well.
arxiv-2505-11635:
Nikhil Kapasi, William Whitehead, Luke Theogarajan, and a co-author introduce a new kind of restricted Boltzmann machine for data with clear, grouped states. Older models use hidden units that are simply on or off. That simple form can struggle with tasks that need richer, multi-valued ideas.

Their model replaces those binary units with units that can take several states, drawn from the Potts model. The paper derives the energy, the learning rules, and training tricks that stop units from collapsing to one state. On memory and recall tests, the new model matched or beat the older one at the same size and cost.
arxiv-2505-12135:
Idriss Malek and seven co-authors build a test that checks whether language models can plan, apart from all the skills that blur other tests. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In most game-like tests, a failure could stem from poor seeing, fuzzy orders, or weak recall. One score hides which skill broke.

Their bench turns a small grid world into pure text, fully open to view. Three tasks split the skills apart: predict the next state, plan a path to a goal, and break a mission into subgoals. Seven top models were tried with no examples. All simulated far better than they planned, and the best nearly aced simulation. Long plans were the breaking point for every strong model. Step-by-step answers showed the models plan by rehearsal, not by true search.
arxiv-2505-12235:
Jia Li and co-authors presented a test-time method for making varied copies of an image in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion models generate images from noise, and that noise quietly encodes shape and texture. Most control methods steer generation with outside signals instead of using what the noise already holds.

Their module, NOFT, fine-tunes the seed or inverted noise through an information bottleneck shaped by optimal transport. It has only about fourteen thousand trainable parameters and trains in about ten minutes. Plugged into Stable Diffusion, it produced highly correlated yet diverse image variants that respect topology and texture. Tests covered two- and three-dimensional generated assets with text or image guidance.
arxiv-2505-12335:
Ziqiang Li and co-authors ask, in a 2025 paper, whether spotting AI-generated images is really a solved problem. Modern generators make synthetic pictures that look strikingly real. That fuels worries about misinformation, deepfakes, and copyright abuse.

Many detectors claim high accuracy, yet they are often tested on narrow data. The authors build a benchmark, AIGIBench, to stress these tools the way real use would. It spans 23 sets of fake images and four challenge types, from cross-source tests to degraded or altered images. Putting detectors through such trials shows which claims survive contact with messy reality. The benchmark gives the field a sterner yardstick than it had before.
arxiv-2505-12435:
Wenqiao Zhu, Ji Liu, Lulu Wang, Jun Wu, and Yulun Zhang steer language model tuning with a self-made guide in a 2025 paper. A known tune method aligns models to human picks but yields weak and shaky gains. Their twist adds a pilot term that steers the slope of each update.

The pilot gives fine control over how picked and spurned replies gain or lose weight. Full maths for the method and its inner works are set out in the paper. Tests across models and bench sets show clear gains over the base method.
arxiv-2505-13035:
Itamar Procaccia and Tuhin Samanta trace energy loss in strained amorphous solids to broken symmetry in this 2025 paper. Glasses and other disordered solids can respond to strain in two ways. Some cycles give the energy back, while others waste it as heat.

The team study just one slow cycle of strain to expose the source of loss. A sharp switch between the two behaviors depends on how the solid was prepared. The switch comes with breaking of shift and rotation symmetry, plus screening effects. They solve one case exactly with a middle-scale theory. Matching micro-scale simulations confirm the picture. The result guides models of damping in glasses and gels.
arxiv-2505-13335:
Liam Kruse, Marc Schlichting, and Mykel Kochenderfer scale rare-event work to high dimensions in a 2025 study. Importance sampling estimates the chance of rare outcomes by drawing from a proposal spread tilted toward them, then correcting with weights. Gaussian mixtures are the usual proposal, but their full covariance matrices become too hard to fit as dimension grows.

Low-rank structure inside the mixture parts cuts that cost while keeping flexibility. The authors build plans from such mixtures so sampling stays feasible in many dimensions. Reliable rare-event estimates serve safety analysis for aircraft, self-driving systems, and finance.
arxiv-2505-13435:
Priyankar Banerjee and co-authors compute light signals that betray coherence in paired molecules in a 2025 paper. Two coupled emitters bathed in vibration can emit light as a pair, but the bath of shaking usually blurs the quantum marks. The team modeled intensity and photon coincidences sorted by mode for dimers at a range of angles.

Even pairs set at right angles gave cooperative signatures under projective measurement. The work folds in the shaking around them through a polaron frame, plus detector smearing, heat, and static disorder. The paired counts stayed clear to read with today's detectors despite the mess. The authors offer the results as a guide for experiments that want to watch the shared motion play out in real molecular systems.
arxiv-2505-13535:
Aniket Bhattacharyya and co-authors teach language models to extract data from visually rich documents. Their method first cuts each page into semantic blocks. Their 2025 paper, BLOCKIE, answers a split in the field. Classic extractors read layout but cannot reason or infer missing values. Raw language models reason well yet misread layout, especially in new formats.

A block is a local, reusable chunk of text that keeps its own meaning. The model then reasons over blocks one by one, a narrower and more portable job. Scores rose one to three points over the best prior systems on public benchmarks. The method held up on formats it had never seen. It could also infer values the page implied but never printed.
arxiv-2505-13635:
David Alemán-Espinosa and Nikhil Kumar study routing flows in a special class of graphs in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In multicommodity flow, many goods must travel through one network at once. A classic theorem says a cut condition suffices to route them in outerplanar graphs, if flows may split. The harder version studied here forbids splitting: each demand must take a single path.

The authors prove that routing is still nearly possible. If the cut condition holds, every demand can take one path, as long as edge capacities may be exceeded by a bounded amount. The bound scales with the largest single demand. Such results guide network design where splitting a stream is not allowed. The paper belongs to combinatorial optimization and graph theory.
arxiv-2505-13735:
Polarimeters at a Brookhaven collider read proton spin from tiny sideways asymmetries, and reading them right demands exact corrections for electric forces. Andrei Poblaguev, writing alone in a 2025 paper, computes those Coulomb corrections numerically. The setting is forward elastic scattering of polarized protons on protons and on nuclei.

The corrections must span many nuclear charges and form factor shapes, and stay flexible while data are fitted. Poblaguev sidesteps a hard calculation with a fake photon mass by tying the non-flip correction to the spin-flip one. Everything then reduces to stable integrals with finite limits in the massless photon limit. An absorptive correction that drives the spin effects is also evaluated with care.
arxiv-2505-14335:
Mikael Chala, Luis Gil, and Zhe Ren push a standard early-universe calculation to unusual precision, in a 2025 paper. Phase transitions in the young universe, like the one tied to the Higgs field, are studied by shrinking the hot four-dimensional theory into a simpler three-dimensional one. That reduction's accuracy limits predictions, including for gravitational waves such transitions might have produced.

In a toy model resembling the Higgs sector of an extended standard model, the team computed transition parameters to cubic order in the small ratio. They layered one-loop corrections for higher-dimension terms, two-loop ones for basic terms, and three loops for the mass term. Bookkeeping covered running couplings and quantum effects from light fields. For strong transitions, the one-loop corrections from new operators rivaled the two-loop ones, while the three-loop thermal mass effects lagged behind.
arxiv-2505-14635:
Benjamin Prada and co-authors join two learning theories in one frame in a 2025 paper. Predictive coding is a brain-inspired rule where each layer learns from its own errors. Minimum description length instead scores a model by how briefly it can be written plus its mistakes.

The team proves layerwise predictive coding descends step by step on that two-part code. Each sweep provably shortens the total code, they show. A fresh risk bound follows, trading fit against code length in a clean ratio. Repeated sweeps settle at a stable point of the shared objective. Biology-flavored learning gains the guarantees of compression theory.
arxiv-2505-14735:
Maysam Rabbani and Elijah Gervais show that newborn birthweight in New York fell during the pandemic and has kept falling since, in a paper from 2025. Studies had disagreed on whether the pandemic years lightened babies at all. Hospital discharge records for the state give the question a large, uniform data set.

Birthweight dropped by about seven grams during the pandemic years. Afterward it did not rebound; it slid to about seventeen grams below the pre pandemic level. Mothers giving birth in the later years were also notably more likely to be flagged at higher risk of death and greater illness severity. Small average shifts in birthweight can echo through a generation's health, the authors note, and the causes of the continued slide need direct study.
arxiv-2505-14835:
Diego Ortiz Barbosa and co-authors outline a recovery system for autonomous drones under attack in a 2025 paper. A drone that detects an attack, such as spoofed signals or hijacked controls, needs a sound plan to save itself, not just an alarm. Their design adds common-sense reasoning on top of detection.

The system weighs what happened and picks a recovery action, such as holding position, landing, or returning home. The authors walk through drone use cases, then discuss how to run the design on small edge devices without opening new security holes. Fast, safe recovery could keep a compromised drone from harming people below.
arxiv-2505-14935:
Navid Hashemi, Lars Lindemann, and Jyotirmoy Deshmukh presented PCA-DDReach in two thousand twenty-five, a faster way to judge where a random system can go. Safety checks for cyber-physical systems often lack exact models, so teams learn from sample paths instead. Past data-driven tools gave safe bounds, but those bounds could be far too wide, above all when test data shifts.

Their method joins a statistics tool that gives proven bounds with principal component analysis, which trims the data to its main axes. That pairing cuts the extra width and scales to larger systems. Planners can check reach and safety with tighter, still honest, guarantees.
arxiv-2505-15335:
Jacob Lund, Jeff Murugan, and Jonathan Shock add spin to the classic billiard problem in a 2025 paper. Billiard models, a ball bouncing in shaped tables, are laboratories for chaos. Giving the ball spin couples its sliding and turning at each bounce.

Across famous tables, spin steadily damped chaos but never removed it in the physical range. In the stadium and Sinai tables, the chaos measure fell with spin while staying positive. Round and rectangular tables stayed orderly as before. A conserved quantity at each bounce explains the pattern, strongest where walls are long and flat. Spin carves islands of order into a chaotic sea.
arxiv-2505-15435:
Zeqing Wang, Shiyuan Zhang, Chengpei Tang, and Keze Wang build TimeCausality, a benchmark for causal reasoning over time in vision-language models, in work from twenty twenty-five. People read irreversible change, like fruit rotting or ageing, with ease. Such reading needs world knowledge, not just event order spotting. Whether vision models share that skill was largely untested. The new benchmark isolates temporal causality as its target skill.

Top open models match closed models on standard visual question tasks. On TimeCausality those open models lag closed rivals by a wide gap. Even the strongest closed model drops sharply on this benchmark. The gap flags temporal causality as a weak spot across the field. Future model training should fold in change-over-time reasoning. Open developers gain a clear target to close next.
arxiv-2505-15835:
Nayan Bhatia and Katia Obraczka repurposed chat-style transformer models to locate devices indoors in a 2025 paper. WiFi signals can pinpoint a phone inside a building for navigation and asset tracking, but fading, reflections, and interference corrupt the signal, and each hardware vendor reports telemetry in its own format. No single model handled all that variety well.

Their system, WiFiGPT, treats telemetry as a language the model can learn, capturing faint spatial patterns in noisy readings. In experiments it acted as a reliable regressor of position, matching leading specialized methods while accepting varied inputs. A unified model could spare each site the cost of hand-building its own locator for every device mix.
arxiv-2505-15935:
AI agents built on large language models now use tools and memory, but models weaken in languages other than English, and agents inherit that weakness. Users of other languages may face unreliable or unsafe agent behavior. The authors propose MAPS, a multilingual benchmark suite for agent performance and security. It translates four established benchmarks, covering real-world tasks, code generation, math reasoning, and agent security, into eleven languages.

The suite holds 805 unique tasks and 9,660 language-specific instances. Testing shows both performance and security degrade when agents leave English, with the drop varying by task and growing with the amount of translated input. The authors offer MAPS as the first standardized frame for judging multilingual agents and as a push toward agents that serve all users equitably and safely.
arxiv-2505-16035:
Alejandro García-Castellanos and co-authors introduced a new solver in 2025 for travel-time problems, such as timing waves through the earth. Their method joins two ideas: neural fields that respect symmetry, and neural solvers for a key equation that gives travel times. One shared network is steered by small codes that stand for each new case.

Because the codes sit in a space with clear geometry, moving a code moves the answer in a way that can be predicted. The method works on flat, round, and curved spaces alike. Tests on wave timing data in two and three dimensions, and on a sphere, beat older neural methods, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-16135:
Tests of machine reasoning often reward memorized patterns rather than fresh thought. The authors answer with Sudoku-Bench, a benchmark of hard and unusual Sudoku variants chosen to demand creative, multi-step logic. Each variant adds its own constraints, sometimes interacting in subtle ways, so a solver must find a novel break-in rather than recall a template. Yet all variants share one compact structure, which keeps scoring clean and consistent.

The benchmark ships with a curated puzzle set, a standard text format for puzzles, and tools that work with thousands of public puzzles. In baseline tests, the strongest current language models solve fewer than 15 percent of the puzzles unaided. The authors present that low score as headroom: progress on this benchmark would signal real gains in long-horizon, strategic reasoning. They offer the bench as an open research environment for that work.
arxiv-2505-16435:
Alexander Boeschoten and co-authors set the quantum limits for reading several light-shape parameters at once in a 2025 paper. Information can hide in the modes a beam is built from. Estimating many such parameters jointly is the task. Errors trade against each other in principle.

The team generalize mode-based estimation theory to the multi-parameter case. A general quantum Fisher matrix is derived, with the conditions for reaching its bound. Each parameter pairs with a detection mode shaped like a derivative of the field. Overlaps between those modes, real parts for correlation and imaginary for attainability, decide success. The criteria guide sensor design.
arxiv-2505-16635:
Zhaomin Wu, Ziyang Wang, and Bingsheng He build a benchmark for learning jointly across databases that sit in separate organizations, in a paper from 2025. Such silos block shared analysis in fields from health to retail. Joint learning methods promise training without pooling raw data, but past benchmarks assumed clean, aligned tables that real life rarely offers.

Their analysis of a large real corpus of public databases showed tables that link unevenly, mismatch, or cannot be joined at all. The new suite, WikiDBGraph, is built from that corpus to mirror the mess. It covers the full pipeline, including the joins and alignment steps that older benchmarks skip. The aim is to test methods against the data problems they will actually face in deployment.
arxiv-2505-16935:
Ayubirad, Akbar, and Ossareh hold gas-split cell push in bounds with a guard tool in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such cells split water for fuel gas cross a wide force range. Fast force swings can push cell push past safe build caps.

Inside, a lean cell build tracks push and flow acts for the guard. The guard trims force asks ere push can cross its set cap. Sim runs show push held in bounds through wild force swings. The guard beat plain smooth tricks on both push and yield. Gas yield rose while aux fuel use fell in the same runs.
arxiv-2505-17035:
Michael Drew and four co-authors estimated the spin of the black hole in galaxy M87 in twenty twenty-five from Event Horizon Telescope images. The famous ring image shows hot gas orbiting the hole. Measuring the inner disk edge's rotation speed from the image gives about fourteen percent of light speed, which converts to a spin parameter near point eight — probably a lower limit.

Polarization data reveal the magnetic field's direction in the disk, a proxy for how the spiraling gas actually moves. Splitting that motion into rotation and infall gives an accretion speed near seventy thousand kilometers per second. The implied feeding rate spans a wide range, and its power range matches the jet's power, consistent with jets powered by accretion itself.
arxiv-2505-17335:
Tahina Ramananandro, Gabriel Ebner, Guido Martínez, and Nikhil Swamy apply separation logic to secure parsing and serializing in a 2025 paper. Bugs in how low-level code reads data formats sit at the root of many security holes. Tools that are proved correct, and that emit C code, could cut that class of flaw at the source.

Their library, PulseParse, offers parser and serializer parts with proofs written in separation logic. The parts join like blocks, and even nested formats parse in constant stack space. The team then build the first formal version of CBOR, a binary data format, plus its schema and signing kin, all on the same base.
arxiv-2505-17435:
Hongyi Henry Jin and three co-authors found in 2025 a cleaner route to fair predictions across many overlapping groups. A predictor is multicalibrated when its stated odds hold true inside every group that matters. Old methods chop the output range into bins and patch values step by step, which adds rounding error and touchy settings.

Their method skips the chopping. It fits an ensemble of shallow decision trees by plain loss minimization, using off-the-shelf boosting tools. Under a stated fairness condition on the data, the method provably reaches multicalibration. Standard training pipelines stay intact.
arxiv-2505-17735:
AI agents built on large language models now handle real tasks, yet they can be steered into unsafe acts through tricky prompts and tools. Xueyang Zhou led a team that built AutoSafe, a system that makes agents safer without collecting dangerous real-world examples. It starts from a threat model that spells out how unsafe behavior grows out of user wording, context, and the agent's own steps.

From that model, the system invents risky scenes on its own, thinks through safe replies, and builds a large training set from them. Agents trained this way scored about forty-five percent higher on safety tests and did far better on real-world tasks too. The team released the project in public for others to build on.
arxiv-2505-17835: Marc Lalonde and Hamed Ghodrati test vision-language models on grading eczema in this 2025 report. Grading atopic dermatitis from patient photos is hard even for trained skin doctors. Automated deep learning has made headway, but the new multimodal models promise more explainable reads. Seven such models were set loose on a test image set to grade severity.
arxiv-2505-18335:
Jian Tang and seven co-authors review, in 2025 work, a quantum edge state in layered crystals that can be peeled and stacked. In that state, charge flows along a sheet's rim with spin locked to path, while the sheet's heart stays still. First seen in wells, the state found a rich new home in these peelable stacks.

Their bare faces let probes read the state in full, and stacking lets builders twist traits and borrow effects from next layers. Twisted stacks add flat bands and strong ties, which can flip the state to kin forms, some split into parts. Two lead sheet families are traced in depth. Uses run from wave-based power harvest to guarded quantum sums.
arxiv-2505-18435:
Mohammadreza Iranpour and Mohammad Rasoul Narimani solve power grid flow problems to true global optimality at larger scale, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The core problem, AC optimal power flow, is famously non-convex, so relaxed methods give good bounds but no guarantee. Pure global search is exact yet slow.

Their hybrid splits the ranges of voltage size and angle step by step. A quadratic convex relaxation bounds each subregion, and any region whose bound beats the best known answer is pruned. Benchmark grids showed fewer subproblems and better answers, above all on large cases. The code builds on an open Julia package.
arxiv-2505-18535:
Dmitry Dudukalov and co-authors analyze how stochastic gradient descent moves near critical points in a 2025 paper. The workhorse optimizer of machine learning wanders a landscape of valleys and passes, pushed by noisy gradients. When it settles, lingers, or escapes shapes what training finds.

One-dimensional landscapes are studied under both tame and wild noise. Descent reliably reaches its basin's floor unless it starts too near a peak. Near a blunt peak it can stick for a long time; near a sharp one it slips away, with calculable odds for each neighboring valley. Noise character and local geometry together script the dance.
arxiv-2505-18635:
Luke G Bennetts reviews how ocean waves travel through floating ice, and what they do to it on the way. Waves can run long distances under ice covers, loosening floes and flexing shelves. As polar regions warm, the meeting of waves and ice grows ever more important for climate science.

The chapter covers three settings: the marginal ice zone of broken floes, ice frozen fast to the shore, and floating ice shelves. It traces the field from its founding work in the 1970s and 1980s to the newest studies. For each cover it names the open questions that matter most. Shared threads across the three settings close the review, along with an outlook on a fast-changing cryosphere.
arxiv-2505-18735:
Guillaume Ballif, Laurent Pfeiffer, and Jakob Ruess gave in 2025 a general recipe for proving facts about stochastic chemical reaction networks without simulating every molecule. Such networks are modeled as Markov chains with huge state spaces. Their method groups states into blocks, then builds two simple one-dimensional processes that provably bracket the real one from below and above.

The brackets are easy to analyze and compute with. They answer whether a steady state exists and how much error comes from chopping the state space down to a solvable size. Formulas produce the tightest such brackets for any chosen grouping. The authors stress that choosing the grouping well decides how sharp the conclusions are, and they demonstrate on an example network.
arxiv-2505-18835:
Samiha Tariq models how mental biases warp money choices using a Bayesian game. The paper from twenty twenty-five notes that classic theory casts investors as fully rational. Real choices bend under loss aversion, overconfidence, and herd conduct. Tariq builds these bends into a game where investors split wealth between a risky asset and a safe one.

Each investor acts with partial knowledge of the others, as in a Bayesian setup. Solving for the Bayesian Nash equilibrium shows how each bias skews the best split. The skews add up to market-wide effects. Tariq links the results to Herbert Simon's idea of bounded rationality. Biases can breed waste, price bubbles, and crashes. The work urges policy that counts the mind's quirks to keep markets steadier.
arxiv-2505-18935:
Ronny Vallejos, Clemente Ferrer, and Jorge Mateu build a new gauge for how well two maps of the same trait agree across a grid of regions. Their case is poverty rates in Chile, where rival methods give rival maps for the same districts. Agreement tools for such grid data had a gap the authors aim to fill.

Their gauge builds on a family version of an older agreement measure, with weights that honor how regions sway each other. A spatial model of that sway, fit the Bayesian way, drives the math. Applied to two Chilean regions, the method yields poverty rates with high-confidence bands. The work should help judge social measures that live on maps.
arxiv-2505-19035: Ahmad Moussavi, Peter Danchev, Arash Javan, and Omid Hasanzadeh gave a new characterization of semi-tripotent rings in twenty twenty-five. These are rings tied to tripotent elements, those equal to their own cube. The authors describe the class in terms of sums and products of special elements. They also explore when a group ring is semi-tripotent. The results supplement a twenty nineteen study by Koşan and co-authors, and the entry stands as a focused contribution to ring theory.
arxiv-2505-19335:
Dora Zhao, Diyi Yang, and Michael Bernstein propose a knowledge ecosystem that lets ordinary users hand custom information to language models. Much of what people want models to know, from personal preferences to workplace policy and community advice, never appears in training data. Their system, Knoll, turns clipped web pages and shared documents into reusable modules.

Users build modules from web clippings or documents on Google Docs and GitHub, adopt modules others made, and let the system insert relevant knowledge during chats with models like ChatGPT and Claude. A public deployment drew over two hundred users doing everything from seeking advice to writing help. Evaluations confirmed that Knoll improved response quality for those tasks.
arxiv-2505-19435:
Zhihong Pan, Kai Zhang, Yuze Zhao, and Yupeng Han route hard questions to the right model and method in a 2025 paper. A model's skill and its reasoning style jointly set its scores. Long reasoning chains cost a lot and can trap models in overthinking. Their frame, Route-to-Reason, picks both per task.

The router learns compact codes for models and for strategies. It then matches them to task difficulty under a budget. The design is cheap, flexible, and plug-and-play in form. Tests span seven open models and four reasoning strategies. The router beat the best single model on accuracy. It also cut token use by more than 60 percent.
arxiv-2505-19535:
Juntong Wang and co-authors build a way to grade videos made by text-guided editing tools, in this 2025 paper. Such tools change a video to match a written request, like swapping a season or a style. Judging the results is hard: no standard test set or grader existed for editing quality. Human viewers remain the gold standard, but they are slow and costly to use at scale.

The team first built a large benchmark: thousands of edited videos from twelve models across eight kinds of edit. Human raters scored them on quality, fit to the request, and how well the scene's structure held up, giving over one hundred seventy thousand ratings. They then trained an automated grader on that data and used it to rank current editing models. The yardstick should help the field compare tools honestly.
arxiv-2505-19635:
Ivan Tyukin and co-authors settle a long fight over whether odd distance measures collapse or spread out in high dimensions. Their 2025 paper studies fractional quasi p-norms, where the exponent sits between zero and one. Distance collapse can break data tools, and past claims clashed.

For wide classes of data spreads, these distances do concentrate, with bounds that hold evenly across the whole exponent range. That kills hopes of tuning the exponent to dodge collapse for such data. Other families, though, still let the exponent steer the collapse rate. Near any well-behaved spread sit countless wild ones that refuse to concentrate. The authors say encodings can exploit that split, by design.
arxiv-2505-20135:
Wenyang Liao and co-authors tailor in 2025 data distillation for replay-based continual learning. Replay methods trust that a tiny stored subset can stand in for full past tasks. Small buffers and rough pick rules break that trust in practice.

Their learnable buffer distills global facts from new data plus old buffer content. A light module writes soft labels for buffer items instead of reworking the whole set. That design dodges heavy compute and overfit risk at once. Tests across data sets hold forgetting down against strong rivals. Soft labels alone carry the distilled global signal into the buffer.
arxiv-2505-20335:
Zishun Yu, Shangzhe Li, and Xinhua Zhang reframe language model shrinking in a 2025 paper. Big language models are costly to run, so builders distill them into smaller ones that copy the teacher's behavior. Most current methods amount to behavior cloning, a plain form of imitation learning. That view has already inspired variants that borrow from reinforcement learning.

Rather than add one more variant, the authors build a general frame around temporal difference learning, a method that updates value guesses from later guesses. Their key observation is that teachers place nearly all probability on a small set of likely next words. Working only on that reduced set makes the learning cheaper and more stable. They show how practical algorithms follow from the frame, with gains to match.
arxiv-2505-20535:
Uros Zivanovic and co-authors adapt the masked autoencoder to messy, unevenly timed data, in a 2025 paper. Transformers usually demand regular grids, so time-series work bolts on special parts that cost speed and simplicity. Their model, RoMAE, instead feeds continuous positions through rotary embeddings, a trick from language models, letting one plain design read irregular series, images, and audio alike.

On a hard astronomy challenge of uneven light curves, RoMAE beat specialized time-series designs. On images and audio it held the classic model's usual level. The team also probes a subtlety: learned embeddings added to the input break the rotary trick's relative-position property. One general learner, they argue, can travel across data kinds.
arxiv-2505-20735:
Jianfeng Yu and Yanyong Hong extend a family of algebraic operators in a 2025 paper. Novikov algebras arise in the study of certain differential equations and Hamiltonian structures. Operators on them, called O-operators, generate new algebra structures from old ones.

The authors define a broader version, the extended O-operator, acting between an algebra and a partner module. Such operators produce fresh Novikov structures on the module. They also introduce post-Novikov algebras and tie them to weighted O-operators. Writing the operators in tensor form leads to extended Novikov Yang-Baxter equations, and the paper maps how all these notions imply one another.
arxiv-2505-20935:
Sanghyun Jo and co-authors fix a common flaw in AI image generators in a 2025 paper. When a prompt asks for several objects, models often drop some, merge them, or mix their traits. The team traces the trouble to the earliest cleanup steps, before object borders settle. Their method, called ISAC, needs no retraining.

ISAC first steadies the layout that self-attention sketches, then ties word meanings inside each region. Across three test suites it beat other training-free fixes. It also sharpened rough boxes from layout tools into clean object masks. Readers get a plug-in upgrade for crowded image prompts.
arxiv-2505-21535:
Ren, Collins, Hu, and Yang propose in twenty twenty-five a way to make transformer AI models run well on memory-based chips. The attention step at the heart of transformers clashes with such chips, needing many cross-multiplications and far-flung memory access. That mismatch adds delay and data traffic on edge devices where these chips promise big energy savings.

Their framework swaps every attention block in a trained image model for a step-by-step module that suits the chip layout. Training by block-wise copying keeps the swap faithful to the original function. Extra pruning trims models to fit small chip arrays. Tests showed accuracy close to the original models, with fewer settings and lower delay.
arxiv-2505-21635:
Haoqian Liang and co-authors teach computers to grasp what an object is by watching things move, in a 2025 paper. Babies learn objects partly this way: parts that move together belong together. The team's framework copies that trick, using motion edges in videos to outline separate objects without any human labels.

Software first estimates motion in raw video and clusters it into rough masks for each object. Those masks then supervise a vision model trained by comparing views. The trained model is tested on depth guessing for single images and on finding objects in three dimensions. It beats both labeled and unlabeled rivals and handles new scenes well. The authors argue that motion-born object sense is a missing layer in today's vision models.
arxiv-2505-21935:
Kaiyu He and Zhiyu Chen present a 2025 survey of whether large language models can discover new knowledge, not just follow orders. Most work so far has sharpened instruction following and step by step deduction. Real discovery needs fresh hypotheses that can be tested and turned into rules.

The survey uses a classic three part frame for reasoning: guessing a cause, drawing out its consequences, and checking them against data. It sorts past work on forming, applying, and testing hypotheses with language models. The authors name the main wins and the open gaps. Their aim is a map for turning today's models into engines of discovery.
arxiv-2505-22235:
Amon Lahr and co-authors published this estimation study in 2025. Kernel regression is a flexible way to learn an unknown function from noisy data points. Users of such estimates need honest error bounds, especially before trusting them in safety-critical systems. The catch is that the noise may be correlated over time and only loosely bounded in total energy. The team derived a bound for this setting that is tight, meaning no valid bound can be smaller.

Their bound returns the worst-case function value still consistent with the data at any chosen input point. It takes a clean form: the mean and spread of a Gaussian process, once the noise level is chosen well. Computing it stays cheap. The authors checked the method against earlier results in the field. They show it stays sharp where older bounds grow loose, which makes it practical for judging estimation accuracy.
arxiv-2505-22335:
Wancai Zheng and five co-authors present UP-SLAM, a real-time mapping system for robots moving through scenes where things move too, in this 2025 arXiv paper. It builds the map from Gaussian splats and splits tracking from mapping so they run in parallel. A probabilistic octree manages the splats, adding and pruning them without hand-set thresholds.

A training-free estimator fuses several error signals to judge, pixel by pixel, what is likely moving, catching new object types without labels. A temporal encoder and borrowed image features enrich the map. Across hard test sets the system beat leading rivals on tracking accuracy and image quality, while keeping a clean, reusable map of the static world.
arxiv-2505-22935:
Jipeng Li and Yanning Shen ask whether graph diffusion models really need to be told the noise level. Conditioning on noise is standard practice, yet corrupted graphs may carry the clue themselves. The team builds theory around Bernoulli edge-flip corruption and extends it to coupled noise on structure and attributes. Tests ran on synthetic and real graphs with GDSS and DiGress models.

Unconditional models matched or beat their conditioned twins. They also used 4 to 6% fewer parameters and ran 8 to 10% faster. The authors argue that high-dimensional graph data often encodes enough noise information on its own, opening simpler designs.
arxiv-2505-23135:
Zhe Ye and co-authors introduce VERINA, a benchmark for code generation that must come with proofs of correctness. Language models now write much software code. Checking that code by hand is slow and costly.

Verifiable generation asks models for code plus specs plus proofs. Past benchmarks tested those pieces only in isolation. VERINA holds nearly two hundred hand-built tasks in Lean. Each task ships with tests and a formal specification. Models are scored on code, specs, proofs, and their fit together. Leading models struggle most with proof generation. The gap shows where research should push next. The benchmark aims to make verified coding measurable and fair to compare.
arxiv-2505-23335:
Zhihan Jin, Matthew Kwan, Lisa Sauermann, and Yiting Wang study a chance problem about polynomials of random signs in 2025. The question asks how much a polynomial can pile its values on one point.
