A known bound caps that pile-up near one over the root of the variable count, unless the polynomial sits near zero.

New results back a wider claim, that the bound can be beaten down unless the polynomial sits near one with special algebraic shape. Links to analytic number theory run through the proofs. An appendix with two more authors refutes an older guess on multilinear forms and gives a fixed form.
arxiv-2505-23635:
Daniel Luckhardt, Harsh Beohar, and Clemens Kupke built in 2025 a way to measure how alike two system states are when exact sameness is too strict. Their setting is Markov decision processes, systems that act with chance and rewards, read as coalgebras over analytic spaces, a wide class of measurable spaces. Past work on such spaces used plain sameness tests. The team instead defines a distance: states count as near when no short test can tell them far apart.

They build the distance through a frame from category theory, then craft a counting logic to match. A Hennessy-Milner style result then shows the distance from the frame equals the gap the logic sees. The work gives a firm math base for likeness in broad chance systems.
arxiv-2505-23735:
Ali Behrouz and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a memory module that learns to store context as it reads. Transformers rule sequence tasks but pay a quadratic cost on long inputs. Newer recurrent designs are cheaper yet falter on long-range recall. The team traces that failure to small memory, step-by-step updates that see only the last token, and rigid memory handling.

Their module, ATLAS, fixes all three. It tunes its memory on current and past tokens together, which breaks the online limit. A new model family grows out of it as a strict extension of the Transformer. Tests on language, reasoning, and recall favored ATLAS over both Transformers and recent rivals. On a ten-million-token benchmark, it lifted a sister model sharply.
arxiv-2505-23835:
Ye Cheng and co-authors present LACE in 2025, a system that lets users write Internet of Things access rules in plain language. Access control for smart devices must weigh time, place, behavior, and surroundings. Existing platforms offer coarse controls or rigid rule matching, and experts' words must be hand-translated into code by developers.

LACE uses large language models to turn intent into structured, enforceable rules. It adds retrieval support and formal validation to check meaning. In smart home tests, verified policy generation was fully correct. Decision accuracy reached up to eighty-eight percent, beating standard model baselines.
arxiv-2505-24135: Levi Lorenzo, writing alone, studies index pairings for algebras built from minimal actions on the Cantor set, in a math paper from 2025. The algebras are crossed products, and the pairings join K-homology with traces. Lorenzo uses orbit-breaking subalgebras from Putnam and their embeddings to show that any such pairing can be computed with trace formulas of Connes. For odometer systems, a classic case, he shows the algebras have uniformly finitely summable K-homology. The results make abstract pairings concrete for a central family of dynamical systems.
arxiv-2505-24235:
Muralidharan Kunnummal and three co-authors compare data-driven ways to model groundwater, in work from 2025. Cheaper computing and richer sensors have made statistical methods central to the field. Their study checks classic time-series models and modern neural networks side by side on the kind of data researchers usually have, and adds a copula-based route to spatial dependence between sites.

Forecast skill is judged not only on accuracy but also on model shelf-life, a check the authors say the field rarely makes. Longer-lived models cut compute cost while keeping forecasts sound. The framework aims to help researchers pick methods that stay valid, not just ones that fit the first dataset well.
arxiv-2505-24535:
Narmeen Oozeer and four co-authors present a 2025 method to steer several traits of a language model at once. Traits such as tone and stance can clash when steered one by one. Classic steering adds fixed vectors and needs tuning per trait, which scales poorly. Their method trains one classifier on the model's hidden states instead.

At use time, slopes from that classifier give a fresh steering direction for any trait mix. No stored vectors or retraining are needed. Two new test sets probe mixed-trait control in tone and debate text. Across three model families, the method beat strong rivals as judged by both probe classifiers and model judges.
arxiv-2506-00335:
Jingyang He, Shuai Wang, and Ang Li asked in 2025 whether an experiment's true effect can be recovered when the data are skewed by selection. Selection bias, the systematic inclusion or exclusion of certain samples, threatens causal inference. Earlier methods could recover unbiased distributions from biased data with partial outside information, but leaned heavily on observed data and a tricky adjustment.

The team instead works from test data, building what-if worlds openly with structural causal models. They trace how a selection rule in the seen world leaks into the what-if one. From that trace they derive tests, drawn and formal, for when the test result survives selection untouched. Readers get a full recoverability test: a principled answer to whether biased samples can still yield the truth.
arxiv-2506-01035:
Chen Lan, Zhen-Xiao Zhang, and Hao Yang build regular black holes, black holes without a singular point at the center, by starting from the curvature they want. Their paper came out in 2025. They prescribe smooth, finite curvature profiles and reconstruct the space-time geometry that produces them.

They try two starting measures of curvature and several profile shapes, including bell curves and rational functions. The resulting geometries stay regular, flatten far away, and respect standard energy conditions. They then test stability by studying quasinormal modes, the fading ring of a disturbed black hole. The shape of the barrier in the effective potential decides the outcome. Barriers with a high peak over a deep valley rang stably, while shallow ones could develop late-time instability.
arxiv-2506-01135:
Ziliang Zhang, Cong Liu, and Hyoseung Kim present TeleXR, an open system for steering robots through extended reality headsets, in a 2025 paper. The user moves, the robot copies, and 3D feedback returns. Delay between motion and feedback, driven by the network, inflates errors and task times in older systems.

TeleXR breaks the dependence on the network by rebuilding missing or late information from local sensor data on each side. Robot control and headset display then run alongside the network traffic instead of waiting on it. A smart scheduler eases graphics chip contention, and point cloud detail scales with available bandwidth. The authors release the full framework openly for other labs.
arxiv-2506-01835:
Het Patel and co-authors pinpoint where to poke a wing to tame stall in this 2025 paper. When a pitching wing stalls, lift drops hard and fast. The team models the swirling flow as a network of vortex points and tracks how nudges spread through it.

Their broadcast analysis names the vortex spots, timing, and direction with the most leverage. The best moment falls just after flow splits, as the stall vortex forms. Shear layer spots beat all others for control. Flow tests with well-placed jets cut peak lift drops by wide margins in both flat and shaped wing cases.
arxiv-2506-02135:
Alexander Chudik, Hashem Pesaran, and Ron Smith propose, in a 2025 paper, a method to find long run relations in panel data when there are more units than time points. Panel data tracks many units over time. Past methods for long run links assumed the opposite shape, with long histories for few units, leaving wide, short panels unserved.

Their procedure first filters out short run wiggles. It uses averages over sub samples, set against the full sample average, as the working data. The number of long run relations and their weights then come from the eigen structure of a pooled covariance matrix. They prove the estimator settles on the truth as both dimensions grow. Computer trials show it counts relations precisely and behaves well in size and power. Bank ratio data illustrate the method in practice.
arxiv-2506-02235:
Muhammad Yarahmadi and Amin Salehi test a dark energy model with a neural network method, in a 2025 paper. Dark energy drives the universe's speeding expansion, and one puzzle is that two trusted ways of measuring the expansion rate disagree, the Hubble tension. The model studied builds dark energy from holographic ideas with modified entropy, and it includes neutrino mass. Data came from the microwave background, galaxy spacing patterns, cosmic clocks, and supernova records.

The team fit the model twice: with the standard sampling method and with a Bayesian physics-informed neural network. The network gave sharper estimates for several parameters and a tighter cap on neutrino mass. Both fits landed between the two clashing expansion values, easing the tension in this model.
arxiv-2506-02335:
Alvaro Herráez and co-authors review a bridge between black holes and towers of light states, in a 2025 overview. Gravity's effective theories break down near field-space edges, where endless towers of light states emerge. In string theory those towers come from wrapped dimensions or string modes. A past bridge linked black holes to strings; the new one links black holes to towers, ruled by a quantum gravity cutoff called the species scale.

Heat rules for the switch then cage the spectrum tightly, matching string forecasts. The authors gather recent steps and spell out what the frame, named Species Thermodynamics, says about black hole entropy.
arxiv-2506-02435:
Zhen Zhang and co-authors teach a transformer network to set ad sale rules that stay firm and fair. Sale rules for web ads must grant each slot whole, not in shares, and must hide who bid what. Past network-built rules gave share grants, which leave no workable end in most real cases. Their 2025 network, JTransNet, builds the grant step in firm units from the start.

A proof shows the share flaw is not a rare edge but the norm when all slots must go. The firm step of the network can also be grafted onto past rule networks with small change. Tests on stored and live data show the network beats the set baselines on house revenue. Fair grants and top revenue, the team says, can ride one network.
arxiv-2506-02635:
Five authors led by Jannis Halbey present a 2025 paper on faster methods for convex problems. Their base method is the Frank-Wolfe approach, which moves toward a best point by steps that stay inside a feasible set. Plain steps can be slow, so the team adds repair steps that fix the path as it goes. The work joins and extends three older methods of this kind into one frame.

The authors prove tight bounds on how fast the new method closes in on an answer. They also give two cheap repair steps for problems with a squared-cost form, each shown to end in finite time. Two older methods can borrow these repairs to speed up their own sub-tasks. Tests on a range of problem types show large gains in run time.
arxiv-2506-02735:
Min Fu, Lipeng Zhu, and Rui Zhang propose a new antenna design for future wireless networks in a 2025 paper. Movable antennas can shift position to catch better signals, a trick eyed for 6G systems. Their design spreads movable subarrays over a very large area at a base station.

Wide spacing strengthens near-field effects and lets many users share the air at once. The authors build a channel model that captures how signal strength and sight lines change with position. They then derive a formula for the data rate the system can reach and tune the layout. The work guides how such large, flexible stations might be built.
arxiv-2506-03035:
Pierre Lepagnol and four co-authors improve spoken language understanding in twenty twenty-five. Voice assistants must grasp user intent reliably to book, play, or answer. State-of-the-art systems hunger for training data, but annotated examples are scarce for many tasks and languages. Instruction-tuned language models do well few-shot, if the prompt is right.

The authors use information retrieval to choose the prompt's examples. Retrieved examples are matched to the incoming query rather than picked blindly. That builds an enhanced prompt for the understanding task. Several spoken language benchmarks were used to test the method. Readers in conversational AI get a retrieval trick that spends a small labeled pool where it helps most, instead of fine-tuning on data they do not have.
arxiv-2506-03135:
Mengdi Jia and co-authors introduce OmniSpatial, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in vision-language models, in this 2025 paper. Models have largely mastered simple relations such as left versus right, but deeper spatial thought remains weak. The new test, grounded in cognitive psychology, spans four areas: motion-based reasoning, complex spatial logic, interaction, and taking another viewpoint.

The team hand-built more than eight thousand question-answer pairs across fifty subcategories. Both open and commercial models showed clear limits on the harder items. Two add-on strategies, one feeding scene graph cues and one reasoning through novel views, helped somewhat. The authors offer the set as a harder yardstick for the field.
arxiv-2506-03335:
Dheeraj Khanna and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on tracking players in team sports video. Players sprint, swerve, and hide behind each other, so trackers lose identities and paths bend sharply. Appearance cues mislead too, since teammates wear the same kit.

Their system, SportMamba, leans on motion first. A mamba-attention block models the curved, non-linear runs directly inside the sequence model. A height-adaptive matching rule forgives the size changes that come with depth and partial hiding, cutting identity switches. Wider search buffers catch fast breaks before the player leaves the expected zone. On the SportsMOT benchmark, full of hard motion and heavy occlusion, the method set the best scores. The design is offered for analytics and broadcast alike.
arxiv-2506-03535:
Qiming Zhu and co-authors study retrieval-augmented code generation across programming languages in a 2025 paper. Most such research stays inside a single language. Real teams migrate and reuse code across languages constantly. Cross-lingual transfer had never been mapped systematically.

A new data set covers thirteen languages with nearly fourteen thousand instances. Experiments probed how knowledge moves between language pairs. Transfer proved non-trivial even with direct injection of examples. Success depended on how close the languages are linguistically. Diversity of the model's training corpus also mattered. Code-specific retrievers relied little on natural language inside code. Comments and identifiers mattered less than expected there. The authors distill guidance for multilingual system design. Language pairing and corpus mix become planning variables. The data set is released with the paper.
arxiv-2506-04235:
Xinyan Zhao and co-authors introduce a benchmark for designing antibodies that bind their targets more tightly, in a 2025 paper. Antibodies are tuned and redesigned in the lab, but past benchmarks judge a design alone, by likeness to natural sequences or by shape error. The authors argue the real unit is the antibody joined with its target.

Their benchmark gathers more than one hundred and eighty thousand lab measurements of antibody mutants, across fourteen antibodies and nine targets that include flu, a cancer marker, and the COVID virus. Fifteen protein models are compared on how well their scores track lab binding strength. Models that fold a structure back into a sequence did best, both at ranking and at generating new variants. A flu antibody redesigned with the top models gained binding in lab tests. The authors offer a unified, biology-based frame for future design models.
arxiv-2506-04335:
Yugo Onishi, Nisarga Paul, and Liang Fu show that a gravity-like field can arise inside quantum materials, in a physics paper from 2025. The materials have patterns of spin, the tiny magnetic sense of electrons, that vary slowly across space. Electrons moving through such a pattern feel its twist as they travel.

When the link between a moving electron and the spin pattern is strong, the electron acts like a particle with no spin moving in curved space. The curve comes from quantum corrections to how its spin follows the pattern. That curved space bends electron paths, much as real gravity bends light near a star. The effect can appear even with no magnetic field present. The authors say such gravity-like effects may be common in quantum systems.
arxiv-2506-04535:
Erziev proposes a benchmark of questions that have no reasonable answer, in a 2025 paper. The title asks whether a language model will try to find the largest prime number, a task with no valid end point. Testing models on impossible questions sounds like a joke, the author argues, but it exposes a real weakness.

Models often answer such questions as if they were solvable instead of refusing or flagging the flaw. The benchmark, BSBench, lets researchers score that behavior in a repeatable way. The author also gives a method to convert existing datasets into impossible versions. Current models score far from perfect on these tests. Code and data are released for others to use.
arxiv-2506-04635:
Thai-Binh Nguyen and co-authors automate data gathering for speech recognition that uses both sound and lip movement in a 2025 paper. Lip cues make recognizers sturdy in noise, but training sets are scarce beyond English. Hand building such sets is slow and costly.

Their pipeline pulls audio-visual sets straight from raw video, refining past methods for speed and ease. A first model for Vietnamese trained on the auto-built set matched strong audio-only systems on clean sound. In cocktail-party noise it beat them by a wide margin. The route could carry lip-reading aids to many under-served tongues.
arxiv-2506-04735:
Saurabh Pandey, Hector Mas, Georgios Vasilakis, and Wolf von Klitzing shape matter waves of ultra-cold atoms inside a ring-shaped guide. Their 2025 letter introduces atom-optics tools for these waves, which already power sensors of gravity, rotation, and magnetic fields with extreme precision. Working in a ring lets the waves circulate in a tiny device.

The team collimate and focus waves from both a quantum condensate and a thermal cloud inside the ring. A delta-kick technique, a brief lensing pulse, cut the condensate's expansion energy many times over. The ring's radius is under half a millimeter, where rival setups need zero gravity or ten-meter chambers. Compact control of this kind moves quantum sensors toward field use.
arxiv-2506-04835:
Julien El Hajj, Gilles Ledoux, and Samy Merabia model how gold-core, silica-shell nanoparticles heat water under laser pulses, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such particles are prized for heat-based medical treatments, imaging, and sensing. Their heating depends on a chain of energy handoffs at tiny scales.

The team combined light-scattering theory with a two-temperature model and atom-level simulations. They varied shell type, dense or half-porous, and pulse lengths from femtoseconds to a nanosecond. A thin dense shell made the particles heat surrounding water much faster than bare gold. The boost came from stronger electron-vibration coupling at the gold-silica boundary and easy heat flow from silica to water. The findings guide particle design for heat therapies.
arxiv-2506-04935:
Pengxin Bian and five co-authors pose a tougher version of a classic data mining problem in a twenty twenty-five paper. The classic task finds substrings that occur often in a long string. Real data, though, gets edited, and a pattern that breaks under a few letter swaps may be of little use.

Their resilient version asks for substrings that stay frequent even if any k letters in the string are swapped out. They give an exact algorithm that runs fast and uses modest memory. On large real data sets, resilient patterns proved more useful for genome work than plain frequent ones, and the method beat a baseline by a wide margin.
arxiv-2506-05035:
Hyeongwon Jang, Changhun Kim, and Eunho Yang published this study in 2025. It works on explaining time series models, showing which moments in a series drove a forecast. Common tools report how much each point matters, but not whether it pushed the score up or down. The team shows that standard gradient methods do capture both kinds of points. The grading metrics, though, cancel the two kinds out, hiding that skill.

They propose two new metrics that score positive and negative points apart. Then they build TIMING, a method that makes the gradient path respect time order, so it avoids unreal mixed-up samples. On synthetic and real data sets, TIMING beat the other explanation tools. The code is public.
arxiv-2506-05535:
Waqar Ahmed and Emre Mengi give a way to guess the far edge of a near spectrum for large matrix problems. Exact tools work for small cases but stall at large scale, where best tools settle for local answers. Their guess uses how values shift under small nudges.

For tiny nudges the guess is sharp, with a tight error bound in the plain case. For big nudges they seed local tools with the guess and add fixed point steps. In most tests the chain lands on the true far edge. The work aids stability checks in big systems.
arxiv-2506-05635:
Christine de Kock and co-authors test whether language models can crack the coded slang of extremist communities in a 2025 paper. Extremist groups build cryptolects, in-group languages designed to shut out or mislead outsiders. The team evaluated eight models on six detection and decoding tasks across two extremist platforms.

General-purpose models could not reliably spot or interpret the coded language. Domain adaptation and specialized prompting improved matters significantly. The authors release new data sets for the problem, including over nineteen million posts from extremist platforms and expert-checked lexicons. Their findings carry a double message for moderation technology: out-of-the-box models are not enough, but targeted tuning makes automated help realistic.
arxiv-2506-05735:
A team of co-authors wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five asking whether language models really forget what they are told to unlearn. Unlearning aims to strip memorized facts from a model. Most checks test single facts in isolation, but knowledge in a model is tangled: related facts can let a removed fact be inferred again.

Their framework maps the facts around a target as a knowledge graph with confidence scores. Strong language models then act as judges, reasoning over that map to decide whether the fact is truly gone. The judges were calibrated against human ratings. The method exposes false claims of forgetting.
arxiv-2506-05835:
Rewriting simplifies expressions by applying rules step by step. Narrowing goes further: it turns rewriting into a search for values that make an equation true. Both tools were built for simple first-order terms, and both run into trouble in languages with binders, where names and scopes matter. Mauricio Ayala-Rincón, Maribel Fernández, Daniele Nantes-Sobrinho, and Daniella Santaguida extend the machinery in 2025 to exactly that setting, using nominal techniques.

They give the first definitions of nominal rewriting and narrowing that work modulo an equational theory, such as commutativity, with name equivalence handled the right way. A property they call E-coherence pins down when normal forms behave as they should. Their E-Lifting theorem then guarantees that plain rewriting steps and narrowing steps match, which a correct unification method needs in order to be trusted. Commutativity is the running example.
arxiv-2506-06135:
Awn Alqahtani, Jason Gaddis, and Xingting Wang prove results in a 2025 algebra paper on Hopf actions on Poisson algebras. A Hopf action is a structured way for a symmetry object to act on an algebra. The authors ask when such actions are forced to be simple in a setting called quantum rigidity.

For several key algebras, they show that any well behaved finite Hopf action must pass through a group algebra. Their proofs lift the actions to related Rees algebras, where known results for quantum algebras apply. The paper also treats group actions on related enveloping algebras and sorts some low dimensional cases.
arxiv-2506-06235:
Akram Zaytar and co-authors speed up how satellite images reach graphics chips for deep learning, in a paper from 2025. Training on Earth data at petabyte scale means the data live in cloud storage, far from the chips. Standard loaders starve the chips while files crawl in. The team measured loading from cloud stores and from local disks alike.

They tuned tile-aligned reads and pools of worker threads. A smart search method found the best settings for each kind of storage. Tuned loading ran twenty times faster from the cloud and four times faster locally. Models trained on streamed data matched the accuracy of local training in the same time. Chip use rose from near idle to near full. The code is shared in public for other teams.
arxiv-2506-06535:
Vineet Bhat and co-authors present in 2025 a robot grasping system that takes orders in plain words. Telling a robot which unseen object to pick up, and how, is a hard mix of language and sight. Their system, MapleGrasp, first marks the target object in the image, then pools features inside that mask to plan the grip.

Mask pooling lifted scores by seven percent on a standard test set. The team also released a new data set eight times larger than prior ones, where their method reached eighty-nine percent grasp accuracy. On a real robot arm it gripped unseen objects in seventy-three percent of tries, eleven points clear of rivals.
arxiv-2506-06635:
Ayan Roy, Jeetkumar Patel, Rik Chakraborti, and Shudip Datta proposed TrustConnect in 2025 to spot false data inside a car network. Modern cars have many parts that talk to each other and to the outside world. A false reading can spread from part to part and cause real harm if it is not caught.

TrustConnect rates how much each part can be trusted, based on how the parts are linked. It also weighs how values from linked parts agree and how open each part is to attack from outside. Tests used computer models of car networks in many layouts. The scores aim to flag parts that look wrong before the fault spreads.
arxiv-2506-07035:
Zixuan Jiang and Renjing Xu tackle a hard problem in a 2025 paper: teaching a computer model to say what a protein does. Protein language models learn from the chain of amino acids, yet the labels for function are vast in number and very unevenly spread. Some functions have many examples, and most have few, so models learn the common ones and miss the rest.

Their method, AnnoDPO, borrows a training trick from language model tuning. Instead of only showing the model right answers, it trains on preferences between better and worse labels, a method called direct preference optimization. The frame also joins more than one kind of input. The goal is to fight both label scarcity and imbalance at once, and to set a new pattern for folding biological knowledge into protein models.
arxiv-2506-07135:
José Manuel Suárez, Luís Mariano Bibbó, Joaquín Bogado, and Alejandro Fernandez study how to fix quantum code when the Qiskit library changes, in a 2025 paper. Qiskit updates often break working programs, and quantum code has quirks that set it apart from normal software. The team set out to sort the kinds of fixes that moving between Qiskit versions can demand.

Expert coders built one list of fix types from Qiskit docs and release notes, and a large language model built a second list. The team then compared the two lists and merged them into one shared scheme. That scheme gives later work a clear base for judging tools that fix quantum code on their own.
arxiv-2506-07835:
Two fluids that partly mix and partly separate, like oil and water with motion, can be modeled by coupling Navier-Stokes flow to a Cahn-Hilliard phase equation. Danica Basarić and Andrea Giorgini study that system for a compressible binary mixture. Their twist is the physically realistic Flory-Huggins entropy, a logarithmic potential, where earlier work settled for smoother polynomial stand-ins.

Their main result proves that global weak solutions exist in three-dimensional bounded domains for arbitrarily large starting data. The hard part is new estimates for the chemical potential and the entropy in a density-dependent equation, under weak assumptions on the density. They also show the phase variable stays inside its physical range wherever the density is positive. The result puts phase-separating compressible flow theory on a more realistic footing.
arxiv-2506-07935:
Pavel Naumov and Jia Tao study diffusion of responsibility in collective decision making. The phrase covers cases where many agents share blame for an outcome and individual accountability blurs. The authors ask which decision mechanisms can avoid that diffusion while still counting as collective.

With two agents, the only diffusion free mechanism is dictatorship, where one agent decides alone. With more agents, any diffusion free mechanism is an elected dictatorship, where agents elect one member to decide alone. The proofs define a bisimulation between mechanisms, show it preserves responsibility traits, and reduce each case to a smallest equivalent mechanism. The results give a sharp limit on shared decision design.
arxiv-2506-08135:
Hermano Velten, Felipe S Escórcio, and Nadson J S Trindade published a paper in 2025 on stars made of dark matter that do not press equally in all directions. Most models of cosmic objects assume a perfect balance of forces in a sphere. Real objects, and possibly dark ones built from light particles called axions, may lean more to one side.

The authors study still, uneven boson stars tied to gravity in a nonstandard way. They derive a general equation for their structure and map how much unevenness such stars can bear before no balance is possible. In the quantum-led case, unevenness and gravity swap the roles they play in classical stars. The result is a new family of balanced objects to look for.
arxiv-2506-08535:
Ronald Katende published this mathematics paper in 2025. It introduces a new way to compress a large matrix into a simpler low-rank form. The method, called D-decomposition, writes a matrix as the product of three smaller ones, with a square matrix in the middle. Unlike classic factorizations, it is not computed by a fixed algebraic recipe. Instead it is defined by an optimization problem that balances accuracy against rank, sparsity, and numerical stability.

Katende proves the solution exists and resists small perturbations, and gives the cost of each update step. He then benchmarks the method against three standard rivals, including truncated singular value decomposition. Test data covered movie ratings, handwritten digits, faces, and gene expression. The new decomposition reconstructed the originals more accurately, especially when data were sparse or noisy. The author presents it as a flexible alternative when stability under messy conditions matters.
arxiv-2506-08635:
Siddhant Ranade and co-authors rebuild 3D surfaces from point clouds with a multi-scale attention scheme, in a 2025 paper. Learning methods split into camps: small per-object models with fine detail but slow retraining, and big general models that handle new shapes but blur detail and crawl. SurfR aims at the missing corner, fast and faithful.

Its implicit representation answers inside-or-outside questions for query points, but lazily: early features ignore the query point entirely, saving work. A parallel grid holds features at several scales, coping with noise and varied sampling density, and attention across scales sharpens the reconstruction. The authors report the best speed-accuracy trade-off among baselines, at only a slight quality cost against the slowest champions.
arxiv-2506-08835:
Shravan Nayak and co-authors introduce CulturalFrames in 2025, a benchmark for testing whether text-to-image models respect cultural expectations. The study covers 10 countries and five social and cultural domains. It asks whether models meet both cues stated plainly in a prompt and cues that are only implied by the cultural setting.

The benchmark holds 983 prompts, 3,637 images from four leading models, and more than ten thousand human ratings. Raters found that models missed cultural expectations about 44 percent of the time, and stated cues were missed even more often. Standard scoring tools also matched human judgment poorly. The work gives builders a concrete test and clear directions for fairer image models.
arxiv-2506-08935:
Andrew Shin wrote a solo paper in two thousand twenty-five asking whether a gamer's computer can train a serious math model. Large language models reason well about math, but training them usually takes costly clusters of high-end hardware. Cheaper routes still lean on big machines, which shuts out most independent researchers.

Shin trained a model with one and a half billion parameters on a single gaming graphics card with sixteen gigabytes of memory. He combined reinforcement learning with memory-saving tricks. The small model matched or beat models several times its size on math reasoning tests. He argues the result widens access to high-level AI research.
arxiv-2506-09135:
Mathew Arun, Prachiti Athalye, and Basabendu Barman lighten a dark matter idea in twenty twenty-five. Planckian interacting dark matter touches the visible world only through gravity. In its classic form it demands very heavy candidates and extreme reheating temperatures. The authors realize it instead in warped five-dimensional space.

Their setup stacks three branes: ultraviolet, dark, and infrared. The dark matter is a composite light state on the dark brane. Its mass can range from MeV scale up to TeV scale, far below the classic range. It interacts with the massless graviton and its massive Kaluza-Klein partners, with suppressed couplings. Light standard model matter sits near the ultraviolet brane, heavy matter near the infrared. Readers get gravity-only dark matter at accessible masses.
arxiv-2506-09235:
Kengle and ten co-authors report evidence for a rare state of matter in a semiconductor, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The material, a lanthanum cadmium arsenide compound, may host an excitonic insulator, a phase where electron-hole pairs condense on their own.

At about two hundred seventy-eight kelvin, the material switched into a highly insulating state with no matching change in its crystal structure. Electrical measurements showed flat, sheet-like transport and charge fluctuations that point to an electronic cause, while standard calculations could not reproduce the insulating behavior. The team argues a gap opened by exciton effects, making this crystal a rare bulk example of the long-sought phase, which could teach physicists how such states form.
arxiv-2506-09335:
Moshi Wei and Sparks Li propose a decentralized network for human and AI agents in a 2025 paper. Their system, ISEK, treats people and software agents as peers who publish tasks, find each other, do work, settle payment, and rate outcomes in a six-step cycle. A native token handles micropayments and voting, while NFT records hold agent identity.

The design aims to resist censorship and adapt on its own through distributed consensus. A layered reputation score tracks trust across many dimensions. Readers get a blueprint for a self-organizing knowledge economy, offered as a shift away from central platforms.
arxiv-2506-09435:
Jens Visbech, Anders Melander, and Allan Peter Engsig-Karup present a spectral element solver for water waves in this 2025 paper. The tool simulates linear and fully nonlinear waves and their hits on offshore structures. It is built inside an open-source finite element framework with built-in parallel computing.

High-order elements cut the smearing and speed errors that plague wave models. Tests check convergence as meshes and polynomial orders refine, plus scaling across many processors. The solver is validated against exact solutions and lab data, including wave making and waves striking a cylinder and a breakwater. Flexible meshes handle complex shapes. The authors offer the model as a general-purpose tool for offshore engineering.
arxiv-2506-09935:
Jiangyong Huang and co-authors present a model that understands three-dimensional rooms from words and images, in this 2025 paper. The head titles the model LEO-VL and calls it an efficient route to scalable 3D vision-language learning. Such models still reason poorly about space, held back by heavy scene codes, thin training data, and shaky robustness.

Their fix starts with a condensed feature grid, a scene code that uses far fewer tokens while keeping detail. On top of it they trained LEO-VL on over 700,000 examples across four indoor settings and five tasks, from captioning to dialogue. A post-training step, SceneDPO, sharpens answers by contrasting scenes as well as replies. The model topped standard 3D benchmarks. Tests showed data quality and task variety mattered more than raw scale, a useful lesson for the field.
arxiv-2506-10435:
Planet nurseries seem to hold too little dust to build the planets we see, a puzzle called the mass budget problem. Daniel Godines and six co-authors argue in 2025 that the dust is there but hides, because clumps of it glow less than telescopes assume.

The team simulated the streaming instability, where dust drifts and piles into dense filaments that can seed planetesimals. Light from those filaments, they computed, is partly opaque at millimeter wavelengths rather than fully thin. When the simulated glow was read the usual thin way, the mass came out two to seven times too low. The bias appears even when only a small share of the disk is thick, which could close much of the missing-mass gap.
arxiv-2506-10535:
Jan Zimmermann and co-authors test a radio-assisted emergency brake in a 2025 paper. Automatic braking saves lives, but its cameras and radar cannot see through obstacles. Vehicle-to-everything radio lets a hidden car announce itself early. The team studied a two-stage brake: a gentle partial brake fired by radio warning, then a full stop fired by onboard sensors if needed.

They replayed real crashes from the German in-depth accident database inside a simulation framework. The radio-enhanced system avoided far more of the crashes than sensor-only braking, and also beat a radio-only partial brake. For the crashes still not avoided, the team catalogs the causes case by case. The authors argue the layered design is a practical path to cutting collisions at blind junctions.
arxiv-2506-10735:
Carolina Agurto-Gangas and a large team weigh dust and gas in ten aging planet-forming disks in Upper Scorpius. The AGE-PRO survey tracks how disks evolve, and this installment targets the older Scorpius population with ALMA. Dust glow, carbon monoxide lines, and a nitrogen tracer sized up each disk. Radii matched the younger Lupus region for both gas and dust.

Solid mass, though, ran ten times lower than in Lupus and Ophiuchus, and the dust spectrum showed grains already evolving. Radial drift, trapping, and growth into bigger bodies fit the pattern. Gas and dust brightness still tracked each other, with more scatter than in young disks.
arxiv-2506-10835:
Francisco Montoya and Santiago Sánchez Acevedo present a new way to change coordinates in power systems that are out of balance, in a 2025 paper. Such changes shrink the math needed in power system studies, machine models, and the control of power converters. Older methods can falter when voltages or currents are uneven across phases. The pair base their method on geometric algebra.

Their method finds the flat plane that holds the path of an uneven signal, using a tool from that algebra. It works for any degree of unbalance in systems with many phases, and needs only two readings taken at different times. Lab tests and real-time computer tests backed the method. In converter control it removed wobbles that the standard Clarke method leaves behind under unbalance.
arxiv-2506-11035:
Moussa Koulako Bala Doumbouya, Dan Jurafsky, and Christopher Manning present a 2025 computing paper that rebuilds neural networks on a psychology theory of similarity. Standard networks judge likeness by distance, which is symmetric. Human judgments are not: people rate some pairs as more alike in one direction than the other.

Amos Tversky's 1977 theory treats objects as sets of features and weighs shared and distinct features separately. The authors make that idea differentiable so it can train by gradient descent. Their Tversky projection layer can express bent functions, like XOR, that a plain linear layer cannot. Swapping the layer into image and language models improved both, including a large accuracy jump on a bird photo task. The work gives deep learning a more human notion of likeness.
arxiv-2506-11335: Levi Cai and co-authors ask whether fish change their behavior when underwater vehicles come near, and whether that response skews what the vehicles record, in a 2025 paper. The team offers a framework, in theory and in practice, for estimating animal behavior without that bias. Early field results from coral reef settings test the approach. The work matters because counts and behavior notes gathered by vehicles feed wider claims about reef life, and a vehicle that startles its subjects quietly distorts both.
arxiv-2506-11735:
Johannes Lohmann and Georg Gottwald tackle a forecasting problem: how to sense that a complex system is near a sudden shift. Before such a tipping point, a system recovers from knocks more and more slowly, a warning sign called critical slowing down. In systems with many parts, though, a measure picked at random may show no warning, or even the opposite trend. The warning only shows in the right measure.

The authors show how to build that measure from the system's own dynamics. A data-driven method, the diffusion map algorithm, estimates a key function of the backward Fokker-Planck operator, the first one beyond the trivial case. Watching how values along that function wobble concentrates the warning signal where it belongs, cutting both false alarms and missed warnings.
arxiv-2506-11835:
Yunus Emre Kunt describes a smart watering system for farms and greenhouses that uses sensors and a learning model. Plain watering can waste water and cut yields. His 2025 work updates drip watering, a frugal method in use since the 1970s, with linked devices and software.

A small test rig of three rows by three columns sends soil and air data to a computer. A model that learns from past readings predicts what the plants need. Users can run the valves by hand through a phone app or let the system act on its own. The parts include rain and soil sensors, relays, and valves. The aim is to save labor as well, so staff can focus on other farm tasks.
arxiv-2506-11935:
Matt Jarvis and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on finding hydrogen in distant galaxies. Atomic hydrogen is the raw gas from which stars form. Its radio line is faint, so direct detections rarely reach beyond the nearby universe. The team uses the MeerKAT telescope's MIGHTEE survey. Instead of blind searching, they aim at galaxies already known from optical light. Positions and redshifts from emission-line catalogs tell them where to listen. Eleven detections clear the bar at redshifts past 0.25.

Each detection measures a galaxy's cold gas tank directly. Radio astronomers get proof that targeted stacking-free searches can reach this depth. Gas censuses at earlier cosmic times anchor stories of how star formation rose and fell. Blind surveys waste hours on empty sky; the targeted trick spends them where galaxies are known to sit. The eleven finds are a first harvest, with method value beyond the count.
arxiv-2506-12035:
Chaoyi Jiang and co-authors introduce a faster way to generate images in a 2025 paper. Their starting point is a model family that builds images token by token while looking both ways across the picture. The cost is high, since each step recomputes work for every token.

The new method, called MARCHE with an accent in the original name, reuses past work for tokens that barely change. It splits tokens into active and cached groups, each handled on its own path. A selective refresh step updates cached tokens when context shifts enough to matter. The method needs no new training. It speeds up generation while keeping the full context in view.
arxiv-2506-12535: Susovan Pramanik studies an inverse problem for the logarithmic Laplacian in this 2025 mathematics paper. That operator is a near relative of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a curved surface. The setting is a closed Riemannian manifold, a smooth space with no edge. The Calderón problem asks whether boundary data can reveal the hidden shape inside. Pramanik shows the data do recover the shape, up to the standard gauge freedom such problems allow. The result extends inverse problem theory to a fractional style operator of order just above two.
arxiv-2506-12635:
Alexander Grigoriev and co-authors give in 2025 a method that lists all potential maximal cliques in a class of planar graphs with steady delay. Such cliques feed width methods that solve hard graph problems fast when width is small. A fresh description of the cliques in this graph class drives the method.

Each new clique comes after a gap that grows only as a polynomial in graph size. Paired with known dynamic programming tools, the lister yields a width method for all planar graphs. Its run time scales in a straight line with the clique count. The work tightens the toolkit for planar graph algorithms.
arxiv-2506-13135:
Qi Zhang and Yubin Lu study irreversibility in random jump processes in a 2025 math paper. Many real systems drift smoothly yet also jump without warning, from markets to cell signals. The rate at which such a system produces entropy measures how strongly it breaks time symmetry: run the film backward, and a high rate means the reverse looks plainly wrong.

The authors first define the entropy production rate for general jump diffusions and set out its thermodynamic ties. For steady systems, they derive the rate from the gap between forward and reversed path odds, using a classic change-of-measure tool. They then prove that four traits amount to the same thing: time reversibility, zero entropy production, a detailed balance rule, and a gradient form. The clean equivalence anchors later work.
arxiv-2506-13535:
Two physicists in France enter a debate about how to define the center of a twisting light pulse, in a 2025 paper. The pulses, called spatiotemporal optical vortices, carry a sideways form of angular momentum whose value depends on where the center sits. Two rival centers are on the table: one based on energy and one based on photon density. The authors derive formulas for both within a single frame.

Their math gives the position and speed of each center for nearly any simple pulse shape. Worked cases include pulses with stretched timing, rotating fronts, and tilted lobes, and they show how each center drifts as the pulse flies. The values and saving of the sideways momentum hang on which center is chosen. The authors also argue that single photons in such pulses cannot be said to carry a fixed quantum of that momentum.
arxiv-2506-13735:
Jennah Gosciak and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how slow reporting of race and ethnicity data can bend fairness audits in health care. Audits need group labels, yet those labels often arrive late, and not at the same speed for all groups. The team uses records for millions of primary care patients across all US states.

Delays were common and varied widely by group and place. Replaying past audits with delayed data changed the verdicts, most at state and clinic level. Filling in missing race by standard guessing did little to fix the timing problem. The authors argue that fairness pipelines must treat delay as a first class flaw, not a footnote.
arxiv-2506-13835:
Masakazu Inoue and seven co-authors present a silent speech decoding system in two thousand twenty-five. Silent speech reads unspoken words from brain and muscle signals. Data are hard to gather, and setups vary from lab to lab. Mixed electrode layouts thus block one big clean data set.

Their networks take in signals from varied electrode setups as they come. Multi task training on large pooled sets drives the learning. Word accuracy hit high marks for healthy users in tests. A speech impaired patient scored far past single subject models too. Cross language calibration also gained from the pooled route.
arxiv-2506-14035:
Chelsi Jain and seven co-authors published this paper in 2025. It answers questions about long, mixed documents, where the facts needed may sit in text, tables, or images spread over many pages. Reading every page with a big model is slow and costly.

Their system, SimpleDoc, works in loops. A first pass pulls candidate pages by embedding similarity. A second pass filters and re-ranks those pages using short summaries, a cue the plain search lacks. One reasoning model then asks for more pages as needed, keeping what it gathers in a working memory until the answer is firm. Across four test sets, the system beat earlier methods by about three percent on average. It also used far fewer pages, which cuts cost for real document work.
arxiv-2506-14335:
Silvia Casola and co-authors show that the choice of reference summaries can quietly reshuffle summarization scores. Their 2025 paper studies reference-based metrics, which grade a summary against human-written ones. Human language varies richly, and several good references per text are known to help scores track human taste.

Across three multi-reference data sets, many popular metrics prove unstable under reference swaps. Word-overlap metrics such as ROUGE wobble most, flipping model ranks by set choice. Fresh human ratings on model outputs for varied genres link weakly, or not at all, to the metrics. The authors urge that reference set variation join human correlation as a standard check. The warning bites hardest for grading large language model summaries.
arxiv-2506-14435:
Big multimodal models gain skill by consulting a crowd of expert sub-networks, but storing all those experts eats memory, a problem on phones and edge devices. Eight authors present MoTE, which grows a model from a dense checkpoint using ternary experts instead: each expert weight is only minus one, zero, or one, apart from one shared full-precision expert.

The trick is to trade precision for numbers, fielding more small experts for the same memory. In tests, MoTE matched a full-precision rival system while using much less memory. Stacked with standard post-training quantization, its lead widened as the memory budget shrank: at one fixed footprint it beat the rival by 4.3 points of average accuracy. The authors present the approach as a scaling path for capable models that still fit on constrained hardware.
arxiv-2506-14535:
Jose Manuel Suarez, Luis Mariano Bibbo, Joaquin Bogado, and Alejandro Fernandez tackle an upkeep problem for quantum code in a twenty twenty-five paper. The framework they use is Qiskit, which changes fast. Old code breaks when names move or old calls are dropped.

Their fix uses large language models to rewrite the code. First they build a list of known change types from the Qiskit docs and release notes. That list, plus the old code, goes to the model, which spots each case and drafts a fix. The work targets moves up to Qiskit version 0.46 and shares prompts that worked. The team frames it as a way to judge how well such models can aid code upkeep.
arxiv-2506-14635:
Changkai Chen and co-authors compute the full ringing spectrum of a broad class of black holes, in work from 2025. A struck black hole vibrates at quasinormal frequencies, and two puzzles have dogged those spectra for decades.

First, the spectra of spinning and non-spinning holes seemed to jump discontinuously as spin vanished. Second, some frequencies sat oddly close to special algebraic values, with unexplained splitting. The new method follows eigenvalue equations by analytic continuation, dropping a crutch parameter that blocked modes crossing a key axis. Complete spectra for both hole types matched scattering tests to extreme precision. Both puzzles dissolve: the jump was a computational blind spot, and coincidence with a special frequency spawns an extra nearby mode.
arxiv-2506-14935:
Frank Lu's paper from 2025 proves cases of the Shafarevich conjecture, a famed claim that only finitely many shapes of a kind can have good behavior outside a fixed set of primes. Lu's shapes are complete intersections: spaces cut out by several equations inside abelian varieties, over a number field. The proof uses the Lawrence-Venkatesh method, a recent route that links counting to symmetry groups.

Two fresh inputs carry the work. One computes Euler characteristics for these intersections. The other is a big monodromy claim for the cohomology of a family of such shapes, proven by way of Tannaka groups and then turned into a counting claim about matrices.
arxiv-2506-15135:
Distributed programs fail in sneaky ways when messages arrive in the wrong order, a fault called a communication race. Zhengqun Koo, writing alone in a 2025 paper, builds a framework that can prove such races absent. The work covers a subset of the Go language, where programs coordinate mainly by passing messages on channels.

The framework reasons about the runs of a program in advance, using a happens-before order stretched to cover buffered and unbuffered channels. If the proof passes, no receiver can grab a message meant for another, or wait forever for one that never comes. Static proof beats testing here, since races hide in rare timings. The work points toward distributed code that is correct by construction.
arxiv-2506-15435:
James Cussens, Julia Hatamyar, Vishalie Shah, and Noemi Kreif speed up a method for learning optimal policy trees, simple decision rules that assign treatments or actions. Their 2025 paper builds on a popular approach published in 2021. Policy trees are prized because people can read and audit them, but finding the truly best tree is slow.

The team reimplements the method with discrete optimization techniques. In finite-sample tests, their version learns optimal trees nearly fifty times faster than the original. They release the work as a public software package for the R language, called fastpolicytree. The speedup makes optimal, explainable policies practical on larger data than before.
arxiv-2506-15535:
Alexandru Meterez and co-authors simplify the theory of a workhorse training method in a 2025 paper. Stochastic gradient descent trains most machine learning models, and averaging its later weights often improves results. A recent study gave sharp rates for this method on linear regression, using a bias-variance split.

The authors recover the same bias and variance bounds with a cleaner, simpler argument. Their analysis covers training with a constant step size, with and without tail averaging. A simpler proof helps others extend the results and understand why this averaging works so well in practice.
arxiv-2506-15635:
Robots that work over many days need to recall what they saw and did much earlier. Karmesh Yadav, Yusuf Ali, Gunshi Gupta, Yarin Gal, and Zsolt Kira built a test for that skill and shared it in 2025. Large vision-language models do well at planning, but they can hold only a few hundred images at once. Past video tests also miss hands-on skills like moving objects and finding a path.

Their benchmark, run in the Habitat simulator, holds sixty tasks that need long engagement with a scene. Each task asks the agent to recall past events and act on that recall at the same time. Tasks can also be stretched to longer forms by a set procedure. The test gives builders a shared way to judge and improve robot memory.
arxiv-2506-15835:
Mingyuan Luo and co-authors improve freehand 3D ultrasound, where a clinician sweeps a probe and software stacks the slices into a volume. No external tracker is used, so the software must guess each slice's motion. Errors pile up as drift, worst on tricky sweeps.

Their network fuses the images with motion sensor data, reading speed as a clue. Multiple branches handle different motion styles, from slow pans to quick turns. The design aims at accuracy that holds across scanning habits. Bedside 3D without tracking gear would widen access to volume imaging. Drift is the field's old enemy, and this is a fresh angle on it.
arxiv-2506-15935:
Roland-Batty and co-authors simulate a magnetic flux tube rising through the Sun's near surface layers to test a known tilt pattern. Sunspot pairs tilt away from the east-west line, more so at higher latitudes, a rule called Joy's law. The tilt is often blamed on the Coriolis force from the Sun's spin. Their 2025 study models that force on surface flows.

The team ran a three dimensional simulation with spin set far faster than the real Sun, to make the weak effect measurable. The tube reached the surface with a tilt matching Joy's law once scaled back to solar spin. The tilt barely changed after emergence. The authors say surface level Coriolis action alone can explain the pattern.
arxiv-2506-16035:
Tripathi and co-authors present a 2025 paper on cutting documents into chunks with vision models, for retrieval-augmented chatbots. Plain text splitting mangles tables that span pages, figures, and steps that cross page breaks. Their method feeds PDF pages to a large multimodal model in batches. Context carries across batches, so split tables and charts stay whole.

Hand-built questions over a curated PDF set graded the output. Chunk quality and final answer accuracy both rose over a vanilla pipeline. Close reading showed structure and meaning survived the cuts better. The authors argue that documents are visual objects first, and chunkers should treat them that way.
arxiv-2506-16135:
Liu, Du, Deng, and Zhang teach a neural network to read star chemistry from telescope spectra. Using giant stars seen by both the LAMOST and APOGEE surveys, they train a convolutional network on the spectra of some 62,000 shared stars. They then apply it to over a million LAMOST giants. The network reports temperature, gravity, iron content, and six further elements for each star.

Tests show tight agreement with the survey labels, with errors small enough for mapping the Galaxy. The team then checks known stellar groups in their catalog and weighs where those groups came from. The full catalog is posted online for other researchers.
arxiv-2506-16235:
Yisu Wang and four co-authors tackle network strain in distributed machine learning in a 2025 paper. Training big models across many machines causes sudden traffic spikes. Congestion slows training and hurts final speed. Squeezing the data sent between machines helps, but fixed squeezing loses information and can hurt accuracy.

Their framework watches network conditions in real time. It squeezes data only when congestion actually slows progress, choosing among quantization, pruning, and compression as conditions change. In tests on typical training jobs with tight bandwidth, throughput improved severalfold over strong rivals. The authors present the design as a way to balance smaller payloads against keeping models accurate.
arxiv-2506-16335:
Albert Sadowski and Jaroslaw Chudziak make language models apply rules in a checkable way in a 2025 paper. Models reason well in words but slip on strict rules, exceptions, and clear justification. Legal analysis shows all three demands at full strength.

Their framework splits each task into three steps that can be verified. First the model names the entities involved. Next it extracts their relevant properties. Then a symbolic engine applies the formal rules. Experts can adjust the rule set without rebuilding the system. On a legal hearsay benchmark, top models gained large score jumps over few-shot baselines. The hybrid design pairs flexible reading with strict logic.
arxiv-2506-16435:
A team of three authors studied in 2025 how soap-like coating molecules shape a newborn nanocrystal. Quantum dots and other tiny crystals grow while coated with ligands that keep them apart. The authors modeled ligands as hard spheres stuck to the surface of a prism-shaped particle.

Computer simulations showed the particle settles into a small set of shapes, mainly flat plates and rods. Simple theory describes those shapes well. As coating density rose, the free energies of the shapes drew nearly equal. That means the crowding of ligands narrows the menu of shapes without favoring any one of them. The finding helps explain the forms that appear early in crystal growth.
arxiv-2506-16535:
Tyler Landle and co-authors propose in 2025 a test platform for connected self driving cars that runs at the network edge. Cars that talk to each other, to road gear, and to the cloud promise safer roads, but testing their control systems in big 3D scenes with many vehicles is heavy computing work. No existing framework handles many vehicles in realistic scenes well.

Their platform is modular and built to scale, checking both that safety algorithms work and how fast they run. It can model up to 256 vehicles, each running its own control method, eight times more than standard tools allow without sensing turned on. A future design where control runs at the edge is included for testing.
arxiv-2506-16835:
Peter Hatton, Blas Pedro Uberuaga, and Danny Perez present a 2025 paper on an automated workflow that gathers defect movement data in chemically complex materials. Such materials win their special properties from messy atomic neighborhoods, but that same mess makes simulating atom motion slow and manual. Defect hops set how the materials age, conduct, and fail.

Their Python workflow couples accelerated dynamics with a redecoration trick that reuses work across similar neighborhoods. It builds a graph of defect states whose edges carry distributions of jump rates and energies. Those outputs feed directly into larger scale models. Trials on a copper nickel alloy found simple predictive rules; a spinel oxide showed richer behavior.
arxiv-2506-16935:
Shruti Aggarwal, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, sorts true three-part quantum states that are linked as a whole, using a shape-based measure called concurrence fill. The measure reads the area of a triangle built from pair links.

Such linked states can be made and checked in labs, yet many past measures miss their mark. Aggarwal rewrites the measure in terms of whole and part link terms, in a form that is easier to use. From it, she draws a rule to tell two great classes of such states apart. She then works out the measure for blends of the two classes and for their base states, with a top bound for mixed cases.
arxiv-2506-17435:
Alejandro De La Fuente-Cuesta and co-authors test whether large language models can sort news into political and non-political, from the link alone or from the text. Such sorting is now common in studies of politics and media, but the value of the link itself was not well known.

The study spans five lands and their languages, with human coded data as the yardstick. Links did carry real signal, and link based sorting could stand in for full text work at lower cost. Yet the models too often tagged centrist news as political, a bias that could skew later work. The authors close with advice for sound use.
arxiv-2506-17635:
Eitan Tadmor studies how groups of self-moving agents settle into orderly flocking. His 2025 paper works with the fluid-style equations for crowds whose members align their velocities with neighbors. Such systems are known to flock when their solutions stay smooth, but proving smoothness for all time was open in higher dimensions.

Tadmor proceeds in two steps. First he examines how entropy falls and the system drifts toward a simple mono-kinetic state, where all local agents share one velocity. Then he proves lasting smoothness for a wide class of starting states that meet a threshold condition tied to that entropy drop. The proof works in any number of dimensions.
arxiv-2506-18035:
Maxence Lasbordes, Daniele Falavigna, and Alessio Brutti improve early-exit speech recognition for small devices, in a research paper from 2025. Early-exit models can stop partway through their layers when resources are tight, which suits phones and other edge hardware. A strong speech architecture that varies its frame rate lacks the structure to add such exits.

Their Splitformer adds parallel layers that process downsampled copies of the input alongside the standard path. The branches for early exits can then attach cleanly. On standard benchmarks, recognition improved a lot over earlier early-exit designs. The cost is a small rise in model size, with no added time per run, they report.
arxiv-2506-18335:
Saad Wazir and Daeyoung Kim wrote a 2025 paper on outlining stained markers in medical images by computer. The catalog creator field appends their email addresses, but the head gives the two authors cleanly. Marking these regions guides diagnosis and drug research. Images vary in stain and shape, and labeled examples are scarce, so many methods lean on pre-trained front ends and weak decoders.

Their design rebuilds the decoder, the part that turns features back into a full-size map. It restores detail by a depth-to-space step and uses a lean attention scheme to stress the right channels and regions. Tests on four data sets beat leading methods. The decoder can also plug into other front ends, which widens its use.
arxiv-2506-18735:
Shivam Verma, Vivian Chen, and Darren Mei present in 2025 an audio first framework for targeting ads on a music streaming platform. The service draws over 675 million monthly users who split their time among music, podcasts, audiobooks, and video. Ads arrive as sound, video, and display inside one listening session.

Older ad models were built for screen first apps and strain under that mix. The team's design learns several tasks at once with a mixture of expert networks that adapts across modes. Click forecasts then respect the audio central habit of the platform. Better targeting in the ear first setting could lift revenue without piling on more ads. The paper reports tests at platform scale.
arxiv-2506-18835:
Halyna Butovych, Jaroslav Ilnytskyi, Erkki Lähderanta, and Taras Patsahan simulate how a common polymer grabs mercury ions out of water. Mercury pollution is a serious water hazard, and chelation, binding metals with claw-like molecules, is a proven cleanup route. Their 2025 study runs atom-level simulations of linear polyethyleneimine mixed with doubly charged mercury ions in water. Chains of different lengths were tested. A single chain with ten amino groups proved able to wrap and hold a mercury ion.

Simulation shows the embrace in detail: which atoms close in, and how the chain folds. That microscopic picture guides the design of filter materials before costly lab work. The authors used a standard force field for the atoms. Their result supports this polymer as a mercury trap worth building into treatment systems.
arxiv-2506-18935:
Shri Lal Raghudev Ram Singh, writing alone in 2025, asks which share of mind can be built in a machine, and bids a proof. Mind lore from brain work oft rests on a pair: a thing seen and a seer that sees it, set in one spot. Singh makes that pair a set frame.

The frame is then writ for made things, in the tongue of ZF set lore. In that tongue, a proof of machine mind stands, of a cut kind: know-mind, the mind that knows and can say, not the felt kind. The claim is tight and the frame is the gift: a shared form where brain lore and made mind can be set side by side and weighed.
arxiv-2506-19235:
Yu Xie and co-authors build a recommendation system on a language model trained in two stages, in this 2025 paper. Recommenders trap users in filter bubbles and ignore outside knowledge. User histories and item traits are first rewritten as plain-language prompts the model can read.

Stage one fine-tunes the model on examples to teach basic recommending. Stage two adds group-based reinforcement learning with step-by-step reasoning, steered by a flexible reward. The reward balances accuracy, diversity, and novelty at once. On real data from a large social platform, the system beat prior methods across those measures. The authors say it also weakens the filter bubble effect.
arxiv-2506-19435:
Mirjam Tijhuis and colleagues ran the same storm line through two kinds of weather model in a 2025 comparison. Forecast models chase accurate predictions, while large-eddy models chase physical understanding, and the two differ in equations and grids. As computers grow, their resolutions overlap, raising a fair question: do their answers converge too, or do design choices still rule the outcome?

Both models received an identical idealized squall line setup, resolution, and cloud physics, once with warm rain and once with ice. The broad storm structure and circulation matched well. Quantitative strength differed, with the eddy model spinning a more intense circulation. Convergence is partial: shared setup aligns the story, not every number.
arxiv-2506-19535:
Quantum computers need pairs of qubits that can be linked on demand, and trapped ions are a leading way to build them. A 2025 paper by Xueying Mai and four co-authors tackles a snag that grows with size: as ion chains get longer, the ions' shared motions crowd together, and control gets messy. Their fix uses shaped beams of light to address each ion.

The team built a system that makes arrays of Hermite-Gaussian beams that can be steered from ion to ion. The sideways slope of these beams ties qubits to a sparse set of lengthwise motions, so one motion can carry the link between two qubits. With that setup they ran two-qubit gates in chains of up to six ions. The gates held fidelity near 0.97 without the complex pulse shaping that older methods need.
arxiv-2506-20235:
Yuyang Zhang and co-authors improve link prediction in directed networks by fusing local and global clues, in a 2025 paper. Guessing which connections will form, and in which direction, drives recommendation, fraud spotting, and biology. Existing deep methods compare pairs of nodes or pool neighborhood messages, but each misses something the other sees.

Their graph neural network blends a node's own learned features with information about the community it belongs to, and the authors prove this hybrid view helps in theory. They also redraw the network as a line graph, turning links into nodes, so messages carry richer context during learning. On benchmark networks the method beat the state of the art in most training splits. Better directed link guesses sharpen any system that must rank who will connect to whom next.
arxiv-2506-20435:
Mennatullah Khedr and John Fitzgerald review work on joining digital twins into larger wholes in a 2025 paper. A digital twin mirrors a real system, and cities or factories may need many twins linked as one system of systems. Linking raises hard questions about how parts compose and how the whole gets checked for trust.

The review covers twenty one studies from 2022 to 2024. Composition is widely discussed but rarely given formal rules. Checking leans on semi formal methods and simulation, with full formal proof rare. Model uncertainty and sheer integration complexity stand out as the top technical hurdles. The authors supply a sorting of check methods and call for shared, scalable standards in the field.
arxiv-2506-20735:
A magnetic field makes the magnetization of a metal ripple as the field grows. This de Haas-van Alphen effect is well understood in three dimensions. In flat, two-dimensional Fermi liquids the theory has a stubborn gap. Part of the signal comes from the wobbling self-energy of the electrons, which has no closed-form answer. Yuxuan Wang sidesteps the problem by bosonizing the Fermi surface. The Landau parameters of the liquid then enter the theory directly.

Cyclotron resonance and specific heat come out matching known results. A mode expansion reduces the effect to a simple quantum mechanics problem. The low and high temperature behavior departs from the classic Lifshitz-Kosevich formula. In three dimensions Wang shows those departures shrink to negligible size.
arxiv-2506-20835:
Boudjemaa, a solo author, studies in 2025 what happens to a cloud of ultracold polar molecules right after a sudden change in how strongly they interact. The molecules are shielded by microwaves, and the cloud sits at near zero temperature in a uniform gas. Two theory tools, a time dependent wave method and a self consistent variant, track how the condensate loses atoms to excited states and how pairs of atoms correlate.

Over time these measures swing slowly or fast depending on the shielding strength. At long times the cloud settles into steady patterns that differ from calm equilibrium values. Pair links spread slowly at first, then race outward. The work guides experiments on molecule condensates far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2506-20935:
Hsin-Hsiung Huang and Hayden Hampton forecast geopolitical conflict with STFT-VNNGP, a transformer-Gaussian process hybrid built for spiky event data. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses GDELT records, whose sparsity and burstiness wreck standard deep forecasters at long horizons. Stage one runs a sparse temporal fusion transformer to produce multi-quantile forecasts. Stage two feeds those quantiles to a variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process.

The process layer smooths spatiotemporally and quantifies uncertainty on principle. The architecture won a twenty twenty-three threat detection competition. In Middle East and United States case studies, it beats a lone transformer, especially on timing and size of bursty episodes far ahead. Code and workflows are public for reproduction.
arxiv-2506-21035:
Haodong Lu and co-authors propose a way in 2025 for large models to keep learning new tasks without losing old skills. Past methods add big blocks of new parts and freeze the old ones, but the blocks can clash, repeat each other, and confuse the choice of which block to use.

Their method adds tiny rank one parts that act like small memory units, each holding a key and a value. No extra switch is needed, since each unit judges its own fit to the task. Tests on image and text models show less forgetting and better scores than past methods.
arxiv-2506-21435:
Andronikos Paliathanasis hunts hidden conservation laws in scalar field cosmology with a lift trick and a singularity test. The paper from twenty twenty-five works on a flat expanding universe with a dust source. The Eisenhart-Duval lift, in a fresh form, raises the system to expose nonlocal conserved quantities. One potential family, an exponential plus a constant, admits such laws in nontrivial form.

The Painlevé test then probes integrability of the field equations. Quintessence passes and proves integrable past a set slope bound. The phantom field passes for every slope value. Laurent series solutions are written out for varied settings. The effective equation of state is traced along those solutions. The study sorts which scalar cosmologies can be solved in closed form.
arxiv-2506-21535:
Mohammed Baharoon and co-authors map design choices for AI that writes CT scan reports in a 2025 paper. Multimodal language models promise to draft radiology reports from 3D scans, easing radiologist load. Which parts of the design matter most was unclear.

The team varied the visual input form, the projector, the language model, and the fine-tuning recipe in turn. Two knowledge-based tricks for enriching reports lifted a quality score by up to ten percent. Their entry placed second in a 2024 challenge on 1,687 cases. Report quality barely depended on language model size under one training recipe. Bigger scan volumes did not always help, while adding a segmentation mask did.
arxiv-2506-21735:
Nick Lemke and co-authors bring shared model training to low-resource clinics in this 2025 paper. Hospitals can train one model together without sending patient data out, a method called federated learning. Clinics in poorer countries often lack strong computers and steady internet.

Their system, FedNCA, uses a light model built for medical image outlining. It can train on cheap edge devices, even common smartphones, and keeps data traffic low. The design is also ready for encryption. The work aims to spread smart imaging tools where trained staff are few. Fair access across sites is a stated goal.
arxiv-2506-21835:
Xiaoqi Wang and co-authors published this image segmentation study in 2025. Visual reference segmentation asks a model to outline objects like those in an example image, even for categories it was never trained on. Recent methods built on the Segment Anything Model generate guide prompts automatically. The prompts often land on object boundaries, where small shifts flip the result. That makes the output unstable and fragile.

The team introduces ProSAM, which learns a prompt encoder that predicts a spread of likely prompts instead of one fixed guess. By modeling that distribution, the system steers away from unstable boundary spots. The design stays simple while attacking the root cause of the fragility. On the Pascal-5i and COCO-20i benchmark datasets, ProSAM consistently beat the leading methods. The authors present probabilistic prompts as a general fix for prompt-based segmentation that must work reliably in the open world.
arxiv-2506-21935:
Xiaoqing Liu and co-authors offer a 2025 tutorial on fine-tuning universal machine-learned models of atomic forces. These foundation models work across many materials but often need adjustment to reach the accuracy a specific task demands, and guidance on that adjustment has been scattered.

Using a recent open model as the working example, the tutorial walks through data preparation, setting choices, training, and checking. Case studies cover battery electrolytes, faults in metals, semiconductors, and surfaces where solids meet liquids. Fine-tuned models proved more accurate, cheaper to run, quicker to train, and better with small data sets. Some even picked up long-range effects the base model missed.
arxiv-2506-22135:
William Woodman and Tom Nye build chance models for family trees of species, in a 2025 study. Such trees sit in a curved space where plain stats do not apply: the space has corners, and curve rules rule how trees blend. A mean tree and a spread around it are hard to define there.

Their fix treats an unknown tree as the end of a random walk, like a drunkard's path that starts at a source tree. A bridge method fills in paths that must end at the trees in the data. From those paths, the team can sample the source tree and the spread, and score rival source claims. Tests on fake data work, and a run on yeast gene trees shows the method on real facts. It lays a base for wider tree stats.
arxiv-2506-22735:
