Willem Conradie and four co-authors develop a formal framework for group decisions in a 2025 arXiv paper. They model how each person filters choices by what they see as relevant. These stances, called interrogative agendas, shape the outcome of group deliberation.

An agenda is cast as a rule that treats two outcomes as the same when they differ only in points the person ignores. The authors map which agendas fit different rules for winning a vote. They then add a structure that links agents and agendas to model how the two interact. They close by marking which interaction rules their framework can and cannot express.
arxiv-2506-22935:
Marc Bara Iniesta presents in 2025 a way to make a core radar tool work with modern gradient-based learning. The ambiguity function maps how well a radar signal can pin down range and speed, and it guides signal design. Its classic form uses steps that block gradient flow, which shuts it out of neural network training.

His frame, GRAF, restates the calculation so gradients pass through the whole chain while the math stays the same. It handles complex values, runs fast with parallel Fourier methods, and stays numerically steady. The result lets designers train signal generators with ambiguity goals built in and tune radar systems end to end.
arxiv-2506-23135:
Yu Shang and co-authors build a robot world model that learns physics alongside video. World models dream up training footage for robots, easing data scarcity. But dreamt clips often bend geometry and motion in impossible ways, above all in contact heavy scenes. RoboScape trains two extra tasks inside the generator.

One predicts depth over time, anchoring three dimensional shape. The other tracks keypoint motion, quietly encoding shape and material feel. The joint training yields clips with stronger visual fidelity and physical sense. The authors then train and grade robot policies on the dreamt data, showing the pipeline's practical worth.
arxiv-2506-23435:
Hayder Tirmazi recounts a failed quest to prove video game speedruns with cryptography. Speedrunners race to finish games fast, and proving a run is real still leans on human observers, sound forensics or hand-checked game maths, all slow and fallible. Tirmazi set out, by his own cheerful account, to build a system that proves a run's authenticity outright.

The paper walks through each attempted design and the way it can be cheated. The failures add up to a lesson: proving live, interactive human input in an untrusted setting is deeply hard. Signature schemes, game integrity checks and provable play all hit limits that the narrative makes plain.
arxiv-2506-23735:
JiaRu Wu and Mingwei Liu present AutoEvoEval in two thousand twenty-five. Their frame grows test data for large language models on its own. Fixed test sets can miss weak spots in how models cope with change. Past growth methods lacked control over change types and depth.

AutoEvoEval has a set of clear atomic change steps. Steps can stack over rounds to make hard, real style samples. Tests span many open and closed models. Single steps cut scores by a clear margin on average. Stacked steps cut scores far more. The pair argue that fixed tests flatter models. Growth aware tests give a truer view of skill.
arxiv-2507-00035:
Alemayehu Negash and Meaza Bogale prove shared fixed point results under weaker rules, in work from 2025. Classic fixed point proofs demand continuity and strong match rules between maps. Looser weak compatibility can still force shared fixed points when contraction is shaped with care.

Three self maps form the main frame, guided by a control function in the contraction. Extra results cover map pairs and cases where the control is upper semi continuous. Repeat maps and map sequences extend the frame to wider use in later work. Sharp examples show why each assumption is needed for the claims. Past theorems from many authors fall out as special cases here.
arxiv-2507-00535:
Dietmar Jannach, Amra Delić, Francesco Ricci, and Markus Zanker argue that systems which suggest choices to groups need a rethink, in a 2025 essay. Group recommenders have been studied for over twenty-five years, gathering each member's tastes and blending them into one list. Few such systems run in the real world. The authors suggest the old designs misread how groups actually talk and decide together.

The essay draws on research about group decision making and on the new powers of generative AI, such as chatbots that can hold a conversation. Instead of one fixed list, a future system could join the group's discussion, ask questions, and adjust as views shift. The authors sketch this agent-style support as one path forward. Their piece invites builders to test these ideas against what groups really need.
arxiv-2507-00835:
Vipin Kumar Sharma, Himanshu Chaudhary, and Sanved Kolekar test an emergent dark energy model against the newest sky data in a 2025 paper. Fresh results from the DESI survey hint that dark energy may not be a pure constant, challenging the standard model. The generalized emergent model lets dark energy switch on with a tunable sharpness.

The team fitted the model to DESI's second data release, supernova collections, and microwave background distances. Depending on which supernova calibration joined, the fit preferred earlier or later emergence. The model matched the data better than the standard at some distances. Model comparison gave it weak to moderate support, keeping the idea alive.
arxiv-2507-00935:
Zhengqi Niu and co-authors build tunable superatoms from a row of eight superconducting artificial atoms linked by a waveguide. A group of atoms in shared quantum states can act as one multi-level superatom when light meets it. The team set two spacings between neighbours, matching Bragg and anti-Bragg scattering conditions.

By tuning the atom frequencies, they reshaped both kinds of superatom and saw unlike optical effects, such as collectively induced transparency and a broad photonic bandgap. Strong coupling between waveguide and atoms let a small system steer light well. The work shows how such Bragg and anti-Bragg superatoms could serve in quantum devices.
arxiv-2507-01435:
In a two-dimensional semimetal built on mercury telluride, two kinds of holes share the stage: massless Dirac holes and massive normal ones. Yuping Huang and five co-authors work out how their interactions reshape how charge flows in a magnetic field. Dirac holes alone add an interaction-driven term to conductivity that is zero for normal spectra, with a steep temperature law, yet leave resistivity and the Hall effect unchanged at leading order.

Mixing the two hole types changes the full picture: conductivity, resistivity, and Hall response all gain interaction corrections, growing as the square of temperature, at times with a log twist. A strong field holds back those corrections to resistivity. The theory came out in 2025 under a head title about interactions-controlled magnetotransport, and gives lab teams clear signs to look for.
arxiv-2507-01735:
Kai Chen and thirteen co-authors report a workshop on corner cases in autonomous driving in this 2025 paper. The event, W-CODA, ran with the ECCV 2024 conference. Corner cases are the rare, odd scenes where driving systems fail: strange obstacles, odd light, rule bending road users. Five invited speakers from academia and industry shared progress and views. The workshop collected papers and ran a two track challenge, one on understanding corner case scenes and one on generating them.

The organizers frame the event as a first bridge between research and the reliability self driving agents need. Multimodal perception, mixing camera, lidar, and language, is the chosen weapon. Corner cases cannot be drilled away with ordinary data, since they are rare by definition. They must be hunted, shared, and synthesized. The authors say the workshop series will continue that hunt.
arxiv-2507-01835:
Seven researchers reconstruct full light spectra from three phone cameras in a paper from 2025. Ordinary photos record three color channels, losing most spectral detail. The setup adds chosen filters to two of a phone's lenses. That yields richer spectral clues than any single camera. Because the views are misaligned, a lightweight module aligns and fuses them first.

The team built the first data set for this task, with matched phone and reference camera images. Spectra came out about thirty percent more accurate than from a plain camera. The alignment module added a further five percent to leading methods. The authors argue commodity hardware can do practical hyperspectral imaging.
arxiv-2507-01935:
Manuel Ladra and Andrés Pérez-Rodríguez build a Frattini theory for evolution algebras, a class where each basis step squares into a mix of others, in a paper from 2025. The Frattini part of an algebra sits inside every maximal subalgebra at once.

The classic nilradical does not port cleanly to this class, so the authors define a supersolvable stand in. With that tool they give exact marks for when the Frattini subalgebra and its ideal shrink to nothing. They also note how the ideal helps study a tightly woven class of these algebras.
arxiv-2507-02035:
Robin Schäfer, Claudio Chamon and Chris Laumann showed in 2025 that a famous topological model hides extra phases of matter near its transitions. The chiral Zp toric code is a standard example of topological order. When perturbed in a fixed flux background, it sprouts descendant states much like fractional quantum Hall states. The team named them Hall-on-Toric states and confirmed them with large computer simulations.

These states carry fractional charges and a larger ground-state degeneracy than the parent phase. Checks on entanglement and a generalized Hall response backed the identification. Strikingly, the states survive without the symmetry usually thought to protect them. The authors say the result deepens the reading of the model's defects as electric and magnetic particles. It also hints that textbook models still conceal rich behavior worth mining.
arxiv-2507-02235:
Meng Xu, Frank Neumann, Aneta Neumann, and Yew Soon Ong bring quality-diversity methods to learning scheduling rules, in a 2025 paper. Real problems often need many good solutions that differ from each other, not just one best answer. Quality-diversity search builds such sets by exploring varied niches.

Most past work used static problems, while scheduling changes over time. The team built a map that links each rule's code to its behavior, so diverse rules can be found and kept. Experiments on fixed and changing training cases show how the map fills over time. The paper also discusses theory gaps and future directions for dynamic problems.
arxiv-2507-02335:
Extra wave twists in gravity signals are hunted by Shun Yin Cheung and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Einstein's theory allows two twist kinds in gravity waves. Rival theories allow up to six. A null stream, a mix of three detectors that cancels the known two, leaves room for extras to show. A smooth random model scans that stream for odd shapes.

Forty-two three-detector events from a shared catalogue fed the hunt. No extras showed in any of them. One event caps the odd share under two fifths of the strain. Einstein's pair still rules.
arxiv-2507-02735:
Sizhe Chen and co-authors harden language models against prompt injection in a 2025 paper. Injected instructions hide inside data an agent reads, and this is ranked the top threat to AI agents. The best open defense, SecAlign, trains on fake injections, but the authors find it quietly wrecks the model's usefulness, above all on agent tasks.

Their Meta-SecAlign changes two things: injection spots vary at random during training, blocking shortcut learning, and the model's own answers serve as training labels, keeping its style intact. Across knowledge, instruction, and agent tests on six benchmarks, the defense kept nearly all plain-model usefulness while beating the older defense on security, even against adaptive attacks.
arxiv-2507-02935:
Guessing what a person means by loose orders is tested by Fardin Saad, Pradeep K. Murukannaiah, and Munindar P. Singh in a 2025 arXiv paper. Good teaming with a software agent needs it to grasp orders that leave gaps. The agent must infer the aims the person left unsaid. The authors call that work an Instruction Inference task and set it in a live goal task.

Their agent, Tomcat, comes in two forms. One learns from a few worked cases with step-by-step thought. One leans on plain common sense. Both ran on three big language models. Scores for aim match and plan quality put the first form near human levels in a study with fifty-two people.
arxiv-2507-03035:
Pete Rigas studies how fast classical bits can be sent over noisy quantum channels when the messages must also be checked for errors and verified as genuine. Two parties, called Alice and Bob in the field's custom, share the channel, while an eavesdropper may listen in. Earlier work had set lower bounds on the sending rate when noise is light. Rigas asks the reverse question: what upper bounds hold no matter how clever the scheme?

He proves strict upper bounds on the bit rate that depend on the size of each player's alphabet of symbols. The proof uses a pruning step that drops letters from the alphabets when they cannot help. The bounds matter, he argues, for sorting out odd claims about such protocols and for building codes that resist noise while rarely accepting a fake message. The work is theoretical and aimed at specialists in quantum communication.
arxiv-2507-03835:
Octavio Junqueira and Roldao da Rocha present a 2025 theoretical physics paper on the matter inside colliding atomic nuclei. Under extreme heat, ordinary matter melts into a soup of quarks and gluons; at lower heat it stays locked inside particles. The pair study how spinning motion changes that melting point, using a gravity-based model of strong-force matter.

Working with an exact solution for a charged, rotating black hole in a curved five-dimensional space, they map where the locked phase can survive. Faster spin lowers the allowed range, and as the matter grows denser the permitted spin falls toward zero. Spin too fast, and matter stays in the melted phase with no transition at all. Their phase diagram refines estimates used to read real collision data.
arxiv-2507-04135:
Stephan Gerster and Giuseppe Visconti raise traffic flow modeling to third order by letting driver hesitation evolve on its own. Classic second-order models freeze hesitation inside a fixed function, which caps what they can say. Starting from a microscopic view of drivers, the authors give hesitation its own evolution law. Drivers then react one way when speeding up and another when slowing down, even at the same density.

That split is the hysteresis seen on real roads. Relaxation terms are added to steer the model toward known limits. The paper ties the new system back to the Aw-Rascle-Zhang model and runs a full stability analysis.
arxiv-2507-04335:
Yexin Yan, Stefan Hillmich, Robert Wille, and Christian Mayr improve a trick for faking quantum computers on classical ones in this 2025 paper. Simulating quantum circuits classically costs resources that explode with size. Decision diagrams compress the simulation by exploiting repeated patterns, but hard circuits like the quantum supremacy benchmarks have almost no repetition to exploit.

Approximate simulation trades a little accuracy for a lot of memory. Earlier methods deleted the least important diagram nodes; this team instead replaces them with similar nodes, slowing the accuracy loss. A hashing technique finds replacement candidates fast enough to keep the overhead small. The result is a better memory-accuracy balance, scaling well as circuits grow deeper. For the supremacy benchmarks the team demonstrates, for the first time, a better-than-linear trade between memory saved and fidelity kept.
arxiv-2507-04535:
Chang Sun and co-authors present a 2025 tool for running neural networks on chips at very high speed. Some networks, such as those used at the CERN particle collider, must answer within millionths of a second. They are laid out fully on FPGA chips, where the math of fixed matrix steps eats much of the chip's space.

Their method, called da4ml, uses distributed arithmetic to carry out those fixed steps with less room and no loss of speed. It matches the space savings of the best known methods while running far faster to compute. The code is open and built into a free library for fast network use on such chips. On realistic compact networks it cut on-chip resource use by up to a third and lowered delay, making some designs possible for the first time.
arxiv-2507-04735:
Francesco Giuliari and co-authors test whether vision-language models can fetch the right fabric photo from a written description, in a 2025 paper. Factories hold product knowledge as fabric samples paired with text, yet no public dataset existed for this retrieval task. The team built one with an automated pipeline that asks large multimodal models to write two kinds of description for each sample.

One kind is free-flowing prose; the other is a structured list of attributes. Three retrieval models, CLIP, LAION-CLIP, and Meta's Perception Encoder, were tested without any training on fabrics. Structured descriptions lifted accuracy sharply, above all for visually tangled patterns, and the Perception Encoder led the field. Plain zero-shot search still struggled, which the authors take as a call for domain-tuned methods.
arxiv-2507-05035:
Konstantin Nikolaou, Sven Krippendorf, Samuel Tovey, and Christian Holm wrote this 2025 study on what scaling laws hide inside neural networks. Such laws link model size and data to scores, yet say little about the inner works. The team studies training through the neural tangent kernel, a tool that tracks how a network's answers shift as it learns.

On standard vision tasks, the same score scaling could hide opposite inner behavior, so scores alone cannot explain how networks learn. The team also tracks how feature learning fades as width grows toward the endless-width limit. In their setups, the widest models that still learn features were far narrower than today's big language models. The authors urge a look past curves to the machinery beneath.
arxiv-2507-05135:
Svyatoslav Pchelintsev and co-authors give household robots a way to fix failed plans by looking at the scene. Language models plan well from text but cannot see what went wrong. Their method, LERa, runs a three-step loop with a vision-language model: Look at a plain camera image and name the error, Explain the correction, then Replan.

The loop needs only the image, the instruction, the first plan, and a failure flag, with no object detectors or preset conditions. On two new chaos-filled home benchmarks, it beat baselines by forty percent in changing scenes. In simulated tabletop tasks it raised success by up to two-thirds, and real robot trials confirmed the gains.
arxiv-2507-05235:
Joschka Braun, Bálint Mucsányi, and Seyed Ali Bahrainian keep summaries on topic by nudging the model's word scores as it writes. Their 2025 paper deals with abstractive summarization with a set theme. Fine tuning works but costs much; prompting often loses focus, above all in small models. Their method reweights the scores of topic relevant words during generation. Three variants are tested.

One adds a fixed boost to those scores. One multiplies them by a factor. The third boosts only scores already above a threshold. Tests used a topical news data set and two open models, of two and eight billion parameters. All three variants raised topic word use. The threshold variant improved focus without hurting summary quality. That trade off plagues other approaches, the authors note. They pitch score reweighting as a cheap, practical control for generated text.
arxiv-2507-05335:
Quantum phases with hidden order are hard to sort when noise enters the picture. Marvin Qi and co-authors offer a new lens for that task in a 2025 paper. They extend a frame that views a thin quantum system as the edge of a thicker one, so phases and shifts between them fit one picture.

Their twist folds the thicker system into two layers, which lets it hold both strong and weak forms of symmetry at once. With that folded view, the team maps some noisy phases to cleaner ones. They also sort a broad class of states and show how noise can turn one kind of phase into another. The frame may help guide future lab work.
arxiv-2507-05535:
Kuan-Cheng Chen and co-authors propose a design in 2025 for trainable quantum circuits that avoids the flat training problem known as barren plateaus. In those plateaus, the training signal fades to near zero as circuits grow, which stalls learning. Their design builds each layer from a single exponential tied to a small symmetry group.

Keeping the motion inside that compact subspace shrinks the space the circuit can reach, by a huge factor. The training signal then fades only mildly, not catastrophically. Exact gradients that run on real hardware come from a generalized shift rule, with no extra qubits or guess based error. Tests on quantum auto encoding and classification show much larger training signals than standard designs. Trainable circuits are a gate to most near term quantum uses.
arxiv-2507-05835:
Balázs Bárány and Manuj Verma compute the fractal dimension of self-similar measures whose generating maps share a fixed point. Self-similar sets and measures live on the real line here. When several contraction maps fix the same point, overlaps pile up in a structured way. Dimension formulas usually demand a separation condition to tame those overlaps.

The authors prove a weak exponential separation holds outside an exceptional parameter set of codimension one. That exception is far thinner than in earlier results, strengthening prior work by the first author with Szvák. As an application, they give the dimension of self-affine measures on a generalized four-corner set. Shared fixed points occur naturally in many constructions, so removing them from the exceptional pile matters. The result widens the territory where fractal dimension is exactly known.
arxiv-2507-06035:
Ioannis Caragiannis, Zhile Jiang, and Stratis Skoulakis wrote this economics paper, published in 2025. It compares the two main ways to pay power producers in energy markets: pay-as-clear, where every winner gets the top accepted price, and pay-as-bid, where each winner gets its own bid.

The goal is to meet demand at the lowest total cost even when producers bid strategically. The authors prove two results. First, no pricing rule can beat both systems everywhere; for any rival rule, some market setup makes each of the two look better. Second, judged by the worst equilibrium outcome, pay-as-bid always caps prices below pay-as-clear. Simulations with learning bidders backed the theory, showing lower average prices under pay-as-bid in several settings. The paper speaks to a live debate in market design.
arxiv-2507-06135:
Federico Lanza, Gaute Linga, Fabian Barras, and Eirik Flekkøy ask what happens when a hot, thick fluid flows into a thin, cold gap. Their 2025 paper studies a flow effect in which cooling makes the moving fluid break into finger-like streams. They study a case where heat loss through the walls is weak but steady.

As the fluid cools, it grows more viscous, so warm parts flow faster and cool more slowly than cold parts. The authors build a depth-averaged model, run simulations in a flat channel, and use stability analysis to find when the fingers grow fastest. Their formulas show how the growth rate and the spacing of the fingers depend on flow speed, cooling rate, and the change in viscosity. The findings also bear on magma moving through narrow cracks and on oil films in machines.
arxiv-2507-06335:
Casey Kennington and David Schlangen argue for artificial intelligence that both understands language and connects it to the world. Models of meaning come in three broad kinds: formal systems built on logic, statistical systems learned from text, and grounded systems tied to perception. Each kind has strengths and gaps. Recent work adds visual knowledge to language models, and many researchers want to add symbolic methods, hoping to combine all three.

The authors champion one model, words-as-classifiers, in which each word is a small classifier trained to judge whether the word fits what is seen. That model is already built into formal and statistical systems and tested in live dialogue. They back it with findings from human thought research and report a small experiment of their own. The paper closes by sketching a unified account of meaning built on this word-level idea.
arxiv-2507-06435:
Rafiu Adekoya Badekale and Adewale Akinfaderin track how world climate talks changed their focus over three decades. Reading thousands of policy texts by hand is slow and misses links between themes. Their 2025 study applies a topic model that follows themes through time. The corpus holds United Nations climate decisions from 1995 to 2023, with 2020 left out since the talks were postponed that year.

Early texts stressed greenhouse gases and world treaties. Later texts turned to doing the work: putting plans in place, sharing skills, building local capacity, and paying for it all. The authors say the model scales well to huge text sets. They suggest the same method could track how language shifts in other policy fields.
arxiv-2507-06535:
Shan Shen and co-authors present a learning method for chip design in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Designers of mixed signal chips need early estimates of stray electrical effects, but design data are scarce and labels are uneven. The team aims to learn features that carry over from one circuit to another.

Their method, called CircuitGCL, learns from the shape of circuit graphs without needing many labels. It also uses new loss rules that balance rare and common labels. Tests on chip designs covered two tasks, one at the link level and one at the node level. The method beat all prior approaches on both tasks by clear margins.
arxiv-2507-07135:
François Gardères and co-authors build FACap in this 2025 paper, a large fashion data set for search by photo plus a text edit. The task, composed image retrieval, asks for pictures matching a reference image changed as the text describes. General models handle color and texture but stumble on fashion's fine vocabulary. Hand labeling by fashion experts is costly, so a big labeled set was missing.

FACap gathers web fashion photos and writes edit texts with a two-stage pipeline using vision and language models. The team also tunes a retrieval model, FashionBLIP-2, with light adapters and multi-way matching. Training on FACap lifted scores on fashion benchmarks, above all for fine-grained edits. The authors release code and pitch the set for online shopping search.
arxiv-2507-07335:
Ankit Jyothish and Ali Jannesari present a 2025 paper on giving graph learning models a better sense of shape. Graph transformers place every node in one flat space. Real graphs mix shapes, though: some parts spread like a tree, others cluster like a ball, so one flat space blurs them.

The authors add a light first layer that sends each node to the kind of curved space that fits its local shape. The choices include flat, ball like, and tree like spaces. Fed into a top graph transformer, this layer raised accuracy by up to three percent on four standard tests. The split also makes the model's view of the graph easier to read.
arxiv-2507-07835:
Maarten Boonekamp, Matthias Schott, and Chen Wang check whether a background process could be skewing one of physics' most argued measurements, in a 2025 paper. The mass of the W boson is a core test of the standard model. Most labs agree with the predicted value, but one recent result from the CDF lab sits far off, which has drawn fresh scrutiny of hidden biases. In the muon channel, Z bosons can fake the signal when a muon escapes notice.

The team built updated simulations and reweighted templates to test how errors in modeling that Z background would move the measured mass. The shift came to at most eight units of a million electron volts, more than the source's quoted error but far short of the full CDF gap. The authors conclude the background cannot explain the dispute, though it deserves care.
arxiv-2507-08035:
Anwei Zhang and Wang built in 2025 a unified quantum theory of how materials respond nonlinearly to electric and magnetic fields together. Earlier theories handled electric drives well but left magnetic ones piecemeal. Their framework uses thermal Green's functions and keeps track of how the field varies in space, a detail simpler theories drop.

Diagrams organize the calculation, and the team extracts general rules for the response coefficients. Applied at second order, the theory yields the nonlinear Hall effect and its magnetic cousin in materials with and without time-reversal symmetry. Both trace back to quantum geometric quantities, with a further share from the Zeeman interaction. The authors present the scheme as a base for hunting new effects. It treats light's push and magnetism in one language.
arxiv-2507-08135:
Chunxi Wang, Maoshen Jia, and Wenyu Jin present DARAS, a deep learning system that guesses a room's echo pattern from speech alone. Their 2025 paper targets room impulse responses, which capture how sound bounces indoors. Knowing them helps speech cleanup, recognition, and virtual sound, but measuring them directly is not always possible.

An audio encoder first pulls hidden features from the recording. A module built on the Mamba sequence model then estimates room traits without supervision. A fusion step blends sound and room features, and a tuning decoder shapes early echoes apart from late reverberation. Listening tests and scores showed DARAS beating older methods by a wide margin.
arxiv-2507-08235:
Smart buildings log mountains of sensor data, yet managers still struggle to learn why energy use spikes. Pinaki Prasad Guha Neogi and co-authors present InsightBuild in this 2025 paper, a two-stage system that finds causes first and explains them in plain words second.

A light statistical module tests which signals drive which, using temperature, heating settings, and occupancy from two real building data sets. A tuned language model then turns those cause links into short, practical explanations. Checked against expert-labeled cases, the pairing produced clear and precise accounts, helping managers spot waste and fix it faster.
arxiv-2507-08435:
David Munoz-Lahoz characterizes all f-algebra products on AM-spaces, in a 2025 paper in functional analysis. An AM-space is a type of ordered vector space with a norm that behaves like a maximum. An f-algebra product is a multiplication on such a space that respects its order structure. A classic result describes these products on spaces of continuous functions on compact sets.

For each AM-space, he builds a canonical new space tied to it. The products on the original space then match one-to-one with the positive cone of the new space. He also finds the unique product, when it exists, that embeds the space as a closed subalgebra of a function space. Spaces with that product get a name of their own. He closes with spaces that admit only the zero product.
arxiv-2507-08535:
Bipul Biswas, Prasanna More, and Hima Nagamanasa Kandula built bendy filaments that move on their own, and watched how softness decides their motion, in this 2025 physics paper. Living systems are full of active filaments, from cell skeletons to cilia, but most knowledge of single filaments came from theory and simulation because controllable lab versions were scarce. The team strung together tiny dielectric beads and powered them with an alternating electric field.

The field drives flows around each bead. Depending on the flow type, a filament either softened, exploring many more shapes, or stiffened, holding straighter. By tuning elasticity and activity separately, the authors showed that the contest between springiness and flow shapes the motion. Floppy filaments wandered by diffusion, while stiffened ones pushed themselves along directed paths. The platform gives physicists a hands-on model for the filaments that stir life at small scales.
arxiv-2507-08635:
Shining complex laser light into a nonlinear material creates new colors at multiples of the original frequency. Raoul Trines and co-authors explain that rainbow in a 2025 paper through the symmetries of the setup. Their earlier work used a beat wave idea to predict the spectrum of harmonics.

Here they show the same spectrum falls out of the full symmetry set of the laser and target. They also reconcile the two views, so each supports the other. The paper ties the story to classic results on crystal diffraction and to theorems by Noether, Floquet, and Bloch. Examples from past literature show the symmetry view applies far beyond one experiment.
arxiv-2507-08735:
Anna Rosenberg, John Kennedy, Zohar Keidar, Yehoshua Zeevi, and Guy Gilboa build in a 2025 paper ensembles of weak image learners for a PET CT task. Training data scarcity dogs many medical vision problems in practice. Their features come from spectral total variation, which reads texture at many scales.

The clinical task predicts hot uptake on PET from CT alone in suspected bone spread cases. Data hold 457 scans with 1,524 matched slice pairs across the set. Weak learners on those features vote as an ensemble for the call. The ensemble scored 0.87 on the curve test, beating neural nets at 0.75. Radiomics features landed between at 0.79 in the same trials.
arxiv-2507-09035:
Micah Warren proves a stability result for optimal transport on curved spaces in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. Optimal transport moves one smooth distribution into another at least cost. Smoothness of the best map can fail, and curvature conditions usually guard it.

Warren fixes a bound on the densities' log slopes and finds a whole neighborhood of measure pairs where transport stays smooth. The proof tracks a key second-derivative bound along a path from an easy case. When the slope stays small, that bound is trapped in one of two zones, and the path starts in the safe zone. So the bound holds all along, giving the result despite unhelpful curvature.
arxiv-2507-09235:
Matija Kocbek presents a 2025 mathematics paper building Ramsey graphs from geometry. A Ramsey graph avoids both large cliques and large independent sets. Explicit builds give concrete lower bounds for Ramsey numbers. The paper extends a known triangle-free family by Codenotti, Pudlák, and Resta. It also revisits a later generalization by Kostochka, Pudlák, and Rödl. A fresh proof bounds the independence number for the older builds.

For the wider family, lower bounds on independence are proven too. Parameter limits mark where better Ramsey bounds could arise, with the triangle case stressed. A linear-time algorithm finds large independent sets inside the family. On a large subfamily it guarantees half the best possible size. Combinatorics readers get both theory and a usable algorithm. Constructive bounds are prized because pure existence proofs give no graphs to inspect.
arxiv-2507-09935:
Hai-Toan Nguyen, Tien-Dat Nguyen, and Viet-Ha Nguyen lift search backed text builds by cuts of texts that match their build. Such tools fetch facts from out side for a language model. But plain cuts often split text into bits that lack a clear sense as one. Search grade drops when cuts snub how the text is laid out.

Their frame joins cuts in steps by rank with groups to make cuts that hold sense as one. At ask time it pulls with marks at both part rank and group rank. Tests on the NarrativeQA, QuALITY, and QASPER sets show gains next to plain cut ways. The team says cuts that heed build lift the odds of facts that are true and on point.
arxiv-2507-10135:
Santiago de Leon-Martinez, Robert Moro, Branislav Kveton, and Maria Bielikova present, in 2025, the first large eye-tracking study of how people browse carousel recommendations. Carousels, rows of themed lists that users swipe through, are now the standard shopfront of online services. How eyes move across them was largely unknown.

The team recorded free browsing and asked where users start, how they move within and between rows, and how taste in genres steers those moves. Their answers feed concrete design advice. The headline tip is to reorder ranked items after a swipe, matching the new positions to how people actually look. Designers get evidence instead of guesses.
arxiv-2507-10335:
Hypergraphs let one edge join many nodes at once, capturing group relationships that plain graphs miss. Jo Andersson Stokke and co-authors extend a core tool, the Laplacian, to hypergraphs whose node values live on curved spaces rather than flat ones. Many real data sets carry exactly such values, like directions or rotations.

Following the classic route, they define function spaces and symmetric products on nodes and edges, then derive the Laplacian from those. Earlier constructions handled only flat, Euclidean features. Their 2025 generalization covers many manifolds scientists actually meet, opening hypergraph analysis to fields from vision to robotics where curved data is the norm.
arxiv-2507-10435:
Xinnan Dai and co-authors open up the transformer to see how it pulls substructures out of graphs described in text, in a 2025 paper. Language models answer graph questions surprisingly well, but the mechanism was obscure. Focusing on substructure extraction, the team reads the model's layers through a lens they call Induced Substructure Filtration.

Experiments and theory together show the filtration view matches the model's inner dynamics layer by layer. The authors extend the idea to thinking in substructures, where bigger patterns are assembled from smaller ones, and show decoder-only models can extract substructures even from rich attributed graphs such as molecules. The work offers a concrete story for how sequence models reason over structure.
arxiv-2507-10535:
Hongchao Jiang, Yiming Chen, Yushi Cao, Hung-yi Lee, and Robby Tan benchmark how well language models judge code written by other models, in a paper from 2025. Model judges now rank answers for training and leaderboards, but coding had no dedicated test of their reliability. Three tasks anchor the benchmark.

Across code generation, repair, and test writing, twenty-six judge models were scored. Recent thinking models clearly beat non-thinking ones, and a small thinking model outperformed specially trained judges many times its size. Still, every judge showed real randomness: swapping the order of two answers swung verdicts. Reliability of model judging in coding remains shaky.
arxiv-2507-10635:
Nicola Assolini and three co-authors open the formal checking of variational quantum circuits, in a 2025 paper. Such circuits blend quantum and classic steps and sit at the heart of quantum machine learning. Like classic networks, they can be fooled by tiny input tweaks. No proof tools yet exist to certify their strength against such tweaks.

The team adapts interval reachability, a classic proof trick, to the quantum case. Quantum rules such as state normalization tie variables together in ways that strain the old trick. A fresh semantic frame lets the checking problem be stated cleanly and its hardness weighed. Tests on standard check sets show the approach can run in practice.
arxiv-2507-11135:
Selma Saidi, Omar Laimona, Christoph Schmickler, and Dirk Ziegenbein propose shared trust methods for autonomous systems in a 2025 paper. Self-driving and other autonomous systems must decide safely in shifting scenes. Systems nearby hold data that could help, but reports can conflict. Picking which peers to trust becomes the core problem.

Classical rules lean on consensus or majority votes. The authors instead weigh each system's quality traits, such as perception quality. Concepts from social epistemology guide how beliefs merge and spread. Only systems judged trustworthy steer the joint decision. Belief states are modeled with compact decision diagrams. Reduction rules shrink those diagrams for efficient computing. The frame aims at reliability in fleets that share data. Transport is the lead setting in the paper. The authors offer the rules as a general base for collaborative autonomy.
arxiv-2507-11235:
Andrey Boris Khesin and Tanya Khovanova survey ways that fans have stretched the card game SET. In SET, players hunt triples of cards that match or split on each trait. Math fans love the game for its clean group roots. Their 2025 paper sorts the known stretches by the rule that marks a winning set.

One family says a win set is a triple whose cards blend to the neutral card under the group law. A second family says a win set is three cards in a neat counting step, low, middle, high. Board size, card counts, and trait counts all shift with the group picked. The close weighs what makes a stretch fun to play: pace, hunt depth, and how often win sets show. The paper is a map for game makers.
arxiv-2507-11635:
Tamojeet Roychowdhury and co-authors test galaxy catalogues for chasing gravitational wave alerts in this 2025 paper. Wave detectors now hear many mergers, but each sky patch is wide and vague. Pointing small telescopes at ranked galaxies is one way to find the flash.

The team simulated the current observing run and used a large galaxy catalogue. Ranking galaxies by mass trims the search list, yet thousands still crowd each view at far distances. Deeper coverage fills whole fields with candidates faster than teams can check. Catalogues thus help most for near events, where lists are short and the catalogue is nearly complete. Tricks to fill missing galaxies are also weighed.
arxiv-2507-11735:
Gabriele Carcassi and Christine Aidala raise a basic question in 2025 about how chance should be counted in quantum physics. Quantum chance does not follow the classic rules, and past fixes use signed counts that can go below zero. The pair look at a different role of counting: tallying how many states a system can be in.

In classic physics, that tally shapes the whole setup of motion and space. When they build the quantum twin of that tally, it turns out not to add up in the normal way, they report. So chance rules built on it may need counts that do not add. The paper lays out the idea and its open puzzles for experts in such counts, hoping to spark joint work.
arxiv-2507-12235:
Saúl Fenollosa and co-authors measure how the radar cross-section of common targets changes with radio frequency. Their 2025 paper serves work on integrated sensing and communications, a 6G idea that joins both tasks in one system. Targets were a guided vehicle, a pedestrian, and a full size car, measured in two industry frequency bands.

Tests ran indoors and outdoors for broad coverage. The team removed background signals and used time gating to isolate each target, then compared values across bands. Results showed the cross-section shifts with frequency and with target shape in complex ways that resist simple scaling. The findings feed into better channel models for future standards work.
arxiv-2507-12335:
Models of the Sun must match three kinds of evidence at once: sound waves inside it, light from its surface, and tiny particles called neutrinos. Morgan Deal and co-authors test how the slow drift of chemical elements inside the Sun changes those matches. They ran two solar model codes and varied the rules for atomic diffusion in each. Extra mixing processes were also weighed, since plain diffusion fails to match how much light elements the surface has lost.

Added mixing fixes the surface problem but tends to lower predicted neutrino flows below what detectors see. A second effect, electronic screening, also shifts the neutrino match. The paper sorts out which choices keep all three evidence types in line. That balance is key to trusting models of other stars.
arxiv-2507-12435:
Yi Li and co-authors rebuild in 2025 neural networks so their causal answers come with honest error bars. Deep networks predict superbly but say nothing valid about treatment effects or survival curves, the quantities decisions actually turn on. Classical fixes bolt bias correction onto a fitted model, at heavy cost or with no guarantee the correction took.

Their framework, Targeted Deep Architectures, builds the correction into training. Almost all weights freeze; a small targeting subset keeps moving along a gradient distilled from the influence functions, the statistical directions that matter for the target quantity. The result aims at the classical virtues: protection against one of two kinds of model error, and efficiency when both behave. Whole survival curves, many parameters at once, collapse into a single universal targeting update. Benchmarks on a standard treatment effect data set and simulated survival data test whether the theory survives contact with practice.
arxiv-2507-12935:
Shirui Zhao and five co-authors speed up sampling based AI with a chip co design in a 2025 paper. The methods at stake, called Markov chain Monte Carlo, sample their way to answers for planning and inference. They cost too much for big jobs, and past speed up chips bend poorly to new tasks or waste gains at the system level.

Their frame first maps how compute, sampling, and memory should balance for each workload. It then lays out a chip of programmable tree units, reshaped samplers, and a cross switch for odd access paths. A new sampler drops the slow math steps of the classic one. Whole task tests beat central and graphics chips by wide margins.
arxiv-2507-13135:
Arnab Chaudhuri shows how heat fed scatters can strengthen early world phase shifts and their wave hum, in a 2025 paper. Some scatters grow as the world cools, a flip of the plain tale. Those scatters feed back on the field well that drives the shift in key ways.

Heat loop terms add a field mass shift that grows with heat grade. Shift marks like birth heat, stored heat, and span all bend in step. Wave hum tales from the bent shifts run more strong than plain tales. Next scope ears may catch those hums in their bands. Field well tales gain a firm heat source here.
arxiv-2507-13435:
Richter, Charlton, Fox, Sameer, and Wakker surveyed diffuse gas in the outskirts of four nearby galaxy groups in twenty twenty-five. Using ultraviolet spectra of bright background quasars taken with the Hubble Space Telescope, they searched for hydrogen absorption near each group's velocity along thirty-five sightlines passing beyond the groups' virial radii.

Absorption appeared on nineteen sightlines, a detection rate above fifty percent. The implied incidence of absorbers per unit redshift runs about a quarter above the general filament population and more than twice the diffuse forest value. Toy hydrostatic models put the gas densities in the same range as the general forest. The overdensity fits a picture where active galactic nuclei feedback lifts gas far beyond group boundaries, though the authors call for a larger survey and simulation comparisons.
arxiv-2507-13535:
John Holmes and co-authors settle when a new wave equation has solutions in a 2025 paper. The RZQ equation is a fifth-order integrable relative of the Camassa-Holm equation. Its nonlocal form resists the usual reading as a perturbed Burgers equation. Well-posedness was open.

For smooth enough starting data, solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on the data. That threshold sits at a sharp smoothness level. Below it, the problem is ill-posed and solutions can fail outright. The solution map is not evenly steady, though it stays Hölder steady in a weaker sense. The results give the young equation a firm footing for later study.
arxiv-2507-14135:
Alan Sherry and Sthitadhi Roy ask whether a strong form of thermal settling holds for quantum states that start out mixed, in a physics paper from 2025. For pure states, local parts of a chaotic system can settle into universal random patterns, a result called deep thermalisation. Mixed states blend many pure states at once.

The authors show that the pure-state picture fails sharply for mixed starts, even with a tiny amount of mixing. They propose a new form of the idea for mixed states. In it, the final pattern comes from a largest-entropy pattern on a bigger system, with part traced away. The shape depends on how much entropy the start held. In a solvable chain model, the new pattern appears exactly at finite times.
arxiv-2507-14235:
Adam Zhang and co-authors watch how community college students use auto grader feedback in a Python course, in a 2025 study. Five colleges' worth of submission logs let the team separate students who read the machine's comments from those who ignored them, a split earlier work rarely made.

Students who checked feedback more often earned higher assignment scores overall. A submission sent right after reading feedback also scored higher than one sent after skipping it. The authors take this as real evidence that auto grader comments teach, and they urge designs that get students to actually read them.
arxiv-2507-14335:
Nicolas Wischermann, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Gabriel Poesia, and Francesco Noseda pair a big general language model with a small specialist theorem prover, letting each do what it does best. Specialized provers are efficient but myopic; general models reason broadly yet cost a fortune to run at scale. Training a large specialist is more expensive still.

ProofCompass has the large model supply natural language proof strategies and, after failed attempts, pick intermediate lemmas for the specialist to try. No additional training is needed. On the miniF2F benchmark it slightly beat the specialist alone while using twenty-five times fewer attempts. The authors present the hybrid as a cheaper route to stronger formal proving.
arxiv-2507-14535:
Huang and co-authors build a statistical engine for learning the parameters of diffusion processes — systems that drift and jitter, from neurons to share prices. Their setting is a family of stochastic differential equations where a numerical splitting trick preserves the model's behavior and yields an explicit stand-in for the likelihood. The catch is computing that stand-in under realistic observation patterns: partial views, noisy views, or both.

The team recasts the problem as a Feynman-Kac flow and estimates its normalizing constant — the quantity needed — with controlled sequential Monte Carlo. Diffusion bridges patch the bias from slicing time. In simulations the method balanced cost and accuracy well, for single best estimates and posterior distributions. A neuroscience application showed it coping with a hard, real problem. For scientists fitting continuous-time models to discrete data, the paper offers a middle path between crude and unaffordable.
arxiv-2507-14735:
Vladyslav Bulhakov and co-authors test how to make a language model better at domain modeling in a 2025 paper. Software teams draw formal models of a field, such as medical data, before building systems. General models can draft them, but fine-tuning is costly and can erase prior skill. The team tries tuning settings and prompts instead.

Search-based tuning on a medical model lifted quality clearly over the base model. Carrying those settings to ten other fields helped in some but not all cases. Adding prompt craft on top improved nearly every field. Readers get a cheaper recipe for adapting models to expert modeling tasks.
arxiv-2507-14835:
Pan Peng and Hangyu Xu study how to share a network summary without exposing private links, in work from 2025. Their focus is cuts, splits of a network into two parts. They ask how many small triangle shapes cross each cut.

The authors give the first private method that builds a fake graph matching those counts well. Its error grows with graph size and with how many triangles touch a single edge. They also prove that no private method can do much better in the worst case. Both results extend to weighted graphs and to larger shapes. Such tools help analysts study social and other networks with less risk to the people in them.
arxiv-2507-15035:
Zhijun Zeng and ten co-authors released OpenBreastUS in twenty twenty-five, a large data set for testing neural wave solvers on breast ultrasound imaging. Ultrasound computed tomography rebuilds tissue properties from scattered sound waves, but solving the wave equation the classic way is slow and sometimes unstable. Neural operators promise speed, yet toy data sets flatter them.

OpenBreastUS holds eight thousand realistic breast phantoms and over sixteen million wave simulations made with real scanner settings. It benchmarks popular neural operators on both forward simulation and inverse imaging, probing speed, scale, and generalization. The team also reports the first in-vivo breast imaging done with neural operator solvers. The resource aims to move neural PDE methods toward real clinical use.
arxiv-2507-15135:
Parisa Tayerani and co-authors simulate how wall wettability steers bubble formation in fast water flow, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cavitation, where vapor bubbles form and collapse, can help or harm ship and turbine parts. The team varied surface water-loving to water-hating around a foil shape.

More water-hating walls sparked earlier bubble growth and thicker vapor layers. At mid settings, such walls fed larger vapor structures and stronger pressure swings. At the strongest setting, they instead held stable wall-hugging cavities that calmed loading. Surface choice thus acts as a passive control knob for flow stability.
arxiv-2507-15535:
Aso and Machida study how viewing angle affects signs of outflow rotation in young star systems, in a 2025 paper. The work uses magnetohydrodynamics simulations with radiative transfer and synthetic observations. A velocity gradient across the outflow axis is the usual sign of rotation.

In face-on-like views, the rotation sign was clear in standard maps and diagrams, matching past observational work. At lower angles, the outflow's own speed along the line of sight distorts the maps. The outflow axis can then be misjudged, and diagrams made with the wrong axis lose the gradient. The authors estimate rotation may be hidden in most outflows by angle alone. Complex real structures add further difficulty.
arxiv-2507-15835:
Diego Buccio, Gustavo de Brito, and Luca Parente tested a claim about higher-derivative gravity in twenty twenty-five. Such theories add curvature-squared terms to Einstein's gravity, a route toward quantum gravity. Recent papers argued that improved beta functions, capturing how couplings run with momentum at one loop, best describe the theories at high energy.

Using the background field method, the authors computed that momentum running explicitly in quadratic and conformal gravity — and checked its gauge dependence. Physical predictions should not depend on gauge choices, but the running they found does. They discuss what this dependence means for the theories' predictivity. The paper is a cautionary check on a fashionable calculational shortcut in quantum gravity research.
arxiv-2507-15935:
Csáki and co-authors solve a fine-tuning headache in theories that erase the strong CP problem, in this 2025 paper. The puzzle asks why the strong force respects a symmetry it need not. Mirror-symmetry fixes usually demand suspiciously perfect parameters.

Their twist lets a hidden sector's condensate do the symmetry breaking on its own. The model adds a heavy quark family and a scalar bridge to a dark copy of the strong force. When the dark sector confines, its pions double as dark matter with the right abundance, fed in slowly. The paper ties the old puzzle to modern confining theory.
arxiv-2507-16035:
Maxime Faymonville, Carsten Jentsch, and Efstathios Paparoditis wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about prediction for time series that take only whole-number values, such as daily counts. For continuous data, forecasters build intervals with a set coverage level. That recipe fails for counts, since the future value jumps between whole numbers.

The authors reverse the approach: pick sets of interest in advance and estimate the chance the next value falls inside. They then measure how unsure that estimate is. Both model-based and model-free estimators get theory, and bootstrap methods mimic their behavior under several settings, including when the chosen model may be wrong. Simulations and real datasets show how the method performs in practice.
arxiv-2507-16135:
Chris Bispels and co-authors published a 2025 number theory paper on covering systems, a puzzle Erdős posed in 1950. A covering system is a set of remainder conditions, each fixing a residue class modulo some number, that together cover every integer. The famous odd covering problem asks whether a covering exists using distinct odd moduli, all greater than one. It remains open.

The authors investigate a loosened variant: one odd modulus may repeat, while all others stay distinct and odd. Allowing a single repetition changes the landscape enough to explore, while keeping the problem's spirit. Such variants map the boundary between what is provable and what is not, and sometimes crack the original problem's resistance by showing which relaxation matters. Covering systems connect to deep questions about how residue classes can tile the integers. The paper is another probe at a seventy-five-year-old wall.
arxiv-2507-16235:
Listening posts that record wildlife soundscapes can track species health, but teaching a computer to spot one bird's call takes piles of hand-labeled recordings. Kaspar Soltero, Tadeu Siqueira, and Stefanie Gutschmidt build those piles by machine in a 2025 paper. Clean background sound is mixed with lone calls of a small owl, and the labels write themselves during the mix.

A model trained on the fake soundscapes held up well on real field recordings. Cutting the variety of source calls down hard barely dented the result, a sign the model learned the call's shape rather than memorizing samples. For ecology teams short on labelers, the recipe offers a way to train a sharp detector from a handful of clean clips.
arxiv-2507-16435:
Partha Kumbhakar and Varadharaj Ravi Srinivasan work on strongly normal extensions in this 2025 algebra paper. These are special field extensions in differential algebra, where fields carry a rule for rates of change. The authors study fields that sit between a base field and such an extension.

They prove that any middle field of this kind contains a notable smaller field. That field is either built from a nonalgebraic solution of a Riccati equation, or it forms an abelian extension after a base change. With this result they reprove and extend work by Goldman and Singer. They also study when linear equations can be solved and how solutions depend on each other.
arxiv-2507-16535:
Shang Liu and co-authors generate three-dimensional Earth scenes at continental scale in a 2025 paper. AI builders can now dream up small 3D objects, but stretching that to thousands of square kilometers of terrain is an open problem. Data and model design both had to change. The team tackled the pair together.

They first built the largest aerial 3D data set yet: fifty thousand scenes across the mainland United States. Each scene spans six hundred meters and carries many views, depth, normals, and labels. Their model then splits the job in two, compressing shape and surface texture into separate compact codes. Diffusion models grow each half, guided flexibly by maps, photos, or nothing. The split keeps computing costs sane at geographic scale.
arxiv-2507-16835:
Rumi Allbert and co-authors grade voice AI interview systems at scale in a 2025 paper. Automated interviews chain speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech into one voice. Each link can add errors, tone shifts, or awkward pauses.

Data came from over three hundred thousand real AI-run job interviews. An automated judge scored talk quality, technical accuracy, and skill assessment. Five live system stacks were compared head to head. One stack, pairing Google's speech tools with GPT-4.1 and Cartesia voice, led on scores and user ratings. Oddly, hard quality scores tracked user happiness only weakly.
arxiv-2507-17435:
Ye-Chao Liu and co-authors present a single toolbox for checking quantum entanglement in a 2025 paper. Entanglement links several particles so they act as one, but proving it in larger systems is hard. Past tools worked only for small or narrow cases.

Their method rests on a step-by-step gradient approach and gives both quick checks and strict proofs, with control of number errors. It handles systems of up to ten qubits and any pattern of links. On a tricky class of states, it closed the gap between known bounds for noise strength. It also set noise limits that older methods could not reach.
arxiv-2507-17635:
Kang Liu and Xiao-Mei Kuang study gauge symmetries in minimal massive gravity in two thousand twenty-five. The model is a three dimensional gravity with an auxiliary field. Covariant phase space methods frame their checks. Three gauge symmetries show up, with algebras that close by field reshuffles.

At a set parameter limit, a new transformation must swap in for the Kosmann derivative. That swap fits Wald's route to exact symmetries and charges. It opens a fresh way to build conserved charges in theories with helpers. The end charge mixes diffeomorphism and gauge parts in a nontrivial blend.
arxiv-2507-17735:
Qibing Bai and co-authors present a system that softens a speaker's foreign accent while keeping their voice, in this 2025 paper. Accent normalization aims to make speech sound native-like without erasing who is speaking, a balance that dubbing and language tools both want. Their pipeline works from discrete tokens learned by self-supervision, rather than from matched recordings of the same lines in two accents. That frees training from costly parallel data.

Speech is first turned into tokens, then converted by a dedicated model, then rebuilt into sound with a flow-matching synthesizer. Tests across several English accents beat a frame-by-frame baseline on naturalness, accent reduction, and voice preservation. A phonetic analysis at the token level backs the design. Two tricks for keeping the original timing suit uses like film dubbing.
arxiv-2507-18635: Mahesh Krishna introduces, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a noncommutative version of equiangular lines, sets of lines passing through one point with equal angles between every pair. Classic results cap how many such lines can fit in a space. He derives noncommutative versions of two fundamental bounds, the van Lint-Seidel relative bound and the Gerzon universal bound. Extending these ceilings into the noncommutative setting opens a fresh corner of line geometry for further work.
arxiv-2507-18735:
Agaev, Azizi, and Sundu compute the fate of a hypothetical molecule built from two heavy mesons. The pair joins a starred and a plain Bc meson into an axial-vector structure, a fully heavy four-quark state no experiment has yet pinned down. QCD sum rules are their tool for weighing such ghosts.

The two-point sum rule gives a mass near 12,770 million electron volts. That weight lets the molecule fall apart into several meson pairs, and three-point rules price each breakup route. Summed, the total width lands near ninety-three million electron volts. The numbers give experimental hunters a target and a lifetime scale to search against.
arxiv-2507-18835:
Enkelejd Hashorva studies in 2025 classes of random fields built by shifts, under a scaling rule for their measures. Random fields assign random values across space, and shift-built classes arise in extreme value work. Past study set extra demands on smoothness and local bounds that this work drops.

Each non-empty class is shown to hold a member with a strong continuity trait. That step proves a key integral stays positive for all class members and their local forms. The defining rule then extends to a wider set of measures, letting canonical members be built by random shifts. Links to tail fields close the argument.
arxiv-2507-19135:
Somdeep Dey, Abhisek Saha, and Soma Sanyal wrote this 2025 paper on a subtle effect in colliding atomic nuclei. The Chiral Magnetic Effect would separate electric charge along a magnetic field in the hot matter made in collisions. Two standard measures try to catch that separation. The team asked whether the measures can tell apart versions driven by two quark flavors versus three.

Using a transport model of collisions, they found both measures shift only modestly with flavor in mid-level collisions. Their power faded or grew with collision geometry and particle speed, limiting their use. So the team trained a neural network on final-state patterns instead. It sorted the flavor cases with over ninety percent accuracy, giving a firmer tool for the hunt.
arxiv-2507-19435:
Bernhard Schmiedmayer and co-authors combine machine learning with first-principles physics in this 2025 paper. Their goal is to predict a nuclear property that reports on the electric field inside a material. Getting that property right for disordered materials at real temperatures is hard for standard calculations.

The approach uses one learned model to act as a force field and run the atomic motion, and a second model to predict the field property while respecting rotations and shifts. Sampling driven by a thermostat lets the method handle hot, disordered samples. The team tested it on a perovskite material used in solar cell research. The predicted temperature of its tetragonal-to-cubic phase change landed close to the measured value. The result points to a practical route for predicting this property in complex materials.
arxiv-2507-19535:
Harry Holt, Sebastien Origer, and Dario Izzo compare two ways to train the neural controllers that steer spacecraft, in a 2025 study. One way copies expert flight paths. The other learns by trial and error, earning rewards for good moves over many test flights.

The team built a fair test rig for the trial-and-error route, with split rates for action and control plus a spread of rewards over time. Copy-trained controllers hugged expert paths closely but were capped by the quality of the paths they copied. Trial-trained ones coped better with random shocks and at times found routes better than the expert ones. Flight teams gain a clear guide on when each training style wins.
arxiv-2507-19635:
Zain Asgar, Michelle Nguyen, and Sachin Katti design a system to run AI agents at scale in a 2025 paper. Agents are fast set to be a top workload for firms and homes. Their work is not one call but a graph of steps: data fetch, model calls, tool use, and format swaps. Those graphs run on mixed gear, chips and graphics cards of many makes and tiers. The system must place each step where it runs best.

Three blocks drive the design. A planner shapes the graph with cost models for compute, memory, and wire width. A compiler splits the graph into fine ops and writes code per gear type. A live boss places ops across the fleet to meet a set service bar. Early reads show mixed old and new graphics cards can tie new fleets on cost. That find may stretch the life of old gear.
arxiv-2507-19735:
Jiaoye Du, Cezhong Tong, and Zicong Yang study differences of weighted composition operators between spaces of analytic functions in a 2025 math paper. Such operators mix a function transform with a weight, and the gap between two of them can be bounded, compact, or in finer classes. The authors first give a simpler proof of known results for Bergman spaces.

They then characterize when the difference belongs to the Schatten class, a scale that grades how fast an operator fades. The compact case on Hardy Hilbert spaces is treated as well. The work sharpens tools for comparing operator pairs across function spaces.
arxiv-2507-19935:
Young-Jin Sim proves that a pair of spinning balls of fluid, flying apart, hold their shape for all time, in a 2025 paper. The balls are Hill's spherical vortices, exact whirlpools of the Euler equations for smooth flow. The pair is set as mirror twins in a swirl-free, symmetric flow, each receding from the other. The risk is that their pull on each other warps or breaks the clean profile.

The proof leans on the pair's interaction energy. Kept small at the start, that tug leaves each vortex's own energy near the lone Hill value forever, and near-maximizers of that energy must look like Hill's ball. A center-of-mass track then prices each twin's speed, with an error bound the author shows cannot be sharpened. The result settles a clean case in the long study of vortex pairs, a bench case for harder swirls.
arxiv-2507-20035:
Thorsten Krause and Harrie Oosterhuis studied how people pick items from recommendation lists in 2025. A click does not always mean a true favorite; sometimes the picked item was just the best among weak rivals. Older choice models assume a fixed rule for how people decide, and a wrong rule can distort what shops learn about taste.

Their method learns the choice rule from data instead of assuming it, using a smooth density estimate. It recovers both what users like and how they choose at the same time. Tests show it can recover the true rule behind a dataset accurately. Better choice rules mean fairer credit for items that were shown but not picked.
arxiv-2507-20335:
Siyu Song and colleagues align educational language models to three goals at once: be helpful, be personal, and be creative. General models answer questions; tutors must guide responsibly, adapt to the learner, and spark exploration. Their framework, EduAlign, starts with a rubric-guided pipeline that synthesizes training data per subject, grade band, and task type. Scoring criteria and generation prompts are refined together, iteratively.

The data train a multidimensional reward model that scores all three virtues separately. A new multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm then optimizes them jointly, weighting conflicts and crediting marginal progress against an ideal point. On seven and thirty-two billion parameter models, EduAlign earned the highest mean ratings on every dimension, from experts and a model judge alike. It also topped the aggregate scores on three education benchmarks among compared methods.
arxiv-2507-20635:
Diffusion welding joins metals without melting them, and the joint is strongest when crystal grains grow across the original interface instead of stopping at it. Camille Godinot and six co-authors model that crossing at the scale of individual crystals, using a level-set method to simulate full two-dimensional microstructures under varied interface conditions.

They formulate two ways to measure how much crossing a simulation produces, then test and compare both against the simulated structures. The goal is control: knowing which process parameters let boundaries migrate across the weld line should help engineers secure the joint's strength and uniformity. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2507-20735:
Andre G Henriques and James E Tener settle half of a long-standing match between two ways to write quantum field theory, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Conformal nets and vertex operator algebras both frame the same class of two-way symmetric quantum theories, one in space-time terms and one in algebra terms. They were long thought to be two faces of one thing, but proof was hard.

The pair show that every conformal net gives rise to a unitary vertex operator algebra of its own. They also show that well-behaved representations of the net, those where turning the system yields tidy finite steps, become proper modules of the new algebra. One direction of the match is thus closed. The paper is pure math, aimed at readers in both camps.
arxiv-2507-20835:
Ganesh Teja Theertham and co-authors present a control method that changes its inputs as rarely as possible in a 2025 paper. The method, called minimum attention control, still must steer a system to its target. The team place it inside a rolling planning scheme that looks ahead, reuses the last plan, and also weighs how well the system tracks its target.

Their solver alternates between two steps: one step is a standard math problem, and the sparsity step has a direct formula. They test the method on a slow four-tank system and a fast fuel cell stack. Against standard model predictive control, their method gave far fewer input changes, at the cost of somewhat larger tracking error. The trade-off suits machines where each adjustment wears parts or costs effort.
arxiv-2507-21135:
Alexander Abanov and co-authors laid out a method in 2025 that reads data as quantum geometry. Their method, quantum cognition machine learning, encodes each trait of a data set in a learned Hermitian grid and maps each data point to a state in a Hilbert space. That translation is not storage: the data set inherits the geometry of quantum states, with a measurable internal size, a quantum metric. And Berry curvature worked out from the data itself.

Because the geometry is global, the method sidesteps the curse of dimensionality that afflicts local, area-based methods. The paper gives the method's full math exposition. It introduces a grid Laplacian whose eigenmaps embed data while keeping geometry, as a substitute for graph methods. It also shows how topological invariants such as Chern numbers can be extracted from data sets. High-dimensional data, they note, can be shown faithfully in small Hilbert spaces.
arxiv-2507-21335:
Monika Shah and co-authors probe how vision-language models handle questions that break the normal rules of polite talk. People cope well when a speaker says too much, too little, or drifts off point, though it costs extra thought. The team ask whether AI models that answer questions about images cope as well, in their 2025 study.

Extra words were added to hand-written questions from a standard image question set. Three top models were tested on the altered questions. Scores fell steadily as the extra wording piled up, unlike the grace people show. The authors say this gap offers a useful way to map where such models still fall short of human talk skills.
arxiv-2507-21435:
Jiaheng Wang and co-authors present MindChat, a brain-computer spelling aid, in this 2025 paper. Such spellers let people with severe motor limits type by brain signals alone. Letter-by-letter typing is slow, and decoding errors grow as words get longer.

MindChat adds a large language model that suggests words and full phrases as the user spells. The prompts are tuned so suggestions fit the context of the chat. In online tests across four dialogue scenes, users saved more than sixty percent of keystrokes. Spelling time fell by more than a third versus standard spellers. The team sees a path to practical daily use.
arxiv-2507-21735:
Han Tang, Bin Dong, Nanxiang Wen, Yidian Chen, and Danning Li simulated the chiral phase change of quark matter in 2025. Their tool is a soft-wall holography model with two light quark flavors plus the strange quark. In equilibrium, the model's phase map matches the famed Columbia plot in rough shape.

Instead of freezing at equilibrium, the team solved the live time evolution of the order parameter, the chiral condensate. That shows how quark matter settles toward balance after a disturbance. Near the transition zone, the settling shows odd behavior at middle times rather than a smooth glide. The study spans separate regions of the quark mass plane to compare settling paths.
arxiv-2507-21935:
Luke Paluso and Alex Kasman connect two corners of modern mathematics: exceptional Hermite polynomials and Calogero-Moser pairs. The polynomials belong to George Wilson's adelic Grassmannian, a space with two faces. One face speaks of differential conditions; the other, of Calogero-Moser pairs, pairs of matrices with a tight commutation rule.

Earlier work placed the generating functions of each exceptional Hermite family inside the Grassmannian by the first route. No one had tried the second. Drawing on the first author's thesis, this note gives a new formula for the polynomials written in Calogero-Moser terms. A theorem then uses the match to build explicit, finitely supported distributions that wipe the polynomials out.
arxiv-2507-22135:
Vanessa Dan studies random family trees in a 2025 math paper. The trees follow the classic Bienaymé–Galton–Watson model, where each person has a random number of children. Dan pins down two totals at once: the whole tree size plus either its leaves or its inner nodes. She asks what shape a huge tree takes under each double condition.

The leaf condition gives one universal limit, the same for every offspring rule. The inner-node condition splits into many outcomes, from one giant hub with most children on it to long stretched trees. Which outcome appears depends on the offspring rule's tail. Random walk tools and counting methods from combinatorics carry the proofs.
arxiv-2507-22335: Li Xia, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, studies games where each of many players runs their own chain of states. All share one aim: to keep the spread of their joint gains low. No player sees the others' states or acts. Since the spread aim is not a sum over steps, the classic step rule fails. Xia draws diff and slope forms for how the aim moves when a plan is nudged. He proves a steady pure best-reply plan exists, and gives a two-level tuning method.
arxiv-2507-22535:
Rishabh Batra, Zhili Chen, Rahul Jain, and YaoNan Zhang construct pseudorandom quantum states and function-like state generators with strong guarantees, in a research paper from 2025. Such generators must fool any quantum adversary, even one that feeds quantum inputs and adapts queries over time. Past constructions lacked one or more of scale, quantum access, or adaptivity.

Their isometric method prepares states that sit arbitrarily close to truly random ones. That yields the first generator with all three traits, from a standard assumption on one-way functions. Their quantum access notion is stronger than prior ones, since adversary inputs may be entangled with side registers. Many variants, from long input to classically accessed forms, follow.
arxiv-2507-22935:
Kathleen Mealey and co-authors test how well software can mine aircraft maintenance records in this 2025 paper. Airlines sit on rich repair logs, but the data is sensitive and full of trade terms. The team broke extraction into steps: spotting names, linking mentions, and pulling out relations. Sixteen language tools, old and new, were run against a public aviation failure dataset.

All trials ran inside a sealed setting, so no data left the building. Even the newest large models showed sharp limits on this trusted task. The authors weigh what keeps such tools from mission-critical use. They close with fixes to raise trust and release their test set for others to use.
arxiv-2507-23035:
Xueying Wu and co-authors present OASIS, a 2025 arXiv paper on speeding up large language models. The catalog lists the work under a different title, but the text itself names and describes OASIS. Big models eat memory and power when they answer, and shrinking their numbers to save space brings a trade-off. Plain shrinking either costs time to undo or blurs the model's answers.
