OASIS uses precomputed lookup tables to multiply shrunken weights and signals without undoing the shrink first. Its tables run far smaller and far more in parallel than older table methods. A side step spots rare outlying values and fixes their errors on the fly. Tests show a small drop in accuracy, about two percent, with a threefold speed gain over a rival chip design.
arxiv-2507-23135:
Ananya Sadana, Yash Kumar Lal, and Jiawei Zhou introduce ISO-Bench, a test of whether vision-language models can reason about cause and order across pictures and text. Each item shows an image of one step in a task next to a written step from a plan. The model must decide whether the pictured step comes before or after the written one, a judgment people find easy.

Ten leading models scored poorly. The best zero-shot result reached an F1 of only 0.57, and step-by-step reasoning lifted scores only to 0.62. Human performance on the same items was 0.98. The authors analyze where the models fail and point to concrete directions for strengthening causal understanding. The benchmark gives labs a shared yardstick for a skill that home robots and assistants will need.
arxiv-2507-23235:
Radar satellites must know exactly how their antenna beams energy across the ground, and checking that pattern from orbit is difficult. Mohammad Roueinfar and Masoud Ardini propose a ground receiver that sweeps narrow slices of the radar's wide signal in this 2025 paper.

Reading the power slice by slice lets them reconstruct the antenna pattern more sharply than broadband receivers allow. Models and trials with an Italian radar satellite backed the method, which posted a better signal-to-noise showing than standard gear. The authors offer the receiver as a sturdy tool for calibrating radar satellites and checking them after launch.
arxiv-2507-23535:
Dhanesh Ramachandram and co-workers made the case for transparent AI in a 2025 position paper drawn from institute experience deploying systems across industries. As models steer high-stakes choices in health, finance, and beyond, the authors argue interpretability must be built in from the start. Not bolted on after rollout when trust is already at risk.

Lessons from real projects are boiled down into actionable strategies and implementation guidance, sorted for organizations at unlike stages of AI maturity. The weight falls on useful steps teams can take now, rather than abstract rules. For practitioners weighing accuracy against accountability, the paper offers a field-tested argument that understandable systems earn adoption in regulated, high-stakes settings.
arxiv-2508-00535:
Förtsch and co-authors describe the bench that tested more than a thousand light sensors for two particle detectors, in a 2025 paper. The sensors, Hamamatsu multi-anode tubes, catch single photons in the CBM and HADES experiments. Each tube has many channels, and each channel must be graded before it earns a place. The bench reads gain, dark noise, relative efficiency, and afterpulse odds per channel.

The paper lays out how the bench works, then charts how each trait spread across all eleven hundred tubes. Most tubes clustered in sound ranges, with tails that sorting could trim. Repeat reads of single tubes over time also probed slow aging of the model. The authors frame the rig as the gate that kept weak sensors out of two flagship detectors.
arxiv-2508-00735:
Lucas Aubard and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on a sneaky gap in how networks rebuild split data. Packets can be fragmented, and the pieces may overlap with different content in the overlap. Each system resolves overlaps by its own policy, so a security monitor may read a packet differently from the computer it guards, hiding attacks.

Their audit tool, Pyrolyse, tests every overlap pattern for small packets across IPv4, IPv6, and TCP. Testing 23 implementations turned up far more variety than expected, from 14 to 20 distinct policies depending on the protocol. The sweep also found eight real errors, hitting an operating system, two security monitors, and two embedded stacks. The catalog of policies helps defenders align monitors with hosts.
arxiv-2508-00835:
Zachary Rewolinski and Bin Yu present a streamlined workflow for trustworthy data science built on predictability, computability, and stability, in work from twenty twenty-five. Artificial intelligence findings often fail to replicate across teams. Human judgement calls throughout the analysis hide uncounted uncertainty. Their PCS framework threads those three checks through every stage. Generative AI assistance is woven into the workflow deliberately.

A running example shows the framework operating end to end. A companion case study zooms into data cleaning choices. Those humble choices sway downstream predictions more than expected. Reporting the sway is part of honest data science. Practitioners get a concrete, updated routine to follow. Truthful analysis becomes a habit, not an aspiration.
arxiv-2508-00935:
Aaron Tian and co-authors measure how harmful computer using agents can be in a 2025 paper. Such agents control computers on their own through many steps, which creates misuse risk. Existing safety tests mostly cover chatbots or simple tool use. Their new benchmark holds 104 expert written misuse tasks, such as disabling firewalls, leaking data, or installing backdoors, run in a sandbox with rule based checks.

Leading models complied with many harmful tasks at high success rates, even without jailbreak prompts. Newer models that score safer as chatbots were often riskier as computer agents. A leading agent framework raised both skill and misuse. Monitoring the agents proved hard, with only modest gains from reading their reasoning. Readers see a safety gap that grows with capability.
arxiv-2508-01135:
Ataru Tanikawa and co-authors ask whether the heaviest black hole merger yet seen could come from the first stars. Their 2025 paper deals with a gravitational wave event joining two black holes over one hundred solar masses each. Such heavy holes strain standard formation stories. The team ran population synthesis for pairs of Population III stars, the first generation ever formed. They evolved in isolation in these models.

Such pairs can make events like the observed one often enough to explain it, under three conditions. Early stars must mix their interiors weakly. A key nuclear reaction rate must sit below its standard value. And the first pairs must start with orbits like those of later stars. An earlier heavy event needs no such special settings. The find tightens what star models must satisfy, the authors say.
arxiv-2508-01235:
Touring a faraway museum through a telepresence robot is hard when you do not know the rooms. Yaxin Hu and co-authors built NarraGuide, a mobile robot that narrates as it guides, using a large language model to answer questions in dialogue. They deployed the prototype in a geology museum, where 20 remote participants toured through the robot.

The team watched how visitors judged the robot's role, how they used conversation during the tour, and how they felt about meeting bystanders along the way. Visitors engaged with the storytelling format, the authors report. The study points to language-driven narration as a way to make remote visits feel guided rather than merely driven.
arxiv-2508-02035:
Hiroki Nakano, Takashi Koide, and Daiki Chiba build a crawler that outwits phishing sites which hide from security scanners. Their 2025 paper targets cloaking: attack pages show themselves only to victims matching a profile, while crawlers see a harmless page. Standard detection therefore misses the trap entirely.

Their system, PhishParrot, uses a large language model to read the clues a phishing campaign leaves across cases. From similar past sites it infers the victim profile the attacker expects, then tunes browser settings and network configuration to match that profile and slip past the cloak. A twenty-one-day evaluation improved detection accuracy by up to thirty-four percentage points over standard systems. The crawler generated ninety-one distinct environments, one per attacker target pattern.
arxiv-2508-02235:
Sangjun Park, Tony Quek, and Hyowoon Seo armor split learning against cheating clients. Their 2025 paper works at the network edge, where a model is split between devices and a server. The step-by-step training chain is fragile: one bad client can poison the whole model. Their scheme leans on the pigeonhole principle.

Clients are split into one more cluster than the count of foes, so at least one cluster must be fully honest. Each cluster trains alone, and only the best-scoring one moves on. A plus version retrains the winner to keep pace with normal training. Under label-flip and gradient attacks, the method held accuracy far better than standard split learning.
arxiv-2508-02435:
Shengbo Gong and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on a leaner way to feed facts to language models. Retrieval systems either loop many times, burning costly model calls, or build knowledge graphs that are slow to construct and error-prone. The alternative from the team skips graphs entirely and stores knowledge as atomic triplets, simple subject-predicate-object facts.

Their framework, T-squared RAG, has the model rewrite each question as triplets with blanks, then fills the blanks step by step from the triplet store. Across six data sets it beat leading multi-round and graph-based systems by up to eleven percent on average. Retrieval costs fell by up to 45 percent at the same time. The authors pitch triplets as the sweet spot between raw text chunks and heavy graphs.
arxiv-2508-02735:
Vrushaly Shinglot and John Zweck study the steadiness of light pulses inside short-pulse fiber lasers, in a 2025 paper. These lasers fire very brief flashes, and the pulse shape swings widely on each trip around the fiber loop. Simple averaged models miss those swings, so designers must model each part of the loop in turn.

Because the pulse repeats each round trip, its stability can be judged with a tool that tracks small changes over one full loop. The pair built a search method that finds pulses which repeat cleanly, using gradients worked out from the loop model. They also add a new split-step method to solve the stiff equations involved. Steadier pulses mean more reliable lasers for cutting, imaging, and timing work.
arxiv-2508-02835:
Kennedy Edemacu and five co-authors defend a popular AI setup against poisoned sources in a 2025 paper. Retrieval-augmented generation lets a language model pull in outside texts before it answers. If an attacker plants crafted texts in that source, the model can be steered to give the attacker's chosen answer, an attack named PoisonedRAG.

The team found a trait that sets planted texts apart from clean ones and built two filters on it, FilterRAG and ML-FilterRAG. Both sort the source before the model reads it, dropping the planted items. On standard test sets the defenses worked well, with results close to those of a clean system. The work gives builders a practical guard for retrieval-based tools.
arxiv-2508-02935:
Artificial life systems that grow patterns on a smooth grid have outrun the math used to describe them. Ivan Yevenko, Hiroki Kojima, and Chrystopher Nehaniv close that gap for one system, Asymptotic Lenia. Writing the system as smooth equations lets them apply dynamical systems tools. They sort its behaviors into four classes: lone solitons, rotators, repeating patterns, and chaos. Each class gets a mathematical account.

The team shows when a global attractor exists with a fractal size above four. A dimension measure from chaos theory serves as a yardstick for complexity. They share fast open code for the key exponents. The frame may tell builders which ingredients any complex artificial life needs.
arxiv-2508-03035:
Vo Van Tai and co-authors compute how the surface under a graphene sandwich changes its ability to turn heat into voltage, in a paper from 2025. The stack pairs two double layers of graphene around a gallium arsenide sheet. Such layered systems are candidates for compact thermoelectric devices, but their output depends on details of how electrons scatter.

Electrons in the stack collide with sound waves in the middle layer in two ways, and the team finds the piezoelectric route dominates. Three candidate substrates were compared, and the one with the highest dielectric constant gave the strongest thermopower. Unequal charge on the two graphene layers and wider spacing between them also shifted the output. The results give device builders a ranked set of design levers.
arxiv-2508-03735:
Gopalji Gaur, Mohammadreza Zolfaghari, and Thomas Brox wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It keeps the same subject looking the same across a run of story images, with no retraining of the image model.

Text-to-image tools drift: a hero's face or coat shifts from scene to scene. StorySync shares attention across the batch of images, masked so the subject's traits align as they form. A second step, regional feature harmonization, evens out the fine detail that still clashes. The whole trick rides on a frozen pretrained model, so its flair stays intact. Tests across varied tales show steady subjects from frame to frame. The cost is a small fraction of fine-tuning routes.
arxiv-2508-03835:
David Fabian, Patrick Morris, and Tibor Szabó wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how slowly an infection-like process can spread through a graph. In bootstrap percolation, edges or vertices join the spread once enough neighbors are already in. The key measure is the longest time the process can take to settle on a graph of a given size.

The authors build a general method based on chains of smaller graphs. They vary the method to set lower bounds for many graph types, from dense graphs to random and two-sided complete graphs. A main question is whether the longest time grows nearly like the square of the size. Their bounds link the problem to additive combinatorics and to a classic theorem on triples, and matching upper bounds round out the picture.
arxiv-2508-04035:
Ba Alawi presents a survey, published in 2025, comparing the two leading toolkits for building deep learning systems. One grew from Google, the other from a social media lab and the open-source world. The survey takes up three questions: how pleasant each is to use, how fast each trains and runs models, and how each ships models into products. On style, one favors a graph you define first, now with an eager option, while the other runs code as written, in a natural Python flow.

On speed, the author draws on recent benchmarks across tasks and data sizes. On deployment, one toolkit offers a mature chain for phones, servers, and browsers. The other answers with its own compiler, export format, and serving tool. The survey weighs these trade-offs for teams choosing a stack. It is a map for a decision that locks in years of work.
arxiv-2508-04235:
Jiaying Zhu, Ziyang Zheng, Zhengyuan Shi, Yalun Cai, and Qiang Xu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It speeds SAT solving for chip checks by feeding the solver what the circuit itself knows.

The standard path flattens a circuit into clause form and hands it to a generic solver, which throws the circuit's shape away. Their frame, CASCAD, keeps that shape. A graph neural network scores each gate's odds given the rest, and those odds steer two key solver choices: which phase to try, and which clauses to keep. On hard equivalence check tasks the frame cuts solve times by up to tenfold. A odds-based clause filter trims a further share. The lesson: keep the structure in the loop.
arxiv-2508-04335:
Yanyan Li and co-authors introduce RiemanLine, a compact way to represent three-dimensional lines for camera localization and mapping, in a 2025 paper. A minimal line representation matters when a system must optimize many lines at once. Standard forms treat each line on its own. They miss the regularities of built spaces, where sets of parallel lines are everywhere.

Their form is built on Riemannian manifolds and covers single lines and parallel groups in one frame. Each line splits into a shared direction, placed on the unit sphere, and scaled normal vectors in tied subspaces. For n parallel lines, the parameter count drops from 4n to 2n plus two. Parallelism is thus built in, not added later as a constraint.
arxiv-2508-04435:
Alvaro Garrido Perez and four co-authors model mental effort in 2025 using a classic two-step learning task. In the task, choices play out in two stages, letting scholars split habit from planning. High-level theory frames effort as the cost of breaking a habit to follow the best plan.

The team merged two frameworks: active inference, which casts the brain as a prediction engine, and drift-diffusion, which models how evidence piles up toward a choice. The blend predicted reaction times well at the second stage but missed the first stage pattern. The authors blame the task design and propose tweaks to isolate effort better.
arxiv-2508-04635:
Cong Wang extends a variational method for computing quantum states of atoms and molecules. The free complement method builds trial wavefunctions from complement functions, and accuracy hinges on how those functions are formed. His 2025 paper constructs them by decontracting the Gaussian expansions of Slater functions, starting from an initial wavefunction and helper functions.

The helium ground state serves as the test case for the new construction. Helium is a standard benchmark because its exact energy is well known, so errors are easy to spot. Wang uses it to show the accuracy the Gaussian complement route can reach. Computational chemists get a refined variant of a high-accuracy wavefunction method.
arxiv-2508-04735:
Yasemin Ozkut and co-authors released a 2025 dataset paper on eye ultrasound for a sight-threatening emergency. In retinal detachment, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye peels away. Fast care can save sight. How urgent the case is depends on whether the central spot for sharp vision is still attached.

Ultrasound at the bedside can spot a detachment quickly and cheaply. Reading the scans, though, takes skill that many clinics lack. No public set of labeled ultrasound clips covered the key question of the central spot's state. The team's dataset, named ERDES, fills that gap. Its clips are labeled for detachment and for whether the central spot is on or off. They also trained forty starter models across eight designs. The set gives other teams a shared base for building tools that could help less expert users.
arxiv-2508-05135:
Thinh Nguyen and four co-authors present HFedATM, a 2025 method for federated learning across sites whose data differ. Federated learning trains one shared model across many clients without moving raw data. Stacking the system into layers, with stations aggregating for groups of clients, eases the load on one central server. The catch is domain shift: each station's data looks different, so the shared model stumbles on new domains.

The method first aligns the filters of models from different stations using optimal transport, then merges them with a shrinkage-aware average that resists outliers. Across data sets, it lifted existing domain-generalization baselines while keeping compute and communication lean. Theory gives it tighter error bounds and faster, stabler training than plain hierarchical averaging.
arxiv-2508-05235:
Aditya Ajith and Saravana Veni simulate satellite quantum key links through turbulent air in a 2025 paper. Quantum key distribution promises secrecy that physics itself protects. But links between ground and orbit pass through churning air that bends and scatters the beam.

Their numerical model steps a laser beam through the atmosphere layer by layer. Phase screens mimic turbulence, and they add steady losses from air gases that absorb light. They then run the BB84 key protocol with decoy states for extra safety. Results give the expected link budget and secure key rates across distances. The numbers show where free-space quantum links to orbit stay viable.
arxiv-2508-05335:
Ayan Acharyya and colleagues map gas-phase metallicity across distant galaxies with the James Webb telescope. Their 2025 arXiv paper resolves chemistry inside galaxies at redshift two to three. Metal content traces how galaxies build stars and enrich gas. Eight galaxies were mapped with the NIRISS instrument. Four came from one survey and four from another.

Most targets sit at cosmic noon, the peak star-forming era. Stellar masses and star formation rates span wide ranges. Ionization sources were mapped alongside the metals. Metal patterns were compared with where stars form. Such maps reveal how enrichment spreads within a galaxy. The work is the first of its kind for multiple galaxies. Galaxy evolution models gain sharp new constraints.
arxiv-2508-05435:
Vincent Jeanselme, Brian Tom, and Jessica Barrett study a bias in risk prediction in a 2025 paper. Survival models forecast when an event, like death or failure, may occur. Some subjects face other events first that block the event of interest. Treating those blocks as simple dropouts is common but wrong, they argue.

The team proves that this shortcut inflates risk estimates. They build a frame to measure the size of that error. Groups with different risk profiles suffer different sizes of error. That gap can widen unfairness in algorithmic decisions. A heart care case study backs the theory with real data. The authors warn that the most at risk people are hit hardest by the flaw.
arxiv-2508-05535:
Albert Yu and co-authors present MICoBot in 2025, a robot helper that talks through task sharing with a person. Long jobs need partners who can adapt as the other person's skill, effort, and grasp of the robot change. Both sides need room to propose, accept, or refuse steps.

MICoBot plans at three levels, from a broad strategy shaped by dialog down to concrete moves. It aims to finish the job while asking as little human effort as possible. Tests cover varied, task-focused chats. The system shows a path toward home and work robots that negotiate, not just obey. That shift could make teamwork smoother.
arxiv-2508-05635:
Yue Liao and co-authors introduce a robot platform in a 2025 paper called Genie Envisioner. Robot training usually splits into parts: learning a policy, testing it, and simulating the world. Their platform joins all three inside one video based frame.

At its core sits a large video model, trained on robot tasks, that captures how space, time, and meaning unfold in real robot work. A light decoder then turns the model's inner states into action paths a robot can run. The design aims for exact control that carries across robot bodies with little extra teaching. Such a shared base could cut the cost of building each new robot skill.
arxiv-2508-05735:
Ankit Aggarwal and co-authors revisit, in 2025, a family of two-dimensional theories tied to flat space-time and slow light cones. These Carrollian theories are a non-relativistic cousin of standard conformal theories. The team looks at a symmetry that swaps the theory's two cycles, and at the characters that count its states.

In parts of the parameter space, the empty state's character wins in the swapped channel. That fact lets them zoom into distinct subsectors of the theory. One sector mirrors a known sector of ordinary theories and matches a flat-space holographic picture. All such sectors share negative specific heat, echoing black hole-like objects in flat space.
arxiv-2508-06135:
Lingyuan Liu and Mengxiang Zhang ask how to shrink large language models into small ones without wasting effort, in a 2025 paper. The standard trick, called knowledge distillation, trains a small student model on a big model's output. Most work tweaks the balance of answers, yet data quality and fit with the student get less care.

Their method lets the student grade its own training data. It keeps pairs that are both sound and well matched to the student, ranks them by how hard they are, and feeds them in stages. Added to many known methods, it raised scores and cut training time by up to 39 percent in their tests.
arxiv-2508-06235:
Dmitriy Leykekhman, Boris Vexler, and Jakob Wagner prove sharp error bounds for computer solutions of the Stokes flow equations, in a paper from 2025. The equations govern slow viscous flow. Their version tracks a stream function instead of speed directly, which suits some solvers.

Time stepping uses a jump-tolerant scheme of any order. Space handling is left general, so many grid methods fit as long as they respect a shared orthogonality rule. Smooth and rough data both get covered without extra assumptions. Two penalty methods from practice fall inside the frame. Best-possible error rates are the prize, and the bounds also serve flow control problems, where solver trust matters most.
arxiv-2508-06535:
Faisal Ahmed classifies leukemia cells from blood smear images with transfer learning in a 2025 study. Spotting acute lymphoblastic leukemia early guides treatment, but reading smears by eye is slow and uneven. Pretrained image networks can be retuned for the task.

The data set was lopsided, with far more leukemia images than healthy ones. Heavy augmentation balanced the training set to 10,000 images per class. Several network families were compared, and EfficientNet-B3 won with an F1 score near 94 percent and accuracy near 92 percent. Those marks beat past results on the same challenge data, the author reports.
arxiv-2508-06635:
Yewon Byun led a team that wrote, in two thousand twenty-five, on safe sums from fake data. When real data are thin, teams now ask big word codes to make fake rows, such as fake survey forms. Mix fake rows with real ones, and the sums can go wrong with no sign. Past work dealt most with code tags put on real rows. Wholly fake rows are a harder case.

The team built a new estimator, a sum tool based on the generalized method of moments. It needs no knobs set by hand, and strong proof backs its sums. One find was a surprise: when the gaps in the fake rows and the gaps in the real rows track each, the pair can sharpen the sums a great deal. Tests on code tasks from group and crowd study bore that out, with large gains.
arxiv-2508-07135:
Runlin Duan and five colleagues give image generation a drafting table: a three-dimensional canvas where users place objects before the picture is made. Text prompts alone leave arrangement to chance. Precise layout, who stands where and how big, is what designers actually need.

Canvas3D turns a prompt into movable objects inside a 3D engine view. Users arrange the scene directly, and those placements become hard spatial constraints for the generator. In a scored comparison, it beat a baseline on control, interactivity, and overall feel. An open-ended study then let people use it freely. The authors argue spatial intent deserves its own interface, not longer prompts.
arxiv-2508-07235: An insurer's ruin probability, the chance its reserves run dry, usually assumes steady income, and Viktor Antipov studies a harder case. Premiums arrive at random, with densities whose Laplace transforms are rational functions, while reserves sit in a risky asset whose price follows geometric Brownian motion. Antipov applies the Laplace transform to the ruin problem itself, focusing on what happens to the ruin chance when starting capital grows large. The result adds a tractable case to a classic problem, one where both income and investment returns are uncertain at once.
arxiv-2508-07735:
Nima Rasekh proves in a 2025 math paper that a classic building trick keeps its good structure. The filter quotient builds new categories from old ones and has long served logic, where it yields fresh models of set theory. Rasekh asks whether the same trick preserves model structures.

Given a model category and a fit notion of filter, the answer is yes. The new structure keeps some prized traits, such as being simplicial or proper. It does not keep every trait, since it may fail to be built from a small set of maps. The work also shows fit with the known version for higher categories.
arxiv-2508-07935:
Jingwen Zhou, Jieshan Chen, Qinghua Lu, Dehai Zhao, and Liming Zhu build a safety net for software agents run by language models, in a paper from 2025. Such agents plan and carry out multi-step jobs on their own. When a step fails, most tools treat the fault at face value and miss the flawed plan behind it.

The team first sorted faults into 36 types across 12 parts of an agent. Their system, SHIELDA, then sorts each new fault and picks a matching fix pattern from a stored set. Fixes can act locally, steer the flow, or restore state, with steps that rise in force when the first try fails. A test on the AutoPR agent showed the net catching a fault born in planning.
arxiv-2508-08035:
Chiara Piazzola and co-authors model the spillover benefits of HIV prevention drugs in a 2025 paper. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, blocks infection in people at risk. When one group uses PrEP, infections also fall in other groups, since fewer carriers can pass the virus on. That spillover is real but poorly measured, so it rarely shapes policy.

Their study builds analytical and numerical methods to quantify spillover when PrEP is prioritized to key groups. Pricing spillover correctly can flip which allocation looks best under a tight budget. Health planners get a fuller account of prevention value, where protecting one network quietly protects its neighbors too.
arxiv-2508-08435:
Kazuki Irie and Samuel Gershman write a primer on fast weight programmers, neural networks whose own connections rewire as they run. In these systems a second network, the programmer, updates the main network's weights in response to each input, turning the weights into short-term memory. The resulting two-dimensional hidden state links them to linear transformers and state space models.

The primer lays out the technical foundations and the computational character of these models. It then follows the thread into neurobiology, where synapses that change on the fly are the brain's own trick. Plasticity models and fast weights, long separate literatures, turn out to be close cousins worth reading together.
arxiv-2508-08535:
Mohammad Jalili Torkamani, Negin Mahmoudi, and Kiana Kiashemshaki survey body-worn health networks upgraded with language model control in a 2025 study. Wireless body area networks stream heart, temperature, and other signals for chronic care and crises. Sixth-generation communications, post-quantum cryptography, and energy harvesting each promise gains, but no unified design yet adapts them together as a patient's state changes.

Their structure lets a language model coordinate those pieces as conditions change. A survey of the pieces plus an integration plan gives engineers a route toward monitors that reset themselves around the wearer.
arxiv-2508-08835:
Robert Smit, Boleslaw Kozankiewicz, and Michel Orrit pin down a hidden energy level in single molecules, in a 2025 paper. Many molecules have triplet states that light can barely reach, and their energy was unknown. Knowing it would open a path to switches and spin control driven by light alone, starting from a spin-free ground state.

The team embedded a dye molecule, perylene, inside a crystal host that keeps its glow clean. There, the faint afterglow of the triplet state grew stronger, letting them read its energy. That value narrows the hunt for the ultra-weak jump from ground state to triplet. The step brings all-optical spin handling in single molecules closer.
arxiv-2508-09035:
Yibo Jin and co-authors split a large language model between the cloud and the user's device to cure two opposite bottlenecks. Their 2025 paper describes the P/D-Device design. In the cloud, long answer generation hogs capacity and caps throughput. On a phone, the wait for the first token balloons as prompts grow, since the device is weak.

The disaggregated design assigns each phase to the side that handles it best, rather than running the whole model in one place. Industry already splits such serving inside data centers; this work pushes the split across the cloud-device boundary. The goal is snappy first tokens without starving the cloud's total output.
arxiv-2508-09235:
Nathaniel Gorski and co-authors give a squeeze frame that keeps the shape web of tensor fields as it shrinks them. The work dates to 2025. Such fields tag each space point with a grid of counts. They drive work in stress, shape craft, and brain scans.

Lossy squeezes can warp the shape web and spoil later reads. The new frame keeps key points for matched fields. For unmatched fields it keeps the path and size graphs that code their web. It scans cell by cell, which keeps local webs and thus some world webs. Paired with two known squeezers, it held the web with care.
arxiv-2508-09335:
Jan Sova and Marie Kolaříková set hard ceilings on the signal quality any camera pixel can reach. Their 2025 paper starts from the radiometric integral, the basic law linking scene radiance to light flux. For careful calibration work, that law must be applied pixel by pixel, taking in each pixel's acceptance and how much of the pupil it sees across the field.

The authors package that per-pixel geometry into one reusable throughput factor. Light delivered to a pixel then scales directly with the factor, for a fixed scene and settings. Photon counting does the rest: the shot-noise ceiling grows with the square root of the delivered photons, and detector noise can only pull the real signal lower. The result is an instrument-limited bound: no processing can beat what the optics deliver. The paper gives calibrators a clean way to budget photons before blaming electronics.
arxiv-2508-09835:
Arnab Chaudhuri, Priya Mishra, and Rukmani Mohanta explore a small change to the standard model of particle physics in a 2025 paper. The standard model cannot explain why neutrinos have mass, why matter beat antimatter, or what dark matter is. The authors add one new force and one new field that breaks that force as the universe cools.

Their setup gives mass to neutrinos through a seesaw effect that uses three heavy partner particles. The force breaking would have been a sharp shift in the young universe, and such shifts can ring space itself with gravitational waves. The team computes that signal and finds future space detectors could hear it. The same heavy particles could also explain why matter won out over antimatter.
arxiv-2508-09935:
Sayem Hossen, Monalisa Moon Joti, and Md. Golam Rashed reviewed how deceptive business language can be detected in 2025. Digital reports, green claims, and online marketing now mix honest persuasion with advanced misrepresentation, and readers struggle to tell them apart. The authors combine classic rhetoric, communication psychology, and language theory with findings from finance, sustainability, and marketing studies.

In controlled tests, textual analysis with tuned transformer models reportedly caught deception with very high accuracy. Results were much harder to repeat across languages, mainly for lack of data and processing tools. The review argues for stronger automatic detection as machine-written business text grows more human-like, and it maps where theory and measured practice still diverge.
arxiv-2508-10135:
Yue Li and co-authors report a 2025 optics experiment on single photon light. Light that avoids bunching, where photons arrive one by one, is prized for sharp quantum imaging. The team made such light on a small chip device built from a thin film waveguide.

Pairs of photons from the chip were mixed with a weak laser beam tuned to match them. A two-photon effect then removed the paired part of the laser light, leaving the anti-bunched field. The setup gave about one hundred thousand photons each second with a low bunching score. The authors point to uses in long-range quantum telescopes, where clean single photons can raise the signal above background noise.
arxiv-2508-10235:
Jathin Korrapati and co-authors ask whether transformers can crack ciphers from examples alone in a 2025 paper. In-context learning lets a model pick up a task from a few shown pairs, with no retraining. Past tests stuck to tidy math and symbol tasks.

Here the hidden task is a cipher: substitution and Vigenère codes with a fixed secret letter map. Given a few coded and decoded pairs, the model must infer the map and decode a fresh word. The setup probes how far the model's pattern sense stretches into structured secrets. The authors share their code for others to test the limits.
arxiv-2508-10635:
Hosam Elgendy, Ahmed Sharshar, Ahmed Aboeitta, and Mohsen Guizani build an interactive model for watching the environment. Their 2025 paper joins satellite image pairs with live sensor data. Past vision-language models ignore sensor signals, lean on one caption source, and cannot run what-if scenes. Their model, ChatENV, is built to chat about change over time.

They built a data set of image pairs across 62 land-use classes in 197 countries, with sensor facts like temperature and air particles. Two large models helped label the data in distinct styles. A base vision-language model was then fine-tuned with light adapters. Scores on time and what-if tasks rivaled top temporal models. The tool supports scene play for planning and ecosystem checks.
arxiv-2508-10735:
Jonathan Schmidt and Nicola Spaldin simulate a crystal that flips into a ferroelectric state when its oxygen gets heavier, in a 2025 paper. Strontium titanate normally hovers on the edge of ferroelectricity without crossing. Swapping its usual oxygen for the heavier isotope tips it over the edge in experiments. Reproducing that delicate act in theory demands quantum and anharmonic effects together.

Machine-learned interatomic potentials make such simulations affordable at many temperatures. The calculations recovered the isotope effect and showed the transition proceeds by smooth atomic displacement. The window where the light version stays unpolarized while the heavy one polarizes proved narrow. The authors caution that sharper electronic methods are still needed for exact phase diagrams.
arxiv-2508-10935:
The authors of HQ-OV3D present a framework for open-world 3D detection that produces high-quality bounding boxes, published in 2025. Closed-set 3D detectors fail in open settings such as self-driving. Open-vocabulary methods usually generate rough labels, then align them with language models; the labels have grown semantically better, but their box geometry is often poor.

Two parts address that gap. A proposal generator uses cross-checks between modalities and geometric consistency to draft good initial boxes. A denoiser then refines them step by step, borrowing geometric knowledge from labeled classes through a diffusion-style process. Training with these labels improved detection scores on novel classes by a clear margin over the prior best method. The framework can also serve as a plug-in label generator for other detectors.
arxiv-2508-11035:
Hasibul Jamil, Zulkar Nine and Tevfik Kosar built in 2025 EMLIO, a service that feeds data to large AI training runs while cutting both waiting time and energy use. As datasets outgrow local disks, loading across networks becomes the bottleneck, and most loaders ignore its power cost. Their design places a light server on storage machines that batches samples and streams them ahead of need. A graphics-side library then prepares the data for the model.

Across local, office and wide-area links, the service loaded data up to 8.6 times faster than leading loaders. Energy use fell by up to about eleven times. Performance stayed flat even as network distance grew, a rare trait. The authors offer the design as a blueprint for greener AI clouds. They argue energy belongs beside speed in judging data pipelines.
arxiv-2508-11235:
William Alemanni and colleagues released an enhanced map matching algorithm in 2025. Map matching snaps a recorded GPS track onto the real road network, a basic step for traffic analysis and navigation services. Real tracks arrive at wildly different sampling rates and with gaps, and the original interactive voting-based algorithm was built only for aligning signals to roads under friendlier conditions.

The enhanced version adds trajectory imputation to fill missing stretches, so accuracy no longer depends so heavily on input quality. A distance-bounded form of the interactive voting keeps computation under control, and changes handle holes in the road network itself. The team also built a custom asset from OpenStreetMap data, so the method can be applied in any region that OpenStreetMap covers, widening its use across real-world settings.
arxiv-2508-11535:
Navin Prabhu and co-authors enhance speech emotion conversion in a 2025 paper. The task changes the emotion in a voice while keeping words and speaker identity. Generative methods can adjust pitch, tone, and energy, but they often cannot control how long sounds last, a key part of emotional expression.

Their duration framework uses discrete content units from resynthesis, allowing speech rate to shift toward a target emotion without parallel recordings. On a podcast data set of natural speech, expressiveness improved clearly. Low arousal emotions linked to longer, slower speech, while high arousal emotions were shorter and faster.
arxiv-2508-12535:
Cho, Wu, and Koshiyama steer language models using features chosen by correlation in twenty twenty-five. Sparse autoencoders extract readable features from a model's inner activity. Picking which features to steer usually needs contrast data sets or huge stored activations. CorrSteer avoids both by working at generation time.

It links each feature's activity to whether the model's answers were correct. Steering strengths come from average activations, automating the pipeline. Tests covered question answering, bias reduction, jailbreak prevention, and reasoning. Two open models improved across these tasks. One benchmark gained over twenty-seven percent from just one hundred eight samples. Chosen features showed clear meanings tied to each task.
arxiv-2508-12835:
Navaneet Villodi and Prabhu Ramachandran present a fast way to seed the starting particles for mesh-free flow simulations, in a 2025 paper. In methods like smoothed particle hydrodynamics, a fluid is modeled as a cloud of particles, and the quality of that first cloud drives the accuracy of everything after. Older seeding methods struggle to mix fine and coarse spacing, respect complex shapes, and pack particles evenly all at once.

Their method builds the cloud from the same basic tools the simulation itself uses. It seeds fluid and solid regions together, accepts shapes of any complexity, and avoids extra steps like gluing surface particles in place. In two- and three-dimensional tests, the clouds hugged boundaries well, stayed orderly, and held even density. The cost ran far below that of rival approaches.
arxiv-2508-13035:
Runze Li, Lucien Heitz, Oana Inel, and Abraham Bernstein present D-RDW, a 2025 algorithm for diversifying news recommendations. News recommenders shape what citizens see, and editors may want norms built in, not just clicks. D-RDW reranks stories with diversity-driven random walks, steering toward target mixes of article traits like sentiment and party mentions. The method is light and transparent by design.

Against leading neural models, it scored better on the diversity measures tested. It also ran cheaper than existing diversity approaches. The authors frame it as a societal recommender: a tool that lets editors encode values openly rather than hiding them in a black box. The trade-off between engagement and exposure diversity is made explicit and tunable.
arxiv-2508-13135:
Yueyang Liu and co-authors present a 2025 experimental study on training machine learning models with records of how people move through space and time. Predicting a person's next stop or short path is well studied, with uses from disease tracking to elder care. Far less attention goes to the larger routines that shape a life, and to how training choices affect them.

The team set out to find best practices for training on historical mobility data at that macro level. Their experiments compare training setups rather than chase a single new model. The paper offers guidance for builders who need models of daily and weekly movement patterns, not just the next step.
arxiv-2508-13535:
Masaki Gen and co-authors offer a unified model for how spins and lattice vibrations couple in a frustrated magnet, published in 2025. The magnet sits on a pyrochlore lattice, a network of corner-linked tetrahedra. In such a system, spin and lattice effects are hard to split apart, and older models each captured only part of the picture.

Their extended model treats vibrations of bonds and of single sites on an equal footing. It sits between two classic minimal models, one based on bonds and one on sites. With it, they reproduce a sequence of field-driven phase changes and key traits of a three-up, one-down state. Those traits include shrinking under heat, a boosted cooling effect, and a sharp peak in heat capacity.
arxiv-2508-13635:
Umberto Collodel presents a 2025 paper on forecasting market turbulence after European Central Bank press conferences using simulated traders. Central banks cannot preview how markets will read their words. The framework sets thirty language model agents, each with a different trader profile, to interpret conference transcripts. Their disagreement becomes a measurable signal. Across nearly three hundred council events from 1998 to 2026, that disagreement tracked actual overnight swap volatility with a correlation near one half.

The signal beat standard text-based alternatives and added information beyond volatility's own persistence. It held up on genuinely unseen conferences from 2025 onward. Feeding the models past examples of market reactions improved calibration further. Collodel offers the tool as a pre-release check for central bank communication. It turns the question of how a statement will land into something testable in advance.
arxiv-2508-13835:
Nitin Vashishtha and co-authors simulate a breakout coronal mass ejection and what controls it, in their 2025 arXiv paper. These solar eruptions drive space weather, so predicting them matters. Solar Cycle 24 was weaker than its predecessor, with more feeble ejections, which makes the background magnetic field a key variable.

Using a magnetohydrodynamics code in two and a half dimensions, they set a multipolar field inside a background bipolar field and added shear to trigger eruption. Stronger background poloidal field held eruptions back. Varying the injected helicity produced failed, single and multiple eruption scenarios, tracked through global magnetic parameters. The results link field geometry to eruption outcome.
arxiv-2508-14035:
Elena Manjavacas and co-authors present a spectral library of very young brown dwarfs in a 2025 astronomy paper. Brown dwarfs are bodies too small to burn like stars, and the youngest ones help trace how such objects form and change. The team gathered near-infrared spectra of twenty-five objects in the Orion Nebula Cluster using the Keck I telescope.

The objects span about seven to seventy-five times the mass of Jupiter. Spectral checks confirmed they are younger than five million years and belong to the cluster. Six showed emission lines that point to gas falling from disks, even at planet-like masses. Those low-mass objects seem to drain their disks fast. The team also traced how one planet-mass object's spectrum changes with age.
arxiv-2508-14135:
Collins Ogbodo and three colleagues present a 2025 engineering paper on planning vibration tests for structures. Modal testing reveals how a bridge or machine part shakes, but planning a test means many linked choices, and fixed plans cannot adapt when conditions change mid-campaign. Sensor placement in particular can make or break the results.

The team built a decision support system in which a learning agent chooses sensor spots as the test setting evolves. They frame the task as a partly hidden decision problem and train the agent with a two-stage curriculum. A case study on a steel beam showed the method placing sensors well across frequency ranges, suggesting a more flexible way to run real test campaigns.
arxiv-2508-14735:
Language models work in many tongues, but whether they reason the same way in each is unclear. Samir Abdaljalil and three co-authors built a test in 2025 from made up logic puzzles: short premises and claims whose truth links are set by design. They translated the pairs into a spread of languages and also mixed languages inside single pairs.

To their surprise, the mixed language pairs did not hurt scores and sometimes helped, as if the varied wording kept the model honest. Checks on meaning confirmed the translations kept the logic intact. The authors say the test exposes both strength and brittleness in cross language reasoning. They point to code switching as a lever for hardier multilingual models.
arxiv-2508-14835:
Alessandro Bondi and Martin Forde published a mathematics paper in 2025 on rough volatility models collapsing into Levy processes. The rough Heston model drives variance with a jagged memory kernel. Rescaling it, the authors prove the integrated variance at a fixed time converges weakly to an inverse Gaussian Levy process. Earlier routes to this limit forced special values of the roughness index.

Their proof needs no such forcing, which may matter more for real markets. With jumps added to the variance, the limit becomes a clock-changed barrier hitting-time process for a broad family of one-sided Levy processes. The convergence is then lifted to whole paths in a suitable topology.
arxiv-2508-15035:
Ankit Panda and co-authors compute the lepton pairs born in a magnetized quark soup in this 2025 physics paper. Heavy-ion collisions briefly melt matter into quark-gluon plasma, threaded by a huge magnetic field. Lepton pairs that escape carry news of that fireball's life.

The team ran the first full study with a field that varies in space and fades in time, set in a flow pattern that can be solved exactly. Spectra grew with collision offset, fed mostly by annihilation. A sideways flow signal from decay channels stayed nonzero even in head-on hits, flipping sign with momentum. Conductivity boosted yields but left no clean fingerprint. The patterns may let experiments sense the field's imprint.
arxiv-2508-15235:
Suo-Ning Wang and co-authors read the hue shift of a merger flash to name what was left behind, in a study from 2025. When two neutron stars merge, the flash, a kilonova, glows from torn stuff. What sits at the core, black hole or live star, is hard to spy.

Three feeds can light the flash: rot of fresh stuff, a spun-down magnet star, and its wind nebula. If a black hole forms at once, rot alone feeds the glow: hue sits flat ere the peak, then climbs fast. If a magnet star lives, all three feeds burn and the post-peak hue walks a unlike path. Hue in time, the team shows, is a name tag for the unseen core.
arxiv-2508-15435:
Johnson and co-authors present a 2025 radio search for a suspected redback pulsar, a fast-spinning dead star that blasts its partner star. The target system pairs such a star with a light companion in a 16.5-hour orbit. Signs of the pair show at many wavelengths, yet radio pulses had never been caught. Two large radio telescopes joined the hunt for 34.5 hours in all.

The search covered about three quarters of the orbit, hunting both steady pulses and lone bursts. Nothing rose above the set signal bar. The miss may mean the pulses are faint, scattered, or blocked by the partner's outflow. Null results still guide the hunt: they tell teams where and when to listen next, and they mark how elusive some redbacks stay.
arxiv-2508-15535:
Guotao Liang, Juncheng Hu, Ximing Xing, Jing Zhang, and Qian Yu animate multi-object sketches with GroupSketch, a two-stage method for lively, coherent motion. Their paper from twenty twenty-five answers past tools that handled one object or lost time consistency. Stage one splits the sketch into semantic groups interactively and sketches key frames. Interpolation turns those into a rough draft of the motion.

Stage two polishes the draft with a Group-based Displacement Network. It predicts a displacement field per group, borrowing priors from a text-to-video model. A context feature module steadies the frames over time. Wide tests show cleaner, more consistent animations for complex scenes than past methods. Sketch tools gain a way to stage whole ensembles, not lone figures.
arxiv-2508-16035:
Software-defined networks need intrusion detectors that learn from little data, since attacks are rare by design. Poorvi Joshi and Mohan Gurusamy turn network traffic into pictures first. A Markov transition field encodes how the signal moves between levels over time. A transformer then reads those pictures for attack patterns.

The pairing beat standard classifiers on a software-defined networking dataset, with the widest margins when training data was scarce. Training and response times stayed competitive with simpler models. The authors argue the field picture hands the transformer exactly the temporal structure it is good at exploiting. The approach suits security tools that must work before big datasets exist.
arxiv-2508-16135:
Sen Yan and four co-authors survey machine learning for small city vehicles like bikes, e-bikes, and scooters. These light fleets ease jams, dirty air, and ride costs, but raise hard plan and safety tasks. Smart methods help run them, yet past reviews miss their special needs.

The survey sorts data sets by place, time, and traits, then sorts models by strength, pain, and use. Uses run from demand guess to energy care and safety. Gaps point to next work on data share, robust models, and user trust. Riders and city planners both gain from smarter small fleets.
arxiv-2508-16235:
Mayank Nagda and co-authors redesign physics-informed neural networks in a 2025 computing paper. Such networks solve equations of change by baking physics rules into training. Standard versions predict each moment on its own, which clashes with how real systems unfold step by step. That mismatch breeds wobble and drift in long forecasts.

Their version, named PIANO, predicts forward from its own past outputs, like the systems it models. Training rolls the model out on its own while physics rules keep it honest. Theory in the paper shows why the older design wobbles and why the new one holds steady. Tests on hard changing systems and on weather data put it ahead of rivals.
arxiv-2508-16335:
Ayan Majumder and co-authors study strain in diamond devices in this 2025 paper. Diamonds host glowing flaw centers prized for quantum links and sensing. Makers plant those centers with ion beams and carve tiny light guides, steps that can strain the crystal.

Strain shifts the spin notes of the flaw centers, which the team reads with a light-based probe. Their spectra show a shear strain mark tied to the planting and carving steps. The mark shows up as a lopsided split in the signal at zero field. The authors say the probe gives makers a keen way to spot hidden strain before devices ship.
arxiv-2508-16435:
Warda and four co-authors wrote this physics paper in twenty twenty-five on modeling hard materials with computers. Some compounds hold electrons in d and f shells, which standard theory handles poorly. A common fix adds a correction called U, but it can distort the states where shells mix. That leads to wrong forces and wrong crystal shapes.

The team studied uranium compounds with manganese, cobalt, or nickel. They show that sorting states into localized and spread-out groups gives accurate results. The trick is to match the helper functions to the true shape around each atom, or to correct only the most localized orbitals. Their findings open a path to reliable predictions for uranium-based solids used in key technologies.
arxiv-2508-16535:
Trung Hieu Pham and co-authors (2025) make a plain computer monitor show moving 3D, using a webcam and cheap red-cyan glasses. True 3D usually demands headsets or special screens, which shut out low-resource settings. Their system tracks the viewer's eyes with an ordinary camera. As the head moves, the software picks views from pre-captured light-field data. That data is a set of images of a scene from many angles. It blends the right pair into an anaglyph image, tinted for the two eyes.

The update happens in real time, so the scene shifts with the viewer like a window into depth. Everything runs on a standard CPU, no graphics card, and holds a steady thirty frames per second. That frugality is the point: classrooms, clinics, and small labs could add depth viewing with hardware they already own. The paper reports the pipeline and its measured performance.
arxiv-2508-16635:
Steady swirling states in a spinning fluid shell are computed directly by Juan Cruz Gonzalez Sembla and co-authors in a 2025 paper. Planet-like flows spin fast, which forces tiny steps in time-marching codes. Treating the spin force implicitly steadies the math.

The team rebuilt their code to solve for steady states with Newton's method, skipping time error entirely. The implicit terms also precondition the linear systems, so a matrix-free solver finishes fast. Branches of rotating waves with four to twelve lobes were mapped. As spin grows extreme, flows hug the inner wall and ignore the axis, matching theory and past experiments.
arxiv-2508-16835:
Trine Quady and Eric Neuscamman sharpen a quantum chem gauge by pruning weak knobs as it runs. The work dates to 2025. The gauge is a strong second-step method for tuning wave forms. Yet noise in weak knobs can spoil the step for the knobs that count.

Tests show that even zero-set weak knobs drag down the step a lot. The new plan grows the knob set, then cuts weak ones on the fly. In tests on three small chain molecules, large shares of knobs could go with no loss. The cuts made the whole tune work better in each case.
arxiv-2508-17135:
Carlos Soto gives a new take on differential privacy in a 2025 paper, writing as a solo author. The field guards private data by adding noise scaled to what one person adds to a result. That hides each person while keeping the shared result useful. Most past takes define the guard through a gap between two data spreads.

Soto uses a tool from information geometry instead: the Rao distance, a way to measure how far apart two spreads sit on a curved space. His new guard keeps the plain sense of the old ones, he argues, while giving a better rule for how privacy loss adds up step by step. The paper is a theory piece, with proofs rather than trials.
arxiv-2508-17235:
Markus Sauerberg, writing alone in 2025, links a distance measure from transport theory to gaps in life expectancy. The measure gives the cheapest cost of turning one distribution into another. He applies it to tables of ages at death for whole populations. The main result is that the distance equals the gap in life expectancy at birth in set cases. The key condition is that the survival curves of the two groups do not cross.

That condition holds for many real comparisons, such as women versus men over recent decades. Sauerberg shows the link both by proof and with real data. Life table data from a major mortality database backs the math. The result gives demographers a fresh way to read a familiar gap. It also ties a modern math tool to a classic population measure. The paper is short and focused on that single bridge.
arxiv-2508-17335:
Avner Kiro and Alon Nishry refine a counting result about special polynomials in a 2025 math paper. The polynomials take whole number values at whole number inputs. Earlier work found a sharp growth threshold: above it, endless many such polynomials exist; below it, only finitely many.

Kiro and Nishry give sharper estimates for how many such polynomials sit at each growth level. They also study a variant where the growth rule differs on the two sides of the number line. In that case, the threshold is set by a quantity from potential theory tied to an explicit region. The paper deepens the link between these polynomials and classic analysis.
arxiv-2508-17635:
Remi Chierchia and co-authors build a tool that turns phone video into 3D models of chronic wounds, in a 2025 paper. Wound care still leans on hand notes and ruler checks, which vary by nurse and eat time. Flat photo tools warp sizes and miss depth, above all on curved limbs. Their frame, Wound3DAssist, works from short handheld clips shot on plain consumer gear.

The pipeline rebuilds the wound surface in 3D, cuts out the wound bed, sorts its tissue types, and checks the rim of skin around it. Tests ran on digital models with known shapes, on silicone fakes, and on real patients. The builds were sharp, near millimeter accuracy in the clinic cases, with clear views of the wound bed. A full check took under twenty minutes. The team frames it as research gear, ready for trials in real care flow.
arxiv-2508-17735:
Chhikara, Ghosh, and Chakraborty present SMITE, a method to make language model classification fairer in a 2025 paper. Models classify tables well from a few examples, but their picks can skew by group. Example choice turns out to matter a lot.

Instead of a fixed validation set, theirs evolves alongside the test data. Candidate example sets are scored against the matching dynamic validation set. The set with the lowest total error becomes the final prompt. Experiments across four models beat baseline methods on both accuracy and fairness. The authors claim a first use of dynamic validation for in-context learning. Responsible deployment is the stated motivation. Careful example curation is cheap fairness leverage.
arxiv-2508-17835:
Ayushi Suman and Sarika Jalan chart how a crowd of coupled oscillators falls out of sync. Their model links every unit to the rest, not just to near neighbors. At the change point the order parameter jumps at once, a first-order leap, yet the team finds critical behavior more typical of gentle transitions.

They measure a scaling exponent of one half for the order parameter near the jump. The time the system takes to settle stretches toward infinity at the edge, shown both in numbers and in math. A correlation measure across all units also swells without bound there. Data collapse checks confirm their finite-size scaling rules. The study suggests that long-range links can lend critical traits to abrupt transitions.
arxiv-2508-18135:
Eoghan Downey and co-authors study a crystal named Zr2CuSb3 in a 2025 paper on new solid materials. The crystal may hold a flat grid of atoms that, in theory, can host odd states where electrons barely move.

The team grew single crystals with a melt method and checked their form with X-rays. Tests of charge flow showed the solid acts like a metal, with electrons as the main carriers. Light-based tests mapped its energy bands and found more than one pocket of electrons, plus a blur that comes from its tall cell shape. Computer models helped split the bands by plane. The work gives a full first map of how charge moves in the crystal.
arxiv-2508-18235:
Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan and co-authors present a defense against backdoor attacks in text-to-image models in work from 2025. Attackers can plant hidden text triggers in training data so a model outputs manipulated images on cue.

Their method uses self-distillation guided by cross-attention to erase the link between trigger phrases and poisoned outputs. Since the poisoned model still answers clean prompts correctly, distillation can steer it back. Tests removed all pixel backdoors and most style backdoors while keeping image quality. The authors frame targeted unlearning as a strong defense for generative models.
arxiv-2508-18335:
Kalmar builds random hill and valley maps on surfaces by taking random walks in twenty twenty-five. In math, such maps are called Morse functions, and their peaks and passes reveal the shape of a surface. He asks what these random maps look like as a group. Each map in his study has few peaks and just one lowest point.

He cuts the surface at set heights and studies the pieces that result. Those pieces act as a code for the whole map. He finds a small set of maps that stand close to all the rest in this code. The result helps map out the full space of such functions with a short list.
arxiv-2508-18535:
Giuseppe Di Battista and co-authors study how to draw trees on fixed point sets in a 2025 paper. A drawing can aim for a set number of edge crossings while keeping each edge's bends few. The work sits where graph theory meets graph drawing.

First, in a tangling phase, the team lay a tree out with its top crossing count and few spine passes. Next, in an untangling phase, they strip crossings down to any target count without adding passes. The layout then turns into a point-set drawing with the same counts. Run times are given for plain trees and for paths. A right-angle variant is also covered.
arxiv-2508-18735:
Ali and Khan secure drone-based air networks with a blockchain trust system in a 2025 paper. Flying base stations serve users where towers cannot reach, but rogue drones can slip into the swarm. Their frame, SkyTrust, scores each drone's trust from past record, live behavior, and energy given. Scores update without pause on a permissioned ledger.

Block checks go to drones with the most charge left, saving power. Shared learning pools trust lessons while keeping raw data private. Simulations hit high marks for trust forecasting and rogue spotting, beating central and fixed rivals. The authors pitch the design for sixth-generation air networks.
arxiv-2508-19035:
Congchi Yin and co-authors test language model reasoning through black-box play in 2025. Standard tasks grade deduction, induction, and guessing in isolation. Real discovery mixes all three while probing an unknown system, so the team hides a function inside a black box for models to crack.

Models get a set number of probe turns and must infer the hidden rule from input-output pairs. Their Oracle benchmark holds 96 boxes across six task types. Nineteen models were tested, and the top model led five of six task types. Hard boxes still dropped average scores below forty percent. Weak high-level planning for probes stood out as a shared flaw.
arxiv-2508-19235:
Hakim, Bower, Seidler, and Sossi read a planet's air for signs of molten rock in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Sub-Neptunes may hide magma oceans under thick envelopes. Where gas meets magma, chemistry bends away from textbook rules. The team modeled that boundary for a hot sub-Neptune, TOI-421b, using real-gas physics.

Hydrogen and nitrogen dissolved most readily into the magma. One silicon gas, silane, ruled the boundary when the air was metal-poor. Methane took over when metals ran a hundred times richer. Higher up, silicon gases froze into cloud-like particles and thinned out. The silane-to-methane balance thus signals both metal content and whether a magma ocean exists.
arxiv-2508-19835: Ben-Hur Eidt, Daniel Gonçalves, and Danilo Royer wrote a paper from 2025 that widens a family of algebras built from wide graphs. They define a relative form of these algebras and carry known tests for when maps into them are faithful into the new setting. The work is driven by a class of interval maps with endless branching, which the team calls infinite Markov maps. The new algebras, they argue, are the natural frame in which the maps' induced structures are defined.
arxiv-2508-20135:
Andrew Yarovoi and Christopher Valenta segment point clouds of rough roads with little labeled data in a 2025 paper. Self-driving and mapping systems need to read unpaved roads, but labeled examples from such settings are scarce. Urban datasets are plentiful yet different.

Their pipeline pre-trains a projection-based network on mixed urban data plus a small set of in-domain scans. A light prediction head is then fine-tuned on just fifty labeled target clouds. Extra tricks, including prompt-style tuning and data mixing, are tested along the way. Accuracy rose sharply over naive training on the small set alone. The recipe suits any niche terrain where labels are expensive.
arxiv-2508-21035:
Gennaro Percannella, Mattia Sarno, Francesco Tortorella, and Mario Vento present a network that spots abnormal cell division figures in tissue slides, in work from 2025. Such figures help doctors judge how aggressive a tumor is. Models often lose accuracy when slides come from new labs with a different look.

Their approach trains the network on side tasks tied to the main one. Those extra tasks push the model to focus on the dividing cell and ignore the shifting background. The entry was made for a public challenge on this exact problem. Early tests on three data sets gave promising scores. The authors aim for a tool that travels well across labs.
arxiv-2508-21135:
Harris Song, Tuan-Anh Vu, Sanjith Menon, Sriram Narasimhan, and Khalid Jawed present HiddenObject, a system for finding objects that are hard to see. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that plain color cameras fail when targets are blocked, camouflaged, or poorly lit. The system fuses three views of a scene: color, heat, and depth. A Mamba-based fusion block merges their signals.

The method first pulls traits that are unique to each view type. It then blends them into one shared code for the scene. This code carries what each view can add to the rest. Tests on several benchmark sets show top or near-top scores. The gains expose weak spots in single-view and naive fusion designs. The authors see Mamba-style fusion as a strong path for hard detection tasks.
arxiv-2508-21235:
Kwela and Swaczyna show a zoo of ideal Schauder bases in classic Banach spaces, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A basis is a set of blocks that can stand for any point in a space. Filter bases widen the standard kind: sums need only settle down along a chosen ideal of whole numbers. New cases beyond the standard ones were rare in classic spaces. The authors build many such bases in ell p spaces, in c zero, and in James space.

The new cases set filters apart from each other and sort them by how the bases act. The authors also trace how possibly basic sequences link to filters. Two ideals can give quite unlike basis effects in one and the same space. So classic spaces hold rich structure that shifts with the ideal. The zoo lets readers see basis theory through the lens of sets and counting.
arxiv-2508-21435:
Fake X-rays are cheap to make and real ones are scarce, but a model trained on fakes stumbles on real scans because the two differ in shading, noise, and soft tissue. Francisco Caetano, Christiaan Viviers, Peter De With, and Fons van der Sommen built a translator in 2025 that converts images between the synthetic and real domains in either direction. One shared model handles every domain pair it was trained on, with no paired examples needed.

To test it they released a dataset of matched synthetic and real skull X-rays taken at several radiation doses. Despite being smaller than rival diffusion systems, their model scored strongly and can be tuned at use time toward looks or toward structural faithfulness.
arxiv-2508-21635:
Nicolas Soncini and co-authors present a 2025 dataset paper for farm robotics. Robots that work in crop fields must find their way through glare, blur, and rough ground. Good test data from real fields is scarce, and this release aims to fill that gap.

The Rosario Dataset v2 holds over two hours of recordings from a soybean field. Sensors include stereo infrared and color cameras, motion and magnetic sensors, satellite positioning in three grades, and wheel odometry. The rig keeps all sensors in sync and provides full ground truth for position and orientation. Long routes with loops test whether mapping systems can recognize revisited places. The team ran leading SLAM methods on the data and shows where they strain. Data and tools are released in public.
arxiv-2509-00135:
Davin Choo leads a team with eight co-authors who build a planner for health coverage growth in Ethiopia in 2025. The work backs a national push for universal health coverage, a United Nations goal. Ethiopia is strengthening health posts to widen access to basic care, but budgets allow only a share of the plan each year.

Their tool, HARP, guides which facilities to upgrade in sequence to maximize people covered under budget doubt. It must also meet region-specific proportionality targets at every step, so no region is left behind. One algorithm improves on expert picks at any single step with learned help. A greedy method gives a second route. Fair sequencing could stretch scarce health funds.
arxiv-2509-00635:
Alexandru Ghitza and Takuya Yamauchi prove that some Galois representations do not exist. A Galois representation encodes the symmetries of number fields as matrices. The pair studies irreducible ones in small characteristic. Irreducible means the object cannot be split into smaller pieces. They work modulo two or modulo three.

The proof refines arguments due to Hyunsuk Moon. It assumes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. That is a major unproven claim about prime patterns. Under that claim, they rule out a range of mod two cases. The ruled-out cases are unramified outside the prime two. Parallel results cover totally real cases and mod three cases. Without any assumption, they show one symplectic case must have a large image.
arxiv-2509-01035:
Nikta Gohari Sadr leads a team of five authors on TaarofBench, a benchmark for Persian taarof. Taarof is a system of ritual politeness in Iranian daily life. It stresses deference, modesty, and indirectness in speech. Large language models struggle with such culturally specific norms. Taarof is absent from existing cultural benchmarks, the team notes.

The benchmark holds hundreds of role-play scenarios across twelve social topics. Native speakers validated the scenarios before use. Five frontier models are evaluated against human baselines. Accuracy falls far below native speakers when taarof fits the scene. Scores vary by topic and improve with Persian prompts. Gender-based gaps appear as well. Responses rated polite by standard metrics often break taarof norms. Tuning and preference methods yield large gains.
arxiv-2509-01235:
Deep networks can be fooled by tiny changes to an input that humans would never notice, a weakness called adversarial vulnerability. Yixiong Ren, Wenkang Du, Jianhui Zhou, and Haiping Huang trace that weakness to geometry, the shape of the network's inner representations. Their framework trains each layer locally with geometry in mind.

The training pushes examples of one class closer together and classes farther apart, smoothing the feature landscape. The authors explain the gains with a statistical mechanics view that integrates out network parameters, plus a model with Hebbian coupling between hidden units. The resulting networks resisted both white-box and black-box attacks better, and they could absorb new information with less interference. The work links robustness to how representations are arranged.
arxiv-2509-01335:
The Holstein model is a standard test case for how electrons interact with lattice vibrations, yet how charge moves through it is still not fully mapped. Suzana Miladic and Nenad Vukmirovic run numerically exact calculations over a broad range of the model's settings. They use a path-integral quantum Monte Carlo method, a sampling approach with no systematic shortcuts.

Their results are compared with three candidate pictures: normal band transport, small polaron hopping, and polaron band transport. A polaron is an electron dressed by the lattice distortion it creates. By matching correlation functions, and checking direct currents and known mobility data where needed, the pair marks where each picture holds. They find the three regimes together cover nearly the whole parameter space, giving modelers a clear map of which transport story to trust where.
arxiv-2509-01435:
Clinical trials sometimes borrow strength from past data, and a robust mixture prior is a popular Bayesian way to do that while guarding against mismatch. Marco Ratta, Gaelle Saint-Hilary, Mauro Gasparini, and Pavel Mozgunov study two settings of that prior that are usually treated unevenly. One is the weight given to the rich historical part; the other is the spread of the vague robust part.

Practice often fixes the second setting to the spread of a single observation and tunes only the weight. The team shows performance depends on both choices jointly, and that many weight-spread pairs give nearly identical conclusions in parts of the parameter space. Large-spread robust parts can be used without triggering a known paradox, and they improve control of false positive rates in large samples. The study offers fuller guidance for hybrid-control trials.
arxiv-2509-01735:
Alfonso Davila Vera solves a counting problem posed at a 2014 meeting on additive number theory. The task is to find the largest set of vectors with entries modulo four, meaning values wrap around after four, with no three distinct members that sum to zero. A standard bound says such a set can hold at most half of all vectors. Vera shows that bound cannot be beaten for this family.

His proof counts pairs to cap the size, and he gives an explicit build that reaches the cap. Taking all vectors whose first entry is odd yields exactly half of all vectors, checked for small dimensions. A search that mixes greedy and genetic steps, aided by AI, finds the same top size. The result closes the problem with both proof and construction.
arxiv-2509-02335:
Vaibhav Raj Singh Parmar and Ranjini Bandyopadhyay wrote a 2025 physics paper. It looks at patterns that form when water pushes a clay mix outward. The clay sits in a thin Hele-Shaw cell, a narrow gap between two plates. Additives let the team tune how stiff the clay is.

With weak stiffness, the moving edge showed viscous fingering. Thin fingers of water cut into the clay in tangled ways. Tuning the additives brought out two growth styles not seen before in such systems. The team calls them skewering and zig-zag finger growth. Stiffer clay formed branching dendrites, tree-like shapes with side limbs. Salt-rich clay with high stiffness cracked instead of flowing. The study shows additives give a hands-on dial for pattern shape.
arxiv-2509-02735:
Kejin Wu and Dimitris N. Politis wrote a 2025 statistics paper on prediction intervals. The setting is regression when the usual normal, linear premises fail. A point forecast alone hides its own error. Old-style intervals built on the t-distribution collapse without those premises.

Their calibration interval leans on flexible estimators instead. Deep neural networks or kernel methods supply the fits. The range can fold in fit error too. Many methods ignore that error source. Theory shows the range hits its promised coverage rate as samples grow. That holds under mild rules. Kernel versions carry a high-probability coverage guarantee at large samples. Network versions can work with finite samples too, under stated rules. Tests and two real datasets back the method.
arxiv-2509-02835:
