Thomas F. Bloom and Ernie Croot present a 2025 number theory paper on integers whose digits stay small in several bases at once. Writing a number in a base splits it into digits; the question is how many integers keep almost all digits below half the base, simultaneously in every chosen base.

For distinct coprime bases that are large enough, the authors prove infinitely many such integers exist. All but a tiny fraction of their digits stay small in each base. The result improves earlier work by Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt in both strength and precision. As a consequence, a conjecture of Graham about divisibility of the central binomial coefficient receives a weak answer. Simultaneous digit control across bases is the heart of the argument.
arxiv-2509-02935:
Khwahish Kushwah and Gabriel S. Denicol derived a 2025 theory of magnetized plasma flow for accretion disks, the swirling gas that feeds black holes and young stars. Their version is relativistic, meaning it respects the speed-of-light limit, and dissipative, meaning friction-like effects can drain energy. It starts from a particle-level equation that tracks how a dilute gas of electrons and ions moves.

Using a method of moments, which summarizes particle motion with a few bulk quantities, they get a wider set of equations than standard versions use. Older treatments keep only the shear stress aligned with the magnetic field. In extreme cases their extra stress parts grow large. They also show the theory can trigger the firehose instability, a wobbling driven by excess pressure along field lines.
arxiv-2509-03035:
Viktor Tsyrennikov made a 2025 case for a credit index called AXI as a partner to the benchmark rate SOFR. When the older LIBOR benchmark ended, loans lost a built-in response to bank credit stress. AXI instead measures what banks actually pay for funding, using real transactions across short and long maturities.

A broader companion index, FXI, tracks AXI closely in calm times and serves as its fallback. In stress episodes the two still moved together strongly, including during a regional bank failure in 2023. Tsyrennikov reports that adding AXI to SOFR pricing cuts funding risk for lenders. It can even support sizable spread discounts for borrowers without hurting risk-adjusted returns. Under stress, SOFR-only lenders failed to recover notable amounts on credit lines.
arxiv-2509-03235:
Jan Dereziński and Pedram Karimi catalogued exactly solvable Schrödinger operators tied to the hypergeometric equation in 2025. Schrödinger operators describe quantum particles in a potential, and exactly solvable ones have formulas for their energies and states. Here the solutions are built from the Gauss hypergeometric function, a classic special function, and potentials may even be complex.

The operators fall into three groups. One reduces to the Gegenbauer equation, a special case; the other two reach the full hypergeometric equation in distinct ways. Each group splits into three families named for geometric settings: spherical, hyperbolic, and de Sitter. For every family the authors compute the spectrum and the Green function, the kernel that inverts the operator. Identities trade spectral parameters for coupling constants across families.
arxiv-2509-03735:
Pair production in ultraluminous X-ray sources, black hole binaries feeding faster than the classic Eddington limit allows, is examined in a 2025 research paper by Gustavo Esteban Romero and two co-authors. In that supercritical regime, photons get trapped in a thick, radiation-dominated disk. A transparent funnel opens along the spin axis, filled with intense radiation and strong fields.

Those conditions suppress primary relativistic electrons inside the funnel. The authors show high-energy electrons can instead appear as secondary pairs through Bethe-Heitler interactions, where relativistic protons strike ambient photons and convert energy into electron-positron pairs. Using self-similar disk models with strong winds, they compute particle acceleration by magnetic reconnection and diffusive shocks, plus the losses that follow. The pairs should produce nonthermal radiation across a MeV band. Future MeV instruments might spot that glow, proving relativistic protons hide in the funnels.
arxiv-2509-04035:
Georgy Lukyanov, writing alone, studies audits and rule-breaking in a 2025 theory paper whose record title is Audit Silence and the Capacity Trap. An inspector chooses how hard to work, yet an audit may still not happen. A weaker inspector checks at a steadily lower rate. Each firm either stays compliant, meaning it follows the rules, or breaks them, and getting caught ends the relationship.

When no audit comes for a long stretch, firms grow more convinced the inspector lacks capacity. Past a long enough silence, breaking the rules follows in every consistent outcome the model allows. Lukyanov also compares audit systems and tracks which firms survive over time.
arxiv-2509-04135:
The ATLAS Collaboration, the international team running the ATLAS detector at CERN, reports a delicate measurement from lead nuclei that barely miss each other, in a 2025 research paper. When lead beams pass very close without colliding, one nucleus can flash light that creates a J/psi particle in the other. That particle quickly decays into two muons, heavier cousins of electrons, whose tracks reveal the event. Data came from the Large Hadron Collider's 2023 running.

Special triggers and track-only reconstruction were needed because the muons move unusually slowly. Rates were measured across the particle's forward-backward range and checked against theory. Results matched theory fairly well but clashed with earlier LHC measurements near the central range, a puzzle for follow-up work.
arxiv-2509-04335:
Renzo Cavalieri and two co-authors compute one family of counting numbers for branched covers in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their objects, called k-leaky double Hurwitz descendants, were defined in earlier work by the same circle. The numbers generalize two older counting schemes for maps between surfaces that branch in controlled ways. Attention here narrows to the one-part case, where the positive branching profile is a single number rather than a list.

Recursion formulas, which build big answers from smaller ones step by step, are derived first. Those recursions then produce closed formulas and structural results for several infinite families of the numbers. Enumerative geometry, the art of counting geometric objects, gains new worked territory.
arxiv-2509-04435:
Rose Kudzman-Blais and one co-author, Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay, revive the study of cartesian linearly distributive categories in a 2025 mathematics paper. These categories were built by Cockett and Seely to give meaning to linear logic in its multiplicative form, a logic that tracks resource use. Two combining operations, like abstract versions of and and or, pass through distributor maps. In the cartesian case both operations coincide with plain products and coproducts. Scholars once thought these matched plain distributive categories, learned otherwise, and lost interest.

With fresh uses for the parent theory, the authors return. Strong structural traits shared by all such categories are shown. Two example classes are studied, while a long-assumed third class, Kleisli categories of exception monads, is shown not to qualify after all.
arxiv-2509-04535:
Minjong Yoo and two co-authors teach robot skills in one domain to transfer to another without retraining in a 2025 research paper. Long multi-step tasks challenge reinforcement learning, especially when the target setting offers little data and forbids model updates. Their framework, ICPAD, learns diffusion-based skills across domains from offline records. Domain-agnostic prototype skills capture common behavior pieces, acting as a shared language, while a skill adapter grounds them in each specific domain.

A dynamic prompting scheme steers the adapter toward the target domain during use. Robot manipulation tests in Metaworld and driving tests in CARLA showed superior adaptation across changes in dynamics, robot body, and task length. Few target examples sufficed, which suits real deployments.
arxiv-2509-04635:
Silicon, germanium, tin, and lead atoms could be laser cooled and trapped under a scheme simulated by Geoffrey Zheng, lead author with five co-authors, in a 2025 atomic physics paper. These group IV atoms share a strong transition between a metastable state and an excited state at an accessible laser wavelength.

The team focus on tin, which suits precision measurement. Their simulations cover slowing an atomic beam, capture into a magneto-optical trap, and further sub-Doppler cooling and compression. They also discuss a realistic experimental setup for producing a dense, cold sample of tin atoms.
arxiv-2509-04735:
Rain, fog, and snow make road scenes hard for segmentation models to read. Dharsan Ravindran, lead author with four co-authors, study two ways to strengthen the Segment Anything Model family for self-driving in a 2025 paper. Their starting point is that these models lack uncertainty estimates, which hurts them where images are ambiguous.

One approach fine-tunes SAM2 with uncertainty metrics built into the loss. The other adapts an uncertainty-aware adapter first designed for medical imaging. Tests on several driving datasets show both help, with the adapter strongest in extreme weather and the tuned model improving across diverse scenes.
arxiv-2509-05035:
Boundary treatment can limit the accuracy of lattice Boltzmann flow simulations. Kaj Hoefnagel, lead author with three co-authors, introduce a volumetric boundary method in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Particle populations are projected onto a discontinuous piecewise linear basis. They are streamed using an exact geometric mapping, for two-dimensional convex, stationary shapes.

Stability is checked with a new analysis tool based on eigenvalues of the streaming step. The method reaches a convergence rate of at least two, improving on precursor methods. For flow around a two-dimensional airfoil, it gives better lift and drag results in their tests.
arxiv-2509-05735:
Robots that learn a world model from fixed logs do worse than robots that keep collecting data, Jiaqi Chen and four co-authors find in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Model-based agents learn environment dynamics once, then plan inside the learned model, so data collection strategy shapes everything downstream.

Across thirty-one environments, online agents beat offline ones. The failure mode is distribution shift: offline data cover too little of the state space, so at test time the agent meets states its model imagines wrongly. Extra online interaction on fixed or adaptive schedules restored online-level performance with limited data. Adding exploration data to large datasets, which today lean on expert demonstrations, is their recommendation.
arxiv-2509-05935:
Some moves between two healthy power grid settings may simply be impossible, and Mohammad Rasoul Narimani and two co-authors offer a way to prove it in 2025. Grid operators steer the system through the optimal power flow problem, which picks settings satisfying physics and engineering limits. The feasible settings can split into disconnected islands, and no legal path joins islands.

Their algorithm first hunts for an infeasible point on the straight line between two feasible settings. It then certifies disconnection by showing, through convex relaxation and bound tightening, that every point on the plane perpendicular to that line at the bad spot is infeasible too. Applied to standard test cases, the method delivers the first certifications of disconnected feasible spaces for several of them.
arxiv-2509-06135: When does a dynamical system persist under small changes? N. Pant surveys the theory behind that question in a 2025 note. Persistence theory has been used across many disciplines to study systems generated by differential equations or maps. Pant's note lays out a roadmap for proving persistence. It is organized around problems from the literature that hinge on the spectral radius or on Lyapunov exponents, the two classic gauges of long-term growth and stability.
arxiv-2509-06235:
Competitive Minecraft teams are the arena of PillagerBench, a 2025 benchmark from Olivier Schipper and four co-authors. Language-model agents shine at cooperation and strategy in calm settings, but competitive multi-agent play is little studied. PillagerBench runs real-time team-versus-team matches with an open interface, multi-round testing, and rule-based built-in opponents for fair comparisons.

Alongside it, the authors field TactiCrafter, a multi-agent system that coordinates through human-readable tactics, learns causal dependencies, and adapts to opponents. It beats baseline approaches and improves through self-play, with its strategic evolution analyzed across episodes. Both benchmark and system are open-sourced to push competitive multi-agent research.
arxiv-2509-06735:
Learning the equations of a living system straight from data is reviewed by Bartosz Prokop and one co-author in a 2025 paper on computing in biology. Dynamical systems theory describes how living parts change together, from tiny chemical clocks to tissue patterns. Curved feedbacks, delays, and many scales make hand-built models hard as readings grow richer.

Three groups of data-driven methods are weighed: regression-based methods, network-based designs, and splitting techniques. Each is judged on three aims: seeing what comes next, finding which parts sway each other, and describing steady states, swings, and shifts. To weigh them fairly, sample methods are run on one shared test case, the Oregonator, a minimal chemical oscillator with design principles common in biology. Strengths, limits, and clarity are weighed so research teams can pick tools fit for complex, many-sided living data.
arxiv-2509-06835:
Traffic sign classifiers can be fooled by nearly invisible tweaks, and Nabeyou Tadessa and two co-authors quantify that risk in a 2025 computer vision paper. Adversarial attacks add carefully crafted perturbations that flip a model's answer. Most earlier studies used simple digit datasets rather than real driving imagery.

A convolutional neural network was trained to classify forty-seven kinds of traffic signs from the LISA dataset. Two standard attacks were applied: the fast gradient sign method, a one-step perturbation, and projected gradient descent, a stronger iterative version. Accuracy fell sharply as perturbation size grew, showing clear susceptibility to adversarial examples. The authors present the study as groundwork for defenses tailored to real-world traffic sign recognition, where a fooled classifier is a safety problem rather than a curiosity.
arxiv-2509-07035:
Wei-Wei Zhang and 3 co-authors propose using a relativistic quantum battery as a probe of the Unruh effect in a 2025 paper. The Unruh effect predicts that a uniformly accelerated observer perceives a thermal bath where an inertial observer sees vacuum. Their scheme uses a uniformly accelerated Unruh-DeWitt battery and quantum work extraction to witness that thermal nature.

Employing an open quantum system approach, the authors analyze coherent and incoherent parts of ergotropy, the maximum quantum work extractable from the battery, driven by a coherent field. Steady values of coherent work extraction in the asymptotic condition are proved to be determined only by the acceleration-dependent Unruh temperature. That asymptotic behavior can show the thermal nature of the effect with respect to a standard equilibrium condition. The phase of the charging field also affects dynamics.
arxiv-2509-07135:
Ruggero Marino Lazzaroni and 4 co-authors present MedBench-IT in a 2025 paper. It is a test set for gauging AI models on the exam that gates entry to medical school in Italy. Tests in tongues other than English, and in narrow fields, are still scarce, and this set aims to fill that gap for Italian.

The set holds more than seventeen thousand expert-written choice questions in six fields, from biology and chemistry to logic, math, and physics, at three levels of hardness. The team ran both closed, paid models and smaller open ones that most labs can run. Past raw scores, they checked how steady each model's answers were when asked twice, how much the order of choices swayed it, and how well step-by-step prompts helped. They also checked if hard-to-read questions hurt scores, and found a small but real link.
arxiv-2509-07235:
Matheus F. S. Alves and 2 co-authors chart the ringing tones of a Schwarzschild black hole in 2025 when a massive scalar field vibrates around it. These tones are called quasinormal modes, and each has a pitch and a decay rate. A non-rotating, uncharged black hole is the test case, and the field mass is varied over a wide range.

Two numerical methods, the Hill-determinant method and the Leaver continued-fraction method, are run side by side and checked for agreement. The study finds three critical field masses where the tone pattern changes character. Past one threshold, modes become long-lived, with almost no decay at all. Such lingering tones could shape how massive fields behave around real black holes. The comparison also shows where each numerical method is strongest, guiding later work on spinning or charged holes.
arxiv-2509-07635:
Paolo Combes and 2 co-authors train neural proxies for sound synthesizers in a 2025 paper. Automatic synthesizer programming helps musicians find presets that match a target sound, but software synthesizers can be black boxes that do not allow gradient-based training. Their method approximates an arbitrary synthesizer with a neural network that maps presets into an audio embedding space from a pre-trained model.

The proxy produces compact, effective preset representations, so an audio embedding loss can guide synthesizer programming systems. The team evaluates which pre-trained audio models give the best representations and compares feedforward, recurrent, and transformer architectures for the proxy. Tests use synthetic and hand-crafted presets from three popular software synthesizers, judged on sound matching. A good proxy turns any beloved synth into a trainable instrument for AI-assisted sound design.
arxiv-2509-08035:
Bright gas streamers in a forming giant galaxy cluster are reported by Nikolaus Sulzenauer and 19 co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The protocluster SPT2349-56 sits at redshift 4.3, when the universe was young. Its extreme starburst challenges slow, bottom-up pictures of galaxy growth, since today's giant ellipticals must somehow assemble within a few hundred million years.

Sensitive ALMA observations of dust and ionised carbon emission reveal a highly structured gas reservoir spread across sixty kiloparsecs. Star formation running at thousands of solar masses per year across concurrent gas-rich mergers fits the picture of rapid assembly. The glowing streamers act as a beacon, showing cold fuel flowing into one of the most extreme construction sites known.
arxiv-2509-08135:
Patrick Kreidl studies which streaming flows to admit onto a link shared with deadline-driven traffic, in a solo 2025 networking paper. Two data centres share bandwidth between elastic jobs with deadlines, like scheduled synchronisation, and profitable but inelastic streams that need steady rates. Admitting a stream pays, but overload can break the elastic jobs' deadlines.

Admission control is cast as a stochastic shortest path problem. Its states discretise the elastic flow's size and deadline, and its actions choose which inelastic flows to accept. Uncertainty covers both available bandwidth and offered loads. Such policies matter commercially: the link owner wants streaming revenue without quietly sabotaging the synchronisation traffic that other services depend on.
arxiv-2509-08335:
Etienne Fouvry and Michel Waldschmidt count how many integers families of binary forms can represent, in a 2025 number theory paper, the third in a series. A binary form is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables; asking which integers arise as its values is a classical representation question. Degree at least three is the range in play.

As the bound grows, the main contribution to the count comes from forms of the smallest allowed degree, while higher-degree forms feed only the error term. The present instalment specialises to fewnomials, forms with only a handful of nonzero terms arranged in a symmetric pattern. Sparse polynomials behave differently from dense ones, and representation counts for them sharpen number theorists' grip on Diophantine problems.
arxiv-2509-08535:
Teams of language-model agents tackle particle physics data analysis in a 2025 paper by Sascha Diefenbacher and 5 co-authors. Modern fundamental physics produces data volumes that demand complex analysis workflows. Machine learning tools in the field are usually special-purpose algorithms with physics knowledge baked in, powerful but narrow and hard to retool.

The authors explore an orthogonal direction: several language model instances, each assigned specific subtasks, jointly solve analysis problems as a team. Agentic division of labour mirrors how human collaborations split a search into selection, fitting, and validation. If general agents can reach specialised tools' performance, the cost of trying a new analysis idea in physics could fall dramatically.
arxiv-2509-08635:
Around many active galactic nuclei sits a ring of molecular gas only tens of light-years wide, and its true shape has stayed blurry. F. Combes and 13 co-authors mapped two of the most massive such tori in a 2025 research paper. They used the ALMA telescope array at its highest resolution. The view reaches scales near one parsec for these nearby galaxies.

In one galaxy, the torus looks like a ring with a gas-depleted center offset from the black hole. In the other, the torus is edge-on, extremely thin, and clearly warped. Both structures are clumpy and slightly lopsided. The classic picture of a simple, thick dusty donut does not survive these images. Sharper maps also improve black hole mass estimates in a size range where standard relations scatter most. The results reshape how astronomers picture the fueling zone of active black holes.
arxiv-2509-09035:
Tung Nguyen and 2 co-authors prove a coarse graph theory analogue about excluding a fat tree in a 2025 paper. Classic results link tree minors with path-width: excluding a tree minor bounds path-width, and conversely. A fat minor is a thickened, coarse version of a minor.

For every finite tree and thickness, constants exist so graphs with no fat copy of that tree are quasi-isometric to graphs of bounded line-width. Quasi-isometry means the graphs look alike at large scale. A converse also holds: some tree and thickness force no such approximation when present. The work is part three of an asymptotic structure series.
arxiv-2509-09235:
Sarah C. Irvine and 5 co-authors extend virtual staining to three-dimensional X-ray histology of bone implants in a 2025 paper. X-ray tomography images tissue without cutting or staining, but its greyscale contrast lacks chemical specificity. Virtual staining uses deep learning to simulate real stain appearance.

Over fifty paired micro-CT and toluidine blue histology images train a modified CycleGAN network for limited paired data. Pixel level supervision and greyscale consistency help preserve fine structure while adding realistic color. The model beats Pix2Pix and standard CycleGAN on several image metrics. Once trained, it stains full CT volumes. New bone formation is reproduced well, though implant degradation layers vary.
arxiv-2509-09635:
The bright star Zeta Ophiuchi spins so fast it bulges, and its spectral lines are broader than rotation alone can explain. A. J. Kalita and 3 co-authors combine space photometry with rapid spectroscopy to find the extra broadening's source in a 2025 research paper. The broadening is blamed on macroturbulence, large-scale surface velocity fields of uncertain origin. The team used the TESS telescope's light curves and a high-resolution spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope.

Pulsations turned out to drive large swings in the measured macroturbulent velocity. Peak-to-peak scatter reached values comparable to the broadening itself. Different spectral lines reported different time-averaged values. Short exposures also systematically read lower than stacked spectra imitating the long exposures used for faint stars. That last point warns of a bias in published measurements for faint massive stars. Macroturbulence, it seems, is partly the star's heartbeat leaking into its portrait.
arxiv-2509-09735:
Willem Huijzer and Jieying Chen wrote this 2025 paper on bias in large language models across two languages. They test whether models treat people differently by background, gender, and age when making decisions and when summarizing text. A large English test set was translated into Dutch, giving hundreds of thousands of prompts for each task, run on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o.

Both models showed clear bias in decision tasks, favoring women, younger ages, and some backgrounds, while summaries showed little bias apart from age effects in one model. Bias patterns were broadly alike in English and Dutch. New prompt instructions could not remove the bias, but the best one cut the gap between favored and disfavored groups by about a quarter on average.
arxiv-2509-09835:
Justin Gwee and 1 co-author solve a risk-sensitive control problem in a 2025 stochastic analysis paper. A system drifts like a linear diffusion, and a controller may push it through a finite-variation process at some cost. The aim is to keep the state near a chosen interval over the long run while spending little effort, with the scoring rule punishing risk rather than just average deviation.

Central banks holding an exchange rate inside a target band face exactly this shape of problem. Gwee and his co-author derive the complete solution under general assumptions by building a smooth solution to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The construction leans on a family of Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problems, whose solutions piece together the optimal policy's behaviour across regions.
arxiv-2509-09935:
Chirayu Agrawal and 1 co-author adapt vision models to new domains without ever seeing the old training data in a 2025 machine learning paper. Source-free adaptation starts from a finished source model and must retune it on unlabeled target examples alone. Standard recipes lean on fully supervised pretraining and match features by angle, a habit that throws away the shape of the model's inner space, where much useful structure lives.

Their SCoDA framework starts instead from a teacher trained purely by self-supervision. A student then learns through feature matching plus a space similarity loss that honours the latent geometry, while the teacher slowly follows the student by an exponential moving average to resist forgetting. Benchmark trials place the method well ahead of earlier approaches.
arxiv-2509-10635:
Rare genetic syndromes often announce themselves in the face, and Ali Burak Ünal with three co-authors make that diagnosis both sharper and more private in this 2025 medical AI paper. Tools like GestaltMatcher read facial features for diagnostic clues, but they grow on centralized photo collections, while hospitals hold their data apart under strict privacy rules.

Their federated GestaltMatcher lets hospitals train a shared feature extractor together without exchanging patient images. Faces map into a common latent space, and a privacy-preserving kernel computation supports syndrome matching and discovery. New hospitals can join and immediately benefit from earlier rounds. In experiments, the federated service kept over ninety percent of the centralized version's performance and stayed robust as the number and mix of participating sites varied.
arxiv-2509-10935:
Ankan Mullick and eight co-authors introduce Spotlight, a new kind of document digest, in this 2025 natural language processing paper. A summary aims for coverage; a spotlight instead picks out the most compelling aspects of a document and shapes them into a short, engaging narrative meant to pull readers into the source. The authors formally separate spotlights from summaries and neighboring constructs.

They built new benchmark datasets for the task and studied it in detail. Their generator works in two stages: fine-tune a large language model on the benchmark, then align it with direct preference optimization. Evaluations show the model selects key elements precisely while improving readability and the engagement value of the original document. For publishers drowning readers in text, spotlights offer a lure that summaries never tried to be.
arxiv-2509-12035:
Type Ia supernovae serve as cosmic distance markers only after their brightness is corrected for color, and S. Ramaiya with four co-authors show in 2025 that the right correction depends on the host galaxy. Their sample comes from the Dark Energy Survey's five-year run, with host data stretching to far-infrared observations.

Sorting hosts on the plane of star formation rate against stellar mass gives three families: low-mass galaxies, heavy star-forming ones, and heavy quiet ones. The color-brightness slope is steepest for explosions in low-mass hosts and shallowest in heavy quiet hosts, a gap far beyond statistical noise. After each group is corrected with its own slope, the quiet-host events end up slightly brighter, so the authors urge future cosmology analyses to standardize by host region.
arxiv-2509-12235:
Hangzhan Jin and 7 co-authors revisit a common claim about training language models in a 2025 paper. The usual recipe first uses supervised fine-tuning, teaching on labeled examples, and then reinforcement learning, teaching by reward. A popular slogan says the first stage memorizes while the second generalizes to new problems.

Tracking checkpoints during training, the team found that performance on out-of-distribution reasoning, problems unlike the training set, often peaks early in supervised training and then falls. Reinforcement learning usually did not beat that early peak; it restored ability lost later, and only from certain checkpoints. Spectral analysis linked the pattern to rotations of singular vectors while singular values stayed fairly stable. Controlling that rotation may improve robustness.
arxiv-2509-12635:
Rotary position encoding tells a transformer where each token sits. But it secretly penalizes distant tokens. Yu Wang and four co-authors prove that in 2025. The bias sits inside the attention scores. It weakens long-context reading. Patch fixes exist, yet they need rescaling or retuning after pretraining.

Their replacement is Token-Aware Phase Attention. It builds a learnable phase function directly into the attention mechanism. Token interactions survive over long ranges. The model stretches to longer texts with light extra pretraining. It also extrapolates to lengths never seen in training. In the long-context regime, it posts much lower perplexity and stronger retrieval than rotary-style baselines.
arxiv-2509-12835:
Arnab Acharya, Titir Mukherjee and two co-authors ask in 2025 whether quantum versions of a bouncing ball system can show chaos. A classic bouncer can split, loop, and turn chaotic, while quantum rules are straight and seem to block such acts.

Models of free, driven, and open quantum bouncers show near-loops, odd non-chaotic patterns, and even chaos when loss is present. The team checks these claims with entropy traces, spectra, spread tests, and a clear chaos test. The results bridge two fields that long seemed apart: quantum rules and chaos, and they hint at new tests for small quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-13435:
Florent Leclercq lectures in 2025 on field-level inference in cosmology, a frame that reads full maps instead of compressed summaries. Uncompressed maps hold more data and dodge summary biases. Bayesian hierarchical models formalize the approach.

Sampling tools for vast, complex posteriors are reviewed in depth. The framework beneath field methods is laid out from base principles. State-of-art uses span varied cosmic probes, from galaxy surveys to background maps. Machine learning roles in lifting field methods grow through the notes. The lectures suit newcomers who need both theory and practice in one place.
arxiv-2509-13535:
S. M. Farah Al Fahim and four co-authors ask a practical question in a 2025 software engineering study. Can large language models improve crash reports? These reports are the error logs developers rely on when a program fails. Many lack the detail needed to debug quickly. The team tests adding fault locations, root-cause notes, and repair suggestions.

Two strategies were compared on several hundred real crash reports. One is a single-shot method using the stack trace. The other is an agentic method that also searches the code repository. Both sharply improved fault localization over the original reports. The agentic version gave stronger explanations and fixes. A small user study confirmed the enhanced reports were easier to understand and act on.
arxiv-2509-13635:
The CMS Collaboration searches for a heavy new particle in a 2025 collider paper, using proton-proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider recorded between 2016 and 2018. The hypothetical particle, called X, would decay into a Higgs boson plus a second new particle, Y, each producing one wide spray of particles called a large-radius jet.

To spot Y, the team scores its jet with an autoencoder that flags patterns unlike ordinary quark or gluon jets, letting one analysis cover many decay scenarios at once. Benchmark cases include Y decaying to W boson pairs, light quarks, or top quarks. No significant excess over standard model background appeared, so the team sets the strictest limits yet on such signals across the mass ranges covered.
arxiv-2509-13835:
Minh Duc Bui and four co-authors show that large language models discriminate against German dialect speakers in a 2025 paper. Over forty percent of Germany's population speaks a regional dialect, and dialect speakers already face negative stereotypes in society. The team ask whether language models have absorbed the same prejudices.

They built an evaluation corpus pairing sentences from seven regional dialects, including Alemannic and Bavarian, with standard German versions. In an association task, every model tested linked dialect speakers with negative adjectives, through both dialect names and dialect use. The same biases appeared in a decision task. Surprisingly, explicitly labeling the demographic amplified the bias more than the subtler cue of dialect text itself, reversing what earlier work on demographic mentions had found.
arxiv-2509-14035:
Hannah Keller and four co-authors present Piquant-epsilon in a 2025 privacy paper. It is a system for estimating quantiles over sensitive data held by many parties. Quantiles drive distributed analytics. Local differential privacy, where each user scrambles their own data, costs too much accuracy. Central privacy needs a trusted aggregator nobody wants to be.

The system splits trust between two servers and uses secure multi-party computation. It avoids the scalability traps of generic secure computation. Carefully chosen intermediate statistics are released instead, which shrinks the secure work. End-to-end differential privacy holds, even against malicious servers. In tests, it estimated five quantiles over a million records in under a minute. Accuracy ran far beyond local methods, and runtimes beat its baselines.
arxiv-2509-14535:
S. Ohkubo and Y. Hirabayashi report in 2025 a secondary rainbow with ripples in carbon on carbon nuclear scattering, seen for the first time. Rainbow scattering in nuclei mimics optics: a bright edge with interference fringes marks a refraction like effect. A second bow is far rarer.

Experimental angular patterns at two incident energies were compared with an extended double folding model. The model builds all coupling potentials from microscopic carbon wave functions. Large angle patterns are tangled because the two carbon nuclei are identical bosons. A clear Airy minimum still marks the dynamically generated secondary bow near the reported angle at the lower energy. Fine scattering structure thus reveals reaction dynamics that simple patterns hide.
arxiv-2509-14635:
Weihan Peng and five co-authors bring in SWE-QA in 2025, a bench for answering questions about whole code bases. Real questions for engineers span many files, the shape of a system and long range links in code. Past code benches stick to small, self held snippets, which miss that depth.

SWE-QA grounds its questions and answers in real world code bases. A system must search many files and join far apart code before it can answer. The bench is made to push work on repo level question answering, a core skill for coding helpers. Repo level grasp splits a snippet completer from a true project partner. Shared hard tests let teams gauge that jump with care.
arxiv-2509-14935:
Punith Reddy Vanteddu and five co-authors tune both the body and the flight controller of a jet-powered humanoid robot in a 2025 paper. The base robot is the iRonCub-Mk3, which must fly along hard paths. Body shape and control settings affect each other, so the team treats design as one joint task.

A planned sweep builds five thousand valid variants in CAD form. Limb lengths, jet mount angles and offsets, and mass layout all change across the set. Grouping the variants picks a small set of stand-ins for costly tests. Flight is scored on a smooth path tracked by a predictive controller. A multi-goal search then trades off the design and control goals at once.
arxiv-2509-15235:
Jialiang Kang and four co-authors speed up vision-language models with vision-aware speculative decoding in a 2025 machine learning paper. Speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose tokens that a large model verifies, a proven accelerator for text models. Applied to vision-language models, earlier attempts gained only modest speedups.

The authors hypothesize that large multimodal models filter redundant image information layer by layer, while small draft models cannot, which starves the drafting process. ViSpec adds a light vision adaptor that compresses image tokens into a compact representation for the draft model, keeping the original positional information intact. A global feature vector per image further guides drafting. Better drafts mean fewer rejected proposals, which is where the real speedup lives.
arxiv-2509-15435:
Chung-En Johnny Yu, Brian Jalaian, and Nathaniel Bastian present a guard for models that read images and text. Such models can state false facts about a photo, a flaw called hallucination. Attacks on the input can also fool them. Both flaws limit trust in real use. Their guard works at run time, with no need to retrain the model.

The guard, called ORCA, loops through four steps: observe, reason, critique, and act. It asks several small vision tools pointed questions and checks where they disagree. It keeps a record of its steps, so choices can be audited. On a known test, it lifts scores by a wide range on some models. It also resists attacks it was not trained against.
arxiv-2509-15735:
Davide Ettori leads a team that spots when a language model starts to go wrong. Models can state false facts or fail on inputs unlike their training. The team read the model's inner signals as it works. Those signals form patterns whose spread holds a compact sign of the model's state.

Their detector, EigenTrack, streams a few summary stats of that spread: how mixed it is, the gaps in it, and its drift from random baselines. A small recurrent classifier reads the stream and flags hallucination or drift early. It needs one pass, with no resampling. It keeps the time order that other inner detectors drop. Users can trade accuracy against delay in a clear way.
arxiv-2509-16235:
How a lone test particle moves through a model galaxy can range from near-regular paths to near-total chaos. Megha Burri and Robert S. MacKay study that motion for a galaxy model proposed by Serge Aubry, mixing theory with computer runs. They find both regimes in the same model, side by side.

A sketch of an explanation for the chaotic regime is offered. The authors also share thoughts on what the results mean for real galaxies. Even a simple galaxy model can thus host a rich mix of order and chaos. The study helps map when galactic motion stays predictable and when it does not.
arxiv-2509-16535:
Darian Figuera-Michal and co-authors tackle a hard plasma problem in a 2025 paper on phase mixing. In a plasma with almost no collisions, mixing creates thin threads in velocity space. Full simulations capture this well but cost a great deal. The team tests whether a much smaller model can keep the key physics.

They join two tools that pick out main patterns and then find simple equations for them. Data come from particle simulations of mixing. The small model filters out particle noise and keeps the main motion. Its equations stay mostly linear and easy to read. Data size drops by a huge factor across tests.
arxiv-2509-16935:
Lavish Ramchandani, Gunjan Deotale, and Dev Kumar Das classify odd cell divisions in a 2025 medical paper. Atypical mitotic figures are rare, abnormal divisions tied to aggressive tumors. Spotting them is hard: cues are subtle, cases are rare, and experts disagree. The team adapt a large vision model with a cheap fine-tuning method.

Their best setup used low-rank adapters and a three-way ensemble. It scored well on a challenge test set and placed near the top of the board. Gaps in specificity and in new domains remain. Cheap adaptation of big models could help pathology labs that lack huge labeled sets for rare patterns.
arxiv-2509-17435:
Xiaoyu Wang and five co-authors fly a drone with nothing but a cheap color camera. Their 2025 arXiv paper works where GPS fails, indoors or under jamming, so the drone must navigate by sight alone. Their method is image-based visual servoing, which steers by the gap between what the camera sees and what it should see.

The framework needs no explicit path plan. It hops between visual targets in the form of AprilTags, a family of printed markers that cameras can track with ease. Collision avoidance comes from depth guessed by an AI model from the single camera's images, with no stereo pair or ground computer. The whole stack runs onboard a Jetson board, which keeps the system self-contained. Flight tests show the drone crossing several targets and dodging obstacles in GPS-denied settings, a useful trait for warehouses and disaster sites.
arxiv-2509-17635:
Mazen Alamir, writing alone, improves a method for learning unknown dynamics from a little noisy data. His 2025 arXiv paper works in continuous time and targets nonlinear systems whose behavior follows a polynomial law with few active terms. The systems in view take one input and one output, with relative degree up to four.

Two recent advances feed the method. The first rebuilds high derivatives of a signal from a noisy time series, which continuous-time identification needs. The second finds sparse multivariate polynomials that fit the rebuilt signals. Joined, they let the procedure name a parsimonious model from a small data set. Alamir illustrates the full pipeline on an electronic throttle control system from the automotive world. The paper speaks to engineers who must model a plant from short, imperfect test runs.
arxiv-2509-17735:
Jannis Clausius, Luca Schmid, Laurent Schmalen, and Stephan ten Brink improve symbol detection on channels that smear symbols into each other. Their 2025 arXiv paper works with expectation propagation, a message passing method that nears optimal detection on many channels. Strong inter-symbol interference breaks its usual start, since the first linear estimate it leans on is poor.

Their detector works in a transformed signal space. Instead of pairing the linear estimator with a symbol-wise demapper, it pairs a channel-shortening filter with a reduced-memory BCJR detector. A deliberate mismatch between the starting messages and the starting covariance speeds convergence in the first round. The test bed is the well-known Proakis-C channel, a standard hard case for interference. The design keeps the method feasible where the full optimal detector is out of reach, while clawing back the accuracy that strong interference steals.
arxiv-2509-17835:
Julien Duron and Hugo Jacob bound how long a clean path must hide inside a flat graph. Their 2025 paper works on planar graphs, which can be drawn with no crossed edges. A clean, or induced, path may use no extra edges between its points.

Past work by Galvin, Rival, and Sands showed a bound for sparse graphs, but flat graphs lacked a tight one. The pair split graph edges into few non-crossing sets along a main path. That split yields a bound that matches the best known upper bound, up to a fixed factor. The growth is slow: log of size, scaled down a step.
arxiv-2509-17935:
Anshul Adve proves that a set of equations from physics does pin down the spectra of curved surfaces. His 2025 paper deals with compact hyperbolic surfaces, whose vibration tones and form links are key data. A physics method, the conformal bootstrap, had used those equations to get sharp bounds on the tones.

The open ask was if each solution of the equations must come from a real surface. Adve proves it does, with no extra terms save that the spectrum is discrete. A core step sorts which group actions can take the needed form. The result gives the physics method a firm maths base.
arxiv-2509-18235:
Jialu Li and 6 co-authors review tools that auto-analyse long home recordings of young kids. Their 2025 paper deals with naturalistic tapes, where families act as they would with no lab staff near. Such tapes can run for hours or days, and they show how kids talk, play, and grow in real life.

Speech tech now takes a first pass at those huge sets. Tasks span who spoke when, what kind of sound a child made, and how many words adults used. Counts can stay rough, yet still yield real clues on growth. The team maps uses, snags, and next gains for the field.
arxiv-2509-18435:
Black holes might sit on a brane, a four-dimensional sheet inside a five-dimensional world. Milko Estrada and Francisco Tello-Ortiz give a method to build such a hole with spin in this 2025 paper. They use the Janis-Newman algorithm in Hopf coordinates to shape the geometry. On the brane itself, the shape matches the standard Kerr black hole of four-dimensional gravity.

Two singular spots appear: one pinned to the brane's center, and one that matches the Kerr ring on the brane. Horizons and the stationary limit stretch into the extra dimension in a flat, pancake-like form. The source in the bulk shifts from a slanted fluid form to empty space with a negative constant. In that limit the geometry joins an anti-de Sitter boundary. No matter is needed on the brane itself. The authors check the energy conditions with a diagonal frame.
arxiv-2509-18635:
Cold brown dwarfs are failed stars so dim and frigid that they serve as stand-ins for giant planets. Jacqueline K. Faherty and 30 co-authors report space telescope views of one such object in this 2025 paper. The target, a halo member poorer in heavy elements than almost any known body, sits within twenty parsecs of the Sun. Its spectrum shows methane and water, as expected.

The surprise is silane, a silicon gas never before caught in such an atmosphere. Silane should vanish into silicate clouds deep below, which is why rich worlds like Jupiter hide it. On this metal-poor dwarf, a clear silane band appears at a measured abundance. Modeling suggests the gas is frozen in at high pressure, just above the cloud layer, then mixed upward. The find ties composition, clouds, and mixing together in one object. It sharpens how scientists read cold planetary atmospheres.
arxiv-2509-19235:
Terahertz wireless links promise huge data rates, but their narrow beams are easily knocked off target by movement. Wamberto J. L. Queiroz and three co-authors analyze how such systems perform when the channel fades, beams misalign, users move, and hardware is imperfect. They work with a fading model named alpha-F, built to fit real terahertz measurements. From scratch, they derive the full statistics of the signal-to-noise ratio.

Those statistics yield new formulas for outage probability, average symbol error rate, and channel capacity. Simplified versions for the high-signal regime show which factors dominate there. An upper bound on capacity rounds out the toolkit. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the formulas behave as derived. The results give engineers closed-form ways to predict terahertz link quality without simulating every scenario.
arxiv-2509-19435:
Delilah E. A. Gates, writing alone, asks whether black holes with accretion disks can out-collide any machine humans build. A particle falling from far away can strike a disk particle near the horizon with enormous center-of-mass energy, in principle. Rapidly spinning black holes with disks are the natural candidates. Earlier work raised hopes for such astrophysical colliders as windows on physics beyond terrestrial reach.

Gates shows that scattering moderates the energy of those near-horizon collisions, trimming the extremes. Once scattering is included, black holes with prograde disks, rotating the same way as the hole, remain the most viable candidates. Retrograde disks, counter-rotating, are disfavored. The result narrows where nature might actually run its highest-energy collisions. It also tempers claims built on idealized, scatter-free trajectories near the horizon.
arxiv-2509-19535:
Graph theory hosts a guard game: guards hold key vertices, an attacker may evict one, and the guard set must reshuffle to stay in control. Gary MacGillivray, Christina Mynhardt, and Virgelot Virgile study the smallest guard family that can survive forever. They compare that number, the eviction number, with the independence number, which counts vertices no two of which touch.

One result shows the gap between the two numbers can grow without bound. The authors build a family of graphs where the eviction number runs about a third higher than the independence number. Their main result uses Ramsey numbers to cap the eviction number by a function of the independence number alone. So while the gap can be huge, it cannot depend on graph size once independence is fixed. The work sharpens what each measure says about a graph's structure.
arxiv-2509-19635:
Free groups are built from letters with no relations, and gluing two copies along a shared part gives an HNN extension. Vasily Ionin studies extensions where the gluing swaps basis elements for their conjugates. For that class, he builds a normal form that gives each element one standard spelling. He also adapts the ping-pong lemma, a classic test that proves a set of elements generates a free subgroup.

His version gives conditions that can actually be checked in practice. He then applies the tools to the pure braid group, which splits into layers of free groups. New families of free subgroups appear inside its first two layers. Free subgroups inside braid groups matter for both algebra and proposed uses in cryptography. The work adds concrete families where only general existence results stood before.
arxiv-2509-19835:
Waves that lose energy as they travel obey damped wave equations, and their long-term fate can flip on fine details. Trung Loc Tang and Dinh Van Duong study a semilinear version with a borderline power nonlinearity. A modulus of continuity fine-tunes the term. Earlier work in one to three dimensions found a sharp condition separating solutions that last forever from ones that blow up in finite time.

The authors extend that threshold to four dimensions. For lasting solutions, they identify the asymptotic profile: the Gauss kernel, the classic heat bell, governs the tail. When blow-up wins, they give a sharp lifespan estimate. Critical cases like this one test PDE theory at its edge. Knowing the exact profile also anchors numerical schemes that track such waves.
arxiv-2509-20235:
Richard Stiskalek wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on cosmology. Astronomers measure how fast galaxies drift apart from pure cosmic expansion. Those peculiar velocities constrain a quantity that tracks how strongly matter clumps. The result can be compared with values from the cosmic microwave background and weak lensing, where a mild tension has been debated.

Stiskalek combines three distance methods inside one Bayesian model: the Tully-Fisher relation, the fundamental plane, and Type Ia supernovae. Each indicator is calibrated jointly with a reconstruction of the local universe. The Tully-Fisher and supernova results agree with the Planck satellite values. The fundamental plane results proved unstable and shifted under different bias treatments. Overall, the low-redshift data do not deepen the known tension, though the fundamental plane needs more scrutiny.
arxiv-2509-20335:
Moments of the Riemann zeta function sit at the heart of analytic number theory. Alexandra Florea surveys what is known about bounding them in a 2025 expository article. The story starts with Heath-Brown's work of 1981 on fractional moments of the function. His ideas reshaped how researchers attack these bounds.

Florea reviews the methods behind that classic paper in accessible form. She then traces how later work built on it across four decades. Recent results now recover the expected growth rate for all moments. Small moments are settled unconditionally. Larger moments still rest on the Riemann hypothesis itself. The survey is written as an entry point, connecting a landmark paper to the current frontier of the field.
arxiv-2509-20435:
Disorder usually kills delicate quantum order, yet Julian May-Mann and three co-authors find a superconducting state that survives it in a 2025 arXiv paper. They start from a pair density wave, a superconductor whose pairing strength ripples through space. In a clean system it also carries charge order. Dirt destroys that charge pattern, leaving the fate of superconductivity unclear.

The authors take a strongly disordered limit: random puddles of the pair density wave sit in a normal metal. When the puddles are dilute, they still lock phases at low temperature. The whole sample then behaves like an ordinary charge-2e s-wave superconductor with zero resistance. This mechanism differs from the vestigial order proposed for weak disorder. It shows one route by which patterned pairing can outlive the pattern itself.
arxiv-2509-20735:
Near the South Pole, an array buried in ice listens for radio pulses from ultra-high-energy neutrinos. Mohammad Ful Hossain Seikh, Dave Besson, and Pawan Giri describe a data-cleaning problem for that array in a 2025 conference paper. The array is the Askaryan Radio Array, known as ARA.

Steady continuous-wave signals from human gear, instruments, and the environment can hide the faint, brief neutrino pulses. The authors review techniques the ARA team has built and refined over the years to spot and filter these steady signals. The array sits deep in Antarctic ice and works across a wide radio band. Cleaner data means more reliable event identification for one of the quietest detectors on Earth.
arxiv-2509-21235:
Thomas Cecil wrote an expository maths paper in 2025 on Dupin hypersurfaces. A hypersurface is a higher dimensional surface. A Dupin surface keeps each principal curvature fixed along its own curvature surface. Principal curvatures measure how the surface bends in main directions. The paper surveys compact proper Dupin examples in a sphere.

Cecil gives a detailed account of two constructions. One came from Pinkall and Thorbergsson in 1989. The other came from Miyaoka and Ozawa, also in 1989. Both examples lack constant Lie curvatures, which are ratios of the principal curvatures. So they refute a 1985 claim by Cecil and Ryan. That claim said all such compact examples must match a simpler constant curvature case.
arxiv-2509-21335:
Sharp borders between fluids that mix completely have puzzled theory for a long time. The paper is the work of Gyeong Min Choi and Heon Sang Lee. Miscible fluids mix fully, like alcohol and water. Sharp interfaces in such fluids have long been observed. Classic theory links sharp interfaces only to phase separation. The authors offer a new minimal framework for the effect.

They add a Fermi-Dirac free energy term to a standard convex bulk term. The mix stays fully miscible. In the gradient balance, the convex part drops out. The new term alone sets a logistic profile by least dissipation. After forming, the interface spreads diffusively and later broadens by ripening. The result gives a unified view of interface dynamics in mixed fluids.
arxiv-2509-21735:
Houliang Zhou and seven co-authors, working with data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, built a model that forecasts how Alzheimer disease will advance in a patient. The model reads brain scans taken over time. Such scan series arrive at uneven intervals, which makes them hard to model. The work appeared in a 2025 paper.

The model is a graph neural network that follows both where brain regions sit and how their activity changes over time. Two stochastic differential equations handle the uneven timing of the scans. The team tested the model on two patient groups, the ADNI group and the OASIS-3 collection. It flags the regions and links that matter most for the forecast. Those flags line up with known symptom patterns, and they point to signs doctors could use for early, personal forecasts.
arxiv-2509-21835:
Xunpeng Huang and six co-authors prove new cost bounds for a popular way of generating discrete data, such as text. The method is absorbing discrete diffusion, which masks elements step by step and then unmasks them. It works well in practice, but theory had not shown it beating a simpler uniform scheme. Their 2025 paper finds the structural reason it should win: the absorbing scheme cleans each masked element exactly once, while the uniform scheme redoes valid ones.

Building on that insight, the authors design an inference method tuned to the absorbing scheme. They prove it reaches a set accuracy with effort that does not grow as the accuracy demand tightens, unlike earlier bounds. The proof also drops a limiting assumption about scores that prior work needed. With lazy updates, the number of score checks grows only in step with the data size.
arxiv-2509-22235:
Dylan Dijk and Haeran Cho study how to model many time series at once when the data have heavy tails, meaning extreme values occur often. Their 2025 paper uses a factor-adjusted vector autoregressive model. A few shared factors capture the broad co-movement of the series, while a sparse model of the same autoregressive kind captures the remaining links between individual series. Standard estimators bend under heavy tails, so the authors build robustness in from the start.

Their method first truncates the data element by element, trimming the extremes, then estimates in two stages: the latent factors first, then the autoregressive matrices. Under an assumption that only a modest moment of the data exists, they derive estimation rates. On simulated data and on forecasting macroeconomic indicators, the estimators performed competitively.
arxiv-2509-22335:
Arjun Prakash and seven co-authors investigate why neural networks lose plasticity, the ability to keep learning new tasks, during continual training. A network that has learned several tasks in sequence often cannot learn the next one without being restarted. Their 2025 paper traces the failure to the geometry of the loss surface at the moment a new task begins. The Hessian, the matrix of curvatures of the loss, undergoes a spectral collapse: its meaningful directions vanish, leaving gradient descent with nothing to grip.

Studying a simplified linearized network, the authors derive exact conditions on the effective rank of a related matrix for training to succeed. They prove that this matrix is spectrally equivalent to a standard curvature approximation, linking two popular views of training dynamics. A Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian motivates two regularizers: one keeps the feature rank high, the other applies a plain weight penalty.
arxiv-2509-22435:
William Colglazier and 4 co-authors test a simple trick to sharpen predictions of molecular dipole moments. A dipole moment shows how charge is spread in a molecule, and only its size, not its direction, was known here. The team trained their model on two tasks at once. The main task was the dipole size. The side task was Mulliken atomic charges, a cheap but rough charge estimate.

Even rough side labels helped a lot. With a small weight on the charge task, dipole accuracy rose by up to three tenths. The model seemed to learn a more physical picture of charge spread. The result backs using cheap, imperfect data to aid a harder target.
arxiv-2509-22535:
The CMS Collaboration reports a search for the Higgs boson decaying to charm quarks, made alongside top quarks. How strongly the Higgs couples to charm and bottom quarks is a key test of the standard model. The search used proton collision data at thirteen teraelectronvolts, a large sample collected at the LHC. Advanced machine learning sorted jets by flavor and classified events.

The bottom-quark decay rate came out close to the standard model prediction. No charm signal stood out, so the team set an upper limit on its rate, several times the predicted value. Combined with an earlier search, the charm coupling bound is the tightest to date. The result narrows how far that coupling can stray.
arxiv-2509-22635:
Luc Boudier and 4 co-authors make synthetic training images for few-shot classification, with no model training at all. Few-shot tasks give only a handful of labeled examples per class. Diffusion models can invent more data, but most recipes fine-tune the generator or need outside tools. Their method, DIPSY, uses an image adapter to translate the few real examples into new, class-sharp images.

Three ideas drive it. Guidance can be steered separately by positive and negative image prompts. A sampling plan picks contrast examples by class similarity. The whole pipeline needs no fine-tuning, captioning, or filtering. Across ten benchmarks, DIPSY matched or beat the best prior results, with the clearest gains on fine-grained classes.
arxiv-2509-22735:
Seán Boddy and Joshua Joseph propose measuring and capping the agency of language model agents. As agents grow more capable, harms from misalignment and loss of control grow more severe. The authors treat agency as a property distinct from intelligence. They define it along three dimensions: how rigid the system's preferences are, how independently it operates, and how long it persists toward goals.

A representation engineering approach would measure and control agency inside the model. That enables regulatory tools: mandated testing, domain-specific agency limits, insurance priced by agency risk, and hard ceilings against societal-scale harm. The authors see the approach as a middle path, keeping some benefits of limited agency while curbing its risks.
arxiv-2509-22835:
Tim Schrader and 3 co-authors trace how ethylene forms on a gold surface, a step toward turning carbon dioxide into useful chemicals. One route to ethylene runs through methylene units that pair up on a catalyst surface. The surface is not a passive stage: its structure shapes the whole pathway. The team studied the dimerization reaction on gold surfaces of varying layer thickness.

Support layers beneath the gold changed the reaction coordinate and the energy profile along it. They also changed how strongly the ethylene product sticks to the surface. Those shifts matter for how nanostructured gold might be tuned for carbon dioxide upconversion. The work is a theoretical investigation of the mechanism.
arxiv-2509-23135:
Learning a reward function from expert demos often swings between reward and policy updates, which destabilizes training. Yang Chen and 8 co-authors unify the calmer, non-adversarial family of methods. Those methods, they show, all maximize the likelihood of expert behavior. That equals shrinking the expected return gap. Their framework, TRRO, guarantees steady improvement in that likelihood.

A practical version, PIRO, comes out of the framework. It mirrors the stability promises of trust region policy methods. On MuJoCo and Gym-Robotics tasks, PIRO matched or beat top baselines. It recovered rewards well and imitated with high sample efficiency. A real animal behavior task also fit the method.
arxiv-2509-23635:
A robot that understands, creates, and edits human motion in one system could serve animation and robotics alike. Ruibing Hou and 4 co-authors built MotionVerse on top of large language models for those three jobs. A motion tokenizer with residual quantization turns smooth movement into streams of discrete tokens. A delay parallel scheme staggers those streams in time, so the model tracks links between them at single-stream cost.

A dual-tower design keeps motion and language parameters apart, which limits interference between the two. Tests cover one person and several people moving together. Ablations back each design choice, and wide experiments show strong results across motion tasks.
arxiv-2509-24135:
Alexander Plakhotnikov studies when quantum Sobolev spaces sit inside Schatten classes. These spaces blend smoothness measures for operators with the norms that define the Schatten families. Past work by Lakmon and Mensah covered part of this picture, chiefly near the case where the index equals two.

Plakhotnikov extends the question to indices away from two. He shows that the quantum Sobolev spaces in view are Banach spaces, so they carry a complete norm. A duality argument then lets him define the matching spaces for indices above two. The embedding question matters because it links how smooth an operator is to how fast its singular values fade.
arxiv-2509-24335:
Image generators that predict one token after another have lagged behind diffusion rivals, in part because their latent values vary too wildly in scale. Guolin Ke and Hui Xue propose SphereAR, which pins every input and output of the autoregressive process to a fixed-radius sphere. With all vectors at the same length, the scale part that drives variance collapse is removed.

Their theory shows the constraint steadies decoding, even under classifier-free guidance. On ImageNet generation, the largest SphereAR set a new best score for its model family. Smaller versions matched or beat much larger rivals. The authors claim a first: a plain raster-order next-token generator ahead of diffusion at like scale.
arxiv-2509-24435:
Predicting the next token has powered large language models, and it also causes their worst habits: weak long-term planning, compounding errors, and slow generation. Charlie Wyatt and 2 co-authors survey the growing family of alternatives. They sort the field into five families, from predicting blocks of tokens at once to planning first and generating after.

Other families move reasoning into a continuous latent space, replace step-by-step output with parallel refinement such as diffusion, or drop the transformer shape entirely. The survey knits these threads into one taxonomy. Its aim is to guide work on models that keep the strengths of token generation while shedding its known limits.
arxiv-2509-24735:
Raphaël Trésor and Mykola Lukashchuk tackle a classic puzzle in chance theory in 2025. When an event has zero chance on paper, such as an exact reading of a smooth value, two fair ways of framing it can give two unlike answers. That clash is the Borel-Kolmogorov paradox.

The authors add a distance measure to the model and define the answer as a limit. As the allowed gap to the event shrinks, each step picks the most even spread that fits. Under their rules the answer is unique and stable under fair reshaping. Tests on old rock magnet data show how rival distance choices can be compared head to head.
arxiv-2509-24935:
Sangeek Hyun, MinKyu Lee, and Jae-Pil Heo ask whether adversarial image generators scale as gracefully as other generative models, and they rebuild the design around two proven choices. Their generator and discriminator are pure transformers, and training happens inside the compressed latent space of a variational autoencoder, where computation is cheaper and image quality survives. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they first diagnose what breaks when the design is naively enlarged: early generator layers sit underused, and optimization grows unstable at larger widths.

Two light fixes follow: extra supervision partway through the generator, and learning rates adjusted for width. With them, models from small to extra-large trained reliably. The largest reached state-of-the-art one-step class-conditional scores on the standard ImageNet test in far fewer epochs than strong baselines, by the authors report. A project page hosts examples.
arxiv-2509-25135:
Daniil Dmitriev, Harald Eskelund Franck, Carolin Heinzler, and Amartya Sanyal study learning from partly fake labels in a 2025 computing paper. Systems that train on their own past answers can trap themselves in an echo chamber. The authors model a foe who sometimes replays the learner's own old labels instead of the true ones. Old errors then look like fresh proof.

Classic learning methods fail badly in this game. The authors define a new complexity measure for a class of rules and prove it exactly captures how many mistakes any learner must make. A closure-based learner hits that bound, and no method can beat it. The result gives a firm yardstick for a risk that grows as models train on their own output.
arxiv-2509-25235:
Nikola Prianikov and three co-authors use machine learning to sort printhead faults at Canon Production Printing. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Each nozzle in a printhead is logged at all times. When some fail, the counts over time and their place in the grid form patterns that hint at the cause.

The team builds traits from time and place, guided by staff who know the machines. They test several standard learning methods on this rich data set. A One-vs-Rest Random Forest scores best of the group. It beats the firm's own rule-based tool on a weighted score, for several kinds of fault.
arxiv-2509-25535:
Yichi Zhang, Fangzheng Xie, Shu Yang, and Chong Wu train a router that sends each question to a suitable language model in a 2025 study. Using the single best model for every query costs too much, so routers pick cheaper or stronger models per request. Training a good router needs reliable scores for candidate answers, and those are scarce.

Expert-checked gold data are accurate but expensive and hard to scale. Preference data are cheaper yet noisier. The authors' meta-router bridges the two supervision types, learning from both at once. Better routing cuts inference cost while keeping answer quality close to the best single model.
arxiv-2509-25735:
Md Nasim, writing for the STAR Collaboration, reported a study from 2025 on how matter flows in smashed gold nuclei. When two gold nuclei crash off-center, the spray of new particles leans to one side. That lean, called directed flow, tells physicists about the hot early stage of the crash. The team measured the lean for three kinds of short-lived particles in crashes at three energy levels.

One of the three, a heavy cousin of the kaon, had never had its lean measured before. Its lean split away from the plain kaon's lean, and the gap grew in head-on crashes. A second particle's lean kept a steady gap from the kaon's at all crash types. The team reads the split as a sign of particles bumping into each other late in the crash. That makes the new measure a useful check on models of such crashes.
arxiv-2509-25835:
Xinzhe Li trims the cost of tree search in language model reasoning, in work from 2025. Searching many branches at test time lifts scores on long tasks, but it burns vast compute. The plug-in frame, Chain-in-Tree, asks at each step whether a branch is truly needed before growing one.

Two light checks make that call: one asks the model point-blank, and one votes across its own tries. Plugged into three known search frames, the direct check cut tokens, calls, and time by three quarters or more on math sets, with near no score loss. The voting check saved as much but wobbled in a few settings. Code is public.
arxiv-2509-25935:
Ying Gu and co-authors model a fading tidal disruption event in an active galaxy in this 2025 paper. In such an event, a star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole. This candidate, CSS100217, faded below its pre flare brightness, unlike typical events. The authors blame time varying obscuration by debris or nuclear clouds.

Their fit assumes the obscuration follows a Weibull pattern over time. It points to a star of about 4.6 solar masses torn by a black hole of about 33 million solar masses. About 1.38 solar masses of debris fell onto the hole in the fit. The host galaxy added little to the pre flare light, matching spectrum analysis. The model shows hidden debris can reshape an event light curve.
arxiv-2509-26035:
Quantum field theory on a spacetime with a wall needs its vacuum states rebuilt to respect the wall. Costeri, Dappiaggi, Juárez-Aubry, and Singh carried out that construction in 2025 for a scalar field living in half of flat spacetime. The boundary carries Robin conditions, a rule mixing the field's value and its slope. Their method extends a classic trick that converts Robin problems into simpler Dirichlet ones.

They obtain formulas for the forward and backward Green functions and prove the solutions are unique with the right support. A local formula then defines the physically preferred states, capturing echoes of singularities off the wall. Finally they prove their local rule matches the standard global one, a Radzikowski-style theorem for this setting.
arxiv-2509-26135:
Maciej Demianowicz tackles, in a 2025 quantum physics paper, an open question about special sets of product states that cannot be extended. Such sets, called unextendible product bases, link closely to graph theory through the pattern of which states are at right angles. The genuine form stays unextendible even when parties are grouped in any split.

Using graph tools and lists of banned sub-patterns, Demianowicz narrows which local graphs such a basis could have. The smallest candidate case, thirteen states across three three-level systems, is then ruled out entirely. Partial results for larger bases and four-level parts are also given. The work trims the search space for anyone hunting a true example.
arxiv-2509-26535:
Yun Zhao and Harry Zheng show in 2025 that neural networks can solve variational inequalities, a class of problems with a free boundary that is hard to pin down. Such problems appear in optimal stopping, like deciding when to exercise an option. Their loss function builds the inequality in directly, so no stopping region must be guessed in advance. They prove networks exist whose loss shrinks to zero.

The pair then apply the method to an investment and stopping problem in finance. A duality trick turns the hard version into a linear one that their method handles. Tests cover American put options in high dimensions. Results support networks as a flexible solver for control problems.
arxiv-2510-00235:
Charity Woodrum and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper in the JADES survey series. It measures star formation and dust in 602 galaxies seen when the universe was young. Spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope give the Balmer decrement, a hydrogen line ratio that reveals dust. Imaging fits supply each galaxy's mass and star formation rate.

The team confirms that dustier galaxies are already the more massive ones at these early times. That mass-dust link barely changes between the nearby universe and redshift seven in their data. The ultraviolet slope, another dust clue, behaves differently at high redshift than locally. For the most intensely star-forming galaxies, the slope stops tracking the Balmer dust measure altogether. The authors warn that ultraviolet slope alone should not be trusted as a dust gauge for such galaxies.
arxiv-2510-00335:
Matthew Marshall and four colleagues published this 2025 methods paper on stripping the coating from optical fibers. Polyimide coatings protect fibers in harsh settings, but technicians must remove them for splicing and sensing. Common stripping tools risk nicking the glass or cost too much for routine labs. The authors test a bath of cheap, common solvents as a gentler route.

Soaking fibers for six hours in two parts methanol to one part acetone loosened the coating fully. The stripped length came out slightly longer than the soaked length. Warming the bath to about forty degrees cut the needed soak to four hours. The paper also charts how mixing ratios, wicking, swelling, and drying shape the outcome. Those details give other labs an empirical recipe to copy safely. The method trades a little patience for far less risk to the fiber.
arxiv-2510-00435:
Dipankar Shakya and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 paper on probing chips from four sides at once. Future wireless devices pack several antennas and radio chains, so test gear must contact a wafer from every direction. True four-port probing at millimeter-wave frequencies does not exist yet in commercial stations. Two new stations, from FormFactor and MPI Corporation, now sit in New York University's terahertz facility.

Probing from east, west, north, and south at once makes calibration the hard part. The team designed an on-chip calibration standard in a 28-nanometer CMOS process. Its short, open, load, and reciprocal elements follow the SOLR scheme up to 125 gigahertz. A virtual multiline method supplied reference values to validate the new standard in simulation. The authors say the stations plus standard open precise radio characterization across wide frequency ranges.
arxiv-2510-00535:
A. Abebe and five colleagues published this 2025 cosmology paper on a modified gravity where dark matter talks directly to geometry. The framework is symmetric teleparallel gravity, driven by a function of the nonmetricity scalar. A coupling lets dark matter exchange influence with the gravitational field itself. Working in a special gauge, the equations recast as a multi-scalar field system.

The authors classify every stationary point of the cosmic dynamics for an arbitrary gravity function. Each fixed point gets a physical reading: matter era, acceleration, or something between. For a power-law theory, a full stability analysis follows. The de Sitter state, steady exponential expansion, emerges as the unique future attractor. The matter-dominated point survives as a saddle, giving the universe a proper youth. A family of scaling solutions even echoes inflationary dynamics, the authors note.
arxiv-2510-00635:
Jiang and seven co-authors test whether erased concepts in image generators are really gone in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety.
