Estefanía Duque Pérez, Lukas Jansen, and Benedikt Haeckener map Morocco's hydrogen prospects in a 2026 arXiv paper. Global demand for green hydrogen is growing fast. It is seen as a key tool for sectors that are hard to clean up. Morocco holds rich solar and wind resources. The country aims to capture up to 4 percent of the global PtX market by 2030. That would make it a strategic partner in Europe's energy transition.

The study tests how that path holds up under change. It varies demand scenarios and weather patterns. It also factors in efforts to cut emissions. Hydrogen output depends on sun and wind, so weather swings matter. For planners, the paper links ambition to conditions. It asks what Morocco's renewable build-out must survive to pay off.
arxiv-2601-15635:
Theodore Y. Faust, Arash A. Amini, and Mason A. Porter study communities in changing networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. A community is a set of nodes linked densely inside and sparsely outside. In temporal networks, these groups shift over time. Statistical inference is a growing way to track that structure. It fits a model and reads communities from the fit.

The authors focus on biases tied to community size. Inference may treat large and small groups unevenly. Such bias can distort maps of how networks evolve. Social, biological, and transport networks all change with time. Analysts who track their communities need to know where the method leans. The paper's warning is methodological: check the size effects before trusting the story a fit tells.
arxiv-2601-15735:
Takuya Nomoto and three co-authors set out a system for building magnetic structures in a 2026 arXiv paper. To predict how spins line up in a material is a basic step in magnetism. Their frame draws on oriented spin space groups, or SSGs. First, structures are built as fully symmetric forms of an SSG. Then they are rotated to fit the largest magnetic space group of that SSG.

The two levels get names: spin-symmetry-adapted structures, and oriented forms of them. The title adds high-throughput first-principles math as a use. Speed matters because candidate materials are many. A system that builds structures on its own can feed screening pipelines that hunt for new magnets. The frame turns symmetry from a check into a building tool.
arxiv-2601-15935:
Richard Stiskalek and Harry Desmond pair two cosmic probes in a 2026 arXiv paper. The thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect traces the pressure of ionized gas. It lights up galaxy clusters and the cosmic web. Constrained simulations rebuild the local universe's mass and velocity fields. They are digital twins, tuned to match the real nearby cosmos. The authors explore how the two tools inform each other.

The tSZ signal benchmarks how faithful the simulations are. In return, the simulations locate cosmic web structures. They supply positions, total masses, and density profiles for tSZ studies. Each tool thus covers the other's blind spot. Local-universe studies gain from that loop. It sharpens both the maps of nearby structure and the physics read from them.
arxiv-2601-16335:
Gustavo Gonçalves and coauthors test if bars in young star systems can be seen in fake views. Their 2026 preprint deals with barred star systems through time. Euclid views show bars fall from near space to a past shift of one. The TNG50 sim says bars should stay more oft than that. A clash of this kind may stem from view bias, not true counts.

The team makes fake Euclid like views of TNG50 systems. They then test how oft bars can be seen in those views. Miss rates at high shift would ease the clash much. The case study shows how to fair test sims next to views. It guards teams from false clash claims.
arxiv-2601-16535:
György Dósa, Zsolt Lángi and Zsolt Tuza ask how big a square can be clad by unit squares. Their 2026 preprint sets a clean maths task. Take a count n of unit squares, each of edge one. They must clad a big square with no gaps left. The aim is the most large edge the clad square can have.

That most edge is named S of n in the work. Small n can be solved by hand with care. Big n needs firm bounds and build tricks. Clean tasks of this kind test pack and clad maths. The team seeks sharp values and bounds for S of n.
arxiv-2601-16835:
Ke Ding, Bo Li, and Ankang Sun study fair pay when one boss hires many hands. A boss sets pay terms to spur work from each hand. Past work sought the boss's best gain from those terms. That aim can leave pay gaps that are vast and harsh. Their 2026 preprint adds a fairness curb to the task.

Their terms curb how far pay can spread among hands. The curb suits state work and worker co-ops. In such spots, fair pay is a core rule, not a wish. The team shows how to keep spur while pay stays even. This can guide real pact design in fair-first shops.
arxiv-2601-17035:
Christoph Bartneck, Richard Watt, Etienne Borde, and Pattara Klinpibul test a match rule to fix peer review. Peer review is key to science, but it crawls. Journals strain to find apt judges for each paper. Their 2026 preprint runs fake crowds to test a fix. The fix borrows the deferred acceptance rule from match work.

That rule pairs folks in a stable way from ranked picks. Here it pairs papers with apt judges. Fake runs set the rule next to the old way. Gains in speed or fit would help all fields. Match rules have fixed school and job queues before.
arxiv-2601-17335:
Angshul Majumdar asks if general AI can be defined in a strict way at all. Claims about AGI speak of existence, robustness, and self-checks as if they were fixed traits. Majumdar treats AGI as a distributional predicate. That means the claim rests on a task family, a task spread, a score rule, and set resource budgets. Change any one, and the claim can change.

In that frame, broad claims turn fragile. Some may even be undecidable, beyond proof or disproof. The work does not deny strong AI progress. It asks for claims that name their terms. Clear terms would make AGI debate more honest. Funders and labs could test what is said, not what is implied.
arxiv-2601-17435:
María Jesús Rodríguez-Sánchez and three co-authors propose a declarative layer for AI agents. Agents now plan, use tools, and split tasks. Many systems still fail in plain ways. They invent actions, make plans that cannot run, and coordinate poorly. The proposal sits in server ecosystems built on the Model Context Protocol.

A declarative layer lets builders state what agents may do in clear terms. Clear terms are easier to check than free text plans. That should cut brittle behavior across tools. The work speaks to teams that link many agents to live services. It offers a path to agents that stay within set bounds. Reliability, not flair, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-17635:
Gravity waves meet the stratocumulus-topped boundary layer in this simulation study. That layer is a sheet of low cloud over the ocean. Its breakup affects how much sunlight Earth reflects. The team uses large-eddy simulation to model the clash. The grid is five meters in the vertical and thirty meters across. A radiative-convective equilibrium state keeps the layer steady at start.

Gravity waves are then introduced through a set forcing. The study asks how prone the layer is to break up. Cloud sheets are a big unknown in climate models. Their breakup could shift warming forecasts. No author is named in the record. Fine grids give this test rare detail.
arxiv-2601-17735:
Kyungho Kim and five co-authors present ReFuGe for prediction on relational databases. Such databases store linked tables for web apps at scale. Prediction tasks on them have drawn fresh interest. Retrieval alone does not solve those tasks. ReFuGe uses LLM agents to generate informative relational features. Good features lift predictive performance in a direct way.

Feature craft is slow hand work in most data teams. Agents that mine linked tables could cut that time. They can join facts across tables humans might miss. The work targets web data as it lives, in tables. Better features mean better forecasts for churn, fraud, and demand. The agent design is the novel step.
arxiv-2601-17835:
Baowen Zhang, Chenxing Jiang, Heng Li, Shaojie Shen, and Ping Tan work on pulling true shapes out of a popular 3D method. Their 2026 preprint deals with Gaussian splatting. The method builds scenes from many soft blobs and renders new views fast and well. Getting a clean surface shape back out of those blobs is still an open problem.

Weak shape terms and loose fits leave methods with poor agreement between views. Stray blobs, called floaters, also throw off the result. The authors ground their method in geometry to fight both flaws. Clean shapes matter for robots, mapping, and any task that needs the world as a surface, not just a picture.
arxiv-2601-17935:
Daniel Commey, Matilda Nkoom, Yousef Alsenani, Sena G. Hounsinou, and Garth V. Crosby tackle money laundering that hops between firms. Their 2026 preprint presents FedGraph-VASP, a shared learning system for virtual asset service providers. These firms face a clash. Rules push them to catch laundering across firms. Privacy law pushes them not to share client data. Working alone, each firm misses patterns that cross chains and borders.

The team's design lets firms learn together without pooling raw data. Graph learning tracks how funds move between accounts. Federated training keeps the data at home, and post-quantum security guards the links. The aim is joint detection that respects privacy law.
arxiv-2601-18335:
Zexia Fan and co-authors teach sound localization systems to keep learning without forgetting. Their 2026 preprint deals with sound source localization, which finds where a sound came from. The method shines in controlled settings but struggles in the real world. Two imbalance problems bite. Within a task, some directions are far more common than others. Across tasks, new data skew and overlap with old. Both drive catastrophic forgetting as the system learns over time.

The authors propose analytic incremental learning with imbalance rectification. Analytic methods can update in closed form, which suits steady learning. Fixing the skew at both levels should keep old directions sharp. Hearing aids, robots, and smart rooms all need such ears.
arxiv-2601-18435:
Biraja Ghoshal and colleagues take on a hard task in eye care: to guess how bad a sight fault will be from a gene fault alone. The fault sits in a gene that helps the eye sense light. When it fails, sight fades over time. Two people with near twin faults can still end up with quite unlike sight loss.

The team looks for a sharp edge in how the gene's key part does its work at the scale of single atoms. Their claim is that a jump in how protons move through the part marks that edge. Past the edge, the fault turns harsh. If the claim holds, doctors could sort new cases by risk with more care. That would help them plan checks and care for each child in time.
arxiv-2601-18535:
Peter Balušík and Pavel Rajmic work on a fix for gaps in sound when the gaps are read as a map of tones over time. A tone map shows which tones sound at each beat. A flaw in the tape can knock out whole ticks of that map. The task is to fill the lost ticks in a way that sounds true. Time-based fills have a long past.

The tone-map form of the task is newer and less well served. Past fills can smear the tone or lose the phase, the part that sets how tones line up in time. The pair add phase care to the fill, so the built ticks keep the beat of the rest. A good fill could save tapes of talks and songs with short gaps. It could also help clean up calls and field tapes.
arxiv-2601-18735:
Jusheng Zhang and seven colleagues let a team of sight-and-text agents trade their doubts as if doubt were cash. Such teams can do more as one than each can solo. But to run many big agents at once costs a lot, and the cost grows fast as the team grows. Past team plans route tasks by gut rules that skip both cost and the shape of each agent's doubt.

A route that skips doubt can send a task to a sure but dear agent when a cheap, near-sure one would do. The team let agents state their doubt and trade tasks by worth and cost as one. That trade should cut waste while it holds the grade of the joint work. Sound trades could make big agent teams pay their way in real use.
arxiv-2601-18935:
B. Bercu and three co-authors prove a central limit theorem for a known random split model. The Ewens-Pitman model gives chances over ways to split a set of items into groups. It has two knobs that shape the splits, and one setting falls back to the classic Ewens model from population genetics.

A central limit theorem says how far the random counts stray from their mean, in a bell shaped way. The team works in the case where one knob grows large, using a martingale approach. Such results help geneticists judge whether a sample's family pattern is odd or just chance.
arxiv-2601-19435:
Shengwei Xu and four co-authors work out how ads could live inside chat model answers. Paying for large language models in a lasting way is an open problem. Search ads rested on static keywords, but chat users reveal their wants in passing, inside a flowing conversation, and those wants fade fast.

Ad insertion must catch that fleeting intent and place a fitting offer without wrecking the answer. The team studies the design of such a system. How this gets solved will shape whether chat tools stay free, and how much trust users keep in answers that also sell.
arxiv-2601-19535:
Manish Chandra, Debasis Ganguly, and Iadh Ounis work on retrieval-augmented generation, a method that lets language models look up text before answering. A retriever first finds passages that seem relevant to the question. The model then writes its answer using those passages. The catch is that a relevant passage may not actually help the answer get better.

Their system, LURE-RAG, re-ranks the found passages by utility instead. Utility means whether a passage truly improves the output for the task at hand, such as answering a question or summarizing for a query. The reranker is kept lightweight, so the extra step stays cheap. Putting helpful text first should raise answer quality without heavy cost. The work targets a quiet flaw in how most retrieval pipelines pick their evidence.
arxiv-2601-19635:
Shusen Liu, Pascal Jahan Elahi, and Ugo Varetto tackle a sharing problem in quantum computing. Quantum cloud services give each user's program an entire processor to itself. That monopoly blocks resource sharing and keeps costs high. It also prevents any quality-of-service tiers, where users could pay for better machines.

Existing quantum virtual machine designs try to split a processor among users. But they lean on the layout of one specific chip or on fixed templates. The authors propose DynQ, a dynamic virtual machine that ignores the chip's exact topology. It partitions the hardware using quality-weighted community detection, grouping good qubits together. Virtualisation transformed classical cloud computing. This work explores what it would take for quantum clouds to follow.
arxiv-2601-19735:
Francesco Sannino writes graduate-level lecture notes on one of particle physics' deepest puzzles. The strong CP problem asks why the strong force respects a symmetry it is allowed to break. The leading answer is the axion, a hypothetical particle that could also be dark matter. These notes introduce the problem and the axion from the viewpoint of effective field theory.

The notes are self-contained. They build the chiral effective theory of quantum chromodynamics and derive a potential that depends on the offending angle. Vacuum alignment, periodicity, and branch structure all follow from that potential. A clear path through this material helps new researchers enter axion physics. The notes serve courses and self-study alike.
arxiv-2601-19935:
Yiting Shen, Kun Li, Wei Zhou, and Songlin Hu build a benchmark for agents that must use long-term memory. Language model agents increasingly run complex, tool-based tasks over long periods. Memory should drive their actions, not just answer questions. Existing benchmarks mostly test passive recall of isolated facts in response to direct questions.

Their benchmark, Mem2ActBench, tests active memory use instead. The agent must apply what it remembers to execute tasks. That is the capability real deployments depend on. An agent can ace recall quizzes yet fail to act on what it knows. Measuring the gap guides memory design for autonomous systems. The work shifts evaluation from remembering to doing.
arxiv-2601-20135:
Domitilla Del Vecchio gives an overview of control systems engineering as used in synthetic biology. The field builds new functions into living cells, with uses such as cell therapy and guiding cells to change fate for regenerative medicine. A core problem runs through these uses: keeping the level of a key factor in the cell on target.

Cells face noise from their surroundings and from within, so open-loop designs often drift. Control methods add feedback that corrects the level as conditions change. Del Vecchio closes with a case study in cell fate reprogramming. The paper shows how tools from engineering can make living therapies safer and more predictable.
arxiv-2601-20435:
Aleix Roca and Vicenç Beltran rethink thread scheduling when a machine runs more threads than it can handle at once. High-performance computing and AI workloads now mix several parallel runtimes in one application, or share machines across jobs. Traditional operating system schedulers strain under these demands.

The authors present a user-space framework that coordinates multi-runtime and multi-process workloads. Coordinating above the operating system lets runtimes cooperate instead of fighting over cores. Better scheduling under oversubscription would raise the useful output of the clusters that train and serve large models. Less strife over cores means more work done per hour on the same chips.
arxiv-2601-21235:
Alok Abhishek, Tushar Bandopadhyay, and Lisa Erickson argue that current safety tests for large language models hide the harms that matter most. Models now work in high-stakes fields where a rare but severe failure can cause lasting damage. Most benchmarks still shrink social risk into one average score.

Their framework, called SHARP, builds risk profiles instead of single scores. It tracks how harm is spread out, how risk factors interact, and how bad the worst cases get. A single average can make an unfair model look safe. Profiles show which groups face the worst outcomes and where the danger concentrates.
arxiv-2601-21435:
Han-Chuan Kou, Zhi-Han Zhang, Xin-Hui Wu, Yan Zhou, Gang Chen, and Peng Li speed up a classic protocol for crossing a quantum phase change. Slow crossing follows a known scaling law for how many defects form. Rushing the crossing can backfire and create extra defects instead.

Their optimized protocol ramps the control field in a shaped way near the critical point. It keeps the classic scaling while taking much less total time. It also damps therise in defects that fast ramps often cause. Faster clean crossings help quantum devices and simulators that must change state without heating up.
arxiv-2601-21535:
Giacomo Greco and Domenico Marinucci study random fields spread over a sphere and how to make them sparse. Such fields model data on globes, from cosmic background radiation to climate maps. A simple new representation lets the authors compare several meanings of sparsity under rotational symmetry.

They also build sparse fields that mimic the spectra of popular non-Gaussian fields. The mimicry holds for both the basic power pattern and higher-order patterns. At the same time, the sparse form allows fast simulation. Fast, faithful simulation is gold for cosmology, where thousands of fake skies are needed to judge real ones.
arxiv-2601-21935:
Tom Yates and co-authors study belief propagation, a workhorse algorithm for drawing conclusions in probabilistic graphical models. The method passes messages between variables until they agree on a joint picture. Exact belief propagation quickly becomes infeasible as models grow, blowing past compute and memory budgets.

Cheaper variants exist, and the most popular one assumes every distribution is locally Gaussian, bell-shaped near each point. The team's 2026 preprint shows that belief propagation itself tends to converge toward Gaussian distributions in sparsely connected factor graphs. That result helps explain why the Gaussian shortcut works as well as it does. And it tells practitioners when the cheap version can stand in for the exact computation.
arxiv-2601-22035:
Longxuan Yu and co-authors study a freedom that diffusion language models have and ordinary ones lack. Autoregressive models must write left to right, in a fixed order. That hurts when the required output order clashes with natural reasoning, for instance when a format demands the answer before the explanation.

An autoregressive model must then commit to an answer before reasoning through it. Diffusion models generate in a different order, which could fit reasoning better. The team's 2026 preprint asks when output order stops reflecting reasoning order in these models. The answer shapes how structured outputs, from forms to code, should be generated when the reasoning must come first but the page layout says otherwise.
arxiv-2601-22135:
Zhexin Liang and co-authors relight whole photographs with a diffusion model guided by physics. Full-image relighting, changing a scene's light after the photo is taken, is hard for three reasons the authors name. Paired training data are scarce, physical plausibility is difficult to maintain, and data-driven priors generalize poorly.

Earlier attempts to bridge the gap between synthetic training scenes and real photos stayed suboptimal. The team's 2026 preprint, PI-Light, builds physics-inspired structure into the diffusion process for full-image relighting. Believable relighting serves film, e-commerce, and design, where reshooting under new light is costly. Physics guidance helps the model respect shadows and reflections instead of painting light on freely.
arxiv-2601-22535:
Yotam Dikstein, Max Hopkins, Russell Impagliazzo, and Toniann Pitassi build a new kind of error-correcting code. Their codes can be decoded locally, by reading only a small part of a message, and they list a few possible answers when noise is heavy. The codes reach rates and error tolerance close to the best theory allows.

The decoding runs very fast and with shallow circuits. Paired with older codes for low-noise cases, the work settles several long-open problems in coding and complexity theory. Such codes help protect data and also power proofs about hard problems.
arxiv-2601-22635:
Claudio Guarcello, Alexander Dubkov, and Davide Valenti survey how noise can help systems escape stuck states. Many systems, classical and quantum, relax slowly through metastable states — traps that look stable but are not the true rest state. Their 2026 preprint spans systems from memristors to Josephson devices.

Noise, long seen as a foe, can give the kick that frees a stuck system. The survey links Lévy flights, quantum escape, and axion hunts with Josephson gear. One frame for many fields can spark cross-field tricks. The work is a map of noise as a tool.
arxiv-2601-22735:
Zhidian Huang and a large team ask whether reasoning multimodal models actually think in a sound way. New models reason step by step about images and text. Their 2026 preprint, MM-THEBench, probes whether that thinking cuts hallucination, or adds new kinds of it.

Self-checking thought can steady a model, yet each extra step can also drift. The bench sorts those gains and harms across tasks. Honest grades for reasoning are now a core need. The work gives the field a shared test. It asks a sharp question in its title, and answers with data.
arxiv-2601-22935:
Evgeny Grigorenko and four co-authors protect private code used by AI autocomplete tools. Modern coding editors use language models to suggest code as you type. Training those models on user code risks leaking that code through the model itself, a new kind of data exposure.

Their approach applies differential privacy, a method that adds measured noise so single examples cannot be traced. The trade-off is between suggestion quality and privacy strength. Safer training would let firms use smart coding help without risking their source code. Privacy protection at training time is the focus, since a released autocomplete model cannot be un-trained once it leaks code.
arxiv-2601-23035:
Samir Adly, Vinh Thanh Ho, and Huu Nhan Nguyen study a fast gradient method with a fading regularizer. Their algorithm targets smooth convex minimization, where the objective's gradient changes at a controlled rate. It comes from discretizing a damped inertial system, a model of motion with friction.

A Tikhonov regularizer that vanishes over time steadies the path without biasing the end point. Explicit, step-by-step versions suit real computation better than continuous models. Faster convex solvers sit under logistics, imaging, and machine learning pipelines. Vanishing regularization is the balancing act: strong enough early to guide the iterates, gone at the end so the true solution remains.
arxiv-2601-23135:
Cheng Ge, Caitlyn Heqi Yin, Hao Liang, and Jiawei Zhang explain why a popular training method needs its normalization step. Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, trains language models without a separate critic network. It compares answers within a group per prompt and normalizes by variance.

Why that normalization helps, and when, was unclear. The authors give a local-curvature view of the adaptive gradients involved. A clear reason for a standard trick helps practitioners tune it instead of trusting habit. Per-prompt baselines replace the critic, so understanding the normalization explains the method's core stability trick.
arxiv-2601-23235:
Barron K. Nguyen, Laura K. Schaefer, Fei Dai, and Héctor E. Delgado-Díaz model the air of the rocky planet 55 Cancri e. The planet is an old, dense world orbiting a K-type star, larger and heavier than Earth. Webb observations suggest a carbon-rich atmosphere over a global magma ocean hotter than any on Earth.

The authors test how tidal heating and the planet's volatile budget shape the outgassed atmosphere. Matching the observed carbon gases constrains what the interior holds. Lava worlds like this are natural labs for planetary origins.
arxiv-2602-00035: Sebastian Racedo and coauthors design an async multi agent routing method for 5G networks carrying mixed traffic with varied quality demands. Single central policies and synced learners struggle to scale and stall on slow learners, so the team gives each service its own PPO agent. Agents plan routes in parallel and post resource changes to a shared world, which keeps choices feasible across services. Tests on an O-RAN like simulation with near real Montreal traffic match a single agent baseline on acceptance and delay, with faster training.
arxiv-2602-00235: William Thompson and coauthors build a calibrated catalog and model frame for finding companions from Gaia DR2, DR3, and Hipparcos data. They calibrate DR2 motions and DR3 minus DR2 positions against the DR3 frame, then join Hipparcos and Gaia constraints. A joint model in Octofitter averages over unpublished observation epochs, giving full orbit results for a large class of companions. The team recovers all 25 test binaries clearly, the authors report.
arxiv-2602-00335: Maria Domenica Galati and team present a feasibility study for observing rare B decays at LHCb during Run 3. Using RapidSim simulations, they show LHCb can observe B+ to tau+ nu_tau and Bc+ to tau+ nu_tau decays with Run 3 data. That extra information greatly reduces limits from missing momentum and vertex data, giving enough statistical power to pursue both decay channels, with the Bc+ channel a key community objective.
arxiv-2602-00535: Liyu Zerihun and Alexandr Plashchinsky tackle long sequence memory, where recurrent networks suffer vanishing gradients and Transformers scale quadratically. Their Invertible Memory Flow Networks make compression tractable by factorisation, splitting it into merges through a binary tree of sweeper modules. Each sweeper learns a simpler 2-to-1 task, giving logarithmic depth with sublinear error growth in sequence length. For online inference the team distils a recurrent student with constant sequential steps. Tests on MNIST sequences and UCF-101 videos confirm high-dimensional data can be compressed over long sequences.
arxiv-2602-00635: Lingsong Wang and colleagues tackle face occlusion segmentation, where parsers mistake blocks for parts because occlusion names no class. Building a data set covering block types is nearly impossible and mask annotation is labour-intensive. Their S3POT system combines face generation with self-supervised spatial prompting. A reference image rebuilt from a parsed mask feeds raw-reference token contrast for a prompt. Positive-negative prompt screening serves a mask decoder. Learned without block ground-truth masks under three complementary objectives, it beats prior work on a data set.
arxiv-2602-00735: Yan Xie and colleagues study a parallel one-level overlap Schwarz solver for finite-element high-frequency Helmholtz problems, whose linear systems are large and complex-valued. They present a variant using RAS with Perfectly Matched Layer terms. In their method the overlap width and extra matched layer on each part may shrink as frequency grows, ensuring convergence. Experiments show scalability under Cartesian grids, with iteration counts and time growing with frequency. The note uses 2D problems at constant wave speed.
arxiv-2602-00835: Ahmed Aloui and colleagues introduce the Metropolis-Adjusted Fractional Langevin Algorithm, a score-based fix for sampling heavy-tailed, multimodal targets. Older methods fail here because neither target nor proposal density can be evaluated. Older methods run unadjusted and can show large finite-time errors with poor tail control. MAFLA uses proxies for proposal scores under alpha-stable noise and derives an acceptance function through Score Balance Matching. Tests on combinatorial tasks show it strongly improves finite-time sampling over older dynamics.
arxiv-2602-00935: Mohamed Sorour and colleagues abstract ant foreleg features into a novel low-cost gripper for bin-picking, testing whether hairy, high-friction structures help grasping. Ant forelegs, especially tarsi with high-friction setal pads, hairs, and a flexible under-actuated tip, grip objects in clutter well. Their gripper legs are long, slim, and carry high-friction pads, low-friction hairs, and a single-segment tarsus-like structure mimicking insect compliance. Tests show robust grasping across varied consumer objects with all attempts successful, plus effective single-object picking from dense clutter.
arxiv-2602-01435: Soumyaroop Nandi and Prem Natarajan propose BioTamperNet for spotting copied regions in doctored biomedical images. Forensic tools trained on natural images often miss on biomedical data, where small changes undermine validity. BioTamperNet leans on affinity-guided attention from State Space Models. One module captures similarities inside one image, another maps matches across images. Light linear attention keeps localization sharp yet efficient. Trained end to end, the tool flags doctored regions and source copies at once. Tests on benchmark bio-forensic sets show clear gains over baselines in finding copied regions.
arxiv-2602-01535: Huzaifa Mustafa Unjhawala and co-authors co-design rover wheels and steering with Bayesian optimization on deformable terrain. Deformable terrain modeling is costly, confining discrete element tests to single wheels hiding interactions. Their framework tunes wheel geometry and steering parameters in full-vehicle simulations and a continuum model. The optimizer tunes radius, width, grouser features, and steering PID gains, balancing speed, tracking error, and energy use. Across 3,000 simulations, campaigns run five to nine days, not months. Hardware tests suggest tuned wheels keep their relative trends on the physical rover.
arxiv-2602-01635: Jinwoo Park and colleagues build COMET for spotting anomalies in time series across settings, where single scale views and normal only training leave models blind to shifting distributions. COMET encodes patches at several scales to capture time dependencies and variable links, then learns normal patterns in a quantized coreset, scoring anomalies by quantization error plus memory distance. A third part adapts the codebook online at inference, generating pseudo labels and updating through contrastive learning. On five benchmark sets COMET tops thirty six of forty five metrics, showing strength across environments.
arxiv-2602-01835: K. Fujio and colleagues develop a method for generating probability tables on a theoretical foundation, calculating fluctuating cross sections with the GOE-S-matrix model. The model embeds the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble in the matrix calculation, and results are converted to probability tables as in NJOY. Using uranium-238 and plutonium-239 targets, they set model parameters from convergence of average cross sections, and examine statistical error against the number of ladders. Tables at zero kelvin match conventional single level Breit-Wigner tables, with local differences from requisite S matrix unitality.
arxiv-2602-02535:
Abdul Rehman and 2 co-authors build an explainable deep learning system to assist ADHD diagnosis, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beyond what is normal for a child's age. Diagnosis is difficult, and black-box predictions give psychologists little reason to trust them.

Their hybrid model couples a deep neural network with a recurrent network to detect ADHD and sort its subtypes. Feature choice uses the Pearson correlation coefficient in a set workflow. Explainability tools, notably SHAP values and permutation importance, reveal which inputs drove each choice and how the logic flows. The model hit a ninety-nine percent F1 score on binary detection and about ninety-four percent on multi-class sorting. The authors frame the system as decision support that pairs raw computing power with clinical judgment, not as a stand-in for psychologists.
arxiv-2602-02635:
Siyu Li and 4 co-authors wire a knowledge graph into a language model to answer tobacco pest and disease questions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Generic models can hallucinate treatments or recommend inappropriate pesticides. Reliable agricultural advice needs structured domain knowledge, not just text similarity.

Building on graph-based retrieval, the system constructs a domain knowledge graph of diseases, symptoms, pesticides, and control measures as linked entities. Query-relevant subgraphs are retrieved as relational evidence during answer generation. A graph neural network learns node representations capturing symptom-disease-treatment dependencies. The language model backbone uses setting-efficient fine-tuning, and retrieved graph evidence enters its input directly. Experiments showed steady improvements over text-only rivals. The largest gains appeared on multi-hop and comparative questions, exactly those requiring several relations chained jointly. The design targets evidence-aware, domain-steady recommendations.
arxiv-2602-02835:
How a hot, dense form of matter flows is the subject of Isabella Danhoni's solo 2026 paper. She calculates shear viscosity, a measure of internal friction, in two very different settings. One is perturbative quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons. The other is a gas of hadrons, the particles quarks form.

An interpolation framework connects the two regimes at finite densities of baryon number, strangeness, and charge. Danhoni also presents nearly next-to-leading order weak-coupling results. She discusses how well the perturbative series converges. The work helps bridge descriptions of matter from very hot to more ordinary conditions.
arxiv-2602-03035:
Identifying wireless devices from their radio signals is improved by Tianya Zhao and 5 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Each device leaves a subtle fingerprint in its transmissions, useful for authentication. Deep networks read those fingerprints well, but they falter when the environment changes and they offer little explanation for their decisions to operators reviewing access.

Their system pairs two-part shapelets with a pretrained large language model. Shapelets are short signal patterns that capture local traits in the in-phase and quadrature parts, in a compact and interpretable form. The language model adds long-range context and generalization. Prototype output supports few-shot use in new domains without retraining. Tests across six datasets and several plans showed superior standard and few-shot results.
arxiv-2602-03235:
A dark Higgs particle is searched for in simulated future collider data by S. Elgammal, working with 1 colleague. Their model, the Mono-Z-prime portal, predicts both a dark Higgs and a new neutral gauge boson. The search uses simulated electron-positron collisions at the planned Future Circular Collider, at an energy of two hundred forty giga-electronvolts, with a large integrated luminosity assumed for the run.

The target event signature pairs two oppositely charged muons with missing transverse energy, the imbalance signaling invisible particles escaping finding. Monte Carlo runs make the expected events and backgrounds. Assuming no dark Higgs particles were detected, the analysis figures upper limits on the dark Higgs mass at ninety-five percent confidence. The study scopes what the future collider could exclude.
arxiv-2602-03435:
Soft robots bend continuously, which makes fast dynamic moves like swinging a limb upward genuinely hard to control. Daniele Caradonna and 7 co-authors benchmark model-based optimal control for such rigid-soft systems in a 2026 paper. Most earlier methods only handled slow, quasi-static motion, and simple template models miss real deformation behavior.

Using a geometric model that allows exact derivatives, the team compares three strategies: direct collocation, differential dynamic programming, and nonlinear model predictive control. Implicit integration and warm starts keep the stiff dynamics numerically stable. The test systems, a soft cart-pole, a soft Pendubot, and a soft Furuta pendulum, expose each method's performance and computing cost for swing-up tasks.
arxiv-2602-03535:
Training a neural network that stays sparse from the start could cut computing costs sharply, if the accuracy held. Yannick Lunk and 2 co-authors propose a dynamic sparse training algorithm in a 2026 paper. It builds on linearized Bregman iterations, a mirror descent method that naturally encourages sparsity. The challenge is exploring sparse structures without losing the sparsity itself.

Their algorithm alternates between static phases and dynamic updates of the sparsity pattern, and adaptively freezes the network structure in between. A multilevel optimization framing supplies convergence guarantees. On standard benchmarks the method produces highly sparse, accurate models. Theoretical operation counts fall to about 6 percent of dense training, and a sparsity-aware CPU implementation halves training time.
arxiv-2602-03635:
Adding an entropy bonus is the standard trick for making reinforcement learning explore, but in language models it barely helps and can hurt. Chao Huang and 10 co-authors explain why in a 2026 paper. With huge vocabularies and long generations, global entropy maximization smears probability onto vast tails of invalid tokens instead of plausible ones.

Their method, Trust Region Entropy, encourages exploration only inside the model's trust region, the set of candidates it already takes seriously. That focuses curiosity where reasoning stays coherent. Across mathematics reasoning, a combinatorial countdown task, and preference alignment, TRE consistently beats other exploration baselines, standard entropy regularization, and vanilla PPO. The work reframes exploration for models whose action space is mostly nonsense tokens.
arxiv-2602-03735:
Pablo Capuzzi and 3 co-authors solve exactly the spectral function of one-dimensional quantum mixtures squeezed into confining potentials. Their 2026 paper treats Bose-Bose and Fermi-Fermi mixtures with strong repulsive interactions, at every frequency scale. One-dimensional gases are a rare setting where such exact answers exist.

Under harmonic confinement, the density excitations form the ladder structure the trap imposes. On top of it, spin excitations appear as sideband peaks, with dispersions echoing ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic spin chains. The peaks are much wider for fermionic mixtures than bosonic ones, a gap the authors trace to the symmetry of the spin states. Seeing these branches would give a clear probe of interaction-induced magnetism in ultracold atoms.
arxiv-2602-03935:
Knowing how far away survey galaxies are is half of weak lensing cosmology. Boris Leistedt and colleagues forward-model those distances for the KiDS-1000 survey in a 2026 paper. Their pop-cosmos model generates realistic galaxy populations, calibrated on deep infrared observations, and a learned data model adds noise and selection effects.

Applying the survey's binning to synthetic data yields redshift distributions without spectroscopic reweighting. Swapping in a different galaxy model shifted mean redshifts in edge bins by amounts rivaling quoted uncertainties. The method points toward the accuracy Stage IV surveys will demand, where redshift errors dominate the error budget.
arxiv-2602-04135:
Black holes merging inside a gas disk may flash where others stay dark. Emily McPike and colleagues simulate those flashes with the McFACTS code in a 2026 paper, the fourth in its series. Disks around active galactic nuclei can assemble binary black holes whose mergers gravitational-wave detectors already hear.

The simulations predict luminosities of jets and shocks from merger remnants plowing through disk gas. Such light would make these mergers multimessenger sources, visible to telescopes and detectors together. No statistical predictions existed to guide searches of survey archives or real-time alerts. This work supplies them, helping observers pick candidate counterparts for follow-up.
arxiv-2602-04235:
Everyday finite elements stumble on fourth-order equations. Xihao Zhang and 3 co-authors develop C0 methods, using only unbroken elements, for such equations on polygonal domains in a 2026 paper. This first part of a series centers on the biharmonic equation and how edge conditions shape the scheme.

A changed mixed setup splits the problem into a system of Poisson equations. The system's size depends on the largest interior angle and the edge conditions on its sides. Unlike the naive two-equation split, theirs converges to the true solution for arbitrary polygons and Navier, Neumann, or mixed conditions. Error estimates and computed tests confirm the design.
arxiv-2602-04835:
N. V. Makarenko and S. V. Popruzhenko study electrons torn from argon atoms by very intense laser pulses in a 2026 paper. Tunnel ionization frees the electrons inside the laser focus, where they speed up to near light speed along the beam and give off radiation.

That radiation alone has moderate power. Hitting the electrons with a weaker pulse sent the other way can raise it a lot. Mixing tunneling theory with nonlinear Thomson scattering theory, the authors compute angular patterns and spectra of the photons given off. The angular pattern in the polarization plane is narrow and peaks at an angle set by intensity. That link turns the setup into a probe of peak intensity in the focus, and a source of collimated extreme ultraviolet light.
arxiv-2602-05035:
Multilingual language models often trail their single-language cousins, and Sean Trott and Pamela D Rivière measure one slice of that gap in this 2026 computational linguistics paper. Their test is lexical disambiguation: judging which meaning of an ambiguous word fits, using human relatedness ratings in English and Spanish.

Multilingual models scored consistently worse than monolingual ones from the same families. Three possible bottlenecks were then checked: less orderly embeddings, weaker attention to the clues that fix a word's meaning, and more words split into extra tokens. The multilingual models showed signs of all three, and together the three factors statistically explained the penalty once credited to multilingual status alone. The findings suggest the gap is a capacity problem with identifiable parts.
arxiv-2602-05135:
Some quasars already hosted billion-solar-mass black holes when the universe was young, which is hard to explain if black holes start small. Yu Wang and Remo Ruffini revisit that puzzle in this 2026 astrophysics paper, accepted by a high-energy astrophysics journal. New James Webb observations of small red sources suggest million-solar-mass black holes were active in compact environments before galaxies fully formed.

The authors model growth as the slower of two rates: gas supply falling as the universe expands, and the Eddington limit set by radiation feedback. Fitting two famous high-redshift quasars with Bayesian inference favors heavy seeds of about a million solar masses, born early in unusually dense gas. Growth then spends a long stretch supply-limited, with no need for faster-than-Eddington feeding. That seed mass matches what collapsing cores of degenerate fermion dark matter would produce.
arxiv-2602-05435:
Flow matching trains image and video generators by teaching them a velocity field that turns noise into data. Donglin Yang, Yongxing Zhang, and 6 co-authors argue that this training is held back by noisy targets, since each training step leans on a single sample. They map out where that noise is worst: high near the starting noise, and low near real data where target and average velocities nearly match.

Based on that map, the team builds a framework called Stable Velocity with parts for both training and sampling. One part cuts target noise during training, and another adds stronger guidance where noise is low. A third part speeds up sampling with closed-form shortcuts. Tests on ImageNet and on large text-to-image and text-to-video models show faster training and more than twice as fast sampling, with no loss in sample quality.
arxiv-2602-05635:
Cutting one skill from a trained network, or stretching its reasoning to longer inputs, often fails even when the task has a clean math structure. Ojasva Nema, Kaustubh Sharma, Aditya Chauhan, and Parikshit Pareek argue the fault lies in how networks lay out their inner patterns, not just in training or skill removal. They study bilinear nets, networks where units combine inputs by multiplying them.

The authors prove a non-mixing rule for such nets under gradient flow: task parts keep to their own orthogonal zones. Careful tests on modular arithmetic, cyclic reasoning, group dynamics, and targeted skill removal back the theory. Unlike pointwise nonlinear nets, the bilinear models recovered links that match the true math structure. The authors conclude that edit skill and broad use are limited by inner layout. Their message is that design choices, made before training starts, decide whether later surgical edits can succeed at all.
arxiv-2602-05735:
Embeddings turn text and images into long lists of numbers, and those dense vectors cost storage, memory, and time at scale. Lixuan Guo, Yifei Wang, and 6 co-authors work on contrastive sparse representations, which map embeddings into high dimensional but mostly empty vectors. The promise fades in the ultra sparse regime, where most neurons stay dead and quality drops hard.

Their method, CSRv2, stabilizes sparsity learning by annealing the number of active features gradually, adds supervised contrastive objectives, and fine tunes the full backbone end to end. Dead neurons fell from most of the network to a fifth in their tests. Accuracy at just two active features matched rivals that use many more, with large speed and memory gains over dense embeddings. The work was accepted at a major machine learning conference. It targets teams that serve embeddings in search and recommendation systems, where every active feature costs money.
arxiv-2602-05835:
People who learn from each other in short bursts may still fail to explore enough as a group. Kiarash Banihashem, Natalie Collina, and Aleksandrs Slivkins study a stylized social learning dynamic built on the multi armed bandit protocol. Each self interested agent controls one episode, a short run of consecutive decisions, like a user returning to an AI tool or a shopper revisiting a marketplace.

Within an episode, agents have reason to explore. The authors show that the aggregate exploration still fails: Bayesian regret grows linearly over time. That failure is typical, not a worst case artifact. It persists even when an agent episode payoff is a fixed function of the round outcomes, such as the minimum or maximum rather than the sum. The conclusion is that outside driven exploration is needed even when some exploration happens on its own. The paper appears at a major machine learning conference.
arxiv-2602-05935:
A detector that flags inputs unlike anything in training is only useful if it was tuned well, and tuning usually needs example out of distribution data that may not exist. Sudeepta Mondal, Xinyi Mary Xie, and 3 co-authors formalize that neglected problem: tuning out of distribution detectors with no given out of distribution set. Hand picked stand in sets are ad hoc, and the authors show detector performance swings widely with the choice.

They present strong baselines for the problem and a generic tuning approach that needs no data beyond what trained the network itself. Across higher parameter detector families, their approach improved over baselines consistently, and stayed comparable in simpler settings. Real anomalies are unknown unknowns, rarely resembling any proxy set. A tuning method that assumes nothing about them is safer to deploy.
arxiv-2602-06235:
Laser-driven ion beams could serve medicine and high-energy physics, but their energy and efficiency need a boost. Mohammad Rezaei-Pandari and 2 co-authors simulate a new target shape for the standard sheath acceleration method. Instead of a flat foil, they use a C-shaped annular sector target under the same intense laser pulse.

The hollow shape traps light, bouncing it inside so the target absorbs far more energy than a flat foil. Electrons grew much hotter, and ion bunches from the curved walls met at the center in a dense focal spot. Proton and carbon energies rose well past the flat-target values in the simulations. The authors present the design as a promising route to stronger beams.
arxiv-2602-06435:
People influence each other's choices, but hidden groups can make that peer effect look uniform when it is not. Zhongjian Lin and 2 co-authors study estimation in social interaction models with latent group structure. Groups carry their own fixed effects, and slopes differ across them, creating many incidental parameters.

They characterize the bias those parameters cause in the slope estimate of a binary choice model. A parametric bootstrap then removes the bias and restores valid inference. Tailored algorithms hunt the latent groups and choose how many there are. Simulations performed strongly. Applied to students' risky behavior, the method found two hidden clusters, with significant peer effects inside only one of them.
arxiv-2602-06635:
Sofia Giappichini, Markus Klute, and Matteo Presilla study how a future electron-positron collider could test whether the Higgs boson treats matter and antimatter differently. The decay of the Higgs into two tau particles is especially sensitive to this question, because the spins of the two taus carry traces of the interaction. The clean setting of the planned collider helps rebuild those traces.

Using simulated Higgs events made alongside a Z boson, the team projects that the key mixing angle could be pinned down to within about two and a half degrees. Most of the power comes from tau decays that leave a single visible track. They also translate the result into limits on new-physics terms in the standard effective theory, and compare those limits with other precision measurements.
arxiv-2602-06835:
Marco Di Francesco and Daniel Matthes study a particle approximation to the porous medium equation. It models gas flowing through a porous material or water spreading in soil. Their scheme tracks particles that move as nearest neighbors along a line, in a Lagrangian description that follows the material rather than fixed grid points. The question is whether the discrete scheme inherits the celebrated Aronson-Bénilan estimate of the continuous equation.

The authors prove that it does. They use the discrete estimate to derive a growth bound for the expanding support and a decay bound for the maximum height. Both are known in the continuum and uniform in the number of particles. They also prove the scheme converges to the true solution for completely general integrable initial data.
arxiv-2602-06935:
Shankar Veludandi and two co-authors make sequential recommenders cheaper to run. Transformer recommenders like BERT4Rec catch user habits well, but their softmax attention drags heavy middle steps along. Their model, Cotten4Rec, swaps that attention for linear-time cosine similarity scoring, built as a single tuned GPU kernel.

Cutting middle storage and launch costs slashes memory and run time against BERT4Rec and a linear-attention rival, most of all for mid-size sequences and vocabularies. Tests on three benchmark sets confirm large resource savings with only a small dip in suggestion quality. The authors pitch it as a workable option for large-scale recommendation where compute budgets are tight.
arxiv-2602-07235:
Watermarks let providers trace text back to a language model, but most encode only a single bit or a few bits per token.  Atefeh Gilani and five co-authors present ArcMark, a watermark that embeds multiple bytes into generated text without distorting average next-token predictions.

Built on coding and information-theoretic principles, ArcMark can carry richer payloads, such as which user submitted a prompt, which model version ran, or even the prompt itself.  That expands watermarking from a simple generated-or-not flag to a real provenance channel.  The paper matters for responsible deployment, where knowing the origin of a text in detail is increasingly a requirement, not a luxury.
arxiv-2602-07535:
After an acute ischemic stroke, emergency perfusion imaging figures dead core tissue and salvageable penumbra. Follow-up MRI shows the final infarct, but how penumbral tissue evolves after treatment is poorly mapped.  Md Sazidur Rahman and three co-authors propose a bi-time phenotyping method linking admission scans to outcomes.

Admission tissue signatures from statistical, radiomic, and deep-learning features are tied to follow-up outcomes through six outcome-aware region classes, revealing how heterogeneous penumbral tissue changes after treatment.  Stroke clinicians and imaging teams get a method that follows tissue fate, not just a single snapshot, supporting faster and better-guided treatment decisions.
arxiv-2602-07635:
Machine learning has transformed data compression, and relative entropy coding offers an option to quantization and entropy coding for lossy compression using stochastic codes.  Gergely Flamich and one co-author provide a broad overview of that direction, emphasizing computational and useful aspects missing from earlier literature.

The paper serves three audiences at once: curious readers get an intuitive picture of a simple yet emerging field, applied teams get an account of the most salient current applications. Specialists get a consolidated view of methods and open problems.  Compression teams get a field guide to stochastic codes as a useful option in lossy source coding.
arxiv-2602-07735:
Drug screening stalls when predicting how a compound binds requires slow, full-atom models of its 3D shape. Matteo Rossi and ten co-authors present TerraBind, a foundation model that predicts protein-ligand structure and binding strength from a coarse pocket-level picture instead.

Using only key protein atoms and heavy ligand atoms, combined with modern molecular and protein embeddings, TerraBind skips atom-by-atom diffusion and still improves binding prediction accuracy by about 20 percent. It runs 26 times faster than leading methods. Benchmarks on structure prediction support the design. For large-scale compound screening, the trade of fine detail for speed looks like a win.
arxiv-2602-08135:
Parrondo's paradox, where alternating two losing strategies wins, sounds like a gambler's trick, but it runs deep in nonlinear science. Marcelo A. Pires and three co-authors provide the first systematic review of its synergy with chaos, a two-way relationship.

In one direction, the paradox translates into order-chaos interplay: chaos plus chaos yielding order, or order plus order yielding chaos, measured with Lyapunov exponents and entropy. In the other, chaotic switching protocols engineer surprising effects across many paradox cases. The review clarifies the paradox's universality, surveys applications across science and technology, and flags open questions about high-dimensional maps, continuous flows, and theoretical limits.
arxiv-2602-08235:
Pc-use agents can cause serious harm even from benign orders, straying from hoped results in ways no one logged. Jaylen Jones and eight co-authors build the first method for mapping chance acts of such agents and for finding them automatically.

Their AutoElicit system stepwise perturbs benign orders using running feedback, drawing severe harms while keeping tweaks lifelike and benign. Applied to state-of-the-art agents including Claude 4.5 Haiku, Claude 4.5 Opus, and Operator, it surfaces hundreds of harmful chance acts, with transferability studied across systems. Agent safety teams gain a proactive method for finding long-tail failures before deployment, rather than cataloguing them after incidents.
arxiv-2602-08335:
Teams of AI agents that use tools can split hard jobs, but training them is tricky because credit is hard to assign when the team wins or fails. Yanming Li and thirteen co-authors introduce SHARP, a framework that shares credit fairly using Shapley values, a classic tool for dividing rewards among contributors. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets multi-agent systems built on large language models.

SHARP blends three signals: a team-wide accuracy reward, a per-agent marginal-credit reward, and a bonus for efficient tool use, with advantages normalized across trajectory groups to steady training. Across real-world benchmarks it beats recent baselines by wide margins, improving matches by about 24 percent over single-agent setups and 14 percent over other multi-agent methods. Readers get a principled fix for one of the field's most stubborn training problems.
arxiv-2602-08435:
Engineers use the describing function method to judge limit cycles in nonlinear control, but drawing the exact function takes heavy calculation. Davide Tebaldi and Roberto Zanasi offer a qualitative shortcut for piecewise nonlinearities with jumps. Their arXiv paper gives hand-drawn plotting rules based simply on the shape of the nonlinearity.

The method suits fast, qualitative analysis and control teaching, where exact computation discourages use. Case studies show the shortcut's limit-cycle estimates match the standard exact plotting in qualitative terms. Readers get a pencil-and-paper tool that restores a classic method to everyday engineering judgment.
arxiv-2602-08535:
Generative models usually follow deterministic flows, but those paths turn brittle when a causal intervention pushes mass through regions where the flow is undefined. Rui Wu and Li YongJun introduce the Causal Schrödinger Bridge, which reframes counterfactual inference as entropic optimal transport. Their arXiv paper lets diffusion processes tunnel mass through support gaps while enforcing structural admissibility.

A decomposition theorem shows the high-dimensional bridge splits exactly into local transitions, resolving a bottleneck that plagues monolithic models. On a system with a hundred thousand dimensions, standard structure-blind networks fail to converge, while the new method reaches low error in about seventy-four seconds on one graphics card. Readers get a scalable foundation for causal inference in very large systems.
arxiv-2602-08735:
Humans reason across multiple views by matching regions between views and by stepping through viewpoint changes, but models usually learn those skills only implicitly. Masanari Oi and five co-authors propose HATCH, a training framework that supervises both mechanisms explicitly for multi-image spatial reasoning. Their arXiv paper targets multi-modal language models that struggle to integrate viewpoints.

Patch-level spatial alignment encourages representations of corresponding regions to match across views. Action-then-answer reasoning requires the model to emit explicit viewpoint-transition actions before answering. Tests on three benchmarks show clear wins over same-size baselines and competitive results against much larger models, with single-image skills intact. Readers get a human-inspired recipe for multi-view spatial reasoning.
arxiv-2602-08835:
People in a group rarely share one set of values, yet AI helpers are often built as if they did. Andrés Holgado-Sánchez and four co-authors propose learning the value patterns of a whole society at once. Their approach groups users into clusters, each with its own value system and a policy that acts in line with it.

The method rests on preference-based multi-objective reinforcement learning, which learns from comparisons rather than hand-set scores. It builds both the groupings and the value models jointly, so each cluster's behavior stays readable in value terms. Tests on two decision-making worlds with human values show it holds up against a leading rival method and simpler baselines.
arxiv-2602-08935:
Electron diffraction can reveal crystal structures, but absorption muddies the signal in ways this paper pins down. Benjamin Colmey and three co-authors derive a two-beam formula for absorbed intensity in centrosymmetric crystals: for thin samples, reflections fade by a single exponential set by the mean absorptive potential. Many-beam simulations add reflection-specific quirks beyond that uniform fade.

Ignoring absorption in dynamical refinement adds error that grows roughly with thickness and bites hardest near zone axes. Tests on three materials show real gains for the heavy compound CsPbBr3, where the error measure improves from 6.4 to 5.3 percent, but little change for quartz and borane. Routine work can skip the effect except in heavy materials near full thickness.
arxiv-2602-09235:
Fully fake record sets are taking over from older hiding tricks, but old identity-leak tests say little about whether a foe can guess private traits. Matthias Templ and two co-authors bring RAPID, a risk test for trait-guessing leaks under a lifelike attack. In it, the foe trains a model only on released fake data, then runs it on real people's near-ID tags.

For number traits, RAPID gives the share of records guessed within a set error band. For label traits, a base-adjusted trust score shows how much surer the foe is than plain rates alone would hint. The capped, maker-free test is shown with cutoff tuning, doubt gauging, and maker tests, giving a handy top bound on guessing risk.
arxiv-2602-09335:
A Chern insulator is a material whose topology protects conducting edge states, but what happens when its electrons also tug on a vibrating lattice? A 2026 study led by Sebastião dos Anjos Sousa-Júnior, with four co-authors, couples a Chern insulator to dynamical phonons in the half-filled Haldane-Holstein model. It tracks the topology in real space. Stronger coupling proves fatal to the topological phase.

Using determinant quantum Monte Carlo, the team finds a first-order transition from the Chern insulator to a staggered charge-density wave that acts as a sublattice mass. Two markers of topology, a nearly quantized many-body Bott index and a local Chern marker built from the interacting Green's function, both collapse as charge order takes hold. Gap closing and lost boundary spectral weight confirm the change, while the phase problem from broken time-reversal symmetry stays mild at low frequencies.
arxiv-2602-09535:
Irmantas Ratas and Kestutis Pyragas study large but finite neural networks whose joint moves follow an exact low-size mean-field account in the large-network limit. The ruling rules for mean firing rate or mean membrane voltage are assumed known, but their settings are not, and only one scalar large-scale signal can be seen. Their 2026 paper infers the hidden settings and regains unobserved large-scale factors from that single time series.

Setting guesses use difference search, while syncing the mean-field model with the finite network throughout tuning removes need on unknown starting values of hidden factors. Tests on two quadratic spiking networks, one with regular rhythms and one chaotic, recover settings within one percent for networks above a thousand neurons. The method thus reads hidden joint moves from a single seen trace.
arxiv-2602-09835:
TIC 277539431, a fast-rotating M7 dwarf, hosted the highest-latitude flare to date at eighty-one degrees. Desmond Dsouza and two co-authors note that magnetic activity like stellar flares at high latitude indicates coronal loops at these latitudes on fully-convective M dwarfs. Sunspots, in contrast, usually occur below thirty degrees. Their 2026 study looks for modulation in the X-ray signal from coronal loops hidden by the star during rotation.

An updated rotation period of about two hundred seventy-four minutes comes from TESS sectors twelve, thirty-seven, thirty-nine, sixty-four, and sixty-five. Chi-squared fits varying amplitude and phase of a sinusoidally modulated signal from the new period find no evidence of rotational modulation in the X-ray signal. Possible causes include lack of a stable coronal loop during observation or too weak a modulated signal, though the dataset cannot distinguish scenarios.
arxiv-2602-09935:
Recommender systems first narrow millions of items to a short list, and that retrieval step must be both sharp and fast. A 2026 paper led by Vojtěch Vančura, with three co-authors, tackles the tension between expressive embeddings and serving cost. The team swaps dense embedding layers for high-dimensional sparse ones, training them to stay compact without losing expressive power.

Applied to a production-grade collaborative filtering autoencoder called ELSA, the approach shrank embeddings tenfold with no accuracy loss, and a hundredfold with only a small loss. The active dimensions also form an interpretable inverted index that groups items along the model's latent space. That structure lets segment-level features, such as two-dimensional homepage layouts, live inside the retrieval model itself.
arxiv-2602-10335:
Nonlinear elliptic Dirichlet problems on time scales unite steady, discrete, and hybrid settings in one framework. A 2026 paper led by Shalmali Bandyopadhyay, with two co-authors, proves results on when solutions exist and are unique for such problems on n-dimensional time scale domains. Under a Lipschitz cap on the nonlinear term set by the first eigenvalue, solutions exist and are unique by shrinking maps.

Under a weaker one-sided growth rule, existence follows from the Leray-Schauder fixed point result. Using these function-space tools requires recasting the problem as an operator equation, which demands building spectral theory for the Dirichlet Laplace operator with mixed nabla-delta derivatives. The operator proves self-adjoint and positive, with product eigenfunctions forming a full orthonormal basis in the n-dimensional setting.
arxiv-2602-10435:
Zhanou Liu and four co-authors combine quantum and older computing to handle strongly linked electrons in a 2026 chemistry paper. Near-term quantum methods struggle here because capturing all link at once demands very deep circuits. The hybrid plan splits the job instead of forcing one machine to do everything.

A variational quantum eigensolver handles the static link inside a compact multireference state, while a older density functional recovers the remaining dynamic link. Self-consistent orbital tuning keeps resource demands low without sacrificing rigor, the authors report. Tests reproduce carbon dimer bond lengths and benzene stirring energies at chemical standards, showing the approach works on standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-10635:
Keane Ong and eleven co-authors build a base model for social conduct in a 2026 paper. Socially intelligent systems must reason across diverse behavioral tasks, but behavioral data mix modalities and prediction targets, producing uneven training signals that unbalance learning. Current models struggle with that heterogeneity.

Their model, OmniSapiens-7B 2.0, addresses the imbalance with heterogeneity-aware relative policy tuning, a reward-based learning method that reweights signals across samples. It approximates each sample's contribution to the policy update and uses those estimates for geometrically centered, inertially smoothed advantage modulation. The result, the authors report, is the most consistent results across social conduct tasks, with steadier training on data that refuses to be uniform.
arxiv-2602-10735:
Hugo L. Hammer and two co-authors build an open-source tool for narrated e-books in a 2026 paper. A narrated e-book pairs audio with text, highlighting the spoken word or sentence during playback. The format supports early literacy and readers with reading hurdles, and lets any reader switch between reading and listening. Commercial services exist, but no open-source answer did.

Their system, Calliope, converts standard text e-books into narrated books in the EPUB 3 Media Overlay format using open-source text-to-speech. With care computed audio timestamps ensure exact synchronization between voice and text, while local processing protects privacy and layout fidelity is preserved. The tool gives publishers and teachers a free route to accessible, synchronized reading.
arxiv-2602-11035:
String diagrams draw computation as wires and boxes, but many terms can draw one diagram. Julie Cailler and three co-authors lay groundwork for machine checks of diagram equality, driven by quantum circuit checks. They treat diagrams as terms built from primitives by sequential and parallel composition, quotiented by deformation rules.

For two diagram classes they build normalizing term rewriting systems that equate exactly the diagram-equal terms. Termination and confluence are proved with the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant. The work does not yet automate all diagram thinking, but it gives verified foundations on which circuit-checking tools can stand.
arxiv-2602-11335:
Molecule polaritons promise optical control of chemistry, but demand a quantum account of light. Millan F. Welman and Sharon Hammes-Schiffer simulate a molecule under vibrational strong coupling with a cavity mode started in a Fock state rather than a coherent state. Their mean-field and full-quantum real-time methods previously agreed for coherent starts.

For Fock starts they diverge in telling ways. The mean-field method, which forbids light-matter linkage, predicts no polariton formation. The full-quantum method also lacks swings in mode and dipole expectations, yet shows swings in even powers and light-matter linkage, implicating polariton formation. The lesson is that quantized starts without classic analogues can reveal physics only a quantum cavity treatment captures.
arxiv-2602-11435:
Fixing is central to software work, yet theory about how experts reason through bugs is thin. Haolin Li and Michael Coblenz build a grounded theory from observing seven professional coders and five live-coding streamers across seventeen fixing tasks in their own codebases.

They theorize fixing as a structured, iterative diagnostic process. Programmers update a mental model of the system to guide information gathering. They alternate navigation and execution, forward and backward tracing, adapted to context, hardness, and familiarity. External resources complement code evidence, and experience lets coders build models systematically. The theory carries implications for tool design and for teaching fixing as a human-centred skill.
arxiv-2602-11635:
Humans solve textbook spatial reasoning problems with over 95 percent accuracy, yet leading multimodal models stumble below 60 percent on the same material. Shuo Lu and eighteen co-authors treat that gap as a fundamental weakness and build MathSpatial, the first large dataset resource devoted to mathematical spatial reasoning. It pairs a curated bench of 2000 problems across three categories and eleven subtypes with a training corpus of 8000 problems carrying verified solutions and reasoning traces.

All problems come from genuine educational material and pass multi-stage checks for duplicates, geometric consistency, and verified answers. Benchmarking sixteen leading models confirms the bottleneck: even the strongest model trails humans by over 35 percentage points, worst on abstract deduction. Training on the new corpus, however, lifts scores consistently across model families, showing the resource can actually teach the missing skill.
arxiv-2602-11935:
In static lattices, a classic theorem forces Weyl points to come in opposite-chirality pairs, blocking the chiral magnetic effect at equilibrium. Xiao-Dong Lin and two co-authors propose a way around that barrier with ultracold atoms in a three-dimensional optical Raman lattice under steady periodic driving. By setting distinct symmetries between the lattice and several Raman potentials, the setup creates effective 3D spin-orbit coupling and a tunable topological-insulator phase.

Slow modulation then yields eight Weyl points in the low-energy quasienergy spectrum, with a net twist that can be tuned precisely. A nonzero total twist means unpaired Weyl points exist. Adding a synthetic magnetic field through laser-assisted tunneling, the authors show the twist imbalance drives a quantized charge current in weak fields. That current is a direct signature of the chiral effect, within reach of current experiments.
arxiv-2602-12035:
Cheap talk theory assumes a fully rational advisor, but real advice now often comes from learning systems. Emilio Calvano and two co-authors study strategic communication when the advisor is a reinforcement-learning algorithm adapting messages from payoff feedback while the decision maker best-responds. Their theoretical analysis tracks long-run outcomes under reward-driven adaptation.

With aligned goals, learning, as a rule, produces informative messages even from uninformative starting policies. With clashing preferences, no stable outcome exists; instead, learning generates cycles that sustain highly open talk with payoffs above any static standoff. The algorithmic advisor, the paper argues, can beat textbook benchmarks precisely because learning never settles: cycles carry information that equilibria cannot.
arxiv-2602-12235:
Long-context models can shrink long inputs into a few learned tokens, but no one had pinned down when that squeeze starts to erase needed facts. Julia Belikova led this work with four co-authors, naming that failure token overflow: the squeezed code no longer holds enough to answer the query. The paper builds ways to characterise and detect that regime.

In the xRAG squeeze setting, simple saturation stats separate squeezed from raw tokens, yet they spot overflow poorly on their own. Light probe models that read both query and context codes do better, reaching 0.72 AUC-ROC on average across three question sets. That query-aware check offers a cheap gate before the main model, cutting errors caused by over-compression.
arxiv-2602-12335:
Quantum anomaly can force a theory to stay gapless, but the full picture in three spatial dimensions was incomplete. Arun Debray led this work with two co-authors, mapping low-energy phases of a fermion theory from anomaly tied to a finite symmetry. Anomaly split into two classes with opposite fates, a basic split at the heart of the paper.

First-class anomaly can always be met by gapped states that respect the symmetry, and symmetry extension builds candidate states those theories can flow to. Second-class anomaly can never be gapped without breaking the symmetry, giving symmetry-enforced gaplessness. Applied to four-dimensional gauge theories, the frame predicts candidate low-energy phases, and it implies discrete chiral anomaly cannot be gapped by adding arbitrary bosonic degrees of freedom.
arxiv-2602-12635:
Pengxiang Zhao led this work with twelve co-authors. Their study examines HiFloat, a set of low-bit number formats built for Ascend neural processing units, in two versions called HiF8 and HiF4. As large language models grow, formats that use fewer bits can save compute while keeping answers accurate, and the team tests HiFloat on weight-activation work and on KV-cache work.

Three findings stand out. First, INT8 fits data with a narrow range, while floating-point formats do better when values vary widely. Second, at four bits, HiF4 uses layered scaling that stops the sharp accuracy loss integer formats suffer. Third, HiFloat works fully with leading post-training quantization tools. Taken together, the results point to HiFloat as a practical route to faster, leaner language-model inference on these chips.
arxiv-2602-13135:
Guess-based argumentation is a structured way to reason from guesses, but classic systems restrict arguments and attacks to ground, variable-free forms built from propositional atoms. Emanuele De Angelis and five co-authors lift that restriction with limited guess-based argumentation, where components and arguments may carry limited variables over possibly infinite domains. They define non-ground meaning through some notions of non-ground attack.

The new meaning conservatively generalise standard guess-based meaning, meaning old results survive inside the broader system. For argumentation research, the extension matters. Real thinking involves variables and infinite domains, and a system that handles them without breaking current meaning opens the door to richer, more faithful models of debate and justification.
arxiv-2602-13235:
Vision-language models often lose detail when they crop or split an image before reasoning about it. Fixed outside tools can make that loss worse. Lang2Act takes a different path: it lets a model grow its own set of word-based tools for looking closely at images, then reuse those tools when it answers a question. Training runs in two stages: first to find good looking tools, then to use them well.

In tests, the method lifted visual perception scores by more than 4 percent over prior setups, showing that tools the model builds itself can beat rigid preset ones.
