The work fits a wider effort to give retrieval-based vision systems finer eyesight, since outside pictures are only useful if the model can still see their small details. Yuqi Xiong leads the work with eight co-authors, and the code and data are shared in public.
arxiv-2602-13435:
A universal zero-cycle is a strong algebraic gadget on a variety, and this paper finds a new obstruction to its existence. As an application, the author constructs a smooth projective complex surface whose Chow group of zero-cycles is representable, yet which admits no universal zero-cycle. The surface gives a two-dimensional analogue of Voisin's recent threefold counterexample to a question of Colliot-Thelene.

A further consequence is the first smooth projective threefold of Kodaira dimension zero carrying a non-torsion Hodge class of degree four that is not algebraic. The construction leans on the geometry of bielliptic surfaces of type two, tying the obstruction to a concrete geometric source. Theodosis Alexandrou is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13735:
Searching a long string efficiently requires an index, and the best indexes are measured against the string's compressibility. This paper describes an index on a string of length n with space proportional to delta log n over delta, where delta is the string complexity, measured in machine words. It searches any pattern of length m in time proportional to m plus occurrences times a small logarithmic factor. Crucially, the index is built in expected time proportional to n log n by a single left-to-right streaming pass, using the same compressed space.

The construction avoids Karp-Rabin fingerprints, and its randomization can be removed with deterministic dictionaries at some slowdown. Search time matches the best known results and space is almost optimal, and this is the first index constructible within such space and time guarantees. Dmitry Kosolobov is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-14435:
Di Zhou, writing alone, widens a 2026 arXiv model of phonon echoes in low-heat glasses. Glasses differ plainly from crystals at low heat, and the phonon echo spurred the two-level-system model, which told many shared glass odd bits. This paper broadens that setup to multi-level systems.

Phonon echoes last when non-linear energy forms and mess are in view. Virtual phonon swap brings many-body links between multi-level systems, yielding non-linear eigen-energies that lift the echo signal. Finite-heat warm wiggles cause dephasing, fading echo size over time. Analytic and number results agree across semi-classic and quantum regimes, backing the multi-level model and marking many-body roles in glassy motion.
arxiv-2602-14735:
Ait Haddou Marwan asks how much class news stays open to local probes when noise mars a quantum classifier. He casts two-way quantum sorting as a choice task with a cap: probes may touch at most k parts at once. His yardstick is the best bias such probes can reach, a local score for how well classes can be told apart.

For n qubits hit by lone depolarising noise, a Pauli-weight shrink rule sets that local score, and it points to a plain predictor he calls the k-local Pauli-accessible signal. Local eyes thus see less than global eyes, and this work says how much less, and why.
arxiv-2602-14835:
Evan Hadfield and Andrew Konya propose the Global Representativeness Index, a total variation distance framework scoring how well a survey sample matches its target population across demographic dimensions on a zero-to-one scale. Response rates and quotas, the usual proxies for sample quality, measure effort and coverage but not distributional fidelity.

Validation on seven waves of the Global Dialogues survey, seventy-five hundred respondents across more than sixty countries, finds fine-grained demographic scores of only 0.33 to 0.4 in the reported range, a sobering read on global samples. Survey research for AI governance and cross-cultural policy gains a standard fidelity metric. Representativeness becomes measurable, not assumed.
arxiv-2602-14935:
A. Plati, F. Restagno, and C. Poulard present the first systematic investigation of stick-slip dynamics in an interleaved system with self-amplified friction. Stick-slip is well studied in simple frictional setups, but complex assemblies with many contact surfaces, where traction forces convert into normal compression and amplify friction, have resisted characterisation.

Using interleaved paper blocks as a model system, the team combines force measurements and image processing to track stick-slip events as blocks are pulled apart at varied detachment velocities. Peak force and event amplitude patterns emerge from the data, as detailed in the paper. Tribology gains a controlled model for friction that feeds on itself.
arxiv-2602-15135:
Bhardwaj and Sastry census passkey adoption across the top 100000 websites. Passkeys are WebAuthn credentials synced across devices, promoted as the future of passwordless login. Built on FIDO2, they remove shared secrets, resist phishing, and gain usability from platform managers. Vendors have baked them into operating systems and browsers since 2022, yet wider adoption remains unknown.

Measuring it is hard because sites implement passkeys in mixed ways. Some show sign-in buttons, others bury options in multi-step flows, and many lean on outside identity providers or JavaScript libraries. With no standard discovery endpoint, the team builds Fidentikit, a browser crawler using 43 heuristics across five categories. The categories cover page elements, DOM structures, WebAuthn API calls, network patterns, and library detection. Applied to the top 100000 Tranco domains, it produces the first large-scale census. Use rises with site popularity and often depends on outside providers rather than native builds.
arxiv-2602-15535:
Verma and colleagues ask how to judge scores that rate hand gestures for biometrics. Past work leaned on error rates, but error rates say little about whether a score itself is good. The authors start from rank order and relevance. A good score ranks gestures well and rewards high scores for top gestures and low scores for low ones. It also tracks the trend of true scores, while disentanglement of identity traits acts as a discount.

Weaving those strands with weights, they define the Advanced Acceptance Score as one holistic gauge. Tests across three data sets and five state-of-the-art models show their gauge picks better scores than older gauges do. The new gauge still tracks older gauges well enough to support its trustworthiness. Code for the measure suite is public.
arxiv-2602-15635:
Sidorov works alone on a scheduling bottleneck: cumulative constraints in constraint programming are usually propagated one at a time, missing interactions between resources and causing severe slowdowns on some benchmarks. His fix is a preprocessing step that infers extra cumulative constraints capturing those interactions, without probing at search time. The method reads cumulative constraints as linear inequalities over occupancy vectors.

It then finds covers, sets of tasks that cannot run in parallel, strengthens their inequalities by lifting, and injects the resulting constraints back into the scheduling instance. Tests on standard RCPSP and RCPSP-max suites show better search performance and tighter objective bounds on favourable instances, with little harm elsewhere. The experiments also uncover 25 new lower bounds and five new best solutions, eight lower bounds coming straight from the inferred constraints.
arxiv-2602-15735:
Le Saux and colleagues test why many solar-like stars show no detectable acoustic modes, especially rapid rotators and magnetically active stars. Acoustic modes are the main probe of stellar interiors, yet Kepler data show a large share of solar-like stars without detectable modes. Recent theory proposes that spin damps convective motion, cutting power for stochastic excitation of low-degree modes.

The team tests that idea with fully compressible hydrodynamical simulations of a solar-like star, running 2.5D simulations with the MUSIC code across rotation rates from zero to eight solar units. Mode amplitudes fall clearly and systematically as spin rises, and damping rates grow in the fastest rotators. Reduced excitation plus stronger damping explains the observed drop in detectability, showing rotation must be accounted for when reading asteroseismic data.
arxiv-2602-16035:
Jibran Iqbal Shah leads a team of seven researchers asking how much self-driving cars should trust their own perception when they plan motion. Perception-based planners already try to carry sensor uncertainty into decisions, but if that uncertainty is miscalibrated, plans can go wrong in ways not yet measured. The team compares two prediction-planning pipelines with different levels of uncertainty propagation on the nuPlan benchmark.

Closed-loop tests on nuPlan challenge scenes show that the pipeline carrying upstream uncertainty through to planning generalizes better to complex scenes. Calibration of that uncertainty also shapes the outcome, not just its presence. For builders of urban driving systems, the paper gives a measured case for treating perception uncertainty as part of planning rather than an afterthought.
arxiv-2602-16335:
Stefan Ratschan leads a team including Mikoláš Janota on certifying satisfiability for formulas with universal quantifiers and uninterpreted function symbols. That combination shows up often in automated reasoning, partly because it can reason about arrays, yet satisfiability for such formulas is in general undecidable. In practice, SMT solvers do well on unsatisfiable cases through heuristics, but for satisfiable cases they rely on building an explicit model, which fails when the smallest model is not small enough.

The authors propose a different route: certify satisfiability with induction arguments. They apply the idea to linear integer arithmetic, producing an algorithm that proves satisfiability for formulas beyond the reach of current SMT solvers. The paper thus gives practitioners a tool for cases where model building stalls.
arxiv-2602-16435:
Arun Vignesh Malarkkan, Wangyang Ying, and Yanjie Fu introduce CAFE for causal feature engineering. Such engineering lets AI build representations from raw data, but existing methods rely on heuristics, producing brittle features that fail on shifted data. CAFE recasts the task as a causally-guided decision process bridging causal discovery and reinforcement learning.

Phase one learns a sparse graph over features and target, yielding soft priors, grouping features as direct, indirect, or other. Phase two uses cascading multi-agent deep Q-learning to select causal groups and operators, with reward shaping favoring plausible transformations and controlling complexity. Across fifteen benchmarks, CAFE improves up to seven percent over baselines, converging in fewer episodes. Under controlled shifts it cuts performance drop fourfold against a non-causal baseline, yielding compact sets with stable attributions. Causal structure as a soft prior, not a rigid constraint, boosts robustness.
arxiv-2602-16835:
Sasha Behrouzi and co-authors present NeST, a neuron-selective tuning frame for efficient post-hoc safety alignment of language models. Full fine-tuning costs much compute and storage, while parameter-efficient routes such as LoRA trade efficiency for uneven safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Intervention methods cut unsafe outputs without changing weights, but they do not shape the internal codes governing safety behavior.

NeST finds safety-relevant feed-forward neurons by activation probing on plain harmful and benign prompts, clusters neurons with similar activation profiles, and trains shared cluster-level updates while freezing the rest. It trains only on plain malicious prompts, without jailbreak-specific attack data, yet generalizes robustly to diverse jailbreaks. Learned updates fold into the original weights with no inference-time overhead. Tests on fourteen open-weight language and multimodal models show strong safety gains.
arxiv-2602-16935:
Justin Albrethsen and co-authors bring in DeepContext, a stateful real-time detector of multi-turn hostile intent drift. Safety guardrails remain largely stateless, treating multi-turn dialogues as disconnected events. That lack of time awareness opens a safety gap where hostile tactics such as Crescendo and ActorAttack slowly bleed malicious intent across turn boundaries to bypass memory-free filters.

DeepContext maps the time trajectory of user intent with a recurrent neural network ingesting a sequence of fine-tuned turn-level embeddings. By propagating a hidden state across the conversation, it captures incremental risk buildup that memory-free models overlook. Tests show it beats existing baselines in multi-turn jailbreak detection, with a state-of-the-art F1 score, substantially above hyperscaler cloud-provider guardrails and leading open-weight models. It also keeps inference overhead under twenty milliseconds on a T4 GPU, ensuring viability for real-time use.
arxiv-2602-17035:
Jing-Hui Huang and Xiang-Yun Hu report a quantitative test of weak-value amplification for longitudinal phase measurements using Allan variance analysis. The work builds on a recent double-slit interferometry experiment with real weak values. Allan variance analysis shows measurement of a few attosecond time delay near the shot noise limit at short averaging intervals.

That result represents two orders of magnitude variance cut compared to a long operating point in prior implementations. Allan-variance noise floor scales with the inverse of the detected photon number, showing shot-noise-limited working with weak-value amplification. That scaling shows that weak-value amplification can outperform usual measurement under fixed detected photon number and detector limits, in the presence of technical noise, as predicted by theory. Results provide strong evidence of near-optimal noise performance within reach with weak-value amplification, setting a new benchmark for precision optical metrology.
arxiv-2602-17335:
Jigao Luo led a three-author team asking whether GPUs truly need new tabular file formats, or just better settings for the old one. Parquet rules modern analytical systems as the columnar format, but its configuration guidance grew from CPU-centric execution. GPU-accelerated processing now spreads, and Parquet files built with CPU-oriented defaults can starve GPU parallelism, turning GPU scans into a bottleneck.

The paper systematically studies how Parquet configurations affect GPU scan performance. Poor GPU performance, the authors show, is not inherent to the format but follows from suboptimal configuration choices. GPU-aware configurations lift effective read bandwidth to very high rates without modifying the Parquet specification. The message is practical: tune the format for the hardware before inventing a replacement.
arxiv-2602-17635:
Nils Hertl and team build Newns-Anderson Hamiltonians from first principles for hydrogen stuck to metal surfaces. This tool is standard for gas sticking to solids, yet its usual build leans on simple guesses such as constant coupling and the wideband limit.

Their route applies projection operator diabatisation to matrices from Kohn-Sham density functional theory runs. They test it on hydrogen on three metal surfaces: Al, Cu and Pt. State counts and charge and vibration lifetimes match prior calculations well. The wideband limit holds for Al but has limited reach for Cu and Pt, a caution for future use.
arxiv-2602-17735:
Benoit Cloitre revisits the golden sieve, a self-reading removal process on rising lists of positive integers that he first gave in 2002. Applied to the natural numbers, the sieve yields the Wythoff pair as a Beatty partition. The paper extends the story to number runs and to new sieve variants.

For runs of a standard linear form, Cloitre shows a link with hiccup lists recently studied by Fokkink and Joshi, and with Fraenkel's paired splits. He also introduces a pull-out sieve that likewise yields hiccup lists, whose action on number runs follows a plain affine shift of hiccup settings. Readers gain a compact update on a self-reading process and its links to paired splits.
arxiv-2602-17835:
Sirui Chen and team introduce Iprox, a two-stage frame for influence-preserving proxies in gradient-based data selection for language model fine-tuning. Supervised fine-tuning hinges on picking training data that most helps downstream scores. Gradient-based methods such as TracIn and Influence Functions spot useful samples, yet scale poorly for multi-billion-parameter models.

Off-the-shelf smaller models serve as common proxies, but they stay suboptimal. Their learning motion is unclear, their sizes cannot flex, and they cannot align further with the target model on influence. Iprox derives proxies from the target model. A low-rank compression stage preserves influence information. An aligning stage aligns gradients and logits, controlling cost while retaining target influence. Tests show Iprox beating off-the-shelf proxies and baselines. On Qwen3-4B, a smaller Iprox proxy beats a larger off-the-shelf one. On Llama3.2, Iprox beats baselines while halving compute.
arxiv-2602-18035:
Serena Dipierro and colleagues study the spectral theory of mixed local and nonlocal operators carrying lower-order terms on the right-hand side. Such problems arise from superposition operators of mixed order whose lower-order terms carry the wrong sign relative to classical elliptic theory. The paper builds the eigenvalue picture for this mixed setting.

When the right-hand side localizes, the results converge to the classical cases, recovering simplicity and sign-definiteness of eigenfunctions in the limit. Disconnected domains behave strikingly differently. Unlike the classical case, every eigenfunction for the first eigenvalue must change sign. The first eigenvalue of a union of disconnected domains sits strictly below those of its individual components. The authors also give examples where the first eigenvalue is simple or non-simple on disconnected domains, backed by a regularity theory that supports the whole analysis.
arxiv-2602-18135:
A large team led by Francesco Clozza tests the X-ray eyes of SIDDHARTA-2, an experiment run at the DAΦNE collider. Their 2026 paper checks a wide-area silicon drift detector system built to read faint X-rays from light atoms holding a kaon, a short-lived particle. Those readings probe how kaons tug on atomic nuclei at low energies.

The team pushed the detector checks to higher energies, up to fifty thousand electron volts, so later runs can study heavier kaonic atoms with brighter lines. They measured how straight the energy scale stays and how sharp the energy readings are across that range. The calibration held to better than one part in a thousand. That result clears the way for wider kaonic atom studies with the same detectors.
arxiv-2602-18235:
Gábor Damásdi builds explicit hypergraph families that stay hard to color in two different worlds at once. His 2026 paper gives families whose uniformity and chromatic number can grow without bound, realized both geometrically and number-theoretically. That dual realization is the paper's engine.

As a first payoff, Damásdi reproves a result first shown by Chen, Pach, Szegedy, and Tardos, by construction rather than chance. Any finite plane set can be forced to hold a same-color axis-parallel rectangle with many points. For rectangles holding two points, he also builds graphs with both huge girth and huge chromatic number. The paper closes by answering a coloring question of Pálvölgyi on integer sets and finite arithmetic progressions, plus an application to partially ordered sets.
arxiv-2602-18735:
Rebuilding a full 3D shape from a partial scan is hard when the missing parts could take many forms. Weilong Yan, with six co-authors, presents LaS-Comp in 2026, a zero-shot, category-agnostic completion method that borrows the geometric priors of 3D foundation models without training a new model for each object type.

Completion runs in two complementary stages: an explicit replacement stage keeps the observed geometry faithful, and an implicit refinement stage smooths the joins between observed and invented regions. A new benchmark, Omni-Comp, mixes real and synthetic partial patterns for a sterner test. Across quantitative and qualitative checks, the method beats previous leading approaches while working with different foundation models.
arxiv-2602-18935:
Libraries are turning to language models for reference services, raising a fairness question. Can those services treat all patrons impartially, regardless of demographic identity? Haining Wang, with two co-authors, audits three widely used open models in 2026. The protocol pairs diagnostic classification, which spots systematic gaps between replies, with linguistic analysis, which helps explain them.

Across the three models, no compelling evidence of systematic distinction by race or ethnicity emerges. Only minor evidence of sex-linked differentiation appears, in one model and one setting. The authors discuss what that means for equitable AI adoption in libraries. Ongoing monitoring matters, they argue, for keeping LLM-based services aligned with social justice goals. Fairness here is not a one-time check, but a standing commitment.
arxiv-2602-19035:
Visual odometry usually assumes fixed viewing rates and calibrated cameras, assumptions dashcam footage routinely violates. Phuc D. A. Nguyen, with two co-authors, introduces OpenVO in 2026, a frame for open-world visual tracking with time motion awareness under limited input conditions.

OpenVO estimates real-world-scale ego-motion from single-camera dashcam footage with varying viewing rates and uncalibrated cameras, allowing robust trajectory dataset building from rare driving events. Time motion data is explicitly encoded within a two-frame pose regression frame, and 3D geometric priors from foundation models are leveraged. Validation on three major autonomous-driving benchmarks shows performance gains of over twenty percent over leading approaches. Under varying viewing rates, errors fall by roughly half to over nine-tenths across metrics. OpenVO thus proves versatile for real-world 3D reconstruction and downstream uses.
arxiv-2602-19335:
The brightest fast radio bursts are rare, so pinning down their top energy takes a huge sample. Vishwangi Shah and 27 co-authors use 2,998 one-off bursts from the Second CHIME/FRB Catalog, the largest sample available. They use it to set a lower limit on the maximum isotropic energy of such bursts. With redshifts unknown for most sources, they work from dispersion measures and fluences plus the likely redshift for each dispersion.

Simulated samples test how outliers, bursts with large host-galaxy or halo dispersion, might inflate the limit. After accounting for them, the lower limit ranges from 1.2 times 10 to the 41st power up to 1.9 times 10 to the 42nd power erg, with a best estimate of 1.2 times 10 to the 42nd power erg. The result matches limits from much smaller samples, tightening constraints on burst engines and progenitors.
arxiv-2602-19835:
The Mumford-Tate conjecture links the symmetries of a variety's cohomology across different mathematical lenses, and hyper-Kähler varieties are a key test case. A 2026 arXiv paper by Zhichao Tang and Haitao Zou studies that conjecture for hyper-Kähler varieties.

The authors link the Mumford-Tate group to a Levi factor inside the connected total l-adic monodromy group. From that link, the conjecture follows after passing to semisimplified forms in every degree, a statement they call the semisimple Mumford-Tate conjecture. Uses include a Hodge-to-Tate implication for powers, proof that the conjecture survives deformation, an l-adic Nagai result for Type I reduction, and a maximality result widened from degree two to all cohomology.
arxiv-2602-20135:
Good test datasets for language models take time and money to build. That bottleneck slows testing of other applications. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mohammad Amanlou and five co-authors introduces KNIGHT, a framework that generates question datasets from external sources using a knowledge graph.

KNIGHT first builds a topic-specific knowledge graph. That graph is a structured, compact summary of items and relations. Once built, it can be reused to set difficulty levels under teacher control, including multi-hop questions, without re-feeding the full source text each time. The graph acts as a compressed, reused state, so generating questions becomes a cheap read over the graph. The framework is shown on Wikipedia and Wikidata, while staying free of any single domain or ontology. As a case study it produces six question datasets in history, biology, and mathematics, judged on fluency, clarity, topic fit, option uniqueness, and more.
arxiv-2602-20235:
Physicists hunting for new particles in collider data need the proton's inner structure, described by parton distribution functions. At large momentum fraction, those functions overlap where new physics would show up, so a wrong choice can hide or fake a signal. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ella Cole and six co-authors asks which PDF sets to trust in searches beyond the Standard Model.

Tight PDF sets give the most sensitivity, but they may already hide new physics. Cautious sets that drop high-energy data avoid that trap, at the cost of wider errors. The paper tests cautious fitting plans and recommends the class best suited to robust searches. It also studies fits solving for new-physics strengths and proton structure together, keeping their links consistent. Readers gain practical guidance for searches that must neither overclaim nor silently absorb the signal they seek.
arxiv-2602-20435:
Heavy-quark effective field theory has succeeded for heavy-to-light meson decays, and Ruiyu Zhou and three co-authors test it on charmed semileptonic decays. They compute transition form factors for Ds decays to eta and eta-prime mesons with a lepton and neutrino, using light-cone sum rules in the heavy-quark framework. A right-handed chiral correlation function tames large uncertainties from eta twist-three distribution amplitudes.

Extrapolating the form factors across the full physical range with a simplified series expansion, the authors predict branching fractions for eta decays. They are about two point three percent with electrons and two point two five percent with muons. For eta-prime decays the figures are about zero point eight six and zero point eight two percent. Lepton flavor universality ratios near one match recent BESIII measurements, and small negative forward-backward asymmetries suggest no significant violation.
arxiv-2602-20635:
It is conjectured that a quantum code corrects a given count of deletion errors exactly when it corrects the same total count of insertion and deletion errors. Ken Nakamura and two co-authors prove this conjecture for general quantum codes, closing a gap left by earlier proofs that covered only special conditions. The proof turns on a key property of inserted states, which the paper establishes first.

The paper shows that a quantum state after an insertion error forms a product state of the original multi-qudit system and the inserted quantum state. Combining that property with previous results yields the full proof. The paper also defines generalized insertion errors by dropping the quantum channel requirement from insertion errors, and it presents properties of those generalized errors.
arxiv-2602-20735:
Kun Ran and eleven co-authors present the award-winning RMIT-ADM+S system for the Text-to-Text track of the NeurIPS 2025 MMU-RAG Competition. They introduce Routing-to-RAG, a research-focused search-augmented generation design built from light parts. It tunes the search plan on the fly, based on guessed query depth and whether evidence suffices.

The system uses smaller language models, letting it run on a single home GPU while handling complex research tasks. It builds on G-RAG, winner of the ACM SIGIR 2025 LiveRAG Challenge, and extends it with modules shaped by close review of outputs. R2RAG won the Best Dynamic Evaluation award in the Open Source category, showing high strength with careful design and lean use of means.
arxiv-2602-20835:
Tensor-triangulated categories appear across geometry, homotopy theory, and representation theory, but they lack a single geometric picture. Drew Heard and Marius Nielsen supply one in this 2026 arXiv paper. To any small tensor-triangulated category in the key sense, and a chosen Thomason subset, they attach a ringed space called the formal spectrum.

The authors set out the basic traits of this build and compute it in cases drawn from algebraic geometry, chromatic homotopy theory, equivariant homotopy theory, and modular representation theory. The result is a shared language for passing between abstract categories and geometric spaces. Readers in any of these fields can see how the same formal picture orders their own cases.
arxiv-2602-20935:
Imagine standing at a point in hyperbolic space while random flat dividers block your view. Zakhar Kabluchko, Vanessa Mattutat, and Christoph Thaele study that sight-line problem in this 2026 arXiv paper, for a family of dividers that runs between fully straight dividers and horospheres. Their main result is a shared rule: the key sight traits do not hinge on the blend setting.

A key density splits two regimes: below it the seen zone has no bound with good odds, above it it is bounded almost surely, with an exact key value. In two dimensions boundedness also holds at the key value. In the bounded phase the mean seen volume matches the known rule for the endpoint case. The proof turns on an integral-geometric count that is itself free of the blend setting.
arxiv-2602-21135:
Altermagnets split spins by momentum, and symmetry decides where that splitting lives. Arindom Das, Arijit Mandal, Nayana Devaraj, and B. R. K. Nanda study symmetry breaking in chromium antimonide in this 2026 arXiv paper, using density functional calculations and symmetry analysis. Pristine material has six-fold rotational symmetry, which vacancy engineering and interstitial doping reduce to two-fold.

Under two-fold rotation, fragmented nodal curves appear across the Brillouin zone, with locations that vary by band, unlike typical nodal planes and axes. Uniaxial strain and the compound RbMnPO4 confirm the pattern. These curves can support anomalous Hall conductivities with Neel vectors in-plane and out-of-plane, opening device possibilities for altermagnets.
arxiv-2602-21635:
Tobias Galla alone authors a paper on a diffusion model for systems with frequent weak resets. The work develops a diffusion model for systems subject to fast random resets by small amounts. Equivalently, it describes systems with frequent but small catastrophes.

Validity is shown by computing the steady spread and mean first-passage times of simple one-dimensional systems. The model captures correlations in multi-particle systems that arise from motion itself. It can also extend the conditionally independent and identically distributed structure recently found in systems with full resets. Finally, resets can induce cycles and patterns, which can be described with the diffusion model, giving a compact tool for weakly reset systems.
arxiv-2602-21835:
Video base models join understanding, generation, editing, and direction following in one setup, a direction for next-gen multi-mode systems. Yet current review benchmarks remain split, each targeting one task with task-specific scores and short or simple clips, missing the joined skills aimed for. Jianhui Wei and eight co-authors introduce UniVBench, a benchmark judging video base models across four core skills: understanding, generation, editing, and video rebuilding. It judges how faithfully a model reproduces video content it has met.

The benchmark widens review complexity with 200 high-quality, diverse, multi-shot videos, each with detailed captions, editing orders, and reference images. All videos are human-created and checked, offering richer cinematic detail than prior benchmarks. UniV-Eval standardizes prompting, order parsing, and scoring, enabling fair, scalable, repeatable comparisons. Grounding review in order-based multi-shot video tasks, UniVBench first measures joined skills, with human notes aligning review.
arxiv-2602-22435:
Artin-Schreier curves are a well-known family in the math of curves, and their rings of invariants encode deep facts about symmetry. Juanita Duque-Rosero and three co-authors present a step-by-step method for computing generators of those rings. The method is concrete and constructive, turning invariant theory for these curves into computation.

The authors give explicit invariants for almost all Artin-Schreier curves of genus up to eight in standard form, plus a few higher-genus curves. That coverage makes the method ready to use for researchers studying these curves' symmetries. Number theorists gain a concrete toolkit where abstract invariant theory once stood alone.
arxiv-2602-22535:
Zitong Yu and three co-authors ask whether AI-based fast MRI scans keep the detail doctors actually need. They trained deep learning model observers, stand-ins for human readers, to judge resolution on a Rayleigh discrimination task. Test signals were planted in the white matter of synthetic brain images. Scans ran at full sampling, roughly fivefold, and roughly sixteenfold acceleration.

The AI reconstruction, a U-Net, scored far higher than the standard root-sum-of-squares method on general image-quality numbers. Yet it fell behind on the task that matters: telling close signals apart. At roughly fivefold acceleration its accuracy dropped about 25 percent for 4 mm signals and 5 percent for 5 mm signals against fully sampled standard reconstruction. Similar declines appeared at roughly sixteenfold acceleration. Better-looking scans, the authors warn, do not always mean better diagnoses.
arxiv-2602-22735:
Yunpeng Bai and two co-authors turn augmented reading into an optimization problem. Reading aids that adapt text layout to help comprehension usually rest on heuristics, opaque data models, or endless human testing. The team grounds design instead in resource-rational models of reading, where a simulated reader spends limited attention, memory, and time under task demands.

Two pipelines follow from that simulated reader. An offline pipeline explores layout options without human subjects, while an online pipeline personalizes interfaces live from ongoing interaction data. Together they promise reading tools that adapt, explain themselves, and scale, judged by systematic simulation rather than trial and error alone.
arxiv-2602-23035:
Viraj Patel and six co-authors model cardiac swirls as linked nodes in a latent graph. Blood flow patterns carry rich information about disease levels and medical treatments, yet imaging and computer methods miss the link structure of orderly flow traits. Their physics-guided setup pairs neural link-based inference with physics-inspired interplay energy and birth-death shifts.

In aortic coarctation runs, learned graphs grow more structured as vessel narrowing progresses. Graph entropy tracks illness level steadily, with an R-squared near four-fifths and a Spearman correlation near one. Aneurysm volume gives the most telling latent picture among shape measures, with entropy tracking illness level steadily and carrying over to several alternative shape measures. Ultrasound flow fields of a left heart chamber under varying assist-device support show the graph capturing the loss of orderly vortex interplay under machine help.
arxiv-2602-23335:
Dany Haddad and 21 co-authors analyze how researchers actually use AI-powered science tools, through the Asta Interaction Dataset. Such tools are joining research workflows fast, but the field has lacked a clear view of real-world use. The data set holds over 200,000 queries and interaction logs from two deployed tools, a literature discovery interface and a scientific question-answering interface, inside a retrieval-augmented generation platform.

Users pose longer, more complex queries than in traditional search and treat the system as a research partner, delegating drafting and gap-finding. They treat generated answers as lasting artifacts, revisiting outputs and cited evidence in non-linear ways. With experience, queries grow more targeted and citation engagement deepens, though keyword-style queries persist even among veterans. The anonymized data set and a new query intent taxonomy are released to guide future assistant design and realistic evaluation.
arxiv-2602-23535:
Adam Block and one co-author study how hard it is to estimate partition functions. They assume sample access to a proposal distribution plus an unnormalized density ratio for the target. Existing guarantees usually lean on structural assumptions about domain or model shape. The authors instead depend only on the proposal-target link.

Their analysis introduces the integrated coverage profile: how much target mass sits where the density ratio is large. Integrated coverage tightly pins down sample complexity for multiplicative estimation, with matching lower bounds. Restated via f-divergences, the bounds show sharp phase transitions with the growth rate of f. They recover classical results and extend to heavy-tailed regimes. Applications improve finite-sample guarantees for importance sampling and self-normalized importance sampling. They also show a strict separation between the complexity of approximate sampling and counting under the same divergence constraints.
arxiv-2602-23635:
Romina Mahinpei and two co-authors study how large language models help and hurt teaching assistants in proof-based courses. Teaching assistants are essential for grading and feedback, yet these tasks are time-intensive and hard to scale. LLM effectiveness in proof-based courses, however, was still unknown.

The team presents a multi-part case study as a technology probe in an undergraduate proof-based course. They compare rubric-based grading decisions by an LLM and by teaching assistants with varying expertise, and examine teaching assistants' perceptions of LLM-generated feedback. They find substantial disagreement between LLMs and teaching assistants on grading decisions, but LLM-generated feedback can still prove useful for submissions with major errors. The paper closes with design implications for human-AI grading and feedback systems.
arxiv-2602-23735:
Fabian Zierler and six co-authors present numerical results from a finite-temperature study of Sp(4) Yang-Mills theory on the lattice. They study its first-order confinement and deconfinement phase transition by reconstructing the density of states via the Logarithmic Linear Relaxation algorithm.

Measurements are performed on lattices with different extents of space and time and aspect ratios. The team estimates the size of discretisation and finite-volume artefacts. Clear signatures of a first-order transition are found. The critical coupling, specific heat, and surface tension are determined for finite extents of the thermal circle, and the results set bounds for the continuum theory.
arxiv-2602-23935:
Bowen Sun and five co-authors present LACE-RL, a framework that balances cold starts against idle carbon in serverless computing. The 2026 paper notes the core trade-off. Keeping function instances warm cuts latency. Reclaiming idle instances cuts emissions. Both grid carbon intensity and workload shift over time, defeating fixed keep-alive rules.

LACE-RL treats pod retention as a sequential decision problem and uses deep reinforcement learning to tune keep-alive durations on the fly, jointly modeling cold-start odds, function-specific latency costs, and real-time carbon intensity. On a public Huawei cloud trace, it cuts cold starts and idle keep-alive emissions sharply versus the provider's static policy. It beats heuristic and single-objective baselines on the latency-carbon trade-off. It approaches oracle performance. The work offers cloud operators a practical lever for greener, faster serverless service.
arxiv-2602-24035:
Stephen A. Cookson and six co-authors build a quality framework for testing gravity with wide binary stars, and find no evidence for MOND, a modified dynamics theory. The 2026 paper targets the low-acceleration regime, where MOND predicts measurable departures from Newtonian gravity in the relative motions of widely separated stellar pairs.

The framework stresses high-quality sample selection, filtering of poor astrometric solutions, contamination control, and careful uncertainty propagation. The authors show that undetected close binaries, chance alignments, and mishandled projection effects can fake MOND-like signals, and they offer a checklist to avoid those traps. Applied to Gaia data, a high-purity sample of nearby wide binaries shows no velocity enhancement of the size MOND predicts, matching Newtonian gravity across separations. Earlier apparent MOND signals shrink as methods tighten.
arxiv-2603-00035: Gahtan, Shpund and Bronstein present a fast differentiable solver for anisotropic asymmetric distance fields under Randers-Finsler metrics on Cartesian grids. A GPU-friendly fast-sweeping forward pass with causality-valid stencils pairs with exact gradients from implicit differentiation. The backward pass solves the adjoint system in one reverse-time back-substitution without unrolling iterations, saving memory and runtime. Closed-form derivatives, feasibility projections and stable gradients enable inverse problems such as recovering metrics and drift fields from sparse arrival times, demonstrated on wildfire spread models.
arxiv-2603-00135: Park introduces shift-share designs, a popular tool in political science, reviewing past work, synthesising recent methods and weighing their value in the field. Although long used in economics, their causal traits only recently came into focus, and papers often apply them without fully probing or testing identifying assumptions, sometimes wrongly. Most papers lean on share exogeneity, leaving shifter exogeneity underused despite its similar spread in economics. Park shows the shifter framework and builds extra theory results for use in political science settings.
arxiv-2603-00535: Zhou and six colleagues turn cone beam CT scans into synthetic CT for radiotherapy dose planning, where beam scans carry heavy artefacts and unreliable density values. Paired scans are often missing or misaligned, and plain rectified flow with random pseudo pairs gives unstable training on small medical sets. Their RAFM method builds retrieval guided pseudo pairs with a frozen DINOv3 encoder plus a global CT memory bank, stabilising unpaired flow training. Under a strict true unpaired protocol on SynthRAD2023, RAFM beats existing methods.
arxiv-2603-00935: Vu, Martinelli, and Lähdesmäki adapt latent-space Bayesian optimization to goals that drift over time, as in design campaigns with shifting tastes or targets. Their TALBO method weaves time into both the surrogate model and the generative representation, keeping the latent space aligned as objectives move. On drifting molecular design tasks it beats strong baselines across drift speeds and stays competitive when objectives actually stand still.
arxiv-2603-01235: Mestre and three colleagues extend checks of ESS beyond staff-loss forecasts to a mixed urban resource sharing system. The second case mixes tabular, time, and place data under multi-interest-group rules, with scored ranks of typical clear-AI groups in both contexts. Results show ESS rankings adapt in step with rule roles, risk shapes, and group setups. They are not domain-set, backing ESS as a general choice-support tool for clear-AI plans.
arxiv-2603-01435:
Heejune Kim studies a model of magnets with many possible states in this 2026 math work. The Potts spin glass gives each spin one of several colors, and the states interact in a random way. A key question is whether all colors stay in balance when the system is hot and disordered.

Kim shows that color balance holds at high heat for three or more colors. The proof uses a second-moment count on a balanced form of the model, plus known facts from a calmer Potts case. For just two colors, a symmetry trick shows that skewed states are very rare at any heat level. Such results help map where order can and cannot form in random magnet models.
arxiv-2603-01535:
Zijin Yin, Bing Li, Kongming Liang, and colleagues build a way to stress-test image labeling models before real use. Their 2026 work concerns semantic segmentation, which labels each pixel by class for cars, medicine, and more. Models that shine on clean test sets may fail when color, size, or weather shifts in the field.

Their pipeline, Gen4Seg, edits real photos with tight control while keeping the true labels valid. Edits change object traits like color, material, size, and place, plus whole-image traits like weather and style. Diffusion models power the edits, and old labels carry over, which cuts the cost of new test sets. From the pipeline come two new test sets drawn from classic photo collections, ready to probe model weak spots.
arxiv-2603-02135:
Jin Yan, Ayumi Ozawa, Yuzuru Sato, and Hiroshi Kori study linked spinning units in this 2026 physics paper. Each unit is a phase oscillator, a simple model of a cycle that repeats. Neighbors are linked with a shared phase shift. The authors ask which end state the system reaches from each start.

As the shift grows, the borders between outcome regions grow more jagged and complex. The team suspects those regions become fully mixed near a key limit. They also track how long a twist count takes to settle. That time grows with system size, and growth speeds up at large shifts. The work maps how one shift value shapes long, slow settling.
arxiv-2603-02435:
Athanasios Efthymiou, Stevan Rudinac, Monika Kackovic, and colleagues merge vision-language models with knowledge graphs in this 2026 paper. Knowledge graphs store facts as entities and relations, often with images attached. Standard embedding methods learn from one modality at a time. That leaves cross-modal alignment weak and assumes every entity has every modality.

Their framework, VL-KGE, uses vision-language models to align modalities in one shared space. Structured relation modeling then works on those unified representations. Tests used a word-image graph and two new fine art graphs built by the team. Link prediction improved steadily over unimodal and multimodal rivals. The results argue that vision-language alignment strengthens reasoning over large, mixed knowledge graphs.
arxiv-2603-02535:
Zheyuan Kuang, Tinghui Li, Weiwei Jiang, and colleagues study how interaction shapes emotion in virtual reality in this 2026 paper. VR reliably evokes emotions, but research mostly measures how strong they feel. How interaction itself changes the experience was less clear. The team extends a validated emotion data set in two ways.

A new scene targets strong, positive arousal and was validated with two dozen users. Every scene then gained interactive elements, creating paired interactive and passive versions. A larger study of eighty-four users combined self-ratings with body signals. Interaction did not just amplify emotion, it redirected it by context. It supported coping in negative scenes and boosted enjoyment in positive ones. Scene-tailored interaction could regulate emotion, not merely evoke it.
arxiv-2603-02735:
Philip Caesar Flores, Stefanos Carlström, Serguei Patchkovskii, and colleagues explain why shining circular light on chiral molecules can sort electrons by spin. Chiral molecules come in left- and right-handed forms, and their ionization yields differ by handedness and spin. An earlier theory needed ten separate parameters to describe the effect.

The authors show the signal comes from just three arrow-like quantities, called pseudovectors, rooted in the geometry of the process. Two arise inside the molecule, in spin space and in real space, and one from the light's direction. The ten older parameters collapse into moments of these three quantities. Because the same arrows govern related processes, the picture should extend to multi-photon cases and any light polarization.
arxiv-2603-02835:
Shubhankar Paul, Atsutoshi Ikeda, Giordano Mattoni, and colleagues grow and measure clean crystals of the altermagnet CrSb. Altermagnets blend traits of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets while keeping zero net magnetization, and CrSb draws interest for its large spin splitting. Their 2026 paper reports crystals grown by a self-flux method, larger and cleaner than earlier samples.

Electrical, magnetic, and heat measurements show a quality ratio well above prior reports and a strong rise in resistance inside a magnetic field. Heat data down to very low temperatures point to weakly interacting electrons and a measurable gap in the magnetic excitations. The crystals show no superconductivity down to near absolute zero. The clean baseline helps judge CrSb for room-temperature spin devices.
arxiv-2603-02935:
Mohammadreza Nakhaei, Aidan Scannell, Kevin Luck, and Joni Pajarinen teach agents to recognize which task they face by how its world behaves. Their 2026 paper addresses offline meta-reinforcement learning, where policies must adapt to new tasks using only fixed past data. Context methods guess the task from recent transitions, but learning good guesses without labels is hard.

Their fix conditions a latent world model, an internal simulator, on the inferred task summary, and trains both parts together. That forces the summary to capture how the task's dynamics differ, not just surface clues. The learned summaries were richer, and adaptation to unseen tasks improved clearly. Gains held across three standard benchmark suites for control and manipulation.
arxiv-2603-03035:
Emil Javurek, Dennis Frauen, Yuxin Wang, and Stefan Feuerriegel give cause-and-effect estimates honest error bars. The usual Bayesian route needs a full chance model of the data, plus messy side parts like who got treated. Their 2026 frame skips the full model entirely.

Prior views sit straight on the causal amounts of interest, such as mean treatment effects. A loss built from the logic of the design then updates those views. Old loss-based tools thus gain full statements of doubt at no extra cost. Plugged into modern machine learning pipes, the method stays robust when the side parts are learned slowly. Tests across settings confirm the error bars are well sized.
arxiv-2603-03235:
Choosing how many clusters hide in data is a classic headache, and the elbow statistic gives the folk solution a rigorous form. Analysts often eyeball a bend in a heterogeneity curve to pick the cluster count, yet real structure can live at several scales at once. This 2026 paper builds ElbowSig, a framework that treats the elbow as a formal inference problem.

A normalized curvature measure, computed from the heterogeneity sequence, is compared against the behavior of genuinely unstructured data. The authors derive that null behavior for both large samples and high dimensions. The procedure works with hard, fuzzy, and model-based clustering alike, needing only the heterogeneity curve. Experiments show sound false-positive control plus the power to resolve layered structure that single-answer criteria miss.
arxiv-2603-03335:
Anna Bair and three colleagues show that single skills inside a language model live in surprisingly few parts. Models reason about mathematics, write code, and handle language, and one might expect each skill to be spread everywhere. Their 2026 study finds the opposite: many capabilities sit in small subsets of attention heads, the components that route information between tokens.

Turning off as few as five skill-specific heads can cut performance on that skill's tests by up to about two thirds, while unrelated tasks stay mostly intact. Finding the right heads is the hard part, so the authors borrow compressed sensing, using strategic knockouts and few evaluations to locate them. Tests across two model families at several sizes confirm a modular pattern, with clear stakes for interpretation, editing, and safety work.
arxiv-2603-03435:
J J Ramos and J E G Silva ask whether cosmic acceleration can come from geometry outside our universe. Their 2026 paper places our cosmos on a thick brane, a four-dimensional sheet inside a five-dimensional bulk, under a modified gravity theory built on symmetric teleparallelism. Solving the field equations for an expanding five-dimensional universe gives the scale factor's behavior over time.

An effective cosmological constant appears on the brane by itself, generated and confined by the bulk's curved geometry, so no fundamental constant needs to be inserted. Both a thin Randall-Sundrum style brane and a thick sine-Gordon brane yield accelerated expansion. Tuning the theory's parameters also produces steady de Sitter growth, contraction, and oscillating histories. Where the brane sits in the bulk decides its fate, offering a geometric reading of the observed constant's smallness.
arxiv-2603-03835:
Z Zhang presents the lattice computation that removed a twenty-year hint of new physics. The muon's odd magnetic moment long sat far away from its Standard Model prediction, and sharpening tests seemed to widen the gap. Then the Budapest-Marseille-Wuppertal collaboration's lattice computation of the hadronic vacuum polarization, the leading uncertainty, overturned the expert consensus and erased the tension entirely.

This 2026 report gives the latest results from the BMW and DMZ collaborations. Their determination of the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution now reaches an accuracy under half a percent, the sharpest yet from lattice methods. The talk-format paper walks through the comparison between the world-average measurement and the lattice-based forecast. A discrepancy that motivated a wave of proposed new particles ends, on this evidence, as a triumph of computing.
arxiv-2603-04635: Aliakbarpour and colleagues design independence testers with prediction help. Independence testing asks whether a joint distribution is a product or far from every product form. In finite-sample work, sample complexity grows polynomially with support size, making the task expensive. Augmented distribution testing moves past worst-case limits using extra prediction tips. The testers stay robust, keeping worst-case soundness, while gaining when predictions are accurate. Work includes a paired tester that cuts sample complexity by prediction error, a wider version, and matching lower bounds showing optimal complexity.
arxiv-2603-04735: Brenner, Cohen-Addad, and Woodruff show AI speeding math work by solving an open physics problem. Their hybrid system joins Gemini Deep Think with tree search and auto number feedback. It derives novel exact answers for gravity wave spectra from cosmic strings. The agent evaluates a core integral for any loop shapes, improving on recent partial attempts. It finds six exact methods, the most elegant using the kernel in Gegenbauer polys to absorb inner spikes. The asymptotic result agrees with numerical results and connects to further theory.
arxiv-2603-05035: Anatoly Belikov and Ilya Fedotov present GELO, a rule for privacy-keeping inference on shared accelerators where adversaries can see KV caches and hidden states. Static obfuscation breaks under multi-run statistical attacks, while cryptographic protections are far too slow for interactive inference. GELO hides hidden states with per-batch invertible mixing, inverting on return so outputs stay unchanged. Because mixing is never reused, attackers face just a one-batch blind source separation problem. Defenses include non-orthogonal mixing to mask Gram matrices.
arxiv-2603-05135: Wenqian Li and team offer SRasP, a crop-global style perturbation network for cross-domain few-shot learning. Current style perturbation methods mitigate domain shift but suffer gradient wobble and settling to sharp minima. SRasP uses global semantic guidance to spot incoherent crops, then reorients and aggregates crop style gradients with global gradients within one image. A multi-objective tuning function trades visual discrepancy against semantic sameness across global, crop, and adversarial features. Stabilized perturbations during training encourage flatter, more transferable answers and better carry-over to unseen domains.
arxiv-2603-05435: Joannes Vermant studies infinitesimal graph-of-groups realisations using cellular sheaves and cohomology, building on Stokes and Vermant's hypergraph versions via graphs of groups as a new stiffness account. Using these tools, the author gives an algebra-based Henneberg-move freedom condition, proving stiffness and flexibility of them are generic traits. Whenever a stiffness problem is posed in a Lie group G with a 1-dimensional connected subgroup H whose normalizer quotient is finite, the Maxwell-count gives a necessary and sufficient condition. That rule governs minimal stiffness, generalising results.
arxiv-2603-05735: Badea and team present an agent thrust-spread measure in electron-positron collisions at 91.2 GeV using ALEPH data. The work proceeds through agent-physics teamwork prompting Claude and Codex. Under physics guidance, agents wrote and ran all code and drafted most text. A fully fixed thrust spectrum comes from repeat Bayesian opening and Monte Carlo fixes. The main point is showing agent analysis with thrust as a benchmark. The work steps toward a theory-test loop where agents assist measures and math and blend insights by matching results.
arxiv-2603-06135: Revilla and colleagues tackle telling legitimate critical speech apart from coordinated conspiracy narratives, where labeled roles and rigid schemas miss diffuse participation. Their pipeline pulls an entity interaction graph from narratives with a BERT encoder and classifies it with a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer. Counterfactual distillation then estimates each node's treatment effect and prunes extras, leaving a minimal predictive subgraph. On the PAN benchmark the model reaches state of the art accuracy with roughly a third of its nearest rival's parameters. It prunes graphs by about three quarters on average.
arxiv-2603-06335: Gabrovšek and Cavicchioli classify spherical knotoids fully through six crossings, guessing it holds up to seven crossings. They extend knot tabulation to knotoids from Turaev. They describe methods for diagram listing, trimming, and telling classes apart with markers including the Kauffman bracket, Arrow, Affine index, Mock Alexander, and Yamada polynomials. They also look at chirality and rotational symmetries, with protein entanglement uses showing the value of such work. The list of markers is long, and each one tells classes apart in its own way.
arxiv-2603-06635: Podstawski studies whether small taught language models can infer properties of linked structures presented as text, testing input form and reasoning strategy. Across local and global graph metrics on three models, scaled errors always exceed the spread of target properties, and rank links stay weak across setups. Graph property guessing thus remains deeply unreliable absent task-specific fine-tuning or design adaptation. The failure is structured, however: neighbour-list codes lower error and improve ordinal order versus edge-lists, while multi-branch thought yields real gains.
arxiv-2603-06735: Mitzner and colleagues build a vessel-aware deep learning method for detecting age-related macular degeneration from OCTA scans. Instead of global image traits, theirs fuses vessel tortuosity maps and dropout maps, drawn from arteries, veins, and tiny vessels, with the OCTA image. Tortuosity tracks odd vessel shape linked to poor self-control of blood flow, while dropout maps mark local blood-supply gaps that precede retinal damage. Artery tortuosity proves steadiest.
arxiv-2603-07035: Liao and colleagues extend a circuit quantisation method to include Higgs modes in superconductors, modes tied to how the energy gap moves. They start from a microscopic model of small superconductors and project it onto its low-energy BCS state space. From this they derive formulas for the Higgs mass, spring constant, and gap oscillation rate, checked by numeric tests. They also compute anharmonic shifts to the Higgs rate for higher excitations of small islands, and compare with earlier long-wave results.
arxiv-2603-07335: Lim and colleagues open up vision-language models with VisualScratchpad, an interface for inspecting visual concepts during inference. Sparse autoencoders pull concepts from the vision encoder, and text-to-image attention links each concept to the words that use it. A heatmap view then points to a small set of latents sufficient for causal ablation tests. Case studies expose three failure modes: weak cross-modal alignment, misleading concepts and unused hidden cues.
arxiv-2603-07735: Mkrtchian, Allahverdyan and Khanbekyan identify a truly new resonance class for light scattered by point-like electric dipoles. They match two-body Green function poles. Exact resonances require breaking the optical theorem, which holds in equilibrium but can break out of balance without breaking causality. A pumped two-level atom reaches exact resonance with the required polar response, while one charge and one magnetic dipole amplify a weak magnet response. Balanced systems admit only near peaks with finite boost, and Drude metal bits never beat the best single-dipole response.
arxiv-2603-07835: Jiang presents DistillGuard, testing defenses against knowledge theft. He introduces three defenses: output perturbation, poisoning, and info throttling. He tests nine setups with Qwen3-14B teaching Qwen2.5-7B across three benchmarks. Against a naive attacker in a same-family setting, most defenses fail: paraphrasing barely hurts student quality, and poisoning mainly hurts chat fluency while leaving skills intact. Only chain-of-thought removal hurts math reasoning, though code generation stays intact. Effectiveness is task-dependent, and current approaches cannot stop knowledge theft.
arxiv-2603-07935: Thani and colleagues tackle audio deepfake detection when a system trained on one dataset meets new sources, where shifts in recording and synthesis drag accuracy down. Their pipeline needs no labeled target data. It starts from pre-trained Wav2Vec 2.0 embeddings, then applies a power transformation, ANOVA-based selection, joint PCA, and CORAL alignment before logistic regression. On transfers between ASVspoof 2019 LA and Fake-or-Real, accuracy reached about 63 percent. Feature selection and CORAL alignment gave the largest single gains, and the full pipeline beat the baseline by about 11 percent.
arxiv-2603-08335: Nguyen and colleagues review coordination between transmission and distribution system operators in the energy transition. Energy change is ongoing in many countries, aiming to reduce need for fossil fuels and carbon dioxide output. Besides green gains, the shift brings hard challenges for grid teams, such as tricky energy system merging, less doubt, and advanced trading models that pay customers. Teamwork between the two grid levels is one of the most important aspects of meeting these problems, enhancing flex use from spread energy assets.
arxiv-2603-08635: Yan-bo Zeng and colleagues train a neural encoder-decoder to produce wave amplitudes for extreme mass-ratio inspirals fast. Old routes choke on about a hundred thousand harmonic modes across four parameters, so direct sums and dense grids both fail. Their model learns step by step from simple circular orbits to generic tilted Kerr orbits, yields full amplitudes in milliseconds, and keeps median errors tiny.
arxiv-2603-08835: Cornelius Emde and colleagues judge whole agentic systems, not just their models. Current benchmarks fix the agent setup, hiding how topology, orchestration, and error handling shape results. Their MASEval library compares full systems across three benchmarks, three models, and three frameworks, finding that picking a framework swings results as much as picking a model.
arxiv-2603-09035: Kelly Blincoe and colleagues map hurdles for New Zealand researchers at software meetings. Far-flung scholars face dear travel, off-kilter term dates, and thin voice, despite conferences being vital for exchange and teamwork. They push mixed in-person and online attendance, cheaper venues, and rule reforms, urging steps toward fair global joining and a stronger research circle.
arxiv-2603-09235: Radim Spetlik and colleagues present HelixTrack, an event-based method that tracks propeller-like objects and estimates their spin rate at microsecond latency. Frame and event trackers drift on propellers because periodic motion breaks their smooth-motion assumptions. HelixTrack warps incoming events into the rotor plane, tracks phase with a Kalman filter, and refines pose by coupling phase residuals to geometry. They also release a quadcopter dataset with egomotion and precise spin ground truth for this new task.
arxiv-2603-09735: Paul Didier and colleagues propose a shared way for wireless acoustic sensor networks to pull speech out of noise. Each small device should match what one central Wiener filter could do with every microphone signal, yet send far less data. Their dMWF method is not iterative and stays optimal even when nodes hear different sources. Simulated speech tests show it beats the DANSE method early on.
arxiv-2603-09835: Naman Gupta and a large team study the order in which chunks of a long document should reach a chain of agents. Each agent holds only a bounded shared memory, so early summaries can lose key facts for later steps. Their method learns a Chow Liu tree of links between chunks, then walks it breadth first. That order beats plain document order and score based order on three test sets.
arxiv-2603-10035: Srirag and coauthors build TriageSim, a tool that turns plain health records into mock emergency triage chats. Real nurse patient talks are hard to study under privacy rules, so their tool makes persona shaped multi turn talks instead. It controls stumbles in speech and choice conduct, making a set of mock transcripts with sound. Checks cover speech, conduct and sound quality, plus clinician review of medical truth on a sample of the talks.
arxiv-2603-10235: Xingru Zhang verifies the AJ conjecture for connected sums of torus knots when two parameters share the same sign. Torus knots correspond to coprime integer pairs, and the conjecture links a knot's recurrence polynomial to its A polynomial. In cases where the pair products match but the pairs differ, the recurrence polynomial gains repeated factors after a key evaluation. Zhang notes these seem to be the first such examples, so the conjecture needs slight modification.
arxiv-2603-10335: Yuedong Yang and co-authors present Fuel Gauge, a method that predicts how long a large multimodal model's chain of thought will run before it starts. The reasoning process, they observed, follows a simple form tied to a hidden fuel-like quantity. Reading that signal early lets systems plan ahead. Two uses stand out: allocating KV cache in advance to cut memory fragmentation, and steering reasoning length to avoid under-thinking or over-thinking. Tests across text, image, and video tasks show strong results.
arxiv-2603-10535: Zichao Li and co-authors tackle length inflation in reinforcement learning for large language models, where models pad reasoning to chase rewards. Past fixes add penalties that create shortcuts, or gate heuristically in ways that do not generalize. Their method rescales rewards multiplicatively in a group-relative way, forming a continuous gate that adapts to reward level. Added regularization tunes length budgets to task difficulty and keeps strong trajectories' advantage intact. Across RLHF and RLVR settings it matched standard GRPO performance while cutting the bloat, beating leading baselines.
arxiv-2603-10735: V Lindholm and the Euclid collaboration study covariance matrices for the galaxy cluster two-point correlation function, built by a fast linear-construction method. The method runs far faster than standard sample covariance, but must prove itself in parameter estimation. Using a thousand mock halo catalogues, the team fitted both covariance estimates, then ran likelihood fits for matter density and fluctuation amplitude. Posteriors from the two methods agreed closely, both with each other and with the true simulation values, with the same widths, validating the fast method.
arxiv-2603-11035: The CMS team searches for heavy Z-prime bosons that decay into pairs of charginos, using proton-proton collision data recorded at 13 TeV during the 2016 to 2018 runs. The target bosons arise from an extra gauge symmetry extending the minimal supersymmetric standard model, and the hunt looks for two oppositely charged leptons plus missing transverse momentum. A parametrized neural network extracts the signal, the data match standard model expectations, and the analysis excludes Z-prime masses up to about 3.5 TeV for bosons decaying exclusively to charginos.
arxiv-2603-11535: Sun and co-authors propose Expert Threshold routing for language models. Token-choice routing sends each token to a fixed expert count and needs extra losses to balance loads. Each expert instead keeps a moving threshold drawn from the global token stream. A token joins an expert only when its score clears that expert's threshold. Loads balance on their own, with no auxiliary loss, and the rule stays fully causal. In pretraining, it cuts cross-entropy loss by 0.067 versus token-choice routing.
arxiv-2603-11735: D'Aprile, Wei, and Zhang classify when a singular Liouville equation on the unit ball admits blow-up solutions. The equation balances the Laplacian of v against a term built from a positive smooth potential V and e to the v. As the parameter lambda tends to zero, some solution sequences shoot to infinity near the origin. The team finds the exact conditions on V for such blow-up at the origin. The result sorts coefficient functions by a second-order rule.
arxiv-2603-11935: Zou and co-authors ask whether language models can write efficient kernels for mobile devices, and build MobileKernelBench to test it. The benchmark stresses operator variety and cross-framework use, with on-device verification. On the MNN CPU backend, today's models stumble: over 54% of kernels fail to compile, amid hallucinations and thin grounding. Their multi-agent system, MoKA, plans with repository awareness and executes step by step. It lifts compile success to 93.7%, with over a quarter of kernels beating native speed.
arxiv-2603-12035: Abbas argues that technicolour can live again inside a Dark Technicolour scheme. The key tool is the Extended Most Attractive Channel idea about which channels pull hardest. Standard Model fermions gain mass from chiral condensates formed by new strong dynamics. Three confining gauge sectors take part, linked by extended gauge symmetries. At low energies the setup falls back to known hierarchy models. That match offers a fresh answer to the flavor problem.
arxiv-2603-12335: Chen, Hill, and Haiman mine higher-order CMB lensing stats for extra cosmological information. Their pipeline ray-traces the MassiveNuS suite and mimics Simons Observatory lensing maps. Nonlinear growth, post-Born effects, and noise all enter in a natural way. The measures include Minkowski functionals, peak counts, moments, and wavelet-scattering scores. Emulators link each measure to matter density, spectrum amplitude, and neutrino mass. Shape-based measures add strong power, cutting errors on all three targets when combined with the spectrum.
arxiv-2603-12435: Olgun and co-authors present DiscoRD, a fast method to find the reliable read disturbance threshold of real DRAM chips. Mitigations key on how many aggressor row activations trigger the first bitflip in a row. Testing every row exhaustively takes far too long for routine use. Their method builds on a study of 212 real DDR4 chips and hundreds of thousands of rows. An empirical bitflip model weighs error chances under a single minimum threshold reading. Error tolerance, scrubbing, and online profiling all prove key to safe, efficient defenses.
arxiv-2603-12635: Dibyajyoti Chakraborty and co-authors use a diffusion model as a stand-in for costly flow simulations. Chaotic flows are hard to forecast, and fixed models miss how outcomes can spread. Their model looks far ahead in time and is trained step by step for stable rollouts. A graph transformer deals with complex shapes in the flow domain. The system also picks good sensor spots from its own error or doubt. New readings are then folded in with no need to retrain.
arxiv-2603-12735: Chao-Qiang Geng and Chao Han study purely baryonic weak decays of heavy baryons in the Skyrme model. These decay channels have never been observed and could test the standard model. They may also reveal new sources of CP violation in the baryon sector. The heavy baryon is pictured as a heavy meson bound to a Skyrmion. For one direct case, the computed branching fraction matches prior estimates in size.
arxiv-2603-12935: Mihaela Rotar and co-authors ask whether fairness in high-stakes recommendations can be prompted into a language model. Models can infer gender or age from names and pronouns, which can bias their picks. Weight-based fixes are costly and out of reach for lay users. The team tests three bias-aware prompting strategies for group fairness. Across models, templates, and datasets, a fairness instruction raised fairness by up to 74%. In some cases, though, it overpromoted specific groups.
arxiv-2603-13035: Mingyu Deng and Shengqian Han design a graph neural network that learns precoders for cell-free wireless systems with association in view. In cell-free setups, which access point serves which user can change, unlike fixed cellular layouts. The best precoder thus depends on channel data plus live association status. Their network builds that status into the design and uses permutation traits to cut training cost. An attention step aids generalization. Simulations beat baseline learners with low training and inference cost.
arxiv-2603-13235: Hang Thi-Thuy Le and co-authors work on continual fine-tuning with task retrieval that needs no learned retriever. A pretrained model must learn new tasks in order and keep skill on old ones. Prompt methods can forget how to retrieve, while fixed methods adapt less well. Their method adapts parameters yet lets input embeddings shift at test time. Bounds tie retrieval error to how task clusters are shaped. Tests under large task shifts show the two parts work well together.
arxiv-2603-13335: Libang Zhao, Qixin Zeng, Hongyin Zhang, and Donglin Wang tackle forgetting in Vision-Language-Action models. Robots in open settings must learn new skills, yet old skills fade fast. The team links this loss to decay in how visual, language, and action data relate over time. Their Info-VLA framework guards that cross-modal structure with two constraints. Replay Anchor Contrastive Learning uses a frozen teacher to set stable alignment anchors. A mutual information term further guards the link between visual and language features.
arxiv-2603-13535: Giorgio Micaletto and Tebe Nigrelli link Balanced Forman curvature to Ollivier-Ricci curvature on graphs. Computing Ollivier-Ricci curvature is costly, since each edge needs an optimal transport solve. They derive explicit two-sided, piecewise-affine transfer moduli between the transport-based and combinatorial curvatures. The bounds use only 2-hop local graph combinatorics, cutting edgewise cost a lot and removing global solvers. Benchmarks confirm large speedups over exact evaluation. Tests on random graphs and real networks show the bands hold widely.
arxiv-2603-13635: Manish Yadav studies how E-I structure emerges in reservoir networks that evolve by performance. He uses the Wilson-Cowan system, a classic model with two populations, excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I), that underlies physiological rhythms. Starting from a minimal seed network, his method grows and prunes a reservoir based only on prediction scores. The evolved networks predict both E and I activity on unseen stimulus amplitudes. They also generalize, with no retraining, to new stimulus patterns. Their structure recovers the true sign pattern for most interaction types.
arxiv-2603-13835: Zheng, Kumar, and Gupta tackle queries that join data across a graph store and a relational store. They define this query class with a unified algebra and build five benchmarks for it. Their middleware, MICRO, runs such queries without copying all data into one model. Its optimizer, CMLero, learns to rank execution plans instead of estimating exact costs. On their tests, MICRO runs up to 2.1 times faster than the XDB federated system overall.
arxiv-2603-14335: Ross, Sundstrom, and Holmes model which mixes of classroom activities predict student learning gains. Their data cover over 10,000 students at 24 institutions. Four time uses prove enough for a solid forecast: lecture, group worksheets, clicker questions, and student questions. One class type stands out, with effect sizes above two. Those classes spend modest shares on worksheets and clicker work and field at least two student questions per hour. Classes with no group worksheets learn about as much as pure lecture classes.
arxiv-2603-14535: Liu, Guo and Gill chart critic loss landscapes to explain online reinforcement learning control. Actor-critic methods can falter when system dynamics shift. The critic network mirrors how well values are fit during learning. Their method projects logged critic weights onto a flat subspace. Match loss is then scored on a grid with fixed state samples. The output is a 3D surface plus a 2D path of the training run. New indices score landscape shape and system results for clean comparisons.
arxiv-2603-14635: Apparaju and Gupta ask where compute pays off in reasoning-heavy retrieval pipelines. Agent memory grows over long tasks, so search must bridge implicit links. Pipelines add query expansion and re-ranking, both costly steps. Tests use the BRIGHT benchmark with the Gemini 2.5 model family. Re-ranking gains much from stronger models, plus 7.5 NDCG@10, and deeper pools. Query expansion gains flatten fast past light models. Extra thinking time helps at neither stage. Spend belongs on re-ranking, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-14735: Yuan and Fang set out a new algebra class, transposed Poisson conformal algebras. The class mirrors transposed Poisson algebras in conformal form. It carries a rich set of identities. Tensor products of two such algebras stay in the class. Links with Hom-Lie conformal algebras come with matching tests. Those tests also tie Poisson conformal algebras to their transposed kin. New builds grow these algebras from older structures. A full list of structures over the W(a,b) family closes the work.
arxiv-2603-14835: Taggart, Loveday and Louis set rules for scoring time-to-event forecasts under fixed-horizon censoring. Forecasts in weather, water, warranty and insurance work face a shared deadline. Values past that horizon arrive only as censored marks.
