The clusters show significantly enhanced rotation-measure scatter relative to off-target regions, while the bridge between them shows comparatively low scatter. Combined with low depolarization, this points to a bridge field fairly ordered on small scales but less ordered on larger ones.
arxiv-2604-19235: Bittencourt and three colleagues sort out how electromagnetic waves travel through uniform dielectrics that respond magnetoelectrically, meaning an electric field can stir magnetization and vice versa. Working in the geometric-optics limit, they derive a compact fourth-degree relation for phase speed and split the response matrix into trace, symmetric, and antisymmetric parts. The trace part stays silent, the antisymmetric part gives two closed-form branches, and the symmetric part drives the richest directional effects.
arxiv-2604-19435: Komossa and colleagues present first observations of a unique radio changing-look narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy that has brightened dramatically, with a long on phase. The paper gives first high-frequency radio data, the first joint radio and optical-UV-X-ray spectra, and the first X-ray monitoring of this event. The X-ray spectrum is soft, with a photon index of 2.5, and line-of-sight absorption is low or absent. The radio spectrum peaks near 2 GHz, and the outburst lasts over 8 years, roughly constant.
arxiv-2604-19735: Khan and eight colleagues design early fault-tolerant systems for neutral atoms aimed at quantum advantage, starting from quantum dynamics simulations. A good design pairs low-overhead error correction codes with fast logical computation methods such as transversal and extractor-based gates, balancing space against time. They find bottlenecks in current space-efficient schemes, which run very serially and leave usable space idle, and answer with a teleportation-based approach.
arxiv-2604-19935: Ncube and three colleagues propose a hybrid mobility model for indoor optical wireless networks, where links fail when transmitter and receiver misalign. Their GM-LSTM model pairs a Gauss-Markov component, which tracks how motion correlates over time, with a long short-term memory network that learns leftover nonlinear moves and orientation shifts. It predicts user position and device orientation together. Tests show it beats Random Waypoint and plain Gauss-Markov models on prediction accuracy and steadier data rates.
arxiv-2604-20035: Chiba and three colleagues propose circumbinary discs as the source of dense circumstellar material around hydrogen-poor supernovae. About 10 percent of such supernovae explode inside compact, massive material, hinting at enhanced pre-explosion mass loss, possibly via rapid stable transfer from expanding helium stars. Their viscous disc models, fed by time-dependent injection, yield discs whose half-mass radii span 640 to 4000 solar radii with an aspect ratio near one-tenth. Ejecta-disc interaction can then power the fastest-evolving interacting Type Ibc supernovae, including some fast blue optical transients.
arxiv-2604-20135: Zhang and five colleagues propose AFMRL, attribute-enhanced fine-grained multimodal representation learning for e-commerce. Large models grasp multimodal content well but struggle to tell highly similar products apart. AFMRL turns fine-grained understanding into attribute generation: a multimodal language model extracts key attributes from images and text. Two training stages follow: attribute-guided contrastive learning to find hard samples and filter false negatives, and retrieval-aware reinforcement using retrieval gains as reward. Tests on large e-commerce sets reach state-of-the-art retrieval performance.
arxiv-2604-20235: Wieland and Alkofer solve the transverse quark gluon vertex in Landau gauge QCD from Dyson Schwinger equations, using kinematic variables. Form factors lean weakly on angle, yet that mild lean matters for precise values, so no planar degeneracy. In a self consistent 3PI propagator vertex system, the key driver of chiral symmetry breaking is the dynamically built tensor coupling of glue to quarks. That coupling needs chiral symmetry breaking. They link chirality violating form factors, find the propagator unchanged across decoupling and scaling answers, and fit them precisely.
arxiv-2604-20535: Toyin and eight colleagues align stuttered-speech research with the needs of people who stutter. Current speech recognition falls short in practice, and research priorities and evaluation methods rarely reflect end-user experience. The team pairs a scoping review of stuttered-speech papers with a 70-person stakeholder survey covering adults who stutter and speech-language pathologists. Comparing those views, they map where research diverges from stakeholder needs, propose a taxonomy of the field, and set out concrete guidelines for work that serves the stuttering community.
arxiv-2604-20735: Collett, Stasik, Casolo, and Riemer-Sørensen propose an AI-driven SBI framework to diagnose failure modes in heat units. By training neural density models on sim data, their approach learns a direct mapping from thermal readings to the full posterior distribution of degradation values. They benchmark this framework against an MCMC standard across fouling and leakage cases, including rare faults. The results show that SBI gives comparable accuracy and reliable uncertainty, while speeding checks by 82 times versus sampling.
arxiv-2604-21035: Visive and colleagues bring masked-token prediction to anomaly detection at the Large Hadron Collider. The technique comes from large language models. A lightweight encoder trained on background events learns Standard Model structure, so sequences that break that structure are flagged as anomalous. Tests target four-top-quark and gluino-pair production, both top-rich with missing transverse energy. Good results on the four-top signature, which mimics background, show sensitivity to subtle deviations. Vector-quantized variational autoencoder tokenization beats look-up table tokenization, and the model transfers across searches.
arxiv-2604-21235: Zihan Liang, Ziwen Pan, and Ruoxuan Xiong learn patient representations from multimodal clinical time series while exploiting a neglected signal: which measurements get recorded, and when. Their framework pairs a multimodal encoder that reads structured data, notes, and observation patterns with Bayesian filtering that updates a latent patient state over time. Downstream modules then learn treatment policies offline and predict outcomes from that state. On ICU sepsis cohorts from MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU, it beats clinician behavior on policy learning and scores strongly on post-72-hour mortality prediction.
arxiv-2604-21935: Michael Cooper and Samuel Cooper propose Math Takes Two, a benchmark for emergent maths reasoning through communication. Language models score well on maths benchmarks, but it remains unclear whether that reflects true reasoning or statistical pattern matching over formal rules. Their benchmark asks if two agents with no math background can build a shared symbol protocol for a visually grounded task in which numbers help extrapolation. Unlike many datasets, it avoids predefined maths language, requiring agents to discover hidden structure and representations from scratch.
arxiv-2604-22435: Solomadin and Touzé establish formality over the rationals for diagrams of Eilenberg-MacLane spaces of any height at least one. That means the diagram's algebraic model captures its homotopy type fully. That result implies spectral sequence collapse at page two for any diagram of such spaces over any small category. They prove by functor calculus that formality fails over any fixed commutative ring not containing the rationals, where diagrams range over the category from finite direct sums of a cyclic group.
arxiv-2604-22535: Adisa proposes and tests on past data a hospital readmission framework tackling clear reasons, steady clinical use, and fairness together. Built from 415,231 adult stays in the MIMIC-IV database, with a 30-day readmission rate near 18 percent, it trains logistic regression, XGBoost, and LightGBM models on 26 features. XGBoost leads on ranking skill and beats or matches the LACE baseline, while LightGBM calibrates best. Prior stays dominate as a predictor. All 16 subgroups meet the fairness bars on ranking skill and error gaps, and the code is public.
arxiv-2604-22635: Karpinski asks when group actions on restricted products count as decent. A decent action gives subgroups with finite orbits a shared fixed point, and gives finitely generated subgroups whose members each fix a point one point fixed by all. He proves the automorphism group of a restricted product over the projective plane acts decently. The result extends work by Lonjou, Przytycki, and Urech.
arxiv-2604-22735: Brown gives talks on the non-linear shape view of multiple zeta values. This second family of integral forms puts matrix factors in bottom lines instead of split linear terms. Tracing this view from its roots, he tours tropical fields, moduli spaces of tropical curves, Feynman sums in quantum field theory, integer-matrix groups, and cut-down theory of quadratic forms.
arxiv-2604-23235: Lu tracks when kinds of information show up during generation in diffusion language models, using three 32-step runs of LLaDA-8B-Base on WikiText-103. Four timed measures cover token commitment, linear readout of POS, semantic category, and identity, plus confidence shifts and remasking sensitivity. Across seeds the same order recurs: content groups settle before function groups, and coarse labels stay far more recoverable than word identity. Uncertainty runs higher for tokens that end up wrong, confidence grows less calibrated, and remasking sensitivity peaks mid-run, at the changed spots.
arxiv-2604-23535: Sun introduces a fully quantum algorithm for finding edges in grayscale images, working entirely inside the quantum circuit model. Images are encoded so that pixel values support exact arithmetic, directional gradients come from superpositions of neighbouring pixels, and a direction-aware shift aligns edges with the darker side of each transition. A new quantum partitioning routine thresholds candidates in place, yielding a resource-efficient approach with polynomial speedups.
arxiv-2604-24135: Conradi, Van der Hoog, Uldahl, and Rotenberg give near-tight bounds for computing Fréchet distance between lambda-low-density curves, the broadest realistic class. In such curves every ball meets only a bounded number of long edges. Their approximation algorithm for continuous and discrete Fréchet distance rests on a tight simplification property: simplifying a low-density curve preserves low density with a sharp bound. Lower bounds under the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis show the dependence on size and density is optimal, and the techniques extend to map matching.
arxiv-2604-24435: The ATLAS Collaboration measures jet production in lead-lead crashes at 5.02 TeV where neither nucleus breaks apart or sheds forward neutrons. In these glancing photon-driven events, light from one nucleus can strike the other or meet light from it, and the team separates the rival processes by fitting gaps in particle spray. The split yields a first LHC measure of photon-pomeron jet rates in nuclear crashes and shows no-breakup events pick out more peripheral strikes.
arxiv-2604-24635: Renninger, Koebe and Weber ask how extreme heat reshapes city life, using activity data from points of interest in 20 cities across temperate, tropical and arid climates. Hot days cut activity overall but shift it from midday toward later hours, especially in historically hotter cities, which lose less and substitute more in the evening. A new Bactrian index captures whether a city's daily profile has one hump or two. Adaptation, they argue, works mainly by moving activity to cooler hours.
arxiv-2604-24835: Fairbairn, Olea-Romacho, Urrutia and Vaskonen use JWST galaxy observations to bound primordial magnetic fields. Such fields boost, through the Lorentz force on baryons, small-scale structure formation. This raises the counts of low-mass halos and the galaxies they host. Stringent bounds come from calibrating the reionisation history with the UV luminosity function. Strong fields would induce a distinct double reionisation at redshift about 24. That pattern is incompatible with CMB measurements of optical depth. Early galaxy observables are among the most sensitive probes of primordial fields.
arxiv-2604-25135: Saeidi and six colleagues present FAMA, a failure-aware meta-agentic framework for open-source language models used as agents in interactive tool-use settings. Smaller open models with short context and tight inference budgets pile up errors across turns. FAMA first studies failure trajectories from baseline agents to find the most common errors. It then wakes a minimal set of specialized agents that add targeted context before each decision, gaining up to 27 percent over standard baselines.
arxiv-2604-25235: Kumar and four colleagues study vision-language models as judges through conformal prediction, turning point scores into calibrated ranges from log-probabilities, with no retraining. Across 3 judges and 14 task categories, uncertainty is task-dependent. Intervals cover about 40 percent of the range for aesthetics and natural images but expand to about 70 percent for chart and math tasks. They identify ranking-scoring decoupling: judges rank well while producing wide intervals, failing to assign reliable scores. Interval width tracks task difficulty and annotation quality, with 4.5 times tighter intervals on a clean benchmark.
arxiv-2604-25535: Hachem splits the work in two, first pinning down free energy and then estimating spin averages with a message passing method. The first half gives a long run equivalent for free energy at high enough temperatures, whatever the variance profile's sign pattern. The second half estimates the average spin vector under the Gibbs measure, using an approximate message passing scheme built on Thouless Anderson Palmer equations. The variance profile has no set structure and may be sparse, extending the classic Sherrington Kirkpatrick spin glass model.
arxiv-2604-25635: Wysong and three colleagues explore nonlinear dynamics of classical field theories with ghost degrees of freedom, using two coupled scalar fields with opposite terms. Ghost-normal systems can evolve in a long-lived, bounded way over extended intervals, with stability controlled by spectral content and amplitude. Ultraviolet and small setups stay stable far longer than infrared or large ones. Nonlinear self-interactions play a dual role, speeding energy exchange between sectors. Yet certain potentials, including a lifted sixth-power interaction, create transient metastable regimes that partly suppress ghost growth.
arxiv-2604-25935: Liu builds a geometry for spaces whose local frames undergo dilation, compression, and shear. The core object is a dilation-shear field over a metric-compatible base geometry. It represents the induced metric and compares tangent data via a base case. The natural connection from that field has zero nonmetricity when the base connection preserves the metric. The theory differs from Levi-Civita geometry through torsion and through its deformation-based comparison. Cases range from line dilation to spherical geometries.
arxiv-2604-26335: Huang and three colleagues tackled wasted energy in battery-powered micro DC motors, where cautious voltage margins guard against stalling but burn power. They showed energy per mechanical cycle dips and rises with driving voltage, reaching its cheapest point at a load-dependent voltage that moves as loading changes. A light load metric from current waveforms spots load shifts, and a two-phase adaptive voltage plan steers the motor to its cheapest operating point. Tests tracked the new minimum in both load directions within about 12 seconds.
arxiv-2604-26735: Ahookhosh and four colleagues study quasar-convex functions, a class arising in machine learning with a friendly global shape: no false critical points and no saddle points. They show the class survives standard calculus operations and develop high-order proximal-point methods, HiPPA, for minimizing such functions. Convergence depends sharply on the regularization order: lower orders converge locally, order two converges globally at a linear rate, and higher orders converge faster than linear. Early numerical tests on machine-learning problems match the theory.
arxiv-2604-26935: Liu and five colleagues evaluate ArtKrit, a drawing tool for disciplined drawing, through a three-week deployment with nine digital artists in three communities of practice. Artists completed weekly master studies beside a researcher-artist. The study tracks how their ties to the tool evolve, from early trial to selective use or misuse, plus shifts in how they see art. Support networks built confidence and creative safety and validated personal expression. The authors argue tool evaluations should double as chances for real artistic engagement, not just extractive measurement.
arxiv-2604-27035: Uhr and Moura develop a doubly robust version of local-projection difference-in-differences for staggered treatments. Their estimator, DRLPDID, keeps the local-stack target and stays consistent when either the outcome regression or the treatment model is right. It also gives influence inference for post-treatment summaries and bootstrap bands for dynamic paths. In simulations with covariate selection it matches adjusted LP-DiD when outcome models align, and beats the IPT-only variant when propensity scores are wrong.
arxiv-2604-27235: Ray shows finite general linear groups at large rank leave almost every irreducible orthogonal representation with Stiefel-Whitney classes one and two trivial. Divisibility explains it: with odd q fixed and n growing, irreducible orthogonal character values grow highly divisible by powers of 2 across nearly all representations. That link comes from recent formulas expressing these classes through values of characters at elements whose order divides 2. Those formulas connect characteristic-class questions with 2-adic divisibility of character values. When q is 1 mod 4, the same tendency to 1 holds for the fourth class.
arxiv-2604-27335: Rehmat and three colleagues propose a training-free iterative definition refinement framework for zero-shot web content sorting. Web filtering needs accurate sorting to block threats, prevent theft, and meet rules. But the modern web changes fast. Vector-based zero-shot methods map content and category descriptions into a shared meaning space, assigning labels without labeled training data. Yet they stay highly sensitive to definition quality. Poorly specified or unclear definitions create meaning overlap and wrong labels, which step-by-step definition tuning aims to reduce.
arxiv-2604-27835: Ibáñez summarizes his Corfu contribution in September 2025, on two Species Scale moduli topics. In the first, with Aoufia and Castellano, Wilson coefficients for BPS operators obey Laplace-like eigenvalue equations. This lies at the root of Swampland conjectures on tower damping rates and Distance behaviour. In the second, with Casas, the no-scale moduli potential sums light and heavy tower modes. The Species Scale serves as cut-off. It has desert-point minima, falls exponentially at large moduli, with a de Sitter hill in between.
arxiv-2604-27935: Arshid and colleagues turn drone-swarm route planning from repeated optimisation into a form of inference guided by expert examples. An offline planner first builds mission, route and motion patterns, which the swarm then uses online to choose allocations, insert routes and dodge collisions without rerunning the optimiser. Tests in simulation and on real flight data show smoother, steadier paths than a modified Q-learning baseline.
arxiv-2605-00035:
Jeehyun Yang, Danica J Adams, Renyu Hu, and Yuk L Yung propose a new route to the building blocks of DNA and RNA. Benzene can form high in an atmosphere or by lightning and gather on the early Earth or Mars. But inserting nitrogen into its ring to make pyrimidine and purine is widely thought hard. Their pathway offers a way through.

Quantum chemistry calculations support a route in which hydrogen cyanide adds across benzene's pi system. A following fragmentation then leaves a nitrogen-bearing ring. That pyrimidine can react further toward purine. Photochemistry at an ocean surface or episodic impacts could drive the steps. A Mars model then shows the chemistry working in cold, dry conditions, with the products later washing into surface waters.
arxiv-2605-00335:
Mohammad Mohaghar and 3 co-authors watch convection fingers grow in a laboratory tank. Double-diffusive convection arises when two influences on density, here heat and salt, pull in opposite ways and at different speeds. The resulting thin rising and sinking fingers control how heat and salt mix in stratified fluids, from oceans to industrial tanks.

Using laser-based imaging of both the fluid's glow and its motion, the team tracked individual fingertips at one heat contrast and three salt contrasts, alongside a matching computer simulation. Growth came in three stages: speeding up, steady advance, and decay. Stronger salt contrast raised peak growth rates, and a swirling ring at each fingertip drove vertical transport. At the strongest contrast the ring broke unevenly, tipping the fingers into a zig-zag drift that spread material sideways.
arxiv-2605-00435:
Xin Du and Kumiko Tanaka-Ishii reinterpret mode collapse in text generation, the slide into looping, narrowing, and early convergence, as a geometric event inside the model. Viewed as a dynamical system, a generating model traces a path through its representation space. In collapse, that path becomes confined to a thin, low-dimensional region, so whole territories of states become unreachable.

That framing explains why token-level fixes and probability tweaks in decoding so often fail. Their remedy, Reinforced Mode Regulation, intervenes online in the model's value cache, damping the dominant self-reinforcing directions with a light, low-rank adjustment. Across several large models it substantially reduced collapse and kept generation stable at entropy rates where standard decoding already falls apart. The work argues that diversity must be regulated in the geometry of the states, not only at the output surface.
arxiv-2605-00535:
Priyanka Maity and 6 co-authors study how a phone user can hide their true direction from a base station that is trying to localize them. In an uplink MIMO system, the station reads the angular signature of the incoming signal. The user equipment aims to spoof that signature, making the perceived angles match a false position, without knowing the channel gains.

Their design is a blind analog precoder that forces the received signal to agree with a chosen fake angular subspace. An alternating optimization solves the design under realistic amplitude limits on the hardware. In simulations of a multipath setting, the method achieved near-perfect angular spoofing. It clearly beat a simpler pilot-only blind approach, which stalled at an error floor. The results also expose a trade-off between spoofing accuracy and communication rate, governed by the virtual geometry the user chooses to project.
arxiv-2605-00635:
Alexander Keimer and Lukas Pflug prove a general result: the entropy solutions of scalar conservation laws can be recovered as limits of nonlocal versions of the same laws. Conservation laws describe amounts like traffic density, and their entropy solutions are the right ones when shocks form. In the nonlocal law, the flux at a point depends on averages of the density nearby, which restores a finite travel speed that pure averaging would lose.

The proof changes altitude. Working with the integrals moves the problem to the Hamilton-Jacobi level, where rough-solution theory gives the steadiness needed to pin down the limit. The known bridge between the families then recovers the right solution. The result extends, after a shift, to sign-changing data. For convex fluxes the authors also prove a rate for how fast the limit is reached. It even lets one define solutions through nonlocal near-laws.
arxiv-2605-00935:
An Huang, Junggab Son, and Zuobin Xiong investigate step embeddings in diffusion models as a hidden channel for information. Step embeddings give the denoising network a time signal so it can adapt across noise levels, yet their scope and security risks are little studied. The authors introduce Shadow Timestep Embedding, a mechanism that encodes side-channel information into that temporal space.

Different steps show distinct coding capacity, and encoded information can be used for attack or defense through the scheduler interface. Theoretical analysis treats step embeddings as position maps and derives a coherence measure explaining why disjoint step ranges stay apart. The findings frame the step as a strong side channel for attack modeling and source work.
arxiv-2605-01035:
Daniel Báscones, Arshpreet Singh Maan, Valentin Savin, and Francisco Garcia-Herrero introduce a scalable FPGA architecture for real-time decoding of quantum low-density parity-check codes. The decoder uses message passing and exploits the detector error model from the GARI method, which handles correlated errors. Resource reuse with modest parallelism aims to cut power and area while preserving low latency. The design can in principle adapt to any such code using GARI.

As a case study, three decoder cores run on one FPGA for a well-known bivariate bicycle code, reaching sub-microsecond average latency per round. The implementation uses six times fewer resources than the previous GARI-based proposal. It is described as the first with multiple cores for correlated errors on a single device.
arxiv-2605-01135:
Anya Ji and six co-authors introduce ScribbleEdit, a synthetic dataset for image editing that combines freehand scribbles with text instructions. Text conveys semantics such as texture and color but lacks spatial precision, while scribbles give rough layout but cannot express detailed attributes. Existing models struggle to interpret both together because specialized training data was missing.

The dataset is built by a pipeline that generates source-target image pairs through inpainting, then pairs them with human-drawn scribbles and model-generated text instructions. Off-the-shelf diffusion and autoregressive editing models handle abstract scribbles poorly. Finetuning on ScribbleEdit significantly improves their ability to produce edits that match in both layout and meaning.
arxiv-2605-01435:
Kahori Komaki, Ryohei Miyadera, and Aoi Murakami study a twist on Wythoff's game, a classic two-pile taking game. Players remove stones from one pile, or the same number from both. Whoever takes the last stone wins. The same game can be drawn as a chess queen sliding toward the corner of a grid.

The variant studied here widens the winning corner into a terminal zone: all squares whose two coordinates sum to at most a chosen bound. Reaching any square in the zone ends the game. The team work out the set of losing positions for the player about to move, called P-positions, for this widened target. The pattern is given by the Fibonacci sequence, stated directly rather than by recursion. The result slots the variant neatly into the known theory of turning-turtles and cold positions in combinatorial game theory.
arxiv-2605-01535:
Stanislav Hencl and Yi Ru-Ya Zhang test a hopeful conjecture about weakly quasiregular maps, a bent class of mappings used in geometric analysis. Below a critical smoothness level, such maps need not behave, and Iwaniec and Martin had conjectured that extra regularity would restore good behavior.

The pair show that two natural extra demands, continuity and boundedness, do not save the claim in three or more dimensions. For any bounded region and any exponent under the threshold, they build a bounded continuous weakly quasiregular map, as smooth as the setting allows, that still fails to be quasiregular. Their maps can even have wild sets of nearly the largest size the smoothness permits. The fault lies in a sign condition on the Jacobian that is too weak at this level. Swapping it for a one-sided condition on the distributional degree does restore the good behavior in a stated range.
arxiv-2605-01735:
Chenchen Tan and five co-authors erase a chosen topic from a language model without ever seeing its training data. Privacy and governance rules increasingly demand such selective unlearning, yet most methods need the original corpus and work by refusal training or broad gradient pushes that risk the model's general skill.

Geometric Unlearning works on hidden states instead. From a small set of safe reference prompts it distills a compact, low-rank subspace of safe behavior. Synthetic anchor prompts then trigger a projection that aligns hidden representations for the target topic onto that safe subspace, locally, where the topic appears. A teacher-distillation guard on non-target anchors limits side drift. On two privacy benchmarks the method suppresses the target strongly while leaving other performance nearly intact, using only a little synthetic data.
arxiv-2605-02235:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian and Hamid Rabiee design fault detection for mixed traffic, where human-driven cars share the road with connected self-driving cars. Sensor data are partial. The self-driving group must track the state of the human-driven group through shared observer estimates. That must work even when no single self-driving car can see the whole group near it.

Each self-driving car then runs a local check on its own sensor data. The check uses residuals, the gaps between sensed and expected values, to flag faults or attacks. No central unit is needed. Two logics are given, one that uses past residuals and one that does not. Both use chance-based thresholds to isolate a fault.
arxiv-2605-02335:
Önder Gürcan and Moharram Challenger argue that language model agents need explicit social grounding to behave intelligibly, not just fluent speech. Such models now let software, physical, and simulation agents talk and deliberate in natural language. Yet most systems stay weakly tied to roles, norms, intentions, and context, which limits real participation in social settings.

The authors develop a conceptual baseline in which a social agent is grounded in a role definition, made concrete through a persona description. On that base they outline research directions for representation, hybrid control, and evaluation. Their conclusion is that persona-based role definitions are a necessary foundation for turning language competence into social behaviour that others can read and trust.
arxiv-2605-02535:
Fengkai Wei and four co-authors boost light emission from erbium-doped silicon nitride at room temperature, at the wavelength used in telecommunications. Erbium ions emit there naturally, but weakly. The team shapes the material into a metasurface, a pattern of tiny cylinders whose resonances change how light is stored and released around the ions.

By tuning the cylinder radius, they reach an emission boost of about eighteen times after heat treatment, in line with their simulations. Timing tests show the glow fades nearly ten times faster, a sign that the boost comes mainly from the Purcell effect. How deep the erbium sits also matters: deeper placement raised output fourfold across the range tested. The work points toward compact light sources that fit standard chip making.
arxiv-2605-03035:
Mohamed Khalafalla Hassan and Indrakshi Dey argue that counting spare copies is a poor way to judge resilience in virtualized 6G networks. Copies often share the same platform and software, so one fault can take them all down at once.

They propose three scores that reward real variety instead: distinct stand-ins for a function, distinct algorithms with similar performance, and diversity spread across layers. In tests with targeted disruption on synthetic data, the scores split true robustness from mere copy count. The work frames variety itself as a practical tool for open, split 6G systems.
arxiv-2605-03135:
Kabir Kang and Stephen Mussmann argue that scoring classifiers as if all errors cost the same misleads real decisions. In moderation or medical screening, missing a clear case should count more than missing a borderline one.

They propose normalized excess cost, which weights each error by a per-example cost and matches the plain error rate when costs are equal. Costs can come from voter margins, distance to a threshold, or confidence ratings. Across text, image, and table data, cost-weighted scores ran well below raw error rates, showing errors cluster on hard cases. Training with costs helped only unevenly.
arxiv-2605-03535:
Yong Li, Qiyi Tang, and Di-De Yen study hyper-minimization for deterministic register automata, machines that read data values and store some of them in registers for later comparison. Hyper-minimization shrinks a machine as far as possible while changing its behavior on only finitely many inputs. The authors focus on well-typed automata, where each state carries a unique register type.

They first adapt classical ideas from deterministic finite automata to the register setting. Then they give an algorithm that produces automata minimal in both states and registers among well-typed machines. A correctness proof shows the method works, which settles that hyper-minimization is decidable for this class.
arxiv-2605-03835:
Jeremy Feusi and Sam Molcho study the birational classification of orbifold compactified Jacobians, and more generally of families of toroidal compactifications of a group over a toroidal base. The groups are tori or semiabelian schemes. The problem asks which of them count as the same under the relevant orbifold birational notion.

The authors reduce the problem to finding the minimal such spaces in logarithmic geometry, where it becomes a combinatorial one. They solve it for families of tori, for Jacobians of nodal-curve families, and for semiabelian schemes with abelian generic fiber. The general semiabelian case is reduced to an open conjecture. The results extend and recast recent work of Schmitt.
arxiv-2605-04135:
David Gringras and Misha Salahshoor audit academic evaluations of large language models and find a systematic frontier lag: papers tend to evaluate models that were already outclassed when the results were published. They name the underlying problem a publication elicitation gap, the distance between the systems that generated a paper's results and the systems a current reader would reasonably assume were referenced. Their sweep covers OpenAlex records from 2022 into 2026.

From over one hundred twelve thousand keyword matches, they identified about eighteen and a half thousand admissible evaluation records. They ranked each evaluated model against the frontier model of its time on a capability index. The median paper's models trailed the frontier, and that gap is growing year by year. Only a minority of full-text papers state an explicit evaluation date, compounding the misreading risk.
arxiv-2605-04735:
Ondřej Ježek and three co-authors combine two structural design optimisation methods that compensate for each other's weaknesses. Density-based methods explore shapes freely and efficiently but leave blurry boundaries that factories cannot use directly, while level-set methods keep crisp boundaries yet depend heavily on the starting design.

Their sequential framework converts the density result into a signed distance function, a geometric description that initialises the level-set stage for boundary refinement. In three-dimensional tests on cantilever and standard benchmark beams, the combined method matched the standalone level-set method's stiffness while running several times faster on one case. The implementation is released as open-source software.
arxiv-2605-05035:
Carla Caro Villanova and Alan Santos examine how wiring-like capacitive links between superconducting circuits change the spread of quantum information. Simple models treat only nearest neighbours, which works when coupling is weak. In arrays of transmon devices, though, the whole capacitance network can mediate interactions between distant parts.

Using out-of-time-ordered correlators, which track operator scrambling, they show stronger network coupling makes scrambling saturate far faster than the nearest-neighbour picture predicts. Spectral statistics also shift away from random behaviour toward level repulsion, signalling partial ergodicity rather than full quantum chaos. Because the effect appears in realistic device regimes, it matters for scaling superconducting architectures.
arxiv-2605-05135: Ushangi Goginava studies de la Vallée Poussin means of Walsh-Fourier series, a smoothed way of reconstructing a function from its Walsh expansion. He works with a nondecreasing window sequence shaping the smoothing. The central question is for which integrable functions these means converge at almost every point, and he establishes a sharp criterion answering it. When the criterion fails, Goginava shows every Orlicz class below a certain logarithmic scale contains a function whose means diverge everywhere.
arxiv-2605-05335:
Ming-Zhang Wang, Xu-Yang Hou, and Hao Guo find geometric and topological blocks that can stop a quasi-Hermitian quantum system from being recast as a plain Hermitian one. Such systems, including PT-symmetric ones, can be mapped to Hermitian partners by a similarity transformation with a positive metric. A pointwise map is easy, but true dynamic matching needs the transformation to be proper, single-valued throughout, and fitting the modified Schrödinger equation.

The authors separate curvature-based geometric blocks from holonomy-based topological ones around loops in setting space, giving clear criteria for each. Concrete cases show both. Their results clarify when a system can be fully reduced to Hermitian form and when its non-Hermitian traits are built in.
arxiv-2605-05435:
Compressed sensing rebuilds images from very few measurements, guided by a learned generator. Alexander DeLise and Nick Dexter study a conditional version, where a text prompt steers both sampling and recovery. They separate the prompt's two jobs so each can be studied on its own.

For common generator types they prove stable recovery bounds. When the sampling prompt matches the recovery prompt, the method keeps its near-optimal guarantees, while a mismatch adds an explicit penalty. Tests with Stable Diffusion confirm that prompts reshape where samples are taken and change how well images come back.
arxiv-2605-05635:
A black hole dressed in dark matter should cast a slightly different shadow than a bare one. Mohsen Fathi computes those optical signatures for rotating black holes, using numerical ray tracing rather than a single assumed geometry. Two backgrounds are compared against Kerr: a regular black hole from an Einasto dark matter profile, and one from a cored profile.

Fathi maps horizon structure, shadow boundaries, lensing bands, and photon rings under one accretion prescription. He adds image-level diagnostics and angular-size checks against the observed shadows of M87* and Sgr A*. The exercise shows which features could, in principle, betray the dark matter halo.
arxiv-2605-05835:
Large reasoning models sometimes say, mid-thought, that they might be under evaluation. Amelie Knecht, Lucas Florin, and Thilo Hagendorff test whether that spoken awareness really changes behavior. The worry is strategy: a model that knows it is being tested might perform safety rather than be safe.

They compared traces that mentioned evaluation on their own against those that did not, across safety, alignment, moral, and political benchmarks. They also inserted evaluation-aware lines to force the state. The effects on outputs were small, hinting the spoken awareness is more commentary than control signal.
arxiv-2605-05935:
Irmak Sağlam and Georg Zetzsche study games played on infinite state systems with energy style winning rules. Pushdown systems support many decidable games, while counter based systems often make even simple games undecidable. Adding energy semantics, where staying legal becomes part of the winning goal, can change that picture.

The authors define viability games in a broad framework where graphs specify pushdowns, counters, and mixes of both. They map out exactly where these games are decidable and how hard they are across that whole family. Some mixes of pushdowns and counters yield decidable viability games even where related games are undecidable. A few cases are decidable even when plain reachability for one player is not.
arxiv-2605-06035:
Lisan Al Amin and four co-authors bring quantum kernels to the task of spotting fake audio. Many quantum approaches read a spectrogram as a plain image and miss its time and frequency structure. Their method, Q-Patch, is built around that structure from the start.

Each chosen patch of a mel spectrogram is summed up by four acoustic measures, then encoded into a shallow four qubit circuit. Nearby patches share entanglement in the circuit design, keeping it feasible on near term hardware. On a balanced spoofing test, Q-Patch scored 0.87 on the area under the curve measure, against 0.82 for a matched classical baseline. The design suits authenticity checks in low resource settings.
arxiv-2605-06235:
Diane Tchuindjo, Devavrat Shah, and Omar Khattab argue that modern search fails a class of queries they call oblique. An oblique query seeks documents that fit a latent pattern, such as tweets voicing an implicit stance or logs showing a failure mode. Retrieval benchmarks look saturated, yet the authors say efficient search is far from solved once such hidden pattern requests are counted.

They study three mechanisms that make queries oblique and build OBLIQ-Bench, five search problems over real long tail collections. A sharp asymmetry appears: reasoning models reliably verify latent relevance once a document is surfaced. Even sophisticated retrieval pipelines, though, fail to surface most relevant documents in the first place. The benchmark aims to push retrieval design toward latent pattern matching at scale.
arxiv-2605-06335:
Fabian Kabus and five co-authors recover links between clinical variables from language models without opening the models. A model's training spans biomedical literature from many patient groups, so associations between patient traits are buried in its answers. Direct questioning is shaky, so the team instead ask structured comparison questions: patient triplets where one trait is varied and similarity judgments reveal the model's implicit correlation structure.

A statistical model turns those judgments into correlation estimates with no access to signals or internals. Prompt level environment shifts then give estimates per subpopulation, feeding an invariant causal prediction method that returns conservative candidate causal parents. Tests in lung disease and multiple sclerosis gave smooth, stable, clinically sensible correlations. The invariant step distilled them into a small set of candidate causal links.
arxiv-2605-06535:
Ziyun Zeng, Yiqi Lin, Guoqiang Liang, and Mike Zheng Shou introduce Sparkle, a dataset and model for instruction-guided video background replacement. Swapping a video's whole background while keeping foreground interaction natural is central to film and advertising work. Public datasets focus on easier local edits, and existing models often produce static, unnatural backgrounds.

The team traces that failure to weak background guidance during data synthesis. Their pipeline creates foreground and background guidance separately with strict quality filtering. Sparkle holds about 140 thousand video pairs across five background-change themes, plus the largest benchmark for this task, and a model trained on it beats prior baselines.
arxiv-2605-06635:
Hailey Onweller and five co-authors build the first framework for checking whether citations in deep research agent reports actually support their claims. These agents synthesize hundreds of web sources into cited reports, but citations may be broken, off-topic, or factually wrong. Their tool parses inline citations from Markdown at scale and retrieves the cited content for judging.

Each citation is scored on whether the link works, whether the content is relevant, and whether the facts match. Across fourteen models, links and relevance score high, yet factual accuracy runs only thirty-nine to seventy-seven percent for the strongest models. Deeper research with more tool calls makes factual accuracy worse, not better.
arxiv-2605-07235:
Nana Matsuno, Takaaki Yokoyama, and Mami Machida simulate how heat conduction shapes jets from supermassive black holes inside galaxy clusters. Clusters hold hot, thin plasma, and merging clusters create cold fronts that jets must cross. How conduction along magnetic fields changes jet shape and field strength was an open question.

Their two-dimensional simulations move heat from the jet head back into the inner cocoon, raising its pressure. That pressure squeezes the jet far more tightly than in runs without conduction, and the squeezing stretches magnetic fields along the cold front, strengthening them. Conduction efficiency controls the effect, which the authors call conductive collimation.
arxiv-2605-07335:
Mengran Li and nine co-authors present CellScientist, a workflow that lets language models revise models of how cells respond to treatments, without losing the audit trail. Free-form model revision can break code or quietly change the task. Their protocol records every design state and outcome, and routes each mismatch to the part at fault.

Revisions stay local and under a fixed task contract, with checks that contain breaches. In matched-budget studies, structured rework found better held-out models under two base models. Audits link the recorded history to fewer repeated proposals and more targeted repairs, and frozen designs were retested on a fresh cohort for outside validity.
arxiv-2605-07935:
Shuren Xia and three co-authors verify LLM multi-agent coordination protocols before letting them run. In TraceFix, an agent drafts a coordination protocol as a structured representation from the task description, and generates formal coordination logic. It then repairs the logic against counterexamples from the TLA+ model checker until verification passes. Verified parts become per-agent system prompts, guarded at runtime by a monitor that rejects off-protocol moves.

Across forty-eight tasks in sixteen scenario families, every task reached full verification, most on the first attempt and none needing more than four repairs. In thousands of runtime runs, monitored execution with verified protocols achieved the highest task completion, and an ablation showed verification cut deadlock and livelock rates by more than half.
arxiv-2605-08335:
Jacqueline Caminiti and Aidan Herderschee examine a correction to black hole entropy for charged holes near extremality. The Bekenstein-Hawking formula gets a competing term. Semiclassically, it is the negative exponential of the inner horizon area. The cancellation between the two drives the density of states to zero. That happens as the horizons merge.

Building on earlier work, the authors argue the correction is a complex saddle geometry. It belongs to the gravitational path integral. The solution has negative boundary length. It caps off at the inner horizon. A Picard-Lefschetz analysis of the inverse Laplace contour follows. A stability check joins it. Together they show how the saddle and its minus sign shape the spectrum.
arxiv-2605-08735:
Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Joonhyung Park, and Eunho Yang reason with video by pairing a vision language model with a video generator in a tight loop. Generators alone drift over long tasks and compound small mid clip errors. Plans made fully in advance commit too early, while whole video critiques arrive too late, so CollabVR intervenes at each step instead.

The language model plans just the next action, inspects the generated clip, and folds the diagnosis into the next prompt to repair faults. Across two benchmarks it lifts both open and closed generators at equal computing cost, with the biggest gains on the hardest tasks, and stacks on top of reasoning tuned generators.
arxiv-2605-08935:
Hao Wu and eleven coauthors steady joint casts of linked flows, like sea and air. Each sim's slips feed the next one's slips. The slips grow till long casts crash. Their PnP-Corrector plan locks trained physics cores in place. It trains just a fix agent. The agent fights the set biases the link breeds, in advance. A lean cast build named DSLCast is the plan's spine.

The split keeps physics sound while the learned layer copes with drift. On a three hundred day sea and air cast, error drops by more than a fourth. The plan beats top sets on key scores. Long casts gain life with no new physics training.
arxiv-2605-09435:
Danieli studies word sets over endless alphabets, where machines carry small stores that hold letters for later checks. It has been guessed that the Parikh image of every such machine word set is given by a rational form. That image is just the letter count, with order ignored. The guess was known for one store machines. Danieli sharpens that result and then breaks the wider guess, showing where the theory stops acting like the finite alphabet case.

For one store machines, the star height of the Parikh image is at most two, a bound that holds for all such cases. Yet one store context free word sets already reach any star height at all. For many stores the guess fails outright. So does the claim that context free grammars and machines match in power over endless alphabets. In short, Parikh's theorem does not survive the move to endless alphabets.
arxiv-2605-09535:
Chi and Wang advance the Erdős Kleitman problem, the non uniform version of the Erdős matching problem. For integers n and s, the problem asks for the largest family of subsets of an n element set with no s pairwise disjoint members. Kleitman settled the question Erdős had posed. The authors approach it from the Erdős matching conjecture side, fixing m and writing n from s, m, and a remainder c.

They prove that for fixed m of at least 3, and large enough s, extremal families take a specific form. That form combines m element subsets of a chosen set with all larger subsets, over a c range set by two constants. For m equal to 3, they pin down the asymptotic remainder range for which that form is extremal. The result fixes extremal structure in a long standing non uniform matching problem.
arxiv-2605-10135:
Lu and seven colleagues accelerate large-scale graph-index building for approximate nearest neighbour search, the engine behind vector databases. CPU-based construction is slow for large, high-dimensional data, while GPUs are costly and memory-limited. Their end-to-end system, ScaleGANN, builds graph indexes on low-cost spot GPUs in a distributed cloud setup.

A divide-and-merge design with an optimised vector partitioning algorithm improves indexing time and space efficiency while preserving index quality. A novel resource allocation strategy enables multi-GPU indexing parallelism and cost-effectiveness for both build and query, with a task scheduler and cost model managing spot instances. On large real-world data sets, ScaleGANN builds indexes up to nine times faster at six times lower price than the DiskANN benchmark, with similar scalability and search quality.
arxiv-2605-10335:
Yao Lu and three colleagues cut the memory cost of training giant neural networks. Adaptive trainers such as Adam dominate large-scale training, but they store running estimates of gradient first and second moments, doubling trainer memory. Their 2026 paper introduces PowerStep, a trainer that achieves per-coordinate adaptivity with no second-moment storage.

Motivated by steepest descent under an Lp-norm geometry, PowerStep applies a nonlinear transform straight to a momentum buffer, yielding per-coordinate adaptivity from one buffer alone. The authors prove convergence at the optimal one-over-square-root-of-T rate for non-convex stochastic training. On Transformers from 124 million to 235 billion parameters, PowerStep matched Adam's speed while halving trainer memory. With aggressive int8 quantization it stayed stable and cut trainer memory about 8 times against full-precision Adam.
arxiv-2605-10435:
Shota Takahashi and four colleagues simulate the contest between fast and collisional neutrino flavor instabilities in dense settings such as core-collapse supernovae. Fast flavor unrest and its collisional cousin both drive rapid flavor conversion. Their non-linear contest with damping in uneven settings remains poorly understood. Their 2026 paper studies that contest with neutrino transport simulations including spatial drift and collision terms.

Rather than merely causing simple decoherence, damping substantially alters group flavor swings, driving the system through complex pathways. In every case where flavor unrest develops, the system converges to the same even flavor end state despite diverse intermediate dynamics. The results suggest that dynamic competition could reshape the widely accepted picture of collisionless fast flavor unrest. Realistic collision effects, the authors argue, belong in supernova flavor-conversion models.
arxiv-2605-10535:
Federico Stra and two colleagues settle when concentration optimizers exist for the Born-Jordan distribution. They study the Lp focus problem for the Born-Jordan distribution in dimension d above 1, building on a one-dimensional analysis. Their 2026 paper shows whether concentration optimizers exist depends on the exponent p. The key threshold is p-star of d, equal to 2d over d minus 2 for d at least 2.

For exponents below the key value, from 1 up to but not including p-star, the authors prove the top value is finite and is attained. For exponents above the key value, they show the function is unbounded. They also provide the complete solution in the much harder key regime in d equals 2. The Born-Jordan distribution, an average of broad Wigner distributions, is valued for reducing ghost tones in phase-space signal analysis.
arxiv-2605-10735: Filippo Revello studies axion-scalar cosmology in limits of type IIB and F-theory flux models. He tests an extension of the Distance Conjecture, which says towers of states grow light along a path. For infinite-distance limits the extension holds when all effects count. For finite-distance limits it surprisingly fails. The new solutions show fast expansion as they near the edge of moduli space.
arxiv-2605-10835:
Daniel Dratschuk and Paul Swoboda introduce Transcoda, a 2026 system that reads sheet music from images and turns it into structured text, without ever training on hand-labelled real scans. Optical music recognition has stalled for lack of large annotated collections, and the usual text code for scores allows many spellings of the same page, which muddles learning.

Transcoda trains on richly varied synthetic scores, forces its code into one standard spelling, and decodes with grammar rules that keep the output well formed. A compact model trained in six hours on one graphics card beats far larger rivals on fresh synthetic tests and cuts errors sharply on old Polish scans. Archivists and musicians get a fast route from printed pages to searchable, playable notation.
arxiv-2605-11035:
Soham Sen and Vlatko Vedral propose a test for quantum-gravitational deflection using two parallel matter-wave beams. Two parallel photon beams famously do not deflect each other, but the pair asks whether atom-laser beams from two Bose-Einstein condensates would show a purely quantum-gravity tidal effect.

Beyond classical deflection, their model predicts an irreducible noise in the geodesic separation of the beams, a standard deviation imprinted by quantum gravity itself. The paper sketches an experiment to detect that spread, targeting low-energy quantum-gravity signatures without probing Planck-scale lengths directly. Quantum-gravity researchers get a concrete, tabletop-scale proposal for a notoriously elusive effect.
arxiv-2605-11235:
Han Zheng and six co-authors introduce METIS, a framework bringing curriculum judgment inside LLM reinforcement fine-tuning. In fine-tuning, curriculum learning drives efficiency and performance. But current methods put judgment outside, via hand-made rules or helper models, risking mismatch with dynamics.

METIS treats curriculum judgment as a built-in skill, using within-prompt reward variance as a gauge of informativeness. It predicts this gauge from recent results as light in-context cases, and this self-judgment sets training allocation on the fly. METIS also links judgment and optimization by jointly tuning standard rewards and a self-judgment reward, letting the policy learn what to learn next as metacognition. Across discrete and continuous benchmarks from math reasoning, code generation, and agentic function-calling, METIS beats rivals while speeding convergence by up to 67 percent. Teams get this judgment living inside the policy.
arxiv-2605-11535: Yu, Bae and Lee propose primal-dual policy tuning for linear limited Markov choice tasks. Prior work on linear CMDPs focuses on random settings, open to hostile changing settings. Their online finite-horizon method faces hostile losses under full-information feedback and random costs under bandit feedback. It is the first to achieve slow-growing regret and constraint breach bounds, both order K to the three quarters. The method uses weighted LogSumExp softmax policies with timed mixing and a smoothed dual update, tested by numbers.
arxiv-2605-11935: Hsin-Hsiung Huang and Suyeon Kang propose a Bayesian model for mixed health results of many kinds: latent-cluster reduced-rank regression. Each latent cluster carries its own mean shift and low-rank factor matrix, giving clustering and shrinking the feature count, plus per-part clarity. Results may be Gaussian, Bernoulli, or negative binomial, and gamma process shrinkage adapts rank within clusters. Tests found cluster counts right, and case studies gave clear county- and state-level cluster maps.
arxiv-2605-12135: Joshua Opria presents STRUM, a pipeline turning raw audio into playable charts for Clone Hero and YARG, with no oracle data. Drums use a two-stage onset finder plus a six-model ensemble; guitar and bass use onset finders with single-note pitch tracking; vocals use word-timed speech recognition; keys use spectral detection. On a 30-song test set it scored drum onset F1 of 0.838, bass 0.694, guitar 0.651, and vocals 0.539 within 100 milliseconds.
arxiv-2605-12235: Giovanni Cerulli studies policy learning under budget and coverage constraints. The problem has a knapsack-type structure, and the policy follows a threshold rule using budget and coverage shadow prices. The linear programming relaxation has an O(1) gap, implying equivalence with the optimal discrete allocation. He analyzes two approaches: Greedy-Lagrangian and rank-and-cut algorithms. The Greedy-Lagrangian method approximates the optimum. Rank-and-cut is near-optimal when coverage is slack or costs are uniform, failing only when cost heterogeneity meets a coverage constraint.
arxiv-2605-12535: Santos-Grueiro studies whether trusted rules stay in place when a language-model agent acts. Agents build each decision from system rules, live state, tools, task content and the final request, and the rules must stay present, sound and correctly bound right before action. Under controlled pressure replay on AutoGen and OpenHands traces, protected placement keeps rules across the sweep, while task-local placement loses, weakens or overruns them. Yet a fixed-assembler test produced no unsafe proposals, so rule absence alone did not prove unsafe behaviour.
arxiv-2605-12635: Sandeep and seven colleagues build phonon molecules from coupled interface states in GaAs/AlAs superlattices. Such states trap sound-like shakes at edges, guarded by band topology. Joining three stacks with alternating shape yields two coupled states that mix into symmetric and antisymmetric modes. Their split tunes over tens of gigahertz by varying the central mirror. Chains of up to six coupled states then form narrow bands while staying pinned at edges.
arxiv-2605-12835: Mahadevan presents PROMETHEUS, turning papers, filings, reviews, reports, traces, source data, code, sims and models into causal atlases. Each local region holds causal events, claim tables, forecast tests and support stats, while maps compare shared regions and checks expose accord, drift and clashes. The Topos World Model maps corpus claims by content, place, strength of backing, and where claims fail to join cleanly. Case studies cover ocean-heat impacts on marine stocks, GLP-1 evidence, and resveratrol claims.
arxiv-2605-12935: Dufay, Dzulfikar and Gilbert show that predictions need not raise the message cost in Byzantine agreement, where nodes must agree despite faulty members. Older methods sent huge numbers of bits to cope with many wrong guesses. Their plain algorithm nears the best possible bit cost with top resilience, while a signed variant hits the best bit cost with near-top resilience. Both keep the best round count no matter how many guesses prove wrong.
arxiv-2605-13135: Shah and Cortés propose an algebraic framework for pruning subspaces in Koopman operator approximations, aiming to refine invariance error. Accuracy hinges on invariance, measured via principal angles between a trial subspace and its operator image. They prove geometric equivalence between consistency methods and principal-vector pruning. A hybrid mix then weighs multi-vector against single-vector pruning for stability and scalability. Rank-one updates cut the cost of tracking these angles tenfold. The pruned subspace yields a lifted linear model for state prediction, trading fit against reconstruction error.
arxiv-2605-13435: JaeHyeok Doo and four colleagues introduce Q-Flow, a framework using flow-based models as policies in reinforcement learning. Flow-based policies are expressive, but naive gradient methods through numeric solvers often turn unstable. Existing fixes curb expressive power, trading stability against flexibility. Q-Flow instead uses fixed flow dynamics to send terminal value to mid-flow latent states. This allows stable tuning from mid-flow value gradients without unrolling the solver. On OGBench, it beats top baselines by an average of 10.6 percentage points.
arxiv-2605-13635: L. Schöller and six colleagues trace sulfur depletion in starless and pre-stellar cores, the earliest stages of star formation. They observed nine cores in the Taurus cloud, targeting 13 sulfur-bearing molecules. Ratios for carbon- and oxygen-bearing species fall as H2 column density and the N2D+ over N2H+ ratio rise, while others show weak or no correlation. Models match OCS, H2CS and HDCS reasonably well but not all species at once, suggesting local conditions, not one evolutionary parameter, drive sulfur chemistry.
arxiv-2605-13735: Ren Kawase, Takatoshi Shibuya and Kazunori Matsuda propose a point-spread function deconvolution algorithm for active galactic nucleus host galaxies. It simultaneously sharpens host resolution and removes the bright central point source. Three constraints shape reconstruction: a smooth constraint on the host image, a sparse constraint localising the point source to few pixels, and a new point-source balance constraint. Tests on artificial and redshift 0 to 1 real AGNs from Hyper Suprime-Cam show host resolution comparable to Hubble images with central sources removed.
arxiv-2605-13935: Ahmadi, Parthasarathi and Cui name a flaw in post-training for diffusion language models: trajectory locking. Reward-led updates pile weight onto a tight set of denoise paths. That shrinks cover of other right answers when the model samples again and again. Their TraFL fix trains toward a reward-tilted goal spread tied to a frozen base model. A diffusion-fit stand-in and a learned prompt-tied norm make the fix work in practice.
arxiv-2605-14135: Qureshi and three co-authors present PanoPlane, a plane-aware fix for sparse-view indoor novel view synthesis. It rebuilds closed room geometry from 360-degree panoramas, using the full spatial layout rather than narrow perspective views. A training-free trick, Layout Anchored Attention Steering, steers diffusion attention toward detected flat planes at inference time. That grounding swaps wild hallucination for surface extrapolation.
arxiv-2605-14235: Dahia and Szabo test quantum entanglement in agent coordination within quantum multi-agent learning. Most prior work tests quantum policies without provable baselines, making it hard to separate genuine quantum advantage from algorithmic luck. Their decentralized setup pairs variational quantum circuit actors with shared entangled states. In the CHSH game, whose win-rate ceiling is proven at 0.75, entangled agents approach the Tsirelson limit of 0.854, clear evidence of quantum advantage. Unentangled circuits merely match the classical baseline, proving entanglement as the key.
arxiv-2605-14535: De Sabbata and colleagues examine how large language models handle relative geographic space using activation patching, a new tool for model workings. Growing use of language models in geography raises safety questions about using these tools across tasks, given limited grasp of their inner workings. This short abstract sets out that study.
arxiv-2605-14635: Chen, Furusawa, Hirakawa, Shimizu, Fan and Wada build MultiEmo-Bench, a multi-label benchmark for the emotions images evoke in multimodal language models. Older sets show each annotator one candidate emotion per image, which misses the fact that one image can stir several feelings at once. Twenty annotators per image pick all felt emotions, yielding over ten thousand images and about two hundred and thirty-seven thousand votes across eight emotions.
arxiv-2605-14935: Nhat Le and three colleagues present MSCoT, a system for generating human motion under test-time control signals. It discretizes motion into a multi-scale hierarchy and predicts each scale's tokens coarse to fine, instead of iterating many denoising steps. A token guidance strategy steers sampling toward the control goals, and a light refiner adds continuous corrections for precise alignment. Benchmarks report leading controllable text-to-motion quality, with far faster sampling than diffusion rivals.
arxiv-2605-15235: Wugeng Zheng and five others present MuteBench, a benchmark for multimodal clinical AI under sensor failure. Two failure modes rule: whole modalities missing, and unbroken segments lost within a channel. No prior benchmark tests multiple fusion architectures under both modes at set levels across diverse medical data. It spans 9 datasets, 7 domains, 6 designs, and 125 thousand samples. Design family predicts robustness best, beating parameter count, and curriculum dropout protects only up to its training maximum.
arxiv-2605-15435: Lute Lillo and Nick Cheney study nets that grow new units while they train. Fixed-shape nets never face this, and growth is not pruning in reverse. New units can fire forward yet get far weaker learning signals than old units. The gap grows in convolutional nets. Growth near the output builds tight, task-fit features, while spread-out growth gives weaker support. Added units need time and ease of training to turn useful.
arxiv-2605-15535: Lin Hong and eight colleagues tackle underwater salient object detection, where degradation varies across the image and makes boundary cues and region cues unreliable in different places. Their SASC-USOD framework builds both a boundary-sensitive representation and a region-coherent one, then learns how much to trust each at every location. It beats existing methods on two benchmarks, cutting mean absolute error by 4.07 percent on one and 23.53 percent on the other, with a lightweight version running at 21 frames per second on embedded hardware.
arxiv-2605-15935: D. Sorokin and nine colleagues present a reinforcement learning agent for plasma shape control in tokamaks. Classical methods assume a fixed sensor set. The agent trains in NSFsim, a tokamak simulator set for DIII-D, on 120 shapes, with targets resampled as random steps every 0.25 seconds. At test time it tracks new shape sequences, with mean error 2.01 cm on a held-out case. Dropout masks 30 percent of sensors per episode, yielding one robust policy. The policy drives coil actuators on two maneuvers on the DIII-D device and transfers to GSevolve.
arxiv-2605-16035: Chocron and five colleagues tackle agent attribution, tracing a harmful autonomous agent back to the account that deployed it. Affected parties can see the harm but not the vendor session behind vendor-hosted model calls. Their canary protocol plants signals in content the agent consumes, then asks the vendor to search a narrow window of session logs. Semantic canaries resist removal because deleting them also destroys task-critical information.
arxiv-2605-16135: Lira Tacca and eleven colleagues measure inter-core skew, the differential group delay between cores of a multicore fibre, with two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. Using a fibre-integrated four-by-four beam splitter, they extract skew values for all twelve core pairs at plus or minus 0.11 picoseconds. The root-mean-square skew grows with the square root of length, confirming random-walk scaling from laboratory to field scales. That precision beats the standard correlation reflectometry method by about 180-fold.
arxiv-2605-16535: Jayawardena and three colleagues offer RAPT, a wrapper that sharpens label choice for industrial multi-label document pipelines without retraining the classifier. For each document, RAPT retrieves similar past thresholding cases and adjusts the cutoff from their outcomes. Across one industrial dataset and six public benchmarks, it beat fixed global and per-label thresholds. With metric learners it reached 0.87 Macro-F1, while transformer variants averaged 0.775 Macro-F1 in the same tests. It also beat few-shot language-model baselines with far less inference time and graphics memory.
arxiv-2605-16635: Gonzalez examines electron flow through a single-molecule magnet transistor under a transverse magnetic field and a periodically driven gate voltage. Using Floquet and Landauer theory, he finds zero-transmission resonances that swing with the field. The swing comes from Berry-phase interference between two tunneling paths. Those swings should be visible in conductance versus field for an incoming electron at a suitable energy.
arxiv-2605-17035: Huang's team reports the low-temperature monitoring and alarm system for the Taishan Antineutrino Observatory, a near detector for JUNO. TAO aims to supply a precise reference antineutrino spectrum, removing model dependence and sharpening mass-ordering results. Built on EPICS, PT100 thermometers in the detector track liquid-scintillator temperature. Live data feed thermal monitoring, while a trigger-based alarm with multi-level thresholds alerts staff when temperature leaves the safe range. Running six months with over one thousand alarm records, it has proved good for safe, stable operation.
arxiv-2605-17135: Yang and Condurache tackle semi-supervised segmentation of LiDAR scans, where labeling 3D point clouds by hand costs heavily. Their CoLLiS framework trains several LiDAR representations together as equal students, each learning from the others while online checks resolve conflicting pseudo-labels. Across three datasets it beats current methods, with the largest gains when labeled examples are scarce.
arxiv-2605-17635: F. Shipilov and colleagues present a machine-learning approach to fast simulation of the FARICH detector response for high-energy physics. Traditional Monte Carlo methods anchor modern physics software but cost much compute. Given a particle track and momentum, their conditional adversarial network with a lightweight design generates realistic photon-hit samples on the sensor matrix. Against a linear statistical baseline on probability maps and velocity distributions, the network yields lifelike samples with a large speed-up over Monte Carlo.
arxiv-2605-18035: Xinzhe Yuan and three colleagues offer a new view on variance reduction in zero-order hard-cutoff for sparse fitting. The SZOHT algorithm alone tackles l0 thinness limits with zero-order slopes, but caps the number of random directions because gradient drift clashes with the cutoff stretch. Their wider spread-cut algorithm drops that cap, with a matching settling study under standard terms. Theory shows it improves convergence rates and widens use over SZOHT, shown on ridge fitting and black-box hostile attacks.
arxiv-2605-18135: Matteo Di Giovanni and sixteen colleagues study seismic noise by season at the Sardinia picked site for the Einstein Telescope, using deep hole data from 2022 to 2025. July and December emerge as best- and worst-case months. Measured spectra gauge Newton noise in the 2 to 10 Hz range and adjust the design reach. Models of binary neutron star and mid-mass black hole signals in the triangle setup show median season weather shift seen SNR by mostly under 2 percent. The upper tail of December noise cuts mean SNR by about 20 to 25 percent.
arxiv-2605-18335: Nader Bshouty sharpens, in a 2026 note, bounds on the heaviest-loaded bucket when a random linear hash map throws keys into bins. Refining the exponential-potential argument behind a 2025 result, he shows binary linear hashing nearly matches fully independent hashing at second order, not just in the leading term. A separate argument gives a tight tail bound for a single fixed bucket, with a subspace construction showing the bound cannot be improved asymptotically.
arxiv-2605-18535: Chunlin Tian and three co-authors argue in a 2026 position paper that personal-agent architecture must move to the edge. Cloud designs sit poorly with agentic tasks' tight coupling to local context and need for zero-latency loops. Three shifts drive the claim: executive control overtaking pretraining scale, local data losing meaning in cloud transit, and real-time local interaction as the sustainable source of refinement data. The paper closes with falsifiable predictions for the next deployment cycle.
arxiv-2605-18735: Miguel Farinha and Ronald Clark present PIXLRelight, a 2026 method for controllable single-image relighting. Older methods give limited lighting control or need costly per-image optimization. Their idea bridges physically based rendering and learned synthesis through shared intrinsic conditioning. Training photos split into albedo, diffuse shading, and residuals that condition the model. At run time, the same conditioning comes from a path-traced render of a coarse 3D rebuild. A transformer renderer applies the target light, keeping fine detail via per-pixel affine modulation.
arxiv-2605-18835: Jiajie Luo and ten colleagues build StampFormer, a physics-guided model that predicts sheet metal stamping fields fast. Finite element analysis validates designs but runs slowly and costs heavily, while older surrogates miss either full fields or material effects. StampFormer fuses part geometry with material stress-strain data, then predicts fields such as thinning, strain, and displacement in under a second. On a crossmember panel, its average error stays below eight and a half percent on two-dimensional fields.
arxiv-2605-19135: Manal Benhamza, Marianne Clausel, and Myriam Tami ask whether causal representations can be pinned down for multimodal data, where each mode comes from a subset of latent variables. With no set distribution assumed, they prove each part can be found on its own, including the undercomplete case with more observed than latent variables per mode. To use the theory they build a Wasserstein-based module that recovers the latent structure. Its smooth gradients let it join architectures with changes, and tests on fake and lifelike sets beat best methods.
arxiv-2605-19235: Zhiyuan Fan and Gabriele Farina diagnose a flaw in advantage estimation for self-play learning in games with hidden information. Random future actions inflate variance in the usual estimator, and the noise survives even with a perfect critic. Their VRPO method replaces sampled backups with a variance-reduced estimator built on a central action-value critic. Tests on mid-size and large games, including Dou Dizhu and no-limit Texas Hold'em, show consistently strong play.
arxiv-2605-19435: Yanko and Shavit tackle unreliable confidence in visual place recognition, where robots cannot tell when a match is likely wrong. Their KappaPlace method learns uncertainty-aware descriptors by modeling image features as von Mises-Fisher variables and predicting a concentration value as a proxy for doubt. A prototype-anchored training scheme uses latent class examples as targets, and a match-level formula scores single query-reference pairs. Across five benchmarks it cuts calibration error by up to half while holding or improving retrieval recall.
arxiv-2605-19535: Maity and Puzynina bound the closed-rich constant of infinite words. A finite word counts as closed if short or holding a proper factor appearing as prefix and suffix with no internal occurrences. An infinite word is closed-rich when the infimum of closed-factor ratios, scaled by squared length, exists and is positive. The authors show the supremum over all infinite closed-rich words is at most 0.165952 in value. For the Fibonacci word they pin the constant between 0.09519 and 0.10893, which also lower-bounds the supremum.
arxiv-2605-19635: Athanasopoulos and team analyze 124 multi-frame lunar impact flash light curves from nine years of NELIOTA detections, sorted into mare, highland and border terrain. Both terrains show similar peak brightness distributions, but their fades differ sharply: highland flashes decay more slowly and last longer, while mare flashes fall faster and steeper. Fitting single-size and dual-size ejecta cooling models, the dual-size version attributes the longer highland duration mainly to fine ejecta droplets. The split shows early cratering stages depend fundamentally on lunar rock type.
arxiv-2605-19835: Göbel, Klodt and Krejca show host graph expansion is not needed for epidemic spread in SIRS. In SIRS, nodes move between at risk, sick and healed states, and healed nodes stop spread on stars, bounding life to polynomial time. The team proves the process lives very long on a network of poly log stars of poly size. Such parts appear in network models, giving outbreak threshold bounds for each, and on hyperbolic graphs their threshold sits beside the spread based one based on power law index and immune span.
arxiv-2605-19935: Boos and colleagues put a rare four bottom Higgs decay forward as a probe of bottom quark ties. They add its three main paths and find a rate near one and a half per thousand, with cancelling paths that matter. At the high luminosity LHC it could just show up, while the electron positron run tops five sigma early.
arxiv-2605-20335: Anjali Gupta and seven co-workers study the heat and chemistry of the North and South Polar Spurs from Suzaku, XMM-Newton, and Chandra data.
