Neutral gas soaks up the spur glow, placing gas past the Galactic disk, not a near supernova remnant. Heat levels: a warm-hot level near 0.2 keV and a hotter level at 0.4 to 0.5 keV. The warm-hot phase shows N/O at 3.6 and Ne/O at 1.9 times solar overall. South Spur N/O 2.9 and Ne/O 1.6 back a shared past and opposite bubble limbs.
arxiv-2605-20935: Gabriel Vigny proves rigidity for the Julia set of Henon-Sibony maps in complex dimension k. Take two such maps f and g, and suppose they share the same forward Julia set. Vigny shows they must then share a common iterate. That extends Lamy's earlier results from dimension two to arbitrary dimension k, settling rigidity in this higher-dimensional setting.
arxiv-2605-21035: Julia De Miguel Velazquez and three colleagues trace a quiet path from seemingly minor design errors to workplace AI incidents. Recent human-computer interaction research reveals a widespread mismatch between how developers design workplace AI systems and what workers truly need from them. Yet little research has studied the effects of that gap or how it may cause harm. The authors analyze 1,524 reports of incidents in which AI systems performed 171 occupational tasks across 12 industry sectors, extracting system traits with a language-model-as-expert approach and a twelve-trait design.
arxiv-2605-21535: Nicholas G. Polson, Vadim O. Sokolov, and Daniel Zantedeschi offer an old look at empirical Bayes. Lindley once quipped that only one thing is worse than a frequentist: an empirical Bayesian. The quip is technically serious. The method uses the same data twice and mixes levels. It produces belief-like summaries whose uncertainty measures differ from a full hierarchy model. David Blei's 2026 IMS Medallion Lecture brings back the program under three labels: mirror patterns, hidden odds via simulation methods, and calibration studies combining trial and observed data.
arxiv-2605-21635: Tommaso Turchi and co-authors address the synergy gap in human-AI pairing. AI now sits inside healthcare, finance, and policy, yet joint performance beating either party alone remains uncommon, and reviews find AI help improves human work without synergy. Most work treats pairing as a building problem focused on interpretability, trust calibration, or interface design, spanning only part of what makes pairing work. They map the wider design space through six linked parts: sociotechnical context, decision-making frames, human participants, AI powers, contact, and whole review.
arxiv-2605-21735: Ness and colleagues re-express sixteen chemical abundances measured for two hundred thousand Milky Way disc red giants as four shared enrichment patterns. The patterns' varying contributions across the disc reveal a low-dimensional chemical structure tied to radius, age, and height above the plane. Grouping stars by pattern mix uncovers enrichment pathways, stratified in age and height. A shift near six billion years ago marks a move toward a more mixed regime with growing delayed-source contributions. The two-branch abundance split emerges naturally inside the shared structure.
arxiv-2605-21835: Xiaofeng Liu and coauthors present an open-source, multi-center, whole-body FDG PET/CT foundation model for tumor segmentation. Methods stay narrow, train on single-center cohorts, or fuse branches late, delaying PET-CT mixing. It uses hierarchical UNet models with early channel-wise concatenation, letting anatomical and metabolic data mix from the first layer. A masked autoencoding with zero-mean imputation avoids false intensity jumps at mask edges. With ten percent of labeled data, the models match full-dataset scratch models on AutoPET lesion segmentation.
arxiv-2605-22535: Chu and team launch TerminalWorld, a data engine making test tasks from in-the-wild shell logs. From 80,870 logs, the engine yields 1,530 checked tasks spanning 18 kinds, from short jobs to 50-step workflows, with 1,280 commands. A Checked subset of 200 tasks is picked by hand. Tests on TerminalWorld-Checked across eight models and six agents show systems still struggle with real shell workflows, reaching only 62.5%. TerminalWorld shows shell skills distinct from expert-picked benchmarks, with weak score link (Pearson r=0.20).
arxiv-2605-22935: Kelly, Mishra, and Strigari ask how dark matter detectors entering the neutrino fog can probe sterile neutrinos, hypothetical particles that mix with muon and tau neutrinos. Current PandaX, XENONnT, and LZ data constrain these mixings only weakly. With modest gains in exposure and systematics, future detectors could add useful, complementary limits. An ideal next-generation facility of about 3000 ton-years could reach parameter space no other search has touched.
arxiv-2605-23035: Guo, Wu, and Yiu use sparse autoencoders to explain why middle layers of language models best predict human brain responses to language. Decomposing GPT-2 XL plus Llama-3.1-8B into tens of thousands of interpretable features per layer, they find semantic features alone recover 94 percent of peak encoding performance. Five semantic subcategories drawn from three neuroscience programs map onto distinct brain regions, confirmed by a formal convergence test. The features also predict human reading times beyond lexical controls, and generalize across English, Chinese, and French.
arxiv-2605-23135: Vella and Blincoe track how AI coding assistants affect professional software engineers over time through a longitudinal mixed methods study. Two questionnaires six months apart yielded 158 participants at first, 101 at second, and a matched cohort of 95. Participants spent less time on most tasks, with 82 percent reporting less on writing code, and focus shifted from creation to verification. The authors name this supervisory engineering work. A productivity experience paradox appears: perceived productivity held stable while worsened experience nearly doubled from 14 to 27 percent.
arxiv-2605-23235: Feng, Tan, and Pilanci propose Convex Language Detection for accent language spotting in speech recognition. Spoken dialogue systems often fail on rare dialects and accents, misidentifying the input language. Standard fine-tuning is costly and prone to overfitting on speech data. Their method puts convex tuning into the spoken dialogue pipeline, run via multi-GPU ADMM in JAX, giving global best guarantees and fast training. Theory proves the convex objective gives certified margin stability. Tests show sample efficiency and toughness to dialect variation, reaching 97 to 98 percent accuracy.
arxiv-2605-23435: Amirhosein Sadr and Mehran Alidoost Nia present MileStone, a framework for compiler phase ordering, the search for a pass sequence balancing run time, code size, and energy use. Fixed optimization levels and heuristics rarely handle all three goals at once. MileStone models ordering as multi-objective optimization, draws programs as graphs, predicts metrics with a graph neural network, and explores sequences with a reinforcement-learning agent under user limits. A growing database of transforms sharpens its predictions, and tests cut run time by up to 45 percent at equal energy.
arxiv-2605-23535: Fang and colleagues formalize fine-grained human-LLM co-writing, where assistants suggest continuations unasked rather than waiting for prompts. Existing tests judge output quality only, missing how users accept, edit, or repair suggestions live, hiding true usability. The authors model writing as a human-in-the-loop Markov decision process and introduce the Co-Writing Fidelity Suite, metrics for user-assistant alignment and cognitive editing effort. A simulation across 16 writing domains with 1688 continuation queries, plus a 30-person study, shows interaction-aware tests reveal effects output-only metrics miss.
arxiv-2605-23935: Fernandez tackles a runtime failure of autonomous agents: acting on authority that no longer holds when the action runs. His model checks authority at action time and adds a third verdict, halt, for cases where authority cannot be pinned down because key facts are unobserved. A recovery loop then pauses execution, gathers the missing facts, and retries the authority check, using drift detection alongside execution control. The design guarantees no action runs without constructible authority, while letting work resume once the defining facts become visible.
arxiv-2605-24535: Luoyu Chen and colleagues tackle jailbreaks that fall outside any fixed training set, where supervised steering methods fail. They simulate varied jailbroken activations by extending refusal-state harmful-request activations through unsupervised latent direction discovery. A steering field trained in that scheme then pushes those simulated states into refusal regions while leaving benign states unchanged. Across three models and six jailbreak families, attack success mostly stayed below 5 percent, with rising subspace coverage explaining the generalization.
arxiv-2605-24835: Ken Goodearl and James J. Zhang classify Poisson fields of rational functions in two unknowns across four chosen sets. They give isomorphism tests, describing automorphism groups for all but the Weyl Poisson field. The paper also looks at embeddings, along with an analogue of the Dixmier Conjecture: is every Poisson endomorphism always an automorphism? The first family answers no, but several subclasses of the other sets answer yes. Finally, they exhibit a Poisson field not the same as any field of the standard polynomial-bracket form.
arxiv-2605-25235: Sohaib Afifi gives an attribution method for neural combinatorial optimization policies that explains choices by constraint group. Dual variables from a linear programming relaxation split the outcome across constraint groups. Counterfactuals are certified via a combinatorial feasibility model, and explanation size is capped by a Bonferroni-corrected Hoeffding test in greedy order. On vehicle routing, the method matches the counterfactual-derived signal at 96.5 percent, and on the orienteering problem at 77.2 percent, ahead of proxy gradients. In flexible job-shop scheduling, both backends agree on certified flips.
arxiv-2605-25335: Lei Wu proves a deep conjecture about singularities for complex hyperplane arrangements, flat hyperplanes passing through a common center. The proof runs through a conjecture of Budur, Mustaţă, and Teitler about the b-function. That conjecture states that minus dimension over degree is a root of the b-function for irreducible essential central arrangements. That root settles the strong monodromy claim for the whole class. The argument is short, turning a conjecture about singularities into one algebraic fact.
arxiv-2605-25535: Yeonjun In and colleagues ask whether language-model memory should keep the same items for every user. They argue that one fixed rule wastes a tight memory budget on passing chats while losing context that matters over long tasks. Their PerMemBench testbed spans multi-year, multi-domain histories for varied personas, and a session-level gating scheme skips storage for transient sessions. Personalization lifts retention when gating is perfect, yet reliable gating itself stays unsolved.
arxiv-2605-25935: Riestenberg, Taha, Trettel and Wienhard settle the last open thinness cases for degree-six matrix groups that track how solutions twist around singularities. They prove two groups, C-32 and C-47, are arithmetic, meaning they fill out their ambient group in a strong sense. A third group, C-55, is thin. The arithmetic proofs were found with AlphaEvolve. The thinness proof uses a ping-pong argument produced by a harness running ChatGPT 5.5, then checked by exact rational arithmetic.
arxiv-2605-26035: Pert, Alrajeh and Russo tackle length generalisation, where models trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. Recurrent models carry positional biases, while transformers have fixed compute depth. The authors propose MLP-LDRU, a log-depth recurrent unit built from associativity-biased operators that mimic recurrence by parallel reduction. On 21 regular-language tasks, it hits 100 percent out-of-distribution accuracy on 18 and at least 99.9 percent on the rest as training length grows. It also competes beyond regular languages on classification-style benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-26535: Jiahe Huang and three colleagues forecast spatiotemporal dynamics with Recursive Flow Matching, or RecFM. Generative models promise physics emulation, but speed trades against fidelity. RecFM aligns trajectories across discretization scales through self-consistency, cutting discretization errors and lifting scores on physics tasks. It claims the first high-quality one- and few-step generation for scientific systems matching multi-step solvers. Across hard scientific benchmarks, RecFM runs up to 20 times faster than leading diffusion emulators while improving accuracy. It cuts mean squared error by over 15 percent against vanilla flow matching.
arxiv-2605-26635: Florian Kohn and three others add a type system that catches timing clashes in stream monitors for sensors. Monitors blend sensor streams that arrive at uneven speeds. Pacing notes let users state sync rules, yet users can demand sync that can never hold. Pacing types check those notes against a formal meaning for a core slice of RTLola and prove monitors free of timing mismatch. The soundness proof itself was machine-checked with the Rocq assistant, adding a second layer of assurance.
arxiv-2605-26735: Lasbordes, Chatelain, and Seddah revisit the gap between reasoning in a model's native language and reasoning in English first, training specialists in both regimes on the same base model across six languages. The native gap shrinks to a small margin, and weight analysis reveals a largely language-agnostic reasoning core in the middle layers surrounded by language-specific outer layers. Swapping the English specialist's middle layers into native specialists closes most of the remaining gap.
arxiv-2605-26835: Long and three colleagues present Helicase, a multi-agent language-model system that builds supply chain knowledge graphs to answer questions no single document can settle. It splits a query into an investigation plan. Search, reasoning, and coding agents then work through verification loops, assembling a query-specific graph with per-fact uncertainty tags. A three-layer uncertainty model tracks confidence at action, trajectory, and memory levels, and a new 80-query benchmark spans single- to multi-hop inference.
arxiv-2605-26935: Maab, Jamil, and Schmitt present DunbaaBERT, a set of Urdu RoBERTa models trained from scratch on a deduplicated 17GB Urdu corpus with three vocab sizes. Tests cover acceptability, news sorting, offensive language spotting, and sentiment analysis. The models rival strong multilingual baselines while staying efficient. Bigger vocabularies do not always help, and the 32k model offers the strongest overall efficiency profile.
arxiv-2605-27135: Gesny and Giboulot compare modern and classic post-hoc watermarking for AI-generated images. Modern neural methods reach a very low false-alarm rate and stay robust to common image changes. They argue fair comparison has been lacking, especially in realistic settings where robustness and security matter more than a very low false-alarm rate. Across classic tweaks and recent clever attacks, their tests show classic watermarking beats modern methods on security while keeping robustness.
arxiv-2605-27235: Tang and co-authors present a masked region diffusion model for layered image creation and editing at scale. Their MRT model, trained on over 10 million design samples, unifies three layer tasks, from text, from images, and from layers, in one frame where selective token masking allows layer-wise work. An overflow-aware canvas layer handles edges and semi-transparent backgrounds so layers can extend past the visible canvas. Distillation yields eight-step real-time generation, and tests show strong gains over prior systems, including commercial ones, on all three tasks.
arxiv-2605-27435: Pu Li, Jiawen Qi, and Qinyu Chen benchmark mobile language model inference across CPU and NPU stages. Their stage-aware decomposition isolates communication, quantization, and compute overheads in the NPU path. CPUs beat NPUs by more than one and a half times in compute-heavy Prefill, while NPUs help only slightly in memory-bound Decode. Heavier offloading raises energy use by up to 51 percent.
arxiv-2605-27535: Yogesh Kumar, Akshay Ankush Yadav, and Susanta Samanta map when linear layers in AES-like ciphers show related differentials. They prove every non-MDS matrix admits such a pair, so avoiding them requires the MDS property, and every odd-order symmetric MDS matrix admits them too. Related differentials are also unavoidable for circulant matrices except when the order is 2 or 10 more than a multiple of 12, and a 3-by-3 criterion uses 15 polynomial constraints.
arxiv-2605-27735: Jamal Slim, Saverio Monaco, Florian Rehm, Dirk Krucker, and Kerstin Borras train a quantum generative model classically and deploy it on quantum hardware for calorimeter images. Their instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machine learns shower profiles at 64 qubits, running on a 67-qubit superconducting processor. The model reproduces correlation structure within about two-hundredths of the encoding floor, with near-perfect correlation on device samples.
arxiv-2605-28235: Hensel and colleagues probe how semiconductor nanocrystals stretch and sing under intense laser light. Pump-probe and X-ray studies of indium phosphide crystals on silicon tips reveal radial breathing modes plus nonlinear mixing above a fluence threshold, modeled by an extended Hooke's law. Oxidation tracks the nonlinear modes, and diffraction pins the crystals as their source.
arxiv-2605-28335: Zuo and colleagues quicken attack-proof joint learning by squeezing gradients before pooling. Their projected shrink-down works out trust weights in a far tinier space via sparse random projection, hitting read-bound speed. Convergence stays best-rate while the attack error floor rises only by a small tunable factor.
arxiv-2605-28635: Marcelo Aron Fetzner Keniger and three colleagues compare three methods for removing telluric and stellar lines in sharp exoplanet spectroscopy. Ground studies must strip Earth's air lines and stellar lines to detect exoplanet atmospheres, with no consensus on approach. They test principal-component detrending, Molecfit, and their own Astroclimes fitter on near-infrared views of tau Bootis b, using injected water signals. It sometimes reaches higher signal-to-noise but degrades signals more, all methods struggle at low orbital speeds, and claimed water signals go undetected in their reanalysis.
arxiv-2605-28835: Hao-Xiang Xu and seven colleagues present GenesisFunc, an auto pipeline making call data. Real tool-call data is hard to obtain and label, while synthetic data suffers shaky APIs, limited tool scale, thin diversity, and weak control. GenesisFunc uses an agent framework making chats across diverse cases with range and quality. A multi-stage check system further lifts data truth. Fine-tuning an 8B model on the made data beats like-sized open-source models in-domain and holds up out-of-domain, reaching skills like API-based models.
arxiv-2605-28935: Franz Sattler presents FunKit, a Mathematica tool that derives and traces functional equations from any master equation. Its terms and rules work across field theories. They cover Dyson-Schwinger and renormalization-group equations, nPI equations, symmetry identities, and Polchinski and Wegner flows, and users can add extensions for narrower systems. It also traces large tensor expressions through the FORM language. It exports expressions to C++, Julia, or Fortran code for number work, with tracing and code export usable apart or together.
arxiv-2605-29335: Yunghee Lee and Byeonghyun Pak rethink Frechet Inception Distance through reference-dataset geometry. FID is widely used to judge image generators, yet lower FID does not always mean better samples. Across six datasets, density and effective rank explain much of how FID changes as sample quality improves. Concentrated datasets yield more favorable FID trends, whereas dispersed datasets can make FID worsen despite better samples. Such metrics should thus be read together with reference-dataset geometry.
arxiv-2605-29435: López and Cartas-Fuentevilla present a non-Abelian gauge field framework using hypercomplex rings. This extension creates non-compact hyperbolic symmetries, which, with the compact gauge symmetries, double the internal degrees of freedom. This allows bipartite gauge systems to be described, and shows how field dissipation works at the dynamical level. Working in a commutative ring lets the algebraic structures come apart and makes it easier to build solutions to the equations of motion.
arxiv-2605-29535: Yilin Feng, Ahmed Burak Gulhan, and Mahmut Taylan Kandemir propose AsymVLM, a pruning method treating vision and text tokens differently at inference. Vision tokens are spatially redundant and flood early computation, while text tokens depend on prior words and pile up during decoding. AsymVLM prunes vision tokens aggressively before the first pass with a learned scorer and per-sample budget. It evicts text tokens only past a fixed limit with a time-based threshold, saving up to 54% of compute while leading on document and chart tasks.
arxiv-2605-29635: Luxuan Li, Chunfeng Cui, and Xiao Wang tackle nonconvex constrained problems with difference-of-convex regularization, with a bending feasible set and a kinking concave part. The hard part is staying feasible while keeping oracle cost low, a gap for single-loop methods here. Their method, MoSSP, takes one stochastic proximal-gradient step that smooths penalty and convex part, with the concave part handled in parallel. Two variants follow, a Polyak-momentum form and a sharper recursive-momentum form, each with proven cost bounds, and tests back them.
arxiv-2605-29735: Peter V. Danchev and Patrick W. Keef extend the study of strongly Hopfian and strongly co-Hopfian abelian groups to genuinely mixed groups. They show that a reduced group that is strongly co-Hopfian in the uniform sense must also be strongly Hopfian in that sense. They also widen a Chekhlov-Danchev result on when a torsion-free group earns the strongly Hopfian tag, stretching it to global Warfield groups. The paper thus pins down how the two Hopfian traits relate once torsion and torsion-free parts mix.
arxiv-2605-29935: Zezhong Qian and six colleagues tackle self-driving models that falter in a new city, where looks, road shapes, and traffic shift. They offer CityTransfer-Bench, a test set split by place that checks sensing, segmentation, and planning across cities. Their CityGen tool adapts a model to a fresh city with no labeled local data, shaping scenes from HD maps plus city-level visual prompts. Tests show steady gains in cross-city toughness across tasks. The pair gives a label-light base for driving systems that must work anywhere.
arxiv-2605-30135: Hyuck Lee, Taemin Park and Heeyoung Kim propose DAMEL, a dual-axis multi-expert method for imbalanced, long-tailed data. Rebalancing tricks cut bias but often raise variance, and existing multi-expert fixes add complex procedures. DAMEL attacks both problems with experts along two axes. On the representation axis it concatenates expert representations and trains a balanced classifier alongside them. On the time axis it averages network weights across epochs for use at test time. Experiments show it reduces both bias and variance.
arxiv-2605-30235: Marco Peer, Anna Scius-Bertrand, Patricia Scheurer and Andreas Fischer present BullingerDB, a benchmark dataset from Heinrich Bullinger's correspondence. The corpus holds 20,898 pages and 499,222 text lines by 796 writers over six decades, with varied styles, Latin and Early New High German text, and writer and time metadata. TrOCR performs best on text recognition at about nine percent character error rate. For writer retrieval they introduce a temporal ranking metric, and coherent retrieval proves achievable, though precision near 78 percent shows style variation still challenges retrieval.
arxiv-2605-30335: Anany Kotawala studies multi-part LLM agent failure: each part sound, yet the joint quote breaks odds rules. He names the gap the compositional residual, the L2 gap to the sound-odds set, worked out at run time. A Boyle-Dykstra fix repairs the quote, and an e-process tracks soundness. Over 1,876 cliques, the gap is above zero on 33 to 94 percent of cliques. This means about a tenth of a nat per bet on 1,770 bets. The gain falls to near zero for self-fixing bettors.
arxiv-2605-30535: Gray and Levine prove undecidability results for the Diophantine problem, deciding whether polynomial equations have solutions, in groups near one-relator groups. They exhibit a generalized Baumslag-Solitar group with an undecidable Diophantine problem, and from it a group with the same property that is quasi-isometric to a one-relator group. They also find a one-relator product of cyclic groups with an undecidable problem, and a one-relator group whose problem with fixed free-subgroup constraints is undecidable. A free-by-free example rounds out the collection.
arxiv-2605-30635: Ruhrberg and colleagues trace cell paths from group snapshots, where cell-killing sequencing blocks tracking single cells over time. Optimal transport aligns snapshots, but standard versions use gene-expression gaps alone, treating cells as lone points and ignoring cell talk. Their CellBRIDGE method adds an aimed, typed contact cost from cell-contact signals to feature-based transport. The result improves cross-snapshot links and path calls on mock and real data. On lung cancer data, muting chosen ligand-receptor pairs shifts paths as aimed pathway blocking would predict.
arxiv-2605-30835: Yamaguchi and Yokura show that the group of homotopy self-equivalences, known not to be a functor in the usual sense, is a Lax functor. For a space X, this group collects self-maps that can be undone up to homotopy, a classic object studied since the late nineteen-fifties. The authors map topological spaces into a two-category of group correspondences, with the self-equivalence group as its Lax functor. The result gives the group a functorial home it lacked.
arxiv-2605-31035: Zou and colleagues improve low-precision formats for large models with MixFP4, a mixed extension to NVFP4. A single FP4 micro-format often mismatches varied block tensor statistics. MixFP4 selects between two FP4 micro-formats per block, reusing NVFP4's scale hierarchy and encoding the choice with no extra metadata via the block scale sign bit. Decoding both micro-formats into a unified compute form avoids duplicating the data path. Across model families, MixFP4 improves quantization robustness and accuracy over NVFP4 baselines with modest overhead.
arxiv-2605-31335: Kong and Yu stress-test gravothermal collapse in self-interacting dark matter halos under baryonic feedback. Dense halos, where heat flow is fast, see the fall slowed only slightly, and it never halts, even under very strong feedback. A mid-density halo's fall can be delayed a lot, but it resumes once feedback ends. The final density profile hinges on episodic feedback history, yielding a broad spread in central densities. The results back reading dense compact objects in strong-lensing data as core-collapsed halos.
arxiv-2605-31435: Linden, Popescu and Short show a spin-half particle can mimic spin-s behaviour. Its Stern-Gerlach pattern then carries the spot count of a spin-s particle, though with a weaker gyromagnetic ratio. Odd features of constrained Hamiltonians and their effective forms drive the effect. The paper sketches what it could mean for condensed matter. It also sets plain non-perturbative limits for a strongly constrained system.
arxiv-2606-00135:
Liu and co-authors probe how tool use by AI agents is scored and taught. Tool calls let a model reach past its own stored facts. Scores guide trust in these skills. Yet small hidden choices can sway the scores a lot.

The team shows that seed choice, prompt text, and chat form all shift results. How past turns are kept also matters. In long chats, ranks can flip when these picks are not fixed. They also find waste in how such skills are taught with reward-based training. Many prompts give no learn signal at all. Costly update steps add more waste. Two new tricks cut train time a lot and keep scores level.
arxiv-2606-00235:
Orban argues that rule-making must turn from a norms craft into a build craft. Fast AI swells the pace of choices groups must make. Human checks on AI work stay slow and capped. When checks cost more than acts are worth, smart groups freeze in place.

Orban names that trap the Freezing Equilibrium. He borrows from meta-stuff in physics, where small built parts set big traits. A short law links group reach to branch counts, source trust, check rates, and shared fails. The law marks a sharp flip from self-healing to self-harm runs. He sorts source trust in three kinds and sets four claims to test. A 12-week trial in grant boards is laid out to test them.
arxiv-2606-00335:
Kharlampovich and Vdovina build all split maps from a closed skin group to two free groups. Such maps come from cuts that split a closed 3D form in two. Perelman's proof put the groups of such forms in sharp light. Which groups can arise is still a core ask in the field.

Split maps that hit each free part in full are the quarry here. The pair build all such maps up to sameness of form. True split maps are those whose tied group form is the plain one. They give births and ties for that tied form in each case. A wide class, with old key cases, is worked through in depth. True split maps prove rare in that class.
arxiv-2606-00435:
Miah and co-authors catch sight-word models that reply with no true sight proof at hand. Such sure-but-blind replies are called mirages in the field. The team study how to flag a mirage before a reply ships. Their aim is a go or no-go call on each reply.

Their tool, TC-LIA, tracks ask-image fit through the layers of a frozen CLIP tool. Four marks sum that track: end fit, late top fit, gain, and slope. No task tags train the tool at ship time. On near 19,000 cases from ten fields, mirage rates start high. TC-LIA cuts them to a small share on its own. A blend with blank checks and self-grades does yet better, and ports across tools.
arxiv-2606-00535:
Liu and co-authors speed up sight-word models with a draft scheme tuned by search. Guess-and-check cuts the wait in text tools by a wide span. Its use in sight-word tools was scant till now. Their frame, DREAM-S, fits the scheme to that mixed case.

A search frame hunts the best draft plan for the gear at hand. It picks how draft and target tools should talk in the run. It also picks the draft tool's own shape for that gear. Teach of the draft leans on mid traits, steered by watch spread. Tests span a range of known sight-word tools. Top speed gains reach near four times past plain runs. Past draft tools are beat by clear spans as well.
arxiv-2606-00635:
Strano and co-authors show how the loss picked for rebuilds reshapes what a VAE keeps hid. Such tools squeeze data to a hid code, then rebuild it. Stock tales weigh rebuild by point-wise fit to the source. Live use pairs that fit with sight and foe losses.

That mix was used with scant grasp of its hid effects. Proof and tests show it cuts how much the hid code holds. The rate-cost tale thus shifts at its root, they argue. Sight and foe losses bend the hid space's shape as well. Codes spread more even, and doubt shares out more flat. Those shifts can hide from rebuild views alone. A tool-led read of loss picks is their urged path.
arxiv-2606-00835:
Genalti, Azize, and Perchet study router choices under deadlines in this 2026 paper. A router with quality-of-service duties must pick, each clock cycle, which dying packet to send. The catch: a packet's value is unknown until it has been processed. So the router must learn while it acts.

They frame this as online packet scheduling with deadlines under partial feedback. A link to the sleeping bandits problem guides their design. Their goal is low alpha-regret, a scaled measure of loss against the best fixed rule. Across levels of slack, with or without randomization, their algorithms hit a regret bound that matches the classic bandit floor. For the key case where deadlines sit at most one cycle out, their deterministic method has the tightest ratio that theory allows. The work ties network engineering to learning theory with firm guarantees.
arxiv-2606-00935:
Santana and Vico test kind words as a rescue for a failing AI agent in this 2026 paper. Their setup puts a small language model, Qwen3.5-4B, in a broken-tool trap. Its bash tool is deliberately wrecked, and the model falls into functional collapse. Mid-collapse, a message arrives: technical, relational, scrambled, or none.

They run 300 episodes in six conditions over 50 matched tasks. Two factors are crossed in a grid: relational structure and sender register, first-person or impersonal. Attention and behavior part ways. Attention chases lexical surprise, with the scrambled note drawing the most. Behavior ranks the true relational, first-person note far above the rest. Neither factor alone copies the full effect. Both main effects count, and their interplay is firm on persistence, at p of 0.046. Emotion probes split off in their own pattern. The study treats tone in agent feedback as a variable with real causal weight.
arxiv-2606-01135:
Ahmed and co-authors make a speech recognizer lean with spiking and event driven design in this 2026 paper. Deep speech models work well on phones and home devices. Their compute and energy costs strain such small hardware. Neuromorphic design promises relief: sparse, spike based computation in place of dense math. No study had weighed the hardware gains of the rival strategies for speech.

Their base is SpeechMamba, a top speech model. An event driven variant with a special activation passes 60 percent activation sparsity. It loses less than one percent accuracy on LibriSpeech. A spiking variant passes 70 percent sparsity with 30 percent fewer parameters than peer spiking nets. A cycle accurate simulator lets them explore design and hardware together. It finds bottlenecks and adds over ten percent more efficiency. The paper maps which neuromorphic route pays for edge speech.
arxiv-2606-01435:
Reddy and Challaram split evidence extraction from answer policy in agent memory. Language model memory systems retrieve relevant evidence well. They still fail when generation mixes too many jobs. Filtering, conflict handling, and output shaping blur in one step. Newer facts carry larger serial numbers in their test set. Yet top systems score just 54 percent on single-hop recall. All 22 reported systems score at most 7 percent multi-hop.

Their pipeline extracts matching evidence into a candidate form first. A separate stage then executes the answer policy. At 262K context, single-hop scores reach 82 to 93 percent. Multi-hop scores reach 27 to 41 percent. Most gain comes from the split itself, they show.
arxiv-2606-01535: Wang discusses energy convergence for a free complement method in quantum chemistry. The method uses complement functions expanded in Gaussians. Each expansion has a count of Gaussian functions, called n_G. The case studied holds n_G fixed and finite. The basis count n then grows toward infinity. Wang asks whether the energy still converges in that limit. The summary states the question and regime in one line. No answer or proof sketch is given there. The note suits specialists in electronic structure theory who use STO-nG expansions.
arxiv-2606-01635:
Qing, Wu, and Du value single response tokens for LLM post-training. Token selection shapes how well post-training works. Past methods rely on local heuristics for that choice. Few treat selection as a principled valuation of tokens. AlphaToken splits valuation into two objectives. Adaptation promotes learning on the target task. Stability preserves pre-trained capabilities in the model. Each objective is made path-aware in their design. Local gradient signals join downstream causal-path signals.

Retention data are usually unavailable for the stability side. A Fisher-drift proxy anchored at the pre-trained model fills that gap. Ghost Dot-Product extends to token-level valuation for efficiency. AlphaToken masks low-value response tokens during fine-tuning. It also masks them during preference optimization. Performance improves and catastrophic forgetting falls.
arxiv-2606-01735:
Qian and co-authors find the local drivers of collective transitions. Complex systems often switch states through the interplay of many parts. Classical stability theory describes such switches in spectral space. Global eigenmodes organize the dynamics there. Their collective nature hides links to single parts, though. Disorder in empirical random networks changes that picture in a key way. It induces spectral localization of Laplacian modes. Modes then concentrate on small subsets of nodes.

A mode-node correspondence ties dynamics to a dominant node and its coupling. Their node-resolved frame predicts transition onsets from that principle. It names the nodes that drive emergent behavior in the system. Reaction networks show exotic states under the same mechanism. The work restores interpretability where classical modal theories fail.
arxiv-2606-02035:
Meena and co-authors build a network that writes chest radiology reports. Reading medical images is a pillar of clinical diagnosis. Writing reports by hand is slow and can vary between readers. Deep learning promises faster, more standard diagnostic output. Fine visual features and clinical coherence remain hard.

Their RL-ACRGNet pairs an encoder with a multilevel decoder. A pretrained DenseNet encoder reads the chest image. An LSTM decoder writes the report step by step. Off-policy reinforcement learning refines the whole system. A dual-network approach shapes visual-semantic embeddings. A metric-based reward guides that refinement process. The authors demonstrate performance gains from the design. Clinical workflow streamlining is the stated aim.
arxiv-2606-02135:
Chen and co-authors link hypergraph Turán problems to extremal set theory. Turán densities measure how dense a hypergraph can be. The hypergraph must avoid a forbidden pattern. Upper bounds on those densities are the target here. Extremal set theory holds classic results on intersecting families.

The team exhibit these connections in a systematic way. Natural families of uniform hypergraphs are constructed. For them, density bounds reduce to classic set problems. The Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem is one such problem. L-intersecting families form another linked case. The Erdős matching problem is also connected. Each reduction transfers known results across the fields. Combinatorialists gain a bridge between two literatures. New bounds follow from old theorems by this route.
arxiv-2606-02235:
Schrottenloher optimizes point addition circuits for elliptic curve discrete logarithms. Shor's algorithm is the main quantum threat to cryptography. Precise cost estimates decide how real that threat is. Many authors have worked to cut those costs. Work splits between logical and physical levels of design.

Factoring RSA keys got cheaper through better arithmetic recently. Elliptic curve discrete logarithms saw a similar jump. Babbush and co-authors cut gate and qubit counts by a factor of two to three. Their result rests on optimized point addition circuits. Those circuits work on elliptic curves over prime fields. Schrottenloher pushes that circuit optimization further here. Resource estimates for quantum attacks gain precision. Cryptographers can judge timelines with better numbers.
arxiv-2606-02335:
Tetsassi Feugmo and Pankaczy present a new way to solve hard physics equations with neural networks. Their method is called the Neural Spectral Element Method. Each network is tested only at fixed grid points. Precomputed matrices supply all derivatives. This setup gives a fixed loss that suits a strong optimizer.

The authors add a coordinate map that resolves thin boundary layers in electrochemistry problems. A neural mortar scheme joins multi-part domains with no mesh. On a four-case benchmark for ion transport, their errors run from ten to the minus four down to ten to the minus seven. They reach that with far fewer points than a standard adaptive baseline. Two network types both hit spectral accuracy. One of them needs about half the early training steps. The work offers a fast, exact route for stiff coupled problems.
arxiv-2606-02535:
Liu and co-authors benchmark big generative models on low-level vision tasks. Such tasks demand pixel-wise control. Image generation and editing have advanced fast. Restoration skills have been studied far less. Their benchmark, LL-Bench, fills that gap.

The set holds 2,469 real degraded images across 16 degradation tasks. Restored outputs number 28,919 images. They come from 10 large generative models and 21 conventional restoration models. Expert pairwise preferences number 152,020, with 28,334 quality scores. A systematic diagnosis maps where generative models fail. Their failure modes differ from conventional tools. Standard quality metrics also clash with human ratings. The team proposes LL-Score, an evaluator built on a multimodal model. It scores restoration quality and flags hallucination. It beats existing metrics and may serve as a reward model for training.
arxiv-2606-02635:
Anderson studies stability on a hybrid time scale that mixes continuous and discrete parts. The scale alternates continuous intervals of length alpha with discrete gaps of length beta. A first-order linear dynamic equation runs on this scale. Its coefficient is a complex constant. The question is whether the trivial solution is stable. That property is also called Lyapunov stability. The Lambert W function drives the analysis.

Results cover coefficient values across the complex plane. The case where the exponential alternates in sign is included. As gap size grows relative to interval length, a bifurcation appears in parameter space. Both delta and nabla forms of the equation are treated. The nabla results connect to Hyers-Ulam stability of the same equations. The work extends stability theory to time scales with uniform gaps.
arxiv-2606-02835:
Caldarella and co-authors study what happens when reasoning models keep thinking after they are already right. Large reasoning models gain from explicit intermediate traces. Longer reasoning is assumed to help. The team asks whether post-correctness reasoning refines or derails. Their protocol evaluates reasoning prefixes directly. Reasoning sufficiency sets the minimum budget at which the model first reaches the correct answer.

Two kinds of overthinking split apart. Verbose overthinking is redundant but harmless. Harmful overthinking breaks an already-correct trajectory. Many multimodal benchmark items need surprisingly little reasoning. Stopping at the first correct prefix lifts accuracy by up to 21 percent. Models are limited by stopping skill as much as reasoning skill. Early stopping halves verbose overthinking. It fails to mitigate the harmful kind. Logical drift and changed visual readings drive the deviations. Findings generalize to language-only benchmarks. Harmful overthinking is framed as a broad reliability risk.
arxiv-2606-03335:
Zhang and a large team build a GPU-parallel benchmark for robot learning across many tasks. GPU simulation gives rich robot interaction, but past benchmarks rarely mix that scale with varied manipulation tasks and standard multi-task scoring. Their benchmark, Hebero, runs in Isaac Lab. One policy can train and be scored on all 40 tasks at once.

To learn from sparse rewards and few demos, the team adds a method that reuses demos for dense tracking rewards and asymmetric value learning. A signal of per-task progress steers it. Demo guidance fades as a task improves, and lagging tasks get more weight in updates. With 50 demos per task, the method hit about 90 percent mean success on state input. Its visual form reached about 93.5 percent. A single policy trained in simulation then did four tasks on a real Piper robot.
arxiv-2606-03535:
Ni and co-authors test whether a language model reranker can judge its own ranking quality. Ranking skill varies a lot from query to query. Predicting that skill before any relevance labels exist is the query performance prediction task. Most predictors sit outside the reranker and run after it. This study moves the estimate inside the reranker itself.

Two training-free routes are tried. One uses self-consistency across sampled rankings for each metric. The other asks the reranker to state its confidence in words. Tests span TREC Deep Learning 2019 to 2022 and four large models. Self-consistency matches the best rival approach and calibrates better in nearly all settings. Stated confidence, by contrast, is badly overconfident. Two supervised fixes, Verb-Num and Verb-List, repair that flaw. They yield calibrated quality estimates for a few extra output tokens. Search teams get a cheaper way to flag weak rankings.
arxiv-2606-03635:
Tzachor, Green, and Ben-Ari benchmark whether models grasp the hidden message of short videos. Online clips carry more than visible objects and actions. Makers embed a purpose or point in the footage. VidMsg tests that implicit message skill. It holds 400 YouTube clips across nine topic areas and 52 target messages. Topics span careers, health, safety, sustainability, and lifestyle.

The build starts from messages, not clips. A language model turns each message into indirect search scenarios. Human annotators keep only clips that convey the point without stating it plainly. The main task pairs messages and clips in both directions for retrieval. A multiple-choice diagnostic adds a second test. Strong current models often fail here. The task needs pragmatic inference and fine separation of close messages. A baseline method, VidVec-Msg, improves message retrieval but leaves large headroom.
arxiv-2606-03735:
Fejziaj, Hassona, and Marszalek review dynamic multi-agent pathfinding and test six algorithms in one frame. The setting mixes moving obstacles, partial sensing, and conflicts between agents. Classic solvers struggle when the world changes mid-route. A unified simulation allows a fair comparison across methods. Dijkstra, D star Lite, Space-Time A star, WHCA star, and M star form the baseline set.

A new method, A double-star, joins the comparison. It splits the work into two phases. Diverse candidate paths are computed offline from geometry alone. Online, space-time planning reconnects the agent to those paths as conditions shift. This template design aims at better solutions where change is frequent and sensing is limited. The study also proposes modifications to the rival methods. Robotics readers get a structured map of a crowded algorithm space. Simulation results in one frame make trade-offs visible at a glance.
arxiv-2606-03835:
Mayeux argues for formalizing all published mathematics as a living benchmark for reasoning. Math stands apart through formal rigor. Claims follow from explicit axioms by checkable steps. Interactive theorem provers support that rigor in a fully formal language. A verified, ever-updated corpus of all mathematics is the benchmark vision.

That view treats mathematics as a structured database of linked results. It raises hard questions about scale and organization of large formal libraries. A case study in categorical algebra shows the work in practice. Dilatations of categories are being formalized here. The topic extends classical localizations of categories. Readers see what one brick of the grand corpus looks like up close. The piece links a grand program to concrete daily formalization work.
arxiv-2606-04035:
Bugaud maps how safety behaviour shifts across domains in open-weight language models. Trustworthy use needs steady, predictable refusals and compliance. He ran seven standardized experiments across seven ethical domains. Five models from 12B to 70B took part. The study logged 4,200 interactions with dual-judge checks.

Each scenario ran in two frames: spot the harm, or help commit it. Compliance ranged from 14.7 percent for trafficking to 85.7 percent for surveillance design. One model gave surveillance designs in every request, yet helped with trafficking far less. A technical framing could bypass safety training with no outward signal. Closed frontier models showed the same shape, at lower levels.
arxiv-2606-04135:
Shiqiao Zhou and colleagues present SARAF in 2026, a forecasting method that borrows the retrieval idea from language models. To predict a time series, it first fetches similar stretches of the series' own past.

Critics note that such stretches may not share the key property of stationarity, where the statistical pattern stays stable over time. The authors answer with a careful theory. They also add a step that deliberately mixes stretches from varied regimes, much like retrieved text from varied sources. On forecasting benchmarks, the method beat prior approaches. It did so mainly by gaining robustness across shifting conditions, not by peak accuracy alone. Diversifying the retrieved past, they conclude, is what makes retrieval work for series.
arxiv-2606-04235:
Tao Jin and Stuart Florescu build a framework in 2026 for collateral choice, with a quantum step inside a proven classical pipeline. Collateral choice is the daily puzzle of pledging assets against margin while obeying legal and risk rules.

The hard part is picking which assets to pledge from a large pool. Their solver uses a quantum routine to propose candidate sets. A classical check then certifies each candidate against all rules. Nothing leaves the pipeline unless it passes the check. On synthetic pools the method found better pledges than standard solvers. The authors stress the certificate step: it makes the quantum part safe to use in a regulated setting.
arxiv-2606-04735:
Veselý and colleagues identify a failure mode in deep reinforcement learning that mirrors a famous human memory bias, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Temporal credit assignment, deciding which past actions caused later rewards, is central to learning. At intermediate eligibility trace depths, they find agents irrationally prefer trajectories with high-magnitude reward peaks over alternatives with higher total returns. They call this Trace-Mediated Peak Bias, and it mechanistically mirrors the Peak-End Rule, where people judge experiences by their most intense moment rather than their overall value.

The bias emerges because eligibility traces amplify distant temporal-difference errors into gradient shocks that fixed-step-size gradient descent cannot normalize, causing global overestimation. Adaptive optimizers, by contrast, mitigate the pathology through second-moment normalization. The paper bridges machine learning and cognitive heuristics with one mechanism explaining both.
arxiv-2606-05235:
Samak Boonpan uses quantum circuit complexity as a measure of particle creation in bouncing cosmologies in this 2026 arXiv paper. A bouncing universe contracts, reaches a minimum size, and expands again instead of beginning in a singularity. Circuit complexity counts how hard a quantum state is to prepare, and tracking it for a quantum scalar field across the bounce could reveal what correlation functions miss.

Earlier studies relied on perturbative approximations, but Boonpan applies the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method to build an exact, non-perturbative framework for how complexity evolves through the bounce. The complexity stays finite at the bounce, dominated by the squeezing of the quantum state caused by spacetime contraction. After the bounce, its growth correlates strongly with cosmological particle production. One contribution, called the chirping term, acts as a geometric memory of the transition, quantifying the information cost of creating particles in a nontrivial spacetime geometry.
arxiv-2606-05435:
Naima Tasnim, Lalitha Sankar, and Oliver Kosut introduce DP-MacAdam in this 2026 arXiv paper, a differentially private training algorithm that unifies two previously separate tricks. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent protects training data by clipping each example's gradient and adding noise. Its fixed clipping threshold is a pain point that needs manual tuning. Clipping methods estimate the gradient's mean and variance to set the clipping. Private Adam variants use the same statistics for momentum, yet neither used the estimates for both jobs.

The authors analyze the algorithm and show that it estimates gradient variances in a bias-free manner, which matters because biased statistics would distort both the clipping and the update direction. In evaluations of privacy and accuracy, DP-MacAdam achieved better model utility than the private baseline and than either parent method, adaptive clipping alone or private Adam alone.
arxiv-2606-05535:
Pratama and co-authors address noisy medical images in a 2026 arXiv paper on question answering. Their system looks at a scan or X-ray and answers plain questions about it. Most systems of this kind link a standard image reader to a large language model. Small flaws in the image can then distort what the model sees. The team adds a cleaning step that is trained to rebuild clean image features from damaged ones.

After cleaning, the features pass to the language model as short prefix tokens. A light training method then adapts the system without retraining the whole model. The authors tested the system on two public test sets, SLAKE and PathVQA. It held up better than rival systems when noise was added to the inputs. Its scores on clean images stayed close to the best competing results.
arxiv-2606-05635:
Kong and colleagues teach a model to crop one photo into a film-style trio in a 2026 arXiv paper. Photo tools usually return a single best crop. Posters and stories, though, often need three views: a wide scene, a medium frame, and a close-up. Each crop also needs a short caption to carry the story. The team defines this triple-shot task and trains a model for it with little expert labeling.

Training runs in three stages. First, guided reasoning teaches basic cropping through worked examples. Next, the model learns from its own high-confidence drafts, scored by a mix of checks. A final reinforcement stage uses a reward built for this task. The team also built TSC-Bench, twelve hundred expert-marked test cases. On shot placement their model scored nearly three times the accuracy of GPT-5. The result points toward automatic storyboarding.
arxiv-2606-05735:
Dihua Jiang and co-authors settle parts of a wavefront set conjecture for classical groups in a 2026 arXiv paper. Wavefront sets record the rough directions hidden inside a representation, a symmetry package for a group. Three flavors exist: arithmetic, trace-based, and one from special models. The conjecture says they agree. The team works over local fields of characteristic zero, including the real and complex cases.

Their first theorem proves a reciprocity between wavefront sets for representations with a generic parameter. Over archimedean fields, a second theorem confirms the conjecture and its refinement outright. The character of the representation then has its fine structure fixed by arithmetic data alone. A composition law ties the model-based flavor in across all fields. As a bonus, the work sharpens Vogan's maximal-orbit principle, a guiding rule in the field. Conditional pieces remain, and the authors mark exactly which ones.
arxiv-2606-06035:
Firmbach, Steinbrecher, Popp, and Mayr make fiber-in-solid models solvable at scale in a 2026 arXiv paper. Embedding thin beams inside solid bodies models everything from collagen tissue to reinforced composites. Lagrange multipliers enforce the coupling, but the discrete system becomes an indefinite saddle-point problem that naive solvers choke on. Augmented Lagrangian preconditioning steadies the system while keeping the constraints exact.

Starting from an ideal block preconditioner, the team derives usable block-triangular variants. Solid, beam, and Schur complement blocks can then be handled on their own. Several Schur complement approximations are tried and compared. Tests showed robustness across model parameters. Iteration counts stayed nearly flat under mesh refinement. Strong and weak scaling both looked favorable. An engineering example, a composite sandwich plate, shows the workload. Mixed-dimensional models are growing across biomechanics and materials science. Solvers that respect their structure are the bottleneck this paper removes.
arxiv-2606-06135:
Lucie Kubíčková and Martin Isoz extend a fluid simulation method in this 2026 arXiv paper on computational fluid dynamics. Engineers optimizing shapes with simulated airflow normally must rebuild the computational mesh whenever the shape changes, which is slow. Immersed boundary methods avoid remeshing by embedding the solid shape inside a fixed grid. The authors adapt one such method, the hybrid fictitious domain approach, to Reynolds-averaged turbulence models, which average out turbulent fluctuations rather than resolving each one.

Their open-source OpenFOAM solver adds wall functions, which approximate flow near solid surfaces, and solves the averaged equations with the SIMPLE algorithm. It matched standard body-fitted simulations across Reynolds numbers from ten to one million, on benchmarks such as flow over a backward-facing step and an Ahmed body. Tests on a NACA airfoil at varied attack angles checked robustness, though the solver tended to overestimate wake size.
arxiv-2606-06635:
Tanvi Thoria and co-authors read the fingerprints of failing reasoning in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a language model reasons step by step and goes wrong, the failure is not one thing. Using token level uncertainty signals from a single completion's log probabilities, they distinguish two processes. In committed failure, the model locks onto a wrong path early; past a commitment point, more trace only hurts detection. In persistent uncertainty, doubt accumulates throughout, and the full trace is needed to spot the failure.

Across twenty three model and dataset configurations, the framework's predictions held in twenty of twenty three cases, far above chance. The classification pays off practically. In the committed regime, self consistency sampling can be skipped on the top thirty percent most confident inputs without losing failure recall. Combining uncertainty features with agreement rates lifted detection in both regimes.
arxiv-2606-06835:
Language models think best in the language they trained on most. Jayarao and co-authors let a model call for help in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system can translate an input into the model's strong language before answering. Translating everything would waste money, though. Models also refuse help too often, out of overconfidence.

The team trained one policy to decide for itself, using reward alone. A confidence gate keeps translation for cases the model truly cannot handle natively. Training covered twenty two languages in three resource tiers and five domains. The gated policy kept the full reward of an always translate policy. It did so at about sixty three percent of the cost. Gains were largest for low resource languages. The policy even handled two invented languages it had never seen, and transferred to nine held out ones.
arxiv-2606-07035:
Nuclear theory drowns in giant matrices whose eigenvalues encode a nucleus's energy levels. De Lucia and a large team solve those problems on a quantum annealer in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their test bed is the equation of motion phonon method, a many body technique for nuclei. Full quantum algorithms for eigenvalues need hardware that does not yet exist.

Annealing offers a nearer term path. The eigenvalue problem is recast as a binary optimization puzzle. A hybrid algorithm then peels off eigenvalues one by one through deflation. Classical steps clean up between quantum rounds. On real D-Wave hardware, quantum annealing beat simulated annealing on ground states. Deflation recovered the full spectrum with high precision. Symmetric test problems reached machine precision under all deflation variants. The paper maps both the promise and the limits of today's annealers for nuclear physics.
arxiv-2606-07235:
Mehrish and Vascon rethink how AI systems gather evidence from long, mixed-format documents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Answers often hide in fragments spread across text, tables, and slides, yet standard retrieval fetches isolated chunks ranked independently. Their system, FlowReader, treats evidence assembly as a min-cost flow problem, a classic optimization method that routes flow through a network at lowest total cost. One scoring signal controls which fragments act as sources, sinks, and connecting paths.

The chosen flow is split into candidate evidence paths, pruned for redundancy, and passed to vision-language model workers that draft the answer. A consistency check can trigger one deeper refinement pass when the first answer looks shaky. On the VisDoMBench benchmark, FlowReader scored best on the two subsets dominated by fragmented evidence, reaching about fifty-eight on table-heavy questions and seventy-three on slide questions in their reported averages.
arxiv-2606-07535:
Krasnodębska, Kusa, and Lipani test whether safety training in one language protects users of other languages, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model aligned to refuse harmful requests in English may comply with the request in Polish or Greek, an inconsistency with deployment stakes. The authors introduce RefusEU, a refusal alignment dataset spanning 12 European languages with a dedicated test set for models. Controlled experiments used Direct Preference Optimization, a method that teaches from preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs, varying the training languages.

Two insights stand out. Aligning in English did not ensure cross-lingual safety, even for identical harm categories tested in other languages. Multilingual training data, by contrast, improved safety while leaving knowledge intact, as measured by a knowledge benchmark. The results argue that multilingual safety cannot be an afterthought bolted onto English training. Dataset and evaluation materials are released, targeting European language coverage that safety research neglects.
arxiv-2606-07635:
Shen and a team fuse brain scans of different kinds to detect early cognitive impairment, in this 2026 arXiv paper on NeuroAlign. Functional MRI shows dynamic brain activity while diffusion imaging maps structural wiring; together they should reveal mild cognitive impairment better than either alone, but their spaces differ and their outputs misalign. Their layered framework models multi-scale dynamic connectivity and aligns dynamic with static and functional with structural embeddings, then lets connectivity-level and region-level features shape each other globally.

An attribution method designed for the system gauges which links and regional markers drive each decision, without needing gradients. Evaluated across 3 cohorts under 5-fold validation, NeuroAlign reached accuracy near 0.83 on the ADNI dataset. Fused features beat the best single feature type. Cross-dataset transfer to an independent cohort was partial, which the authors report as evidence of domain gaps between scanning sites.
arxiv-2606-07935:
Song and co-authors announce the fourth edition of a challenge on generating facial reactions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task: given someone speaking, produce the facial reaction a listener would plausibly show, with many valid answers rather than one correct face. The REACT challenge series has standardised this multiple appropriate facial reaction generation problem, and the 2026 edition raises the bar.

Two data additions headline the update. Personality labels for the Big Five traits let systems generate reactions conditioned on who the listener is, not just what was said. The new MARS dataset broadens the scenarios available for training and testing. The challenge also adds a second task, predicting electroencephalography signals, the brain's electrical activity, as a reaction. Together the changes push reaction generation toward personalised, multimodal modelling: a system should eventually react like a particular person, in face and in measurable brain response, not like a generic listener.
arxiv-2606-08035:
Hangui Lin and co-authors diagnose a coordination failure inside vision-language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains such models to reach correct answers, but scores only the outcome. Token-level analysis shows what goes wrong mid-reasoning. The model fails to alternate between extracting visual evidence and synthesising text, staring at words when it should look. This breakdown is causally linked to wrong answers.

Their method, DyCo-RL, builds the alternation into training. A Fisher-Rao geodesic distance measures how much each token's attention shifts within its modality, so tokens can be assigned visual or text roles. Training checks whether each token's attention matches its role, and reweights the learning signal by that alignment. The model is rewarded not just for being right, but for looking at the right thing at the right step. Experiments show this improves visual reasoning over outcome-only training.
arxiv-2606-08135:
Siyu Nan and co-authors improve how language models write code inside large existing repositories, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Repository-level generation is hard because new code must call the right existing functions across a codebase far too big for the model's context window. Retrieval systems fetch candidate functions to reuse, and planners sketch steps. Two flaws persist: plans are written with no behavioural guidance, so they drift from what the code should do. And retrieved functions are reused blind to their actual implementation logic.

Their framework, TICoder, fixes both ends. A test-driven iterative planning mechanism uses the repository's test cases as behavioural specifications, refining the implementation steps against them before code is written. An implementation-aware reuse mechanism then reads how candidate functions actually work, not just their names and signatures. The pairing is the point: tests discipline the plan, implementations discipline the reuse.
arxiv-2606-08335:
Karl Zhu and colleagues optimize the design and operation of green ammonia plants in this 2026 arXiv paper. Green ammonia is made with renewable electricity. But the Haber-Bosch process at its heart has a minimum load. The synthesis unit cannot run below a certain throughput without shutting down. Wind and solar output fluctuate, so guaranteeing that minimum is the central challenge. The authors build a robust optimization framework that plans for worst-case conditions within stated bounds.

A strategic model sizes the plant while allowing flexible operating modes such as hot idling and shutdowns. A scenario-reduction method clusters weather patterns and generates adversarial renewable trajectories to test plans against. An operational model then adapts decisions on a rolling horizon as forecasts update. In computations, the framework produced plans that stayed feasible in out-of-sample simulation. Existing approaches failed the minimum-load requirement in those tests.
arxiv-2606-08535:
Yun-Hsuan Huang, Bui, and Chuang sharpen satellite images with a lightweight network in this 2026 arXiv paper. Remote sensing faces a spatial-temporal trade-off. Finely detailed imagery is acquired infrequently, while frequent observations are coarse. Single-image super-resolution enhances coarse images without changing schedules. But many transformer-based models are expensive and sensitive to limited or biased training data. Their architecture, NGram-MoSE, targets both efficiency and texture continuity.

An N-gram context injection mechanism strengthens consistency across the local windows the transformer processes. A mixture-of-experts design scales capacity through sparse activation, consulting only a few subnetworks per patch. Together the two ideas aim at super-resolution cheap enough for routine use over large areas.
arxiv-2606-09335:
Agneedh Basu and colleagues dissect why speech recognizers stumble, testing state-of-the-art models on Indian languages under messy real-world conditions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recognition performance varies with language, speaker, and recording chain, but systematic factor studies for Indic languages are rare. The authors analyze decoded outputs from several open-source models in zero-shot settings across Hindi, Bengali, Kannada, Telugu, and Marathi. They correlate word error rate with speaker traits like word length and speaking rate, and probe audio factors in depth for Hindi.

Bandwidth is the most critical audio factor: narrowband 2G GSM audio degrades recognition sharply, while wideband stays close to clean accuracy. Bit depth shows a threshold, stable at 10 to 12 bits, collapsing at 8 bits and below. Competing background speech causes the strongest degradation of all, with Whisper models comparatively robust. Neural restoration introduced harmful artifacts, making plain resampling the safer choice for telephony.
arxiv-2606-09735:
Wendy Tam peers inside a language model to see what safety tuning did to its political lean in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tuning method is RLHF, training from human feedback, the standard way to align models with stated values. Tam compares the inner maps of Llama 3.1 8B before and after that tuning. The question is whether a partisan tilt was erased or just masked.

The tilt's structure survived. RLHF squeezed the spread of the partisan signal, so output reads balanced, but the direction itself stayed in place. Sparse autoencoder maps showed policy features that fired in the base model went dark in the tuned one. Steering tests then proved the break was causal: the path from tilt to output was cut, not the tilt. Tricks that guess a user's lean can switch the path back on. The mask, Tam warns, is thin, and the same may hold for other values.
arxiv-2606-09835:
Akbaba and co-authors pack a hands-on data workshop into a box that non-experts can run alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data physicalization turns numbers into objects people build and touch. Such workshops spark rich talks, but their worth has hinged on a skilled researcher in the room. The team worked with a Swedish social aid group whose staff wanted to run the sessions themselves.

Together they co-designed the kit for youth leadership groups. The box holds both stuff and steps: the materials to build with, and a script that walks a host through each stage. Three pilot runs tuned the set, and two more case studies checked that it travels. The paper lists what the box must carry, from clear task cards to spare parts for when builds go wrong.
arxiv-2606-09935:
Isbarov and colleagues test whether AI agents inside software pipelines can be hijacked by hostile text, in a 2026 arXiv paper on security. Their setting is CI/CD, the automated systems that review code and maintain projects on GitHub. These agents read untrusted content while holding strong permissions. That mix makes prompt injection, where planted instructions steer the agent, a supply chain risk.

Their open-source framework, GitInject, builds throwaway repositories and triggers real workflow runs, so limits and credential handling behave as in production. Across four AI providers, the team documented eleven named attacks, covering config-file injection, credential theft, judgment manipulation, and outages. Every provider tested fell to at least one attack class in its default setup. The worst flaws came from how the pipeline infrastructure handles credentials and configuration files, not from any single model's behavior, and the authors give the cheapest workflow-level fix for each attack.
arxiv-2606-10035:
Prodinger studies a coloring game played on Dyck paths, the lattice walks that step up and down without dropping below zero, in a 2026 arXiv paper on combinatorics. Nodes along the path receive black and white labels, and the white-height counts a weighted measure of the white labels. Using generating functions, the standard tool that encodes counting sequences as power series, he computes the average white-height over all paths of a given length.

For two different labeling models, the average white-height grows like one half times the square root of pi times n, where n is the half-length of the path. A final section links walks with double steps to 2-Motzkin paths, another family of lattice walks, where white-height is again the natural quantity. The paper is short and deliberately elementary, aimed at students learning the trade of analytic combinatorics.
arxiv-2606-10235:
Kushwahaa and colleagues use dying stars to trace the warp in the Milky Way's disc, in a 2026 arXiv paper on galactic astronomy. The team uses two populations: carbon-rich stars about a billion years old, and oxygen-rich intermediate-mass stars only a few hundred million years old.

The downward warp traced by the oxygen-rich stars matches the warp found from Cepheid variables, as expected from their similar ages. The more numerous carbon-rich stars reveal the warp clearly across a wide range of azimuthal angles, and their warp reaches larger amplitudes than the Cepheids' across those angles. Together the populations constrain the warp at intermediate stellar ages, adding a new point to the relation between stellar age and warp amplitude. That age dependence helps astronomers test explanations for the warp, from satellite interactions to misaligned gas accretion.
arxiv-2606-10335:
Jung and his team reconstruct fluid flow fields in a way that respects the physics the data came from, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computing. When input data break physics, through low-fidelity simulation or unmodeled errors, rebuilds can show wrong equation residuals, violated balance laws, or shaky derived values. Their physics-informed B-spline method embeds the governing constraints directly into the rebuild process.

The method builds compact, smooth field forms from tensor-product B-splines, the standard piecewise polynomial basis. It finds the spline control points by weighing data fit against the residuals of the partial differential equations, plus initial and boundary conditions. The method offers simulation scientists a middle path: smoother and more usable than raw gridded output, yet answerable to the equations the flow must obey.
arxiv-2606-10835:
Lee analyzes a blended target update for linear Q-learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Q-learning steadies itself with a target network, a lagging copy refreshed only periodically, but hard periodic updates can still destabilize linear value models. The lambda-target update averages the periodic update maps with geometric weights, sliding between two known schemes as lambda runs from zero to one.

At lambda zero it is the plain one-period update; as lambda approaches one it becomes projected Q-value iteration. Both endpoints solve the same projected Bellman equation yet generate different error systems. Lee derives a joint spectral radius certificate for the whole family, plus implementable sampled versions of the update.
arxiv-2606-11135:
Zhao, Bouffard, and Joós address a protection problem created by solar and battery inverters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Distribution networks increasingly host inverter-based resources, which supply little short-circuit current during faults. Traditional overcurrent relays, which trip on excess current, can no longer be trusted to spot faults quickly in such networks.

They propose pre-fault voltage discrimination. It uses the voltage recorded just before a disturbance to tell real faults apart from normal switching events and transformer inrush, the surge when a transformer energizes. On that foundation they build a time-domain fault detection algorithm using traveling wave information, the fast transients a fault launches. Offline simulations and controller hardware-in-the-loop real-time tests validated the design. It stayed dependable against small fault inception angles, secure against normal switching, and faster than traditional relays.
arxiv-2606-12035:
Tian-Ci Tian and five colleagues describe quantum devices without rerunning them in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowing what a quantum device actually does, process description, underpins benchmarking and error checks. Shadow methods recently extended from states to processes, letting many properties be predicted from few measurements, but only singly.

Their framework, shadow engineering, encodes each shadow into sparse transfer matrices. From those, arbitrary combined process chains can be predicted in advance, without running it on hardware. They prove modest sample needs, far better than full process tomography. Shadow data is simply reused, so overhead is minimal. Tests on a superconducting quantum processor show the approach for error mitigation and Hamiltonian dynamics. The authors describe the result as virtual quantum process control: complex changes handled on a normal computer while the quantum hardware stays untouched.
arxiv-2606-12135:
Fournier and Zhou extend mean-field theory to crowds whose links themselves keep changing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mean-field theory replaces a huge interacting crowd by one typical member facing an averaged environment. Here each particle follows a noisy diffusion, random wandering with drift, while the weight on each link between two particles also evolves noisily. Each weight's motion depends on the states of the two particles it joins.

Starting data are assumed dissociated, a product form where separate random ingredients generate each particle and link. The authors build the limiting equation by averaging over an independent neighbor and prove it has a unique solution. The dissociated structure survives the dynamics, an echo of the classic propagation of chaos. Under stated conditions, coupling estimates show a typical particle and link converge to the limit as the crowd grows. The crowd's overall distribution of state pairs and weights converges too.
arxiv-2606-12335:
Noble and Royle prove a 1988 conjecture for planar graphs after it failed everywhere else, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Las Vergnas conjectured a divisibility pattern in the Tutte polynomial, a graph-counting polynomial, tied to a graph's bicycle dimension, a measure of its cycle structure. The claim says certain derivatives of the diagonal Tutte polynomial at minus one come out as multiples of powers of two. Counterexamples killed it for general graphs and binary matroids. Computation hinted planar graphs, drawable without crossings, might obey it.

The authors define a stronger property, the LV property, and prove it for a wider class: delta-Y-reducible graphs. They analyze how a delta-Y exchange, a local graph surgery, shifts the polynomial's coefficients. Planar graphs are all delta-Y-reducible, so the conjecture follows for them at once. A conjecture surviving only in the flat world now has a proof shaped to that world.
arxiv-2606-12435:
