Leibniz-dendriform and Zinbiel-dendriform algebras split well-known operations into two parts, and their bialgebra theories come with their own Yang-Baxter style equations. Pre-Lie algebras sit one level up, with commutators giving Lie brackets.

Tensoring a Leibniz-dendriform bialgebra with a quadratic graded Zinbiel algebra yields a full pre-Lie bialgebra, Sun shows. The mirror construction pairs a Zinbiel-dendriform bialgebra with a graded Leibniz algebra. The reverse holds too: affinization by a special Leibniz algebra detects exactly the Zinbiel-dendriform bialgebras. Answers of the two Yang-Baxter equations then lift to full solutions of the S-equation in the induced pre-Lie algebra.
arxiv-2608-00035:
Song, Lepori, and Pavlick test whether language can reshape visual representations. Human vision bends toward the task at hand. That shift aids sorting and search. Models face the same tasks, but their visual codes were seen as fixed stores. Language was thought to act on them from outside.

They show two cases of language-driven recoding. First, a shared reference code marks which objects matter for a prompt. Steering vectors for that code steer model predictions in a causal way. The code holds across objects, tasks, and image styles. Second, later layers boost task-relevant traits in visual codes. A causal test shows that boost shapes the model's reply mix. Vision tokens are thus dynamic, not static stores.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol3-18:
Audubon issued volume three of his Ornithological Biography in 1835. The work stands as the prose companion to The Birds of America. Species accounts march on through the birds of the young republic. Audubon's years in forests, swamps, and coasts stand behind every page.

He records how each bird feeds, nests, migrates, and sings. Encounters with hunters, settlers, and wild weather enliven the science. The accounts mix exact detail with a storyteller's pace. Volume three holds the middle of the five volume set. Its pages widen the record his pictures made famous. Naturalists quote these observations to this day. The America he crossed has vanished, but not from here.
berzelius-theorie-proportions-1835:
Berzelius states his full atomic-weight system in his Theory of Chemical Proportions, in French from 1835. Decades of exact trials stand behind the tables in this capstone work. The great Swedish chemist sums up a life spent weighing the elements with unmatched care and patience.

His system gave later chemists the firm numbers they needed. On such weights the periodic table would one day be built with confidence. He also defends his views against rivals in clear, firm prose. The book closes an era in which one man's laboratory set the measures for a whole science coming of age.
boerhaave-elements-chemistry-1735:
Herman Boerhaave's Elements of Chemistry, in Peter Shaw's 1735 English version, was the eighteenth century's leading textbook of the science. Boerhaave taught at Leiden, and students crossed Europe to hear him lecture. He made chemistry a fit and honored study for a university, not a mere trade secret.

Order, clarity, and trial mark every part of his vast course. Furnaces, salts, metals, and medicines fall into one clear system here. Shaw's version carried the master's voice to the English-reading world in full. The book laid a foundation stone of Enlightenment chemistry, and its influence ran through lecture halls for decades after.
buchner-dantons-death-1835:
Georg Büchner wrote Danton's Death in 1835, at the age of twenty-one, while hiding from police pursuit. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Danton, hero of the French Revolution, has tired of blood and wants the Terror stopped.

Robespierre and Saint-Just, cold and certain, move to destroy him for that mercy. Danton drifts, jokes, and despairs, yet will not flee or fight in time. Büchner built the play from historical sources, letting real speeches carry the scenes. Its weary, brilliant talk sounds startlingly modern. Critics now rank the play as the birth of modern political drama.
calderon-life-is-a-dream-1635:
Pedro Calderon de la Barca wrote Life Is a Dream in 1635, a Spanish verse drama of the Baroque age. Prince Segismundo has been locked in a tower since birth. A prophecy said he would become a cruel king. His father the king tests him by giving him one day of freedom.

Segismundo acts with rage, is returned to the tower, and is told it was all a dream. Later a revolt frees him for real, and he must choose how to rule. The play asks whether life itself is a dream. It is the most famous drama of Spain's Golden Age.
christian-phrenology-1835:
A chart of the phrenological organs opens an 1835 attempt to make phrenology Christian. Each organ is listed with its use, its abuse, and the effect of its weak development. Amativeness, love between the sexes, heads the propensities. Its abuse is lust, its lack a dislike of the other sex. Philoprogenitiveness, love of children, follows the same pattern.

Combativeness abused becomes cruelty and war. Acquisitiveness abused, joined with secretiveness, may lead to theft. The argument then turns theological. Human beings, the text insists, are moral agents addressed by every page of the New Testament. Powers can be neglected or debased, but they can also be trained. The chart's neat rows try to hold brain science and free will in one frame.
cia-0000009835:
American prisoners of war passed through Viet Cong hands in Quang Ngai province, a February 1972 item reports, in a civilian context the title cuts short. Quang Ngai, on the central coast, had a dense Viet Cong network among its villages. Prisoners in transit were often the most exposed to view.

Transit sightings gave brief, dated fixes between camps that stayed hidden. A group seen passing told officials its men were alive that week. The civilian angle in the heading suggests villagers, not soldiers, supplied the sighting. This file preserves one such passage near the war's end in the south.
cia-0000011835:
Katanga, the mineral-rich province of the Congo, had broken away from the new Congolese state, and in November 1961 the CIA mapped its possible futures. Moise Tshombe led the secession, backed by Belgian interests and foreign mercenaries. United Nations troops were fighting to end the split, which had already drawn in both Cold War blocs.

The paper weighs the courses open to Tshombe, the central government, and the UN force. It treats Katanga's copper and uranium as prizes that raised the stakes for everyone. The study captures a crisis that became a byword for the chaos of decolonization in Africa.
cia-0000013835:
Allied prisoners in Viet Cong hands are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1967. The southern captivity held more than Americans. Australians, Filipinos, and others who served beside the United States shared the jungle camps, along with Vietnamese whose fate the files tracked less fully. The paper counts the southern roll as far as sources knew it, name by name where names could be had.

The southern roll was always incomplete, and the paper says so by its gaps. Every name entered was a family's hope given form. For readers, the survey shows the captivity as an allied burden, borne in the same cages.
cia-0000014135: The new look of the Ongania administration in Argentina is the subject of a CIA report dated May 3, 1967. The report reads the government's fresh face after its first phase in power. Military rulers in Buenos Aires drew steady watch from Washington in those years. Notes like this tracked how such a regime presented itself and where it seemed to head.
cia-0000014735: Unknown subjects, a husband and wife, anchor a CIA file dated November 1, 1962. The pair had worked at American Westinghouse around 1950, per the title. An unnamed couple in a defense linked plant was exactly the sort of lead agents chased. The file shows the spy hunt still turning over old stones in 1962.
cia-0000015235: UFO research is the named topic of a CIA file dated March 1, 1976. The case number and the researcher's name are both cut out as deleted. Redacted files like this fed years of public doubt about what the agency knew. Even with names gone, the date shows UFO work still on desks in the mid 1970s.
cia-0000015435: Dr. Edward Condon visited NPIC, the national photo reading center, in a visit recorded by the CIA on January 4, 1967. The catalog title gives the visit date as February 20, 1957, which clashes with the 1967 file date and Condon's known study period. Condon was then leading a major review of the UFO question. The visit put photo experts and their methods in front of him.
cia-0000020435: Signs that Chile's junta government was softening toward political prisoners are weighed in a CIA record dated in 1974. The junta had seized power in 1973 and filled prisons with its foes. Any easing mattered to families, to exiles, and to foreign governments pressing for mercy. The careful word indications shows analysts judging a thaw from hints, not from firm promises.
cia-0000022335: Commentary on the Powers trial fills a CIA record dated in 1960. Comment pieces told readers what the Moscow trial meant, beyond the charges and pleas. The agency gathered such views to gauge world opinion as the case ran. A commentary file is a mood record, showing how the U-2 affair played in print while the court still sat.
cia-0000028335: Nicaragua faces the prospect of a refugee exodus, a CIA paper dated in 1981 weighs. The contra war was just beginning, and fighting would soon empty border villages. Forecasting an exodus meant judging war, fear, and the roads north together. The paper came early in a flow of people that grew all decade and reached the United States.
cia-0000045235:
Reuters blamed leftist rebels for the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. A wire attribution early in a case sets the story's frame. Later reports argue inside the frame the first ones built.

Inside, the agency's judgment on responsibility is preserved. Reuters wrote for editors in a hundred capitals at once. Its verdict reached them all before any court could sit. First frames are hard to break, and this one held through the whole long course of the case. The file keeps that early framing from August 1985, when the question of who had taken the president's daughter was still being settled in public print.
cia-0000045935: An appeal urged the United States to put an early end to the missing-men issue, and a CIA item dated January 2, 1992, kept the text. The accounting for Americans missing in Vietnam still stood between Hanoi and normal ties with Washington. The item shows the push, growing on both sides, to settle the war's last open question.
cia-0000049235:
The role of Roberto D'Aubuisson in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA paper from 1981, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. D'Aubuisson, a former army major, was then building the movement that became ARENA and standing accused, already, of directing death squads. The paper tries to fix one man's place in a widening war.

Inside, his part is weighed against the institutions around him: the army that trained him, the rich who funded him, and the squads that answered him. That weighing mattered because later judgments, including the Truth Commission's own, returned to the same question. The paper is an early draft of the verdict history would reach.
cia-0000049335: Declassified CIA document 0000049335, dated November 3, 1980, takes up the Salvadoran military's attitude toward compromise. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and focuses on how the military viewed a negotiated path. It remains a brief agency item whose title states its question clearly, part of the early declassified record on El Salvador's political choices.
cia-0000095035: Czechoslovakia; the Dubcek Pause is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000095035, dated May 4, 1968. The title names the country's leader and a pause, in a few words. The brief file is a dated agency item on Czechoslovakia that spring, its compressed heading carrying the whole description the catalog record offers. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000098735: Wilhelm-Pieck University renamed Rostock is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098735, dated March 3, 1990. The title records a name being dropped and a city name taken instead. The brief file is a short renaming notice, preserved as a small dated marker among the agency's records from Germany's year of change.
cia-0000112335: Airship-like Ufo Sighted Over Murmansk is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112335, dated August 2, 1990. The title describes a sighting in shape terms: an airship-like object over Murmansk. Murmansk is the only place named in the short heading itself. The brief record is a sighting item, filed among the late Soviet UFO items in the release as filed there.
cia-0000112835: Collaborators In- Shanghai Area is the heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112835, dated October 4, 1945. The title names a group, collaborators in the Shanghai area, with a stray dash in the heading. No single person is named in the title itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the stray mark.
cia-0000119735: Dated September 1956, a CIA paper surveys the present political situation in Hungary. Budapest was nearing a boil that autumn, though no one could name the day it would spill over. The paper takes the country's temperature on the edge of revolution. Situation surveys like this one fed the stream of Hungary reporting that would swell into daily crisis coverage within a matter of weeks.
cia-0000124335: A September 1958 CIA report describes a Moscow industrial and farm exhibit that featured models of Sputniks and electronic gear, the heading breaking off. The Soviets put their technical triumphs on public show that year. The report sets out the showpiece items as observed. Exhibit reports doubled as shopping lists of Soviet pride, telling analysts which machines Moscow wanted the world to admire and therefore what it valued in itself.
cia-0000132235: Situation report 552, from January 1991, covers political developments, including Iran's foreign minister Velayati preparing to hold something the heading cuts off. Velayati was working the diplomatic circuit during the crisis. The report tracks his moves that day. Velayati's movements were followed because Iran's neutrality was valuable to both sides, and every capital he visited was guessed at in the next day's reporting.
cia-0000132635: Cuba putting off its planned meeting of poor nations fills item 14 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated June 5, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word indefinit, short for indefinitely. Havana's bid to lead the third world was on hold for the time. The short item reports the delay and the reasons given for it.
cia-0000135835: A report dated 2 March 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on a situation report on PBSUCCESS for the week of 20 to 26 April. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000135935: A CIA cable from 3 January 1954, now declassified, deals with a reported need for fabricated operational documents, false papers ordered up as a line item. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136135: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 1 April 1954, covers a possible arms shipment and the instructions that went with it, for ONTRICH, info SKILLET. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136335: Operators 24, 27, and 38 reported in the radio material summarized here for 27 June 1954, the last day of the Arbenz government. One operator suspended activity for lack of a battery, while Chacon reported himself thirty kilometers west and said enemy morale was falling, with air attacks causing many desertions. Captured artillery and expected two-pronged attacks from Zacapa also appear. The summary catches the rebel advance in fragments, as headquarters heard it.
cia-0000136935: Leaflet drop flights prompt questions from headquarters in April 1954. Before any more such flights, headquarters wants facts. What is the position of the pilots? How many are there? What plans exist? It also asks about staffing. Air operations now play a bigger role. Should LINCOLN get more qualified air officers? BRODFROST may soon be in the forward area. The station may need backstopping and review for field flights. Paper propaganda still needed pilots.
cia-0000137335: Castro holds overwhelming popularity among Cuba's lower classes. This CIA briefing reports it for the 401st NSC meeting on 23 April 1959. Agrarian reform is alienating business groups. Rent and utility cuts do the same. No sign of organized opposition has yet appeared. His charge about Batista-era arms was not repeated on the visit. The United States sent tanks and planes at a peso apiece, he had claimed. At least two communists sit in his entourage. Raul Castro attacked the United States sharply on 20 April.
cia-0000139035: Soviet Mongolia will issue modern weapons in Chahar. This July 1946 report on a mission to Kalgan states it. The weapons are for training civilians. Three divisions of Soviet Mongolian troops will direct the training. They number about 4,500 men. They will also designate stationing areas for Chinese Communist troops. The areas lie in Chahar and along the Peking-Suiyuan Railroad. Inner Mongolian banners will accept Mongolian advisors from Outer Mongolia. Three to five advisors are expected. A note clarifies that Soviet Mongolia means the Mongolian People's Republic.
cia-0000139135: President Rafsanjani is using the Gulf crisis, this Middle East brief reports. The brief is dated 30 August 1990. He encourages movement toward resolving the Lebanese hostage situation. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait drew world condemnation. He tries to capitalize on that mood. A pro-Rafsanjani Tehran paper urged the West to respond. Irish hostage Brian Keenan had been released. The West should press Israel to free Shaykh Obeid, the paper said. Other Arab prisoners should be freed too. Tehran's demand for four Iranians was not repeated this time.
cia-0000141135:
Gar Thorsrud and Jack Pfeiffer talk through the Bay of Pigs failure in a recorded talk kept in CIA files, with a catalog date of 1976. Thorsrud tells how Charles Cabell and Richard Bissell went to Secretary of State Dean Rusk's office to protest a scrubbed second air strike. Rusk phoned President Kennedy at Glen Ora, his Virginia estate.

Rusk backed the call to scrub the strike, and both men chose not to plead their case to Kennedy themselves. Talk then shifts to Lyman Kirkpatrick's probe and one raw question: could any of the Americans shot down over Cuba still be alive? The talk lays bare how the doomed operation was run, and judged, from the top.
cia-03002335:
Afghanistan and Pakistan open the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 22 October 1955. The lead item passes on a claim of evidence that Kabul was inciting the Pushtoon tribes against Pakistan. Kabul had ordered its Pushtoonistan propaganda resumed on 18 October, weeks after a settlement. The bulletin judges a small tribal rising possible, but regular Afghan troops unlikely to cross the border.

Britain, in the second item, urges American aid for Egypt's Aswan high dam. Foreign Secretary Macmillan wants Washington approached urgently, to forestall Soviet moves. Eden calls the proposal major and wants a contract signed within days. A delayed Moroccan government, an Indonesian party weighing Communist support, and Japan's push to trim the China embargo list fill the rest.
cia-03153735:
France opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 7 December 1957, by urging an independent European nuclear weapons capability. Paris now favours a joint programme apart from the United States, and if needed from Britain. West Germany seems interested in a bilateral effort. Anger over Anglo-American arms deliveries to Tunisia is named as a spur. France means to push its own programme regardless.

Danish officials are impressed by Kennan's neutral belt concept in the second item. Renewed labour agitation threatens the Gaillard government. Indonesia's situation and the fighting in Spanish Ifni follow, with insurgent strength now estimated at four thousand. Communist terrorism is expected in South Vietnam on 19 December. Guided missiles are possibly installed on two Soviet submarines. Suslov criticises Japanese Communists for weak mass influence.
cia-03155135:
Disarmament opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 12 July 1957. Britain is reconsidering whether Communist China must join a first-step agreement. Australia and New Zealand dissented sharply at the Commonwealth conference. Menzies argued Peiping's expansionism makes binding China essential. London has agreed to study the question again. A French legislative committee moves toward recognising Communist China, and Canadian officials consider the same.

A Soviet UN official, in the fourth item, claims the recent purge makes better American-Soviet relations possible. He promises flexibility, though no change in basic aims. Settlements would come item by item, little by little. Italian Communists react to the purge in the next item. The Shah returns to Iran ahead of schedule. Indonesia's situation follows, and a Watch Report annex closes the issue.
cia-06828435:
Cafe menu for the week of 6 November 2017 at the OHB Main Cafe marks Native American Heritage Month. A traditional Native American meal was set for Tuesday, November 7, late in the morning through early afternoon. Everyday lines include a chipotle bacon chicken ranch panini and Vietnamese-style banh mi burgers with fries. Both are priced just under seven dollars.

Chicken enchilada appears all week at seven dollars and forty-nine cents. Monday pairs chili lime baked chicken with roasted lemon dill tilapia, beside beef and rice soup, spinach soup, and beef chili. Wednesday turns meatless with stuffed yellow peppers, plus an Asian inspired flank steak. Thursday entrees on the second page include baked fresh cod with harissa sauce, Moroccan chicken tagine, and fragrant beef curry. Friday brings Cherokee-style fried chicken and Native-style roasted salmon.
coriolanus-pg1535:
William Shakespeare's Tragedy of Coriolanus, in this modern-spelling text with full scene locations, opens on a Roman street where citizens, starving and angry, name Caius Martius chief enemy of the people. The contents map his rise: Corioles besieged, the gates, the Volscian camp, and triumph at Rome. Menenius, the hero's garrulous friend, tries to talk the crowd down in the middle scenes.

Coriolanus wins his name in battle, loses Rome by contempt, and returns at the head of its enemies, crying peace, peace, peace to a Forum in confusion. This text parallels the old-spelling Coriolanus elsewhere in the library, offering modern readers the Roman tragedy of pride and ingratitude in a cleaner page.
croll-basilica-chymica-1635:
Oswald Croll, a German physician in the circle of Paracelsus, wrote Basilica Chymica, shown here in its 1635 form. Croll taught that chemical medicines, made by art, could heal better than the old herbal mixtures alone. His book became a leading guide to Paracelsian pharmacy.

Recipes give salts, oils, and spirits drawn from metals, plants, and minerals, with the steps for making each one. Croll also set out the doctrine of signatures, which held that a plant's shape hints at its use. Doctors and apothecaries used the book across Europe. It shows chemical medicine taking shape inside an older world of signs and likenesses.
doe-osti-2998720-measured-reaction-rate-:
Nicholas Whitman, Robert Weldon, Matthew Gooden and Jesson Hutchinson of Los Alamos National Laboratory report reaction rate ratios from the PFUNS criticality experiment. PFUNS used shells of highly enriched uranium at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center in February 2024. Its aim was to shrink doubt about the high-energy tail of neutrons thrown off when uranium-235 splits.

Two irradiations exposed about 40 measured reactions in more than 20 foil materials held in the shells' hollow centre. Focus here is the first run: pairs of fission foils, one bare and one wrapped in cadmium, plus metal foils with short-lived products. Bare and covered foils agreed within uncertainty, since the neutron spectrum was so hard. Ratios for depleted uranium foils fell between older Lady Godiva and Flattop-25 values. Full results from both runs will feed a final spectrum adjustment.
dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life-volu:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Dynevor Terrace opens its first volume with Charlotte, a leafless horse-chestnut in a dusty field, and a row of houses filling with families. The contents sketch the colony: an old schoolmistress, the two ministers, the family compact, and a halting proposal. The Frost household, kindly in frost, anchors the terrace. New inhabitants arrive: the Conways, with Isabel, and a fantastic viscount to unsettle every drawing room. Childe Roland and the hero of the barricades widen the cast toward France and revolution's aftershocks.

Yonge, the author of The Heir of Redclyffe, builds her chronicle on small decisions of conscience. The clue of life in her subtitle is the ruling principle each young person must find and keep. Readers starting the volumes get her method pure: households as moral weather, and courtship as a test of principles.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol1-1835:
John Elliotson sets out the human body in the first volume of his Human Physiology, from 1835. Elliotson was London's most fashionable physician and a star lecturer. His textbook bridged orthodox medicine and the mesmerism that would soon define, and then destroy, his public standing in the medical world.

Organs, tissues, and functions are laid out in systematic order here. The writing aims at students yet carries a controversialist's spark beneath. Within a few years, mesmeric trials would cost him his hospital post. The volume shows establishment medicine at its most ambitious, by a man standing, unknowing, on the edge of a spectacular fall from grace.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol2-1835:
Elliotson continues his systematic textbook in the second volume of Human Physiology, from 1835. The body's functions unfold in ordered detail for the medical student. Its author writes on the very eve of the scandal that would exile him from respectable medicine into the mesmeric camp for good.

Senses, nerves, and the machinery of life fill these careful pages. Elliotson's fame as a lecturer rests on clarity like this throughout. Orthodox in form, the book hides no hint of coming disgrace. Readers meet the establishment's physiology at full stretch, from a physician whose later fall makes the calm competence of these volumes read almost sadly.
elliotson-human-physiology-vol3-1835:
Elliotson completes his Human Physiology with this third volume, from 1835. The system of the body stands whole at last for his students. Within a few years, his public mesmeric demonstrations would cost him his hospital post and his good name among the faculty of London medicine.

Generation, growth, and the mind's link to the body close the course. The physiology itself remained a landmark text despite its author's disgrace. Elliotson later founded the Zoist to plead the mesmeric cause in print. The three volumes together capture a moment when one textbook could carry a man from fame to exile, while the work outlived the scandal.
europmc-pmc10353935:
Patel and colleagues built a better gene-based risk score for heart artery disease in 2023. The Genes & Health Research Team and the Million Veteran Program shared data for the work. A polygenic score adds up many small gene effects into one risk number. The new score, GPSMult, drew on gene data from five ancestry groups.

The data held over 269,000 cases and over 1,178,000 controls. Patel also folded in gene data for ten risk traits, such as blood fats. In UK tests, the top fifth of scorers had three times the risk of the middle group. The score beat all past scores in African, European, Hispanic, and South Asian groups. It also flagged 3% of healthy people whose risk matched that of patients.
europmc-pmc1044835:
Iacoboni and colleagues used brain scans in 2005 to test how people read the aims of others. Mirror neurons are brain cells that fire both when a person acts and when they watch the same act. Past work tied them to naming an act. The team asked if they also grasp why the act is done.

Twenty-three people watched hand grasps in the scanner. Some clips showed a grasp with no setting, some a setting alone, and some a grasp in a setting that hinted at drinking or cleaning. Iacoboni found a clear rise in signal for grasps in a setting. The hot spot sat in the lower front of the brain, in mirror areas. The result says the motor system infers aims on its own.
europmc-pmc10558035:
Huang and Li built compleasm in 2023, a faster tool to grade how complete a genome build is. A genome build may miss genes, which then warps all later work. The standard grader, BUSCO, checks for a set of genes kept near unchanged across species. It runs slowly, most of all on huge genomes.

Their tool pairs a fast protein aligner with the same gene sets. Huang reports a 14-fold speed gain on human builds. It also scored the full human build at 99.6% complete, close to the 99.5% from gene labels. BUSCO had scored the same build at just 95.7%. The code is free on GitHub for any lab to use.
europmc-pmc1084335:
Bolzer and colleagues mapped every chromosome inside human cell nuclei in 3D in this 2005 paper. Chromosomes are the bundled strands of DNA that carry genes. How they sit inside the nucleus, the cell's control centre, may affect how genes are used. Past studies clashed on whether their layout follows a fixed order.

The team built tools to chart all chromosomes at once in skin cells. Small chromosomes sat nearer the centre, they found, while large ones sat nearer the edge. This held in resting and growing cells and in a second cell type from birth fluid. The pattern followed size, not gene richness, in these flat nuclei. The authors note that round nuclei in other cells follow a distinct rule, so layout rules vary by cell type.
europmc-pmc11223835:
Galaxy Community reports the 2024 state of a global platform for data analysis in biology in this paper. Galaxy lets researchers run complex analyses through a web interface without local computing power. Most services are free to use, and the user base broadens each year. Stability, tool variety, training, and support draw users in.

Recent work applies user experience design to improve accessibility and tool discovery. A redesigned ToolShed, the platform's app store, is part of that push. Two technical directions stand out: access to graphics processors for cutting-edge methods, and support for licensed tools. The Galaxy Training Network has grown its course portfolio and linked lessons directly to tools. Job scheduling and the interface were improved. The authors also describe resourcing public services to run more shared workflows.
europmc-pmc1523235:
Cells that build tissue, fibroblasts, behave unlike twins in each body site. Rinn and co-authors mapped their gene programs in 2006, sampling 43 sites across the human body. The question was whether each site is specified on its own, or reads its place on a body map.

A set of 337 genes sorted all samples by their site of origin. The genes varied along three axes: head to tail, limb base to tip, and skin versus deep tissue. Many were pattern genes, including HOX genes whose embryo layout persists in adult cells. Rinn argues fibroblasts keep a lasting memory of position.
europmc-pmc1635535:
A jumping gene from fish can haul cargo too big for virus tools. Balciunas and co-authors harnessed the Tol2 transposon in 2006. Viruses and transposons insert DNA into genomes, but falter beyond about 8,000 letters.

Tol2 efficiently integrated pieces larger than 10,000 letters into human cells. The team trimmed it to a minimal form, miniTol2 at 5,800 letters, that still works in zebrafish and human cells. Both forms fixed a missing enzyme in an animal model of hereditary tyrosinemia, a liver disease. Balciunas offers Tol2 as a nonviral truck for large therapeutic genes.
europmc-pmc1762435:
Oxygen-starved cells tune their blood vessel signals with tiny RNAs. Hua and co-authors mapped that tuning in 2006 for VEGF, a key vessel growth factor, in a human tumor cell line. Computer analysis predicted 96 microRNAs could regulate VEGF.

Expression profiles across five cell lines showed only some candidates were actually present to act. Different cells used different subsets of the 96. Some microRNAs co-regulated several vessel factors at once. Multiple microRNAs could cooperate at separate binding sites or compete for one. Hua lays out coordinate and competitive principles for how microRNAs jointly govern a gene.
europmc-pmc2125335:
Henry F. Moore tested the drug ethylhydrocuprein, optochin, against pneumococci in 1915, in the dish and in animals, alongside other microbes. In very high dilution its hydrochloride stops the growth of all four pneumococcus groups and kills them within eighteen hours. No group is notably harder or easier to kill than another.

The sharpness of the action is the finding. On bacteria other than pneumococci the effect is slight or absent; streptococci feel it most and still far less. Plain quinine hydrochloride also kills pneumococci in the dish, but only at much stronger concentrations, and it hits other organisms too. The base form also protects infected animals, the paper's mouse experiments charting survival, drug deaths, and septicemia deaths side by side. Readers get an early, targeted antibacterial, prized as much for diagnosis as for cure.
europmc-pmc2126335:
Herbert Haessler and Marianne G. Stebbins asked whether bile itself slows blood clotting, as jaundice is known to do. They reported in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1919. They added bile salts in graded amounts to whole blood, to plasma, and to fibrin solutions. In each mixture they timed how long clotting took.

Within limits, clotting time rose in direct proportion to the amount of bile present, across all three test materials. Tracing the steps of clot formation, they located the block at the last step. Bile interferes with the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin, the final mesh of the clot. It does not interfere with the formation of thrombin, the agent that drives that conversion. The finding gives the slow clotting of jaundice a precise address in the clotting chain. The blood's own dissolved bile salts can act there directly.
europmc-pmc2130935:
Simon Flexner and Harold L. Amoss argued that ordinary herpes virus can itself attack the rabbit's brain as fiercely as the so-called encephalitis virus. Their paper is the second in a series on experimental virus encephalitis, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. The claim cut at a standing division in the field.

Certain workers had held that two distinct viruses exist: one causing epidemic encephalitis in man, the other causing febrile herpes. Flexner and Amoss show that undoubted herpes strains from man exist which, in the rabbit, show brain-attacking power not exceeded and rarely equalled by any encephalitis strain. A newer view, urged by Levaditi and others, gathers both into one family of closely related viruses, some strains loving the nervous organs and others the skin and cornea. Their evidence supports the family view: the difference is one of strain temperament, not of kind.
europmc-pmc2140435:
Jacques Loeb studied the linked behavior of osmotic pressure and viscosity in gelatin solutions in a 1921 paper. The two properties often move in opposite directions under the same treatment. Loeb argues protein solutions are true solutions of separate ions and molecules, sometimes with tiny solid particles mixed in that can soak up water.

Osmotic pressure, he holds, comes from the separate protein ions, which alone can set up a Donnan equilibrium across a membrane. Viscosity comes from the tiny solid particles, whose swelling is ruled by that same equilibrium. Warming a gelatin solution turns particles into ions; viscosity then falls while osmotic pressure rises, in mirror image. That reciprocal trade is the paper's central evidence.
europmc-pmc2140535:
Wallace Fenn wrote part four of his phagocytosis studies in 1923, on carbon and quartz in fluids of varying acidity. White blood cells eat the two dusts at different rates, and part three had shown carbon winning in serum. Here the acidity of the fluid is swung from acid to alkaline to see whether the ranking flips.

In acid solutions the cells ate quartz more readily than carbon; in alkaline solutions carbon won. With acacia gum present, carbon was always preferred, even in acid. Manganese dioxide particles were eaten with extraordinary speed and even seemed to attract the cells, while carbon and quartz did not. Penicillium spores were eaten more readily than quartz. Very small quartz grains broke the surface tension prediction, pointing to another factor.
europmc-pmc2141035:
Ultraviolet light kills bacteria, and Frederick L. Gates asks which surrounding conditions change that killing power. His 1929 study, the second in a series, works with Staphylococcus aureus and varies light intensity, exposure time, wavelength, temperature, and the acidity of the setting.

Doubling intensity does not neatly trade against halving time, so the Bunsen-Roscoe reciprocity law fails strictly, especially for young active bacteria. Direct killing reaches out to wavelengths between 302 and 313 millimicrons and was seen down at 225. The reaction barely speeds with heat, pointing to a light-driven chemical process rather than a heat-driven one. Acidity between pH 4.5 and 7.5 makes little difference, though stronger alkaline conditions show an effect.
europmc-pmc2225435:
García-Lerma and a large team tested HIV prevention drugs in macaques in 2008. With no effective vaccine, pre-exposure prophylaxis, taking antiretroviral drugs before exposure, is a leading prevention idea. The team used a repeat-exposure model with fourteen weekly rectal virus challenges. Six monkeys per group received daily emtricitabine alone, an oral two-drug combination, or a stronger injected combination. A fourth group got the strong regimen only around each challenge.

Risk of infection fell 3.8-fold with the single drug and 7.8-fold with the oral combination, compared with eighteen untreated controls. Both reductions were statistically significant. The work used a macaque model of rectal transmission of the virus. All six monkeys on the strong daily regimen were protected. All six on the intermittent regimen were also protected. Breakthrough infections showed blunted virus levels, and drug resistance appeared in two of six cases.
europmc-pmc2491635:
Strobl and colleagues fixed a bias in how random forests rank the importance of input factors in 2008. Random forests are models built from many decision trees, prized when inputs are many and tangled together. Their importance scores guide screening in fields like gene studies, but the scores favour inputs that move together with others.

The authors traced the bias to two causes. First, tree building itself prefers such linked inputs when choosing splits. Second, the standard score shuffles one input on its own, handing its linked partners an extra edge. Their fix shuffles each input only within groups matched on its partners, so each factor is judged on its own effect alone. In tests, this conditional score tracked each factor's true impact far better. They urged its use when tangled inputs make the standard ranking hard to trust.
europmc-pmc2527135:
Jones and colleagues studied in 2008 what a gene-tagging enzyme called Dot1L does in developing mammals. Dot1L adds a chemical mark, methylation, to one spot on histone H3, a protein that packages DNA. In yeast the mark helps silence genes near chromosome ends, but its role in mammals was unclear, so the team bred mice lacking the enzyme.

Embryos without Dot1L grew poorly, showed blood vessel defects in the yolk sac and swollen hearts, and died around day 10 of development. Stem cells taken from them had lost the H3 mark entirely. They also carried weaker silencing marks at chromosome centres and ends, wrong chromosome counts, overlong chromosome ends, and slow growth. The work ties Dot1L to keeping silent DNA regions intact during development.
europmc-pmc2581435:
Towner and a large team of collaborators reported in 2008 the discovery of a new Ebola virus species behind a haemorrhagic fever outbreak in western Uganda. In November 2007, cases appeared in Bundibugyo District. The known Ebola species, Zaire and Sudan, kill 53 to 90 percent of patients, so identifying the culprit fast mattered. The team tested blood from the first 29 suspected cases.

Standard antibody and antigen tests plus a new random-primed sequencing method identified an Ebola outbreak caused by a previously unknown species, named Bundibugyo ebolavirus. Its genome is only distantly related to Côte d'Ivoire ebolavirus from western Africa. It diverges enough from all known ebolaviruses to matter practically. The authors warn that diagnostic tests, antivirals, and vaccines designed against the known species may miss or fail against this one.
europmc-pmc2628535:
Brenk and colleagues described in 2008 how they assembled screening libraries for drug discovery against neglected diseases, working from 2.3 million commercially available compounds. A new discovery operation for diseases of the poor needed libraries chosen with limited money and staff. The team defined rules to drop unwanted chemical groups and criteria to enrich for lead-like compounds, molecules simple enough to optimise later.

They selected 222,552 compounds for a computer-screening library. A diverse general screening library took 57,438 more. A focused set aimed at kinase enzymes took 1,697, built from key fragments mined from the literature and patents. Testing showed the general library spanned broad lead-like chemical space with high purity and suitable solubility for biochemical screening. The authors draw lessons for compound selection in resource-limited academic settings.
europmc-pmc2631735:
Hooper reviewed in 2001 the emerging mechanisms by which bacteria resist fluoroquinolone antibiotics, a widely used drug class. These drugs kill by jamming two bacterial enzymes, DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, that manage DNA tangles. Resistance had followed broad use, and Hooper catalogues the routes bacteria take.

Most resistance comes from mutations in the target enzyme genes that blunt drug binding. Bacteria also mutate genes controlling the pores that let drugs in and the efflux pumps that throw drugs out. Species needing only one mutation, like Staphylococcus aureus, turned resistant first. Species needing several mutations followed later. These include Campylobacter and the gonorrhoea bacterium. Animal drug use and person-to-person spread helped them along. Hooper warns pneumococcus resistance, then low, needs close watching.
europmc-pmc2674935:
Hessell and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a famous HIV-blocking antibody could protect monkeys at strikingly low blood levels. The antibody, 2G12, locks onto sugars on the virus surface and neutralizes many strains. Most such antibodies need high levels to protect, which had dimmed hopes for an antibody-based vaccine. Earlier hints suggested 2G12 might be an exception.

The team dosed five monkeys and exposed them to a monkey-human hybrid virus through the vagina, mimicking sexual transmission. At blood levels so low they barely registered, three monkeys were fully protected, with no sign of infection at all. One showed a delayed, smaller infection, and one was not protected. Comparisons with a rival antibody found no edge for 2G12 in reaching the vaginal surface or in calling in killer cells, leaving its unusual strength unexplained.
europmc-pmc2677735:
Xilouri and colleagues showed in 2009 that faulty alpha-synuclein harms brain cells in part by jamming one of the cell's recycling routes. This protein clumps in Parkinson disease. Cells clear proteins two ways through their acid sacs: a bulk route, and a targeted route called chaperone-mediated autophagy, which walks single proteins to their doom.

In rat and human cell lines switched to make the faulty protein, the targeted route faltered and overall protein clearing fell. In mature nerve-like cells, both normal and faulty protein slowly killed, and the harm partly depended on the jammed route. The bulk route ramped up to compensate. In real neurons grown from rat brain, only the faulty form caused both the jam and the extra death. Easing the jam lessened the killing, pointing to a drug target.
europmc-pmc2685735:
Terwilliger and colleagues improved in 2009 the way crystallography software judges its own work while solving protein structures. To read a protein's shape from X-ray data, scientists build an electron-density map, a cloud picture of the molecule. Automated solving makes choice after choice, and each choice needs a reliable score for how good the current map is.

The team tested ten candidate scores against known answers. The winner was skewness, a measure of how lopsided the density values are; good maps skew in a characteristic way. They wrapped that score in a Bayesian method, which weighs new evidence against prior expectation, inside the PHENIX AutoSol wizard. The wizard now picks paths and stops bad branches with better judgment. Sharper self-scoring matters because structure solving is increasingly done by software alone, overnight, on hundreds of targets.
europmc-pmc2721635:
Melman and co-authors tested in 2009 whether parasitic worms from Kenya had grown less sensitive to praziquantel, nearly the only drug used against schistosomiasis, a widespread worm disease. Heavy reliance on one drug raises fears of resistance. They took Schistosoma mansoni isolates from workers in Kisumu who face constant exposure through their jobs.

Larvae from patients treated before were less sensitive in lab tests than larvae from untreated patients. One isolate from a man never cured despite many treatments was clearly less sensitive in mouse and adult-worm assays too. A sub-line kept apart for three years regained sensitivity, which suggests the trait fades without drug pressure but could spread as treatment expands.
europmc-pmc2740835:
Lemey, Rambaut, Drummond, and Suchard introduced in 2009 a Bayesian framework for phylogeography, the study of how viruses spread across places over time using their genetic family trees. Past work mostly used model-free shortcuts that gave little sense of timing. Probabilistic evolution models, by contrast, can date dispersal events while allowing for uncertainty in the tree itself.

Their method maps locations onto sampled, time-scaled trees and uses a variable search to pick the simplest set of dispersal routes that fits the data. Priors can encode sampling patterns or rival hypotheses about spread. Tests on bird flu H5N1 origins and on rabies in West African dogs showed timed routes and epidemic cycles that sustain the virus locally.
europmc-pmc2777335:
Sprong, Cacciò, and van der Giessen, with the ZOOPNET network and partners, genotyped in 2009 Giardia duodenalis isolates from people and animals to judge how often animal strains infect humans. This gut parasite causes giardiasis worldwide and spreads through stool, water, and food. Its seven genetic groups differ in host range, and two of them occur in humans and many mammals.

They characterized nearly one thousand human and over fourteen hundred animal isolates, building almost four thousand sequences from four gene loci into a shared European database. At coarse resolution, both human-infecting groups looked zoonotic, able to pass from animals. Under strict multi-locus definitions, though, only two genotypes of one group clearly qualified, and none of the other. Mixed genotypes within single isolates appeared repeatedly. Real zoonotic potential is evident, they conclude, but its size is still unmeasured.
europmc-pmc2810335:
Khallou-Laschet and colleagues tracked how macrophages, the eater cells inside artery plaques, change character as fatty deposits grow in mice prone to clogged arteries. Macrophages come in an attacking type, M1, and a repair type, M2. The 2010 team told them apart by which version of an enzyme called arginase each type makes.

Young plaques held almost only repair-type cells, which helped vessel wall cells multiply in lab tests. Older plaques flipped to mostly attack-type cells, and worse disease tracked with that flip. Lab experiments showed fully set cells could still swap types, so the change likely happens inside the plaque rather than by new arrivals. Reversing it might slow disease.
europmc-pmc2845135:
Seyfried and Shelton argued in 2010 that cancer is, at root, a metabolic disease of broken cell energy systems. Normal cells draw most usable energy from oxygen-based burning in mitochondria, the cell's power units. Most cancer cells instead lean on a cruder sugar-fermentation route, even when oxygen is plentiful, a pattern noticed by Warburg generations ago.

The authors review evidence tying that energy failure to nearly every cancer hallmark, from runaway growth to spread. Gene instability itself, they contend, may flow from faulty energy metabolism rather than sitting at the top of the chain. If the view holds, prevention and treatment would shift toward guarding mitochondrial function and starving the backup energy route tumors depend on.
europmc-pmc2877735:
Van Vliet, Harmsen, de Bont, and Tissing argued in 2010 that gut microbes help drive mucositis, the painful gut injury that often forces cancer treatment to pause. The classic model of mucositis runs through five phases of damage and healing and gives microbes no role. Yet gut bacteria clearly shape several bowel diseases, and chemotherapy itself slashes the gut's anaerobic bacteria just as mucositis peaks.

The authors set out five candidate pathways linking the microbial community to each stage of injury, from the first tissue damage to bacterial escape through the broken lining. Microbe shifts could amplify inflammation, weaken the mucus shield, and slow repair. Testing those routes could open probiotic or antibiotic strategies to protect patients and keep chemotherapy on schedule.
europmc-pmc2936535:
Hershberg and Petrov asked whether mutation itself leans in one direction across bacteria, in a 2010 evolution study. Mutation supplies the raw variation for selection, yet its habits were thought to differ widely between species.

They used clonal disease bacteria that evolve under unusually weak selection, letting mutation patterns show with little filtering. Across five pathogens from four broad groups, mutation consistently favoured the bases A and T, even in genomes rich in G and C. Changes from C or G toward T or A drove the trend. Base makeup, they argue, must also reflect selection.
europmc-pmc2948035:
Guerrero-Bosagna and colleagues examined sperm DNA in rats three generations after a pregnancy exposure to vinclozolin, a hormone-disrupting farm chemical, in a 2010 study. Earlier work showed such exposure produced disease in later generations without direct contact.

Scanning promoter regions genome-wide, they found dozens of stretches with altered chemical marking in the third-generation sperm, and confirmed a set of them with a second method. Most confirmed regions shared a common short DNA motif, rare among random promoters. One case turned out to be a copy number change rather than a marking shift, hinting early marks may seed later genetic faults.
europmc-pmc2987835:
Bos and colleagues hunted effector proteins from the green peach aphid, a sap-sucking pest, in a 2010 functional genomics study. Aphids inject saliva that calms plant defences such as sap tube clogging, and the responsible molecules were unknown.

Starting from salivary gland gene tags in public data, they picked forty-eight candidates sharing features with known pathogen effectors and tested each in a model plant leaf. One, named Mp10, triggered leaf yellowing and local cell death and made a virus carrying it recognisable to tobacco defences. A plant helper protein long tied to disease resistance proved necessary for that response.
europmc-pmc2993935:
Martínez and co-authors fed volunteers two kinds of resistant starch and tracked changes in gut microbes in a 2010 trial. Resistant starch escapes digestion and feeds bowel bacteria, but its forms differ chemically and may act differently.

Ten people ate crackers carrying one starch type, a modified type, or plain starch for three weeks each in a blinded rotation. Gene tag sequencing showed both resistant types shifted the faecal community in distinct ways. The modified type lifted whole bacterial groups and multiplied certain bifidobacteria up to tenfold in some people, while the natural type favoured other named species.
europmc-pmc3020935:
Rossin and co-authors tested whether genes in genome regions tied to immune diseases physically interact as proteins, in a 2011 study of rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease. Scans had flagged over a hundred and fifty regions, but the disturbed biology behind them stayed murky.

Building protein interaction networks from genes inside the flagged regions, they found far more links than chance allows, confirmed by several shuffling tests. Network members clustered in tissues relevant to each disease. Proteins in the networks but outside the flagged regions also proved enriched for new associations, giving the networks power to nominate fresh disease genes.
europmc-pmc3031535:
Harvey and coauthors showed in 2011 that plants keep a backup weapon against viruses when their first defense is knocked out. Plants fight viruses by chopping viral RNA, using proteins called Argonautes. The main fighter, AGO1, is itself targeted by proteins that many viruses carry. The team tested plants missing each of ten Argonaute proteins against two real viruses.

Plants missing AGO2 became far sicker than normal plants and let both viruses build up faster early on. Healthy plants raised their AGO2 levels after infection. The authors propose a layered defense: when viral blockers disable the first layer, that loss frees the second layer to switch on. The backup does not cover every virus, since a third virus was unaffected. The model helps explain how plant and virus counter moves evolve together.
europmc-pmc3072935:
Gagliardi, Brouwers, Palda, Lemieux-Charles, and Grimshaw asked in 2011 why clinical guidelines are so often ignored. These documents are the evidence summaries meant to guide care. The team also asked whether guidelines could be built for easier use. They coined a framework of implementability: features of a guideline that help or hinder its uptake. The team built the framework from the implementation literature, then checked twenty high quality guidelines against it.

The framework holds twenty two elements grouped under headings such as usability, adaptability, and how use is evaluated. Most guidelines were long walls of graded evidence and tables. Few offered versions for different readers, plain summaries, patient discussion aids, cost notes, or tips for local promotion and monitoring. No topic area did consistently better. The authors say closing those gaps may require new setups for who writes guidelines and how. Testing the framework comes next.
europmc-pmc3118335:
Sascha Keller and colleagues tested tiny cell-made sacs from body fluids as a diagnostic tool in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Translational Medicine. Cells shed these sacs into blood, urine, saliva, and other fluids, and each sac carries proteins and RNA from its parent cell. The team asked whether that cargo survives well enough to read.

Sacs purified from pregnancy fluid, saliva, and urine carried the expected marker proteins, and their RNA stayed intact, shielded by the sac wall from enzymes that would destroy it. RNA from pregnancy fluid even revealed a gene variant and the sex of the unborn child. Since collecting fluids is gentle, the authors present sacs as a promising window into the body's gene activity.
europmc-pmc3186735:
Mark Tremblay and colleagues reviewed sitting behaviour and health in school-age children in a 2011 paper. Evidence was growing that sitting harms health independently of exercise, but youth data had never been gathered fully. More than two hundred studies covering nearly a million participants met their criteria.

Across study types, more sedentary time tracked with worse health in a dose-wise fashion. Television dominated the measures, and more than two hours daily was tied to poorer body composition and fitness, lower self-esteem, weaker social behaviour, and lower school achievement. Trials that cut sitting time lowered body mass index modestly but significantly. The authors conclude any reduction in sitting helps, with television time the clearest target.
europmc-pmc3263635:
Marianne Baird and colleagues examined creatine kinase as a marker of exercise-induced muscle damage in this 2012 paper in the Journal of Nutrition and Metabolism. The enzyme leaks into the blood when muscle is injured, and its blood level is widely used to diagnose heart attacks, muscular dystrophy, and brain disease. Its use after exercise is more controversial.

The authors review the evidence and opinion on whether raised levels after physical activity genuinely reflect muscle damage and whether they should worry anyone. They stress that unchangeable traits such as ethnicity, age, and sex shift the enzyme's baseline, so the upper limit of normal may need resetting for different groups. They also call for standardized testing protocols and stronger guidelines, arguing the field's scientific integrity depends on treating this everyday measurement more carefully.
europmc-pmc3265535:
Kathrin Ziegelbauer and colleagues pooled the evidence on sanitation and intestinal worm infections in this 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine. More than a billion people carry soil-transmitted helminths, the roundworms, whipworms, and hookworms that spread where human waste contaminates soil and water. The infections cling to poverty, poor hygiene, and missing or inadequate toilets.

By combining the available studies, the authors find that access to sanitation is associated with a clearly reduced risk of catching these worms. The result strengthens the case for building and using proper sanitation. It is not only a matter of dignity and general hygiene. It is also a measurable defense against a vast, neglected burden of disease. It also gives control programs a firmer evidence base for investing in sanitation alongside deworming medicine.
europmc-pmc3289635:
Poland and his co-authors introduced a cheaper way to map genes in barley and wheat in 2012. Both crops have huge genomes, which makes full sequencing slow and costly for breeding work. Their method uses two cutting enzymes to sample only part of the genome, then reads those pieces for many plants at once.

Applied to breeding populations, the approach placed tens of thousands of single letter variants onto existing reference maps for both crops. The authors also built a fresh wheat map using only markers from the new method. Because each sample costs little, they argue the technique can support association studies and breeding programs that select plants using DNA markers.
europmc-pmc3325235:
Kohane and colleagues used electronic health records to count the other illnesses that travel with autism, in a 2012 study. Earlier estimates came from studies of fewer than two hundred patients, too small to measure rare conditions well. Querying records across four Boston hospitals, the team profiled more than fourteen thousand people under thirty five with autism spectrum disorders.

Epilepsy stood out, affecting roughly one in five patients, many times the hospital wide rate. Schizophrenia, bowel disorders, brain structure differences, sleep problems, and a muscle disease all appeared far more often than in other patients. Some conditions, including schizophrenia and inflammatory bowel disease, grew more common as patients moved from childhood into young adulthood. The authors say care for autistic patients must plan for this broad medical burden, not just developmental support.
europmc-pmc3329435:
Bloemberg and Quadrilatero presented a faster way to type muscle fibers in rats, mice, and people, in a 2012 methods paper. Muscle is a patchwork of fiber types that differ in speed and fuel use, and the proportions vary from muscle to muscle. Older staining methods are slow and can blur types together, while antibody based fluorescence can reveal several fiber proteins at once on a single slice.

Using multicolored glowing antibodies, the team sorted pure and mixed fibers across ten muscles each from rats and mice, plus a human thigh muscle. Mixed fibers, carrying two fiber proteins at once, turned up in every species and formed a sizable share in some muscles. The paper also reports fiber sizes and fuel burning enzyme activity by type, offering a reference dataset alongside the protocol.
europmc-pmc3369835:
Zug and Hammerstein re-ran a contested estimate in 2012: how many insect and other arthropod species carry Wolbachia bacteria. These microbes live inside host cells and twist how their hosts reproduce. An earlier study had put the share of infected species at about two thirds.

Using a newer survey that tested more animals per species and picked species more randomly, the pair arrived near forty percent. That is lower than before, yet still a striking share of land arthropods. Within a species, they found, usually nearly all or very few animals are infected. Wolbachia also stayed the most common reproductive parasite in the survey.
europmc-pmc3414035:
Li and colleagues reported new variants of a pig coronavirus in 2012 after outbreaks swept vaccinated Chinese herds the year before. The virus causes porcine epidemic diarrhea: severe gut illness, vomiting, and watery diarrhea that kill suckling piglets in droves. Infection rates had jumped despite wide vaccine use, suggesting the field virus had changed.

The team sequenced the full spike gene, the virus's key weapon, from samples collected at nine hard-hit farms with heavy deaths. Three new variants emerged from the sequences. Older pigs sickened mildly and recovered, but every suckling piglet caught the disease. Because the current vaccine rests on an older strain, the findings explain its partial protection and press for updated vaccines.
europmc-pmc3543235:
Obesity doubled its global share in a generation, and Gretchen A. Stevens leads a large collaborating group estimating overweight and obesity trends for 199 countries from 1980 to 2008 in 2012. Comparable country numbers had been missing, so the team models mean body mass index first, then converts it to prevalence with stated uncertainty.

Age-standardized obesity rises from 6.4 percent in 1980 to 12.0 percent in 2008, with half the rise in the final stretch. By 2008 one in three adults worldwide is overweight and one in nine obese. At least one in five women is obese in 117 countries, and one in five men in 73. The increase accelerated after 2000.
europmc-pmc3600435:
Yochai Wolf and colleagues reviewed the brain's resident immune cells through one receptor in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2013. Microglia, the patrol cells of brain and spinal cord, carry large amounts of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1. Its partner signal, fractalkine, is made in the brain almost only by neurons, forming a private line between the two cell types. High receptor levels also give researchers a handle for seeing and steering microglia.

Physiology first: the signal pair helps microglia tend synapses and keep the peace in the healthy brain, and its tone changes under injury and disease. Genetic tricks that hitch fluorescent markers or control switches to the receptor's gene let labs watch microglia live and test their jobs one by one. The review weighs what those experiments have shown, for calm times and for challenges, and where the line's role is still disputed.
europmc-pmc3707035:
Zhou and colleagues tested whether exosomes from human umbilical cord stem cells can protect kidneys against the chemotherapy drug cisplatin, whose usefulness is limited by kidney damage. Rats given cisplatin developed the expected injury: rising waste markers in blood, dying tubule cells, and oxidative stress.

Injecting the stem cell exosomes into the kidney cut all of these, and in cultured kidney cells the exosomes likewise reduced cell death and oxidative damage while restoring growth. Two signalling pathways explained the split: a stress pathway driving death was quieted, and a growth pathway was switched on. The authors propose the exosomes as a cell-free treatment candidate for drug-induced kidney injury.
europmc-pmc3708335:
Gaggini and colleagues review non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. They trace its tight connections to insulin resistance, abnormal blood fats, and heart disease. Fatty liver ranges from harmless fat storage to inflamed, scarring disease, and it now affects perhaps thirty percent of adults in Western countries, often undetected because liver blood tests stay normal.

The review follows the mechanisms. Fat stored in the liver travels with fat in the heart and pancreas. Free fatty acids fuel lipotoxic damage. The same metabolic faults drive atherosclerosis. The authors present fatty liver not as a side note to metabolic syndrome but as part of its engine, with direct consequences for coronary risk.
europmc-pmc3721235:
Nicole Rapicavoli and co-authors reported a mouse study in eLife in 2013 on a long non-coding RNA called Lethe. Pseudogenes are gene copies long thought to be dead, yet many are still copied into RNA. The team asked which of these RNAs switch on when an inflammation signal, TNF-alpha, reaches mouse cells.

The signal changed hundreds of long non-coding RNAs, including 54 from pseudogenes. Lethe stood out because it switched on only for set triggers and worked as a brake on the inflammation switch NF-kB. It binds a part of that switch and stops it latching onto DNA. Lethe levels also fall with age, a state when NF-kB activity rises. The authors present such RNAs as active regulators of inflammation, not leftovers.
europmc-pmc3760635:
Stephen Gould and Graça Raposo wrote an editorial in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2013 on the messy naming of extracellular vesicles. These tiny sacs secreted by cells matter for cell traffic, immunity, development, and diseases from cancer to HIV. At the first meeting of the field's international society, in Gothenburg in 2012, the authors chaired a session on names.

Dozens of names exist, many tied to a vesicle's job or its cell of origin. Even broad terms split people: exosome has at least three rival definitions, based on how the vesicle is made, its supposed function, or how it is spun out in a centrifuge. The session reached no shared naming system, agreeing only to guard each other's freedom on the issue and to lay out the concerns in print.
europmc-pmc3846635:
Rob Horne, Sarah C. E. Chapman, Rhian Parham, Nick Freemantle, Alastair Forbes, and Vanessa Cooper pool studies on medicine beliefs in PLoS One in 2013. Many patients skip doses of long-term drugs. A frame called Necessity-Concerns says the choice turns on two beliefs: how much the drug is needed, and how much it may harm.

The team kept studies that used a standard beliefs survey next to a measure of actual drug taking. Across many long-term illnesses, stronger need beliefs went with better taking, and stronger harm worries went with worse taking. The pooled odds back the frame as a useful guide. Care that asks about beliefs, and answers worries with facts, may lift adherence more than dose charts alone.
europmc-pmc3989735:
Meritxell Rosell, Myrsini Kaforou, and co-workers compare brown and white fat in mice, in a 2014 paper in the American Journal of Physiology. Brown fat burns energy as heat, while white fat stores it. Cold can push some white fat toward a brown-like state, a change called browning.

The team measured gene activity in fat depots at warm and cold settings, and set cold-linked genes beside genes that mark brown fat. From that match they defined a gene pattern for the in-between form, called brite fat. One gene, for a signal called neuregulin 4, stood out. It rose in white fat in the cold, and cell tests showed it helps nerve fibres grow. A cell culture system that keeps depot traits let them study the shift in the dish, with gains hoped for obesity and type 2 diabetes care.
europmc-pmc4014635:
Tomasz Zielinski, Anne M. Moore, Eilidh Troup, Karen J. Halliday, Andrew J. Millar, and Shin Yamazaki compare ways to estimate the period of daily rhythms, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Body clocks run on a near-day cycle, and pinning down the exact period is a core step in clock studies. Many methods exist, with unlike assumptions and unlike levels of care needed.

The team runs an online system, BioDare, that stores and analyses clock data. Six period methods ship inside it, from classic periodograms to entropy-based tools. Each is explained in plain steps, then tested on fake signals with known periods and on model-made gene data. Rebuilding all six in one language let the team time them fairly. No method won everywhere. The paper ends with guidance on which method fits which data type, and on how to design clock experiments that yield clean period reads.
europmc-pmc4026735:
Aniruddh D. Patel and John R. Iversen set out a theory of how the brain hears a musical beat, in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience in 2014. Every human culture makes music with a beat, a steady pulse that times movement and dance. One older view held that beat hearing rests on broad brain skills shared with many animals.

Patel and Iversen argue for a tighter circuit. Hearing a beat, in their view, needs fast talk between hearing areas and movement-planning areas, even when the listener sits still. The movement areas mimic the pulse and send back timing forecasts for the next beat. They call this the action simulation for auditory prediction idea. It rests on a rear hearing pathway that looks stronger in humans than in other primates, perhaps as a side gain of vocal learning, and yields clear cross-species tests.
europmc-pmc4046135:
Bhagwan Yadav and colleagues build a scoring system that ranks drugs by how selectively they kill a patient's cancer cells, in Scientific Reports in 2014. Labs test hundreds of compounds on cells across many doses. Turning those curves into one fair score per drug is tricky, and noise can warp simple measures.

Their drug sensitivity score models the full dose curve and folds several traits into one number. It proved steadier than standard measures against technical noise. The sharper test came with leukaemia samples. Comparing patient cells with healthy controls picked out drugs that hit the cancer and spared normal cells. It also split patients into sensitive and resistant groups. Repeated testing tracked how responses shifted as disease advanced and returned. The team releases the tool as open source. The aim: turn lab screens into choices fitted to one patient.
europmc-pmc4049835:
Chin-Sheng Yu and seven colleagues present CELLO2GO, a free web server that predicts where a protein works in the cell and what it does, in PLoS ONE in 2014. A protein's address inside the cell hints strongly at its job. Lab checks of address and function are slow, so prediction tools fill the gap.

The server merges two approaches. One predicts location from sequence traits and the species of origin. The other searches for look-alike proteins with known annotations in a database drawn from UniProt. When relatives are found, their gene ontology terms are tallied across three views: compartment, molecular function, and biological process. Results come back as pie charts, for one protein or a batch. Even when no relative carries a recorded location, the predictor still offers a confident guess.
europmc-pmc4054835:
Yohei Sasagawa and six colleagues present Quartz-Seq, a method for reading the active genes of single cells, in Genome Biology in 2013. Cells of one type differ from each other in gene activity for non-genetic reasons. Measuring that spread cell by cell, across the whole genome, had been noisy and fiddly.

Quartz-Seq uses a simpler protocol than rival methods and repeats more faithfully between runs. It is also more sensitive, catching more of each cell's message pool. With it, the team separated different cell types and different phases of the cell cycle within one type. The finer test grouped cells of the same type in the same phase, and real differences between them still showed through. The paper offers the method as a sharper lens on cell individuality.
europmc-pmc4067335:
Shengsong Xie, Bin Shen, Chaobao Zhang, Xingxu Huang, and Yonglian Zhang built sgRNAcas9, a software package for designing guide RNAs for the CRISPR-Cas9 editing system. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. CRISPR cuts DNA at chosen sites, but unwanted cuts elsewhere in the genome remain a major worry.

The package searches for target sites under user-set rules and predicts possible off-target cut sites across the whole genome. It sorts those sites into three classes and can batch-design the short DNA pieces needed to build guide constructs. It also pulls flanking sequences so users can design lab tests that check for edits. Choosing cleaner targets in advance, the authors argue, makes editing experiments safer and easier to interpret.
europmc-pmc4086135:
Janette Nickel, Robert Preissner, and colleagues updated SuperPred, a web server that links drug-like compounds to their protein targets and treatment classes. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The approach rests on the similar property principle: look-alike molecules tend to act on the same targets.

Since the first release, known compound-target pairs had grown from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands, allowing confidence estimates. The new version adds measured binding strengths, 3D shape similarity, fragment counts, and physical-chemical agreement, and tests which molecular fingerprints work best. Retrospective checks on approved drugs classified them correctly about three times in four, an improvement of several points. For similar novel compounds, the server can forecast treatment areas and new leads.
europmc-pmc4107735:
Nicolas A. Crossley, Edward T. Bullmore, and colleagues tested whether the brain's most connected hubs are the places where disorders strike. Their study appeared in Brain in 2014. Brain networks hold a minority of highly connected hub nodes that are valuable for integration but costly to run.

Using diffusion imaging from healthy volunteers, the team mapped the normal hub layout. They then meta-analysed published MRI studies across twenty-six brain disorders. Anatomical abnormalities across disorders tended to concentrate at hub locations rather than at ordinary nodes. Hubs form an interlinked rich club carrying long-distance traffic between brain modules. Their central position, the authors argue, may explain why so many different disorders leave marks in the same high-cost regions.
europmc-pmc4148835:
Michael C. Phillips, writing alone, reviewed the molecular mechanisms by which cells export cholesterol. His minireview appeared in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2014. Most body cells cannot break cholesterol down, so shipping it out to high-density lipoprotein particles is essential for balance.

Macrophages, the cells that clog arteries when overloaded, use four exit routes. Two are passive: simple diffusion through water and a facilitated path through a scavenger receptor. Two are active, driven by membrane pumps called ABCA1 and ABCG1. The ABCA1 route, which loads fat and cholesterol onto the protein apoA-I, is how new HDL particles are born. Phillips details the workings of all four pathways and their roles in preventing the overload that builds arterial plaque.
europmc-pmc4168435:
Matteo Stoppa and Alessandro Chiolerio surveyed wearable electronics and smart fabrics in Sensors in 2014. Cloth with wires and circuits woven into it can bend and stretch in ways rigid boards cannot. Such cloth can sense the wearer and the world nearby, then adjust what it does to fit the moment.

Their review covers the materials used, from conductive yarns to printed circuits, and the ways makers build them into garments. Each method trades off flexibility, comfort, low power use, and ease of joining with other parts. The authors see future clothing that quietly tracks activity and health, and they set out what must improve before such gear is cheap and tough enough for daily wear.
europmc-pmc4176335:
Pedro H. Oliveira, Marie Touchon, and Eduardo P. C. Rocha studied bacterial defence systems in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Restriction-modification systems cut foreign DNA at set sites while shielding the cell's own DNA. Scientists had long debated whether these systems mainly block incoming genes or help mobile DNA elements settle in a genome.

The team mapped the systems across 2,261 prokaryote genomes. The systems turned up often alongside mobile elements and other defences, yet they were rare inside plasmids and almost absent from phages. Their count per genome rose with genome size, then levelled off near two. Looking at 43 pan-genomes, the authors found lone defence genes seldom came from broken-down systems. The pattern suggests the systems travel with mobile DNA more often than they bar its way.
europmc-pmc4214635:
Fadi F. Hamdan and eleven co-authors searched for fresh mutations behind intellectual disability in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Genes are thought to explain much moderate to severe intellectual disability, yet many cases stay unsolved. Mutations arising new in a child, not inherited from either parent, are prime suspects.

The team read the protein-coding genes of 41 affected children and both their parents, confirming 81 new mutations. Twelve sat in genes already tied to the condition, solving about 29 percent of cases. Twelve more sat in genes never linked to it before, and those genes' products connect in networks with known disability genes. No case traced to an inherited mutation. The authors conclude new mutations are a major cause worth testing first.
europmc-pmc4235735:
