Philippe Gérard wrote a solo review on gut microbes and sterols in Pathogens in 2013. The microbes of the human gut hold far more genes than their host, and they process molecules human enzymes cannot touch. Two sterol families show the range of that chemistry: cholesterol and the bile acids.

Gut bacteria turn cholesterol into coprostanol, a form the body cannot absorb and simply excretes, though only some people carry the microbes that do it. Bile acids get far richer treatment: bacteria split, oxidize, and rearrange them into over twenty different secondary forms, in every human gut. These conversions have been known for decades, Gérard notes, but their effects on health and disease are only now being traced.
europmc-pmc4301835:
Jing Yan, Lin Liu, Yun Zhu, Guowei Huang, and Peizhong Peter Wang pooled studies on whether breastfed children are less likely to become obese. Their meta-analysis appeared in BMC Public Health in 2014. Single studies disagreed, with some finding a clear protective link and others none.

The team searched three databases and combined twenty five studies covering more than two hundred thousand children. After adjusting for other factors, breastfed children showed a lower risk of obesity overall, though the strength of the link varied between studies. The authors report checks for publication bias alongside the pooled result. The paper gives health planners a measured estimate rather than a yes or no claim.
europmc-pmc4334535:
Edward Geisinger, Ralph R Isberg, and David Weiss studied the capsule of Acinetobacter baumannii, a hospital pathogen famed for drug resistant infections. Their study appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2015. Every clinical strain carries the same gene cluster that builds its sugar capsule, which shields it from blood killing and raises its virulence, but whether the capsule also resists antibiotics was unknown.

Mutants that cannot build the capsule lost some of their built-in resistance to peptide antibiotics. Worse, low doses of certain antibiotics made normal bacteria produce more capsule, hardening the shield further. Another mutation in shared sugar building steps weakened resistance across drug classes. The work warns that sub-lethal drug exposure can toughen this pathogen.
europmc-pmc4339735:
Tim Rohe, Uta Noppeney, and Christoph Kayser showed that the brain solves a causal puzzle step by step when it merges sight and sound. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology in 2015. A sound and a sight may come from one event or two, and the brain must decide before it can place them; people make this call in line with Bayesian probability rules.

Volunteers located sounds and flashes while their brains were scanned. Early hearing and vision areas represented position as if the signals were separate. A higher area, in the parietal lobe, represented them as if shared. Decoding the scan patterns layer by layer revealed this hierarchy at work, the first neural account of causal inference in perception.
europmc-pmc4366535:
Jimmy Berbée and co-authors tested whether switching on brown fat protects arteries, in Nature Communications in 2015. Brown fat burns large amounts of fatty acids, lowering blood fats and obesity, but its role in cholesterol and artery disease was unclear. The team activated brown fat in mice bred to mimic human fat handling, using a drug that stimulates a specific receptor, then tracked blood fats and artery lesions.

Activation raised energy use and lowered blood triglycerides and cholesterol. Brown fat pulled fatty acids out of fat-rich particles faster, which sped the liver's clearance of the cholesterol-rich leftovers. In mice lacking the liver clearance route, the same activation gave no protection. The benefit thus depends on a working liver pathway, a point any future therapy must respect.
europmc-pmc4377835:
Rashmi Prasad and Leif Groop reviewed the genetics of type 2 diabetes in Genes in 2015. The disease arises from a mix of genes, gene regulation, and environment, with diet and activity the best-known outside factors. Genome-wide scans and new sequencing had, by then, firmly linked more than 120 gene variants to the disease or to related traits. Yet together they explain only a small share of the disease's heritability, the part passed through families.

The review weighs ways to find the missing share, from deeper sequencing to finer trait measures. One pitfall stands out: diabetes may lump together distinct subgroups under one label, which blurs genetic signals. Sharper definitions of the disease and its subtypes could sharpen the hunt. The authors also cover gene-environment interplay and what found variants can teach about mechanism.
europmc-pmc4383435:
Huilan Xu, Li Ming Wen, and Chris Rissel reviewed how parents shape young children's activity and screen time, in the Journal of Obesity in 2015. Parents guide habits early in life, when activity patterns and sedentary routines first form. The team searched six databases in November 2013 for studies from 1998 onward. Thirty studies met their rules, covering parenting practices, role modeling, parents' views, parents' confidence, and general parenting style.

Parental encouragement and support raised children's physical activity across studies. When parents cut their own screen time, children's screen time fell as well. Sharper parenting practices, stronger parental confidence, and changes in style also looked promising for both goals. The review gives program designers a short list of parent-focused levers, while noting that most evidence comes from observation rather than trials.
europmc-pmc4389235:
Nikolaos Patsoukis and co-authors showed how the immune brake PD-1 rewires T-cell fuel use, in Nature Communications in 2015. When T cells switch on, they normally shift their metabolism toward sugar burning to power rapid growth and attack. PD-1 is a receptor that restrains T cells, and blocking it revives anti-tumor responses. The team asked what PD-1 engagement does to the fuel choices of activated T cells, and how that shapes their fate.

Cells receiving PD-1 signals could not engage sugar burning or amino-acid use. Instead they burned their own fats faster, raising a fat-transport protein and a fat-splitting enzyme, with glycerol and fatty acids released as signs. A second brake, CTLA-4, blocked sugar burning without raising fat burning. Forced sugar dependence during effector growth explains why PD-1 stalls that growth, and fat burning may explain the long life of PD-1-signaled cells.
europmc-pmc4396535:
Julie Kohn, Marsha Lampi, and Cynthia Reinhart-King reviewed why arteries stiffen with age, in Frontiers in Genetics in 2015. Stiff large arteries strain the heart and track with cardiovascular disease, and stiffening is usually measured for the whole vessel, as pulse wave speed in the clinic. The review argues the story continues at microscopic scale: the vessel wall's scaffold, the extracellular matrix, is crosslinked and deposited in excess as years pass, and its altered architecture sets up disease.

The authors describe measurement at both scales, from clinical pulse readings to laboratory micro-tests. Stiff walls impair the endothelial lining, and changes in scaffold proteins feed plaque formation. Newest work shows lining cells sense stiffness directly, and their health suffers as it rises. Stiffening thus harms vessels twice, by load and by signal.
europmc-pmc4421935:
Manfredo Atzori and eight co-authors released a data set in Scientific Data in 2014 to help build better robotic hand prostheses. Losing a hand limits daily life, and hands driven by muscle signals from the skin often feel clumsy. Users must learn odd signal patterns, and control stays far from natural.

The database pairs surface muscle signals from the forearm with hand movement and force measures. Research groups worldwide can use the same records to test methods that read intended grips and finger moves, and to compare results fairly. Tests in the article show the data match real-life signals and that current methods can already sort many hand tasks from them.
europmc-pmc4480835:
Maximilian Hecht, Yana Bromberg, and Burkhard Rost introduced SNAP2, a predictor of what gene variants do, in BMC Genomics in 2015. Knowing which natural DNA changes alter a protein, and which are harmless, is a central challenge for personalized medicine. Computer classifiers try to sort effect from neutral variants, but their accuracy leaves room for better tools.

SNAP2 is a neural network trained on a refined data set of more than a hundred thousand experimentally labeled variants, screening many protein features for signal. In cross-validation it beat rival methods and even combinations of them, sorting variants correctly in most cases, with its strongest calls much more reliable still. Evolutionary information from related sequences gave the strongest signal, yet the method still performs well without it, which speeds predictions hugely and allows whole-genome comparisons. A calibrated score guides which variants merit lab follow-up.
europmc-pmc4489235:
Jianguo Xia, Igor Sinelnikov, Beomsoo Han, and David Wishart released MetaboAnalyst 3.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The web server helps researchers analyze metabolomics data, the full set of small molecules in a sample, with heavy statistics and graphics that need serious computing power. First launched in 2009, the service had grown a lot in traffic, processing tens of thousands of jobs a month.

Version 3.0 was rebuilt from scratch on newer web technology for speed, capacity, and smoother interaction. Three modules were added. One judges biomarker performance with receiver operating curves. One estimates sample size and statistical power so studies can be planned properly. One analyzes pathways jointly for genes and metabolites. Older tools for data processing, statistics, and plotting remain, now integrated with the new features for systems biology and clinical translation work.
europmc-pmc4495335:
Javier Blesa, Ines Trigo-Damas, Anna Quiroga-Varela, and Vernice Jackson-Lewis updated the role of oxidative stress in Parkinson's disease in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy in 2015. Parkinson's is a chronic, worsening brain disease marked by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in a small region called the substantia nigra. Why those neurons die remains elusive, but oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen, is a leading suspect.

Faults in complex I, the first station of the cell's energy chain, account for much of the harm. Toxins and pesticides from the environment, dopamine itself, and mutations in Parkinson's-linked proteins all disturb mitochondria and raise reactive oxygen. The mini-review walks through these classic pathways, the molecular events that make dopamine neurons unusually vulnerable, and how disease-related gene products change a cell's response to oxidative stress during degeneration.
europmc-pmc4552735:
Daniel Enderle leads a twelve-author team presenting a simpler way to harvest RNA from blood vesicles, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Cells shed tiny sacs called extracellular vesicles into blood, and the RNA inside them may serve as disease markers. The standard isolation route, hours of ultracentrifugation, is laborious and uneven between labs.

The team built a spin column kit that pulls vesicle RNA from up to 4 milliliters of serum or plasma. The yield matched or beat ultracentrifugation, with strong purity and a sharp preference for vesicle RNA over free-floating RNA. Rare transcripts stayed detectable thanks to the larger input volume. The method aims to make vesicle RNA studies reproducible enough for diagnostic use.
europmc-pmc4580335:
Marie E. Bechler, Lauren Byrne, and Charles ffrench-Constant test who decides the length of insulation on brain wiring, in Current Biology in 2015. Oligodendrocytes wrap axons in myelin sheaths, and sheath length sets how fast signals travel. Lengths differ between brain regions, and the standing view credited axons with instructing the wrappers, by analogy with the peripheral nerves.

Working with oligodendrocyte precursor cells from different sources in culture, the team found sheath length followed the precursor cells' origin, not the axons offered. Length behaved as an intrinsic property of the oligodendrocyte lineage itself. That flips the search for control signals toward the wrapping cells' own programming, with consequences for how signal timing is set across brain circuits.
europmc-pmc4585135:
Guillaume Hoeffel and Florent Ginhoux review where tissue macrophages come from, in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015. Macrophages, the immune system's resident eaters, guard every tissue. For decades they were assumed to descend from blood monocytes made in adult bone marrow. New fate-tracking evidence overturned that simple story for many tissues.

Some macrophage populations are seeded before birth and renew themselves in place. Yolk sac precursors first give rise to microglia, the brain's macrophages, without passing through a monocyte stage. Later, fetal monocytes from liver-seeded precursors supply most other adult tissue macrophages. Bone marrow production matters less for these residents than textbooks held, a shift with consequences for how tissue immunity is studied and treated.
europmc-pmc4593435:
Li-Min Luo and eleven colleagues reported a 2015 study of ticks and severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus in China. The disease is a serious fever illness first reported in China in 2009. The Haemaphysalis longicornis tick was suspected of spreading the virus, but proof was missing. The work appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases.

The team collected ticks in Shandong Province and tested how the virus moves through tick life stages. They showed the virus passes from one tick stage to the next and from mother ticks to their eggs. Ticks could also pass the virus to mice through a bite. These findings support the tick acting as both carrier and reservoir, which matters for control work in rural areas where cases occur.
europmc-pmc4593935:
Louise V. Wain and a large group of colleagues published a 2015 genetic study using UK Biobank data. They examined smoking behaviour, lung function, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD. The study sampled people at the high, middle, and low ends of a breathing measure called FEV1. Heavy smokers and never smokers were both included.

Genetic data from about 50,000 selected participants were scanned for links to lung function and smoking traits. Low lung function shared many genetic causes between heavy smokers and never smokers. The scan also found new gene regions tied to lung function and smoking behaviour. Results like these help explain why some people develop severe lung disease while others with similar habits do not.
europmc-pmc4601135:
Gabriel Renaud and colleagues presented a 2015 program called schmutzi, built for ancient human DNA. Old DNA is short, damaged, and often mixed with modern DNA from handlers. Those problems make it hard to rebuild the genuine ancient mitochondrial genome. The paper appeared in Genome Biology.

Schmutzi works in rounds, estimating modern contamination and rebuilding the ancient sequence at the same time. It uses the damage patterns at fragment ends and the length spread of fragments to tell old molecules from new ones. Tests showed accurate rebuilding even when contamination passed half the sample. With enough coverage, it also gives trustworthy contamination estimates, which helps archaeologists judge whether an ancient genome result can be believed.
europmc-pmc4652635:
Alessandra Montecucco, Francesca Zanetta, and Giuseppe Biamonti published a 2015 review of the molecular mechanisms of etoposide, a widely used cancer drug. Etoposide derives from a toxin in the American mayapple plant. It was first synthesized in 1966 and approved for therapy in 1983. The review appeared in EXCLI Journal.

The drug poisons topoisomerase II, an enzyme that cuts DNA to untangle it and normally reseals the cuts. Etoposide traps the enzyme mid-task, leaving DNA breaks that trigger wide changes in cell behaviour and often cell death. The authors walk through how the breaks form and how cells respond. Understanding these steps helps explain both the drug's power against tumours and its side effects, including secondary cancers.
europmc-pmc4659935:
In 2015, Muhammed Murtaza and colleagues' case study that tracked how breast cancer changed over time by reading tumour DNA in blood appeared. One woman with spread breast cancer was followed for three years on two rounds of targeted drugs. The team read eight tumour samples and nine blood samples taken over 1,193 days.

Levels of each mutation in blood matched the clone family tree read from the tissue samples. Mutations held by side branches rose and fell with how each spread site met the drugs. Blood tests thus caught many sites changing at once, something repeat tissue sampling cannot do in practice. The case shows how blood-based tests might steer the choice and order of drugs as cancers adapt.
europmc-pmc4692135:
Peter K. Robinson wrote a solo primer on enzymes for Essays in Biochemistry in 2015. Enzymes are the protein catalysts that speed up the chemistry of living cells. Taken out of cells, they also run many industrial jobs, from making sweeteners and adjusting antibiotics to powering washing powders and medical test devices. Robinson's chapter lays out the core ideas a newcomer needs and then surveys those uses.

The chapter covers how enzymes are named and grouped, their structure, and the math of how fast they work. It explains inhibition, the ways other molecules slow enzymes down, and methods for purifying enzymes from source material. A short history runs from the coining of the word enzyme in 1878 to the finding that some RNA molecules can also act as catalysts. The result is a compact entry point to a field that joins biology with industry.
europmc-pmc4786435:
Claire M. Gillan and five co-authors test a new way to cut up mental illness in eLife in 2016. Compulsive behavior, seen in obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction, is blamed on weak goal-directed control: the system that weighs outcomes before acting, whose failure leaves rigid habits in charge. Yet weak control also shows in disorders with no clear compulsion, which blurs the story.

Instead of sorting people by diagnosis, the team measured symptoms and thinking tasks online in two large general-population samples. Weak goal control tied most tightly to one symptom cluster: compulsive acts and intrusive thoughts. The tie was specific, standing apart from other symptom groups. The result backs sorting patients by thinking traits, grounded in biology, rather than by label alone.
europmc-pmc4800035:
Nicholas D. James leads a large author team in The Lancet in 2016 reporting survival results from the STAMPEDE prostate cancer trial. Hormone therapy has anchored care for advanced prostate cancer since the 1940s. STAMPEDE tests many add-on drugs in one standing trial; this report covers two, the bone drug zoledronic acid and the chemotherapy docetaxel, each alone and combined.

Nearly three thousand men starting hormone therapy were assigned across the four arms. Median survival on standard care was about seventy-one months. Adding docetaxel stretched it to about eighty-one months, a clear gain, though with more serious side effects; the combined arm also gained. Zoledronic acid alone gained nothing. The authors set docetaxel as part of standard care for fit men starting hormone therapy, and drop the bone drug for this use.
europmc-pmc4828635:
Mark A. Rider, Stephanie N. Hurwitz, and David G. Meckes Jr. present a cheaper way to harvest exosomes in Scientific Reports in 2016. Exosomes are the tiny parcels cells release, prized for the diagnostic clues they carry in blood and other fluids. Gathering them cleanly has been slow and costly, with commercial kits giving impure yields.

Their method, ExtraPEG, borrows a virus trick: the polymer polyethylene glycol pulls the parcels out of large fluid volumes with a slow spin, then one small high-speed spin polishes the catch. Protein and RNA yields sufficed for the standard profiling methods, and the parcels kept their biological activity under the microscope. The method adapts to different fluids and parcel types, and can feed finer purification steps.
europmc-pmc4833835:
Prince Marowa, Anming Ding, and Yingzhen Kong review expansins in Plant Cell Reports in 2016. Expansins are small proteins that loosen plant cell walls without cutting them: they ease the grip between wall strands so the wall can stretch. Found in all plants and a few other organisms, they come in four families.

That loosening is needed nearly everywhere a plant grows, from seed sprouting to fruit ripening, and the review gathers the reports gene by gene and crop by crop. The payoff is practical. Tuning expansins has been tied to better yield, softer or firmer fruit, and stronger stress tolerance in test plants. The authors outline where breeders and engineers might put the proteins to work in crop improvement.
europmc-pmc4848535:
Mubasher M. Shah, Yuanguang Liang, Jay J. Cheng, and Maurycy Daroch reviewed the green microalga Haematococcus pluvialis in 2016, the richest natural source of astaxanthin. That red pigment is a strong antioxidant, stronger in natural form than the factory-made kind, the review notes. Demand spans health supplements, cosmetics, food, and fish farming, where the pigment colors flesh.

Coverage runs from the alga's life cycle and chemistry to how it builds and stores the pigment under stress. Growing, harvest, and drying methods get close review, since cost decides whether farms can compete. The alga turns red and rests when conditions harden, and coaxing that switch at scale is the core craft the review teaches.
europmc-pmc4896435:
Carl Lachat and a large expert group issued STROBE-nut in 2016, a reporting extension for nutrition studies. Diet research draws fire for weak reporting, which blurs what was eaten and how effects were judged. The group of 21 experts ran a three-round Delphi consultation with 53 outside experts to agree on added items for the standard observational study checklist.

In total, 24 recommendations join the checklist, covering diet assessment methods, food detail, and serving sizes with weights or volumes so effect sizes can be compared. Clearer reports would let readers judge diet-health claims fairly. Journals that adopt the list raise the floor for a field where small effects and big claims often collide.
europmc-pmc4904035:
Chang-Ro Lee and co-authors reviewed the global spread of carbapenemase-making Klebsiella pneumoniae in 2016, a bacterium that defeats last-line carbapenem drugs. Three enzyme families drive the spread: KPC, NDM, and OXA-48-like. NDM was first spotted in Sweden in 2008 and raced worldwide within years. Two bacterial clones, ST258 and ST11, carry much of the load.

Each enzyme's home range differs, yet all three now appear on most continents, often on mobile DNA that jumps between strains. The review covers spread patterns, the gene settings that aid travel, treatment options that remain, and detection methods. Naming the vehicles of spread is the first step to roadblocks, from hospital screening to plasmid-aware tracking.
europmc-pmc4919035:
Bronwen L. Aken leads a large Ensembl team in describing the system that annotates vertebrate genomes. Their methods paper appeared in Database in 2016. The system had annotated over 70 vertebrate species by then. It also builds the automatic gene sets for the human and mouse GENCODE projects, which many labs use as a shared reference.

The system aligns cDNAs, proteins, and RNA sequencing reads to a target genome. From those alignments it builds draft transcript models, then checks and filters them. What survives becomes the final gene set, posted on the Ensembl website. The paper walks through each step in detail, including newer methods for short and long noncoding RNAs. The authors stress strict input choices, since loose inputs lower the quality of the whole gene set.
europmc-pmc4978735:
Kelly Houston and four co-authors review how plant cell wall genes respond under stress. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. The cell wall frames the plant, feeds growth, and forms the first line of defense against pathogens. It must still flex and remodel fast when development or attack demands. Genes that build or cut wall parts change their activity under many stresses, which suggests the wall itself is part of the stress response.

The review gathers genetic and gene expression data from both dicot and monocot plants. Signatures of wall change under stress proved complex, with many genes moving at once. Yet wall genes often answered different pathogens and abiotic stresses in similar ways, even across the monocot dicot split. The authors propose that shared wall programs help plants tolerate stress. They flag those shared genes as targets for hardier crops.
europmc-pmc5035035:
Hao Chen and six co-authors present a software package for mass cytometry in PLoS Computational Biology in 2016. Mass cytometry tags antibodies with metals instead of dyes, letting researchers measure more than forty markers on each single cell. The flood of high-dimensional data is hard to clean, view, and sort by hand. Their package, cytofkit, strings the whole analysis into one pipeline inside the free R-based Bioconductor system.

The pipeline handles pre-processing, shrinks the data into readable maps, finds cell subsets on its own, and works out how the subsets relate. A point-and-click window and an interactive app let bench scientists run it and explore the results without coding skill. On blood and tonsil test data, the tool recovered known lymphocyte groups and split helper T cells into finer subtypes across tissues. The same pipeline also works for standard flow cytometry data.
europmc-pmc5035135:
Kathryn L. Mills and ten co-authors track structural brain growth in NeuroImage in 2016. Brain scans taken over years let researchers chart how the brain is built between childhood and adulthood, but single studies have disagreed on the exact curves. To settle the pattern, the team repeated the same analysis in four separate long-running samples, covering ages eight to thirty with 391 participants and 852 scans.

The four samples converged. Cortical grey matter volume peaked in childhood and fell steadily through the teens, with the fall slowing in the twenties. White matter volume rose until mid-to-late adolescence before leveling. Head and whole-brain volume kept growing into adolescence on their own distinct paths. The authors also show that correcting for head size changes the story, above all for sex differences, and they advise future studies to show results both with and without that correction.
europmc-pmc5116235:
Roddy Walsh and a large team, including the Exome Aggregation Consortium, rechecked genes blamed for inherited heart muscle disease in Genetics in Medicine, with the hosted text dated 2017. They compared gene data from 7,855 cardiomyopathy patients with 60,706 reference samples to see which rare variants can be trusted as causes.

For some genes long listed as culprits, rare variants turned out so common in healthy reference samples that calling them disease causes would often be a false alarm. For other genes, labs may be too cautious and dismiss real causes. The authors propose stricter ways to judge which genes and variant types are readable at all, arguing the same checks will sharpen genetic testing across many inherited diseases.
europmc-pmc5180335:
A review in The British and Foreign Medico-Chirurgical Review, dated 1862 in the hosted text, examines J. Russell Reynolds's 1861 book on epilepsy and other chronic convulsive diseases. The reviewer notes epilepsy had lately drawn intense attention, with new work on the body's functions beginning to clarify this class of disorders.

Reynolds, the reviewer says, does full justice to his predecessors, so the 360-page book works both as a record of his own experience and as a reliable reference. Reynolds prefers sorting disease by how it limits life and warps function, over sorting by the organ involved. His scheme divides convulsive diseases into three kinds. First come home-grown forms such as epilepsy proper. Then come secondary convulsions arising from other organs. Last come forms rooted in general nutrition changes.
europmc-pmc5189935:
Céline Lefebvre and a very large clinical team map the mutations found in metastatic breast cancer. They sequenced the exomes of 216 tumor and blood pairs drawn from the SAFIR01, SAFIR02, SHIVA, and MOSCATO trials. The metastatic profiles were then compared with 772 primary tumors from the TCGA collection. Twelve genes stood out as significantly mutated in the metastatic samples.

ESR1 acted as both a driver and a metastatic gene, with an odds ratio of 29. ESR1 mutation or amplification appeared in 31 cases and in 19% of hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative tumors. Mutations in the mTOR pathway genes TSC1 and TSC2 were also enriched, and APOBEC-driven mutagenesis rose in the same tumor subgroup. The authors note real limits: no bone metastases were sampled, and the cohort size constrains how far the findings reach.
europmc-pmc5266735:
Oleg I. Yakhin, Aleksandr A. Lubyanov, Ildus A. Yakhin, and Patrick H. Brown gave a global review of plant biostimulants in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Biostimulants are products applied to crops to lift productivity, sourced from bacteria, fungi, seaweeds, higher plants, animals, and humus-rich materials, and made by many different processes. That diversity has left the field without a settled definition or solid rules.

The authors propose a definition. A biostimulant is a formulated product of biological origin. It improves plant productivity through the fresh, combined properties of its constituents, not merely through known nutrients, growth regulators, or protective chemicals it contains. Because a single mode of action may never be pinned down for such mixtures, research and regulation should demand proof of efficacy and safety. A broad mechanism, not one precise pathway, should suffice. The category, they add, may itself surface new biology.
europmc-pmc5302835:
Carlo Bressa and nine colleagues compared gut microbes in active and sedentary women in PLoS ONE in 2017. Exercise prevents and treats chronic disease, and one route may run through the gut microbiota, now tied to many such diseases. The team sequenced the 16S rRNA gene. Samples came from women who met at least the World Health Organization's recommended activity level, and from sedentary counterparts.

Eleven bacterial genera differed between the groups. Targeted counting found more of three health-linked species in active women: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia hominis, and Akkermansia muciniphila. Body fat percentage, muscle mass, and activity level each tracked with several bacterial groups. The authors claim the first showing that particular genera track sedentary behavior measures. They stress that dose and type of exercise matter, as does simply breaking up sitting time, for shaping the gut community.
europmc-pmc5350035:
David A. Brown led a panel of heart experts in a consensus paper on the failing heart in Nature Reviews Cardiology in 2017. Heart failure strikes millions and still carries a grave outlook. Most drugs ease symptoms but do not fix the flaws inside heart muscle cells. Many patients keep living muscle that works poorly, so repair is at least in reach.

The panel points to the cell's powerhouses, the mitochondria, as a prime target. In failure, their energy chains falter, harsh oxygen waste rises, and fuel choice shifts to weaker paths. Their shapes and splits go awry, and ion balance inside them drifts. The paper sets out how each flaw feeds the weak pump. It then surveys young drugs that aim at the powerhouses, with the goal of lifting heart function at its root rather than masking its fall.
europmc-pmc5364735:
Justin Xavier Moore, Ninad Chaudhary, and Tomi Akinyemiju tracked a risk cluster in United States adults in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2017. Metabolic syndrome joins five ills: a wide waist, high blood fats, low good cholesterol, high blood pressure, and high blood sugar. Three or more mark the syndrome, which lifts the odds of heart disease and cancer. The team read national survey data from 1988 to 2012.

Across that span, the share of adults with the syndrome rose by more than a third, from about a quarter to about a third of all adults. Gaps by race and sex stood out in the last span. Black men fared better than white men, while Black women fared worse than white women. Low schooling and older age each raised the odds on their own. The authors urge care aimed at the hardest hit groups.
europmc-pmc5428335:
Nishita and co-authors link a tumor signal to the cell's shipping hub, the Golgi complex. Their research article appeared in Scientific Reports. The signal runs through a receptor called Ror2. It responds to the protein Wnt5a. Active Ror2 signaling helps tumors invade nearby tissue. It does so in part by forming invadopodia. Those feet-like structures deliver enzymes that chew through tissue barriers.

The team found a new partner in this path: IFT20. The protein is best known for transport inside cell cilia. These tumors lack cilia, yet IFT20 still drives their invasion. It helps the Golgi form its ribbon shape. It does so by shaping microtubule growth at the Golgi. A tidy ribbon lets the cell ship cargo in one direction. That directed traffic supports migration and invasion. IFT20 also speeds transport through the Golgi itself.
europmc-pmc5482335:
Naska, Lagiou, and Lagiou present a review in F1000Research on ways to measure diet in large health studies. What people eat is hard to record well. Memory slips and flawed food tables add error to self-reports. Yet most big studies still rely on such reports. The authors take stock of current tools and their limits.

Methods split into live recording, such as food diaries, and recall tools. Recall tools include food frequency questionnaires and 24-hour recalls. The review also covers dietary biomarkers, which can check self-reports. Big studies often mix methods and run validation sub-studies, they note. Web and phone tools may ease the burden. Error checks still remain essential.
europmc-pmc5573035:
Zaman and co-authors present a review in Cureus on antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics were once seen as wonder drugs. They are now used in farming and animal care as well as medicine. Microbes have grown resistant at an alarming rate, the authors warn.

Infections such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, and gonorrhea grow harder to treat. Some are at times impossible to treat. Resistance tracks the level of antibiotic use. Careless use is the main driver, they argue. Options for hard cases stay few, and deaths are high. Public knowledge on the topic is still scarce. The authors call for wise drug use and broad education. Readers get a plain summary of a global threat.
europmc-pmc5596335:
Hammond, Bowron, and Edler probe what water does to a deep eutectic solvent, in Angewandte Chemie. Such solvents mix salts with neutral partners to form green reaction media. They soak up water from air with ease. The team asks when added water stops being a guest and breaks the solvent's own structure.

They studied the classic mix of choline chloride and urea across a wide water range. Neutron scattering mapped the tiny structure at each level. Even small amounts of water changed the layout. Yet the solvent's structure held up to about 42 percent water by weight. Water hid in pockets around the choline ions. Near 51 percent, the structure gave way. Past that point, the mix is best seen as a watery solution. Readers learn why reporting water content matters.
europmc-pmc5639435:
Mari and co-authors wrote a perspective article in Chemical Science. It surveys ruthenium complexes paired with light against cancer. Ruthenium compounds have drawn interest for decades. Two were in phase II trials as drug candidates. Their shapes can be tuned toward chosen cell targets. They also tend to harm the body less than platinum drugs.

Light gives doctors control over when and where drugs act. In photodynamic therapy, a sensitizer makes toxic oxygen species under light. In photoactivated chemotherapy, light frees an active drug instead. It can eject ligands or crosslink DNA. The article covers recent gains in both fields. It favors compounds tested in cells with known action.
europmc-pmc5645435:
Thistlethwaite and co-authors report a phase I trial in Cancer Immunology, Immunotherapy. It tested first-generation CAR T cells against advanced cancers. The target antigen was CEACAM5, found on many gut tumors. Fourteen patients were recruited before early closure. Cohorts got rising cell doses after drug pre-conditioning. Systemic IL2 support followed each infusion.

No objective clinical responses were observed. Engraftment rose with stronger pre-conditioning in cohort four. Yet the cells faded fast, declining within 14 days. Cohort four also saw brief, acute lung toxicity. CEACAM5 on lung tissue may explain that harm. Raised cytokine levels signaled immune activation in those patients. The trial closed early over toxicity and poor persistence.
europmc-pmc5682335:
Cipriano and co-authors present a systematic review in Frontiers in Psychology. It surveys nonsuicidal self-injury, or NSSI. The term means deliberate damage to one's own body tissue. No suicidal intent is present, and the act is not sanctioned. The team searched PubMed and PsycARTICLES under PRISMA rules. English articles from 1998 to 2016 were screened.

NSSI is most common in adolescents and young adults. Onset usually falls between ages twelve and fourteen. Reported rates vary widely across study groups. Links with borderline personality disorder are often noted. Eating disorders also appear alongside it frequently. Causes seem rooted in childhood trauma and other disorders. DSM-5 lists NSSI as a condition needing further study.
europmc-pmc5689835:
Kirkham and co-authors present a standards paper in PLoS Medicine. It sets minimum rules for building core outcome sets. A core outcome set lists outcomes every trial should report. Hundreds of such projects exist, with no quality check. The COS-STAD project aimed to fix that gap. An open survey first generated candidate items. A two-round Delphi survey then refined the list. Nearly 250 experts from key stakeholder groups took part.

Consensus needed strong support in every stakeholder group. A final discussion settled the agreed standards. The result is 11 minimum standards for all projects. They cover three domains: scope, stakeholders, and consensus process. Developers use them when planning new outcome sets.
europmc-pmc5701135:
Cosenza and co-authors report a mouse study in Scientific Reports. It tests stem cell vesicles against osteoarthritis damage. Mesenchymal stem cells protect cartilage in animal models. Most of that benefit flows through released mediators. Those mediators ride inside tiny extracellular vesicles. The team compared two vesicle types from bone marrow cells. Exosomes and microparticles were split by spinning steps. Effects were tested on arthritis-like cartilage cells.

Both vesicle types revived cartilage marker genes. They also curbed breakdown and inflammation markers. Treated cells resisted death, and immune cells calmed down. Injected into arthritic mouse joints, both protected tissue. The benefit matched whole stem cells themselves.
europmc-pmc5705535:
Williams and co-authors present the CompTox Chemistry Dashboard, a public data resource. Their article appeared in the Journal of Cheminformatics. The dashboard comes from the US Environmental Protection Agency. It serves environmental science and toxicology users. Demand for curated open chemical data keeps growing. The system links substances to their structures.

The database holds about 760,000 substances. Data cover physical properties and environmental fate. Exposure, usage, and toxicity data are included. Bioassay results are also integrated. Users can search chemicals in batches. Downloads come in several formats. Advanced search supports mass spectrometry work. The authors describe strict quality controls. Curation has run for fifteen years.
europmc-pmc5725835:
Carr and co-authors report a study of vitamin C levels in very sick patients. The work was done in an intensive care unit in Christchurch, New Zealand. The team tracked 44 patients over four days. Many had septic shock, a severe form of infection.

They report low vitamin C in most patients despite standard tube or vein feeding. About one third met the mark for frank deficiency. Patients with septic shock had lower levels than the others. Low levels also went with higher signs of inflammation. The authors link the gap to raised need driven by that inflammation, not to low intake alone.
europmc-pmc5729535:
Kalkavan and Green review how mitochondria trigger orderly cell death. The key step is permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane, called MOMP. Once that barrier opens, proteins stored inside spill out. Those proteins switch on caspases, the enzymes that dismantle the cell.

The review covers cytochrome c and SMAC, two of the released proteins. It also covers the BCL-2 family, which sets the balance between life and death upstream. Partial membrane opening, the authors note, can cause harm without full death. Better maps of these checkpoints may guide new cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc5753035:
Richter and co-authors test glyoxal as a fixative for cell staining and fine microscopy. Paraformaldehyde is the standard fixative, but it can hide targets and warp cell shape. Glyoxal is a smaller, less toxic aldehyde. It had not been tried in a systematic way for modern fluorescence work.

Glyoxal fixed cells faster and linked proteins more strongly, they report. Cell shape was kept better than with standard methods. Several labs checked the results against paraformaldehyde protocols. Most targets stained better after glyoxal fixation. The authors back glyoxal as a sound swap for the standard.
europmc-pmc5774635:
Phillippo and co-authors set out how to adjust indirect treatment comparisons for population gaps. Standard methods assume trials match on traits that change a drug's effect. Newer methods use patient level data from some trials to fix that gap. Agencies that judge drug value now see them often.

Two named methods, MAIC and STC, remain largely untested, the authors warn. The paper spells out the assumptions each comparison type needs. Anchored comparisons, with a shared control arm, rest on weaker claims than unanchored ones. Advice follows on when to use adjustment and what checks must support it.
europmc-pmc5818535:
Lautenschläger and co-authors show calcium tuning how alpha-synuclein grips vesicles. Alpha-synuclein is a small protein at nerve endings. It was known to bind tiny fat bubbles by its front end. Calcium's role at its tail was less clear.

Using NMR methods, the team maps a second grip at the tail. Calcium binding there boosts the protein's hold on membranes. In synapse samples, calcium steers the protein to the terminal. Too much calcium or protein herds vesicles into clumps. Readers get a new control knob for a protein tied to Parkinson's disease.
europmc-pmc5829835:
Taylor and co-authors count traumatic brain injury care and deaths for 2013. Brain injuries bring short and lasting harm, including disability. Crashes, falls, and assaults cause most of them. The report compares 2013 with 2007 across the United States.

About 2.8 million injury-related events occurred in 2013. Emergency visits made up roughly 2.5 million of them. Hospital stays added about 282,000, and deaths about 56,000. Rates peaked in people aged 75 and older. Small children and young adults followed. Men faced higher rates than women in every count. Readers get the national scale of a common, preventable harm.
europmc-pmc5834035:
Vidal and co-authors test whether a blood draw can stand in for tumor tissue when guiding colon cancer care. Their study appeared in Annals of Oncology. Doctors must know a tumor's RAS status before choosing antibody therapy. Tissue biopsies are slow and sample one spot only.

The team ran the OncoBEAM assay on plasma from 115 patients with metastatic disease. Blood and tissue results agreed in 93 percent of cases. Repeat draws then tracked RAS mutations during therapy. Levels mirrored how well treatment worked. New RAS mutations also surfaced early in patients turning resistant to anti-EGFR drugs.
europmc-pmc5835235:
Gabard-Durnam and co-authors present HAPPE, free software that cleans brain-wave recordings on its own. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. EEG from children is short and full of artifacts. Hand cleaning is slow and varies from person to person.

The pipeline filters, rejects bad channels, and strips artifacts in fixed steps. It then issues standard quality scores for every file. In tests it beat seven rival approaches. It removed more artifact while keeping as much true signal. Reference scores from 867 files show how it handles messy real-world data.
europmc-pmc5864935:
Lebreton and co-authors measure plastic in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Their article appeared in Scientific Reports. The patch is a vast zone of floating plastic between California and Hawaii. The team combined ship surveys with aircraft surveys. A model, tuned to those data, estimated the total load. They report at least 79 thousand tonnes of plastic there. That figure is four to sixteen times earlier estimates.

Debris larger than five centimetres held over three-quarters of the mass. Fishing nets made up at least 46 percent of it. Tiny microplastics were only 8 percent of mass. Yet they formed 94 percent of some 1.8 trillion pieces. Plastic there is growing fast, the team concludes.
europmc-pmc5869935:
Desai and co-authors review immune cells in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Medicine. This lung disease scars tissue for unknown reasons. Half of patients may die within three to five years. Most experts agree immunity does not start the disease. Yet immune activity seems to shape how scarring proceeds.

The review covers innate cells such as macrophages and monocytes. It also covers adaptive responses from T cells and B cells. Signals from microbes and from injured tissue can switch these cells on. Each cell type is weighed against genes, environment, and outcomes. Possible therapies get attention throughout. The authors close with open questions for future work.
europmc-pmc5974435:
Roux and Topisirovic review signalling pathways that regulate mRNA translation. Their review appeared in Molecular and Cellular Biology. Translation is a key step in gene expression control. It is also one of the cell's most costly processes. Many pathways converge on the translation machinery under stress or growth signals. The PI3K/AKT and MAPK routes are the best understood. Both engage mTOR to tune parts of the machinery.

When these pathways fail, faulty translation can drive disease, the authors note. Diabetes, brain disorders, and cancer are linked. The review also highlights newer regulators of the apparatus. Phosphorylation of machinery parts is a recurring theme.
europmc-pmc6010835:
Fleming and co-authors review real-world uptake and engagement with digital self-help interventions for depression and anxiety. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Such programs work well inside controlled trials. How people use them outside research was seldom reported. The team searched four databases plus hand sources. Eleven articles on seven public interventions qualified. Measures of use varied widely between reports.

Registrations ranged from 8 to over 40,000 per month, they report. Between 21 and 88 percent of users engaged at all. Moderate use reached only 7 to 42 percent. Sustained completion was rarer still in practice.
europmc-pmc6093935:
Yao and co-authors map genetic control of blood proteins tied to heart disease. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The team scanned 71 cardiovascular proteins in 6,861 Framingham participants. Protein levels link genes to disease. Which links are causal stayed unclear.

Over 16,000 protein-linked variants were mapped. External samples confirmed many of them. Thirteen proteins shared variants with coronary disease risk. Mendelian randomization supported causal roles for several. Eight proteins predicted future heart events in the cohort. The team released a public database of the results. Readers get candidate drug targets with genetic backing.
europmc-pmc6212435:
Dobnikar and co-authors profiled single smooth muscle cells from mouse vessels. These cells give vessel walls their strength. They also play a key role in hardening of the arteries. The team used single-cell gene reads plus lineage tracing. The study appeared in Nature Communications.

Cell profiles matched each region's developmental history. Cells varied in genes linked to vascular disease. Those genes affect inflammation, adhesion, and movement. The team found a rare cell group marked by Sca1. Those cells lose contractile genes over time. They gain genes for response to inflammation. The same group appears in artery plaques. The authors say such profiles may flag disease risk early.
europmc-pmc6215335:
Iglesias and co-authors built an atlas of the human thalamus. The thalamus holds many small nuclei. Each nucleus has its own function and connections. Mapping them in live brain scans is hard. The study appeared in NeuroImage.

The team traced 26 nuclei by hand in tissue slices. They used tissue from six autopsy samples. Ex vivo MRI gave the frame to rebuild the slices in 3D. Photos taken during slicing helped align the stack. The atlas is stored as an adaptive mesh. Its nucleus volumes match past tissue studies well. Applied to live scans, it segments nuclei reliably. It also detected thalamus changes in Alzheimer's disease. The atlas and tool are shared in public.
europmc-pmc6299935:
Ge and co-authors built iDEP, a web tool for RNA sequencing analysis. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. RNA sequencing shows which genes are active in a sample. Making sense of the data takes many steps and skills. Biologists without coding training often struggle with it.

IDEP links 63 R and Bioconductor packages in one site. It adds pathway and gene databases for 220 species. Users can explore data, find changed genes, and map pathways. They can also download the code to repeat the work. The team shows two worked examples. One probes a knocked-down gene in lung cells. The other tracks how the guard protein p53 shapes radiation response. Both gave known paths and fresh, testable ideas.
europmc-pmc6318335:
Haberman and co-authors profile gene activity in the gut lining of children with ulcerative colitis. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Samples came from 206 children before treatment began. The team also profiled gut microbes from stool. Findings were checked in adult and child cohorts. Those cohorts held 408 more participants.

Active disease showed a marked drop in mitochondrial genes. Energy-making functions in the lining were suppressed. Worse disease brought more innate immune and tumor-linked genes. A gene set helped predict who would respond to steroids. The same set tracked response to two biologic drugs. Microbe shifts lined up with the gene patterns. The work may guide care for nonresponders.
europmc-pmc6344535:
Eraslan and co-authors build a neural network that cleans single-cell RNA data. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications. Single-cell sequencing reads gene activity cell by cell. Noise from amplification and dropouts clouds the signal. Genes often read as zero when they are active. The team designed a deep count autoencoder, called DCA.

DCA models the count nature of the data directly. It accounts for excess zeros and wide spread. Nonlinear links between genes are captured too. The method scales in a straight line with cell count. It can thus handle datasets of millions of cells. Tests on simulated and real data showed clear gains. Downstream analyses worked better after DCA cleaning. It also beat older imputation tools on speed.
europmc-pmc6413235:
Chiavaroli and co-authors present an umbrella review in Nutrients on the DASH diet. DASH stresses fruit, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, and low-fat dairy. It limits salt, red meat, sweets, and sugary drinks, and is widely advised for heart health.

An umbrella review joins many past systematic reviews into one verdict. The team graded proof on DASH and heart and metabolic outcomes. Work was done to update European diabetes guidance. Across reviews, DASH links to lower blood pressure and better metabolic markers. The authors sort which outcomes rest on strong proof and which on weak.
europmc-pmc6419435:
O'Cathain and co-authors offer a methods overview in Pilot and Feasibility Studies. Health interventions must be built before they can be tested. Many published ways exist to build them, but no map tied them together.

The team gathered approaches from books, websites, and articles after 2007. They also used approaches cited in intervention reports from 2015 and 2016. From those they built a taxonomy, a sorting scheme for the approaches. Each type differs in the steps it takes and the evidence it uses. The taxonomy should help teams pick a build method that fits their question.
europmc-pmc6423835:
Wang and co-authors present clinical guidelines for diagnosing and treating gastric cancer, issued by the Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology in 2019. China carries one of the highest gastric cancer burdens in the world, and the group argues that Western guidelines do not fit Chinese patients well. Differences in tumor biology, treatment patterns, and drug access all shape the recommendations.

Graded recommendations fill tables covering diagnosis, combined treatment, and follow-up visits, with notes explaining each choice. A panel of senior specialists weighed evidence from China and abroad, regional differences, and the cost of care. Clinicians gain a practical reference built for the patients and resources they actually face.
europmc-pmc6425035:
Harutyunyan and co-authors examine how the H3K27M mutation, found in a deadly group of gliomas, disrupts chemical marks that normally silence genes. The mutation swaps one building block in histone H3, a protein that packages DNA. Tumors carrying it lose much of a repressive mark called H3K27me3, yet the exact failure was unclear.

Using primary tumor lines and CRISPR-edited controls, the team found the PRC2 complex still arrives at its usual sites but cannot spread the mark outward from them. Removing the mutation restored normal spreading, slowed cell growth, and stopped tumors forming in mice entirely. The results pin the mutation as both a driver and a requirement for these cancers.
europmc-pmc6510035:
Hody and co-authors review the risks and benefits of eccentric muscle contractions. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. An eccentric contraction lengthens a muscle while it works against a load. Walking downstairs and downhill running use this action. It produces high force at low energy cost.

Unaccustomed eccentric work can damage muscle. It also causes delayed-onset soreness, called DOMS. Repeating light sessions with rising intensity is the main guard. The authors trace damage and repair at cell and molecular level. They then survey uses in sport, rehabilitation, aging and chronic disease. Gaps in the mechanism still limit training design, they note.
europmc-pmc6523135:
Hohmann and Dehghani review the cytoskeleton, the inner scaffold of animal cells, writing in Cells. Three filament families build it: actin, microtubules and intermediate filaments. Together they let a cell divide, haul cargo, crawl, grip surfaces and hold or change its shape, reshaping within minutes as cues arrive.

The review walks through each family in turn. It covers how the filaments assemble and fall apart, what controls them, and the structures they form, from the pushing sheet of the lamellipodium to stress fibers. It then covers how the three networks interact and jointly drive cell movement. A final section asks how cytoskeletal changes in glioma, a brain tumor, may fuel its spread through tissue.
europmc-pmc6588935:
Han and co-authors trace a new route by which the RNA-editing enzyme METTL3 feeds bladder cancer, writing in Molecular Cancer. METTL3 installs m6A marks on RNA, and tumors often carry too much of it. The team found METTL3 sharply raised in bladder cancer, with high levels tracking poor patient survival.

Beyond its known work on messenger RNAs, METTL3 here targets a microRNA precursor. Partnering with the processing protein DGCR8, it marks pri-miR221/222 with m6A and speeds its maturation. The mature microRNAs then suppress PTEN, a brake on cell growth. Removing that brake let bladder cancer cells multiply faster in culture and in mice. The authors present the chain as a fresh therapeutic angle on a common cancer.
europmc-pmc6616535:
Keller reviews laboratory markers used to judge malnutrition. His article appears in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Clinicians long relied on blood proteins like albumin. Prealbumin is now often preferred for its shorter half-life. Yet inflammation suppresses both proteins strongly. That makes them reflect illness more than food intake. Modern guidance favours history and physical examination first. Lab values should only complement that exam.

Other candidate markers have seen little uptake. Urinary creatinine and 3-methylhistidine track muscle breakdown poorly in practice. IGF-1 falls in malnutrition but lacks specificity. Still, markers like prealbumin predict surgical outcomes and death. Keller presents them as prognostic aids, not diagnostic proof. Careful interpretation is the review's central message.
europmc-pmc6678835:
Shang and co-authors summarise the bioactive compounds and biological functions of garlic. Their review appears in Foods. Garlic is a globally consumed spice and old remedy. Its key actives are sulfur compounds. Allicin, alliin, and diallyl sulfides lead the list. Ajoene and S-allyl-cysteine also feature. Saponins, phenolics, and polysaccharides add further chemistry. Processing changes the profile substantially. Black garlic gains polyphenols during its heating.

Studies credit garlic with a wide benefit range. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects are best documented. Antibacterial, anticancer, and heart-protective actions follow. Liver, gut, nerve, and kidney protection are also reported. The review details mechanisms behind each function. Functional foods and nutraceuticals are the target outlets.
europmc-pmc6708235:
Engebretsen and Bohlin explain how to make sound predictions with the glmnet software. Their guide centers on elastic net regression, a method widely used in studies that scan the full set of chemical marks on DNA. Such data hold far more measures than people, which makes plain models fail.

Elastic net methods accept a small amount of bias to gain much steadier predictions. The paper walks through each step in the R language with plain examples. It shows how to pick between related methods such as Lasso and Ridge. It also shows how to keep models small while holding down prediction error.
europmc-pmc6711235:
Chow and co-authors report a possible fifth family line of the yeast Candida auris. This drug-resistant yeast has spread through hospitals in more than 35 countries. Known cases fall into four major groups, each tied to a region. The team sequenced a yeast sample taken from a patient in Iran.

The Iranian sample sat far from all four known groups. It differed by more than 200,000 single-letter DNA changes. The patient, a 14-year-old girl with an ear infection, had never left Iran. That makes local origin likely. A fifth group would change how health teams trace and contain this hard-to-treat yeast.
europmc-pmc6722135:
Schyns and co-authors mapped the macrophages that live in mouse lung tissue. Macrophages guard tissues, but the lung's interstitial macrophages were poorly known. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, the team separated the cells that sit between air sacs and airways. They found more variety than expected.

Two long-lived groups stood out. CD206-positive cells cluster near airways, maintain themselves, and make calming signals. CD206-negative cells sit near air sacs and present antigens to other immune cells. A third group of monocytes enters from the blood and seems to seed the second group. The map may guide future macrophage-based therapies for lung disease.
europmc-pmc6769035:
Terrén and co-authors review natural killer cell metabolism inside tumors. NK cells kill tumor cells without prior training, making them attractive for immunotherapy. Against solid tumors they still perform poorly. The tumor microenvironment suppresses them. It also starves them of nutrients and oxygen while flooding them with waste such as lactate.

This metabolic squeeze dulls NK cells' killing functions. The review covers their needs for glucose, amino acids, and oxygen. Some evidence suggests cutting a tumor's amino acid supply need not hurt NK cells. That opens a possible strategy: starve the tumor, feed the killer. The authors say NK fuel needs must be mapped fully before such therapies can be designed well.
europmc-pmc6783435:
Nievergelt and co-authors ran an international genome-wide study of posttraumatic stress disorder. PTSD risk after trauma is partly heritable, but firm common gene variants had eluded researchers. Their meta-analysis pooled over 30,000 PTSD cases and 170,000 controls of multiple ancestries. They also split results by sex, a step earlier work often skipped.

Genetic heritability estimates ran from 5 to 20%, varying by sex. Three loci reached genome-wide significance, two in European and one in African-ancestry analyses. Three more appeared in men only. One hit was PARK2, a Parkinson's gene involved in dopamine control. A combined genetic risk score predicted re-experiencing symptoms in veterans. Diverse samples proved essential.
europmc-pmc6815535:
Su and co-authors review cell death in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Reactive oxygen species are harsh molecules made during normal cell work. In excess they attack the fats in cell membranes. That chain reaction, called lipid peroxidation, can push a cell to die. Cells hold defences against it, but those defences can fail.

The review traces how the products of this damage set off three forms of cell death. Apoptosis and autophagy are long-known routes; ferroptosis is a newer iron-linked one. The authors explain the steps in each path. They also link this damage to states seen in critical illness, where it may worsen organ injury.
europmc-pmc6823935:
Maresova and co-authors offer a scoping review in BMC Public Health on the burdens of old age. Populations worldwide are growing older. Long-term diseases and physical limits rise with age. Together they strain health systems, families, and public budgets.

The review first lists the main challenges older people face, from chronic illness to loss of independence. It then gathers what studies say about seniors' own needs and worries. A final part discusses answers that can protect quality of life, such as support for daily activities. The authors aim to give planners an up-to-date map of the problem and of research done so far.
europmc-pmc6826135:
Johnson and Stolzing review fat metabolism and ageing in Aging Cell. How the body handles lipids, its fats, seems to shape how fast it ages. Many treatments that alter fat pathways lengthen life in small animals. The review gathers that evidence across species.

Blocking genes for ceramide and related fats extends life in worms and flies. Raising certain fat-cutting enzymes does the same. Removing fat tissue lengthens life in rats, and tweaks to fat-carrying proteins help flies and mice. Human studies of very old people point the same way, with some fat-related gene forms more common in centenarians. The pair argue this pathway deserves a central place in ageing research.
europmc-pmc6927135:
Townes and co-authors rethink how single-cell RNA data should be cleaned and reduced. Their study appeared in Genome Biology. Such data record gene activity cell by cell. Many data sets now carry unique molecular identifiers, or UMIs, which tag each original molecule. Standard cleaning steps can invent false variation.

Using negative controls, the team show that UMI counts follow multinomial sampling, with no extra zero inflation. That finding supports simpler, better matched methods. They propose a generalized form of principal component analysis for count data. They also rank genes by deviance to pick informative features. On data sets with known answers, their approach beat common practice at grouping cells correctly.
europmc-pmc6974435:
Tan and co-authors review how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, differ from place to place. Their review appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Microglia were once treated as uniform. Recent work shows they vary across brain regions in number, shape, molecular profile, and job.

Why that variety exists, and what it does, remain open questions. Large-scale and single-cell gene studies disagree on some regional signatures, adding to the puzzle. Local neurons and other glial cells likely shape each microglial population. Varied microglia may also react differently to the same disease signals, helping explain why disorders strike some regions and spare others. The authors trace how microglia first arise, then weigh possible mechanisms. Grasping this geography, they argue, could seed new therapies for brain and mental disorders.
europmc-pmc7019735:
Gombart, Pierre, and Maggini review micronutrients and immunity in the journal Nutrients. The immune system needs many vitamins and minerals to work at each stage. They list vitamins A, D, C, and E, several B vitamins, folate, zinc, iron, copper, and selenium. Shortfalls, even mild ones, can weaken the body's defences.

The review traces what each nutrient does. Some support skin and gut barriers. Others help immune cells grow and act, or aid antibody work. The authors weigh trial evidence on supplements with several nutrients at once. Vitamins C and D and zinc have the strongest support, they report. They also call for better trials on dose and mixes in different groups.
europmc-pmc7058535:
Yuan and co-authors characterise mitochondrial genomes in human cancers in Nature Genetics. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants and matter greatly in cancer, yet their small genomes are often skipped by sequencing studies. Within the pan-cancer whole-genome consortium, the team combined mitochondrial genome data with matching RNA data across thousands of tumours.

The analysis covers 2,658 cancers across 38 tumour types and presents the most definitive landscape of mitochondrial mutations so far, including several hypermutated cases. Truncating mutations were markedly enriched in kidney, colorectal, and thyroid cancers, suggesting they can help drive those diseases. The team also found frequent transfers of mitochondrial DNA into the nuclear genome, some disrupting genes targeted by therapy. Mitochondrial copy number varied widely and tracked with clinical variables. Co-expression patterns connect mitochondrial genes to energy production, DNA repair, and the cell cycle, laying groundwork for clinical uses.
europmc-pmc7064135:
Galluzzi and co-authors set consensus guidelines on immunogenic cell death in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. Dying cells were long assumed to be immunologically silent. It is now clear that cells dying under stress can start an adaptive immune response with lasting memory, if they show enough antigenicity and adjuvanticity, the qualities that alert the immune system.

The panel offers an updated operational definition of immunogenic cell death, then lists the intracellular and environmental factors that decide whether a death provokes immunity. Assays for detecting the phenomenon in the dish and in animals are summarised, with guidance on interpreting each one. Dozens of specialists signed the document, reflecting how central the concept has become to cancer immunotherapy. Standard definitions matter here: trials and drug claims built on immunogenic death need shared tests, or results cannot be compared across laboratories.
europmc-pmc7137535:
Cheng and co-authors describe how Hong Kong hospitals escalated infection control during the first 42 days of the COVID-19 outbreak, in Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology. Their bundle combined active lab surveillance, early airborne isolation, fast molecular testing, and tracing of exposed staff. The period began on 31 December 2019.

Of 1,275 patients tested under the surveillance rules, 42 (3.3%) were confirmed infected. Locally acquired cases jumped from 7.7% of confirmations in one stretch to 93.1% in the next, and 28 patients came from 8 family clusters. Eleven of 413 staff who cared for cases had unprotected exposure and were quarantined 14 days; none became infected, and no hospital transmission was observed.
europmc-pmc7164635:
Yan and co-authors solve the structure of human ACE2, the cell protein SARS-CoV-2 grabs to enter cells, together with the viral binding piece, in Science. ACE2 normally works in a pair, chaperoned by a membrane partner called B0AT1. The team captured the full-length human protein in that natural complex.

In this setting ACE2 forms a dimer, and the second structure shows how the virus's receptor-binding domain docks onto it. The geometry suggests two spike proteins could bind one ACE2 dimer at once. Because this grip is the first step of infection, the detailed picture offers a template for drugs and antibodies designed to block the handshake.
europmc-pmc7170235:
Fawns-Ritchie and Deary check whether the UK Biobank's brief touchscreen tests of thinking measure what they claim, in PLoS One. UK Biobank holds data on more than 500,000 adults. Its short tests, taken alone on a touchscreen, are used in many studies despite thin proof of their quality. They recruited 160 people, mean age about 63, to take both the Biobank tests and trusted standard tests.

The Biobank tests matched their standard counterparts moderately well, with correlations averaging about one half. A general ability score built from the Biobank set matched the standard-based score closely, at over four fifths. Fifty-two people retook the tests after four weeks, and repeat scores matched at just over one half on average. The authors judge some of the tests solid despite their brevity, while others are weaker.
europmc-pmc7191035:
Gómez-Benito and co-authors review animal models of Parkinson's disease built around alpha-synuclein. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. This protein clumps into Lewy bodies in the Parkinson's brain. Dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra die off. Mutations in the protein's gene cause inherited forms of the disease.

Good models must copy both the cell loss and the spreading clumps. The review covers models that add the protein by gene or injection. It tracks how clumps appear and neurons decline over time. Some models show gradual loss of dopamine markers after injection. Others miss parts of the human picture. The authors judge each model's strengths and gaps. Such models remain central to testing future treatments.
europmc-pmc7197635:
Wen and co-authors chart immune cells in patients recovering from COVID-19. Their study appeared in Cell Discovery. They used single-cell RNA sequencing on blood cells from patients in recovery. The mix and state of immune cells during recovery were unclear. Patients were grouped into early and later recovery stages.

T cells dropped sharply in early recovery, while monocytes rose. One monocyte type carried strong inflammatory gene activity. Specific inflammatory monocytes marked with IL1-beta were more common early on. Antibody-producing B cells showed expanded clones in some patients. These patterns faded as recovery advanced. The map helps explain the slow immune reset after infection. It may guide care for patients with lingering symptoms.
europmc-pmc7221535:
Artasensi and co-authors review drugs that hit several targets at once in type 2 diabetes. Their article appeared in Molecules. Diabetes is a long-term condition affecting a growing share of adults. Around 90 to 95 percent of patients have the type 2 form. Single-target drugs often fail to control blood sugar and its companion problems together.

Multi-target drugs aim at several systems in one molecule. The review covers agents acting on incretin and glucagon pathways. It also covers drugs that activate PPAR receptors, which steer fat and sugar handling. Heart and vessel complications get attention alongside glucose control. Inflammation inside artery walls is another target discussed. The authors argue that one well-designed drug may beat several narrow ones.
europmc-pmc7302735:
Snijder and co-authors settle where coronaviruses copy their RNA inside a sick cell. Their study looks at the so-called replication organelle, a set of changed cell membranes the virus builds. Bubbles with a double wall are its hallmark. Sick cells show other shapes too, and which one makes the RNA was in dispute.

The team imaged several coronaviruses in 2D and 3D. All of them made much the same membrane changes. Small open balls, once thought to belong to just a few virus types, showed up as well. When new viral RNA was tagged and viewed, lots of it sat with the double-wall bubbles. None sat with the small balls. The bubbles are the hub of the work, and a target drugs could aim at.
europmc-pmc7320135:
Parhi and co-authors show that a common mouth bacterium can settle in breast tumors and make the cancer worse. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Fusobacterium nucleatum was already known to frequent colorectal cancers, where it predicts poor outcomes. It reaches tumors through the blood by using a bacterial lectin, Fap2, that grips a sugar displayed on tumor cells.

That sugar, Gal-GalNAc, rises as human breast cancer progresses, and bacterial DNA in breast tumors matched high sugar levels. In mice, injected bacteria with working Fap2 colonized mammary tumors, while Fap2-deficient bacteria could not. Colonization suppressed tumor-infiltrating T cells and sped tumor growth and metastasis. Antibiotic treatment counteracted those effects, suggesting the bacterium or its grip protein could be a treatment target.
europmc-pmc7378635:
Liang and co-authors build a gene signature to predict survival in liver cancer, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. Hepatocellular carcinoma varies so much between patients that prognosis is hard. The team focused on genes tied to ferroptosis, an iron-dependent cell death that the drug sorafenib can trigger.

Most ferroptosis-related genes, 81.7 percent, were expressed at different levels in tumors than in nearby normal tissue. From 26 genes linked to survival, a statistical method built a 10-gene signature. Patients scored high-risk died sooner than low-risk patients in the training data, and the pattern held in a second cohort. Readers get an example of turning a cell-death pathway into a prognostic score.
europmc-pmc7397035:
Jordá and Puig review how yeast controls production of ergosterol in Genes. Ergosterol is the fat that gives fungal membranes their fluidity and strength, and making it costs the cell heavy energy. Too little cripples growth and stress adaptation, so levels are tightly governed in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Several regulators coordinate the pathway's genes, sensing sterols, oxygen, and iron. Control also runs through feedback inhibition and by moving enzymes around the cell. The review covers making, transporting, and detoxifying sterols, plus responses to sterol loss, low oxygen, salt stress, and iron shortage. The topic has a medical edge: ergosterol is the target of many antifungal drugs, so its regulation shapes drug resistance too.
europmc-pmc7402635:
Lee and co-authors compare immune responses in COVID-19 and influenza in Science Immunology, using single-cell RNA sequencing of blood immune cells. Both viruses can turn severe, but their immune signatures differ. The comparison aimed to isolate what is special about severe COVID-19.

Severe COVID-19 samples showed hyper-inflammation linked to type I interferons, standing out against influenza profiles. The interferon-driven state appeared alongside the inflammatory surge rather than instead of it. That pairing matters for treatment timing: blocking inflammation while interferon signaling runs hot is a delicate act. Readers get a cell-by-cell contrast between two respiratory diseases that hospitals must tell apart each winter.
europmc-pmc7503635:
Wang and co-authors summarize the virulence, biofilm growth, and drug resistance of Klebsiella pneumoniae. This gram-negative bacterium causes urinary infections, blood infections, pneumonia, and liver abscesses. Resistant and hypervirulent strains now spread fast.

The review sets out how the bacterium harms the host. It covers the capsule and other factors that help it invade and persist. Biofilms, its surface cities, shield it from drugs and immune attack. Resistance paths to key antibiotics get a full survey. Whole genome sequencing and global proteomics open new views of these traits. The authors say grasping these mechanisms is a core task for medicine now. New clues may guide treatment of infections that current drugs fail to clear.
europmc-pmc7560135:
Rajula and co-authors compare standard statistics with machine learning in medicine. Machine learning aims for the most accurate predictions. Standard models aim to infer links between variables.

The authors weigh strengths and limits of each approach. Standard methods suit cases with many patients and few variables. They also suit fields with strong prior knowledge. Machine learning suits data-rich and fast-moving fields. Examples include omics, imaging and drug development. Personalized treatment is another strong area for learning methods. The authors favor joining the two approaches. A one-way choice is not advised. Examples cover diagnosis, drug work and treatment outcomes.
europmc-pmc7833635:
Boson and co-authors study how the SARS-CoV-2 envelope and membrane proteins handle the spike protein. Virus particles carry four structural proteins. They are spike, envelope, membrane, and nucleoprotein. Each part and their interplay shape particle assembly.

The E and M proteins steer where spike travels inside the cell. Spike gathers at the ER-Golgi zone when either is present. That trapping stops cells from fusing into syncytia. A tail motif on spike is needed for M-driven trapping. E instead bends the cell's shipping routes. Both proteins also shape the sugar coat on spike. E, M, and N together gave the best output of virus-like particles. The work maps the steps of particle building.
europmc-pmc7886435:
