Dalglish and co-authors present a methods paper on document analysis in health policy research. Documents are one of the most used sources in the field. Yet guidance on how to work with them well has been thin. The authors offer a structured approach drawn from their own research.

Their method is called READ, after its four steps. The steps are: ready your materials, extract data, analyse data, and distil your findings. Practical advice runs through each step. The authors also discuss how documents are made and what that means for reading them with care. Two case studies, from Pakistan and Niger, show the method at work. In both, documents gave insight that interviews alone could not. The paper makes a case for rigorous document work.
europmc-pmc7913135:
Shekhar and co-authors report a survey of COVID-19 vaccine acceptance among health care workers in the United States. These workers were among the first in line for vaccination. Their attitudes shape both uptake and public trust. The team collected responses in late 2020, before the vaccine rollout began.

Of 3479 complete responses, 36% said they would take the vaccine as soon as they could. A larger share, 56%, were unsure or wanted to wait for more safety data. Only 8% said they would not take it at all. Acceptance rose with age, education, and income. Women, Black and Latinx workers, and rural workers were less ready to take it at once. Safety, effectiveness, and the speed of approval were the top concerns. The study flags where outreach should focus.
europmc-pmc7915135:
Naresh and Lee present a review of biosensors built with nanostructured materials. A biosensor pairs a biological sensor with a device that turns its signal into an electric one. Such tools serve disease diagnosis, pollution checks, and food and water testing. Demand for small, fast, and sensitive devices keeps rising.

The main hurdles are clear capture of the signal, stronger transducers, and miniaturisation. Nanomaterials can help on all three fronts. Their high surface area and strong conductivity boost sensitivity. The review covers nanoparticles, nanowires, nanorods, carbon nanotubes, and quantum dots. Each type brings its own strengths to a sensor design. Some nanomaterials can even act as the transducer itself. The authors trace how biosensors evolved and where the field is heading.
europmc-pmc7980035:
Fan and co-authors report a study of the 3C-like proteinase of the SARS coronavirus. This enzyme cuts the virus's long protein chain into working parts. It is a prime target for drug design against SARS. The team cloned, made, and purified the enzyme. Then they mapped which cuts it makes and how fast, to guide the design of blockers.

Only the paired, dimeric form of the enzyme is active, they found. That makes the pairing surface itself a drug target. The enzyme cut all 11 test peptides drawn from its natural cut sites. Its own two cut sites were cut fastest. Substrates with a large water-shy residue at a key spot reacted well. Peptides with more sheet-like shape also reacted faster. The outbreak behind the work caused 8422 cases and 916 deaths. The study lays ground for inhibitors against this and kindred viruses.
europmc-pmc8137635:
Nakase and co-authors present Japan's updated evidence-based guidelines for inflammatory bowel disease. The term covers ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease together. Patient counts in Japan have climbed since 1950. Genes, environment, and gut bacteria all feed the cause. Seventeen experts revised the prior guideline set in full. They sorted the work into three question families.

The document carries 69 questions in total for clinicians. Background questions number 39, clinical questions 15, and future research questions 15 in the final structure. Each clinical question passed through GRADE evidence grading. A Delphi consensus process then set recommendation strength. Topics run from first diagnosis to long-term treatment choices. Guidance is written for physicians at the point of care. Heterogeneity between patients gets repeated emphasis. No two bowel disease courses run quite alike. Tailored, evidence-based care is the document's whole argument.
europmc-pmc8186235:
Liang and co-authors test how plastic particles of mixed sizes harm the gut in mice. Micro- and nanoplastics pollute the environment worldwide. Small particles are hard to detect, so real exposure mixes sizes.

The team dosed mice with polystyrene particles of 50, 500, and 5,000 nanometres. They compared single sizes with mixed exposure. Mixed particles weakened the gut barrier more than expected. The damage ran through reactive oxygen species that drove gut cell death. The authors argue that size-by-size safety tests understate the risk. Joint exposure needs its own study.
europmc-pmc8279135:
Chicco, Warrens, and Jurman argue that R-squared beats rival metrics for judging regression models. Regression predicts a continuous target from other variables. It fills a large share of machine learning work.

No single standard metric had won consensus. Studies lean on error measures such as MAE, MAPE, and RMSE. The authors compare what each metric really tells. R-squared, the coefficient of determination, conveys more, they argue. It shows how much of the target's spread the model captures. Their case rests on worked comparisons across the metrics. Analysts gain a clearer default choice.
europmc-pmc8293835:
Peschel and co-authors present NetCoMi, an R tool for building and comparing microbiome networks. Sequencing data let researchers chart links between microbes. Workflows for that span many separate steps.

NetCoMi unifies the full path in one package. It handles zeros, normalises data, and computes microbe associations. Comparing networks between groups is built in. That matters when health and disease states differ. Before this tool, no single package covered the whole flow. The authors aim to make network work routine and repeatable. Microbiome teams gain a shared standard method. Group comparison is where the package earns its keep.
europmc-pmc8494635:
Kozareva and co-authors build a gene-based atlas of cell types in the mouse cerebellar cortex. This brain region guides motor learning, balance, and thought. A complete list of its cell types was still missing. New high-throughput profiling made one possible.

The team defined cell types across single lobules of the adult mouse cerebellum. Purkinje neurons showed strong regional variety, most of all in rear lobules. For some interneurons, variation ran as a smooth gradient, not neat groups. Unipolar brush cells showed that pattern, matched by graded electrical traits. Molecular layer interneurons split into two clear types. The atlas gives the cerebellum a firm cell map.
europmc-pmc8573635:
Asher and co-authors track world trends in asthma symptoms among school-aged children. Asthma is the most common chronic disease of childhood. The Global Asthma Network Phase I study asked whether that burden is shifting. It reused the methods of the earlier ISAAC surveys.

In all, 119,795 young people from 27 centers in 14 countries took part. The groups covered ages 6 to 7 years and 13 to 14 years. Pupils filled written questionnaires at school. The team estimated 10-year change rates for wheeze, severe symptoms, and night cough. Trends were read by region and by country income. Response rates ran high in both age groups.
europmc-pmc8607935:
Camell and co-authors test drugs that clear aged cells in old mice infected with a coronavirus. Aged, or senescent, cells build up with age and release harmful signals. The team found these cells react strongly to SARS-CoV-2. Their signals also weaken virus defense in nearby healthy cells and raise viral entry proteins.

Old mice got a virus related to SARS-CoV-2. Treatment with senolytic drugs cut the load of aged cells. Death rates fell in the treated mice. Their antiviral antibody levels also rose. The work suggests that clearing aged cells could help older patients face severe viral illness. It links cell aging to the high risk seen in old age.
europmc-pmc8674135:
Seyyed-Kalantari and co-authors show that medical AI systems under-diagnose patients from underserved groups in chest X-rays. AI tools now match experts on many imaging tasks. A missed diagnosis can delay care, so bias here carries real harm. The team tested top vision models on three large X-ray datasets plus a merged set.

The models missed disease more often in women and in Black patients. Low-income patients also faced higher miss rates. Miss rates rose further for patients in more than one such group, such as Hispanic women. The authors warn that clinic use could widen care gaps. They call for bias checks before these systems guide treatment.
europmc-pmc8738735:
Yang and co-authors trace how lactate drives the release of the alarm protein HMGB1 from macrophages in sepsis. High blood levels of both lactate and HMGB1 track with severe sepsis and death. Whether lactate itself promotes HMGB1 release was not known. The team studied infected mice and cultured macrophages.

Macrophages took up lactate through transport proteins. Inside, lactate spurred two chemical marks on HMGB1. Marked HMGB1 left the cell in small vesicles and raised vessel leak. Cutting lactate output or blocking its receptor lowered HMGB1 in blood. Survival in septic mice improved with those steps. The authors propose this route as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc8741835:
Kong and co-authors review how doxorubicin causes acute heart damage, with focus on oxidative stress and cell death. The drug is a strong cancer treatment, but it puts survivors at risk of heart harm. Many factors feed this damage. Free radicals and cell death routes stand out as the main drivers.

The review maps where the free radicals come from. It then traces the death pathways they switch on in heart cells. Each route gets a full account of its steps. The authors aim to explain the cell-level chain behind the harm. They also seek new ideas to prevent or reverse it. Heart protection during cancer care is the end goal.
europmc-pmc8836235:
Morana, Wood, and Gregory set out a paradox at the heart of cancer biology. Apoptosis is the body's tidy program for cell death. It removes damaged cells and keeps tissues in balance. That makes it a natural brake on tumors. Yet aggressive cancers often show high levels of apoptosis. The same process seems to help tumors grow.

The review explores both faces of this cell death program. Dying tumor cells can condition their surroundings. They can sway immune cells such as phagocytes. Those responses may feed surviving tumor cells and blunt therapy. The authors also compare apoptosis with other death programs. They ask how each shapes the tumor microenvironment. The piece gives readers a nuanced view. Cell death in cancer is neither pure friend nor pure foe.
europmc-pmc8964935:
Jovic and co-authors give a brief overview of single-cell RNA sequencing and its uses. The method reads gene activity one cell at a time. It exposes variety that bulk sampling averages away. Since its debut in 2009, it has spread across biology and medicine. It reveals cell types and functions inside complex tissues. Cell atlases of whole organisms are a flagship product.

The overview traces the technology's rise first. Experimental workflows get a step-by-step account. Data analysis pipelines follow, from raw reads to meaning. Applications in health and disease are highlighted. Cancer and development both feature as examples. The authors close with remaining challenges. Cost, noise, and scale still limit the method. Its power to reshape diagnosis is their closing claim.
europmc-pmc8977435:
Zhao and co-authors review targeted protein degradation, a drug strategy that removes proteins instead of blocking them. Classic drugs tune a protein's activity. Degraders hand the protein to the cell's own shredders. PROTACs led the field into the clinic's sights. They link a target to the proteasome pathway. Other designs route through the lysosome instead. LYTAC, AUTAC, ATTEC, and AUTOTAC each take that road. Molecular glues add another twist.

The review sorts the strategies by machinery. Proteasome routes come first. Lysosome routes follow in detail. Each method's mechanism is explained plainly. Disease applications close the survey. Cancer leads the list of targets. The authors hope to prime both biologists and chemists. Proteins once called undruggable are the lure. Removing them beats inhibiting them, when inhibition fails.
europmc-pmc9240035:
Thompson and co-authors measure long COVID burden and risk factors across 10 UK longitudinal studies and health records. How common the condition is in the community was unclear at the time. The team coordinated analyses of survey data from 6,907 people with self-reported COVID-19. They added records for 1.1 million people with diagnostic codes.

Between 7.8% and 17% of survey cases reported symptoms for 12 weeks or more after infection. A smaller share reported symptoms that limited daily life. Higher age, female sex, and white ethnicity raised the risk in both data sources. Poor prior health, excess weight, and asthma also raised it. Results for heart and metabolic factors were less clear. The study aids planning for services.
europmc-pmc9392735:
Zagami and Carey survey the pitfalls and progress in triple negative breast cancer. This subtype lacks estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 growth signals. It makes up 10 to 15% of breast cancers and holds the worst outlook. It strikes Black and pre-menopausal women more often than others.

Chemo remains the chief systemic weapon, now strengthened by immunotherapy. Drugs for inherited BRCA mutations have added real options since 2019. Still, no tumor-specific targeted therapy exists for most patients. Financial strain and treatment burden weigh heavily on patients. The authors call for work on targetable flaws and on blocking immune evasion. They look forward to retiring the negative name itself. New labels, they hope, will name what can be treated.
europmc-pmc9779435:
Guo, Yin, Liu, and Wang trace how fatty liver disease develops and which natural products may help. The disease is now the most common chronic liver condition. About a quarter of the world's people carry it today. Fat builds up in liver cells without alcohol as the cause.

The review lays out the steps that drive the disease. Lipid pileup starts the harm in the liver tissue. Oxidative stress and cell stress add to the injury. Fat poisoning of cells deepens the damage over time. Mild cases can harden into inflamed, scarred liver stages. Scarring can end in cirrhosis or liver cancer. The authors then survey natural products tested against the disease. Plant compounds lead the list of candidate helpers. Lab and animal results back several of them. The review frames natural products as a real treatment option.
europmc-pmc9797335:
Khan and co-authors review macrophages and microglia inside glioblastoma and the therapies aimed at them. The brain tumor is the most aggressive of its kind. Its surroundings suppress immune attack to a high degree. Macrophages and microglia dominate the immune cells present there.

These cells feed most of the tumor's hallmark traits. They help it hide, grow, and resist treatment. Older tools could not sort their many forms well. Single-cell methods now split them into clear subpopulations. Each subpopulation carries its own tumor shaping job. The cells also bend and shift between states. That plasticity complicates any plan to target them. The review sums up current drug ideas against these cells. Reprogramming them is one leading line of attack. Blocking their recruitment signals is another path weighed. The authors expect cell maps plus lab tests to speed cures.
europmc-pmc9849135:
Iketani and co-authors test how SARS-CoV-2 can become resistant to nirmatrelvir. Nirmatrelvir is an oral antiviral that targets the viral 3CL protease. Other treatments have already faced resistance, so the team checked this drug early.

The authors passaged the virus in nirmatrelvir with two methods, one at large scale. Resistant viruses emerged in both, with many mutations in the protease. One large run yielded 53 lineages with changes at 23 residues. Most lineages traced back to T21I, P252L, or T304I as first steps. The E166V change gave about 100-fold resistance but cut viral fitness. Added changes restored that fitness. The findings guide design of next protease inhibitors.
europmc-pmc9877435:
Singh and co-authors review butyrate-producing gut microbes and their role in gut health. Butyrate is a short-chain fatty acid made by groups such as Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Eubacterium. It matters more for gut function than acetate or propionate, the other major acids.

Butyrate feeds colon cells and helps keep the gut lining intact. It supports barrier proteins, limits inflammatory cytokines, and blocks some cancer-linked pathways. Producer microbes also secrete antimicrobial compounds that shape the gut community. Some make anti-carcinogenic products such as shikimic acid. The review weighs these microbes as candidate live therapeutics. It also sets out open questions for their clinical use.
europmc-pmc9917735:
Sæbø and co-authors test how assay choices change hemolysis results used to judge cytotoxicity. The hemolysis test checks whether a compound breaks red blood cells. It is a common first screen for drugs and blood-contact materials. Protocols in the literature vary a great deal, which hinders comparison.

The team varied blood source, control detergents, cell levels, and incubation time. Blood source species alone shifted results up to fourfold. Detergent choice changed calculated ratios up to 2.7-fold. More cells and longer incubation raised hemolysis counts as expected. Based on these tests, the authors propose an optimized protocol. Their aim is to standardize future hemolysis studies.
finney-lectures-revivals-1835:
Charles Grandison Finney was the lawyer turned evangelist who led the Second Great Awakening across upstate New York. His Lectures on Revivals of Religion, published in 1835, turn his practice into a teachable method. Finney insists that a revival is not a miracle dropped from heaven.

A revival, he argues, is the right use of means: preaching that presses for decision, prayer meetings, and the anxious bench for seekers. Critics called his methods machinery, but his converts filled churches and fueled reforms from temperance to abolition. The lectures remain the manual of American revivalism as science and method.
frus-1861-d135:
On 6 July 1861, William H. Seward sent William Dayton a letter full of hopes for a quick win. The letter is document 135 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July orders from Washington carried hopes of a quick win in Virginia. Seward's tone to Paris was bold in those weeks. The letter belongs to the last confident days before Bull Run taught both capitals that the war would be long. Bold words abroad rested on the loans and levies Congress voted that July. Loans and levies at home were the hard facts beneath his boldest phrases. Hard facts at home underwrote every bold phrase.
frus-1861-d235:
From his post abroad, Mr. Murphy wrote to William H. Seward on 27 May 1861. It stands as Document 235 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d35:
On 21 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote once more to Henry Sanford in Belgium. The letter is document 35 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By late August the Union cause abroad rested on habit as much as hope. Seward's task was to keep neutral courts neutral, month after month. A routine letter to Brussels may look slight, but a hundred such letters were the wall the Confederacy could not climb. Routine, in this record, was not the foe of policy but its chief tool. The wall held because a hundred hands kept laying its plain, dated bricks.
frus-1862-d135:
On 29 August 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 135 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d235:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 September 1862, the same day Seward wrote twice to him. The Stuart letter is Document 235 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Same-day traffic in both directions marks a live matter moving between the legation and the Department. September 1862 gave both offices urgent business, with Lee in Maryland and Europe debating whether to step in. A letter in this exchange belongs to the small group of papers that show Anglo-American dealings at their most active that summer. Each note was numbered and docketed by clerks, which is why the file reads so evenly.
frus-1862-d335:
Document 335 is the second Dayton report dated 14 October 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent both reports to Secretary of State William H. Seward the same day.

An envoy's second letter of the day often carried the softer material: impressions, private remarks, the tone of a room. In Napoleon III's Paris, such things were policy, since one man's leanings drove the state. This report's value lies in that register, complementing the formal account in its mate. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d35:
Circular No. 9 went out from the State Department on 17 March 1862. It stands as Document 35 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see how Washington kept many far-flung posts working from a single set of orders. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d435:
On 9 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gabriel García Tassara, Spain's minister in Washington. The note is Document 435 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Seward wrote a week before Antietam, while Lee's army stood on Union soil and every foreign legation in Washington waited on the result. His notes to ministers like Tassara in those days carried a steady message: the government was unshaken and expected its rights respected. Spain, with Cuba in play, heard that message directly. The letter is part of the September file in which Seward held the diplomatic line until the army could help him.
frus-1862-d535:
Answering the Dutch minister's same-day notes, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Roest van Limburg on 9 June 1862. The letter is Document 535 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward's answering note closed the first round of the June exchange, though the Dutch file ran on through the autumn. His method with resident ministers was to meet formal notes with formal notes, each complete in itself, so that the record could speak later. That is exactly what the printed volume does with this run of letters. A reader who follows the sequence from Document 527 gets a short, complete course. It teaches how the Union handled a friendly power's complaints during the blockade.
frus-1862-d635:
Townsend Harris, the first American minister to Japan, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State Lewis Cass on 1 August 1860. It is Document 635 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the oldest paper in this run of the Japanese file.

Harris wrote before the Civil War, under President Buchanan. He wrote from the post he had won by the treaty of 1858. That treaty opened Japan to American trade. His letters from Edo reported the hard birth of that new relationship. Ports were opening and officials were learning new forms. A lone minister was insisting on the treaty. The State Department printed such back papers with the 1862 volume because the Japanese correspondence ran as one story across the change of administrations.
frus-1863p1-d135:
March closed as it had run, with a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams dated 28 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 135 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward closed the month as he had run it: by feeding the London brief in short, clear sheets. His pair of 28 March answered the flood of Adams mail that month. This letter opens the pair. It shows Washington's hand on the brief at the end of a hard month, when the ship fight and the claims all pressed at once.
frus-1863p1-d235:
Washington's orders to London on 13 July 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 235 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d335:
In Washington on 10 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 335 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d35:
Judah P. Benjamin, the Confederate secretary of state, wrote this letter to John Slidell on 26 September 1862. Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris, charged with winning French backing. The letter is document 35 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

These papers are the other side's mail: letters from Richmond's state office to its men in Europe, printed in the Union's own record. Benjamin's letters armed his envoys with the South's claims and hopes. This one shows the Confederacy's foreign push at its height. It was run from Richmond by a man who wrote with great skill for a cause that needed friends abroad.
frus-1863p1-d435:
The date 31 March 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d535:
A dispatch dated 26 May 1863 went from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d635:
A 8 October 1863 dispatch from the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams reached William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d135: Charles Bohlen wrote a second memorandum on November 16, 1943, a week after his first in this series. It is Document 135 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Bohlen was traveling with the president's party as its Russian hand, and his papers helped shape the American approach to Stalin. The record gives the author and the date only. The memorandum is preserved in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d235:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure A, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the paper went straight to the President and was never approved by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Seven items are listed for the Americans to raise. They are Chiang's account of the situation in China, China's view of Soviet help in the war, and the state of operations against Japan. The rest are Chinese aid for the north Burma campaign, air bases, supplies, and the equipping and training of Chinese forces. A second list prepares Roosevelt for Chinese questions, most of them postwar, about bases, mutual security, and continued American aid after Japan's defeat.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d335:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a secret priority telegram from Cairo on 27 November 1943, numbered 10064. It reports his talk of the day before with Foreign Secretary Eden about the European Advisory Commission in London.

Eden, McCloy says, plainly prizes the commission and will not see its authority cut down, and he wants a small, good American staff sent to London at once to help Ambassador Winant. In exchange, Eden agrees that the commission's draft recommendations go to the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment before reaching governments. He also drops the push to move the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London. McCloy calls the deal entirely satisfactory and the best arrangement possible, and asks for Stimson's views.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d35: On October 4, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Stalin, in a letter kept as Document 35 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October was the month the three foreign ministers were to meet in Moscow, and the leaders' letters that fall ran alongside the planning for it. The record names the date and the two men only. Printed in the Foreign Relations series, the letter forms part of the final approach to Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d435: Document 435 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note, not a wartime paper. State Department historians wrote such notes to guide readers through the file. A note can supply background, name the people involved, or point to related papers nearby. The volume covers the Cairo and Tehran conferences of late 1943. There Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin planned the war's next phase. Readers meet this note as a signpost placed by the editors.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d535:
Ambassador Averell Harriman closed the year with another report to President Roosevelt from Moscow on December 30, 1943. It was his fourth direct cable in ten days. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A year-end report from Moscow let Roosevelt take stock of the alliance as 1944, the year of the great invasion, was about to open. Harriman's stream of cables had made him the President's chief interpreter of Soviet behavior. For readers, this message ends the volume's December run with the Soviet question still at the center of Allied fortunes, exactly where Tehran had left it.
frus-1944-quebec-d135:
General William O'Dwyer, chief of the Economic Section of the Allied Control Commission for Italy, reported to Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. Years of Fascist and Nazi rule and battle destruction had left the Italian people in serious plight. His report moves through health, jobs, and transport before turning to Italy's political status.

O'Dwyer warned that malnutrition would bring serious illness between January and July 1945 unless food and shipping increased. Demolished power plants meant mass unemployment, and without food and power he foresaw rioting and anarchy. He urged ending the confusion between defeated enemy and co-belligerent, abolishing the Control Commission in liberated Italy, and handing government to the Italians and civilian experts.
frus-1944-quebec-d235:
Deane wrote to General Spaatz on September 15, 1944, urging that no date be set for reducing the American shuttle-bombing bases in Russia. The Soviets had told London they would cooperate in Warsaw aid under a prearranged plan, and Deane and Burrows had asked the Red Army staff for an immediate meeting. No Soviet reply had yet come, while the Red Army stood in Praga, across the river from Warsaw.

American participation would probably be limited to the single Frantic 7 mission, Deane judged. Even so, closing the bases now would make further missions impossible before the battle was decided. Politically, he and Harriman agreed, that would put America in a most disadvantageous position, and might suggest the insurgents had been abandoned.
frus-1944-quebec-d35:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on August 29, 1944, as the Quebec Conference came within a fortnight. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill's late-August letters rehearsed the arguments he would carry to Canada: the endgame in Europe, the treatment of Germany, and Britain's place in the Pacific war. He liked to arrive at a conference with his case already stated in writing. For readers, this message shows the Prime Minister loading his brief for Quebec, in a correspondence that had become the alliance's chief instrument of decision.
frus-1945-50-intel-d135:
The National Intelligence Authority wrote to Representative Clare Hoffman on 26 June 1947. A letter from the secret board to a member of Congress is a rare outward paper in the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Congress held the money and was then writing the law that would replace the authority with a statutory agency. Answering a representative's inquiry put the board's case on a new kind of record: one the public's branch could read. Readers can mark the widening circle here. A system born in secret directives now had to explain itself to legislators. It was the open season of the National Security Act, weeks before that act remade it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d235:
A memorandum from the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 2 September 1948. The State Department prints it as document 235 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d335:
Formal minutes cover the 3d Meeting of the National Security Council, held on 12 December 1947. It survives in print as document 335 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

A set of minutes does one job well. It fixes what a body took up and what it settled, in the order the items came up. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d35:
Stone of the Budget Bureau wrote to Appleby, the bureau's assistant director, on 26 October 1945. The Budget Bureau's papers run through the volume like a spine. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By late October the bureau was deep in the arithmetic of the postwar intelligence house: which units survived, at what strength, on whose budget. Stone's inside memorandum shows the bureau talking to itself as it formed the advice the president would hear. Readers should not mistake these dry papers for minor ones. In Washington, the bureau that prices a plan often decides whether the plan exists at all, and this volume proves the point repeatedly.
frus-1945-50-intel-d435:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 9, issued on 10 March 1950, is document 435 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The out of order date is itself a clue to how the series grew. Older numbers were revised or filled in long after higher ones appeared. Placed at the end of the volume's run of directives, No. 9 shows the Council still working through its first set of rules on the eve of the Korean War. The volume's editors placed the directives together, so readers can trace the rule book as one growth.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d135:
Ends and means for Germany's economy are set out in a briefing book paper of 11 January 1945. “Economic Policies Toward Germany” was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It looks past the first occupation months to the lasting aims.

In the end, the paper says, the goals are to end German self-sufficiency and strip away the tools of economic aggression. For a long control period, policy must first cut Germany's war potential and help the victorious countries rebuild. Economic disarmament would bar the making of arms and all aircraft, wreck the special plants for them, and watch for secret war work. Limits on key goods and on metal and chemical exports are also weighed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d235:
Wait, Stettinius advised on Iran on 18 December 1944, gently setting the President's plan aside. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, answers Roosevelt's direction that Harriman raise the Soviet quarrel with Stalin. News from Tehran had changed the picture.

Ambassador Morris reported on 8 December some hopeful news. Since the Iranian government resigned last month, no Russian act can clearly be read as fresh meddling. The trouble touches Iran's home affairs, where an approach now might stir the Russians to a harder policy than ever. As long as the tension may be easing, sending Harriman to Stalin would be a mistake. The Department watches events closely and keeps Harriman posted, ready when the right moment comes.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d335:
No record of what was said at this meeting has ever been found, and this note says so at the start. Times and names come only from the official trip log, which shows the talks ran until 4 p.m. Years later, in 1954, H. Freeman Matthews added a written memory of the session.

Matthews could not recall the subject. But he noted that most such meetings briefed the President on the morning's foreign ministers' session. They also readied him for the afternoon agenda. The note is honest about the hole in the record. It fills it with nothing stronger than a careful guess.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d35: New Year's Eve brought a Churchill message to Roosevelt on 31 December 1944, filed as document 35. It appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. A prime minister writing on the last night of the year underlines how continuous this diplomacy was, with the winter conferences now only weeks away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d435:
Late on February 9, 1945, after the plenary, Britain tabled its revised formula on the Polish government. A new situation, it begins, has been created by the complete liberation of Poland by the Red Army. That calls for a fully representative provisional Polish government, more broadly based than was possible before western Poland was freed.

The government should rest on the provisional government then functioning in Poland, plus other democratic Polish leaders from inside Poland and abroad. It should be called the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. Molotov, Harriman, and Clark Kerr would consult in Moscow, first with the present government's members. This text became the spine of the final Yalta formula.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d135:
Robert Murphy reported on the delegation's housing from Hoechst on July 10, 1945. His telegram is document 135 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Washington's invitation and its request that he arrange quarters for the State Department party.

The arrangements look reasonably satisfactory, Murphy says. The Secretary will likely live in the President's villa and use a second villa as his office, with rooms for Dunn, Clayton, and Matthews. Three more villas will billet the rest of the party, each person with an individual room, and small bungalows are set aside for Harriman, Pauley, and Murphy. A small apartment house gives some twenty rooms of office space. Officers who knew Yalta and Tehran judge the setup far more convenient than those conferences.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d235:
A briefing paper urged bringing Italy back into world bodies quickly, in a paper dated July 6, 1945. The paper is document 235 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It seeks British agreement that the United States and Britain should lead in restoring Italy to international life without waiting for a final settlement of her status.

Italy should join the United Maritime Authority now, the paper argues, rather than after signing a peace treaty, as the British prefer. She should also return to the International Labor Organization. On the world security organization, it recommends asking British support for a public American pledge: if Italy declares war on Japan, Washington will back her admission at the earliest date. Such steps, it says, would raise Italian morale and strengthen moderate elements, without weakening Allied claims in the final settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d335:
Agreed allied propaganda in Germany is urged in a memorandum by the Joint Staff Planners. Reports from supreme headquarters, it says, showed that clashing official announcements from the several zones had already affected German minds. In the American zone, Germans heard one version of policy; elsewhere, they heard others.

If the lack of coordination went on, the planners warned, harmful reactions could spread through every zone. The memo sets out the American policy for control of public information in Germany, agreed by the Joint Chiefs, the State Department, and the Office of War Information. Its plea is simple: the four occupiers should tell Germans one story, not four.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d35:
Molotov wrote to correct the record in this letter to Harriman of May 26, 1945, given here in translation. During that day's conversation between Stalin and Hopkins, the place for the pending heads-of-government meeting had been mentioned. It had been said that Stalin's message to Truman spoke of the region of Berlin.

For accuracy, Molotov writes, the Berlin area was named not in that message. It appeared in his own answering telegram to Joseph Davies. Davies, citing a conversation with the President, had recently raised both the meeting and its place. The letter is a footnote in ink — and a sign Moscow was already steering the summit toward Berlin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d435:
Suggested American policy toward Poland is summarized in a briefing book extract dated June 29, 1945. On population transfers, the summary draws a firm line. The United States should help, where its aid is requested, with the transfer of minority groups. Managed movement is one thing; forced movement is another.

Washington should not permit, the paper says, the forced repatriation of Poles now in the West. Nor should it allow the uncontrolled deportation, by Poland's unilateral action, of the eight to ten million Germans formerly living in the areas claimed by the Soviet-sponsored Polish government. The extract is one section of a longer Poland paper printed in several parts.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d535: Mail weights between two embassies are reported in Ambassador Murray's airgram from Tehran of July 11, 1945. It answers a Department request of the previous December. The table gives mail sent from the American embassy at Tehran to the American embassy at Moscow in June 1945. Figures are in pounds, for June 9, June 25, and June 30. Courier mail totaled 1,011 pounds. Navy courier mail made up 648 of that. Non-courier mail totaled 3,199 pounds, with 251 pounds of Navy mail inside it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d635:
James Dunn, an Assistant Secretary of State, sent Secretary Byrnes a memo from Potsdam on July 14, 1945. Extracts form document 635 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Dunn reports a two-hour talk that day with Sir Alexander Cadogan, the top career man in Britain's Foreign Office.

The extract kept here covers Iran. Cadogan set out Britain's wish to get out of Persia, as the text also calls Iran. London proposed a concerted withdrawal of British and Soviet forces by stages, starting with Tehran. British officers wanted a small force left to guard the oil fields. Foreign Secretary Eden, Cadogan said, would insist all troops go, leaving a trained police force, if that would coax the Russians to withdraw in full. Cadogan warmly backed a gradual exit by all three forces.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1035: Ambassador John Winant sent this telegram from London to Philip Mosely at Potsdam on July 18, 1945. It is the full text of the message printed in extract just earlier in the volume. Winant reports that no word has reached the Soviet embassy in London from Moscow. Without that word, the Soviet side cannot clear or sign two pending papers. One is the agreement on additional requirements to be imposed on Germany. The other amends the agreement on zones of occupation in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1135:
From London, Ambassador Winant cabled the Acting Secretary of State on 23 July 1945. A week into the Potsdam talks, his embassy kept up its reports on British politics and press response to the summit. The election that would change Britain's government hung over every report.

Winant's dispatches gave Washington a read on its closest ally that no other post could give. He knew the British leaders, their parties, and their press at first hand. This cable is one part of that running London account. It helped the home office judge how much weight British words at the table would carry at home.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1235:
A second Sato cable to Togo bears the date 25 July 1945. The pair of reports shows the Moscow embassy working to the last hour before the Allied terms appeared. Sato summed up his channel's state: open in form, empty in fact.

The exchange between these two men is the volume's secret spine. Allied leaders read it through codebreaking while they weighed how to end the Pacific war. Each Sato report told them Japan's bid for Soviet help was failing. This one, from the eve of the declaration, confirmed it. Tokyo would face the Allied terms with its Moscow hope already spent.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1335:
From Tehran, Ambassador Wallace Murray sent a second cable in two days to the acting secretary of state, dated 28 July 1945. His post in Iran put him close to Soviet and British moves in the region. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Back-to-back cables from one embassy show a post working a fast-moving story, not a single event. Readers can watch how an ambassador framed facts for Washington readers who were busy with the Potsdam talks. The pair of Murray cables, read together, gives a ground-level view of diplomacy in Iran at the end of the Second World War.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-135:
Emile Despres, adviser on German economic affairs, wrote this memorandum on July 29, 1945. Germany's economy lay at the center of the Potsdam bargaining. What the beaten country could produce, pay, and export shaped every other question. Despres gave the delegation expert counsel on that ground. His memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An adviser's memo states a problem and weighs the choices. Despres wrote as a specialist for men who had to decide quickly. Readers see the economic thread of the talks in expert hands. The paper shows how deeply the settlement rested on questions of coal, food, factories, and cash.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-35:
Department of State minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945, at 11:30 a.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov sat in the chair, and the morning's story was mostly one of papers not ready.

The German economic paper came first on the agenda, but it was not yet finished. The question had to go over until tomorrow. The Polish paper was no further along, Vyshinsky reported. His committee had met the day before and that morning without producing a report, though he hoped for results by night. The third item, the Council of Foreign Ministers, bred a procedural tangle instead. Byrnes thought a subcommittee had the draft in hand. Molotov answered that no subcommittee had been appointed, and asked whether a general drafting committee covered all questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d735:
Byrnes wrote to Grew, his acting deputy in Washington, on July 21, 1945, in document 735. The Secretary reported from the conference's first week. Grew needed the feel of the talks, not just their texts. This letter kept the home office aligned. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Letters from the Secretary to his deputy show trust in action. Byrnes could not run Washington from Potsdam, so he armed the man who did. Readers learn what the travelers thought worth cabling home. The document also reveals workload: a summit abroad and a department at home, bound by a daily flow of paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d835:
Kennan answered the Acting Secretary from Moscow on July 17, 1945, in document 835. The chargé replied as the Potsdam Conference opened in Germany. Kennan's letters from this period are prized for their clarity. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A Kennan reply joined reporting to judgment. He did not merely list events; he read them. Readers get the Soviet capital interpreted by its sharpest American observer. The document shows the embassy's value while its chief bargained abroad. Moscow still had a voice in Washington that week, and it spoke in Kennan's prose.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d935:
William Clayton's statistical paper of July 26, 1945, works through the math of one-time reparations removals. It finds 40 percent of German factory and mining output in the Russian zone. Most of that industry, though, uses small units of light trades like textiles and printing, which peacetime Germany should keep.

The zone's true removal potential is therefore put at 30 percent. The Ruhr holds 42 percent of the German total. If Russia is owed half of all removals, 20 percent must come from elsewhere. The paper proposes assigning half the Ruhr removals, with only half of that counted as reparations. The rest would be traded for goods from the Russian zone.
frus-1969-76v17-d135:
An editorial note in Volume XVII of the 1969-1976 series sets out how Kissinger's secret trip to Beijing was arranged. The channel ran through the Government of Pakistan. A June 11, 1971 message from Premier Chou En-lai, relayed by President Yahya Khan, fixed the visit for July 9 to 11. Pakistan pledged foolproof arrangements for secrecy. Kissinger's public plan showed stops in Saigon, Bangkok, New Delhi, and Islamabad.

The note prints his coded instructions to Ambassador Farland in Islamabad. Only a small circle knew of the side trip. Cover plans placed his staff at a hill station while he flew on to Beijing. The note is a compact record of secret diplomacy in motion.
frus-1969-76v35:
Volume XXXV of the 1969-1976 series takes national security policy from 1973 to 1976. The main run of documents covers force plans and budgets under Nixon and Ford. A second section covers intelligence and the trial of rival analysis teams. Short sections follow on phone and data security. The last covers the Hughes Glomar Explorer and its secret bid to raise a sunken Soviet submarine.

The papers show strain between the Pentagon and Congress over money. The rival analysis section records the Team B exercise and its darker view of Soviet aims. The Glomar chapters are a rare print record of a famed covert recovery effort.
gao-gaoreports-b-296335:
Great South Bay Marina protested a National Park Service award at Fire Island in GAO decision B-296335, dated July 13, 2005. The winner was Fire Island Concessions. The deal was a concession pact for the seashore. The firm said its bid was the best value. The agency first said GAO had no power here.

GAO denied the protest but took the case. The pact also required build and repair work worth over 1 million dollars. That work gave GAO power to hear the fight. The agency then sent no report. GAO ruled on the thin record at hand. Broad claims of a better bid, with one point shown, were not enough.
gao-gaoreports-b-297235:
Global, a 1st Flagship Company, protested a Navy award for idle ship care in GAO decision B-297235, dated December 27, 2005. The winner was George G. Sharpe. The work was to run and keep East Coast idle ships. The base was in Philadelphia. The firm had a top tech bid. It was cut from the field on cost.

GAO sustained the protest. The field held just the winner. That bid was not fit on its first form. The firm's bid was shut out as its cost was 15 percent higher. But the cost review held flaws and false starts. Tech points weighed more in this call. A one-firm field built on flawed cost math cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-298235:
DeTekion Security Systems protested a Bureau of Prisons award in GAO decision B-298235, dated July 31, 2006. The winner was Sigcom-GDI Fencing Solutions. The work was to design and build electric fence systems. Sites were seven prison sites. The call set a best value pick. The firm said the pick was in truth low price with a pass bar.

GAO denied the protest. The pick lead found the two bids near equal on tech in a sound way. Staff marks split the bids less than they seemed to. A lead may set aside staff marks when the record backs a new view. With tech tied, low price could rule.
gao-gaoreports-b-298835:
Tessa Structures, LLC protested a Federal Highway Administration award to Fort Myer Construction Co. The invitation for bids covered bridge repair work. The bridges sit on the George Washington Memorial Parkway. GAO decided B-298835 on December 14, 2006.

The agency had rejected Tessa's bid as nonresponsive. It doubted the firm could finish in the days its bid stated. GAO read that doubt in a distinct way. A doubt about ability to perform goes to fitness, not bid form. For a small firm, such a call must go to the Small Business Administration. That office weighs fitness through its own review. The agency skipped that step. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-304335:
Agency reports of Antideficiency Act breaches gained a new filing step in this GAO circular letter, B-304335, dated March 8, 2005. The letter went to agency heads and others concerned. The Act bars spending past the funds on hand. It also bars spending past set shares of those funds. A breach must be reported at once to the President and Congress.

A 2004 law change added one more step. The same report must also go to the Comptroller General on the same day. GAO will keep a central file of all such reports. The letter gives an email address for PDF copies. It also gives a mail address in Washington. It notes that the budget office will add the step to its Circular A-11.
gao-gaoreports-b-305835:
Overtime and time off for three top Capitol Police chiefs are the subject of this GAO opinion, B-305835, dated July 19, 2005. The three posts have pay set by law. They are the Chief of Police and the Assistant Chief. The third is the Chief Administrative Officer. The police board asked what extra pay the three could earn.

GAO held that the Chief and the Assistant Chief qualify for neither benefit. Their pay tops the cap set for such extra pay. The Chief Administrative Officer fails the test for overtime pay. That officer could earn time off instead. But that takes a finding of special need by the Chief. The opinion sorts out who at the top can earn more than base pay.
gao-gaoreports-b-310535:
Utility Tool & Trailer, Inc. lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-310535 on January 3, 2008. The Army sought 5-ton dual axle trailers for Iraq and Afghanistan. The award went to Schutt Industries, Inc. UTT bid a high price with fast ship times. The winner bid low with a slower pace. UTT said the pick strayed from the call's terms.

GAO denied the protest. The agency weighed the price gap against a slight speed edge. It found the gap too steep for the gain. That math was fair on the facts. A small speed edge need not beat a large price gap.
gao-gaoreports-b-311035:
Evans Security Solutions, Inc. lost its protest — GAO decision B-311035, dated March 19, 2008. The firm raised four claims in its fight. One claim struck at the agency's own power to do the work. The firm claimed a right to first call as a small firm in a slack-jobs zone. It said like gear should mean like tech scores. It said the call terms slighted small firms.

GAO let no claim stand. A peer firm stood next in line, so the first claim could do the firm no good. No rule gave the firm the first call it claimed. Gear is one point of many in a tech score. The terms claim came past the close date.
gao-gaoreports-b-311235:
United Way of the National Capital Area saw its protest thrown out. GAO decided B-311235 on May 16, 2008. The case deals with the Combined Federal Campaign in the capital zone. A local panel picked Global Impact to run the drive. United Way said the pick race was not fair. It asked GAO to judge the race and the pact that came from it.

GAO dismissed the protest. The local panel is not a federal agency in law. GAO may judge buys by state arms, not by such a panel. The act may look like a buy for the state. Looks do not grant GAO the power to hear the case.
gao-gaoreports-b-400135:
Lockheed Martin MS2 Tactical Systems lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-400135, dated August 8, 2008. The buy sought a drone craft to watch the seas. Past work scores drove the pick in large part. A sub of Lockheed was to do near half the work. That sub had a past of staff and stock woes on like drone jobs. Costs and dates had slipped on those jobs.

GAO denied the protest. The winner's edge on past work had a fair base. Its team drew marks past the fair line on most jobs. Lockheed's team drew bare pass marks on 11 of 26 jobs. The sub's woes were not shown to be cured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-335:
Grants Management, GAO-05-335 of April 18, 2005, asks if a 1999 law has eased the maze of federal grant rules. In fiscal year 2003, the government gave about $400 billion in grants. About 1,000 grant plans, run by many agencies, each set their own forms and rules. That maze can slow the aid work the cash is meant to buy.

The 1999 law told agencies to build one shared path for grant seekers. GAO asks how far that build has got. It asks how the budget office, agencies, and grant seekers work as a team. More acts are due to smooth the path, the title holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-435:
Interior traffic checkpoints run by the Border Patrol are assessed in GAO-05-435, a report dated July 22, 2005. The Patrol used fixed and temporary checkpoints on roads in the southwest border states. Their job was to catch people who had entered the country outside legal ports of entry. GAO looked at the role of checkpoints, what was known about their costs and gains, and how their results were judged.

The Patrol ran 33 permanent checkpoints in 8 of its 9 southwest sectors. Temporary checkpoints could move to block side routes and react to tips. People near checkpoints often cited less crime and vandalism, though some cited traffic delays. GAO found that the Patrol did not routinely weigh checkpoint results or costs. The performance data that existed pointed to wide gaps between sectors. The report shows why checkpoint resources were hard to place where they were most needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-535:
Stock prices quoted in pennies instead of fractions are judged in GAO report GAO-05-535, dated May 31, 2005. U.S. markets made the switch in early 2001. The smallest price step fell to 1 cent for stocks. Many credit the change with helping small investors. Others fear it hurt large funds and the firms that make markets. GAO measured effects on both groups and on those middle firms.

Trading costs fell hard after the switch. Small investors gained from much narrower spreads between buy and sell quotes. Costs for large investors fell between 30 and 53 percent. Of 23 large firms asked, 87 percent said costs fell or held steady. But markets grew harder to read, since fewer shares are shown at each price. Big traders adapted by slicing orders and using electronic venues. Middle firms suffered: revenue fell over 50 percent for exchange specialists and over 70 percent for NASDAQ market makers. Other forces shared the blame.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-735:
The Social Security Administration's 800-number service is the subject here. GAO covered it in GAO-05-735, dated August 8, 2005. Each day, thousands of people call to file claims or update records. The number went nationwide in 1989. It is now a main contact point for millions. GAO checked how easily callers got through. It also checked how right and how polite agent replies were.

GAO found gains, but demand still outran the service. A new network let any caller reach the next free agent at any site. More self-service options were added. Yet callers still chose agents: about 51 million of over 71 million callers in fiscal year 2004. Of those, 8.7 million never got through. GAO also found gaps in how well agents followed agency rules, and it urged more steps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-935:
Airport security directors and their authority fill GAO-05-935, a report issued September 23, 2005. Federal security directors oversee screening at over 440 airports. They must work closely with airport parties to keep sites safe. GAO asked how clear their roles and authority are. It checked the partnerships they build. And it asked their views on recent changes meant to support them.

GAO found roles are clearly defined in guidance. Authority is not. The key delegation is outdated and unclear beside other parties' powers in an incident. It even grants command of a law enforcement force that was never created. Airport parties told GAO the limits were never explained to them. Confusion flared at one airport during an incident. Partnerships at visited airports work well, GAO found. The agency said in August 2005 it was updating the guidance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-435:
A scorecard decides many home loan applications, and this one is the government's own. GAO's April 13, 2006 report, GAO-06-435, reviews the Federal Housing Administration's mortgage scorecard. The system is called Technology Open to Approved Lenders, or TOTAL. Since 2004, lenders have used it to judge applications for FHA-insured loans. The housing agency built it between 1998 and 2004.

GAO found the way the scorecard was built was generally reasonable. Some choices could limit its power, though. Data were not current, and updates were not planned on a regular cycle. Private sector practice shows more benefits are possible. Readers get a tool's strengths and missed uses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-535:
Negative views of the United States in the Muslim world set the stage here. GAO's GAO-06-535 report, issued May 3, 2006, reviews U.S. public diplomacy toward Muslim audiences. The State Department leads such work. Its aims include explaining U.S. policy, countering false claims, and building mutual understanding. Polls showed continued negative sentiment toward the United States. GAO was asked to examine the effort.

GAO measured resources and programs aimed at the Muslim world. It checked whether posts use a strategic approach. It also named challenges that remain. Efforts lack certain communication elements, GAO found. They also face significant challenges. Readers get programs, strategy gaps, and obstacles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-635:
Medicare payments for radioactive sources used in cancer treatment are examined in GAO report GAO-06-635, issued on July 24, 2006. The treatment, called brachytherapy, places radioactive sources near a tumor during a hospital outpatient visit. Medicare normally pays a set rate meant to cover all items used in a procedure. It pays separately for some items that are too new to be in its rate data, and for some older items as well.

GAO reviewed how the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services sets those separate rates. The agency's general practice is to base rates on the average unit cost across hospitals. GAO concluded that rates for certain radioactive sources could be set in advance in this way. Prospective rates, GAO said, would be more predictable than paying billed charges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-735:
When a sponsor's sex crimes can be revealed is the subject of GAO-06-735, released on June 14, 2006. In fiscal year 2005, citizens and lawful residents filed about 730,000 petitions to bring family members to the United States. Petitioners sponsor spouses, fiances, and children. A question arose over warning the incoming relative when the petitioner has a sex offense record. GAO reviewed the rules and the practice of the agencies involved.

GAO found that hundreds of convicted sex offenders had petitioned for spouses, fiances, and other relatives, including children. Agencies had a framework for disclosing a petitioner's criminal sexual history to beneficiaries. GAO set out the circumstances under which disclosure may occur. The report speaks to a hard balance between family immigration and personal safety.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1035:
Schools stuck in fix-up status under the No Child Left Behind Act are studied in GAO report GAO-07-1035, dated September 5, 2007. In the 2006-2007 school year, about 4,500 of 54,000 Title I schools had missed yearly progress aims for 4 or more years. At 4 years a school faces corrective action. At 6 years it must be restructured.

GAO profiled those schools and the steps they took. It weighed help from districts and states. It checked how the Education Department aids states in that work. Two web polls and visits to five states feed the findings. Clearer guidance is needed, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-335:
A small fund that preserves the Capitol's art and grounds passed its audit on the numbers. GAO reported in GAO-07-335, dated March 13, 2007. GAO audited the Capitol Preservation Fund's statements for fiscal years 2005 and 2004. The audit ran under a statute that assigns GAO the task. GAO checked fair presentation and legal compliance. It also weighed controls tied to the fund.

The statements were presented fairly, GAO found. No material weaknesses appeared in the controls tested. Tests found no reportable breaches of the provisions checked. Two lesser control problems sit at the Library of Congress. The Library provides financial services linked to the fund. Its controls over cash payments and financial reporting need work. GAO plans to report those points to the Library directly. They are classed as reportable conditions, not material weaknesses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-35:
Farm conservation programs can shelter rare species, but landowners weigh real costs before signing up. GAO gathered their views in GAO-07-35, a report dated November 15, 2006. Several farm programs face renewal in 2007. GAO surveyed over 150 officials and landowners by phone. Six farm programs were under review. GAO also studied teamwork between the farm and wildlife agencies.

Money draws landowners in, respondents said. Scoring boosts for species projects help too. Many landowners value conservation for its own sake. The barriers are plain: scarce funds head the list. Fear of new regulation ranks high. Paperwork and eligibility rules add friction. Some fear habitat work will crimp farm operations. Teamwork between the agencies runs on staff drive, GAO found. A draft pact between them lacks follow-up checks. The farm service agency is not a party. Its reserve program holds about $1.9 billion and 36 million acres.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-535:
College sports rosters by sex are counted in GAO-07-535, a GAO report issued July 12, 2007. Since the 1970s, women have passed men in college enrollment. Their sports participation has climbed as well. Public debate asks two things at once: do women now play at rates like men's, and have men's chances shrunk as women's grew? GAO took up the count on the Comptroller General's authority.

The study tracks teams and players in National Collegiate Athletic Association sports at 4-year colleges. Its window runs from the 1991-1992 school year through 2004-2005. Both sexes are charted sport by sport and in total. The design is descriptive: it shows the shape of change over 14 years without ruling on fairness or law. Athletic directors and policy staff get a shared fact base for an argument often fought with single-campus stories.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-735:
Border checks for fake goods are reviewed in GAO-07-735, dated April 26, 2007. Customs and Border Protection leads the fight at U.S. ports. Fake and pirated goods cost firms billions and can harm health. GAO studied how the agency picks shipments to inspect. It checked goods for authenticity and tracked seizures and fines. The report covers fiscal years 2001 to 2006. It is the public form of a sensitive report with the same title.

The agency's computer scans flag shipments from known suspects. That method misses most noncommercial mail and courier traffic, though. Port staff also pick shipments by instinct and experience. Manual picks can cover any route but take scarce staff time. GAO found the agency's data on results were weak. It urged better data and clear measures in the agency's plan. It also urged use of port data to guide the work. The agency largely agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-35:
State and local information fusion centers are the subject of GAO report GAO-08-35, dated October 30, 2007. Fusion centers pool data to spot and stop crime and terror threats. GAO interviewed officials at 58 centers and at federal agencies that partner with them.

Officials at 43 of the 58 centers said their centers were up and running as of September 2007, and 34 of those had opened since January 2004. Most centers cover crime as well as terrorism, and state police or state investigation bureaus run most of them. At least 34 working centers had federal staff assigned. GAO recommended that the federal government spell out its long-term role and whether it will fund the centers' upkeep. The Department of Homeland Security agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-535:
Language and cultural care for veterans is described in GAO report GAO-08-535, dated May 28, 2008. The Department of Veterans Affairs serves a veteran population growing more diverse in race, ethnicity, sex, and age. A department directive tells medical centers to assess language needs and build access services where needed.

By June 2007, all medical centers reported action on the directive. Centers GAO visited offer translated materials, lists of bilingual staff, and, at five of six, phone interpretation by contract. Use of these services is low so far, though officials expect demand to rise as today's diverse force becomes veterans. Centers also train staff yearly on culturally fit care and tailor services to veteran groups. GAO made no recommendations in this report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-635:
Federal disability programs rest on old ideas about work and health, GAO warned in 2003. GAO-08-635, dated May 20, 2008, checks steps taken since then by two big agencies. It covers the Social Security Administration and the Department of Veterans Affairs. It also asks how well they team up with other agencies that serve disabled people.

Both agencies changed some rules to reflect new medicine and to help people return to work. Still, few people on benefits go back to work, and claim backlogs persist. Help often comes late, after habits and health have shifted. GAO suggested Congress weigh a joint group of agency leaders to build one shared plan.
gautier-mademoiselle-maupin-1835:
Theophile Gautier published Mademoiselle de Maupin in 1835, a French novel famous for its preface as well as its story. The preface argues that art need not serve morals or use. In the tale, a young woman travels disguised as a man named Theodore. Two lovers are drawn to Theodore without knowing the truth.

Letters and confessions slowly reveal desires that cross the lines of the age. Gautier writes lush, jeweled prose about beauty in all its forms. The novel shocked many readers of its time. Its defense of art for art's sake shaped later writers, including Oscar Wilde. It remains a landmark of French Romantic fiction.
gogol-taras-bulba-1835:
Nikolai Gogol published Taras Bulba in 1835, a historical novel about Cossacks in Ukraine. Old Taras is a fierce Cossack leader with two sons, Ostap and Andriy. He takes them to the Cossack camp and then to war against Poland. Battles, raids, and sieges fill the story.

Andriy falls in love with a Polish noblewoman and betrays his own side. Taras must answer that betrayal in the harshest way. Ostap shows steady courage to the end. Gogol writes with energy and pride in Cossack freedom. The book is a rousing, violent tale of loyalty, family, and war on the steppe.
hor-phrenologic-being-three-phrenologica:
John Epps, a London doctor, wrote these three phrenological essays, issued in 1835. Phrenology read character from the skull's organs. Epps applies it to morality, to happiness, and to veneration. The Reverend John Pierpont adds notes to this edition.

Epps laments that no Englishman since Gall and Spurzheim truly represents the science. Combe alone, he allows, comes near. New readers are sent first to Combe's System of Phrenology. The essays mix skull lore with Scripture and moral counsel. A translation note on the Hebrew text shows the period's learned style. Readers get a period piece of a science now discarded, argued in earnest.
hutcheson-considerations-on-patronages-1:
Francis Hutcheson published his Considerations on Patronages in 1735, entering a live fight in the Church of Scotland. Lay patrons claimed the right to appoint parish ministers, while many churchmen held that congregations should choose their own pastors. Hutcheson, a Glasgow professor and Presbyterian minister's son, defended the church's side.

The pamphlet argues from both Scripture and the nature of religious office that forced appointments corrupt the ministry. It joins deep thought about conscience and authority to the hard politics of Scottish church life. Hutcheson is better known as the philosopher of the moral sense, and that wider thought shows here in his care for free consent. The piece shows the Scottish Enlightenment at work in the pulpit's defense, where philosophy met parish quarrels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-glusk-lecz:
Abba Glusk Leczeka is a poem by Adalbert von Chamisso, published in 1832. Its hero Abba, at the age of sixty, went to Berlin, drawn by the fame of Moses Mendelssohn. He wanted to gain secular knowledge. At home in Glusk, the orthodox community had driven him out for his free views, and he wandered as a preacher.

At Wilna, the poem says, thirteen works of his were burned in the synagogue courtyard for their radical bent. A rabbi saved Abba himself from worse harm. Scholars named in the entry split on the model. Kayserling takes Abba as a verse form of Solomon Maimon, while Stanislavski holds he was the Glusker Maggid himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abiud-335: Abiud was a son of Zerubbabel. Matthew i. 13 names him among the ancestors of Joseph, husband of Mary, mother of Jesus. The entry notes a puzzle: he is missing from the list of Zerubbabel's sons in First Chronicles iii. 19, 20. No deeds or dates are recorded for him. His place in the text rests on that one line in Matthew's genealogy and on the gap in Chronicles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-eli:
Abraham ben Elijah of Wilna was a Russian Talmudist and author born at Wilna about 1750. He died there on Dec. 14, 1808. His father was Elijah, the gaon of Wilna, who guided his schooling and shaped his scientific bent.

In 1802 he edited Midrash Agadat Bereshit and like works, with notes. His preface gave a first full history of midrashic writing. His larger Rab Po'alim, printed in 1894, indexes over one hundred and twenty Midrashim. He also wrote a Hebrew geography, printed at Berlin in 1821. Like his father, he never served as rabbi but held community posts.
