jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrest-paul-d-p: Paul d'Abrest was the pen name of Friedrich Kohn, a journalist born at Prague in 1850. He studied at the Lycée Bonaparte in Paris. He wrote for papers such as "Le Petit Journal" and "Le Siècle." Later he reported from Vienna for the "Temps." In the Russo-Turkish war he covered events for the "Siècle." The French state then sent him to Bosnia to study its wealth. His books include a work on Vienna and a life of General Hoche. He died near Vienna in July, 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achselrad-bened: Benedict Achselrad was a preacher of Lemberg in the first half of the seventeenth century. His full name was Bendet ben Joseph ha-Levi. He wrote works of sermons and moral teaching. "Ben Da'at" came out at Hanau in 1616. It holds one hundred and fifty talks on the Psalms. A work on the Ten Commandments came out the same year. His Genesis sermons came out at Cracow between 1632 and 1648. That last book is part of a larger work on the whole Torah, never printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-b-awya-or-a: Aha b. Awya, also called 'Awa, was a Babylonian halakist of the third generation of Amoraim. He once visited Palestine, where he attended the lectures of Rab Assi and seems to have met Rabbi Johanan. Back in Babylonia he was a disciple of Rab Hisda and appears frequently in controversy with Rab Ashi I.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akiba-ben-josep:
Akiba's Book on Letter-Ornaments is a small Midrash fathered on Akiba ben Joseph. Haggadah said Akiba found meaning in every curl on the letters of the Torah. The work treats those little curves and flourishes. It also treats the odd letters of Scripture that are written larger or smaller than the rest.

The piece serves as a kind of supplement to Akiba's Alphabet. Its date can be no later than the start of the ninth century. A sample shows its method: the letter Bet, with two strokes, stands for the two courts of judgment, on earth and in heaven. The tall Lamed bends its head like God, high above all yet looking down. The work first appeared in print at Mantua in 1613. A complete text came out at Paris in 1866.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-of-ap:
Alexander of Aphrodisias was a Greek commentator on Aristotle. He flourished at the turn of the third century. His surname, the Exegete, marks his trade. The other name comes from Aphrodisias in Caria, his birthplace. Arabs and Greeks held his authority high. Maimonides urged Ibn Tibbon to study the commentaries closely.

Beyond the commentaries, Alexander paraphrased Aristotle's book on the soul. There he set out a new theory of intellect. The mind begins as a bare capacity, the material intellect. Study turns it into an acquired intellect, formed by ideas it takes in. The force that wakes it, he held, is the universal spirit, God Himself. At death that link ends, and the acquired intellect falls back into nothing. Arab and Jewish thinkers fought the doctrine, as it struck at the soul's immortality. Averroes answered it, and Levi ben Gerson sided with Alexander.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aliens-1235:
Aliens in the Bible go by more than one Hebrew name. One word means a foreigner in a broad sense. The key word is ger, a resident alien. A ger had come to live for good among the people. A second word marks a less settled guest. The entry sorts these terms by verse.

Early ties between groups were free and open. Marriages across groups were common in that age. Full rights later narrowed to natives alone. Still, many laws shielded the alien from harm. The entry tracks loans, land rights, and courts. It finds a slow trend toward wider rights. That trend runs from early law to Ezekiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altschul-altsch:
Altschul is a family name borne by Ashkenazic Jews worldwide. The name comes in four main spellings. All forms seem to share one root. That root is the Old Synagogue of Prague. The first men of the name served or backed that house. Prague stayed the chief seat for centuries.

A ban in 1542 drove many from the city. They spread to Poland, Lithuania, and Italy. Later kin reached England and America. Full family trees can not be built, the entry warns. Records are too thin for that task. Three charts give what can be proved. Short lives of key members fill the long entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aphek-the-battl:
Battle of Aphek is the entry's name for an event told in First Kings, chapter 20, verses 26 to 34. The entry calls it one of the most notable fights in the long war between northern Israel and the Arameans of Damascus. Beaten in the hills of Samaria the year before, the Syrians chose the lowland this time.

Their camp was likely Aphek, at the north end of the plain of Sharon. Israel beat them again, shut them inside the town, and took their surrender. Ahab treated them with mercy and let them go home to Damascus. A truce of over two years followed, but war returned in 853, and Ahab died at Ramoth-Gilead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archipherecites: Archipherecites is the Greek form of an Aramaic title meaning heads of the school. A pirka was literally a chapter, hence a discourse. The word occurs in Justinian's Novella number 146, On the Hebrews, of the year 553. In it, the archipherecites, the elders, and the teachers are forbidden to use their power of anathema. The ban aimed at one use: stopping the reading of the Greek Bible version in place of the Midrashic or Targumic interpretation. The entry rests on Gratz's history and a law collection it cites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artom-benjamin-:
Benjamin Artom, chief rabbi of London's Spanish and Portuguese congregation, was born at Asti in Italy in 1835. Left fatherless as a child, he was raised under an uncle's care and trained by rabbis at Trieste and elsewhere. At twenty he was teaching Hebrew, Italian, French, English, and German. He served first at Saluzzo near Genoa, then at Naples, before London called him in 1866.

He was installed on December 16, 1866, over the Spanish and Portuguese congregations of the United Kingdom. Within a year he preached in English with force. His chief care went to his congregation's schools, the Sha'are Tikvah and Villareal schools, which he organized and oversaw. Orthodox in view, he still welcomed moderate reform and worked to unite split factions. He died at Brighton on January 6, 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-leon-1935:
Leon Asher, a German physician, was born at Leipsic on April 13, 1865. His father, David Asher, served for years as secretary to Chief Rabbi Nathan Adler in London. The son studied medicine at Leipsic from 1885 to 1890 and took his degree. In 1891 he went to Heidelberg as a laboratory assistant under Kuhne and Quincke.

In 1894 he joined the Bern Physiological Institute in Switzerland, and in 1895 he became a lecturer at the university there. Summers from 1896 to 1898 he spent in Hering's laboratory at Leipsic. In 1901 Bern made him professor of medicine. His research ranged across nerve and muscle physiology, the senses, and tissue change. His work on lymph, backed by the Berlin Academy of Sciences, won wide acceptance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augusti-friedri:
Friedrich Albrecht Augusti was a German author. He was born at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1691 and died at Eschberge on May 13, 1782. His birth name was Joshua ben Abraham Herschel. He left home young, meaning to travel to the Holy Land. On the road, Tatar robbers seized him and sold him as a slave in Turkey.

A wealthy Jew from Podolia ransomed Augusti at Smyrna. He spent years in Poland and picked up secular learning and Latin there. In 1720 robbers beat him and left him for dead at Sondershausen. During his recovery a clergyman converted him to Christianity. He was baptized on Christmas day, 1723, before the duke of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. He studied theology at Gotha, Jena, and Leipsic. From 1734 he served as minister of Eschberge until his death. His books treat the fabled Sambathian river and the Karaites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ba-al-plural-co:
Ba'al is a Hebrew word for the possessor or owner of a thing. Joined to other nouns, it marks a tie between a person and an object or a trait. Many such phrases live in the Bible, and Polish-German Jews still used them when the entry was written. Ba'al ha-Bayit, master of the house, had worn down in speech to Baalboos.

The Talmud sorts scholars by the word: masters of the Talmud, of the Bible, and of the Mishnah. Other phrases name a party to a lawsuit, a penitent sinner, a counselor, and a man in pain. Medieval writers used the word in a curious way. They cited an author by the title of his best book. So Alfasi is the Ba'al of the Halakot, and Jacob b. Asher is the Ba'al ha-Ṭurim. The entry ends with a long list of Ba'al phrases in common use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-band-moritz-243: Moritz Band was an Austrian writer and art critic born Oct. 6, 1864. He began writing for the press while young. His work was mostly feuilletons, comic sketches, and sporting news. The entry is largely a list of his books. They run from an encyclopedia of the bookseller's trade in 1887 to operettas such as "Rosl" in 1888 and "Die Sphynx" in 1900. Comedies, a novel, and a handbook of cycling sport from 1895 fill out the list. He also edited two art collections, in 1889 and 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnato-barnett:
Barnett Isaacs Barnato, commonly called Barney Barnato, was an English "diamond king," promoter, and speculator. Born in London on July 5, 1852, he died by suicide on June 14, 1897, jumping from the steamship "Scot." His father was a small general dealer. Barney and his brother Henry were educated at the Jews' Free School, Spitalfields. Henry reached the Kimberley diamond-fields in 1871 and dealt in diamonds as Barnato. Barney followed in 1873 with about £50 and took the same surname.

In 1874 the brothers began as diamond-dealers. In 1876 Barney bought four Kimberley claims that soon brought $9,000 a week. He floated the Barnato Diamond Mining Company for $575,000, paying 36 per cent a year. In November 1895 the lord mayor banqueted him, and he gave $50,000 for Spitalfields' poor. The Jameson raid shook his interests and broke his health. On the voyage home he eluded his attendants and jumped overboard.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-adolf-2735:
Adolf Beer was an Austrian historian and educator born at Prossnitz, Moravia, on Feb. 27, 1831. He studied at five universities and trained for public life. To serve that aim he left the Jewish faith and embraced Christianity, the entry reports.

Beer taught history at several schools, then joined the Ministry of Public Instruction in Vienna. Voters sent him to Parliament in 1873 and kept returning him. In 1893 his Jewish descent blocked a cabinet post he was offered in talks. His books range over trade, finance, schooling, and modern history. The historian Ranke praised his powers of expression as early as 1872, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-b-e-co: Belmonte Colaco was a lawyer and writer in Surinam, in the Dutch West Indies. The entry names three printed works by him and nothing of his birth or death. One book treats reform of the governing system in the Dutch West Indies and came out at Leyden. A second reports the work of a Surinam benevolent society, printed at Paramaribo. A third takes up the interests of the Dutch West Indies against a named Dutch writer on slaves and free men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedikt-moriz-:
Moriz Benedikt, an Austrian nerve doctor, was born at Eisenstadt, in Hungary, on July 6, 1835. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1859 and at once served as a surgeon in the war with France and Italy. War service came again in 1866, against Prussia and Italy.

In 1868 he gained a chair of neurology at Vienna and kept it for life. His main work lay in nerve disease and in treatment by electric means. He also ranked as a pioneer of the new study of crime, basing his views on study of the mind and the body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berebi-and-in-g: Berebi was a title of learning in the age of the Tannaim. It went chiefly to scholars who were sons of scholars, or to members of the patriarch's family. The entry weighs how the word was formed and what it truly meant. It warns against taking it to mean a mere student of a great teacher. Bar Ḳappara is named as the scholar who bore the title most often. The entry also corrects a claim that a separate tanna named Berebi ever existed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-berna: Bernard Bernstein, an actor, was born at Warsaw in 1861. He sang in the chorus of the Polish opera there and played his first comic part in 1882, in a Goldfaden comedy. He acted in Jewish theaters in Russia until that stage was banned there in 1883. He then played in Galicia and in Rumania, mostly in comic roles. In 1892 a New York theater engaged him, and he won his best success as Shamai in The Jewish King Lear. He lived in New York in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bishop-of-the-j: Bishop of the Jews was a title for a Jewish official. It was used in the Rhine country and England. That use fell in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. At Cologne it equaled parnas, the synagogue warden. England had three such bishops per large community. Scholars infer they were the three dayyanim. Those judges formed the community's bet din. The title later hardened into a surname. French Jews bore the name Evesque or Levesc. Exchequer tallies suggest it simply means Cohen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenthal-niss:
Nissen Blumenthal was a Russian cantor born in Jassy, Rumania, in 1805. He died in Odessa on Feb. 9, 1902. Trained for the rabbinate, he used his fine voice and musical gift as a cantor instead.

Blumenthal sang at Berdychev and Yekaterinoslav before Odessa called him in 1841. He held the chief cantor post at the Brody congregation there for fifty-five years. He brought planned singing and written music into Russian synagogues. His fortune went to the choir of the temple he made famous. Critics praised his music as deeply Jewish in character.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bongoron-or-bon: David ben Yom-Tob Bongoron, or Bonjorn, was an astronomer at Perpignan in the middle of the fourteenth century. Judah Mosconi names him among the greatest astronomers of that time. Steinschneider links his name to a divorce case reported by Isaac de Lattes and Hisdai Crescas. Steinschneider also supposes him to be David ben Yom-Tob ibn Bilia. That man was an astrologer and philosopher. He was father of the astronomer Jacob Poel, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandes-georg-m:
Georg Morris Cohen Brandes was a Danish author and critic born in Copenhagen on Feb. 4, 1842. He graduated in 1859 and soon left law for literature and philosophy. A gold medal essay on fate among the ancients came in 1863.

Brandes sided with free thought in the church and science fights of his day. His 1866 pamphlet denied that orthodoxy could square with science. His method of criticism came from Taine, and his outlook from Mill and positivism. Later lectures made him the father of modern Danish literary criticism, the entry says. In 1902 a royal patent made him professor on his sixtieth birthday.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-broglie-victor-:
Victor-Claude, Prince de Broglie, was a French statesman born at Paris in 1757. He opposed Jewish emancipation during the French Revolution. In 1791 he published an opinion against admitting Jews to civil status. He argued that a reformed Jewish oath proved Jews had given up citizenship rights.

The entry recounts how the representative Prugnan defeated Broglie's exclusion bill on Sept. 27, 1791. Prugnan held that Jewish civil law and religious law were linked, so the oath did not settle citizenship. Broglie was beheaded in 1794 for plotting against the Revolution. The entry also reports a later legend that he asked forgiveness before death, and notes it has no historical basis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burgel-nathan-b: Nathan Burgel, son of Abraham, was a rabbi at Tunis about 1750 and a pupil of Isaac Lumbroso. People from far and near brought him hard cases to decide, since he ranked as a rabbinical authority. Late in life he went to Jerusalem. He died there soon after arrival, in December 1791. His printed work held new explanations on the Mishnah order Kodashim and on the treatise Horayot. It appeared at Leghorn from 1776 to 1778. The entry notes that the Wilna Talmud edition later reprinted it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calm-marie-pseu: Marie Calm, a pen name of M. Ruhland, was a German author and a voice for women's voting rights. Born at Arolsen on April 3, 1832, she ran a seminary for poor girls at Cassel. She was an early member of the general German women's union. Her books covered household economy and manners. The entry also lists her poems from 1871 and novels from 1876, 1880, and 1883. She died at Cassel on Feb. 22, 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cardozo-4035: Cardozo names an American Sephardic family, probably linked to the Cardozos of Amsterdam and London, though that link has not been made out. The family traces itself to Aaron Cardozo, a London merchant who went to New York about 1752. Among his descendants were noted citizens of Charleston, South Carolina, and a New York state judge. A short pedigree sketch follows, giving the chief branches and leaving out lines that had died out or married out of the faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chilmad-4335: Chilmad is a name in the list of nations that supplied goods for Tyre, in Ezekiel xxvii. 23. The Septuagint form points toward Carmania. The Targum renders the name as the Medes, and Rashi follows that view. David Ḳimḥi reports his father's view that the word holds a root meaning taught. George Smith linked the name to Chalwadh. The entry judges the Targum view the simplest and perhaps the most sound. Other corruptions crowd the same verse, it notes, which may explain the hard form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-toby-4535: Toby Cohn, a German physician and medical author, was born at Breslau on Dec. 26, 1866. He studied at the Elisabeth gymnasium there and at the universities of Breslau and Freiburg. From September, 1891, to January, 1893, he assisted at Wernicke's university clinic for neuropathy. Since then he had assisted Mendel at Berlin. The entry lists seven works, all on nerve and muscle disorders. They run from a study of water flow in the medulla in 1894 to a guide on electric diagnosis and therapy in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-creeping-things: Creeping Things is a loose phrase in the Authorized Version for two Hebrew words. The first means what creeps, with feet too small to see, or none. It covers land and water animals alike. The Revised Version renders it as teemeth or moveth in several verses. In the Talmud it names worms in the gut. The second word means what swarms. It fits weasels, mice, and lizards on land, and swarming life in water or air. Its core sense is vast, breeding multitudes of small animals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-czechowic-marti: Martin Czechowic was a Polish Unitarian priest, born at Zbaszynie about 1530. He died in 1613. He changed his faith more than once. A Roman Catholic priest at Kurnik until 1555, he then joined the Bohemian Brotherhood at Wilna. In 1575 he wrote against infant baptism. That year he also published a book meant to answer Jewish objections to Jesus as Messiah. Rabbi Jacob Naḥman of Belzyc replied in print in 1581. His defense was able and logical, and Czechowic answered it in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-benjamin-: Benjamin Ferdinand David was a French deputy born at Niort, in Deux-Sèvres, on March 30, 1796, and he died there on January 24, 1879. He studied medicine and served as an assistant navy surgeon on cruises to the Gulf of Mexico in 1813-14. He represented Deux-Sèvres in parliament across several terms between 1834 and 1870, and he was mayor of Niort in 1840. The entry notes that he favored the coup d'état of December 2, 1851, and backed the imperial government through the Second Empire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-decapolis-the-t:
Decapolis, the Ten Cities, was a district of Palestine made up of self-governing cities. Pliny lists them as Damascus, Philadelphia, Raphana, Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippos, Dion, Pella, Gerasa, and Canatha. All but Scythopolis lie east of the Jordan. Other ancient writers count the cities differently, and Ptolemy names eighteen.

The people of the Decapolis were mostly pagan. Pompey cut the cities off from Jewish territory in 63 B.C. and put them under the governor of Syria. Gadara and Hippos passed to Herod for a time, then became free again under Augustus. The entry also notes Pella as home of the first Christian community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-anton-5: Anton Deutsch was a Hungarian journalist and writer on economics, born at Budapest on October 21, 1848, and the entry on him is short. He studied in Budapest and Paris. Since 1870 he had worked for the "Pester Lloyd," and the paper's economic articles came from his pen. His most important writings are named as a history of twenty-five years of Hungarian economics and finance, and a history of the Hungarian fairs. The entry cites Hungarian reference works and gives no list of other writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-divination-5235:
Divination means reading the future from signs, movements of things, or visions in ecstatic states. The entry says it rests on belief that spirits dwell in the elements of life. Those spirits were thought able to share knowledge of what is coming. Jewish law forbids the practice outright.

Leviticus bans enchantments, augury, and consulting familiar spirits or wizards. Deuteronomy lists the diviner among acts called an abomination. The entry traces the Hebrew term to the casting of arrows, as Nebuchadnezzar does in Ezekiel. It also notes Balaam's use of divination. Forms drawn from clouds, trees, and lots fill out the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edrehi-moses-54:
Moses Edrehi was a Moroccan cabalist and teacher of modern and Oriental languages. He was born in Morocco early in the nineteenth century. He lived at Amsterdam and in England. His sermons for the festivals, Yad Mosheh, came out at Amsterdam in 1809.

Edrehi wrote on the River Sambatyon and on the Ten Tribes beyond it. His Historical Account of the Ten Tribes appeared at London in 1836. He firmly believed the tribes still lived somewhere in western Asia. At Edinburgh in 1829, Blackwood's Magazine sketched him with kind humor. His long beard, Eastern dress, and mix of tongues drew the writer's eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eilenburg-issac:
Issachar Baer ben Israel Leyser Eilenburg was a Polish rabbi. He was born at Posen about 1570. He died at Austerlitz, in Moravia, in 1623. His father trained him well in Talmud. At Prague he studied under Rabbi Liva. Back in Posen he learned under Mordecai Jafe.

About 1600 Eilenburg became rabbi of Göritz and its district. About 1620 he took the Austerlitz post. His Be'er Sheba comments on Talmud treatises that lack tosafot. It came out at Venice in 1614, in seven parts. Each part bears a Ner, or lamp, title. He also wrote a supercommentary on Rashi's Pentateuch notes, printed at Prague in 1623-24.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-of-hagr: Eleazar of Hagronia was a Babylonian scholar of the fifth century. The Babylonian Talmud names him only twice. Once he drew divine punishment for taking rabbinic power in another man's district. The other tale is set in a drought at Hagronia. Raba had called a fast, but no rain came. He asked if any man had dreamed that night. Eleazar told a dream of good greeting from a good Lord. Raba took it as a sign of favor. Fresh prayer was offered, and rain soon fell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ernesti-johann-: Johann August Ernesti was a Protestant theologian and classical scholar born August 4, 1707, at Tennstadt, Thuringia. He died at Leipsic in 1781, where he taught classical studies, rhetoric, and theology at the university. The entry credits him with pressing for strict word-based reading of the Bible. His Bible work lay mainly in the New Testament. He was no great Hebrew scholar, the entry admits, yet he wrote tracts on Herod's Temple, on Hebrew traces in Greek, and on Josephus. Those pieces were later reprinted in his collected shorter works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fatalism-6035:
Fatalism is the doctrine that every event is fixed in advance and must happen, and the entry asks where Judaism stands on it. Josephus is the first witness called. He sets the Pharisees between two camps: the Sadducees denied God's hand in human affairs, while the Essenes gave all to destiny. The Pharisees split the difference, the entry says.

For them, a person's inner life stayed free, but his outward lot was set. The Mishnah puts it in one line from Hananiah ben Dosa: all is foreseen, but freedom is given. R. Hanina adds that all is in God's hands except the fear of God. A Talmud tale of a heavenly voice naming a child's spouse, field, and house forty days before birth shows the fixed side at its strongest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-formon-zaddik-b:
Ẓaddik ben Joseph Formon was a Turkish Talmudist and translator of the middle of the sixteenth century. He turned Bahya's Ḥobot ha-Lebabot into Judæo-Spanish. Its title in that tongue means Duties of the Hearts. The translation was first printed in Roman letters at Amsterdam in 1610.

David Pardo, who printed it, claimed that he was himself the translator. Fürst ascribes the work instead to Joseph Pardo, rabbi of Amsterdam. An edition in Hebrew letters came out at Venice in 1713. Formon is quoted in the responsa of his fellow scholar Solomon Cohen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freemasonry-633:
Freemasonry is a secret society bent on brotherly feeling and good morals among its members. In its modern form it arose in London in 1717. From there it spread through the British Isles and to the Continent. It reached North America about 1729. The order claims descent from the craft of working masons. By that link it traces much of its sign language and rite to Solomon's Temple. One high grade turns on the legend of Hiram's death.

The terms and signs of the craft are full of Jewish matter. Names like Urim and Thummim and Sephirot appear, and the pillars Jachin and Boaz hold a chief place. In the Scottish Rite, papers are dated by Hebrew months and the Jewish era. Jews were active in the order in America and France. In Germany, by contrast, Jews were long kept out of the lodges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furst-livius-64:
Livius Furst, a German physician born at Leipsic on May 27, 1840, was a son of the Orientalist Julius Furst. He studied at Jena and Leipsic and took his medical degree in 1864. After further study at Prague and Vienna, he practiced at Leipsic. Child medicine became his main field. He ran the university children dispensary there from 1865 to 1886.

Furst served as a surgeon in the wars of 1866 and 1870-71. In 1878 he founded a laboratory for animal lymph at Leipsic. He left the university in 1889 and later moved to Berlin. His many books treat child care, feeding of infants, vaccination, urine tests, and women health.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gazara-or-gazer: Gazara, also spelled Gazera, is named in the entry as a walled city in Palestine on the borders of Azotus. It lay not far from Emmaus-Nicopolis, to the west. Schurer is cited as having proved that Gazara is the same place as the Gezer of the Bible, at Joshua xvi. 10. The entry is brief and gives no events, rulers, or later fate for the town beyond that place fixing and that name match.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goshen-6635:
Goshen was the region of Egypt where the Israelites lived during their stay there. It lay on the eastern edge of Lower Egypt. Shepherds would call it "the best of the land," the entry notes, since Pharaoh's cattle grazed there. Genesis also calls it the land of Rameses. Its Egyptian name was Ḳsm. It first appears in a papyrus of dynasty 12.

The entry fixes Goshen as the 8th, or Arabian, nome. It lay west of the Bubastide nome, between a Nile branch and a canal at Belbeis. Its capital may have shared the region's name. The entry weighs the Septuagint's reading, Heroonpolis, and finds it wrong. It then traces the "land of Rameses" name to Rameses II's colonies east of Goshen. The Wadi al-Ṭumilat fits the biblical picture best.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guimaraes-6935: Guimarães was a city of Portugal. In the fourteenth century it held a wealthy Jewish community. Its quarter stood where the fish-market, the "praça do peixe," now stands, and reached to Holy Ghost street. A few years before the expulsion from Portugal, the community paid a yearly tax of 25,000 reis. Maranos lived in the city for centuries afterward. The poet Manuel Thomàs was born there. So was Manasseh ben Israel's wife, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggiah-festiva: Haggiah was a Levite of the family of Merari. The entry gives him in one line: son of Shimea, and father of Asaiah, from I Chronicles vi. 15. In the Septuagint his name takes other forms, which the entry spells out in Greek. Nothing more is recorded here: no office, no acts, and no dates attach to Haggiah beyond his place in this one family line of Levites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamburger-wolf-:
Wolf Abraham Benjamin Hamburger, born on Jan. 26, 1770, was a Talmudical scholar and head of the yeshibah in Fürth who died on May 15, 1850. He was a fellow of Moses Sofer, who names him in the "Ḥatam Sofer." His books are many: "Sha'ar ha-Zeḳenim" and the three parts of "Simlat Binyamin," chiefly responsa, plus funeral orations printed at Fürth.

Hamburger was one of the last yeshibah heads in Germany who held no congregational post. His wife's business kept the house while he taught. Strictly Orthodox, he still shunned ecstasy and mysticism. When Reform rose about 1830 with government backing, his school was closed and he was forced to leave the city. His pupils include Seligman Baer Bamberger, Isaac Löwy, and David Einhorn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanun-7235: Hanun is a name the entry assigns to three men. The first was a son of Nahash, king of Ammon. He dishonored David's messengers. That dragged the Ammonites into a war with David, which ended badly for them (II Samuel x). The second Hanun worked with the people of Zanoah. He repaired the valley gate in Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah iii, 13). The third was the sixth son of Zalaph. He also helped repair the wall (Nehemiah iii, 30).
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hellenism-from-:
Hellenism is the taking up of Greek speech, manners, and culture, above all by the Jews. It runs from the fourth century before the common era into the first centuries of the common era. Alexander's victories bound East to West. Greek became the shared tongue of nearer Asia, and Greek art and thought traveled with it.

The long article maps where the pull was strongest. Greek cities lined the coast and the east bank of the Jordan. Place names and personal names turned Greek, Jason for Joshua and the like. Even in strongholds of Judaism, Greek ways reshaped law, public life, and daily habit. Loan words in Hebrew and Aramaic prove the depth of the change.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzfeld-albrec:
Albrecht Herzfeld, born at Vienna on June 7, 1840, was an Austrian actor and son of Adolf Herzfeld. Educated at the Vienna gymnasium, he began in wholesale trade as an apprentice. Like his father, he left trade for the stage. He first acted at Linz in 1857.

After volunteering in the Austro-Italian war of 1859, Herzfeld played at Brünn, Leipsic, Mannheim, Vienna, and Stuttgart. He left the stage in 1889. He later lived in Carinthia, then Ratisbon from 1900, writing for the stage. His son Leo, born in 1872, also acted, at Hermannstadt in Transylvania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-jenny-77:
Jenny Hirsch, born Nov. 25, 1829, at Zerbst, was a German author and advocate of women's rights. After her parents died she lectured at a girls' high school and opened a private school. In 1860 she moved to Berlin to help edit a women's journal.

From 1864 Hirsch wrote on her own and joined groups aiding women. She helped found a national women's union from a Leipsic congress. She served the Lette-Verein, which helped women support themselves, for seventeen years. Her books include a translation of Mill on women, plus novels under her name and pen names. She edited two women's papers. She died at Berlin on March 9, 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-homberg-herz-78:
Herz Homberg, born at Lieben, near Prague, in Sept. 1749, was an Austrian educator and writer. He studied Talmud at Prague, Presburg, and Gross-Glogau. Reading Rousseau's Emile at seventeen turned him toward teaching. At Berlin he tutored Mendelssohn's eldest son from 1779.

Under Joseph II, Homberg returned home to build German-Jewish schools. In 1784 he became superintendent of all such schools in Galicia. In 1793 Francis II called him to Vienna to draft laws on the moral and political status of Jews. That work won him a great gold medal in 1797. Later he served as censor and reader maker, with mixed success. He died on Aug. 24, 1841.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huna-b-joshua-7:
Huna ben Joshua was a Babylonian teacher of the fifth generation who died in 410. Raba was his chief teacher and sometimes praised him, sometimes blamed him. He also studied under Abaye. His close companion was Papa, and the two were rarely apart in school or out of it.

When Papa headed the school of Naresh, Huna presided over its general assembly. Later teachers often ruled by the pair's joint opinions. Huna was rich and careful in his habits. He never walked four cubits bareheaded. He ate so slowly that Papa ate four times as much in the same span. He outlived Raba by fifty-seven years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ezra-abraha:
Abraham ben Meir ibn Ezra was a scholar and writer born in 1092 or 1093 who died on January 28, 1167. Toledo was his birthplace, and Cordova his lasting home in Spain. The great men of Spanish Judaism were his friends, above all Judah ha-Levi. In Spain he made his name first as a poet and thinker.

About 1140 he left Spain, grieved by his son Isaac's conversion to Islam, and wandered for near thirty years. At Rome and across Christian Europe he spread the science of Spanish Judaism to Jews who knew no Arabic. His Bible commentary reports talks with Judah ha-Levi and argues with Karaite views. He called himself a Spaniard to the end and mourned his homeland in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-vives-al-lo:
Joshua ben Joseph ibn Vives al-Lorqui, baptized as Hieronymus de Santa Fe, was a Spanish physician turned anti-Jewish writer. As a Jew his name was Joshua ha-Lorki, from Lorca. The entry warns he is hardly the same man as the Joshua who wrote to Paul de Burgos. He knew Talmud well, though he was no rabbi.

To prove his zeal, he offered to show from the Talmud that the Messiah had come as Jesus. He got Pope Benedict the Thirteenth, whose physician he was, to stage a public debate with learned Jews. His two attack books were printed together as Hebraeomastix. Jews answered him in print. His own family suffered later. One son killed himself in prison to escape burning, and others were burned as Marranos in 1497 and 1499.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaiah-8235:
Isaiah, in this entry, is the greatest of the Hebrew prophets of whom written works remain. He lived at Jerusalem, was married, and had children who served as signs. The book's heading names Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah as the kings of his time. The entry warns that such headings are late and carry no real authority. Still, the man shows through his words, above all in the vision of chapter vi.

The entry recalls his counsel to Ahaz: Judah should not pay Assyria for work Assyria would do for its own sake. It also notes his acted prediction, in chapter xx, of the fate of Egypt and Ethiopia. A second part gathers the rabbis' Isaiah: ranked just after Moses, he cut the commandments to six and then to two, justice and charity. It retells the tradition that Manasseh had him sawn apart inside a cedar tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-issachar-tribe-:
The Tribe of Issachar article traces the tribe that descended from Issachar, Jacob's son. The counts given for it differ by book: 54,400 in Numbers, 64,300 later in Numbers, and 145,600 in Chronicles. Its land was the fourth lot in Joshua, north of Manasseh and south of Zebulun and Naphtali, west of the Jordan. It held sixteen cities and the rich plain of Esdraelon.

Issachar's princes stood with Deborah and Barak in the battle against Sisera on that plain. The judge Tola was a man of Issachar, and Baasha, founder of the northern kingdom's second dynasty, came of its house. In rabbinical telling, the tribe was a tribe of scholars. Raba said no Jewish student lacked descent from Levi or from Issachar. Its 200 chiefs, one passage says, led the Sanhedrin, and its people joined wealth with learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-javal-emile-853:
Emile Javal, a French physician and deputy, was born at Paris on May 5, 1839, as a son of Leopold Javal. He studied medicine and mineralogy and took his degree in 1868. He gave his work to eye medicine, devised a sharp way to test for astigmatism, and became a leading name on strabismus, or squint. In 1877 he directed the eye laboratory of the Sorbonne.

Javal entered the Academy of Medicine in 1885 and sat in the Chamber of Deputies for Yonne, where he fought the Panama scheme. His books cover squint, school hygiene, and eye measurement, and he translated a major German work on optics. In 1900 he was struck with blindness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-criterio: Jewish Criterion was an American weekly newspaper started at Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on Feb. 8, 1895. S. Steinfirst and Joseph Mayer founded it, and Rabbi Samuel Greenfield was its first editor. In 1899 Charles H. Joseph followed him and in 1900 became the paper's owner. In 1901 J. Leonard Levy took the chief editor's chair, with Joseph as his helper. The entry closes with the paper's aim: it is published in the interest of Reformed Judaism. No sample views or debates are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-john-casimir-87:
John Casimir was king of Poland from 1648 to 1668. He won the throne with Cossack help, yet the Cossack leader then demanded that no Jew live on Cossack lands. When Jews who had fled the massacres came back, the king let those baptized under fear of death return to Judaism. Hundreds of orphaned children were brought back as well, with parchment rolls of their descent hung at their necks.

In February 1649 he confirmed the old rights of Jews in Wilna, Brest, and many other towns. Later decrees guarded leaseholders, gave one town a second market day, and let a synagogue be built if kept modest. One 1653 decree also barred Jews of Wilna from keeping Christian servants, on pain of fines and loss of their synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-noah: Joseph ben Noah ha-Basri, in Arabic Abu Ya'kub Yusuf ibn Nuh, was a Karaite scholar of the eighth and ninth centuries and a brother of Nissim ben Noah. He rendered the Pentateuch into Arabic and wrote notes on it. A short form of that work was made by Abu al-Faraj Harun. Hadassi reports that Joseph allowed only two bases for religious law: Scripture itself, and agreement across the whole body of laws. He rejected proof by logical deduction. Later writers mixed him up with Joseph al-Kirkisani.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judd-max-origin: Max Judd, born Maximilian Judkiewich, was an American maker, consul-general, and chess player born at Cracow on December 27, 1851. He came to the United States at eleven and lived in St. Louis from 1873. He made cloaks wholesale until 1893, when President Cleveland named him consul-general at Vienna. In chess he took prizes at state and national meets from 1869 on. He beat Showalter in a match in 1889 and took first prize at the Western Chess Congress in Chicago in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kattina-9235: Ḳaṭṭina was a Babylonian amora of the second line, in the third century. He is known both for law and for lore. He studied under Rab, also called Abba Arika. His rulings show up often in the Babylonian Talmud. Some come down in his own words. Others reach us through Ḥisda and Rabbah b. Huna. He taught that the world runs in spans of 6,000 years. Between the spans lie 1,000 years of chaos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohut-adolph-94:
Adolph Kohut, a German writer born on Nov. 10, 1848, at Mindszent in Hungary, was a brother of Alexander Kohut. He spent three years at the Jewish Theological Seminary in Breslau, then studied philosophy, literature, and Oriental languages. He took his Ph.D. at Jena in 1877. Journalism filled his early career, with editorships in Berlin, Breslau, Düsseldorf, Kiel, and Dresden.

More than 200 books and monographs stand to Kohut's name in the entry. He wrote lives of composers, a standard life of the poet Theodor Körner, and lives of Bismarck and Emperor William I. His attacks on Bismarck in print got him expelled from Prussia on Sept. 13, 1884, until a pardon came in 1889. Works on Jewish subjects include books on Humboldt, Heine, Mendelssohn, and Lassalle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kovno-or-kovna-:
Kovno, a Russian fortified city where the Viliya meets the Niemen, had Jews living and trading there by the end of the fifteenth century. Tax farming on wax and salt went to Jewish holders in 1528 and 1558. Trade fights with Christian merchants fill much of the early record, with kings ruling for and against Jewish traders by turns.

Persecution and recovery mark the eighteenth century. A court ruling of Sept. 14, 1753, confined Jews to one district, and a mayor's riot in 1761 burned their houses. Damages of 15,000 florins were awarded in 1782. By 1902 the community reached 37,196 people, about half the city, with twenty-five synagogues, a large hospital, and thousands of Jewish artisans counted by trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lapidoth-lappid: Lapidoth, whose name means torches or flames, was the husband of Deborah, named in Judges iv. 4. That is the one firm fact the short entry gives from the Bible text itself. The Rabbis identify Lapidoth with Barak, whose name means lightning. He is also known as Michael, a view the entry ties to Ḳimḥi, Budde, and Wellhausen. The entry adds a grammar note: the name is an intensive plural with, in all likelihood, a figurative sense. No dates, place, or acts of his own are stated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leitner-gottlie:
Gottlieb William Leitner, a professor of Arabic, was born at Budapest in 1841 and died at Bonn on March 22, 1899. He was schooled at Constantinople and at King's College, London. His gift for tongues won him work as an interpreter in the Crimean war, with the rank of colonel.

Leitner taught Arabic, Turkish, and Modern Greek at King's College from 1859, then became professor of Arabic and Mohammedan law. Later he led the Lahore Government College and set up the Punjab University, serving as its first registrar. He founded journals and free libraries, wrote on Indian subjects, and in 1866 led a Punjab expedition into the little known land between Kashmir and Afghanistan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-solomon-b-: Solomon ben Isaac Levi was a rabbi and scholar of the sixteenth century. He was born in Smyrna. He became director of the academy Ez Hayyim at Salonica, and later went to Venice. He knew philosophy, natural science, and mathematics, as well as Talmud and law. He was famed as a preacher. His many works include a commentary on Abot, five sermons for each weekly portion and feast, and a commentary on Talmud, Midrash, and Zohar. His responsa came out at Salonica in 1652.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewysohn-abraha:
Abraham Lewysohn was a Hebraist and rabbi of Peiskretscham, in Upper Silesia. He was born on Dec. 6, 1805, and died on Feb. 14, 1860. He left a great mass of manuscripts behind him. They hold several hundred sermons in Hebrew and German, notes on the Talmud, and verses.

His printed works include "Mekore Minhagim" of 1846, a critical study of religious customs. The entry notes that the book was later plagiarized at Vienna. He also printed sermons and lives of two early sages, Joshua ben Hananiah and Rab. His history of the Tannaim and Amoraim stayed in manuscript, save for its introduction.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-littauer-lucius: Lucius Nathan Littauer was an American congressman and manufacturer born in Gloversville, N. Y., on Jan. 20, 1859. He graduated from Harvard University in 1878 and joined his father's glove-making business, which he took over in 1882. In 1896 he was elected to Congress as a Republican from New York. He was reelected to each Congress after that and served on the Committee on Appropriations. Sources cited include the Congressional Directory and the American Jewish Year Book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-leopold-101:
Leopold Löw, the leading reform rabbi of Hungary, is profiled at length in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Czernahora, Moravia, in 1811, he studied at several yeshivot before turning to philology and theology at Presburg, Pesth, and Vienna. He became rabbi of Gross-Kanizsa in 1841. He died at Szegedin in 1875.

Much of the article covers his fight for the emancipation of Hungarian Jews, won in 1867. Löw was the first to preach in Hungarian in the synagogue, and his journal Ben Chananja pressed the cause for years. The entry describes his arrest after the revolution, his pardon, and his long Szegedin rabbinate. It also surveys his studies of Jewish law and custom, which argued that Judaism had always developed over time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabans-the-1:
The Maccabaeans, an association of English Jewish professional men, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Founded in 1892, the club aimed at social fellowship and cooperation. Its stated goal was to advance the higher interests of the Jewish people. The idea came from Herman Cohen, who became its first honorary secretary.

The article explains how membership was shaped. Admission was soon limited to Jewish professional men, though that term was read widely. The committee could also elect ten men a year honored for public service or work in letters, science, or art. Solomon J. Solomon served as first president. The club met often to hear and debate papers on Jewish questions. Out of those meetings grew the Jewish Lads' Brigade, the Jewish Athletic Association, and the Education Aid Society. The entry records a club that turned talk into new institutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malki-raphael-m: Raphael Mordecai Malki, a rabbinical scholar and physician of Palestine, gets one of the shortest entries in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He lived at Safed about 1627. The article notes that he was versed in astronomy and philosophy as well as in rabbinic learning. His one named work is a commentary on the Pentateuch, titled Perush al ha-Torah. The notice rests on a single cited source, Hazan's work on the scholars of Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marriage-laws-1:
Marriage laws in Jewish tradition form the topic of a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Solomon Schechter and Julius H. Greenstone wrote it. It starts from the rabbinic reading of Genesis. The rabbis held that the first positive commandment in the Bible is the duty to marry and have children. So marrying young counted as a religious duty.

The entry sets out the rules in detail, citing the Talmud and Maimonides. Eighteen was the age the rabbis named. A man still unwed at twenty could be pressed by the court. Study of the Torah was nearly the only excuse the rabbis took for delay. The entry also covers when the duty counts as met, why women were exempt, and the care needed in choosing a worthy wife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-mendel-:
Menahem Mendel ben Baruch Bendet was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the eighteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 notices him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. He is noticed chiefly as the editor who carried the Vilna Gaon's work into print. Born at Shklov, he was a pupil of Elijah of Wilna. He published his master's commentaries on Proverbs, the Shulhan Aruk, and Abot. He published them on the Sefer Yezirah and the Passover Haggadah too. His notes to the minor treatises appeared besides.

After the Gaon's death he emigrated to Palestine. He settled at Safed. There he lectured on Talmud in the house of study founded in the Gaon's memory. His own literary legacy went the other way. Ten works of a mystical character, the entry reports, are all still unpublished. He died in Palestine, the Gaon's disciple to the end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-metals-10735:
Metals known to the ancient Hebrews — gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead — are surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss, published in 1906. It opens with a puzzle: Deuteronomy calls the Promised Land rich in ore, yet Palestine itself had almost no metals and imported nearly all of them.

Section by section, the article traces where each metal came from, from gold of Ophir to iron from the north, and unpacks the Hebrew names and Talmudic lore for each. Gold gets seven Talmudic varieties, silver doubles as the word for money, and tin likely arrived through Phoenician trade. Later parts list metal terms in the Talmud, from unstamped silver coins to Corinthian brass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milk-hebrew-hal:
Milk in the Bible and Talmud is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer, Julius H. Greenstone, and Cyrus Adler, published in 1906. A land flowing with milk and honey is its most famous phrase: milk stands for life's necessities, honey for its luxuries. The article gathers every kind of evidence, from poetry to dairy practice.

Goats and sheep supplied most of Israel's milk, the writers note, because the hill country suited cows poorly, so cows' milk stays rare in the text. Milk was kept in buckets and skins and served as a refreshing drink at meals, as Abraham served his guests in Genesis. Ben Sira ranked it among the principal things needed for human life, and Deborah called it a cup fit for nobles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molln-molin-109:
Mölln, better read Molin, is a Mayence family name that is really a personal name. It is perhaps a pet form of Moses. The Jewish Encyclopedia explains it in 1906 through Isidore Singer, Eduard Neumann, and Gotthard Deutsch. Its famous bearer is Jacob ben Moses Mölln, the MaHaRIL, born about 1365. The tangle of his names, the entry warns, has caused much confusion.

Jacob was a pupil of Shalom of Austria at Wiener-Neustadt. He won a name while young for learning and piety. His rulings on ceremonial law were sought from afar. At Mayence his school drew many pupils. Chief among them was Jacob Weil, whose own responsa became authoritative. Teacher and pupil stand at the head of the Ashkenazic tradition the article goes on to trace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morwitz-edward-:
Edward Morwitz was a physician who became one of the leading German-language newspaper men in America. Cyrus Adler and Louis E. Levy wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Danzig on June 11, 1815, he studied medicine at Berlin and graduated in 1840. After taking part in the revolutionary movement of 1848, he had to emigrate, and he settled in Philadelphia in 1850.

In Philadelphia, Morwitz bought the Philadelphia Demokrat in 1853 and gave up medicine for journalism. He added weekly and Sunday papers, founded German papers across Pennsylvania, and built a Newspaper Union covering more than three hundred periodicals. For nearly eleven years he also published The Jewish Record, mostly at a loss. He died in Philadelphia in 1893, a power in the Democratic politics of his state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-palerm:
Moses of Palermo was a Sicilian translator from Arabic into Latin in the later thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. A document in the Naples archives tells his story. In 1277 Charles of Anjou ordered that Moses be taught Latin for a special task.

The task was to translate a set of medical works kept at the royal castle in Naples. Moses is known by name for one surviving translation: a work on curing the diseases of horses, ascribed to Hippocrates. It was printed at Bologna in 1865, with two old Italian versions. The entry preserves a Jewish scholar working for an Angevin king.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musa-ibn-tubi-a: Abu Imran Musa ibn Tubi was a Spanish-Arabic poet of Seville, in the first half of the fourteenth century. In Hebrew he is called Moses ben Tobiah. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn, knows him for one poem. His Al-Sab'aniyyah is an Arabic poem of didactic character. Solomon da Piera later translated it into Hebrew as Batte ha-Nefesh, and both texts were printed together in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nieto-david-115:
David Nieto was haham of London's Sephardic community. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Venice in 1654. He died in London on Jan. 10, 1728. He first practiced medicine and preached at Leghorn.

His Paschologia of 1702 compared three churches' calendars. In London he succeeded Ayllon as ecclesiastical chief that year. His Divine Providence treatise of 1704 stirred fierce opposition. Foes charged him with Spinozism, then a name for atheism. Zebi Ashkenazi, called to judge, decided in his favor. His Matteh Dan defended the oral law against Karaites. He fought the Shabbethaian heresies without pause or rest. He first fixed Sabbath eve's start for England's latitude.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nut-11635:
Nut is a word study from the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Cyrus Adler, and M. Seligsohn all had a hand in it. The piece looks at two Hebrew words. One is egoz, and the other is botnim. Both words stand for nuts in English Bible texts.

Egoz is read as the walnut, brought from Persia. It is named once, in the Song of Songs. Botnim is read as the pistachio nut. It is named among the gifts sent to Joseph in Egypt. The piece adds notes from the Talmud and Mishnah. Nuts were a treat, and oil was pressed from them. Shells gave a dye for cloth as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-morit:
Moritz Daniel Oppenheim was a German painter of scenes and faces. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hanau in the year 1801. His parents were strict in the Jewish faith at home. He died at Frankfurt am Main in 1882.

Moritz took his first art lessons at Hanau as a boy. At seventeen he entered the art school at Munich. He read in Paris, then went on to Rome. There he sketched the life of the Rome ghetto. He drew its home and faith life in full. In 1825 he settled at Frankfurt am Main. His canvas of David at Saul's court drew crowds. Goethe's word won him a title of professor in 1832. His Jewish scenes made him famed across his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ozer-ben-meir-1: Ozer ben Meir was a Polish rabbi from a famed line. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the great grandson of Solomon Luria, a sage. He died at Zolkiev in May of the year 1710. He served as rabbi at Clementow, a Polish town. He wrote a work on the code called the Yad. He wrote new notes on tracts of the Talmud as well. Some of his works came out years after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pasternak-leoni:
Leonid Osipovich Pasternak was a Russian painter born in Odessa in 1862. He trained in Odessa, Moscow, and Munich. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He also took a law degree, though art became his life.

His painting A Letter from Home won praise in Paris in 1889. Tretyakov bought it for his gallery. Students Before the Examination took a gold medal and joined the Luxembourg Museum. Pasternak also drew scenes for Tolstoy's novel Resurrection. From 1894 he taught at the Moscow school of painting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perizzites-1203:
The Perizzites were a tribe of Canaan in the Bible. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They lived in the south of Palestine. Abraham found them there when he entered the land.

Jacob feared them after the crime at Shechem. Later, Simeon and Judah beat them in battle. Solomon never made them pay tribute. Ezra still lists them among the peoples of the land. The name is missing from the table of nations. Newer scholars think it covers all folk of unwalled towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-arnold-121:
Arnold Pick was an Austrian psychiatrist of Moravian birth. He was born at Gross-Meseritsch on July 20, 1851. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at Berlin and Vienna. His field was the pathology of the mind.

Pick took his degree in 1875 and entered asylum work. He served at Wehnen, then at the Prague state asylum. In 1880 he became chief physician at Dobrzan. Six years later Prague made him professor of psychiatry. His books map diseases of the brain and nerves. One was written with Kahler in 1880.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polak-jakob-edu:
Jakob Eduard Polak was an Austrian doctor who worked in Persia. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia in 1818, he studied medicine at Prague and Vienna. In 1851 he sailed to Teheran to teach at a new army school.

Polak soon won the trust of Shah Nasir-ed-Din himself. He first taught in French through a helper who translated. Within a year he could lecture in Persian. He wrote a Persian book on the human body. He also made a medical word list in three tongues. He founded a state clinic with sixty beds. His book on Persia and its people came out at Leipsic in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-precedence-1233:
Precedence means the rank and first place given to persons by rule. The Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such rank can rest on custom or on set law. The Bible shows a clear order of rank in the home. The husband stood above the wife, they note.

The male was put before the female in that order. The first-born son took a double share of the estate. The child of a bondwoman ranked lower than others. In Egypt the whole tribe of Levi stood apart. Its men were freed from bondage there, the article says. The entry works through rank in home, court, and synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pul-12435:
Pul was a king of Babylonia in the eighth century B.C. Emil G. Hirsch and Samuel Fuchs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He seized the throne in the year 745. He held it until the year 737. He is one and the same as Tiglath-pileser the Third. King lists name him as Pulu in short form.

Rawlinson first put that link forward in 1863. Lepsius proved it on his own six years later. On taking power, Pul brought peace back to Babylonia. In 738 he took Kullani, thought to be Calno of the Bible. He laid tribute on Syria as far south as Samaria. His own stone records name the kings who paid him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahab-broad-125:
Rahab of Jericho hid the two spies sent by Joshua. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Her house stood in the city wall. It had a window facing outward.

The article retells Joshua chapter 2 in close detail. Rahab hid the men on her roof and misled the king. She asked that her whole family be spared in return. She then lowered the spies by a scarlet cord. When Jericho fell, Joshua kept that promise to her. A second part covers how later rabbis discussed her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ricardo-david-1:
David Ricardo was an English political economist born on April 19, 1772. Joseph Jacobs and J. H. Hollander wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London. He died on September 11, 1823.

The article traces his family from Italy to Holland to London. His father Abraham grew rich on the stock exchange. David was the third child of a large family. His schooling was sound and practical, the writers say. His father designed him for a financial career. At fourteen David joined his father's exchange business. Even young, he showed a taste for abstract reasoning. He pressed for final analysis in every question. He held opinions firmly yet stayed open to proof. The entry introduces a thinker formed by the market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenau-william:
William Rosenau was an American rabbi born at Wollstein, Germany, on May 30, 1865. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He trained at Hebrew Union College and earned a doctorate at Johns Hopkins.

Rosenau led Temple Israel in Omaha, then Congregation Oheb Shalom in Baltimore from 1892. He held office in the Central Conference of American Rabbis for years. At Johns Hopkins he taught rabbinica, and he sat on Baltimore's board of education. His books cover Hebrew turns in the English Bible and Jewish ceremonial customs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rules-of-elieze:
The Thirty-Two Rules of Eliezer b. Jose ha-Gelili are rules for reading the Bible's non-legal passages. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Many of the rules also serve in legal interpretation.

The entry lists and explains all thirty-two rules one by one. Some turn on small particles: one word can widen a verse, another narrow it. Others cover arguing from lesser to greater, or repeated words bearing special meaning. Still others treat shortened speech and clauses split across a passage. Together they form a toolkit for drawing teaching out of Scripture's wording.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabeans-11435:
The Sabeans were the people of Sheba, an ancient kingdom in southeastern Arabia. Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. They are known from the Bible, classical writers, and native inscriptions.

Genesis gives Sheba, their ancestor, three different pedigrees in its genealogies. One line makes him a grandson of Cush, through Raamah of Arabia's coast. Another makes him a descendant of Shem, through Joktan the patriarch. A third makes him a grandson of Abraham by Keturah, his later wife. The Psalms and prophets stress Sabean wealth and busy trade in gold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-haym-13:
Haym Salomon was an American financier born at Lissa, Poland, in 1740. Cyrus Adler and Herbert Friedenwald wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He left Poland after its partition in 1772 and settled in New York.

When the Revolutionary war began, Salomon sided with the American cause. The British jailed him as a spy after taking New York in 1776. His languages won him a post in the Hessian commissariat instead. From there he helped French and American prisoners escape their captors. In August 1778 he fled New York, leaving property, wife, and infant behind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-nasi-:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Nasi. He was an exilarch, the official head of the Jews, in Bagdad. He probably held that post sometime between 773 and 816. Until recently, scholars knew he existed only from one hard manuscript passage. Part of that passage was printed in the Maẓref la-Ḥokmah.

The passage says the pious took the groundwork of the prayer book from Aaron ben Samuel ha-Nasi. Aaron had left Babylon. A fourteenth-century Paris manuscript adds more. It says Moses, who wrote a prayer work, was Aaron's pupil. The Chronicle of Ahimaaz gives Aaron a large role in Italy. Taken together, these scraps prove that Samuel himself was real.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-savannah-13235:
Cyrus Adler and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Savannah. The Georgia city stands on the Savannah River. General James Oglethorpe founded it in 1733. Georgia was meant as a refuge from religious persecution. The colony's trustees warned Oglethorpe not to encourage the Jews. The general ignored them.

The first Hebrew settlers arrived in 1733 itself. Among them was Dr. Nuñez, whose good work Oglethorpe praised. Savannah's Jews prospered in peace until the Revolution. Many scattered then, and several enlisted in the rebel army. After independence they returned and rebuilt. Their president, Levy Sheftall, sent greetings to President Washington. The letter was warmly answered. The Mickwa Israel congregation, founded soon after the first landing, anchors the community's story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwab-moise-13:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moïse Schwab. He was a French librarian and author. Schwab was born at Paris on September 18, 1839. He studied at Strasburg's Jewish school and Talmud Torah. From 1857 to 1866 he served as secretary to Salomon Munk. Since 1868 he has been a librarian at the Bibliothèque Nationale.

Schwab's chief work renders the Jerusalem Talmud into French. It runs to eleven volumes, printed from 1871 to 1889. He began it before Frankel's introduction existed. Critics praised and blamed it in turns. He finished the huge task alone. His other books cover Jewish history and the ethnography of Tunisia. He wrote a bibliography of Persia and studied early Hebrew printing. In 1880 the ministry sent him to Bavaria to hunt old Hebrew presses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serah-13435:
Serah was the daughter of Asher, one of Jacob's twelve sons. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on her. She is counted among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Her name appears again in a census taken in the wilderness.

Serah stands alone as the only woman in those family lists. That odd fact made rabbis build legends around her. One tale says she first told Jacob that Joseph still lived. Jacob then blessed her with life without end. Another tale has Moses ask her where Joseph's remains lay. The entry shows how a brief name grew into lasting story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shekanzib-13535:
Shekanzib was a small town near Nehardea in Persia, perhaps on the Tigris. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its women were famed for beautiful songs of mourning. They sang those songs at burials in the town.

Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi barred his children from living there. He called it a town of mockers, the entry reports. Yet Rab Nahman married a woman from Shekanzib. Sherira Gaon tells that Rabba fled there for safety. He ran when Papa ben Nazar captured Nehardea. The brief entry mixes praise, blame, and refuge around one little-known Babylonian town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sid-sidi-arabic:
Sid, or Sidi, meaning lord or noble in Arabic, is a common Eastern Jewish family name. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the name. Several rabbinical authors bore it across the Balkans. Abraham Moses Sid was born at Nish in 1842.

Abraham wrote many works, though few reached print. His printed books cover ethics, Passover law, and Ruth. The Nish synagogue library kept four more works in manuscript. Judah Sid served as chief rabbi at Philippopolis under Ottoman rule. He headed its tribunal as president there as well. His Ot Emet treats rules for reading the weekly Law lessons. His Ner Mizwah comments on the Pentateuch itself. The entry gathers one name's learned bearers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhat-torah-th:
Simhat Torah, the Rejoicing over the Law, is the second day of Shemini Azeret. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It falls on the 23rd of Tishri and closes the Feast of Sukkot. The name came into use only in later times. It marks the day the yearly Torah reading ends.

As soon as Deuteronomy ends, Genesis begins again at once. All the scrolls are taken from the Ark in the morning. A hymn is sung for each scroll in turn. Those who read the last and first parts are honored. Gifts, dinners, and even dancing in the synagogue grew around the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sofia-the-triad:
Sofia, once called Triaditza and Sredec, is the capital of Bulgaria. Gotthard Deutsch and M Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lies 350 miles from Constantinople. Jews lived there before the ninth century. In 811, Jewish prisoners from Thessaly joined that early community.

More Jews came from the Byzantine empire in 967. Others arrived from Germany in 1360 and Hungary in 1367. When Murad I took Sofia about 1389, four synagogues stood there. They served Byzantine, Ashkenazic, Italian, and native Jews in turn. Spanish Jews founded a Sephardic synagogue after 1492. The false Messiah Shabbethai Zebi later wrote to his brethren of Sofia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-max-emanu:
Max Emanuel Stern was a Hungarian Hebraist born at Presburg on November 9, 1811. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His father taught at the Jewish primary school in Presburg. When his father went blind, Max took over his classes at fourteen. He died at Vienna on February 9, 1873.

Stern studied at night and wrote Hebrew poems and translations of Proverbs. In 1833 he became a corrector for a Vienna printing press. He later led the Jewish-German school at Eisenstadt. His epic poem on Elijah appeared under a pen name in 1840. From 1845 he published a Hebrew periodical backed by the Imperial Academy. The emperor gave him a gold medal for literature and art. The entry traces a Hebrew writer honored by the state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sussmann-ezra-b: Ezra ben Jekuthiel Sussmann was a Polish scholar of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. His one known book is Hoshen Yeshu'ot, printed at Minsk in 1802. It comments on the Pirke Abot, the rabbinic ethics tractate. Bibliographies by Benjacob, Fürst, and Zedner record the work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhuma-b-abba-:
Tanhuma ben Abba was a Palestinian amora famed for sermons. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He belonged to the fifth generation of amoraim. Huna ben Abin was his main teacher. He likely lived at Nave in Perea.

Tanhuma ranked among the foremost haggadists of his time. One Talmud tale shows his wit before an emperor. The ruler proposed that all become one people. Tanhuma answered that circumcision divided them by Rome's choice. The emperor threw him to wild beasts for winning. The beasts left him unharmed in the story. A bystander who mocked was not so lucky. Tanhuma also ordered a public fast in his town. The entry blends legend with a preacher's public record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terni-mattathia:
Mattathiah Nissim ben Jacob Israel Terni was an Italian rabbi and poet. M. Seligsohn wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Terni served congregations at Florence, Urbino, Pesaro, and Sinigaglia. He worked in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

His writings center on Jewish law and marriage rules. Sefat Emet collects his halakic decisions, printed at Leghorn in 1797. Midbar Mattanah gathers responsa in four parts. An appendix in Italian appeared at Urbino. He also left a volume of poems. The entry is brief, drawn from standard bibliographies. It still fixes his posts, dates, and main books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toledo-14435:
Toledo, capital of Old Castile, held one of Spain's oldest Jewish communities. Joseph Jacobs wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews lived there by the sixth century at least. The Toledo Council of 589 already legislated against them. Later councils banned intermarriage and public office for Jews.

Jews reportedly helped the Arabs take Toledo in 715. Under Arab rule their position seems to have been strong. Congregation minutes stayed in Arabic into the late 1200s. Judah ha-Levi and Abraham ibn Ezra were born in Toledo. The city became Europe's hub for translation from Arabic. Alfonso X granted Jews full equality with Christians. Friction between the faiths soon followed anyway.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tubal-cain-1453:
Tubal-cain, brother of Jabal and Jubal in Genesis, stands at the dawn of metalwork. Emil G. Hirsch, Ira Maurice Price, and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Lamech sons founded several industries and arts. Scholars dispute the exact Hebrew text of Genesis 4. Some call part of it a marginal gloss.

The Septuagint omits one key word of the verse. Dillmann and others think Tubal once stood alone. Cain, they argue, was added later as a title meaning smith. Tubal matches an Assyrian people southeast of the Black Sea. The Tibareni traded bronze goods with Phoenicia, Ezekiel notes. That trade supports the older reading. Later tradition adds still more inventors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valls-raphael-1:
Raphael Valls was a Spanish Marrano put to death by the Inquisition. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Valls was burned at the stake at Palma, Majorca, on May 6, 1691. The court treated him as the rabbi of the Chuetas, Majorca's hidden Jews.

Two of his followers died with him. They were his pupil Raphael Terongi and Terongi's sister Catalina. All three held fast to Judaism. Local poets wrote verses about their deaths. Women on the island still sang those verses years later. The entry keeps their names and story from being lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-mathieu-1:
Mathieu Weill was a French mathematician and school leader. He was born at Hagenau, Alsace, on May 24, 1851. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Burg, Strasburg, and the Polytechnique. He trained at the military school of Fontainebleau. He rose to lieutenant of artillery.

Weill resigned his commission in 1877. In 1881 he began teaching math at Collège Chaptal. In 1898 he became the college's principal. He published essays in French math journals. His textbooks cover analytic geometry in one course. A four volume set treats arithmetic, geometry, algebra, and trigonometry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wurzburg-15035:
Wurzburg is the chief town of Lower Franconia in Bavaria. Gotthard Deutsch and Moses Lob Bamberger wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town ranked as a city from the year 741. A Jewish group lived there from the 1000s at least.

The first firm proof of Jews there dates to 1119. The Crusade of 1147 brought great pain to them. Fresh attacks came in 1298 and again in 1349. In that last year Jews died by fire in their synagogue. Men, wives, and small children chose death that way. In 1565 a bishop cast the Jews out of the town. The grave yard was seized and shut soon after. The group at Heidingsfeld took up the work from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zemah-ben-hayyi:
Zemah ben Hayyim was gaon of Sura from 889 to 895. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the stepbrother of Nahshon ben Zadok of note. He came to the chair on the death of that man.

He is known most of all for one court reply he made. Men of Kairwan had asked him of Eldad ha-Dani then. Eldad was a far guest who claimed a lost tribe root. The reply of Zemah treats that guest in nine points of law. It ends with a plea for the gaps in Eldad's tale. Zemah held those gaps to be mere slips of mind in age. One more reply of his lives on in a law book. No facts of his own life are known to men now at all.
mellon-ms-6-alchemical-miscellany-1435:
Mellon MS 6 is an Italian paper manuscript of about 1435. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the slim book, with 17 leaves. One hand wrote most of it, in a gothic antique script.

Two known works treat the magic traits ascribed to gems. They also treat the meaning held to sit in carved stones. Mixed in are steps to mend spoiled wine and tint glass. One step claims to ripen grapes early, and one to make an ass bray loud. Red ink marks most heads, capitals, and paragraph signs. Damp has marked the lower edges through the whole book.
nasa-tm-19680016260-lunar-explorer-35:
Norman F. Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center reports on Lunar Explorer 35 in this May 1968 paper, presented at COSPAR in Tokyo. The spin-stabilized spacecraft entered lunar orbit on 22 July 1967. It weighed about 104 kilograms and circled the Moon in about eleven and a half hours.

Its instruments included magnetometers, plasma probes, and detectors for energetic particles and cosmic dust. Bi-static radar tests probed the electrical properties of the lunar surface using reflected radio signals. Ness reports that the spacecraft operated continuously after launch. Its data gave scientists new views of the Moon's space environment and surface properties.
on-the-functions-of-the-brain-and-of-eac: Franz Josef Gall wrote this work on the brain, printed in 1835. Winslow Lewis translated it from the French. Gall argues that head shape reveals talents and traits. The hosted sample preserves only Google Books boilerplate text. It gives no readable pages of Gall's work itself. Readers can confirm the title, author, and translator from the metadata alone. Volume one treats the origin of moral and mental faculties in man.
openalex-w1999469035:
Tiina Sarkinen, Martijn Staats, James Richardson and colleagues tackled a practical problem in PLoS ONE in 2012. Herbaria hold huge numbers of dried plant specimens. Those specimens could serve DNA studies. Yet getting usable DNA from them is often hard.

The team compared shop-bought DNA extraction kits on herbarium specimens. They judged each method by DNA purity and yield. They also checked success at copying three DNA markers of different sizes. Methods differed a lot in performance. Clean DNA mattered more than the amount gained. Short DNA pieces copied far more often than long ones. How a specimen was prepared also affected success. The results help researchers choose methods for old plant material.
openalex-w2027420135:
Ian MacGregor-Fors and Mark Payton wrote a methods paper for ecologists in PLoS ONE in 2013. Ecologists often compare diversity between two places. Common software cannot run standard tests on richness estimates. Field workers needed a simple, valid shortcut.

One shortcut uses overlap between confidence intervals. If two intervals do not overlap, the values differ. The authors simulated how uneven intervals behave. They searched for an interval level that mimics a standard test. Intervals at the eighty-four percent level worked well. They matched the usual five percent test level. The paper gives step-by-step guides for two free programs. The guides cover EstimateS and Distance, both widely used for wildlife data.
openalex-w2076380535:
Sonia Silvente, Anatoly Sobolev and Miguel Lara compared how two soybean types respond to water shortage. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Soybeans supply protein and vegetable oil worldwide. They need steady water through the growing season. Drought at key stages cuts yields deeply.
