Melt convection washes partitioned solute away from the front, which paradoxically promotes solute trapping as the front outruns diffusion. The model explains the observed swing from ultra-fine cells to coarse ones. Trapping, once a defect, becomes a tool: faster freezing could cut crack risk in hard-to-print superalloys and steer alloy design.
pmc-10694135:
Sunju Lee and nine co-authors study white matter tract health in normal pressure hydrocephalus in a 2023 paper. In this brain condition, fluid builds up and harms walking, thinking, and bladder control. A scan sign called DESH, for fluid spaces that swell out of proportion, may help flag how a patient will do.

The team split patients by DESH score and set their diffusion scans next to matched healthy controls. Tract measures were read across many brain regions. The high-DESH group showed clear changes in key tracts, and the paper links those changes to the grade of the patients' symptoms.
pmc-10694935:
Camdon Fary and five colleagues compare early knee motion after robotic-assisted versus manual total knee replacement, in a 2023 study. They matched 216 robotic cases with 216 manual cases of similar age, sex, health, and body mass across several centers. Flexion and extension were measured before surgery and at one and three months after.

The robotic group gained more flexion at both checkups, by about seven degrees at one month and five at three. Only the robotic group ended the quarter above its starting flexion, and its patients had roughly double the odds of reaching 90 degrees of bend at one month. Complication rates matched. The authors credit the robot's precise cuts for the faster recovery.
pmc-10695535:
Chang Liu and Lei Ma compare blood-thinning strategies for chronic coronary syndromes by pooling trial evidence, in a study published in 2023. Patients can receive aspirin alone, various two- or three-drug combinations, or newer anticoagulant pairings, and head-to-head trials between all options will never be run. A Bayesian network meta-analysis lets the authors rank the options using ten randomized trials.

Outcomes included major cardiovascular events, death, heart attack, and major bleeding. In direct comparisons summarized here, no strategy clearly beat the others on the main cardiovascular endpoint. The ranking machinery still helps clinicians weigh small efficacy differences against bleeding risk, which is the everyday trade-off in this population. Full results extend beyond the summary available here.
pmc-10695935:
Networks usually link pairs, but real groups meet in threes and more, and reconstructing those group links from messy pair data is this study's puzzle. Ariane Lizotte and two co-authors build a Bayesian method in 2023 for hypergraphs whose edges join pairs and triples, observed only indirectly and with error. A sampling algorithm does the inference.

Tested on synthetic and real networks, the hypergraph model rebuilt the true structure more faithfully than a plain graph model could. The authors present the method as a minimal case that exposes the general problem's hard parts. Higher order structure, they show, is recoverable when the model admits it exists. Ignoring triples, by contrast, distorts the map.
pmc-10696035:
Chang, Cao, Lin, and Huang test a fermented mung bean preparation and three variants in twenty twenty-three. Praeparatum mungo is a traditional fermented food, called PM for short. Variants add turmeric, the enzyme bromelain, or added minerals during fermentation. The team set their antioxidant and related effects side by side. All three variants were made from the same base and were tested in the same way.

The bromelain variant, PM/B, held the most phenolic compounds and showed the strongest radical scavenging. The mineral variant, PM/IE, led on another radical test and on iron chelation. The turmeric variant, PM/T, best inhibited tyrosinase, an enzyme tied to pigmentation. The base extract calmed inflammation in stimulated mouse macrophages without killing them. These additions clearly boosted the properties of the base product. The authors see cosmetic and health applications ahead.
pmc-10696235:
Bananas bruise easily in handling, and bruises shorten shelf life in ways that depend on storage warmth. Mai Al-Dairi and co-authors swing a pendulum at bananas with three set energies in this 2023 study, then store the fruit at three temperatures for twelve days.

Harder hits made bigger, softer bruises. Water loss and leakage from cells depended most on storage temperature, then on time, then on hit strength. Fruit kept at the middle temperature colored most evenly, while warm storage sped up ripening gas release after hard hits. The team shows bruise softness alone can forecast much of the quality loss.
pmc-10696735:
Ljiljana Majnarić Trtica and co-authors model what drives loneliness in older patients, in a 2023 study. Loneliness speeds health decline, and long-term illness can deepen it, yet the two had rarely been studied in one frame. The team set out to build that joined picture.

The study covered 189 patients over sixty who attend primary care clinics. More illness load, anxiety, low positive mood, and few hobbies each predicted stronger loneliness. Poor social support, weaker thinking skills, and holding back feelings added to the risk as well. A second analysis traced how mood and thinking carry the effect of illness into loneliness. The authors suggest care that eases anxiety, lifts mood, and builds social support.
pmc-10696835:
Yi Chen and colleagues published a 2023 population study of HIV transmission as antiretroviral treatment expanded. Using genetic networks that link similar virus samples over time, they could see which patients' infections were connected to new cases. The question was whether wider treatment, which suppresses the virus, also slows its spread through a community.

Patients on treatment had notably lower transmission risk than those not treated, and the benefit grew when the virus stayed fully suppressed for years. Stopping treatment erased the advantage entirely. The molecular evidence reinforces a simple public health message: staying on effective therapy protects both the patient and everyone around them.
pmc-10697735:
Hongjing Xie, Xuewei Cao, Shuanglin Zhang, and Qiuying Sha present a method for testing gene links to many traits at once when cases are vastly outnumbered by controls. Large biobanks hold many traits per person, but most people are healthy for any one trait, and that imbalance inflates false alarms in standard tests. Joint testing across traits can raise power if the imbalance is handled.

Their method first builds a layered network from people who have at least one of the traits. A fast grouping step then clusters traits that travel together. A combined test finally checks each merged trait group against a gene variant. The pipeline is built for speed on biobank-scale data.
pmc-10699835:
Cervantée Wild and co-authors ask families how child health data should be held in a 2023 study. Linking large health datasets promises public gains, yet children's own views are rarely heard. The study ran in Aotearoa New Zealand through a community health service.

Five focus groups heard from Māori and non-Māori children, youth, and their caregivers. Young people and parents met in separate rooms so each could speak freely. A mixed research team ran the sessions and read the transcripts for themes. Storage, linking, and consent each drew firm expectations. Data stewards gain a clear brief: children want a say in their own records.
pmc-10700335:
Saif studies how a toy epidemic dies out along a line of sites, in a 2023 paper. The model cycles people through susceptible, infected, refractory, and susceptible again on a one-dimensional lattice. Oddly, the system shows two thresholds between active spread and total die-out: one at low infection odds, one at high.

Simulations say the low threshold behaves like directed percolation, the standard class for such transitions. At the high threshold the outcome grows hypersensitive to starting conditions, a mark of a sudden, discontinuous jump. Distribution checks and finite-size analysis back the reading. One road to silence, it turns out, comes in two very different styles.
pmc-10700535:
Shrinathan Esaki Muthu Pandara Kone, Kenichi Yatsugi, and Hideo Iizuka present a 2023 study of a motor powered through the air with no wires. Wireless power can feed phones and implants, but motors wobble as speed changes. Their system borrows a symmetry idea from physics to hold voltage steady.

Theory and bench tests agree: the motor runs stably across changing spin speeds. Coil misalignment also failed to break it. The design uses paired coils tuned to the special symmetry point. The authors say such robust wireless motors could serve self driving vehicles and other moving machines. Stable power without cables is the prize.
pmc-10701435:
Michael Omini, Deema Alsalih, SarahBeth Votra, and Dimitra Bourboulia present a lab protocol in a 2023 paper for studying a secreted cancer related enzyme. The enzyme, a tyrosine kinase, appears outside cells in the fluids of several human cancers, where it can modify other proteins. Prior large scale work found over one hundred possible target proteins.

The protocol walks through collecting the fluid cells secrete, plus cell extracts, then using antibodies and a nickel based pull down to capture the enzyme and its partners. Final steps detect protein interactions and phosphate tags added to targets. The method can be adapted to other secreted kinases. Full execution details are in the paper and its cited sources.
pmc-10701935:
Qin leads a team reporting prenatal cases where two chromosome problems appear together in a 2023 paper. Four fetuses carried both mosaic aneuploidy and uniparental disomy, where both gene copies come from one parent. Predicting outcomes for such mixes is hard.

A battery of tests, from karyotyping to exome sequencing, mapped each case. One fetus with low-level mosaicism looked normal before birth. The other three had poor outcomes, tied to imprinted regions or higher mosaic levels. At least two separate genetic accidents produced each combination. The authors stress testing for both problems at once when imprinted chromosomes are involved. Counseling for such pregnancies is crucial. Outcome hinges on mosaic level, tissue, and the genes involved.
pmc-10702335:
Carla Letícia Gediel Rivero-Wendt and co-authors test a farm disinfectant for harm to fish in a 2023 study. Chloramine T is used on fish farms to kill bacteria on gills and skin. Its chemical reactivity raised concern about side effects on fish themselves, so the team exposed adult zebrafish to three dose levels for four days.

At the top dose, cell nucleus flaws rose, which signals genetic harm. Shape changes in nuclei appeared at low and high doses. Gill and liver tissue showed low to moderate damage at all doses. A brain enzyme tied to nerve signals did not change. Readers get a caution that a common farm chemical is not harmless.
pmc-10703335:
Hye Jeon and Hae Yoo hunt gene variants that tie gout to daily habits in Korea. Gout, a searing joint inflammation from urate crystals, runs in families and lifestyles alike. Genome scans across two Korean cohorts, thousands of people in all, found fifteen linked variants. One in a known urate transport gene was new.

Several variants also tracked habits: smoking span, drinking amount, and exercise dose. A combined genetic risk score interacted with smoking duration to shift gout odds. The work suggests genes and habits do not merely add up; they amplify each other. The authors see tailored prevention for high risk carriers.
pmc-10704635:
Niklas Nilsson and colleagues review two surgical fixes for old Achilles tendon tears, in a synthesis from 2023. Tears left untreated past four weeks count as chronic and need graft style repair. Two donor choices dominate: a calf sheet flap or a hamstring tendon graft.

Thirty-six studies with over seven hundred patients met the review entry rules. Both fixes scored well on tendon and ankle function scales after surgery. Flap patients healed wounds with more trouble than graft patients in the set. Graft patients instead saw more injuries to a nearby skin nerve. Study quality ran mostly low, so firm ranking needs better trials.
pmc-10704835:
Hang Zhu and co-authors mapped genes tied to trace element levels in maize grain in a 2023 study. Maize feeds people and livestock worldwide and supplies minerals such as manganese, iron, and molybdenum. Breeding grain richer in these elements is a nutrition goal, but the genetics are scattered and small in effect.

The team grew one hundred seventy maize lines and measured grain mineral content. Two genome-wide association models scanned for DNA spots linked to each element. Dozens of spots emerged for manganese, with fewer for the other elements. Each spot is a breeding handle: markers let breeders select mineral-rich lines without slow lab assays of every harvest. The catalog supports biofortified maize for regions where mineral deficiency is common.
pmc-10705335:
Alon Vigdorovits, Maria Magdalena Köteles, Gheorghe-Emilian Olteanu, and Ovidiu Pop review artificial intelligence in cancer pathology for poor health systems in this 2023 paper. Pathology is the base of cancer care: it names the tumor and increasingly predicts how it will answer treatment. Yet in resource-scarce systems, pathology funding comes last.

Digitized slides change the odds. Once tissue images are digital, AI tools can sort tumor types, predict gene changes from the picture alone, and count biomarkers faster than tired human eyes. The review surveys those directions and gives examples of tools already built. The authors see a chance to leapfrog: clinics short on specialists could still deliver modern cancer diagnosis, if the digital base and the tools are chosen well.
pmc-10705735:
Çağlar Ünal and co-authors report a single-center experience from 2023 treating spread neuroendocrine tumors with a gentle drug schedule. Metronomic dosing gives the chemotherapy drug temozolomide in small, frequent doses rather than big bursts, paired here with bevacizumab, a drug that blocks tumor blood vessel growth. The study focused on patients whose tumor growth index stayed under fifty-five percent.

Records for thirty patients showed a median time without tumor growth of about sixteen months and median survival near twenty-six months. Disease was controlled in about eighty-seven percent and shrank measurably in about sixty-three percent. No severe grade four side effects appeared, which suits older or frail patients. The authors call for larger trials to compare the pairing with standard therapy.
pmc-10705835: Hussain and co-authors report harm from krokodil, a street form of the opioid desomorphine. Their patient developed a skin ulcer that would not heal. He also suffered a sudden heart rhythm problem. Clots formed in the veins of both his arms. Their 2023 case sets out learning points for clinicians. The drug can cause chronic ulcers, new rhythm problems can appear in its users, and arm vein clots can follow as a complication.
pmc-10706935:
Weijian Han and a team of co-authors study how mast cells respond to harmless copies of a farm animal virus, in two thousand twenty-three. Mast cells are immune cells that can sense the copies through a sugar-binding receptor. The copies mimic foot-and-mouth disease virus without causing disease.

The team mapped which parts of the cell's DNA packaging opened or closed after the sensing. Open regions pointed to several signal paths, with one path standing out. Blocking the receptor lowered key signal and messenger levels in the cells. The work suggests that DNA packaging shifts help set which messengers the cells release. That idea may guide new vaccine design for the disease.
pmc-10707235:
Rosanna Mallamaci and co-authors test whether spirulina protects nerve-like cells from heavy metals, in this 2023 Europe PMC paper. Spirulina is a microalga sold worldwide as a dietary supplement, with antioxidant and metal-binding properties. The team exposed human neuroblastoma cells to cadmium, mercury and lead, alone and mixed with spirulina, for up to three days.

All three metals lowered cell survival, with the ranking of harm shifting over time. Spirulina treatments at several doses considerably raised survival of metal-exposed cells. A second assay, tracking enzyme release from damaged cells, matched the survival pattern. The authors present the work as early in vitro evidence for a protective effect worth further study.
pmc-10708835:
Mengsi Wang and seven co-authors predict leg joint torque with two learning methods. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, aims at walking in the side plane. Torque is the twist force at hip, knee, and ankle. Old methods need floor force plates or complex body models, both of which slow real use.

Inputs come from skin sensors on five leg muscles plus three joint angles. One model reads sequences over time, and the other is a flexible curve fitter. Both land most errors below fifteen percent. Their scores track true torque closely across joints. The work supports smart braces and rehab tools that must sense effort fast.
pmc-10709435:
Xiao Ling and colleagues searched in 2023 for CT-based radiomic markers that predict survival in oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer where non-invasive prognosis tools are limited. Records and scans from one hundred forty-nine patients were mined for image features tied to outcome, alongside clinical facts.

A screening pipeline picked a small feature set, which fed survival models that tested fairly well. Two image features stood out, along with cancer stage and alcohol use. Patients split by one feature had sharply different three-year survival, about ninety percent versus about half. The second feature split survival in the opposite direction. The authors say such markers could help tailor treatment plans.
pmc-10709535:
Jane Waldfogel and co-authors compare what preschool children get at home across six rich countries, in a 2023 study. Family income and center based care at ages three and four set up later schooling. Parental education splits both, but policy may soften the split.

Matched data covered the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Japan. Gaps by parental education appeared everywhere, yet their size varied with each country's policy design, partly as predicted. How education is measured matters too: counting only the mother's schooling shrinks income gaps and widens care gaps. The study ranks among the first cross country checks of its kind.
pmc-10709635:
Sushadi and co-authors extend the fertile life of stored chicken semen in this 2023 study. Liquid semen storage matters for poultry breeding and for conserving breeds whose sperm freeze poorly. Yet even short storage in a tube cuts fertility fast, unlike the weeks sperm survive inside the hen's storage tubules.

Calcium inside sperm steers energy use, so the team added calcium-removing agents to the storage fluid. Two agents, one acting outside the cells and one inside, each prolonged fertility, confirmed by live fertility tests. The agents reshaped power-plant metabolism and energy spending in different ways, tied to a two-phase control of the motor protein that drives sperm tails.
pmc-10709935:
Shih-Kai Hung and co-authors ask which breast cancer patients gain most from radiation after breast-conserving surgery. Their 2023 study sorts tumors by molecular subtype, the pattern of markers in the cancer cells, giving groups such as luminal A and HER2-enriched. Earlier work left open whether the gain from radiation differs across these groups.

The team drew on a Taiwan health insurance database and studied 59,502 patients treated from 2006 to 2019. Within each subtype, they matched patients who had radiation with similar patients who did not, then compared local and regional return of the cancer, spread to distant sites, and survival. Their design aims to show which subtypes truly benefit from added radiation and which may safely gain little, a question that shapes care after surgery.
pmc-10710635:
Brain tumors of childhood now sort by their gene marks, and the surgeon's plan must sort with them. Akira Gomi, Hirofumi Oguma, and Kensuke Kawai look back in 2023 at forty-one young patients cut at their center over two decades. The new world rule book splits child growths from adult ones, and targeted drugs wait on the gene read. Their set held mostly the slow kinds.

The tame, boxed-in growths and the child-type spread ones filled the slate; the adult-type spread kind never showed. Most of these carry a kinder fate than adult growths, the team note. For growths near the sight path, a small bite for the gene read can beat a bold cut. For the seizure-linked kinds, a full cut can free the child of fits. Gene first, knife second is the drift.
pmc-10712035:
Elena Kraus and four co-authors explore how women with chronic illness weigh pregnancy and birth control, in a 2023 interview study. More women of child-bearing age now live with long-term conditions that raise pregnancy risk. Yet their rates of unplanned pregnancy match those of low-risk mothers. The team spoke at length with twenty-eight pregnant women with prior conditions at a specialist hospital. Surveys and health records added context for each woman.

Four themes stood out: felt risks and gains of pregnancy, felt risks and gains of birth control, drivers of birth control use, and a sense of choice over one's own fertility. Most saw birth control as fine to use but worried about side effects on body and mind. More found pregnancy a source of pride than a health threat. The authors say prior illness alone did not steer choices much.
pmc-10712135:
Won-Kyu Rhim and co-authors review engineered cell vesicles for healing medicine in a 2023 paper. Extracellular vesicles are nano parcels shed by cells that mirror their source cell traits. Labs now tune those parcels to carry repair cues on purpose.

The review sorts culture tricks that steer vesicle yield and punch, from starved media to 3D growth and low oxygen. It then sorts split routes, from fast spins to flow filters. Four build styles, gene edits, loaded goods, in cell loading, and hybrids, round out the kit. Uses span kidney, joint, nerve, and immune ills in early work.
pmc-10713535:
Mateja Perović and co-authors show that learning the exceptions to a rule shifts across the menstrual cycle. Their 2023 study tests 171 people on a category task where most items follow a rule but a few break it. Ovarian hormones are known to affect the brain, yet their role in such learning was underexplored.

Participants in the high-estradiol phase learned exceptions faster and better than those in the low phase. They also outpaced a male comparison group on exception learning. The authors link the effect to estradiol's action on pattern separation and completion in the hippocampus. They argue that cognitive neuroscience should routinely account for cycle phase and sex-related variables.
pmc-10713635:
Sedlak and coauthors build DNA tools to study the Colorado potato beetle. The beetle is a major pest of potato crops worldwide. The team sought markers on the sex chromosome of the beetle. Those markers can show how diverse wild groups are.

They found ten strong markers from past DNA data. Tests used 420 adult beetles from 14 sites in Czechia and Slovakia. Tests also used 866 larvae from five single-mother broods. Six markers varied in length across beetles. The team found far fewer gene mixes than math would predict. Spread of types was uneven across sites.
pmc-10714535:
Evans and co-authors build a rule set to derive growth stage from rolls. Stage at first find is a key fact for growth care. Yet wards oft fail to send stage facts to growth rolls. Rolls in Australia show thin stage facts for womb growth now. The team set rules to let roll staff work stage from roll facts. Rules rest on the AJCC TNM frame in its eighth form. A pro group of care leads, counters, and code staff blessed the rules.

Base fullness of the facts the rules need got scored per state. The share of cases a stage could be set for was counted too. Stage splits by lump size, node spread, and far spread in the frame. The rule set takes the name RD-Stage in the text. It aims to fill the stage gap in roll data sets.
pmc-10716135:
Yingjun Sang and colleagues plan routes for oil sample transportation using an improved version of the A-star pathfinding algorithm. Their 2023 study fixes sharp turns, weak direction guidance, and excessive computed nodes in the classic method.

Their directional search variant adds an angle constraint to the evaluation function, converting sharp turns into obtuse angles for smoother paths. An enhanced distance function strengthens guidance toward the target, shrinking the search space and planning time. Redundant path nodes are removed for a more concise route. An improved step-size adjustment further trims node counts and boosts efficiency. Simulation experiments compared the new algorithm against the traditional one on route quality.
pmc-10716935:
Alice Murage and Julia Smith published a study in 2023 on how the pandemic hit recent immigrant women working in hotels and food service in Canada. These women faced layered insecurity at the meeting point of gender, race, migration, and labor. The team used in-depth interviews and a work precarity framework to sort their experiences. The question was how shaky work shaped wellbeing during the crisis.

The pandemic deepened prior marginalization in three forms: unstable hours and jobs, low income from work, and unsafe conditions at work. Work insecurity stood out as a driver of poor mental health. The authors urge policy steps in recovery that cut the inequities the crisis exposed and rebuilt.
pmc-10719335:
Hang Zhou and co-authors used gene data to link eye thickness with Parkinson's symptoms beyond movement, in a 2023 study. The retina thins in Parkinson's, but whether that ties to symptom severity was unclear. Their method, Mendelian randomization, treats gene variants as natural experiments, comparing people born with thinner or thicker retinal layers on paper.

Thinner nerve fiber layers tied to lower odds of constipation and to slightly milder total symptom scores. A thinner inner layer also tied to less constipation, yet to higher depression risk. The mixed pattern warns against simple stories. Still, the eye may offer a cheap window on the non-motor face of the disease.
pmc-10720235:
Stephen Adesina and colleagues study why fracture patients in a low-resource setting fail to return for follow-up, and what can be done about it. Most traumatic injuries occur in low- and middle-income countries, yet the literature comes chiefly from wealthy countries, partly because follow-up is so poor. Clinical and radiographic review after surgery is essential to monitor healing and catch complications.

The prospective study enrolled five hundred ninety-four patients with long-bone fractures treated with SIGN nails. Before discharge, staff explained the importance of follow-up, encouraged attendance even when patients felt well, and validated addresses and phone numbers. Patients who missed appointments were contacted by phone; those who repeatedly failed to attend rescheduled visits received home visits. The study identifies predictors of non-attendance from socio-demographic and clinical data. It also tests whether mobile phone contact and home visiting raise attendance rates.
pmc-10720335:
Mei-Yan Gao and a team of co-authors report a layered material that sorts a family of petrochemical feedstocks. Their twenty twenty-three article deals with C8 aromatics: the three xylene isomers and ethylbenzene. Splitting these near-twins now takes energy-hungry distillation, so a sorbent that grabs them by shape would save a lot.

Their network, built from zinc and two linker molecules, acts like clay that swells in steps. It takes up about a fifth of its weight in the liquids. Crystal studies show it shifts between narrow, middle, and wide pore forms as guests enter. In mixed feeds it picked out three of the four isomers over ortho-xylene, a first for such sorbents.
pmc-10723135:
Tyler Sowers and five co-authors test a soil treatment that locks lead and arsenic into minerals the stomach can barely dissolve. Digging up poisoned soil is costly and damaging, and chemical fixes for both metals at once are rare. Their method seeds soil with potassium jarosite, nudging the metals to convert into jarosite-family minerals such as plumbojarosite and beudantite. Pot experiments checked conversion across temperatures and doses.

Every treatment variant formed the target minerals and cut the share of metal that gut-like acid could mobilize. Warmth helped, but the jarosite seed itself mattered most. Treated soils dropped below ten percent accessible lead and arsenic, down from roughly seventy and sixty percent untreated. The authors present the approach as a rare single fix for two major poisons. Field trials are the stated next step toward real cleanups.
pmc-10725635:
Ayogeboh Epizitone, Smangele Pretty Moyane, and Israel Edem Agbehadji propose in 2023 a data driven model for health information systems that can last and adapt. Shocks such as pandemics have pushed health care toward digital systems. Those systems now produce endless complex data. Their study reviews the literature through the data lens, following standard rules for systematic reviews.

Five parts of the model are set out: data sources, data actions and decisions, and data science methods. The order in which methods are placed, and how insights are put to use, complete the set. The authors argue these parts are essential for a robust system that can keep serving care under change.
pmc-10725835:
Kathryn King and co-authors scan the trial evidence on helping patients actually take their long-term medicines, across three immune diseases, in a scoping review from 2023. Non-adherence is rife: up to three quarters of bowel disease patients, most arthritis patients, and half of multiple sclerosis patients skip doses meant to hold remission. The team gathered randomized trials from 2012 to 2021.

Twenty-four trials with 3,024 patients qualified, ten of them pilots. Only nine clearly improved adherence. Every winner used tailored, personal education or counseling from a trained professional, mostly face to face. Technology-led programs also leaned effective, and simple tools like diaries and calendars helped. Few trials rested on an adherence theory. The authors call for personal, theory-grounded designs.
pmc-10726135:
Jonathan Deans and thirteen co-authors show how one liver gene's two versions split the day's work in a 2023 paper. The gene, a master regulator of liver identity, is read from two starting points, yielding two protein isoforms. One dominates adult liver; the other was thought to appear only before birth and in liver cancer.

The team found the second version present in normal adult liver at two times of day. Mice engineered to make only that version ran a distinct program of gene activity and chemistry, shaped by different partners, including clock proteins. Removing the core clock gene changed the second version's rhythm but not the first's, exposing a feedback loop. The division of labor was stark: version one drives sugar production, version two drives ketone production, and females need it for normal ketone levels. The ancient two-starter design, the authors propose, keeps the liver's daily balance.
pmc-10727335:
Ngo and coauthors tally extra bed days and costs from harms after heart ablation. Catheter ablation treats a common faulty heart rhythm. Harm rates and types after the step are well logged. Their toll on stay length and hospital cost was unknown.

The set held more than 20,000 adults in Australia. Mean age was near 63 years, and women were near a third. Most stays lasted just one day in the group. Cost data came from a national hospital cost pool. Harms in the 30 days after discharge were tracked. Models gauged extra cost per harm type in 2021 dollars.
pmc-10728335:
Honey is often stretched with cheap syrups, and Oroian and co-authors compared two ways of catching the fraud. They spiked tilia honey with corn, rice, agave, maple, and inverted sugar syrups at 5, 10, and 20 percent. One approach tracked classic chemistry: moisture, acidity, conductivity, sugars, and a heat-damage marker. The other listened to the honey's electrical response across frequencies with gold electrodes.

Both data types separated pure from adulterated samples when fed to pattern classifiers. A support vector machine sorted them much more cleanly than partial least squares analysis. The team presents impedance sensing as a fast screening partner to lab chemistry.
pmc-10729235:
Shumaila Furnaz and co-authors study outcomes of children's heart surgery in Pakistan in a 2023 paper. The data come from a quality registry at the national heart institute in Karachi. Care for children born with heart defects is hard to deliver where resources are thin, and local outcome data guide where to improve first.

More than thirty-three hundred operations were reviewed. Most patients were boys, and most were between one and seventeen years old. About seven in one hundred patients died in the hospital. Infection after surgery was also common. Death risk rose for the youngest children, for those with low blood oxygen, and for the most complex operations on a standard risk scale. Teenagers fared better than young children. The authors say infection control and care for high-risk cases are the top targets.
pmc-10730935:
Tommaso Davini and co-authors ask whether head trauma after birth is an overlooked cause of fluid-filled cavities in the brains of dogs and cats. Such cavities, called porencephaly, are usually blamed on development before birth. The team searched two centers' records over seventeen years for animals with MRI-proven lesions.

They gathered 32 cases, 23 dogs and nine cats. About a fifth were six years or older when diagnosed. The scans were re-read for brain lesions plus signs of past injury to the skull and muscles. The study hunts for scan features that separate trauma-born cavities from inborn ones, and checks how often these patients have seizures.
pmc-10734035:
Lis Corral-Gómez and four colleagues propose estimating diesel spray momentum from the easier measurement of fuel injection rate. Momentum flux governs how fuel mixes with air in the chamber, but measuring it directly is complex. Their method targets sustainable synthetic fuels in small engines for light aviation and drones.

They tested single-hole nozzles of three sizes with a conventional diesel, a gas-to-liquid fuel, and hydrotreated vegetable oil in a common-rail system. Feeding measured injection rates into their simple model reproduced momentum flux values with very good precision against earlier direct measurements on multi-hole nozzles. The authors offer the procedure to researchers modeling sprays of new renewable fuels without specialized rigs.
pmc-10735335:
A support group for people grieving after years of dementia caregiving worked well, but two leaders could not scale it and its members were mostly White. Zachary Baker and co-authors describe, in this 2023 conference abstract, how they built a wider team to carry the group to more people. Community partners joined the design from the start, shaping goals and the funding bid.

The team chose to focus first on African American caregivers, where local ties were strong. On a partner's advice, they also paused to ask whether unmet needs truly existed, rather than assuming them. That step honored community strengths and made the research stronger either way. Even a finding of no unmet need would teach lessons worth sharing with other groups.
pmc-10735435:
Darlingtina Esiaka examines what shapes dementia risk in older Black men, in a study from 2023. Beyond biology, schooling, neighborhood, and income shape cognitive aging. Black men are starkly underrepresented in dementia research, which blocks tailored prevention.

Within-group analysis used survey data from 178 men aged seventy and older, plus ongoing collection from a younger cohort. Less neighborhood disorder, such as vandalism, linked to better executive function scores. Better sleep quality also linked to stronger executive performance. The author frames the work as a step toward early risk and protection markers in this group.
pmc-10735535:
Molei Liu and co-authors read whole-body health from saliva protein dynamics in a 2023 pilot study. Organs talk to each other constantly, and the protein chorus in saliva may echo that conversation. Six patients with severe mitochondrial disease and six matched healthy people gave timed samples around waking.

Nearly three thousand proteins were tracked across the morning recalibration. The pattern of proteins rising and falling together differed sharply between groups. Network analysis distilled features that tracked health status, correlating with self-rated health up to a solid level. The team proposes proteome dynamics as an accessible window on intrinsic health, worth testing at scale.
pmc-10735635:
Megan Mullins and co-authors ask whether memory problems change cancer care in this 2023 study. They linked a national survey of older Americans with Medicare claims from 2000 to 2016, covering breast and prostate cancers. They also surveyed cancer doctors, giving each a case sketch of a patient with either mild memory loss or normal thinking.

Women with dementia had far lower odds of getting radiation for breast cancer than women with normal thinking. Doctors were also less likely to advise chemo for a breast patient sketched with mild memory loss. Prostate care showed no such gap. Many doctors overestimated how often mild loss turns into dementia, and they leaned more on family wishes in those cases. The authors flag a bias worth correcting.
pmc-10735735:
Yan Du and co-authors present a 2023 study of what shapes diet and movement habits in older adults with type two diabetes. Talks with fifteen mostly Latino adults, near age seventy, closed a twelve-week self-watch study. Two readers coded the talks by a five-level social frame.

Traits ran from know-how and self-trust at the person level to kin and doctor sway, gear access at senior homes, culture norms, and policy. Traits at one level bent those at others, so one-level fixes fall short. The team calls for layered programs that work all five levels at once.
pmc-10735835:
Colin McKenzie, Shinya Kajitani, and Kei Sakata published an economics study in 2023 on why health behavior changes at retirement. The team studied Japanese men and women using fourteen waves of a national survey of middle-aged and older people. Outcomes covered drinking, smoking, exercise, and mental distress. Pension age rules served as instruments to handle the fact that retirement is a choice.

Retirement did not change stated intentions to limit drinking or smoking or to exercise enough. Mental distress fell for both sexes after retirement. The share of men drinking fell, and smoking shares fell for both sexes, while moderate exercise rose. The authors read the pattern as stress relief at work's end, not income loss.
pmc-10735935:
Chunhong Xiao and co-authors track how nursing home residents with dementia resist mouth care over time, and what that means for oral health. People who push back against care often end up with poor teeth and gums. Their 2023 study followed seventy-five residents for twenty-one days, rating resistance morning and afternoon. A trajectory model sorted residents into patter groups.

Three resistance paths appeared at each time of day. Starting resistance, care length, and antipsychotic count best predicted group membership. High-resistance groups had the worst oral health and the fewest finished cleanings, though oral health improved in every group. The authors suggest fitting care timing to each person's daily pattern.
pmc-10736135:
Yulin Yang and co-authors linked prison history to pain in later life in a 2023 study. Time behind bars dogs health across the years, from hearts to minds. Whether it also shapes how much pain older adults live with was barely studied.

The team drew on a national survey of United States adults aged 50 and up, with waves from 2012 to 2018. Pain paths were compared between those who had been incarcerated and those who had not. Models tracked how pain rose or eased over the years. The work argues that pain care for older adults should reckon with prison's long shadow.
pmc-10736235:
Shoulder pain and weakness are common in older adults and can make daily tasks hard. Ranyah Almardawi, Derik Davis, and Denise Orwig test whether a simple hand grip strength measure tracks shoulder trouble in older women. Grip strength is cheap and quick to test, and it often stands in for overall muscle strength and function.

The team studied 36 women aged 62 to 84. They measured grip with a hand device and asked each woman to rate her shoulder function on a standard survey. Grip strength and shoulder scores moved together: women with stronger grips reported better shoulder function, with a clear link between the two. The authors suggest grip testing could serve as a simple screen for shoulder problems, pending tests in larger groups.
pmc-10736335:
Megan Wilson, Isaiah Spears, Sara Norton, Ryan Bogdan, and Thomas Oltmanns study unfair treatment and sense of purpose in older adults in 2023. Purpose means a felt sense of goals and direction in life. The sample held 1,630 adults with a mean age near 73 years.

Unfair treatment went with lower purpose across the group, and race did not change that link in these data. More schooling softened the tie, which hints that learning can guard purpose. Purpose also blunted the tie between unfair treatment and poor health, a sign it may act as a shield in later life.
pmc-10736435:
Zhuoer Lin, Yi Wang, Thomas Gill, and Xi Chen wrote a study from 2023 on whether attending segregated primary schools in childhood leaves a mark on the mind in old age. Most past work looked at segregated housing, not classrooms. The team linked state school separation scores from the late 1960s to a national survey of Americans over fifty. More than thirty thousand adults, Black and White, entered the analysis, matched by where they lived as children.

Higher childhood exposure to school segregation predicted lower thinking scores and more impairment after fifty, for both groups. The hit was larger for Black participants. Schooling and later wealth explained much of the link, between forty and seventy percent. Yet a clear effect survived even rich late-life controls. The authors argue that desegregating schools, within and between districts, is also long-range brain health policy.
pmc-10736635:
Elizabeth Zambrano Garza and a team of co-authors show that rumination, the loop of negative self-focused thought, spills between close partners. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic supplied a season of deep uncertainty.

One hundred forty older Canadian adults and a close other each kept evening diaries for ten days. Most partners were spouses. On days a person ruminated more, their own mood soured, matching known results. The new finding crossed the pair: a partner's rumination also raised the other's negative mood and cut positive mood. The effects were small per day but steady. The authors argue well-being research must treat rumination as a shared weather, not a private storm.
pmc-10736735:
Nancy Kusmaul, Amy Roberts, and Mercedes Bern-Klug report in 2023 on how nursing home social service heads handle clashes at work. These staff weigh the needs of residents, kin, and care staff, often when those needs pull apart. They also stand with families at the end of life.

The team read open replies from a national sample of such heads. Two prompts asked what they like in the job and what they would change. The replies show what these heads prize when rights clash and whose claims they put first. Home chiefs gain insight into a role that quietly holds much of home life in balance.
pmc-10736835:
Marie Savundranayagam and six co-authors studied whether care organizations are ready for a virtual reality training program in a 2023 paper. The program teaches frontline care workers to communicate with people living with dementia in a person-centered way. Before rolling out such a tool, leaders need to know what helps or blocks adoption.

The team interviewed nine managers from home care and long-term care settings in Canada. Using a standard framework for putting new practices in place, they sorted the answers into themes. Four themes stood out: openness to virtual reality as a training tool, the logistics of staffing and training time, a culture that supports staff growth, and outside pressures to keep organizations sustainable. The findings tell program designers what to fix first, from scheduling to leadership buy-in, before the headsets arrive.
pmc-10736935:
Joanne Murabito and co-authors test how easy a smartphone app for health data is for older adults to use. Published in 2023, the study worked with two groups of 15 older adults: one from the Framingham Heart Study and one more diverse sample. Average ages were about 72 and 71 years. Few past studies check app usability in this age group.

People completed surveys, a body map task for pain sites, and thinking tests on the phone while thinking aloud. Coders scored errors from the recordings. Most people were satisfied with the app, and scores for function and look were similar in both groups. The majority finished self report tasks without trouble, the authors report.
pmc-10737035:
Ayumi Honda, Yin Liu, Elizabeth Fauth, and Sumihisa Honda survey working family caregivers in Japan in two thousand twenty-three. Many adults both hold jobs and care for an older relative at home. The study asks whether clashes between the job and the care role drag down life satisfaction.

One hundred forty-one caregivers under sixty-five who lived with their care recipient took part. A regression model weighed the clash, the burden of care, and their interplay. The clash itself raised the risk of poor satisfaction. Among those who felt it, two or more burdens made poor satisfaction far more likely, with odds over five times higher. Among those without the clash, extra burdens made no such split. The authors urge support at work.
pmc-10737235:
A 2023 study from Taiwan tests case management for family caregivers of people with early cognitive decline. Caregivers of persons with mild cognitive impairment or early dementia carry heavy strain, and structured support programs are one proposed remedy. No author is named in the record.

Dyads of caregiver and care recipient were recruited from memory clinics and assigned to an experimental or control group. Thirty-eight dyads received case manager services over four months, while thirty-three received general health education, with data collected at three time points. The design shows whether a dedicated case manager measurably eases caregiver burden.
pmc-10737335:
Cancer treatments save lives but can leave older survivors at higher risk of dementia. Jayden Haggler and co-authors asked in 2023 whether gut microbes help explain that risk. They studied 110 adults aged sixty and over from a gut-and-brain aging consortium, sequencing the gut microbiome and testing thinking skills with standard screening tools.

Cognitive impairment appeared in 46 percent of cancer survivors versus 38 percent of others. Comparing by thinking status alone, one microbe, Escherichia coli, ran higher in the impaired group, while a yogurt-linked species ran higher in the healthy group. Several other species were enriched in survivors, and one of them also tracked with impairment among survivors. The authors suggest treatment-shaped gut signatures may feed into cognitive decline, and that understanding them could guide therapies for treatment side effects.
pmc-10737435:
Monica Beck and Amelia Gallagher build a nurse training program in a 2023 paper on spiritual care. Nurses often hold back from asking older cancer patients about spiritual needs, though such talks improve outcomes. Lack of training, skill, and time are the usual reasons given for that silence.

Their program, Lift the Spirit, teaches communication for spiritual histories. It rests on national palliative care guidelines: respect for patient and family beliefs, reflection by the provider, and screening with a validated tool. Seventeen nurses tried a learning module in a pilot. The study checks whether the program is workable and welcome, ahead of wider use.
pmc-10737535:
Shannon Richard, Du Feng, Dieu-My Tran, Brenna Renn, and Jinyoung Kim published a study in 2023 on metabolic syndrome and lifestyle factors among Hispanic adults in the United States. This group faces high rates of the syndrome, a cluster raising heart and diabetes risk. The team reanalyzed a large community health study of over fourteen thousand adults from seven heritage backgrounds.

Low physical activity and disordered sleep breathing tracked membership in the syndrome group taking medication. Heavy drinking lowered the odds of that group. Smoking history showed no clear link. Gender reshaped several ties, including diet and alcohol effects, and heritage differences ran through every measure. The authors flag midlife as a prime window for prevention work.
pmc-10737635:
Grace Rose and co-authors review trials that pair exercise care with mind based care in a 2023 paper. Exercise care aims to keep older adults able and active. Low drive and low self trust can keep people from joining in, which cuts the gains.

The team searched four data bases and screened near five thousand papers down to thirty one trials. Each trial was read through a world health frame for function and daily life. Most trials checked body function, and most checked acts and social roles too. The review sums up what paired care has shown so far and where proof stays thin.
pmc-10737835:
Heng Wu compared old-age income and health in China and the United States in a 2023 study. Frailty, a state of weakness and low reserve, hits older adults hard. Income in old age rests on three legs: public pensions, private pensions, and savings. Wu asked how each source of income ties to frailty under two unlike welfare systems. Data came from matched retirement studies in each nation.

Health was scored with a five-item frailty scale. Outcomes split a great deal by nation and by income type. Public pension, job pension, savings, and other supports each showed their own pattern. The paper adds to debate on how welfare states shape health gaps in later life.
pmc-10737935:
Jason Grullon, Daniel Soong, and Roger Wong present a 2023 study of social isolation and dementia risk across racial and ethnic groups in the United States. Being cut off from others has been linked with thinking decline. Past work rarely used proven isolation measures or split the results by group.

The team used eleven years of a national aging study, from 2011 to 2021. Their sample held 6,155 adults aged sixty five and older who lived in the community. A longitudinal isolation score was built from a validated measure. Black, Hispanic, and Asian older adults showed higher average isolation than white peers across the span, the authors report.
pmc-10738035:
Ryan Dougherty and co-authors link hand and body strength to brain shrinkage in a 2023 aging study. Weak motor skills track with smaller brains and poorer thinking, but whether fine hand control and whole-body movement age the brain in the same way was unclear.

The team analyzed 726 participants in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, most in their seventies, with 525 scanned again over about five years. Dexterity came from a pegboard test, and gross motor skill from grip strength and movement batteries. Both skills tied to roomier brain regions and smaller ventricles at the start. The study also weighed blood vessel damage and daily activity, separating what hand and body each say about the aging brain.
pmc-10738135:
Zach Gassoumis, Jeanine Yonashiro-Cho, Elizabeth Avent, and Laura Mosqueda study what raises or lowers the risk of mistreatment for people living with dementia. Their 2023 paper draws on interviews with care groups, each pairing a person with dementia and their care partners. Dependence on others for daily tasks creates openings for abuse, neglect, and exploitation.

Nearly a quarter of the people with dementia in the sample had experienced mistreatment. Emotional abuse was most common, then neglect, then financial exploitation. Early analysis ties higher odds to the person's own alcohol or substance misuse and to education differences. Risk can sit with the person, the partner, or their shared setting, so protection has to scan all three.
pmc-10738535:
Harris-Love and colleagues reviewed in 2023 studies linking ultrasound brightness of thigh muscle to knee strength in older adults. Brighter muscle on ultrasound, called echogenicity, signals poorer muscle quality. Across twelve studies, brighter quadriceps went with weaker knee extension. The links were weak to moderate. Averaging several thigh muscles gave stronger links than any single one.

Correcting the readings for fat thickness under the skin also sharpened the results, though not in every study. The authors see ultrasound as a promising screen for age-related mobility problems. They urge future work to report all thigh muscles, with and without fat correction, so results can be pooled properly.
pmc-10738635:
Valerie Greer, Terry Fulmer, Ashley Cadiz, Christopher Hernandez, and Linda Edelman report on a symposium about building age-friendly ecosystems, in this 2023 paper. The age-friendly movement adapts neighborhoods, health systems, and campuses to serve older adults better. The online gathering brought national experts and regional aging stakeholders together to take a place-based view.

About one hundred thirteen people attended, including twenty-seven health professions students, and most said the event deepened their grasp of age-friendly ideas. Talks, panels, and group work pointed to gains from shared language and shared measures across neighborhoods, campuses, and clinics. Planned outputs include a website, a resource guide, and a book. The authors frame the meeting as a base for wider teamwork on fair, healthy aging.
pmc-10738735:
Stacy Yun and Sara Qualls study depression among Korean older adults who care for a spouse in a paper from 2023. The data come from a 2017 national survey of older Koreans. Three hundred sixty-nine caregiving couples were analyzed, with partners in their eighties on average. The team tested how family values, burden, social support, and coping relate to depression, using a cultural stress model.

Lower perceived social support was the strongest predictor of depression. Older age, less schooling, and fewer living relatives also mattered. Burden raised depression mainly by eroding felt support. Cultural values and coping styles played smaller roles. The authors urge creative ways to raise felt support, above all for rural caregivers with thin networks.
pmc-10738935:
Care robots can ease the load on families and staff, but only if older adults will accept them, and Hee Jeong Yoon and co-authors survey what tips that acceptance in Korea. Their 2023 study questioned more than five hundred community-dwelling adults over sixty. Acceptance was modeled against background, health, and technology factors in layers.

Schooling and town living raised acceptance, as did better self-rated health and daily functioning. Among technology factors, digital literacy helped while stress about technology hurt. The authors urge programs that raise digital skills and calm tech anxiety, especially for rural, less-educated, and frailer elders, before robots are rolled out.
pmc-10739035:
Rozmin Jiwani and co-authors study group yoga and mindfulness for South Asian women, in a research report from 2023. South Asian adults in the United States report high rates of mental distress, and women face higher risk than men. Many women read mental strain as body illness and avoid care, so a group program may fit better.

Thirty women aged forty-five and older joined weekly ninety-minute sessions for twelve weeks. Sessions mixed yoga poses, meditation, and mindfulness practice. Early data at six weeks showed strong attendance and gains in mindfulness scores. Most women in the group were overweight at the start. The report tests whether the program is workable and helpful.
pmc-10739135:
Elise Bisset and Susan Howlett tested whether dietary nitrate and aerobic exercise can slow frailty in female mice, publishing in twenty twenty-three. Earlier work by the pair showed exercise alone softens frailty in older females. Here they added sodium nitrate to the drinking water. Adult and aged mice received the supplement, a running wheel, both, or neither for three months.

Blood pressure was unchanged by nitrate or exercise at either age. Older sedentary mice grew frailer over the study, while nitrate, exercise, and the combination each prevented that rise. Exercise also helped younger mice, but nitrate did little for them. Age-related weight loss in older mice was likewise prevented. Mortality was highest in sedentary older controls and lowest in exercised mice given nitrate. The results suggest nitrate may help prevent frailty mainly in old age.
pmc-10739535:
Beth Fields and co-authors try out a phone app that uses augmented reality to assess whether a home is safe for aging in place, in a 2023 study. Professional home assessments are scarce and costly, above all in rural areas. Sixteen people, occupational therapists, older adults and their caregivers, and housing professionals, were mailed a phone with the tool installed and later surveyed on its ease and acceptability.

Users found the app easy to handle and fit for measuring features of the home. The authors see it as one route to wider, cheaper assessments as the older population grows. Impact on real health outcomes remains for later studies to test.
pmc-10740735:
Suzy Park and co-authors published this study in 2023. It tests a bone implant coated with a rubbery, body-friendly polymer that remembers its shape. The polymer, PGS, can be squeezed into a temporary form and then, warmed by the body, springs back: a grip that could anchor implants in the fragile bone of osteoporosis patients.

The team tuned how the coating is cured and washed, then ran the standard safety test with muscle precursor cells. The coated implant proved friendly to cells in culture. Mechanical tests showed the memory effect paid off: coated implants resisted being pulled out of test material far better than bare ones, and held their position well. The authors believe the multifunctional coating could improve fixation for fracture repair in weak bone, a common failure point in orthopedic surgery. Animal and clinical tests would be the next steps.
pmc-10740835:
Nicoletta Capuano and co-authors review nanoparticles against germs in root canal care in a 2023 paper. Root canal work struggles to clear stubborn bacterial films from the tooth inner maze. Tiny particles can break cell walls, leak membranes, spark reactive oxygen, and stall DNA copying through slow ion release.

The review weighs chitosan, silver, graphene, glass, and metal oxide particles, among others, for use inside the canal. Their varied attack routes and strong safety record could help dentists beat drug resistant films. That promise is why the authors urge wider uptake in endodontic care once trials firm up.
pmc-10741435:
Mengyao Lu and four co-authors review the genes that raise the odds of more than one primary cancer in the same person, in a review published in two thousand twenty-three. About one in six cancer survivors develops a second, separate cancer. Old clinic rules often fail to tell a new cancer from a spread or return of the first. Gene sequencing now gives a sharper way to judge.

The review walks through known risk genes, among them repair genes tied to colon and breast cancers and the guard gene TP53. It also covers shared risk spots that affect many cancer pairs at once, and gene faults that steer second cancers after treatment. The authors map how these genes link across tumor pairs to guide screening of survivors.
pmc-10741735:
Jakub Pietrzak and co-authors review scope based care for a blocked bile duct at the fork where it leaves the liver, caused by cancer. A stent placed to drain the bile is a main form of comfort care for such blocks when they are of the higher types.

The review walks through the routes by which a stent can be placed, from through the skin to through a scope. It sorts the stent kinds, from plain plastic to metal and even radioactive forms. It weighs draining one side or both, and the two ways paired stents can be set. A look ahead at new methods in this field closes the review.
pmc-10742235:
Michelucci, Sforna, Franciolini, and Catacuzzeno reviewed in twenty twenty-three how low oxygen in a brain tumor links to two ion gates and to tumor harm. The tumor kind, glioblastoma, is the most fierce brain tumor in folks. Its low-oxygen zones track with fast spread and strong death block.

Two gates that move charged parts are turned up in these tumor cells. One lets a salt part flow when cells swell, and one lets a key mineral flow with charge cues. Oxygen level sets both gates, and that set feeds spread and death block. The team sees both gates as drug targets.
pmc-10742335:
Daniele Santi and co-authors pool studies on gut germs and sleep in a 2023 review. Germs in the gut talk to the brain through a gut-brain axis, and that talk may steer sleep. Sleep ills have been tied to off-balance germs, so the team asked two things. Do germ mixes differ in poor sleepers, and do probiotics help sleep?

The search ran to July 2022 and kept human studies in English. Germ mix range did not differ in a clear way between poor sleepers and sound sleepers. Data gaps blocked some planned checks. Probiotic users did report far better sleep on a standard sleep score than dummy pill users. A day sleep score showed no gap. The authors read probiotics as a real aid to felt sleep quality, while they flag patchy reports in the field.
pmc-10742435:
Francesco Tiralongo and co-authors sweep in 2023 scan signs of a hot gut pouch flare, the top side ill of pouch disease and a true belly call. The flare spans mere swell to grave gut leak, so a true read counts. Dye scans rule that read for their sharp marks.

Signs split to gut wall marks and out side marks in the sweep. The scan also stages the ill by two in use grade sets. Fake foes span gut tumors, pouch tip swell, blood starved gut, and kin belly ills. A set form for scan tales caps the work, to firm words cross crews.
pmc-10742835:
Emily Josyfon and four co-authors study feelings and senses in autistic adults who use a specialist clinic, in a 2023 survey study. Many autistic adults also face low mood and anxiety, which cut into daily life. Two traits may add to that load: alexithymia, which makes feelings hard to name, and unusual responses to sound, light, and touch. The team asked one hundred ninety clinic users to fill in standard scales for all three areas.

Two thirds of the group scored in the alexithymic range. Trouble naming feelings tracked with worse low mood, and trouble spotting feelings tracked with worse anxiety. Sense differences also tracked with both mood and anxiety scores. Part of the sense effect ran through the feelings scores. The authors suggest care that builds feeling awareness and eases sense strain.
pmc-10743035:
Moon-Hyung Choi and co-authors compare two MRI methods for prostate checks in a 2023 paper. One method, fingerprinting, reads tissue traits in numbers from a quick scan. The other tracks how a contrast dye moves through tissue over time. Both aim to tell cancer from harmless tissue.

In 68 patients, three-quarters of whom had cancer, two readers marked the suspicious spots. One fingerprinting value after dye was much lower in cancer in both prostate zones. Dye-flow measures were higher in cancer in the outer zone only. Some fingerprinting values tracked the dye measures closely. The authors conclude the two methods reflect different sides of how tissue takes up dye, and that fingerprinting may add useful numbers to prostate exams.
pmc-10743135:
Aeree Sohn and co-authors chart a decade of HIV knowledge and stigma in South Korea in a 2023 study. Their focus is men who have sex with men, a group at higher risk and a target of prevention work. Five repeat surveys ran between 2012 and 2022, letting the team watch attitudes move over time rather than in a single snapshot.

General knowledge of HIV ran high across all five rounds, though some misconceptions held on. The first block of questions kept a steady level of understanding through the decade. Personal stigma fell steadily. Willingness to share daily life with people living with HIV, from eating together to living together, rose across the surveys. The authors argue the gains call for active policy to match: counseling, testing, education, and prevention programs that lock in the trend.
pmc-10743635:
Lorenzo Guidotti and co-authors test natural compounds that might shield hearing cells from chemotherapy in this 2023 study. Cisplatin cures many solid tumors but damages ears, kidneys, and nerves. Its harm flows from DNA cross-links and a flood of reactive oxygen.

The team treated an auditory cell line with cisplatin plus protective candidates. Two antioxidant products and a sulfur compound from vegetables were tried. Viability tests and enzyme assays measured the rescue. Protecting the ear without blunting the drug's cancer kill is the tightrope. Early cell results decide which compounds deserve animal trials. The work serves patients who trade hearing for survival.
pmc-10743935:
Camila Quel de Oliveira and co-authors evaluate activity-based therapy for people living with spinal cord injury, in a 2023 case series. Such therapy trains movement patterns below the injury level, and clinics worldwide offer it at patients request despite mixed evidence. Fifteen people with chronic injury joined a community program, with sitting balance, mobility, and quality of life measured before and after, plus interviews about their experience.

Sitting reach improved by about nine percent, mobility scores rose clearly, and quality of life edged up. No harmful events were tied to the program. Interviews gave two themes: the disability felt less limiting, with life feeling more like it was before the injury, and the program felt better than usual rehabilitation. The authors conclude that community activity-based therapy improved clinical outcomes and left participants highly satisfied, while noting the small group studied.
pmc-10744235:
Jiajun Zhang and co-authors build a search tool that finds images with like irregular patterns. Factories and hospitals both need to pull past images that match a new one: a past fault on a line, or a past case of disease. Their 2023 paper draws a set of shape traits, called DefChars, from the odd patterns in each image rather than from color or texture alone. The traits come from morphological analysis, a way of probing shapes with simple probes.

Search then ranks stored images by how close their pattern traits sit to the query image. The team tests the framework on industrial and health data sets. Fast, pattern-based search can flag repeat faults and like cases early. The authors present shape traits as a sturdy signal where patterns are messy and uneven.
pmc-10745435:
Ruimin Yang, Shahbaz Ahmad, Hongyan Liu, and six colleagues isolate a cholesterol-eating bacterium in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Cholesterol drives artery blockage and heart and vessel disease, so microbes that degrade it interest drug developers. From the gut of healthy people came a strain identified by gene sequencing as Enterococcus faecium YY01. In culture it cut an initial cholesterol load from one gram per liter to half a gram in five days, growing fastest on glucose and beef extract.

Sequencing the strain's genome revealed likely machinery. Three genes stood out, coding for a choloylglycine hydrolase, an acyltransferase, and an alkyl sulfatase, which together convert a bile-acid step product through choline-CoA toward bile acid production. The hydrolase ties into both primary and secondary bile acid synthesis. The authors present YY01's pathway map as a starting point for bacteria-based strategies against high cholesterol.
pmc-10745635:
Bongliba Sangtam and Hanwook Park review bubble behavior in a clean hydrogen device in a paper from 2023. The device splits water with a proton exchange membrane to make green hydrogen. It gives off no carbon, yet gas bubbles that build up inside can block the flow and cut output.

The review explains how bubbles form, grow, and break free during the process. It also covers the tools used to watch and measure them. Bubble behavior shifts with heat, flow, and the shape of the cell. Knowing these patterns helps engineers design cells that waste less energy. The goal is a higher yield of green hydrogen from the same power.
pmc-10745735:
Yoocheon Lee and Doohyeok Lim report a new transistor design in a 2023 paper, with work checked in a device simulator. Their feedback field-effect transistor can act as either a p-type or an n-type device. Past designs that could switch type in this way needed more than one gate.

Here a single gate triggers the feedback step at the center of the device. That gives steep switching, the authors report. The device showed a very high on and off current ratio and strong on current at low gate voltage in both modes. Its memory-like behavior may suit other electronic uses, they add.
pmc-10745935:
Han Dong and co-authors design a glowing probe that lights up in the presence of a harmful molecule inside cell powerhouses. Their twenty twenty-three article targets peroxynitrite, a reactive species that can damage cells when it builds up. Watching it inside mitochondria, where much of it forms, needs a probe that goes to the right place.

Built on a rhodamine dye, the probe DH-1 brightened about thirty-four-fold when it met peroxynitrite. It homed to mitochondria well and spared other species. Cell imaging in two cell lines tracked the molecule's rise and fall. The team also caught its generation during ferroptosis, a form of cell death. The probe was gentle on cells and easy to make.
pmc-10746435:
Pan Qin and eight co-authors study a secretion machine in a fish-killing bacterium, in this 2023 paper. The germ causes visceral granulomas in farmed fish such as large yellow croaker, costing growers heavily. Many related pathogens inject proteins into host cells through a type III secretion system, a nanoscale syringe. Its role in this germ was unclear.

The team deleted two parts of the syringe's tip and compared the mutant's secreted proteins with the normal strain's, using mass spectrometry. The deletion cut release of a key effector protein and also disturbed flagella, the whipping tails bacteria swim with, plus biofilm growth. Follow-up tests confirmed weaker swimming, sticking, and film building. The authors conclude the syringe and the flagella talk to each other, a link that helps explain how this germ causes disease.
pmc-10747035:
Martin Kulhánek and co-authors review plant nutrition research, published in 2023, arguing that new methods grow best from old lessons. The review first honors long term field experiments, which reveal what feeding strategies do over many seasons in a way short trials cannot. It then surveys modern analysis tools, from imaging inside soil to chemical fingerprinting of microbes and enzymes.

Later sections cover breeding better roots, precision farming, placing fertilizer where plants reach it, natural stimulants, waste materials as nutrient sources, and nanotechnology. Environmental risks close the review, above all salt building up in soil. The authors push for local, precise feeding paired with organic inputs and strong crop varieties.
pmc-10747435:
Ren Chen and co-authors published this horticulture study in 2023. Indoor plant factories usually light lettuce only from above, so lower and side leaves sit in shade and age early. The team added side lighting for two extra hours a day in the six days before harvest. They tested red, blue, mixed red-blue, and red-blue-green LED light against a no-side-light control in a hydroponic setup.

Side lighting of every color loosened the canopy and raised fresh weight. Shoot weight rose roughly a fifth to a third depending on the color mix. Blue light stood out for nutrition: it raised chlorophyll, sugars, and starch in lower leaf layers while cutting nitrate. The full three-color mix boosted sugar in the top layer. Responses differed by leaf layer and plant position. The authors recommend side lighting to fix the edge effects of top-only lighting.
pmc-10747535:
Juliene Oliveira Campos de França and co-authors make magnetite and poly(lactic acid) composites with the help of sound waves. Such composites are promising for medical treatments, but the magnetic particles clump and spread unevenly. The team's method uses ultrasound and a single iron precursor, with no surfactants or organic solvents, at room conditions.

The products held 18 and 33 percent magnetite by weight. Heat tests showed two stages of breakdown, which suggests part of the polymer binds to the particles through hydrogen bonds and gains stability. Light-based tests backed that reading, showing shifts tied to the polymer's end groups and the iron-oxygen bonds. In the 18 percent composite, the polymer shielded the magnetite from oxidation under a strong laser. Microscope images confirmed particles spread through the polymer without extra reactants. The authors present the route as a clean way to make these biomedical materials.
pmc-10747735: Christine Hanssen Rinaldo and Morten Tryland opened a 2023 special issue on the state of virus research in Norway. The land's spread-out people and wild lands long kept many virus threats at bay. But bird flu strains reached wild birds and farms from 2020 on, and Newcastle disease came back in 2022. Ten papers were taken for the issue. They span viruses of humans, animals, fish, bugs, plants, and germs, with the COVID-19 years shaping much of the work.
pmc-10747835:
Kazuki Yoshida and co-authors show a way to fool a wrist sensor in a 2023 paper. Smartwatches use light to track the pulse wave in the blood, a signal called a photoplethysmogram. Such sensor data can affect insurance and health care choices. If the signal can be changed, a person could gain an unfair benefit.

Their attack puts pressure on the upper arm with a computer controlled blood pressure cuff. That changes blood volume and can erase pulse peaks. Tests at rest and after exercise, across five watch models, showed the displayed heart rate fell below the true rate. No skin contact attack was needed.
pmc-10748335:
Luana di Leandro and co-authors review how to brew toxins for therapy in 2023. Lab made toxins can kill cancer cells or germs with precision. Making them is tricky because the toxin can poison its own host cell. Bacteria, yeast, and mammal cells each offer trade offs as factories.

The review sorts expression tactics that keep yields high and hosts alive. Uses span antimicrobials, cancer drugs, and vaccines. Three targeting styles are set out, from antibody guided toxins to suicide gene setups. Named examples range from plant and animal toxins to bacterial toxin parts.
pmc-10749435:
Saede Atarbashi-Moghadam, Mohammad Jafarian, and Shaghayegh Dowdani reported in two thousand twenty-three a rare case of cancer spread to the jaw with no findable origin. A man in his sixties complained of numbness in his chin and lower lip. Jaw imaging showed a hazy eaten-away area near a molar root remnant.

Under the microscope the tissue was a mucus-making gland cancer unlike normal jaw tumors. A whole-body scan lit up several bone sites, and marker tests hinted at a gut origin, yet no primary tumor was ever found. Dentists learn that chin numbness can signal hidden cancer spread.
pmc-10749935:
Vanessa Pühringer, Bernd Jilma, and Harald Herkner pool world counts of grave whole-body allergy hits. Their sum appeared in twenty twenty-three. Four bases were swept for folk-based rate works, and forty-six made the cut. The pooled world rate sat near forty-six per one hundred thousand folks per year, with a wide span.

Works from allergy hubs and ward stays read low. Kids bore less risk than the whole folk run. A year growth near seven percent was drawn from the set. The team say it is a first full pool to twenty seventeen.
pmc-10750035:
A classic calculus fact, that sine of x over x tends to one, trips up many first-year students. Weldeana, Sbhatu, and Berhe test 251 freshmen across three cohorts of engineering and technology students on the basic limit theorem, then interview fifteen of them, with and without hints. Students stumbled at reading the problem's surface, picking the right strategy, and carrying out the rules cleanly.

For each student who reached a right answer by a sound path, about two reached right answers through invalid steps. Hints were essential: students needed on average eight or so rounds of dialogue to repair their thinking. The authors blame thin or misapplied prior knowledge and offer cues as a teaching tool.
pmc-10750235:
Nagavalli Chilakam and co-authors set out a protocol to review mosquito disease costs in poorer countries in a 2023 paper. Mosquito-borne diseases impose billions in yearly global costs. Systematic evidence on their economic burden is scarce. Households bear much of that burden out of pocket.

The review will synthesize costs across low and middle-income countries. Direct and indirect costs will be compiled together. Estimates will be broken down by disease, country, and patient. Out-of-pocket spending and catastrophic expenditure are key outcomes. Impoverishment and national output effects will also be reported. Searches span major medical databases and grey sources. Bank and health agency websites are included in the plan. The protocol follows standard systematic review practice. No results appear yet, by design. Policymakers are the intended audience for the final synthesis.
pmc-10752235:
Deborah Nadal and six colleagues published a practice guide in two thousand twenty-three on care after a possible rabies exposure. Rabies kills once symptoms start, yet it is fully preventable with prompt, correct treatment. Access and technique remain uneven worldwide.

The guide walks providers through five steps with simple visuals. First, wash the wound with soap and water for fifteen minutes. Then judge whether immune products are needed, and inject them deep in and around every wound. Next comes the World Health Organization's one-week skin vaccination course, which saves doses and time. Clear talk with patients runs through every step to keep them returning. The authors aim to make sure no life is lost to poor delivery.
pmc-10753235:
