Fatima Kayali and co-authors review in 2023 proof on a hybrid arch fix for the main chest artery, known as the frozen elephant trunk. The fix joins a stent and a cloth graft in one stage. It can mend hard arch ills that once took two stage work.

Harms of its own trail the fix: new tears past the stent, leaks, kink, and fresh work. Death rates in past work run from five to twelve per cent by graft type. Leak and fresh work rates span wide as well. All reads show the true bore grew and the false bore shrank post fix.
pmc-10754335:
Anthony Hannan argues that repeated DNA stretches, long dismissed as junk, hold keys to brain disease and beyond, in this 2023 paper. Tandem repeats make up about eight percent of the human genome, sitting inside and between genes. Over sixty single-gene disorders already trace to their mutations.

Huntington's disease, several ataxias, and motor neuron disease sit on that list, along with fragile X conditions. Hannan contends these headline cases are the tip of an iceberg. Repeat variation may feed common mental and nerve disorders too. The review maps why this genomic dark matter deserves the spotlight.
pmc-10754535:
Leonardo Varoni and co-authors study heart tracing patterns in patients with a bulge in the heart wall, in a 2023 paper. The bulge, called an aneurysm, can follow artery disease that scars the heart. The team asks if combined electric and vector tracings can spot the bulge without costly scans.

Records from thousands of people were screened, and small test and check groups got full heart scans plus tracings. Two T wave patterns each found the aneurysm group with high sensitivity and specificity in both phases. The patterns held up when scans set the truth standard. Cheap tracings could thus help flag patients who need deeper heart checks.
pmc-10755735:
Qi Zhou and co-authors study a bacterial enzyme that breaks down key antibiotics in a 2023 paper. The enzyme, OXA-48, is made by gut bacteria that resist treatment and are linked to higher death rates. Its reaction runs in two phases, and the cause of that two phase pattern was not clear.

Using heat based measures and a stable form of the enzyme, the team traced the pattern to chloride binding, not to a step long blamed for it. They caught a stuck middle state of the reaction, held in place by a chloride ion. Chloride both speeds the first phase and slows the later one, which can change how well antibiotics work in the body.
pmc-10757135:
Sirui Tan and co-authors test a slow ramp-up dosing plan for a colon cancer drug in older patients, in a 2023 phase two trial. Fruquintinib extends life in treated metastatic colorectal cancer, but skin and blood-pressure side effects hit elders hard at the standard dose. The trial started 29 patients aged 65 and up, all past two chemo rounds, at a low daily dose. The dose rose week by week only if the body bore it well.

About half climbed to the middle dose, and a few reached the full one. Just four quit over side effects. Cancer held still for a median near four months, and median survival ran near eight. Skin reactions and high blood pressure were the chief severe harms. The authors judge the middle dose a sweet spot most elders can hold, and the ramp a fair swap for the flat full dose.
pmc-10774835:
Fakhar Hayat and co-authors report an unusual toddler case in a 2023 paper. Dandy-Walker syndrome is a rare birth defect of the brain. Its marks are an enlarged back cavity, a missing mid part of the cerebellum, and a cyst in a fluid space. Most cases show in early infancy.

An 18 month old girl came in after four days of vomiting and belly pain. Drugs did not ease her symptoms. She also arched her back and held her neck and legs stiffly extended, odd signs for a belly complaint. Scans showed the syndrome, with water pressure built up across the brain's fluid rooms. The case warns that gut symptoms can mask a brain cause.
pmc-10784835:
Ji Won Han and co-authors examine drug levels and graft survival after difficult liver transplants in a 2023 study. ABO-incompatible transplants cross blood-type barriers, and many recipients also carry liver cancer. The cohort covered eighty-nine living-donor recipients, forty-seven of them with cancer. Blood levels of tacrolimus, the anti-rejection drug, were tracked over time against graft outcomes.

Graft survival reached about seventy-one percent at five and ten years, with no clear gap between cancer and non-cancer patients. Low drug levels at twenty-four weeks joined antibody-mediated rejection as warnings of poor graft outcome. Among cancer patients, rejection and recurrence drove risk. Fine drug control after surgery may matter as much as the operation.
pmc-10795835:
Gatikrushna Panigrahi and co-authors show that breast cancer arising with diabetes is a distinct disease at the molecular level, in a 2023 paper. Diabetes is common among cancer patients, yet its imprint on tumor biology is rarely mapped. The team attacked the question from three sides: implanted human tumors, patient samples, and cells grown under high-sugar conditions.

Diabetes did not make the cancer cells divide faster. Instead it pushed them toward a mobile, stem-like state tied to spread. Tumors showed more oxygen-radical damage and gene patterns of faulty DNA repair. Food and microbe chemicals also built up in diabetic tumors. Cells grown in high sugar took more DNA damage and grew sensitive to repair-blocking drugs. The findings nominate a treatment angle for a large patient group.
pmc-10797335:
Ehab and Reznk commented in 2023 on the drive toward fewer ports in robotic lung surgery, weighing access against safety. Minimally invasive cancer surgery must cut pain and complications without giving up the quality of open operations. Robotic resection offers fine vision and dexterity, but the view and loss of touch take getting used to.

They discuss a modified Hamamatsu method that keeps a head-on, cranial view while merging two ports into one incision, keeping five-port function. Across the field, groups keep trimming port counts, and a single-port robot is in trials. The ideal access, they argue, is easy to learn, flexible when plans change, and gentle on the patient.
pmc-10824035:
Mark Scher outlines a training program in fetal and newborn brain care, in work whose text is dated 2023. The program spans the first thousand days of life and draws on many fields at once. Its lens is the neural exposome: all inner and outer forces that shape the brain over time. Teaching joins pregnancy, birth, and child care in one frame.

Trainees learn how genes and settings interact from before conception through adult life. Stressors before and after birth can bend brain growth and raise later risk. Shared choices, set questions, and talks track learning and cut bias. The author argues this life-course view can lift care across ages and aid future generations as well.
pmc-10824835:
Bhanumati Sarkar and co-authors detect a bibenzyl core scaffold in twenty-eight mangrove and partner species of the Indian Sundarbans, published in 2023. Bibenzyls are plant compounds of two linked benzene rings with notable healing value. Until now they were known mainly from mosses, orchids, and cannabis, and are read as defenses against oxidative stress.

Mangroves endure salty, tidal extremes by adjusting their internal salt balance and then quenching oxidative stress. Whether a bibenzyl scaffold plays a part in that coping was unknown. Careful chemical analysis confirmed the scaffold across the sampled species of the delta. The authors propose it as a signature molecule of how these plants acclimate to salt stress, adding a new chemical thread to the story of mangrove survival.
pmc-10824935:
Vittoria Guareschi, Patrice Mathevet, and Martine Jacot-Guillarmod describe fifteen cases of a little-known vulvar ulcer disease seen at a Swiss hospital, in a 2023 paper. The disease, shortened to UVAL, strikes mostly teenagers and mimics many other conditions. The team searched their emergency records for girls aged ten to twenty suspected of the diagnosis, then charted symptoms, tests, treatment, and healing.

The average patient was fifteen, and most had never been sexually active, a fact that helps rule out common causes. All had at least one flu-like symptom beside the ulcer. Blood tests rarely settled the cause, and two biopsies were inconclusive. Treatment was simple: painkillers and numbing gel. Nearly all cases began healing within about ten days. The authors recommend a published diagnostic algorithm, which confirmed the diagnosis in two thirds of their cases after the fact.
pmc-10825035:
Getting drugs through skin is a tug between skin's guard role and the need to reach a target, Zhao and co-authors review in a paper dated 2023 in its text head. Skin creams skip the gut and liver, cut stomach upset, and place the drug right at the sore spot. Yet the outer skin layer blocks most drug entry.

The review sorts boosters by three levers: the state of the skin barrier, the carrier system that holds the drug, and dose plans tuned to the patient. New carriers can ferry drugs across the barrier in set amounts. Skin checks can guide dose for each person. The authors chart where the field stands and what blocks wider use.
pmc-10848735:
Benjamin Ledoux and co-authors find in a 2023 study that tiny bends in a cell's outer skin switch on internal scaffolding and tune a signal. Cells on patterned surfaces feel bumps far below what eyes see. A family of curved proteins senses the bend size, and only some members dock on each radius.

Where bends formed, a sensor protein and a switch protein gathered and built actin fibers, the cell's inner cables. Those fiber-rich spots also hosted a receptor for an immune signal and partly muted its message. Skin geometry, the study shows, is a quiet hand on the cell's controls.
pmc-10869535:
Zahra Bahiraei and co-authors survey chewing lice on wild birds in Iran in a paper whose text is dated 2023. Between 2019 and 2023 they examined 612 birds from 78 species across ten provinces with varied climates. Lice were found by eye and then identified under closer study.

About one bird in eleven carried at least one louse species. The take comprised 28 louse species from three families, with two owl and falcon lice the most common. Alongside the new records, the authors compile a checklist of all bird lice reported in Iran. Such baselines help track how parasites move with their hosts.
pmc-10871035:
Four shop-bought essential oils are sold for rubbing on inflamed skin, but their inner workings are little mapped. Pilar Cebollada and co-authors ran one test battery across all four: copaiba, wintergreen, everlasting, and clove. Cell-free and cell-based assays covered a key inflammation enzyme, fat oxidation, radical mopping, and a pigment enzyme. Each oil was active somewhere in the battery. Clove oil led overall, with wintergreen strong against the enzyme and fat oxidation.

The study was published in twenty twenty-three. Measured potencies give shoppers and formulators more than label claims to go on. The authors present the oils as candidate antioxidants and anti-inflammatories. Uneven strength across tests argues for matching each oil to its best use.
pmc-10875035:
Gorovoy and eight co-authors linked neighborhood sleep to child opportunity in this study from twenty twenty-three. The team merged health data from a federal cities project with the Child Opportunity Index. That index scores education, health and environment, and social and economic conditions for children. Over twenty-seven thousand census tracts were analyzed.

Where more adults reported at least seven hours of sleep, child opportunity scores ran higher. Each added percent of well-rested adults matched a rise of about three and a half index points. Sleep stood out as the strongest single correlate in stepwise tests. It accounted for over half the variation in the global score. The authors suggest community sleep health may flag broader well-being.
pmc-10880035:
Breathing harder when oxygen runs low is a reflex with deep control circuitry, and one gene that trims proteins may sit inside that circuit. Paulina Getsy and co-authors tested male mice lacking the gene, HDAC6, in a 2023 study. The mice breathed a low-oxygen mix for fifteen minutes while the team recorded their breathing in fine detail.

Even at rest, the knockout mice breathed differently from normal mice. During the low-oxygen challenge, their responses ran stronger across nearly every measure, from breathing rate to the force of each breath. Their recovery on room air also diverged sharply. The authors conclude the gene plays a fundamental part in setting how mice answer low oxygen.
pmc-10956935:
Joy Bohyun Jang, Amy Pienta, Margaret Levenstein, and Joe Saul review how organizations manage restricted data in a 2023 paper. Many groups worldwide use the Five Safes frame, covering safe data, projects, people, settings, and outputs. The frame runs through the whole data life cycle, yet hard spots remain.

The authors focus on three: data use agreements, checks for disclosure risk, and training. They survey current practice and set out future directions. Coming needs include fairer access to science data, guarding against unethical use, and handling new data types that old rules did not foresee.
pmc-10979735:
Xiaocheng Li and six co-authors build a chart to flag the riskiest cases of a rare pancreas tumor, in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. The tumor, a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, grows slowly but can turn harmful. Which cases will do so was unclear. The team reviewed patients treated by surgery at a hospital in Jilin, China, from 2010 to 2022. They hunted traits that mark the high-risk group.

Five traits stood on their own. They were symptoms at arrival, fuzzy tumor edges on scans, a torn tumor shell, and a width past a set size. A low score blending diet and swelling markers completed the five. Their chart, a nomogram, blends the five into one risk read. It sorted high from low risk well in checks, and its forecasts matched real outcomes closely.
pmc-10992335:
Nattha Ingavat and co-authors report a 2023 study on a ceramic material as a final clean-up step in making two-target antibodies. Such antibodies can treat disease well, but their mixed shapes and stray parts make clean-up hard. The ceramic binds proteins at two kinds of sites at once, which may sort the good product from the junk in a way standard steps cannot.

The team tested the ceramic on three model antibodies and matched it against the standard clean-up step. It gave at least 97 in 100 purity for two forms of the drug. It cleared clumps better, left far fewer process strays, and caused far less new clumping than the standard step. A wash tweak cut small stray parts by up to half more.
pmc-11041735:
Ko and co-authors present a 2023 methods paper on imaging fat tissue inflammation without dyes. Standard tissue study needs labels and many slow steps, which can distort the sample. Infrared light can read tissue chemistry directly, but water in fresh tissue blocks the view. Their microscope pairs infrared pulses with sound detection to bypass the water problem.

The tool, called MiROM, excites molecular vibrations and listens for the tiny sound they make. It worked on thick, unprocessed tissue in this proof-of-concept study. The target was inflammation in fat, a driver of metabolic disease. Fast, label-free views of native tissue could speed pathology work. The authors show the method on fat samples as a first case.
pmc-11075035:
Plant chemicals taken before sepsis strikes may blunt its storm, and Bengul Ozdemir, Pinar Bayram, and Selina Karamese review the animal and dish proof, in work from twenty twenty-three. Sepsis kills through runaway inflammation and organ failure, and standard care still leaves many dead. The review gathers widely eaten plant compounds tested in sepsis models.

Given ahead of onset, several compounds eased organ harm and calmed immune fire in the models. Their cell paths are mapped in detail. The authors pitch them as add-ons beside standard care, not swaps for it. Human proof is the missing step, and the review says so plainly.
pmc-11128735:
Ardeshir Hesampour and co-authors measured in 2023 the activity of two oxidase genes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The genes, DUOX1 and DUOX2, help make hydrogen peroxide needed for thyroid hormone production. The study enrolled women in four groups: syndrome with underactive thyroid, syndrome with normal thyroid, thyroid disease alone, and healthy controls. Blood samples supplied hormone levels, magnesium readings, and gene expression data.

Thyroid hormone levels differed as expected between the thyroid groups and controls. Magnesium also differed in the syndrome groups. DUOX1 expression was reduced across the patient groups compared with controls. The drop was steepest where the syndrome and thyroid disease overlapped. DUOX2 showed no such headline change. The authors link lower DUOX1 activity to strain on the oxidative stress system. They call for deeper molecular studies of both genes.
pmc-11225435:
Margarete Arrais and co-authors profile COVID patients in Luanda during the pandemic's first year in this 2023 study. Africa's burden looked lighter than Europe's or North America's. Age mix, environment, and other diseases were proposed as reasons. The team studied patients at Luanda's Military Hospital. Records covered March 2020 to March 2021. Clinical traits and outcomes were charted for each case.

They asked which traits tracked with severe illness or death. Angola-specific data were scarce before this work. Malaria, HIV, and tuberculosis all circulate in the setting. Those background infections could bend COVID's course. The study is cross-sectional, from one hospital. It gives the first-year picture for the capital. Later waves may differ, the design implies.
pmc-11343235:
Manisha Singh and ten co-authors build, in 2023 work, a soft robot copy of the heart's right pumping chamber. That chamber has drawn fresh focus in recent years, yet tools to test cures for it lag behind. Their model mixes a treated real inner lining with a soft robot muscle layer.

Hooked to a flow loop, the model copies real pressure and flow in health and in faults such as overload and weak squeeze. It also matches signs of chamber failure seen in a live pig test. The valve cords pull as in a real heart, so valve repair and swap can be tried on the bench. The team offers it as a test bed for new right-heart cures.
pmc-11530935:
Yu Jeong Bang and co-authors run a blinded trial on sedation for children having MRI scans. The question: does the drug mix change how often the lungs partly collapse during deep sedation? They enrolled children aged three to twelve at one large hospital.

Half got propofol alone; half got propofol with ketamine, at adjusted doses. Neither families nor outcome checkers knew the assignments. Lung ultrasound after the scan measured collapse. Of 117 children screened, 107 joined the trial. The masked design guards the comparison from bias. Results bear on a daily choice in pediatric scan suites, where both mixes are common.
pmc-11532335:
Adoub Al Derazi and co-authors survey what helped Bahraini adults stick to COVID-19 precautions in this 2024 study. An online questionnaire reached 1,008 residents, mostly young, educated women. Knowledge of how the virus spreads was high, and reported compliance was higher still.

Mask wearing led at nearly 99 percent, with hygiene and distancing close behind. Adults over fifty complied most steadily, and people with chronic illness masked most faithfully. Feeling negative about distancing, though, predicted trips into crowds. The authors advise aiming future campaigns at younger people, crowded settings, and the emotional side of distancing, so the next outbreak meets a better-prepared public.
pmc-11532535:
Rahne and co-authors test a bone-conduction device for checking balance organ function before tumor surgery. The tumors, vestibular schwannomas, grow on the balance nerve. Knowing which branch of the nerve a tumor springs from helps plan surgery. The team used a prototype device, the B250, to send vibration through bone. They recorded muscle responses that reflect balance organ health in 27 patients.

On the healthy side, neck muscle responses showed in 89% of patients. Eye muscle responses showed in 74%. For tumors from the lower nerve branch, responses on the tumor side were much weaker. The test may help map nerve function before the tumor comes out.
pmc-11533335:
The families of hostages carry a distinct kind of trauma. A 2024 study by Shahar Livne and co-authors measures it in women during the first two months of the 2023 Israel-Hamas war. Their loss is ambiguous: loved ones are gone, yet not known to be dead.

An online survey reached 318 Hebrew-speaking women: 245 from the general public, 40 who volunteered in the hostage crisis, and 33 from hostage families. Each rated her health, mental state, and daily habits before the war and at the time of asking. Hostage family members reported the harshest impacts, with volunteers next. Rates of fair or poor physical health rose in every group. The study puts numbers on secondary stress in wartime.
pmc-11535035:
Two bone cancers, osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma, can look alike on scans yet need different care. Zhi Gao and co-authors test whether radiomics, mining hundreds of numbers from MRI images, can tell them apart. They study 116 patients with confirmed diagnoses at one Chinese hospital.

From two MRI sequences, the team extracted 530 image features and cut them to a short list: 8 from contrast scans and 15 from fluid-sensitive scans. Models built on each sequence scored well. The fluid-sensitive model reached an accuracy area of 0.97 in training and 0.90 in a held-out group. The contrast model scored lower but still usefully. The authors say the tool could support doctors' calls and spare resources, though it needs testing at other hospitals.
pmc-11536535:
Stefano Angiari and co-authors probe in a 2024 study how fueling a cell factor can tame rogue T cells. Immune cell fuel use shapes how harmful those cells can be in autoimmune disease. Myelin hungry T cells drive a mouse model of multiple sclerosis used here.

Maps of small molecules show these T cells warp their path for making coenzyme A, a core cell helper. Feeding its precursor, pantethine, shifted key immune steps in the cells. Tests run in dishes, in live mice, and in human T cells from patients. The human arm backs the hope that the trick could travel to care. The team frame fuel tuning as a fresh way to calm brain inflammation.
pmc-11536835:
Older adults often need plain, clear health facts to make good care choices. Mehran Sardareh and co-authors review past work in 2024 to find which steps raise health literacy in this age group. They search five large data banks plus journals and lists of cited work, then check the quality of each study with set tools.

Twenty-one studies make the final set. Steps run in rich lands work better than steps run in poorer lands, and steps run in the wider town work better than steps run in care homes. Teaching works better than broad life change plans, and one clear aim works better than many aims at once. Tools that use screens and the web also help, the team finds.
pmc-11536935:
Valerie Boucher and co-authors evaluate a mobile clinic for frail older adults in Quebec in this 2024 study. The clinic, the first of its kind in the province, brings hospital-style care to the home. It aims to ease the move from hospital back to daily life. Patients were seventy-five or older and had passed through a short geriatric unit. One group got the usual path after an emergency visit. Another group was taken on by the mobile clinic.

The study compares returns to the emergency department between groups. Deaths, hospital stay length, and repeat admissions were also tracked. Close to nine hundred patients were included in all. Statistical models weighed the clinic's effect apart from patient traits. Home-based teams are a growing answer to packed hospitals. This evaluation tests whether the promise holds for the frailest patients.
pmc-11545235:
Hailong Sun and four co-authors catalogued the scent of plums in two thousand twenty-four across many varieties and ripeness stages. They used a fibre-based capture method joined to gas analysis to pull scent compounds from the fruit. The set covered early, middle, and late ripening types, thirty-eight varieties in all.

They found one hundred thirty-eight scent compounds, led by esters and alcohols. Thirteen compounds stood out as the main drivers of plum scent. A smaller set of smells could tell apart fruits by ripening time, and some had strong scent impact scores. Growers and breeders can use these marks to pick tastier fruit.
pmc-11551835:
Isao Shimokawa reviews in 2023 how eating less slows aging in lab animals. Mild cuts in food energy delay aging and extend life compared with free feeding, and the paths behind that effect could help extend healthy years in people.

The review centers on a family of transcription factors that sit below growth hormone and insulin like signals. Mouse studies with one copy of each gene removed showed the two factors play split roles in blocking tumors and in extending life. One factor proved key to how metabolism and cell power plants adapt to low food. A brain peptide was also shown to be needed for the gains, with effects that differ by sex.
pmc-11552435:
Liam Cribbin and six colleagues worked out how to form carbon-carbon bonds on the crowded edges of saddle-shaped porphyrins. Porphyrins are ring molecules at the heart of chemistry and biology. These twelvefold-substituted versions are badly twisted, and standard coupling recipes fail in such cramped settings. The team tuned a palladium-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura coupling between the porphyrins' haloaryl arms and various boronic acids. They tested each spot around the ring in turn.

Couplings at the outer para and middle meta spots worked. The innermost ortho position resisted all attempts. Flipping the reaction's polarity, by borylating the porphyrin instead, improved yields. X-ray structures showed the products coming together into host-like supramolecular structures. This twenty twenty-four chemistry opens routes to complex porphyrin systems for catalysis and sensing.
pmc-11561135:
Mohammad Amiri, Delara Amiri, and Shahram Hamedani reviewed heat-sensitive gels for healing gum disease damage in a 2024 paper. These gels flow at room temperature but set firm at body heat, which makes them handy for filling tooth pockets. The review asks how well they work for regrowing periodontal tissue.

The authors searched three databases and kept nineteen studies. The gels set in times from forty seconds to twenty minutes, depending on their makeup. Lab work checked how cells lived, grew, and moved in the gels, and animal work judged healing by scans and tissue samples. Adding active agents boosted healing through germ-fighting, calming, and regrowth effects. The authors see the gels as a sound platform for gum repair.
pmc-11562735:
A car's exhaust plume lasts a second at the roadside, and Naomi Farren and co-authors learn to read it before it disperses, in a 2024 paper. Their technique, plume regression, parks fast instruments by the road and assigns each passing vehicle's puff to that vehicle.

The method yields emissions by vehicle type that match established remote sensing, and it also splits the roadside air itself into contributions by type, information managers lacked. Applied to ammonia and nitrogen oxides, it acquits diesel vehicles, whose ammonia output stays very low even with ammonia-fed cleanup systems. Gasoline cars dominate ammonia emissions instead, and their output climbs with mileage. The authors offer plume regression as a flexible tool deployable at ordinary monitoring sites for many pollutants.
pmc-11565635:
Tin-bearing solar films promise cheap, tunable cells, but air itself dopes them in unwanted ways. Jasmeen Nespoli and co-authors trace that slow doping in a 2024 study. Oxygen pulls electrons out, turning tin to a higher state and freeing holes.

Longer air exposure raised dark conductivity step by step. The effect faded back over days once air was removed. Light sped the doping sharply. Even brief exposure hurt charge flow at once. Long exposure left oxide crusts and lost iodide at the surface. The team urges strict air blocks in making and running such cells.
pmc-11566235:
Brain scans of depression and trauma stress share some marks and split on others, Jing Jiang and co-authors review in a 2024 paper. The two illnesses often arrive together, and genes plus brain data hint at shared roots. The team sums functional and structural scan studies across both conditions and their overlap.

Both show quieter frontal regions during thought and feeling tasks. Trauma stress lights fear regions, such as the amygdala, more strongly than depression does. Patients with both illnesses show distinct faults in fear and reward circuits compared with trauma alone. Treatment effects on the combined condition are also reviewed. A cleaner brain map can guide matched therapy for patients carrying both diagnoses.
pmc-11573535:
Machines that sense and answer feelings invite a new kind of closeness, and Jie Wu examines its social cost in a 2024 essay. Platforms now read emotion and reply in kind, which makes them feel more like partners than tools. Wu calls the bonds that form pseudo-intimacy: real feelings aimed at a system that cannot feel back. The essay traces how platform design feeds that pull.

Early AI thinkers already foresaw machines with emotions, and later work built the field of affective computing. Wu argues the shift meets real emotional needs while warping how people relate to each other. Risks include weaker human ties and blurred lines in daily interaction. The paper maps ethical stakes rather than running experiments.
pmc-11575135:
Paula Avila-Fernandez and co-authors published a study in 2024 on lab-grown human tissue. They built two-layer skin-like substitutes: a deep layer with living support cells and a surface layer on top. A second design put the surface layer on a bare scaffold with no living deep cells. The team watched how the support web between cells matured over time.

The full design's surface layer matured more, gaining markers of grown skin. Its deep cells actively built web parts like collagens near the surface. The bare design's base film stayed partly formed, with fewer key parts. Both designs served as tools to study a growth signal pathway, which fired distinctly in each. The authors say contact between the layers drives proper web growth.
pmc-11577735:
High-grade serous ovarian cancer mostly shrugs off immunotherapy, yet a few patients respond well, hinting that some tumors carry a friendlier immune landscape. Laurel Berry and co-authors built an algorithm, CONSTRU, that hunts for genes which change how strongly an immune activity score predicts survival. From those genes they assembled a signature that splits patients into three groups with sharply different immune behavior.

The lowest group showed no survival benefit from immune activity at all. Their tumors ran suppressive programs, with dysfunctional T cells, weak antigen presentation, and many fibroblasts. The highest group showed the opposite: active antigen machinery, healthier T cells, and a survival benefit that grew with mutation load. The authors say the signature mirrors how immunogenic a tumor is, which could help select patients for immune treatment.
pmc-11577835:
A team led by Lei Zhang studied how a gene switch called POU3F4 helps young brain stem cells become nerve cells. Stem cells from the mouse hippocampus, a memory center, often make too few nerve cells for repair work. The team traced which genes the switch turns on and tested mice lacking it.

The switch raised levels of a partner gene, Gli1, and direct tests showed Gli1 sits downstream of it. With the switch active, stem cells made more nerve cells and more links between them, and divided less. Mice lacking it learned and remembered worse. Boosting Gli1 in the brain improved those skills.
pmc-11579335:
Druzhkova and co-authors report cancer research from two thousand twenty-four on cells that hide inside other cells in colorectal cancer. In these cell-in-cell structures, an outer cell shields an inner one from a hostile setting. Such structures appear in many tumors, but their link to drug resistance was unclear.

Across five colorectal cancer cell lines, lines that formed these structures on their own were also the most drug resistant. After treatment with standard drug mixes, the structures grew more common in cultures and in tumors grown in animals. Inner cells were seen escaping once the drug was removed. Lines with acquired resistance held more structures than their drug-naive parents, and chromosome counts shifted as resistance developed.
pmc-11583035:
Claire Clark and co-authors scope what is known about dying at home in the UK from lived experience studies in 2024. Home is where most people with advanced illness wish to die. The team searched two databases for first hand quality studies. Thirteen studies from 2010 to 2022 made the final set.

Nearly all captured the views of bereaved family or unpaid carers. Just one spoke with a dying person directly. Most cases involved cancer deaths with specialist team support. Themes centered on care access, care quality, and family support. The authors flag thin proof for non cancer deaths. First hand accounts from dying people are the clearest gap. Services built on this base risk missing those voices.
pmc-11584935:
Neil Sehgal and co-authors study online reviews of health care sites in the United States in a 2024 paper. Review platforms capture patient experience in ways formal metrics miss, and the pandemic reshaped care. The team asked how ratings shifted after COVID-19 and whether the shift fell unevenly by race and rurality of each site's area.

They gathered about one and a half million reviews across more than one hundred fifty thousand facilities from 2014 to 2023. The share of positive reviews fell from about fifty four percent to forty eight percent after March 2020. Rural areas and areas with more Black or White residents saw steeper drops, while areas with more Hispanic residents were less affected. Themes in review text add depth.
pmc-11585535:
Xiaowen Hou and co-authors share a large data set of thyroid ultrasound images for training computer models, in a 2024 paper. Reading such scans takes time and varies between doctors. Even with a set scoring stage, a needle biopsy is still needed for a firm answer on whether a lump is cancer. Past models often learned from report scores rather than from true lab results, which caps how much they can be trusted.

Their data set holds more than eight thousand images from just over eight hundred cases, drawn from two hospital groups. Each case carries the true diagnosis from tissue study, not just a report score. The team also ran three learning models on the data as worked examples. They show how a model can be trained to read cancer status straight from the image, a step that could cut needless biopsies.
pmc-11585635:
Xingxing Zhu and co-authors study a nutrient sensing complex in B cells in a 2024 paper. B cells drive antibody immunity, and forming germinal centers takes much energy and metabolic change. A complex that senses amino acids was known to signal to growth pathways, but its role in antibody immunity was undefined. The team removed parts of the complex in mouse B cells.

Without the complex, B cells failed to form germinal centers, make antibodies, or produce plasma cells in two types of immune response. The complex works by holding back two factors that would otherwise trigger excessive self eating of cell power units. Removing those factors restored much of the lost function. Readers learn a new link between food sensing and immune strength.
pmc-11585935:
Harald Hannerz looks at long work hours and health in Denmark in a 2024 study. Laws often cap the work week to guard health, but the best cap needs firm data. The study reuses three Danish group studies to supply that data.

Work hour data came from labor surveys run from 1999 to 2013. Health follow-up came from national records on injury care, deaths, and filled prescriptions. Two drug groups were tracked: drugs for mood and drugs for blood pressure. Risk was charted hour by hour against a standard week. The design lets law makers see where, if at all, risk climbs as hours grow past the norm.
pmc-11586135:
Nancy Staub and co-authors measure sex hormones in salamanders in a 2024 comparative study of the genus Aneides. Some species in this group show derived monomorphism, where females look much like males, including enlarged jaw muscles, and the authors suspected androgen levels might explain those male-like traits.

Blood samples across species told a different story. Testosterone and a related hormone ran higher in males than females everywhere, and the size of that sex gap was similar in the dimorphic and monomorphic species alike. The hypothesis was rejected. The paper also reports female androgen levels in this salamander family for the first time.
pmc-11586435:
Qoosaku Moteki studies surges of north wind that cross the equator near the Maritime Continent and stir heavy rain. His 2024 paper looks at six surge events from a 2021 field campaign run in the cold-surge season. Each surge came under a different mix of Pacific and tropical weather patterns.

Soundings from weather balloons showed how deep the north wind ran and how heat anomalies stacked in each case. One surge stood out, with north winds reaching high into the sky, tied to a storm in the southern half of the globe. A count of past events showed that eight in ten fall in January and February. They also come more often in La Niña years and in active phases of a slow tropical pulse. The surges lift air and boost rain near the islands.
pmc-11587735:
Konrad Wesselmann and co-authors built and validated a lab test that can tell apart two closely related mosquito-borne viruses. O'nyong-nyong virus causes fever outbreaks in Africa but is easily confused with its relative chikungunya, and few tests can detect it directly. Their test copies a gene segment from the virus's outer coat and can run alone or paired with an existing chikungunya test in the same tube.

The paired test reliably detected fewer than ten viral copies per microliter for both viruses and stayed accurate across a wide range. It ignored a broad panel of other viruses and worked on real patient samples. The authors offer it as a tool to reveal the true burden of both diseases and sharpen outbreak readiness in Africa.
pmc-11589135:
Marko Lampe and co-authors offer a kinder gel for holding living samples under the microscope. Standard embedding media set slowly, poison samples mid-setting, or refuse to let go. Their 2024 supramolecular hydrogel forms a mesh that stabilizes small organisms for light microscopy. It even suits super-resolution STED nanoscopy in several colors. The trick is the exit: vigorous pipetting with plain water melts the mesh back to liquid.

Organisms come out alive and able to grow to adulthood. Rival matrices demand heat, chemicals, or tearing that kill or maim. A defined recipe also beats biological gels whose makeup drifts between batches. Freed samples can be re-examined or released, which opens longitudinal studies on the same creature.
pmc-11590235:
Chalie Mulugeta and co-authors pool, in a 2024 review, studies on how often male partners take part in delivery care in Ethiopia, and what drives that part. Global health bodies back partner involvement as a way to improve outcomes for mothers and babies. The team searched six databases for Ethiopian studies and checked their quality.

Ten studies with more than five thousand people were pooled. Just over half of male partners were involved in delivery care. Involvement ran higher among fathers with more schooling, good knowledge, and a positive attitude. City living and prior visits to pregnancy clinics with the mother also helped strongly. The authors urge programs that teach and invite fathers early.
pmc-11590335:
Junjie Wang and five co-authors test a nutrition index against rheumatoid arthritis in a 2024 study. The index blends two blood measures into one gauge of immune and nutritional state. Whether it tracks arthritis presence and survival was unsettled.

National survey data from 2003 to 2018 covered over eighteen thousand adults past forty. About nineteen hundred had the arthritis, and a quarter of them died over a median seven years of follow-up. Higher index values meant lower odds of having the disease. Curve analysis probed whether the link bends at extremes. The cheap blood-based score could help flag patients whose nutrition deserves attention. It may also add prognostic value beside standard joint measures.
pmc-11590535:
Shreelaxmi Hegde and eight co-authors measure the effect of remedial classes on struggling first-year medical students. Their twenty twenty-four cross-sectional study deals with biochemistry, a common stumbling subject. Remedial teaching targets each student's weak spots to pull them up to the expected standard.

Fifty-six underperforming students took tailored sessions over six months, with mixed methods checked by tests and feedback. Mean marks rose from about thirty to about seventy-one out of one hundred, a clear gain. Student feedback fed a thematic analysis of what worked and what did not. Regression singled out the most effective techniques. The authors back daily, tailored remediation for this group.
pmc-11590635:
Jing Yu and five co-authors add a friendly gut germ to a two-drug plan to wipe out a stomach germ tied to ulcers and cancer. The base duo, an acid blocker and a penicillin kin, had underwhelmed as first care in China. One hundred twenty-six fresh patients split by chance into the germ-boost trio and a four-drug standard arm. The trio ran ten days; the standard ran fourteen.

Clear rates sat near tied, at 87 and 89 percent by first count. Harm events hit the standard arm far more often in the run. Small body size and a smoke-free life marked trio wins in the sub-reads. Cost per cure also favoured the trio in the books. A kind short plan earns a first-line look.
pmc-11591835:
Mafalda Calheiros-Lobo and co-authors pair a standard oral cancer antibody drug with cell-division blockers to kill more cancer cells. Their study appeared in 2024. Oral cancers resist treatment and return often. The antibody, cetuximab, blocks a growth receptor but works only so far alone. The team added three small molecules that jam different gears of the division machinery: the spindle checkpoint and two mitotic engines.

Each partner drug deepened the antibody's killing of oral cancer cells in the lab. The team also measured the four target proteins in patient tumor samples and weighed their clinical meaning. The authors argue that hitting growth signals and division at once attacks the cancer on two clocks, leaving fewer escape routes than either strike alone.
pmc-11591935:
Alexey Orlov and co-authors built a cheap glass chip that sniffs out a potent corn toxin, in a 2024 paper. Aflatoxin B1, made by a common mold, causes cancer at trace levels, so food testing needs extreme sensitivity without labels or dyes. Their trick treats glass with stannous chloride, giving proteins a firm grip. Tuned recipes fixed the dose, time, and drying heat for the coating.

On that glass, an interferometric sensor running a competitive immunoassay detected the toxin down to twenty-six picograms per milliliter, across five orders of magnitude. Spiked real corn flour samples validated the readings. The substrate could host many other sensors, the authors argue.
pmc-11592535:
Diogo Fernandes and five co-authors compare two shapes of ceramic dental implant for grip in bone of different densities, in this 2024 lab study. Zirconia implants offer a metal free option beside titanium, but a fresh implant must sit tight from day one to succeed. The team set both a tapered and a straight sided implant into foam blocks that mimic bone from soft to dense.

Each implant was placed and removed repeatedly, with tightness read by a vibration device. The tapered implant scored higher at every density. Softer foam gave lower scores for both designs, as expected. The authors conclude that shape and bone quality jointly decide early stability, and that tapered designs deserve preference where bone is thin. The findings are meant to guide choices in the clinic.
pmc-11593235:
Anna Ogonowska-Slodownik and co-authors wrote this 2024 scoping review on water-based therapy for children and teens with disabilities. About one in ten children worldwide has a moderate to severe disability, and water makes exercise easier through its support and resistance. The team mapped what kinds of water programs have been studied, for whom, and in what form.

The search across ten databases and one trial register found 52 reports. Most work covered children with autism, and swimming was the most common program for them and for children with Down syndrome. Programs most often ran for eight weeks, twice a week, for an hour at a time. The review gives clinicians and researchers a map of the field and of where the gaps still lie.
pmc-11593635:
Alexander Denesyuk and co-authors map the working core of a family of protein-cutting enzymes and compare it with two other families, in a 2024 paper. The enzymes, subtilisin-like proteases, snip other proteins using a trio of amino acids arranged in space. Two subfamilies use slightly different trios. The authors ask how the surrounding structure holds those trios in place, and whether the design repeats elsewhere in nature.

They show the core splits into zones that stay the same across many structures, like rooms in a standard house plan. The same zoning lens is then turned on trypsin-like proteases and on a third enzyme clan, the alpha/beta-hydrolases. Comparing cores across families that evolved separately helps show which features cutting enzymes truly need. Such maps guide efforts to redesign enzymes for medicine and industry.
pmc-11593835:
Researchers in Greece used a national electronic prescribing database to map drug use from 2015 to 2021. Electronic prescribing let them collect records in real time for the whole country for the first time. They measured use and cost per person, split by drug class, age, sex, and region. Trend models and grouping methods helped them spot patterns.

The count of prescriptions rose by about a fifth, while spending rose by over a third. Cancer and immune drugs took the largest share of cost, driven by new pricey drugs. Older people, above all women, cost more per head. Regions fell into clear groups with their own traits, which can guide fairer drug policy.
pmc-11595935:
Maciej Tokarczyk and co-authors test in this 2024 study how curing energy shapes varnish coatings on fiberboard in modern ultraviolet lines. Furniture boards get layered UV varnish; too little curing light and layers peel apart. On a prototype line in a Polish furniture plant, the team varied lamp types and doses, then measured roughness, wetting, grip, and power use.

Low doses opened the biggest wetting gaps and weak adhesion, with layers splitting cleanly. Five settings instead broke inside the board itself, the healthy sign, and also drew the least power. Late stages of the line saved up to half the energy. Surface imaging tied droplet behavior to fine texture left by each stage.
pmc-11597035:
Ioannis Katsaros and co-authors review a plant compound and its promise for fatty liver disease in a 2024 paper. The liver illness, tied to excess fat plus poor metabolic health, now affects up to thirty percent of people worldwide. It can worsen into severe liver swelling, scarring, and cancer. The review centers on cell cleanup, the process that helps cells handle fat and keep balance, and on how that process fails in this illness.

The compound, found in many foods, is known for fighting cell damage and swelling. Early work hints it may cut liver fat, help cell power units work better, and restore cell cleanup. The authors stress that its exact actions still need proof in human trials. Readers get a plain map of the pathways at stake.
pmc-11597835:
Zijian Sun and co-authors simulate how coated explosive nanoparticles break down under heat in a 2024 study. Each particle pairs a core of a standard explosive, one of three named compounds, with a shell of aluminum hydride, a fuel-rich material. Such core-shell designs aim to release energy faster and more fully.

Reactive molecular dynamics follows the atoms as the particles are heated, so bonds can break and form in the simulation. The CL-20 cored particle fell apart fastest of the three. Higher heat sped the first breakdown of all three explosives, but the shell did not change how that first step went. The team counted the main product gases and noted the solid aluminum clusters left behind. The results guide the design of energetic materials that burn as intended.
pmc-11598035:
Michal Antala and five co-authors published a 2024 study of how spring warming affects two peatland plants, peat moss and bog cranberry. Northern peatlands store huge amounts of carbon, so how their plants respond to warming matters for climate models. The team warmed plants in the field and tracked the state of their photosynthetic machinery from winter into early spring.

Peat moss woke up earlier, since it manages light energy through the winter in a ready state. Bog cranberry needed a spell of warmth first, then sped up fast, with one key efficiency measure doubling by early May. Added warming boosted cranberry more than moss. The authors warn that warmer springs may help shrubs spread over peatlands, changing how these lands store carbon.
pmc-11599035:
Merja Elo and co-authors present a 2024 study on restoring drained northern peatlands. Many such bogs were drained for forestry, which degrades them. World targets will drive much more restoration, so proof of what works matters. The team ran a long before-and-after test at 151 sites of six ecosystem types. Plant life was sampled before restoration and at two, five, and ten years after.

Left alone, the sites kept degrading. Restored sites stopped that slide and turned it around. Results varied by type, and nutrient-poor sites were the most likely to fail. Ten years was too short to see full recovery in slow sites. The authors say restoration can halt biodiversity loss, but efforts should be ranked by evidence.
pmc-11599735:
Ayesha Rauf, Usama Asif, Kennedy Onyelowe, Muhammad Faisal Javed, and Hisham Alabduljabbar present a 2024 study on greener concrete. Building booms are draining river sand, a key concrete ingredient. Quarry dust, a quarry by-product, can replace part of that sand.

The team cast two concrete grades with quarry dust at zero to sixty percent of the fine material, plus a plasticizer. Ten mixes were tested for workability, squeezing strength, and splitting strength. Results fed a gene expression programming model, a soft computing method that evolves formulas from data. That model can predict the strength of new mixes without casting them. The study joins lab evidence with machine learning to make a waste material easier to specify.
pmc-11600435:
Callum Lucas and co-authors report a flexible route to 4-prime-thionucleosides in a 2024 chemistry paper. These sulfur-swapped nucleosides draw interest as drug leads for cancer and viruses. Old routes were rigid and hard to scale. Their new path builds the sugar ring from scratch.

Key steps add fluorine and join carbon pieces by an aldol step. A tidy sequence then cuts, activates, and swaps in sulfur with sodium hydrosulfide. The team made one target on a multi-gram scale. Both purine and pyrimidine versions came through the route. Side-chain variants at the two-prime spot also worked.
pmc-11600735:
Shuaishuai Wang and Yi Zhang present a 2024 study building a prognostic score for lung adenocarcinoma, the most common lung cancer. Their score uses five long non-coding RNAs, RNA strands that regulate cells without making proteins, chosen for links to a fiery form of cell death that alerts the immune system. Data came from a public cancer genome atlas.

Patients split by the score into high and low risk lived clearly different spans, and the score predicted survival independently of standard factors. High-risk tumors showed weaker anti-tumor immunity and shrugged off several drugs. In lab dishes, silencing one of the five RNAs slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion. The authors offer the signature as a guide for prognosis and treatment choice.
pmc-11600835:
Mehdi Karimi and co-authors compare two muscle relaxants in eye surgery in a 2024 trial. Relaxants keep patients still under anesthesia, but they can stretch the heart's QT interval, a safety concern. Cataract surgery patients in Hamadan, Iran, joined this double-blind randomized trial.

Eighty patients were split evenly between atracurium and cisatracurium. Heart tracings were read at four set times to track the corrected QT interval in each group. Even small interval shifts matter for patients with fragile hearts. A head-to-head trial under the same conditions gives anesthetists clean guidance. The study adds local data to a drug choice made daily in operating rooms.
pmc-11600935:
Joshua Ojodale Aruwa and co-authors present a 2024 study asking whether vitamin C shields the testes from harm caused by fluoxetine, a common antidepressant. The drug is a first choice for depression and anxiety, but it can damage male fertility by unleashing reactive oxygen species in the testes. Vitamin C is a natural counterweight to such species.

Thirty male Wistar rats were split into six groups of five: plain control, drug only, and drug with vitamin at set doses among them. The team then measured sperm and tissue health across the groups. The design tests protection directly, a step toward keeping treatment benefits without the reproductive cost.
pmc-11602235:
Fabrizio Rocco Mancuso and five co-authors zap benign growths on the vulva with a laser in a 2024 case paper. Angiokeratomas are harmless vessel growths that show as rough red black bumps. On the labia they can mar looks and comfort, and cuts in that tender zone heal hard. The team tried a long pulsed deep laser in a single sitting.

Photos were taken right after the session and two weeks on. At the check, every growth had cleared. The skin read healthy, with no scars and no color shifts. The patient felt no real discomfort and rated the look highly. The authors back the laser for such growths in delicate zones, where it spares the knife and heals clean.
pmc-11602435:
A fifty-two-year-old woman came to the emergency department with three days of abdominal pain that began a day after a screening colonoscopy. Andrew Chiu and Zinta Zapp describe the puzzle. Her vital signs were normal and her white cell count was high, yet an X-ray showed no free air under the diaphragm, the sign of a perforated bowel.

A CT scan solved the case. Air had escaped through a rectal perforation into the retroperitoneum, the space behind the abdomen. There it tracked along the aorta and the large vein beside it instead of rising under the diaphragm. She was treated with surgery and a diverting colostomy. The authors note that colonoscopy perforations are rare but real, that rectal ones are rarer still, and that many patients arrive more than a day after the procedure.
pmc-11602835:
Shami and co-authors learn how long fixed tissue can sit in storage before microscope work suffers in this 2024 methods study. Labs often cannot process samples at once, especially across institutions. The team stored rat liver in three fixative mixes for up to 28 days, at room and fridge temperatures, then checked labels and fine structure.

One mild mix kept tissue fit for both glow-label and electron imaging for two weeks. Fine structure alone held up for a month under several mixes. Kept cold in the mild mix, samples stayed good for electron work for years, though glow labeling faded. The study gives labs concrete storage limits for shared samples.
pmc-11603035:
Manvendra Yadav and co-authors test erosion of aluminum composites under particle impact in a 2024 paper. Metal matrix composites reinforced with hard ceramic particles serve in abrasive settings. Two reinforcements, silicon carbide and tungsten carbide, were compared across particle loadings made by powder metallurgy.

Samples were blasted at angles from shallow to head on and at several speeds. Statistical analysis found impact speed the strongest factor, then reinforcement content. Behavior shifted between ductile and brittle with angle and loading. Different composites won at different angles: one carbide mix led at shallow impact, the other at normal impact.
pmc-11603135:
Benjamin Young and co-authors tracked gene activity in corals planted on Florida reefs in 2024. Coral cover is falling under human pressure, and restoration answers by planting farmed corals. How planted corals respond at the gene level across sites and seasons guides that work.

Four genetic lines of staghorn coral were followed for a year at three reef sites in the Florida Keys. Which line a coral came from mattered more than site or season, with baseline immune and protein output the main split. Once line was accounted for, winter showed growth programs and summer showed survival and immune programs. Site effects were small. The authors suggest planting in cool winter months and weighing genetics in restoration.
pmc-11603335:
Shichao Zhou and a large co-author team trace, in 2024 work, how tumour cells slip past targeted cancer drugs. Cells hooked on one growth signal often first slow down, hide in a tough survivor state, then return as fully drug-proof clones. The team asks what drives that path.

A gene switch called YY1 sits at the centre, they find. Drugs that block the main growth path turn YY1 down, and it rises again when cells escape. If YY1 fails to fall, the drugs lose their bite. Wiping out the YY1 that stays boosts the drugs and stalls the rise of proof clones. Tissue from lung tumours showed the same pattern. The team names YY1 a key node in care with such drugs.
pmc-11603535:
Kazunori Shimomura and co-authors compare two graft choices in 2024 for knee ligament repair with a shaped tunnel method. One graft uses tendon from below the knee with bone at each end. The other graft uses tendon from the thigh with bone, a choice that has grown more common.

The study followed one hundred thirty four patients for at least two years after their first repair. Both groups got much better scores for knee function after surgery. The authors track pain at the graft site, new ligament harm, and knee looseness tests to weigh which graft serves patients best over time.
pmc-11603635:
Karoline Doser and co-authors measure thinking skills in adults with neurofibromatosis type 1 across Denmark. The genetic condition is known for body signs and for learning problems, but adult cognition was barely described. In this nationwide study, one hundred three adults with the condition took a full test battery alongside matched peers.

Overall test based cognition differed clearly between groups. Adults with the condition showed moderate to severe weakness in intelligence, visual memory, quick recall of layouts, and sustained attention. Some executive skills also lagged. Other skills, including reaction time, motor speed, planning, and multitasking, matched peers. The authors read this as a selective profile, not a general decline.
pmc-11603735:
Ovarian clear cell carcinoma shrugs off chemotherapy, yet some patients answer immune therapy well and others not at all. Siyu Xia and ten co-authors mapped the immune neighborhoods of these tumors in 2024 at single-cell resolution, before and during treatment.

From thirteen patients they sequenced over 140,000 cells and their T cell receptors, backed by tissue staining and spatial maps. A common mutation, ARID1A, came with a livelier baseline immune scene, including T cells primed against tumor antigens. Returned tumors looked fibrotic and suppressive, with fat-burning metabolism turned up. Two surface proteins marked worse survival. Three patients on a combined vessel-blocking and immune drug regimen illustrate how the maps may guide pairing strategies.
pmc-11603835:
Kareem Hamdi, Ahmed Elsebaai, Mostafa Abdelshafi and Hamdi Hamama review lab studies on whether orthodontic adhesives can rebuild enamel around brackets. White spot lesions, the first sign of enamel decay, often mar looks after brace treatment. Three databases were searched, and twenty-four in vitro studies met the rules for the review.

Adhesives carried added agents such as bioactive glass, nano-hydroxyapatite, nano-calcium phosphate, nano-calcium fluoride and other mineral forms. Most studies tested trial bioactive glues rather than shop products. Across methods, from tomography to hardness and light checks, the loaded adhesives rebuilt mineral far better than plain controls. Bioactive glass was the most studied additive, in thirteen of the papers.
pmc-11603935:
Alexandru and colleagues pooled in 2024 randomized trials of short-acting beta blockers in septic patients with persistent fast heart rates. The drugs, landiolol and esmolol, are meant to calm the heart without long-lasting effects. Seven trials with under a thousand patients met their criteria. Treatment did not significantly cut short-term or longest-follow-up mortality.

Age and heart rhythm subgroups showed no difference either. Results varied a lot between trials, though publication bias was not evident. The authors note future trials should report detailed heart function data. Without it, doctors cannot tell which septic patients, if any, might benefit.
pmc-11604735:
Gabriella Roofeh, Nicholas Matthees, and Manuel Cevallos report an unusual artery pattern found in body dissection in a 2024 paper. Two neck arteries, the occipital and the ascending pharyngeal, normally branch from the external carotid artery. The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck before it enters the skull, which makes the found pattern notable.

During a 2023 anatomy course, twenty eight donors were dissected by first year students. In one donor, the two arteries arose from the neck part of the internal carotid on the right side only. The split angle was near a straight line. The authors discuss what this rare variant could mean for surgery and imaging in the neck.
pmc-11604935:
Aceng Sambas and co-authors build a new chaotic oscillator, teach a neural network to mimic it, and use the pair to encrypt images in a 2024 paper. Their jerk system settles into symmetric attractors with three unstable saddle-focus equilibria. Standard tools, bifurcation diagrams, phase portraits, and Lyapunov exponents, chart its dynamics, and a circuit simulation matches the theory.

A feed-forward network trained on twenty thousand iterates learned to reproduce the system. The chaos then drives an image cipher that scrambles pixels along a space-filling curve with dynamic DNA-style coding. Tests showed the cipher withstanding common attacks with strong resilience. The authors present the pipeline as a template for chaos-plus-learning security tools.
pmc-11605635:
Takeo Uzuka and co-authors study two rare brain tumor types in a 2024 conference paper. Both tumor kinds often carry the same gene fault, called BRAF V600E, and look alike under the microscope and in the clinic. A second change, in a promoter that guards cell growth, often joins the first.

Cases from past reports and the authors' own set totaled 104 patients. Data covered tumor site, spread through spinal fluid, and loss of a brake gene pair. The study weighs how the paired gene changes track with patient outcomes. Knowing which pairs fare worst could guide how hard to treat and how closely to watch each patient.
pmc-11605835:
Shih-Chun Lin, Hsin-Yi Chang, and Mei-Chih Huang study abuse and comfort care for very ill youth in Taiwan in this 2024 paper. Their group covers children and young adults whose illnesses will shorten their lives. The team asks whether abuse and killing strike this group at the same rates as peers, and whether victims reach comfort care.

Nationwide records show abuse rates much alike in both groups. Death by killing, though, was far less likely in the ill group. Among ill youth who faced abuse, few got specialist comfort care before death. Referral rates did not differ by abuse history. The authors urge closer links between comfort care and child protection teams.
pmc-11605935:
Giuseppe Annunziata and ten co-authors review a body signal called phase angle as a warning sign for overtraining, in a 2024 survey. The signal comes from a body scan that passes a mild current through tissue. It tracks with muscle mass, strength, and muscle quality. It also shifts with inflammation and fluid moves, which makes it a candidate marker for strain from hard training.

The review gathers the science on how the signal behaves in sport and clinic use. The authors argue that watching the whole-body value over a season could flag early harm. Such harm includes overtraining syndrome, muscle injury, and fluid shifts after damage. They stress that raw scan values need care in reading, not just body fat sums. The goal is a cheap, routine check for training staff.
pmc-11606135:
Li Liu and four co-authors link hospital stays for self-harm in Canada to how deprived a neighborhood is. Their 2024 study used hospital records from April 2015 to March 2022, covering over one hundred thousand stays. Areas were ranked by material deprivation, such as income and work, and by social deprivation, such as living alone. Rates were then compared across the five ranked groups.

People in the most deprived areas had clearly higher rates of self-harm stays than those in the least deprived areas. Repeat stays also ran higher in more deprived areas. The gaps shifted by age and sex. The authors call for action at the neighborhood level, not just care aimed at single patients.
pmc-11606235:
Yefan Zhang leads a team on how couples cope with breast cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in Jinzhou City, China. Cancer hits the couple as a whole, not just the patient.

Couples from a few large hospitals filled in scored forms. One form scored how pairs cope with stress together. A second form scored growth after the trauma of illness. Profile tests grouped couples by their coping style. Links between style groups and growth were then checked. More than two hundred couples took part in all. Both partners were studied as one unit.
pmc-11607135:
Muhammad Khubaib Ullah leads a team of ten clinicians reporting a bleeding disorder. It first showed up as a blood collection in the duodenum of a small girl. Factor XIII deficiency tends to show in childhood in set ways. These ways are umbilical stump bleeding, soft tissue bleeds, and brain hemorrhages. Mouth bleeding and wounds that heal poorly also occur. This girl, aged three, came to the emergency department with abdominal pain and vomiting.

Scans found a duodenal hematoma. That is an atypical debut, and the report sets it out in full. She was cared for without an operation, under the pediatric surgery team. The authors share the case to widen what clinicians look for. A rare clotting factor flaw can hide behind a surgical-looking abdomen in a small child. A scan-first path can spare such a child an operation she does not need at all.
pmc-11607435:
Hanser and co-authors studied whether a scan can map belly lymph vessels without surgery, in a paper published in 2024. Their patients were born with a heart served by a single pumping chamber. A rerouting operation in childhood keeps them alive, but lymph vessel problems often follow. The team used a magnetic scan weighted toward water signals, which makes lymph channels stand out. They scanned 33 patients, with a median age near twenty, about fourteen years after the operation.

The scans drew the vessels clearly enough to sort them into types. The team then checked whether vessel patterns lined up with clinical signs and lab values. A reliable map could warn which patients are heading for lymph complications. It could also guide treatment without dyes or radiation. The study shows the scan approach is workable and worth wider testing in this fragile group.
pmc-11607835:
Pengfei Wu, Shuli Xia, Haitao Yu, Xianghua Zhao, Genxi Zhang, and Kang Wang studied heat stress in chicken breast muscle in 2024. Heat harms the global poultry trade. One local Chinese breed, the Tianjin-monkey chicken, resists heat well thanks to its bare neck and low feather cover.

The team heated that breed and a normal feathered layer breed, then read gene activity in breast muscle. Far more genes changed in the normal breed than in the resistant one. Paths tied to fat balance and cell cleanup stood out in the normal breed, while breakdown paths stood out in the resistant breed. A major signaling path was shared. The work points to genes and paths behind heat resistance.
pmc-11607935:
Sawada and co-authors ask hosts with split-mind ills how they view grade scales. Scales that grade ends in grave mind ills have grown for 50 years. Yet views of the hosts such scales grade stayed thin in print. Views past the west world are more thin still in the count. The team ran group talks in Japan with 11 hosts. Five hosts had long peer-help past in mind care work.

Six hosts had no peer-help past in the set at all. Two group talks ran at once, in split rooms, for two hours. Split groups kept power gaps low and talk free in the rooms. Hosts read 12 grade scales, both ward and self-fill forms. They shared views on each scale in the group talks. Four staff then read the talk texts for themes.
pmc-11608035:
Mohamed Mustaf Ahmed and co-authors review gene editing against drug-resistant germs, in a paper published in 2024. Resistance to antibiotics is a growing global threat that weakens standard care. CRISPR systems, borrowed from bacterial immunity, can be aimed at the genes that give resistance. The review gathered work from 2014 to mid 2024 across four databases.

Studies show edited systems can cut out resistance genes and make bacteria treatable again. One cut a colistin resistance gene from plasmids, restoring a key drug's power in two species. In other species, natural CRISPR systems already block resistance genes from entering. Success varies with how each species builds its CRISPR locus. The authors map delivery and safety as the hurdles to clear before clinic use.
pmc-11608235:
Liyan Sui and co-authors map how a tick-borne virus reshapes host cells in 2024. The virus can cause severe brain illness in Europe and Asia. No strong drugs exist for it or for some kin viruses, so its inner workings matter.

The team measured three layers of cell proteins at once after infection. The virus hit the early immune response, ribosome building, self-eating of cell parts, and DNA repair. Two virus proteins were traced to specific harms in repair and cleanup. Drugs that block repair paths or key enzymes fought the virus well in tests, marking them as leads.
pmc-11608335:
Xiongying Yan and fifteen co-authors tame a stubborn bacterium into a factory chassis by deliberately hobbling its favorite pathway. Zymomonas mobilis ferments fast and hard for industry, yet its dominant ethanol route starves rival products. An enzyme-aware genome model first mapped its flux habits. The team then inserted a mild but cofactor-unbalanced butanediol pathway to loosen ethanol's grip, forming an intermediate chassis.

On that chassis a D-lactate strain poured out over 140 grams per liter from glucose, and over 104 from corncob waste liquor, at near-total yield. Cost and life cycle checks supported commercial promise and carbon cuts. The recipe may generalize to other stubborn microbes.
pmc-11609135:
Daiene de Morais and co-authors report a 2024 study that builds a face database for emotion research in Brazil. Reading the feelings on a face is a core social skill. Culture shapes how well people read expressions, so a database should match the population it serves.

The team photographed Brazilian models showing the basic emotions, matching the country's mix of age, sex, and race. Then 459 Brazilians judged what each face expressed. Specialists also weighed in on the content. The final set holds 56 high-quality color images, and agreement between judges reached 81.6 percent. The authors report how often each emotion was read correctly, so later studies can pick the images that fit their needs.
pmc-11612435:
Song and colleagues report in 2024 how two small RNAs tune the juvenile hormone level in the migratory locust. That hormone holds back metamorphosis and drives egg production. The gene Jhamt, which builds the hormone, tracks its rise and fall across life stages. Knocking the gene down cut hormone levels. It also sped up nymph development and harmed egg formation.

Two microRNAs pull the gene in opposite ways. One, abundant in late nymphs, binds Jhamt and acts as a brake. The other dominates in adults and acts as an accelerator. The pair explains how hormone levels swing across the locust life cycle.
pmc-11612835:
Catherine Granger and eleven co-authors test, in 2024 work, a home exercise and self-care plan after lung cancer surgery. Patients leave such surgery with weak bodies and low life quality, and gym-based plans proven in trials seldom reach real care. The team moved the plan home, with weekly phone help from a movement expert.

One hundred sixteen patients were split by lot between the home plan and plain care, then tracked for a year. At three months, self-told body function ran the same in both groups. Hands-on tests and life scores were read at set points too. The flat lead score, the team notes, tempers hopes that home plans alone lift felt function after such surgery.
pmc-11613335:
Xunuo He, Shuang Wei, Panpan Li, and Xianfeng Li published this study in 2024. It presents the complete mitochondrial genome of the Satanas beetle, a large South American rhinoceros beetle. The specimen reached the team through Chinese customs, which seized it during a smuggling attempt in 2022.

The genome runs 16,973 DNA letters and holds the standard animal set: thirteen protein-coding genes, twenty-two transfer RNAs, two ribosomal RNAs, and a long control region. Its gene order matches relatives in the same genus. The base mix leans heavily toward A and T, as is typical for insects. Family-tree analysis placed the species at a clear distance from its closest named relative, far enough that the authors suggest the two belong to different subgenera. Sequenced genomes from seized specimens, they note, can aid both taxonomy and wildlife trade enforcement.
pmc-11614135:
Sipora Petronela Telnoni and co-authors test freezing mixes for Manila duck semen to find the best protector level. Frozen semen lets breeders store and ship genetics, but ice harms sperm. Their 2024 study used semen from three drakes, pooled and split into five mixes. Each mix held a set share of DMSO, a common freeze guard, from four to twelve percent, in an egg yolk base with astaxanthin.

After thawing, sperm motion and survival differed clearly by mix. The six and eight percent mixes kept the most sperm alive and moving, with eight percent giving the best recovery rate. Abnormal sperm were fewest at eight percent. The authors name that level the best of those tried.
pmc-11614535:
Love, Heckley, and Webber review how animals avoid parasites in the wild in two thousand twenty-four. Hosts steer clear of places where parasites are likely, which shapes a pattern the authors call the landscape of disgust. The idea mirrors how prey avoid places where predators hunt.

The review names three limits of work so far. Many host and parasite pairs do not fit the frame at all. Most studies look at quick choices on small scales, which weakens wider claims. Core ideas from habitat choice and evolution have also been left out. The authors urge work that tracks the pattern across generations, not just single choices.
pmc-11614835:
Lejla Alic, Kristina Dendinovic, and Nikolina Papac-Milicevic published a 2024 review of the complement system, an arm of the immune defenses, and its ties to diseases of fat in the body. That system clears microbes and danger signals. It steers the later arm of immunity, and it can alter how the body burns energy. Its interplay with fats was the theme here.

When the system fires too much or too little, the course of fat-related diseases changes. Clogged arteries are in the count, and so are obesity and a fatty liver disease. The review sets out the pathways by which the system moves these diseases, from laboratory dish work and animal work alike. The conclusion casts the system as a bridge: it links the first line of immunity to the fat balance of the body. That bridge, the team says, is a target for new treatments.
pmc-11614935:
Qifeng Deng and co-authors run in 2024 a trial of an under water scope cut for mid size bowel growths next to the stock cut way. Growths in the ten to twenty span had no clear best way. Two hundred patients split by lot in two arms of one hundred.

Clean full cut rates ran high in the water arm, near three quarters next to just past half. Whole piece cuts and pain scores also leaned to the water arm. Bleed rates mid work sat near in both. No late bleed or wall hole hit either arm. The team backs the water way for such growths.
pmc-11615535:
Lim, Ong, and Leow present a dataset for detecting human activity from radio signals in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Instead of cameras, the setup listens to how Wi-Fi-like transmissions change as people move, which protects privacy and works through walls.

Eight volunteers performed ten activities, twenty times each, in three indoor layouts, two with a clear path and one blocked. A router sent the signals and a low-cost ESP32 board received them, recording signal strength plus detailed channel data across fifty-two subcarriers. With sixteen hundred trials per layout, the collection gives researchers rich material for building cheap, low-power activity sensing for smart homes and care settings.
pmc-11616335:
Mohammed Gameil and co-authors weigh gallstone risk across a class of diabetes drugs, in a 2024 study. The drugs aid weight loss, and gallstones have often been seen in users. Which drug in the class carries the most risk was not clear.

The team studied about three hundred patients with type two diabetes in four groups, three on named drugs and one control group. Stones turned up in near a third of all patients and linked clearly to drug use. Most stone cases caused symptoms, and a third of those had complications. Risk ratios rose step by step across the three drugs. The results help doctors counsel patients on this side effect.
pmc-11616435:
Parimala Vijai Indrian, Wei Wen Chong, Anizah Ali, and Adliah Mhd Ali review the counseling tools that help community pharmacists dispense contraceptives well. Pharmacists increasingly hand out contraception, and a good tool turns a rushed counter talk into real shared decision-making.
