Their 2024 systematic review searched five databases plus grey sources for tools and strategies pharmacists use when choosing and dispensing contraceptives with patients. The aim was to find tools that fit patient-centered outcomes.

The right contraceptive is the one a person will actually use, so counseling quality is clinical quality. Tools range from charts to structured question sets; the review judges which have evidence behind them. The authors write for pharmacy practice leaders and educators. Their synthesis can standardize a conversation that varies wildly today. It treats the pharmacy counter as a real site of reproductive care.
pmc-11616635:
Byron Breedlove, writing in 2024, introduces a journal cover drawn from an ancient Egyptian tomb painting. The fragment shows Nebamun, a scribe, hunting birds in the marshes. It dates to about 1350 BCE. The piece comes from his tomb chapel, now held by the British Museum.

Breedlove describes how the art was made. Walls were coated with mud and straw plaster, then a finer smooth layer. A team of artists sketched each scene before adding detail. Pigments came from soot and ground minerals. The sealed tomb's dry air kept the colors vivid for over three thousand years. The essay ties fine craft in the artwork to fine attention in care.
pmc-11617835:
Yeiwon Lee and co-authors pooled trials on whether strong statin treatment around heart bypass surgery prevents a common rhythm problem afterward, in a 2024 meta-analysis. The problem, new atrial fibrillation after surgery, strikes many bypass patients. The team searched four databases for studies of high-intensity statins given around the operation.

Nine studies with 3,072 patients qualified, using either of two statin drugs at high doses. Reported rates of the rhythm problem ranged from 11 to nearly 49 percent. Pooling showed the statin groups had clearly lower odds than controls, near 0.43. The benefit held in the main subgroups the authors checked, including by drug type.
pmc-11619135:
Azadeh Dehghani and co-authors pool all prior pooled studies to size up overweight and obesity across Iran. Their 2024 umbrella review searched major databases for meta-analyses published up to November 2023. Twenty-four such studies passed the quality screen. Rates were split by age and sex to give a national picture.

About eighteen percent of Iranians were overweight and eleven percent obese. Among children and teens, overweight ran near twelve percent and obesity near seven. Adult rates ran far higher, near twenty-seven and seventeen percent. Boys carried more excess weight than girls, while adult women edged men. The authors urge national prevention programs.
pmc-11619435:
Lucas Horn and a large team pair a chemokine blocker with chemotherapy against stubborn head and neck cancer. The cancers studied lack HPV links and often return after care. They run high in the call signals IL-8 and its docks, CXCR1 and CXCR2. Their 2024 study tests a small-molecule blocker of both docks, SX-682, in dishes and in mice.

In dishes the blocker made tumor cells easier for the drug docetaxel to kill. In mice the pair gave strong tumor control and outright cures in graft models. The win came with a rise in a small RNA tied to less spread. Immune makeup inside the tumors also shifted. The team backs trials of the pair for this hard group.
pmc-11621335:
Kai Chen, Xin Chen, and Yuxi Su review the safety of fixing the humeroradial joint with Kirschner wires in children, in a look back at Monteggia fracture cases. Joint fixing holds elbow stability during surgery, and wires are the common choice in kids despite breakage fears. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

Hundreds of young patients at one center were tracked for skin irritation, wound infection, joint looseness, and bone healing. Elbow function was scored on a standard scale. Fixing lasted weeks on average. A small few had wire breakage and needed a second surgery, and a few had wire end irritation. Most elbows scored excellent or good.
pmc-11621635:
Ji-In Seo and five colleagues present a 2024 research letter on an itchy side question in psoriasis care: do systemic treatments invite fungal skin infections? Arguments cut both ways, since immune-damping drugs could help fungi while psoriatic skin's fast turnover and antimicrobial peptides resist them. The team mined Korean national insurance claims for adults treated systemically between 2014 and 2018, matched against people without skin disease.

They tracked new fungal infections, from athlete's foot and ringworm to nail fungus and candida, per thousand person-years, and modeled risk by treatment class: biologics, classic immunosuppressants, and acitretin. Adjustments covered age, sex, and other illnesses. The nationwide scale gives the comparison a firm statistical footing that earlier, narrower studies lacked.
pmc-11622035:
Silver particles far too small to see can kill germs, which makes them useful for food safety. Pei-Jun Li and co-authors made such particles with pectin, a plant gel, in a 2024 study. They used two forms of pectin, one plain and one treated to add nitrogen groups. Three treated forms were made with rising doses of the treatment.

Under a strong microscope, the particles from both forms were about twelve to thirteen units wide on average. The best treated form held more silver and killed two common germs far better than the plain form. Its lowest dose that stopped growth was sixteen times lower. Treated germs leaked protein and sugar and showed more signs of stress. The results point to better germ control for food uses.
pmc-11623935:
Dey and co-authors show weak-base drugs slow in cells when they take a charge. Drugs must reach their aims in cells to do their work. That takes a wall cross, then free spread in the cell sap. The team read spread pace for dye drugs next to flesh parts. Scope shots and bleach-back reads gave the pace marks in cells. All flesh parts spread free in the cell sap in runs.

Drug pace tied hard to the pKa mark of each drug. Weak-base drugs came back less post bleach in the reads. They spread 10 to 20 times more slow in cells than in wet. More than half of all drugs in use are weak-base in kind. Such drugs take a charge in the cell sap at work. That charge makes a form that can't cross walls back out.
pmc-11624235:
Ten biochemists study how amino acids speed the shutdown of a rat liver enzyme in a paper from 2024. The enzyme, called Enpp3, breaks down nucleotide building blocks and needs zinc to work. A chelating agent, EDTA, strips metals and slowly inactivates it. Earlier work found that one amino acid, glycine, hastens that shutdown. The team now tests many other free amino acids.

Most amino acids sped the shutdown without harming the enzyme on their own. Two stood out as exceptions, one blocking the effect and one causing shutdown itself. Tests also confirmed that the preparation held Enpp3 and close relatives. The authors suggest amino acids nudge the enzyme into a new shape.
pmc-11624735:
Peng-Fei Zhang and co-authors set out a trial plan for treating advanced stomach cancer with chemo plus a dual immune drug before surgery, in a protocol from 2024. Removing the tumor after drug treatment is now standard for locally advanced disease of the stomach and the junction with the food pipe. The added drug, cadonilimab, blocks two immune checkpoints at once.

The single-arm phase II trial will enroll 37 patients at one center. Each gets three cycles of two chemo drugs plus the immune drug, then major stomach surgery within four weeks. The main measure is how often no cancer remains in the removed tissue. Survival, safety, and complete removal rates are also tracked. Enrollment began in September 2023 and was set to finish in July 2025.
pmc-11624835:
Florent Eymard and co-authors set out the plan for a trial of platelet-rich plasma for knee arthritis, in a 2024 protocol paper. Injections of a patient's own concentrated platelets are widely used for worn knees, yet major societies do not recommend them, since trials disagree and some show no benefit. The PIKOA trial aims to settle the question cleanly.

The trial will enroll two hundred ten adults over forty with painful, moderately worn knees at several centers. Each receives three weekly injections of either plasma or salt water, with patients, doctors, and injectors all blind to which. Pain change at fourteen weeks is the main measure, backed by function scores, painkiller use, quality of life, and blood markers of cartilage wear and repair through six months. The plasma's cell mix is recorded for every patient.
pmc-11625235:
Stefano Comità and co-authors published a protocol in 2024 for enriching reticulocytes, immature red blood cells, from low-volume human blood samples. Such isolation is crucial for blood research. It was designed for small samples from healthy people and from people with alpha-thalassemia, an inherited condition that reduces hemoglobin production.

The method has two main stages. First, the blood is centrifuged through two density gradient media that separate cells by weight, yielding a fraction rich in them. Next, a negative magnetic step removes granulocytes and platelets, leaving them purified. The authors also detail how to recover two further cell groups from the original sample: peripheral blood mononuclear cells and mature red blood cells. The enriched cells suit deep multi-omics work on genes and proteins, a big plus when blood volume is scarce.
pmc-11625435:
Shibei Lv and Rubao Guo write a letter on a trial plan for neck pain care, dated 2024. The plan tests acupressure plus neck moves for a stiff neck state, scored by muscle ultrasound scans. Lv and Guo praise the new pairing but raise points the trial team left open. Scan scores hinge on the skill of the person who runs the probe, they note.

All scans should thus come from one trained expert under a set protocol, which the plan does not state. The pair also asks why the age range stops at forty to sixty, when the state now hits younger people. Dose of the twice-daily care is also queried.
pmc-11626535:
Akhtar and co-authors mine public gene data for early warning markers of stomach cancer in this 2024 study. Gastric cancer is common worldwide, including in Pakistan, and late diagnosis cuts survival sharply. The team hunted genes that change reliably across many datasets.

They reanalyzed ten microarray datasets with standard tools and intersected the results. Seventy-one genes appeared across dataset combinations. Five genes showed up in every dataset: ATP4B, ATP4A, CCKBR, KCNJ15, and KCNJ16. Pathway analysis tied the gene set to stomach acid secretion. Three extra datasets confirmed the five genes' altered levels in tumors. Survival and pan-cancer checks added context for using them as biomarkers.
pmc-11626935:
Ran and co-authors report in 2024 a frog model of inherited melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer. Most animal models rest on one well known gene fault, while the rare inherited form tied to another gene lacked models. Gene editing was used to knock out two guard genes in a tropical frog.

The frogs went on to develop melanoma on their own at high rates, plus pancreatic and other tumors. Their melanomas shared traits with human inherited cases. Growth involved shifts in cell state programs and several signal paths named in the head. The frog offers a fresh test bed for a cancer form that had few lab models.
pmc-11629135:
Victoria Navarro-Compán and co-authors compare women's and men's paths through a spinal arthritis in a 2024 survey study. The disease, axial spondyloarthritis, stiffens the spine over years. The survey spans thousands of patients in twenty-seven countries.

Data from 5,555 patients fed the comparison, with women at fifty-five percent. Women waited about two and a half years longer for a diagnosis than men. A key gene marker of the disease showed up less often in women. Women reported a heavier disease burden and worse mental health links. They also used standard drug classes more often. The authors urge clinics to spot the disease in women sooner and weigh its full load.
pmc-11629535:
Yao Liang and seven co-authors build a one-tube test to find a parasite in soil, water, and cat waste, in a 2024 paper. The parasite spreads from cat feces and can harm people who swallow its eggs. Fast, exact field tests guard public health. The new test joins three tools in one tube: a loop copying step, a gene-cutting system, and a paper strip readout.

The test caught nine types of the parasite and told them apart from eleven other parasites. It could spot a tenth of one egg in a sample. On 112 field samples, it matched known infection rates in full. Results show by color or glow, with no lab visit needed for a first read.
pmc-11630735:
Rachel Keller-Evans and co-authors compare two ways of hunting gene fusions in tumor samples, in a study published in 2024. Fusions, where two genes are wrongly joined, can drive cancer and guide treatment. Whole transcriptome sequencing reads everything at shallow depth, while comprehensive genomic profiling reads selected RNA deeply.

In validation samples and real clinical cases, the broad method missed fusions that the deep method caught. The research whole-transcriptome assay failed to report thirty percent of the fusions found by profiling in fusion-positive tumors. Shallow coverage around thirty to fifty times depth struggles most when tumor content is low. The authors warn that breadth-first sequencing, however attractive for discovery, can under-serve patients whose therapy hinges on finding one specific fusion.
pmc-11631435:
Muriel Ritsch and four co-authors examine data problems in the study of viral remnants inside host genomes, in a paper from 2024. These remnants, left by ancient infections, can affect health and reveal deep viral history. Yet they are often missed in genome studies, and reports about them are scattered across fields and databases under shifting terms.

The authors sort the barriers: uneven focus across remnant types, complex biology, and poor data gathering. They propose a user-friendly finding tool and targeted fixes to shared databases, plus common guidelines for reporting. A dedicated open database is the ideal, they note, but shared fixes may come faster.
pmc-11631835:
Sagar Pardeshi and five co-authors review new ways to deliver a glaucoma drug to the eye, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The drug lowers eye pressure, but it washes out fast and needs frequent drops. That burden hurts how well patients stick with treatment.

One route wraps the drug in ring-shaped sugar molecules that help it dissolve and linger. Another packs it into tiny carriers: polymer beads, fat particles, bubbles, or fine emulsions. These release the drug slowly, pass the eye's surface better, and ease irritation. Trials of drop and liposome forms matched standard therapy, with hints of better comfort. The authors see these systems as a path to simpler, kinder glaucoma care.
pmc-11631935:
Anna Pigott and co-authors argue that universities stay quiet on the climate crisis partly because feelings have no place in them, in a 2024 paper. Schools and colleges both teach about the crisis and add to it through their own habits. Calls for deep change are common, yet the means to change get far less attention.

The authors draw on their Climate Lab project, a run of workshops from 2021 to 2023 for scientists, engineers, and others. The sessions made room for grief, fear, and hope about the planet, in person and online. Sharing those feelings, they argue, can break silence and inertia where facts alone have not. The paper offers methods other institutions can borrow to start the same shift.
pmc-11634035:
Matthew Graff and co-authors compare whisker layouts in three mammals in a 2024 study. Harbor seals, house mice, and brown rats all sense touch through whiskers, but their counts and layouts differ a lot. The team built a shared way to chart whisker shape and angle in three dimensions across the face.

In all three species, whiskers grow shorter and more curved from back to front. Their tilt shifts in smooth lines with face position, though seals show a twist in that pattern that rodents lack. The shared rules hint at deep roots for whisker design. A seal head model built from the charts can now host tests of whisker sensing.
pmc-11634335:
Esteves and co-authors study implanted chest catheters in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Such ports are flushed with salt water on a schedule to keep them working. During the pandemic, many patients skipped hospital visits and left their ports unflushed for long stretches.

The team checked sixty-six patients whose ports were removed after chemotherapy ended. They split the group by whether the last flush was more or less than ninety days before removal. Blockage and germ growth rates were much the same in both groups, and no gap reached clear significance. The authors also tracked travel costs for each trip to the hospital for flushing.
pmc-11634935:
Jakob Thestrup and co-authors ask children what they think of health workers in a study from 2024. Talking well with young patients is a core skill, yet it is often skipped in training. Children rarely get a say in how that training is designed.

The team used story and play-based interviews with eight preschool children. An online survey reached fifty-four more children and teens, aged five to eighteen. Themes from the answers feed goals for a shared training course. The course would serve all professions that treat children. Young voices pointed to warmth, clarity, and being heard. Training built on patient views may stick better than lectures alone.
pmc-11635335:
Júlia Nascimento da Silva Mulder and co-authors map the proof on teledentistry, dentistry done at a distance, in a paper from 2024. Video visits, remote checks, and online training all fall under the term. Use surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and has kept growing since. The team gathered systematic reviews to chart what is known and what is not.

They sorted the work into eight kinds of intervention and eight kinds of outcome. Information tools made up the largest share of links, with online learning next. Training outcomes and patient-centered outcomes drew the most study. Quality ratings were mixed: about a third of reviews scored high, but half scored very low. The map shows where proof is thick and where it is thin. Funders and clinics can aim new work at the gaps.
pmc-11635535:
Sradha Kotwal and co-authors lay out a global kidney trial network and a platform trial design in a 2024 protocol paper. Chronic kidney disease affects almost one billion people worldwide and is a top health priority. New drugs and adaptive platform trials, which can test many agents in one frame, offer a chance to find good combinations faster.

The network is a registry that recruits patients from kidney and hormone clinics and has run since 2020. The platform trial, called CAPTIVATE, is a large placebo controlled study that draws patients from the network. Its first patient was randomized in late 2024. The paper describes the design, structure, and baseline results.
pmc-11636535:
Qiu-Si Tian and co-authors study a protein that helps colon cancer hide from the immune system, in a 2024 paper. The protein, CD47, sits on cell surfaces and keeps immune balance. Its levels have been tied to cancer outlook. The team asked how it shapes tumor growth and the immune mix around the tumor.

Surgical samples came from 96 patients with colon adenocarcinoma. Most were stained and counted under a microscope, and six got a richer multi-color study. Public gene data from two large atlases were joined in. Tools linked protein levels to patient traits, survival, and immune cell shares. A marker that flags immune escape could guide who gets immune therapy.
pmc-11637335:
Francesca Frisco and co-authors test whether feeling your body as yours depends on where you think it is, in a 2024 study. Volunteers wore two lab illusions: a virtual rubber hand and a full-body view from inside an avatar. Each came in matched and shifted forms, so the seen body sat either on the real one or off it. A virtual knife then stabbed the avatar while skin sweat was tracked.

Both tricks raised ownership, though the shifted full-body form did so weakly. Only the shifted full-body setup bred disownership of the real body, most when the legs were off. People also dragged their felt body spot toward the shifted avatar, but not when the two bodies matched. Position sense and ownership tracked each other in the full-body data. The authors conclude that where you place your body feeds whether you claim it.
pmc-11637535:
Ahmed Daqour and co-authors report a forty two year old woman whose lungs flooded after brain surgery. She sat upright for removal of a tumor near the brainstem, a posture that lets air slip into veins. Mid operation her exhaled carbon dioxide plunged, the classic warning of an air embolism.

The team ruled out other causes and laid the lung edema on the embolism. Supportive care alone carried her through, and the condition cleared within about a week. The case urges surgical teams to expect this rare twist and act fast.
pmc-11638335:
Kazuma Nakajima and co-authors watch a pigment fade during a cell death in a 2024 study. Ferroptosis kills cells through iron driven fat damage and may help fight cancer. Few markers can flag cells dying this way or predict which cells are prone to it. The team tracked biliverdin, a natural reducing pigment, using a light based sensor borrowed from bacteria.

Biliverdin levels fell as ferroptosis ran its course. The fall was specific: other death forms did not show it. Starting levels also predicted how sensitive a cell would be to the death trigger. A cheap pigment readout could thus sort cells by risk and confirm the death type, two tasks that now need costlier assays.
pmc-11638435:
Clemens Spielvogel and co-authors use smart models to spot prostate tumors that have broken out of the gland before surgery in a 2024 study. Surgeons who spare the nerves near the gland give men a better life after, but that plan fails if the tumor has spread past the edge. Scans alone miss such spread too often.

The team trained models on scan traits, blood marks, tissue facts, and age facts for 107 men. Their best model scored 0.88 on a standard grade in both tuning and fresh tests. Human scan reads scored far lower on the same men. Such tools could help surgeons pick who can safely keep the nerve-sparing plan.
pmc-11639835:
Daniele Masarone and co-authors tell of a heart case where the obvious answer would have meant the wrong treatment. A patient arrived referred for surgery to strip the stiffened sac around the heart, after ultrasound confirmed every classic sign of constrictive disease.

Before booking the operation, the team ordered a cardiac MRI. It confirmed the squeezing pattern but also showed the sac was hot with inflammation, the mark of a transient form that can melt away. Drugs replaced the scalpel, and the patient improved steadily on scans and symptoms alike. The authors argue every such case deserves a check for how long-standing it is: chronic disease needs surgery, a fresh flare needs medicine, and imaging tells them apart.
pmc-11639935:
Olimpia Barbato and eight co-authors measured a pregnancy signal in underfed sheep in a 2024 study. Pregnancy-associated glycoproteins, made by the placenta, mark pregnancy in ruminants. Fifty-nine ewes were fed either full energy needs or half, from day 24 to day 100 of pregnancy, the placenta's peak growth window. Blood was sampled monthly through a month after lambing, tracking the signal, hormones, and fuel markers.

As expected, more fetuses meant more signal. Diet mattered too, in the surprising direction: underfed ewes ran higher signal levels than fully fed ones, about eleven against eight units on average. The authors read this as the placenta compensating, growing its function under restriction. The marker may thus report placental health, not just pregnancy.
pmc-11640135:
Eva Erzar and co-authors count calming regulatory T cells inside two kinds of nodal T-cell lymphoma and ask whether the count tracks survival, in work from 2024. The tumor's immune neighborhood shapes how these cancers grow. Regulatory cells can shield a tumor or restrain it, and their role here was unsettled.

Biopsies from 105 lymphoma cases and seventeen reactive nodes were stained for a marker of the regulatory cells. Scorers tallied the marked cells by eye and tested several cut points against survival. The cells appeared in nearly all samples. Lower counts pointed one way on survival and higher counts another, by subtype. The study sorts where the cells help and where they hurt.
pmc-11640335:
Irene Ferri and co-authors profile mealworm larvae raised on chestnut shell waste, in work from 2024. Insect meal is a rising protein source for feed and food. What larvae eat shapes their chemistry, so waste substrates need checking.

Larvae grew for fourteen days on wheat bran alone or with chestnut shells mixed in. A mid-level shell share lifted crude protein above both other groups. Magnetic resonance profiling mapped acids, sugars, and fats in the larvae. Shell-fed larvae showed new compounds and lost one acid entirely. Their metabolic profiles clustered apart from the control group. Farm waste could thus upgrade insect protein.
pmc-11640435:
Chia-I Hou and co-authors used virtual reality to nudge people away from beef, in a 2024 paper. Heavy red meat eating raises cancer and heart risks and cost the world hundreds of billions in health spending in a recent year. The team asked whether an immersive experience could shift attitudes, and whether empathy is the lever. One hundred forty-two participants took part in a controlled experiment.

People with higher empathy felt more present inside the virtual scene. That presence changed their stance against beef eating, which in turn shifted their overall attitude toward consumption. The chain was statistically supported. The authors conclude that virtual reality can serve as a persuasive health tool, especially when tailored to the viewer's empathy level. One limit: they measured attitudes right after the session, so whether the change lasts is unknown.
pmc-11640535:
Isaac Demaree and co-authors study how two related ion channels interact, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. TRPC5 channels let cations into cells and raise nerve cell excitability. A sister protein, TRPC1, joins with TRPC5 and damps its action, but the way it does so was unknown.

Using electrical recordings and molecular simulations, the team varied the mix of the two proteins. More TRPC1 meant less cation flow through the joint channel when triggered by histamine. Simulations showed two charged lysine residues of TRPC1 facing the channel pore. Swapping those lysines for neutral ones weakened the damping. Magnesium outside the cell also curbed flow. The work explains a key control on this channel pair.
pmc-11640735:
Robert Browne and a large team of co-authors published a review in 2024 on how to save frog and toad species during a time of mass loss. The work links the fate of these species to broad care for the living world. It argues that guarding wild homes alone will not be enough to stop the losses.

Inside, the authors set out tools that are in use now and tools still in growth. They cover hormone help for breeding, cold storage of sperm and eggs, lab joining of sperm and egg, and banked cells kept for later use. They also weigh gene care, public support, and hard moral and faith questions. Readers get a full plan for how breeding work in care can help species last.
pmc-11641135:
Coman and coauthors test immune marks for sepsis course in critically ill patients. Sepsis mixes excess swelling with immune shutdown in the body. Cell death marks may track how grave the illness is. The team tracked three marks and lymphocyte subsets.

The study held 87 critically ill patients in total. Checks ran on day one and day five of care. A cutoff for one mark came from healthy contrasts. All patients showed low lymphocyte counts at entry. Helper T cell shares fell as death marks rose. Marks may help forecast sepsis progression early.
pmc-11641235:
Yuxin Song and co-authors compared fast gene-scan methods for disease resistance in rainbow trout in 2024. The disease, columnaris, harms farmed trout. Standard mixed models failed to control false hits for this trait, so the team tested three generalized tools on the same fish data.

Scans covered nearly twenty-six thousand DNA markers. The fastest tool found seven linked markers, while the other two found four and three. Together they explained about nine percent of trait variation. Heritability came out far higher than an earlier estimate, at 0.71 rather than 0.35. Three nearby genes and one further gene now guide marker-based breeding.
pmc-11641535:
Magdalena Wojciak, Natalia Swiatonowska-Lonc, and Kinga Wegrzynowska-Teodorczyk review cardiac rehabilitation and frailty in a 2024 paper. Frailty, a state of low reserve and strength, often rides with heart disease in older adults and worsens outlook. Rehab that trains movement can push frailty back, yet standard programs may need upgrades for frail patients.

The review compares classic rehab, multi part training that adds balance and breathing work, robot assisted limb training, and pre surgery conditioning. Endurance work alone is not enough; strength, mobility, and daily activity coaching matter too. Programs started early and built broadly improved clinical state and cut frailty while staying safe. The authors urge home exercise habits as the long tail of care.
pmc-11642035:
Rina Almuhaitb and co-authors charted in 2024 how abnormal uterine bleeding is classified and managed in women of reproductive age at one Saudi university hospital. The complaint is common, and a world classification, PALM-COEIN, sorts its causes from structural ones like polyps and fibroids to functional ones like ovulation failure.

Five hundred records of women aged twenty to fifty were reviewed. Most patients were in their twenties, and about two thirds were overweight or obese, in the figures reported. Ovulatory dysfunction was the leading named cause, ahead of fibroids. Hormonal treatment, above all the combined pill, tracked with better outcomes in the association begun in the results. The head byline runs to nine names against ten in the catalog, so the team framing is used. Readers get a clinic's case mix with its treatments attached.
pmc-11642235:
Water left over from firefighting carries a nasty mix of ash, chemicals, and half-burned material, and it often runs straight into soil and streams. Anna Rabajczyk and five co-authors review a cleanup candidate in a 2024 paper: hydrogels, water-swollen polymer networks that can be tuned to grab pollutants.

The review asks how hydrogels can be functionalized, loaded with microbes or bioactive substances, to suit post-fire water. It weighs what the materials can capture, under what conditions they work, and where they fail. Capturing the water at the scene, before it spreads, is part of the plan. The authors map the promise and the limits of hydrogels for a job that climate-driven fires make more common every year.
pmc-11642435:
Qinglin Liu and five co-authors present a 2024 materials study on building aluminum-lithium parts layer by layer with a friction-based printing method. The process reheats earlier layers with each new pass, so the microstructure and strength vary through the part. The team examined a sixteen-layer component of a high-strength aerospace alloy, comparing its last, middle, and first layers.

Heat cycling reshaped the strengthening particles differently by depth. The top layers kept the most of the key phase and measured hardest and strongest, with the best stretch before breaking. Strength and hardness declined steadily toward the bottom. The authors explain the gradient through the precipitate patterns each layer's heat history produced. The work guides how such printed parts should be designed and where their weak zones lie.
pmc-11642535:
Raquel Sainz-Amo and co-authors track blood markers under a strong multiple sclerosis drug in a 2024 study. Natalizumab calms relapsing MS powerfully. Two serum proteins report nerve damage and glial activation. Their course on treatment may grade response.

Fifty-four patients, mostly women in their thirties, were sampled at start, six, and twelve months. Seventy-six healthy controls set the reference. The nerve marker fell by about two-thirds within six months and more by a year. Patients free of disease activity dropped earlier and deeper. The glial marker also fell in the wider group. Blood tests may soon certify drug response without scans.
pmc-11642635:
Toshihiro Sato and others tracked clozapine blood levels in schizophrenia patients in 2024. Clozapine helps hard-to-treat schizophrenia greatly. Blood levels vary between patients though. Enzymes and transporters may drive the spread. Patients in Japan were little studied before this. One transporter gene was the focus.

Lab uptake tests used transporter variants. Docking math backed the uptake gaps. Clozapine proved to be a transporter substrate. Gene variants may shift drug handling. That finding is claimed as first. Dosing might one day be tailored to each person. Blood checks remain key meanwhile. Transporter genes join body chemistry in explaining it.
pmc-11642835:
Road crews can recycle old asphalt in place by heating and reusing it, a green method whose surface can still age and crack. Yao Guan and co-authors studied that aging in 2024, exposing recycled mixes to heat with oxygen and to a year of ultraviolet light in the lab. They tracked strength at high and low temperatures and resistance to water damage.

Aging bought little gain in heat strength, while crack resistance fell sharply. Ten years of heat aging cost far more bending room than the year of light exposure. The team built a formula to forecast the decline and proposed measures of how far light aging has gone. They urge stronger anti aging steps for recycled roads.
pmc-11642935:
Vincent Torelli and co-authors review one center's experience imaging a rare heart inflammation disease, in a 2024 study. The disease, cardiac sarcoidosis, seeds grainy clusters in heart muscle. It can scar the heart, disturb rhythm, and cause failure. Biopsy is the standard proof but often misses the disease. The team looked back at ninety-two patients seen at their center. Most were men, with an average age near sixty-two.

Eighty patients had a glucose-based scan. Eighty-four percent had a magnetic resonance scan. One heart segment showed uptake most often on the first scan. The same segment led on scar imaging. Patients showing both uptake and scar, in a mismatched pattern, faced about double the risk of major heart events. The authors argue combined imaging can replace biopsy in many cases. It also helps track treatment over time.
pmc-11643235:
Katarzyna Gaweł-Bęben and co-authors published a 2024 study testing whether two plant extracts together fight prostate cancer cells better than either alone. Maca, a Peruvian root crop, comes in color types with different chemistry. Saw palmetto extract is a common supplement for prostate health. The team combined selected maca types with a carbon-dioxide extract of saw palmetto.

First, chemical fingerprinting mapped what each maca type contains, and the types differed clearly in their active compounds. Then the extracts, alone and combined, were tested on human prostate cancer cells and normal prostate cells in dishes. The point was targeted killing: harm the cancer, spare the healthy tissue. Combinations of specific maca types with the palmetto extract showed the sought synergy. The authors frame the work as early, dish-level evidence for plant-based prevention strategies.
pmc-11643435:
Jia Li and colleagues review high amylose rice and blood sugar after meals, in a literature review from 2024. Rice is a staple across East Asia, and heavy white rice intake links with higher diabetes risk. Rice rich in amylose is digested more slowly and tends to give lower sugar peaks.

Seventeen clinical trials were reviewed for meal sugar levels and glycemic index. Most trials found lower meal sugar and lower index scores with high amylose rice. Trial size, design, rice type, and amylose share all varied across studies. Stronger sugar control tended to track higher amylose content in the rice. Long term intake data stay scarce, so the authors call for more study.
pmc-11643535:
Xiaowei Zhuang and co-authors tune tin zeolite catalysts that turn glucose into lactic acid in a 2024 paper. Lactic acid feeds many chemical chains, and sugar conversion beats older routes. The team builds beta zeolites at varied silicon to aluminum ratios, then loads tin into the framework by high energy mixing. A battery of probes maps structure and acid sites.

Below a ratio of forty-five, lower aluminum means more tin held and more acid sites of both kinds, they find. Past that point the gains stall and reverse. The best batch converts about ninety-seven percent of glucose with a lactic acid yield near thirty-nine percent in seven hours at high heat.
pmc-11643635:
Zhang and co-authors test in 2024 whether products made from human birth tissue can ease pain after surgery without opioids. Pain after operations is a heavy burden, and opioids carry grave side effects. A membrane product from the womb lining had shown early promise in the clinic.

In mice, the product applied at the wound dulled lasting pain sensitivity, with no opioid like harms. It worked by quieting pain sensing nerve cells through a surface gate. The team then purified the active matrix part, which beat the raw product in purity and ease of use. The pure part reshaped cell scaffolds and cut nerve firing.
pmc-11643835:
Painful nerve damage is a common burden of type 2 diabetes, and certain toxic fats in the blood may feed it. Alfonso M Durán and two co-authors test whether a diet supplement rich in DHA, an omega-3 fat, can lower those harmful lipids. Forty people with diabetes joined a program of weekly lifestyle classes plus daily DHA and EPA capsules for three months.

Blood analysis afterward showed several neurotoxic lipids clearly reduced, while markers shifted in a protective direction: a cell-death protein fell, and proteins tied to cell cleanup and fat transport rose. The work builds on an earlier finding from the same program that pain eased over the three months. The authors frame omega-3 fats as a plausible lever on the lipid side of nerve pain. The study appears in 2024.
pmc-11643935:
McCarthy and a team of colleagues compared two timings for a slow-release sugar during exercise in adults with type 1 diabetes, in a 2024 trial. The volunteers used automated insulin pumps. The sugar, isomaltulose, was taken either as one serving before cycling or as three small servings during it.

Eight participants completed both arms of the crossover trial, riding for forty-five minutes each time. Blood sugar during exercise ran higher and steadier when the sugar came in small servings during the ride. With the pre-exercise serving, blood sugar fell; with the during servings, it rose slightly. Gut and pancreatic hormone levels stayed lower in the during arm. The body also burned less carbohydrate and more fat in that arm. The authors say splitting the sugar through the session guards blood sugar better. The result flags meal timing as a real lever for exercising patients.
pmc-11644035:
Wanlu Bian and co-authors model how coupled light modes in tiny metal disks create strong chiral signals, in a 2024 paper. Such signals matter for sensors because they react sharply to the medium around the structure. The design pairs two elliptical disks in a stacked, rotated layout.

By tuning the gap and shape, the authors couple a simple dipole mode with a higher order mode. That coupling produces a Fano resonance, a sharp asymmetric feature in the spectrum, along with a strong difference in how left and right circular light are absorbed. The layout with the largest asymmetry factor gave the strongest signal. The signal also shifted sensitively with the refractive index nearby, above all in visible and near infrared light. The authors propose it for high sensitivity sensing.
pmc-11644235:
Jiyeon Kim and five colleagues tested whether elderberry extract can restore testosterone in aging rats. As men age, oxidative damage to Leydig cells lowers testosterone and brings deficiency symptoms. Plant-based alternatives to hormone therapy are in demand. The twenty twenty-four study fed an elderberry extract powder to aged rats with low testosterone. Its main compounds were rutin and fructose-leucine. Total and free testosterone, plus sperm motility, were measured.

The extract raised testosterone levels and improved sperm motility in the rat model. The authors traced the effect to regulation of three enzymes that make or convert testosterone. Safety markers for the prostate, liver, and kidneys were also checked. The results position elderberry extract as a candidate functional ingredient for testosterone deficiency, pending human evidence.
pmc-11644335:
Bao, Yan, Han, and Schick study modified clay nanotubes in plastic composites, in work from twenty twenty-four. Halloysite is a natural clay that forms tiny tubes. Adding it to polypropylene can stiffen the plastic, but poor mixing limits the gain.

A silane coating called APTES was grafted onto the tubes by wet and dry methods. The wet method in water worked best. Coated tubes spread better in the plastic and bonded more tightly at the interface. Flow, crystal, and heat tests all improved, and strength rose clearly. The best filler level was found to be low. Coating is a cheap step with a large payoff.
pmc-11644435:
Marco Zanelli and six co-authors study 3D printed parts reinforced with basalt fiber in a 2024 paper. Long continuous fibers can lift printed plastics from prototype grade to structural grade. Basalt fiber is natural in origin, strong, and resists heat and chemicals, yet it had rarely been studied in printing.

The team printed a combined material with a standard filament method and tested it for heat and pulling strength in the plane. Along the fiber direction, strength was fifteen times that of the plain plastic. Across the fibers, strength was far lower, making the material strongly directional. The authors say fiber paths must be planned with care for real structural parts.
pmc-11644535:
Keiichiro Kawabata and co-authors hunt what foretells food ills a year post a plague stay in Japan wards. The plague leaves a tail of ills, food lack in the flock. Their 2024 read rides a big mend study: just over one thousand grown sick folks who left ward care. A poll at one year logs life shifts; a stock sieve scores food lack.

Just under a fourth of the set scores in the food-lack band. Base facts, ill harsh tier, and one-month tail signs are raced as foretells in a chance fit. Early food aid could be aimed by such marks ere lack roots. Long tails need year-tier watch, not week-tier.
pmc-11644635:
Kenan Yang and co-authors turned, in a 2024 study, natural wood into a sponge that drinks oil from water in any weather. Thick crude resists ordinary sorbents because it barely flows. Their sponge is chemically carved from wood, then coated to repel water fiercely while loving oil, with iron oxide particles worked in.

The surface shed water at a contact angle over 154 degrees and cleaned itself of grime. Sunlight heated it to 74 degrees, and a small voltage pushed it past 120, melting thick oil into easy reach. Under suction or gravity it separated flowing oils continuously. The materials are cheap and the sponge degrades, unlike plastic rivals. The authors aim it at spills and factory wastewater alike, day or night.
pmc-11644735:
Mariya Dimitrova and co-authors compare in 2024 the strength of false teeth made by 3D printing with teeth bought ready made for dentures. Printed teeth are a step forward in digital dentistry, but they must stand up to biting forces as well as factory teeth do. The team tested four groups of thirty teeth each.

One group was printed from a resin cured by light. The other three were well known brands of factory teeth. Tests measured how each kind resists chipping and breaking under a pull force. A printed tooth that matches factory strength would let labs make dentures in house at lower cost. The results give dentists a base for trusting printed teeth in daily use, or for holding off where they fall short.
pmc-11644835:
Imran Hossain, Murat Tahtali, Ugur Turhan, and Kamanashis Biswas analyze blockchain integration in drone networks in a 2024 paper. A private blockchain promises security and decentralized control for fleets of unmanned aerial vehicles. The costs in speed and delay need measuring before adoption.

Simulations varied fleet size, transaction load, area, altitude, and data rate. In the blockchain network, throughput fell as drones and transactions rose, while delay stayed flat up to a point. The plain drone network gained throughput but added delay under load. Area and altitude changes mattered little for the chain but raised delays in the plain network.
pmc-11644935:
Li Tan and co-authors present a 2024 neural network model for sorting knitted fabric by its surface pattern. In garment factories, naming fabric texture by eye is slow and error-prone, yet the step guides automation and quality checks. Older machine methods leaned on hand-picked features, which took time and capped accuracy.

Their model builds on a design in which each layer feeds all later layers. A learnable weight scheme, steered by channel attention, picks the most useful signal channels and trims the rest. Varied learning rates keep that picking sharp through the whole training run, which also prunes the model. Since no public data set existed for the task, the team built one, named KF9. Their model beat a tuned rival network by five points of accuracy.
pmc-11645135:
Laxman Ghimire and Hongbo R Luo comment, in a 2024 piece, on a study naming a brake protein that keeps lung neutrophils from over-firing. After infection or injury, neutrophils can flood the lung and spill compounds that shred tissue. The study under discussion pinned the brake as SHP1, a tyrosine phosphatase.

Mice lacking SHP1 only in neutrophils grew severe lung inflammation, bleeding, and higher death in both sterile and germ-driven injury. Their lungs held big clusters of neutrophils inside vessels and many extracellular traps. Without the brake, a kinase called SYK ran unchecked and drove the chaos. The commentary frames SHP1 as a balance point for acute respiratory distress care. Tuning it may calm lungs without disarming defense.
pmc-11645335:
Heather Zierhut and co-authors review how community-based participatory research has been used in genetics services. Their 2024 review covers work from 2006 to 2023. The method brings patients and community members into the design of care, with the aim of fairer access to genetic counseling and testing.

Searches of five databases found sixteen papers that met the rules, most of them qualitative and most from the United States. Cancer and genetic education were common topics. Community partners most often helped with recruiting and with reading results, and least at other stages. The authors map where partners are brought in early and where their role stays thin.
pmc-11646435:
Early liver cancer can be attacked by blocking its blood supply while heating it from inside, and Yu-Tang Chen and co-authors ask whether that combo works as well when cancer returns. Their 2024 study pools 158 patients from three hospitals, split into first-time and recurrent groups. Both got chemoembolization plus radiofrequency ablation between 2019 and 2024.

Response rates were nearly equal, about 98 and 95 percent, and survival at one, three, and five years matched too. The recurrent group, though, relapsed sooner, a gap that proved strong. Liver reserve and whether the cancer was new drove relapse risk, while a blood protein level drove survival. The authors back the combo for both groups, with closer watching after recurrence.
pmc-11646635:
Xiaodong Lan and eight co-authors wrote this 2024 review and pooled analysis on using mild electric current to help diabetic foot ulcers heal. These wounds are slow to close and cause heavy distress and cost. Many small studies report that the current helps, but the team wanted to check how firm and steady that proof is.

The team searched five databases and kept only trials that assigned patients by chance to the treatment or to a placebo or standard care. Ten trials with 451 patients qualified. The treated group healed at a rate about twenty points higher, and more ulcers closed fully. Both gains were firm by standard tests. The authors credit better blood flow and nerve function in the legs, and they note that the best current settings are still unsettled.
pmc-11646935:
Brenda Owusu and co-authors write an editorial on a quiet inequity: health care is going digital, and Black older adults risk being locked out. Managing diabetes or heart disease now runs through patient portals, telehealth visits, and apps, yet gaps in devices, connectivity, and digital confidence track with race, income, and schooling. The authors frame digital health literacy as a social determinant of health in its own right.

They argue providers cannot simply adopt new tools and hope; training, access, and trust must be built deliberately for this population, or disparities will widen behind a friendly interface. Justice theory gets a mention: fairness demands more than equal offers of technology. The editorial calls the divide bridgeable, but only with intentional effort aimed at the communities it harms.
pmc-11647335:
After a spinal cord injury, many nerve cells die by a runaway process called necroptosis, and that loss blocks recovery. Xiong Cai and co-authors tested in 2024 whether a growth factor named FGF20 could protect those cells in mice. The factor supports nerve growth in healthy development, so the team gave its human form to injured mice.

Treated mice moved better on standard tests and kept more living neurons at the injury site. Signs of new nerve growth rose, and the scar that walls off the injury formed more slowly. Measures of necroptosis fell as well, matching the survival gains. The authors propose FGF20 as a candidate treatment worth carrying forward.
pmc-11647935:
Makoto Akashi, writing alone, surveys the history of radiation emergency medicine from its beginnings to its future. The field covers dose assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of people injured by radiation exposure or contamination. Akashi notes the story starts before Roentgen's famous X-ray report: Crookes tubes had already emitted X-rays and injured skin. Early users handled radiation with no sense of its danger.

Radioactive materials were discovered soon after, and contamination incidents followed. Devices grew sophisticated, new radionuclides multiplied, and nuclear physics made artificial radioactivity and reactors possible. Each advance reshaped the medical response required. The twenty twenty-four perspective connects that history to present practice and future needs, arguing the discipline evolves with the technology it serves.
pmc-11648335:
Remy Poncet and Olivier Gargominy wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about a gap in records of the microbes that live on and in people. Bacteria tied to human health are widely studied in labs. Yet records that say where, when, and in whom a microbe was found are rare in shared databases.

The authors argue that this gap slows work on disease prevention and on how human, animal, and environmental health connect. They point to a French national system for nature records as a ready model. Medical staff could use such a system to log and share records of human-linked bacteria with little extra effort.
pmc-11649235:
Quan-Son Eric Le and co-authors dissect how learning shapes the full range of mouse defense behaviors in this 2024 paper. Classic fear conditioning studies mostly measure freezing, which hides other responses. Mice heard a two-part sound cue paired with footshock, while control groups got unpaired or reordered versions.

Paired mice froze to the first sound part, then switched to explosive jumping and darting at the second. Control groups froze less and rarely jumped, though they showed tail rattling and darting, signs of non-associative learning. During extinction, freezing faded and escape moves softened, except in one reversed group whose freezing resisted. The authors conclude both learning types shape defense, but only pairing unlocks the full repertoire.
pmc-11649335:
Radwan Haffaf and co-authors present a case report from two thousand twenty-four on treating a severe jaw mismatch in a teenager without surgery. In class three malocclusion, the lower jaw sits too far forward, and the pattern is among the hardest problems in orthodontics. Causes are mixed, so many treatment routes exist.

The patient was near the border where surgery is often advised, but a non-surgical plan was chosen based on skeletal age and the patient's own wish. Treatment used rapid widening of the upper jaw, then fixed braces with elastic bands. Over fifteen months the upper jaw moved forward, a stuck tooth erupted on its own, and the bite corrected. The authors report a pleasant, working result.
pmc-11649835:
Plaza, Santangeli, Cancellario, and Lambertucci map in twenty twenty-four how a severe bird flu virus could first reach Oceania. The virus has caused the worst spread in animals ever recorded and has reached almost the whole world. Yet no cases had been found in Oceania when they wrote, which leaves time to prepare.

The team listed wild bird species known to have caught the virus elsewhere. They then mapped where those birds live. Oceania hosts few such species overall, so its broad risk looks low. But more than fifty of them live along the coasts of Australia and New Zealand. That overlap marks the most likely entry path the authors urge planners to watch.
pmc-11650035:
An EFSA expert panel reports a 2024 safety review of a food enzyme made by a modified fungus. The enzyme breaks down fructans and is meant for grain processing, in baked goods and other cereal foods. The panel checked the modified strain, the product's purity, and lab safety tests. The enzyme carries no live cells or DNA from the maker strain.

Toxicity tests raised no alarm. Rats fed the highest dose for 90 days showed no harm, giving a wide safety margin over expected human intake. Estimated intake in Europe topped out well below that dose. A search found no match to known allergens, though one allergen source is used in making the enzyme. The panel judged allergy risk low and cleared the enzyme for its stated uses.
pmc-11650135:
The gels that give noodles, jellies, and sauces their body form when starch cooks and cools, and Yongqiang Gong and co-authors review how to make those gels stronger. Their 2024 paper first explains the two-step birth of a gel, swelling and bursting granules, then chains re-linking as the paste cools. Native starches often gel weakly, which limits their use.

Composition of the starch, cooling conditions, added ingredients, and physical or chemical modifications all tune the result. Stronger gels serve food quality and nutrition, and they reach beyond the plate into packaging and 3D food printing. The review gathers the toolbox in one place.
pmc-11650335:
Xiaochen Huang and co-authors study bladder and urinary tract cancers that make only small amounts of a growth protein called HER2. Their study appeared in 2024. Such HER2-low cancers are easy to overlook, since attention goes to tumors with heavy HER2. The team re-scored samples from 75 patients at one cancer hospital, using stains and gene probes, and checked the results against a large public cancer database.

HER2 showed in about 83 percent of tumors, and about 61 percent of all cases were HER2-low. HER2 level tracked with the tumor's stage. Patients with HER2-low tumors fared worse, and the trait predicted poor outcome on its own. The authors argue the low group deserves its own treatment research, as new HER2-targeted drugs reach patients who were once ruled out.
pmc-11650735:
Alexey Koval, Cédric Boudou, and Vladimir Katanaev challenged claimed drug compounds in two thousand twenty-four that were said to block Frizzled receptors. These receptors sit in the Wnt pathway, a prized cancer and regeneration target. Several past reports claimed selective blockers, but most lacked a truly selective test to back the claim.

The team built a selective assay for single Frizzled types and retested the reported compounds. Most failed to block their claimed target when a Wnt signal drove it. Instead they showed off-target effects, no activity, or even blocked the test reporter itself. Only one peptide passed the selectivity test. The authors urge strict functional checks in drug hunting.
pmc-11651135:
Shiyu Li, Yan Ding, and co-authors build a test to flag children with Kawasaki disease who will not respond to a key first drug, in a 2024 study. Poor response raises the risk of heart vessel harm. Early flags thus have real worth for care teams.

The study held more than one hundred forty children from one hospital. One cell death gene read low in poor response cases. Some blood marks also split the groups in clear ways. A joint model caught most poor response cases with fair care on false flags. The team sees the joint test as fit for clinic use.
pmc-11651435:
Ruolin Hou and co-authors ask if a family of enzymes helps cause joint disease in a 2024 study. Joint disease here is rheumatoid arthritis, a long-term ill where the immune system harms the joints. Past data linked the enzymes to the disease, but cause was not clear.

The team used gene traits as a natural test of cause, with checks on the strength of the proof. Higher levels of one enzyme, named once as Cathepsin B in the source, tracked with a small rise in disease risk. Tests in the reverse path found no such link. The authors suggest the enzyme may serve as a sign of the disease.
pmc-11652135:
Bahia Galal Abd El-Razik Siam and five co-authors surveyed how well people with high blood pressure care for themselves at primary health centers in Unaizah city, Saudi Arabia. The 2023 study drew 372 patients who had been in follow-up care for at least six months. A checked questionnaire covered personal details, health history, and daily self-care habits such as diet, weight control, and taking medicine on schedule. The average age was about 41 years, and two thirds of the patients were women.

Just over half had never checked their own blood pressure at home. Weight control was the strongest habit, then healthy eating, then steady use of medicine. Scores rose with how often patients did these activities, and they differed by age, sex, schooling, and work status. The authors urge staff to teach home blood pressure checks and joint care of related conditions.
pmc-11652435:
Hyun-Tae Kim describes the smell organ of the javelin goby in a 2024 anatomy study. Fish rely on smell to find food and avoid danger, and the organ's build reflects its habitat. The javelin goby lives in tidal zones where pools warm up and lose oxygen between tides. Kim examined the organ under stereo and light microscopes, looking for traits fit to that harsh cycle.

Seven features stood out. The front nostril is a tube, and a single lengthwise fold lines the chamber. Two side sacs assist water flow. Immune cells sit low in the sensory lining, which carries rich blood supply underneath. Smell receptor cells bear four to five small fingers each. Even the red blood cells are rod-shaped. Together, the traits hint at design for stagnant, low-oxygen pools.
pmc-11652535:
Dávid Száraz and five co-authors present a case report from two thousand twenty-four on jaw bone death linked to bone drugs. A woman with osteoporosis had taken alendronate for three years and a statin as well. After just one low dose of denosumab, she quickly developed advanced necrosis of the jaw.

Part of her upper jaw was removed, and she healed fully with no return of the problem. The team also reviewed past reports of similar cases after a single low dose. They found only a small number, most after prior use of related bone drugs. The authors urge care before starting denosumab, with all risk factors weighed first. The case shows a rare harm can follow even one small dose.
pmc-11652935:
Margherita D'Alessandro and five colleagues test chitosan, a fiber from shellfish, as a functional ingredient in factory-made sliced bread. Chitosan changed the dough: it grew more elastic and resistant to stretching, firmer, and harder to mold. The stronger dose showed the biggest effects. Baked loaves had larger pores, more color from browning reactions, and higher firmness and available moisture.

Microbe counts stayed within acceptable limits, though chitosan did not suppress spoilage organisms as hoped. The pleasant surprise was prebiotic activity. The enriched bread better supported growth of helpful gut bacteria in simulated intestinal fluid. The authors weigh factory practicalities against the possible gut-health selling point.
pmc-11653535:
Five authors, led by Wenjie Hu, test in 2024 whether a gut made molecule can shield rat brains when blood flow returns after a stroke. The molecule, a byproduct of an amino acid handled by gut microbes, resembles stress hormones in shape. In the rat model, treated animals had smaller dead zones and better behavior scores.

The molecule latched onto a hormone receptor on the brain's immune cells and quieted it. Those cells then released far less of three swelling signals, and fewer nerve cells died. A drug that switches the same receptor on erased the benefit, pinning the effect to that switch.
pmc-11653835:
Hermioni Amonoo and co-authors survey how residents and faculty experienced a group mentorship scheme called mentorship families. Their 2024 study comes from a psychiatry residency, where one-to-one faculty mentors run short for large cohorts. The program grouped eleven faculty members with forty-five residents, four or five trainees per family.

A cross-sectional survey after the first year gauges what the arrangement delivered: guidance, belonging, and peer support in one structure. Group mentorship spreads a scarce resource, senior attention, while adding the horizontal ties that carry trainees through hard rotations. The authors report perceptions from both sides of the family table to judge whether the model deserves keeping.
pmc-11653935:
Madhawa Pradeepa Nawarathne and Chathuranga Dharmarathne review plant-based control of dengue mosquito larvae in this 2024 paper. Dengue is a harsh viral disease spread by two Aedes mosquito species. Killing larvae is the most effective control point in the mosquito life cycle. Synthetic chemicals work but raise health and environment worries. Plant extracts offer a greener option, being cheap and target-specific. Tiny particles made with plant extracts are a newer twist.

The review gathers studies on extracts from many plants. It compares their larva-killing compounds and strength. Particle versions can carry the compounds and release them slowly. Safety for non-target life is a key plus claimed for these tools. The authors weigh the evidence for field use in dengue regions. Such reviews help control programs pick candidates for trials.
pmc-11654135:
Yueqing Wang and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on gaps in diabetes care in Shandong, China. Good care is a chain: screening, diagnosis, treatment, and finally hitting health targets. People fall off the chain at each step. The team measured how many adults with diabetes remain at each stage.

They re-analyzed a 2018 national survey of chronic disease in China, using its Shandong sample of interviews, exams, and lab tests. The cascade counts people from first blood sugar test through to full control of sugar, pressure, and fats. Each drop between stages marks a fixable gap, such as people tested but never told their result. Health planners can use the map to aim effort where the losses are largest.
pmc-11654335:
Jiuyang Xu and co-authors report an adult whose rare immune disorder first looked like a lung infection. The disease, X-linked lymphoproliferative disorder, leaves boys vulnerable to a common virus and usually appears in childhood. Few patients reach adulthood undiagnosed. This man arrived with fever, breathlessness, and nodules scattered through his lungs.

Gene sequencing and family tracing confirmed the diagnosis. His chest scans showed both lungs studded with nodules that partly shrank under steroid treatment. High-dose steroids, plus broad drugs against the mixed infections that had moved in, controlled his symptoms. Tissue studies found unusual cell growth and T cell buildup in the lungs. The authors stress that gene testing belongs in the workup of young patients with unexplained infections and possible immune defects. The case also adds rare detail on how this disease marks the lungs.
pmc-11655235:
Xiaoxiao Bao and co-authors report a cervical cancer that closely resembled a rare HPV-related tumor of the nasal cavity, published in 2024. That tumor type is a two-part epithelial growth tied to human papillomavirus infection. It almost always arises in the nose or sinuses; only two cases elsewhere, in breast and vulva, had been reported.

A 69-year-old woman came to hospital after more than a year of vaginal bleeding and tested positive for high-risk HPV. Biopsy showed a high-grade lesion with invasion, and she had radical surgery. Pathology, staining tests, and HPV testing led to the diagnosis of a multiphenotypic cervical carcinoma resembling the nasal tumor. She received no added radiation or chemotherapy. After a year of follow-up there was no recurrence or spread. The authors note these tumors tend toward slow local growth despite high-grade looks.
pmc-11655535:
Wangqu, Xue, and Chen surveyed in twenty twenty-four how media lean, app hopping, and low mood link in young college folks in China. App hopping means swift moves twixt many apps and sites in a rich media world. They asked more than one thousand two hundred students in a rich east zone.

Traits of hopping shaped how much folks leaned on media for their needs. The kind of that lean then shaped low mood in its turn. The chain gives a fresh lens on media use and mind health. It also fills a one-sided view from past work on lean and mood in a pair.
pmc-11655635:
Yang and colleagues report in 2024 that a small RNA, miR-378, worsens rheumatoid arthritis in mice by amplifying cell stress. The RNA is abundant in patients' joint tissue and tracks disease severity. Mice engineered to overproduce it developed faster joint swelling and bone damage in an arthritis model. Their joint tissue showed stronger endoplasmic reticulum stress, more blood vessel growth, and more bone-eating cell activity.

The team traced the effect to a stress protein the RNA suppresses. Blocking the RNA with a delivered inhibitor eased disease in mice. The authors nominate miR-378 as a drug target.
pmc-11655735:
Wang and co-authors compared two commercial kits for making a prostate cancer imaging tracer, in a paper published in 2024. The tracer, a gallium-labeled molecule that homes to prostate tumors, is scanned by PET to find disease. Both kits were recently approved, and demand for the scans has surged, helped by a matching therapy. Labs using germanium generators must choose which kit to run daily. The authors prepared the tracer with each kit in routine production.

They measured how consistently each kit labeled the molecule and what the workflow felt like. The comparison offers practical guidance: yield, reliability, and handling. A kit that fails a morning run costs a patient a scan slot. Routine, boring consistency is the real product here. The paper speaks to radiopharmacy managers making a recurring purchase.
pmc-11655835:
Vaishali Bhardwaj and co-authors profile the suppressor immune cells that gather in the bone marrow of patients with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, a slow blood cancer. The marrow's non-cancer cells shape whether immunity can fight the tumor, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells are prime suspects. Their 2024 study sorts and sequences the non-malignant marrow cells of patients against healthy controls.

Suppressor cells marked by low HLA-DR were clearly expanded in patients, mostly the polymorphonuclear kind. Single-cell profiling gave them an inflammatory, immune-damping signature, wired through interferon and tumor necrosis factor signals. The picture is a marrow coached to tolerate the cancer. Hematologists get named cell populations to target if they want the immune system back in the fight.
pmc-11655935:
Pei Luo and co-authors study an orchid compound against colorectal cancer with network methods and lab tests in 2024. The compound is an alkaloid from a medicinal orchid. Network pharmacology maps its likely gene targets. Cancer gene lists come from a public database. The overlap set holds more than one hundred fifty genes.

Those genes cluster in growth, death, and signal tasks. In cell tests, the compound slowed cancer cell growth and movement. Gene and protein checks show two signal paths were damped by the compound. Those paths are known drivers of this cancer. The authors say the compound has real anti cancer promise. More work can test it as a treatment base.
pmc-11656235:
Elena Ivanova and sixteen co-authors exposed the bacterium Escherichia coli to intense terahertz radiation from a synchrotron to see whether the cells merely endure it or actively adapt. The health effects of this radiation band are unsettled. Their beam covered a wide span of terahertz frequencies for over ninety minutes at room temperature.

Growth dipped at regular intervals during exposure, then viable counts recovered. Under the microscope, about a fifth of the cells showed deformed outer skins, with contents leaking out. A day later, the protein profile of survivors had shifted toward membrane repair and salt-stress handling. The authors read this as a prompt, evolved stress response rather than passive survival: the same machinery the cells use against other hardships. The work informs safety thinking as terahertz devices spread.
pmc-11656435:
Wang and colleagues asked in 2024 whether how fast a stroke's dead tissue grows early on predicts dangerous bleeding after clot removal. They defined early infarct growth rate as core volume on imaging divided by time since onset. In their registry of large-vessel stroke patients, about one in nine suffered symptomatic brain bleeding within three days. Faster growth independently raised that risk.

The link was linear, and adding the growth rate to standard risk factors improved prediction clearly. The authors suggest the measure can flag patients needing extra caution after thrombectomy. It uses scans already taken before treatment.
pmc-11656835:
Jun Yong Kim and co-authors build a hybrid speck to treat worn joints in a 2024 study. Joint wear, called osteoarthritis, breaks down cartilage and stirs swelling. Sacs shed by stem cells can aid repair, but past ways to upgrade those sacs risked harm to cells or loss of the good factors inside.

Their method fuses the sacs with fat-based specks in a mild bath, keeping inner factors whole. One speck type also holds a calming drug and a tag that homes to cartilage. A growth factor was loaded high in the sacs as well. In rats with a hurt knee joint, the hybrid guarded cartilage and calmed swelling for a long span.
pmc-11657135:
Charley Wilson and co-authors survey how childhood hardship and neurodivergence combine to shape adult life in England, in a 2024 study. Neurodivergent people may face more adverse childhood experiences, from abuse to household strife, than others. Past work counted few hardship types and leaned on formal diagnoses. This team asked more than five thousand adults in one region directly.

Neurodivergent adults reported each hardship type more often than their peers, and stacked up more of them overall. Poor health, low mental well-being, arrest, and jail all ran higher in that group. Hardship counts alone also raised most of those odds. Joined together, the two factors added risk past what either gives alone. The authors urge services to prevent hardship in neurodivergent children and to answer it early.
pmc-11657435:
Jiajia Yu and eleven co-authors hunted for urine markers that can diagnose lung tuberculosis, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Current tests for the disease are slow or invasive, and better tools are needed for sound decisions. Urine is easy to collect, so its proteins and small molecules are attractive candidates.

Samples came from tuberculosis patients, lung cancer patients, pneumonia patients, and healthy controls. Thousands of proteins and over a thousand metabolic features were measured. A five-protein panel sorted tuberculosis from each other group with high accuracy. A five-metabolite panel did nearly as well, topping the protein one against healthy controls. The authors say combined urine panels could enable non-invasive diagnosis with strong sensitivity and specificity.
pmc-11657635:
Seyedmostafa Sheikhalishahi and co-authors train machine learning models to forecast which surgery patients in intensive care will need a blood transfusion, in work from 2024. Getting blood ready in time matters for outcomes and for blood bank planning alike. Too-early guesses waste stock, and too-late ones endanger patients.

Records for 9,118 surgical intensive care patients came from an Amsterdam database. The models used thirty-two clinical variables, drawn from windows that stretch from before admission to six hours after. Two algorithms were compared head to head, and the boosted tree model won, most clearly for a twelve-hour horizon. Longer data windows helped up to a point. The authors weigh data span as a design choice.
pmc-11658535:
Joël Fokom Domgue and a large team of co-authors published a 2024 survey study on colposcopy services for cervical cancer care in Africa. Cervical cancer hits the continent hard, in part because organized screening is scarce. Women who screen positive need a colposcopy exam to guide next steps, yet its use in the region was little documented.

The team surveyed health providers involved in cervical cancer prevention across Africa in 2021 and 2022. One hundred thirty providers from 23 countries replied. They reported their training, whether they perform the exam, and what prompts them to use it. The results map the training and practice gaps that screening programs must close. Without follow up exams, positive screens cannot turn into saved lives.
pmc-11658935:
Andri Papaleontiou and co-authors adapt a parent questionnaire about children's eating into Greek, and check that it still works. The scale, About Your Child's Eating, probes how feeding interactions feel between parent and child, for better or worse. Two hundred Greek-Cypriot parents took part: half with children who had feeding or swallowing trouble, half without.

The translation followed World Health Organization steps for cultural fit. Parents in the difficulty group scored far higher on problem-related items than the typical group, as the scale intends. Overall consistency was strong. The authors conclude the Greek version can help clinicians spot strained feeding relationships in Cyprus. Such spotting matters, since feeding is a daily, repeated negotiation that shapes nutrition, growth, and family calm.
pmc-11659235:
Jing Zhao and eleven co-authors pair a virus with antibiotics against a drug-resistant gut bacterium. Their 2024 study targets Shigella dysenteriae, a cause of severe dysentery. Careless antibiotic use has bred strains that shrug off standard drugs. Phage therapy, using bacteria-killing viruses, offers a fresh route.

A phage named Henu10 was fished from sewage and fully profiled. Its genome, shape, and family ties were mapped. Bacteria that evolved resistance to the phage were then bred on purpose. Those resistant strains paid for their armor: weaker gripping, more stress sensitivity, thinner biofilms. They also fell easier to some antibiotics. The trade-off suggests phage-plus-drug pairs can corner the bacterium.
pmc-11659635:
Òscar Guadayol, Rudi Schuech, and Stuart Humphries asked how long a swimming bacterium should be to chase food well. Elongated shapes are common among ocean bacteria, and the team suspected a trade-off: longer cells explore faster but may harvest less neatly. They watched treated gut bacteria of different lengths swim toward a food-like chemical in a microfluidic channel with a steady gradient.

Cells of middling length gathered most tightly at the source. A model matched to the experiments explained why. Very short cells lose their sense of direction, while very long cells run slowly and briefly. The best shape depends on how stable the chemical landscape is. In simulations of the nutrient halo around an algal cell, long cells using a run-and-reverse style did best. The authors say the stability of the chemical scenery helps decide which cell size evolution favors.
pmc-11659735:
Meiying Cai, Na Lin, and co-authors chart small code cuts and dups on one arm in unborn babes from a vast ward pool, in a 2024 study. That arm swaps bits with kin strands with ease, which spawns such cuts. Birth traits vary wide post birth, so womb calls stay hard for staff.

Tens of thousands of womb tests feed the pool, with scores of hits. Two hot zones hold most of the hits in the set. Bone odd marks lead the scan signs in the top zone. Soft marks lead in the next zone, a soft flag kind. Most live births show no odd marks at all. Cuts lone should not end a birth path.
pmc-11660535:
Hany Heiba and co-authors tested a mixed oxide catalyst in 2024 for cleaning arsenic from water using light. Arsenite is the more toxic, harder-to-remove form of arsenic, and light-driven oxidation converts it to a safer form. Their material pairs tin-doped titanium oxide with titanium-doped tin oxide at a junction.

Light tests showed the junction holds separated charges about twice as long as plain titanium oxide, and makes more of them. The oxidation itself ran in under a microsecond. Blocking experiments showed hydroxyl radicals did most of the work, with superoxide radicals second. Scavengers cut yields sharply, confirming the ranking. The authors present the junction as a strong candidate catalyst.
pmc-11662335:
Miyu Wang and co-authors report a 2024 trial on adding eye tasks to gym class for young children. The hope was to lift distance sight, moving-target sight, and the eye's focus shifting, all of which slump as screen time grows. In a Suzhou primary school, 168 third graders were split into two groups for sixteen weeks of exercise.

One group trained with visual targets flashed for three seconds during their exercise cycles; the other group exercised as usual. After the term, the target group had gained on all three eye measures, while the usual group gained only on focus shifting. Moving-target sight also acted as a bridge, carrying part of the gain to the other two measures.
pmc-11663435:
