Essa Samuel and co-authors review advanced treatments for complex regional pain syndrome in a 2024 paper. The disorder brings burning pain far beyond any injury, plus swelling, color shifts, and stiff movement. Usual drugs often fail it, so wired, injected, and unconventional options draw hope.

Four databases yielded twenty-three studies covering more than two thousand patients. Nerve-root and spinal cord stimulators cut pain by large shares in most reports, with gains in mood and life quality alongside. Block injections and odd-lane therapies showed mixed but sometimes real relief. The review calls the field promising yet thin, and asks for stronger trials.
pmc-11664235:
Eleven authors, led by Yunjie Wang, tested a targeted drug on brain tumors in this 2024 paper. Some gliomas lack a gene called MTAP. That loss floods the cell with a byproduct that weakens an enzyme, PRMT5, making the pair a synthetic lethal target: hit the weakened enzyme and only the tumor dies.

A drug that binds the weakened complex, MRTX1719, killed such tumors in dishes and animals while sparing normal cells. But reports hint that in real brains, healthy neighbors that still carry MTAP may soak up the byproduct, draining the tumor's weakness. The team checked which normal brain cells near the tumor still make MTAP, and how that changes the drug's punch. The findings matter for dosing a promising therapy.
pmc-11665635:
Matija Jelenc and co-authors measure heart valve roots in healthy adults in this 2024 study. A heart operation swaps a failed aortic valve with the patient's own lung valve. The swap lasts only if the lung valve's shape is kept sound, yet normal lung root data were scarce.

The team read more than five hundred chest scans and kept fifty with clear views of both roots. Lung and aortic leaflets matched in size, but the lung root's shape set its leaflets lower. The lung ring also stretched and shrank across each heartbeat by a wide share. The authors say fixing the moved valve to aortic, not lung, sizes should keep its leaflets in true form.
pmc-11667135:
Anushree Joshi, Jallavi Panchamia, and Apurvakumar Pandya set out a 2024 protocol for a choice study on rural work among specialist doctors in India. Rural health centers face an acute lack of specialists in medicine, child care, women care, and surgery. Policy needs to know which job traits would draw specialists to stay.

The method asks doctors to pick between mock job offers that vary by pay, place, and perks. A first qualitative phase mined past work and talks to pick the job traits and levels for the test. The full design mixes that phase with the choice survey in sequence. The end goal is reward packages that pull specialists into underserved areas.
pmc-11668635:
Muhammad Hazeem Akashah and co-authors report gout in the larynx in this 2024 paper. Gout deposits uric acid crystals in joints, and rarely in the head and neck. The patient was a 50 year old man with a long history of gouty arthritis. He came in with painless front neck swelling for two weeks.

Ultrasound suggested a cartilage tumor of the thyroid cartilage. A CT scan instead showed fluid and chalky deposits that pointed to infected gout. Surgery and tissue tests confirmed crystal deposits typical of gout, called tophi. This was the first such case reported in Sabah, Malaysia. The authors review how this rare condition forms and how it is treated, to raise awareness among clinicians.
pmc-11668735:
Khola Noreen and colleagues measure HPV vaccine uptake across South Asia. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-four. Cervical cancer burden in the region ranks among the highest worldwide. Few countries there run national HPV vaccine programmes.

Searches across four databases gathered thousands of candidate papers. Seventeen studies with over ten thousand people qualified. Pooled vaccine uptake came out in the single digits. That low rate leaves most eligible people unprotected. The team also modelled which factors predict getting vaccinated. Cost, awareness, and programme absence all shape the picture. Regional health planners gain a stark baseline for action.
pmc-11668935:
Hossein Mohammadi and seven co-authors published this brain study in 2024. It tracks glutamate, a key chemical messenger in the brain, while people learn and hold items in short-term memory. The team watched two brain areas: one in the front of the brain and one toward the back.

Fourteen healthy adults did a verbal memory task inside a scanner that can measure brain chemicals. The glutamate signal rose during the task in both areas, and it tended to rise more as the memory load grew. The front area showed a rise of about twenty percent, and the back area about thirty-three percent. The results suggest that harder thinking calls on more of this chemical, even in the right side of the brain.
pmc-11669435:
Shivendra Tangutoori and co-authors report a lymphoma case that squeezed the chest's great vein while wearing several disguises, in a 2024 paper. Hodgkin's lymphoma usually announces itself with fever, night sweats, and weight loss. This patient, a man in his early fifties, instead suffered eight months of worsening cough and breathlessness. He arrived with a drooping eyelid, a swollen neck, and engorged chest veins, signs of two syndromes at once.

Scans showed a bulky chest mass and fluid around the lung. Biopsy confirmed classical Hodgkin's lymphoma, staged at the highest level. His blood also carried a striking excess of eosinophils alongside chronic itching, both uncommon in this disease. Modern combination chemotherapy shrank the tumor and relieved his symptoms markedly.
pmc-11670235:
Alexandre Pierre Vaudano, Françoise Schwager, Monica Gotta, and Sofia Barbieri map the feedback loops that pattern a worm embryo's first cell. In Caenorhabditis elegans, two RNA-binding proteins, MEX-5 and MEX-6, gather at the front of the cell. They help place other factors, including the kinase PLK-1, and support the cell's front-back polarity.

Though the two MEX proteins are close cousins, the team found their gradients are tuned in different ways. PLK-1 lifts MEX-5 only indirectly, by steadying the cell cortex. It shapes MEX-6 by touching the protein directly. The picture that emerges is a circuit: the kinase ties the MEX proteins to the cortex so polarity is set up faithfully and held in place.
pmc-11670935:
Abigail Smith and co-authors present a 2024 study on an early gene signal in polycystic kidney disease. In this disease, kidney tubules slowly turn into fluid-filled cysts and the kidneys fail. Late stages are well studied, but the first steps of cyst formation are not.

The team deleted a key disease gene in mice and tracked gene activity before and right after cysts appeared. Seventy-four candidate genes emerged. Comparing them with single-cell data from human patients singled out one gene, TACSTD2. Its protein is scarce in healthy kidney cells but rises in the cells lining cysts. The gene is also known from cancer research, where tumors show the same pattern. The authors flag it as a treatment target.
pmc-11671035:
De Qing Görtzen and Ferdi Akca review in 2024 the naming chaos around minimally invasive heart bypass surgery. Each new variant coined its own term as the field grew, which muddies study and talk. The review gathers every term in use across the years into one map.

A database search in August twenty twenty four swept robotic and plain routes alike. Forty unique terms name the same broad family of procedures. Groups sort by how the artery is harvested and joined, with four main forms. One direct form leads the counts, with closed-chest full scope work next in study volume.
pmc-11672335:
Yilin Lang and co-authors test whether sealing a hidden leak between the heart's sides can calm vestibular migraine. Forty-one patients with the dizziness migraine variant and medium-to-large right-to-left shunts had the shunt closed, through the heart's foramen or by plugging a lung vessel malformation, depending on where the leak lived.

One month later, attack frequency and duration for both dizziness and migraine had fallen sharply, and every symptom score improved. The two closure routes performed alike. Red blood cell measures correlated with how much relief patients got, and men benefited more than women. The authors read the shunt as a real contributor to this migraine type and the blood markers as early candidates for predicting who surgery helps.
pmc-11672435:
Shiori Kitaya and co-authors pair ultraviolet light with a containment hood to disinfect hospital rooms more deeply. Drug-resistant bacteria linger on bed rails and shadowed corners, where plain UV-C beams fall short. Their test room held agar plates seeded with two hardy germs, a carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter and MRSA, on lit and shadowed surfaces alike.

With the hood in place, MRSA colonies fell sharply even in the shadows that bare irradiation had missed. The hood traps and reflects the light where it is needed, so germs on indirect surfaces die too. The team also checked how much ultraviolet leaked outside the unit during use. The pairing offers hospitals a stronger terminal clean for rooms that housed resistant infections.
pmc-11672835:
Timothy Holder and co-authors used wearable sensors to study dog-assisted therapy sessions in a 2024 paper. Dogs now assist in care for many conditions, from cancer fatigue to post-traumatic stress. Programs are widespread, yet outcomes for the humans and for the dogs themselves remain open questions.

The team fitted wearable devices to track both partners during sessions. Movement, heart signals, and proximity data reveal how the interaction unfolds moment by moment, beyond what observers can note. Such records can show which session patterns calm or stress each side. The work aims at therapy that is proven good for the dog as well as the person, a welfare standard the field has lacked.
pmc-11672935:
Fake blood must carry oxygen like the real thing, but its cargo spoils by rust-like decay. Rerkshanandana and co-authors wrap blood protein in tiny grains and add guard enzymes to slow that decay. Their 2024 study builds the grains by a rain-and-set method and loads them with two front-line guards and a vitamin.

The guards are the same ones a living cell uses first: one that kills a harsh oxygen form, and one that turns peroxide into water and air. The grains were cycled through oxygen on and off, then read for total and loaded protein. The wraps shielded the cargo through sixteen rounds of peroxide hits. Total protein held steady across the cycles. Such grains could one day store and ship as a blood stand-in.
pmc-11673035:
Qinyi Zhang and co-authors study dengue virus infection in macrophages in a 2024 paper. Dengue is the most widespread mosquito borne virus. It can cause mild fever or progress to fatal bleeding and shock. Macrophages are main target cells and lead the innate immune response against the virus.

Infected macrophages showed a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis, with inflammasome activation and membrane pore formation. Sequencing across infection stages found dozens of microRNAs changed in both early and late stages. Several named microRNAs were flagged as possible regulators of the death pathway, offering targets for understanding dengue severity.
pmc-11673135:
Tsabeeh Salah Mahmoud and co-authors improve breast imaging in a 2024 paper. Multispectral transmission imaging shines several light colors through breast tissue, but absorption and scatter leave images faint and noisy. Stacking many frames cleans the image, yet breathing and camera shake misalign the frames and blur the stack.

Their fix aligns frames first with a hybrid search that pairs a genetic algorithm with a swarm method, sped by a squared constriction tweak. Tests at four wavelengths hit about ninety-nine point nine percent alignment accuracy with faster runs. Readers get cleaner breast images for later sorting and diagnosis steps.
pmc-11673435:
Enrico Apa and co-authors present a 2024 study on the mental health cost of being deaf in one ear for working adults. Single-sided deafness wrecks sound localization and speech understanding in noise, but its psychological toll is less charted. The team compared fifty-four employed adults with the condition, free of other major illness, against ninety-five normal-hearing peers. Both groups took hearing handicap, communication, well-being, and social functioning questionnaires.

The deaf-in-one-ear group scored worse on most measures of psychological well-being and social functioning. The differences were statistically clear across most subscales of the tests. The authors say the study firmly establishes poorer mental health and social adjustment in this population. They recommend a multidisciplinary approach: counseling, acceptance support, and role modeling to raise quality of life. Workplace awareness, they imply, is part of the fix.
pmc-11673935:
Yoosun Kim and co-authors run, in a 2024 pilot study, a test of how muscle activity affects reading of touch cues while walking. The cues were mild electric pulses standing in for a haptic signal. Three healthy adults walked on a treadmill as the experiment ran.

Pulses landed on a calf muscle and on an upper arm muscle, timed to slices of the step cycle. Recognition patterns varied from person to person. The arm, mostly idle in walking, showed more variable recognition than the hard-working calf. A warping method compared muscle signals with what participants felt. Such findings guide where on the body a wearable should buzz a walker who cannot look down.
pmc-11674035:
Vlad David and co-authors compare children's forearm fractures before and during the pandemic at one Romanian hospital, in a study from 2024. Lockdowns changed how children played, traveled, and reached care, so injury patterns and treatment choices likely shifted too. A side by side year comparison can show exactly what moved.

Records covered just over fourteen hundred children, split between 2019 and 2021. Ages and backgrounds were much the same in both years. Broken bones sat at steeper angles in the pandemic year, while other injury features barely changed. The authors also compared how the fractures were managed in each period. The study gives pediatric trauma teams a record of how a crisis year bent, but did not break, routine fracture care.
pmc-11674535:
Maryna Khorkova and co-authors study creativity, movement skill, and daily activity in young school children in a 2024 paper. The group held 195 children aged eight and nine, girls and boys in near-even split. The trait was tested by a drawing task, its movement form by a standard action test, fitness by parts of a European test battery, and daily activity by a screening form.

Boys and girls differed in motor fitness scores, but not in activity level or in either form of the trait. In neither sex did activity or fitness link to the test scores. The authors caution that, at this age, simply adding more activity may not grow the trait on its own. Richer, more varied movement tasks may be the lever that matters.
pmc-11674735:
Chieh Kao and Yang Zhang probe sex differences in how brains register emotional tone of voice in a 2024 pilot study. The melody of speech carries feeling, and brains flag changes in it automatically, before conscious attention. Whether that automatic response differs by sex and emotion was unclear.

Twenty-two young adults heard streams of words spoken angrily, happily, sadly, or neutrally while watching a silent film. Brain responses showed both early detection and later attention-grabbing signals for emotional voices. Women responded more strongly to angry than sad tones; men, to angry over happy. Happy voices grabbed the most attention, but only in men. The authors caution that the small sample needs confirming, and note the results complicate any simple female-superiority story.
pmc-11674835:
Çağlar Türk and co-authors reviewed ten years of care at one hospital in a 2024 study. They looked at infants born with an open spine defect who also had fluid buildup in the brain. Each child had the spine defect closed and then a shunt placed to drain the fluid.

Records covered many infants followed for about five years on average. About three in ten had shunt problems, from blockages to infections. Infections often led to more operations, and boys faced more long-term infections than girls. The authors stress close follow-up after surgery, since early care for shunt failure or infection can change a child's course.
pmc-11675035:
Gabriella Guelfi and co-authors review in 2024 how aging unfolds in dogs, from single molecules up to whole-body change. Aging starts at birth and slowly erodes the body's power to adapt, leaving older dogs slower to heal and more prone to disease. Twelve hallmarks now frame the field, from worn chromosome caps to a faltering immune system.

The review adds a thirteenth hallmark: poor water balance. Cells, organs, and behavior all shift as water control slips with age. The authors walk through each hallmark in dogs and point to where vets might step in. A better grasp of dog aging could guide care that keeps old dogs healthier for longer.
pmc-11675435:
Valentina Schiavoni and co-authors review a cell pathway as a possible target for new kidney cancer care, in a 2024 paper. Kidney cell cancer is the most common type of kidney cancer. It tends to act in an aggressive way, with spread to other sites and a poor outlook. Most cases are found by chance, often late, when spread has already begun.

Care is made harder by the fact that this cancer often resists both drug therapy and radiation. The pathway under review centers on a factor called Nrf2, which runs the cell's response to oxidative stress. Its level is raised in many tumors. The authors weigh signs that blocking or tuning this path could give new options for care and for judging risk.
pmc-11675535:
Suryadeep Dash and co-authors record from motion-sensing neurons in a bird's brain area that feeds visual flow signals to the cerebellum, asking whether a neuron's favorite direction changes with speed. Standard tests fix one middling speed, so the question stayed open. They measured over a hundred neurons in zebra finches across an enormous speed range.

Cells responded best at moderate speeds. At those speeds, most cells preferred one direction. At the fastest speeds, nearly half answered every direction, and only a fifth stayed choosy. Few cells were all-direction at every speed, so most neurons truly retune with speed. The authors suggest the area flags unexpected drift or looming collisions during flight.
pmc-11675735:
Zsigmond Papp and co-authors sort plant-based drinks by their scent fingerprints, in a 2024 study. Oat, soy, and other plant drinks fill more shelves every year, and makers need fast checks that a batch is what the label claims. Full lab analysis is slow and costly, so the team tested two scent-based tools on 111 samples.

One tool separates vapor chemicals with ion mobility; the other is an electronic nose with dozens of sensors. Math models then tried to group the drinks by type from 58 scent compounds or the nose's readings. The nose separated more drink types cleanly than the vapor method in their tests. Cheap scent screening could catch swapped or spoiled products before they ship.
pmc-11675835:
Leonardo Lima studies two quantum effects side by side in layered ferrimagnets in a 2024 theory paper. These materials hold spins in mixed patterns, with some neighbors aligned and others opposed. He looks at the spin Nernst effect, where a heat flow drives a spin flow, and asks how it links with entanglement, a measure of quantum connection.

Working with exact computer solutions on small lattices, Lima traces how the coupling strengths between spins shape both the wave bands of the material and the entanglement measure. He also studies how those couplings drive shifts between phases. The results are compared with an older wave-based theory to check where the two agree.
pmc-11676035:
Atsushi Yamashita and co-authors test a new imaging dye in a 2024 paper. Surgeons use near-infrared dyes to see blood flow and lymph nodes during operations. The one approved dye glows at one wavelength only, which limits the detail a camera can capture at once.

The new dye, indocyanine blue, glows about one hundred nanometers lower, in the seven hundred range. It dissolved well and cleared from the body fast in tests, giving clean views of vessels and lymph nodes. Paired with a second dye aimed at tumors, it allowed two-channel views of tumors and nodes together. The authors say the added channel could sharpen guidance during surgery for many patients.
pmc-11676235:
Stanisław Pałubicki, Jarosław Plichta, and Krzysztof Nadolny map how heat input shapes weld size in a duplex stainless steel. The steel, grade 1.4462, joins ferritic and austenitic phases and serves in construction and offshore work where strength and corrosion resistance count. Welding current, arc voltage, and speed together set the heat delivered in the MAG process. The team measured how those settings change the cross-sectional area of the joints.

Mathematical models tied heat input to weld area closely enough to explain and predict joint size. A regression function and its three-dimensional response surface plot the relationship. The authors offer the models as a base for tuning process parameters and controlling weld quality.
pmc-11677035:
Charlotte Day and co-authors test lab-made antibodies against the NMDA receptor for their effect on long-term brain plasticity. Antibodies to this receptor appear in encephalitis and autoimmune epilepsy. Their exact role in nerve excitability is still unsettled.

The team raised antibodies against chosen parts of the receptor's GluN1 unit. Peptide purification then enriched the receptor-specific fraction. Binding and specificity checks confirmed the antibodies hit their target. The purified set was applied to brain tissue models. Plasticity measures showed an inhibitory effect from the antibodies. That finding helps explain symptoms in antibody-driven disease. It also gives drug hunters a cleaner test reagent for labs that study these brain disorders in mice and in cell work.
pmc-11677335:
Samih Haj Ibrahim and co-authors present a 2024 method to model how a water drop freezes on a surface carved by laser. Such surfaces can delay ice build-up, which matters for planes, power lines, and cold gear. Tests alone are slow, so a sound model that sorts good patterns from bad ones has clear worth.

The model works in two steps: first the drop settles into its rest shape on the surface, then cold terms are added to freeze it. The team built models of plain, lined, and angled patterns from lab samples and ran the freeze for each. Freeze times did not match lab times with full care, yet the model ranked patterns well. It also lets users study wetting and freezing on rough ground in fine detail.
pmc-11677735:
Meng and five co-authors study a stainless steel with added aluminum in molten carbonate salt in a 2024 paper. Such salts are candidates for next-generation solar power storage. Structural metals must resist both harsh corrosion and creep at high heat.

Tests ran at high temperature with several aluminum levels. Adding aluminum lowered the corrosion rate, with one mix cutting it by about a quarter over a long test. Aluminum changed the inner corrosion layer and helped form a dense protective surface film early on. It also improved strength and stretch at high heat. One mix showed the best tensile traits and the slowest creep. The work guides alloy choice for solar plants.
pmc-11677935:
Chappell and colleagues pin down a fungus that rots parsnip roots in this twenty twenty-four study. The crop is a niche but rich one for UK farms, and root rot is its top loss. How wide the chief rot fungus spreads and how it splits was not well known.

Inside, strains from the UK, far Europe, and New Zealand were grown, stressed, and gene-read. All strains could rot both roots and leaves of the crop in tests. Strains grew from cold to mild warmth and made two spore types in that span. Gene trees split strains into loose groups with no tie to host or place. The team finds no proof for more than one true species in the set.
pmc-11678135:
Yue Gao and co-authors paired a cancer drug with a ring-shaped host molecule to fix its flaws, in this 2024 study. The drug, cisplatin, kills tumors but dissolves poorly and breaks down fast in water. The team used host-guest chemistry, where the ring cradles the drug.

Tests with light and vibration tools confirmed the pairing, at a best ratio of one to one. The complex dissolved far better and stayed stable longer in pure water, and even better in salt water. In lung cancer cells it killed more strongly than the raw drug. The authors offer the pairing as a route to stronger, steadier chemo.
pmc-11678235:
Water filters built from plastic membranes foul and tear; plant fibers might make them stronger and greener. Seren Acarer Arat and co-authors reinforce polysulfone membranes with cellulose nanocrystals and nanofibers. Both fillers come from renewable plant material. The team varied the filler share and type, then measured pore structure, roughness, strength, and flow. Fouled membranes were cleaned and retested to judge recovery.

One recipe, with a light dose of nanocrystals, passed the most pure water. A nanofiber-heavy version proved stiffest. Computer models of the composite's mechanics matched the bench results. The study weighs a familiar trade: flow against strength, with fouling behavior in between. Tuning the plant-fiber dose lets engineers pick their point on that trade for real filtration duty.
pmc-11678335:
Kim and Kim studied wasp parasitoids of pine beetles in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Pine wilt disease, spread by Monochamus beetles, kills Korean pines. The team catalogued fifteen parasitoids of the two beetle carriers. Two larval parasitoid wasps were followed in the field near Pohang from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty.

One wasp, Cyanopterus flavator, parasitized up to about six percent of one beetle species. Both wasps preferred that carrier, though only one preference was statistically firm. Peak attack matched the season when beetle larvae sat just under the bark. Tree height patterns lined up with larval density as well. The authors say the timing and height data can guide releases for biological control.
pmc-11678435:
Haohao Miao and co-authors build and test a simulation potential for tantalum-rhenium alloys, in a 2024 paper. Layered parts of these two refractory metals promise strength at extreme heat, suiting them to aerospace engine nozzles. To study how atoms mix and strengthen at the layer boundary, modelers first need a reliable rule for how the atoms push on each other.

The team derived an embedded atom method potential by force matching, then checked it against quantum calculations and lab tests. Predicted crystal sizes and surface energies landed close to the reference values, with small errors throughout. The sound potential now lets researchers simulate how atoms diffuse and strengthen in these heat-proof composites.
pmc-11678535:
Denis Aiudi, Alessio Iacoangeli, and co-authors try a glow scope in brain vessel cuts for bulges and knot webs, in a 2024 study. A dye glow view in the main scope is the stock aid for such cuts. A hand scope with a spy glow mode may stand in for cost or stock gaps.

Five sick folks with bulges or knot webs feed the early tale. All bulges seal off in full with no neck scraps left. All knot webs clear in full with no scraps left as well. The spy scope shows the dye glow in sharp view through the cuts. Picked plain cases suit the aid best, they say.
pmc-11678635:
Deep burns on hands and feet often need skin grafts, which means a second wound where skin is taken. Kohei Aoki and co-authors report a gentler method in a 2024 pilot study. They treated four patients with an enzyme gel that dissolves dead burn tissue, followed by a spray of the patient's own skin cells.

The patients ranged from infants to a 28-year-old, and the burns covered a small share of the body. Care took place between August 2023 and July 2024, and no one needed added surgery afterward. The wounds closed early, and scar scores stayed very low over about a year of follow-up. The patients were pleased with how their hands and feet looked. The team also wrote pain and sedation plans for both adults and children.
pmc-11678735:
Valentina Meloni and eight co-authors formulate a prostate cancer PROTAC drug into films that dissolve on the tongue, in a two thousand twenty-four drug-making paper. ARV-110 belongs to a molecular class beyond the classic rule-of-five, and its poor solubility blocks easy delivery.

Polyvinyl alcohol films were made two ways: hot melt extrusion, screened first by vacuum compression molding, and solvent casting. The drug's heat stability allowed both. Films were tested for disintegration in man-made saliva, drug release under body-like settings, and mechanical strength. All formulations raised solubility with fast disintegration and good stress resistance. The authors lay the groundwork for orodispersible delivery of proteolysis-targeting chimeras in general.
pmc-11678835:
Jinghui Cheng and co-authors design glowing probes that switch on when zinc is present in a 2024 study. Zinc ions matter in cells, and a fast visual test for them aids biology and medicine. The team built a family of paired Schiff base compounds with varied bridges and decorations.

Light tests mapped how each compound absorbs and emits across the visible range. Some reached very high fluorescence efficiency in solution. One probe uses a proton-shift trick to light up on binding zinc. The probe was then tried inside living cells and on paper test strips. Both settings showed a clear turn-on signal. Such strips could bring zinc checks out of the lab and into clinics or field kits.
pmc-11678935:
Panagiota Kalligosfyri, Eleni Lamprou, and Despina Kalogianni review fast sensor technologies that read cancer clues from body fluids, in a 2024 paper. Liquid biopsy hunts tumor traces in blood and other fluids, sparing patients the knife and allowing repeat checks over time. The prize is early diagnosis and treatment matched to the patient.

The review covers optical sensors that read color, glow, or light shifts, and electrochemical sensors that reach very low detection limits. Color tests win on simplicity, glow tests on speed, and surface-wave methods on label-free reading. New amplification tricks push sensitivity further. The authors track how these tools edge toward bedside use, where quick, cheap, robust answers matter most.
pmc-11679035:
A research team made activated carbon from the stones of amla fruit and tested how it pulls phenol pollutants from water, in this 2024 study. Phenols are common industrial contaminants, and the chemical groups attached to them may change how well they stick to carbon. The carbon was made with a low-heat water treatment of the fruit stones.

The finished carbon had a wide inner surface and took up three test phenols from water. A standard model fit the uptake well, and the nitro-bearing form was captured most, then the chlorine form, then plain phenol. The process drew in heat and ran on its own once started. Results slightly beat a store-bought carbon used for the same job.
pmc-11679335:
Tao Yan leads a team of eleven authors comparing crucian carp raised in rice paddies against pond-raised fish, and the paddy fish come out biochemically ahead. Rice-fish co-culture is an ancient Chinese farming model whose product quality claims deserve measurement. Digestive enzymes, antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism enzymes, and muscle nutrients were assayed in both groups.

Paddy fish showed higher digestive enzyme activity and stronger liver antioxidant enzyme activity. Nearly every glucose-handling enzyme measured ran higher in paddy fish, with one key enzyme markedly lower, indicating a rewired glucose economy. Muscle nutrient content differed as well. The authors conclude the traditional system produces measurably different, arguably healthier fish, giving farmers data behind the premium paddy-raised label.
pmc-11679435:
Giacomo Villa and co-authors test a cheap belt sensor as a jump gauge, in a study from 2024. Jump height is a stock leg mark in sport and care. Gold gauges, cam webs and force floors, stay in labs. A slow belt sensor at the low back could free the test if its math holds.

Eighteen sound souls did five two-leg and ten one-leg countermove jumps, read by all three rigs at once. Three math ways turned belt reads to height. Twin-step math won: it tied gold at near nine in ten and sat a hair off, with top trust. Wing and flight ways held for two-leg jumps but waned on one. A field gauge, the team reads, is in hand.
pmc-11679535:
Alexander Arkhipov and co-authors assemble a chromosome level flax genome from nanopore reads in this 2024 paper. Flax is grown for seed and fiber, with 30 chromosomes and a genome near 460 million bases. Past assemblies fell short of full telomere to telomere coverage. Long nanopore reads can span the hard repetitive parts.

The variety K-3018 was sequenced to about 120 fold coverage. Two assemblers were run on the long reads. One produced 54 large pieces with a strong continuity score. In that assembly, eight chromosomes were single pieces with telomere repeats at both ends. Five more needed only two pieces each. The resource supports breeding and gene studies in this dual use crop.
pmc-11679935:
Yang Zhang and six co-authors study how long-term aerobic exercise protects the liver, in a research paper from 2024. The focus is fatty liver disease linked to poor metabolism, where the body resists insulin. Exercise is known to cut liver fat, but the exact path was unclear.

The team tracked tiny particles called exosomes in blood after a twelve-week exercise plan. A small molecule inside them, tied to fat tissue, acts on a gene called ROCK1. Tests in patients and in mice fed a high-fat diet backed the link. Exercise lowered liver fat and improved insulin response, and this molecule helps explain why.
pmc-11680235:
André Filipe Pastor leads a team of nine authors in 2024 in putting forward the laboratory opossum as a new animal model for Zika virus research. The Zika epidemic exposed a gap: monkey models are costly and scarce, and ordinary lab mice resist the virus unless specially bred.

The small marsupial Monodelphis domestica fills the gap neatly. Infected opossums mount a strong immune response, carry the virus widely through the body, and keep it for a long time. Those traits mirror what researchers need to study in people. The team argues the opossum is a practical, faithful stand-in for testing vaccines and treatments.
pmc-11680335:
Sofie Peere and co-authors report a foaling that beat long odds. A six-year-old Standardbred mare carrying identical twins, a rare outcome of embryo transfer, developed hydrops, a dangerous swelling of fluid around the foals. One twin died in the womb at about eight months. Such pregnancies usually end with both foals, and often the mare, lost. At 332 days the mare delivered with assistance, and the outcome surprised the team.

The surviving foal was born alive, healthy, and normally sized, and the dead twin was intact rather than decayed, which is itself unusual after weeks in the womb. Mare and foal left the clinic a week later. The authors believe this is the first report of a healthy foal from a monozygotic twin pregnancy with hydrops after transfer of a single laboratory-made embryo.
pmc-11680435:
Aya Saitoh and co-authors survey vaccine education and hesitancy among Japanese healthcare students, in this 2024 cross-sectional study. Future clinicians shape public acceptance of vaccination, so their training and attitudes matter. Over five hundred final-year medical, nursing and pharmacy students answered an anonymous online questionnaire in March 2023.

About forty percent voiced concern over new vaccine risks, and average immunization knowledge sat near sixty percent correct, with medical students slightly ahead. Medical students also felt far more prepared for clinical practice than nursing or pharmacy peers. Substantial shares doubted government information or recommended vaccines. The authors call for earlier, stronger immunization education across all three programs.
pmc-11683335:
Micaela Chacon and Neil Dixon review in 2024 genetically encoded biosensors for a circular plastics economy. Current plastic production harms climate and pollutes, so the whole value chain needs reform. Biology can make plastics from renewable feedstocks and help recycle or upcycle them at end of life.

Biosensors built into cells can speed the design-build-test cycle for such processes. The review sums up sensors that respond to plastic building blocks and monomers. It also covers uses in both making and breaking down plastics. The authors present the tools as a resource to support a circular bioeconomy for plastics.
pmc-11683635:
Murad Hajiyev, Ahmed Ibrahim, Mohammed Alotaibi, and four colleagues tune oil-recovery chemistry under pressure in this two thousand twenty-four study. Surfactant flooding can mobilize trapped oil by driving surface tension ultralow, but mixes are tuned on dead oil at ambient conditions. The team ran high-temperature salinity screening and high-pressure phase tests on live oil containing methane, varying pressure and the gas-to-oil ratio.

Pressure and gas content shifted the optimum. At lower gas ratios, more pressure raised the water uptake ratio in the microemulsion while oil uptake fell; at higher gas ratios both ratios dropped versus dead oil. Optimum salinity decreased as gas ratio rose, from about seventeen thousand parts per million at a ratio of one hundred eighty to about fourteen thousand at two hundred eighty. Microemulsion formation weakened with more gas. Mixes must be tuned for live reservoir conditions, the authors conclude.
pmc-11683735:
Kawazu and a large team present a trial from twenty twenty-four on mindfulness yoga for children who refuse school. Forty-three children aged ten to fifteen join across several centers. Half get usual care; half add a four-week video yoga program. Anxiety is scored with a standard children's scale at four time points. Overall anxiety shows no real gap between groups. One subscale, fear of physical injury, improves with yoga. Pulse rate also runs lower in the yoga group.

The program proves safe for these children. Benefits look narrow rather than broad, the authors conclude. Longer-term effects need further study. Blending yoga with other therapies is a future question.
pmc-11685135:
Ao Shen and seven co-authors build a prediction chart for how completely pituitary tumors can be removed through the nose, in this 2024 study. Surgery for these gland tumors uses an endoscope through the nasal passage, and total removal varies with anatomy. The team reviewed 626 patients treated at one center over four years.

Landmarks around the tumor, above the gland and beside it in the cavernous sinus, were cataloged from pre surgery scans. Total removal was achieved in ninety-one percent of cases. Statistical selection distilled eight landmarks that matter most, and a chart built from them predicted outcomes with excellent accuracy in both training and check groups. Removal extent, age, tumor grade and size, and crossing certain landmarks also tracked later recurrence. The chart helps surgeons counsel patients before operating.
pmc-11686535:
Felipe Schütz and colleagues study fat-eating cell processes in fatty liver disease using rats. Their experimental study from twenty twenty-four feeds rats a special diet. The diet lacks choline and carries high fat for weeks. Rats on it develop the severe liver condition under study.

Liver tissue markers of fat breakdown inside cells were measured. Blood microRNA signals were checked alongside those markers. Several fat-handling proteins fell in diseased livers. One master switch for cell cleanup rose instead. Gene-silencing molecules in blood shifted with the disease. The pattern links faulty fat disposal to disease progression. Such markers might one day help stage liver disease without biopsy.
pmc-11686735: Yuan Xie, Yanli Gu, and Liang Chen report a rare fungal infection of the heart's lining sac in a 2024 paper. The condition, caused by a common mold, has vague symptoms, is seldom caught, and often kills. Their case report presents one patient in detail. They also review similar published cases to draw lessons for practice. The authors stress that doctors should keep this diagnosis in mind, since catching it early and starting treatment promptly offer the best chance of a good outcome.
pmc-11688035:
Shenglan Tang, Xuelu Jiang, and Xue Wang report two cases of a rare cervical gland growth. Their case report and review appeared in twenty twenty-four. The growth, called lobular endocervical glandular hyperplasia, is often missed. It lacks clear signs and mimics more common cervical problems.

One patient had months of abnormal vaginal bleeding. Scans showed a mixed cystic mass in her cervix wall. The second patient suffered cysts returning after three operations over years. Both women needed fertility-preserving treatment choices. Surgeons removed lesions with image-guided and vaginal approaches. Follow-up outcomes are reported for both cases. The review helps gynaecologists recognise this underdiagnosed condition.
pmc-11688835:
Jeremy O'Connell profiles a young drug company, Juvena Therapeutics, in a 2024 showcase piece on small business research funding. The company was founded to restore tissue health by fixing protein signals between cells. It received backing in 2021 from a federal small business program run by the National Institute on Aging.

Juvena maps proteins that stem cells release, screens them with an AI-enabled platform, and engineers the best finds into biologic medicines. The grant paid to polish its lead compound, widen its screens, and gain strict peer review feedback. Since then the company has raised close to sixty million dollars in venture funding. The piece holds the firm up as an example of how early public grants can carry a biotech startup toward private money and real products.
pmc-11688935:
Farida Ejaz and Courtney Reynolds share lessons from a five-year Texas study on preventing self-neglect, in this 2024 report. Partners from research, a large health system, and adult protective services screened older and disabled patients at 19 clinics. Those at risk got four months of case management or usual care.

In all, 477 patients took part, most of them Hispanic and low income. Home visits drew higher response than clinic interviews, even with cash incentives. Patients were mostly not self-neglecting but carried many unmet needs, such as food access and home fixes. Needs were met 65 percent of the time. The authors stress soft wording, home checks, and referral follow-through.
pmc-11689035:
Rachel Koffer and co-authors propose that a healthy old age needs variety, not just volume, of experience. Ageing research usually counts how much people do: activities, stressors, feelings. The X-versity theory instead asks how experiences are spread: rich and balanced across kinds, or piled into one.

The symposium lays out a framework tying daily diversity to person-environment fit and ageing outcomes. Studies of activity, stressor, and emotion diversity show spread shrinking with age and tracking resilience. The authors also flag measurement choices, time scales, and contexts that future work must handle. Their pitch is that daily-life data sets already hold the categories needed; researchers should count balance, not just totals.
pmc-11689235:
Shannon Freeman and three co-authors study what helps or blocks aging tech in a new rural dementia home, in a 2024 journal article. Rural and northern elders with dementia merit the same fine care as city peers. Tech built for aging, from light that tracks the day to indoor gardens, may lift life and let people stay put.

The team ran a process check in the home with a northern tech hub and health leaders. Garden walls, day timed lights, and a screen led exercise plan were set in place. Talks with staff, leaders, firm reps, and leads named the blocks: far off place, the tangle of dementia signs, and elders new to tech. Help came from firm teamwork, keen clients, and plain teaching packs. The word guides rural roll outs.
pmc-11689335:
Sarah Neller and Radion Svynarenko explore in this 2024 study how a past spell of caregiving shapes well-being in later life. Most research stresses the toll of care work; this team also hunts for gains. They link life history survey data on caregiving of six months or more with well-being measures gathered from 2016 to 2022 in a large retirement study.

The effects came out mixed. Past caregivers reported lower life satisfaction, yet stronger compassionate goals and a firmer sense of purpose. They also feared aging less. The authors suggest building on the gains: programs could help caregivers keep the purpose and compassion while easing the losses, a fuller picture of care's long shadow.
pmc-11689735:
Hyunkyung Yun and Ellen McCreedy study how nursing home records capture agitated behavior across racial groups in this 2024 paper. Standard assessments under-report such behavior, which hinders trials that rely on routine data. Adding doctor orders and transfer forms from electronic records raised detection by about a quarter in earlier work.

Data covered 19,705 residents in 312 homes run by one large non-profit, from January 2020 to August 2022. Black residents were more likely to live in homes that used electronic records often, while Latinx residents were less likely. In those high-use homes, Black residents had behaviors recorded far less often than White residents, in both the standard and electronic records, despite more memory impairment.
pmc-11689835:
Jill Juris and co-authors build a checklist for intergenerational technology programs in universities in this 2024 paper. Such programs pair students with older adults, boosting digital inclusion for the elders and giving students service learning. A shared planning tool could help new programs last.

The team reviewed 17 sources on program elements such as planning, access, safety, staffing, and training, and interviewed twelve stakeholders from universities and a mentoring organization. The result is the IG TECH checklist, a set of questions to guide staff decisions when setting up a program. The work was funded by a foundation focused on ageing.
pmc-11690035:
Noah Webster, Laura Zahodne, Toni Antonucci, and Kristine Ajrouch ask in a 2024 study whose schooling shapes brain health in old age. It is well known that more schooling links to better brain health for the person. Far less is known about schooling of friends, family, and the local area.

The team drew on 161 adults age 60 and older in the Detroit area, first seen in 2015 and again in 2021. Each person's own schooling linked to better brain scores five years on. So did the share of close contacts who held a degree. The share of degree holders in the local tract did not link to scores. Brain checks by phone covered memory, language, focus, and working memory.
pmc-11690135:
Amit Shrira and co-authors study how daily ageist attitudes and bad mood move together, and whether that link differs by country. The data come from the Subjective AGES project, with 379 adults aged 50 to 90 in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Israel, and Türkiye. Each person reported their attitudes toward aging and their negative feelings daily for 14 days.

On days when a person held more ageist attitudes, they also felt worse. The strength of that daily coupling varied: it sat in the middle in the United States, ran weaker in the United Kingdom and Germany, and ran stronger in Israel and Türkiye. The authors link the pattern to health care access in Europe and to falling social status in fast-changing societies. They set out next steps for the project.
pmc-11690335:
Paola Zaninotto and Matthew Prina introduce in 2024 a symposium on how surroundings affect the health of older adults. Talks in the set cover body, mind, and dementia. One talk maps what is known about city settings and brain health, with gaps in the evidence and strong spots such as air pollution and social setting.

Other talks cover long term air pollution and dementia risk in Denmark, industry fumes and thinking in England, and night light and low mood, which showed no link. A final talk covers extreme heat and faster biological aging. The set argues that these exposures need action to cut harm in later life.
pmc-11690435:
Elisa Ogawa and co-authors tested whether a gait therapy program also lifts thinking skills in veterans, in this 2024 study. Slow walking and weak thinking each predict poor outcomes in aging, and the two are linked. The program, built to speed gait, ran for eight weeks.

The analysis covered 51 veterans with slow gait, split between the program and a wait-list group. One fluency skill, naming words by class, improved in the program group and fell in the wait-list group. Two other fluency skills did not differ. The authors say the program may aid the effortful word search part of thinking, and call for fuller trials.
pmc-11690735:
Carlisle Shealy, Pamela Teaster, Jullie Gray, and Laura Sands asked care managers what they gain from belonging to their professional association. These managers, called Aging Life Care Professionals, coordinate services for older adults and families. Their nonprofit association offers training, professional development, and ethical standards, but its value to members had not been studied.

The team interviewed 35 members online, starting with chapter presidents and then recruiting more through referrals. Members said they joined for networking, connection, and friendship, and that ties with other members kept them in the group. They valued the credibility the association lends their work, plus referrals, business resources, and conferences. Members also asked for better inclusion of newcomers and diverse colleagues, and training matched to career stage.
pmc-11690935:
Ruben De Man and co-authors count mutations in single lung cells and link them to aging in a 2024 study. Age is the top risk factor for lung disease, and mutations that build up in cells over life may drive part of that risk. The team read mutations from single-cell gene data in healthy donor lungs.

Nearly two hundred thousand cells from thirty-two donors formed twenty-five cell types. Mutation load ran highest in the thin air-sac cells and in lung macrophages, and it rose with age. Loads tracked genes for cell cleanup and DNA repair, plus a known marker of cell aging. In key cell types, high load came with fading identity genes. The work ties mutation buildup to the transcriptional drift of aging lungs.
pmc-11691135:
Phyllis Greenberg, Isaac Asirifi Boateng, Sheila Moriarty, and Claudia Burgos Zuniga described a student project on older adults and homelessness in two thousand twenty-four. In two thousand twenty-three, nearly one in four people facing homelessness in the United States was over fifty-five. Numbers are expected to nearly triple by two thousand thirty.

Gerontology and social work students in central Minnesota joined a Project Homeless Connect event for a semester. They prepared information for the public and officials, raised funds, and packed bags of basic goods like food, socks, and coats. At the event they helped participants reach services and learned their stories. Many participants said being asked their name made them feel seen.
pmc-11691335:
Yanjing Liang and co-authors trace the alumni of a healthy aging center at the University of Washington. The de Tornyay Center has backed nursing scholars since the late nineteen nineties. It has mentored well over a hundred students and funded their research and travel. The team surveyed former scholars on where their careers went.

Most replies came back from graduates now in practice, teaching, or research, often in mixed roles. Alumni credit the center with sharper research skills and key career guidance. Their work spans top journals, major grants, new care models, and leadership during the COVID years. The authors use the map to shape the center's next plan.
pmc-11691435:
Jung Yoen Son, She'Lon Tucker, Carol Vos, and Janet Larson measured how much assisted living residents move and sit, in a 2024 pilot study. Low movement and long sitting speed decline and push elders toward nursing care. The team asked whether a long study with two body-worn trackers, one on the wrist and one on the thigh, would work in four Michigan homes.

Forty-two people signed up; about six in ten finished both week-long rounds six months apart, and most found the gear acceptable. Over the half year, hard exercise fell by eight minutes a day, and sitting crept up. The pilot shows the design is workable for a larger study.
pmc-11691535:
Talk that walks a loved one through old tales can stir a mind that the mind ill has dimmed, since far tales oft stay bright. Xianglan Jin and co-authors hear how such home talks felt in a 2024 read of a small first run. Nine pairs, a patient and a kin hand, were quizzed at the run's end.

Pairs praised the talks as a kind spur for the ill mind. Home was the right hall, they said; the dose, an hour or so twice a month through half a year, sat well. The ill kin were keen to tell their tales. Most hands asked for school in how to lead such talks. The team back kin led home talk, with aid at the hand's back.
pmc-11691935:
Talia Gilfix and co-authors presented this 2024 first-year report from a Boston study of healthy aging. The initiative follows adults over fifty-five in independent-living communities. It measures things people can change: movement, thinking, strength, daily function, habits, and mood. Each person gets prompt feedback to act on.

Year one held 173 participants. Patterns split by age and sex in telling ways. Memory gaps between men and women at ages eighty to eighty-four vanished by the late eighties, as women's rates caught up. Fall risk in women nearly doubled across the late seventies, while men's risk fell for those who stayed agile to eighty. The report argues for looking at each domain from several angles.
pmc-11692235:
Alexa Bragg and Chanee Fabius track how caregiving networks for older adults with disability changed between 2015 and 2022, and how the changes differ by race and ethnicity. Families and unpaid helpers often share tasks, with several people assisting in the same area of care. The study uses a national survey of Medicare beneficiaries. It compares non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and non-Hispanic White groups living in the community.

Few traits of the older adults changed, but Black and Hispanic adults faced steady gaps in income, Medicaid enrollment, and probable dementia. Fewer children served as caregivers in 2022 among Black and White adults. The share held steady for Hispanic adults. More extended family members helped across all groups. Sharing was most common for household tasks, at about 30 percent in both years. Hispanic adults shared self-care help more than the other groups. The findings point policy toward these shifting support structures.
pmc-11692335:
Howard Degenholtz and co-authors study in 2024 whether a teaching nursing home plan changed the staff who work in nursing homes. The plan added student training with nursing schools, a quality model for care of older adults, and an online learning network. The team used payroll data and staff surveys from 2022 and 2023.

Results were mixed. Feelings of being worn out fell, but other signs of strain rose, and views of managers fell. At the same time, nurses and aides left their jobs less often than staff at matched homes nearby. Readers learn both what the plan helped and what it did not change.
pmc-11692435:
Prasad Padala and co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether one session of magnetic brain stimulation can ease the load on people caring for a spouse with mild memory loss. Caring for a partner with cognitive decline is known to strain mental health, yet spouses at the mild stage are rarely studied. The trial enrolled thirty-two patients with mild cognitive impairment, along with their caregivers, inside a blinded study of stimulation against apathy.

Every patient first received a single real stimulation session, two weeks before the main course. After that one session, caregiver burden scores and patient apathy both improved significantly. Memory scores did not move. The authors suggest that this non-invasive stimulation may lighten the caregiver's load early, and that a single session could forecast who benefits from the full course. They call for the main trial's results to confirm the signal.
pmc-11692535:
John Shean and co-authors describe building dementia training with the people it serves in a 2024 paper. Dementia grows commoner, and students entering public health need training that is interactive and easy to reach. A partnership among the Alzheimer's Association, the CDC, and Emory centers produced a free online curriculum, A Public Health Approach to Dementia, with four modules launched across 2023 and 2024.

Students, researchers, professors, and practitioners all shaped the material. Early modules cover dementia's public health impact, health equity, and caregiving. The first two drew hundreds of learners each, with launch webinars pulling over nine hundred registrants apiece. About nine in ten learners reported more knowledge afterward and said the training would help their work. The authors offer the build process as a model.
pmc-11692635:
Kelly Munly, Jared Frederick, and Harriett Gaston describe joint teaching to prepare students for work with older adults, in work published in 2024. Human development students needed life course context before a practicum in long term care. History faculty joined the effort as part of a wider push for age friendliness on campus and nearby.

Seventy-two students in two classes heard history sessions on older adults' life paths. Topics covered the Great Migration and economic moments that shaped later life across generations. Students then wrote reflections online before their practicum work. Early review of those reflections suggested stronger understanding and readiness. The authors frame life course theory as the base for both design and aims.
pmc-11692735:
Diane Berish and seven co-authors report how rural health workers rated an online training series on age-friendly care, in a 2024 program review. Older adults in rural Pennsylvania face gaps in care access and support. The program used video case rounds, where far-flung providers learn from experts and each other. Sessions taught a four-part frame for older care: what matters, mind, medicines, and mobility.

Yearly surveys from 2020 to 2023 drew small groups of replies. Most who replied said the sessions built their skill and knowledge for older care. Every respondent in each year said they would urge colleagues to attend. Top-rated topics shifted by year, from mobility checks to dementia care. The authors call the format a proven way to reach rural teams. They present four years of steady feedback as support.
pmc-11692835:
Howard Fink and co-authors ask how much of the extra healthcare cost of dementia and thinking problems is really driven by frailty and daily-life disability, in a 2024 study. The team linked four long-running cohorts to Medicare claims, covering 8,165 community-dwelling beneficiaries with an average age of 79.

After adjusting for age, race, region, and other illnesses, people with dementia or cognitive impairment cost several thousand dollars more per year than those without. The team then asked what share of that extra cost frailty and functional limits could explain. Depending on the measure used, the shares ran from about a third to nearly two-thirds. A combined measure explained the most: about 63 percent of the extra cost in women and 58 percent in men. The authors conclude that most of the added cost rides on frailty and lost function, not on the brain diagnosis alone.
pmc-11693035:
Allison Kuipers and co-authors identify predictors of change in carotid artery measures in a 2024 study of long lived families. Ultrasound of the neck artery can reveal early vascular aging. Families selected for longevity may show what slows that aging.

About six hundred seventy participants had ultrasound at baseline and again after roughly six years. Wall thickness and artery diameter both grew over time. Yearly wall thickening was faster in those under sixty five than in older participants, while diameter growth did not differ by age. Models tested lifestyle, metabolic conditions, and medication as predictors of change.
pmc-11693135:
Ray Merrill analyzed in 2024 how often American cancers are recorded without a stage, and how that rate depends on who reports the case. Treatment hinges on stage, yet some cancers, above all in older patients, are never staged. Merrill used over five million cases from twenty-two registries covering 2015 to 2021.

About nine percent of male and seven percent of female cases were unstaged. Rates were far higher in men, rose with age, and varied by the type of reporting source and by cancer deadliness. The pattern marks where registry practice, not biology, leaves the record blank.
pmc-11693335:
Kira Sheldon and Elizabeth Luth study why people refuse free palliative care in a 2024 paper. Such care, offered in the community under some Medicare plans, eases symptoms and supports families of the seriously ill. Yet many eligible people turn it down when offered at no cost.

The team interviewed 22 plan members and caregivers who had refused, plus five care team members. Three broad reasons emerged, led by linking palliative care with the very end of life. Others found the benefit unclear. Naming the reasons gives programs a chance to explain the service better and time the offer so it does not feel like giving up.
pmc-11696435:
A team of authors report coated nanotubes for cleaning polluted water in a 2024 study, with Seyed Ahmadi among the lead authors named in the record. The tubes are made of titanium oxide, a light activated cleaner, coated inside and out with two conducting polymers. The goal is faster breakdown of a toxic pollutant, 4-nitrophenol, under visible light.

Many tests confirmed the coating's structure and light traits. The coating kept light generated charges apart longer, which raised cleaning power. The best mix, three quarters of one polymer and one quarter of the other, destroyed over ninety nine percent of the pollutant in two hours. Its large surface area and narrow energy gap helped drive that result.
pmc-11707835:
Shreya Upadhyay and six co-authors review how chemokines, the chemical signals that guide immune cells, shape the course of leishmaniasis. Their review came out in 2024. The disease is caused by parasites that live inside the very immune cells sent to kill them.

Control of the infection depends on T cells reaching the right tissues in the right mix. When chemokine signals are distorted, that traffic goes wrong and the parasite persists. The review gathers what is known about which signals and receptors shift in the skin and organ forms of the disease, and how different T cell subsets are affected. Understanding this signaling system, the authors argue, is a route to immune-based therapies for a neglected tropical disease.
pmc-11708835:
Renuka Kolli, writing alone, draws on journal archives to explain the roles of proteins that ride and regulate microtubules in plant cells. The 2025 article introduces microtubules, the largest filaments of the cell skeleton. They grow and shrink in fast cycles and serve as tracks for moving cargo.

Helper proteins control their birth, stability, and linking, while motor proteins haul vesicles and organelles along them. The article illustrates these roles with archived studies, starting with organelle movement in growing pollen tubes. Tip growth and the cell division frame are also covered, per the title. The piece serves readers who want a guided tour of classic findings, rather than a report of new experiments.
pmc-11709535:
Martine Therrien and co-authors screen fatty acids for their effects on the brain's immune cells. Lipid handling goes awry in Alzheimer's disease, and many risk genes act in microglia, those immune cells. The team grew human microglia from stem cells and dosed them with dozens of fatty acids. Gene readings sorted the replies into five patterns.

One pattern marked a toxic, fat stressed state, reached without a known risk gene's help. Cells from many donors were then pooled to hunt gene variants that soften or worsen the stress. The hunt named regulators of the toxic state. The authors aim at shields for synapses and early markers.
pmc-11709635:
Tanya Steel tells her family's story in a 2025 personal essay on caregiving. Her husband Robert died at fifty-eight from a genetic form of frontotemporal dementia that had stalked his family for generations. He had feared the disease since youth, when it took his father. In his early fifties his teaching work slipped, his inner map of places faded, and his habits grew rigid.

Doctors first called it depression, more than once. A car accident he fled, wildly out of character, finally led to a specialist who named the disease and its gene. Steel writes as a wife who supported the family while her twin daughters neared college. Her account shows what at-risk children and spouses live with while answers lag.
pmc-11709835:
Alzheimer's disease varies wildly between patients, and blood tests that capture that variety could sort people into the right trials and treatments. Lenora Higginbotham reviews in 2025 what a large consortium learned by working backward from brain tissue to body fluids.

Across hundreds of brains, network analysis of proteins found tidy modules, groups that rise and fall together, reflecting synaptic, metabolic, vascular, and inflammatory trouble. The brain-to-biofluids strategy then hunted those same modules in spinal fluid and plasma, where a needle can reach. Machine learning stitched the layers together. The review argues the peripheral shadows of brain modules are among the most promising accessible markers of the disease's many faces.
pmc-11709935:
Andres Duarte and co-authors looked at mood and daily functioning in Hispanic older adults at risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias in 2025. Hispanic groups carry a heavier dementia burden than non-Hispanic white groups, and neuropsychiatric symptoms are known to worsen how patients function day to day. Yet most evidence comes from white samples. The study drew people from a Florida Alzheimer's research center, administering a geriatric depression scale and a changed medical dementia rating.

The sample joined just over one hundred fifty Hispanic people with about one hundred non-Hispanic white people, aged sixty to ninety, spanning cognitively normal adults and people with mild mental impairment. The authors' central finding, announced in their title, is that depression greatly forecast medical functioning in the Hispanic group. A link with effects for caregiver burden and quality of life. And a case for screening mood early in dementia risk care.
pmc-11710135:
George S Bloom maps where a marked form of the tau protein gathers in the brain, and what that marking does. The mark, a phosphate at one spot called threonine 217, can be read in blood and spinal fluid. It ranks among the best early warning signs for Alzheimer's disease.

Bloom surveys human brains across disease stages, mouse model brains, and cultured nerve cells. Careful antibody checks prove the signal truly names this one marked form. The mark shows up in neurons at the earliest tangle stages and spreads wider as disease advances. Outside amyloid and tau clumps can raise its level in cells. Tests in other cells show the mark loosens tau's grip on microtubules. The work grounds a blood test in real brain biology.
pmc-11710235:
Martin Darvas reports a 2025 conference abstract on a three-drug mix aimed at aging itself in Alzheimer's disease. The mix joins acarbose, rapamycin, and phenylbutyrate, each aimed at a different aging process. Old mice ate the mix in their chow, then received virus injections that seeded amyloid and tau changes in the hippocampus.

At 27 months, the seeded mice did worse than control mice on two memory tasks. They alternated less in a Y-shaped maze and froze less in a fear test. Mice on the drug mix performed better on both tasks. The results support treating aging pathways, not just single disease proteins.
pmc-11710335:
Dustin Hammers and co-authors test whether two common gene variants speed decline in early-onset Alzheimer's in a 2025 paper. The early form strikes between ages 40 and 64 and makes up only about five percent of cases. Variants in the BDNF and COMT genes have been tied to thinking changes in other settings.

The team followed 88 amyloid-positive patients for twelve months. Carrying the BDNF variant predicted steeper drops in memory and executive function scores. The analysis adjusted for age, schooling, sex, and ancestry. Effects on the age when symptoms began were also checked. The work helps explain why patients with the same diagnosis decline at different rates.
pmc-11710435:
Annie Lee and co-authors search for genes that change how blood vessel risks affect Alzheimer disease, in a 2025 study. Vessel risks, such as high blood pressure and diabetes, raise the chance of the disease. Most patients also show vessel damage in the brain. The team asked which genes interact with those risks.

The study spans several ancestry groups, which broadens its reach. It scans the full genome for gene-by-risk interactions. Past work by the group found one gene that interacts with a combined risk score. That gene affects how support cells clear a harmful protein. Stroke history was also factored in as a risk. Findings of this kind may explain why the same vessel risks harm some people more.
pmc-11710535:
Idris Demirsoy and co-authors link self-rated memory slips to brain scans in this 2025 study from the A4 trial. The trial enrolled older adults with no clear thinking problems but with amyloid buildup in the brain. Each person and a study partner filled in a short form about changes in memory and daily function over the past year.

People with higher levels of tau protein in a key brain area reported decline on six form items. Seeing a doctor about memory worries and getting lost on trips stood out. Partners, by contrast, flagged only one item. The results suggest that early self-reports may track brain change sooner than partner reports.
pmc-11710635:
Emily Reeve and co-authors report a 2025 mouse study of stiff large arteries and brain vessel function. Stiff arteries are a sign of vessel aging and track with thinking loss. Extra pulse force can harm the lining of brain vessels, but long term effects and sex gaps were unclear.

They studied mice bred for stiffer arteries at young and old ages, next to normal mice. Brain arteries were tested for how well their lining could widen them. Young males with stiff arteries fared worse than normal peers, but old males did not. Old females showed the opposed pattern. A vessel relaxing gas explained the gaps. The authors say timing of risk differs by sex.
pmc-11710735:
Sara Holec and co-authors build cell lines that can tell tau strains apart by disease. Tau protein folds into distinct shapes, or strains, and the shape picks the disease. Past cell tests could split strains by protein version but not within one version. Their 2025 study seeds kidney cells with single-letter changes in the tau gene. The changes were picked by modeling to block one disease's strain and not another's.

Corticobasal degeneration and progressive supranuclear palsy are the test pair. Growth setups were tuned in tiny wells with mouse tau seeds first. Human patient samples then face the panel. If a line grows one strain and shuns the other, strain-specific tests become possible.
pmc-11710835:
Annie Du and co-authors measure a clotting protein in the brains of people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 study notes that adults with Down syndrome have a high genetic risk of Alzheimer's. Most develop its brain changes in their forties. They have low rates of vessel risk factors, yet show vessel harm in the brain, such as tiny bleeds.

That pattern hints the blood brain barrier may leak, letting blood proteins into brain tissue. The protein studied, fibrin, marks such leaks and drives immune harm. Tissue from the back of the brain was stained and scanned. Twelve adults with both conditions were compared with twelve controls. The first group showed far higher fibrin in both white and grey matter.
pmc-11712135:
Anne Turner and co-authors build an online picture tool to help people with memory loss talk through care choices. Their 2025 study deals with a hard gap: weak language and thought skills can block such people from stating what care they want. In video calls, each person worked through three cases with the tool on a shared screen. One case recalled a past care choice, and two posed future choices as skills fade and needs grow.

The tool lets the host drag icons for people, places, safety, feelings, and acts onto a canvas, or type words there. Fifteen people with mild loss or mild to mid dementia took part. Design stressed ease, low mind load, and images that rang true.
pmc-11712335:
Neurologist Ignacio Illán-Gala set out a plan in 2025 for a shared research archive on Alzheimer's disease and related disorders in Spain. The plan, called ARMA, links memory clinics through an electronic data capture system tied to medical records. Its aim is to sharpen diagnosis and track how these diseases change over time.

The project runs for four years and starts in two memory units. It tests fluid and scan markers against real patient data, then builds a trial platform meant to recruit a wider mix of patients. The team also plans tools that spot bias in who joins trials, so study results fit more of the people who live with these diseases.
pmc-11712435:
Pritam Das reports a 2025 laboratory study of a vessel growth receptor in Alzheimer's disease. Recent gene studies found the receptor, VEGFR-1, turned up in patient brains, while its sister receptor ran low. Higher levels of the first receptor tracked faster decline. Das asked whether the receptor itself harms neurons.

In donated brain tissue, the receptor clustered in damaged nerve fibers near amyloid plaques. Low oxygen or amyloid clumps raised the receptor in human nerve-like cells and mouse neurons, and the cells died. Silencing the receptor's gene saved the cells. Forcing extra receptor also killed neurons on its own. Das points to a signal chain that could be a drug target.
pmc-11712535:
Jose Hernandez Preciado and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on memory and thinking problems among the Wayuu, an Indigenous people of the Colombian Caribbean coast. Such problems are reported more often in Indigenous groups, yet data on the Wayuu were scarce. The team compared one hundred Wayuu adults with one hundred non-Indigenous neighbors.

Brain wave tests sorted thinking into normal and three grades of impairment. Moderate impairment was far more common in the Wayuu group than in their neighbors. Being Wayuu and having epilepsy stood out as strong predictors in their models. The authors say local health services need screening that fits this community's language and life.
pmc-11712635:
Ravindran and co-authors report early findings in 2025 on how sleep and heart rate swing night to night in people with mild Alzheimer's disease and their caregivers. Sleep change is common in the illness and wears on both patients and those who care for them. Home records over many nights can show that swing in real life.

Sixteen patients, eight caregivers, and twenty three healthy older adults took part for up to two weeks. Sleep diaries and a touch free bedside device logged over six hundred nights in total. The team compared group gaps and each person's own swing. The work sets up longer studies of sleep and care.
pmc-11712735:
Parris Pope and co-authors test a drug for Alzheimer disease in a 2025 study. The drug, XPro1595, is a lab built protein that soaks up just the harmful form of a swelling signal. Past work marks that signal as a driver of brain harm.

Twenty patients got one of three doses each week for twelve weeks. The team read the full protein mix in spinal fluid before and after. Some protein groups shifted in step with dose, which hints the drug hit its target. Brain tissue from past donors served as a check set. The small early trial sets up larger tests of dose and effect.
pmc-11712835:
Tiffany Luo, Chencai Wang, Benjamin Ellingson, and Ceylan Cankurtaran present a 2025 study that uses link prediction to track cortical atrophy in Alzheimer's disease. Markers that can flag how the disease will move are in demand as new treatments come forward.

The team built morphometric correlation networks from structural MRI scans of patients and matched healthy controls, taken at two times a few years apart. Scans came from a large Alzheimer's imaging database and were processed to map cortical volume. The model then asks which links in the network best predict where brain tissue will thin next.
pmc-11712935:
A 2025 paper by Tavia E. Evans and co-authors looks at how inherited risk relates to loss of volume in parts of the hippocampus over time. Small zones inside this memory area may not share the same gene pattern, so tracking them apart could reveal disease change sooner.

The analysis covers 1,051 ADNI participants, from healthy controls to people with Alzheimer's disease, scanned every six months for up to eight years. The team built gene risk scores with and without the APOE region and modelled change in each zone. Their work asks whether sex and disease stage change how strongly genes drive this shrinkage.
pmc-11713035:
Hamid Sohrabi and co-authors ask whether years of education delay Alzheimer disease in the cognitively normal oldest old in a 2025 study. Education is the classic proxy for cognitive reserve, yet findings past age eighty are mixed.

Over one hundred adults aged eighty and up from two Australian studies had brain amyloid scans, thinking tests, gene typing, and blood markers. Early results show no firm link between education years and baseline thinking. Education also did not track brain amyloid load. Amyloid-positive and negative groups, and gene risk carriers, held similar schooling years. The authors probe whether amyloid mediates any reserve effect in this very old group, where reserve may behave differently.
pmc-11713135:
Mostafa A Khalifa and co-authors wrote a 2025 review of gepirone, a drug for major depressive disorder, a condition that affects more than 280 million people worldwide. Older drugs can carry heavy side effects, so the value of newer options needs a clear test. The review gathers all trial evidence for this drug against placebo.
