The authors searched major databases for trials from 1987 to 2024 and kept only randomized trials in people diagnosed by standard criteria. Seven trials met their rules. They checked each trial for bias with a standard tool and combined the results to judge how much the drug eased symptoms compared with placebo.
pmc-11713235:
An enzyme called asparaginyl endopeptidase, or AEP, cuts proteins inside cell compartments and has been linked to damage in nerve cells. Meenakshi Singh, Joyal Xavier, Sampada P Tamhankar, and Raj Amin search for small molecules that can block the enzyme in this 2025 study. No such blockers are in hand yet, and the team works by computer screening rather than bench chemistry.

The authors screened CNS-focused molecule libraries against the enzyme's active site using two virtual methods, then ran motion simulations to see which candidates stayed bound. Promising molecules were tested further on cells engineered to make extra AEP. The study walks through the enzyme's cutting machinery in detail, including the three key residues at its active site. The shortlist of candidates offers starting points for lab work on drugs for nerve disease.
pmc-11713335:
Rifaldy Fajar and co-authors use machine learning to study COVID-19 vaccines and Alzheimer's disease in this 2025 paper. Some evidence links virus-driven inflammation in the body to faster brain decline. The authors ask whether vaccination might slow the course of the disease instead.

The team followed ten thousand adults aged sixty-five and older with early-stage disease across five regions. Half had received a COVID-19 vaccine and half had not, matched for age, sex, and health. Over two years the team tracked thinking scores, gene data, and brain scans. Their models compare the rate of decline between the two groups to test for a protective effect.
pmc-11713435:
An antibody drug for Alzheimer's disease gets a fresh pooling of its smaller trials in a 2025 meta-analysis by Ameer Fadhil Abbas Al Wssawi and co-authors. Solanezumab was designed to clear beta-amyloid, the protein that clumps in the Alzheimer's brain, and its big trials gave mixed readings.

The reviewers screened over twelve hundred reports and kept a small set of randomized trials outside the main EXPEDITION program, covering nearly five thousand patients in all. Outcomes were the standard Alzheimer's rating scales for thinking and daily function. Several of the pooled studies reported gains on the cognitive subscale. The authors present the combined picture as a reason to keep probing where the drug might help, despite the field's disappointments.
pmc-11713535:
Laili Soleimani leads a large team in this 2025 study on whether speech betrays the neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia. Depression and apathy are common, corrosive, and hard to measure objectively with current tools. The team recorded fifty-four older adults describing a standard picture, then mined the recordings for acoustic and word-choice features.

More severe self-reported depression came with a higher average voice pitch. Worse overall symptom scores tracked with simpler speech: more unfinished words, less novel vocabulary, and, oddly, pleasanter word content. Symptom severity also leaned toward more dominant-sounding speech. The authors stress the analysis is preliminary, with a small sample. Still, the pattern supports a hopeful idea: a short voice sample, cheap to collect, might one day flag behavioral changes in early dementia without a clinic visit.
pmc-11713635:
Isabelle Burke and co-authors test whether training the nose can sharpen memory in older adults who feel their minds slipping. Subjective cognitive decline worries patients before tests show anything. Smell and memory share deep brain wiring, and training smell memory in the young once spilled over into visual memory. Their Mind Your Nose trial asks if the trick survives aging.

Fifty-two volunteers, average age in the early seventies, trained daily for twenty days. One group worked odor memory tasks; the other, visual ones. Both then faced tests of each skill, a standardized smell test, and a visuospatial memory battery. The design pits cross-training against same-training head to head. Aging researchers get a playful intervention with a serious transfer question.
pmc-11713835:
Frank Lai and co-authors ask how caregivers feel about their own aging, and what that feeling predicts. Their 2025 cross-cultural study surveys sixty spousal caregivers across Western, Asian, and mixed backgrounds. The study measures self-perception of aging alongside strain and physical and mental symptoms.

The pattern was stark: the worse the strain and symptoms, the darker the view of aging, with physical symptoms the strongest correlate. Together the three burdens predicted over half the variation in aging outlook. Culture and gender interacted in how outlook formed, with Western caregivers scoring higher than others. Sixty people make this a preliminary map, and the authors label it so. Still, the direction is useful: supporting caregivers' bodies and minds may protect their relationship with aging itself, which loops back into care quality. Interventions could target the outlook, not just the workload.
pmc-11713935:
Feng Han and co-authors link resting brain wiring to memory readiness in aging, in a 2025 study. The default mode network, active at rest, supports memory work, and its links thin with age. Young adults whose rest wiring contrasts sharply between high-order and low-order zones tend to remember better.

The study scanned 16 young and 42 older adults at rest, then during a task pairing objects with scenes. The contrast measure subtracted low-order wiring strength from high-order strength per person. That contrast tied to age and to task success. Wave counts traveling between layers also tracked memory and key region activity. A rested brain's internal contrast may set how well it can learn on demand.
pmc-11714035:
Bradley Christian and Matthew Zammit report how amyloid and tau scans track disease growth in adults with Down syndrome, in a 2025 conference paper. An extra copy of the chromosome that holds the amyloid source gene gives this group a very high risk of Alzheimer's disease by their forties.

A joint study has followed adults with Down syndrome past age twenty-five, scanning amyloid and tau over time. Next to the usual form of the disease, the path here runs fast: the gap from first protein build up to mild loss and dementia is shorter and well mapped. Drug trials for this group are now starting. The talk shows how the scan time line can guide trial design and dose choices.
pmc-11714135:
Miriam Lucar Flores and co-authors lay out a 2025 plan to adapt a dementia support program for Peru. Dementia strains patients, families, health systems, and society, and no cure exists. Phone and internet tools can aid training, safety checks, and learning. A care navigation model from a rich nation offers guided, personal support by phone and web.

The plan first reworks the model's care guides with input from experts, providers, patients, and caregivers in four Peruvian regions. Co-design shapes the fit to local needs and culture. Then a trial will test the adapted program in 120 patient and caregiver pairs over nine months. Half will get the program and half will not.
pmc-11714335:
Ari Alex Ramos and co-authors chart twelve years of dementia research in Brazil through a bibliometric lens. Their 2025 study answers a gap: past maps of the field leaned on rich countries, with Latin America barely covered. The team sorted each paper into research areas set by the World Health Organization.

From more than five thousand Scopus records, about twenty-five hundred papers qualified. Output grew at roughly ten percent a year, close to health publishing overall. Diagnosis and disease mechanism work took two thirds of the field. Care, drug work, and risk studies trailed, while trials and cost studies were scarce. Southeast Brazil dominated affiliations. Women led most first authorships but few senior slots.
pmc-11714435:
Mark Eldaief and co-authors test spinal fluid markers in early-onset Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. This form of the disease starts before old age and can waste the cortex in a known pattern. Doctors need fluid signs that track that wasting. The team drew on 92 patients and a set of seven markers from spinal fluid.

Some markers count nerve fiber harm, others count synapse loss or the disease's core proteins. Each patient's wasting was scored against healthy controls, adjusted for age and sex. The team checked which markers tracked the signature wasting pattern. Past work linked a few markers to thinking loss in this group. The authors guessed those, not the core protein markers, would track the wasting.
pmc-11714535:
LATE is an age-related brain disease in which a protein, TDP-43, piles up in memory regions, but it can only be confirmed after death. Alex Wesseling and co-authors ask in 2025 whether brain scans could betray it earlier. They paired post-mortem scans with tissue measures in fifty-one donors who had Alzheimer's or Lewy body diseases, seventeen of whom also had LATE.

Donors with LATE showed smaller amygdala and hippocampus volumes, even after accounting for the other diseases' proteins. The more TDP-43 in tissue, the smaller the scanned volumes. The link held in Alzheimer's donors but not in the Lewy body group. Two young-onset cases also carried LATE, widening its suspected reach.
pmc-11714635:
Henry Bockholt and co-authors show that brain network patterns separate people with CADASIL who have symptoms from those who do not, in a 2025 study. CADASIL is an inherited disease of small brain arteries. It is a key model for how vessel damage disrupts brain communication. Strokes and dementia follow in many patients.

More than two hundred participants joined longitudinal assessments despite pandemic hurdles. Resting brain scans yielded static and dynamic network measures. Symptomatic and quiet carriers differed on both kinds of measure. Network change may precede or mirror clinical decline. Such markers could stage the disease without waiting for strokes. Trial designers gain endpoints that move faster than disability. Families carrying the gene get a research window into their future.
pmc-11714735:
Miriam Rabl and co-authors test blood markers for mood and behavior symptoms in memory clinic patients in this 2025 study. Such symptoms are common in older adults, can appear early in dementia, and predict worse outcomes. The team measured three blood proteins tied to nerve damage and brain inflammation in 151 clinic patients, some with normal thinking and some with mild loss.

At the first visit, none of the markers tracked current symptoms once age and thinking were accounted for. Over about two years, higher levels of two markers went with new or worse symptoms and with faster decline in daily function. Adding symptoms plus all three markers to a basic model sharpened forecasts of future symptoms and decline. The authors suggest the mix could aid clinic decisions.
pmc-11714835:
Caroline Skirrow and co-authors test an automated speech test in 2025 for spotting early thinking decline in people with a brain risk marker. New Alzheimer treatments need proof of the marker plus real symptoms, and blood tests for the marker are entering care. Yet marker-positive people vary widely in thinking, so a sensitive, scalable test is needed.

The team studied eighty-four marker-positive adults in British and American studies, split between mild impairment and unimpaired. A phone-style story recall test scored how much of each story people retold, in clinic and at home. The paper weighs how well that score separates the groups and predicts mild impairment, aiming at screening that can run anywhere.
pmc-11714935:
Dorota Religa examines the care received by people with Alzheimer's disease who live alone in Sweden, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. About 150,000 people in Sweden live with dementia, and two-thirds of them have Alzheimer's. Religa asks whether those living alone get the same standard of diagnosis and treatment as people living with others.

The analysis uses the national SveDem quality registry, covering 26,163 community patients diagnosed between two thousand seven and two thousand fifteen. Nearly half lived alone, mostly older women. After adjustment, living alone meant lower odds of receiving brain scans such as CT and MRI. The findings suggest solo dwellers receive less complete dementia care.
pmc-11715035:
Temitope Hannah Farombi, co-authors, and the Africa Dementia Consortium wrote on the role of media in gene studies. Dementia is on the rise in Africa as the share of old people grows. Myths still paint the state as witchcraft, which breeds shame and keeps families from care. The group runs a gene study that needs wide, fair sign-up across the continent.

They looked at how print, radio, TV, and social apps were used in one world health month push. Posts, shows, and news pieces carried facts on the disease to many kinds of crowds. The push helped draw people in and kept them in the study. It also fought shame by framing dementia as a health state, not a curse. The team holds that smart media work is a core tool, not an extra, for such studies in Africa.
pmc-11715235:
Boxin Sun and co-authors read brain signals to spot the flow faults tied to early memory loss. Their 2025 study uses EEG, a scalp record of brain waves, while people judge which way dots move. The group held 56 older African American adults with memory complaints. Half had normal cognition and half had mild cognitive impairment.

Each task was split into three spans, from first sight of the dots to the button press. For each span the team mapped which brain areas drove which others, and with what delay. They used a causal cross-mapping method on the signal source maps. The aim is a set of flow patterns that split the two groups. Such patterns could aid early checks for Alzheimer's-linked change.
pmc-11715335:
Yoshikazu Nakano, An Vo, Nha Nguyen, Chris Tang, and David Eidelberg study how brain networks change as Parkinson's disease affects thinking. They use a known activity pattern for cognition in Parkinson's, drawn from brain scans, and measure how its regions link to each other. Their 2025 study covers 102 patients sorted into four groups, from normal thinking to dementia.

All patients took thinking tests and had metabolism scans of the brain. A measure called assortativity, which tracks whether busy regions link to other busy regions, was much the same in normal and mildly affected patients. It rose in patients with wider mild problems and rose further in dementia. The authors say the measure may warn which patients are moving toward dementia and deserve closer watch.
pmc-11715435:
Sai Chintapalli and co-authors split Alzheimer brains by type with fake image nets in a 2025 paper. No two Alzheimer brains wear the disease in quite the same way. That spread clouds diagnosis, outlook, and care plans.

Their method maps how far each brain strays from a healthy norm. A GAN net repaints a sick brain as its healthy twin. The gap between the pair scores that person own disease load. Six thousand healthy brains from a world set trained the net. Fake sick brains helped teach it where norms bend. Personal maps may sort patients for trials with more care.
pmc-11715535:
Eric V Belcea and co-authors set out a plan for a blood test system, AHEADx, that could flag Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms start. Tiny sacs called exosomes, shed by brain cells, ride in the blood and carry molecular signs of harm. Three such signs are known to rise up to ten years before the first symptoms. No tool yet can both isolate the exosomes and read their cargo in one fast step.

The planned system joins acoustofluidic sorting on a chip with photonic PCR on the same chip. The first unit isolates the exosomes in under a minute at high yield and purity. The second reads about 20 markers in under six minutes from a tiny sample. The team will validate the system on blood from 100 patients and 100 healthy donors with known spinal fluid results. A success would bring early checks into a normal office visit.
pmc-11715635:
Jiachen Chen and co-authors chart the inflammation behind frailty and dementia risk in this 2025 study. Frailty, the slow loss of strength and reserve with age, raises the odds of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Which immune signals drive that link was unclear.

The team studied 741 Framingham participants, dementia-free at entry and followed about sixteen years. Blood samples carried 209 inflammation markers, from immune cells to signaling proteins. Half the group built a frailty signature; the other half tested it. The validated pattern was then checked against who developed dementia. The work may yield blood tests that flag risk while prevention still helps.
pmc-11715735:
Ting-Wen Chu and five co-authors ask whether the thickness of retinal layers at the back of the eye can warn of cognitive decline in older adults in Taiwan. Eye scans are quick and painless, so a true link would aid early detection. Their 2025 study follows non-demented older adults over seven years. All were free of dementia when the study began, in 2015 to 2017.

The cohort held 264 adults who had retinal scans at baseline and cognitive tests every two years through 2022. One retinal layer showed a curved link with scores: both thin and thick values went with worse results. The link held for global scores, memory, and executive function, and it stayed clear in women when the sexes were split. The retinal nerve fiber layer showed no such link. The team names the one layer a hopeful early marker.
pmc-11715835:
Tamil Iniyan Gunasekaran and a large team hunt structural DNA variants in families with Alzheimer's disease, in work from 2025. Standard gene scans explain only a slice of the disease's heritability, and large insertions and deletions are a suspect for the rest. Genome data from about four hundred families of two ancestry groups were mined with several variant callers, then checked for variants that travel with the disease.

Well over a hundred thousand variants were found, and hundreds of insertions and deletions segregated with illness in most families. The affected genes are active in brain tissue. Most segregating variants were small, under a thousand base pairs.
pmc-11716135:
Svetlana Ukraintseva and six co-authors link past infections, a gene variant, and shrinkage of the brain's memory center in older women, in this 2025 study. The hippocampus shrinks early in Alzheimer's disease. The gene, NECTIN2, carries a variant that raises Alzheimer's risk and also affects vulnerability to infections.

Using UK Biobank data on 11,765 people, the team related infection history and the variant to hippocampal size measured by MRI at ages sixty-five to eighty. In women carrying the risk variant, past infections came with about two percent smaller hippocampi on both sides, a combined effect larger than either factor alone. Results in men did not reach significance. The authors suggest the variant may deepen infection-related brain harm, and that the sex gap deserves study. They frame the work as a hypothesis for laboratory follow-up.
pmc-11716235:
Sarah Abbas and co-authors test a blood marker as a trial gauge for Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. The marker, a protein from brain support cells, has been tied to harmful brain deposits and to thought loss, and drug trials already track its fall as a side signal.

Ninety four impaired adults with confirmed deposits came from two cohorts. Blood marker levels at start and follow up were compared, and hazard models asked whether change in the marker foresaw later decline. The study judges whether the marker earns a formal place as a secondary trial endpoint.
pmc-11716435:
Susanne Röhr, Rosemary Gibson, and Fiona Alpass link poor neighborhoods to faster cognitive slide in New Zealand. Their 2025 paper follows adults aged forty-eight to seventy-five with no impairment at the start. A national deprivation index graded each home area. Thinking was tested with a standard exam, then again two years on.

Living in a poorer area tied to lower scores and steeper decline, even after personal income, schooling, and lifestyle were weighed. About a fifth of the sample lived in high-deprivation zones. Women, the less schooled, and those with unhealthier habits also fared worse. The authors urge dementia plans to treat place itself as a risk factor worth funding against.
pmc-11716535:
Lee and co-authors test a blood marker's meaning across ethnic groups in a 2025 study. A plasma protein fragment, P-tau217, flags Alzheimer type brain change with high accuracy. Most validation cohorts, though, were ethnically narrow. The team asked whether the marker's link to memory scores depends on ethnicity, comparing Hispanic and Latino elders with non Hispanic White peers across the cognitive range.

If the link shifts by group, cutoffs tuned on one population could misread another. Subjective decline and mild impairment cases joined healthy elders in the sample. Blood tests promise cheap, wide screening for dementia risk; fairness across groups decides whether that promise holds for everyone.
pmc-11716635:
Takanobu Ishiguro and four co-authors split a Parkinson-like disease into subtypes using spinal fluid markers. Their 2025 study concerns progressive supranuclear palsy, a movement disorder that can overlap with Alzheimer's pathology in the brain. Nineteen diagnosed patients gave spinal fluid, and the team sorted them by the standard marker scheme for amyloid, tau, and nerve damage.

Twelve patients fell on the Alzheimer's continuum and seven did not. The continuum group had become ill later in life, scored worse on a standard cognition test, and more often showed stiffening along the body's axis. One damage marker also tracked daily functioning across all patients: higher levels meant lower independence scores. The authors argue the fluid profile marks real clinical differences inside one diagnosis, and that the damage marker may serve as a gauge of disability in this disease.
pmc-11716735:
Damage to the brain's white matter raises dementia risk, yet many people with such damage never develop the disease. Surabhee Eswaran and co-authors asked whether strong social ties soften that risk, in a 2025 study from a long-running heart health cohort. They also checked whether the answer changes by sex and by race.

The study followed 1,679 adults who were free of dementia in mid-life. In the early 1990s, participants reported on their social relationships and were classed as strong or poor in ties. Brain scans two decades later measured white matter integrity, and cases of dementia were tracked through 2019. The team weighed how ties and scan measures each fed into risk, within race and sex subgroups. The work treats mid-life friendship and support as factors that may blunt the harm of brain change.
pmc-11716835:
Annelie Scharf and co-authors count the care needs that dementia leaves unmet in a 2025 German study. People living with dementia at home often need more help than they get, yet who falls through the gaps, and why, was poorly mapped. The baseline of a multi-center trial offered a detailed snapshot.

Four hundred seventeen participants, mostly with mild to moderate impairment, averaged about eleven diagnoses and nearly seven medications each. Roughly two in three carried at least one unmet need, about two to three apiece on average. Needs piled up where social support ran thin, education was lower, bodies and daily function were frailer, and health felt worse. Among women, depression, money strain, and living alone added more. A recent visit to the family doctor, by contrast, trimmed men's unmet needs.
pmc-11716935:
Jenna Adams and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how the whole shape of the brain changes with age. Rather than looking at single regions alone, they track where the surface of the brain presses inward and where it stretches outward, and how the two sides drift apart.

The team worked with more than two thousand scans from adults aged forty-two to ninety-seven. Shape measures were compared across age groups and against a rating of clinical impairment. The authors also checked how shape change lined up with scores on thinking tests. Their approach treats aging as a change in the brain's overall form, not just shrinkage in a few spots.
pmc-11720435:
Taslima Begum and five co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, what lab work shows about the harms of kratom. Kratom is a plant from Southeast Asia used in folk care, and its main active part is mitragynine. Rules on its sale differ by country, yet people keep taking it on their own for many health problems.

The team gathers lab studies, animal work, and case reports on the plant's toxic effects. Bench studies point to effects on the enzymes that break down drugs, while animal work shows direct harm to the liver, kidneys, lungs, and brain. The review also covers how such harms are managed, where the proof is thin, and what studies should come next.
pmc-11724735:
Swollen blood and lymph vessel tangles in the eye socket are hard to treat. Surgery near the eye risks vision, and earlier injections often fail. Kit May Chow, Kala Sumugam, and Amali Ahmad report three patients treated with bleomycin injections into the lesion. The patients were a 7-year-old girl, a 37-year-old woman, and a 56-year-old man. Two cases were recurrences after failed sclerotherapy. All received several doses.

Lesions shrank clearly in all three. Eye bulging eased, and pain relief followed. No eye or body side effects appeared. Symptoms did not vanish entirely. The authors still rate the drug a safe, useful option when cutting is not feasible.
pmc-11726735:
Mária Csernoch, Carolin Hannusch, and Piroska Biró study how people modify correct and erroneous digital texts, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. End users generate enormous hidden waste through flawed digital artifacts. Their group built an objective system measuring the entropy of digital texts. Fifty-three participants edited documents under set task requirements.

Erroneous documents took more time and information to modify than correct ones. That extra effort is measurable waste. Breaking edits into atomic steps exposed uncertainty and idleness, adding further waste. The authors call attention to the scale of this hidden cost. They blame educational approaches and general ignorance for the low skill levels. A standard evaluation system, they argue, is needed for further analysis of digital work.
pmc-11727035:
Okpala Chibuike, Xiaopeng Yang, and Ayman El-Baz build a hybrid vision model for lung disease classification, in work published in 2024. Vision transformers capture broad context in an image but can miss fine detail. Convolutional networks capture local detail well but struggle with long range links across lung regions.

Their design stacks convolutional blocks and transformer blocks in one modular unit. A gated attention step mixes channel, spatial, and element wise cues to stress key features. A multi-scale fusion module then joins features at different scales. Tests reached very high accuracy across four pulmonary conditions. Long tests and ablation studies supported the design, which also showed good calibration for medical image use.
pmc-11727635:
Ioannis Gastouniotis and seven co-authors studied a heart strain marker in people with type 2 diabetes but no known heart disease, in research published in 2024. The marker, a peptide the heart releases under strain, guides heart failure care in known cases. Its value before disease appears was unclear. Their group held 100 clinic patients who took breathing tests, heart scans, and the blood marker test.

Patients in the top third of the marker had lower peak breathing scores than those in the low third. Their hearts also showed more stiff filling traits on scans. One scan measure tied to lower breathing scores as well. The authors say even mild rises in the marker flag early heart strain in diabetes. It could select who needs close monitoring before clear heart failure arrives.
pmc-11727835:
Radu-Andrei Moga, Cristian Doru Olteanu, and Ada Gabriela Delean published this dental study in 2024. Braces move teeth with force, but most of that force is soaked up before it reaches the tooth's pulp and its nerve-vessel bundle. No one had measured how much gets through. The team ran 180 computer simulations on the lower second premolars of nine patients.

Five moves were tested, from push-in to tipping, at low and high loads. Two stress rules gave like maps, with the nerve bundle taking 5.7 times the stress of the pulp. Rotation proved harshest on the bundle. In sound gums, just 2.85 percent of a high bracket load reached the bundle, and half a percent reached the pulp. The authors say tooth tissue shields the inner parts well, soaking up nearly all the load.
pmc-11728035:
Ahmed Alsibani and co-authors pool proof on which scan best finds hidden neck lymph spread in head and neck cancer, in work from twenty twenty-four. Standard scans often miss hidden spread in nodes that feel normal. Spread status drives surgery and radiation choices for these patients. Four scan types face off: CT, MRI, PET-CT, and ultrasound. Dozens of studies feed the pooled analysis across databases.

Close to four thousand patients anchor the patient-level results. PET-CT shows the best overall balance of hits and correct clears. Its odds score for correct calls tops the rival scans clearly. Node-level results split the honours a bit more by measure. MRI catches the most true spread at node level in the pool. PET alone clears healthy nodes most reliably at that level. PET-CT still leads on the combined odds score overall.
pmc-11728135:
Kamil Feliksik and co-authors tune a ceramic by swapping in calcium, in a 2024 paper. Their base material, barium titanate, is a workhorse for capacitors and sensors. Replacing part of the barium with calcium at three levels changes its grains, crystal phases, and response to heat and electric fields. The ceramics were baked by a standard solid-state route and examined under a microscope and X-ray checks.

The middle recipe grew small uneven grains yet gave the strongest heat-driven electric current. More calcium pushed the material's key switching temperature lower. The richest mix also sprouted a second crystal phase. The authors map these trade-offs for anyone designing heat sensors or energy harvesters from this family.
pmc-11728235:
Filip Franciszek Karuga and five co-authors run a preliminary study of small RNA signals in patients with sleep apnea, some of whom also have type 2 diabetes, in this 2024 paper. Apnea, where breathing stalls in sleep, doubles diabetes risk, and repeated low oxygen is a suspect link. The team measured two tiny RNAs and two proteins that all respond to low oxygen.

Forty-eight patients were sorted by sleep test results and diabetes status. One RNA ran higher in the morning in patients with both conditions, and the other ran higher in apnea patients in the evening. Levels of the RNAs also tracked with insulin resistance scores and with the calming protein SIRT1 in opposite directions. The authors frame the pattern as an early clue to how apnea nudges metabolism toward diabetes.
pmc-11728335:
Behzad Parsi and co-authors present, in a 2024 paper, a model for moving a flat panel with droplets that respond to voltage. The trick, called electrowetting on dielectric, changes how a droplet wets a surface when voltage is applied. Panels moved this way could retune radio gear on the fly, shifting frequency and bandwidth in real time. Speed depends on a tug of war among drive force, moving mass, and drag.

More droplets raise the drive force but also add weight and drag. Their math model weighs those trades and predicts the panel's top speed. Lab tests matched the model closely across voltage levels. A 3D simulation adds detail on flow inside the thin droplets. The design is flat, small, cheap to make, and can embed radio circuit boards directly.
pmc-11728435:
Boyu Sima and ten colleagues build an electromagnetic surface that can switch between absorbing microwaves and converting their polarization. The design stacks tightly coupled dipole antennas over a ground plane loaded with interchangeable radio-frequency circuit boards. Swapping the back board swaps the function, making the surface modular and reconfigurable.

The array works across roughly four to thirteen gigahertz with wide scanning angles. With the absorption board it absorbs across most of that band for both polarizations; with the conversion board it converts polarization over a similar range. Simulations and experiments agree. The authors point to active stealth, adaptive camouflage, and intelligent communications as applications for the modular surface.
pmc-11728535:
Qingyong Bian and co-authors field-tested irrigation amounts in 2024 for drip-watered maize under plastic mulch in arid southern Xinjiang. Water is scarce, so each drop must count. Four watering volumes were compared for soil moisture, plant growth, and yield. More water raised soil moisture, water use, and plant size, and lifted yield by up to about thirty-nine percent.

But the gains per drop shrank at the top volume. A scoring method picked the third volume as the sweet spot. It saved a fifth of the water of the largest volume while giving up under one percent of yield. The findings guide watering plans where supply is tight.
pmc-11728635:
Alexander Pogrebnjak and co-authors study tunable coatings of titanium, zirconium, molybdenum, and carbon, in a 2024 paper. The catalog list is truncated, so team framing is used. Coatings were laid on silicon with a dual sputtering setup, and the carbon share was steered by the graphite target current.

Microscopy showed a single phase with columnar grains, a strong texture, and many nanotwins and stacking faults. A suite of surface tools confirmed the makeup and nanostructure. Computer modeling probed how the four part solid mix behaves with electron count. The best films were very hard and wore very slowly, aided by a thin amorphous carbon layer. Such coatings suit parts that face heavy wear.
pmc-11728835:
Abdo Meyiah and co-authors test tweaked plant compounds on immune cells in a 2024 study. The base compound comes from frankincense resin, a tree sap used in old cures, and it is known to calm immune acts. Chemists hung a fresh ring group on it to make four kin forms, each with its own traits.

The team grew human T cells, the immune cells that lead attack, and dosed them with each form. They tracked how fast the cells split and how strongly they woke. The tests show which forms curb or stir T cells most, a lead for drugs that tune immunity.
pmc-11731435:
Fatemeh Karimi and four co-authors published a trial in 2024 on whether yoga helps mothers of premature babies produce more milk. Mothers of infants in intensive care often struggle to pump enough, and stress works against supply. At an Iranian hospital, seventy-eight first-time mothers of babies born before thirty-four weeks were randomized to yoga or usual care.

The yoga group practiced thirty minutes each morning for six days under a therapist. Afterward their average pumped volume reached about thirty-four milliliters against about eleven in the control group, a clear difference. The milk's composition, though, did not change in any measured component. More milk, same recipe, is the plain summary, and the authors present yoga as a cheap, drug-free aid for a stressful ward.
pmc-11734135:
Abdullah Ghunaim and four co-authors present a tricky heart tumor biopsy case in a 2024 paper. Masses in the heart's left atrium are usually benign growths called myxomas. When features look malignant instead, doctors need tissue proof before choosing treatment.

The patient was a seventy-one-year-old woman whose presumed myxoma showed worrying traits. Biopsying a left-sided heart tumor is notoriously hard to reach safely. The team guided a needle using combined CT and live X-ray imaging through the skin. The sample revealed a malignant spindle cell tumor, not a myxoma. That answer spared her an operation aimed at the wrong disease. Treatment for the true cancer could start early, guided by a firm diagnosis.
pmc-11735335: Danielle C Brown and co-authors present a single instructive case of a white epidermoid cyst. These rare cysts stand out by glowing bright on T1-weighted MRI scans and by their pearly white surface when removed. The 2024 report walks through the patient's presentation, the imaging workup, and the management chosen at their center. The authors stress that recognizing this uncommon variant matters, because a correct diagnosis steers treatment and helps avoid later complications.
pmc-11739535:
Ayako Shimada, Shinnosuke Ohnaka, Masanao Nakashima, and Atsushi Nagai report a 2024 case of lung cancer spread to the small bowel, treated with an immune drug and then surgery. Gut spread from lung cancer is rare, and care paths in the immune drug era are vague. A man aged fifty-nine came in vomiting from a bowel spread spot.

The immune drug shrank the spot, but a narrowed gut still blocked food, so drip feeding ran on. After a line infection flared again, surgeons cut the tight stretch and built a bypass. The cut tissue showed the tumor gone, with immune cells in its place.
pmc-11745035:
Roberto Nava and co-authors measure fear of COVID-19 among psychiatric patients in Italy, in this 2024 study. Two hundred sixty-nine patients at two clinics took a standard fear scale. The team compared strong-fear and low-fear patients and hunted for what predicts a high score.

Being female, falling ill younger, and having better insight into one's illness each predicted stronger fear. Current substance abuse predicted weaker fear. Patients with schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses scored lowest of all. The authors say such maps can guide support for psychiatric patients during health crises, whose effects linger past the emergency.
pmc-11771835:
Sunithi Thearawiboon and Chanapong Rojanaworarit studied in 2024 whether tooth loss and tooth decay relate to diabetes complications in Thailand. Their hospital sample held 438 patients with type 2 diabetes. Most had teeth with decay, and a small share had no teeth at all. Outcomes covered eye and foot problems plus kidney disease.

Kidney disease appeared in about a tenth of patients and foot problems in over a third, while eye problems were rare. Patients with no teeth showed higher rates of kidney and foot problems than those with clean teeth, but the gaps were not firm in statistical tests. Decay alone showed smaller gaps in the same direction. The authors frame the pattern as a hypothesis for larger studies, not a settled link.
pmc-11782035:
Yuncao Fan, Wei Chen, and eleven co-authors link eating marine fish with lower odds of depression paired with heart disease. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, surveys adults in Taizhou, China. Nine hundred thirty-two people aged twenty-five to ninety-five enter the analysis. Diet histories sort fish intake into three bands. Heart scans and a mood scale define the paired condition.

About one in nine participants has both conditions. Heavier fish eaters show lower odds of the pairing. The link holds after statistical adjustment for other traits. Fish nutrients are the suspected bridge between mood and heart. The authors call for prospective work to test cause and effect.
pmc-11784035:
Fernando Fariñas-Guerrero and co-authors survey skin germs carried by veterinarians in Spain in 2024. Staph germs live on pets and can pass to people who handle them. Vets face daily contact, yet few studies check their carriage rates. The study covered healthy vets in clinical practice in the province of Malaga.

Volunteers gave swabs from the nose and hands. Labs checked for three staph species and tested their drug resistance. One species is a known animal germ that can infect people. Knowing carriage rates helps clinics set hygiene rules that protect staff and animal patients alike.
pmc-11788135:
Awadia Gareeballah and co-authors review a simple ultrasound rule set for ovarian tumors in a paper whose text is dated 2024. Growths on the ovary are common, and telling a harmless one from cancer is the central challenge. The rule set uses five ultrasound signs that point to cancer and five that point to a benign growth.

The team searched five databases for studies that tested how well the rules sort tumors. Pooling those studies gives a shared verdict on accuracy. A rule set that any trained scanner can apply could speed referral of true cancers and spare women with benign growths from needless surgery and worry.
pmc-11790635:
Zhen Li, Changming Han, and Hongwei Zhao published a case study in twenty twenty-five of a young boy whose epilepsy traced to a gene variant never before reported. His condition, epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures, involves sudden jerks and drops. Whole-exome sequencing hunted the cause in the SLC6A1 gene, which moves a calming brain chemical.

The boy had early delays in intellect and language, a fever seizure as a toddler, then mixed seizure types with inattention and hyperactivity. Sequencing found a single-letter missense change in SLC6A1, arising new in him rather than inherited. Treatment with levetiracetam left him seizure-free for eight months at reporting. The case extends the known variant list for this epilepsy and links genotype to presentation.
pmc-11791535:
Brandon Joa and co-authors present MOUD 2.0 in a 2025 paper, a clinical algorithm for buprenorphine treatment of opioid use disorder in primary care. Most patients first meet care in primary clinics, yet few get proven treatment there.

Long-acting injectable buprenorphine may lift adherence and retention in low-barrier settings. The algorithm sorts patients by adherence and retention, with urine tests plus self-report, and gives steps for each class. It was built from literature and expert views, refined with clinic staff and patient input. The paper also sets a plan to test rollout at a housing and integrated care clinic. Patients serve as their own controls in the evaluation design.
pmc-11792735:
Fahimeh Pakravan and co-authors compare a mushroom extract gel with a standard antifungal gel for denture mouth sores, in work from twenty twenty-four. Denture stomatitis is a fungal sore under dentures that causes pain. Fifty patients with mild to moderate sores join a blinded trial. Half get a gel from Ganoderma lucidum mushroom extract. Half get the standard clotrimazole gel for comparison.

Pain and recovery are scored at one week and two weeks. Early full recovery runs a bit higher in the mushroom group. That edge does not reach statistical significance in the trial. Skipping dentures overnight multiplies recovery odds several times over. More severe sore type cuts recovery odds sharply by contrast. The mushroom gel matches the standard gel overall in effect. It may suit patients whose fungi resist standard azole drugs.
pmc-11802435:
Minyan Wang and six colleagues published a burden-of-disease analysis in two thousand twenty-four comparing China and Japan. Diet shapes the toll of heart disease, cancer, and diabetes. The team used Global Burden of Disease data spanning nineteen ninety to two thousand twenty-one.

Cancer and heart disease burdens fell in both countries over the three decades, while diabetes kept rising. Too much red meat was the leading diet risk for cancer in both. High salt intake drove heart disease burden, above all in China. For diabetes, red meat led in China and processed meat in Japan. Oddly, higher meat intake looked protective in some comparisons. The authors chart the trends and urge diet policies fitted to each country.
pmc-11807735:
Qinwei Pan and co-authors free shoot growth by blocking a gene-silencing enzyme in a 2025 study. Plants can regrow whole shoots from root callus, a near-magical rebuild. The epigenetic rules governing that rebirth were largely obscure.

Blocking histone deacetylases with trichostatin A during callus growth boosted shoot formation. Treated unwounded roots even skipped the wound signal and sprouted shoots anyway. Wound pathway genes switched on alongside the effect in wounded roots. Chromatin loosening seems to prime cells for a new identity. Nursery and lab propagation could exploit the trick for stubborn species.
pmc-11815335:
Andrew Maurer leads a team of eleven in a 2024 study of green turtles feeding in San Diego Bay. Green turtles roam widely and eat both plants and animals, so what draws them to one patch over another was murky. Knowing their picks can guide how the bay is managed.

The team tracked 29 turtles by satellite from 2013 to 2023, gathering more than 5,000 location points. They compared the spots turtles used with the range of spots on offer, weighing local traits such as food and shelter. The models show which parts of this city bay the turtles favor while feeding.
pmc-11852335:
A failing heart after surgery can leave a patient in shock with few good options. Ai Sakai, Kenji Iino, Yoshitaka Yamamoto, and Hirofumi Takemura describe one such case in a 2024 report. Their patient had severe narrowing of the aortic valve with weak blood flow, plus heart muscle disease from poor blood supply. A pump called Impella can support the heart as a bridge, but the usual entry routes need healthy vessels.

This patient had limited vessel access, so the team placed the pump through the brachiocephalic artery in the neck. The patient was managed with success after surgery. The authors say this route may let high-risk patients have surgery that would otherwise be too unsafe. One case cannot prove a rule, but it adds a workable option.
pmc-11870135:
Gianmarco Troiano, Isuri Fernando, and Alessandra Nardi survey travelers about accepting the dengue vaccine, in a pilot study published in 2024. Dengue, a mosquito-borne virus, sickens millions yearly, and a live vaccine exists for travelers to risky regions. Whether travelers actually take it was the question.

At an Italian travel clinic over three months, fifty-eight travelers bound for twenty-three countries answered anonymously. Trips averaged about seventeen days. Only five travelers refused the dengue shot, most calling it unnecessary and one citing cost. Sex, age, and trip length did not sway acceptance. The authors caution that the sample is small, but acceptance looks high among clinic visitors, and the few refusals rest on underestimating the disease rather than fearing the vaccine.
pmc-11874835:
Eseosa Osaghae led a large team building teaching material on COVID-19 vaccines in a 2025 paper. Vaccine uptake gaps by race persist, and people with rheumatic conditions face extra risk because their immune systems are often weakened. The team worked with community partners in two cities to design lessons that trusted local voices could share.

They made two online curricula with the same core facts but different framing. One stresses racial justice and names how past and present racism feeds hesitancy. The other uses a standard medical framing. A future trial will test which version better helps community opinion leaders spread uptake in Black communities.
pmc-11887835:
Gabriele Gaggero hunts, in a 2024 review, for journals where medical image reports can be published free of charge. Image reports are short articles built around one striking picture, such as a scan or a microscope view, and they teach faster than full case reports. Many journals charge fees that block authors without funds.

Following standard review rules, the search sifted a vast pool down to 102 journals that were free, open access, and indexed in top databases. Of those, thirty-nine actually accept image reports. Oncology and general medicine led the list. Rules on image count, word length, references, and author numbers varied widely, and the review tabulates them for authors.
pmc-11888635:
Shahad Abdulrahman Alshamrani, Bushra Fahad Alobaid, and Hamad Mohammad Alharkan compare how temporary dental crown materials hold their color. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Patients wear interim crowns for weeks, and staining from food and drink can spoil the match with real teeth.

Sixty-four discs were made from four material types: a hand-mixed acrylic, a bis-acryl resin, a milled acrylic, and a three-dimensionally printed resin. Discs soaked in water, cola, coffee, or tea for up to thirty days under warm, humid, dark conditions. A clinical color meter tracked the shifts. Material, drink, time, and their mix all mattered. Bis-acryl and printed discs stained most; coffee and tea stained worst.
pmc-11889435:
Devyansh Nimodia and Anand Hatgaonkar present a short clinical image report from 2024. Their subject is a 31-year-old man who came to an emergency unit after a road crash. Scans showed a rare birth defect of the neck spine, with extra bone growth.

The scans found fused neck bones, a raised shoulder blade, and cord damage after the crash. The team linked the pattern to Klippel-Feil syndrome type II. They note the classic signs of short neck, stiff neck, and low hairline at the back. Care is mostly supportive, with braces or traction, and surgery is saved for pain or loss of stability.
pmc-11891135:
Melanie Etti and a large study group audit hepatitis B screening in pregnancy in Uganda in a 2024 paper. Antenatal visits offer a prime chance to catch the virus early. Treatment then protects the baby from infection at birth.

The study followed women delivering at a government hospital in Kampala. Records showed how many infected women were actually diagnosed in care. Missed chances to test and treat were counted across the pathway. Globally, only about one in ten carriers knows their status. Readers see where a screening program leaks, step by concrete step.
pmc-11895735:
Graham Huggan and five co-authors open a 2024 special issue on extinction studies across many fields. Extinction sounds final, yet the word means quite distinct things across time and place. A few centuries ago, most people doubted that species could vanish at all. Now more than a million species stand under threat.

The editors argue that the new field needs both life science and culture. Stories, tongues, feelings, and values shape how loss is grasped, not facts alone. The recent pandemic showed how human, animal, and germ lives hang together. Framing extinction as a crisis of the mind, as well as of nature, guides the essays that follow.
pmc-11919235:
Qianshuo Mao and co-authors review the hunger hormone ghrelin and its role in mental disorders in a 2024 paper. Ghrelin is a twenty-eight amino acid hormone, and its receptor is found in the brain, pituitary, and adrenal glands, above all in the hypothalamus. Through that receptor, ghrelin shapes many of its biological effects.

Ghrelin is closely tied to the onset of psychosis. It can influence dopamine, GABA, and serotonin signaling through the hormone axis linking brain and adrenals. The review covers both the harmful roles of this system in mental illness and what blocking or tuning it might offer as therapy.
pmc-11922835:
Si-Yi Wang and six co-authors tested in 2024 whether a mix of lactic acid bacteria improves alfalfa silage grown on salty soils. Feed shortages press livestock farms, and salty land is one place to grow forage. The team ensiled wet alfalfa from salty and normal soils for sixty days, with and without a four-strain bacterial mix. They then checked feed quality and the microbe mix inside.

Silage with the bacteria held more dry matter and lactic acid and showed a lower pH. The added bacteria took over as the dominant group, and total microbe variety shrank. Gains appeared on both soil types. The authors conclude the mix can lift silage quality and help farms use salty land for feed.
pmc-11926135:
Mosleh Hmoud Al-Adhaileh leads a team of nine authors in 2025 in building a deep learning aid for diagnosing chest disease from X-ray images. Pneumonia from viral infection is hard to spot on a chest film because it resembles other lung conditions, and current reading methods have limited accuracy.

Their system, DLAAD, starts from a proven mobile-sized image network and adapts it by transfer learning to chest radiographs. The aim is a tool light enough for ordinary medical devices yet sharp enough to help doctors separate pneumonia from look-alike diseases. The study reports the model's design and its diagnostic performance.
pmc-11931335:
Dipendra Pandey and co-authors measure how common osteoporosis is among postmenopausal women attending a district hospital in Nepal. Their 2024 study enrolled women from three districts at Trishuli Hospital. Bone density was scanned at the hip and lower spine with a standard absorptiometry machine, and risk factors were tested with adjusted statistical models.

Of 384 women, eighty-two, about twenty-one percent, had osteoporosis. Women with the disease averaged about sixty-eight years old, twelve years older than those without. Age stood out in the analysis, alongside other clinical and lifestyle factors the team examined. The findings give local planners a baseline for screening older women in a setting where bone health is rarely checked.
pmc-11935535:
Wenxian Wang and co-authors test whether fat around the heart predicts trouble in weak-heart patients in this 2024 study. The patients have heart failure with mid-range or preserved pumping strength. Fat packed around the heart is suspected of feeding the disease, but its effect on outcomes was unknown.

The study followed 692 patients scanned at two Chinese centers between 2016 and 2022. Heart imaging measured the fat volume and scar-like tissue change. The team tracked deaths and first heart failure admissions. Linking a simple scan measure to real outcomes could sharpen risk checks. The multicenter design gives the finding broader weight.
pmc-11996635:
Efrat Eilam questions a central habit of climate teaching in a paper published in 2024. Sustainability and climate education often set student behavior change as an explicit goal, and Eilam argues that this aim deserves scrutiny. Making behavior the target raises moral and ethical worries about pressuring students, and it may weigh on their well-being.

Several critical lenses are turned on the behavior-first approach. In its place, the paper proposes folding behavior into ethics education. Instead of treating conduct as a lever to pull for outside ends, teachers would treat it as something with its own educational worth, worth examining for its own sake. The reframing keeps agency with the student.
pmc-12046635:
Adam Rose and co-authors re-weigh sea wind power for California, as the state aims for clean power by 2045. Sea wind is new to the mix, and its facts shift fast: rig costs, sea room, and shore ties all bend by place. Their 2024 update sifts tech, social, and cost studies to rate if sea wind can hold its own in the state's blend.

Per-unit cost calls had long slid down, but fresh tech and trade winds have pushed them back up of late. At the same time, the worth of cut carbon has leapt by a wide span as harm prices rise. Side gains, from jobs to air health, join the sums. The net read is a call in flux: dear now, but with gains that grow as carbon costs bite.
pmc-12246735:
Yongqiang Zhang and colleagues ask whether a simple blood index can predict kidney injury after heart catheter treatment. Their meta-analysis from twenty twenty-four covers contrast-induced acute kidney injury. That injury often follows percutaneous coronary intervention. The candidate marker is the systemic immune inflammation index, built from routine blood counts.

The authors searched four major databases for cohort studies on the index. Eight studies with just over six thousand participants met their rules. Pooled results showed moderate sensitivity and lower specificity for predicting injury. The summary curve suggested fair overall accuracy, with little sign of publication bias. Clinicians gain a cautious case for using the index to flag higher risk patients.
pmc-12345635:
Milan Dodig and co-authors report a 2024 lab study on how insulin may drive scar tissue build up in the liver. In liver cells called stellate cells, insulin had not been well tested as a direct cause of collagen growth, the protein that stiffens a scarred liver. The team grew these cells from normal mice and from mice bred to carry high insulin levels.

Insulin raised collagen output in the cells when sugar levels were high, but not when they were low. The effect ran through a surface protein pair that helps cells grip their surroundings, not through a well known insulin signal path. Blocking that pair stopped the effect. Cells from the high insulin mice also made more collagen, and the authors warn that long term high insulin may add to liver scarring risk.
pmc-12352335:
Vandana Sharma and Rammohan Shukla study ribosomal protein genes under stress in mouse brains in a 2024 paper. These genes build the cell's protein factories, and they tend to switch down under stress across many species. How that conserved response plays out in brain stress models was not well mapped.

Public gene data from several mouse stress models and brain regions were reanalyzed. Changes ran both up and down, for both cytoplasmic and mitochondrial gene sets, with no neat pattern by region. Downward shifts still outweighed upward ones overall. The team also probed side roles of these proteins at synapses. Stress may tune protein output in the brain in finer ways than first thought.
pmc-12660335:
Elizabeth Yeh and co-authors present a 2025 report on summer research programs at an Indiana cancer center. Cancer death rates have fallen sharply since 1991, and keeping progress going needs a steady stream of trained researchers. The center ran its first hands-on summer program in 2002 and has hosted more than 300 students since.

What began with federal training support has grown into three nationally funded programs. Early cohorts drew high school and early college students; the newer ones also reach middle schoolers, high school science teachers, and medical students. The authors describe how the programs are organized and share early results from the expansion. Their aim is to grow a skilled, committed cancer research workforce for the long term.
pmc-12661835:
Dan Liu and co-authors test whether synthetic data can rescue machine learning on small health datasets. Published in 2025, the study uses generative models to augment small tabular datasets, a trick proven on images but unmeasured on tables. Simulations on thirteen large datasets let the team vary sample size and check what augmentation really adds.

Gains landed where baseline scores were low and categories ran wide. No single generative model won across the board. On seven real small datasets, augmentation raised scores by about sixteen percent on average, beating plain resampling. The diversity of the synthetic rows, not just their count, drove the benefit. The authors frame augmentation as regularization for data poor health research.
pmc-12662235:
Kenneth Chukwuebuka Egwu and co-authors argue in 2025 that the fight against drug-resistant germs in poorer countries must face three social forces: corruption, poverty, and inflation. Resistance hits low-resource regions hardest, yet most plans stress drug stewardship and public campaigns. Those plans, the authors say, skip the conditions that shape daily choices.

Bribery can bend drug sales and checks, poverty can push people toward partial or fake drug courses, and inflation can price full treatment out of reach. The team calls for a people-centred approach that helps patients handle those pressures, not just germ facts. They present the piece as the first to join all three forces to resistance.
pmc-12663135:
Yingjie Zheng and co-authors build an AI system for early autism screening and tailored support plans for children, in this 2025 paper. Early help can improve development, but current methods scale poorly and adapt little to each child. Their system pairs a deep neural network for detection with a learning agent that adjusts support over time. Data sets covered toddlers through teens.

The detection network reached about ninety-seven percent accuracy on test sets, beating classic models. Checklist scores and background traits ranked among the strongest signals. The support agent then simulated twelve monthly rounds of care on virtual data. Social skills rose up to a quarter, and problem behavior fell up to thirty percent in the simulation. The authors present the system as a data-driven aid, while noting the support results come from simulated, not real, children.
pmc-12664135:
Gregory Neil Kawchuk and four co-authors report a survey study from 2025 on the mental health of chiropractors in Canada. The team adapted a survey first built for doctors by the Canadian Medical Association. They sent it to chiropractors and students across the country in early 2023 and report here on the part that dealt with mental well-being.

More than two thousand people replied. Most said they were doing well, yet the rates of strain were high: about a third reported burnout, and more than a quarter said they had at some point thought about suicide. Young women early in practice and students scored worst, while older men with long careers scored best. The authors use these profiles to argue for support aimed at those most at risk.
pmc-12669735:
Aritra Sinha and Alexander Wietek use computer models to study stripe order in cuprate superconductors, in work from twenty twenty-five. Stripes are neat rows of charge that form at low heat in these materials. They are the lowest-energy state of a key grid model for these solids. At higher heat, stripes give way to odd metal and pseudogap states that are still poorly understood.

The team models a square grid and tracks how charge clumps as the grid cools. Well above the stripe state, large loose clumps of charge grow and drift. The charge response rises to a broad peak but stays finite. On further cooling, the clumps stop growing and lock to the stripe spacing. So clumping starts the path, but stripe order cuts it short at low heat.
pmc-12685235:
Ka Shing Yow and a large team of co-authors report a 2025 study of a health screening follow-up program led in part by young volunteers. Older adults often miss follow-up care after screening and struggle to keep new habits. In the HealthStart program, trained youth volunteers coached older adults on health and digital skills for three months after screening, guided by health care volunteers.

The team tracked nearly two hundred older adults and spoke with participants and volunteers in depth. The share who saw their regular doctor rose from well under half to well over four fifths. Two thirds met their health goals, and most said they were pleased with the program. The mix of youth energy and skilled backup seemed to help older adults act on screening results.
pmc-12686035:
Hussein Elsayed and co-authors (2025) design a magnetic field sensor built from a phononic crystal, a layered material that controls sound waves the way optical crystals control light. The layers alternate between Terfenol-D, a material whose stiffness shifts with the magnetic field around it, and PMMA, a common acrylic. When the field changes, the crystal's forbidden band for sound waves shifts too. Reading that shift tells the field's strength without touching the source.

The layered stack traps sound energy and concentrates it, which sharpens the sensor's response. The team models the design, configured as repeating Terfenol-D and PMMA unit cells, and tunes its geometry for sensitivity. They present the device as a simple and accurate way to monitor magnetic fields, with the added benefit that the same structure can steer acoustic waves. Such sensors could serve in industrial monitoring and medical or navigation equipment.
pmc-12686135:
Francesco Mezzetti and colleagues pilot non-invasive genetic monitoring of the hazel dormouse. Their 2025 study works in Italy's Agri Valley. The dormouse is a tree-dwelling rodent tied to habitat quality. Low numbers and shy habits make it hard to study. DNA from shed material offers a low-impact way to track it.

Hair tubes collected samples without trapping or handling animals. The team judged how well genotyping worked on those hairs. They also checked the reliability of chosen microsatellite markers. Sample size in hairs mattered for result quality. Such checks are vital before wider rollout of the method. The work supports gentler monitoring for a species of conservation concern.
pmc-12686435:
Shifting the pitch of light on a chip, fast and at visible colors, is a missing piece for quantum tools and laser ranging. Jacob Freedman and co-authors built such a device in 2025 in a standard chip factory. Their modulator pairs a vibrating element with a light guide in one tiny structure that traps both light and sound.

The device handled more than half a watt of visible light and shifted its phase strongly at gigahertz speed. It needed far less microwave power than earlier devices of its class, about a hundred times less by one measure. The phase shift per volt was the lowest ever reported for this kind of modulator. The authors say the design can scale, since it was made on a large wafer line.
pmc-12687035:
Wajid Ali and co-authors wrote a pooled review from 2025 on comfort-focused care for people with high blood pressure in the lung arteries. The disease grinds patients down and often ends in death. Guidelines urge comfort care early, alongside disease treatment, to ease the symptom load. Yet few patients receive it. The team gathered studies to name the barriers and to test whether such care links to survival.

Nineteen studies qualified. Patients held back because they felt not sick enough, thought comfort care meant the end of life, or feared burdening family. Doctors pointed to scarce funding and thin training in the field. The pooled death analysis, drawn from just four studies, found no clear survival split between those who got such care and those who did not. The studies also varied a great deal. The team urges health systems to build comfort care into standard treatment paths.
pmc-12687935:
Qusai Belbaisi and co-authors present a 2025 case report on a rare small bowel cancer, leiomyosarcoma. A 73-year-old man arrived after eight months of belly pain, constipation, and anemia. Scans showed a mass partly blocking the small bowel, and surgery found an ulcerated tumor reaching into the mesentery. The growth was removed whole and the bowel rejoined.

Lab work confirmed a high-grade tumor of smooth muscle origin, with markers separating it from look-alike stromal tumors, though one faint marker overlapped confusingly. The authors review the literature and stress that vague symptoms delay diagnosis, surgery remains the main treatment, and careful pathology prevents mislabeling.
pmc-12690835:
Millions of Egyptians drink from the Nile, yet city growth and shifting seasons push pollution into the river. Ahmed Saied, Adel Mousa, and Abdullah Abdo sample water at four sites in Giza through the year in 2025. They compare a commercial rapid test system with classic culture methods. Both track coliform bacteria and other microbes, and the team also measures temperature, acidity, cloudiness, and dissolved solids.

Counts peaked in summer, when oxygen demand also ran highest. The rapid system consistently found 8 to 10 percent more bacteria than the older methods. Microbe levels rose and fell with temperature and cloudiness. The authors call for stronger monitoring, above all in the risky summer months.
pmc-12691135:
Jaewang Lee and Jong-Lyel Roh review an enzyme that guards mitochondria against a type of cell death, and its use in cancer care, in this 2025 paper. The death type, ferroptosis, is driven by iron and fat damage. The enzyme, DHODH, was found in 2021 to suppress that death inside mitochondria. It also makes a building block for DNA, linking two cell jobs. The review gathers the growing work on that dual role.

By restoring a protective form of coenzyme Q, the enzyme blocks fat damage in mitochondria. Tumors may lean on that shield to survive stress. Blocking the enzyme could then strip the shield and kill cancer cells. The authors weigh that promise against what is still unknown. They cover mechanism, tumor growth links, and treatment outlook in turn. The piece is a synthesis meant for cancer researchers.
pmc-12691835:
Arielle Morris and nine co-authors wrote a review in 2025 that links three things: how people bond, how they steer their feelings, and the shields they use to guard the self. People with safe bonds tend to steer their feelings in loose, apt ways. Those with less safe styles lean on weaker ways, and their shields give a clear view of those habits.

The review brings past work and past thought on how the three parts lock in with each other. It shows how growth and group norms shape bond styles. It weighs the ways to test for these traits and gives tips for staff who treat sick minds. The team says staff can read a sick person's shields to learn their bond class. They say this joined view makes tests and care plans sharper.
pmc-12692035: Jia Li, Xiaohong Tong, Zhiyong Li, and Yuxuan Hou introduce a journal special issue on the genetic regulation of plant growth and protection. Plants in the wild face drought, cold snaps, and pests, all of which cut growth and yield. The 2025 editorial frames the issue around the genes that help plants grow under such stress and fight back against attack. It sets the theme for the collected studies.
pmc-12693235:
Sang Yoon Kang and co-authors ask whether amino acid supplements help older adults regain blood protein after hip fracture surgery. Low protein in the blood is common after such breaks and can slow healing. Their 2025 study reviews records from one large hospital for patients treated from 2022 to 2023.

After matching, 53 patients who got the supplements three times a day for six weeks were compared with 53 who got standard care. Blood protein rose more in the supplement group by six weeks. Stay length, blood transfusions, and confusion rates did not differ between groups. The authors call the result early and hopeful, and ask for larger trials to confirm it.
pmc-12693935:
Golden root, Rhodiola rosea, is sold as an energy herb, but solid dose data in trained athletes are thin. Majid Koozehchian and co-authors ran a double-blind crossover trial in twenty-seven resistance-trained adults. Each person cycled through no capsule, a placebo, a low dose, and a high dose, then tested lifting and thinking on day seven.

Both doses raised leg press strength over the no-capsule baseline, and the low dose lifted bench press as well. Repetitions to failure and power output improved at one dose or the other. A color-word test of mental focus improved under every supplement condition. Cycling power, the Wingate test, showed no steady effect. The 2025 trial supports short-term gains.
pmc-12694435:
Aurup Ratan Dhar and co-authors measure the nutrient footprint of Indian diets in a 2025 study. Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but losses along the food chain pollute water and air. India, with its mix of vegetarian and meat-eating regions, offers a sharp test case.

Using national diet surveys, the team produced the first state-level footprint map. Averages came to about 13 kilograms of nitrogen and just over one kilogram of phosphorus per person yearly, with wide swings between states. Meat-eating regions scored clearly higher. Poor fertilizer efficiency and household food waste, near four percent, drove much of the excess. The authors link diet policy with farm practice.
pmc-12694535:
Gilson Borges and colleagues reviewed wearable studies in young children with Down syndrome in two thousand twenty-five. Wearables measure activity and sleep objectively. No systematic review had covered this age group. Five databases were searched thoroughly. Bias risk was checked with established tools. Only nine studies survived screening.

Children showed small movement changes over time. Upper body moved more than lower body. High-intensity activity lagged behind typically developing peers. Sleep quality was poor across studies. Children slept about an hour less than controls. That is far below global recommendations too. Sensor methods varied widely between studies. Standard procedures are needed for population research.
pmc-12695935:
A team of seven researchers reported in 2025 on extracts from Sargassum horneri, a brown seaweed rich in plant sterols and other active compounds. Earlier work had linked the seaweed to lower swelling and lower body fat, but the steps behind those effects were not clear. The team tested an alcohol extract and its parts in lab cells and in obese mice fed a high-fat diet.

In cells pushed into a swollen state, the team tracked signs tied to swelling and fat gain. In the mice, they checked weight and related body changes. The work ties the effects to two cell signal paths, named in the title, and helps show how the seaweed might aid care for swelling and excess weight.
pmc-12696035:
Ang-Jun Liu and co-authors pool the trial evidence on turmeric compounds as add-on therapy for two autoimmune diseases, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Curcumin, the active extract, is widely sold for inflammation. The team searched three databases for randomized trials comparing it with placebo or standard care, judging success by disease activity and blood inflammation markers.

Only seven trials with 314 patients qualified. Across them, curcumin showed no significant effect on joint disease scores or on either of the two blood markers. The trials also disagreed with each other far more than chance allows, which weakens any pooled answer. The authors conclude that current evidence shows limited and inconsistent benefit. They call for larger, better-designed trials before turmeric extracts can be recommended as adjunct therapy. For patients now spending on these supplements for arthritis or lupus, the review is a caution against expecting proven relief.
pmc-12696135:
Yiyao Zhu and a team of co-authors studied outcomes for lung cancer that has spread to the membranes around the brain, in two thousand twenty-five. They reviewed forty-three patients at one hospital over about nine years. Patients were split by whether the cancer had also spread into the brain tissue itself.

Median survival was the same in both groups, at five months. The group without brain tissue spread had higher one- and two-year survival, though the gap was not firm. Missing a certain vessel-blocking therapy, spread to the adrenal gland, and a high blood ratio all marked a worse outlook. Combined treatment eased symptoms and improved life quality across several measures.
pmc-12698235:
Anne Louise Elkjaer Christensen and colleagues compared two knee operations in a matched study published in two thousand twenty-five. Patients with arthritis on one side of the knee can receive either a partial or a full knee replacement, and the better choice is debated. Patient surveys tracked pain and function before surgery and across the first year.

Partial replacement patients, matched with similar full replacement patients, reported better outcome paths over the year when gains were summed across all check-ins. Scores came from standard knee, joint awareness, and activity questionnaires. Surgeons and patients get recovery-shaped evidence, not just a single end-of-year snapshot, for a common decision.
pmc-12699035:
Asmaa Atta and co-authors test whether approved antifungal drugs could be reused against breast cancer in a 2025 paper. Breast cancer is the top cancer killer of women in their region, and fresh drugs are slow to arrive. One growth switch, VEGFR-2, drives the blood vessel growth tumors need, and the azole drug family is known to interact with such switches. Repurposing approved azoles could skip years of safety testing.

The team screened market-approved azoles with computer modeling against the switch, then checked the leaders in lab tests. Itraconazole, a common antifungal, stood out as a strong blocker of the target. Blocking it should starve tumors of new vessels and slow growth. The authors call for animal and clinical studies to see whether the promise survives contact with real patients.
pmc-12699835:
Alice Godden, Benjamin Rix, and Simone Immler compare jumping genes in polar bear groups in 2025. A newly found group in south east Greenland lives in a warmer zone, much like the future that melting sea ice promises for the species.

Jumping genes, or transposable elements, can switch on as part of how a genome answers stress. Gene activity data from the warm south east group and a cooler north east group were compared. The warm group showed more, younger, and more varied active jumping genes, above all from one family. Genes that differed in the warm group linked to aging and metabolism pathways. The authors offer the data as a resource for bear conservation.
pmc-12700335:
Sophie Dennard and co-authors study how people with psychosis get on with experience sampling, a method that pings them through the day for short reports. The work sits inside the AVATAR2 trial. Their 2025 paper mixes numbers and interviews: completion data from trial members, plus talks with users about why they kept up or dropped out.

The team tests whether age, ethnicity, gender, or symptom severity track with completion rates. Interviews then give the human side: what the pings felt like, what helped, and what grated. The aim is to shape digital assessments that people with psychosis find fair and usable. Mental health researchers get both the rates and the reasons behind them.
pmc-12700535:
Masahiro Shuda tells how a skin virus and the skin own fate chiefs lock in a loop that keeps a rare skin cancer alive, in an essay from 2025. Most such cancers bear the virus, whose growth gene drives them. Why the virus picks this skin kind was a long ask.

A work in the same book shows the cancer needs two fate chiefs of the nerve skin line. The virus growth part rides with those chiefs at hot spots of the gene map. Hot spots also sit by the virus own home in the cell, and the chiefs drive the virus gene in turn. The loop ties the cancer to its skin line. Drugs that cut the loop are the pitch.
pmc-12700835:
Tongtong Wang and co-authors study home rehab for people with spinal cord injury, in a 2025 paper. The team wants to know how patients manage care at home and how those paths differ. Seventeen patients were chosen on purpose for deep talks, and the talks were worked through a set seven step method.

The team built patient personas, or model profiles, from six parts of life, from basic traits to social support and care access. Three profiles emerged: self driven patients, patients who lean on others, and patients who feel torn and in pain. Nurses can use the profiles to tailor home care to each kind of patient, rather than give all the same plan.
pmc-12703035:
Ziyat Abdel and co-authors test cholera germs held in a Kazakhstan vault in a 2025 paper. Strains were saved from field and lab sources from nineteen seventy to twenty twenty four. How well drugs still kill them was not known as a set.
