Twenty six strains were tested against fifty nine drugs by disk and strip tests. Gene kits probed for drug proof genes of two drug classes. All strains stayed open to key drugs like doxycycline in the tests. The vault set gives a base line for drug watch in the region. Such checks guard the drugs that cholera care leans on.
pmc-12703635:
Ayisha Ejaz Bhutta and co-authors present a 2025 case report on a rare birth emergency. The wall of the womb can split during labor, most often where a past caesarean scar sits. Here the patient was a first-time mother with an unscarred womb carrying identical twins, which makes the event far more unusual.

After one twin died in the womb, labor was induced and both babies were delivered. Fever, retained tissue, and heavy bleeding followed, needing several rescue steps. A month later she collapsed with fresh bleeding, and scans showed the front wall of the womb was gone. Surgery repaired the defect and saved her fertility. The authors urge vigilance even without classic risk signs.
pmc-12704335:
Juan Diaz-Ricaurte and eleven co-authors revisit a little-known poison dart frog in a 2025 paper. The frog, Ameerega ingeri, was described from only four preserved specimens and was thought to live only in Colombia. Its colors in life, habits, range, and family ties stayed murky for decades, and it was often confused with close relatives.

Field work brought new records that widen the frog's known range. The team describes its body and tadpoles in detail, records its mating call, and notes what it eats and where it lives. Gene and sound data together pin down its place in the frog family and set it apart from look-alikes. Using the new data, they also judge its risk of extinction and propose a formal threat listing. The study turns a museum mystery into a species science can actually protect.
pmc-12706235:
Myo Oo and co-authors count tobacco use in Cambodia in a 2025 study. Tobacco is a top cause of deaths that could be stopped. The team mine a national health survey from twenty twenty one and twenty twenty two.

Over twenty eight thousand adults aged fifteen to forty nine were logged. Nine in ten used no tobacco at all in the data. Smoking sat near seven in one hundred, mostly among men. Smokeless and dual use fill the rest of the count. Traits like sex, age, and schooling were matched to each use type. The counts guide where anti tobacco work should aim.
pmc-12707235:
Jingwen Wu and co-authors study the fibrinogen-to-albumin ratio as a marker for long-term death risk in older patients with coronary artery disease. Their 2025 prospective study follows patients for ten years.

In total, 819 older patients were enrolled from a national geriatric cardiovascular study in China. Patients in the highest ratio group had the shortest overall survival, with a median of about three hundred days. Those in the lowest group lived far longer on median. Multivariate Cox regression marked the ratio as a crucial factor for long-term mortality. The team also built a model to predict survival probability from it.
pmc-12707335:
Gonzalo Cuentas-Canal and co-authors report groundwork for a hypertension trial in Puno, Peru, in a 2025 paper. The ANDES trial rides on HEARTS, the Americas-wide push to control blood pressure and diabetes in primary care, and the team checked how ready the region truly is.

They surveyed 414 health facilities and found readiness under thirty percent for both hypertension and diabetes care. Small posts and basic centers lagged far behind larger ones. Interviews with fifty-five health workers blamed low priority, broken supply chains, and thin training. A companion survey of 204 patients scored how faithfully they take their medicine and keep appointments. The portrait tells the trial exactly where support must land first.
pmc-12707635:
Brian L Weiss and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study of how a bacterial tenant inside tsetse flies sabotages the fly's reproduction. Tsetse carry inherited bacteria ranging from helpful to parasitic. One, Spiroplasma, lengthens reproductive cycles and weakens stored sperm.

Bacteria and sperm compete for fat-derived fuel molecules called acylcarnitines. Infected females raised fuel production in fat tissue after mating. Sperm-storage organs ramped up fuel-handling genes too, yet sperm viability still fell. By starving sperm of shared fuel, the symbiont cuts fly fertility, a quirk that could aid tsetse control.
pmc-12708635:
Alexander Magunia and co-authors build a high-pressure gas rig to watch intense X-ray pulses reshape as they cross dense gas, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The rig holds target gas up to six bar inside a near vacuum. Little beam is lost outside the target zone.

In dense neon, a Raman scatter signal grew past the leftover main pulse in the beam's core. The core beam was nearly all soaked up, which let the scatter part stand out. In principle the two parts can be split in space. The setup opens nonlinear X-ray studies in thick gas. Readers in laser labs get a working design with a first proof.
pmc-12708735:
A blood marker of body-wide inflammation might help explain migraine, but past hints are mixed. Betel Tesfay and seven co-authors test the link in a 2025 study of adults with migraine and healthy peers matched by sex. Blood levels of the marker were read with a checked lab test.

Patients were split by type: with or without aura, long-term or in bouts, and by whether a headache was live at the time blood was drawn. The main test asks how far marker levels in patients sit from those in healthy peers, as a percent gap. Models that allow for other traits refine the check. Subgroup tests then probe whether any one type of migraine drives the link. The design aims to settle a basic question with care.
pmc-12709835:
Nine authors led by Oladunni Oluwoye lay out a trial plan to lift family engagement in early psychosis care. Team care for a first psychosis spell works best when kin join in, yet many kin stay at the edge. A past pilot plan, called FAMES, used culture-fit talks to draw kin in and showed gains. This trial tests that plan at scale in nine care sites, rolled out in three waves.

Each site first takes a plain care group of kin-patient pairs, then a like group on the new plan. Scores track engagement first, then stress and strain in kin. Inner marks such as drive and trust are read to show how the plan works. An equity pack helps sites fit the plan to each culture. Gains by group will show if the pack earns its keep.
pmc-12711035:
Yuexia Lu and eight co-authors asked whether how much B vitamin people eat relates to infection with a common stomach bacterium, in this 2025 study. The bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, infects much of the world and can drive stomach disease. Past work mostly looked at vitamin levels in blood, not at what people actually eat.

The team used a national United States health survey from 1999 to 2000, covering 3,485 people with diet records and infection blood tests. People with the infection ate less of several B vitamins than those without it. Those eating the most B1, B2, niacin, B6, and folate had clearly lower odds of infection, while B12 showed no firm link. Age and ethnic background also shaped the pattern.
pmc-12711435:
Giovanni Trentanovi and co-authors use machine learning in 2025 to predict which trees Eurasian beavers will gnaw in central Italy. Beavers reshape river woodlands by dam building and feeding. Their gnawing can change forest makeup along riverbanks in lasting ways.

Data from three Italian rivers covered tree size, species, and distance from the bank, plus damage signs. Three learning methods predicted damaged versus undamaged trees with high accuracy. They held up well even when trained on a fifth of the data. A second step predicted damage severity with similar accuracy, despite fewer examples.
pmc-12711935:
Valentina Poletti and Eleonora Volpato review why asthma patients stick with, or abandon, biologic drugs in a 2025 paper. Biologics are injected antibodies that calm severe type 2 inflammation in asthma. They work well in trials, yet real-world adherence varies. The authors searched three databases for studies on the mental and social factors at play.

Fourteen studies from 2018 to 2025 qualified, most from the United States. Adherence was mostly moderate to high but swung by drug. Cost and insurance hurdles blocked many patients. Those with mild symptoms or low faith in the drug quit more often. Fear of injections, denial, depression, and stigma recurred as barriers, though little studied. Feeling the drug worked, reassurance, and shared decisions helped patients stay on. The authors call for mental health checks and education built into care.
pmc-12712635:
Robin Thomson and co-authors present a taxonomy paper, published in 2025, describing five new species of microcaddisflies from Ecuador. These tiny aquatic insects belong to the genus Rhyacopsyche, of which only six species were known from the country before. Each new species is introduced with detailed illustrations of the male genitalia, the structures specialists use to tell such near identical insects apart.

The additions lift Ecuador's count for the genus to eleven and the world total to thirty-seven. The paper follows the classic form of species description, comparing each newcomer with its closest relatives and recording where it was found. For a group this small and regionally rich, each addition sharpens the map of freshwater insect diversity in the Andes and beyond.
pmc-12713235:
Jinpeng Xu and co-authors mapped what China's medical insurance fund supervision aims to achieve in a 2025 policy study. What supervision targets shapes which methods get chosen and how well they work. The team gathered more than a hundred national level policies tied to supervision goals. They ranked goal frequency and used network analysis to chart how the goals rank and cluster.

Fund security was the most cited goal, followed by ending insurance fraud and protecting citizens' rights. Goals about efficiency and economy ranked above public facing goals such as participation and justice. The goals clustered around three cores: keeping funds safe, fighting fraud, and guarding rights. Fairness and justice were the most tightly linked pair. The authors present supervision as a web of many related goals rather than a single target.
pmc-12713635:
A cyst in the fatty web that holds the intestines is rare, and one filled with blood rarer still, at roughly one case in a hundred thousand people. Hossam Abdulghafar and four co-authors report such a case in 2025: a fifty-five-year-old man with ten days of worsening abdominal pain.

He arrived with a swollen belly, constipation, nausea, and vomiting, and scans showed a large lobulated mass with bloody content plus signs of blockage high in the gut. Emergency surgery found the hemorrhagic cyst in the small bowel's mesentery, near the duodenum-jejunum joint, and removed it. His recovery was uneventful. The authors stress that full excision guards against recurrence.
pmc-12715135:
Micol Rothman and Gina Woods introduce a special collection on metabolic bone disease in overlooked patient groups in this 2025 editorial. Postmenopausal osteoporosis dominates the field, they note, yet many other groups face bone loss with little guidance. The collection gathers reviews where trials and guidelines are scarce. One paper weighs bone building drugs for cancer patients, a group long limited to anti resorptive drugs over safety fears. It weighs trial data on hormone based and antibody based agents for both cancer related bone loss and bone spread.

A second review covers bone disease in cystic fibrosis, as longer lives make fractures a real concern. A third takes an organ by organ view of bone loss after solid organ transplant, where immune suppressing drugs drive early damage. The editors frame the set as practical guidance for clinicians treating patients the standard playbook skips.
pmc-12715235:
Natalie Miller and six co-authors ask why deep distress raises the risk of death in people living with cancer. The team drew on two large groups: more than thirteen thousand adults in a British study and near six thousand in a Finnish one. Distress came with a higher risk of death from any cause and from cancer itself. The team then tested what might carry that link.

Body-wide inflammation explained up to about a fifth of the tie. Diet, drink, and body weight did not. Cancer stage explained part of the link, yet distress still stood as a strong marker on its own. The paper points to inflammation as one path from mind to outcome.
pmc-12716435:
Derrick Wood, Joseph Roy, and Bari Ballew wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five arguing that simpler models detect ovarian cancer more accurately. Two blood proteins are known markers for the disease, and combining them with a standard regression already gives very high accuracy. A newer, complex model added features from free DNA in blood and claimed gains.

The authors re-examined that model's training data and found a technical flaw. A large share of the cancer samples carried odd chromosome values unlike the rest, which skewed the reported results. After removing those samples, the complex model no longer beat the simple protein-only models. The authors conclude the DNA features are not justified, and that simpler models tend to generalize better.
pmc-12717035:
Tomoya Nakanishi and co-authors study belly chemotherapy in a 2025 paper on stomach cancer. When stomach cancer spreads to the belly lining, outlook stays poor even with standard drug treatment through the blood. Giving a drug straight into the belly has shown benefit, but many tumors resist it.

Thirty patients having a staging scope between 2017 and 2023 joined the study. Wash fluid from the belly was tested for immune cell types and for checkpoint markers that tumors use to hide. The team linked those immune profiles to how well the belly drug worked. The local immune scene may explain who gains from the route.
pmc-12717135:
Sanghoon Lee, Kevin Cruse, Viktoriia Baibakova, Gerbrand Ceder, and Anubhav Jain mine past papers for synthesis recipes in a 2025 study. Solid-state synthesis makes many inorganic materials, from batteries to thermoelectrics. The method lacks a general theory, so past records are a key guide. Prior mined sets often ignored whether extra impurity phases formed.

Using a large language model, the team extracts over eighty thousand syntheses from the literature. Nearly nineteen thousand list impurity phases. The set confirms expected heat based patterns for when impurities form. It also flags odd cases where impurities appear even when the target is far more stable.
pmc-12717235:
Lamine Elkarous, Mohamed Hechmi Jeridi, and Montassar Dhouibi built a system to name firearm types from gunshot sounds in two thousand twenty-five. Telling guns apart by sound is hard because echoes, noise, and setting change each shot's fingerprint. A working system also needs to run in real time.

Their system records shots with small microphones, cleans the signal, and pulls out a mixed feature set from sound spectra. A deep network that blends convolutional and recurrent parts then classifies the firearm type. Tests showed the system could work in real time with a good balance of accuracy and speed. Extreme conditions still hurt its results, the authors note.
pmc-12719635:
Yilong Hu, Yunfeng Chen, and Hailiang Zhao build a warning model for severe gallbladder disease in a 2025 multicenter study. Gangrenous cholecystitis, where the organ's wall begins to die, is hard to spot before surgery. Records came from 744 patients at one hospital, split into training and testing groups, plus 300 later patients at a second hospital for outside validation.

Twenty pre-surgery variables were screened down by two methods, then fed to six machine learning models. A random forest model won, scoring well in training and holding up in outside data. A standard analysis ranked which patient traits drove each warning. Flagging dying tissue before the knife could change how fast and how widely surgeons operate.
pmc-12720435:
Butt, Vaid, Taylor, and Darbyshire review in twenty twenty-five how health researchers involve people from under-served communities, in a review led by public contributors themselves. Such groups bear the most illness yet are least often involved, even though funders require inclusive involvement. Contributors from those communities were trained in review methods and ran the whole project, scanning United Kingdom studies across two searches.

Three themes drove success: involving people relevant to the topic, building real relationships with researchers, and handling practicalities like pay and venues well. The practices matched national involvement standards even when papers never cited them. The authors also show contributors can lead research tasks when trained and supported. Funders' rules, they imply, need such groundwork.
pmc-12722435:
Osvaldo Laurido-Soto and co-authors ran a randomized trial of vagus nerve stimulation through the ear in patients with severe stroke caused by a blocked large artery. Inflammation after stroke worsens brain injury, and stimulating this nerve is known to calm body-wide inflammation, but it had not been tested in acute stroke. Thirty-five patients received either real or sham stimulation twice a day for five days, starting about a day after the stroke was last known to be absent.

The stimulation changed levels of the inflammatory marker IL-6 compared with sham, and on day three several other markers, including IL-1β and IL-17α, also differed between the groups. Safety outcomes such as slow heart rate, low blood pressure, infection, and death showed no significant difference. The authors read the trial as early evidence that the treatment is safe and biologically active.
pmc-12722535:
Nicolett Nyambe, Carolie Cloete, and Andrit Lourens assessed tuberculosis infection control at public health sites in Namibia in 2025. Their study covered the Karas region and asked what health workers know, feel, and do about stopping spread of the disease in clinics. It also asked what helps or blocks good practice and what policies were in place.

The team used a mixed design, pairing an online survey of TB staff with group talks. Survey data were summed as scores for knowledge, attitudes, and practice, and checked for links with worker traits. Group talks added detail on daily barriers and supports. Readers get a ground-level audit from a high-burden setting. The mix of numbers and voices can guide training, supplies, and policy fixes that staff will actually use.
pmc-12722735:
Yunxi Li and co-authors borrow, in a 2025 study, the mathematics of landscape ecology to predict which colon cancers will spread later. After curative surgery, some stage II and III cancers return at distant sites. Scans hold clues in the tumor's spatial texture.

The retrospective study covered patients operated between 2016 and 2020 at one center. Software measured habitat patterns in tumor images, at patch and landscape scales. Statistical models tied certain spatial traits to later spread. Thirty-one of ninety-three patients developed distant recurrence. A landscape score built from the winning traits sorted patients by risk. Imaging that reads like terrain could flag who needs closer surveillance after surgery.
pmc-12722835:
Qingjiang Huang and co-authors examine why burn survivors withdraw from social life, in a 2025 study. Scars and changed skin disturb a person's body image, and body image quietly carries much of our nonverbal communication. The team recruited two hundred eighty-six burn patients and measured body image distress, social avoidance, inner resilience, and family support.

Patients with stronger body image disturbance avoided people more. Resilience softened the blow: patients who adapted flexibly suffered less avoidance for the same distress. Family support worked upstream, feeding a kinder view of one's body and stronger resilience alike. The authors frame the chain with a fear-avoidance model borrowed from pain research. For burn units, the implication is that tending families and building resilience may return patients to society as surely as tending skin.
pmc-12723835:
Yixing Luo and Yang Yang present a 2025 study combining network analysis with machine learning to find gut microbe markers of inflammatory bowel disease in children. Sturdy stool-based biomarkers remain scarce, most of all for Asian children. Bacteria that shift with treatment could sharpen diagnosis.

Fifty children, most with bowel disease, gave stool samples for gene sequencing at a Beijing hospital. Sick children showed lower microbial variety. Network mapping highlighted interacting bacterial groups, and four machine-learning methods ranked the taxa that best flagged cases. Tools that show their working explained the rankings. The combined approach picks candidate biomarkers for testing in larger groups of children.
pmc-12723935:
Jinge Xu, Junyu Li, Junwen Zhang, and Yongsheng Yu tested an old stomach drug, pirenzepine, against prostate cancer. Immune drugs that free the body's attack on tumors help many cancers but often fail in prostate cancer. The team looked for a partner drug to boost them, testing cells in dishes and tumors in mice.

The drug slowed cancer cell growth, spread, and colony forming, more so at higher doses. Tumors drew in more killer immune cells, and pairing the drug with an immune drug worked better than either alone. Tests point to a virus-sensing protein, switched up by the drug, as the driver. The authors propose trials in patients.
pmc-12724235:
Xiaosong Li, Rucheng Yao, and co-authors map where a cell state shift is strong in liver cancer and tie it to immune escape, in a 2025 study. The shift lets cancer cells move and spread more well. Space maps show where in the tumor that shift peaks.

The shift ran hot at tumor edges and linked to worse survival. Hot zones held fewer killer immune cells and more suppressive cells. One gene stood out as a top driver in all models. Lab tests showed that gene sped cell move and spread, while its block flipped those gains.
pmc-12725535:
Yu-Ting Chi and co-authors set out a 2025 plan for a study of two kinds of stapler used in robot-aided surgery. Staplers cut and seal tissue in small-cut surgery, and new robot staplers add fine bending and live reads of how hard tissue is pressed. Whether they beat the older bedside staplers in real care is still not clear.

The plan uses a large US hospital data set for adults who had full robot-aided surgery from 2019 to 2023. Cases cover lung, bowel, stomach, and weight loss surgery, each to be read on its own. The main check is leaks after surgery, with other checks for harm, time, blood need, stay length, and cost. A weighting method will help balance the two groups.
pmc-12727435:
Sebastien Chaigne argues, in a 2025 essay, that heart research stays stuck by studying one piece at a time. The cardiovascular system works as a network, from molecular signals up to whole-organ function. Yet most studies isolate a single pathway in a simplified setting, a habit the author calls one-dimensional. That habit has brought real progress, but it has also slowed the kind of change that comes from seeing the whole system at once.

Chaigne urges a shift toward a three-dimensional view that joins data across scales and fields. Models should treat the heart and vessels as interacting parts, not loose fragments. Funding habits come in for criticism too, since grants reward narrow, safe projects. The essay is a call for the field, and those who fund it, to embrace complexity rather than strip it away.
pmc-12727535:
Martin Rihtaršič and co-authors report a chemistry study from two thousand twenty-five on using common nitroarene compounds as light-driven catalysts. Energy transfer catalysis lets chemists reach excited molecular states without harsh high-energy light. The usual route is building special sensitizers whose energy matches the target.

The team found that what matters is not the catalyst's energy but where its excited state sits. When the excitation centers on the aromatic ring rather than the nitro group, catalysis works far better. They proved the idea on two reactions: flipping alkene geometry against its natural preference and joining pairs of double bonds into rings. A simple energy-gap measure helps predict which nitroarenes will work, speeding the hunt for new catalysts.
pmc-12727735:
Kiki Ochieng and four co-authors survey gut worms in African clawed frogs in a 2025 study. These frogs anchor ecosystems and laboratories across Africa, but parasites, habitat loss, and climate change press on them together. The team sampled two frog species in Kenya's Lake Victoria Basin.

Over eight months, 480 frogs were collected from streams and ponds with traps and nets, and water conditions were logged. Three worm groups turned up: one tapeworm genus in the intestine and two roundworm genera in gut and stomach. Infection rates ran from about a quarter of frogs to ninety percent depending on worm and host, with roundworms most common and most varied. Diversity indices differed between hosts and sites. The baseline matters because frogs are living indicators: shifts in their parasite communities can warn of wider ecological change in the basin.
pmc-12729135:
Atsebaha Gebrekidan Kahsay and colleagues published a 2025 study of Salmonella on Ethiopian dairy farms. Salmonella passes from animals to people. Drug resistance makes it harder to treat. The team worked in the Tigrai region. They sampled milking cows and the people who handle them.

Nearly two hundred farms took part. Stool samples came from cows and from farm contacts. Lab tests isolated Salmonella and checked drug sensitivity. Questionnaires recorded farm practices and risks. Matching cow and human samples shows farm-level spread. Results can guide hygiene and safer antibiotic use.
pmc-12729235:
Paul Oladele, Wenxuan Dong, Brian Richert, and Timothy Johnson test how the route of a fecal transplant changes its effect in piglets. Their twenty twenty-five article deals with weaning stress in pigs, which brings weight loss, diarrhea, and gut barrier harm. Donor microbes can help, but delivery in pigs is invasive and uptake is hard to predict.

Forty weaned piglets got donor material by mouth, by rectum, or mixed into feed, with a saline group as control. All transplant groups gained faster in the first days, and their gut communities shifted toward the donor. The oral route gave the highest colonization and lowest rejection. Route also changed how well uptake could be predicted.
pmc-12729735:
David Fennell, Yulei Guo, and Richard Butler survey tourists at China's panda breeding base about animal welfare, governance, and conservation, published in 2025. Wildlife viewing anchors much tourism, yet concern for the animals involved keeps growing. Frameworks exist to judge how attractions treat their animals, and the study applies one empirically.

Over a thousand visitors rated the base's welfare management, governance, and conservation work. Overall judgments were positive. Two factors colored the scores: how much panda social media a visitor had seen beforehand, and how much the visitor knew about animal welfare. The authors argue that mediated experience shapes on-site judgment. They suggest drawing tourists into education and evaluation, including through digital platforms, to lift both awareness and real welfare standards.
pmc-12730435:
Aloraini, Alghamdi, Alqarawi, and Alanazi review a new heart procedure that uses electric pulses to fix a common rhythm fault. The method, called pulsed-field ablation, destroys faulty tissue without heat and aims to spare nearby structures. Their 2025 review weighs it against older heat and cold based methods.

Trials show rhythm control much like the older methods, with less harm to the food pipe and to a nerve near the heart. Procedures also tend to be faster. Early data suggest the method could serve as a first line treatment for this rhythm fault. The authors still call for longer follow up and larger real world studies before its place is settled.
pmc-12731135:
Monsikan Chaiyakit, Rangsun Parnpai, and In Cho study how the herbicide atrazine harms sperm production, using a lab-grown human model instead of animals. Atrazine is sprayed widely and disturbs the body's redox balance. The team grew sperm-producing cells from human stem cells, including lines with the Huntington's disease mutation, which makes cells extra sensitive to oxidative stress.

Cells were exposed to atrazine for thirty days, then guided to mature for fifteen more. Effects depended on both dose and cell line. Normal cells showed early suppression of development without much cell death. One Huntington's line was highly sensitive: low doses switched on death pathways, and the high dose silenced sperm genes. The second line mounted a strong antioxidant defense at low doses but lost balance at the high dose. The authors trace the harm to a tug-of-war between oxidative stress and cell death signals.
pmc-12731335:
Zdenek Stuchlik and Jaroslav Vrba study disks of charged gas circling a black hole. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The black hole is of the simplest kind, with no spin or charge of its own. A dipole magnetic field, like a bar magnet's, threads the space around it. Gravity and magnetism then pull on the gas in rival ways.

By tracking single charged particles, they sort the motion into three regimes. When the field is weak, gravity rules and orbits stay orderly. When it is strong, magnetism rules instead. In between, the motion turns chaotic. They show how a neutral disk can become ionized and split under these forces. They also compare a dipole field with a uniform one, finding big gaps in the strong-field regimes.
pmc-12732135:
Yongchul Kwon and co-authors report, in a 2025 study, gym lessons designed to draw in students who are usually shut out of sport. Such students may be sidelined by ability, drive, or background. A group of teachers, working as a learning community, co-designed maker-based lessons in which students build, measure, and analyse, not just perform.

Three lesson types emerged: ones built on measuring and analysing body data, ones on feedback about performance, and ones in play and game formats. Sidelined students took on roles as creators and analysts, and also joined the physical activity more as performers. Teachers shifted from skill drills toward reflective practice. The authors call the model cheap and adaptable for wider reform.
pmc-12732535:
Medical researchers review a fast-moving form of leukemia in this 2025 paper on acute promyelocytic leukemia. The disease is a distinct subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. It is marked by a swap of material between two chromosomes, which joins two genes into a fusion gene called PML::RARA.

That fusion blocks young blood cells from maturing and drives the cancer. The review sums up what is known about how the disease works, how doctors find it, and how they treat it. Early death is still a major problem, largely due to severe bleeding problems the disease causes. The authors explain how the fusion protein breaks up nuclear bodies and blocks retinoic acid signals. That block leaves cells stuck and resistant to normal cell death. The paper ends with practice advice drawn from the evidence.
pmc-12732835:
Belisa Marin Alves and co-workers checked a screen risk tool to stop blood clots in ward patients. Clots in veins are plain and can kill, yet care to stop them stays in low use. A Brazil ward brought in a broad plan built on the Maynard risk model. The prior and post study ran from 2017 to 2019. It took in 772 adults who stayed past 48 hours in cure or surgery wards.

The model put most patients at mid risk, near 76 percent, with near 23 percent at high risk. Padua and Caprini scores served as guide marks for cure and surgery patients. Guard care counted as fit when it matched ward rules. The 2025 study tests if set screen sorts lift fit guard care in truth.
pmc-12733335:
Xiaohua Li and co-authors compare pigment chemistry across three varieties of a medicinal orchid, in this 2025 study. Gastrodia elata is a prized traditional Chinese medicine, and flower and stalk color help classify its types. The team combined chemical profiling of pigments with gene activity reads. They asked which pigment family drives the color differences.

Carotenoids, not the red-purple anthocyanins, turned out to carry the color gap. Four specific carotenoids varied most between varieties. Fifty genes differed in the flavonoid path and seventeen in the carotenoid path. Five genes were flagged as key drivers, and a MYB regulator family tracked closely with carotenoid content. The findings guide future breeding to enrich useful pigments in this crop.
pmc-12733435:
Ji Liu, Millicent Aziku, and Dahman Tahri trace how early childhood education lifts teenagers' test scores through calmer behavior and fewer skipped classes. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Preschool's long shadow on cognition is documented but its pathways are not. They used a giant international assessment data set of fifteen-year-olds.

Early education predicted stronger non-cognitive skills and better scores directly. Stronger non-cognitive skills, in turn, meant less truancy and higher performance. Truancy itself dragged scores down. Girls gained more from early education than boys did across these paths. The chain suggests preschool pays off partly by building habits, not just knowledge. Skipping school emerges as a measurable leak in the pipeline. The authors argue early provision carries equity benefits. Access in childhood compounds into adolescence.
pmc-12734035:
Alice Jeanningros, Stephane Bouchard, and Alexandra Potvin-Desrochers review in 2025 virtual reality exposure therapy for fear of movement in Parkinson's disease. Activity eases symptoms and may slow the disease, yet many patients stay sedentary. Fear of movement is a little-studied barrier that may explain part of that gap.

Searches found no studies that target this fear directly in Parkinson's patients. The authors widened the review to related nerve and muscle conditions. Meta-analyses there show moderate to large drops in fear after virtual reality work. They close with directions for building such a program for Parkinson's care.
pmc-12734135:
Donoso and a large team test skipping the biopsy for skin cancers that look clear cut under a dermoscope in twenty twenty-five. The usual path biopsies first, then treats, which means extra visits and cost. Records covered near four hundred basal cell cancers at one center. Some went straight to removal, while others had the standard biopsy first.

The direct group proved right more often, with most removed spots confirmed as cancer. Wide margin cuts cleared in nearly all direct cases. Trouble clustered in high risk and repeat cancers. The authors back direct removal for low risk cases and older patients. It saves visits, time, and money, they say.
pmc-12734435:
Shupeng Guo and four co-authors present a method for standardizing pore images from metal 3D printing, in a 2025 paper. Laser melted parts often contain pores that weaken them. Learning models could predict those defects, but image data come from many sources at many scales, and gathering new data is costly.

Their method detects and strips scale bars, rescales images to true physical size, and evens out resolution while keeping pore shapes intact. Tests on published and lab datasets show the pipeline merges unlike sources into a consistent set. That consistency makes old imaging collections reusable for training. The authors offer the framework as a base for shared, growing materials datasets. They target cheaper defect prediction and process tuning.
pmc-12735135:
Ksenia Latosińska and co-authors tune the lathe turning of a titanium alloy made two ways in two thousand twenty-five. Ti6Al4V parts can be cast or laser-sintered from powder, and the sintered kind's fast heating leaves a distinct inner grain. That grain changes how the metal cuts.

Trials varied cutting settings and tracked force, surface roughness, and chip shape for both stock types. Hardening during the cut and the effect of the cut layer's cross-section shape were also gauged. Their optimization seeks the lowest cutting force that still leaves a fine finish. Reshaping the cut layer, they found, let turning run with sharply lower specific force. A worked shop example shows the method in use.
pmc-12735435:
Adhithya Mullath Ullas and co-authors review diet and bone health in a 2025 paper. Thirty studies, mixing trials and cohorts with over half a million adults, compared Mediterranean, calorie-cutting, high-protein, low-carb, and ketogenic diets on bone density, fractures, and turnover signals.

No diet clearly changed bone density at any measured site. The Mediterranean pattern did link to fewer hip and total fractures. Cutting calories raised bone breakdown markers, while vitamin and calcium status barely moved under any diet. Readers get a measured verdict: eating style guards against breaks more than it builds density.
pmc-12735735:
Maria Anastasiou and co-authors test whether tiny RNA molecules in blood can warn of heart damage from cancer therapy in a 2025 study. Women with HER2-positive breast cancer often receive drugs that can harm the heart. A blood test that flags risk early would let doctors act sooner.

Forty-seven patients were checked for heart damage at the start of care and then every three months for over a year. A panel of 84 microRNAs was measured in baseline blood samples. Forty-five of them differed between patients who did and did not develop heart damage. Two stood out as single predictors. The team also trained five machine learning models on the RNA patterns to classify risk, pointing toward a combined blood and computing test.
pmc-12736335:
Łukasz Balewski and co-authors published a review paper in 2025 on drug design around the isoquinoline scaffold, a two-ring structure with a nitrogen atom. Compounds built on it show a wide spread of effects, with cancer work leading lately. They can block growth signals, stir cell rust, halt division, or jam the pumps that make tumors drug-resistant.

The review also gathers reports of germ-, fungus-, and virus-fighting members, plus early anti-Alzheimer and anti-inflammatory findings. The nitrogen atom makes the core a good grip for metals, and copper, iridium, and platinum complexes show strong activity. The survey covers synthetic advances from 2020 to 2025 and other medical uses.
pmc-12736435:
Xinyi Wang and co-authors set up a lab method to clone pin oak trees, a species prized for parks and wild lands but hard to copy. They grew plant tissue on a standard woody-plant medium and tuned the growth chemicals step by step.

One blend of two growth chemicals made shoots multiply fastest, over fivefold. A rooting blend put roots on 83 in a hundred shoots. A third blend coaxed the tissue lumps called callus from 91 in a hundred samples, with modest browning. One added compound, fipexide, helped callus at low doses and blocked it at higher ones. The recipe gives growers a base for fast pin oak cloning and for saving its germplasm.
pmc-12736535:
Irati de Goñi and co-authors present a 2025 drug design study aimed at glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor in adults. Tumors resist treatment and return, partly because they vary so much and harbor stem-like cells. The team built single molecules that strike several targets at once, a strategy meant to outflank that variety.

The new family joins parts of two parent drugs into one indole-based frame. The hybrids block two enzyme groups and a third enzyme class, while also acting on two receptor types. Four molecules were made, and the two strongest were studied in depth. Early results show the multitarget design works as planned in the lab. The authors see a path toward drugs that hit the tumor on many fronts at once.
pmc-12736835:
Ahmad Almatroudi presents a 2025 review of tiny silica carriers built to deliver drugs in the body. The carriers are sponge-like grains with a large inner surface and pores that can be tuned in size. They can hold a drug, shield it on its trip, and let it out at the right place. Recent designs mix the silica with plastics, fats, metals, or living matter to add new traits.

The review covers how the carriers are made, how their surfaces are changed, and how they are checked in the lab. It gives weight to carriers that react to cues such as acid, light, or cell signals and release their drug then. Uses covered run from cancer drugs and gene delivery to germ killers, vaccines, and brain care. The author weighs fresh lab and animal results and notes what still blocks use in patients.
pmc-12737035:
Chizhov, Goriaev, Belus, and Svistunov present a study from twenty twenty-five on an additive that delays scorching in plastic crosslinking. Peroxide curing can start too early, ruining processing. TEMPO family additives quench radicals but also thin the final network. A two-headed version can both quench and re-link chains. The team vary its dose in polyolefin mixes. Low doses raise final network density while delaying curing onset. Delay reaches over half a minute under moving conditions.

Oxidation resistance of cured parts rises modestly as well. A simple kinetic model predicts the delay well. The authors confirm the additive as an efficient scorch guard. Predictable behavior aids factory use.
pmc-12737135:
Rong Feng and co-authors measure lung strength in rural homemakers of the Fenwei Plain in China. Homemakers face smoke and stale indoor air at close range, day after day. Their 2025 study tested 72 women in one county near Xi'an, in both winter and summer.

Age wore lung strength down most, with clear steps down across age groups. Second-hand smoke and poor room airflow also dragged scores down. Women with aired rooms and no smoke near them scored best. No clear season pattern showed up. The authors urge smoke warnings and better home airflow for local women. Such steps are cheap and sit in the hands of each home.
pmc-12737235:
Zhiwen Zheng and co-authors tune a wolf pack hunt math to plot joint paths for drone fleets, in a study from 2025. Fleet paths must dodge hits, keep rank, and cost least in hard skies. Their hunt adds three tricks to the wolf base: peer learn twixt non lead wolves, a bird style wide roam with leap flights, and lead wolf weights that shift with fit.

On two stock test sets the tuned hunt beat seven peer hunts and took top rank in a signed test. Fleet sims then gave smooth, safe, low cost paths from start to goal for each drone. The tricks cure the base hunt faults of crowd loss and trap in poor peaks.
pmc-12737335:
Huang and co-authors use in 2025 hollow protein fibers to template platinum and palladium nanostructures with enzyme like activity. Engineered virus protein fibers offer stable, well defined shapes for guiding metal growth. Placing metal on the outer surface or the inner channel on demand was the hard part.

Selective mineralization put noble metal structures on either face of the fiber. Co depositing both metals gave bimetallic nanowires in the same frame. Those wires acted like peroxidase enzymes in tests. Paired with a cholesterol enzyme, they enabled cholesterol detection. The work links template control to a sensing use.
pmc-12738435:
Md Saiful Islam Saif and a team of co-authors distill ninety-two blood cytokines into a four-protein score predicting who benefits from immunotherapy in head and neck cancer. Their paper appears in two thousand twenty-five as a biomarker study. Picking responders to anti-PD-1 drugs remains guesswork.

Pretreatment sera from thirty-eight discovery and forty validation patients with recurrent or metastatic disease were profiled. The score, built from CXCL1, MCP-4, interleukin-6, and CD40, predicted survival with concordance near zero point seven one and zero point seven nine in the two cohorts. High scores doubled the adjusted death hazard. The score outperformed tumor mutational burden and PD-L1 testing. A blood draw, the authors suggest, may guide immunotherapy choices.
pmc-12738535:
Deniz Özdemir Çelik and Melek Belevcikli test dental age methods in children with type 1 diabetes in a 2025 study. Dentists estimate a child's age from tooth development on panoramic X-rays. Diabetes might shift that development, but proof was thin. Films from fifty-eight children, half with diabetes and half healthy, aged four to fifteen, are scored three ways.

All three methods give similar ages for diabetic and healthy children, they find. The Willems method proves most accurate in every subgroup. Cameriere slightly underestimates age, while Demirjian overshoots. Well controlled diabetes seems to leave dental age on track, and using methods together adds safety.
pmc-12738635:
Li, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, built a decision method to judge management accounting information when facts are not clear. Management accounting gathers financial and non-financial data for planning and control inside a firm. Judging its quality means weighing vague criteria that can conflict. Plain numbers handle that task poorly.

The method uses circular fermatean fuzzy sets. These sets record how much a point belongs, how much it does not, and a circular spread for doubt. Two known techniques are extended into this fuzzy setting. CRITIC weights criteria by their contrasts and correlations. WASPAS ranks the options. A case study weighed five alternatives on five attributes and picked internal accounting as best. Checks with changed weights and with other methods supported the method, the author reports.
pmc-12738735:
Mi-Kyung Oh, Kyung-Rok Yu, and a large team engineer tiny cell packets to calm bowel inflammation. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets inflammatory bowel disease. Current drugs often miss full remission and suppress the whole immune system. The packets come from stem cells of the cord jelly layer.

Two changes arm the packets for a dual strike. A surface protein engages a brake on active T cells. A small RNA inside cuts a protein that feeds inflammatory T cell growth. The balance then shifts toward calming regulator cells. In mice bred to mimic human immunity, the packets homed to inflamed gut. Disease signs eased there, the team reports.
pmc-12738835:
Chien-Hao Sung and eight co-authors build a sharper way to estimate how much carbon campus green spaces take up. Their twenty twenty-five article measures net primary productivity, the carbon plants store as they grow. The method blends machine learning, drone flights, and satellite data.

A Random Forest first maps the green space with high accuracy. Drone sensors supply a key leaf signal, while satellite images give temperature, sunlight, and water stress. All feed a standard carbon model, CASA. Against the classic model, theirs fit field data better in two seasons. The team argues that campus green space can act as a small urban carbon sink, and that the method can guide city planning.
pmc-12739135:
Ying Lau and five co-authors test an online resilience training for health workers in a 2025 trial. Health staff faced heavy strain during the pandemic and in complex care settings, with burnout widespread. Their six session digital program was built from prior reviews and psychological theory, and experts rated its content highly.

Four hundred ten health workers in Singapore were randomly assigned to training or control groups. Resilience was the main outcome, with work engagement, intent to leave, and harmful work behavior also tracked at three time points. The training group improved in resilience right after the program and at three month follow up. The authors suggest such training can supplement staff support, pending longer studies.
pmc-12740135:
Alachew Adino and Seyoum Mengistou read the health of an Ethiopian river through its smallest animals, in a 2025 study. The Little Akaki River in Addis Ababa suffers heavy sediment loads that smother stream life. Tiny invertebrates react fast to such stress, which makes them living gauges. The team sampled seven sites across gravel, sand, mud, plants, riffles, and pools in the spring of 2024.

They collected 5,575 animals from eleven orders and 32 families. The richest site held 21 kinds; the poorest held the fewest. Habitat quality tracked closely with the share of sediment-shy groups and with overall diversity. A sediment-sensitivity index also rose with richer, healthier scores. Most sites proved heavily sedimented, and sedimented sites were also the polluted ones, the authors conclude.
pmc-12740935:
Dario Messenio and co-authors probe how eye pressure disease affects the brain's visual centers in this 2025 study. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve, but its effects may reach the visual cortex itself. Blood flow there should rise when the eyes work; that coupling was little explored.

A light-based brain scan tracked blood responses in 203 eyes across four groups: eye hypertension, open-angle glaucoma, normal-tension glaucoma, and healthy eyes. Full eye exams accompanied the scans. Comparing groups shows whether the brain's response fades with the eye's disease. Such signs could become early markers, caught before vision loss shows in standard tests.
pmc-12741435:
Ouadii Abakarim and seven co-authors report a hard-to-treat blood disorder case in this twenty twenty-five paper. A woman in her mid-seventies had two diseases at once: a mast cell disorder and a slow blood cancer. Her platelet count was low, which makes many drugs risky.

A first drug pair was stopped because it harmed her blood counts. The team then used a targeted drug at a reduced dose, plus a steroid to support platelets. Within two weeks her swollen glands shrank, her spleen and liver shrank, and her platelets returned to normal. The case offers a workable plan for similar fragile patients.
pmc-12742135:
André Pekkola Pacheco and five co-authors model whether treating sleepless hearts pays for itself, in this 2025 economic study. About half of coronary heart disease outpatients suffer insomnia, and poor sleep worsens their prognosis. Group cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia works, five weekly sessions teaching patients to rebuild sleep, but cardiac clinics do not routinely offer it.

Using data from a Norwegian coronary cohort of 528 patients, the authors simulate a hundred outpatients with insomnia receiving the group therapy versus usual care. The ledger counts possible savings from avoided repeat procedures and hospitalizations after new heart events, and from reduced sick leave, valued conservatively. An early economic evaluation of this kind does not prove savings; it shows whether a full trial is worth funding and where the money would move. For a health system, sleep may be a cardiac intervention hiding in plain sight.
pmc-12743235:
Alireza Jalali and co-authors set out in 2025 twelve hands on tips for bring smart tools into medical training. Such tools can tailor lessons, speed research, and cut desk work for staff. The tips rest on past work and on real cases from the field.

Tips span teach, research, desk, and ethics zones. They urge fit to each learner, fast feed back, and fake cases for class drills. Smart help with lit hunts, data work, and draft prep gets its own pass. Plain sight, fair play, and clear blame lines close the set as ethics guards.
pmc-12745235:
Shicheng Yang and co-authors ask whether a few days of a diabetes drug can guard the kidneys during heart stent work, in this 2025 paper. Contrast dye used in the procedure can injure kidneys, especially in diabetics with weak kidneys. Long courses of the drug class are known to help; short ones were untested.

Hospital records from 2024 split patients into a short-course dapagliflozin group and a control group. Kidney function was tracked before the procedure and at two points after. The main measure was how often contrast injury struck each group. The study weighs a cheap, brief shield for a common risk.
pmc-12745435:
Juan Liao and co-authors present a 2025 study on gut microbes and skin color in a prized black-boned chicken from the mountains of Sichuan. The depth of black pigment in these birds drives their market value. Whether gut microbes help set that pigment, by supporting energy use, was poorly understood.

The team profiled gut microbes in dark-skinned and light-skinned birds, using gene sequencing of cecal samples. Blood chemistry was mapped at the same time. Dark birds held a richer mix of microbes, with ten groups differing between the two sets. Many of the shifted groups link to energy-making pathways. The study ties microbe makeup to pigment in this breed.
pmc-12745835:
Smriti Kochhar and co-authors published a case report in twenty twenty-five on treating necrotizing pancreatitis with hydrogen peroxide flushes in a patient too fragile for standard procedures. The disease destroys pancreatic tissue and usually calls for endoscopic cleaning, but her heart and lung problems made that dangerous. Doctors improvised through drains already placed in her skin.

The thirty-two-year-old woman received peroxide instilled into the dead tissue collections through percutaneous drains, which loosened and washed out the debris. Follow-up over a full year showed a lasting response with no harmful effects and no further endoscopic work. The authors ask for proper studies to set dose and schedules, since guidance for this approach does not yet exist.
pmc-12746735:
Yang Liu, Hong Fan, Guohua Wei, Yinyin Shu, and Jigang Zhang studied brain-wave-guided anesthesia for older hip fracture patients in two thousand twenty-five. Delirium after surgery affects up to half of such patients. The authors asked if guiding anesthesia with an electroencephalogram, a record of brain waves, could cut that risk.

They reviewed patients aged sixty and over treated from late two thousand twenty-two to mid two thousand twenty-four. After matching, the guided group had far less delirium on days one and three, though the gap faded by day five. Guided patients also recovered thinking scores sooner, left recovery and hospital sooner, and reported higher satisfaction. The authors link the gain to less drug and less burst suppression.
pmc-12747535:
Xiaomei Fu, Fasi Wu, and Xiaobo Liu argue for a living archive in a 2025 paper on heritage care. Old sites sit outdoors, where microbes colonize stone and wood and slowly eat them away. Weather cannot be stopped, but microbe damage can be fought. Past studies often stopped at naming the microbes present, short on proof of what they actually do to materials.

The authors call for a bio archive that stores heritage microbe samples and data for the long term. Multi omics tools can then link microbes to the chemical harm they cause. Such an archive would let conservators compare sites and pick treatments with solid evidence. The plea fits a wider push for greener, science led care of shared heritage.
pmc-12748535:
Albert Lecube and thirteen co-authors test a hopeful assumption in Spain: that teaching people obesity is a disease would melt the bias against it, in this 2025 survey. One thousand adults, a representative sample, answered a telephone interview probing knowledge, stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination, alongside their beliefs about what causes obesity.

The public is split on causes: 40.8 percent blamed weak self-control, while 59.2 percent called obesity a disease. The disease camp understood its many causes better and backed public funding for treatment more strongly. None of that softened their attitudes. Discriminatory views ran equally in both camps, and about thirty percent of everyone admitted negative stereotypes or acts of weight-based discrimination. Calling obesity a disease, the authors conclude, is true but insufficient; stigma lives in deeper narratives and structures that information alone does not reach.
pmc-12748735:
Yuxuan Zhu and co-authors compare how three image reconstruction methods render fat inflammation signals around the heart's arteries on CT scans. The fat attenuation index flags coronary inflammation early. Scan processing choices might shift that reading quietly.

Patients were grouped by the plaque their scans showed. Groups ranged from clean arteries to calcified plaque. Each scan was rebuilt with all three algorithms. Deep learning reconstruction faced two older methods head on. Fat values, image noise, and the index were measured. The three artery segments were scored for every method. Differences between algorithms could mislead risk calls. The study tells clinics to mind their settings closely.
pmc-12749235:
Eleven researchers report a study from two thousand twenty-five on hiding data inside folded DNA shapes. DNA origami folds a long DNA strand into a planned shape, and hidden patterns in the folds can store information like a code. Reading that code back fast and correctly is the hard part.

The team paired a fast imaging method, called DNA PAINT, with an automatic grouping method that needs no labels. The pairing read out two and three dimensional origami codes with accuracy up to eighty-nine percent. Simulations helped them allow for the bending of the shapes. They also set rules that promise full recovery of the stored message.
pmc-12749335:
Qihui Wu and six co-authors teach drones to track targets through sudden anomalies in a 2025 paper. A tracker that locks a moving target fails when the scene breaks pattern, and learned trackers eat data and compute while generalizing poorly. Their method borrows the brain's two gear decision style: a fast lane for plain tracking and a slow lane for trouble.

The system, called CEL, swaps modes when its anomaly spotter fires. Rule reasoning and an anomaly clearing module then steer the chase back on course. A new scoring form handles the muddy reads anomalies cause. In sim and real drone tests it beat top rivals by wide spans: success rate up more than three fold and task speed up by half. The authors see embodied smarts as the path.
pmc-12749535:
Gao, Wu, Bian, Liu, and Jing survey a family of proteins that seal the gaps between cells, across many cancers, then zoom in on one member in lung cancer. These claudin proteins guard barriers in tissue linings and often misbehave in tumors. Their 2025 study mines cancer databases for the family's levels and links to outlook, with lab tests on the chosen member, claudin-12.

Claudin-12 ran high in lung adenocarcinoma, the main lung cancer type, and tracked with later stage, spread to nodes, and shorter survival. In dish tests, lowering the protein slowed tumor cell growth, movement, and invasion, and raised cell death. The authors present claudin-12 as a candidate marker for detection and a possible drug target. They note the work rests mostly on database analysis plus cell tests.
pmc-12749735:
Marcus Westerberg and co-authors ask whether age and illness counts can stand in for a fitness grade that cancer registers rarely hold, in a 2025 study. Trials often select patients with the ECOG grade, which rates how active a patient is. The team used Swedish register data on 3,966 men treated with hormone therapy for advanced prostate cancer, where the true grades were known.

They built models from age plus three illness indices, two of them new and based on diagnosis codes and filled prescriptions. The best model sorted fit from unfit men with good accuracy. In a mock cohort, using the model to screen men cut the share of unfit men included from one quarter to a small fraction. The authors say such a stand-in can make register studies fairer.
pmc-12749935:
Irene Pancrazi, Davide Tritini, Hassan Ahmed, and a team of co-authors report on coral colonies moved out of the path of a huge construction project in the Maldives. A new connectivity project joining islands required dredging and land building that would have buried the reef, so colonies were transplanted to a calmer urban reef nearby.

Two years of monitoring brought cautiously good news. About two in three colonies survived, and bigger colonies clearly outlived small fragments. One genus grew faster and shrugged off heat better, while the other bleached more easily yet held its tissue. Warmer water slowed growth across the board, and most losses came from tissue wasting rather than predators. The authors call relocation a workable short-term rescue when paired with smart choices.
pmc-12750635:
Ma and co-authors track immune cell patterns in sepsis, a life-threatening state where the body's response to infection harms its own organs. Their 2025 study compares 220 sepsis patients with 70 healthy controls, then follows the patients for twenty-eight days to see which cell patterns predict survival.

Sepsis patients showed more of some white cells and fewer of others than controls. Two simple measures, the share of neutrophils and a ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes, flagged sepsis about as well as the standard inflammation test. Patients who died kept higher values of those measures on days seven, fourteen, and twenty-one. Survivors showed lymphocyte and monocyte shares climbing back over time. The authors name day seven as a key window for judging outlook.
pmc-12750835:
Mathilde Labouret and co-authors trace the course of a children's fever syndrome in this 2025 study. The syndrome brings repeated fevers with mouth sores, a sore throat, and swollen neck glands. It is the most common cause of periodic fever in children. Doctors usually expect it to fade on its own over time.

The team reviewed records for more than two hundred patients at a hospital near Paris. Only about one quarter had gone a full year with no fever episode. Most children still had active symptoms at last contact, and some who seemed cured later relapsed. Among those who recovered, symptoms lasted about five years. Recovery came at a median age of about eight years.
pmc-12750935:
Drew Duckett and a large team built and tested a DNA-based tool to predict whether a brain tumor will return, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Meningiomas are common tumors of the brain's lining. Their behavior is hard to forecast from looks alone, and chemical marks on DNA carry extra clues about risk.

Using samples from over two hundred patients, the team grouped tumors by those chemical marks and built a classifier that assigns risk groups. It also reports how confident each call is. In the test group, the tool scored high accuracy, and most samples got confident calls. Unlike earlier tools, it uses DNA marks alone and was checked in a clinical setting. The model is shared in public.
pmc-12751135:
Esra Agaoglu, Imran Yılmaz-Karaman, Furkan Acıkbas, and Hilal Kaya Erdogan study partner violence among women with psoriasis. The skin disease is long-lasting, and stress can feed it. No prior study had asked how many of these women face violence at home. The team surveyed 134 women in care, scoring their skin severity, quality of life, and trauma symptoms.

Nearly half the women had faced at least one form of partner violence, most often emotional abuse. Those women reported worse skin-related quality of life and more trauma symptoms. Trauma strain also tracked worse skin scores. The paper urges skin clinics to ask about violence and count it as part of care.
pmc-12751335:
Allylestrenol is given to support pregnancies at risk, yet its safety for the developing young needs direct testing. Lai Jiang and co-authors run a preliminary study in pregnant rats. One hundred thirty-eight mated females received the drug at three dose levels, or control treatments including standard progesterone forms. The team tracked hormone levels in the mothers. They then followed the pups' early development.

The highest dose lowered estradiol late in pregnancy. Two lower doses raised testosterone compared with controls. A standard marker of developmental disruption, the anogenital distance in pups, showed no change at any dose. The authors present the work as a first pass: the drug leaves most measured endpoints alone, but the hormone shifts at higher doses mark where closer study should look.
pmc-12751535:
Sean Van Helden and many colleagues published a 2025 analysis of an antibiotic called eravacycline against gut bacteria named enterococci. These bacteria cause common hospital infections with high death rates. Strains that resist key drugs, like vancomycin, are on the rise.

Eravacycline is a new member of the tetracycline family, approved for complex belly infections. The team pulled out the enterococcus cases from past trial data. They judged how well the drug cured these infections and how safe it was. Subgroup checks like this show where a drug's label may stretch. Doctors need sound options when standard drugs fail against resistant strains.
pmc-12752335:
ShaoChun Liu and co-authors pool trials of creatine plus weight training in older adults in a 2025 review. Muscle loss with age erodes strength and independence; training helps, and creatine might add more. Eight randomized trials with 482 people, training two to three times weekly for eight to one hundred four weeks, passed the screen.

Creatine plus training beat placebo plus training on leg strength and lean tissue mass, but not on upper body strength. Gains leaned on program length in subgroup checks. The authors frame the pairing as a modest, real aid against age related muscle loss.
pmc-12752435:
A virus best known for cervical cancer also drives cancers of the throat, anus, and genitals, and a vaccine now targets it. Mary Mallon and co-authors reviewed which virus types appear in those other cancers in this 2025 paper. The setting is the United Kingdom and Ireland. Since 2019 both have used a nine-type vaccine for prevention.

The reviewers searched two large medical databases and screened over four thousand papers. Thirty studies passed the full checks and gave data for extraction. Bias was scored with a standard tool, and pooled results were computed in statistical software. The types found tell whether the current vaccine covers the strains behind these cancers locally. That answer shapes screening and vaccine policy.
pmc-12752735:
Dandan Zhong and co-authors review how aging and metabolic disease drive each other. Their twenty twenty-five paper maps a harmful cycle of decline that links the two. Old cells, faulty power plants in cells, and long-term swelling all play a part.

Other drivers include changed nutrient sensing, gene-control marks, broken daily rhythms, and gut microbe shifts. New treatments aim at this shared axis, from drugs that mimic fasting to ones that clear old cells. Multi-omics tools and gut-based care also show promise. The authors warn that tissue targeting and long-term safety still block wide clinical use.
pmc-12752835:
Dhruvanshu Patel and co-authors checked in 2025 whether a no cut stomach tightening procedure still helps reflux patients whose food pipe squeezes weakly. The endoscopic procedure is proven in patients with normal squeezing, but weak movers were feared to swallow worse afterward.

Records covered 164 patients, twenty-nine of them with weak motility and stubborn reflux. After the procedure, quality of life scores for overall symptoms, heartburn, and regurgitation all improved sharply. Use of acid blocking pills fell, with most patients stopping them. Swallowing difficulty did not rise. Some patients did restart acid drugs within months. The authors call the option safe for this group.
pmc-12753735:
Sohag Kumar Mondal and co-authors build an automated blood cell reader from microscope images in two thousand twenty-five. Counting and sorting blood cells by hand is slow and error-prone, yet the task steers diagnosis of anemia, leukemia, and allied diseases. Their system sorts nine cell types from smear photos.

A U-Net model first cuts each cell out of its messy background, and a light neural network then names it. Cleaning steps sharpen and vary the training images. The cutting stage scored high on pixel accuracy and overlap measures. The full chain aims to give labs a fast, steady stand-in for manual counts.
pmc-12753935:
Xinchen Wan, Xue Wang, Yanjun Liu, Longyan Hong, Zhandi Zhao, and Pengbo Guo review a form of cell death in infections of the reproductive tract, in a 2025 paper. The death mode, ferroptosis, runs on iron and on the rust-like damage of cell fats. It ties to worn mitochondria, loss of a guard enzyme, and broken handling of iron and amino acids.

Infections of the reproductive system involve many germs and complex pathways, and ferroptosis now appears inside several of them. The review maps how the process drives harm in these infections and related disorders, including immune cell loss in HIV. It also surveys early ideas for drugs that block or harness the process. A fresh angle on stubborn infections could widen treatment choices.
pmc-12754935:
Jiaoyu Deng and Dianbo Xu comment on a data study that named two marker genes for diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease caused by diabetes. The original team used computer analysis of gene data and checked its findings in a public data set. Deng and Xu say that check set was described wrongly.

Records show the set holds tissue from the retina of dead donors, not blood from living patients. Its groups were also more mixed than reported, with donors who had diabetes but no eye disease. That shift matters: the results support a role for the genes in the retina itself, not as blood tests. The comment also asks for deeper work on how the genes affect immune cells in the eye.
pmc-12755835:
Anton Leontyev and Takashi Yamauchi probe, in a 2025 study, how feelings shape impulsive behavior. Impulsivity has parts: choosing a quick small reward, failing to stop a bad action, and losing focus. Feelings are known to feed all three, but theories disagree on the path. One theory says feelings mainly weaken stopping power; another says they break attention first.

Across two studies, the authors stirred happy and sad feelings with pictures and tracked behavior, in part by following the computer mouse as people answered. In people without a clinical diagnosis, feelings made behavior more impulsive by breaking attention control rather than by weakening stopping. One trait, acting rashly when happy, stood out in stopping control. The findings favor the attention account of how emotion drives impulsive acts.
pmc-12756135:
Pengfei Zhang and Roger Cheng ask how few questions can sort every primary headache in this 2025 pilot study. The world headache manual lists disorders through long checklists of traits. The team turned each trait into a yes-no variable and hunted for the smallest set that still separates all the diagnoses.

Their algorithm boiled the needed traits down to twenty-three unique features. Those features collapse into fifteen questions, covering duration, frequency, suddenness, one-sidedness, sharpness of memory of onset, pain quality, and triggers like cold, pressure, and exercise. An even smaller set might exist but sits beyond their computing reach. The authors say the short list could speed up clinic interviews.
pmc-12756735:
Tarak Hidouri and colleagues studied layered semiconductor films as candidates for a new kind of solar cell layer. The films stack a gallium oxide layer on gallium arsenide, with a boron-bearing layer in between in some samples. Using light emission tests at varied power and temperature, plus computer simulation of a full cell, the team examined defects that glow. How those defects might form an intermediate energy band inside the material. Such a band could let a cell harvest lower-energy light in two steps. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five.

Emission was dominated by paired defect transitions shaped by disorder at the layer boundary, where boron and gallium atoms mix and defects cluster. Simulations of the proposed cell design suggested conversion efficiency above twenty percent with strong voltage and current values. The authors also see promise for light detectors in visible and infrared ranges.
pmc-12757235:
Guangqiang Hu and co-authors review PD-1 and PD-L1 immunotherapy for prostate cancer. Their 2025 review covers a common cancer that the immune system barely notices, often called cold. Surgery and radiation handle early disease, but relapse and spread remain common, which keeps the search for new options urgent.

Drugs that block the PD-1 pathway free T cells to attack tumors, and they have scored clear wins in melanoma, lymphoma, and lung cancer. In prostate cancer, single-drug results stay weak, and no firm rule picks who might benefit. Trial evidence hints that combined regimens could do better. The authors weigh the trial record and set out the open questions: better patient selection and smarter combinations.
pmc-12760035:
Romil Parikh, Dana Urbanski, Chanee Fabius, and three colleagues study case management for disabled older adults in this two thousand twenty-five paper. People with physical disabilities using publicly funded long-term services report more unmet needs. Whether a case manager to coordinate services changes outcomes was unclear. The authors studied about sixty-seven hundred respondents aged sixty-five and older from a national aging survey, comparing emergency visits and community life by disability and case manager status.

Physical disability appeared in sixty percent of respondents, who were more likely to lack a case manager. Without one, disability meant clearly higher odds of emergency visits and lower odds of community activity and enjoyment. With a case manager, those links shrank toward nothing: visit odds became hard to tell apart, and community gaps narrowed. The authors argue coordinating services buffers the disadvantage linked to disability in long-term care.
pmc-12764335:
Langhua Xiao, Guilian Zhang, and Guirong Liu lead a team testing whether rational emotive therapy calms first-time mothers' anxiety and improves how their labors go. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The therapy targets the irrational beliefs that inflate distress. Pregnancy anxiety is common and can shadow delivery itself.

Sixty anxious first-time mothers were randomized to routine care or weekly therapy for twelve weeks. Afterward the therapy group scored far lower on anxiety and depression scales. Their first and second labor stages ran significantly shorter. Natural delivery was far more common in the therapy group. Cesarean and forceps rates dropped correspondingly. The third stage of labor did not differ between groups. The authors present belief-focused therapy as an obstetric asset. Mind and labor, in this trial, moved together.
pmc-12764635:
Renata Przydatek-Tyrajska and co-authors studied skin mite damage care in two thousand twenty-five. Tiny Demodex mites live in human hair follicles. In excess they cause chronic skin inflammation. The team checked how common infestation was in clinic patients. They also judged which beauty-medicine treatments eased the aftermath. One hundred patients joined the study.

Infestation turned up in just under half the group. Those patients needed anti-parasite therapy first. Follow-up watched skin recovery after treatment. Medical peelings were the most used helpful procedure. Mesotherapy and botulinum toxin also improved appearance. Supplement care supported the skin's recovery further. The study links parasite control with cosmetic repair steps. It guides clinics facing stubborn mite-related skin damage.
pmc-12765935:
Zihan Qin and co-authors use single cell gene reading to find cells that drive kidney scarring in diabetic kidney disease in a 2025 study. The disease is a leading cause of end stage kidney failure, and scarring is its core damage, yet the cells behind the scarring are not fully mapped. The team reanalyzed public data from human kidneys.

They found a group of fibroblast cells, high in a gene called TMSB10, much expanded in diseased kidneys. Those cells were rich in genes for scar material and for a known scar signal path. Lowering the gene in lab cells and in diabetic mice cut scar markers by about half or more and reduced scar build up.
pmc-12766835:
Sheng Yang and a large team map the immune landscape of KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer cell by cell, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. KRAS mutations drive many colorectal cancers and help them evade immunity. Single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were combined to see which cells sit where and what they signal to each other.

Mutant tumor cells were found recruiting a particular monocyte type through one signaling axis. Nearby fibroblasts laid down collagen that engaged receptors on the tumor cells and kept lymphocytes out. Together these players built an immunosuppressive spatial niche around the tumor. The map suggests targets for therapies tailored to this common cancer subtype.
pmc-12767235:
Beatrice Prampolini, Cansu Ceren Eryilmaz, and Loredana Marcovecchio review blood vessel risks in teens with type 1 diabetes in a 2025 paper. The main harm from the disease comes through vessel damage, which shows in full during adult life. Yet many teens already carry risk factors, and early silent stages can be found with screening.

The review lays out three lines of defense: tight blood sugar control, action on heart and metabolic risks, and early screening plans. Care then joins insulin tuning, lifestyle support, and timely drugs when damage appears. The authors stress that habits and checks set in the teen years shape vessel health for decades. The piece serves clinic teams and families planning long term care.
pmc-12768635:
Hannah O'Keefe and Chris Marshall compare twenty-five large language models for use in horizon scanning, the work of spotting new health technologies early. Such work needs tools that extract data well and cope with messy sources. The team built a frame of thirty-two features in ten groups.

They used a chain of smart tools checked by humans to score each model. Only six features varied much across models. Most could run on site, but few were open source, and only five handled noisy data well. Most charged by use, letting units tailor budgets. The authors say units must weigh hosting, support, price, and data skill when picking a model.
pmc-12768835:
K Paola López-López and two co-authors wrote a 2025 study that builds a math model to rate how well breathing machines are used in a hospital. The team worked with data from a lung diseases hospital in Mexico. Their sample covered 66 machines used during the year 2023.

The model weighs eleven factors, from how many patients each machine served to how many hours it sat out of service. Three scores rate supply, demand, and daily running, and they merge into one score for clinical use. Each machine then falls into one of four levels, from low to high use. The team found that 42 percent of the machines had low use and 39 percent had fair use. The model gives hospital staff a clear way to spot machines that sit idle and shift them where they are needed.
pmc-12770535:
José Rocha and co-authors build a light converter that sets itself up, in a 2025 paper. Such devices turn one set of light patterns into any other set through a series of planes. Design is usually done in a digital model, but even a small gap between model and real device cuts performance hard.
