Their device tunes itself in minutes, soaking up unknown misalignments and flaws into the design as it goes. A fast light modulator that updates a thousand times a second speeds the setup. A new shaping method handles many light modes at once. The team shows arbitrary transforms and a universal mode sorter on the platform.
pmc-12771135:
Narjit Kaur Paramjit Singh and co-authors published this 2025 study on tooth decay in Malaysian children with cerebral palsy. These children face higher decay risk from movement limits, feeding issues, and strained caregivers, but which factors matter most was unclear. The team studied 110 children and teens at two Kuala Lumpur hospitals.

Decay in baby teeth, at about seventy percent, matched the national average. In permanent teeth, though, decay hit about seventy-seven percent, more than double the national rate for twelve-year-olds. Care received was strikingly low, the team report. Records of movement level and palsy type, plus a caregiver burden survey, fed a model hunting the strongest predictors. The results argue for dental plans built around these families, not generic advice.
pmc-12771835:
Hartley and co-authors pool studies on the mental strain carried by families after a loved one survives intensive care. Relatives often leave the hospital with lasting anxiety, low mood, and distress of their own. The team merged fifty studies and measured symptoms three months after the admission, using standard scales and a statistical method that weighs uncertainty openly.

About thirty-eight percent of family members had anxiety at a level that matters clinically. About twenty percent met that bar for depression. Average distress scores sat in a range linked to real suffering. Including bereaved relatives did not shift the estimates in the checks possible. The authors say families rank alongside patients as people needing follow-up care after critical illness.
pmc-12772035:
Wenjia Li and co-authors score China's policies for joining elder care with medical care. Their 2025 study reads 12 policy texts issued from 2016 to 2024. A scoring model with nine main traits and 44 sub-traits turns each text into a number.

The mean score came out at 6.76, with eight policies rated excellent and four rated good. Traits like care for carers and clear leadership scored well. Care systems, policy tools, and care capacity scored worse. The authors urge more joined-up thinking and a better match of supply with demand. They also call for more training of care workers and fresh ideas for the care trade.
pmc-12772535:
Abnormal tangles of vessels in the brain's outer lining can bleed or steal blood flow, and sealing them from inside is the first-line fix. Gaultier Marnat and co-authors report a study, published in 2025, of one sealing agent used for that job. The agent is a liquid polymer that hardens on contact and does not stick to vessel walls.

The study ran at fourteen centres in Europe from late 2017 to late 2019. It enrolled patients with a single such tangle who were set for treatment with the agent. Other tools could be added when needed. The team tracked how fully the tangles closed and what harms arose. Real-life data of this kind help doctors judge where the agent fits among its rivals.
pmc-12774535:
Jing Cai and co-authors build lab models of breast cancer from patient tissue, described in work published in 2025. Drug response varies a lot from patient to patient, and tumors often resist care and return. Older lab models do a poor job of guessing how one person's tumor will react. The team wanted models tied to each patient.

Tumor and nearby tissue were taken during surgery. Cells were grown flat first with a method that keeps them alive longer. The cells were then placed in tiny gel spheres to form 3D models. The team compared the flat and 3D forms with marker tests and drug checks. Such models could help pick drugs for each patient.
pmc-12775135:
Andresen and a large team tested in twenty twenty-five a drug that blocks a scar protein, to aid heal of gut joins in pigs. Crohn's ill oft leaves gut scars that narrow the tube and need cuts. The blocked protein helps scar build in many tissues.

They made two joins in each of forty-five pigs and shot each join with the drug, a known aid, or a plain fluid. The drug was well borne at both doses over up to four weeks. Scar at the join fell by near a fourth with the drug. Muscle cells shifted from a scar form to a work form in drug joins.
pmc-12776135:
Xinyu Huang, Maolin He, and co-authors build a risk model for bone cancer from genes tied to cell phase splits, in a 2025 study. Phase splits let cells sort parts in droplike zones, a new hot zone in cancer work. Its role in this bone cancer was still near bare, though.

Cell and bulk gene sets were crossed to find phase tied genes with odds worth. A seven gene model split risk groups with clear immune splits as well. Lab tests show one gene runs high in cancer cells and drives their growth. The model gives a fresh frame for risk sorts in this cancer.
pmc-12780435:
Xi Lin and a large team test whether a protein in chest fluid can identify cancerous fluid buildup around the lungs, in a 2025 study. The protein, neuron-specific enolase, had shown mixed results in earlier work. The team enrolled patients with unexplained pleural effusion at two Chinese centers and measured the protein blind, then checked accuracy against final diagnoses.

Cancer patients did show higher protein levels, but the test separated the groups only modestly, and the best cutoff differed sharply between centers. Decision analysis found little added value. Digging into past studies, the authors found accuracy rose when more heart failure patients were included, which may explain the earlier optimism. Their verdict: the marker is not useful for this diagnosis.
pmc-12784035:
Facebook use is heavy across the Arab world, yet researchers there lacked a locally validated yardstick for how intensely people use it. Hilmi Jelleli and eight co-authors translate and test a multidimensional Facebook intensity scale in 1,068 Tunisian adults, alongside measures of life satisfaction, happiness, and physical activity.

Factor analysis supported a four-part, thirteen-item scale with a single higher-order score, and the scale proved consistent and valid. Heavier Facebook intensity went with lower life satisfaction, lower happiness, and less physical activity. The authors offer the instrument for research, clinics, and digital well-being programs in Arabic-speaking settings, while urging tests in other Arab cultures and over time. The study appears in 2025.
pmc-12784535:
Tianyu Zheng and co-authors review the blood vessel cells that help tumours hide from the immune system. Their 2025 review covers tumour-associated endothelial cells, the lining of vessels inside a tumour. Beyond plumbing, these cells tune which immune cells enter and how they behave.

Signals from the lining can shut down killer cells and favour suppressive ones. That helps tumours resist both chemo and immune therapy. The review sorts the mechanisms and the drug targets they suggest. Early work on vessel-directed treatment is weighed. The authors close with the gaps that block clinical use, from marker choice to delivery.
pmc-12784935:
Mariia Maiorova, Yulia Kipryushina, and Konstantin Yakovlev offer a shortcut for finding which versions of one gene are active in sea urchins. Their twenty twenty-five paper focuses on Otx, a gene with several messenger RNA forms. Labs usually hunt isoforms with slow bench assays.

Huge short-read archives already sit in public banks. Mapping those reads onto just the one gene, instead of the whole genome, cuts the work and the noise. Tissue and stage patterns of each form can be screened before any new lab work. Gene specialists studying development get a cheap first pass for any single gene of interest, not only this one.
pmc-12785435:
Tugba Onyilmaz and six co-authors look back over ten years of care for a scarring lung disease in a 2025 study. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lungs and kills many patients, and even with newer drugs, guessing who will fare worst stays hard.

The team reviewed records for 268 patients seen at one large center between 2015 and 2024. Most were men, with a median age of seventy-two. Over a median follow-up of two years, forty-four percent died. Those who died were older and more often had heart artery disease or lung blood clots. The authors sort which traits traveled with death so clinics can plan closer watch and care for the highest-risk patients.
pmc-12785535:
Zhen Zeng and co-authors test how processing changes Chinese sweet tea in a 2025 study. The leaf, from a tree in the beech family, is brewed as green or black tea and drunk as a hot brew or a longer decoction. Green tea kept the most plant compounds, with high levels of two measured classes. Black tea lost about forty percent of one prized group to oxidation during its making.

Simulated digestion showed green tea kept strong antioxidant power despite a bitter edge. In lab fermentation with gut microbes, the teas boosted helpful short-chain fatty acids. Black tea decoction tripled one of them and enriched two beneficial microbe groups. Processing and brewing style together set the drink's taste, what the body can reach, and its prebiotic promise.
pmc-12786535:
Tomasz Drzymała, Ewa Rudnik, and Sylwia Lewicka baked and stretched fibre-laced cement mortars meant for tunnels, in a 2025 study. Polypropylene fibres can matter in tunnel fires, where heat threatens the lining. Two fibre shapes and sizes, at two doses, went into fine mortars. Thermal analysis watched the samples dry, decompose, and hold together from room temperature to six hundred degrees.

Fibre-bearing mortars proved more thermally stable than plain ones. Within the tested range, neither fibre type nor dose shifted that stability much. The team also weighed strength after heating. The work guides mix design for linings that must survive both load and furnace heat.
pmc-12786735:
Six engineers study how laser power changes welds in a titanium alloy in a paper from 2025. The alloy, called Ti80, is used where strength and low weight matter. They welded plates and then checked weld shape, inner structure, and strength. Computer models of heat and stress were run beside the lab tests so the two could be compared.

Higher power changed the weld cross-section shape and changed pore counts. The weld zone grew harder than the base metal. At the highest power tested, joints were strong and broke in a ductile way. The model predicted peak stress within about two percent of measured values. The work links welding settings to joint quality.
pmc-12786835:
Kuribayashi and co-authors present a 2025 study on vitamin C and delirium after heart surgery. Surgery on a bypass machine stirs oxidative stress, which may breach the brain's barrier and spark confusion. The team compared two groups at one hospital across two time spans. Forty patients got standard care, while forty-four later patients got two grams of vitamin C on arrival in intensive care.

The groups matched on health and surgery factors at the start. Organ trouble and inflammation after surgery looked similar, though one marker ran higher in the vitamin group. Delirium struck the vitamin group far less often, the results show. The authors call the study exploratory and urge a proper trial.
pmc-12787935:
Amged Elhassan and co-authors test 3D printed sandwich panels whose layers lock together inside the print, in a study from 2025. The panels pair a soft TPU core with stiff skins of nylon, PLA, or PET. Print settings let the team add interlocking joints at the skin-core border, with no extra parts.

Five core patterns were printed at 20 percent density and bent in three-point tests. Grid and gyroid cores bore the highest loads, while cross and honeycomb cores bent in a steadier way. Adding the interlocks lifted peak load by up to 15 percent, bend by 48 percent, and energy uptake by 51 percent. The PET and TPU pairing absorbed the most energy, at 2.45 joules per cubic millimeter.
pmc-12788135:
Senhao Niu and five colleagues design a navigation system that keeps vehicles located when satellite signals vanish, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Urban canyons block GNSS signals frequently in city streets. Inertial systems drift with no correction to hold them true. That drift puts autonomous driving at risk each time it strikes.

Their hybrid pairs deep learning with an adaptive Kalman filter. A temporal convolutional and bidirectional memory network fabricates pseudo-satellite measurements from inertial data in the gaps. An iterated extended Kalman filter with regulated noise then fuses those estimates as they come in. The filter keeps re-estimating its own noise statistics as it goes, for robustness. The team reports sustained positioning through the gaps in signal. The approach is aimed at the messy, stop-start signal world of real city streets.
pmc-12788435:
Swatantra Patel and co-authors compare three stains for mouth cell smears, weighing quality, speed, and cost, in work from twenty twenty-five. The classic Papanicolaou stain is the cytology workhorse, but it is slow and reagent hungry. Two fast, cheap variants promise relief.

Thirty healthy volunteers each gave three smears, one per stain method. Three observers graded cell shape and stain quality without knowing the method. Shape quality tied across all three. One fast method, the modified ultrafast variant, won on overall stain quality and was quickest and cheapest. Both fast methods matched or beat the classic. The authors back them where speed and budget press.
pmc-12789635:
Masoud Amiri, Maryam Imani, and Hassan Ghassemian present in 2025 a deep feature fusion frame for finding targets in hyperspectral images. Such images carry many color bands, which makes target search hard amid varied backgrounds and few target samples. Class imbalance adds to the strain.

Their frame joins two branches in small image patches. One branch uses attention to catch links within and across patches, while the other pulls local space-color patterns. Self and cross attention steer focus toward likely target zones. A guided filter cleans the output maps. Tests on four benchmarks beat top past methods, with gains up to fifteen percent.
pmc-12793035:
Trevor Denton and co-authors survey hospitalized older patients about using a phone app that prompts them to move, in a 2025 study. Lying in bed during a hospital stay can cause lasting loss of independence. An app that reminds patients to stay active might cut that risk, if patients are willing and able to use it.

Of eighty eligible patients invited, sixty nine joined the survey at a large academic hospital. Most wanted to stay active, owned a mobile device, and over half said they would use such an app. Willing patients had more health conditions, more education, and greater comfort with devices than unwilling ones. A hands on test asked each person to set an alarm on their own device. The authors map who might adopt such tools.
pmc-12798935:
Alicia L Salvatore, Michelle Axe, and Matthew K Hoffman studied unmet social needs among pregnant patients arriving at a Delaware hospital's obstetric triage unit, in a paper published in 2025. Needs such as money strain, food, housing, and transport shape health, yet pregnancy care rarely screens for them at the door.

Over three months, about three hundred patients completed an eleven-question screen. Nearly half reported at least one need, and seven percent reported four or more. Money strain, food insecurity, and housing and transport trouble were the most common. Black and Hispanic patients, and those with public or no insurance, carried clearly higher burdens. Screening proved workable, though privacy and referral paths needed care. The authors back routine screening tied to real support services.
pmc-12800135:
J Brémont and co-authors find a hidden law in how wanderers explore space, in this 2025 paper. Random walks model everything from animals hunting food to stock prices, but most real walkers remember where they have been, which breaks the classic math. The team defines a simple event called a flip: the moment a walker, having reached one edge of its visited ground, next breaks new ground at the opposite edge.

For classic memory-free walkers the flip chance matches a known splitting formula. The surprise is that for walkers with memory the flip chance follows a simple universal rule anyway, falling as one over the step count. Tests in simulated memory models and in real data banks confirmed the rule. The team explains why it holds and stretches it to flat maps and fractal ground.
pmc-12800235:
Roshanak Kian and co-authors study how the liquid a drug sits in changes its light behavior and shelf life. Their 2025 work covers two anxiety and seizure drugs with ring-shaped parts rich in nitrogen. Both were tested in fourteen liquids that range from water-like to oil-like.

One drug shifted its inner charge far more when lit, shown by a bigger swing in its electric shape. Two math models showed that liquid acidity and basicity drive most of the effect. A new index from the team tracks how well each drug holds up. One drug stayed steadier in oily liquids, the other in water-like ones. The results guide storage and mix choices.
pmc-12800735:
Erik Storholm and co-authors design a two-year study of how partner violence shapes HIV prevention among transgender and nonbinary people. Their 2025 protocol notes that this group faces partner violence at twice the rate of cisgender people. How that violence changes testing habits and use of preventive medicine remains poorly understood.

The first phase interviewed 32 people with recent violence experience plus 10 service providers. Those talks shaped a national online cohort of 600 HIV-negative, partnered participants. Surveys and home test kits will track condom use, infections, and preventive drug uptake every few months for 24 months. The authors aim to trace both risk and protective paths, so programs can be tailored to real relationship dynamics.
pmc-12801535:
Natalia Stepanova and co-authors link blood magnesium to clotting risk in dialysis access in a 2025 study. The access, a surgically joined artery and vein, often clots and fails, and magnesium guards vessels in other settings.

Records from 408 patients at two centers span up to five years of follow up. A fifth suffered a first clot. Patients in the middle and top magnesium thirds faced roughly half the clot risk of the lowest third. Older age raised risk on its own. The team suggest magnesium checks could join routine access care planning.
pmc-12801635:
Susan Mutile Kavai and a large team of co-authors survey typhoid bacteria in sick children in Nairobi County, Kenya. Typhoid fever strikes about twenty million people a year, mostly in poorer countries, and drug resistance keeps eroding treatment. Their 2025 study examines Salmonella Typhi from febrile children and profiles its resistance genes. The H58 strain, a known multi-drug resistant lineage, proved common. Resistance to fluoroquinolones, a backup drug class, is also emerging.

Findings like these steer local prescribing and vaccine planning. Watching resistance in an endemic area is the only way to catch a strain before it spreads widely. The authors supply current numbers for Kenyan clinics. Their work joins treatment policy with lab surveillance in one report.
pmc-12801935:
Díaz-Narváez and co-authors measure empathy among health sciences professors across Latin America. Teachers model the empathy students will later show patients, so their levels matter. Over eleven hundred professors in six countries completed a standard empathy scale built for health professions, and the team classified scores and compared them by gender.

More than half the professors landed in the medium to very low range. Women scored slightly higher than men overall and on the perspective-taking dimension, though the gaps were small. The scale behaved consistently across genders, supporting fair comparison. The authors are blunt about the headline: the mentors of future clinicians are, on average, only middling in measured empathy. They call for deliberate empathy support in academic settings, not just in student curricula.
pmc-12804735:
Irmaleny, Dharsono, and Ash-shafa compare two fluoride treatments for teeth that have lost minerals. One is silver diamine fluoride, and the other is fluoride varnish. Their 2025 lab study used 27 upper premolar teeth, split into three groups.

All teeth were first softened on purpose, then treated or left as a control group. After a week in a fluid like saliva, all groups got harder again. The silver based treatment gave the highest hardness scores. A follow up test found a clear gap between the two treatments. The authors say the silver based option may guard early decay better. Hardness was checked before softening, after softening, and again after each treatment was applied.
pmc-12804935:
Yuquan Chu and co-authors build a neural network that forecasts traffic flow by fusing place and time patterns at once. Their 2025 model answers a common flaw in older designs. Most rivals read time trends and road layout apart, then merge them late, losing links between the two.

The model uses a cross-attention step borrowed from transformer networks. It pulls space and time traits from past data in sequence and blends them as it goes. Tests ran on four varied traffic datasets. The model beat standard methods on those tests. The authors say reading the two pattern types jointly is what lifts forecast accuracy. They offer the design as a fresh route for smarter transport systems.
pmc-12808435:
Yumi Yamamoto and co-authors tested in 2026 a radioactive tracer meant to image an inflammation enzyme. The tracer is a radioiodinated form of nimesulide, a drug that blocks cyclooxygenase-2. The hope was to picture that enzyme in the brain with SPECT scanning. Tests in normal mice, though, showed weak brain entry and a poor match to the enzyme's true distribution.

The story flipped in a mouse model of peripheral inflammation. There the tracer gathered selectively in inflamed tissue, and blocking drugs for the enzyme cut that uptake. The tracer stayed pure and stable in the body, but strong binding to blood albumin likely kept it out of the brain. The authors reposition it as a tracer for inflammation outside the brain. They also note design lessons on chemical groups and stability.
pmc-12808635:
Adam Alvarez-Monell and co-authors build an ultra-processed food diet for rats in a 2025 study. The diet uses real products that human teens commonly eat and drink. Teen rats of both sexes were fed the diet after weaning.

One trial gave thirty different products, one per day, plus standard chow. A second trial combined chosen products into four set menus. Forty-eight rats were split by sex and diet for six weeks. Body metabolism and behavior were both measured. Processed feeding raised several harm markers. Readers see a lab model for testing how teen diets may affect brain and body.
pmc-12811035:

Six researchers lay out a study protocol in 2025 to test both together. Adults with primary headache at hospitals in a national pilot project choose combined care or usual single-tradition care. The team will follow them for twelve weeks at several centers.

Outcomes include headache days per month, pain scores, quality-of-life scales, and a headache impact test. The economic side counts cost per quality-adjusted life year gained. The authors aim to give policymakers real-world evidence on whether collaborative care earns its cost.
pmc-12811735:
Ghita Bennis and co-authors test the treatment impact of dobutamine stress ultrasound in chronic coronary syndrome at a Moroccan hospital in a 2025 study. The radiation-free test spots inducible ischemia, and guidelines favor ischemia-guided care, yet real-world impact data stay scarce.

Records covered all stress tests over one year; patients with positive or unclear results who went on to vessel imaging formed the study group. About four in five of them had significant artery narrowing. Treatment paths ranged from drugs alone to stents and bypass surgery. Ischemic burden on the stress test was weighed against vessel anatomy, and guideline risk classes were checked for accuracy. The work grounds test use in local practice.
pmc-12812235:
Anas Ahmed and co-authors review in 2025 how hormone-mimic pollutants can harm the kidneys. Such chemicals sit in plastics, sprays, foam, and metals, and they meddle with the body's hormone signals. Kidneys filter waste from blood, so they meet these chemicals again and again.

The review pulls human, animal, and computer studies that link eight classes of these chemicals to kidney harm. Stress inside cells, swelling, and cell death are the shared paths to long kidney disease, the authors note. Four big databases were searched to late 2025, and study quality was graded with set tools. A joined-up map helps health staff see this slow risk clearly. It also shows where proof is strong and where it is still thin.
pmc-12812335:
Marta Campos and colleagues report a rare benign tumor found in pregnancy and handled with no major surgery. Retroperitoneal cystic lymphangiomas are rare, and in pregnancy rarer still, by far. Their patient was thirty-one, at thirty-six weeks of pregnancy, and a large retroperitoneal tumor was found by chance on a routine ultrasound.

One week later she gave birth to a healthy newborn by cesarean section. Cut-out surgery, the standard care, was first proposed. But after the birth the lesion shrank on its own, an atypical course. With that change, the team used drainage through the skin, then sclerosis, in place of a cut-out. The team says this is only the second known case of its kind, found in pregnancy and handled with success by a less invasive route than full cut-out. A tumor that is already shrinking may not need the largest operation.
pmc-12812635:

One builds models of quality of life from disability research, and the other, the neurodiversity view, grows out of autistic self-advocacy and argues that difference is not defect.

The authors sort the overlap and friction between the two outlooks into three areas: language and identity, daily support practice, and research itself. Six shared principles emerge, among them that supports aid participation rather than threaten identity, and that help should build autonomy without forcing people to act normal. They also insist autistic people take part in research at every stage. The result is a shared frame for providers, researchers, and policy makers.
pmc-12812735:
Tian, Su, Shen, Zhou, and Sun report a study from twenty twenty-six on scope-based treatment for older patients with airway tuberculosis. The disease narrows airways of the lung in this group. The team treated one hundred forty-two older patients with scope methods. Those methods include balloon widening, clearing, and stent placement. Follow-up ran for a median of just over two years. Most cases were technical successes, and most patients felt better. Breathing test scores rose sharply after treatment.

Four traits predicted a poor outcome on their own. They include a scarred narrowing type, severe narrowing grade, and long narrowed spans. Re-narrowing struck about one in four patients later. Patients aged seventy-five or older survived at lower rates. The authors give a risk score and stress careful patient choice.
pmc-12815835:
Jiaqi Liu and co-authors (2025) lay out a study that will mine speech for signs of schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Disordered thought shows in how people speak, and speech traits may serve as objective markers of illness. The team will enroll 300 patients at one center, plus matched healthy controls. Each person will take a long guided interview with a psychiatrist. The tasks include reading passages, naming animals quickly, describing pictures, and speaking about inner experience. Every session is recorded.

Software will then extract many features of the speech, from word choice to sound patterns. Machine learning models will search those features for combinations that flag the disorder and track its severity. Clinical scales will rate symptoms alongside, so the speech markers can be checked against expert judgment. The paper is a protocol: it describes the design before results exist. The authors hope the database becomes a base for diagnosis tools.
pmc-12815935:
Freddie Márquez and co-authors validate blood tests for Alzheimer's in Latino adults in a 2025 cohort study. Plasma biomarkers promise early detection without spinal taps, but most validation happened in non-Latino populations, leaving open whether the markers behave the same in the largest United States minority group.

Over five thousand seven hundred community-dwelling adults over fifty gave blood and took cognitive tests spanning learning, memory, fluency, and processing speed. Four markers, covering amyloid, tau, nerve injury, and brain inflammation, were each regressed against the scores. The authors report the blood signals track cognition in this population too, supporting wider, fairer screening.
pmc-12816635:
Cássio Siqueira and co-authors present a 2025 study on a magnetic catalyst made by heat breakdown. Spinel ferrites are valued for their magnetism and now serve as reusable catalysts. The team formed a copper-iron oxide from metal chelates bound to a common ligand. Heat studies under oxygen and nitrogen charted how the chelates fall apart.

Baking at four temperatures up to 1050 degrees gave the oxide as a fine powder. X-ray, microscope, and magnetic tests confirmed its form. The nanoparticles drove a ring-forming reaction between a diamine and varied aldehydes with excellent yields. A magnet then fished the catalyst back out for reuse. Gram-scale runs worked as well. The route offers a practical, recyclable catalyst for fine chemical making.
pmc-12817335:
Paula Schuster-Winkelmann and co-authors test a mouse model that carries human immune cells from arthritis patients. Their 2025 paper tackles rheumatoid arthritis, a long-term disease in which the immune system attacks the joints. Human forms of the disease vary a lot, which makes animal models hard to trust.

The team placed blood cells from patients into mice with weak immune systems. They then triggered disease signs with a bacterial product and antibodies. The mice showed joint swelling, bone loss, human autoantibodies, and gene activity in known disease pathways. Two common arthritis drugs eased the signs and lowered inflammation marks. The model gives drug researchers a closer stand-in for human disease than standard mouse models.
pmc-12817535:
Johanne Triantafyllou Lorenzen and co-authors study how Danish schools for young people outside work and training can get students moving more. Their qualitative study, published in 2025, looks at preparatory schools set up in 2019 for this group. These students tend to be less active than their peers, and little was known about activity programs in such schools.

The team interviewed three school leaders and ran focus groups with teachers and students at three schools. Five themes emerged, covering student needs, school structures, access to facilities, and legal limits. Activity fit the schools' core purpose, the authors found, but rules and buildings often blocked daily use. Programs, they argue, must fit this group closely.
pmc-12817735:
Wenbo Zhao and co-authors pool the evidence on hip scope surgery for soccer players in a 2025 review. The sport's twisting loads batter the hip joint. Keyhole surgery promises a faster return to play, but how much it helps this group was unclear.

Twelve case series covering 361 players met the bar. On a standard hip score, players gained about twenty-eight points after surgery. Pain scores fell by nearly five points, and daily-life scores rose by about twenty-four. Roughly ninety-one percent returned to play. Most studies were rated high quality, the rest moderate. The pooled numbers support the scope as a strong route back to the pitch.
pmc-12820335:
Wang Li and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, record tandem solar cells stacking perovskite on a copper indium gallium selenide bottom cell. The pairing matches sunlight bands well and stays thin, stable, and radiation hard, but the layer joining the two cells often wastes energy.

Their composite joining layer mixes a doped zinc oxide, a whisper of gold, and a nickel oxide paired with a phosphonic acid anchor. The design calms interface defects, aligns energy bands, and speeds charge recombination where the cells meet. The champion device reached about twenty-eight percent efficiency at larger area and over thirty percent in small cells, externally verified.
pmc-12821835:
Yun Ying Choo and five co-authors compare two Zika virus strains in tiny lab-grown brain models. Zika can harm the brain of an unborn child, but how it does so is not fully known. The team infected human cerebral organoids with the wild virus and with a weakened strain. Both strains grew in the models with no clear change in shape.

Gene reads at the single-cell level told a sharper story. The wild strain stirred a stronger immune response and infected many cell types. The weak strain mostly infected one stem-like cell type. The paper ties strain harm to how wide and how strong the host response runs.
pmc-12821935:
Naghshi, Janati, and Khodayari-Zarnaq study manager testing reform in Iran, in work from twenty twenty-five. Assessment centers test manager skills for health system posts. Their worth depends on constant checks and updates, yet past work focused on daily operations.

What key people expect from reform had been missed, the authors say. They ran a qualitative study in twenty twenty-four with twenty-nine interviews. Managers, policy experts, and psychologists were picked by purposive and snowball sampling. Content analysis pulled out shared expectations. The map of what stakeholders want can guide a redesign that staff will trust and use, not just a technical fix.
pmc-12822035:
Peiqi Tang, Ying Xin, Maojun Liu, Cheng Zeng, and Xinqun Hu link a belly fat score to heart risk in diabetes in a 2025 paper. The score, METS-VF, gauges visceral fat from routine measures. Data came from the large ACCORD trial in type 2 diabetes. The team tracked major heart events and total deaths.

Over a median span near nine years, about 19 percent died. Higher scores tied to more heart events and more deaths. The link bent in a J shape with clear turning points. Above those points, risk rose steeply with the score. The score predicted best in patients not taking aspirin. The authors back it as a risk marker.
pmc-12822235:
Sureyya Yigitalp Rencber and Nilgun Ulutasdemir explore in 2025 how faith helped young survivors of a vast earthquake rebuild their lives. The quake, called the disaster of the century in Turkey, shook the survivors' bodies, social lives, and inner worlds. The team asked whether prayer and spiritual practice served as a coping resource in recovery.

They spoke in depth with twenty-two nursing students who lived through the quake, using an approach that seeks the core of shared experience. Two main themes emerged: the effects of the quake, and the religious and spiritual practices used to cope. Survivors leaned on such practices, yet still found coping hard, a point the authors say support programs should heed.
pmc-12822335:
Sunday Akinde and co-authors tracked the coronavirus variants that spread through Osun State, Nigeria, in this 2025 study. The samples came from patients during the second wave, between January and June of 2021. The team read the full genomes of the virus from nose swabs gathered at eight sites.

Forty-five of sixty samples yielded complete genomes. Five lineages appeared, with the Eta and Alpha variants most common. Many genomes carried changes in the spike protein, the part the virus uses to enter cells. Some changes are known to help the virus spread or dodge antibodies. Family trees sorted the genomes into three clusters. The work shows why local genome tracking matters.
pmc-12824535:
Mohammed Abdul Salam, Joshua Birru, and Sarbari Swaika report a heart attack triggered by allergy after a nonvenomous snakebite in this 2025 letter. The patient was a sixty-five-year-old snake rescue worker. He arrived with chest pain and had fainted at home. His heart tracing showed a heart attack pattern in the inferior leads, and a scan showed weak motion in the same wall. A swollen leg led staff to the story: he had been bitten by an Indian rat snake, a nonvenomous species he identified himself.

The diagnosis was Kounis syndrome, where an allergic reaction triggers a coronary event. His clotting test was normal and no nerve signs appeared, supporting a nonvenomous bite. A harmless snake is a new precipitant for such allergic heart attacks. The authors stress careful history taking: the bite explained swelling that a heart focused exam might have missed.
pmc-12825235:
Abdelwahab, Aboraiah, and Elsayed (2025) tested whether an AI chatbot improves nursing students' skill at electronic fetal monitoring. Reading fetal traces demands knowledge and judgment, and the chatbot was meant to give focused, personal practice. In a quasi-experiment at an Egyptian university, 84 maternity nursing students were split evenly. One group learned with the chatbot, the other with traditional teaching. Both were tested before, after, and at follow-up.

The chatbot group improved significantly more in knowledge, practical interpretation, and confidence in clinical reasoning, and also in academic motivation. The gains held at follow-up. Over 90 percent of the chatbot group reported high satisfaction with its feedback. The authors conclude that chatbot education beat traditional teaching on every measure they tracked. They present it as a promising support for teaching a skill where accurate decisions matter.
pmc-12825935:
Wenhao Deng and co-authors published this 2023 study with a twist: a plant's alarm scent can help the pest it should repel. When insects chew leaves, tobacco releases green leaf volatiles, sharp-smelling compounds meant to drive herbivores off or summon their enemies. The team found whiteflies instead thrive on the signal.

Attacked plants turned up a gene, hydroperoxide lyase, that builds these scent compounds from fatty acids. Plants engineered to make more of the gene released more scent and hosted happier whiteflies. Spraying the compounds on plants directly raised whitefly survival and egg laying, and drew more whiteflies in. The authors conclude the pests have learned to read the plant's distress call as a dinner bell, a quirk growers may need to outwit.
pmc-12827435:
Kulthanachairojana and co-authors price a bedwetting drug for Thai children against an older rival and no treatment. Nighttime wetting burdens families, and no economic study existed for Thailand. Their model covered children over seven who had failed behavior therapy and alarms, comparing desmopressin with imipramine over a lifetime horizon.

Desmopressin gave the most quality-adjusted life years at the highest cost, yet its cost per gained year, about 2,300 to 2,400 dollars, sat well under Thailand's willingness-to-pay line near 4,734 dollars. Simulations put its chance of being cost-effective near three in four. Rolling it out nationally would cost about 27 million dollars over five years, a budget question the authors leave to policymakers.
pmc-12827535:
Jianwen Li and co-authors published this study on green space, wealth, and bone loss, dated 2025 in the head though the catalog lists 2026. Greenery near home links to many health gains, but its tie to osteoporosis, the thinning of bones, was little studied. The team also asked whether social and economic standing changes that tie.

They drew 6,544 rural adults from a Henan cohort. Satellite greenness scores measured exposure, and status combined marriage, schooling, and income. Adults in the greenest areas had clearly lower odds of weak bones than those in the least green. Higher status also linked to lower risk. The paper argues that green planning and social support should be weighed together in bone-health policy for rural areas.
pmc-12827635:
Qi Tang and four co-authors studied suicidal thinking in hospitalized older adults in a study published in 2025. Their patients live with physical limits, and the team focused on experiential avoidance: the habit of pushing away unwanted thoughts and feelings. Avoidance has been tied to darker emotions and higher risk. The study of 717 patients asked whether depression carries avoidance's effect, and whether resilience blunts it.

Avoidance did track with suicidal thinking directly. Depression symptoms carried part of that link, as a partial mediator. That strength softened both paths: the stronger it ran in a patient, the weaker the ties from avoidance to dark thoughts and from depression to the same. The authors urge care teams to target avoidance and low mood while actively building such strength in this group.
pmc-12827935:
Mina Karbalaeimahdi, Hooman Minoonejad, Seyed Hamed Mousavi, and Reza Rajabi review phone apps that judge spinal posture from photos in a 2025 paper. Such apps could make posture checks cheap and portable, but their accuracy needs proof. The team gathered studies that built or tested photo-based posture apps.

Twenty-nine studies with about nineteen hundred participants met the rules. For the angle between head and spine, repeat and cross-rater reliability were both excellent. Other measures, such as hip and head tilt, ranged from moderate to excellent. Small samples and uneven reporting temper the verdict. On balance, the authors support clinical use of these apps while urging better study standards.
pmc-12829135:
People with wide friend webs may run their brain nets in a leaner way during social play, and Mengfei Han and co-authors tested that link in work from twenty twenty-five. Players took part in a trust game while their brain nets were mapped. Web size in real life was charted with layered network tools, and learning models joined the hunt.

Wide-web people showed a sharper hub in a mid brain zone tied to clash watch. A sight zone ran less sharply, as did a memory zone in the model picks. Links between a clash zone and smell and touch zones ran stronger. The authors read the pattern as sharp clash watch plus damped sight and memory load, a mix that may free social gains.
pmc-12829335:
Isabella Cooper and co-authors switch off ketosis in women who had lived in it for years and watch their hormone markers move, in a 2025 study. Ten lean, healthy premenopausal women who had kept nutritional ketosis for about four years went through three three-week phases: their usual state, a carb-fed phase that suppressed ketosis, then a return. The focus was a binding protein that governs how much sex hormone stays active.

Suppressing ketosis shifted the protein and related hormone measures within weeks. The authors read the changes through insulin's grip on the liver, where the protein is made. The study speaks to debates on ketogenic diets, fertility, and cancer risk.
pmc-12830635:
Sucharitha and colleagues present a deep dictionary method for finding similar medical images. Their twenty twenty-five paper targets fast-growing hospital image archives. Manual labels cannot keep up with that growth. Clinicians still need quick retrieval for diagnosis, planning, and research.

The system first extracts features with a deep neural network. Two layers of dictionary learning then group and refine image patterns. A clustering step updates groups until they settle. Sparsity cuts noise and sharpens differences between categories. Tests used chest X-ray and standard medical image collections. Scores for precision and related measures improved over prior methods. The authors share their code for others to test and extend.
pmc-12830735:
Fahman Saeed, Sultan Aldera, and Mohammad Alkhatib present a forecasting model for peak electricity demand, in a 2025 paper. Grid operators need sharp peak forecasts to cut costs. Their model pairs a signal-splitting method with a transformer network. An entropy guide picks which signal parts to keep. The network's depth adjusts to the forecast horizon.

Attention heads start from the split signal parts, aiding clarity. Tests covered next-hour, next-day, next-week, and next-quarter forecasts. Rival models included other neural designs and a simpler transformer pairing. Error scores favored the new model across the board. The authors credit design choices matched to the data's time patterns. They argue such adaptive builds suit real power systems. Interpretability is claimed as a further benefit of the design.
pmc-12831235:
Waweru leads a large team studying a microbe that lives inside malaria mosquitoes, in work from twenty twenty-five. Microsporidia MB is a symbiont found in Anopheles mosquitoes. It can block Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, from being transmitted, and it spreads through mosquito generations.

Those traits make it a candidate for symbiont based malaria control. The mechanism inside the mosquito was not fully known. The team measured changes in mosquito gene activity and gut microbiota when the symbiont is present. Understanding its inner effects is needed before field releases can be judged safe and effective.
pmc-12831435:
Elizabeth Obeng-Aboagye and eight co-authors find serological evidence of concurrent Lassa virus and SARS-CoV-2 exposure in Ghana. The pandemic exposed weak infectious disease surveillance in West Africa, where Lassa fever persists. Overlapping symptoms create diagnostic challenges and the possibility of missed co infections.

Archived serum from a nationwide survey supplies 434 samples across six regions. Antibody prevalence is 64.29 percent for SARS-CoV-2 and 20.28 percent for Lassa virus. Among SARS-CoV-2 positive subjects, 20.79 percent also carry Lassa antibodies. Household size strongly predicts dual exposure, with medium and large households showing much higher odds than small ones. Greater Accra shows significantly lower odds of dual seropositivity.
pmc-12831535:
Deepesh Saxena and Tarannum Jindal report a single patient's dental repair in a 2025 case report. The patient had a Seibert Class III ridge defect, a loss of both width and height in the jaw bone that holds teeth. Such defects make it hard to build a false tooth that looks right, works well, and stays clean. The team chose an Andrews bridge, which joins a fixed part with a part the patient can remove for cleaning.

The whole bridge was designed on a computer and made by machine, with no hand-built lab steps. The digital route cut lab errors and made the fit more exact. The finished bridge gave the patient better facial support, clearer speech, and easier cleaning. The authors present it as a sound option when surgery or implants are not open to the patient.
pmc-12835135:
Nadeem Sarwar and co-authors build a guard system for smart device networks in a 2025 paper. The fast growth of linked home and city devices brings security risks, since the networks are mixed and spread out. Odd traffic patterns can signal an attack in progress.

Two public datasets were merged and cleaned to form one test ground. Several machine learning models were trained to flag odd traffic. A decision tree model led the group, with scores near the mid nineties for accuracy and for how many flags were right. The pipeline for cleaning and shaping the data is set out in full for reuse.
pmc-12835535:
Aqsa Mahmood and five co-authors fly drones over wheat fields and teach the images to name the diseases below. Wheat feeds nearly half the world, and its fungal enemies are usually scouted on foot, slowly and subjectively. Their framework pairs a pretrained vision network with a bench of classical classifiers.

Features extracted by the VGG-16 network are classified by support vector machines, random forests, decision trees, gradient boosting, and naïve Bayes in turn. The training set was custom-built for stripe rust, powdery mildew, scab, and other wheat diseases visible from the air. The hybrid design bets that deep features plus simple classifiers beat either alone for field use. Precision agriculture is the stated destination.
pmc-12836435:
Karter Morris and co-workers report an unusual hand cord in a keen pistol shooter, in a 2025 case report. A sixty-five-year-old man developed a visible, fixed cord along the palm edge of his dominant hand's first web space. It appeared within a year of regular pistol shooting and caused no pain or loss of function.

Ultrasound showed uneven thickening of the palm's fibrous sheet in that spot. The picture resembled Dupuytren's disease but sat in an atypical place with no family or medical history to explain it. The team used the working label pistol shooter's palm and chose monitoring over surgery. They propose repeated grip stress as a possible trigger worth watching.
pmc-12836935:
Penghui Li, Yuan Xue, and Xinyu Gu review how an RNA mark and non coding RNAs interact in gastric cancer in this 2025 paper. The mark is called m6A, and it can be added and removed from RNA. Non coding RNAs help control tumor growth, spread, and cell death. Each side of the pair shapes the other.

The mark controls how stable and mature non coding RNAs become. Those RNAs in turn guide pathways that drive cancer growth and spread. Levels of marked RNAs differ between tumor and normal tissue. That gap could serve as a diagnostic or prognostic marker. Blocking the enzymes that add the mark may destabilize harmful RNAs. The review maps this two way talk as a source of new treatments.
pmc-12837035:
Ting-Yu He and six co-authors follow pain over time in older adults and link it to thinking and mood, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Chronic pain is common in later life and often sits beside low mood and fading memory. Whether the pattern of pain matters, and whether it differs for men and women, was unclear.

The team used a large United States study of health and retirement, with over twenty thousand people for pain tracking. They sorted pain paths into three shapes: steady low, steady high, and fluctuating. The mix of shapes differed between the sexes. Outcomes were then checked in a smaller group using phone-based thinking tests and a depression scale. The design lets pain patterns speak to later decline.
pmc-12837235:
Two brain diseases, spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 and a cerebellar form of multiple system atrophy, look alike early on and are often confused. Yuanyuan Xiao and seven co-authors built a tool in 2025 to tell them apart from how a person walks and stands.

Patients and healthy controls wore smart insoles that recorded gait and balance, and the team drew 98 measures from the recordings. Several learning methods were trained on those measures, and an explanation tool showed which measures drove each call. The authors aim for a cheap, wearable aid that can support diagnosis when gene tests or brain scans give no clear answer.
pmc-12837335:
Junming Li, Jing Li, and Haiyan Zhao tested computer-aided teaching for eye plastic surgery in medical undergraduates, in a 2025 study. Their tools let students build three-dimensional models from scans, cut them apart on screen, take measures, and plan fake operations. Fifty-eight students from one class at a medical university in Kunming were split at random. Half learned with the computer tools, and half with standard teaching, over one term.

The computer group scored higher on theory exams and on hands-on skill tests. Their satisfaction with the teaching also ran higher, by about ten points in percentage terms. The gaps were large by standard effect measures. The authors say the tools simplified teaching and sharpened students' grasp of space inside the eye socket. They present the method as a way to teach complex surgery before students touch a real patient.
pmc-12837635:
Hong-Yan Li and co-authors graded sepsis care guidelines in two thousand twenty-five. Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection. Many groups publish guidelines for treating it in adults. Their advice varies, and quality varies as well. The team collected recent guidelines from databases and societies. Work published since two thousand eighteen was eligible.

Eleven guidelines passed the screening for review. Two rating tools scored how each guideline was built. One tool judged method rigor, the other judged advice quality. Scores were strong for clear scope and purpose. Other domains, like who was involved, scored unevenly. Key advice points were extracted and compared across guidelines. The study shows clinicians where guidance agrees and where it splits.
pmc-12838035:
Reading prostate MRI scans takes expert time, and experts do not always agree. Huiqi Chen, Erwang Li, Paul Christos, and Yuan-Shan Zhu pooled the evidence in 2025 on whether artificial intelligence matches radiologists at spotting major prostate cancer on MRI. Their meta-analysis covered ten studies with more than twenty thousand patients, all comparing AI and human readers head to head.

Pooled accuracy was nearly equal: AI was a touch more sensitive and a touch less specific than radiologists. The overall score difference was small and not significant. The authors see promise in faster, more uniform reading and in mixed human-AI workflows, but call for large prospective trials with shared protocols.
pmc-12838435:
Shariati, Hashemi, Peyvandi, Jebali, and Entezari present a study from twenty twenty-five on a peptide vaccine against ovarian cancer. The vaccine packs signal pieces from three cancer-linked proteins into tiny fat bubbles. The best piece of each protein is picked by computer analysis. Mice receive three weekly shots at two dose levels. Antibodies and immune messengers rise with dose. Mouse serum then faces human ovarian cancer cells in dishes. Death signals climb and cell survival falls there.

Humanized mice carrying patient tumors show shrinkage after vaccination. Bubble size and loading quality are reported in detail. The authors present it as a candidate multi-target vaccine. Further development steps remain ahead.
pmc-12843035:
Lina del Mar Angel-Salazar and co-authors report a new fruit disease of oil palm in Colombia in this 2025 paper. White fruit rot has appeared since 2021 in the main palm-growing regions. The team visited six sites, gathered samples of sick fruit, and grew the organisms found on them.

Most isolates proved to be one fungus, which formed white cottony growth and small round resting bodies. Only that fungus caused disease when placed on healthy fruit, both in the lab and in the field. Sick bunches in the field showed the same signs as natural cases. The paper marks the first record of this fungus attacking oil palm in Colombia.
pmc-12844735:
Dorota Bartusik-Aebisher and four co-authors review the element boron in health in a 2025 paper. Boron appears in the body only in traces. Even so, it touches bone strength, hormones, and immune balance. Its odd chemistry lets it form many active structures.

Most dietary boron comes from plant foods. The kidneys clear it, and urine levels track intake closely. Evidence links it with bone density, brain function, and calmer inflammation. Exact molecular routes for those effects remain partly murky. Medical uses range from enzyme blockers to antimicrobe agents. Boron carriers also serve in a targeted radiation cancer therapy. The review maps delivery and detection methods for the element.
pmc-12845635:
Alexandra Weaver and co-authors survey seven years of European grains and forages for mold toxins that taint animal feed. These poisons can harm animal health and farm income, and the harm can grow when many kinds show up in the same feed at once.

From 2018 to 2024 the team tested more than twenty-six hundred samples for fifty-four toxins at once. Grains held on average about four to seven kinds per sample. Barley from the Nordic zone had some of the highest levels of one toxin family. Two toxin groups most often showed up together, in more than half the grain and maize silage samples.
pmc-12847735:
Micka Ullman and co-authors share a year of cave weather data from Israel in a 2025 paper. Cave air shapes the chem and life processes that keep or spoil old remains. The Israel Cave Climate Project logged that air in a set way across the land.

Twelve caves in desert, steppe, and sea side zones were logged each hour for a year. Heat and damp reads come with cave shape facts and rich dig records. All caves are lime stone and hold remains from many eras. The free full data set lets others study how cave air guards or harms old finds.
pmc-12847935:
Afsari and coauthors compare sperm from testes with sperm from semen on DNA harm. Past studies gave conflicting results on that contrast. DNA breaks and telomere length may sway fertility success. The team did a detailed side-by-side analysis.

Sixty men split into four groups for the study. Groups held normal men, men with mixed sperm faults, and two surgical groups. One surgical group had no sperm in semen at all. Tests gauged vitality, shape, DNA breaks, and telomere length. Stains and dispersion assays gave the lab measures. Results may guide which sperm source clinics should use.
pmc-12848035:
Ning Mu and co-authors expose a helper protein driving lung cancer spread in a 2025 study. Hedgehog signaling runs wild in non-small cell lung cancer, feeding its growth. The molecules governing that signal during tumor development were still largely unknown.

The protein HHIPL2 turns out high in these tumors and tied to poor outlook. Removing or adding it slowed or sped cancer growth and spread in tests. It works by teaming with an RNA-binding protein to stabilize a partner message. That chain keeps Hedgehog signaling switched on inside the tumor. Blocking HHIPL2 could give drug designers a fresh choke point.
pmc-12849135:
Thelma Marley, Deirdre Barrow, and Olivia McDermott examine how the European Union's device regulation ripples through global markets in this 2025 paper. The rules raised demands on makers, and some countries lean on the European mark for their own approvals. Effects outside Europe were unforeseen.

The team assessed one large maker's worldwide portfolio and interviewed fifteen European medtech firms. The regulation had cut device availability abroad and piled up registration work everywhere. Firms shared the same worries across the sector. Later amendments may ease the transition or add fresh side effects. The authors offer recommendations for makers planning certification and lessons for policymakers. They stress guarding supplies of critical devices in all markets.
pmc-12849235:
Augustus Aturinde, Geofrey Amanya, and Robinah Ikwangu map tuberculosis patterns across Uganda from 2020 to early 2025, in a 2025 study. The country aims at steep cuts in TB deaths and cases by 2030, and district-level data can show where effort is most needed. The team analyse national programme records with trend, clustering, and forecasting methods.

Reported cases rose sharply, from under thirty thousand in 2020 to nearly seventy-three thousand in 2024, and rates per head more than doubled. Clusters persisted in the northeast, in districts near Lake Victoria, and in newer hotspots around the oil-rich Lake Albert region. Eastern and southwestern districts stayed consistently low. Forecasts point to continued high burden in the same areas. The authors offer the maps as a guide for targeted action, surveillance, and planning on the path to the national targets.
pmc-12849435:
Ameeta Retzer and co-authors develop in 2025 a method for building core outcome sets for population health trials. Such sets help compare studies and cut waste, and they are common in medical research. Their use in population health is less settled, since those interventions are complex and involve many groups with a stake in the results.

Three work packages shape the method: a review of public health evidence and outcome reporting, a review of existing sets and guidance, and a workshop with experts on using routine data. The study also names priority topics for new sets and asks how to get finished sets into wider use.
pmc-12849635:
Parnian Kubor and three co-authors weigh the cost and value of home comfort care for people with end stage cancer in Iran. One group got home care run by a charity that uses smart tools to plan staff and visits. A matched group got usual clinic and hospital care.

Home care cost far less over six months and cut hospital days. Far more home care patients died at home, as many wish. The math shows home care wins on both cost and results. The authors urge health plans to cover such care and note smart planning helps it scale.
pmc-12849735:
Changliang Gong and co-authors hunt for gene variants that steer how much fat ends up in cow's milk. Their 2025 study scans the full genome of 2,709 Chinese Holstein cows, using breeding value estimates for milk fat share as the trait under study.

The scan found one hundred four strong variant sites, with a dense cluster in a gene region long tied to fat output. Eight sites sat inside genes, and four changed the protein code in ways predicted to steady the proteins. A check in a second herd confirmed three sites between genes, and lab tests showed one of them changes how a key fat-making switch binds. The findings offer targets for breeding cows with richer milk.
pmc-12851635:
Bartholomew Olash reports a case of vasculitis and severe neutropenia caused by levamisole-adulterated cocaine. Levamisole, once used in the United States as a drug for rheumatoid arthritis, is now a common cutting agent in cocaine. As a street adulterant it can drop white blood cell counts, scar the skin, inflame blood vessels, and harm the brain. The literature stays sparse, yet the cutting grows more common, so cases are likely underreported.

The patient showed both systemic and skin vasculitis, plus a severe loss of neutrophils, the white cells that fight bacteria. That loss let a body-wide infection take hold, complicated by septic shock. Olash walks through the signs that point to the adulterant over other causes. The call is for heightened vigilance among clinicians, since the harm can be stopped if the cause is caught early.
pmc-12854335:
Rong Bao and co-authors use genetic evidence to test whether type 1 diabetes itself lowers intelligence. Their 2025 study applies Mendelian randomization, which treats inherited variants as a natural experiment, free of many confounders. Whether the disease harms thinking, or merely travels with other risks, had stayed uncertain.

The analysis found a causal link from the disease to lower intelligence scores and a raised risk of intellectual disability. Several extended methods, built to catch hidden bias, agreed with the main result. Genetic signals also tied the disease to slower structural brain growth, including smaller key memory regions. The authors say the evidence is robust that the disease itself plays a role. They call for work on mechanisms, since protecting cognition could improve patients' daily treatment and life quality.
pmc-12857235:
Takuya Koizumi, Akinori Maruta, Yosuke Ohashi, Takuji Iwashita, and Masahito Shimizu wrote this case report, published in 2025. It describes how doctors handled a gallbladder infection that returned four years after a permanent stent had been placed to drain the organ.

Stenting through an endoscope is used when surgery is too risky, but infection can still come back. In this patient, the team threaded a new drain through the bile duct into the gallbladder, using the old stent as a guide for the wire. They added a second drain through the nose, so the gallbladder was drained both inside and outside at once. The patient recovered smoothly. The authors say the old stent, far from blocking the fix, made it easier, and that double drainage suits cases where the bile is infected and thick.
pmc-12858935:
Mangrove mud is rich, airless, and teeming: a dark engine of the world's element cycles. Ying Liu and fourteen co-authors read its crew genome by genome in 2025, from thirty-eight mud samples across six Guangxi sites. Cores ran from the top skin down to ninety units deep.

One shared pipeline built, grouped, and pruned the reads into 2,965 clean genomes. Bacteria make up 2,383 of them; the old archaeal line adds 582. In all, seventy-eight great branches of microbe life show up. The set is a reference shelf: who lives in this mud, what they can do, and how the crew shifts with depth and site. Fellows of carbon and nutrient cycles can now be named, not just counted.
pmc-12859135:
Zeyu Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 study on a blood marker for glioma, a common and deadly brain tumor. Doctors lack a simple blood test that predicts both survival and life quality after surgery. The team studied a protein called ORAI1, which controls calcium entry into cells.

They drew on two large tumor databases, with 309 and 563 patients, plus blood samples from fifty patients at their own center. High levels of the protein marked patients with more advanced tumors and shorter survival. Those patients also reported more pain and worse sleep in the first days after surgery. The marker thus links tumor biology to daily well-being, and it can be measured from a blood draw.
pmc-12859835:
African swine fever devastates pig herds, and its virus is hard to study without good lab tools. Zhibo Liu and co-authors made a lab antibody against one viral protein, called A151R, which helps the virus copy itself and take shape. They built the antibody with cell fusion methods and tested what it binds. Staining infected cells showed the protein at work early in infection, near the sites where new virus is built.

The antibody did not block infection, so its value is as a research tool. The team pinned down the short protein stretch it grabs, an eight-letter segment shared across strains. One letter in that stretch proved key for binding. A shared surface target helps labs track the virus across outbreaks.
pmc-12860035:
Victor Chaumeau and co-authors surveyed mosquitoes that bite people and livestock in six villages in Myanmar's Karen state in a 2025 study. The forest hills there carry a heavy burden of mosquito-borne disease. Control work is hampered because basic data on which species bite, and when, are missing.

The team cataloged the species found biting humans and their animals and charted biting patterns across the villages. Such detail shows which species matter for malaria and other infections, and whether they bite indoors or out, early or late. Control programs can then target nets, spraying, or animal sheds where they count most. The survey fills a data gap for a region where elimination campaigns are active.
pmc-12876235:
Fatimah Ayete Labi and a large team test whether early nutrient supplements change gray matter in Ghanaian children long term, in a study listed as 2025. Undernutrition in mothers and children links to atypical brain growth. Small lipid-based supplements improved growth and development in earlier work, but brain shape effects were unknown.

They scanned 231 children around age ten from a randomized Ghana trial. One group got supplements before birth through toddlerhood, and the other got standard iron and folic acid before birth. Whole-brain analyses found no clear group differences in total gray matter volume or cortical thickness. Region checks followed the same pattern.
pmc-12879335:
Brinda Balasubramanian and co-authors study how gut stem cells respond to inflammatory stress in bowel disease in a 2025 paper. Stem cells in the gut lining and their fast dividing progeny drive repair and renewal of the surface. How they behave under the chronic swelling of inflammatory bowel disease was not fully understood, so the team joined several data types.

Bulk gene data came from the largest biopsy cohort to date, plus single cell data and tests in patient derived gut organoids. Active swelling linked to fewer classic stem cells and more of a repair type population. Stem and progeny cells from patients kept lasting gene changes even in non swollen tissue, and a new swelling linked cluster appeared.
pmc-12882535:
Dinuka Ariyaratne and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 tracking the family tree of dengue virus type 2 in Sri Lanka. Dengue has hammered the island for three decades, and knowing which lineages drive outbreaks guides control and vaccine planning. The team sequenced virus samples from patients across two windows, 2016 to 2018 and 2022 to 2023, and placed them on a global tree.

All the island's samples belonged to one lineage of the cosmopolitan genotype. They sat close to strains from the same years in South and Southeast Asia, which points to regional traffic. Fifteen changes in the coat protein and twenty-two in a secreted protein turned up. Seven coat and ten secreted changes appeared in every sample. Some of those marks are known to raise virus growth, secretion, or escape from immunity. The team urges stronger routine sequencing to catch shifts early.
pmc-12883635:
Rui Weng and ten co-authors measure neck joint angles in people with slipped neck discs, in a study dated 2025 in the text itself. The neck facet joints guide motion between neck bones, and uneven angles have been tied to disc slips. The team measured two angles at three neck levels in two hundred seventy-one patients with a single slipped disc. They compared the values with those of one hundred thirty-two healthy peers of like age and sex.

Patients had a smaller overall neck curve and lower disc height at the sore level. Uneven left-right angles at one mid-neck level stayed linked to slips after strict checks. The second angle ran lower, more level, at two lower levels in patients. The authors say these angle traits may help mark risk and guide prevention. They call for care in reading early, loose results.
pmc-12883835:
Qin Wang and colleagues tested gene sequencing for fungal infections in two thousand twenty-six. Their patients had received kidney transplants. Fungal infections there are rare but deadly. Standard lab tests miss many of them. The team compared broad DNA sequencing with conventional methods. Suspected cases were tracked over two years.

Sequencing found far more fungal species overall. Its positive rate greatly exceeded culture results. Mixed infections appeared only through sequencing. Common fungi were caught more often by sequencing too. Donor-derived infections were identified in several patients. Treatment changes followed the richer information. Transplant teams gain a stronger diagnostic tool. Faster answers can guide antifungal choices sooner.
pmc-12891835:
Xiangyun Xu and five co-authors report a surgical study on kidney stones lodged in the lower calyx of the kidney, published in two thousand twenty-six. Stones there are hard to reach and clear. The team looked back at the records of one hundred eleven patients treated at one hospital. All had scope surgery through the urinary tract with laser stone breaking. One group used a new flexible suction sheath; the other used a standard sheath.

The suction sheath group cleared stones at a higher rate, about ninety-six percent against about eighty-one percent. Their operations also ran shorter. Suction helps wash out dust and bits as the laser breaks the stone. The authors argue the tool makes this hard stone surgery safer and more complete. The study is a look back at past cases, not a randomized trial.
pmc-12894235:
Shanshan Yang and co-authors published a 2025 review of daytime sleepiness in two chronic illnesses: Parkinson's disease, the shaking illness of age, and chronic kidney disease. Daytime sleepiness dogs over four in five of such patients. A three-way axis, gut to kidney to brain, is thought to feed it. How that axis works was still thin.

The team searched five databases for work from 2000 to the end of 2025. Sixty-eight studies made the cut, with over fifteen thousand patients in all. Probiotic pills cut the daytime sleepiness score by a wide margin. Plans guided by the own biomarkers of a patient did over three times better than standard care. The evidence grade sat at moderate. The conclusion calls for plans built per person, not per illness.
pmc-12903235:
Liza Bergström, Julie Cichero, Mariam Jaghbeer, and Anna-Liisa Sutt publish a listening based swallowing assessment protocol in a 2025 paper. Clinicians can learn much by listening at the neck to breathing and swallow sounds, a method with strong evidence for catching unsafe swallows. Yet no standard protocol or training materials existed.

The guide updates the team's earlier unpublished version with fresh literature and new analysis. Twelve trained speech pathologists described the sounds that swayed their ratings of recorded swallows, and ratings were checked against camera based swallow exams. Five checkpoints structure the assessment: breathing sounds before the swallow, the swallow sounds themselves, swallow count, the exhale after, and breathing sounds after. Sample recordings accompany the guide as training material.
pmc-12906735:
Sushant Aryal and co-authors describe a tutor training program that supports a shift to problem-based learning at Patan Academy of Health Sciences, in a 2025 paper. Tutors are key to such programs, and new faculty need strong preparation. The academy built a four-phase program for that purpose.

Phases cover orientation, shadowing a tutor, supervised tutoring, and supervised student assessment. Training blends theory with hands-on practice and is led by faculty with formal training and long experience. Trainees are judged by trainers and certified when they meet standards. The authors say the program has raised the quality of problem-based learning at the academy, with regular checks.
pmc-12909235:
Tasahil Albishi and a large team of co-authors tested ways to enrich cassava flour in a lab study published in 2025. Cassava is a staple food, but its flour can carry a natural poison and offers limited nutrition. The team soaked cassava roots in mixes made from moringa leaves, cloves, and turmeric to see if the flour got safer and healthier.

Eleven treatment mixes were compared with plain and unsoaked controls. The treatments changed the flour's makeup and strongly raised its protective, antioxidant activity. The best mixes cut the poison level by about seventy percent and lowered the blood sugar impact by about half. The water left over from soaking was also checked for safety. The results suggest that cheap plant additives can upgrade cassava flour in the lab, though real-world food tests would come next.
pmc-12920935:
Zeshan Zulfiqar and nine colleagues present a 2025 feeding study on an unlikely bone medicine for geese: perennial ryegrass. Meat geese suffer leg deformities and weak bones, and gut microbes are increasingly blamed for bone loss through inflammation. Ryegrass has antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties, so the team fed it to geese and compared them with commercially fed birds.

Ryegrass-fed geese had denser, more mineral-rich tibias and calmer guts, with more bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. Inflammatory signals fell, bone-building markers rose, and a key inflammatory switch in bone tissue quieted, while oxidative stress markers improved. The authors frame the benefit as a gut-to-bone relay: feed the microbes, calm the inflammation, spare the skeleton.
pmc-12926735:
Michael Willoughby and a large team of co-authors link baby head growth to later thinking skills in this 2025 study from Kenya. Head circumference is a cheap sign of early brain growth, but its tie to specific mental skills is rarely tested in poor countries. The team followed one hundred eighty-two children from infancy.

They charted head growth from one month to two years, then tested executive function and fluid thinking at age four. Children whose heads grew more in infancy scored better on both, even after accounting for starting size and family factors. The link held across groups, including children exposed to HIV before birth. The signal was clear within the first fifteen months, favoring early checks and support.
pmc-12981235:
Belle Zaccari and five co-authors run in 2023 a randomized trial of trauma-sensitive yoga for women veterans living with post-traumatic stress disorder. Women veterans carry twice the burden of the disorder of either veterans overall or women in general, and inflammation is increasingly tied to its symptoms.

The trial assigned women to group yoga classes adapted for trauma survivors or to a comparison condition. The team tracked symptoms of PTSD and depression alongside blood markers of inflammation. Yoga had already shown promise on both fronts, and this study tests the two effects together in one design.
pmc-13018335:
Six dentists in India used three-dimensional scans to link root canal quality with lingering infection at the tooth root tip, in a study published in 2025. Such infection can persist quietly after treatment and doom the tooth. The team reviewed scans of 174 treated molars, upper and lower. They graded how well each canal was filled and sealed and checked for missed canals.

Infection at the root tip showed in fifty-four percent of the molars, more often in lower ones. Molars whose fillings had proper length and density showed far less infection. Poor crowns on top of the tooth and canals the dentist had missed both tied strongly to more infection. The authors stress that a tight crown seal matters as much as the canal work itself. Their message is that careful, complete root canal care pays off in lasting tooth health.
pmc-13023035:
Paul Spaltenstein and co-authors report in 2026 the full chemical synthesis of the B subunit of cholera toxin, in both its natural and mirror image forms. The subunit, a ring of five copies, binds a fat molecule on gut cells and starts the toxin's entry, in a disease that infects millions each year. The team built the protein in three segments joined step by step, then folded it into the five part ring.

The natural form bound its target as expected. The mirror form is now ready as a bait in a mirror image screening method. That screening could yield mirror image peptides that block the toxin, a fresh route to treat and prevent cholera. The work is a landmark for total synthesis of a large protein assembly.
pmc-13044235:
Mahamadou Sagara and co-authors report, in a 2025 study from Rabat, Morocco, which patients with rheumatoid arthritis respond well to biologic drugs. Response to these strong medicines varies a lot, and doctors in North Africa had little local data on what predicts success.

The team reviewed 153 patients treated at a military teaching hospital during 2024, most of them women with an average age near fifty-eight. Two factors stood out in their checks. Patients with a certain antibody in their blood responded better, and so did patients who started a biologic within a year of diagnosis. The results back early, well-matched treatment for this joint disease.
pmc-13086635:
Thiago Gonçalves-Souza and co-authors map what drives frog and toad diversity across South America, in this 2026 study. They cover three great biomes: the Amazon rainforest, the Atlantic rainforest, and the Cerrado savanna. Diversity here means more than species counts.
