The team also weighed how related the species are and what body traits they carry, since each lens tells a different story about a place.

They modeled diversity in grid cells against today's climate, the stability of climate over the past one hundred twenty thousand years, water loss rates, and land shape. Present weather mattered, but so did history: places with stable past climates held distinct mixes. The work helps target protection toward areas that guard all three kinds of diversity at once.
pmc-13087535:
Irfan and colleagues surveyed in 2026 health workers in Gaza about moral injury, the harm done when events violate core values. Blockade, attacks on facilities, and scarce supplies force hard choices daily. In their sample, most respondents were young and many were unpaid volunteers. Witnessing immoral acts and betrayal by leadership scored highest among injurious events.

The strongest aftereffects were broken trust and lost faith in humanity, more than shame. The authors warn that lasting moral injury threatens staff retention and care quality in a system near collapse. They call for protecting medical neutrality, material support, and structured moral-repair programs.
pmc-13092235:
A research team tests oxygen therapy for restricted fetal growth in this 2026 study. When a fetus grows too slowly for unclear reasons, care options are few, and the team asked whether high flow oxygen added to a blood thinning drug and standard support could help.

The study enrolled 117 women at one center from 2022 to 2025. They formed three groups, chosen with the patients: standard care alone, standard care plus the drug, and both plus daily high flow oxygen. The full treatment group delivered about two and a half days later and had babies about 240 grams heavier at the median than standard care alone. Gains were modest, the authors note.
pmc-13096635:
Weijie Zhang and co-authors published a 2026 study on risk prediction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a thickened-heart condition. Some patients develop heart failure even though the heart's squeezing fraction stays normal, a pattern called preserved ejection fraction failure. How much that pattern worsens outlook was unclear. The team used machine learning to sort patients by risk.

The study gathered 2,802 patients from three major hospitals. Records spanned symptoms, imaging, and outcomes. The learning models grouped patients into risk strata and tested which features independently predicted bad outcomes. Preserved-fraction failure emerged as its own risk factor, not just a fellow traveler of other problems. The finding matters because such patients can look stable on the headline measure while carrying real danger. The authors argue risk tools for this disease should weigh the failure pattern explicitly, so follow-up and treatment can match the true risk.
pmc-13105535:
Haiying Lv and co-authors write a letter weighing a study on drinking water and kidney stones. The study, based on a national health survey, linked tap water with fewer stones and bottled water with no clear tie. The letter writers praise the work but warn against reading the link as cause. Kidney stones come in kinds that form under opposed conditions.

One kind grows in acid urine, another in alkaline urine. Since waters vary in acidity, one source could cut one kind's risk while raising the other's. The survey lacks stone type data, so the mix blurs the picture. Wealth, kidney function, and blood uric acid may also skew the results.
pmc-13129935:
Katherine Rosella Kinnard and Ehtesham Khalid share four patient cases from 2026 that raise doubts about one blood test for a muscle weakness disease. The disease, myasthenia gravis, weakens muscles when signals from nerves fail to reach them well. Two common antibody tests find most cases, but some patients test negative on both, so doctors turn to a third antibody test.

That third test, aimed at a protein called LRP4, can come back positive in ways that mislead care. Each of the four patients had full checks, with tests for all three antibodies and other exams. The cases show where the LRP4 result fit the picture and where it did not. The authors urge care in reading a positive result on its own.
pmc-13134935:
Rime Laassar and three co-authors report a hard case where a blood cell storm hid two other illnesses, in a 2025 journal article written in French. The storm, macrophage activation syndrome, can kill if missed. Its call rests on at least five clinic and lab signs, and a marrow test can show guard cells eating blood cells.

Their patient was followed for a slow blood cancer that weakens the immune shield. Fever and lab chaos fit the storm, and the marrow check backed it. Careful search then found pleural tuberculosis as the trigger that set the storm off. The authors warn that in such weak patients, hidden infections must be hunted even when a known blood illness seems to explain all.
pmc-13135435:
Neil Wallace and Aila Hauger published a 2026 case report on spotting a rare hernia type at the bedside before surgery. In an Amyand hernia, the appendix sits inside a groin hernia sac. The condition mimics a trapped or strangled hernia and is usually discovered only once the surgeon is inside.

Their patient was a 46 year old man with a long standing, partly reducible groin hernia. A bedside ultrasound in the emergency department showed a bowel containing hernia with fluid around it. CT then confirmed an inflamed appendix within the sac. The team removed the appendix through a scope and repaired the hernia openly, without complications. Early ultrasound, they argue, speeds diagnosis and improves planning.
pmc-13138335:
Yang Gao, Emily Ho, and Jared Toettcher present a review the catalog lists under 2026. Embryo development needs events timed and placed with precision. Classic proof came from bold moves: grafting tissue or shocking a spot with heat. Light-based tools, called optogenetics, now offer finer control in space and time. A growing suite can switch cell behavior with light pulses.

The review highlights the tools and their uses in embryos. It weighs current limits and future promise in plain terms. Light control avoids the wounds that grafts and heat cause. Repeated, reversible pulses let one embryo serve as its own control. Developmental biologists get a guide to a fast-moving toolbox. The authors frame light as the next standard perturbation, much as genetics became the last one.
pmc-13139435:
Gao Wang, Yingying Huang, Lars Muckli, and Daniele Faccio published a 2026 paper on drawing with a brain-computer interface. Such interfaces read brain activity to let users control devices without moving. Implanted systems are advancing fast, but there is a clear need for capable wearable, non-invasive alternatives with minimal hardware.

Their system lets a user draw by repeatedly choosing among visual probes shown on a screen. Each probe flickers at its own frequency, and the user's steady-state visual evoked potentials, measured brain responses at those frequencies, reveal which one they are attending to. Policies inspired by Gabor filters or learned by machine learning update the probes adaptively. Over iterations, the selections converge on the picture the user imagines.
pmc-13139535:
Nidhal Ben Khedher and eight co-authors model heat and mass flow of a nanofluid over a stretching cylinder for drilling uses, in a 2026 paper. The fluid carries graphene oxide bits in water and behaves with a memory-like flow rule. Radiation, mixed convection, and waste heat all enter the model. Both steady and pulsing regimes are solved, since drilling flows can throb.

Equations were solved with finite differences and an elimination method, then plotted with standard tools. Raising the flow memory value lifted speed, heat, and concentration. Stronger radiation widened swings in heat and speed. At high memory values, surface drag and mass flow rose while heat flow fell. The authors map each dial's effect for drill fluid design.
pmc-13140735:
The European Food Safety Authority gives its year report on crop-spray traces in food for two thousand twenty-four. The report, issued in two thousand twenty-six, is owed by Union law each year.

Samples came through three paths: a joint Union plan, state plans, and checks on imports. Each path found a small share of samples past the set bounds, with imports the worst of the three. The team gauged how much of the traces people take in, short-term and long-term. For most groups and most sprays, the risk was low. The report ends with advice to risk chiefs on how to firm up the checks.
pmc-13141135:
Van der Helm-van Mil and Raza wrote a 2026 review on the stages that come before rheumatoid arthritis. Care for the joint disease has improved over the past decade. Growing interest now turns to stopping the disease before joints are even inflamed, by treating people in its early, hidden phases.

Trials in people at high risk show promise, but full prevention is not yet possible. The early phase varies as much as the disease itself. Some people have joint pain and scan signs of inflammation for long periods. Others develop arthritis with little warning. Risk comes from genes and from exposures such as smoking and work dust. Not all at-risk people go on to get the disease. The review maps what is known and what trials must still answer.
pmc-13141335: A retraction note published in 2026 retracts a 2011 Virology Journal article by Sibnarayan Datta and co-authors on how hepatitis C virus resists interferon alpha in cell culture. The editor states the article was retracted over multiple image overlap concerns between figure panels. The authors could not provide the original data when asked, so confidence in the study was lost. Six named authors agree to the retraction.
pmc-13142235:
Jungmin Ha, Minjeong Ko, Yong-Beom Lim, and Ho Jeong Kwon designed a peptide drug against artery plaque in 2026. The peptide targets the contact zone between two cell organelles, where calcium signals and clean-up control meet. Faults at that zone help drive lipid-based vessel disease.

The lead peptide binds a bridge protein and loosens a three-protein complex, which trims calcium flow between the organelles. That shift switched on a clean-up program and restored cell recycling under fat stress. In mice fed a Western diet, the peptide improved blood lipids and shrank aortic plaque. Heart fat deposits also fell. The contact zone shape tracked recovery, which may serve as a response marker.
pmc-13144835:
Lulu Zhang and co-authors chart how injurious falls rise around the onset of heart and metabolic diseases, in a 2026 study. Falls harm many older adults, yet their timing against disease onset was unclear.

Using Swedish registry data, the team followed over ten thousand people with new disease and an equal matched group without. Fall rates began climbing about three years before diagnosis and peaked in the diagnosis year. Rates stayed high for up to ten years after. People who died during follow-up fell far more, above all in their last two years. The authors cast falls as an early warning sign and a target for timely prevention.
pmc-13144935:
Vadym Perepelytsia and co-authors report stroke prevention care for neck artery injuries in wartime Ukraine in this 2026 abstract. Injuries to the vertebral artery from trauma are an under-known cause of stroke in modern warfare. Four years of war gave a large group in which to study injury patterns and vessel-based treatments.

The study followed 104 patients with combat injuries to this artery from February 2022 to February 2026. Most injuries came from blast and shrapnel, and a small share from gunshots. The most common severity grade was the highest full blockage grade, in about 59 percent. Vessel-based treatment was done in 72 percent, most often closing the injured artery. Overall death during follow-up was about six percent.
pmc-13145235:
Aleksandra Ekkert and co-authors compare flow restoring care for strokes at the back of the brain with strokes at the front. Their conference abstract from 2026 follows patients for a full year, longer than most past work. Past results on the back group have been mixed and hard to settle.

The study held 306 patients, with 101 back strokes and 205 front strokes. Early death was less common in the back group, at two percent versus close to eight percent. Good function at three months was also more common in the back group. At one year, death and median scores still favored the back group, though adjusted tests weakened the gap.
pmc-13145435:
Marina Charalambous gives guidance in 2026 for bringing people with stroke in as true research partners, not tokens. Stroke survivors often get limited or consultative roles. Recruitment trouble, speech barriers, and rigid governance rules keep them at the edge.

Talks with stroke survivors who had done research before, some with trouble speaking, fed a thematic analysis. The study sorts what helped them and what blocked them. It then sets out six recommendations: build rapport, learn communication needs, foster a support system, offer accessible training, tailor resources, and back communication groups. The guidance also covers ethics approval, consent, pay, and lasting involvement. It aims to transfer across complex intervention studies.
pmc-13145635:
Ainur Turzhanova and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on bypass surgery for a fully blocked neck artery inside the skull's supply line. Such patients face repeat stroke risk even on best drug care. The surgery joins a scalp artery to a brain artery to lift flow.

Eleven patients with scan-proven low flow got the bypass at one center. Every bypass stayed open on later scans. Flow rose clearly in all brain zones checked, by a wide mean margin. The donor scalp artery and its branches grew after surgery. One patient had a brief spell of mood and thinking upset after the operation. The authors back paired flow and vessel scans to guide case choice.
pmc-13145735:
Laura Gomez Pintado Cano and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on blood cell ratios and swelling marks in patients seen at a warning-stroke clinic. The immune system shapes vessel disease in the brain, and cheap blood tests might help sort true events from look-alikes. The team compared three groups seen at one hospital.

Ninety warning-event patients, a small set with minor stroke, and a control set with mimic signs were checked in the acute phase. One white cell type and a key cell ratio both ran lower in warning-event patients than in controls. Patients whose warning event came back had lower counts of a second cell type. A settling-rate test also split warning-event subtypes.
pmc-13145835:
Preventing a second stroke is the subject of a 2026 conference abstract by Maryam Haneef, reporting an audit in a London general practice. Repeat strokes strike about nine to fifteen percent of patients within a year, and much of that risk comes from factors that can be controlled.

The audit checked records for patients with a new stroke or mini-stroke in 2024 and 2025, and found twenty-five cases. Blood pressure met target in 48 percent of patients, while 44 percent stayed above target and some were never rechecked. Cholesterol and blood sugar checks showed similar gaps, with about a quarter never reassessed. The audit shows where structured six-month reviews in primary care are falling short.
pmc-13146235: Leticia Requiao and co-authors reported in a 2026 conference abstract on carotid web, a shelf-like tissue in the neck artery that can cause stroke in young adults. Among 2,400 stroke patients at a Brazilian center, twenty-five cases were tied to carotid web. Most got aspirin, and forty percent had a widening procedure. Scores at discharge were much better than at arrival.
pmc-13146335:
Creeann Phillips and co-authors report in 2026, in a conference summary, on vein patterns seen on scans of patients with a double blockage tied to stroke. When both a neck artery and a brain artery are blocked, how well surface veins fill may show how severe the stroke is. The team rechecked data from a trial that compared two clot drugs.

Among 127 patients, those with a vein score of zero had worse stroke scores and more poor backup blood flow. Yet the vein score did not link to how patients fared at ninety days. The summary gives a focused look at whether this scan sign can guide care in a hard stroke type.
pmc-13146435:
Wookjin Yang and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on a diabetes drug class and recovery after clot removal for stroke. The drugs help the body pass sugar in urine. Early lab work hints they may also help the brain, but proof in severe stroke has been thin.

Data came from four stroke centers in Korea, Italy, and Switzerland, covering diabetic patients who had clot removal. About one in nine patients used the drug class after stroke. With three ways of balancing the groups, drug use linked to better function scores at three months. The authors say the pattern was steady across patient subgroups and merits a strict trial test.
pmc-13147035:
Alexander Martin and co-authors present a 2026 conference study following up a talk-based program for stroke survivors five to six years on. The Taking Charge sessions had lifted independence and body health at one year in the TaCAS trial. Four hundred patients had drawn one session, two sessions, or none.

Death data covered the whole group, and form data covered about two thirds of survivors. Body health scores still leaned toward the program group by a like step as at one year. Independence odds leaned the same way. Both gaps had slipped below firm proof at this span. Daily activity, survival, and repeat stroke barely split. The authors read the gains as held in size, if not in firmness.
pmc-13148135:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes presents a 2026 safety opinion on a glutaminase enzyme made by a modified bacterium for use in food making. The enzyme is meant for seven processes, and exposure in Europe was estimated at modest daily levels. No match to known allergens was found, though a small allergy risk cannot be ruled out.

One gap blocked a clean verdict. The maker did not prove the enzyme is free of DNA from the production strain, which carries copies of drug resistance genes. No living cells were found, and no other concern arose. Still, without proof on DNA, the panel could not conclude the enzyme is safe.
pmc-13148335:
Johnathan Meaders and co-authors find a hidden pool of a cell division kinase parked on chromosomes, in a 2026 study. Faithful cell division needs chromosomes to attach to spindle fibers from both sides. The kinase Aurora A helps manage those attachments. In the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, it works with an activator called TPXL-1. Most of that pair was thought to sit at spindle poles.

The team found a second pool bound to chromatin, between sister attachment sites. Structural modeling shows the activator grips a nucleosome patch directly. Breaking that grip removed only the chromatin pool. Chromosome alignment then suffered in telling ways. The finding redraws how division accuracy is enforced. It may inform cancer drugs that target Aurora kinases.
pmc-13149035:
Xiao and nine co-workers wrote a 2026 study imaging the flat energy bands of magic-angle graphene as interactions reshape them. Two graphene sheets twisted to a special angle host very flat bands. Those bands breed rich quantum phases, but their true form stayed murky. A quantum twisting microscope gave sharp views in both momentum and energy.

Off the magic angle, bands matched single-particle theory closely. At the magic angle, interactions remade them fully. Light and heavy electron traits appeared in distinct momentum zones. Adding charge set off cascades and revivals tied to each trait. A stubborn low-energy signal hinted at an uncounted degree of freedom.
pmc-13149635:
Mojtaba Heydari-Majd and co-authors wrap seaweed peptides in tiny fat bubbles to carry them safely through digestion, in a 2026 paper. The peptides come from the red alga Gracilaria corticata, cut loose by digestive enzymes, and they can fight oxidation. Three enzymes were tried for the cutting; the one called alcalase freed the most peptide and loaded the bubbles best.

The loaded bubbles measured under eighty nanometers across and stayed evenly sized and stable. Their antioxidant strength survived packing. In fluids mimicking the stomach, barely seven percent of the cargo leaked out, while in intestinal fluid the release rose in a controlled way to about ninety-five percent. The team offers the system for functional foods.
pmc-13149835:
Christin Hannse Reinhardt and Christoph Kröger test whether demonstration videos teach therapy techniques better than texts, in this 2026 study. One hundred twenty-three psychology undergraduates read about either psychodynamic or systemic therapy methods. Half then watched a video of their method in action; the others reread the text. All faced a mock patient, graded by trained raters.

The systemic video group far outscored its text group. The psychodynamic video, though, gave no edge over text. The authors guess that methods leaning on hidden reasoning need more groundwork than a single video gives a beginner.
pmc-13151935:
Sumali Jayaweera and four colleagues characterize a mangrove soil bacterium that fights fungi, and tune its production, in a 2026 paper. Streptomyces strain RMIT01 came from the root zone of a grey mangrove in a Victorian sanctuary. The team wanted its identity, its chemistry, and its best working conditions.

Standard media tests and microscopy confirmed classic Streptomyces traits, and genome sequencing gave a 7.6 million letter genome. Comparisons suggest RMIT01 is likely an undescribed species. It suppressed the yeast Candida albicans in culture. Grown in starch casein medium with sea salt at twenty-five degrees for six days, it produced its widest inhibition zone. The genome carries clusters for known antifungal compounds and rarer ones. The authors present the strain as a candidate source of new crop and clinic protectants from an overlooked habitat.
pmc-13152935:
Cleyton Silva de Araújo and co-authors report the complete genome of a new papillomavirus found in a spotted paca, a large rodent from the Brazilian Amazon. Wild rodents are rarely sampled for these viruses, so their diversity is poorly mapped. Tissue from a growth diagnosed as a virus-caused papilloma yielded the virus, provisionally named Cuniculus paca papillomavirus 1.

The genome is a circle of 8,803 bases carrying the standard early and late genes of the family. Its L1 gene matches its closest known relative, a porcupine papillomavirus, at only 63.10 percent identity, well below the cutoff for a new type. Family-tree analysis places it as a separate lineage beside that porcupine virus within a scattered group of rodent papillomaviruses. The finding widens the known range of the virus family in South American wildlife.
pmc-13153335:
Seven authors report in a 2026 letter how a rare branch of the internal thoracic artery shaped care of chest bleeding. The branch, the lateral costal artery, shows in about one to two of ten people and runs along the chest wall. A 33-year-old man had a chest mass sampled by needle biopsy.

A month later he arrived in shock with heavy blood in the chest and a low blood count. Scans showed the variant branch ran at the base of the tumor, with small false bulges in its wall. The case warns surgical and vessel teams to spot this branch before chest work.
pmc-13156135:
Ramírez-Paz-y-Puente and a team of colleagues reported in twenty twenty-six on two possible testosterone receptors in a bacterium that infects ruminants. The bacterium, Actinobacillus seminis, causes swelling of the epididymis and pregnancy loss. Testosterone was known to boost its growth and tools for attack, hinting it can sense the hormone.

The team pulled two proteins from bacteria grown with testosterone. Mass analysis identified them as LsrB, from the inner cell region, and OmpF, from the outer membrane. Computer docking showed both can bind testosterone. Blocking the sensing lowered bacterial growth and attack traits. Moving one gene into another bacterium improved its growth with testosterone present. The authors suggest host testosterone helps drive the infection.
pmc-13157535:
Xingxing Wang and six co-workers wrote a 2026 study on a gene-linked factor in liver cancer. The factor, called CRLF3, is known from blood and nerve work but not well studied in this cancer. The team asked how much of it shows up in tumors. They also asked if its level tracks patient outcomes.

They used large cancer data sets, lab stains and gene tests on tissue. Levels were higher in tumor tissue than in normal tissue. High levels tracked with worse survival and with later stage disease. Gene set tools hinted at paths the factor may act through. The authors see it as a possible marker for outlook.
pmc-13158435:
Daniel Morgado-Carrasco and co-authors trial a moisturizer for dry skin in a 2026 study. Thirty-five adults with xerosis, mostly women, applied a cream with panthenol, niacinamide, and a licorice-derived soother to one shin twice daily for twenty-eight days, leaving the other leg untreated as a control.

The treated leg held far more water, up seventy-four percent by day twenty-eight, and lost less water through the skin. Flaking fell and surface smoothness rose. Skin doctors rated dryness and itch improved in everyone. The authors note the lack of a plain-cream control limits credit to the active mix. Readers get a well-measured emollient result.
pmc-13161635:
Xolani Mazibuko and co-authors profile the microbes living in landfill soil in South Africa in a 2026 study. Landfill microbes break down waste and blunt pollution, yet their makeup in many regions is unmapped. The team took four soil samples at the Buffelsdraai site and read all their DNA at once. Three great groups dominated the census.

One sample teemed with variety, hinting at strong waste-processing power. Another ran poor, likely stressed by metals like nickel and cobalt in the soil. Two samples sat between, with one group, Actinobacteria, holding ninety-nine percent sway. Gene maps showed machinery for digesting carbohydrates and fats, plus tools for breaking down foreign chemicals. The authors name Actinobacteria a prime target for cleanup work. Their profile stands as a baseline for South African landfill ecology.
pmc-13162435:
Yin, de Lange and their co-authors track amine compounds in blood and spinal fluid of rats bred as an Alzheimer model. Their work, listed for 2026, follows changes by age and sex over most of the rats' lives.

Lab profiling measured dozens of amines in both fluids at four ages, in model rats and normal controls. In blood, a few amines rose clearly in young adult male model rats, with trend-level shifts at other ages. In spinal fluid, no amine passed strict thresholds, though patterns by age and sex appeared. Links between the two fluids tended to be stronger in model rats.
pmc-13164235:
Viktor Aleinikov and co-authors wrote this 2026 review on printed spine implants used after tumor surgery. When a tumor is cut from the spine, surgeons must rebuild the front column. Three-dimensional printed parts, shaped for the patient, are now used for that rebuild. Reports on their risks, though, are scattered and uneven.

The team searched three major databases for studies from 1980 to early 2026 that reported problems or repeat surgery after such implants. They checked study quality with a standard checklist for case series. Eleven studies held usable data. Because the studies differed too much to pool, the authors summed them up in words. The review shows where printed implants fail and what better reporting should capture.
pmc-13165535:
Xiaoze Yuan and Jiabao Wen tackle radio access for drone swarms in a 2026 paper. Swarms need many fast, stable links at once, often while an opponent jams the airwaves. Classic access rules clog under dense traffic, and learning methods can stall when conditions keep shifting.

Their algorithm trains many agents together but lets each act on its own in flight. A three-stage lesson plan starts with avoiding collisions, then balancing load, then resisting jamming. Rewards shift by stage to guide steady learning. The swarm learns to share spectrum with little central control. Tests in the paper check both anti-jamming strength and learning speed against older methods.
pmc-13166735: Tarek Zieneldien's poem "Homing instinct" turns on a mango tree from childhood. The speaker was born beside the tree and grew reaching for its sour green fruit, always close but never close enough, until oceans stood between them. When unnamed news arrives, the pull home proves too strong to resist. The speaker weighs dying abroad against dying at home. The wish is to rest under the grandmother's tree, knocking down fruit with fallen branches. The last lines ask to hear what comes next in the native tongue.
pmc-13170735:
Laura Leuenberger and co-authors published a study in 2026 on fatty acid metabolites in the blood of patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome. The syndrome is a lung failure state driven by dysregulated lung inflammation. The syndrome can arise from many different causes. One class of fats, polyunsaturated fatty acids, and their downstream products steer lung inflammation, but they were not defined here.

The team measured these fats in blood from ninety patients, plus two inflammatory markers. The fats' products ran low in the most severe cases. No difference was found between patients who lived and those who died. The profiles did differ by cause. Patients whose syndrome arose from sepsis, a body-wide infection, stood apart from those whose syndrome followed trauma. Some products tracked the inflammatory markers. The authors suggest the fats may indicate cause and hint at failures in how the lung resolves inflammation.
pmc-13172635:
Hong, writing alone in this 2026 review, asks whether bone-building drugs are safe for people who have had cancer. As survival improves, weak bones and fractures loom larger for survivors, since cancer care itself thins bone. The drugs in question, hormone-like agents and one antibody drug, grow bone well and cut fractures in the general public.

Yet fear holds them back in cancer care. Early animal work hinted that hormone-like drugs might seed a bone cancer or stir tumor growth, though long human studies have not borne that out. In practice, the drugs are avoided in active cancer, spread to bone, or high calcium. For survivors long clear of disease, careful use may be weighed. The author urges case-by-case balance of fracture risk against cancer risk.
pmc-13173035:
Amanda Woodworth and co-authors apply a standard coding tool to research impact claims in a 2026 paper. Funders want rigorous proof that research benefits society. Self-reported benefits can inflate without strict criteria. Six research hubs tested a shared coding approach for their data.

Investigators reported benefits from eighty-six pilot projects. Reports were surveyed up to seven years after awards. A benefit counted only when strict criteria thresholds were met. Most pilots ran one year with modest award sizes. Two hundred seventy-four potential benefits were claimed in total. Coding confirmed only thirty-four as demonstrated benefits. Clinical and medical benefits were the commonest confirmed type. Feedback rounds improved coder agreement across hubs. The tool boosted reproducibility of impact judgments. The authors offer the method for cross-institutional comparisons. Honest impact accounting is the stated goal.
pmc-13175135:
Vitoria Leite Di Domenico and her team sift gains in lab-made breed glands drugs for breed tech in cud-chewing stock. Their 2026 review takes in lab-made drugs that stand in for goods drawn from beasts in the bred herd trade.

Twelve field studies met the bar to come in. They split twixt a lab-made follicle-stimulating hormone and a lab-made chorionic gonadotropin. The first one hit marks for mass egg shed that matched the marks of stock plans. The next one drove growth of the egg sac, shed of the egg, and young borne in cows and sheep on a par with the clean form drawn from beasts. Lab-made drugs cut use of beasts, give a steady grade of goods, and make herd work plain to run. The review joins fresh trade-age studies with finds from the team's own work.
pmc-13176635:
Jung, Park, Kim, and Kang hunted blood marks in twenty twenty-six for pancreas cancer and its kin growths, which are oft found too late. Blood samples from one hundred folks fed a mass read of serum proteins. Mark picks used three screens, then a fresh set for checks.

A six-protein panel split sound folks from the worst growth kind with high truth. It also split sound folks from full cancer well in the check set. Both reads held high right-call rates for the sound group. The panel could aid non-cut finds, they say.
pmc-13177635:
Kyler Nault and co-authors report on mental health care for the Red River Metis community. Their 2024 study is based on a survey done during health talks in 2022 and 2023. In all, 144 citizens took part. The team used a method shaped with the community, and split replies by age, sex, and other traits.

People named addiction, trauma, and stress as the main causes of poor mental health. Only one fifth said they now use such services. More than two fifths said they were not pleased with the care on offer. Most called for more services made for their own community. Not knowing what exists and cost were key blocks.
pmc-13177735:
Michelle Jamieson, Jan Savinc, and Iain Atherton ask what jobs Britain's registered nurses and midwives actually hold, in a study from 2024. The professions face shortages and trouble keeping staff. If many registrants work outside direct care, policy aimed at drawing them back needs to know where they went and why.

The nursing regulator's register, covering some eight hundred thousand people, was linked to the 2021 census for England and Wales. Census answers revealed each registrant's main occupation, including whether it involved clinical practice. Regression models then weighed how personal traits relate to working in care or elsewhere. The study aims to size the pool of trained staff outside practice and the drivers that keep them there.
pmc-13178735:
Malu Borges and co-authors review what fluoride does to the developing brain when doses climb past the public health sweet spot. Their 2026 systematic review gathers cell, animal, and population studies of fluoride neurotoxicity. Fluoridated water prevents cavities at controlled levels; the question is where benefit ends and harm begins, especially before birth and in early childhood.

Across study types, excess exposure was linked to oxidative stress, failing cell powerhouses, cell death, and clogged cleanup pathways, ending in damaged neurons and weaker cognition. Two protective proteins emerged as possible moderators of the damage. The authors stop short of verdicts on community water levels, and the review's design cannot set a safe threshold. What it does is consolidate the mechanism evidence in one place. For regulators, the message is monitoring: exposure during early brain development deserves the closest watch, and the margin deserves honest measurement.
pmc-13179335:
Why some mammals live decades while close cousins last years may be written less in their genes than in the staying power of their cells' inner machinery. Domagoj Cikes argues that case in a 2026 perspective. Long life demands organelles, the cell's working parts, that stay faithful for a very long time, and gene-only studies miss the protein, fuel, and fat networks that keep them running.

He proposes a comparative atlas: gather cells from mammals of widely different lifespans, measure their organelles in depth, and mine the results for shared resilience tricks. Those tricks, he suggests, could seed therapies that stretch human health rather than merely lifespan.
pmc-13179635:
Viktoria Greeck and co-authors study a failure of immune control in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 paper. In that disease, the immune system attacks the coating of nerves. B cells, which make antibodies, play a key role, and regulatory T cells are meant to keep them in check. Most past work on this pairing came from animal studies.

The team drew cells from forty patients and ninety-eight matched healthy donors. In lab tests, the regulatory cells strongly curbed B cell growth and release of a signal called IL-6 in healthy donors. That curb was weaker with patient cells, and it needed direct cell contact. Early B cell responses were the same in both groups. The authors say the known control flaw in this disease reaches B cells too, which may help drive the illness.
pmc-13180635: Pedro Marques and three co-authors share a 2026 image case of a 57-year-old man who passed far too much urine and drank without pause. His thirst began a week after a steroid shot for back pain. Blood tests showed high salt with sound sugar and kidney marks. A brain scan showed a bright spot at the back of the pituitary gland had gone dark, a sign of lost hormone store. The case ties a steroid shot to a brief loss of the hormone that holds body water.
pmc-13181335:
Liver cancer is often found late, when scans and blood tests miss small early tumors. Ruohan Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 trial of a blood test built to catch the disease sooner in people at high risk. The test reads chemical marks on DNA that floats free in the blood. Three markers, in the genes RNF135, CHFR, and PAX5, carried the final test.

The team found the markers by screening tumor samples and then narrowing a list of thirty down to the best few. They tuned the test on one group of 280 people and locked it on a second group of 124. After that, the locked test went into a large forward-looking trial across many centers. A blood test that works at scale could shift care toward earlier, more treatable stages.
pmc-13181935:
Spintronic logic moves magnetic domain walls, tiny borders between magnetic regions, as its bits. Peng Zhang and co-authors drive those walls with electric fields instead of magnetic fields or currents, which waste energy and aim poorly. Their device bonds a nickel film to a piezoelectric crystal; voltage strains the crystal, the strain crosses into the nickel, and the nickel's magnetic preferences shift.

In simulations, that strain control created, moved, and parked domain walls exactly where wanted. The team assembled the moves into the basic Boolean operations of computing, showing a working logic-in-memory design on paper. Because voltage replaces current, the approach promises far lower power than today's domain-wall schemes. The authors present strain-driven walls as a scalable route to dense, fast, non-volatile computing that keeps its state when power dies.
pmc-13182235:
Jungang Kang and co-authors test an earthworm extract as a farm-ready alternative to antibiotics for gut infection in animals. Their 2026 study targets Escherichia coli enteritis, which costs livestock producers heavily while antibiotics face resistance and residue limits. The hydrolysate is a protein digest made from earthworms.

In dishes, the extract killed the bacteria at modest doses. In infected animals, three days of treatment repaired intestinal injury and rebuilt the mucosal lining. Protective junction proteins rose, while inflammatory signals and their MAPK pathway drivers fell. Gut bacteria shifted toward helpful genera and away from harmful ones. The authors read the extract as a multi-target therapy: germ killing, inflammation control, barrier repair, and microbiome tuning in one feed additive. Field trials would be the next test.
pmc-13183035:
Yan Jiang and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on whether salt intake causes gut diseases. Observational links between sodium and digestive disorders are common, but cause and effect are hard to prove. The team used Mendelian randomization, a method that uses genes as natural experiments.

Genetic variants tied to the ratio of sodium to creatinine in urine served as stand-ins for salt intake. Data came from large genome-wide studies. The main analysis found a causal push toward two outcomes: diseases of the esophagus, stomach, and upper gut, and irritable bowel syndrome. The links survived corrections for multiple testing. Other gut outcomes showed no firm effect. Several backup methods and sensitivity checks generally agreed with the main result.
pmc-13183135:
Yifeng Huang, Jiansen Xie, and Gengsheng He present a study dated 2026 on gallstone surgery in patients with narrow bile ducts. Stones can slip from the gallbladder into the main bile duct. In thin ducts, the standard fix, opening the duct and leaving a drainage tube, is awkward and slows recovery.

Records covered 182 patients treated at a hospital in Guangdong, China, from 2021 to 2024. Ninety patients had a newer method: a tiny cut where the cystic duct joins the main duct, closed with stitches and no tube. Ninety-two had the tube method. The newer group cleared all stones, with short operating times and little blood loss. The authors judge it a good option for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13184635:
Nobuyuki Yamamoto and co-authors follow Japanese lung cancer patients through a modern treatment sequence, watching closely for lung inflammation, in a 2026 study. Patients with unresectable stage III lung cancer receive chemotherapy with radiation, then the immunotherapy drug durvalumab for up to a year. That drug class can inflame the lungs, a side effect called interstitial lung disease, and Japanese patients seem especially prone. The AYAME study enrolled patients across many centres from 2019.

Over three years of prospective follow-up, the team recorded how often the lung disease appeared, how severe it got, and how it was managed. Among 511 patients analysed for safety, a striking seventy-five percent developed some degree of it. Statistical modelling hunted for patient traits predicting the more serious grades. The results frame consent and monitoring for a standard treatment in Japan.
pmc-13185935:
Lin Wang and eight colleagues make food packaging film from peach gum, sodium alginate, and shrimp shell powder, in a 2026 study. The shells are a waste product, and adding their powder to the plant-based film could both strengthen it and cut waste. The team varied the powder from zero to ten percent of the mix and tested strength, barrier properties, and water resistance.

At six percent powder, the film performed best overall: tensile strength rose 55 percent, while water vapor and oxygen passage fell by about 60 and 67 percent. The film also resisted ultraviolet light and heat well. Wrapped around fresh-cut pears, it cut weight loss and slowed browning, and the authors pitch it as biodegradable packaging.
pmc-13186235:
Agatha Nyambi and co-authors test a short HIV knowledge quiz in a Black Canadian population for a 2026 paper. Knowledge shapes whether people take steps to protect themselves, and the eighteen-item quiz they study is one of the most used tools in the field. The question was whether it still measures well in this specific community in Ontario.

More than thirteen hundred Black Ontarians completed the quiz. Its questions hung together well, with a consistency score in the good range. Knowledge scores differed by age, schooling, work status, and gender, as a valid tool should reveal. People in Toronto scored higher than those in Ottawa, and those answering in English scored higher than those answering in French. The authors judge the quiz valid for this population and call for teaching aimed at the gaps it exposed.
pmc-13187535:
Bruna Egumi Nagay leads a large team testing light-activated coatings for dental implants, in this twenty twenty-six study. Germ films on implants can trigger a stubborn gum disease that loosens the implant. Coatings that kill germs when lit could help, but mixed germ films are hard to clear.

The team made a coating in a single plasma step that reacts to visible light. They paired it with a blue dye therapy that also uses light to kill germs. Together the two attacked germ films faster than either alone. The work points to quick, drug-free treatment for infected implants.
pmc-13187935:
Gregory Burkman and Gerald Naccarelli review treatment choices for patients who have both heart failure and atrial fibrillation in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The two conditions often occur together and worsen each other. Care must weigh standard heart failure drugs against strategies that control heart rate or restore normal rhythm.

The review explores whether guideline heart failure drugs also calm the irregular rhythm. It then surveys drug and ablation options for the rhythm problem itself. Weakened and preserved pumping function are treated separately, since the balance of options differs. Recommendations are given for each subtype, aimed at clinicians matching therapy to the patient.
pmc-13189635:
Habib Moshref Razavi, Dale Purych, and Wilson Yeung report a case of tick-borne relapsing fever in a 2026 paper. A fifty-one-year-old man comes to hospital after two weeks of fever, chills, headache, cough, gut symptoms, rash, and blurred vision. Insect bites while gardening at a rural British Columbia cabin precede the illness. Blood tests show anemia and low platelets.

A blood smear shows spirochete bacteria, which is rare in Lyme disease despite a reactive Lyme test. A PCR test confirms Borrelia hermsii, the relapsing fever germ. Antibiotics clear the symptoms within a week, and blood counts return to normal by two weeks, they report.
pmc-13189735:
Adriana Domínguez-Oliva and co-authors review how enriched housing reshapes rodent brains in a 2026 article. Lab rats and mice kept in complex cages, with more space, objects, company, and novelty, cope better with challenges and learn faster. The review gathers what is known about the chemistry and anatomy behind those gains.

Much of the story runs through three messenger chemicals, dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine, which steer alertness, mood, motivation, and movement. Enriched living tunes how much of each the brain makes and where, and the tuned chemistry supports better memory and learning. Structural changes ride alongside: brain regions grow more connected as the animals explore their richer world. The authors frame enrichment as both a welfare duty and a scientific variable that labs ignore at their peril.
pmc-13190535:
Danpeng Wang and three co-authors pool the evidence on what predicts coronary slow flow, in a meta-analysis published in 2026. In this condition contrast creeps through heart arteries even without a blockage, and cases surface more often as angiography spreads. Twenty-three studies covering about 2,300 patients and 3,400 controls were combined.

Seven factors raised the odds: higher triglycerides, total cholesterol, white cell counts, platelet counts, a platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, body mass index and current smoking. Each effect was small alone, but all are measurable in routine care and several are changeable. The authors frame the list as input for risk models and for trials of lipid, inflammation and lifestyle treatment.
pmc-13190735:
Uchit Sangroula, Victor Vinas, Michael Odhiambo, and Thomas Pettersson fuse in a 2026 study machine learning with decision analysis for water network health risk. Leaks and breaks lose water and let germs slip into pipes. A World Health Organization safety plan frame structures their Swedish case study.

Three classifiers guess pipe break odds from network data for the risk model. Flow modeling and microbe risk math then size the health fallout of each break. A ranking method weighs fix options by nearness to an ideal fix profile. Prediction, fallout sizing, and choice ranking chain into one workflow for utilities. The aim is sharper spending on the riskiest pipes first.
pmc-13190935:
Rao and co-authors (2026) review smart materials that separate oil from water by switching how wettable they are. Oil spills and industrial oily wastewater threaten ecosystems, and a surface that flips between water-loving and oil-loving on command offers a controllable way to split the two. The review first lays out the theory of wetting and separation, then compares four families of specially wettable materials.

Eight kinds of triggers get a chapter each: heat, acidity, light, electricity, gas, ions, solvents, and combined triggers. For each, the authors weigh the switching mechanism, the strengths, and the limits in real separation work. They also compare making methods, from layered self-assembly to electrospinning. The review closes with the field's open problems and likely directions, presenting responsive wettability as a maturing strategy for spill and wastewater cleanup.
pmc-13191435:
Xuelian Chen, Lihui Xie, and Bing Li compare gut bacteria in elite athletes from two sports in a 2026 study. Gut microbes are tied to performance, but whether the sport itself shapes them was rarely tested.

The team sequenced gut microbes from 27 professional taekwondo athletes and 11 divers. Overall diversity and broad structure were much the same in both groups. Yet the mix of microbes did differ between the sports, and 12 metabolic pathways stood out as different. Some fat-building pathways ran lower in the taekwondo group, while several breakdown pathways ran higher. The authors say the sport's demands may leave a specific mark on the gut, even at the top level.
pmc-13191735:
Ridhima Aggarwal, Ritu Bala, and Tarlok Singh Lobana present a chemistry study dated two thousand twenty-six on new palladium catalysts. Catalysts of this metal drive a famous reaction that joins two carbon-based pieces, the Suzuki-Miyaura coupling. The team built a family of catalysts without the phosphine parts that many versions rely on.

Their four catalysts differ by one small group attached to a nitrogen atom. All are stable, easy to make, and reusable. They coupled a range of aryl halides with phenylboronic acid in open air. The study reports how each variant performs, aiming for practical catalysts for carbon bond building.
pmc-13194435:
Tittu Biju, Anusree Ambady, and Thomas K V name a weariness that constant retraining can breed. Artificial intelligence keeps rewriting knowledge jobs, and workers are told to reskill without pause. Their 2026 paper argues that the endless cycle itself carries a human cost, above all for mid-career professionals whose standing rests on hard-won expertise.

The authors call the cost reskilling fatigue. Drawing on two work-stress theories, they sketch a loop: shifting tools erode skills, fresh learning demands pile up, energy and confidence drain, and workers learn defensively just to avoid falling behind. Rather than restoring calm, the loop deepens anxiety and weakens mastery. As a remedy they propose shared, bounded fixes: learning tied to real roles, protected study time, clear skill priorities, and slower, phased adoption of new AI tools across the whole organization.
pmc-13194635:
Kandeepan Karthigesu, Robert Bertolo, and Robert Brown test if adding antioxidants cuts oxidant generation in nutrition fluids for newborns, given by vein. Their 2026 lab study deals with babies who need total parenteral nutrition. That need comes after birth that is too early, or from flaws in the gut.

Levels of peroxide in the standard fluid rose by a share that counts as light got more strong. A mix of vitamins C and E, glutathione, copper, and zinc, at set levels, cut peroxide levels by a share that counts. Vitamins C and E as a pair showed a lowering effect in which each added to the other. Other mixes of trace elements were also tested, to set them side by side. The team aims at a new admixture with a lower load of oxidants. Those oxidants may drive problems in newborns.
pmc-13195035:
Genes found in only one branch of the family tree, called orphan genes, evolve fast, so their jobs may not survive the move between species. Patel and co-authors study goddard, an orphan gene that fruit fly sperm production cannot do without. They swap in the gene copies from other fly species and ask which ones restore fertility in flies lacking their own copy.

A distant desert species' copy fully rescued fertility, yet some closer relatives' copies failed. All copies still touched the sperm tail parts, but the failures bound more weakly and sat in different cell spots. Computer analysis tied rescue to shared flexible-region traits. The results show function can outlive heavy sequence change.
pmc-13196835:
Varvara Pantelidou and colleagues offer a 2026 case report on two cancers found at once. A 58-year-old woman came in with a lump in her right breast. Scans showed growths in both breasts, and biopsies found distinct breast cancer types on each side.

A full-body scan then flagged a spot in her left lung. A needle test showed it was a separate lung cancer, not spread from the breast. A joint care team chose staged surgery. Both breasts were removed first, then part of the left lung a month later. Two years on, the patient stays free of disease. The authors stress joint team review, since no shared rulebook covers such paired cases.
pmc-13196935:
Shaoguang Ren and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study on mobile phone use and rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is an immune disease that swells and harms the joints. The team used UK Biobank data, a large health database, to test whether phone habits link to new cases.

They tracked close to 480,000 adults for a median of about fourteen years. Just over six thousand new cases appeared in that span. Phone users had a modestly higher risk than non-users. Risk was also higher for people who talked on a phone more than thirty minutes a week. The authors note that habits of use, not just owning a phone, may matter, and that more work is needed on cause.
pmc-13197235:
Benjamin Simsa and co-authors test whether today's large language models can pull data out of research papers accurately enough for meta-research. Hand extraction is slow and error-prone, and the tasks range from copying plain facts, like sample sizes, to judging softer points. The team ran five leading models through an automated pipeline over 43 papers in network psychometrics, a field that maps links between symptoms.

Accuracy ranged from about 80 to 91 percent across the models. Scores were higher for facts stated plainly in the text and lower where judgment was needed, and most models could signal doubt in the contentious cases. The authors compare cost against accuracy and list the kinds of variables that suit automatic coding, plus common pitfalls to avoid.
pmc-13197435:
Moritz Berger and colleagues present a 2026 methods study on measuring emotional intelligence in elite swimmers. Emotional intelligence means reading and managing feelings, a trait tied to sport success. Ratings on scale questions can be skewed when athletes answer by habit, such as always picking extremes.

The team applied latent trait models, math tools that infer a hidden trait from answers. Richer models also accounted for each swimmer's response style and doubt. Those models fit the data better than simple scoring models. Ignoring answer habits, they argue, can distort how a swimmer's emotional skill is judged. Better models may sharpen mental support in elite sport.
pmc-13198035:
Lakshmi Sravanti and Hesham M Hamoda share lessons on social media for child mental health in a 2026 commentary. They draw on running the accounts of IACAPAP, a global body for child and adolescent psychiatry. Social media can spread mental health literacy and fight stigma, yet it raises ethics and trust risks with young audiences.

They describe the group's aims: health promotion, teaching, and advocacy across platforms. Content is tailored to each platform's style. From this work they propose the ABLE-GA framework. Its six parts cover alignment, boundaries, language, ethics, governance, and adaptation. The guide aims to help peer bodies use digital platforms with care.
pmc-13198135:
Jakub Piwowarski and co-authors report a case in a 2026 paper where a routine heart tracing exposed hidden amyloidosis. The patient, a seventy six year old, had lived for over twenty five years with a stable blood condition that can, in rare cases, seed harmful protein deposits in organs. New vague symptoms gave no clear lead.

A standard twelve lead tracing showed low voltage signals and a pattern that mimics an old heart attack. Those signs raised suspicion of protein deposits in the heart muscle. Further tests confirmed light chain amyloidosis of the heart. The authors stress that a cheap, common test can spark the right workup even when symptoms stay unclear.
pmc-13198535:
Niklas Grieger and three co-authors test a fully automated pipeline for analyzing sleep recordings, in this 2026 case study. Human experts normally score sleep stages and spot brief events called spindles by hand, a slow job where readers often disagree. The team chained two proven learning models, one for staging and one for spindles, and let them run without human help.

The test was whether the pipeline could repeat the findings of an expert study of bipolar disorder. It did so in kind if not in exact numbers, including the key gap in fast spindle rates between patients and healthy controls. The work took minutes rather than months. Both models also matched or beat the level of agreement between human readers. The tools are shared openly through a privacy keeping platform.
pmc-13198635:
Émile Blanchette and Laurent Fradet present a 2026 case report on a rare bone growth in the tongue. A lingual osseous choristoma is mature bone found where it does not belong, in tongue soft tissue. Just over one hundred cases appear in print, and vague signs make it easy to miss.

Their patient was a 45-year-old woman with a slowly growing lump on the back of her tongue, spotted at a routine dental visit. She had no pain, bleeding, or trouble swallowing. The firm, pale lump looked like a benign fiber growth. Removal under local numbing gave both diagnosis and cure: lab study showed mature bone in the tongue tissue. Two years on, no return appeared.
pmc-13200035:
Five researchers led by Riccardo Geletti present a dataset of sound-based profiles of the sea floor off southeast Italy, in the Otranto Channel. Ships towed listening cables during three surveys spanning decades, the oldest from nineteen seventy-one. The profiles image layers under the seabed at varied depths and detail.

The set pairs sharp, shallow views with deeper ones, and the oldest line was reworked with modern methods. All lines were cleaned with shared steps to cut noise and keep true signal strength. The authors stress reuse of old data, since new surveys face high cost and tight rules. The set aids fault, gas seep, and hazard studies in the southern Adriatic Sea.
pmc-13200535:
Li Ying Khoo and Sarinder Kaur Dhillon present a review dated 2026 on using artificial intelligence to find COVID-19 biomarkers in gene activity data. Blood gene patterns can flag disease state and severity, but the data have far more variables than patients. Classic statistics strain under that load, while AI methods handle it better.

The authors searched five databases for studies from late 2019 to March 2025 and kept sixty-three papers. They sorted the field's landscape, then exposed shared flaws: weak data quality, small samples, and shaky validation. A proposed workflow aims to fix those gaps step by step. The review closes with the hurdles between a promising gene signature and a test doctors can use.
pmc-13200935:
Hailin Lu and six co-authors test a simple blood ratio as a sign of calcium buildup in the belly aorta. The ratio divides neutrophils, a white cell type tied to swelling, by HDL, the so-called good cholesterol. Their 2026 study used survey data from United States adults in 2013 and 2014. Scans gave each person a calcium score, and the team checked how the score tracked with the ratio.

Adults with the highest ratios had higher calcium scores and far more severe buildup than those with the lowest. The link held after adjusting for other risk factors and in extra checks. The link was not a straight line, though. The authors propose the ratio as a cheap marker that could flag people for closer heart checks.
pmc-13202035:
Family ties and friend ties both steer teen loneliness, and Kathryn Bates and co-authors mapped those links in a large British cohort, in work from twenty twenty-six. More than two thousand five hundred young people gave data twice: bullying and family strife in early teens, loneliness and connection later. A poverty-margin score was built from local pay data.

Talking over worries, with family or friends, sat at the web's center, along with early bullying. Feeling left out tied to friends' letdowns in detail. Feeling cut off tied to family gaps. The map shifts a bit under heavier poverty margins. Help, the authors argue, must work both ties at once.
pmc-13202435:
Tiny gaps in metal ion size steer crystal design in a 2026 study headed by Kenika Khotchasanthong on lanthanide coordination polymers. The research article makes ten compounds from lanthanide chlorides and chloranilic acid, forming two-dimensional layered networks whose patterns depend on which lanthanide is used.

Larger early lanthanides produced a honeycomb network, while smaller later ones formed a brick-wall pattern, a direct effect of lanthanide contraction. Adding a bridging molecule to the brick-wall form created a pillared, guest-filled three-dimensional layout in two cases. The ytterbium brick-wall material also captured more carbon dioxide than the honeycomb form, linking ion size to gas storage performance.
pmc-13202535:
Sabine Köppen and seven co-authors compare sperm quality in Swiss army recruits in a 2026 paper. One cohort was examined in the peri-COVID period, and the other over an earlier decade-plus span, amid reports of a global decline in sperm quality. Samples were analyzed under world guidelines, and the recent cohort also gave hormone measures. Language region and settlement type were checked for geographic patterns.

By world reference values, notable shares of the recent cohort fell low on count, movement, or shape. Yet overall, concentration, total count, movement, and shape stayed similar to the earlier cohort. The authors conclude quality held stable apart from men with recent infection, pending larger studies.
pmc-13203635:
Hong Zhu and a large team tested in 2026 how soil type and added microbes change what earthworms do for degraded land. Earthworms rebuild soil structure and cycle nutrients, but helpers like fertilizer and bacteria may amplify or blunt their work. The experiment crossed four soil setups, including mining waste soil and fertilizer mixes, with two bacterial inoculants.

Worms lost weight in plain soil but gained it when surface fertilizer met the mixed inoculant. Mining waste did not harm the worms. Burrowing improved structure and mixed nutrients throughout. The bacteria shifted soil conductivity and clumping but not nutrient levels, and their effects depended on the soil base. The authors offer the combinations as guidance for restoring worn-out land.
pmc-13203735:
Belma Nalbant and six co-authors built a living-tissue incubator that can be steered over Wi-Fi, in this 2026 study. Growing replacement blood vessels in the lab needs a bioreactor: a chamber that feeds cells, turns them gently, and keeps conditions like a body's. Existing systems are often sealed boxes the researcher must babysit in person.

Their modular, rotating reactor was printed by fused deposition, wired to a cheap ESP8266 controller, and fitted with a touchscreen, so its state can be watched and adjusted remotely. Into it went tube-shaped gels of agarose and chitosan seeded with human aortic muscle cells. Over fourteen days the cells stayed alive, spread evenly through the tubes, and showed healthy energy activity under the microscope, while toxicity fell over time. Connected, printable hardware lowers the cost of entry into vascular tissue engineering.
pmc-13204335:
Mafalda Meunier leads a team of fourteen in a 2026 study on steering immune cells against leishmaniasis, a parasite disease spread by sand flies. Dendritic cells spark the T cell arm of immunity, so they are a natural lever for tailored care. The team primed these cells with tiny parcels shed by the parasite.

In lab dishes, the primed cells switched on sensing genes and showed more of the surface flags that present targets to T cells. T cells grown with them shifted their mix in response. The authors frame the work as a step toward patient-matched immune therapy for this disease.
pmc-13204735:
Three lung diseases share some roots yet call for quite different care, and Najla Ghrairi, Youssef Zied Elhechmi, and Soumaya Ben Saad map that ground in a 2026 review. Asthma, long-term blocked airways, and lung scarring all involve worn tissue, stress inside cells, and immune signals gone off track.

Asthma care has been reshaped by shots that block single immune signals, with more targets on the way. Blocked-airway care adds new inhaled drugs and shots for one patient subgroup. For lung scarring, two drugs slow the loss of lung power, and fresh work aims at the signals that switch on scar cells. Across all three, the review backs care matched to each patient's traits and markers, rather than one fixed plan for all.
pmc-13205135:
Víctor Rivilla, Miguel Sanz-Novo, and David San Andrés review stereoisomerism among molecules found in interstellar space. Stereoisomers share the same atoms and bonds but differ in shape, like left and right hands. Telescopes keep finding new molecules between the stars, and shape turns out to matter for their chemistry.

The review gathers sixteen known pairs of stereoisomers, spanning molecules of five to twelve atoms. Some pairs differ only by a twist, others by a fixed geometric flip. The pairs were seen in settings from cold clouds to hot regions. Their abundance ratios range widely, and many sit far from what simple heat-based rules predict. The authors argue that selective formation and destruction paths, light-driven flips, and release from dust grains must shape the ratios. They call for lab spectra and models that treat shape with care.
pmc-13206235:
Yu Wang and six co-authors examine protein from the maitake mushroom's fruiting body as a food ingredient, in a 2026 study. How a mushroom is grown changes its yield and makeup, but effects on its protein's working properties were unclear. The team extracted protein from mushrooms grown in four culture media and compared the batches. Tests covered shape, surface behavior where oil meets water, gelling, and digestion.

The batches differed clearly: one showed higher structural turns and glow under light tests, another pressed harder at the air-water surface, and a third gelled at the lowest concentration. Such differences decide whether a fungal protein can foam, gel, or emulsify in foods. Growers may one day pick a medium for the protein traits they want, not just for yield.
pmc-13206535:
Alberto Grossi and seven co-authors map the literature on light therapy that patients can wear. Light treatment can aid healing, and new light sources have made flexible, wearable devices possible. The team searched three databases for work from nineteen seventy to two thousand and twenty-five and kept 110 papers. Output began in the early two thousands and peaked in the most recent year counted.

Mid-period work used new light films to build bendable and even implantable devices. The newest work links light therapy to body sensors that adapt treatment and report back remotely. The authors judge the field fast-moving but still young, with wearable devices not yet fully proven in the clinic.
pmc-13206635:
Tharntip Sangsuwan and co-authors survey e-cigarette use and mental distress among university students in southern Thailand, in a 2026 paper. The region lives with long-running armed conflict, which may color both habits and mental health. The team gathered answers from 901 students at two campuses of one university.

About seven percent of students used e-cigarettes. Men, tobacco users, and those living alone were far more likely to vape, while Muslim students reported lower use than Buddhist peers. Users also scored higher on depression, anxiety, and stress scales. The authors link vaping with psychological strain in a conflict-shadowed setting and call for support that treats the two together.
pmc-13206735:
A body-wide scarring illness can announce itself as kidney failure alone, Manuela Montatore and co-authors report in a 2026 case study. An eighty-year-old man arrived with severe kidney failure and no past kidney trouble. Scans of the belly found nothing wrong outside the kidneys.

Since contrast dyes were unsafe for his kidneys, the team leaned on dye-free ultrasound, CT, and MRI together. Images showed many patches in both kidneys that looked inflammatory rather than cancerous. Tissue checks pointed to the IgG4-related disease family. The case shows how layered imaging can crack a diagnosis when the usual contrast route is closed.
pmc-13206835:
Kyung-Hee Kim and Byong Chul Yoo ask why attacking tumor acidity keeps failing in this two thousand twenty-six review. Tumors turn their surroundings acidic, a trait seen as a clean drug target. Lab studies showed many ways to blunt that acidity slowing tumors. Blocking lactate output, jamming proton pumps, buffering, and acid-triggered drug release all worked in animals. Yet patients gained little that lasted.

The review lists the barriers. Acidity varies across one tumor and shifts over time. Cancer cells reroute their metabolism and keep spare pH controls. Body-wide effects limit dosing. Newer solutions aimed at these walls are surveyed. The paper serves translational oncologists tired of promising starts.
pmc-13207335:
Chen and co-authors compare tiny parcels shed by three kinds of cells as candidate treatments for Parkinson disease. The parcels, called exosomes, carry proteins and gene snippets that can aid repair, and their quality depends on the parent cell. Their 2026 study draws parcels from reprogrammed stem cells, from connective tissue stem cells, and from a common lab cell line, then compares yield, content, uptake, and healing effect.

Parcels from the reprogrammed stem cells won on every measure the team used. Parcels from the connective tissue stem cells came second, and those from the lab line trailed. Parkinson disease still lacks strong treatments, which gives the ranking practical weight. The authors offer the data as guidance for picking source cells in future parcel therapies.
pmc-13208135:
Gelatin capsules come from animals, so plant-based shells are in demand, yet the leading plant material makes weak, costly capsules. Yuting Dong and co-authors tackled that problem in 2026 with a three-part blend built on the plant polymer HPMC, plus gellan gum and a seaweed extract. They tuned the recipe and the process with systematic tests.

The finished capsules fell apart within fifteen minutes across four acidity levels that mimic the gut, meeting the 2025 Chinese standard. Two test drugs dissolved from them as well as from store-bought gelatin capsules. Microscope images traced how the shell breaks down. The authors offer the blend as a low-cost route to making plant-based capsules at factory scale.
pmc-13208235:
Patricija Plačenytė, Nataša Giedraitienė, and Mantas Vaišvilas review tests for autoimmune encephalitis, a brain illness where the immune system attacks the brain. Their 2026 review notes that finding the right antibody is the core of diagnosis. Yet many patients test negative or show few other signs.

The review compares test methods and asks whether blood or spinal fluid gives the better yield. It also covers backup markers in spinal fluid for hard cases. New tools, from sharper lab methods to learning models, may speed up naming the illness. Faster naming means faster calming treatment. The authors stress that clinical judgment must sit at the centre of the diagnostic process for each patient.
pmc-13209935:
Yifan Li and eight co-authors built a DNA test that can name and count four poultry meats in one tube, to fight food fraud. Mixed or swapped meat is a known cheat in food trade. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team found a DNA stretch shared by poultry birds, with steady edges and a middle part that varies by species. Shared primers copy the stretch, while four probes flag chicken, quail, duck, and goose apart by light color. Tests on made up DNA mixes showed the method was sharp, exact, and steady, with a very low catch limit. The authors offer it as a tool for food watch agencies.
pmc-13210435:
Neural networks that run on small edge devices, like cameras and sensors, often stall when a new model first starts up. Yuchang Gu, Diming Zhang, and Taiyu Lu tackle that cold start in a 2026 paper. Their scheduler, EdgeOpt-Sched-CS, decides the order in which a network's parts run on the device, aiming for low delay and low memory use.

Instead of learning that order from scratch, the scheduler borrows knowledge from similar networks it has seen before. Each network is summed up in a compact signature, matched against past ones, and then tuned lightly on the job. Across tests with image networks, transformer models, and small language models, the method cut total cold-start delay by about 11 to 20 percent. It also reached steady behavior faster, with only small added cost.
pmc-13211235:
In China's Gurbantunggut Desert, a flush of tiny plants races through life in early spring, greening the dunes before the heat arrives. Yang Xue and co-authors tracked these ephemerals with twenty years of satellite greenness data. They taught models to recognize the plants' brief life cycle and mapped where the plants grew each year.

Coverage grew overall from 2001 to 2022. The length of the snow season and the driest quarter's rain ruled the pattern, together explaining most of it. Snow and rain both helped the plants spread. Under future climates, mid-density zones should push north and west, with new habitat opening by mid-century. The authors advise protecting the shifting edges where species will migrate.
pmc-13211335:
Guanlin Li and co-authors review how pollution and temperature extremes team up against asthma in a 2026 paper. Climate change and dirty air threaten breathing jointly. Real people face mixed doses, not single pollutants. How the factors work as one remains poorly known.

Classic particles and gases anchor the evidence review. New contaminants like microplastics join the analysis. Heat and cold extremes amplify pollutant effects on airways. Oxidative stress starts the central damage pathway. Inflammatory signaling and an uneven immune state follow from it. Epidemiology and toxicology are joined. Mixed doses may exceed the sum of single threats. The authors push beyond single-pollutant research habits. Risk checks for mixes are what they urge for policy. Steps to act should work as one too. Asthma burden will grow as the climate shifts if not. The review maps mechanisms for future studies.
pmc-13212835:
Yanfang Yang and co-authors test whether one gene's faults mark out the most dangerous breast cancers in this 2026 study. The gene, SMARCA4, helps run the machinery that opens and closes DNA. Its role in breast cancer spread and survival had not been measured in a large real-world group.

The team drew on records of 4,032 patients and found mutations in about one percent, forty-nine people. Those patients showed far more spread to bone and lymph nodes than patients without the fault. Their survival was shorter, and the usual comfort of hormone-sensitive or HER2-positive status faded in this group. Their tumors carried more mutations overall and often paired the fault with two other cancer genes. The authors name the mutation an independent warning sign, raising death risk by about sixty percent, and propose it as a marker for closer watching.
pmc-13213235:
Abishek Arora and a large team probed how common antidepressants affect growing nerve cells in a 2026 study. These drugs, called SSRIs, are often used in pregnancy, and past results on child development after exposure are mixed. Maternal illness itself clouds those results, so a cell model helps isolate the drug effect.

Stem cells from four human lines were grown toward nerve cells while exposed to four drugs. Two drugs lowered cell energy and harmful oxygen forms, a sign of altered powerhouses in the cells. Three fat-like molecules rose under most drugs in the cells. The same molecules ran high in cord blood from a large birth cohort where mothers used the drugs. The team links them to early signs of developmental disorders.
pmc-13213335:
Kaipeng Zhang and colleagues explore in 2026 whether fat-based nanoparticles can help largemouth bass handle sugary feed. Bass digest carbohydrate poorly, so cheap high-starch diets often cause liver trouble, and particle size might decide how well any additive works.

The team made particles in five sizes and dosed fish on high-glucose feed. Sugary feeding disturbed liver sugar pathways, switching on genes that make glucose while disrupting storage genes. Middle-to-large particles, roughly 150 to 200 nanometres across, switched on an intestinal sugar transporter gene, with the 150-nanometre size performing best in the reported tests. Tuning particle size could make functional feeds practical for bass farms.
pmc-13213735:
A tumour cell's inner rooms talk by touch and by signals, and breaking that talk can kill the cell. Yan Su and six co-authors force the talk into a flood in 2026. Their compound, a ruthenium build, settles in three rooms at once: the protein workshop, the power plant, and the waste sac.

Under a super-scope, the contact pads between workshop and power plant grow. Calcium pours out, swamps the power plant, and tips the cell toward death. The surge also wakes an immune arm, so drug and immunity strike as one. The team frames it as whole-cell therapy: aim at the wiring between rooms, not at one room. Cancer's chatter becomes its trap.
pmc-13213935:
Jonas Kunst, Tomasz Besta, and Milan Obaidi answer critics who re-ran their cross-national study with spatial corrections, in a 2026 reply. The original work linked national traits to lower offensive extremism. The commenters added models that account for neighbors resembling each other, and most headline findings survived, which the authors welcome.

They push back on three points. Terrorism's link faded under the correction, but terrorism clusters by region by nature, so removing the shared pattern may erase the signal itself. Claimed spillovers from neighbors' wealth and inequality lack a clear mental mechanism, they argue. And the neighbor definition used gives island nations no neighbors at all. Their verdict: spatial dependence is real, but this correction travels poorly.
pmc-13214435:
L. Zimniak and colleagues run a 2026 trial on whether smartwatch nagging gets bowel surgery patients moving sooner. Early walking after colorectal operations speeds recovery, yet patients in a traditional ward without a formal enhanced-recovery programme often stay in bed.

Sixty-two patients were randomised to hourly active reminders on a smartwatch or to passive step tracking alone, with everyone wearing a tracker.
