The reminded group took significantly more steps across the first five days and reported stronger motivation to move. Complications and hospital stay length did not differ between groups. Cheap wearable prompts, the authors conclude, can substitute for some missing programme structure after surgery.
pmc-13214535:
Rita Salameh, Antoine Leybros, Stéphanie Szenknect, and Rachel Pflieger wash copper from soil with sound aid in a 2026 study. Copper sticks to soil from farm and factory use and ranks among the top metal pollutants. The team paired plant-based wash fluids with ultrasound at two pitch levels.

A spiked sandy loam soil was washed whole and in two grain splits. Plain citric acid freed about three-fifths of the copper in an hour. Sound sped the wash and lifted yields, most sharply on fine sand. Sound also broke up clumps and moved copper-bearing bits. The work maps how wash chemistry and sound team up.
pmc-13214935:
Jaden Roe and colleagues set norms for ultrasound imaging of the quail embryo heart. Bird embryos mirror mammal heart development but sit in eggs where experiments are easy. The team used a high-resolution small-animal scanner on Japanese quail at day ten of incubation.

Their protocol measures right ventricle wall thickness, pulmonary artery width, and blood flow speeds through the outflow paths. Quail hatch in about seventeen days and form a true four-chamber heart, making them a fast stand-in for mammal studies. Baselines like these let researchers spot abnormal development in later experiments.
pmc-13217435:
Hacer Alataş and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of how the antioxidant power of women's diets relates to inflammation and insulin resistance in polycystic ovary syndrome. In that condition all three problems intertwine.

The study compared 129 women with the syndrome against 135 matched controls. The syndrome group ate a diet with clearly lower total antioxidant capacity, scoring 11.8 against 14.3, while showing higher inflammatory markers and insulin resistance nearly double the control level. The models found that richer antioxidant intake was tied to lower insulin resistance both directly and through reduced inflammation. Syndrome status, inflammation, and low antioxidant intake each predicted worse insulin resistance on its own, backing antioxidant-rich diets as a management lever.
pmc-13218135:
Ling Ding and colleagues outline a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of subgroup claims in sepsis trials. Sepsis is life-threatening organ failure driven by a disordered response to infection, and immune-modulating drugs are a hopeful treatment family. Trial after trial has failed to show a benefit, partly because patients respond unevenly. That unevenness makes subgroup findings tempting but easy to overread.

The review will gather randomized trials of immunomodulatory drugs in adult sepsis, plus their published secondary analyses, searching five databases and trial registries. Four reviewers will screen studies independently, extracting one subgroup analysis per trial with standardized forms. Credibility of each claimed subgroup effect will be rated with a dedicated instrument for effect modification analyses. The team summarizes which drugs show differing effects across patient groups and pool effects where studies overlap. It will compare subgroup reporting between trials with significant main results and those without.
pmc-13218235:
Yue Pan and colleagues present a 2026 study on raising the projection contrast of an infrared scene projector. Such projectors display infrared scenes to test thermal imaging systems in the lab, a method called hardware-in-the-loop simulation. Diffraction from the mirrors of a digital micromirror device scatters light and washes out contrast, capping how demanding the test scenes can be.

Working with a dual-micromirror infrared optical engine, the team calculated the diffraction directions of the orders, aiming to use as much light as possible. They tuned a two-element prism group so light strikes at the angle the diffraction math requires. Tracing the stray beams from mirrors in the off state showed the irradiation stayed close to the level expected without diffraction. Bench tests matched the simulation results. The authors note the same contrast-boosting approach can be carried over to other devices built on micromirrors.
pmc-13219235:
Yifan Wang and co-authors map gel research for worn spine disks with AI in a 2026 paper. Disk wear is the top cause of long back pain world wide. Gels may regrow disks where past care can not, but the field map was murky.

Over one thousand papers from a decade were sorted by an AI frame. Proof sits most in animal stage work, with just a hand full at late translation. Three pillars are ripe: calm swelling, frame like gels, and core regrowth. Ring repair lags as the chief block. The map tells funders where the field is stuck.
pmc-13219435:
Shreyas Indurkar, Betül Kayacik, Peng Liu, and Esther Kuehn ask where the brain files touch memories in a 2026 study. We recognize objects by feel and carry emotional touch memories, but their code was unresolved. Memory could be stored in body-centred coordinates, pinned to skin. Or it could sit in external coordinates merging touch with where the hand sits in space and what the eyes see.

Volunteers learned patterns delivered, then retrieved them with hands in the same posture or crossed over, and in matching or changed surroundings. If outside coordinates ran the system, crossing hands or shifting the scene should have hurt accuracy. Performance showed no such influence, fitting body-centred storage: the pattern is remembered on the body, not one in the room. The authors connect the result to experience, where memories in trauma and somatic symptoms stay tied to body sites instead of remapping outward.
pmc-13219735:
Dania El Rahal and co-authors release an open scan dataset of the aorta for AI research in a 2026 paper. Sixty real world CT angiography scans cover normal and diseased aortas. Six balanced groups span young and old normals, aneurysms, tears, and varied scan types. Auto generated masks label the aorta in every scan with no hand fixes.

Two radiologists checked group labels and curation quality. Files ship in a standard format under an open license. Uncorrected auto labels let teams test error patterns and refinement tools. Small size and single center origin mark the stated limits. Shared data like this speeds fair comparison of vessel tracing algorithms.
pmc-13219835:
Ignacio Llada and colleagues read the body chemistry of steers grazing toxic fescue, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The grass hosts a fungus making ergot alkaloids that sicken cattle. Eighteen steers rotated among toxic, novel-endophyte, and clean pastures, then switched after fourteen days, while urine, saliva, blood, rumen fluid, and feces were profiled.

Toxic grazing left a clear metabolic signature: rumen fermentation acids spiked, fat-burning pathways sagged, and amino acid pathways rose, as if the body changed fuel. Amine byproducts of those amino acids marked the exposed animals, and the alkaloids themselves, mostly clavine types rather than the famous ergopeptines, washed out within two days of leaving toxic pasture. Previously exposed steers later resembled never-exposed ones: the chemistry forgives quickly once the grass changes.
pmc-13219935:
Seetha Radhakrishnan and colleagues, writing for a Canadian Society of Nephrology working group in 2026, examine how the 2025 KDIGO guideline on childhood nephrotic syndrome fits Canadian practice. Nephrotic syndrome is the commonest glomerular disease of childhood, a filter disorder that leaks protein into urine, and the guideline was refreshed. The working group paired its reading with a survey of pediatric kidney centres.

The group endorsed most of the recommendations and praised standardizing definitions of the disease and of treatment response, along with prednisone induction protocols. Two areas were flagged as muddy: how relapses should be treated, and which drug to choose for children who relapse frequently or depend on steroids to stay well. Canadian data informed the discussion. The authors are candid about one limitation: they did not grade the quality of proof behind the guideline, so the commentary is an applicability exercise rather than a re-appraisal.
pmc-13220335:
Giacomo Falcucci and four co-authors simulate water flow around clusters of glass sponges and find teamwork written into the current. Euplectella aspergillum, a deep-sea sponge with a lattice skeleton, is usually studied alone. Abyss footage, though, shows the sponges growing in bouquets of several bodies. Supercomputer flow physics on grouped models revealed the catch.

Downstream sponges feed better in a bouquet while upstream ones pay nothing for the favor. The passive entanglement lifts feeding, breeding odds, and resilience for the whole cluster. The authors call it the first case of a group-level flow advantage from pure passive interaction.
pmc-13220835:
Javier Domínguez-Ortega and colleagues test whether sampling compartments sharpens the inflammatory fingerprint of severe asthma in the 2026 BRISA study. Sorting asthma by its inflammation type guides biologic therapy, and nasal cytology, scraping cells from the nose, would be a painless substitute for inducing sputum. Whether the nose mirrors the lower airways in severe disease was the open question.

Twenty-two patients with severe asthma gave nasal samples, induced sputum, and blood for inflammatory proteins, and were split by their blood eosinophil count. Patients with higher eosinophils had worse lung function, more exacerbations, and higher periostin levels. Only sixteen produced sputum, spanning eosinophilic, neutrophilic, mixed, and quiet patterns. Nasal cytology agreed weakly with the sputum pattern, while blood and sputum eosinophils tracked each other well. The authors conclude nasal sampling cannot replace sputum for phenotyping severe asthma, though it may add information beside blood markers.
pmc-13222035:
Emelie Simone Okouango and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare skin disease in a baby. The disease, juvenile xanthogranuloma, is a benign growth disorder that mostly strikes infants. It often shows as a single skin lump and fades on its own. Widespread forms are rare and can be hard to treat.

Their patient was a four-month-old infant with the widespread form on the skin only. Tests of the tissue confirmed the diagnosis. The lumps spread so fast that doctors gave steroid therapy to the whole body. The case shows why doctors watch for links to other illnesses. It also shows that even a benign disease can need strong care.
pmc-13222635:
Zeyu Zeng and co-authors build an early warning model for severe Mycoplasma pneumonia in children, in a 2026 single-center records study from Shanghai Children's Hospital. Records covered 2,381 children treated between late 2019 and late 2023. A drug-resistance mutation common in this infection was tracked with clinical and laboratory features.

About seven in ten children developed severe disease, and nearly half carried the resistance mutation, which clustered in the severe group. A seven-measure model using fever duration and six blood measures predicted severity with strong accuracy. For carriers, early use of other antibiotics shortened hospital stays compared with waiting. The model could help doctors triage children sooner.
pmc-13223035:
Qianchun Dai, Li Yuanheng, and Chengsheng Tong published an economics study in 2026 on subways and business teamwork with universities. Subways move more than riders, they argue. They also help skilled people and new ideas gather and flow across a city. Using records for Chinese listed firms over more than a decade, the team compared firms before and after subway openings reached them, applying a method that tracks changes across places and years.

Firms linked to new subway access showed a clear rise in joint work with universities and research institutes, and the result held under added checks. The team traces the gain to three routes: a stronger culture of cooperation inside firms, a higher share of skilled staff, and faster digital change. Gains were larger for private firms, high-tech firms, and smaller firms. The authors offer the findings as support for transit building as an innovation policy tool.
pmc-13223135:
Fei Fan and colleagues treated tic disorder in rats with a plant compound in 2026. Tic disorder starts in childhood commonly. It is a chronic neuropsychiatric condition. Jujuboside A may ease its symptoms. Mechanisms were unknown before this work. A rat model reproduced the disorder.

Tissue damage eased under the compound. Gut microbe balance shifted favourably too. Helpful bacterial groups grew in share. Less helpful groups declined under treatment. Gut serotonin signalling also changed measurably. A serotonin-making gene switched on more. The gut-brain route looks central here. Clinical translation needs much more work.
pmc-13224135:
A honeypot is a decoy computer left open for attackers, and every break in attempt teaches defense. Viktor Boiko and Oleksandr Niiakyi release in 2026 four months of logs from a high interaction SSH honeypot they built themselves. The trap mimics a real login service and records not just knocks at the door but everything typed after entry.

The set holds more than 145,000 events, with addresses, tried passwords, and full command payloads, including rare fileless attacks run through shell sockets. Sessions can be rebuilt end to end from the identifiers. The authors aim it at training detection models and sharpening alert rules. Botnet habits and hands on intrusions both leave their traces here.
pmc-13224235:
Franklin de Lima and co-authors present in 2026 a video case of a two-year-old with a trapped pocket of spinal fluid in the brain. Born very early, the child had bleeding in the brain that led to fluid buildup. A shunt treated it, but later the fourth ventricle swelled shut, pressing on the brainstem.

Surgeons worked through a small scope. They opened a new drain path in the third ventricle and tunneled a catheter through the narrow channel to free the fourth. Scans then showed the pressure released and the brainstem decompressed. The child went home on day five and stayed well at six months of checks. The video shows the technique step by step.
pmc-13225535:
Haozhu Chen, Ji Fei, and Kaiwei Zhang map how joint lining cells mature in knee arthritis, in work from 2026. Knee arthritis wears down the joint and stiffens movement. The lining cells that coat the joint change as disease grows, but their paths were unclear.

The team reanalyzed single-cell data from three patient samples. The data held over ten thousand genes across eight cell subgroups. Paths traced seven routes by which the cells mature over time. Nearly three thousand marker genes marked the subgroups. The lining cells sat early in the joint's cell order. Key genes and pathways named here could guide targeted drugs for the disease.
pmc-13225935:
Erfan Golestannejad and co-authors trace a long RNA chain in colon cancer in a 2026 paper. Long non coding RNAs tune cancer by soaking up small RNAs. One such long RNA was high in colon tumors in bank data.

The chain runs from the long RNA through a small RNA to a matrix gene. That gene helps build the frame round cells and aids cell move. Tissue tests on tumors and near healthy parts backed the bank finds. Frame density in slices was read by eye and score. High long RNA may flag tumors set to rebuild their frame and spread.
pmc-13226135:
Hirokazu Sawamura and colleagues present a 2026 case of stubborn lymph fluid leaking after groin lymph-node removal for melanoma in a 70-year-old woman. The usual fix requires injecting dye through a remaining lymph node, but none were left to puncture. A nuclear-medicine scan instead mapped two disrupted lymph pathways running beside major leg veins.

Guided by that map, the team punctured the fluid collections directly and sealed them with a medical glue mixture. The first sealing was not enough, because leakage persisted along the second pathway. Treating a small pouch there, which proved to connect with the drainage tube, stopped the external leak within several days. The case offers a fallback route when standard access is impossible.
pmc-13226235:
Haitao Zhang and co-authors test a handheld cold plasma device on nerve-type cells, asking how its gentle ionized gas steers their growth and specialization. Cold atmospheric plasma tunes cell fate through oxidative stress, a promise for cell engineering that is still poorly mapped for this newer piezoelectric device. The team treated neural stem cells, astrocytes, and a neuroblastoma line, then measured growth, death, and differentiation.

Effects ran both ways depending on settings and cell type. Most strikingly, the plasma pushed neural stem cells to mature into both neurons and glial cells. Gene sequencing tied the effects to a buildup of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and to switching on a major growth pathway, with several other signaling routes also engaged. The authors present the device as a physical dial for neurogenic cell fate.
pmc-13226535:
Alnaghaimshi and colleagues ask how mental health phone apps should be adapted for Arabic-speaking migrants in Australia. Apps could widen access to care, but only if their language, faith cues, and family values fit the people using them. Evidence to guide that design has been thin, so the team surveyed a community directly.

pmc-13226935:

pmc-13227635:

pmc-13229935:

pmc-13233335:

pmc-13233735:

pmc-13234635:
Long Kang and co-authors build an atom-level model of bituminous coal in 2026. Coal's structure is disordered and mixed, which makes faithful models hard to assemble. Fragment-based models and sparse data both limit how real the result can be.

pmc-13235635:

Till now, no one could make a neat, large set of one twist alone to test that claim.

pmc-13236935:

pmc-13237335:

pmc-13237435:

pmc-13238335:
Amber Postma and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on what it takes to raise a child with Dravet syndrome. The rare gene-based disease brings hard-to-treat seizures, slow growth of skills, and behavior problems. Care falls on the parents day and night. The team first held group talks with parents, then gave forms to a wider set.

pmc-13238535:
Hatem M. After an intestinal amoeba infection, his diarrhea worsened sharply, with exhaustion, weight loss, and stomach pain. His history already stretched beyond the gut.

Antibody tests suggested celiac disease without biopsy proof, muddying the picture further. pmc-13239635:
Tawanda Makusha and co-authors review in 2026 care that treats the whole family, not just the child, for children and teens living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. These young people still face gaps in testing, steady drug use, and support. Family-based care may close some of those gaps.

Most joined drug supply with family testing, counsel, and mind support. Community models looked strong for keeping families in care, though long-term proof is still thin.
pmc-13239835:

Across the group, a disturbed night meant more pain the next morning. Sleeping longer than usual meant less pain the next day, above all in the evening, and this link appeared only among Black caregivers. The authors propose better sleep as a route to easing pain.
pmc-13240335:
Anjing Liang and co-authors study the dual role of LBH589 in triple-negative breast cancer in a 2026 paper. This drug, also called panobinostat, blocks histone deacetylases, enzymes whose faulty activity drives breast cancer growth.

pmc-13240835:

pmc-13241435:

pmc-13241535:

pmc-13241635:

pmc-13251035:

pmc-13252735:

pmc-13252835:

pmc-13253935:

pmc-13255535:

pmc-13255635:

pmc-13256035:

Stats linked gut microbes and their products to hormone and metabolic pathways, hinting they may steer recovery. pmc-13256635:
Maria Clara Gama de Souza Silva and co-authors review in 2026 how oxidative stress and gut–skin axis imbalance contribute to immune-mediated skin diseases such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. pmc-13256935:

pmc-13257035:

pmc-13257235:

pmc-13257835:
Hao Li and co-authors model magnetic polishing for rough internal channels in printed metal parts in a 2026 study. pmc-13258035:

Two ways of scoring agreed closely, which firms up the count for clinics planning therapy slots.
pmc-13258335:
Heyi Guo and colleagues examined a failed bubble tube pulled from a glass curing furnace. The Inconel 690 tube had spent years bathed in molten glass hotter than a thousand degrees, with gas bubbling through it. Their 2026 failure analysis asks why the metal wasted away unevenly.

pmc-13258535:
Fnu Samiksha and coauthors review fungal cell wall sugars called beta glucans in a 2026 article on gut and immune health. Immune sensors on cell surfaces recognize these sugars and switch on defense activity. Eaten glucans also feed gut microbes, which then produce helpful short chain fatty acids.

Evidence links the compounds to support in bowel inflammation, metabolic problems, lung infections, and cancer care. In cancer settings they may strengthen antibody drugs and vaccines. Uneven sources and formulas make human trial results hard to compare. Few large, well standardized trials exist so far. Readers see both the promise and the proof still needed before routine medical use.
pmc-13259135:
Yifeng Huang, Xikang Lu, and Daode Zhang monitor cutting tool wear across changing machine settings in a 2026 study. Vibration and spindle current signals were fused as multi channel inputs. A deep model with attention read those signals for wear states.

Training moved in stages from source settings to target settings with few labeled examples. Fusing three signal channels beat single and dual channel inputs clearly. Repeated tests with random restarts confirmed the advantage held steady. Competing adaptation methods trailed the staged approach on their custom dataset. Factory engineers gain a wear monitor that survives setting changes without full retraining.
pmc-13259435:
Ziheng Xia and colleagues fuse physics with deep learning to recognize aircraft from radar echoes. A high-resolution range profile compresses a target into a one-dimensional signature of peaks. Purely data-driven networks read it well but stumble in noise and explain little. Their 2026 model runs two branches in parallel.

One branch learns features straight from the raw profile, while the other estimates the peaks' positions and strengths explicitly. Cross-attention blends the two views before the verdict. On measured ten-class aircraft data, the fused model classified more accurately and held up better under added noise. Its peaks lined up with real energy hotspots, keeping decisions interpretable.
pmc-13259535:
Maialen Vázquez-Polo and coauthors teach primary school children about celiac disease in a 2026 education study. Nearly three hundred pupils aged ten to twelve in northern Spain joined the month long program or a regular curriculum control. Eight inquiry based sessions covered the disease and gluten free eating.

Knowledge scores rose clearly in the program group and held one month later. Pupils explained the disease better, judged gluten content, and sorted foods correctly more often. Inclusive behavior choices also improved at follow up. Pupils additionally reported understanding scientist work better. Schools gain a tested program that builds empathy for classmates with dietary disease.
pmc-13259735:
Alshimaa S. Othman and coauthors compare premenstrual symptoms and coping in women with menstrual migraine in a 2026 study. Six hundred one women were classed by diary records across at least three cycles. Headache impact, symptom screening, and coping questionnaires supplied the measures.

Menstrual migraine patients scored higher on both symptom severity and headache impact. The severe mood disorder form appeared somewhat more often in that group, though the gap missed significance. Having that diagnosis added several points to headache impact scores in adjusted models. Lower awareness and acceptance coping also tracked with heavier headache burden. Neurologists gain targets for combined cycle and migraine care.
pmc-13260035:
Stephany Rocha Ribeiro leads a 2026 study of tick- and parasite-borne germs in free-living opossums in São Paulo State, Brazil. Blood samples came from 115 opossums of two species, ninety-five white-eared and twenty black-eared opossums. The team used microscope checks and DNA tests to look for three groups of pathogens: Babesia, Hepatozoon, and Ehrlichia. Positive samples were sequenced and placed on family trees to identify them.

Five samples, or 4.35 percent, tested positive for Babesia, all from white-eared opossums collected in Botucatu. Two samples, or 1.74 percent, were positive for Ehrlichia, and no Hepatozoon DNA was found. The sequences matched known South American marsupial strains closely, in one case exactly. The authors call this the first molecular detection of both germs in this opossum species in Botucatu, and urge continued surveillance.
pmc-13260335:
Eike Matthias Wacker and co-authors present a 2026 software study of TOFU-MAaPO, a pipeline for large metagenome datasets. A metagenome is the combined genetic material of a microbial community. Over 600,000 metagenomes sit in public archives such as the Sequence Read Archive, but shared, repeatable analysis tools are lacking. Their single-command pipeline cleans raw reads, assembles genomes, and annotates them, working on local files or pulling data straight from the archive.

In benchmarks against three existing pipelines, the new workflow produced twelve percent, and forty-two to seventy-seven percent, more high-quality assembled genomes, depending on the rival tool. In a large test run, it pulled down 16,462 human gut metagenome samples and classified them against a standard naming database in under fifty-five hours on a cluster of machines. The tool is free online for research groups.
pmc-13260535:
Grigorios Thermos and co-authors present a 2026 case series of cocaine-induced plasma cell dermatomucositis, an emerging inflammatory condition with ulcerated, nodular lesions around the nose and lips. The series looked back at six patients from two United Kingdom pathology archives. Records, medical photographs, and tissue reports were reviewed to define its features and rule out other diseases. Cocaine exposure was confirmed in every case by history or toxicology testing.

The group had five men and one woman, with a mean age of 50.3 years at diagnosis. Patients typically showed raised, ulcerated masses in the nasolabial area. Tissue analysis in every case found dense collections of plasma cells, a type of immune cell, grouped around vessels. Medical and surgical treatments generally brought partial improvement. The authors, in the first UK series, urge thorough clinic and tissue correlation because the condition mimics common lesions.
pmc-13261535:
Elysia Grose and colleagues present a 2026 prospective study of smell outcomes after endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic sinus inflammation with nasal polyps. Loss of smell is a hard-to-treat symptom in this condition. The team measured outcomes with both a symptom questionnaire and an odor identification test.

The single-center study enrolled 36 adults operated on between July 2022 and May 2024; 45% were female and the mean age was 48. Mean SNOT-22 symptom scores fell from 57 before surgery to 22, 15, and 25 at 1, 3, and 6 months. Odor identification improved from 5.2 of 16 odors to 7.9, 8.3, and 7.7 at the same visits. pmc-13262235:
Rajesh Das and co-authors report a stable manganese formate framework made by precursor tuning, working with metal-organic frameworks of the ReO3-type family. These are promising porous materials, but most members resist being opened up, the step that clears their pores. Aluminum formate has stood alone as ready to open until now.

The activated material held up well under heat in tests, and carbon dioxide uptake matched the aluminum benchmark closely. The metal is earth-abundant and redox-active, adding new promise. Uses could span gas storage and catalysis, and spin-based tools may also build on this material.
pmc-13262735:
Ivan Rosas and thirteen co-authors report a 2026 study of a cell feeding process that seems to drive lung scarring. The disease, called IPF, slowly scars the lungs and has few treatment options. Under stress, cells can gulp large sips of the fluid around them to gather food.

The same drug reduced scarring in mice with injured lungs. The effect ran through how cells take in amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
pmc-13263035:
Lingbo Liu examines whether hospital telehealth volume tracks with artificial intelligence adoption in a 2026 journal article. Telehealth and AI are both signs of digital change, but their link was unclear. The study covered 6,173 United States acute care hospitals, using national survey and cost data to sort hospitals into three AI adoption tiers for clinical and office work.

Telehealth volume was the strongest predictor of both AI tiers, especially for clinical AI. More than half of hospitals did not report telehealth data, and these clustered in the lowest clinical AI tier. Predicted clinical AI adoption rose steeply with telehealth volume at low levels, then leveled off. Rural hospitals gained less predicted benefit than city hospitals at the same telehealth volume.
pmc-13263235:
Henri Laugel and Wolfgang Link argue that faba bean populations already hide the inbred plants breeders need in a 2026 journal article. With 50 markers and a strict threshold, they correctly picked 36 of the 61 highly inbred plants, with six false picks. A cheap pre-screen cut genotyping costs by up to 46 percent.
pmc-13263335:
Felicitas von Usslar and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on freeing cellulose fibers from hardwood without destroying the wood. Cellulose fibrils are a renewable material, but extracting them usually means pulping the whole piece. The team instead worked on libriform tissue, the strong fiber cells of hardwood.

They combined partial removal of lignin, the glue-like polymer in wood, with a surface treatment using an ionic liquid, a salt that is liquid at low heat. The treatment acted only at the surface, so microfibrils peeled away while the wood's structure and fiber direction stayed intact. The authors present this selective release as a new tool for designing advanced wood-based materials.
pmc-13263535:
Muneera Al-Jelaify and co-authors report a 2026 guideline adaptation for calming and pain control in critically ill children. The adapted guideline covers how to score sedation and pain at the bedside, choose and adjust medicines, and wean children off them safely. It adds tools for spotting withdrawal and delirium, plus three step-by-step management algorithms and a push for early movement. The authors note the tools need testing for wider use.
pmc-13263735:

pmc-13263935:

pmc-13264035:

Stronger seasons reduced feasibility, mainly through phosphorus limits, until animal manure was added as a digestion input. pmc-13264135:

pmc-13264235:

pmc-13264335:

pmc-13264635:

pmc-13264835:

pmc-13264935:

pmc-13266035:

pmc-13266135:

pmc-13266735:

pmc-13267035:

pmc-13267435:

pmc-13267535:

pmc-13267835:

pmc-13268435:

pmc-13268935:

pmc-13269035:
Chunhua Chi and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on genes linked to colon cancer that grows out of long-term bowel inflammation. pmc-13270635:

pmc-13270835:

They present this joined strategy as the plant's adaptation to poor soils.
pmc-13270935:

pmc-13271135:

pmc-13271435:

The tracing showed a right bundle branch block shape, rightward axis, and backward signals to the upper chambers at a fixed one-to-one pace.

That pattern puts a rare ventricle rhythm high on the list, yet common blocking drugs failed to settle it. Early beats from the ventricles neither reset nor stopped the rhythm. The authors show feature by feature why the tracing cannot cleanly separate a top-chamber rhythm with detoured conduction from the rare ventricle rhythm, and why drug response matters.
pmc-13288535:
Miguel San Sebastian and co-authors measure asthma in Sami people in Sweden. National registers supplied the data. It holds 13,311 Sami people. Each was matched to four non-Sami peers. Matches used age, sex, and home area. Records ran from 1993 to 2018.

Sami men and women got more specialist asthma diagnoses. Rates sat a bit above their peers in both groups. Sami men also had more hospital stays for asthma. Women showed no such gap. Past survey hints of extra burden held up. The authors urge work on causes. They also urge targeted public health steps.
pmc-13288635:
Yifan Xing and colleagues find a hidden translation starter inside a childhood virus genome in a 2026 study. Enterovirus A71 causes hand, foot, and mouth disease and sometimes severe brain complications. Viruses usually start protein building at one entry site near the genome's start. The team screened the whole genome with reporter constructs to hunt for extra entry elements. Two candidate regions turned up inside protein-coding stretches.

One element, between the 2A and 2B coding regions, drove protein production without the normal entry site. It also shifted how much of two viral proteins the cell made and tilted the balance of genome copies. Quiet mutations that changed no protein letters but bent the RNA shape cut replication and virus output. Those changes weakened binding between the RNA and the viral copying enzyme. The authors say such shape-breaking mutations could help design weakened vaccine strains.
pmc-13288835:
Behnam Honarvar and co-authors present a 2026 field study from Iran on why small families hold back from having more children. Falling population growth and rapid aging have become national concerns there. Small families make up roughly half of all households, so their choices shape the trend.

The team surveyed 280 people with no children or one child in Fars province in 2024. They came from 29 counties and filled out an online survey. Questions covered personal factors, social and cultural factors, and economic factors. Statistical tests then weighed which factors best predicted reluctance. The results are meant to guide policy makers as they design support and incentives. The study ties private family choices to wider social pressures.
pmc-13289135:
Scott Newbould and colleagues give a 2026 study plan on weight change before gut cancer surgery. The study sits in a UK prep service called Active Together. That service blends exercise, food, and mind support. How weight shifts affect surgery is unclear.

The study will recruit 100 adults with obesity. All face curative gut cancer surgery. Visits will run at diagnosis and before surgery. Staff will measure body mass and makeup. Surveys will track food status and life quality. Surgery facts will come from routine records. Stay length and problems will be logged. One-year survival will also be tracked.
pmc-13289235:
Aneesa Vanker headed a 2026 cohort study on indoor air pollution and tobacco smoke before birth in South Africa. The work sits inside the Drakenstein Child Health Study, a birth cohort in a periurban area. Pregnant participants joined between 20 and 28 weeks, and the analysis covered 1143 live births in total.

Exposure checks covered fine particles, carbon monoxide, other gases, and cotinine in urine as a smoke marker. About 17 percent of births were early and 15 percent had low birth weight in this cohort. Active smoking by the mother linked to lower weight-for-age scores in babies. Particle and carbon monoxide levels above ambient standards also tied to more breathing distress at birth, though some links were trends. Cleaner home air in pregnancy emerges as a clear priority.
pmc-13289435:
Xiyue Ge and co-authors review in a 2026 paper a cell protein called caveolin-1 and its role in cancer. The protein marks small pits in the cell surface and shapes signals, fat use, and immune response. It shows up in both tumor cells and immune cells and runs high in many cancers.

High levels appear in breast, liver, lung, and pancreas cancers, plus brain tumors and skin cancer. In some stomach cancers the pattern flips, so context rules the protein's effect. Fat shifts driven by the protein can blunt immune attack and help tumors resist drugs. The authors say that spread of effects makes drug design hard, and that care must be tuned to each cancer type.
pmc-13289935:
Emma Michel and colleagues revisit a 2026 puzzle on apathy and impulsivity using a stop-signal task in healthy young adults. Questionnaires show the two traits rise together, defying a simple seesaw theory placing them at opposite ends of one drive spectrum. The authors test whether each trait maps to a distinct action step: stopping versus starting, measured in the same task.

A total of 144 adults did the stop-signal task under consensus rules and filled validated scales for impulsivity dimensions and apathy facets. Bayesian analysis confirmed global apathy and impulsivity scores rose together as expected. Stopping speed did not track urgency impulsivity, and starting speed did not track initiation apathy, against predictions. The paradox survives behavioral testing.
pmc-13290335:
M Daud AK and co-authors characterize foot-and-mouth disease virus in Acehnese cattle in a 2026 study. The virus returned to Indonesia in 2022 and keeps sparking outbreaks. Samples came from sick cattle in Aceh Besar District during 2024. Blood antibody tests and RNA tests targeted different parts of the virus. One positive sample's VP1 gene was sequenced and placed on a family tree.

Antibody tests reacted in some sick cattle and in none of the healthy ones. RNA tests confirmed the virus in seventy percent of swab samples. The sequenced isolate fell in the Middle East-South Asia topotype, Ind-2001e sub-lineage. It matched Indonesian outbreak strains from 2022 at about 96 percent of its letters. Close relatives also circulate in several Asian countries. The authors say combined blood and molecular watch is needed for outbreak tracing and vaccine matching.
pmc-13290435:
A hands-on six-week course turned wary health care educators into more confident AI users, Justin Peacock and colleagues reported in 2026. Their qualitative case study follows a continuing professional development course built to help educators use generative AI in teaching, administration, research, and clinical work.

Drawing on three data sources analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis, the team found that 16 of 21 learners began the course apprehensive or fearful about AI. Working directly with the tools alongside peers shifted their outlook: participants gained confidence, began applying AI in daily tasks, and started advocating for it to others. Peacock and colleagues argue that practice-based, peer-supported training, rather than lectures alone, is what moves educators past fear.
pmc-13290635:
Four doses of a common urinary antibiotic were enough to injure one woman's liver, Mahir Sampat reports in a 2026 case report. Nitrofurantoin is a first-line drug for lower urinary tract infections, and its liver injury is usually tied to long-term use, which makes this early case stand out.

The patient, a 52-year-old woman, developed symptoms after just four doses, and her blood tests showed a disproportionate rise in AST compared with the usual injury pattern. Scored with the updated RUCAM causality tool, her case reached six points, supporting a probable drug cause. Once the antibiotic was stopped, she recovered completely and quickly. Sampat argues the case should put liver injury on the radar even for short nitrofurantoin courses.
pmc-13290835:
A stomach that empties unpredictably wrecks insulin timing, Francesco Galeano and colleagues explain in a narrative review from 2026 of diabetic gastroparesis. The complication, driven by nerve damage in long-standing diabetes, delays gastric emptying without any physical blockage and often goes unrecognized.

The review traces the damage chain: chronic high glucose, oxidative stress, glycation products, and inflammation injure gut nerves and deplete the pacemaker cells that coordinate stomach muscle. The clinical sting is a timing mismatch: food arrives late while injected insulin acts on schedule, causing early low blood sugar and late highs, with wider swings overall. Galeano and colleagues survey diagnosis, diet changes, and drugs, then weigh glucose monitors, automated insulin pumps, and future glucose-responsive insulins as ways to close the gap.
pmc-13291035:
Micayla M. Kane, Sydney E. Sneed, and Erin E. Kaiser sort surgical animal models in a 2026 review. Their topic is vascular cognitive impairment. The illness spans mild memory loss to vascular dementia. It often mixes with Alzheimer’s disease in patients.

Surgical models block or narrow brain vessels in varied ways. Each method sets a distinct harm pattern. Blood flow loss, white matter harm, and memory loss differ by method. No single model fits the whole illness. The review matches each method to a subtype. Labs can then pick a model that fits their question. Better matching should sharpen future drug tests.
pmc-13291135:
Stronger cannabis products and uneven health system readiness across Europe are linked to mental health harm in a 2026 narrative review led by Justyna Śniadach. Use has risen over the past decade alongside high-strength THC goods and more psychiatric presentations, yet monitoring and addiction services vary widely between western countries and the rest of the continent.

Literature, health reports, and national data from 2010 to 2025 show cannabis as the most used illicit drug in Europe, with use now growing fast in central and eastern areas. High-strength products are tied again and again to psychosis, anxiety, panic, and use disorder in the sources reviewed. Western systems spot such cases better, while stigma and thin screening hide much of the burden further east, the authors conclude.
pmc-13291235:
Antibody genes are shuffled to build vast immune variety. Fujung Chang leads a 2026 study on how DNA loops guide that shuffling in young B cells. A protein ring called cohesin pulls DNA into loops. Two forms of the ring carry different parts, STAG1 and STAG2.

Mouse B cells served as the test system. One form kept gene joining balanced at an early stage. Losing it let the other form grab more DNA. Early long loops then formed too soon. Gene use skewed toward near segments as a result. At a later stage, both forms worked together instead. The study shows stage matters in how these rings cooperate.
pmc-13291335:
A tiny laser can now emit clean, single-direction light. Yifan Li leads a 2026 study of a crystal laser with special bound states. Such states give sharp, low-power lasing. Their swirling polarization has blocked clean output for years.

Normal fixes twist the crystal pattern slightly. Real device size still spoils polarization purity. The team used dispersion to tame the swirl instead. Their compact laser kept single-mode output. Beam quality stayed high at the same time. Polarization purity reached a very high ratio. Chip lasers for comms and displays could use this trick. Precision tools may gain a small, pure light source.
pmc-13291735:
Yasue Fukuda and colleagues model mobile health app acceptance in aging Japan in a 2026 survey study. Japan has the world's oldest population, yet only about a fifth of adults use health apps regularly. The online survey reached 960 adults in November 2023, spread across seven age bands. An extended acceptance model added eHealth literacy, self-efficacy, perceived risk, and distrust to the classic drivers. Structural modeling then tested how these pieces connect.

The model explained about 72 percent of the variation in intention to use health apps. Ease of use mattered most, followed by support conditions and expected benefit. Social influence worked upstream, lifting literacy, confidence, and ease judgments together. Age and sex split several pathways in opposite directions. Digital literacy, for instance, raised distrust in young adults yet lowered perceived risk in older ones. Distrust cut intention only among the middle-aged. The authors advise age-tailored promotion.
pmc-13292235:
Chang Chen and co-authors review biomolecular carriers for boron neutron capture therapy in a 2026 article. In this radiotherapy, boron loaded into tumors splits under neutron fire and kills cells from inside. The carrier decides whether enough boron reaches the tumor. The only approved carriers so far are biomolecular, led by boronophenylalanine, cleared in Japan. The review sorts carriers by their biological vehicle.

Amino acid carriers ride a transporter that hungry tumors overuse. Nucleoside prodrugs switch on inside dividing cells and lodge boron in DNA. Sugar-based carriers exploit glucose transporters, while peptides slip in through receptors or direct penetration. Liposomes gather in leaky tumors and can carry targeting decorations. Albumin systems draw rising attention for their safety and high boron loads. The stubborn challenge is sheer dose, since each cell needs vast boron numbers. Protein carriers may finally clear that bar.
pmc-13292335:
Tommaso Piseddu and Fedra Vanhuyse map a 2026 evidence base on how climate risk moves real estate values. Their systematic map coded 130 academic and grey documents published between 2014 and 2023. Coding covered geography, valuation methods, asset types, and whether studies tackled physical hazards or the low-carbon transition.

Physical risk dominates the literature, led by flood studies, mostly American, that lean on official hazard maps and hedonic price models. Adaptation work using damage functions forms a smaller branch. Transition risk research is thinner still, clustering on energy performance rules, labels, and renewable energy side effects. Geographically, Europe's work concentrates in the United Kingdom, Germany, and Italy. The corpus studies one- and two-family houses far more than any other asset class.
pmc-13292435:
Wajahat Mirza and co-authors weigh a 2026 surgical trade-off in a GRADE-assessed meta-analysis: robotic versus open nipple-sparing mastectomy with immediate implant reconstruction. Restricting the pool to prospective studies left just three. The team compared total operating time first, then major complications, nipple tissue loss, and hospital stay, grading certainty with GRADE methods.

Robotic operations ran longer by a mean of 64.01 minutes in the pooled estimate, with wide uncertainty around it. Major complications, nipple-areolar ischemia or necrosis, and length of stay showed no significant differences between approaches. Heterogeneity ran high for operating time, and overall certainty rated low. The authors conclude the robot costs time without proven perioperative gains so far, while stressing how thin and imprecise the prospective evidence remains.
pmc-13292535:
Javaria Waheed and colleagues test how a feed enzyme changes nutrient release timing, in a 2026 laboratory digestion study. Phytic acid in plant feeds locks up minerals and protein for single-stomached animals. The enzyme phytase breaks that lock, but its effect on release timing was unclear. Soybean meal, canola meal, and corn gluten meal were digested in glassware with graded enzyme doses. The team tracked acid breakdown, mineral freeing, and amino acid release curves.

Phytase sharply raised acid breakdown in every ingredient, nearing its ceiling at a mid-level dose. Phosphorus and calcium freed up alongside, rising steadily in canola but plateauing in the other meals. Amino acids escaped fast then leveled in soybean and canola, while corn gluten released them in two waves. Release speed barely tracked acid breakdown, pointing to the ingredient's own matrix as the real governor. The enzyme mainly shifted timing rather than total protein digestion.
pmc-13292935:
Daniel Schneider, Kristen Harknett, and David Arbelaez assess, in a 2026 study, Fair Workweek laws in United States cities and one state. These laws aim to give hourly staff steadier hours and more notice of shifts in shops and food service.

Using survey data and models that compare places over time, the team found more advance notice, more rest between shifts, and fewer last-minute changes after the laws began. Other parts of job quality did not get worse to offset those gains. Effects varied widely by place, which the authors tie to how strongly each local law is enforced. Wider gains may need firmer enforcement.
pmc-13293435:
James C. Barton and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, antibody levels in people with hemochromatosis who carry two copies of a common iron gene change. These carriers face higher infection risk, yet their IgA and IgM levels had not been reported as a group.

Data covered 73 patients, 36 men and 37 women, with an average age of 51 years at diagnosis, an age the authors give. IgA levels matched those in general European groups, with no clear links to patient traits. IgM ran lower than in comparison groups, fell with age, and rose with daily alcohol intake. The work clarifies one piece of infection risk.
pmc-13293735:
Nathan J. Savage and John S. McKell test whether ultrasound measurements of the ulnar nerve can grade a common elbow nerve problem, in a 2026 analysis. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is usually staged with electrical tests, which sort patients into several severity tiers. The authors asked whether the nerve's cross-sectional area on ultrasound could separate those tiers, using records from 299 elbows of 262 patients sent for electrical testing.

Ultrasound size separated neighboring severity tiers poorly, shifting the odds only modestly between them. It performed better as a simple yes-or-no guide: very small measurements argued against disease, while large ones, above roughly fifteen square millimeters, argued strongly for it. Age and sex shaped the electrical findings without changing that reading. The authors recommend using ultrasound probabilistically rather than as a grading tool.
pmc-13294335:
Yuriria Cortés-Poza and J Rogelio Pérez-Buendía model flower pattern landscapes with a forest metaphor in a 2026 study. Stable petal and organ identities arise from a gene switch network in Arabidopsis thaliana. Each stable pattern anchors a tree of paths that flow into it, and the full set of trees forms an epigenetic forest. Wild type plants were compared with three single and three double homeotic mutants.

Measures tracked basin size, path depth, fate variety, dominance, and distance from wild type. Mutants warped the forest in distinct ways: one narrowed reachable fates, one deleted a whole identity class cleanly, and one raised fate variety despite losing reproductive organs. Double mutants often broke simple addition rules.
pmc-13294435:
Jamal Kazmi and a large team review atom-thin materials for brain-like computing in a 2026 article. Standard chips waste energy shuttling data between memory and processors, while two-dimensional materials offer tunable gaps, fast switching, and spike-friendly behavior. Resistive, ferroelectric, and phase-change memory cells built from such sheets can mimic synapse strengthening and fading.

Gate control lets one device hold many strength levels, cutting power for learning hardware. Remaining hurdles include growing clean large films, taming defects, and scaling arrays without losing uniformity. Uses in health monitors, edge devices, and quantum-linked systems are sketched as next frontiers.
pmc-13295035:
Boonlom Thavornyutikarn and co-authors improve a printable plastic blend for three-dimensional printing in a 2026 study. Polypropylene random copolymer warps and sticks poorly during printing, limiting its use. Clay nanotubes, a crystal-starting additive, and post-print heating were combined to fix those faults.

Nanotubes up to five percent by weight steadied filament shape and helped prints grip the build plate without glue. The crystal starter sped up solid setting, while nanotubes mainly raised stiffness at some cost to impact strength. Gentle reheating after printing partly restored that strength and refined crystal structure. Together the three steps offer a workable recipe for stronger, steadier prints.
pmc-13295235:
Mohamed I Elsayed and colleagues test gentle anti-mould dips for navel oranges in a 2026 study. Green and blue moulds caused by Penicillium species spoil fruit during cold storage and later shelf display. Silicate salts and a helpful Streptomyces strain were tried alone and mixed.

Fruit were dipped for 15 minutes, chilled for 50 days, then held three days at shelf conditions. Untreated fruit reached heavy mould by the end, while single dips held disease to low single figures. The triple mix showed no visible disease at all across the full period and kept fruit quality measures steadiest, marking it as a strong storage option.
pmc-13295535:
Zhongying Li and colleagues test immune training in whiteleg shrimp in a 2026 study. Shrimp lack the lasting antibody memory of vertebrates, yet a first mild exposure can still sharpen later defence. Two spaced doses of killed Vibrio bacteria were given, and blood cell gene activity was read afterwards.

The second dose switched on wide gene changes in the shrimp blood cells. Growth and division genes rose alongside direct immune weapon genes compared with untrained animals. The pattern supports a memory-like training effect in shrimp defence. Candidate genes named by the work may help breeders select shrimp lines that resist this costly farm disease.
pmc-13295835:
Gillian Flower and colleagues measure heat-linked hospital admissions across England in a 2026 study. Extreme summer heat may send people to hospital for far more than classic heat illness. Records of over four million summer admissions from 2008 to 2019 were matched with fine-grained weather data.

The studied conditions alone accounted for more than 3.7 million admissions, heavily weighted toward people aged 75 and above. Comparing the hottest days with mild ones showed raised admission risk for kidney failure, metabolic upsets, infections, and lung disease flares. Many heart conditions showed the opposite pattern instead. Risk climbed steeply with age across the map.
pmc-13295935:
Tetine L Sentell and a multinational team argue, in 2026, for physical activity rooted in local culture, such as ethnic dance and traditional games. Health guidance often overlooks such activities even though evidence for their benefits keeps growing.

Their narrative review surveys a vast, scattered literature spanning dance, sport, Indigenous health and community design. Because formal searches would return hundreds of thousands of papers, the team first craft a shared definition of culturally relevant activity and set its boundaries. They say clearer concepts will help planners fund and use such activity in population health.
pmc-13296335:
Laura Pérez Sánchez and colleagues present a 2026 method for bioprinting curved corneal tissue without the usual stepped surface. Flat slicing in standard printing loses the cornea's natural dome shape and leaves a stair-like finish. Their approach finds the surface from the model's geometry and generates curved printing paths that follow it.

Corneal constructs printed both ways were compared using micro-computed tomography scans. The non-planar prints matched the intended parabolic profile far more closely than the flat-layer prints. They also showed high optical transparency, which matters for tissue meant to restore sight. The work offers biofabrication teams a route to smoother, better-shaped corneal grafts, though clinical testing remains ahead.
pmc-13296535: Frontiers Production Office issued a correction in 2026 to a study of crop rotation effects on cut chrysanthemums, their soil and root microbes. The notice fixes three back-matter items only. A funding statement that wrongly denied support now names a Ningxia research programme and a flower laboratory. The author contribution list is expanded and corrected. The data statement now points readers to sequence data held under accession PRJNA1468310. The item is a correction notice alone, with no findings of its own.
pmc-13296935:
Jianjun Kang and co-authors devise, in 2026, a bedside test where the target enzyme builds its own detector particles. Acid phosphatase is scarce and fragile in samples, defeating ordinary assays, so the team let it convert a starter chemical into vitamin C, which then sparks iron oxide nanoparticle growth.

The coated particles mimic an enzyme and turn a dye dark in proportion to the target, readable by instrument or phone camera within forty minutes. Detection reached very low levels and worked in human serum. The authors pitch the scheme as a general trick for scarce, fragile markers.
pmc-13297435:
Angela Messina and a large team profile sugar chains on antibodies in people with Ring 14 syndrome, a very rare chromosome disorder, in a 2026 study. The syndrome brings drug-resistant epilepsy, learning disability, and repeated infections, hinting at immune faults beneath. Antibody sugar patterns from six patients were compared with those of healthy peers of like age.

Patient antibodies carried fewer of two sugar types, a pattern also seen in inflammatory autoimmune disease. The shift appeared in antibodies only, not in blood proteins as a whole, which marks it as selective. One patient improved on antibody infusion therapy, a clue the team follows for cause. The profile opens new angles on how the syndrome works and how it might be treated.
pmc-13298235:
Rice bran oil can be gelled into a spreadable fat using natural waxes, show Ali Yassoralipour and co-authors in a 2026 formulation study. They built thirteen oleogels with beeswax, carnauba wax, or blends of the two, and benchmarked them against commercial margarine.

Carnauba gels crystallized and melted at higher temperatures than beeswax gels, and the blends landed in between while forming connected crystal networks. More wax meant thicker, stronger gels, and the hybrids matched the hardness of stronger carnauba gels while binding over 94% of their oil. The gels carried more unsaturated fat than margarine but oxidized faster, a trade-off the authors flag for product development.
pmc-13299735:
Torben K. Heinbockel and Vonnie D. C. Shields review plant essential oils as options besides synthetic insect repellents, in a 2026 survey. These oils mask human scent or throw off insect scent detection, and many also fight microbes. Their green image and healing uses add buyer appeal beyond pest control.

Short protection time remains the chief weakness, since active compounds evaporate quickly. Coating and nano-scale delivery aim to stretch lasting power. Because oils are complex mixtures, resistance may evolve differently than against single-ingredient products. Commercial viability still needs wide safety testing, uniform comparisons against approved repellents, large field trials, and official sign-off.
pmc-13300435:
Nur Oğuz Davutoğlu and co-authors study inflammatory markers in immune thrombocytopenia, a disorder where the immune system destroys platelets, in a 2026 retrospective paper. The single-center review covered 166 adults diagnosed between January 2015 and December 2024, testing routine blood ratios and other laboratory values against complications, death, treatment response, and relapse.

Complications occurred in twelve percent of patients, and about seven percent died during the observation period. Death was tied to older age, male sex, and other illnesses, alongside lower hemoglobin and albumin and higher platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio and D-dimer levels. The standard inflammatory ratios showed little power for predicting complications, though the platelet ratio did track with mortality. Response to immunoglobulin therapy and later relapse each carried their own laboratory signatures. The authors suggest cheap routine tests can help sort patients by risk.
pmc-13300635:
Long exposure to homeopathic Gelsemium dilutions changed how cultured human nerve cells handle energy, Imane Lejri and colleagues report in a 2026 lab study. SH-SY5Y cells were kept for fourteen days with mixes diluted to 9C, 15C, and 30C strength. The team measured cell breathing, oxidant levels, survival, neurite growth, and two signaling proteins.

Treated cells made more ATP and drew more oxygen than untreated controls, while oxidant stress fell. They also survived better and grew longer neurites. Two switch proteins, Akt and mTOR, carried more phosphate tags, hinting at one shared control path behind the changes. The authors frame the work as early groundwork for studying stress-linked brain disorders in a dish.
pmc-13300935:
Andrei Mihnea Rosu and co-authors review catheter closure of paravalvular leaks with Amplatzer devices in a 2026 narrative review. These leaks around replacement heart valves can cause heart failure and blood cell destruction, and reopening the chest is risky after earlier surgery. The authors walk through device design, imaging guided strategy, and the registry and cohort evidence for a device family prized for fitting irregular, crescent shaped defects.

Reported results show high technical success with real relief of symptoms and hemolysis, plus reasonable medium term durability in well chosen patients. Outcomes still hinge on leak shape, the prosthesis involved, access route, imaging quality, and operator experience. The evidence base has no randomized trials, uses inconsistent outcome definitions, and rarely compares devices head to head over long periods. Even so, the authors keep Amplatzer platforms as a practical mainstay for complex leaks in experienced centers.
pmc-13301135:
Kidney care for IgA nephropathy is shifting from blanket support toward targeted attack, Abdulaziz Alroshodi charts in a 2026 review. The disease is the world's most common glomerulonephritis and a frequent road to kidney failure. Older care rested on blood pressure control, renin–angiotensin blockade, and steroids with their heavy side effects.

Newer supportive drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors and the dual blocker sparsentan, protect the kidney without suppressing immunity. Gut-targeted budesonide, complement inhibitors, and immune modulators now cut proteinuria in trials. Missing head-to-head comparisons, thin long-term safety data, and high prices still cloud choices, the author cautions, so careful rollout and more research remain essential.
pmc-13301535:
Heart fitness rebounds on a schedule after a heart attack, Kristina Skroce and colleagues chart in a 2026 rehabilitation study. Stable post-STEMI patients and inactive healthy adults both completed twelve weeks of supervised high-intensity interval training, four four-minute bouts per session, three times a week. Testing at four-week marks tracked fitness, heart function, blood markers, and walking distance.

Peak oxygen uptake rose about twenty-two percent in the heart group and twenty-three percent in controls by week twelve. Ejection fraction in patients jumped early, reaching 57.5 percent by week four, while a cardiac stress marker stayed flat and inflammation eased. Body fat and six-minute walk distance improved in both groups, supporting the program's safety in low-risk patients.
pmc-13301635:
E Efimova and co-authors ask whether switching off resynchronization pacing harms patients on heart pumps in a 2026 study. Most pump patients with these devices never responded, and its benefit on mechanical support is unproven. The center reviewed 158 patients. Forty-eight, about thirty percent, had the pacing switched off, most often for a failing left sided lead, at a median of about eighteen months.

Ventricular arrhythmia rates in the first year matched, near thirty-seven versus forty percent. Survival without transplant, though, favored switching off, with three year estimates around eighty-one percent against forty-nine percent. The link held after adjustment for sex, age, and disease type, while overall survival did not differ. The authors caution that reasons for switching off varied and the design looked back in time. Still, the data give no sign that turning the pacing off costs these patients rhythm safety.
pmc-13301735:
Alessandro de Sire and co-authors compare two rehab styles after steroid injections for chronic shoulder pain in a 2026 randomized pilot trial. Patients with subacromial bursitis and pain rated at least four of ten received three weekly ultrasound guided injections into the bursa. They then had ten sessions of proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, a hands on technique using diagonal movement patterns, or standard exercise based physiotherapy. Pain, disability, quality of life, and range of motion were tracked out to twenty-four weeks.

Both groups improved, which is the practical news: the injections plus either therapy helped. The facilitation group edged ahead on outcomes at some time points, functional scores and shoulder movement. The advantage never held across all the measures, so the authors refuse to declare a winner. Their summary is that facilitation may add something for certain patients and moments, and a larger trial would be needed to prove it.
pmc-13301835:
A A C Velraeds and colleagues describe the first Dutch experience, reported in 2026, with a leadless pacemaker placed in the heart's upper chamber. The device suits people whose natural pacemaker, the sinus node, works poorly. Older wired systems often pace the lower chamber unnecessarily, which can weaken the heart over time.

Ten patients received the atrial device from October 2024 onward, and every implant succeeded. Most had sinus node dysfunction, and several needed testing at multiple positions before fixation held. Threshold readings settled quickly, average projected battery life was just over nine years, and no complications appeared during short follow-up. No patient needed lower-chamber pacing, though the authors stress that a larger cohort must confirm these early results.
pmc-13302535:
S Kotoulas and co-authors analyse, in a 2026 sub-analysis, the rhythm drug flecainide in patients whose frequent extra heartbeats had already resisted beta-blockers. Heavy extra-beat burdens can weaken the heart, and guidelines place beta-blockers first despite limited effect. All patients in the parent study had declined catheter ablation.

Patients with earlier beta-blocker exposure numbered thirty-two, against fifty-six who had never taken one. Flecainide cut burden by about eighty percent on average in the pre-treated group, and nearly two thirds of them achieved at least a ninety percent reduction. Results in the never-treated group were somewhat weaker, and adding a beta-blocker alongside gave no extra gain. No major side effects occurred during follow-up.
pmc-13303235:
Older heart patients sort into three tiers of medication safety skill at home, Furong Jiang and colleagues map in a 2026 survey from a Sichuan hospital. Three hundred ninety-three patients who had undergone coronary stenting answered scales on medication competence, health literacy, and family functioning between February and June 2025. Latent profile analysis carved the population into competence groups.

Just thirteen percent landed in the high-competence tier, while thirty-one percent sat low and the rest in between. Schooling, age, health literacy, family support, and how often relatives remind patients about pills separated the groups. The authors recommend tiered nursing follow-up that strengthens literacy and recruits the family.
pmc-13303635:
Jinlong Gao, Lulu Yan, and Jun Ma report a 2026 study of magnetic carbon particles designed to split water out of heavy oil mixtures. Stable water-in-oil blends resist separation and slow transport and refining, and earlier magnetic particles performed poorly on heavy oil.

Particles coated with polyethyleneimine were made and tested by the standard bottle method. At a modest dose, the treated blend cleared water well within an hour at moderate heat. Microscope views showed particles rushing to the oil-water boundary and breaking the surface film through charge effects and hydrogen bonding. Better green separators for the oil industry could follow.
pmc-13303935:
Li Dai and Xiaoyan Sun review smart drug carriers that release antibiotics only where infection cues appear, in a 2026 synthesis on drug-resistant infections. Standard antibiotics spread through the whole body, often missing infection sites while exposing harmless microbes.

Infected tissue tends to be acidic, rich in reactive oxygen, and full of germ-linked enzymes, and carriers can be built to react to each signal. The review compares passive carriers, triggered carriers, and free drugs, and weighs barriers such as biofilms, hidden germs inside cells, and drug pumps. Triggered release could raise local doses while sparing the rest of the body.
pmc-13304935:
Yousun An, Nicholas Norris, Donglai Li, and Jenny E. Gunton review ketogenic diets for obesity and diabetes in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Cutting carbs sharply shifts the body from burning sugar toward burning fat and making ketone fuels.

That shift may dull hunger, ease weight loss, and improve sugar control and insulin response. Lower insulin demand could also rest the insulin-making pancreas cells. Pairing the diet with diabetes drugs may add benefit, but one drug family raises a rare acid-buildup risk needing close watching. Gut microbe changes, long-term safety, and staying power remain open questions.
pmc-13305235:
Karol Skotniczny leads a 2026 randomized comparison of how sweat loss during exercise affects thigh muscle tissue by starting hydration level. Hard exercise drying the body by a few percent can dull performance, but resting tissue effects were unclear.

Thirty active men were split between guided drinking and normal habits, checked weekly by urine strength. All cycled at half power until losing about three percent of body weight. Ultrasound stiffness measures and twitch tests covered the front thigh muscle and nearby layers before and after. Only the deep wrapping layer softened after exercise, regardless of group. Twitch traits held steady.
pmc-13306035:
André Pereira and a large Portuguese team test in 2026 whether an invasive freshwater clam can polish municipal wastewater for reuse. Corbicula fluminea filters large volumes, so the team exposed clams to real secondary-treated effluent carrying drug residues and resistant bacteria. They also tracked changes in the clams' own tissues and microbes.

Within a day, clams removed more than seventy percent of three tracked chemical contaminants, with average removal near thirty-nine percent overall. Counts of multidrug-resistant bacteria fell significantly despite real wastewater slowing clearance. Clam tissues recovered their microbe counts and community mix after exposure. Giving an invasive species a useful treatment role could aid control efforts, the authors argue. The work frames biofiltration as a low-technology polishing step for water reuse.
pmc-13306135:
Victoria Fleming-Batayneh and a large consortium examine inflammation in 188 adults with Down syndrome in a 2026 analysis. Adults in this group often carry extra weight and face early Alzheimer disease pathology, both tied to inflammation. Blood markers were compared with body mass, age, and brain amyloid measured by PET scans.

Most participants met criteria for obesity, and higher body mass linked consistently to higher levels of several inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Older age related mainly to higher beta-2 microglobulin. Amyloid burden showed a narrower link, with interleukin-6 only. The authors highlight weight monitoring and management as the clearest lever for lowering inflammation in this population. They call for later work on brain inflammation as Alzheimer pathology advances.
pmc-13306735:
Sharafa Bankole modelled signal distortion in 5G transmitters with two linked neural networks in a 2026 study. Power amplifiers bend signals in ways that shift with past input, and one giant network wastes computing power on field hardware.

The cascaded design splits the job between two smaller real-valued networks, each handling part of the dynamic behaviour. Accuracy held while total parameter count fell sharply against a single large model in reported comparisons. The authors argue the split approach suits base stations and other gear where space and energy stay tight.
pmc-13307635:
Castilla Bolanos and co-authors measure the chemistry of lab grown mini brains in this 2026 paper. Cerebral organoids are small brain like tissues grown from human stem cells. They offer a way to study human brain metabolism without animal models. The team applied a specialised magnetic resonance method that reads metabolite levels in intact tissue.

They identified and quantified 17 metabolites in organoids aged from 85 to 312 days. The chemical profile resembled fetal rather than adult human brain. Lactate ran high, two amino acid signals sat at near equal levels, a maturity marker stayed low, and an unusual compound called hypotaurine was abundant. Castilla Bolanos presents the pipeline as a platform for studying how metabolism goes wrong in brain disease models.
pmc-13308035:
Magda López Saldaña and colleagues report in 2026 a seventy-eight-year-old man whose oesophagus turned black and necrotic a week after heart attack care complicated by cardiogenic shock. He returned to hospital vomiting blood and unstable. Endoscopy showed extensive dead tissue in the lower gullet ending sharply at the stomach junction.

Scanning confirmed wall thickening without perforation, which kept surgery off the table. Care rested the gullet completely with intravenous feeding, strong acid suppression, and support for cardiac output. A repeat endoscopy seven days later found the lesions fully healed. The condition kills often, but deaths usually stem from the underlying illnesses rather than the gullet itself. The authors credit fast stabilisation of blood flow plus conservative treatment. Their review places the case within the two-hit idea of poor perfusion meeting acid injury.
pmc-13308235:
Stephanie Ali Fairbairn and colleagues link a gene regulator called Kaiso in 2026 to why some triple-negative breast cancers hide the androgen receptor that drugs could target. Tumour data from women of African ancestry and white women were compared, since the first group carries a heavier burden of this cancer type. Laboratory knockouts tested cause and effect.

High Kaiso with low androgen receptor tracked with poorer survival across breast cancer subtypes. Women of African ancestry showed lower receptor levels and more of the fully negative subtype. Removing Kaiso in cancer cells raised receptor expression, weakened a metastasis-linked target gene, and made cells more sensitive to the receptor blocker enzalutamide. Migration and invasion also fell after knockout. The authors propose Kaiso itself as a drug target for these hard-to-treat cancers.
pmc-13309235:
Loay Soliman, Mohamed Elramly, and Ahmed Shehatah scan in 2026 the right side of the heart in 150 hypertensive patients over forty, asking how left-sided thickening spills across. Dual-source CT measured left muscle mass, wall patterns, and right chamber volumes and pumping strength. Hypertension research usually stops at the left ventricle.

About half the patients kept normal left geometry, while the rest split among three abnormal patterns. Heavier left ventricles correlated with larger right volumes and weaker right pumping on both measures used. Right function declined step by step from normal geometry toward concentric hypertrophy, the most severe pattern. The authors read the pattern as early two-sided heart involvement in hypertension. Spotting left remodelling early, they argue, could flag patients before right heart failure, a known marker of poor outcomes, sets in.
pmc-13309635:
Morteza Hadizadeh and co-authors trace gene activity tied to the GFAP gene across glioma stages in a 2026 study. Gliomas, above all glioblastoma, mix many cell types, which fuels drug resistance and return after treatment. GFAP marks star-shaped brain support cells and may shape tumor cell paths.

Single-cell gene data from a public set were merged and grouped with standard software. Tumor cells, immune cells, and support-cell precursors formed clear groups in grade III tumors, new glioblastomas, and returned tumors alike. Six genes stayed shared and steady across all stages, with activity tied to tumor persistence and return. Path modeling showed support-like cells shifting toward cancer cells. The authors flag the shared genes as leads.
pmc-13309835:
Muhammad Shoaib Khan and colleagues follow 220 patients in Peshawar in 2026 through eight weeks of vonoprazan, a strong acid-blocking drug, for erosive inflammation of the gullet. Everyone received the same daily dose, and repeat camera examination graded healing against the Los Angeles scale. Sex and the presence of a hiatus hernia were tested as outcome shapers.

Nearly eighty-seven percent finished treatment with no visible erosion, a high healing rate for a group where over half began at severe grades. Healing was essentially identical in men and women. Hernia changed the picture sharply: about sixty percent of hernia patients cleared fully, against about ninety-six percent without hernia. The drug blocks acid by a newer mechanism than standard suppressors, acting faster and longer. The authors recommend it broadly while flagging hernia patients for closer follow-up.
pmc-13310035:
Toktam Pour and five co-authors map the late effects that follow colorectal cancer years later, in a 2026 scoping review. Survival keeps improving, so more people live long enough to meet problems that emerge five or more years after diagnosis. The review searched three databases for studies reporting late effects with risk estimates against cancer-free controls. Nine observational studies qualified, and their quality was scored with a standard scale.

The synthesis gathers which late effects are documented, from new cancers to organ damage, and what raises the risk. Long-term survivors are often discharged from close follow-up just as these risks ripen. A clear map helps survivorship clinics decide what to keep screening for, and for how long.
pmc-13310435:
Kanyanuth Boonyoung and co-authors pool global data on dry mouth in older adults, in a 2026 review. Aging brings body changes that often harm oral health. Two related problems are xerostomia, the feeling of a dry mouth, and hyposalivation, truly low saliva flow. Both can erode daily quality of life.

The team searched four large databases for studies of adults aged sixty and older. Studies tied to diseases or radiation known to dry the mouth were left out. Over one hundred studies with a huge pooled sample were kept after quality checks. Statistical pooling gave overall rates for both problems. Subgroup checks then hunted for reasons the rates varied so much between studies and places.
pmc-13310635:
Ruchik Kevadiya and co-authors report appendix tissue disease that imitated appendicitis in a young woman in a 2026 case article. Endometriosis usually grows inside the pelvis, but rare growths on the appendix can trigger right-sided belly pain that looks surgical. Missing the true cause risks the wrong operation plan.
