The 19-year-old arrived with right belly pain, nausea, and lightheadedness, plus tenderness and a classic stretch sign on examination. Blood tests showed no infection signal, and scans suggested either appendicitis or a burst ovarian cyst. Surgery found blood in the belly, endometriosis spots, and a likely burst follicle, and tissue study proved endometriosis on the appendix surface. The authors urge keeping the diagnosis in mind for young women.
pmc-13310735:
Chunli Lu and colleagues study how parenting passes across three generations in Chinese families in a 2026 survey. Grandparent style may shape parent style, which then links to child behavior. The team asked how family closeness or conflict carries that chain, and how the chain relates to inward and outward child problems.

Data came from 2,120 families with children, parents, and reports on the oldest generation. Warm and firm parenting passed on through family affection, then linked to fewer child problems. Harsh control passed on through family conflict, then linked to more child problems. Strengthening warm firm care and breaking harsh cycles may help the youngest group.
pmc-13310835:
Amr Ali Mohamed Abdelgawwad El-Sehrawy and co-authors review clot risk in blood cancers called myeloproliferative neoplasms in a 2026 paper. These cancers carry a high clot burden that blood counts and heart risk factors fail to explain. Mutant blood cells may drive swelling that in turn feeds both clone growth and clotting.

A sensor inside cells, the NLRP3 inflammasome, sits at the center of the proposed loop. Mutant stem cells, swollen white cells, sticky platelets, and vessel walls form what the authors call a thrombotic niche. Standard cell lowering care leaves much risk behind. Drugs that calm swelling or block the sensor look promising but lack direct trial proof.
pmc-13310935:
Máté Krisztián Kardos and a large team publish river basin chemistry data from Central Europe in a 2026 dataset paper. Two farm heavy catchments, the Koppány in Hungary and the Ledava in Slovenia, face waste inputs and erosion. Tracing how pollutants move needs matched data across rain, water, soil, and sediment.

Sampling covered calm flows and flood peaks, with grab and automatic river sampling plus passive sediment traps. Labs measured major ions, nutrients, toxic elements, rare earths, and stable and radioactive isotopes. Fine soil and sediment parts were used for solid tests. Open data support checks of transport models at catchment scale.
pmc-13311135:
Jia Hui Megan Loh and co-authors report pregnancy care in a woman with a rare sugar processing disorder in a 2026 case study. Mannose phosphate isomerase deficiency harms protein coating in the body but spares brain growth, and oral mannose treats it well. Proof for pregnancy care is scarce, and mannose is often stopped for safety doubts.

The woman was diagnosed in infancy and took mannose through childhood, with spotty use as an adult. Liver scarring, gut protein loss, bone thinning, and anemia built up over years. Two pregnancies without mannose both ended in emergency cesarean births of healthy infants, though the first held more complications. Team care and liver checks proved vital.
pmc-13311935:
Natalie Finch comments in a 2026 article on a grounded theory study of psychiatric nurses caring for patients with both mental illness and addiction. Such patients fare worse across health domains, and nurse stigma can block good care.

The discussed study by Bertrand and Morvillers gathered nurse views inside psychiatric settings. Finch draws practice lessons: staff need quality supervision plus training and backing to use proven behavior change methods. For research, she urges multi-site, long-term studies that can weigh the many factors shaping nurse experience. Better support for nurses, the note argues, is a patient safety issue too.
pmc-13312235:
Kap Sum Foong and colleagues write a 2026 letter to the editor on penicillin allergy labels and antibiotic prescribing inside prisons and jails. Stewardship work has largely skipped carceral settings, even though infections and antibiotic exposure run high there and resistance spreads easily in crowded, under-resourced facilities.

Working from a statewide census of 20,483 people held by the Wisconsin Department of Corrections from 2021 to 2023, the authors found allergy labels in 1,852 people, or 9.0 percent, close to general population estimates. They then built a matched cohort of people with and without labels to compare prescribing, sorting antibiotics by their risk of fueling Clostridioides difficile infection. The letter extends the team's earlier finding that labels push prescribers toward riskier drugs, this time with population-level prevalence behind it.
pmc-13312335:
Gamze Ergun and co-authors examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether simple blood complement levels can forecast the course of IgA nephropathy, the world's most common primary glomerular kidney disease. Complement activation helps drive the disease, but whether serum C3, C4, and their ratio predict outcomes was unsettled.

The single-center study followed 116 biopsy-proven patients for a median of 37.5 months, and 39 of them lost at least half their kidney function or reached end-stage disease. Those patients started with lower serum C3 and a lower C3/C4 ratio, while C4 alone did not differ. Both markers also tracked with biopsy severity features, and low values marked worse kidney survival. The authors propose C3 and the ratio as extra prognostic markers beside established ones.
pmc-13312535:
Ming Ge and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, a living delivery system that protects farmed shrimp against covert mortality nodavirus. Viral disease inflicts heavy losses on aquaculture, and this virus drives a covert mortality syndrome in the widely farmed shrimp Penaeus vannamei. The team built an RNA interference defense carried by the shrimp's own live feed.

Using a piggyBac transposon platform, they engineered the rotifer Brachionus plicatilis to stably produce short hairpin RNA matched to the virus, first proving heritable gene expression in this non-model organism. Shrimp fed the engineered rotifers carried significantly lower viral loads on PCR testing, and under deliberate virus challenge they died at lower cumulative rates than controls, with no harm to growth. The authors propose transgenic rotifers as a scalable hatchery platform for antiviral protection.
pmc-13312635:
Adam Numis and co-authors hunt for blood markers that can warn which newborns will develop epilepsy after a brain injury with seizures. Their 2026 study drew on two hospital cohorts of infants with seizures confirmed by brain-wave monitoring. Doctors now lack a sound way to spot the highest-risk babies early.

Blood samples taken within days of the seizures were tested for proteins tied to swelling and nerve injury. Babies who later developed epilepsy had higher levels of two such markers in both cohorts. Adding the markers to standard clinical signs sharply improved risk forecasts. Related gene-signal patterns also differed between the groups. The authors say a blood test could one day guide closer follow-up for the infants most at risk.
pmc-13312835:
Yuelin Wang and colleagues explore, in a 2026 study, whether an artificial intelligence reading of eye photographs can estimate arterial stiffness without the usual dedicated device. Pulse wave velocity is the gold standard for stiffness and a strong cardiovascular risk marker, but it needs special equipment. The retina, meanwhile, offers a direct window on small blood vessels that a camera and algorithm can reach anywhere.

The team gathered patients at Peking University Third Hospital who had fundus photos and velocity testing over five years. The system measured vessel patterns, optic disc shape, and lesion counts automatically. In a training set of 3,088 visits, stiffness tracked with vessel density, artery-to-vein ratios, curvature, and deposits on the retina. Predicted values agreed well with measured pulse wave velocity in validation, supporting eye-based screening as a telemedicine route to cardiovascular risk checks.
pmc-13312935:
Man Amanat and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study, rapid whole-genome sequencing for hospitalized adults whose neurological problems defy ordinary workups. Such patients often endure long, expensive evaluations without an answer. Evidence for fast genome sequencing in adults, as opposed to sick infants, has stayed limited, so the team reviewed a structured program at Mayo Clinic.

Between June 2022 and September 2025, 96 inpatients completed rapid sequencing, and 57 of them formed the neurology cohort analyzed here. Thirteen of those 57, or 22.8 percent, received a genetic diagnosis that matched their presentation, spread across genes including IFIH1, C9orf72, and FGF14. The authors also hunted for clinical features that predict a positive result and tracked how often the answer changed management, aiming to show where rapid sequencing earns its place in adult neurology.
pmc-13313235:
Lesley Bell-Sakyi heads a team that built new fly cell lines in a 2026 paper, working with Drosophila willistoni, a tropical fruit fly from Costa Rica. Hundreds of fly cell lines exist, yet nearly all come from one species, Drosophila melanogaster, and none from tropical flies.

A simple method turned three larval cultures into lasting lines named DWL/LULS68, DWL/LULS70, and DWL/LULS72. All three carried Wolbachia, a bacterium that lives inside fly cells, typed as strain wWil. Long treatment with tetracycline cleared the bacterium and gave clean sublines from each line. Gene tests, chromosome counts, and probe staining proved the cells truly came from D. willistoni. The lines are expected to aid study of this species and its bacterial partners in many ways.
pmc-13313335:
Connor R. King and colleagues propose a new account of a gene-reading pattern in a class of RNA viruses in a paper from 2026. These nonsegmented negative-strand RNA viruses read their genes in a fading gradient, with early genes read most and later genes read less.

The old stop-start account blames the copying enzyme pausing at gene joints. The team instead built the RNA Polymerase Association Mechanism model, a random-process frame with two settings for how far the enzyme holds on and how much it can backtrack. The model matched the fading pattern across many such viruses and in shuffled variants of the VSV virus. Its process measure also tracked with genome length, as the authors report. A shared mechanism across this virus class could sharpen antiviral design.
pmc-13314335:
Breeding buffalo in Indonesia depends on semen that survives freezing well, and breeds may differ in that trait. Sigit Bintara and co-authors studied three local breeds in 2025, Silangit, Toraja, and Sapala. They measured thawed sperm quality with computer tools and profiled the small molecules in the semen with high-resolution lab methods.

Silangit bulls showed higher sperm viability and membrane integrity, while the other breeds had fewer abnormal sperm shapes. Each breed also carried its own pair of marker molecules, tied to energy use, membrane repair, or defense against cell damage. Tests confirmed the markers could sort the breeds. The authors say such markers could guide fertility prediction and selective breeding.
pmc-13314735:
Heather E. Whitson and a large team compare two ways to score physical resilience in older adults in their 2026 study. Resilience here means how fully a person bounces back after a health stress, a key idea in aging and frailty research.

The team used data from 170 older adults who had planned knee replacement, tracking pain interference over 6 months after surgery. One method draws the recovery path itself; the other grades recovery against what was expected. The 10 people rated high by the path method also beat hopes by the second method, as the authors report. Among 82 people rated moderate, the second method spread widely, and among 78 rated low most matched too, by the counts given. The check helps aging studies pick a measure.
pmc-13315135:
Andrej Teren and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether blood biomarkers can sharpen two decisions in chronic coronary syndrome: who has obstructed arteries, and who gains from reopening them. The team enrolled 2,251 patients undergoing coronary angiography for disease and measured five biomarkers, then followed the cohort for a median of 12.6 years. Obstructive disease, at least half blockage of a major vessel, was present in 888 patients, or 39.4 percent of the group.

For diagnosis, only high-sensitivity troponin T added information, and its help grew as clinical likelihood shrank, boosting accuracy by 10.4 percent in the lowest-likelihood group. For prognosis, NT-proBNP dominated, predicting death across every treatment path. A threshold of 150 picograms per milliliter split the cohort sharply. Below it, survival was good with or without reopening. Above it, risk soared nearly sixfold yet revascularization cut mortality by about forty percent. The authors propose the pair as a triage duo.
pmc-13315435:
Nayeem Mia and co-authors review in 2026 how to set up safe cell lines and cell banks for cultivated meat. Cells grown for food need the same care as any starter culture, since contamination, stray agents, genetic drift, and tumor-like growth could all affect safety and quality.

Comparing regulatory filings showed wide gaps in how cell lines are checked and banked, and no shared food-grade standard exists yet. That gap creates doubt for regulators and slows sales across borders. The authors propose a risk-based framework for food-safe cell lines and banking to guide future shared rules.
pmc-13315535:
Xuetao Liu and co-authors asked in 2026 whether a protease enzyme that survives feed pelleting can still lift amino acid use in broilers. Enzymes often lose power during feed making, so the team first screened thirteen serine proteases with a cold pelleting method and picked three with low, medium, and high tolerance.

Day-old chicks then got normal-protein feed, low-protein feed, or low-protein feed plus one protease, as mash or pellets, for 14 days. Pellet feed raised daily gain compared with mash, and no diet-by-form interplay appeared for growth or digestibility. The setup tests whether heat-tough enzymes keep their benefit in real pellet diets.
pmc-13315935:
Mengmeng Wei, Chunyan Wang, Sheng Geng, and Benguo Liu used natural deep eutectic solvents in 2026 to pull protein from safflower seeds in a greener way. Of five betaine-based mixes, betaine with glycerol at a one-to-two ratio worked best, giving protein of 85.66 percent purity and a 56.66 percent yield.

Tuning raised yield to 66.45 percent at 29 percent water, 52 degrees, and a one-to-twenty-four solid-to-liquid ratio. Compared with the standard alkali and acid method, the new extract was lighter in color. It kept more helix structure and intact subunits, and beat it on solubility, emulsifying, and foaming at low pH, plus oil holding.
pmc-13316535:
Andrew Duncombe wrote a 2026 editorial opening a themed issue on acute medical units, arguing that senior doctors must make key choices right at the hospital front door. He compares a delayed expert reply to a letter left sitting in an inbox, where slow action brings poorer results.

The issue, guest edited by Anika Wijewardane, gathers best practice on unit leadership, digital systems, bedside testing, and care centered on patients, plus a debate on virtual wards. Duncombe also flags wider journal content on health systems, training, and quality work, and notes a call to train more bioinformatics specialists for the health service's digital shift. His message is simple: early expert judgment sets the tone for the whole stay.
pmc-13316835:
Pushpita Roy, Syed Md Asadul Hoque, and Wai Wai Mroy report a 2026 case of Wilms' tumor, a childhood kidney cancer. It arose in a 26-year-old South Asian woman during her second trimester of pregnancy. Adult cases are vanishingly rare, and pregnancy narrows every treatment choice.

A large mass behind the abdomen was found by chance, and surgeons removed the kidney during pregnancy. Tissue checks confirmed high-risk nephroblastoma. Close monitoring followed, and she delivered a healthy early baby by cesarean section, then began chemotherapy. Despite surgery and several drug rounds, the cancer spread widely and care turned palliative, with some symptom relief. The case stresses team care and swift action to protect both mother and child.
pmc-13317335:
Nana Akwasi Owusu Mensah and a Ghanaian team measure, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how much childhood sight loss drags down quality of life. Eye problems can stall learning and play, yet Ghanaian evidence on the lived burden was scarce.

In Ashanti Region districts, 581 children aged 2 to 18 years received full eye exams and quality-of-life scoring across body, feelings, friends, and school. Children with sight loss scored lower in every area, by both their own and parents' reports, with school and feelings hit hardest. Sight loss predicted poorer overall scores even after adjustment, while social factors like sex and insurance did not. The authors press for earlier detection and school vision support.
pmc-13317535:
Yanyu Hu and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether early change during talk therapy for insomnia predicts who ends well, better than starting scores alone. The therapy is the first-line cure for chronic insomnia, yet a third of patients finish poorly.

Records covered 1,059 patients who completed face-to-face group therapy, with outcomes checked right after treatment and a year later. Models adding early treatment data beat baseline-only models for short-term results, lifting accuracy from 0.630 to 0.741 in the test set, and week-two sleep score change was the single best signal. For the year mark, the edge faded and age led instead. A two-week check-in, they suggest, can flag who needs a plan change early.
pmc-13320035:
Martin Petermann, Puneet Monga and Géza Pap report, in 2026, early results for custom-made shoulder socket implants in patients with severe bone loss. Reverse shoulder replacement needs a stable socket component, yet badly worn sockets defeat standard implants. Patient-specific implants promise precise fit and firm initial fixation, but clinical evidence is scarce.

The first twelve patients at one institution were followed for an average of three years. Standard shoulder scores and movement in every direction improved significantly from before surgery. X-rays showed no loosening or bone dissolving around implants, though mild notching appeared in some patients. Complications affected a quarter of the group, including one dislocation, one blood collection and one arm bone fracture. The authors call the results promising while urging longer follow-up.
pmc-13320235:
Seung Hyun Han and co-authors study heart drugs called beta blockers in kidney patients with no past heart disease in a 2026 national records study from Korea. Kidney illness lifts heart risk, and these drugs are widely used to guard the heart, yet their worth when no heart disease has yet shown was in doubt.

Insurance data from 2012 to 2015 found kidney patients with low filter rates, then matched drug users to non users in a one to two ratio. After matching, 9067 users and 17094 non users were tracked for death and major heart events. Users faced higher risks on both counts in the matched counts, with the gap widest at the lowest filter rates. One drug in the class stood out with higher harm than its peers.
pmc-13320335:
Kavish A.V. Kohabir and co-authors build a gene scissor test for a common herpes virus that skips the copy step in a 2026 proof of concept study. The virus hides for life in blood cells and can wake to harm unborn babies and people with weak immune defenses. Finding its DNA in blood at the bedside is hard because levels run tiny and strands come broken, which breaks copy based tests.

Their test uses the scissor enzyme own signal boost, aimed at many virus sites at once to lift catch rates. One enzyme variant cut a bright tag four times faster than standard tags, which pushed the catch floor to a very low level in bulk tests. A chip version kept the sharpness, a step toward cheap point of care checks.
pmc-13320435:
Yanan Sun and co-authors rewire a giant enzyme line that builds a ring shaped antibiotic in a 2026 study. The line is a chain of work stations that pass a growing chain along and snip it into a ring at the end, and its huge size makes redesign risky. A rare triple end station layout was found in this line, which hinted the end station could be moved without breaking the ring step.

The end station was shifted to new spots along the line in a set of rebuilt lines, and each still cut rings, now with set backbone lengths by design. The cutter kept its taste for the same anchor point across all lengths tested. Moving end stations may be a clean way to mint new ring drugs.
pmc-13321435:
Yu and co-authors studied whether a needle biopsy changes the readings of a special scan in thyroid cancer, in a paper published in 2026. The scan uses a two-layer detector to measure tissue traits in numbers. The biopsy draws cells through a thin needle and is a standard step in diagnosis. If the needle pass stirs bleeding or swelling, the scan numbers after it might mislead. The team reviewed 689 patients with this cancer.

Patients fell into two groups: scanned before the biopsy (222) or after it (467). The team matched the groups on other traits so the comparison stayed fair. They also ran extra checks that weight cases to balance the groups. The goal was to learn whether biopsy order shifts the numbers, and when scanning is best timed. The answer helps clinics order the two tests so that scan-based judgments stay sound.
pmc-13321535:
Tao Wang and six co-authors test whether a brain aging score from MRI scans can forecast how stroke patients fare. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The score compares the brain's predicted age with the person's real age, and a big gap signals faster aging.

The team studied one hundred fifty patients with acute stroke from blocked vessels. Those in the faster-aging group arrived with worse stroke scores and larger areas of damage. They also carried more small vessel disease in the brain. A year later, that group had worse function and lower thinking test scores. Stroke severity at arrival and white matter damage each predicted the one-year outcome on their own.
pmc-13322935:
Yehinson Barajas Ramón and colleagues review heat imaging in soccer, in a 2026 systematic review on fatigue, injury risk and recovery. Following PRISMA guidance, they searched major databases to June 2025 and judged study quality with standard tools.

From 510 records, 20 studies of high method quality remained. Those studies used infrared thermography to read skin temperature as a sign of structural or metabolic fatigue, to flag injury risk factors and to follow recovery after training and matches. The authors judge the tool valid, reliable and non-invasive for these tasks, while noting that study designs and measures varied. Standard routines for imaging and reading would help teams compare results.
pmc-13323135:
Shuangrui Sui and co-authors relate resilience and social support to mental health in breast cancer, in a 2026 analysis of 1,052 inpatients and follow-up patients. Data came from a parent care-management project, with scales for resilience, support, anxiety, depression, fear of progression and symptom burden.

Resilience linked only weakly to social support, yet linked clearly to lower anxiety, depression and fear of progression in their correlations. Regression models gave resilience a stronger weight than social support for mental outcomes. A four-quadrant model, splitting patients by physical symptom burden and psychological status, sorted clinically distinct risk profiles. The authors propose using that split to target support where both burdens run high.
pmc-13323235:
Xiang Chen and co-authors show that a VEGFR3 blocker can undo drug resistance driven by the ABCG2 pump, in a 2026 cell study. Overactive ABCG2, also called breast cancer resistance protein, pushes chemotherapy drugs out of cancer cells and drives failure in lung, breast and colon cancers.

In lung and colorectal lines bred to overexpress ABCG2, the compound (S)-SAR131675 restored sensitivity to pump-carried drugs such as mitoxantrone and topotecan. Intracellular drug levels rose because efflux slowed, while the amount and location of ABCG2 protein stayed unchanged. The team presents the compound as a lead for treatments that pair resistance reversal with cancer therapy.
pmc-13324135:
Zhenzhen Zhao and team issued a correction to their earlier paper on how TGF-beta drives pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition in subretinal fibrosis through the Smad2/3 and Akt/mTOR pathways. The 2026 notice, published in Experimental and Molecular Medicine, addresses a single figure error in the original 2022 article. It states plainly what went wrong and what was fixed, without revising any of the paper's claims.

In Figure 4c, the fibronectin staining image for the rapamycin-treated group had been replaced by mistake with a duplicate of the DMSO control image. The corrected version restores the proper original image for that panel. The authors stress that the fix concerns representative illustration only and leaves all data analyses, results, interpretations, and conclusions untouched. Readers should therefore treat the original findings as unchanged, with only the figure panel corrected.
pmc-13324435:
Suzanne M Underhill and Susan G Amara issue a 2026 correction to their study of acetylcholine receptor stimulation and dopamine transporter internalisation. Figure 1A as published contained a mistake: its first two panels, showing TH and DAT immunolabelling, had already appeared in a prior publication.

A corrected figure and legend replace the faulty panels. The legend reports that, in primary midbrain cultures, PMA and carbachol cut dopamine transport through a protein kinase C route, since the blocker BIM stopped their effect. Amphetamine and methamphetamine also cut transport, but BIM did not block them, pointing to separate internalisation paths. The notice closes by stating the original article has been updated.
pmc-13325135:
Nicholas M. Marshall and co-authors design polyurethane foams that fall apart at low heat in a 2026 materials study. Standard foam packaging is a thermoset that resists recycling, which blocks foam-in-place packing for risky cargo.

New foams used polyols built from polypropylene carbonate and fresh polycarbonate designs meant to break down easily. Foams blown with the usual water and MDI mix degraded poorly. Cutting the water and isocyanate blowing share improved breakdown a lot. A strong acid catalyst and aliphatic isocyanates in place of aromatic ones helped further. The authors see uses in low-waste packaging and in wrapping hazardous loads that must later be freed cleanly.
pmc-13325735:
Keisuke Tachiyama and co-authors measure fading nerve responses in spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy in a 2026 study. The fading pattern is well known in ALS, but its spread in this slower, X-linked motor neuron disease was unmapped.

Records covered 40 patients tested with 3 Hz stimulation on five muscles. Every patient showed a drop over 5 percent in at least one muscle. Shoulder and upper arm muscles faded most often, with the deltoid at 86 percent and the trapezius at 70 percent of patients. Hand muscles trailed at 37 and 25 percent for the two sites. The deltoid drop was also the largest. The pattern mirrors ALS despite the gentler course.
pmc-13326335:
Wu Yinhang and three co-authors review the forgotten kingdom in colorectal cancer: the fungi of the gut, in a 2026 paper. Bacteria dominate microbiome research, but fungi are the gut's second-largest eukaryotic residents.

Cancer patients carry a skewed fungal community. Certain harmful species, including Aspergillus types, grow richer as tumors advance. Friendly fungi thin out, losing their protective effect. The imbalance may feed tumors directly and by rewiring bacteria-fungi teamwork and local immunity. The review gathers the species patterns and their links to clinical features. It closes on promise and difficulty: fungal markers for diagnosis, and therapies that tune the fungal mix.
pmc-13326435:
Nuha Al-Aghbari, Arif Maldar, and Mubashir Angolkar study who died of COVID-19 in one Indian hospital in a 2026 paper. Age and other illnesses are known risks, but how they combine was less clear. The team reviewed 642 confirmed patients admitted in Belagavi during late 2020 and 2021.

Patients aged fifty and over had about double the odds of dying compared with younger patients. Breathlessness and kidney disease were strong warning signs, and higher blood sugar and pulse each added risk. Having several illnesses at once did not raise risk on its own in the main model. No clear interplay between age and multiple illness was found, though older patients with many illnesses still faced the highest predicted risk.
pmc-13327435:
Hannah Alderson and four co-authors check whether a magnetic resonance measure still reads axon width after spinal cord injury, in a 2026 study. The measure, a change in water diffusion over time, promises a non-invasive ruler for nerve fibers.

Rats received a contusion injury, and eight weeks later their cords were scanned and then examined under electron microscopy. The diffusion measure tracked true axon diameter strongly across regions near the injury. Two relaxation-based measures did not. One relaxation measure did relate to the diffusion measure itself, suggesting they sense different tissue traits. The authors call the diffusion ruler robust under injury conditions. That supports its use in tracking damage and repair.
pmc-13327535:
Samarpita Sen and Daniel St Johnston report a cautionary finding on a popular protein-mapping method in a 2026 study. Peroxidase-based proximity labelling tags nearby proteins with biotin, and users assume the tag spreads only about 20 nanometres. Working in fly follicle tissue, they marked proteins at the top, side, and base of cells.

Standard conditions gave a strong base signal even when the tagged protein sat at the top or side, because the reactive radicals travel many micrometres rather than dying out fast. The basement membrane soaked up radicals, acting as a sink. Lowering the label dose or shortening reaction times restored faithful maps, so the authors urge careful tuning before trusting spatial results.
pmc-13328335:
Jie Zhang studies socio-emotional learning inside physical education in a 2026 survey analysis. Lessons that build emotional and social skills are spreading through school subjects, and PE offers a natural stage for them. Data came from 452 high school students aged 14 to 18 across three Chinese provinces, using checked self-report scales.

Emotional regulation carried the link between such learning and student wellbeing, while peer relationship quality did not act as a clear go-between in the models. School climate changed the strength of the route: supportive schools showed a stronger indirect effect through emotion control. Building feelings skills into gym class pays off most where the wider school feels safe and warm, Zhang concludes.
pmc-13328435:
Keyi Dong and co-authors pool evidence on a nutrition index as a heart failure forecast in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The prognostic nutritional index, built from albumin and lymphocyte counts, had given mixed signals across studies. Searches through March 2025 found fourteen cohort studies with 14,166 patients.

Patients with higher index values died less often overall, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.72 against lower scorers, and heart-related death also ran lower, at 0.77 on the same scale in their pooling. First hospital stays for heart failure were less likely too, with an odds ratio of 0.73 across the studies. A two-part blood score may earn a routine place in risk talks.
pmc-13328635:
Shuai Li and co-authors calculate how thick a wall of rock must separate an open pit's slope from the underground workings eating toward it. Their 2026 study models a Chinese mine where a hanging-wall orebody is recovered beneath a slope, simulating five isolation pillar thicknesses with three-dimensional software and a strength reduction method.

All five designs passed the formal stability grade, but deformation told the real story. At thirty meters of pillar, maximum displacement collapsed from over eighty millimeters to about thirty-four; thicker pillars bought little more. Stress and plastic zone patterns at that thickness stayed safely contained. The authors recommend roughly thirty meters as the balance point between slope safety and ore recovery, since every extra meter of pillar is ore left in the ground forever. Mining design is full of such thresholds; this paper prices one precisely.
pmc-13328735:
A birch bark compound dressed with sugars fights breast cancer cells more sharply, in a 2026 chemistry study by Grzegorz Detlaff and co-authors. The compound, betulin, already slows several cancer cell lines, and chemists improve such natural products by reshaping them.

Using a classic rearrangement, the team attached unsaturated sugars to betulin, then hydrogenated some into a saturated family. Shapes of the new molecules were analyzed against the rearrangement's selectivity. Killing tests ran on breast cancer, prostate cancer, and normal skin cells. Attaching sugars from three particular sources clearly strengthened the attack on breast cancer cells, with good selectivity over the healthy line. A structure-activity reading explains which features carry the gain.
pmc-13329535:
Zoi Koukou and Efstathia Davidia Stergiou reviewed blocks to inclusive sexual and reproductive care for LGBTQ+ people, focused on midwife and birth services in Greece. Their 2026 narrative review notes law and policy gains for same-sex couples and gender-diverse people. Reforms do not always show in day-to-day health care work. Midwives and birth staff greatly shape access to inclusive and affirming services.

The review weighs structural, cultural, and job factors. It tells of system-wide and person-to-person blocks: bias, thin provider knowledge, money limits, law and policy setting, and place gaps. Fresh systematic reviews flag money blocks, provider knowledge gaps, and wide bias as repeat drivers of unfair care. Falsehoods in today's news world may wear down trust and tangle access for sidelined groups. The team calls for proof-led, rights-based plans for inclusive, fair, and affirming reproductive health care.
pmc-13330035:
Zhennan Chen, Yabiao He, Qiaomin Qiu, Songtu Zhang, and Qiang Xie report a hybrid surgical fix for shattered or torn-off shoulder bone knobs, in a study published in 2026. These fractures make up about a fifth of upper arm fractures and often come with dislocations and tendon tears. Badly shifted breaks need surgery to keep the arm working smoothly.

Twelve patients treated between 2023 and 2025 received both strong stitching and a slim locking plate in one operation. All fractures healed, at about eleven weeks on average, with no pulled anchors or failed implants. Shoulder scores rose steeply and pain scores fell close to one on a ten-point scale. The authors present the combined construct as a stable answer for breaks that single methods handle poorly.
pmc-13330335:
Leilei Yuan and co-authors find why colposcopy sometimes misses early cervical lesions that a biopsy later catches. Colposcopy guides most screening follow-up, so its blind spots matter. Their 2026 study reviews 448 patients with precancerous lesions who had both the scope exam and a biopsy between 2022 and 2024, treating the tissue result as truth.

Overall the scope exam was right about two times in three. Five traits independently raised the odds of a miss. They were age over forty, no bleeding after sex, low-grade results on the cell test, infection with HPV types other than type 16, and lesions inside the cervical canal. The miss rate peaked near sixty-eight percent in patients over fifty-five with low-grade cell results, though that subgroup was small. The authors advise extra care, and likely biopsy, when these traits stack up.
pmc-13331235:
Andrea Hinojosa-Azaola and colleagues review dance as both training and risk in a 2026 narrative article. Dance loads bones, muscles, nerves, metabolism, and heart systems hard. Gains include bone reshaping, stronger muscles and control, better balance and flexibility, and changed body makeup in children and adults alike.

Injury rates run high, mostly in the lower limbs from overuse: sprains, muscle tears, and stress fractures lead the list in the summed reports. Growth spurts, heavy training, pointe work, hard floors, loose joints, and low energy intake raise risk. Work cover often misses training injuries. Early hints suggest dance therapy may help fibromyalgia, yet proof stays thin, the authors caution.
pmc-13331635:
Sankalp Arora and co-authors study relapse after a targeted drug for a blood cancer, in a 2026 letter. The drug, blinatumomab, added to standard chemo improved results in a B-cell leukemia type. Patients lack the Philadelphia chromosome change in this form of the disease. Trial data showed strong survival for those who reached clean remission.

What happens to patients who still relapse was unknown. The team reviewed adults who reached first remission on blinatumomab-based treatment. They chart which traits predict relapse and how patients fare afterward. The cohort is large for this setting. Such maps help doctors spot high-risk patients early and plan what to do if the disease returns. The letter frames a gap left by the trials.
pmc-13332035:
Min Xu examines 2026 how multinational firms adapt strategy when AI rules diverge between the Atlantic world and China. AI governance has moved from a back-office compliance chore to a force that shapes where and how firms deploy systems. Yet most firm-level evidence has stayed conceptual or tied to a single country, leaving open how companies actually rework deployment, compliance routines, and public signaling under fragmented rules. The study targets that gap across the European Union, the United States, and China.

Its comparative dataset covers twelve multinational firms, tracing changes in deployment design, compliance work, and external messaging. The work matters for managers who must run one company under several AI regimes at once, and for scholars building theory on strategy under regulatory splits. It turns a much-debated divergence into concrete, comparable firm behavior.
pmc-13332735:
Yu Zhang and co-authors asked whether chest muscle measures on routine CT scans can flag which patients with a COPD flare will fare worst, in a 2026 retrospective study. Muscle wasting is common in chronic lung disease, but its warning value during acute exacerbations was unclear.

The study covered 464 consecutive patients scanned within 48 hours of admission, of whom 44 died in hospital and 86 needed a breathing machine. Both pectoralis muscle size, adjusted for height, and muscle density ran lower in those who died or needed ventilation. Each added unit of muscle index cut the hazard of death by about a third in adjusted models. Adding both muscle measures to the standard DECAF and BAP-65 scores lifted their accuracy for death from around 0.70 to 0.89. The authors propose reading muscle from scans already taken as an early risk tool.
pmc-13333035:
Mohammad A Sahi and colleagues study 2026 how tumor stage and molecular subtype shape five-year survival in breast cancer in Pakistan. Breast cancer is biologically diverse, and stage at diagnosis plus receptor-defined subtype strongly affect prognosis. In Pakistan, late presentation is common, partly from limited awareness, socioeconomic barriers, and uneven access to diagnosis and treatment. The team reviewed women diagnosed in 2020 with biopsy-confirmed invasive breast cancer at clinical stages I through III, without distant spread, treated with curative intent.

Survival was measured from diagnostic biopsy to death from any cause or last follow-up, estimated with Kaplan-Meier curves, compared with log-rank tests, and modeled with multivariable Cox methods. The study shows which stages and subtypes fare best and worst in a single tertiary center. It gives Pakistani clinicians and planners local survival benchmarks, and it underscores earlier detection as the lever most likely to lift outcomes.
pmc-13333335:
Koramit Suppipat and colleagues report building a local CAR T cell service in Thailand in a 2026 feasibility study. Their aim is to give relapsed large B cell lymphoma patients a treatment that commercial products price out of reach in poorer countries. Their answer was to manufacture the cells at the point of care on an automated closed machine.

Between 2020 and 2025, 12 patients with a median age of 45.8 years were treated, with a median vein-to-vein time of 12 days. Making succeeded for 11 patients, and one received a dose outside specification. Products showed balanced helper and killer cell ratios and many memory-type cells. Cytokine release syndrome hit 5 patients, severe in one, and mild nerve toxicity hit one. At three months, 58.3 percent had responded and 33.3 percent fully, with one-year overall survival of 90 percent. The median cost was USD 111,231, which the authors call proof local production can work and cost less.
pmc-13333735:
Acharya Balkrishna and co-authors tested an essential oil against Sporothrix globosa, a fungus that causes sporotrichosis and sometimes resists standard drugs, in a 2026 laboratory study. The oil comes from the leaves of Artemisia gmelinii.

Chemical profiling by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry showed the oil rich in oxygenated monoterpenes and related compounds. In broth tests the fungus grew less as oil dose rose, showing dose-dependent susceptibility. The team measured oxidative stress with a fluorescent probe, checked cell shape with staining, and quantified ergosterol, a key fungal membrane component. Tests on biofilms, the dense growth form that shelters fungi, were included as well. The findings point to membrane and oxidative damage as the oil's likely routes of attack.
pmc-13333835:
Tope Abraham Ibisanmi and co-authors search by computer for compounds that block MvfR, a regulator in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Their study starts from the threat of multidrug resistance in this bacterium, which calls for new treatment strategies.

The team profiled recent clinical isolates for resistance genes and virulence factors. MvfR stood out because it controls quorum sensing and biofilm formation. They modeled its shape with AI tools, docked a library of compounds against it, and compared it with known homologs. Drug-like traits were profiled, and long simulations tested how top candidates stay bound. The goal is a lead for next-generation antimicrobials.
pmc-13334035:
Lucena and six co-authors study quality of life in type two diabetes in northern Brazil, in work from twenty twenty-six. Diabetes is growing fast in Brazil, most of all in underserved areas. Daily function and quality of life are key outcomes that primary care often overlooks.

Ninety-nine adults in primary care units in Tocantinopolis took part. Tests measured arm and leg strength, flexibility, mobility, and fitness. Surveys captured health related quality of life and activity levels. The team linked results with social and clinical traits. Local data like this can help small clinics set rehab and support priorities that match patient needs.
pmc-13335535:
Afnan Elmubasher and co-authors test wood treated with graphene as a fuel for laser-driven flight, in a study from 2026. In this form of propulsion, a laser blasts bits off a surface to push a craft. Standard fuels struggle to give strong push under a steady, mild laser. The team used pale wood stripped of lignin and laced with graphene sheets.

Plain wood already beat all past fuels on push per unit of density. The graphene version soaked up far more laser light and lit off at the lowest beam strength yet seen. It also proved far stronger than plain wood, with a top strength-to-weight rate. That rate tops many materials used in flight structures. The authors say such light, plant-based fuels could serve in space. More tests can check how they hold up in real missions.
pmc-13335835:
Nada Ben Amor and co-authors reviewed the physical chemistry of PFAS adsorption at surfaces in a 2026 article. These forever chemicals persist in water and resist cleanup, and adsorption is a promising removal route hampered by poor understanding of how the molecules behave near solids.

The review starts with single-molecule interactions at surfaces, then moves to collective effects such as ionic bridging, self-aggregation, and competition from natural organic matter. Classical models for adsorption thermodynamics and kinetics are laid out, including what sets reaction order. Batch and kinetic experiments are mined for the roles of surface type and PFAS structure. Finally the authors weigh how pH, salinity, co-pollutants, and organic matter shift performance, giving engineers a firmer basis for sorbent design.
pmc-13336435:
Zexin Cui and colleagues study 2026 strain-tuned changeable optical information handling in flexible graphene/PDMS. All-optical information handling, with super-fast response and resistance to electric noise, plays a key role in future comms and computer tech. Graphene, with top non-straight optical properties and machine flexibility, emerges as a top pick for flexible light devices.

However, graphene-based light components are usually fixed in function and lack changeable use. The authors mix graphene with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) to make a flexible graphene/PDMS mix and study its SSPM effect under machine strain. Results show that the non-straight optical response of the mix can be tuned on the fly by strain. Under 532 nm laser light at power 35 W per square centimeter, the mix shows SSPM rings. As tensile strain rises from 0 percent to 40 percent, the ring count falls from 8 to 0.
pmc-13336535:
Sooyeon Noh and co-authors made hydrogels that visibly report their own stress in real time in a 2026 materials study. Seeing strain inside soft materials is valuable, but classic mechanophore systems switch only past a threshold and recover slowly, so they cannot track changing loads.

Their design uses host-guest pairs, beta-cyclodextrin and adamantane, as supramolecular switches inside the gel network. Guest-bearing polymers flip between hydrated and dehydrated states as the complexes join and part under stretch. That microscopic switching turns the whole gel from transparent to opaque, with opacity changing linearly and reversibly as stress rises and falls. The continuous optical readout could serve soft robotics, wearable sensors, and tissue engineering, where watching force develop matters as much as measuring it afterward.
pmc-13336735:
Huidi Yu and colleagues uncover a surprise antiviral switch in a 2026 study of the protein p300. This enzyme tags other proteins and helps switch genes on, including some tied to virus defense. Removing p300 from mouse lung lining cells did not weaken defense, as expected. It made antiviral responses stronger against two test viruses.

Cell work showed p300 normally tags a key defense kinase, TBK1, at two sites and blocks its activation. Virus infection raises p53, which raises the enzyme SIAH1, and SIAH1 marks p300 for destruction. Without p300, defense signals and interferon output rose while viruses copied less. The chain explains how infected cells lift a brake on their own defenses.
pmc-13336835:
Gang Wang and a large team publish a complete genome of a land slug in a 2026 study of life on dry ground. The tropical leatherleaf slug, Laevicaulis alte, descended from water ancestors and now fights drying out, new germs, and breathing air. Its mucus is central to moving, staying wet, and defense.

Combining three sequencing methods gave a gap-free genome with low variety and whole-centromere chromosomes. Chemical profiling showed shifts in fats, immune control, and stress handling compared with a close water relative. Gene data highlighted candidates for mucus making and land adaptation, with the VEGF family linking vessel growth, tissue repair, and mucus output. The dataset frames how molluscs colonized land.
pmc-13336935:
Yiming Li and colleagues report a simple way to make surfaces almost perfectly black over a wide range of light, published in 2026. They spray a blackout ink coating, cover it with tiny self-arranged spheres, and etch through the gaps the spheres leave. As etching goes on, shadows around the spheres shift, shaping the surface into rows of small parabolic cups.

Changing the etch time tunes the curve of the cup walls, which controls how well the surface traps light. The cups held average reflection to 0.89 percent across light from 300 to 1700 nanometers, on flat and curved glass, metal, and plastic alike. Such coatings could cut stray light in cameras, measuring tools, and space instruments without costly lithography.
pmc-13337435:
Si-Man Chen and colleagues identify a missing peacekeeper cell behind repeated miscarriage in a 2026 study. Macrophages in the womb lining normally keep tolerance and help the lining change for pregnancy. Single-cell profiling of human lining and decidua tissue found a FOLR2-positive subset with calm, tissue-resident, vessel-helping traits.

In repeated loss cases, that subset shrank sharply, while inflammation rose and vessel and adhesion contacts weakened. Boosting FOLR2 made the cells calmer and better for vessels; silencing it did the reverse. The cells and lining stromal cells also feed each other's growth in a positive loop. Restoring this subset could help explain and later treat repeated pregnancy loss.
pmc-13337635:
Murad Almadani, Leontios Hadjileontiadis, and Ahsan Khandoker build a transformer model that reads heart coupling between mother and fetus in both directions in a 2026 study. Such coupling may flag fetal stress early, but older methods looked one way and leaned on handcrafted measures. Two identical transformer networks, trained separately, learned mother-to-fetus and fetus-to-mother links from heart rate variability.

Timing differed by direction: mother-to-fetus coupling peaked at a 3 second delay while fetus-to-mother peaked at 5 seconds in the delay analysis. The fetal-to-maternal signal ran consistently lower in abnormal cases. A classifier using both directions plus pregnancy week reached a ROC-AUC of 0.91 in the reported evaluation. The authors call the evidence proof of concept, pending larger, cleaner cohorts.
pmc-13337835:
Chu Huang and colleagues review a three-way link in biliary atresia, a newborn liver disease, for 2026. Blocked bile ducts bring bile buildup, scarring, and eventual cirrhosis, and the disease is the top cause of newborn bile buildup. Its exact cause stays unknown.

Bile acid patterns, gut microbes, and vitamin D levels change across disease stages, the review shows. Those three factors may reinforce each other in a loop that drives harm. Treatments aimed at bile acids, microbes, or vitamin D could shift the course, early evidence suggests. Clearer work on the loop's molecular steps is still needed before firm therapy follows.
pmc-13338035:
Xi Yang, An Yan, Xing Liu, and Yun Zhou mapped cell splits in a fern's male sex organ. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with the fern Ceratopteris richardii. Ferns make free swimming sperm in small multicell sacs on a lone plant stage. Seed plants send sperm by pollen, a far path. How those fern sacs form and fill was near blank. The team used live, no harm imaging with a confocal scope plus 3D math reads.

They rebuilt full lineage maps of the sac from first split to ripe sperm. Set split rules and fate paths came into view. Readers in plant growth get a rare cell by cell film of sex organ build in a seed free plant.
pmc-13338135:
Mahsa Asghari, Ali-Reza Moradi, and co-authors watch powder dry with laser speckle maps and no touch, in work from 2026. Food and plant powders must be watched as they lose damp, since damp drives flow, cake, and shelf life. Corn starch serves as the test powder for its wide use and damp pull.

As dry goes on, speckle grades show inner moves fade in a set trend. Weight and skin scans back the light reads in full. Dry runs in two steps, a fast loss then a slow ease to rest. Skin micro cracks form and firm up as dry ends.
pmc-13338435:
Sepalage Chathurika and co-authors published a qualitative study in 2026 on how first-time pregnant women in Sri Lanka stay active. Being active while pregnant leads to better health for mother and baby, yet most women do not reach the set goals. The team held in-depth talks with 19 women at the clinics of a large hospital. Five themes came out of that work.

Most women did less than they had done before they were pregnant. They named fear of harm to the baby, discomfort, family advice, and a stress on rest in their culture. Some did no more than self-care tasks. Some sat more, and some turned to rest and leisure. The authors call for advice at pre-birth clinic visits that fits the culture of the women, so they can stay active in a safe way and feel sure of it.
pmc-13338735:
Chiaki Kuwada and colleagues tested whether ultrasound texture plus machine learning can spot a rare jaw muscle disorder, in a 2026 pilot study. Masticatory muscle tendon-aponeurosis hyperplasia stiffens chewing and is hard to confirm without invasive checks. The team scanned the masseter muscle in seven patients and seven matched healthy controls, taking 84 image slices in all.

From 107 texture features, logistic regression reached 0.83 sensitivity, 0.90 specificity, and 0.95 area under the curve, while random forest reached similar marks with 0.93 specificity. Both models separated patients from controls well despite the tiny cohort. The pilot suggests ultrasound radiomics could give dentists a non-invasive aid, pending validation in larger groups.
pmc-13341035:
Daisy Maharjan and co-authors study testicular tumors in this 2026 paper. They look at pure forms of two tumor types that grow from an early in-place lesion. Most such tumors are mixed, so pure cases raise a question: does the shift to a new type happen early, inside the tiny tubes where sperm cells grow?

The team tested 67 pure tumors with stains for marker proteins. The early lesion kept the marks of the first type in every case, and did not show marks of the new types. Nearby invasive tumor did show the new marks. The authors conclude the shift most likely happens outside that early niche, not inside it.
pmc-13341335:
Mahesh M Umapathysivam and colleagues probed testosterone and type 2 risk in 2026 in men with no diabetes at baseline. Low blood testosterone has been linked causally to type 2 risk, with protection reported up to 461 nanograms per decilitre. Yet it was unclear if a top limit exists for that effect. It was also unclear if age, waist size, or baseline blood sugar change the link.

Men with no diabetes, cancer, or testosterone treatment from the MAILES cohort took part, with baseline and five year checks. The team tested how waist size, age, and baseline A1c shape the testosterone to type 2 link. The findings refine who might gain most from testosterone linked prevention research.
pmc-13341435:
Ultrasound features separating harmful from harmless carotid webs are identified by Chenyang Dai and research partners in a 2026 study. Carotid webs are shelf-like tissue flaps that can trigger stroke; the team reviewed 45 patients confirmed by angiography between January 2021 and September 2024, 15 of whom had related strokes.

Symptomatic webs ran longer (5.80 versus 4.41 mm) and thicker (1.88 versus 1.38 mm), and curved shapes appeared in 80.0% of stroke cases versus 43.3% of silent ones. Narrowing was usually mild in both groups. Length and thickness survived multivariable testing as risk markers, giving sonographers concrete measurements to watch.
pmc-13341635:
Blood-test-guided blood thinner dosing after spine trauma surgery is evaluated by Dallas L. Sheinberg and colleagues in the 2026 retrospective study. Patients received weight-based enoxaparin from 24 hours after surgery; one cohort had anti-Xa levels checked after the third dose and adjusted toward 0.2 to 0.4 IU/mL.

The 354-patient comparison tracked symptomatic clots, bleeding needing transfusion, spinal bleeding, hospital stay, and walking at discharge. Standard dosing can leave patients under the protective range, raising the question of whether guided titration holds clot rates down without unacceptable bleeding. Spine trauma patients sit at especially high clot risk, making the balance delicate.
pmc-13342435:
Angela O Suen and co-authors offer a 2026 narrative review on clinic care for older adults living with chronic lung disease. Conditions such as COPD and interstitial lung disease fall hardest on older people, yet lung care has long focused on the disease rather than the whole person.

The authors propose the Age-Friendly 5Ms framework: What Matters, Medications, Mentation, Mobility, and Multicomplexity. Each element helps align treatment with patient goals, cut drug harms, support mind and caregivers, and protect movement and independence. A case of an 81-year-old woman with COPD grounds the advice, giving clinics a practical roadmap for care that fits later life.
pmc-13342635:
Jianxin Ran and co-authors test tissue flossing, a tight band wrapping method, as an add-on to balance training for chronic ankle instability, in work published in 2026. The condition follows ankle sprains and weakens muscle control. Flossing had shown short-term gains, but its long-term value was unknown.

Thirty-four patients were split between eight weeks of balance training with flossing and balance training alone. Tests covered muscle reaction time and activation, strength, and standing and dynamic balance. After training, one activation measure showed a group-by-time effect, but follow-up checks found no clear gap between groups. Reaction time and static balance improved in both groups over time. The authors conclude the added flossing gave no firm extra benefit on most measures.
pmc-13342735:
Ankur Mittal and co-authors report an outsized tonsil stone. Their 2026 case describes a unilateral tonsillolith, a calcified mass grown inside a tonsil crypt, removed under general anesthesia after imaging revealed its true size.

The scan showed a dense lump over twenty-three millimeters long beside the jaw angle, far beyond the usual pea-sized stones. Surgeons opened the tonsil region and lifted the stone out in fragments; the pieces were hard, irregular, and pale yellow. The authors place the case in the idiopathic class of soft-tissue calcification, where minerals settle without a clear trigger. They stress early diagnosis: a loose stone this size risks infection, choking, and referred ear pain.
pmc-13343635:
Hossein Ghasemi and co-authors pin down what social undermining means inside nursing, in a 2026 concept analysis. Undermining is the quiet sabotage of colleagues: withheld help, sly put-downs, credit quietly stolen. It erodes trust and confidence, yet nursing papers have used the term loosely. The authors applied a classic eight-step method to clarify it, reviewing English and Persian literature from 2000 to 2025 across major databases.

They define the behaviour as intentional, covert, and repeated, slowly corroding teamwork. Its triggers include rivalry and insecurity in individuals, plus workload pressure, felt injustice, and weak management in organisations. Its costs run from exhaustion to worse patient care. By fixing the concept's edges, the paper gives nurse managers and researchers a shared yardstick for spotting and studying the behaviour.
pmc-13343735:
Samira Abdolbaghi and colleagues tackled multilayer plastic recycling in 2026 by stripping oxygen from EVOH barrier plastic. Films pairing EVOH with polyethylene rule food packaging, yet recycling fails since phases split on reprocessing. A catalyst that cuts C-O bonds while keeping the plastic backbone could turn EVOH toward polyethylene like stuff.

pmc-13353635:

pmc-13355035:

pmc-13355735:

pmc-13356035:

pmc-13356635:

pmc-13360435:

pmc-13368435:
