pmc-13380835:
Wajeeha Iqbal and colleagues describe a 2026 case where heavy bleeding into the chest after a lung biopsy exposed a hidden clotting disorder. Their patient was a 75-year-old man who had a needle biopsy of a lung spot, guided by scans. Some bleeding is a known risk, but bleeding on this scale is rare.

He needed transfusions, a procedure to block a bleeding vessel, chest drainage, and keyhole chest surgery. During the same admission he developed spontaneous bruising deep in other muscles. Blood tests then revealed acquired haemophilia A, where the immune system attacks a clotting factor. The team stresses investigating bleeding that is out of proportion to a procedure.
pmc-13381735:
Yixin Wang and ten colleagues build a framework for measuring how industry and ecosystem services push on each other across China's Loess Plateau. Growth brings technology and cities, but also drained resources and pollution. Industry itself depends on healthy ecosystems. The team proposes treating the link as a true two-way system.

Their design uses spatial equations that run at once to capture feedback loops, rather than one-way impact. The paper is mainly a research framework and modeling proposal. It is meant to guide ecological protection and high-quality development strategy in a fragile region. There, erosion control and economic growth must be planned together.
pmc-13381935:
Yun Ho Roh and co-authors profile a bacterium pulled from an Antarctic lichen, the first of its genus found in that setting. The strain belongs to Streptacidiphilus, acid-loving actinobacteria known for rich chemistry. Life inside a polar lichen demands cold skills most kin lack.

The strain grows at near-freezing cold and across a wide alkaline span, unlike its described relatives. Its genome runs about ten million bases with more than nine thousand genes. Thirty-one biosynthetic clusters promise natural products, one of the richest sets in the genus, and some clusters appear in no other member. Extracts kill common bacteria and a yeast in dish tests. Lacking nitrogen fixing, the strain still chews many large molecules, hinting it recycles matter inside the lichen mat.
pmc-13383135:
Liandi Huang's team built a two-stage nanoparticle that treats dry eye by calming swelling and mopping up mitochondrial oxidants, in a 2026 study. Dry eye disease feeds on a vicious cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress, and eye drops wash out fast. The team's CFMPDA particle carries the anti-inflammatory drug fuziline inside a polydopamine scavenger shell with CCL2-targeting antibodies.

First the particle anchors to the inflamed cornea through CCL2, resisting clearance in proportion to disease severity. Then it homes to mitochondria to deliver combined anti-inflammatory and antioxidant therapy at the oxidant source. In mice, the platform suppressed inflammatory markers and T cell infiltration while quenching oxidative damage, showing synergistic benefit.
pmc-13383935:
Sailesh V. Tummala and co-authors add a flexible bone graft to a standard shoulder repair for Hill-Sachs dents in a 2026 technical note. These dents form when the ball of the shoulder strikes the socket rim during dislocation. Left alone, they can cause standard repairs to fail.

After the main repair, the team prepares the dent under camera view and sets anchors at its edges. A soft bone graft slips through a back portal into the dent, then tightening stitches press it firmly into place. The graft acts as a living scaffold, joining the ease of the knotless method with real structural filling.
pmc-13384335:
Kritika Singhal and colleagues explore why clinicians in India struggle to convey risk and lifestyle advice in a 2026 interview study. Fourteen doctors from cardiology, general medicine, and family medicine at one large hospital took part. Rising rates of hypertension and diabetes make such counseling a daily task.

Five themes emerged, covering disease burden views, language gaps, patient barriers, and daily communication habits. Doctors tailored advice to literacy, age, and income, but heavy patient loads left little time for structured risk talks. Many relied on informal methods and welcomed formal training plus standard tools to make risk messages clearer.
pmc-13384735:
Tillie Schumann and colleagues report a rare clitoral abscess in a teenager, linked in time to grooming and heated workouts in a 2026 case report. A 17-year-old girl first came in with vulvar swelling and pain that oral antibiotics failed to settle. Scans in the emergency department found a 2.6 centimeter abscess beside the clitoris.

Her history included infrared sauna workout classes and routine genital shaving, a pairing not flagged in earlier reports. Two days of IV antibiotics brought no relief, so surgeons drained the abscess. Four days later the wound was healing well, and the authors call for more data on how such abscesses form.
pmc-13385635:
Farahnaz Amini's team charted health care use before pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 matched cohort study. The prodrome of childhood-onset MS was little known, especially by sex and age. Using Ontario administrative data from 1991 to 2020, the team compared 451 pediatric-onset patients with 1420 matched controls up to 18 years before the first demyelinating event.

Hospitalizations rose by the year before onset for ill-defined, other-contact, mental, and respiratory causes, with rate ratios at or above 3.6. Physician visits rose far earlier: respiratory from year minus 14, endocrine and injury from minus 13, ill-defined from minus 12, and nervous system and mental from minus 11. Nervous system visits showed the largest sex gap, flagging early prodromal signals.
pmc-13386235:
Seyed Hossein Hosseinimehr and colleagues test dynamic neuromuscular stability exercises in older men in a 2026 randomized trial. Thirty men aged 61 to 76 years were split between an exercise group and a no-treatment control group. The exercise arm trained three times weekly for eight weeks, with balance and leg strength measured before and after.

The training group gained on every outcome, covering steadiness, a timed stand-and-walk test, and repeated chair stands. Adjusted gaps between groups were clear on all three measures, and they held after accounting for age differences. The authors suggest the method as an effective fall-prevention option for aging men.
pmc-13386935:
Zeinab Merzaei and colleagues test how IBS-linked E. coli strains act on gut lining cells in a 2026 lab study. Irritable bowel syndrome brings pain and changed bowel habits, and gut microbe shifts are part of its picture. Caco-2 cells, a standard gut lining model, were exposed to strains from patients and from healthy sources.

Patient strains invaded cells more strongly and provoked higher levels of two inflammatory messengers. They also raised sensing receptor genes TLR-4 and TLR-5 while cutting tight junction protein expression. The pattern fits a leakier, more inflamed gut lining, which may feed bowel symptoms.
pmc-13387735:
Takahiko Nagamine wrote a short letter in 2026 that puts forward a new model for severe gut slowdown caused by certain drugs. The drugs at issue are clozapine and related sedatives, which are used to treat schizophrenia. Nagamine argues that both drugs act like a brake on the spinal cord center that controls bowel movements.

When that brake is pressed twice, the gut can slow so much that it stops, a dangerous state called Ogilvie's syndrome. The letter cites real world data showing more laxative use in patients on these drugs. It suggests easing the brake by adjusting sedative dose and by caring for gut microbes, so the worst outcomes can be prevented.
pmc-13388935:
Yidan Chen's team built an electronic skin that copies the layered build of the human fingertip, aiming for robots that can feel what they grasp. Natural skin pairs an interlocked outer-inner structure with dense touch sensors. Most artificial skins miss that layered integration of shape and function.

Their gel blends gelatin with sodium lactate and clay nanosheets, shaped with a sandpaper template to mimic dermal papillae, the tiny bumps under skin ridges. The sensor responds in 47 milliseconds across a wide pressure range. A hand-shaped array fitted to a robotic hand grasped objects without damage while mapping pressure across many channels.
pmc-13390435:
Alessia Sala's team weighed set oral misoprostol against dinoprostone for starting labour in 873 single-baby term births with poor cervix scores, treated between 2021 and 2024. Few studies had tested misoprostol since standard dosing arrived, so the team assessed safety, impact, and timing in routine care.

Start-to-birth and time-to-active-labour did not differ clearly between the 528 misoprostol and 345 dinoprostone patients. Misoprostol patients nevertheless had a higher vaginal birth rate and lower after-birth bleeding risk, backing the set oral protocol as safe and effective for starting labour. The comparison covered routine care between 2021 and 2024.
pmc-13391235:
David Heath, Kyungchul Kim, Amyn G Pardhan, and Jacinta Cover synthesise, in 2026, evidence on giving feedback that actually improves surgical performance. Feedback underpins skill growth and safe decision-making, yet busy clinical work in Australia and New Zealand still makes high-quality feedback hard to deliver consistently.

The authors searched big medical databases for work on feedback in surgical training. They gathered proven models into hands-on guidance for teachers and trainees. Trainers gain firm ways to make feedback prompt and clear. Good feedback is of use at once. It is not a vague end-of-term note that no one can act on. The tips suit busy wards, where time to teach is short.
pmc-13391435:
Deelip Kumar Singh and co-authors report, in 2026, a rare chain of events where kidney infection bred a false aneurysm that burst under the kidney capsule. Infection-driven weakening of a renal artery, forming a pseudoaneurysm with bleeding under the capsule, has seldom been described.

A 42-year-old woman whose type 2 diabetes was poorly controlled arrived with right flank pain, fever, and worsening kidney function. Scans showed infection in both kidneys, a large and growing blood collection under the right kidney capsule, and a pseudoaneurysm on a renal artery branch. Urologists and radiologists gain a diagnostic and treatment review for a dangerous mimic that can be mistaken for a tumour bleed.
pmc-13392635:
Jermnak and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of Hericium erinaceus, a medicinal mushroom, tested against canine mammary cancer, a common and often spreading tumor in female dogs. The team worked with two cancer cell lines, CHMp-13a and CHMp-5b, plus normal kidney cells for comparison. They asked whether a methanol extract of the mushroom could slow growth, trigger cell death, and block the shape changes that help tumors spread.

The extract slowed both cancer lines in a dose- and time-dependent way, hitting CHMp-13a hardest while largely sparing normal cells. Treated cells showed more apoptosis, meaning programmed cell death: the pro-death gene BAX rose while the protective gene BCL-2 fell, pointing to a mitochondria-driven pathway. Migration and invasion tests also weakened. Earlier Thai surveys found mammary tumors in 24.5 percent of canine biopsy samples, most of them malignant, which shows why gentler treatments deserve testing.
pmc-13393835:
Haitao Lu and others compare rod lengths for mending thigh breaks just below the hip in a 2026 engineering study. These breaks are hard to fix, and surgeons pick from long, mid, and short rods placed inside the bone plus a plate that rebuilds the outer wall.

A 3D model built from one man's CT scan tested 320, 240, and 160 millimeter rods under push, bend, and twist loads in strong bone and in weak, porous bone. Under straight push, the mid rod showed the least peak bone shift. Surgeons now have hard numbers to match rod length to bone strength in this tricky break.
pmc-13393935:
Ayşenur Gür and colleagues test a blood ratio for early kidney injury detection in crush syndrome in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Prolonged muscle compression can trigger life-threatening kidney failure, and rapid risk sorting in the emergency department remains hard.

At a Level I trauma center from 2019 to 2025, adults with crush syndrome were assessed for creatinine-defined kidney injury, with the lactate dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio calculated at admission. The study asks whether this routine ratio discriminates kidney injury early enough to guide care. Emergency teams gain a candidate triage signal from labs already drawn at arrival.
pmc-13394035:
Aimee R Mills, Antonio de Souza, Toan Pham, and Odunayo O Mugisho tested MOTS-c, a small peptide made by mitochondria themselves, as a dampener of inflammasome activity in diabetic rats. Diabetes was induced with a high-fat diet plus streptozotocin, a standard model, and the team tracked the NLRP3 inflammasome, an inflammatory alarm complex, in blood and heart tissue. Cardiovascular disease drives most diabetic deaths, and chronic inflammasome firing is a suspect.

Treatment lowered fasting blood sugar and a general inflammation marker, and selectively rebalanced circulating inflammatory signals. In the left ventricle, the inflammasome's core parts and its activated cutting enzyme all fell. Two key inflammatory messengers correlated with cholesterol and uric acid levels, tying metabolic state to alarm activity. The authors present MOTS-c as a candidate for cutting cardiovascular risk in diabetes by cooling both body-wide and cardiac inflammation.
pmc-13394735:
Maria Fogelberg and colleagues build, in 2026, a new way to read fetal heart traces during labour. Low blood acid at birth can harm a baby, yet current reading guides miss many cases. The team studied 1,092 births in southern Sweden, mixing babies with acid blood and babies who were well. They tested which trace patterns truly tracked with acid levels.

Their two new models caught far more acid cases than the Swedish and world guides. They also raised more false alarms than those guides. One pattern, heart rate sitting below its base line for much of half an hour, added the most. The authors say the models need fresh testing before ward use.
pmc-13395235:
Amrit Baral and others tie weed use styles to weed use illness in a 2026 study of US survey data. As weed laws ease and weed goods spread, weed illness climbs, and whether use style counts beyond how oft and how strong was unclear.

The team used a big US drug-use survey from 2022 to 2023. It found use styles clearly tied to illness rates and depth, with mixed styles and breathed-in styles bearing the worst risk. The paper urges doctors and law chiefs to weigh how weed is taken, not just how oft or how strong, when they judge risk and craft rules.
pmc-13396035:
Amr Abu Elfadle and colleagues report results from two centers on stenting a large vein inside the skull. The aim was to stop pulsatile tinnitus, the whooshing sound that a narrowed vein can cause in time with the heartbeat. Their 2026 study covers 30 adults treated between January 2018 and December 2024.

Each patient had a narrowed transverse sinus, one of the main drainage channels for the brain, and received a stent to reopen it. The team recorded symptoms, scans, and the pressure drop across the narrowed segment before and after the procedure. They also lay out the combined symptom, imaging, and pressure framework their centers use to pick candidates in everyday practice.
pmc-13396235:
Eric S. Christenson and co-authors ran an early-phase trial pairing two drugs against advanced colorectal cancer that resists immunotherapy, and report it in 2026. The cancer type, called microsatellite stable, almost never answers to checkpoint drugs alone, but blocking the PI3K pathway might change the immune climate inside tumors.

Patients received copanlisib, which blocks PI3K, plus nivolumab. One group of 17 had normal PIK3CA genes and another of 22 carried mutations in that gene, since the pathway matters most there. The pair was tolerated and doses were set, yet the main goal was missed: no responses in the first group and two of 22 in the second at six months.
pmc-13396335:
Fengrui Zhang and others name MKRN3 as a tumor curb in ovary cancer in a 2026 study. Early first bleeding has long been tied to higher ovary cancer risk, but the chain from a puberty gene to this cancer was unknown.

Ovary cancer gene files showed MKRN3 oft lost through deep gene cuts, with loss and low reads tied to grim odds. The gene steers tag-and-trash of CSDE1, and its failure frees tumor-driving programs. The paper ties puberty timing genes to ovary tumor curbs in a fresh chain, with drug hints to chase.
pmc-13396435:
Hadi Farajvand and co-authors address a scheduling problem inside federated learning, where many small devices train a shared model without sending their raw data away. Their 2026 study works in a layered setup: internet-of-things devices report to edge servers, and training proceeds in a semi-synchronous rhythm that tolerates slow members.

The authors optimize two choices at once, which devices cluster together and which edge server each cluster reports to, alongside shifting data so clusters stay balanced. Poor clustering wastes battery and bandwidth and drags accuracy down. Their approach aims at higher model quality per unit of resource, an issue that grows as edge networks scale.
pmc-13397635:
Yuan and co-authors profile, in 2026, how the coastal shrub Suriana maritima survives drought on tropical coral islands. The shrub is an ecological fixture of the Xisha Islands. The team integrated gene expression and metabolite measurements across water stress. Leaves were sampled after 15 days across control and three drought levels, and the team tracked what bounced back on rewatering.

Severe drought switched on defense machinery. Genes for chitinases, late embryogenesis abundant proteins, and the detox enzymes glutathione S-transferase and glutathione peroxidase all rose. Hormone signaling shifted too, across abscisic acid, jasmonic acid, gibberellin, and ethylene. Photosynthesis genes were shut down under severe stress but switched back on fast after rewatering, showing the shutdown reverses rather than reflecting damage. Small molecules shifted too, with amino acids such as tryptophan and valine building up while many flavonoids declined. The authors describe a resource-shifting plan that trades growth for survival.
pmc-13397735:
Yushu Liu and others decode lactylation heterogeneity in glioblastoma with machine learning in a 2026 study. This most common adult malignant glioma carries a dire prognosis, and lactylation, a novel protein tweak, steers tumor growth through multiple routes yet stayed fragmented in glioblastoma research.

Joining single-cell data with bulk cohorts, the team built a lactylation-linked gene score and read high and low score subgroups. Ten machine learning algorithms plus Cox modeling then named G6PC3 as a core prognostic gene. Cell communication reads probed its interplay paths. The paper names a lactylation-linked aim for glioblastoma therapy.
pmc-13398135:
Alexis Barbry and colleagues check whether a quick fitness test battery for schoolchildren measures what it claims. Their 2026 study puts the Diagnoform Kid battery against established reference tests in 184 children grouped at ages 6 to 7, 8 to 9 and 10 to 11. Fitness is a health marker worth tracking, but schools need batteries that are fast and simple to run.

Paired tests covered the same skills: shuttle runs for endurance, jumping games for agility and power, sprints for speed and reach tests for flexibility. Matched pairs correlated as hoped, and scores moved sensibly with age and sex. The authors judge the short battery fit for school screening, while noting where its shortcuts cost precision.
pmc-13398535:
Ryan Peters and colleagues run a quantum neural network to predict which cancer fragments the immune system will notice. Their 2026 study, named Q-CHIPP, tackles neoantigen prediction for HLA presentation, a precision medicine task where datasets stay small and noisy and classical models generalise poorly. Quantum hardware is young, so the team had to steady it before trusting its answers.

Noise-taming tricks (Pauli twirling, dynamical decoupling and controlled shot sampling) stabilised training on a real quantum device, helped by a warm start from classical work. The quantum convolutional network then learned patterns in peptide data within those tight limits. The paper reads as a field test: can today's fragile quantum machines already earn a place in immunology pipelines?
pmc-13399035:
Noriyuki Konishi and Jian Feng Ma pinpoint the amino acids that park a rice manganese transporter on one side of root cells. Their 2026 study works on OsNramp5, one of two transporters that pull manganese from soil at the root's outer and inner skins. Both sit polarised, facing outward, but the parking instructions written in the protein were unknown.

Swapping parts with non-polar cousins showed the tail region inside the cell carries the signal. Mutating single residues found aspartate 500 and four valines (at positions 494, 495, 498 and 506 in the chain) doing the critical work. Swaps keeping a branched shape preserved parking, while slim residues lost it, hinting the cell reads bulk, not chemistry, at those spots.
pmc-13399235:
Sidnei Umberto Bertholdi and colleagues compared single-drug against combined treatment for infections caused by Acinetobacter baumannii that resist carbapenem drugs, in a 2026 study from two Brazilian hospitals. This germ resists nearly all standard drugs and haunts intensive care units, causing bloodstream infections and pneumonia in ventilated patients, with very high death rates. Whether adding drugs helps has stayed unsettled.

Three quarters received combined therapy, usually built around polymyxin antibiotics; sulbactam-based regimens accounted for 16.3 percent of cases, as the authors report. Death rates were nearly the same for both strategies, at 73.3 percent for single-drug and 73.1 percent for combined treatment in the reported figures. In adjusted analysis, only the APACHE II score predicted death. The authors suspect illness severity, not drug strategy, drove the outcomes, and they call for future trials.
pmc-13399335:
Nkgomeleng A. Lekodeba and co-authors modeled what near-point-of-care GeneXpert testing would cost and buy for sexually transmitted infections in South Africa, in a 2026 analysis. South Africa now treats these infections syndromically, judging by symptoms alone. GeneXpert machines can identify chlamydia, gonorrhea, and trichomonas directly. The team asked whether wider testing pays for itself.

Their model ran over one year from the provider's viewpoint. It compared syndromic care against testing aimed at symptomatic patients, pregnant women, and people coming for HIV tests. Syndromic care cost an estimated 24.1 million dollars a year. Testing symptomatic patients alone ran to between 102.1 and 207.8 million dollars in the scenarios modeled. Testing did cut excess antibiotic use by up to 88 percent. Two expanded scenarios looked cost-effective, at 863 and 1,064 dollars per extra person correctly diagnosed and treated, as the authors calculate. They recommend targeting symptomatic and high-risk groups rather than blanket coverage.
pmc-13399435:
Tulio Konstantyner, Marina Carvalho de Moraes Barros, and Fabio Carmona reflect on what artificial intelligence is doing to scientific publishing, in a 2026 editorial. Their essay weighs genuine gains against risks they think the community is underestimating.

On the benefit side, they credit AI with chewing through large datasets and automating chores like literature searches and formatting. The dangers occupy more of the essay. Fluent machine text can fake rigor, and fabricated or biased content can slip through when nobody verifies it. Heavy reliance can dull researchers' and reviewers' own critical skills, a deskilling effect the authors name explicitly. They warn that uploading confidential manuscripts to outside tools breaks confidentiality. Their closing stance is caution: use the tools, but keep human judgment in charge.
pmc-13399735:
David Painter and six co-authors log five seasons of arm injuries in an elite college summer baseball league. Trainers in the Cape Cod Baseball League recorded upper extremity injuries from practices and games in 2018, 2019, and 2021 through 2023. The tally reached 162 injuries, about 32 per season, at a rate of 2.22 per 1000 athletic exposures. No clear trend ran across the five years.

Overuse caused 75.9% of injuries, far ahead of trauma, and muscles and tendons took 60.2% of the damage. Nearly 40% were reinjuries of an old problem. The shoulder led the sites, and most injuries cost playing time.
pmc-13399835:
Matthew R. Bryan and colleagues systematically reviewed surgery for chronic quadriceps tendon ruptures, the disabling tears of the tendon that straightens the knee, in a 2026 review. Chronic here means at least three weeks from injury to operation. Searching EMBASE, PubMed, and Cochrane between October 2023 and November 2024 under PRISMA rules, the team kept clinical studies of Level IV evidence or better in native knees.

Only ten studies, published between 1981 and 2022, qualified. Reported repair failure rates ranged widely, from zero to 33 percent across those series. Extensor lag, the knee's inability to fully straighten actively, was reported as a complication in five of the ten. Their title carries the clinical message: patients repaired late report lower satisfaction and worse results. They call for comparative studies with standardized outcomes before any technique can be recommended over another.
pmc-13400235:
Ruggenenti and team write, in 2026, a letter reappraising two trials of obinutuzumab as first-line therapy for primary membranous nephropathy, a kidney disease causing nephrotic syndrome. They question the comparator arms. The MAJESTY trial pits the anti-CD20 antibody against tacrolimus in 142 patients, and the BEGIN trial against cyclosporine in 155 participants, though calcineurin inhibitor monotherapy is no longer recommended care.

Their argument rests on the earlier MENTOR trial, which showed rituximab clearly superior to cyclosporine, leading 2021 KDIGO guidelines to make rituximab first-line for high-risk patients. On that evidence, they contend any new agent should be tested against a rituximab-based standard, not a superseded drug. Otherwise approval may rest on beating a straw comparator. They also note cost counterarguments are weaker than assumed: B-cell-driven dosing protocols can cut rituximab cost up to fourfold, and biosimilars could halve it again.
pmc-13400435:
Moira Shea and colleagues report, in 2026, on workplace skin screening for firefighters in Boston, a group at raised risk of skin cancer. Few studies had asked what firefighters know about sun safety or how confident they feel checking their own skin. Early detection depends on those habits.

Over 1,500 city firefighters were invited, with 424 attending in 2022 and 524 in 2023. Most lacked a regular dermatologist, and many rarely used sunscreen. Firefighters who came twice scored higher on a ten-question knowledge quiz and felt more confident doing self-exams than one-time attendees. The authors credit contact with skin specialists during screening for the gains, even without formal lessons.
pmc-13400635:
Marta Paterlini reports, in 2026, on the uncertain future facing thousands of researchers hired under Italy post-pandemic recovery plan. The European-funded program poured over eleven billion euros into research and created many new posts. It raised hopes of replacing Italys long pattern of short contracts with durable careers.

As the first contracts expire, researchers describe facing a familiar cliff edge, only higher than before. The recovery money expanded hiring fast without changing the underlying career structure, which rests on temporary fellowships and fragmented funding. Accounts from staff at the national research council illustrate the gap between promise and outcome. The article places Italys experience within a wider European debate on research careers.
pmc-13400735:
Hyeonggyeong Cha and colleagues build, in 2026, an ultralight brain stimulation system for mice that is controlled by infrared light. Studying stimulation therapies in freely moving animals is hampered by wires and heavy wireless modules, which distort natural behavior. Their design drops radio modules entirely and takes commands from light instead.

Two light-sensitive switches tuned to different infrared wavelengths control surface stimulation and deep brain stimulation independently. The full devices weigh under one and a half grams and under half a gram respectively. Bench tests showed even light spread and no heating during long use. Mice wearing the devices moved normally, and stimulating a motor area made them circle reliably, proving the system drives behavior.
pmc-13400835:
Wen Dai, Zebo Hu, Wenjian Mao, Jia Wu and Jun Hong test, in 2026, whether a simple blood ratio at admission predicts relief from an acute gout attack. Gout flares are intensely painful, and knowing who will settle within weeks helps planning. The ratio divides fasting blood sugar by albumin, a nutrition and inflammation marker.

Records for 260 patients admitted between 2022 and 2023 were split into model-building and validation groups. Among several candidate ratios, this one survived statistical selection and stayed independently linked to relief within 28 days. Flexible and machine learning models agreed. Adding the ratio improved prediction over the model without it, which the authors propose as a cheap, routine-data tool for gout care.
pmc-13400935:
Qiancai Lin and colleagues analyze, in 2026, how the pattern of blood lactate over three days predicts survival in intensive care patients with pneumonia. A single lactate reading is a weak guide; its trajectory may say more. Data came from a large public critical care database.

Among 2,091 patients, modeling found four trajectories: low and stable, moderate and slowly falling, rising then falling, and very high then falling fast. The worse patterns came with greater illness severity, more organ support and higher 28-day mortality. A single lactate value lost its link with death after adjustment, but trajectory group stayed independently predictive. Patterns, the authors argue, beat snapshots for prognosis.
pmc-13401535:
Nicola Clemente and James C W Khaw wrote a 2026 correspondence responding to a histology paper by Muro and co-authors. The paper covers the intersphincteric region of the anal canal, the tissue plane between the anal sphincters where fistula tracts travel. They welcome the work as a challenge to the old view of that region as a simple anatomical plane.

The authors work in imaging and surgery for complex anal fistulas. They argue Muro's high-resolution findings fit several concepts they have proposed. These include the Garg fascia, the outer-sphincteric space, and a fistula type they abbreviate RIFIL. They highlight Muro's description of the longitudinal muscle as a mosaic rather than a uniform sheet. Its dense part ends at about 54 percent of the internal sphincter length, and they explore what lies below that point.
pmc-13401735:
Nelson F Freeburg and a very large team of co-authors profiled the immune aftermath of CAR T cell therapy in recurrent glioblastoma in a 2026 study. Glioblastoma, the commonest malignant brain tumour in adults, carries a median survival under fifteen months, and nothing works reliably once it returns.

A recent phase one trial delivered engineered CAR T cells into the brain's fluid spaces and saw promising tumour shrinkage and prolonged survival in some patients, yet relapse stayed common. The team profiled spinal fluid and tumour samples collected over time from responders and non-responders. Their focus is the patient's own immune compartment: how the endogenous immune system behaves after the engineered cells are given. Whether its patterns separate patients who benefit from those who do not. The work aims to explain relapse and guide the next round of cell therapy design.
pmc-13402235:
Ulrika Lindgren and co-authors describe a 40-year-old woman whose muscle disease turned out to be an adult form of a childhood storage disorder tied to the CLN8 gene. She first had seizures, then passing weakness and muscle pain, with moderately raised muscle enzymes. Over time weakness grew steady and mental fatigue set in. Her case did not fit the usual childhood picture of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Muscle biopsy showed fibers stuffed with autophagic vacuoles, plus fat and scar tissue replacing muscle. Stains showed strong buildup of autophagy markers and stored material typical of this disease family, and her blood cells carried fingerprint-like inclusions. Gene testing found two CLN8 changes, one from each parent, and protein analysis showed autophagy and muscle repair systems switched up. The report adds muscle disease as a possible adult face of CLN8 faults.
pmc-13402335:
Merav Catalogna and colleagues ran a pilot study on whether three weeks of digital training can reshape motor wiring in Parkinson disease. Thirty-two patients on levodopa were split between an active app and a placebo app. The active program trained spatial navigation using both body-centered and map-based strategies under reduced senses, with added psychological and rehabilitation parts.

Brain imaging afterward showed stronger white matter signal in the right ventrolateral posterior thalamus and tighter functional coupling between that spot and the motor cortex, alongside better motor scores. Network analysis found richer local efficiency around motor areas, hinting at better structural integration. The authors treat every result as preliminary: the group was small, and a larger, properly powered trial must confirm that such short training truly rewires motor circuits beyond drug effects.
pmc-13402635:
Harshini Weerasinghe and a large team show how Candida fungi starve macrophages of glucose, then burst them open to escape. Macrophages and fungi compete for glucose inside the body, and that contest warps the immune cell energy system. In glucose-starved macrophages the protein NINJ1, known as an executioner that ruptures membranes at cell death, switched on and tore the membrane without help from the usual death programs.

Among host death factors tested, NINJ1 did most of the fungal damage. The amino acid alanine rescued starved cells better than glucose itself, by stopping NINJ1 from clumping into its active form. Infected mice showed disturbed amino acid handling and lower blood alanine, matching the lab picture. Membrane rupture also let the fungus slip out together with its toxin candidalysin. The work names a starvation-driven escape hatch and a possible nutrient-based defense.
pmc-13402735:
Mohammad Alsayegh and co-authors compare two newborn samples as records of metal exposure before birth in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Metals like lead can cross the placenta and build up in the fetus. First stool, called meconium, and newborn hair both serve as non-invasive records.

Fifty healthy full-term babies in Syria gave paired samples within a day of birth. All four metals tested showed in both sample types. Levels ran consistently higher in meconium than in hair. Yet the two records barely tracked each other, except a weak tie for cadmium. The authors say the samples capture different facets of exposure and cannot swap for each other.
pmc-13402935:

Earlier work had linked this system to anxiety and reward. Their 2026 study tests genetically modified mice in a battery of behaviour tasks.

They also responded less to reward-predicting cues in an operant task. Eating at home, novelty preference, and fear memory were unaffected. The authors conclude VGLUT3 in serotonin neurons supports some reward learning but not anxiety-like behaviour.
pmc-13403635:
Stéfany Araújo Fraga and colleagues asked in 2026 how nursing students picture nurses as a group. Their study drew 114 students at a public university in Rio de Janeiro. Students gave free word links for the idea of a nurse, and software mapped the pattern.

Three words sat at the center of the picture: care, empathy, and health. Around them sat love and knowledge, plus weariness and feeling undervalued. Duty, help, and dedication filled a nearby zone. The mix shows pride in caring work, side by side with worry about strain and low regard in the real job.
pmc-13403735:
Jia Liu headed a 2026 study on how low oxygen inside breast tumors helps them shrug off radiation. The cancer type studied lacks the three usual hormone targets, which narrows drug choices. Low oxygen raises harsh oxygen by-products inside cell power units.

A gene switch protein, BHLHE40, turned out to sit in those power units and sense the by-products directly. Chemical change made its copies pair up, and low oxygen also raised its levels two ways. The protein then switched on cell shields that blunt radiation harm. Blocking this sensor could make radiation work better for women with this hard cancer type.
pmc-13404635:
Ke-Yu Liu and co-authors present a 2026 protocol testing mecobalamin alongside standard injections for retinal vein occlusion. A blocked retinal vein causes swelling at the centre of vision, treated first with drugs that block vessel growth signals. Those injections do not protect nerve tissue and must repeat often, at high cost.

The single-centre trial at a Chongqing hospital will enrol 120 patients and assign them evenly by chance. One group gets conbercept injections plus oral mecobalamin, a nerve-protecting form of vitamin B12, for six months. The other gets the same injections plus a dummy pill. Everyone is then followed for a year to compare vision, swelling and safety.
pmc-13404835:
Lumie Sabanai Shintaku leads a Brazilian study, reported in 2026, ranking what shapes quality of life in rheumatoid arthritis. Care happens in real clinics, where disease stage and treatment vary widely. Knowing which factors matter most can guide where clinicians focus effort.

Eleven public specialist centres enrolled 1,079 adults meeting standard classification criteria for the disease. Quality of life was scored with the SF-12 survey and disability with the HAQ-DI questionnaire. Most patients were women, and the average age was about 57 years in the reported data. Regression models compared standardised effects, letting the authors rank clinical and social predictors by strength rather than by statistical significance alone.
pmc-13404935:
Min Seung Choi and co-authors survey South Korean ambulance providers after a national doctors' dispute disrupted care, in 2026 work. A 2024 government plan to expand medical school places triggered resident strikes and a severe hospital crisis. Crews often drove patients far for treatment, and some patients worsened or died during delays.

The cross-sectional study asks whether witnessing such deterioration links to burnout, low mood and poor sleep. Earlier work on moral injury in emergency staff frames the question. Providers reported their exposure to deterioration blamed on system gaps, alongside standard mental health measures. The authors examine how strongly those experiences track with each outcome in a workforce under unusual strain.
pmc-13405635:
Laissa Viegas Cardoso de Barros and co-authors model how tooth decay affects life quality for Brazilian preschoolers, using SB Brasil 2023 data, in 2026 work. Five-year-olds were examined by trained dentists and parents answered questions on pain, visits and schooling. A standard questionnaire scored oral health impact on daily life.

Structural modelling traced paths between decay severity, pain, urgent care need and quality of life. Worse decay and pain each pushed children toward urgent treatment need in the reported coefficients. Decay also worsened quality of life directly, and indirectly through pain, in both child and parent reports. An open bite and mother's schooling complete the web of influences the authors test.
pmc-13405835:
Álvaro Becerra and co-authors gather the evidence on matico, a Chilean healing plant, in a 2026 systematic review. Buddleja globosa features in Mapuche and Aymara traditional medicine, yet its chemistry and effects had never been synthesised. Four databases were searched to March 2026 under PRISMA rules.

Fourteen studies, mostly Chilean and spanning 1989 to 2026, yielded 27 active compounds from leaves, roots and flowers. Named finds include verbascoside, luteolin relatives and amyrin triterpenes, plus four newly reported compounds. Antioxidant action was the most frequently reported effect. Quality grading of the non-clinical studies tempers how far the traditional uses are yet supported.
pmc-13407135:
Satoru Kaneko, Yukako Kuroda, and Yuki Okada review, in 2026, how to judge human sperm quality beyond the usual count and movement checks, with an eye on sperm injection treatment for infertility. Earlier work from the group used density gradients to separate lively sperm without DNA damage from still sperm carrying fragmented DNA.

New dye- and lectin-based tests probe the sperm's outer and acrosomal membranes, internal oxidative stress, and internal cavities, sorting cells that look pre-decline from those already breaking down. For injection, the authors describe the ideal candidate: oval head, intact membranes, healthy energy production, and no DNA damage or vacuoles. Setting firm thresholds is hard because several faults often coexist in one cell, a problem the review maps out.
pmc-13407435:
Bruno Maetz and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot in France testing a behavioural hearing check for babies and toddlers against specialist assessment. Screening at nine months and two years is mandatory in France. Yet follow-through is low and methods vary. The Petale test is given by family doctors or paediatricians. The study checked its accuracy in children aged nine months to three years.

Of 157 children analysed, 119 completed both the new test and the specialist reference test. Petale flagged hearing trouble in 36.9 percent, but it caught only about two-thirds of true cases, and agreement with the specialist test was weak. Its negative results were more reassuring, ruling out trouble correctly in over 90 percent of clear cases. Satisfaction was near universal among clinicians and parents, and the test is quick and cheap, so the authors see promise if accuracy improves.
pmc-13407835:
Rafael Gómez-Fernández and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether blood markers regain their crystal-ball power when mouth cancer returns. Ratios measured before surgery predict survival in mouth cancer. Recurrence is a different biological moment, though. The team analysed markers measured at relapse. They covered 70 of 168 treated patients whose cancer came back.

Seventy percent of the relapsed patients died within five years. One marker stood apart: plasma fibrinogen, a clotting protein, ran higher in those who died, with medians of 595 against 464, and it alone kept its own statistical weight after adjustment. The fashionable neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio faded to non-statistical weight at recurrence. The authors label the single-centre analysis early-stage and call for larger multi-centre testing before fibrinogen guides decisions.
pmc-13407935:
Mariana Charleaux de Ponte and co-authors examine, in 2026, how sex shapes kidney inflammation in diabetic mice. Diabetic kidney disease advances through inflammation. The BTBR ob/ob mouse mirrors the human condition closely. The team therefore compared males and females, studying the kidney's filtering units and its tubules on their own rather than grinding up the whole organ.

Diabetic mice leaked albumin into urine in both sexes, yet proteins of the filtering cells were set differently by sex. Whole-kidney inflammation markers looked unchanged, which masked the real story: inside the filtering compartment, macrophages had infiltrated and a cell-attracting gene was switched on, especially in males. Tubule tissue showed its own sex- and metabolism-dependent inflammation patterns. Section by section, sex-aware analysis is the authors' prescription for sharper therapies.
pmc-13408435:
Ashraf Hefny and co-authors review in 2026 what broken first or second ribs signal after blunt chest injury at a community hospital in Al Ain. Fractures that high up take serious force, so they often warn of wider damage inside the chest. Records covered admissions from late 2014 to early 2020 drawn from the hospital trauma registry.

Of 958 admitted chest trauma patients, 86 had fractures of the first or second rib, and road collisions caused nearly three quarters of those cases. The fracture group carried significantly higher overall injury severity scores than other chest patients. Deaths were somewhat more frequent in the fracture group, though the difference could reflect chance. The authors urge close monitoring whenever these upper fractures appear, since they mark high-energy impacts.
pmc-13408835:
Djamel Nehar-Belaid and a large immunology team chart in 2026 how the healthy human immune system changes from a two-month-old baby to a person of one hundred five. Blood immune cells from 167 healthy donors were profiled gene by gene, with chromatin data for a subset. Lifespan atlases of this depth are rare, and infancy is the least mapped stretch.

Some cell families rose and fell across life, swelling in childhood, peaking in young adults, then fading. Killer T cells changed most, trading naive cells for battle-worn types with age, while the oldest donors accumulated distinctive veteran populations. Infants stood apart, with more of certain monocytes and dendritic cells, interferon programmes switched on by default, and an expanded pool of a particular naive T cell. Inflammatory pathways climbed with age as interferon pathways ebbed. The map is a reference for vaccine and ageing research.
pmc-13409035:
The EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens delivers a 2026 safety opinion on a freeze-dried gut bacterium proposed as a food supplement for adults. The strain, Anaerobutyricum soehngenii CH106, would be sold at a maximum daily dose counted in billions of active units. European novel food law requires the authority's verdict before marketing.

The panel found the identity, production, composition, and stability information sufficient and saw no genotoxicity concern. A human study giving half the intended dose for three months raised no safety flags. In a ninety-day rat study the highest male dose tested showed no adverse effects, leaving a margin over the proposed human dose that the panel considered comfortable. The opinion clears the scientific path, while the legal authorisation decision rests with the European Commission.
pmc-13409235:
Mansour Alshehri and colleagues measure in 2026 how foot shape and grip strength relate to standing on one leg in one hundred four healthy young Saudi adults. A dropping arch is suspected of undermining balance, yet local evidence was missing. Arch status was scored with a sit-to-stand navicular drop test, strength with a hand dynamometer, and balance by timing a single-leg stance with eyes open and closed, alongside walking and chair-stand tests.

Greater arch drop went with shorter balance times on both feet once other factors were accounted for, the link stronger on the right side. Stronger grip, by contrast, predicted longer balancing, suggesting it marks general muscular fitness rather than anything foot-specific. The authors position arch screening and strength work as plausible levers for balance training in young adults, within a cross-sectional design that cannot prove cause.
pmc-13409335:
Pablo Miaja and co-authors test in 2026 how far an antibody against a brain protein called SFRP1 can go as an Alzheimer's treatment, and when in the disease it should be given. Their earlier work had implicated the protein as a multi-pronged driver of the disease and shown that neutralising it eased mouse pathology. Transgenic mice carrying human Alzheimer's genes received the antibody at different disease stages, by injection behind the eye.

Radioactively labelled antibody showed the drug engages its target around the body and does reach the brain, though at much lower levels and with clearance inside a day. A small-molecule blocker of the same protein was compared alongside. Pathology was then read out by immunoassays and tissue imaging to map the treatment window. The study is a pharmacology-first step: dose, distribution, and timing settled in mice before anyone argues for human trials.
pmc-13410335:
Tobias Atkin and colleagues argue in 2026 that trials for cannabis use disorder should stop judging success by total abstinence alone. Twenty years of drug trials have produced no reliably effective medicine for the condition. Full abstinence is hard to reach, may not match what patients want, and can hide real gains.

Many trials were labeled failures even though patients cut their use and felt or functioned better. Alcohol and tobacco research moved ahead by accepting measured cuts in use as valid outcomes. The authors propose shared reduction-based measures for cannabis trials, tied to mental health, physical health, and daily function. Abstinence would stay on the record as a secondary outcome rather than the sole bar.
pmc-13410535:
Ioannis Sykaras, Maria Kantilafti, and Stavri Chrysostomou review in 2026 whether eating in the Mediterranean style protects kidneys in diabetes. Kidney damage from diabetes is the chief small-vessel complication of the disease and can end in kidney failure. The diet, rich in plants and olive oil, is known to help heart and metabolic health.

Following standard review rules, the team searched three databases and kept six studies of adults. Most found that closer adherence to the diet tied to lower odds of kidney damage, with reported links varying widely. Two studies found no clear link at all. Few studies, mostly watch-and-see designs from a narrow region, keep any verdict tentative for now.
pmc-13411135:
Marieli Thomazini Piske Garcia, Valeria Valim, and Luís Carlos Lopes-Júnior lay out in 2026 a plan to review second COVID-19 booster shots in older adults. Aging immune systems and other illnesses leave seniors at high risk of severe disease. Evidence on a fourth dose, covering benefit, safety, and immune response, remains scattered.

The registered protocol will search six databases without date or language limits. Trials and strong comparison studies in people aged 60 and over qualify for inclusion. Standard tools will grade study quality and certainty of the pooled evidence. Results will be told as a narrative, with combined statistics where methods allow. The aim is practical guidance for vaccine policy aimed at high-risk groups.
pmc-13411535:
Oluchi Ezekannagha and colleagues pulled together 39 studies from 2001 to 2024 to map nutrition gaps in Sierra Leone for women, children, and teens. National surveys and program reports exist, yet evidence on vitamins and minerals stayed patchy, leaving policy makers to guess where need runs deepest.

Wasting and stunting stayed high, anemia passed 60 percent in young children, and data centered on iron, vitamin A, and iodine while zinc and vitamin D went largely unmeasured. The review hands planners a gap map for the next national survey and for targeting food and supplement programs.
pmc-13412035:
Yulin Tang and colleagues pooled 17 trials with 2344 sedentary older adults in 2026 to test whether programs built on behavior theory actually get people moving. Sitting too long harms heart and metabolic health, yet generic advice often fails, so the review compared theory-guided programs against control groups on sitting time, activity, and health markers.

Theory-based programs cut sitting time. They added about eight minutes of brisk activity and about 867 steps per day, and nudged body mass and blood sugar markers in a healthier direction. The paper backs structured, theory-led coaching over simple reminders for older adults who sit most of the day.
pmc-13412135:
Hui Wang and co-authors track ten years of MRSA at a Chinese cancer hospital in a 2026 surveillance study. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus spreads in healthcare settings and resists many standard antibiotics, yet long records from cancer hospitals are rare. The team reviewed isolates gathered at Sichuan Cancer Hospital from 2015 through 2024, noting wards, specimen types, and drug test results.

Of 1,550 Staphylococcus aureus isolates, 433 were MRSA, a detection rate of 27.94 percent for the decade. Rates peaked in 2018, then eased, though year-to-year swings were not statistically significant. Head and neck surgery yielded the most cases, and lower airway infections led among hospital-acquired ones. Four last-line drugs still worked against every isolate tested.
pmc-13412635:

The combined group improved most, suggesting the two interventions add up.
pmc-13413235:

Four profiles emerged, from simple question-and-answer users, a quarter of the group, to critical co-thinkers at about one sixth.

A high-depth, high-dependence subgroup made up about a quarter of respondents, skewed toward women and computing majors. Since everything rested on self-report, the authors read the results as perceptions and urge training in reflection over tool skills.
pmc-13413435:

pmc-13415435:

No treatment related toxicity signs appeared in the animals.
pmc-13415535:

Pros showed stronger links and larger rind volume in the lower attention network, and firmer white matter in the upper one. Links in the thalamus network ran lower. Working memory scores tied to one thalamus link across all who took part.
pmc-13415735:
Shun Ling and colleagues tested a cell-surface receptor, PLXNA3, in bowel cancer in 2026 to see if it drives growth and spread. Earlier computer studies had flagged it as a possible warning marker, yet no lab work had confirmed its role, so the team paired public tumor data with cell experiments.

High PLXNA3 marked worse survival, later stage, and spread, and silencing it in cancer cells slowed growth and movement. The paper nominates PLXNA3 as both a prognosis marker and a treatment target for colorectal cancer for future trials to test.
pmc-13416135:

pmc-13420335:

pmc-13421735:

pmc-13422635:

pmc-13422835:

pmc-13423935:

pmc-13424135:

Incidence climbed significantly over the period. Rates ran highest in Asian women, at 10.33% of the cohort. Black or African American women came next, at 8.33% of the cohort. American Indian or Alaska Native women stood at 8.05% of the cohort. pmc-13424235:
Sebastian Hauser, Marit Veit, and Kerstin Leopold compare suspension reagents for a gentle X-ray method that measures elements in medical samples in this 2026 paper. The comparison judges accuracy, reliability, and greenness together. Acid works well but is harsher on lab and environment. A milder winner would widen the method's appeal. pmc-13425035:

pmc-13425535:
Yuyun Eka Kartika Sari and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter adding a public administration view to research on oral microbes and chronic kidney disease. pmc-13426335:
Deqiang Ren and coauthors built molecular identity cards for cultivated Dendrobium officinale orchids in Guizhou Province in a 2026 genetics study. pmc-13426735:

pmc-13427435:

pmc-13427735:

Each one counted in the final model of survey responses. The authors argue these habits can blunt damage to nature. They can also build strength against climate shocks and support broader development goals in Somali communities. They urge leaders, green agencies, and other groups to build plans around the four habits. Care for nature should not be treated as an extra.
pmc-13427935:

Brain tissue showed more cell death and oxidative damage as peak pressure rose. Rats in the middle band, the authors suggest, suit future treatment experiments best. pmc-13429135:

pmc-13429535:

Their average age was near 17 and average body mass index about 46, deep in the severe obesity range. Girls made up about 59 percent.

pmc-13430635:
