Sweden ranks near the top worldwide for this skin cancer, yet a prior report found a drop starting in 2015 for people under fifty. Sun habits and the arrival of residents with darker skin both stand as proposed causes.

The team counted every confirmed invasive case in people aged twenty to fifty-nine from 1998 through 2024. More than seventeen thousand cases fell in the younger band, with a like count in the older band. Cases split by growth pattern, since some forms track sun exposure while others grow apart from it. The study weighs how much each pattern shifted and whether newcomer groups can explain the turn.
pmc-13430735:
Togha and colleagues mapped in 2026 the web of links among symptoms, triggers, and pain sites in cluster headache. It is a rare disorder of severe one-sided head pain with watering eyes and a runny nose. Using records from the Iranian national registry, the team built statistical networks from yes-no data on 321 patients. They stress-tested the webs by resampling to see which links hold up.

Togha found the symptom web's strongest links joined eye watering with runny nose, and a shrunken pupil with runny nose. Yet its ranking of central symptoms failed the preset stability bar. The trigger web was too unstable to read at all, and the authors say so plainly. The pain-site web held up best, with neck and back-of-head pain linked positively and lower jaw and cheek pain opposed. The study models honest limits for this exploratory mapping method.
pmc-13431735:
Zhang and co-authors review in 2026 how clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, an age-related growth of blood stem cell clones carrying acquired mutations, raises cardiovascular risk. The condition was once treated mainly as a warning sign for blood cancer.

The review shows that risk depends strongly on which gene is mutated. Loss of TET2 favors inflammatory signaling through interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-6, while DNMT3A changes reshape immune cell programs in a different way. ASXL1 mutations skew blood cell production and link to harmful heart remodeling, and the JAK2 change drives clot-promoting inflammation. Because several types converge on the same inflammatory signals, the authors discuss blocking interleukin-1 or interleukin-6 as a targeted prevention strategy. They note that gene-stratified outcome trials are still needed.
pmc-13432935:
Chen and team weighed three European Kidney Function Consortium equations for gauging kidney filtration. One uses creatinine alone, one cystatin C alone, and one both markers together. They asked which best predicts death in the general population. All three were applied to 4,519 American survey adults. They were tracked for a median of 211 months through 2019.

All three scores flagged all-cause and cardiovascular mortality on their own. Lower filtration showed a risk link that steepened sharply in the models. The cystatin C equation sorted risk far better than the creatinine version. Net reclassification improved by 15.9 percent for all-cause mortality. Only seven people needed testing per correct re-sorting. The joint equation also beat creatinine alone, at 8.9 percent. Yet adding creatinine to cystatin C did slightly worse than cystatin C alone. The edge came mainly from sorting right the people who lived.
pmc-13433335:
Salameh and colleagues surveyed Lebanese adults in 2026 about childhood abuse, body awareness, and mental health. They focused on alexisomia, which means trouble sensing and reading signals from one's own body. Their one-time snapshot study enrolled 1,205 adults in July 2024 through snowball sampling, where participants recruit others. The team tested whether alexisomia sits between abuse and later depression or stress.

Adults who reported more childhood abuse also reported more alexisomia, depression, and stress. Statistical mediation tests, which check whether one factor carries an effect, confirmed the pathway for both outcomes. The direct link from abuse to depression and stress also stayed strong. The authors urge care that builds body and emotional awareness, such as mindfulness training, for adults with trauma histories.
pmc-13433935:
A large group in France, Belgium, and Switzerland reports a data challenge on blood cell sorting in a 2026 paper. Sorting white blood cells by shape is a core lab skill, yet it leans on expert eyes and varies by site. The challenge tested machine models on a shared, expert marked image bank.

Twenty labs built a bank of more than sixty-nine thousand images in 23 classes. In all, 245 teams from schools, hospitals, and firms took part. The best model reached high balanced accuracy, well past the base model. Common cells were sorted near perfectly, while rare and look alike classes stayed hard. All data and models were released openly.
pmc-13434135:
Yuchen Huang and colleagues describe a 2026 screen that tests whole sets of drug like compounds against many proteins at once. Older screens test one compound at a time and need each compound made in advance. Their mix and test plan lets proteins pick out the best fit before full synthesis.

The team found blockers for three enzymes and mapped more than 2,600 sites on proteins that new drugs could target. Work on one protein, VCP, led to a strong blocker that slowed tumors in animals. A fast gel test checked more than 800 variants in two days. The plan raises screening speed ten to twenty fold.
pmc-13434535:
Jang and colleagues analysed in 2026 how child maltreatment passes between generations in South Korea, and which factors raise or lower that risk. Parents who were maltreated as children are more likely to maltreat their own children, but the link is not the same for all families. Using a 2017 national survey of families with children, the team sorted parents into hidden groups based on how strongly their own childhood harm linked to current maltreatment.

Jang found three groups: one with no link, covering most parents, one with a partial link, and one with a full link across harm types. Views accepting corporal punishment split the first two groups. The full-link group stood out for low mood, parenting stress, partner violence and control, and weak family ties. The authors urge screening that pairs parents' own histories with fixable factors, so support can be matched to risk.
pmc-13434735:
James H Holt and coauthors probe why stem cells keep their virus alarm nearly off in 2026. Human pluripotent stem cells barely react to alarm cues, while their grown daughter cells react well. Lifting a silencing hub part in stem cells tests what the hub holds down.

With the hub part gone, jumping genes woke and alarm genes rose without any alarm signal. The hub sits on both alarm genes and the jumping genes that might trip them. The authors propose a three layer lock on triggers, sensors, and responders. The lock may stop stem cells from harming themselves with false alarms. Early growth seems to need quiet more than speed.
pmc-13436535:
Paul and colleagues altered the cyanobacterium Synechocystis to produce hydrogen straight from photosynthesis. They fused a hydrogenase enzyme onto photosystem I, the light-catching complex, through its PsaF subunit. Fusing the enzyme places hydrogen production at the very source of light-driven electrons. It skips carbon-based middle steps altogether.

Their first try dialed down the PsaC subunit to reach a more energetic electron cluster. It produced no hydrogen at all in the altered strain. Focus shifted to subunit PsaE. Models hinted it sat in the way of electron transfer from photosystem I to the fused hydrogenase. Removing PsaE from the fusion strain made light-driven hydrogen production possible in the tests. The authors conclude PsaF is a viable, sound anchor point. Taking out steric blockers is a general design lesson for living light-based hydrogen systems, they add.
pmc-13437335:
Siena Brazier and a large team asked whether free access to a running wheel could rescue brain cells in mice missing a growth brake. The gene PTEN normally restrains a growth pathway; without it in Purkinje cells, those cells overgrow, waste energy, and slowly die, with autism-like traits in the animals. Their 2026 study let such mice run at will, comparing them with resting cage mates.

Running mice balanced and moved better on motor tests. Their Purkinje cells kept more of the tiny power plants and recycling units healthy cells need, and fewer cells were lost. A stress-energy sensor in the cells rose with running. Surprisingly, the overactive growth signal climbed even higher, which the authors flag as a puzzle. Sex gaps in social and other behavior also narrowed in the runners. The team reads exercise as a real, if partial, lever for this class of brain disorder.
pmc-13437435:
Cesari and colleagues build ultrasmall gel particles from cyclodextrins, ring shaped sugars whose hollow centers can carry greasy drugs that water rejects. Many cancer drugs fail that water test. Their 2026 study links the sugar rings into nanogels with a small bridging compound. It loads them with two poorly soluble agents, osthole and combretastatin A-4, a drug that attacks tumor blood vessels. Tests in ovarian cancer cells then judge safety and killing power.

Combretastatin A-4 became the lead cargo after screening and computer docking. The gamma form of the sugar, with the largest ring cavity, loaded the drug best even though the fit was imperfect. Empty nanogels harmed no cancer cells, showing the carrier itself is gentle. Loaded nanogels kept the drug's cell killing power and beat the plain sugar carrier form. The platform, the authors argue, merits development for other water shy cancer drugs.
pmc-13437935:
Wang and colleagues review the evidence in this 2026 article for a compound mouth gel pairing chamomile extract with lidocaine, a local anesthetic. The gel promises three actions at once against oral diseases: pain relief, reduced inflammation, and faster wound healing, an attractive combination for conditions from gum disease to mouth ulcers.

Searching seven Chinese and international databases through August 2025, the team screened 1,413 articles and kept 27 studies for the final synthesis. Those studies reported encouraging results across periodontal disease, mucosal conditions, wisdom-tooth socket inflammation, dry socket, and implant-related inflammation. The reviewers pull back on enthusiasm, however: sample sizes were small, methods varied widely, and overall study quality rated only moderate to low. Their verdict is that the gel shows preliminary therapeutic potential and now needs rigorous, high-quality trials to confirm real clinical value.
pmc-13438135:
Sandra Bos and colleagues followed dengue antibodies in Nicaraguan children for eighteen months to learn how each kind rises and falls. Dengue's four virus types circulate together, and antibodies from one bout can worsen the next. Their 2026 study used hospital samples from four points after illness began. It split the response into eighty-four subsets by antibody class, target piece, and whether antibodies matched the infecting type or crossed over.

The subsets kept separate clocks. After a first infection, cross-reactive antibodies against the virus coat rose over time instead of fading, a surprise with stakes for later bouts. Matching and crossing subsets behaved differently, as did answers aimed at different parts of one protein. Even eighteen months out, many children carried three antibody classes. The authors argue lumping antibodies into one curve hides what decides protection, and that vaccine trials should track subsets over long windows, not early snapshots.
pmc-13438635:
Jenny Dorich and colleagues studied health literacy in adults living with brachial plexus birth injury, nerve damage during delivery that can leave lifelong weakness. One to three babies per thousand sustain it, and a sizable share never fully recover. Their 2026 analysis returned to a larger outcomes project, merging questionnaire scores from 147 adults with survey comments from 183 and deep interviews with twelve.

Average literacy scores sat midrange, yet the spread was wide. Some adults described care that left them lost: jargon-heavy visits, no roadmap after childhood clinics ended. Others described teams that explained, checked understanding, and planned ahead, and those accounts read as templates. The authors argue the variation itself is the finding, mapping exactly where care can improve without new drugs or surgery. Clearer communication and adult-focused guidance could lift the whole experience of a condition medicine cannot cure.
pmc-13438735:
K P Suchithra's team built DMEFNet in 2026, an uncertainty-aware network for classifying heart sounds in valve disease. Phonocardiograms are cheap and non-invasive, yet noise, patient variation, and overlapping sounds can mislead automated diagnosis. The model fuses one-dimensional heart sound traces with two-dimensional time-frequency images, and four uncertainty methods were compared to flag shaky predictions.

On a public heart valve data set, uncertainty ran low when predictions were right and higher for ambiguous or noisy cases, with good calibration overall. Clinicians get a trust layer for automated heart sound screening: confident calls can proceed, uncertain ones can go to human review. Real clinic recordings will test whether calibration holds outside the lab.
pmc-13439335:
Serdal Deniz, Derya Evgin, and Rıdvan Karabulut study what helps parents care for the teeth and diet of children with disabilities. These children often need complex feeding and mouth care, and parents carry most of that load. Their 2026 study surveyed one hundred ninety-five parents. It measured how confident parents felt, how much family support they had, and how they handled daily nutrition and oral health tasks.

Standard statistical tests and a regression model sorted the links among these factors. Confidence and support stood out in the early results as tied to better daily care. The authors aim to show clinics where help lands best: coaching that builds parent confidence, or services that back up the whole family. The work adds rare data on a group that dental and diet services often miss.
pmc-13439535:
Maja Simonoska Crcarevska and her co-authors present a 2026 evaluation of pharmacist-led asthma care in North Macedonia. Asthma control stays poor worldwide, often due to wrong inhaler use and overuse of reliever puffs. Community pharmacists see patients often and can coach them. The study covered 1,247 patients across 127 pharmacies, checking control scores, reliever use, and inhaler technique with device checklists.

Poor inhaler technique strongly predicted poor asthma control. Among patients followed over visits, correct technique climbed from about seventy-two percent to near ninety percent by the second visit. In those attending three visits, it reached ninety-eight percent. As technique improved, its link to control faded, which the authors read as the wider care package working. They support building pharmacist-led asthma care into national plans. The package included adherence help, lifestyle advice, and monitoring.
pmc-13440235:
Naidu, Shetty, and Dsouza review whether augmented reality guidance makes root-end surgery faster and more exact. The surgery needs precise finding of the root tip and careful bone cutting. Even with 3D scans and microscopes, plans and real cuts can drift apart.

Augmented reality lays 3D body data over the surgeon's view in real time. The review followed PRISMA 2020 rules and searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies were grouped by accuracy, speed, safety, and workflow outcomes. Proof so far is limited and mixed in method, so the authors weigh what can safely be claimed.
pmc-13440635:
Jingyi Yang and colleagues design protein-coated nanoclusters that strip a breast cancer's defences before attacking it, reporting mouse and cell work in 2026. Triple-negative breast cancer resists many drugs, partly by hoarding glutathione, an antioxidant shield, and partly by hiding from immunity. Their clusters, built from copper zinc sulfide wrapped in albumin, respond to tumour acidity in sequence. First they release hydrogen sulfide gas that drains the antioxidant shield.

Copper ions follow, triggering cuproptosis, a copper-driven cell death that dodges usual apoptosis resistance. Zinc ions then act as an alarm, helping cells notice leaked mitochondrial DNA and switch on the STING immune pathway. Tumours in mice drew more killer T cells and matured more immune sentries. Pairing the clusters with PD-L1 blockade, a standard immune release drug, strongly suppressed both implanted tumours and lung spread.
pmc-13440735:
Taliah Prince and colleagues sort Australian teenagers into wellbeing profiles and ask how early cyberbullying sorts with them, reporting in 2026. Online abuse is common in the teen years and tracks with poor mental health, yet whole-person patterns were unclear. Data came from a longitudinal brain study of 86 adolescents. Clustering combined distress, body dissatisfaction, social connectedness, wellbeing, and quality of life in mid-adolescence, while records from earlier waves captured online abuse involvement.

Three profiles emerged: flourishing, broad impairment, and appearance-specific concern. Early cyberbullying involvement aligned with the broad impairment profile, not the looks-focused one. The flourishing group held steady, while the broad-problems group shifted widely across domains. Eating disorder symptoms concentrated in the appearance-specific profile, appeared in the broad impairment one, and were absent among the thriving group. The authors read online abuse as a broad-risk marker and body worry as a narrower pathway.
pmc-13442535:
Kuan Lu and colleagues report early results for a joint spine method called Endo-OLIF in a 2026 study of worn lower-back disease. The method pairs a side-entry fusion with a scope view, so surgeons can clear nerve squeeze while they fuse the joint. Records covered 29 people treated from February 2022 to November 2023, each at one or two spine levels.

No surgery hit a nerve root or tore the nerve sac during the work. Two people, 6.9 percent of the group, had brief thigh numbness or hip bend weakness that faded with time. Pain scores and a back function index tracked gains across a mean follow-up span of 15.6 months in this series. The team presents the joint method as a workable low-cut route, while noting the small, one-center record set.
pmc-13443535:
Halah Abdulaziz Al-Alshaikh presents a 2026 framework for spotting anomalies in smart healthcare data without shipping sensitive patient records to the cloud. Her system, called FL-EAD, lets distributed devices train a shared model locally and exchange only model updates. An energy-aware rule picks which devices join each round based on battery and communication cost.

A hybrid model pairing an autoencoder with attention-based memory networks captures both spatial and temporal patterns in the data streams. Tests on a public healthcare IoT data set showed gains over both centralized methods and standard federated learning in accuracy, F1 score, energy use, communication load, and detection speed. The design offers hospitals a private, scalable watchdog, though live deployment trials remain.
pmc-13443935:
Andrés H. Catalán and colleagues present a 2026 interpretable model for flagging single anomalous log lines in large distributed systems, where sheer volume defeats manual review. Their sentiment-aware transformer builds on a BERT variant tuned for log language, needs no parser, and maps subword evidence up to word-level importance scores via SHAP.

The model reached F1 scores up to 99.96 percent on familiar systems and 96.97 percent on unseen ones, while processing about 3,750 log lines per second. Operators can see which words drove each verdict, a transparency gain over opaque detectors. The authors argue that scale, semantic robustness, and interpretability together decide whether such tools earn trust in production.
pmc-13444335:
Kaur and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a baby with a growing neck lump. The cause proved to be neuroglial heterotopia, brain-type tissue growing outside the skull. Such tissue rests are rare and are not true tumors. In this child, the mass pressed on the airway and worsened breathing.

The patient was a 12-month-old girl with a lump on the left side of her neck. MRI scans showed a cyst-filled mass reaching deep toward the throat space. The scans found no link between the mass and the brain itself. After surgery, tissue tests showed mature brain-type cells in fibrous tissue. The authors stress tissue testing, since scans alone cannot prove this diagnosis. Early removal also eased the pressure on her breathing and airway over time.
pmc-13445935:
Bahman Aghaei and coauthors develop a 2026 by-culture adapted scale gauging Iranian nurses' skill in giving bad news to kin of dying patients. Talks with 18 nurses plus a review of 37 studies yielded three domains, prep, conveying the bitter truth, and comfort, shaped into a 26-item tool tested with 284 nurses.

The scale showed strong content soundness, a clear three-factor structure covering two thirds of variance, and high steadiness. Items caught by-culture set tactics such as gradual truth-telling, good timing, gentle language, and kind comfort. Teachers gain a fitting tool for training and grading, with follow-up and telling checks still ahead.
pmc-13446035:
Angelo Maria Sabatini sets out a strict workflow for fair contests between text classifiers, using Dante's Divine Comedy as the test case, in a 2026 methods paper written in R. Literary text mining leans on word-count classifiers, yet common shortcuts can rig the race: picking features before the split, or judging on mean accuracy alone. The workflow blocks leaks and shares the same random splits across rivals.

Two standard classifiers, a penalized regression and a linear support vector machine, run head to head under the rules. Paired tests, a pilot-based power check, and a trap run with scrambled pairs guard the verdict. The author argues that small score gaps should be weighed with clarity and stability, not crowned on accuracy alone, a stance that travels well past Dante.
pmc-13446535:
Melissa Connolly and colleagues pool the practice of three European labs on prenatal genetic testing for Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, in a 2026 study. The overgrowth syndrome stems from faulty gene imprinting, and womb testing is tricky because the marks often occur in mosaic patches. Requests for the test have grown as scan signs like a belly wall gap raise the question.

The labs reviewed six hundred forty-six prenatal samples tested with methylation assays at the known imprinting centers. About one in ten samples showed a syndrome-typical disturbance, a spectrum like that seen after birth. Just over four in a hundred samples failed, near all of them native tissue draws. The authors back testing when scans or family history point that way, with the caveat that mosaic faults can hide.
pmc-13447335:
Kavi Raj Chataut and coauthors analyze a 2026 look-back study of a decade of surgery and drug treatment for neck spine infection at two spine centers. The team went over 33 patients treated by surgery from 2014 to 2024, tracking implants, lineup, side ills, stay length, nerve signs, pain, and one-year living.

Staphylococcus aureus led germs at 39 percent, and ventral pressure relief with fusion led surgery. Nerve pain and neck pain got better in 24 of 33 patients, while implant slack showed in 15 percent and one-year deaths reached 9 percent, all in older multi-ill patients with sepsis. Surgery plus drugs proved strong short to medium term, the authors conclude.
pmc-13447735:
Marina Lim and Seungmin Lee measured how often Cambodian children aged six months to five years suffer wasting and stunting at the same time. Wasting means being too thin for one's height, and stunting means being too short for one's age.

Using a national health survey from 2021 and 2022 covering 3,420 children, they found about one child in fifty had both problems together. Low birth weight raised the odds nearly fivefold, and having an underweight mother or living in the poorest homes more than doubled them. Girls faced lower odds than boys, and no feeding measure from the survey linked to the combined condition. Lim argues that help should target mothers' nutrition, safer births, and poverty in the same programs.
pmc-13447935:
Weng, Fan, and Tang built a deep learning add-on that forecasts how reservoir landslides creep over time from rainfall, water level, and groundwater data, aiming to sharpen early warnings. Standard forecast models weight every variable and moment equally inside fixed windows, although a rainstorm last week matters differently from one last year.

Their Dynamic Weight Generator learns how much weight each variable gets at each timestep inside the history window, rescaling inputs before any standard prediction network sees them. They bolted it onto four backbones, convolutional, recurrent, transformer, and Mamba architectures, and trained everything end to end for displacement prediction. Across all four, the weighted versions beat their stationary counterparts on the reservoir landslide benchmarks reported. The generator effectively captured lag effects that vary by variable, such as delayed groundwater responses, and the authors offer it as a general upgrade for temporal forecasting.
pmc-13449035:
Govender and colleagues test vitamin B3, in the form called nicotinamide, as an add on treatment for Raynaud phenomenon, where cold triggers painful white or blue fingers from narrowed vessels. Their 2026 study enrolls 38 adults, 20 with the primary form and 18 with a form tied to scleroderma, a disease that stiffens skin and vessels. Each person passed through three two week phases: baseline, vitamin twice a day, then a washout with no vitamin, while diaries and tiny vessel imaging tracked change.

Adherence was near complete and side effects were few and mild. Imaging of nail fold capillaries, the tiny vessels at the finger base, improved after the vitamin phase in both groups, with more normal and fewer abnormal vessels. Quality of life and attack severity improved clearly only in primary Raynaud, and gains lasted past the washout, which hints the vitamin may reset vessel function for a time.
pmc-13449735:
Bo Wu and colleagues reply in 2026 to commentators on their study of obesity measures and type 2 diabetes risk in a rural Chinese population. They use the exchange to spell out their scoring system. Their Lipid-Obesity Metabolic Score adds one point each for abnormal body mass index, waist-to-height ratio, triglycerides, and protective cholesterol, sorting people into low, middle, and high bands with clinical cutoffs. Two other indices, built from sex-specific formulas, predicted diabetes cases.

Across 1,554 cases, each standard-deviation rise in the visceral adiposity indices carried hazard ratios of 1.02 to 1.03 in adjusted models. The home-grown score separated risk more visibly: the middle band carried a hazard of 1.29 and the high band 1.93 against the low band. The authors also take up the letter's points on sex and age differences, liver enzymes in the causal pathway, and repeated measurement over time, arguing dynamic assessment beats a single snapshot.
pmc-13450235:
Elsa Varela and a large Mediterranean team assess in 2026 whether managing landscapes, rather than only fighting flames, can tame the region's worsening fires. Fire in the northern Mediterranean is growing worse under climate change, land left empty, and fuel buildup. Firefighting alone cannot address the social and natural drivers. The authors evaluated ten fire-risk initiatives across four countries against five dimensions: many uses, synergies and trade-offs, cross-sector joining, taking part, and adaptive management.

The strongest programs planned across functions at once, were steered by many actors, and learned as they went. Strong leadership, backing from institutions, and shared governance emerged as the helpers behind that coherence. Weak points clustered around tracking trade-offs and aligning plans across sectors and scales. The authors call for deeper investment in teamwork and steering capacity, arguing that landscape approaches can make Mediterranean fire policy more multi-use, adaptive, and accepted.
pmc-13450435:
Simmonds and Coromilas describe a 60-year-old woman with granulomatous cheilitis. It is a rare condition of painless, repeat lip swelling. Her disease flared on the biologic adalimumab. It was rescued by checking drug levels. The condition has no standard treatment, and effects of tumor necrosis factor blockers often fade over time.

Her swelling had lasted for 16 months, with a perioral rash, before biopsy showed non-caseating granulomas in the lip tissue. Workup ruled out inflammatory bowel disease and sarcoidosis, the main mimics her doctors needed to clear first. Several drugs were tried before adalimumab brought control. When the flare later rose, drug-level checks guided a dose change that brought the response back, without switching drugs. The authors argue level-guided dosing merits wider use in dermatology. Checking levels of such drugs remains rare there, despite limited other options.
pmc-13450535:
Haily Fritts and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare, slow-growing skin T-cell disorder showing up in many spots at once. The disorder, recently given its own class, most often forms a single lump on an ear, hand, or foot. It looks fierce under a microscope yet acts mild, so a wrong label can lead to harsh needless treatment.

Their patient was a man aged 48 with no major health history. The write-up stresses the checks that set the mild disorder apart from fast, deadly skin lymphomas that share some cell marks. Care teams are urged to blend exam, tissue, and gene findings before picking a treatment plan.
pmc-13451335:
Roy Harpaz and co-authors show in 2026 that young zebrafish change how they school based on the crowds they grew up in. Group order grows from simple rules between fish, yet how past crowd life tunes those rules was unclear. The team raised larvae in dense or sparse groups, then watched later group shape in real and virtual setups.

Fish from dense groups later swam closer together, while fish from sparse groups spread out. The shift built over tens of minutes and held for hours. Larvae seem to gauge crowd size by how often looming shapes cross their eyes, and they set their social pull to match. A model fed with that past visual record traced the group shifts well.
pmc-13452235:
Safa Bejaoui and co-authors weigh in 2026 what is known about heat stress rewriting DNA marks in cattle. Heat cuts cow welfare, fertility, and yield, and its marks on gene switches may carry part of that harm. The review sorts work across breeding, immune, liver, blood, and growth settings.

Whole-genome mark studies do not agree on one shared direction of change. At set spots, though, marks recur on stress, immune, fuel, hormone, and growth genes. The authors judge a pooled score unfit for now, since heat loads and mark stats are logged too unevenly. They call for shared heat gauges, open data grids, and mark reads tied to real traits.
pmc-13452335:
Chang Hee Baek and co-authors compare in 2026 the two kinds of shoulder swap for worn shoulder joints whose cuff tendons still hold. Which implant suits whom, by age above all, stays disputed. The team matched 44 pairs of patients across the two swaps on age, sex, start scores, motion, and cuff fat, with at least three years of follow-up.

After the swap, the main shoulder score and side scores showed no firm gap between the two kinds. Age splits at seventy also found no age sway on which kind did better in this matched set. Each kind carries its own risk list, from bone stress breaks to gland loosening, which the study logged side by side.
pmc-13453035:
G X Gbenou and ten co-authors feed a tropical legume forage to Fulani zebu cows and track both milk and methane, the gut gas that warms the climate. The forage, Stylosanthes hamata, is a protein rich plant already widely used for tropical livestock. Their 2026 study covers suckler cows, mothers still nursing calves, in sub Saharan Africa.

Cows on the legume supplement ate more and digested their feed better than cows without it. Milk output rose as well, which matters for herders who sell or drink the surplus. At the same time, methane per unit of feed and per unit of milk both fell. The authors present locally grown legumes as a rare win both ways: more food from each cow with a lighter climate load.
pmc-13453235:
María del Carmen Reche and five colleagues test cheap mite diets for a predatory bug used in crop protection. Macrolophus pygmaeus hunts pests, but growers must feed it before prey arrives. The standard feed, moth eggs, is pricey, and brine shrimp cysts vary in quality.

The team tried seven astigmatid mite species on both a commercial strain and a wild strain of the predator. They tracked survival, growth, weight, lifespan, and egg output. Moth eggs still won, but two mites, Acarus siro and Carpoglyphus lactis, supported fair growth and breeding. Wild predators coped better with poor diets. The authors see room to tune feeds and breed strains that thrive on them.
pmc-13453835:
Guang-Yao Li and five co-authors chart traumatic brachial plexus injuries, tears of the shoulder nerve bundle, across 19 hospitals in Guangxi, China. Their 2026 study reviews cases from 2017 to 2022, with 665 patients in the final count. The injury often follows road crashes and can leave an arm weak or useless.

Men made up 480 of the patients, yet the female share climbed from 15.6 percent in 2017 to 34.1 percent in 2022. Traffic caused 45.86 percent of injuries, and e-bike crashes passed motorcycle crashes as the top mechanism. Closed injuries made up about 91 percent, and half the patients also had fractures. Surgery within three months gave a 78.5 percent recovery rate, clearly ahead of late surgery. Freeing the nerves from scar tissue gave the best recovery of the operation types.
pmc-13454035:
Min Li, Rong Ou, and Wanhui Zheng map three decades of research on high intensity focused ultrasound, a treatment that cooks tissue with sound and no cuts. Their 2026 bibliometric study mines the Web of Science with three mapping tools, tracking which countries, centers, and topics drive the field. Growth tells the story in three acts: slow from 1994 to 2002, rapid from 2003 to 2012, then steady and high from 2013 to 2024.

The United States and China lead in both output and impact, while Europe publishes less yet earns strong quality marks. Hot topics span basic and clinical work, technique tuning, and safety checks. The authors see rich openings as uses widen and imaging guidance improves. They also call for bigger shared trials and common standards before the method settles into routine care.
pmc-13454135:
Seyed Hamed Godasiaei and others probed sound-bubble cooling on nano fins in 2026, for hot computer chips. Phase-change cooling with sound-driven bubbles and nano-coated pin fins holds big promise, but the heat physics and best fin shapes were not fully mapped. The team joined lab tests with smart-model checks on plain and nano fins.

Nano-sheet fins lifted the heat-flux limit by just over seventy percent next to plain fins. The heat-move rate rose by just over one hundred sixty percent. A deep net model fit near-perfectly. Heat flux ruled bubble motion in the model checks, while nano fins spurred bubble birth and eased pressure loss. Chip engineers gain a proven cooling plan for high-power chips.
pmc-13454335:
Jiayun Liu and seven colleagues published, in 2026, a mapping study of research on diagnosing tremor and telling its causes apart. Tremor is among the most common movement symptoms, yet past work sat in scattered pockets. The team searched two large databases for work from 2016 to August 2025 and charted the field with network tools.

The search found 1,145 papers and 47 trials. Output grew year by year, and citations peaked in 2021. The United States published the most, Germany linked the most fields, and Yale led among universities. Trials focused mostly on essential tremor and device-based methods. Lujia Feng leads a large team reporting, in 2026, that a vitamin-like compound may shield the eye in an inherited blinding disease. Retinitis pigmentosa slowly kills light-sensing cells and the layer that feeds them. Using rats with a gene fault tied to the disease, the team found misshapen power plants, the mitochondria, inside those eye cells.

Levels of NAD+, a molecule cells need for energy, had fallen in the sick eyes. The same pattern appeared in human eye cells grown with the same gene fault. Feeding rats a building block of NAD+ protected their retinas in scans and vision tests. Cell work traced the benefit to a pathway linking an enzyme to the mitochondria. The authors propose that failing mitochondria help drive the disease, and that restoring NAD+ deserves study as a treatment.
pmc-13454535:
Shengwen Xu leads a fourteen-author global study, from 2026, of what decades of mineral fertilizer do to soil microbes. The authors stress that communities were reorganized, not impoverished: variety held, and fungal disease agents did not gain ground.
pmc-13454635:
Jijin Wu and nineteen colleagues trace, in a 2026 mouse study, how two opposed wires from the front of the brain jointly govern vulnerability to stress. Lasting stress tips animals toward resilience or susceptibility for reasons that were unclear. The circuit runs from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the lateral habenula, a small hub tied to disappointment and low mood.

The circuit carries both an exciting and a calming projection. In susceptible mice, stress strengthened the exciting input and weakened the calming one, leaving hub cells overactive. Artificially copying that imbalance made animals more susceptible, while restoring balance built resilience. The authors name this dual-pathway failure as a mechanism of stress-related illness and a possible drug target for depression.
pmc-13455235:

Yaoyu Yin, Xinchen Kang, and Buxing Han review, in 2026, an unglamorous ingredient that quietly steers carbon dioxide conversion: the ionomer film inside the catalyst layer. Veronika Ploke, Bernad Batinic, and Stefan Stieger check, in a 2026 psychometric study, whether a well-known well-being questionnaire still measures well when asked every day instead of once. The daily version held together best as a single total score and for emotional well-being, which also swung most within a person. Social well-being barely moved day to day and proved hardest to capture in diary form. Erika Kellerova and co-authors studied how spinal cord injury in rats disturbs the signaling of angiotensin II, a hormone system involved in blood pressure and stress responses. The authors conclude that intact sympathetic innervation governs how the stress axis adapts after cord trauma.
pmc-13457635:
Xiao-Wen Chen and colleagues test whether a woman's traditional Chinese medicine constitution type forecasts depression around childbirth. pmc-13458235:
Fatimah Ali Hasan and colleagues test aloe and date palm seed sprays as natural boosters for cumin in a 2026 study. pmc-13458535:
Tao Han and colleagues test a Chinese service quality survey for online hospitals in a 2026 study. Content soundness drew on 50 experts, shape soundness held in factor checks, and overall trust topped a Cronbach alpha of 0.980. Age, hospital grade and felt service quality linked with staff morale, while the quality-morale link held only for high-hope staff and varied by department. pmc-13458835:
Gershon Spitz and co-authors examined whether a common hidden parasite infection changes long-term outcomes after serious brain injury. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, infects roughly a third of humanity and stays dormant in the brain for life. Their 2026 study recruited 89 survivors of moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, each at least ten years past injury, plus 32 matched people without brain injury. They tested blood for signs of the parasite while scanning brains and mood.

Among survivors, 35 people, about 39 percent, tested positive for latent infection. They also reported higher anxiety. The brainstem shrinkage partly explained the infection-to-anxiety link statistically. Among uninjured controls, infection was not tied to anxiety or cognition.
pmc-13459235:

Using survival analysis, the team calculated the stroke incidence rate and tested which patient characteristics independently predicted a first stroke during follow-up.

Strokes occurred at a rate of 5.53 per 100 person-years in this patient group. Six predictors stood out after adjustment: living rurally, a family history of stroke, the heart rhythm disorder atrial fibrillation, being overweight, and high total or LDL cholesterol levels. The authors recommend lifestyle counseling and closer attention to patients carrying these risk factors.
pmc-13459835:
Woo Sub Kim and co-authors developed a new angle for judging heel alignment on the ordinary standing leg X-rays already taken after knee surgery, sparing patients a special hindfoot view. It correlated moderately with the Saltzman reference angle at 0.443, statistically significant, and weakly with a foot arch angle at 0.331 in the validation subset. pmc-13460135:
Ruben Methorst and colleagues studied in 2026 how pain presents differently in women and men with acute type A aortic dissection, a tear in the aorta that demands urgent surgery. Charts covered 460 patients treated at Leiden University Medical Center between 1992 and 2025, after excluding incomplete records and diabetes cases. Symptoms were compared against how far down the body each tear extended.

Chest pain flagged the condition strongly in both sexes. Women more often reported nonspecific back pain, breathlessness, and collapse, and they tended to juggle several symptoms at once. Men's tears reached farther, and greater extent tracked with leg paralysis and abdominal pain, especially in men. Patients whose tears stayed contained sometimes had no symptoms at all, complicating recognition.
pmc-13460235:
Lichen Zhang and colleagues compared in 2026 removing part of a lung lobe against removing the whole lobe for non-small cell lung cancers up to three centimeters wide. Their eastern China center reviewed 685 consecutive patients operated on in 2014 and 2015, including tumors with hazy ground-glass features, then matched 229 pairs to balance the groups. Ten-year overall and recurrence-free survival nevertheless matched closely between approaches, with hazard ratios near one and wide uncertainty ranges in both simple and adjusted models. The authors conclude that the smaller operation is appropriate for these small tumors when patients are chosen carefully.
pmc-13460735:
Markus Brissman and co-authors followed young children treated for obesity in Sweden to learn whether early weight change leaves a metabolic fingerprint four years on. pmc-13461435:
Li Jiang, Xiaowen Yao, Yuning Deng, and Pengfei Li analyzed in 2026 whether muscle wasting and body weight shape treatment tolerance and survival in extranodal natural killer and T-cell lymphoma. This is a rare aggressive cancer. Their retrospective cohort held 347 newly diagnosed patients, with muscle measured on scans at the third lumbar vertebra against sex-specific cutoffs, and weight grouped by Asian body mass criteria.

About a third of patients were sarcopenic, and they suffered more blood and gut toxicity during treatment than patients with preserved muscle. Sarcopenia raised the risk of death by well over half on its own. It did not clearly predict disease progression. Underweight patients fared worst of all, while overweight patients did best. The combination of muscle loss with low weight carried the highest mortality risk in exploratory analysis.
pmc-13461535:
Borzouie and Manafiazar measured a 2026 feeding study of brown seaweed added to beef heifer diets to cut methane, a potent greenhouse gas from cattle digestion. Borzouie found dose dependent shifts that grew clear at the one and two percent inclusion levels of diet dry matter. pmc-13461735:

pmc-13461835:

When several ribs break in two places, the chest wall moves the wrong way with each breath, risking breathing failure and lung infection. Pain scores fell from six out of ten to two, and blood oxygen measures improved greatly. Discharge came on day eight. pmc-13462135:
Shufang Pei and co-authors build an artificial intelligence model to tell two look-alike thyroid growths apart before surgery. It beat standard models and scoring systems, and it cut both total and needless biopsy rates in the study's comparisons.
pmc-13462235:

pmc-13462935:

The authors say the word conservative undersells today's precision. Surgeons now follow natural tissue planes, spare vessel networks, and shape the breast envelope in three dimensions, with reconstruction planned as part of the operation. They define the approach as full gland removal along natural embryologic and fascial planes. The proposal matches language to how the surgery is done now.
pmc-13463035:
Sanna Leinonen and co-authors report a survey from 2026 on glaucoma care in short-sighted eyes. For diagnosis and monitoring, the top needs were telling disease change from myopic change, and judging scan and vision tests in such eyes. pmc-13463135:

pmc-13463835:

pmc-13464235:

pmc-13465135:

pmc-13465235:

pmc-13465335:

pmc-13465935:

pmc-13466535:

pmc-13466635:

pmc-13467735:

pmc-13468035:

pmc-13468335:

pmc-13468535:
Xin Zhao and co-authors climb an elevation gradient in 2026 to learn what makes Fargesia rufa bamboo rhizomes send up shoots, a food giant pandas depend on in breeding season. pmc-13468735:

pmc-13468935:

pmc-13469135:

Control uses an adaptive neuro-fuzzy system tuned by a chicken swarm algorithm, while a doubly fed wind generator feeds the DC link through a rectifier. Grid connection covers lulls in sun and wind, and tests showed lower harmonic distortion, high efficiency, and reliable two-way flow. The converter should help off-grid-leaning stations deliver steady charging from mixed renewables.
pmc-13469835:
Yamal Jamal-Ismail Ortiz and co-authors outline in 2026 a pilot program that gives older people living with HIV self guided lifestyle education through QR codes. Frailty is common in this group and can shift over time, while diet and exercise support is hard to deliver at scale. Patients at a hospital clinic in Marbella, Spain, received a leaflet whose codes open curated videos on Mediterranean eating and exercise routines.

Frailty was scored with the standard Fried phenotype before and after six months. The team also tracked sleep, resilience, loneliness, mood, activity, diet adherence, and blood markers of inflammation and immunity. Because the pilot has one arm and no comparison group, changes are summarized descriptively with paired tests. The authors frame the work as an early feasibility check for low cost digital support.
pmc-13469935:
Reza Sepahvand and colleagues compared genetic programming with the HEC-HMS conceptual model in 2026 for simulating rainfall-runoff in Iran's Khorramabad basin. Runoff forecasts guide reservoirs and flood design, yet space-time variation breeds error. Both models simulated four flood events, with HEC-HMS calibrated first and genetic programming trained on the same events, plus sensitivity tests dropping sub-watersheds one by one.

Genetic programming fit peaks far better, with R-squared from 88% to 94% against 65% to 79% for HEC-HMS. The edge held under data-rich conditions with long records, the authors stress, not as a universal verdict. Sensitivity analysis flagged sub-watersheds critical to total flood discharge, giving managers both a stronger forecaster and a map of where runoff originates.
pmc-13470535:
Zhou and co-authors show that unpredictable signals around birth blunt reward responses in males across two species. Their 2026 paper links early adversity to anhedonia, the loss of pleasure and motivation central to several mental illnesses, and isolates unpredictability itself as the active ingredient. A longitudinal human study followed 158 mother-child pairs, while a controlled mouse study randomised litters to unpredictable maternal care.

In humans, the randomness of maternal mood signals during late pregnancy, measured as entropy, predicted adolescents' self-reported reward responsivity. In mice, experimentally fragmented care reduced young adults' responses to palatable food. In both species the effect appeared in males but not females. It survived adjustment for income and maternal mental illness in humans and for litter effects in mice. The authors argue unpredictability is a distinct, sex-dependent early risk signal for reward circuitry.
pmc-13470735:
Zijun Yu leads a ten author team testing in 2026 a filter block made from biomass ash for pulling nitrite nitrogen out of water. Ash left from burning plant matter was baked briefly at high temperature into a porous, chemically stable block. Bench tests varied the water nitrite level, temperature, contact time, acidity, and the ratio of water to filter material.

Uptake per gram peaked at a moderately high starting concentration, warm temperature, eighty minutes of contact, and acidic water. The surface proved uneven, and the capture mixed surface sticking in layers with chemical binding, mostly the former. The process also absorbed heat and proceeded on its own. In flowing tests the ash block beat coconut shell charcoal, ceramic pellets, and natural zeolite by wide margins. The authors pitch it as waste recycling that cleans water.
pmc-13471435:
Mi and co-authors ran a randomized trial testing whether adding mindfulness training to aerobic exercise helps heart patients recover after stent placement. Their 2026 trial enrolled 150 patients after percutaneous coronary intervention, the catheter treatment that opens blocked arteries, with a mean age of 50.79 years.

Half the patients received mindfulness sessions plus aerobic training while the other half trained aerobically only, and both groups were checked before and after. The combined group improved far more on treatment adherence, fear of movement scores, and heart rate variability, the beat-to-beat timing shifts that signal autonomic balance. Exercise tolerance and anxiety and depression scores also favored the combined program, backing mindfulness as an add-on in cardiac rehab.
pmc-13471535:
Uğuz and co-authors surveyed young adults in Türkiye about loneliness, the social support they feel, and how hooked they are on AI chatbots. Their 2026 relational study collected online questionnaires from 610 adults aged 18 to 30, with a mean age of 23.84 years and 54.6% women, and tested the links with structural equation modeling.

Loneliness was positively associated with chatbot dependence, and perceived social support significantly carried part of that association in the mediation test. In plain terms, young people who felt unsupported by real relationships were the ones most likely to lean compulsively on chatbots. The authors recommend strengthening real social connectedness and teaching digital self-regulation, rather than simply restricting the technology, as the practical response.
pmc-13471635:
Valeria Zakurazhnaya and colleagues compare in 2026 blood markers of brain degeneration and inflammation across first episode psychosis, chronic schizophrenia, and health. Whether early psychosis is biologically distinct from the chronic illness remains unclear. Eighteen non standard markers were measured in forty nine first episode patients, eighty chronic patients, and eighty healthy volunteers using a multiplex assay.

The first episode group carried a signature the others lacked: lower levels of two markers, higher levels of a cell adhesion molecule, and a building block protein found less often. The chronic group, by contrast, barely differed from healthy controls on most markers. Their marker network was densely interwoven, while first episode patients showed one strong pairing. The authors read early psychosis as its own biological state, not a mild version of the chronic one.
pmc-13471735:
Isabelle Heinzen and co-authors build in 2026 a family of conducting polymers decorated with ring shaped crown ether groups and map how the decoration trades order against ion flow. Five versions of the polymer PEDOT carried crown ether shares from none to all of their side chains. These mixed conductors, which move both electrons and ions, underpin bioelectronic devices that must dope and undope quickly in salty fluids.

More crown ether sharpened electronic delocalization and nanoscale order, yet the structure compacted, pores shrank, and ions moved worse. The voltage window for doping narrowed, and the salt anion, not the sodium cation the rings were meant to catch, set the doping onset. A half decorated version won overall, pairing the highest charge storage with fast switching. In chloride solutions its doping ignored film thickness, a plus for scaling.
pmc-13472035:
Shaza Bishti and co-authors review how the surface finish of all-ceramic implant bridges affects their success in the mouth, in a 2026 systematic review. Bridges can be carved from one solid block, given a thin surface layer, or fully veneered with layered ceramic. The review covers three-to-four-unit bridges and full-arch sets, all held by implants.

Twelve prospective studies qualified, all on strong zirconia in back teeth or full arches. Success at three years ran near 89 percent for short bridges and about 76 percent for full arches, while survival stayed above 96 percent for both. Chipping was the key split: solid and thin-layered short bridges chipped far less than fully veneered ones. Full arches chipped often and rest on thin evidence, so the authors urge care there. No verdict was possible for softer layered zirconia types.
pmc-13472235:
Fangfang Dai and co-authors review in 2026 how a chemical tag on RNA, called m6A, goes wrong across female reproductive disorders. Enzymes that write, erase, and read this tag tune the life of RNA messages in ovaries, womb lining, and placenta. The review maps altered tagging onto preeclampsia, miscarriage, failed implantation, gestational diabetes, early ovarian insufficiency, polycystic ovary syndrome, and endometriosis.

In each condition, shifted tag control reaches into placental growth, the invasion of early pregnancy tissue, womb receptivity, and the behavior of ovarian and lining cells. Hormone receptors and growth signals appear among the tagged targets. The authors gather a fast moving literature into one diagram friendly account. They present the tagging system as a shared lever that future diagnostics and treatments might grip across many disorders at once.
pmc-13472835:
Alonso-Vargas and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of teaching models in physical education, such as sport education and cooperative learning, and their effects on student motivation. Twenty studies in children and adolescents were pooled under standard review guidelines, with extra analyses testing whether sport type, duration, or school stage changed the effects.

Model-based teaching was linked to clearly higher autonomous motivation and intention to be active, higher satisfaction of competence and autonomy needs, and lower amotivation, the state of not caring at all. Effects were weaker for individual sports and health-focused content than for team sports. The evidence certainty was low and studies varied a lot, so the authors stay cautious. Still, how PE is taught, not just what is played, appears to shape whether students want to move after school ends.
pmc-13473035:
Meng and co-authors used genetic causal inference to nominate new drug targets for lung cancer, integrating gene-expression and protein data across three large consortia. Their 2026 multiomics study screened 2,645 candidate genes with strong genetic instruments, then demanded that the gene signal and the cancer signal share the same causal variant.

Four genes passed every filter with colocalization probability above 0.80 on the posterior scale: SERPING1, THBS3, FLT4, and CHEK1. Their directions differed by subtype: higher FLT4 expression raised adenocarcinoma risk, while higher CHEK1 looked protective in squamous cell carcinoma. SERPING1 and THBS3 appeared to promote non-small cell lung cancer progression, in a disease family that makes up roughly 85% of all lung cancers.
pmc-13473135:
Aylin Tanriverdi Eyolcu and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether walking patterns measured by a wearable sensor could predict how far heart failure patients can walk. Functional capacity, usually judged by a six-minute walk test, guides treatment and prognosis, yet clinic tests take time and staff. Seventy patients wore an inertial sensor while walking. The team fed stride and movement measures into four machine learning models, each tuned by four optimisation methods, with results checked by ten-fold cross-validation.

A hybrid pairing particle swarm optimisation with a CatBoost model performed best, explaining most of the variation in walking distance, with an average error of about 11 metres. Right stride length and overall walking speed carried the most weight in predictions. The authors present gait-based prediction as highly accurate in this small sample, while stressing that it needs testing in larger groups before it can support clinical decisions.
pmc-13473535:
Saket Gupta, Neeraj Kumar, and six co-authors apply a tuning-free optimizer to power grid operations. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses the Jaya algorithm on the optimal power flow problem. Grid operators must balance cost, losses, emissions, and voltage stability. Nature-inspired solvers help, but most need fiddly control settings.

Jaya needs no algorithm-specific parameters at all. Candidate solutions simply drift toward the best and away from the worst. That simplicity removes costly tuning rounds. The authors test several grid goals in turn. Rival methods supply the comparison baseline. Precise solutions support the case for parameter-free tools.
pmc-13474335:
Juan Rozas, Pablo Henríquez, and Aldo Mascareño present a data paper, published in 2026. It publishes the voting record of Chile's two recent constitutional bodies. The Constitutional Convention sat from 2021 to 2022. The Constitutional Council sat in 2023. Both drafted proposed constitutions. Voters later rejected both drafts. This release makes their internal divisions measurable.

The data set covers 205 members. It holds 5,919 plenary roll-call votes. Member background details are included. Ideology scores are estimated three different ways. One way is a dynamic model tracking movement over time. The bodies were elected under contrasting rules. The first had gender parity and reserved indigenous seats. The second used party lists. Researchers can compare the two with this data.
pmc-13474535:
Qian Ren and co-authors chart a tick-borne fever illness across China from 2010 to 2024 in a 2026 report. The illness, shortened to SFTS, lowers platelet counts and can kill older patients. National watch data held more than thirty-four thousand cases from thirty provinces over fifteen years. Trend tools measured how fast reports rose and where cases clustered.

Reports climbed over time with swings year to year, and the illness spread into areas once free of it. Anhui province became the top reporter in the last two years of the span. Death rates rose steeply with age, reaching about nine percent past age eighty-five. Health teams gain a map for vaccine planning and tick control.
pmc-13474835:
Perez-Patiño and colleagues tested whether training family doctors improves how vertigo gets diagnosed and coded in primary care records. Their 2026 trial randomized 20 health centers in southern Barcelona province, with 10 centers getting training and 10 serving as controls. Doctors in the training group took 14 hours of online lessons plus a single in-person session on vertigo management and coding.

The study drew on records covering 545,938 patients in 2019 and 513,638 in 2022, before and after the training period ended. Trained centers used specific vertigo diagnoses more often than controls, at 0.30 percent of patients against 0.25 percent for the comparison centers. The clearest gain was for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a brief spinning sensation triggered by head movement, where adjusted odds of a specific code more than doubled in trained centers.
pmc-13475135:
Alanis Rodriguez Rosario and co-authors build in 2026 a mouse model of skin squamous cell carcinoma that keeps a working immune system, then use it to hunt new drug targets. Immune therapy for this skin cancer now leans on one checkpoint drug family alone. Past models missed either the true gene faults of the human disease or its immune setting, slowing the search for more options.

Their mice carry a switchable faulty p53 gene and a deleted guard gene in skin lining cells, and grow tumors that look and behave like patient tumors. Cell lines from those tumors share gene changes with the human cancer. In those models the team tested several immune drugs alone and in pairs and at varied timing, including a STING activator. Two checkpoints, VISTA and CTLA-4, emerged as workable targets, and the same markers checked out in human tumor samples.
pmc-13475635:
Eriona Petro and co-authors survey access to essential medicines in Albania on price, supply, and affordability. The survey follows a standard World Health Organization method. It uses a global core list of key medicines as its yardstick.

Field teams visited private pharmacies across six urban areas. They checked a set of core medicines at each site. Prices were compared with international reference prices. Affordability used the daily wage of the lowest-paid state worker. Average availability sat just below the global target level. A deeper analysis split results by medicine and site. The findings show where Albanian patients face cost or supply gaps. They give officials a clear base for policy fixes.
pmc-13475735:
Li and co-workers in China showed in 2026 how lung cells call up a zinc gate when a drug wounds their DNA. Zinc helps fix DNA harm, and cells keep its level on a tight leash. The drug was bleomycin, a germ killer known to nick DNA. In human airway cells, the team tracked the full clan of zinc gates after a dose, then cut or raised the lead gate to test its worth.

One gate, ZIP1, rose first and most of all. Cells with less of it coped worse with the harm, and cells with more coped better. The call up ran through a known alarm path. The drug raised TNF alpha, a heat signal, which woke NF kappa B, a gene switch. That switch holds two dock sites at the gate's gene. Block the path at either step, and the gate stayed low.
pmc-13476235:
Everaldo B de Souza and a large team project heatwaves in 2026 for Belém, a large city in the eastern Amazon. Climate models were screened for skill over the city, then corrected against local station records. Heatwaves were counted with a threshold drawn from a thirty-year baseline. Four global pathways from low to high emissions framed the futures.

Recent decades already show more heatwaves, with a sharp rise in the last ten years. Near-future change looks modest and uneven across pathways. Under the highest pathway, late-century heatwaves more than double in yearly count. Longest events stretch from about nineteen days to about sixty-five days.
pmc-13476435:
Hitoshi Murakam and co-authors test in 2026 whether income inequality tracks with broad health signs across Japan. Data covered all forty-seven prefectures at five points from 1999 to 2019. The Gini measure of inequality was set against several population health indicators. Models adjusted for average income, density, and year, and tried three panel styles.

Infant death showed a clear link with inequality in the pooled model judged best fitting. A log-income variant backed the same finding, adding trust in the result. Other health signs did not show firm links in the report. Narrowing income gaps may still matter for the youngest lives.
pmc-13476935:
Ning Chen and co-authors search for genetic targets in age-related macular degeneration in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. This eye disease is a leading cause of vision loss, yet firm drug targets for prevention are lacking. The team joins genome and protein data to nominate candidates.

A pooled genome study of more than twenty-eight thousand cases found ten candidate loci, seven of them new. Protein analyses supported twenty-three plasma proteins as risk or protective factors. Two genes stood out as top risk candidates across several data layers. Immune traits, notably certain regulatory T cells, seemed to carry part of the risk. Fifteen genes looked druggable, though the authors stress that lab validation is still needed.
pmc-13477035:
Gregory L Gedman and a large team read ancient dire wolf genomes in 2026 to place the extinct predator on the dog family tree. Two well-kept fossils, one over thirteen thousand years old and one over seventy-two thousand, gave the DNA. Family trees were built against ten living dog relatives. Dire wolves looked like gray wolves yet had never sat firmly in the tree.

About two thirds of dire wolf ancestry traced to a line sister to wolves, coyotes, and dholes together. The last third came from near the base of the wider dog group. Blending after species split thus shaped the dire wolf deeply. Ancient DNA can settle identity debates that bones alone cannot.
pmc-13477135:
Jeremy Chan and colleagues tracked in 2026 valve choices and outcomes for UK patients aged 50 to 70 having first-time isolated aortic valve replacement. They analysed 11,010 patients from 2013 to 2025, a period spanning the pandemic, comparing mechanical and biological prostheses.

Biological valve use rose from 57.5 percent in 2013 to 71.3 percent in 2024. Mechanical valves showed lower death rates, with ten-year survival about 81 percent against about 76 percent, plus less infection and fewer repeat procedures. They also brought more strokes and major bleeding. Lifetime management stays complex, and the authors call for long-term randomised trials.
pmc-13478035:
Breno Torres da Silva and colleagues report a 2026 parasite survey in lowland tapirs in southeastern Brazil, the first to detect the gut ciliate Balantioides coli in this species by molecular methods. The tapir is Brazil's largest land mammal and is classed as vulnerable. Samples came from captive animals and from free-ranging or reintroduced animals, including a reserve population rebuilt after local extinction.

Forty-five fecal samples were tested by microscopy, culture, and DNA methods. About 69 percent carried some parasite, and ciliates were the most frequent group at 60 percent. DNA testing confirmed Balantioides coli in 24 samples, an infection rate of about 53 percent, with sequences matching known references closely. Worm eggs and coccidian parasites also appeared. Because this ciliate can infect people, the findings matter for tapir health programs and reintroduction planning.
pmc-13478335:
Brandilyn Peters and ten colleagues examined in 2026 how gut microbes relate to walking trouble in Hispanic and Latino adults aged 50 and older. Walking decline hits women more often, but sex-specific microbial roles were unknown.

In women with impairment, microbe variety was lower and makeup shifted, while men showed no such pattern. Fifteen species tracked trouble in both sexes, with Streptococcus and Lactobacillus enriched and Eubacterium depleted, plus 84 women-only species. Linked metabolites hinted at roles in imidazole propionate, bile acid, hormone, and energy pathways. Gut microbes may shape physical function and its sex differences.
pmc-13478635:
Hajime Gotoh and four colleagues built in 2026 heavy-atom-centered triangulenes by a directed triple-lithium step. Placing heavy main-group elements at the centre of rigid carbon frameworks had stayed out of reach, leaving their chemistry largely untried.

Starting from nitrogen-bridged ring starts, they built antimony-, bismuth-, tin-, and lead-centered triangulenes with deep bowl shapes stacked in columns. Despite strained bonds, the compounds proved stable to heat and chemicals, a payoff of rigid confinement. The antimony member also switches back and forth between trivalent and pentavalent states, opening a general route to heavy-atom architectures in curved carbon systems.
pmc-13478835:
Xu and co-workers in China graded in 2026 the short videos that parents find when they search whether sleep drugs for child surgery can harm the young brain. Fear on this point is common before a child's operation. The team pulled the first hits for two lay search terms on two big apps, Douyin and Bilibili, with fresh accounts. Two sleep drug doctors then scored each clip for truth, clarity, and how fit it was to guide a choice.

Of two hundred clips pulled, ninety five fit the brief. False claims sat in more than half of them. The top flaw was false comfort: flat claims that the drugs are plain safe, with no talk of dose or length. Clips from sleep doctors, hospitals, and news desks scored best, while likes and views said naught about worth. Longer clips scored higher on most scales.
pmc-13479535:
Ayelign Mengesha Kassie and coauthors published a 2026 implementation research protocol for a community-based care model serving culturally and linguistically diverse Australians with chronic disease. Nearly a third of Australia's population comes from such backgrounds. Language barriers, cultural mismatch, and low health literacy block access to screening and treatment for conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes.

A four-phase approach based on an established implementation framework moves from exploration through preparation to rollout. The package targets screening for hypertension and diabetes plus starting treatment for people diagnosed. The authors aim for a model other regions can adapt rather than a one-off local fix.
pmc-13479635:
Seyedeh-Tarlan Mirzohreh and colleagues present a 2026 meta-analysis of how diabetes affects people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the thick-heart disease. Diabetes might worsen rhythm risk, stiffening, and heart failure in these patients, but pooled evidence was missing. Eight studies with roughly 47,600 patients in all made the cut. Results were pooled as odds ratios, and heart structure from sound-wave scans as scaled gaps. Every study passed a set bias check, and the trust in the pooled proof was graded with the GRADE method. Subgroup and stress-test checks probed whether results held across settings. The pooled work tells heart doctors how much extra watchfulness diabetes should prompt in this group.
pmc-13479735:
Ying Shen and coauthors published a 2026 molecular study of faulty placental cell fusion in preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy blood pressure disorder. Protein profiling of placental tissue flagged NCK1, an adaptor protein, as reduced in early-onset cases.

In cell experiments, NCK1 rose naturally as placental cells fused, and adding more of it repaired fusion defects caused by low oxygen. The protein stabilized PPARG, a gene regulator, and increased a chemical RNA mark on its message. Removing PPARG erased NCK1's benefit, while restoring it rescued fusion on its own. A third partner, EIF3D, links into the axis through phosphorylation changes. The chain offers new targets for a disease treated today mainly by early delivery.
pmc-13479835:
Hernán-David García-Botina and colleagues present a 2026 cohort study of social frailty and death among older Colombians. Social frailty means shrinking social resources and participation, separate from physical weakness. Data came from the national SABE aging survey of 2015, restricted to four departments and 3,213 adults aged sixty and older with verified vital status.

The social frailty index combined daily functioning, social participation, emotional isolation, and perceived healthcare access. Follow-up through official records established who had died. Models tested whether socially frail elders died sooner after accounting for other risks. Evidence from middle-income countries is scarce, so a Colombian estimate helps planners there decide whether befriending, transport, and participation programs deserve a place beside medical prevention in aging policy.
pmc-13480435:
Kudva and colleagues asked in 2026 whether how Black women lived before breast cancer shapes their sleep in the years after care. Black survivors bear worse sleep than white kin, a drag on life grade and health. The team drew on a follow up study of Black survivors, 682 women in all. Life pattern scores came from home visits held pre illness. Sleep was scored two years post care with a stock sleep form.

Mean life scores sat low, at three of a top seven. Six in ten women met the mark for poor sleep. The top life group, folk who ate, moved, and weighed most in line with guide rules, ran a fifth less poor sleep risk than the base group. Gains showed in felt sleep grade and day drive. The authors urge life help as part of care.
pmc-13483435:
Clifford and colleagues review delivery technology in this 2026 article for a workhorse class of antivirals, nucleoside and nucleotide analogs, the drug family behind many HIV, hepatitis, and herpes treatments. These drugs only work after the cell bolts three phosphate groups onto them, and the first step is a notorious bottleneck that leaves much of each dose inactive.

Packaging the already-phosphorylated drug inside nanoparticles could skip the queue. The review surveys carriers built from lipids, polymers, dendrimers, and polysaccharides that shield the fragile cargo from degradation, improve cell uptake, and release it at chosen tissues, borrowing lessons from cancer nanomedicine. Equal weight goes to the analytical headaches: proving what is inside each particle, how much active drug survives formulation, and whether release happens where intended. The authors judge the approach promising but measurement-limited.
pmc-13483535:
Yang and team tested whether fluid from a friendly vaginal bacterium can slow cervical cancer cells grown in dishes. Their 2026 study bathed three cervical cancer cell lines in the fluid the bacteria had grown in, then measured growth, movement, death rates, and signs of DNA damage inside the cells.

Treated cells grew and migrated less than untreated ones across the lines tested in this work. Death rates rose modestly, reaching roughly one fifth higher than controls in two lines by 48 hours. Treated cells accumulated R-loops, tangles of RNA and DNA that stress the genome, plus a marker protein that flags DNA breaks. Gene-activity scans pointed to one stress protein, HSPA5, as a possible player. Yang frames the fluid as a lead for microbe-based cancer strategies.
pmc-13483635:
Wenjing Dai and co-authors test how early separation from the mother and later disrupted day-night cycles jointly affect young rats. Published in 2026, the experiment sorts animals into four groups covering neither stress, either stress alone, or both stresses combined. Behavior in an open arena and gut microbe makeup were compared across groups.

Rats exposed to both stresses spent more time in the exposed center of the arena than any other group, a pattern the authors read as weakened risk judgment. Each stress left its own microbial fingerprint, spanning bacteria, viruses, and fungi, while a shared core community persisted. Early separation drove most of the fungal reshaping. The work shows that two common developmental stresses do not simply add up, since the combined group looked distinct from either single-stress group.
pmc-13483735:
Guillaume B Cardin heads a 2026 genetic search for mouth cancer arising in young adults who neither smoke nor drink. The retrospective Canadian cohort covers 160 surgical patients of European ancestry treated between 2010 and 2024. Genome-wide comparisons isolate young never-smoking non-drinkers, all-ages never-smoking non-drinkers, and young cases with any risk profile.

Young cases most often involved the tongue. One rare variant showed a suggestive link to the young never-exposed group, yet fell short of the strict genome-wide significance bar and sits inside long non-coding RNA genes. No supported rare signals appeared in the other two comparisons, and none of the flagged variants appears in a clinical variant database. An exploratory thirteen-variant risk score behaved independently of exposure status. Small subgroup sizes limit certainty throughout.
pmc-13483835:
Mingyang Yuan, Xiaotian Ma, and Zheng Xu search for which patient and injury features predict specific problems after wrist fracture surgery. Their 2026 retrospective study reviews operations for distal radius fractures at one hospital between January 2022 and June 2025. Matching balances the complication and non-complication groups at 60 patients each for fair comparison.

Outcomes at six months cover wrist movement, grip strength, and a standard arm disability score alongside complication counts. Candidate predictors span fracture pattern, open injury status, wait time to surgery, surgical approach and duration, fixation choices, and conditions such as diabetes and bone thinning. Pinpointing which features attach to which complication, from chronic pain syndromes to tendon trouble, could let surgeons tailor consent talks and follow-up intensity to the person in front of them.
pmc-13485035:
Saptarshi Paul demonstrates nanoparticle making with nothing but sprayed water droplets, a zinc-dusted conductor, and room air. Published in 2026, the method sprays microdroplets of dissolved metal salts onto a conductive surface seeded with zinc particles. Inside each droplet a galvanic swap reaction deposits copper, silver, platinum, or gold particles directly onto the surface.

Particles averaged under 61 nanometers across and formed within minutes, with no applied voltage, no heating, and no organic solvents. Growth couples the local swap reaction with sideways charge movement across the conductor beneath. Alloy particles formed as well as single-metal ones. Because particles land already attached to a substrate, the route suits catalyst and sensor coatings where loose powders would need extra fixing steps anyway.
pmc-13486435:
Mustafa Kaçmaz examines how diabetes stiffens the heart muscle cell from the inside, joining insulin signaling to the giant spring protein titin. Published in 2026, the synthesis walks from insulin receptor activation through relay proteins that align fuel supply with mechanical demand. Healthy signaling also protects the scaffolds that hold contractile units and cell junctions together.

When insulin resistance sets in, calcium handling by the filaments shifts, contractile protein mixes change, and titin variants plus their phosphate tags remodel. Calcium cycling falters, energy factories underperform, and oxidative stress rises. Measured consequences include weaker squeeze reserve, slower relaxation, and higher passive stiffness. A multiscale frame helps explain why diabetic hearts fail with preserved ejection yet poor filling.
pmc-13487835:
