Zhibo Huang and co-authors present a 2026 platform for making dumbbell-shaped small interfering RNA, a short RNA form designed to silence a chosen gene. Ordinary forms break down quickly and cost a lot to make by chemical methods. Their system uses a shortened intron from a bacterial virus, placed inside a probiotic strain of Escherichia coli, to join RNA ends into a closed dumbbell shape.

Tests reached about 85 percent cyclization in lab work and in living cells, with yields near 60 milligrams per liter in a small fermenter. Molecules with a 23 base-pair stem silenced target genes for more than ten days. The authors argue the method could lower production costs for future RNA treatments.
pmc-13488135:
Yan Zhen and colleagues develop a blood marker for combined depression and anxiety in a 2026 case-control study. The two disorders often occur together, and diagnosis still rests on interviews about symptoms, with no accepted lab test. The candidate marker joins a prostaglandin, a fat-like inflammation signal, with glutathione, a key antioxidant, which ties together two systems thought to go wrong in these illnesses. Blood from thirty-nine patients and thirty-eight matched healthy people was profiled.

Five related molecules differed between groups, and the joined marker stayed independently linked with illness after adjustment in the reported models. Its accuracy looked strong in this small sample, split into training and test parts. Larger, independent checks are still required, the authors imply through their design.
pmc-13488635:
Jade Monteiro and co-authors measure fibromyalgia's added burden in lupus patients in a 2024 study. Fibromyalgia strikes people with systemic lupus far more often than the general public. It still goes undiagnosed in many of them, leaving pain untreated.

The study surveyed lupus patients at a university hospital in Paraíba, Brazil. Diagnosis followed the 2012 international collaborating clinics criteria. Quality of life scores were compared between patients with and without fibromyalgia. Cross-sectional design captures one honest snapshot of daily burden. Naming the overlap is the first step toward treating both conditions together.
pmc-13489935:
Laura Chung and Susan Buchanan review ethylene oxide use on foods and the safety dispute around it in a 2026 policy article. The gas sterilizes medical gear worldwide and fumigates foods like spices in some countries to kill germs, yet it is a known carcinogen and banned for food in other countries. Exporting nations stress trade and foodborne illness prevention, while importing nations stress public protection at home.

Residue limits for the gas and its breakdown product differ so widely that shipments get rejected at borders. Exporters push for shared international tolerance levels to keep trade moving. The authors map the conflicting rules and health concerns, arguing that harmonized standards are missing and needed before the friction can ease.
pmc-13490335:
Saikang Tang and co-authors compare combination treatment against artery-directed therapy alone in advanced liver cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. The base treatment, chemoembolization, delivers chemotherapy into the tumor's artery and blocks it. The combination adds an immune drug, tislelizumab, plus targeted kinase-blocking pills. Sixty-two patients treated between 2018 and 2023 were split into groups of thirty and thirty-two with similar starting profiles.

Median time before the cancer grew was about triple in the combination group in the reported figures, and the advantage held after adjustment and multiple check analyses. Response and survival measures also favored the combination, and four patients shrank enough to reach curative treatment. Severe side effects appeared only in the combination group, at a modest rate, with no treatment deaths.
pmc-13490735:
Keri Schmidt, Alexandra P. Schurch, and Elisa Dultz map how two sister proteins build the nuclear pore basket in budding yeast in a 2026 study. The pore is the sole gateway between nucleus and cytoplasm, and its inner face carries a filament basket that helps export RNA and organize chromosomes. Earlier work centered on the largest basket protein, Mlp1, leaving its partner Mlp2 understudied, so the team probed each protein's attachments in living cells.

Mlp2 anchors to the pore frame on its own, and the two proteins grip each other through coiled regions that stabilize the pair. The start ends of both proteins recruit a third partner, Pml39, which in turn pulls in extra Mlp1 copies. The proposed ratio per pore spoke is four Mlp1, two Mlp2, and one Pml39.
pmc-13491135:
Xu-Jin Wu, Ju-Yu Tang, and Nian-Zhe Sun write a 2026 letter to the editor on a study of laser primed cell parcels for healing diabetic wounds. The study under discussion used a low energy fractional carbon dioxide laser on fat derived stem cells. The mild heat raised the parcels those cells shed in a helpful fat signal, by about 1.8 times.

That signal switch set off a chain in vessel lining cells. The cells grew, moved, and formed tubes more readily. In diabetic mice, wounds then closed faster. The letter writers call the work a significant advance in diabetic wound healing. They highlight how a single, carefully controlled light exposure did the priming. As a letter, the piece praises and frames the study rather than adding new data of its own. Its value lies in expert context for readers of the journal.
pmc-13491535:
Anne-Marie Burn and co-authors validate a web tool that screens school pupils for mental health difficulties in this 2026 study. Catching problems early speeds access to support. Their tool, ARTEMIS-A, adapts its questions to each pupil from a bank drawn from standard measures.

More than three thousand pupils aged eleven to sixteen from nine schools helped calibrate it. About one hundred pupils also took a gold-standard diagnostic assessment for comparison. The tool needed a median of just four questions and about a minute per pupil. Its scores agreed well with the clinical ratings. Pupils, parents, and staff all found it acceptable and easy to use.
pmc-13491835:
Sarkies and colleagues describe a 2026 Australian study of a shared care model meant to raise genetic testing among relatives of people with familial hypercholesterolaemia, an inherited condition causing very high cholesterol. Under the older approach, a counsellor at a Sydney lipid clinic offered testing directly. Under the new model, patients handed relatives an expression of interest form, counsellors contacted them, and testing packages went to both the relative and their general practitioner.

The study compared a control period with 25 index patients and 6 tested relatives against an implementation period with 81 index patients and 56 tested relatives. Cascade tests per index case rose from well under one test to about double that rate, a change the authors found statistically significant. However, the share of index patients producing at least one tested relative did not differ between the two models.
pmc-13492435:
Maciej Wójcik, Paweł Błaszkiewicz, and Sebastian Wójcik describe in 2026 the targeted ablation of a racing heart circuit that looped through both upper chambers after earlier surgery. Atypical post-surgical tachycardias that run steadily without warming up or cooling down should raise suspicion for such a two-atria loop, called biatrial tachycardia. High-density mapping of both chambers separated the true circuit from tissue that was merely being swept along.

Mapping traced the loop through connections between the atria, including the Bachmann bundle, fitting a recognized type in the Kitamura scheme. The team then used a balloon-in-basket catheter delivering pulsed field energy. It switched on selected electrode pairs to modify broad areas while sparing delicate neighbors, such as the sinus node and the nerve to the diaphragm. The case shows precision mapping guiding selective energy delivery in a crowded neighborhood.
pmc-13493435:
Hatice Kadı Kardaş leads a ten-author team measuring in 2026 how hard a surgeon can crush nose cartilage before the graft dies. Rhinoplasty reshapes cartilage by crushing, yet nobody knew the force threshold where living cells give up. Using cow nasal cartilage and a custom crushing rig with a force gauge, the team applied two hundred to six hundred newtons, then cultured the pieces for four weeks.

Untreated cartilage scored highest for living tissue under the microscope. Viability slid steadily as force rose, staying acceptable through three hundred newtons before dropping sharply and significantly at four hundred and beyond. At the heaviest force, scores fell to less than half of control values. The device gives surgeons, for the first time, a number to respect rather than a feel to guess.
pmc-13493535:
Liu and colleagues reviewed how coating titanium bone implants with silk fibroin, the protein of silk fiber, turns metal into biologically active scaffolding, in a 2026 review. Titanium bears load and is printed into porous implants for bone defects, but its biological blankness slows the bone growth needed to lock an implant in place. Silk fibroin offers compatibility with tissue, breakdown, adjustable strength, and drug-carrying capacity.

Liu surveys the protein's structure, drug-release behavior, and degradation, then the evidence that fibroin coatings, hydrogels, and composites on porous titanium promote bone-cell attachment and growth. They calm inflammation and improve implant integration in cell and animal studies, in healthy and diseased bone alike. Composite strategies push further: adding the bone mineral hydroxyapatite boosts bone conduction, metal ions tune immune responses, and hydrogel systems meter out drugs. The authors see silk hydrogels married to porous titanium as the shape of implants.
pmc-13493835:
Das and co-authors trace the evolution of one protein across Trypanosoma, the parasite genus behind sleeping sickness and Chagas disease. The protein carries a GAS8 domain and helps organise the cell's internal skeleton and the whip-like flagellum the parasite swims with. Such machinery usually changes very slowly. The 2026 team looked for exceptions across ten species, rebuilding family trees and testing each branch and position for signs of selection.

One branch stood out: the lineage leading to a sheep parasite carried a statistically supported burst of change after strict correction for multiple testing. Two single-letter changes in the protein, both outside its core domain, were flagged as likely products of that episode, while a third looked suggestive only. Other methods gave weaker support, so the authors frame the result carefully. Even locked-down skeleton proteins may fine-tune a few positions when a lineage adapts.
pmc-13494135:
Annabel Shin Ling Tong and Gary Yu Hin Lam present a 2026 interview study of social life among Chinese autistic students in higher education in Hong Kong. Little prior work asks autistic students themselves how social contact feels or what support helps, and most studies come from Western settings. The authors interviewed eight students and read their accounts closely for personal meaning, using a method built for that purpose.

Four themes stood out. Students wanted to connect yet often found the effort draining and the results poor. They described a constant balance between hiding autistic traits and showing them. Formal services and informal ties both helped them cope. Students also asked for a wider mix of support, from skills training to approaches that respect neurodiversity and personal choice. The authors note cultural shades in masking and social taste that Western studies miss.
pmc-13494235:
Pierce and co-authors examine how ivermectin, the antiparasitic drug, acts on human GABA-A receptors, the brain and body switches that calm nerve activity. In parasites the drug opens a different channel, but in mammals it also reaches GABA-A receptors outside the brain, which the blood-brain barrier does not shield. Their 2026 experiments expressed two receptor subtypes in frog eggs and measured electrical currents as they applied the drug alone and with other receptor activators.

Ivermectin switched on the alpha-5 subtype powerfully at very low concentrations and, unusually, never tired the receptor out, even during twenty-minute applications that exhaust normal activators. Receptors already worn out by high doses of GABA itself woke back up when ivermectin arrived. Combined with GABA or the anaesthetic etomidate, effects simply added rather than multiplying, and pentobarbital added nothing or slightly reduced the response.
pmc-13494635:
Guo Zhao and colleagues map, in a 2026 article, a faster route for engineered cancer drugs from lab bench to clinic. Cancer drug work has long moved in a straight, split line, from target hunting to animal tests to human trials. Near ninety percent of candidates fail along the way, a rate stuck for two decades. The authors blame the breaks between stages as much as tumor biology.

They propose joining three fields into one system. Artificial intelligence would design molecules and sharpen diagnosis from the start. Synthetic biology would build living treatments whose action can be timed and placed in the body. Tiny delivery carriers would ferry drugs past tumor defenses to where they must land. Organ-on-chip models, digital twins, flexible rules, and automated manufacturing would close the loop. The article weighs what each part adds, where current practice falls short, and steps to speed adoption.
pmc-13495035:
Yanping Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of a new delivery system for wedelolactone, a plant compound that guards the liver but dissolves poorly and reaches it weakly. Their target was sepsis-induced liver injury, a harm that follows severe infection and drives deaths in intensive care. The team loaded the compound into exosomes, sacs shed by cells, taken here from mouse immune cells.

Tests showed the loaded sacs kept a sound shape and homed to the liver far better than the free compound. In sepsis models, the loaded form shielded the liver more, calming inflammation, boosting antioxidant defenses, and blocking ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and fat damage. Blocking a master switch called Nrf2 erased the gains, which pinned the effect to that pathway. Safety checks came back clean, and the authors offer the platform as a base for future care.
pmc-13495135:
Jamie LaMantia and a team of co-authors review how poverty, insurance, and public aid shape outcomes for diabetic foot ulcers, in two thousand twenty-six. Social drivers of this disease affect who gets ulcers and how they fare, but the pathways were poorly mapped. Their scoping review searched major databases for American studies across two decades.

Thirty-five studies fed a conceptual model of the pathways. System factors often sat between poverty and outcome, while a patient's ability to follow care advice shifted the effect. Team-based care might blunt the amputation risk tied to poverty or lack of insurance. The model also shows feedback loops, both helpful and harmful, and is offered to guide fairer analysis.
pmc-13495335:
Seven authors describe an unusual two stage fix for a failed hip implant in this 2026 case report. The cup part of an artificial hip had slipped early into the pelvis, a rare event that puts nearby organs and blood vessels at risk.

Most past care removed the slipped cup first and rebuilt the joint later. Here the team reversed the order: they rebuilt the socket first with bone graft, a cross plate, and a dual mobility cup. Only then did they remove the old cup and screws through a path behind the gut. The report argues that this order can make a hard case safer and gives surgeons a plan to copy.
pmc-13495435:
Lisa Kawatsu and Kazuhiro Uchimura analyze, in a 2026 study, whether tuberculosis deaths in Japan rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. The pandemic disrupted TB care worldwide, and Japan's TB burden sits mainly in older adults. The team used national surveillance records for every notified case from 2017 to 2022 and tracked TB death within a year of notice across three periods.

Death rates climbed from the pre-pandemic period to the Omicron period. The rise was driven by adults aged sixty-five and over, whose rate rose steeply. Adjusted models tied an Omicron-era diagnosis to higher death risk in that older group. Younger patients showed a like point estimate with wide uncertainty, so the authors warn against reading the age split as real. They urge stronger TB care paths for older adults and guarded services in future emergencies.
pmc-13495535:
Garvit Nama, Ali Elmdaah, and Reemah Almadah trace, in a 2026 case report, a woman's ten-year road to a diagnosis of systemic sarcoidosis. The disease grows clusters of inflamed tissue in many organs and mimics infection and cancer. The patient, a 38-year-old woman of Bangladeshi origin, first fell ill in 2010 with chest and body-wide symptoms, and tuberculosis was the standing suspicion in a region where it is common.

Over the decade she lost hearing in both ears, developed chronic eye inflammation and swollen glands, and built up fluid and thickened tissue in her belly. Repeated tests stayed inconclusive, and she received tuberculosis treatment on guesswork more than once. Only in late 2023 did a biopsy of the belly tissue, showing the disease's signature granulomas, plus a clear response to steroids, settle the answer. She remains on maintenance steroids without fresh flare-ups.
pmc-13495835:
Yusuf Surucu leads a large team describing, in a 2026 study, a system that keeps a full-thickness flap of human abdominal skin alive outside the body for up to three weeks. Animal models translate poorly to human skin, and lab-grown substitutes lack real anatomy. The team pumps nutrient fluid through the flap's own vessels inside a custom bioreactor, refining surgery, vessel mapping, and feed recipes to keep the tissue working.

Heat and dye imaging confirmed flow through the flap. Sugar use and waste output tracked its metabolism, while tissue slices, gene profiles, and reactivity tests checked health, and stem and skin cells grown from it stayed viable. The platform then hosted radiation and chemical injury studies, fat metabolism work, and melanoma and breast cancer models grown in real human skin. The authors offer it as a stand-in that could cut animal testing.
pmc-13498935:
Zhang and four co-authors described three new Penicillium mold species from farm soil in Yunnan, China, in twenty twenty-six. Penicillium is a large fungal genus found widely in soil. Eight strains from mountain farm soils did not match any known species.

The team compared the fungi's shapes and sequenced four gene regions to build family trees. Both lines of evidence marked the strains as three distinct new species. Each sits in a different series within its section of the genus. They are named for the places Longyang, Longling, and Zhenyuan. Comparisons with close relatives confirmed their placement. The authors say the find expands known Penicillium diversity and clarifies how these soil molds are distributed in Yunnan's mountain farms.
pmc-13499535:
Ling-Cheng Kung and co-authors pilot sugar patterns on antibodies as markers in fibromyalgia in this 2026 study. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain and fatigue, and its biology is murky. Sugar chains attached to the IgG antibody differ in many diseases, so the team asked whether they track this illness and its course.

Thirty patients and thirty healthy controls were assessed for sleep, mood, pain, and function, with patients rechecked after six months. Baseline antibody sugar traits barely differed between groups. Over time, a few sugar traits shifted alongside symptom scores, and a reduced model tied three sugar markers to mood and function changes. The authors present the work as a pilot pointing to patient subgroups.
pmc-13499835:
Alex E Henney and co-authors ask in 2026 whether nerve damage from type 2 diabetes signals higher risk of serious liver outcomes. Diabetes drives fatty liver disease progression, and neuropathy marks advanced injury to small vessels, so the team used a large federated health records network. Adults with diabetes were grouped by whether records coded no neuropathy, peripheral nerve damage, autonomic nerve damage affecting organs, or both, then matched on background, metabolic, and illness profiles.

A clear gradient emerged after matching. Risk of major liver outcomes, covering liver failure events, pressure complications, liver cancer, and transplant, rose stepwise across the groups. The combined group's hazard was more than triple that of diabetes alone in the reported ratios. Links held across individual outcomes and after time-based checks, and neuropathy outweighed another microvascular complication, eye disease, as a liver risk marker.
pmc-13499935:
Adit Chotipanich and Panote Kasemsuwan review in 2026 surgical modifications to a neck flap used for rebuilding small and medium defects after head and neck surgery. The infrahyoid flap carries skin and underlying neck muscle on a blood vessel stalk, and surgeons value its colour match and same-field donor site. Drawbacks include unreliable skin blood supply, size limits, and a short stalk, so their systematic search from 1986 to 2025 gathered published variations of the technique.

Twenty-two studies covering 728 patients yielded five families of modification, covering incision design, stalk handling, vein preservation, adding the thyroid gland to the flap, and pairing with microsurgery. Freeing the strap muscles from the jawbone anchor was the most used trick, and pooled flap loss rates for the leading methods sat near one to two percent in the reported estimates. Without head-to-head studies, the authors stop short of crowning an ideal version.
pmc-13500135:
Budi Wardiman and co-authors review in 2026 whether leftovers from cassava processing can safely serve as energy feed for dairy cows within a circular farming economy. Dairy systems face pressure to cut reliance on human-edible feed and lower environmental burdens, and ruminants can upgrade low-value plant residues into milk and meat. Cassava generates huge residue volumes across tropical Africa and Asia, yet its waste streams, from starch pulp to peels, differ in nutrition and risk.

The review weighs that variability, since each stream carries its own feeding value and hazard profile, including safety constraints that must be managed before diets can rely on them. Stabilisation technologies that preserve and standardise residues receive attention as the route to consistent quality. The authors frame the practical questions for producers as which streams suit dairy diets, how much batches vary, and which processing and quality controls make use safe.
pmc-13500435:
Michael S Awadalla reports in 2026 a quality control audit of frozen embryo transfers at a single private fertility practice in Cincinnati, Ohio. Only genetically screened embryos with the normal chromosome count were transferred, one at a time, between January 2023 and July 2025, which removes embryo quality as a variable and exposes process factors. Variables under review covered the transfer protocol, the genetic testing laboratory, the physician performing transfer, and the embryologist handling the embryo.

Fetal heartbeat rate, the main early success marker, linked significantly to the preparation protocol in the analysis. A modified natural protocol avoiding oral medication reached the highest rate, above the centre average. The testing laboratory and the day of embryo biopsy also mattered statistically. Neither the transferring physician nor the embryologist showed an association, a reassuring finding for consistency of hands-on technique at the centre.
pmc-13500535:
Xing Guo and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a reconstruction algorithm named ZeeFree. The tool erases stair-step artefacts from coronary CT angiography, the stepwise misalignment that slices of a moving heart leave in later scans. Ninety-five patients were scanned prospectively on a new dual-source scanner, and images were rebuilt with and without the tool for blinded checks. Doctors graded artefact severity, image quality, and diagnostic confidence on five-point scales. Subgroups split by heart rate and body mass.

Most stair-step artefacts vanished in the rebuilt images in the reported share, and scores for severity, quality, and confidence all improved clearly, holding across both subgroup splits. Agreement between tool-based narrowing estimates and invasive angiography, the reference standard, was strong. The authors conclude the tool clearly upgrades heart image usability on this scanner line.
pmc-13501635:
Wensi Chen leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 school screening study from Guangzhou on spotting children whose hyperopia reserve is running low. That reserve is the natural long-sightedness of young eyes, and losing it early predicts later short-sightedness. Checking it properly needs dilating drops, which are impractical for whole schools. The study enrolled 1,650 children aged 6 to 15 in Zengcheng District and gave each both a quick non-dilated refraction and the full dilated reference test.

Reserve insufficiency affected 14.1 percent of the youngest band, 10.5 percent of the middle band, and 3.9 percent of the oldest band. The quick measure correlated with the reference more strongly as age rose. For detecting insufficiency its area under the curve was 0.661, and a cut-off of minus 0.50 dioptres caught 82.4 percent of cases while holding a negative predictive value of 95.7 percent. The authors stress it is a triage step only, never a diagnosis.
pmc-13501735:
Dilek Yıldırım Tank and Nurten Taşdemir report a 2026 education study on teaching basic life support with a homemade manikin instead of costly simulation equipment. The quasi-experimental study enrolled 148 undergraduate nursing students. Theory came through e-learning, and hands-on practice used the low-cost manikin built for home use. A structured test measured knowledge before training, right after, and one month later, while two blinded experts scored observable resuscitation performance at the same later points with perfect agreement between them.

Knowledge climbed sharply: the mean score rose from 5.08 before training to 7.99 immediately after on the test's scale. One month later it eased to 7.40 yet stayed well above baseline, showing retention. Performance scores started high at 16.54 on the checklist scale and dipped slightly but significantly to 15.62 at follow-up, remaining satisfactory. The authors recommend the homemade manikin route for resource-limited nursing programmes.
pmc-13501835:
Ji Chen leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 study of the TONSOKU gene in Cyathula officinalis, a Sichuan medicinal herb whose roots are the drug. The gene, called CoTSK, encodes a nuclear protein linked to genome maintenance and root development in other plants. The team mapped its domains, family relationships, and location inside cells, then tested what it does. Bacteria carrying the gene survived an alkylating chemical 2.5 times better than controls, while gaining no protection against a DNA stress, showing the defence is damage-specific.

Expression profiling found the gene most active in stems, unlike its relative in a sister species that favours leaves. When the gene was placed into mutant Arabidopsis plants lacking their own version, root growth recovered to between 30 and 42 percent of normal length, though stem and rosette defects persisted. The authors nominate the gene as a breeding lever for coordinating stem and root growth.
pmc-13502435:
Xiuqi Liu and a team of co-authors review the anatomy behind two stubborn foot stress fractures. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. The navicular and the base of the fifth metatarsal hold up the foot's inner and outer columns, yet both heal badly when cracked.

Each bone sits in a vise of mechanical load with a thin blood supply. That pairing explains slow healing, failures to knit, and repeat breaks. The authors walk through the structure and force patterns site by site, with illustrations. Treatment choices follow from which pattern of damage is present. High-risk groups, like athletes, stand to gain most from the clarified picture. The aim is sharper diagnosis and fewer lingering injuries.
pmc-13503635:
Nguyen Le, Yan Liu, and Chanhyun Park argue that past rates of heart deaths among breast cancer survivors were computed the wrong way, in a 2026 paper. Heart disease is a leading killer in this group, so the numbers guide care policy.

Earlier work divided deaths by all women in the United States, not by survivors. That made survivors look safer than the general population, though their heart risk runs high. The authors rebuild the rates for 1999 to 2020 using survivor counts from cancer registry data. Their age-adjusted rates now sit above the general population's, matching clinical sense. The trend still fell about 1.8 percent per year. Correct denominators, they say, keep survivorship care funded.
pmc-13503735:
Ken Ka Pang Chan leads a large survey of lung doctors on how they test for and treat tuberculosis of the chest lining, in a 2026 paper. The illness is hard to prove, and no shared guide rules practice in regions where TB is common. Fluid from the chest often holds too few germs to grow in a lab.

The survey drew 414 doctors from 15 countries or regions, nearly all with medium to high TB loads. Four in five often weigh the illness when they see new chest fluid on one side. Tests and care varied widely from doctor to doctor. About three in five want firm proof from tissue or germ growth before starting TB drugs. Most had seen a first call of likely TB reversed after drugs failed.
pmc-13505135:
Xun Xia and colleagues report the long treatment course of a 63-year-old man with Parkinson's disease who needed full upper-jaw implant rehabilitation. He had severe gum disease, little remaining upper jaw bone, and a history of failed implant work elsewhere. His remaining upper teeth were removed and an All-on-4 restoration, held by four implants, was placed at once.

Complications followed over several years. Implants on both sides loosened or failed and were replaced with tilted implants, combined with sinus floor lifts to add support. The final fixed prosthesis was eventually completed, and it stayed stable through fifty-five months of follow-up, with much better chewing than before treatment. The authors set out lessons on planning, periodontal care before surgery, and regular maintenance for similar patients.
pmc-13505635:
Ando and colleagues examine how DELLA proteins, brakes on plant growth, switch genes on in this 2026 study. DELLA proteins accumulate when the growth hormone gibberellin is scarce and partner with many transcription factors, but how they activate genes was murky. Using a proximity-labeling screen, the team searched for proteins that sit close to DELLA inside the cell nucleus.

The screen found HAC1, an enzyme that adds acetyl tags to histones, the spools DNA wraps around, loosening genes for activation. That tagging proved necessary at target sites where DELLA works with its partner GAF1. One target was ERF2, a gene that represses growth, and the authors showed the DELLA-HAC1 partnership controls it directly. Blocking this chain changed plant growth, tying the molecular interaction to the whole plant's size.
pmc-13505935:
Santosh Kumar Srivastava and colleagues rewired a friendly gut bacterium so it can sense human stress hormones and answer with a chosen output. Harmful gut bacteria already eavesdrop on norepinephrine and epinephrine through a two-part sensor called QseBC. The team moved that system into Escherichia coli Nissle 1917, a well-known probiotic strain.

Gene activity profiling confirmed the borrowed sensor switched on in response to the hormones. The researchers then rebuilt the sensor's output promoter, trimming it and swapping control elements, which produced stronger and dose-sensitive responses. Targeted changes to the sensor protein pinpointed the parts needed to recognise the hormones. As a proof of function, they linked sensing to release of a molecule that blocks a stress-related receptor, and confirmed its activity in lab tests. The work lays out design rules for microbes that react to host stress in programmed ways.
pmc-13506235:
An enzyme floating in the blood, butyrylcholinesterase, drops in critical illness, and Treml and co-authors ask whether its level predicts who will die in intensive care. They pool the actual patient records, not just published averages, from six cohorts.

The pooled set held 482 adults, most with sepsis, of whom 39 percent died in hospital. Patients who died arrived with lower enzyme levels, and each hundred-unit rise in the day-one level cut the odds of death slightly but reliably. A threshold of 1615 units per liter separated higher-risk patients, whose death hazard ran 1.69 times the rest. The signal faded by day four, so timing matters. The authors present the enzyme as a cheap, integrative marker for early risk judgment in the ICU.
pmc-13506635:
Ashley Smith and co-authors report a 2026 study of a gene that sorghum plants need to make pollen. Sorghum is the fifth most grown grain in the world, and seed firms rely on control of male fertility to make hybrid seed. Yet the genes that guide the growth of the pollen-bearing part, the anther, are still poorly known in this crop.

The team studied both normal plants and a mutant whose anthers stay small and white and make no pollen. They sorted anther growth into thirteen stages based on cell landmarks seen in thin slices. Their work pinpoints the gene at fault, called SbTDR, and shows where the mutant's growth goes wrong. The findings give breeders a clearer map of how fertility is built in sorghum.
pmc-13507135:
Jingyun Li and colleagues develop, in 2026 work, a climate-aware method to set the best mix of solar and wind power in future grids. The solar-wind ratio is the solar share of combined solar and wind capacity. Their framework joins climate projections with an hourly investment and dispatch model, so plans face realistic weather and demand swings.

Best ratios differed strongly by latitude and shifted only modestly under climate change. Plans copied from past habits often missed the best ratio, and that mismatch raised costs more than climate-driven resource change alone. Extra capacity was also needed in many regions. Region-specific, climate-responsive mix planning is central to cheap, reliable clean power.
pmc-13507235:
Tomohiro Mimura, Yusaku Nakazono, Noriyuki Kida, Hitoshi Koda, and Takaaki Tsunokawa study, in 2026 work, how kick rate reshapes joint coordination in underwater dolphin kicking. Swimmers use this wavelike motion after starts and turns, where race outcomes often hinge. Eight male swimmers kicked at 80 to 120 percent of their best personal rate while 3D cameras tracked motion.

Speed rose with kick rate but flattened past the personal optimum. At high rates, hip and knee moved in opposite phase more often, yet the time needed to reverse the kick stayed nearly fixed. Squeezing that fixed reversal into shorter cycles squeezed trunk wave motion late in the downbeat. Protecting trunk motion may matter more than raw kick speed.
pmc-13507335:
Kannan Swathy leads a 2026 team that tests seed extracts of Annona squamosa, the custard apple, against the tomato leaf miner Tuta absoluta, a moth pest devastating tomato crops worldwide. Chemical sprays face rising resistance, so plant-derived options draw interest. Extracts made with five solvents faced eggs and larvae in bioassays.

The hexane extract performed best, fully blocking egg hatching at the top dose and killing most larvae within two days. Treated larvae showed lowered protective catalase and raised detox enzyme activity, signs of chemical stress. Earthworm safety tests showed minimal harm, unlike a standard synthetic insecticide that killed nearly all worms. Two fatty compounds dominated the extract and docked strongly onto a key insect enzyme in models.
pmc-13508235:
Muaaz Alajlani, Afraa Alnokkari, and Loai Aljerf survey how pharmacy students in Syria use artificial intelligence tools for study, in 2026 work. AI tools are spreading through higher education, yet little is known about their use in war-affected, low-resource settings. The survey ran in January and February 2026 and drew 295 students from public and private universities. Questions covered how often students use such tools, what they use them for, and what support their schools give.

Nearly nine in ten students used AI tools for academic work, and almost all of them favored ChatGPT. Top uses were explaining concepts, looking up drug facts, and making practice questions. Students rated the learning benefits fairly high. Institutional support, though, scored very low, and nearly all students said guidance and training were absent. Almost everyone learned these tools alone. Senior students felt more confident with them than juniors did.
pmc-13508335:
Luca Timoceanu and five co-authors report early vision gains after surgery for a full-thickness hole in the center of the retina, in 2026 work. The operation removes the eye's gel, peels a fine membrane, and fills the eye with gas while it heals. Records covered 193 eyes treated at their center, with vision checked about a month after surgery. Holes were classed as small, medium, or large by a standard scale. The team also weighed which gas was used and how long patients were told to lie face down.

Two thirds of eyes gained at least two lines on the vision chart within that first month. Gains did not differ by hole size, gas choice, or face-down time. Hole closure, though, fell sharply for large holes compared with small ones. The results help set patient expectations for the first month of recovery.
pmc-13509135:
İsmail Tekbaş and co-authors tested two plant oils as aids for healing wounds inside the mouth. Black seed oil, from Nigella sativa, and grape oil, from Vitis vinifera, are both rich in compounds that affect inflammation. Sixty rats received a small full-thickness wound in the palate and were dosed daily with one of the oils, saline, or nothing, with healing checked over three weeks.

Blood levels of inflammatory signals differed between treated and control animals, and the oil groups showed less ulceration and faster skin regrowth over the wound. Wound areas also shrank faster with the oils than with saline. The authors conclude the oils support mouth wound healing by tuning inflammatory signals, in what they believe is the first head-to-head animal test of the pair.
pmc-13509535:
Dmitry Skvortsov, Aliya Khudaigulova, Danila Lobunko, Sergey Kaurkin, and Galina Ivanova test gait training for people recovering from a stroke that blocked blood flow to the brain, in a 2026 pilot study. Twenty patients received nine sessions of visual feedback training paced by a metronome, aimed at making steps on each side mirror each other more evenly, on top of standard care. Twenty other patients received standard care alone.

Detailed walking measures showed the uneven pattern typical after stroke in both groups at the start and at the end. The trained group showed a hopeful trend toward more even stepping, yet the change fell short of statistical proof. The control group showed no change on that measure. The authors call for a larger trial with enough patients to settle whether the method truly helps.
pmc-13509635:
Bulent Mamikoglu, Pankajavalli Ramakrishnan, Fawaz Al-Mufti, and Gerard Gianoli weigh reported outcomes for rebuilding the wall of a large vein near the ear to treat pulsing tinnitus, in a 2026 review. The operation is a skull-base procedure called sigmoid sinus wall reconstruction. The sound in this condition matches the heartbeat and can stem from a thinned or opened vein wall. The authors searched databases and graded the studies by design, group size, follow-up length, and safety reporting.

Ten studies passed into the final set, most small and backward-looking. Only one group was followed for more than five years on average. In that group, the pulsing sound vanished in about two thirds of ears. Most ears kept a good result years later. Direct pressure readings before and after surgery were rare. The authors call the results hopeful yet thin and urge shared standards for judging success.
pmc-13509835:
Pablo Rodriguez and nine co-authors ask how sampling for germs should be handled in children with septic arthritis, a joint infection that needs fast action, in a 2026 review. Drawing fluid from the joint remains the key urgent step, serving both diagnosis and drainage. The review works through nine clinical questions and builds a risk-based plan shaped by age and by how sick the child appears.

The germs behind these infections change with age, with one kind ruling before age four and staph bacteria ruling after. For children under four with a mild picture and a positive throat test for the early-childhood germ, the authors float non-invasive checks as a possible path, with close review within three days. For older children, joint sampling under anesthesia stays the standard. The plan is offered as a hypothesis, not as guidance backed by major societies.
pmc-13512035:
Hanna Vertanen-Greis and colleagues report a field study, published in 2026. It is a proof-of-concept study of Finnish teachers' voice symptoms. It asks whether symptoms track the indoor air quality teachers perceive at work. Teachers frequently blame stuffy classrooms for hoarseness and voice strain. The team compared self-reported symptoms with clinical voice measures. Environmental readings were compared too.

Poorer perceived air quality was associated with more voice symptoms. Longer exposure time was as well. No matching links appeared in the clinical voice examinations, though. The measured environmental data showed no matching links either. Perception and symptoms seem to travel together without simple physical proof. The authors recommend monitoring affected teachers. Longer studies with real-time air data are also recommended.
pmc-13513335:
Iga Koscinska-Shukla and a large team check whether scans and symptoms agree after steroid shots for wrist nerve compression in Sjogren's disease, in work dated 2026. The autoimmune disease often brings nerve trouble, and carpal tunnel syndrome is common within it. How standard shots work in this group was little studied.

Twenty patients with the disease and the wrist syndrome, plus nineteen with the syndrome alone, received ultrasound guided injections. Nerve thickness on scan, symptom scores, and arm function scores were tracked. The title names the key finding: scan change and felt relief did not always move together. The split matters when doctors judge success by images alone.
pmc-13514735:
Maria-Delia Florean and co-authors test in 2026 whether simple blood markers can predict which sinus patients relapse after surgery. Their disease, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, is a long-lasting inflammatory condition that often returns despite a thorough operation.

They followed sixty-nine patients for up to three years after first-time sinus surgery, measuring four blood proteins before the operation. High blood eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, proved the strongest single warning sign of recurrence. Three proteins, periostin, eotaxin, and procalcitonin, also ran higher in patients who relapsed, and procalcitonin separated the groups best in accuracy testing. The authors propose adding a small blood panel to routine follow-up to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13517635:
Shuang Xu, Zhenyu Yin, Min Huang, and Liubin Xing propose a dual strategy switch migration method for failure recovery in software defined satellite networks. Low Earth orbit networks shift topology fast and suffer node and link failures, which can interrupt the control plane and unbalance controller loads. Migration moves switches between controllers to restore service.

A multi objective model jointly optimizes control link delay, controller load variance, and migration ratio. Two algorithms serve distinct regimes. One robust method favors long term load balance and stability in calm periods. One efficient method favors fast convergence under large failures, with millisecond level delay recovery and low migration overhead. Simulations confirm the split roles across failure intense and stable periods.
pmc-13517935:
Maya Ermakova leads a fourteen-author team building miniature antibodies for polio vaccine testing in a 2026 study. Inactivated polio vaccine works only if its D-antigen, the virus shell in its potent native shape, survives production, so factories need precise measuring tools. The team raised camelid single-domain antibodies, tiny VHH fragments, against the D-antigen of Sabin type 1, the vaccine strain.

The fragments bound the native antigen strongly. One clone, S1-C7, sharpened the test kit enough to tell the vaccine strain from its wild Mahoney cousin. Ordinary antibody mixes could not do that. It even neutralised the virus in a dish. Another clone, S1-D9, recognised all three polio serotypes, hinting at a shared shell feature and a future universal detector. Ermakova's team offers the panel as quality-control instruments for the eradication endgame, where every batch's antigen content matters.
pmc-13518035:
White and colleagues reported a 2026 case of severe tetanus that began with a rooster peck to a finger. The patient was a 65-year-old poultry hobbyist with type two diabetes and no tetanus vaccination in over ten years. Tetanus toxin, made by bacteria in soil and manure, blocks the nerves' braking signals and causes rigid, spasming muscles, and animal injuries are a rarely recognized route of infection.

White describes progressive jaw stiffness, abnormal tongue sensation, and slurred speech at presentation, with scans ruling out stroke and deep neck infection. Worsening respiratory distress needed a breathing tube passed through the nose with a camera's help, followed later by a tracheostomy, an opening in the windpipe. Despite antibiotics, tetanus immunoglobulin, and sedation, spasms returned whenever sedation lightened. The authors use the case to press vaccination awareness for under-immunized agricultural workers and early airway planning in severe disease.
pmc-13518435:
J Weber and three colleagues revisit a long-standing needle taboo after armpit lymph-node surgery in a 2026 German review. Removing axillary nodes for breast cancer or melanoma can damage lymph drainage, and guidelines have long told clinicians to spare that arm: no blood draws, no drips, no pressure cuffs, for life. When the other arm fails, staff resort to foot veins or central lines, both worse options carrying their own pain and clot risks.

Older caution rested on small case reports. Newer data, the authors argue, show that single venous punctures and catheter placements on the operated side are safe when no lymph swelling exists yet. Their practical rule: after a failed attempt on the safe side, try the operated arm before reaching for awkward sites or a central line. Weber's team frames the shift as evidence catching up with a precaution that outlived its data.
pmc-13518835:
A research team transplants lab-grown human heart muscle into injured monkey hearts, in a 2026 study. The cells, reprogrammed from induced pluripotent stem cells and delivered as small aggregates, formed substantial, well-structured grafts three months after injection into infarcted cynomolgus monkey hearts. Early rhythm disturbances caused by the grafts faded with time.

How well each cell batch contracted and conducted in the dish predicted both its rhythm risk and the heart's recovery in the animal. A fluorescent tag strain showed disturbed wiring yet still engrafted, giving a tool for study. The aggregates matched results that once took ten to twenty times more loose cells, and production could be decoupled from surgery timing.
pmc-13519135:
Wallax Ferreira and co-authors profile a protein cutter in 2026 as both driver and telltale of bladder cancer. Using public multi-layer data banks, they map how the cutter, CTSV, is controlled by gene marks and chemical tags, and how it lines up with tumor traits and immune mix.

The cutter ran high in bladder tumors, most in the flat, spread-prone kind, they report. High levels tracked with higher grade, spread to nodes and beyond, drug resistance, and shorter survival. Gene activity links tied it to the tumor's immune landscape as well. A mark that shows in tissue and tracks the course could, if it reaches fluids, sort patients by risk without a scope.
pmc-13519535:
Faith is often described as a shield against substance abuse, yet people in treatment may lean on faith while still using. Camila Chagas and four co-authors explored that tension in 2026 through interviews with homeless people in Brazil and Portugal.

Forty interviews, split evenly between the two countries, traced how each person linked their drug use history with their religious life. Faith could offer a felt sense of protection, mark a moment when change felt needed, or ease the suffering that came with addiction. The authors note a paradox: practices usually counted as protective, such as church attendance, could act as risk factors for people in such exposed social positions.
pmc-13520235:
Qiongling Zhao leads a nine-author genome scan in 2026 of Phyllanthus emblica, a medicinal and edible fruit tree of tropical Asia whose genetics were barely mapped. Leaf samples from 112 accessions collected in China and India yielded 73,405 high-quality DNA markers through a reduced-representation sequencing method.

Family trees split the accessions into two major groups and four source-based subpopulations. Diversity varied sharply, with one source group far richer than others, suggesting uneven use of the breeding pool. Scans flagged regions under selection holding genes for protein turnover, stress response, and hormone transport. A first association study for leaf shape found 85 linked spots, enriched for leaf development and cell wall genes, seeding marker-assisted breeding.
pmc-13520335:
Elnaz Afshari and Neda Soleimani design on paper in 2026 a single vaccine aimed at both Salmonella and Shigella, two food-borne bacteria with no licensed vaccine yet. Their computer-based design joins short immune-triggering fragments from six shared bacterial proteins.

Fragments were screened for immune coverage, safety signals and stability, then linked onto a bacterial flagellin scaffold that also boosts immunity. Modelling suggested a stable, water-friendly construct of suitable size, with favourable structure checks. Immune simulation predicted a strong response. Because all work so far is computational, laboratory and animal testing would be the essential next step before any health claim.
pmc-13520535:
An and colleagues published a 2026 meta-analysis of nerve injury after total hip replacement, a rare complication that is hard to treat once it happens. Pooling case control studies should reveal which patients and surgical choices carry the most risk. The team searched four databases for work published up to April 2025.

Twelve studies covering nearly 1.18 million patients met the criteria for pooling in this analysis by An. Simple comparisons linked injury to younger age, obesity, female sex, fractures, longer operations, repeat surgery, and spinal disease. After fuller adjustment only three factors stayed clearly linked: female sex, a posterolateral surgical approach, and spinal disease. Arthritis type and diabetes showed no clear link, and the spinal disease result weakened when single studies were removed.
pmc-13520635:
Chailapakul and colleagues built a BRCA1 mutant hamster cell line in 2026 to compare how BRCA1 and BRCA2, two cancer-linked genes, each handle DNA damage. Using CRISPR editing on V79 cells, they created a weakened BRCA1 line missing nine building blocks, and set it beside a BRCA2 mutant and normal cells.

Both mutants failed to gather the repair protein RAD51 at damage sites and lost the high-fidelity repair route, and each grew extra sensitive to damaging agents. With different profiles: the BRCA1 line feared a topoisomerase trap and a PARP blocker most, the BRCA2 line feared other drug classes more. The BRCA1 line also carried an unstable chromosome count, while the BRCA2 line stacked up chromosome breaks and kept them unrepaired longer after radiation. Both lines failed the checkpoint that should pause division. The authors offer the matched pair as a model for mutation-specific drug design.
pmc-13521235:
Alvin P Chan and colleagues find in 2026 that blocking fat absorption in mice prevents obesity yet worsens fatty liver inflammation, separating weight gain from liver harm. The fat-blocking drug orlistat is used for obesity, while effects on steatohepatitis remained unclear.

Mice ate a high-fat liver-disease diet with or without orlistat for 32 weeks. Drug-treated mice stayed leaner through fat malabsorption, yet liver enlargement, fat build-up and scarring still progressed. Liver chemistry showed lost essential unsaturated fats, more saturated fats, plus stronger fat-making and inflammatory signals. Imaging, blood tests and tissue checks all agreed that leanness did not protect the liver here.
pmc-13521835:
Guangping Zeng leads a team of fourteen authors asking whether AI-synthesized contrast MRI scans are good enough to use on real throat cancer patients, and for which patients. Contrast dye carries risks and costs, so generating the contrast image from ordinary scans is attractive, but clinical performance data were lacking. Their network had been pretrained on nearly seventeen hundred patients from fourteen institutions.

Three hundred thirty-three patients from six institutions had virtual contrast images synthesized from their plain scans. Three radiologists graded quality, with anything below four of five deemed unacceptable. Acceptability fell with larger tumors, advanced stage, and complex shapes: stage one tumors passed universally, stage four only about seventy percent of the time. The study converts those patterns into patient selection criteria.
pmc-13521935:
Mei and colleagues reported in 2026 a family of ultra-thin metallic materials that pull gold out of waste electronics liquid with striking speed and selectivity. Recovering precious metals from e-waste is valuable but current methods are inefficient. The materials are two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides, sheet-like compounds of metals and sulfur, in their metallic phases, including compounds of molybdenum, tungsten, tantalum, and titanium.

Mei found the sheets removed almost all gold ions from solution in about fifteen seconds. Their pull on gold dwarfed that on rival ions such as copper, nickel, and sodium by a factor of a hundred thousand or more. The titanium compound held the most gold, roughly ten times the capacity of most benchmark materials. Scaling up, the team made membrane sheets and recovered a small amount of high-purity gold from 30 discarded computer processors.
pmc-13522435:
Dong Woo Shin, Sujin Oh, Yun Ji Hong, and Kyoung Un Park profile microbes in blood products collected for cell therapy in a 2026 laboratory study. Forty specimens from eight donors were examined, covering several plasma types, a white-cell layer, and saliva. Genetic sequencing of a bacterial marker gene was used to identify organisms down to species level.

Plasma specimens held a wider mix of microbes than saliva, and the different specimen types formed distinct clusters. One streptococcus type dominated across specimens, while another organism appeared only in plasma. Skin swabs grew nothing after disinfection, suggesting skin carryover alone cannot explain the DNA signals. The profiles may help staff judge molecular test results during cell manufacturing.
pmc-13522835:
Camila Schultz Marcolla and co-authors published a 2026 study of a nationwide survey on fermented foods in Canada: who eats them, and what people think of them. Fermented foods are made by microbes at work on food. They may support long-term health as chronic illnesses rise. Yet no national count of their use was available.

Over four thousand adults were surveyed in one fall. A fourth said they had tried all eighteen fermented foods on the list at least once. Cheese and fermented milk foods led by far. Fermented fish and fermented grains sat last. Use varied by age, sex, income, and education. Older adults, and those with low income or education, ate less. Taste was the leading driver, health next. Home fermentation was rare, at under one in ten. Two in three want to learn more.
pmc-13523235:
Babatunde Ogunmiloro tests an artificial intelligence stroke aid delivered through a messaging app in a 2026 preliminary study. Expert neuroimaging is scarce in many underserved regions, and early stroke treatment is often missed. Two image models were trained on more than six thousand annotated brain CT scans covering normal scans and two stroke types, then checked on a separate public dataset.

The stronger model reached ninety-nine percent accuracy in internal testing and held up well on external sets, with especially strong detection of bleeding strokes, a distinction that guards against dangerous clot-busting treatment. The chosen model was built into a Telegram bot that answers in real time and deletes uploaded data automatically for privacy. The author acknowledges limits, including slice-level data splitting, and frames the results as preliminary.
pmc-13524135:
Kulkarni and colleagues reported in 2026 the first Indian case of antenatal sepsis, a severe infection during pregnancy, caused by Bordetella hinzii, a rare bacterium linked to poultry. The patient was a 27-year-old pregnant woman with sickle cell anaemia and a mild thalassemia trait, both inherited blood disorders that weaken defences. She arrived breathless and swollen, and her unborn baby had stopped moving.

Kulkarni found the baby had died in the womb at 24 weeks of pregnancy. Blood tests showed severe anaemia, high white cell counts, and strong inflammation markers. Cultures grew the rare bacterium, confirmed by an automated lab system. The strain responded to several strong antibiotics, including meropenem, but resisted others such as ceftriaxone. The mother improved on standard early treatment. The authors stress fast, advanced microbe testing for rare infections in high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-13524235:
Zhanbin Wang and co-authors assess, in a 2026 study, toxic elements in farm township soils in northwest Hebei, China, tracing where they came from and what risk they pose. Rural soil quality underpins food safety and countryside renewal plans. The team measured eight potentially toxic elements in surface soil and compared them with provincial background levels. A source-splitting model then divided the pollution among industry, traffic, nature, farming, and air fallout.

Industry dominated the load, with traffic second. Four elements exceeded background levels at most sites, while four others sat below. Cadmium and mercury drove the ecological risk, worst in the study area's center. Health risk modeling found adults broadly safe but flagged a share of children for cancer risk. The authors name industry and traffic as the control priorities.
pmc-13524335:
Yingying Lu and colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, caveolin-1 as a third host factor needed for a Bacillus cereus toxin to kill cells. Hemolysin BL is a three-part pore-forming toxin and a major cause of this bacterium's harm in food poisoning and severe infection. Two host receptors were already known, yet mice lacking both stayed only partly protected.

Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in mouse and human cells pointed to caveolin-1, a membrane protein tied to tiny surface pockets called caveolae. Imaging and binding tests showed the protein sits with the toxin at the cell surface and physically associates with it. Mice missing all three factors were completely resistant to toxin challenge. The authors define a three-part host system and propose caveolin-1 as a determinant of susceptibility.
pmc-13524735:
Khairul Fadzli Samat and five co-authors mix carbon black into a heat-to-electricity film to make it stronger and more efficient, in a 2026 paper. The base material, bismuth telluride, is the standard for harvesting waste heat near room temperature.

The films were plated from solution with soot-like carbon particles worked in. Electrical conductivity more than doubled, while the voltage response to heat held up, lifting the power factor by 15 percent. Heat flow through the film fell by over half, as the particles scattered it. Together those changes tripled the material's figure of merit. Hardness rose about a quarter and stiffness about twofold. The authors offer the recipe for small harvesters that must survive handling.
pmc-13526035:
Michela Polici leads a large team in a 2026 study testing whether body composition measured on scans predicts cancer-related death in colon cancer. Patients had stage II or III disease treated with upfront surgery, and baseline abdominal CT scans were segmented automatically by artificial intelligence software. Seventy-six measures covered visceral and under-skin fat, bone, and liver density.

The cohort held 293 patients, and about one third died from their cancer. Higher average density values for visceral fat and under-skin fat correlated directly with cancer-related death in slice-based analysis, and visceral fat density held up in volumetric analysis too. Adjusted survival models confirmed visceral fat density as an independent predictor in both approaches. The authors present fat quality, not just quantity, as a prognostic biomarker worth prospective testing.
pmc-13526135:
Santo and colleagues report real-world results for a radioactive targeting drug in the hardest prostate cancer cases: metastatic, castration-resistant, and visibly hungry on FDG scans, a marker of aggressive disease. The treatment, lutetium-177 PSMA-I&T, delivers radiation to cells carrying the PSMA surface protein. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 25 such patients who had both PSMA and FDG scans before treatment, letting the team test which scan features predicted benefit.

Just under half the men achieved at least a thirty percent fall in PSA, the blood marker of prostate cancer activity. A little over a third halved it, respectable figures in this pretreated group. Two scan ratios predicted that response: strong average PSMA uptake, and PSMA uptake dominating FDG uptake by a wide margin, each reaching statistical significance. Total tumour burden, measured by imaging volume or blood markers, predicted survival outcomes.
pmc-13526535:
Changying Jing and co-authors chart hormone cell ancestors across species and organs in a 2026 study. Pancreas and gut hormone cells steer body metabolism together. How those lineages form differs across mouse, human, dish, and organ settings. The team profiled ancestor cells with single cell gene and control readouts.

Shared and distinct control networks appeared across the settings compared. Some diabetes linked genes showed only in embryo stage pancreas ancestors. Dish grown gut like cells also formed an odd cell type not seen in bodies. Cell cycle and skeleton programs shifted in shared ways during formation.
pmc-13527235:
Dennis L. Parker and colleagues implement, in a 2026 imaging methods study, a way to measure absolute brain temperature from the chemical signatures of brain metabolites. Temperature guides care after brain injury and during heating or cooling therapies, yet measuring it inside the head noninvasively is hard. Their sequence, called GREPSI, combines a fast spectroscopic scan with a signal-shifting trick.

The shifting method removes the huge water signal and locates metabolite peaks whether or not water suppression is used. Tests on a brain phantom across temperatures from twenty-two to forty-two degrees matched the water bath within two percent at the top end, with precision near two tenths of a degree. Scan time ran two to five minutes for an eight-slice slab, and a healthy volunteer produced values in the normal range.
pmc-13528035:
Jie Zhang and four colleagues mine nursing notes for patterns of problems during outpatient dialysis in a 2026 study. The records came from one center and covered January 2024 to April 2025. The focus was low blood pressure during sessions, a common dialysis complication. Two reviewers pulled the data separately. The team checked which patient traits lined up with ever having the problem.

Older age came with slightly lower recorded odds of in-session low pressure. Kidney failure from diabetes also linked with lower odds than the comparison group. Other complications showed no firm links. The authors stress the limits of chart review. Session settings were not in the notes, so cause cannot be claimed. They propose nurse-led watch protocols built on such notes. Future work should pair live blood flow monitoring with structured checks.
pmc-13528135:
Benjamin Gordon and fifteen colleagues trace how a signal protein helps breast cancer reach lymph nodes in a 2026 study. The protein, Jagged-1, switches on the Notch pathway in nearby cells. Tissue arrays compared first tumors with their matching node deposits. Mouse models tested whether the protein drives spread. Cell barrier tests showed how vessel walls react.

Tumors rich in Jagged-1 invaded lymph vessels and nodes more in mice. A decoy that blocks the vessel growth signal VEGFR3 cut that spread. Jagged-1 loosened the lymph vessel lining in dishes. Tumor cells then crossed more easily, and lining cells turned inflammatory and sticky. Node deposits held more Jagged-1 than the first tumors. High levels there meant higher relapse risk. The authors pitch Jagged-1 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13529035:
Aafreen Bari and six colleagues examine infected corneal inflammation after a fast cross-linking treatment in a 2026 study. The treatment stiffens the cornea in keratoconus, where the eye bulges into a cone. Records came from a large Indian eye center. Of 723 eyes treated from 2021 to mid-2024, fourteen developed infiltrative keratitis. That is a rate near two percent.

Cases clustered in summer and rainy months. Patients from upper-middle income homes formed the majority. Being sixteen or younger more than doubled the relative risk. The commonest germ grown was a skin staphylococcus. Scans showed most damage sat in front of the treatment line. Clearing took about eighteen days on average. Three scan patterns appeared, from flattening to brief steepening. Early care, including steroid drops, ended with good vision, the authors report.
pmc-13529635:
Uk-Su Choi and four colleagues size tiny brain hubs tied to hormone and social signals in a 2026 MRI study. The hubs sit in the front hypothalamus and make oxytocin and vasopressin. Deep learning software carved the region into ten parts. The sample was small, twenty-three non-clinical adults. Trait scores for autism and ADHD were collected.

Two neighboring hubs, short-named PVN and SON, grew or shrank together. That pairing fits a shared hormone axis. Smaller SON volume tracked with higher autistic traits. It also tracked with stronger ADHD symptoms. Path checks suggested PVN effects flow through SON. The authors call the results preliminary, given the tiny sample. Still, they offer rare living-brain evidence for a hormone circuit in these traits. Bigger samples must test the claim.
pmc-13529735:
Valero-Cortijo and colleagues went fishing in the medicine cabinet for a drug that protects gut lining cells from a suicide signal gone wrong. In inflammatory bowel disease, the immune messenger TNF-alpha can flip colon cells from survival mode into apoptosis, orderly self-destruction, when an internal safety checkpoint fails. Their 2026 screen ran 2,421 approved compounds through colon cells engineered to lack that checkpoint. They hunted for anything that restored protection rather than merely blocking TNF from outside, as current biologic drugs do.

One winner stood out: potassium dehydroandrographolide succinate, a derivative of a traditional plant remedy. It rescued more than four fifths of the endangered cells by shutting down the caspase-8 death pathway specifically, while leaving a second death route untouched. Two obvious signalling explanations were tested and ruled out, leaving the mechanism open. The authors propose it as a complement to anti-TNF therapy.
pmc-13530135:
Ying Ma and colleagues set soil safety benchmarks in 2026 for an oasis on the Tibetan Plateau, where farming and grazing press on fragile high land. Standard soil checks give no clear cutoff values and handle patchy ground poorly. The team turned to multifractal models, which capture uneven patterns across space.

More than 1,500 samples from the Delingha-Ulan Oasis yielded background levels and screening values for 20 elements. Nine elements showed spiky patterns hinting at local contamination, while iodine stood out with extreme enrichment. Mercury, nitrogen, and phosphorus shifts pointed to wolfberry farming and herding as likely sources.
pmc-13530435:
Faizan Ahmed and four co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on a study of breast milk expression. Manshanden and co-authors found that five extra minutes of a feeding-like suction pattern raised pumped milk volume in the first four days after birth. The gain was 1.44 milliliters on average. The letter calls the finding intriguing but not yet ready for routine use.

Without random assignment or a same-time control group, the extra milk may reflect longer pumping rather than the pattern itself. The mothers also varied widely in why they pumped, from prematurity to separation. The study ran at one hospital with strong lactation support. The writers urge multicenter trials with equal-length sessions to isolate the pattern effect.
pmc-13530535:
Epner and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 217, outcomes from a multicenter database for arthroscopic repair of panlabral tears. These are shoulder socket rim tears wrapping 270 to 360 degrees around the joint. These huge tears are rare, inconsistently diagnosed, and feared for recurrent instability.

The series included 63 patients, median age twenty-three and overwhelmingly male, mostly contact and overhead athletes. At two years, median shoulder scores sat in the excellent range, with the standard shoulder score at ninety-five and instability-specific scores similarly high, all significantly improved over baseline. Three quarters returned to play, and over ninety percent of those returned at their previous level or higher. Recurrent instability struck about nineteen percent overall. Only two patients suffered a frank new dislocation and five needed further stabilization surgery, rates the authors note compare favorably with earlier series.
pmc-13531135:
Hajime Oyoshi, Kazuto Kano, Kenji Hotta, and Kouta Hirotaki fine-tune a step in cancer radiotherapy setup in a 2026 study. Surface-guided therapy tracks the patient's skin surface to position them, using a surface built from their CT scan.

The surface depends on a density threshold chosen when the scan is turned into a contour. The team tested thresholds across a wide range on two phantom models and two camera systems. Side-to-side and head-to-foot readings barely moved with the threshold. Vertical readings, though, shifted much more. Extra checks covered the planning software, image size, and scan position. Their results guide clinics toward threshold settings that keep the surface monitor honest.
pmc-13531235:
Khote and co-authors mapped drug resistance markers in malaria parasites from Congo and Tanzania, watching for artemisinin resistance. Samples came from treatment studies in both countries, which use unlike first-line drug pairs. Gene reads covered three key resistance genes. The standard form of the artemisinin marker gene ruled, and none of the known proven variants showed up.

Partner-drug markers split between the countries in ways that mirror their chosen treatments. One chloroquine-linked variant varied wildly between Congolese sites. The authors call for ongoing lab surveillance as it emerges in other spots in East Africa.
pmc-13531435:
Elijah Marsh Jung and a large team profile transporter genes in the human placenta in a 2026 paper. Transporters of the SLC and ABC families move nutrients and shield the fetus from harmful compounds. Their full profile at term was poorly known, as was any effect of fetal sex.

Using RNA sequencing, the team profiled placentas from ten pregnancies, sampling two regions of each. They detected 276 SLC transporters, with four standing out at the highest levels. Thirty-seven ABC transporters were also found, mostly tied to drug and lipid transport. One region held far more differing genes than the other. The study maps which carriers are active at birth.
pmc-13531535:
Cecilia Morel and co-authors hunt in 2026 for prescription clues that appear before a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in England. Linked practice and registry records covered 12,990 patients diagnosed between 2011 and 2018. Eight drug groups that treat early disease features were tracked across the five years before diagnosis.

Insulin prescribing rose first, about 19 months before diagnosis, and earlier in women than in men. That timing hints at diabetes caused by the tumor itself. Reflux, pain, and sickness medicines rose in the final year. Each rise marks a window where checking for cancer sooner might help a small share of patients.
pmc-13531635:
Ran Wang and Jinping Lai report a rare bowel cancer that first showed up as a large ovary mass in a 51-year-old woman. Scans found a 16 cm growth on her right ovary, and surgery suggested it had spread from the gut. Yet scopes of the stomach and colon found no source tumor.

Months later, a blocked and burst small bowel revealed the true source: a mixed tumor in the jejunum, part gland cancer and part nerve-type cancer. Gene testing found a new fusion joining two genes, never before reported in this tumor. Despite further drug treatment, the woman died seven months later.
pmc-13531735:
Tiia Mönttinen and colleagues compare in 2026 a rapid recovery path with standard care after keyhole appendix removal. Ninety-six adults with uncomplicated appendicitis at one Finnish hospital entered the prospective study in sequence, first standard care, then the fast track. Phone interviews days after discharge captured pain, sleep, and satisfaction.

Fast-track patients went home a median six hours sooner and reported less sleep disruption from pain. Worst and lightest pain scores favored the fast track, while middle pain ran slightly higher, leaving pain verdicts mixed. Satisfaction stayed high in both groups, and nearly all fast-track patients would recommend the approach.
pmc-13531835:
Shi-Wei Lin and co-authors build in 2026 a CT-based prediction model for a rare kidney cancer subtype defined by gene rearrangements. Records and scans covered 746 kidney cancer patients across several centers, including 77 with the target subtype. Thousands of image texture features were distilled from tumor and normal kidney regions.

A chart combining both image scores with age and stage predicted the subtype strongly in training and held up at fresh centers. Calibration and usefulness checks also passed. Such a tool could flag the subtype before surgery without a biopsy, guiding tailored treatment planning for a cancer that imaging alone rarely names.
pmc-13532335:
Li and eight co-authors built a field test for a pig virus in this paper from twenty twenty-six. Porcine adenovirus type 3 harms swine herds, and farm-side detection tools are scarce. Their platform, nicknamed RADIANT, skips lab extraction entirely. Amplification and a CRISPR enzyme reaction run in one pot, finishing within thirty minutes.

The authors pitch the kit for surveillance in low-resource settings. They also see it as a template for portable CRISPR diagnostics in animal health.
pmc-13533835:
Chapple and colleagues published a 2026 study on a hidden transport route inside myelin. Myelin wraps nerve fibers in fatty layers that speed up signals. The team found that tiny cargo still moves through channels inside that wrap. They named the route TRAM, short for transport route across myelin.

Mice missing key motor proteins saw the traffic stall almost fully. Stalled traffic was followed by damage to the nerve fiber itself. pmc-13534435:
Eric Bertrand Kouam and colleagues survey in 2026 cowpea farming across two zones of Cameroon. Cowpea is a key food crop in tropical Africa, yet output faces drought, pests, and poor soils. The team questioned 300 farmers in 15 divisions about their systems, limits, and seed choices.
