Land purchase, animal traction, group membership, and seed access raised uptake of improved types, guiding breeder and outreach priorities.
pmc-13534535:
Zhaoxiang Zeng and colleagues screen in 2026 for microplastics in the soft core of spinal discs from patients in Wuhan, China. Plastic particles have been found in many human tissues, yet this sheltered disc core was barely studied. Tissue from 51 disc surgery patients was digested, filtered, and scanned with Raman imaging.

Nine polymer particles were confirmed across five patients, most smaller than 100 micrometres, with types spanning foam and rubber-like plastics. Blanks and surgical materials were checked to cut false matches. Readers get early proof that particles can reach this tissue and a method for larger studies.
pmc-13535035:
Madison Nordin and co-authors review digoxin dosing during a form of dialysis in this 2026 paper. Digoxin is a heart drug with a narrow safe range. Some intensive care patients receive it while a machine filters their blood around the clock. Almost no guidance exists for dosing in that setting.

The team found six patients with fourteen drug level checks between them. A low dose given every forty-eight hours kept all levels below the safety line. Both high levels followed large loading doses. Two patients had slow heartbeats, and both were also on a second rhythm drug. The authors stress that firm dosing rules remain unproven and monitoring stays essential.
pmc-13535335:
Hiroki Ikeuchi, Masao Hirano, and Masashi Kabasawa report a 2026 case of fast-moving infective endocarditis after surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot. This heart infection can advance quickly when prosthetic material sits inside the heart. Here it struck both sides of the heart, hitting several valves at once.

A standard heart scan through the chest wall missed the infection, but a scan done with a probe in the throat found it. The authors stress that finding it early, and operating in time, keeps the infection from spreading far inside the heart. For doctors the warning is plain: a clear surface scan does not rule out deep valve infection after repair of a heart defect present from birth.
pmc-13535535:
Patients' own voices rarely shape staff training in imaging wards, and Ilona Lavender and Mohamed Badawy report how one department wove them in, in work from twenty twenty-six. The work ran across two years in a large hospital imaging unit. Patient stories entered workshops and study sessions.

Patients also co-wrote information sheets, filled a dedicated experience role, and sat in unit rule-making. The team weighed each step against known guidance on real partnership. Lessons stress clear aims, care for the tellers' own wellbeing, and a shift from token seats to shared say. The report is a how-to for wards that scan people at raw moments.
pmc-13536535:
Esedullah Akaras and Ugur Sozlu survey in 2026 physiotherapy students in Turkey on climate change awareness and anxiety about the future. Young health workers will face climate health effects, yet their readiness and worries were little known. An online survey reached 394 students at state universities with two standard scales.

Students showed moderate climate awareness and notable future anxiety, with a weak positive link between the two scores. Female students, environmental volunteers, and frequent social media users for climate news scored higher on awareness. Prior environmental training showed no clear link, guiding curriculum planners.
pmc-13536635:
Sejoong Ahn and colleagues validate in 2026 the updated SOFA-2 organ failure score in emergency department patients with septic shock. The new score revises cut-offs and adds modern organ support types, but it had been tested mainly in intensive care. Two prospective registries gave over 4,000 patients for head-to-head scoring.

pmc-13536735:
Jiaxing Wang and co-authors survey eating disorders and suicide risk among Chinese college students in a 2026 study of 18,578 students surveyed in late October 2023. Questionnaires covered background, eating problems, low mood, anxiety, and suicide risk. Statistical models identified factors tied to eating disorders overall, plus factors tied to suicide risk among students who had eating disorders.

About one in seven students met criteria for an eating disorder. Higher weight, town or city living, childhood separation from parents, higher maternal schooling, low mood, anxiety, and prior suicidal thoughts or attempts each tracked with eating disorders. Among affected students, about one in five reported suicidal thoughts or attempts. The authors urge routine suicide checks for students with eating disorders and joint care for mood symptoms.
pmc-13538235:
Pooja Rao leads a large team on money strain in young cancer survivors. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses both counts and talks. Young survivors face money harm in ways that are their own.

A small group of survivors filled a money strain score form. They also sat for talks on money after cancer care. Mean strain scores sat in the mid range of the scale. Talks showed family talk and support varied a lot by case. Strain hit future plans for folks of all ages in the group. Mixed methods give a fuller view.
pmc-13538335:
Psychotria rubra is a plant used in southern China, and early reports link it to relief from low mood. Li Yin and co-authors set out in 2026 to learn how the plant might act against depression. They combined gene data work, computer models of molecule binding, and tests in stressed mice, rather than relying on one method alone.

The team compared gene patterns in blood from people with depression and healthy peers, then screened key genes with machine learning. Computer runs tested how plant compounds fit those gene targets. In mice, several plant compounds were given after three weeks of stress, and mood tests, brain signals, and cell damage markers were tracked.
pmc-13538635:
Eight authors report a hard case from 2026: a brain infection from herpes simplex virus in a patient with a weak immune system. The patient had received donor blood stem cells and fell ill again one and a half months after the first bout, while still on guard drugs. Scans and spinal fluid tests confirmed the return of the virus.

The patient, who had been in a coma with brain swelling and tissue death, grew more alert and began to move. Scans showed no new spread, virus in spinal fluid fell to zero, and no major side effects appeared.
pmc-13538935:
Zengkun Fang and co-authors chart two decades of research on exercise therapy for Parkinson's disease, mapping who publishes what and where the field is heading. Their study appeared in 2026. They mined a major citation database for papers from 2004 to 2024 and ran the set through mapping and text tools. Output rose every year, with a surge after 2019. The United States, Italy, and China lead in volume, and a Dutch university tops the institution list.

Keyword mining exposed the field's clusters and rising terms. The authors say the map helps newcomers find the active fronts, from gait training to brain effects, and helps funders spot crowded ground. Bibliometric maps, they note, show the field's shape better than any single review can.
pmc-13539335:
Seven authors study fatty liver risk in nonobese Chinese adults with type 1 diabetes in this 2026 paper. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction is often linked to obesity, so risk in lean patients with this form of diabetes can be missed.

The team used a blood based steatosis index in 47 adults of normal weight. About 28 percent scored above the high likelihood cutoff. Those patients needed higher bolus and total daily insulin doses than low scoring patients, while reaching like blood sugar control. The authors argue this liver condition is under-recognized in lean type 1 patients and deserves screening and care.
pmc-13539535:
Gyo-Bin Choo and co-authors report a dog whose brain tumor switched off its thirst, in a 2026 case report. The nine-year-old mixed breed arrived limp, vomiting, and shaky, having stopped drinking on its own. Blood tests showed severe high sodium, while hormone checks ruled out a salt-retaining disorder and instead suggested pituitary-driven hormone excess.

After careful fluid correction, MRI found a pituitary macroadenoma pressing toward the hypothalamus, the brain's thirst center. Drugs for the hormone problem plus assisted drinking steadied the sodium, and later scans showed the tumor slightly smaller. The case warns vets that a dog which will not drink may harbor a brain lesion, not stubbornness.
pmc-13539735:
Jiahong Xu and four co-authors review, in a 2026 article, why triple-negative breast cancer spreads to bone and how printed three-dimensional models might help researchers study that spread. Triple-negative disease lacks the hormone receptors that many breast cancer drugs target, so treatment options stay narrow.

The review first explains the cycle in which tumor cells prompt bone breakdown, then looks at printed scaffolds built from gels that can hold tumor, blood vessel, and bone cells together. Such models offer a place to test new drugs and delivery methods. The authors also note printed implants and surgical guides, plus the technical hurdles that still block wider clinical use.
pmc-13539935:
Yuki Hirai and seven colleagues present a 2026 case report of lung surgery complicated by two rare birth defects of blood vessels in the same patient. A 68-year-old woman had cancer in her right lower lung lobe, plus an extra artery from the aorta feeding its base and upper lung veins draining to the wrong place.

Three-dimensional reconstructions mapped the vessels before a keyhole operation removed the lobe. Surgeons tied off the aberrant artery twice and divided it with a stapler, and recovery went smoothly. The tumor proved to be an early-stage adenocarcinoma. A year later scans showed no return of cancer and no swelling at the cut vessel.
pmc-13540835:
Arezo Khadiv and colleagues compare gut bacteria in a 2026 study. The bacteria are Escherichia coli strains from two groups. One group has irritable bowel syndrome. The other group is healthy. The team hunted genes that help bacteria cling to the gut. They also hunted genes for stealing iron.

Gene tests covered sticking factors and iron systems. They also covered toxins and protective capsules. Six genes were much more common in the syndrome strains. That held true after strict correction for many tests. Two genes ran the other way, turning up more in healthy strains. No strain carried two key adhesion genes at all.
pmc-13540935:
Victor M Cnossen and colleagues compare two kinds of trial volunteers in 2026. One group joined controlled human infection trials. In those trials, healthy people are deliberately given a pathogen. The other group joined standard first-in-human drug trials. The two designs look alike on paper. The infection studies ask more of the body.

Seventy infection volunteers answered a validated questionnaire. Ninety-eight drug trial volunteers did the same. Money motivated the infection group less. Altruistic reasons ran stronger in that group. Infection volunteers also endured more severe symptoms. They said expected symptoms truly shaped their choice to join. Views on fair pay and fair burden matched across groups.
pmc-13541835:
Acton and colleagues run a careful supplement trial on ubiquinol, the absorbable form of coenzyme Q10, a molecule that ferries electrons inside mitochondria, the cell's power stations. The oxidised supplement form has repeatedly disappointed in exercise studies. pmc-13542035:
Rieke Gerdes and co-authors run a small pilot study in 2026 on brain tumor scans. Meningiomas are tumors that often carry a receptor that a tracer drug can target in PET scans. The tracer used here has perks over older ones, such as longer life and sharper images, but it lacks formal approval. The team compared scan uptake in tumor tissue with lab stains for the receptor in samples from twelve patients.

Scan uptake tracked the lab stain closely, and high stain tumors took up much more tracer than low stain ones. Two ways of drawing tumor volume from the scan both missed the true size in some cases when set against MRI. Readers learn both the promise and the sizing limits of this scan method.
pmc-13542135:
Ocean eddies are swirling currents that can trap and carry material far below the surface. They measured plastics from fifty meters down to twelve hundred meters and combined the data with models of coherent water structures.

Both eddies held up to three times more microplastics in the upper two hundred meters than nearby waters. Tiny fragments under two hundred micrometers dominated. Fibers were more common in the cyclone, and larger fragments in the other eddy. The authors argue that eddies actively redistribute plastics through the water column, not just at the surface.
pmc-13542235:
Jifang Sun, Chengbo Xu, and Fang Xie describe a 2026 computer vision method for spotting teacher behaviour in classroom images, designed as a sensing layer for future virtual and mixed-reality teaching spaces. Their system builds on the YOLOv8 detector, which locates objects in a single pass over an image. Tests on a classroom dataset the team collected themselves gave precision, recall, and average precision that competed well with several widely used detectors. The authors present detection as groundwork: reliable perception of what a teacher is doing must come before automated feedback or synchronised virtual classrooms can work.
pmc-13542935:
Mathias Holmsgaard Eskesen and colleagues published a 2026 population study of bloodstream infections in people with B-cell blood cancers in North Denmark. The team linked cancer registry and health records for patients diagnosed between 2013 and 2022. They described which organisms caused infections and searched admission data for factors predicting a positive blood culture or death soon after infection. Statistical selection picked the strongest predictors.

Gram-negative bacteria overtook gram-positive ones during the decade, driven by Escherichia coli, which caused roughly a quarter of positive cultures. Low neutrophil counts, high inflammation markers, sepsis, low blood pressure, and kidney failure all raised the chance of a positive culture. pmc-13543335:
Six reviewers examine how reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules made in cells, help drive breast cancer and how they might be turned against it, in a review published in 2026. At very high levels they can kill cancer cells outright.

The review traces the main signaling paths through which these molecules push tumors to grow and spread. It weighs plant and lab-made antioxidants, such as melatonin and curcumin, noting both promise and mixed safety data during treatment. Newer ideas include nano-scale carriers that react to these molecules and ways to force a rust-like cell death in drug-resistant tumors. The authors point toward tailored redox care guided by gene data.
pmc-13543435:
Laura Braun and colleagues published a 2026 review of inherited risk for lymphoma, the blood cancers arising in lymphoid tissue. Finding the weaker variants demands large, well-described case and control sets, which the authors argue family-based cohorts supply better than unselected population sampling. Better risk recognition could steer counselling, watch for treatment toxicity, and prevent second cancers in predisposed patients.
pmc-13543835:

pmc-13544635:

Existing analysis routes were often tied to one marker type, slow at scale, or poor at storing results for long-term monitoring projects. pmc-13545235:

pmc-13545335:

The authors see teaching promise in these tools but warn that reliability is not yet sufficient.
pmc-13545635:

The authors suggest the pairing could sharpen decisions made before surgery.
pmc-13546035:

pmc-13546435:

pmc-13546535:

pmc-13546635:

Its level also tracked which immune cells crowd the tumor, and computer scores hinted at how patients might answer immune therapy. In dish-grown liver cancer cells, lab assays probed what the protein does to growth and spread. The authors pitch VPS45 as both a warning flag and a possible target.
pmc-13546735:

Networked links let institutions share cases and subspecialist opinions. Slide archives become searchable data libraries for teaching and research. Comparing with other large rollouts, the authors distill general rules: design around workflow, integrate the data, keep systems interoperable, and organize diagnosis as a network service.
pmc-13547035:

They trained seven models on over a thousand patients, then checked the best on a fresh group. Simple logistic regression won, and sticking to the plan was the strongest shield against relapse. A learning policy that raised dose as a gut marker rose beat the choices doctors had made, on model-based scoring. The authors urge real trials before clinic use.
pmc-13547235:

pmc-13547335:

pmc-13547535:

pmc-13548335:

pmc-13548535:

pmc-13548635:

pmc-13549435:

pmc-13549835:

pmc-13550635:

pmc-13550935:

pmc-13551735:

pmc-13552835:

pmc-13553635:

pmc-13554435:

pmc-13554835:

pmc-13555135:

pmc-13556435:

pmc-13556535:

pmc-13556635:

pmc-13556735:

pmc-13556835:

pmc-13556935:

pmc-13557335:

pmc-13558535:

pmc-13558635:

pmc-13558835:

pmc-13559235:

pmc-13559435:

pmc-13559635:

pmc-13560235:

pmc-13561535:

pmc-13562135:

pmc-13562335:

pmc-13563735:

pmc-13563835:

pmc-13564535:

pmc-13565535:
