The registry scale turns a ward-level worry into national rates. Orthogeriatric teams get a prevalence figure and an outcome price tag for a complication they aim to prevent.
pmc-13567135:
Carlos Rodriguez and co-authors make plant-derived coumarin compounds with green methods and test them against cattle ticks, in this 2026 paper. The tick species drains herds across the tropics, and chemical controls are losing ground. Coumarins offer a possible alternative chemistry.

Nine variants were built without solvent, using a reusable acid catalyst. Adult female ticks were dipped and survival was tracked with standard models. Hydroxyl-bearing variants, especially at two ring positions, killed ticks at the lowest doses. Docking and structure-activity modeling pointed to the same features: hydroxyl groups and polar side chains at one key position.
pmc-13567235:
Piotr Łabuński, Lucjan Witek, and Paweł Obal measured how temperature changes the vibration damping of two sticky materials on aluminum beams, in a 2026 study. Such materials are used to calm vibration passively, and their softness shifts with temperature. The team tried two ways of applying them: a free layer on the surface, and a layer sandwiched under a stiff skin.

Butyl rubber and a bituminous material were tested from room temperature down to two degrees below freezing. The sandwiched form damped better at room temperature, above all with butyl rubber. As temperatures fell and the materials stiffened, the free layer caught up or won in several modes.
pmc-13567635: Rui-Feng Wang and Kangning Cui wrote on advanced remote sensing and artificial intelligence techniques in agriculture and forestry. Their 2026 article opens by noting that rapid advances in sensing, computation, and automation are reshaping how plants and agricultural systems are observed, analyzed, and managed. That framing sets the topic: remote sensing data joined with AI methods for farm and forest work.
pmc-13568335:
Alfredo Rondinella and Elia Marin propose, in a 2026 paper, a framework for how polymer materials used in medicine break down in the body. Such materials do not fail by one route alone. Water attack, oxidation, enzyme cutting, fatigue, wear, protein sticking, and fat uptake often act together, across the surface, the bulk, and the tissue around the implant.

The framework draws those routes as a directed network of coupled steps. It separates true breakdown reactions from surface factors that modulate them. Damage at the molecular level is then linked to how long the material keeps its function. Function is defined by the job at hand, such as strength, mass, shape, or surface performance. A qualitative matrix shows how each step can amplify or damp the next. From it, the authors name recurring breakdown patterns across major medical polymer families.
pmc-13568735:
Li and co-authors remove a broken dental tool from a hard spot with a printed guide in a 2026 case report. A 20-year-old woman had a root canal file tip snap off and slip past the tooth root, near the sinus floor. Scans placed the fragment exactly. Normal retreatment could not reach it, so surgery with a custom guide was planned.

The guide led the team straight to the fragment for removal. The root tip was cut, the cyst cleaned, and the canal sealed from below. Two years on, the dark lesion had nearly vanished and the tooth worked normally. The authors claim the first such guided rescue at the sinus floor.
pmc-13569635:
Abbey L Landini's team checked the safety of nebulised ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone after children's airway surgery, in a 2026 retrospective review. The antibiotic-steroid mix, borrowed from ear care, is widely used off-label to calm swelling and granulation after airway operations, yet rigorous safety data were lacking. The team reviewed 399 children treated at a tertiary centre between 2019 and 2023, most after surgery for narrowing below the vocal cords.

Children received the inhaled drug for about twelve days on average, and no cases of adrenal suppression, glucose disturbance, or airway over-reactivity appeared. One child on chemotherapy had suspected fungal infection with negative pathology, and endoscopy showed no major swelling. The authors judge the drug well tolerated in medically complex children while calling for prospective trials of benefit and dosing.
pmc-13570135:
Mahsa Seydi and co-authors study in 2026 what brain traits track with fall risk in older adults who live with long-term low back pain. Thirty-three adults aged 50 and over took tests of body function, daily step counts, and quick thought skills. A belt sensor logged how they walked in daily life, and three kinds of brain scans were taken.

How well they walked tied to how well tissue conducts signals in deep brain zones and in the small brain at the back. Plain size and fiber measures did not show that link. Test scores for strength and balance tied to fiber density in sight paths and to the size of deep brain zones. The team says signals and build each add a piece, and that knowing these paths may help craft care to cut falls.
pmc-13570235:
Jonathan Broad and co-authors measure the early effect of a pregnancy vaccine against a lung virus on baby hospital stays in England, in a 2026 study. The virus, RSV, fills infant wards each winter with bronchiolitis. Mothers vaccinated in pregnancy pass protection to newborns.

The program began in September 2024. Time series tracking through March 2026 covered babies under three months old. All cause bronchiolitis admissions fell by about thirty-nine percent against expectation. Admissions tied to the virus itself fell by about sixty-three percent. Critical care admissions were tracked beside ward stays. The authors read the drops as early proof the program works.
pmc-13570535:
Yang and co-authors show estrogen loss worsens Alzheimer's disease through a neuronal enzyme signal in mice. Women face higher Alzheimer's risk and worse pathology than men. The drop in estrogen after menopause is a suspect, but the molecular link was murky. Removing ovaries in female 5xFAD mice sharply worsened amyloid buildup. Thinking deficits, brain inflammation, and synapse loss all grew. Blocking estrogen receptors copied those effects.

Gene reads across brain cell types showed wide rewiring after estrogen loss. A lysosomal enzyme, cathepsin S, rose sharply, as did the risk gene ApoE. Cutting that enzyme's level partway prevented much of the harm. The work names a target chain from hormones to pathology.
pmc-13570735:
Marietjie Botes and others put out a 2026 policy article on mental privacy in South Africa. Brain data tools are spreading fast. Mental health apps also gather sensitive data. South African culture adds shared and spiritual sides. Folk healing shapes many people's care.

The authors review legal and ethical gaps. European and American models fit poorly there. Consent often needs family or local leaders. Abuse risks rise where gaps are deep. They propose making the national privacy law stronger. Brain and mental data should count as protected classes. Consent steps that fit the culture are also urged.
pmc-13571335:
Paul K. Jain and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a catastrophic air embolism during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy, a camera procedure with an otherwise strong safety record, in a 74-year-old woman. Moments into the procedure she suffered a heart attack pattern, airway bleeding, and cardiac arrest.

Heart imaging showed clear arteries but a large pocket of air trapped at the tip of the left ventricle. Her course grew worse with severe brain swelling, seizures, and loss of blood flow to a limb. High-pressure oxygen treatment, the usual rescue, was ruled out by her underlying lung damage. The report warns teams that this rare complication can imitate a heart attack and defeat standard rescue options.
pmc-13571635:
Felipe Arbelaez and co-authors report a 2026 clinical trial protocol and study of a new oral drug for endometriosis pain. The condition causes pelvic pain, painful periods, and pain during sex. The drug blocks an enzyme that makes a hormone locally in tissue.

Women aged eighteen to forty nine with moderate to severe pain were assigned at random to one of three drug doses or a placebo for up to twelve weeks. The main measures were change in overall pelvic pain and the share with side effects. Secondary measures covered period pain, other pelvic pain, and rescue drug use.
pmc-13571735:
Lili Zhao, Liangbin Hu, and eight co-authors turn kiwifruit pruning waste into aroma material. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, profiles the scent gases of kiwifruit branches. Branches are cut in bulk each year and mostly thrown away. The team compares six branch samples with a store-bought scent reference tied to silver vine.

Sixty-four scent compounds were named across the samples. The reference smelled clearly distinct from any single branch. Twenty-six key compounds split into four scent modules for blending. A mix of two branch types came closest to the reference. Eight compounds carried most of the target scent. Waste branches may thus serve the flavor and scent trade.
pmc-13572035:
Jiaqi Li and co-authors trace the evolution of a digestive enzyme family, the alpha-glucosidases, across bees and their relatives in the Apoidea. These insects pollinate widely and face varied nectars across regions, so their sugar-handling enzymes matter for survival. The team compared sequences from many species across six families.

The family split early into three branches that now differ in where they act and what they do. Honeybee members show large structural variety. Many sites near the enzyme's binding pocket carry marks of positive selection and functional divergence, likely shaping how the enzyme grips and cuts its targets. The authors conclude the family expanded and diversified under adaptive pressure tied to diet.
pmc-13572335:
Ying Hu and colleagues follow, in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study, 231,148 women to test whether spontaneous miscarriage predicts early death, and whether later lifestyle changes that risk. Lifestyle was scored from diet, smoking, activity, and body weight, and deaths before the standard premature cutoff were tracked over a median of about twelve years.

One miscarriage showed no link after full adjustment, yet two miscarriages raised the hazard and three or more raised it further, with cardiovascular deaths prominent. Simply ever having miscarried was not significant once lifestyle counted. An unhealthy lifestyle amplified the risk in women with repeated losses. The pattern marks recurrent miscarriage as a signal for long-term health surveillance, with lifestyle a modifiable lever.
pmc-13572435:
Yu-Yu Chen and co-authors present a delivery-ready platform for removing phosphate tags from proteins in a 2026 paper. Adding or removing these tags steers much of cell life, and forced removal could treat disease. Chimera molecules that drag a phosphatase enzyme to a target protein exist, but good small-molecule hooks for the enzyme are rare and can blunt its action.

Their platform, TogoPhosTAC, ships a prebuilt complex inside fat bubbles called lipid nanoparticles. The cargo can be the complex itself or the RNA that makes it. In cells it stripped tags from a growth receptor and from two proteins tied to brain disease, alpha-synuclein and tau. In mice it lowered harmful tau tagging in the brain after delivery through the nose or by injection.
pmc-13572535:
Siv Therese Bogevik Bjørkedal, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 interview study of young people who used headspace Denmark. Headspace is a civil society service where trained volunteers counsel youth on mental health, outside clinics. Most past research has centred on clinical care, so the civic route was little studied.

Thirteen young people aged 14 to 25 took part in deep interviews about their visits. They called the space safe and welcoming, a place to share thoughts they could not voice elsewhere. Counsellors felt caring and truly keen, more like a trusted friend or family member than a clinician. Rooms felt cozy and home-like, a sharp contrast to clinic settings. The authors argue that volunteer care adds value of its own, not just extra hands for a stretched system.
pmc-13572835:
Neutrophils swarm to infections first, yet cancer researchers have largely overlooked them as a therapy base. Shao and co-authors review how lab-grown tissue systems could change that. Microphysiological systems, from 3D spheroids and organoids to organ-on-a-chip devices, let scientists watch human neutrophils interact with tumors in real time. Unlike animal models, these setups give precise control over the cell surroundings and use human cells.

The review surveys what each platform has revealed about neutrophil behavior in cancer. It also covers early attempts to steer the cells against tumors. The authors close with the hurdles blocking clinical use, and how these systems might clear them.
pmc-13573135:
Nele Krüger, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 chemical method that breaks one of the strongest bonds in organic chemistry at room temperature. Carbon-fluorine bonds resist attack, so joining aryl fluorides to other carbons has needed harsh heat or fierce reagents. The team paired a palladium catalyst with a lithium base to do the job gently.

The catalyst carries a methyl naphthyl frame, and the base forms enolates, reactive carbon partners, in place. Ketone, ester, nitrile, and even amide partners all joined to plain aryl fluorides. Computer models showed why the mild route works: lithium ions grip the fluorine atom, which eases the palladium's entry into the bond. That grip explains a reaction long thought out of reach at such soft conditions. The method widens the stock of building blocks for drug and material synthesis.
pmc-13573235:
A sensor paste that spots a plant compound at trace levels is built by the authors in work dated 2026. The paste mixes carbon with a four-metal oxide blend, topped with creatine for a sharper response. Rutoside, a health-linked plant compound, is the target of the hunt. Three current methods set catch floors in the low nanomole range. Selectivity, steadiness, sensitivity, and repeat runs all got careful checks across the study.

The paste also read rutoside in a lemon sample well. Surface, shape, and crystal checks backed the build's form. Food tests gain a cheap, sharp tool from this work.
pmc-13573335:
John Keven and fourteen co-authors assess how mass distribution of insecticide treated nets affects coverage and use in Papua New Guinea. The country ran five nationwide net distributions in 15 years, yet malaria cases are rising and survey indicators for net ownership and use look unusually low. Knowledge gaps limit interpretation of that paradox.

Household surveys cover 12 villages in three high burden provinces, with 815 households and 5,671 people. Fieldwork runs in the months before and after the 2024 distribution. Teams record questionnaires, inspect all nets in homes, and match nets to individual users. The before and after design shows how distribution changes ownership, access, and actual nightly use on the ground.
pmc-13573435:
Ringga Rahmi Prima, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 case-control study of home conditions and tuberculosis in Padang City, Indonesia. Poor housing has long been tied to TB, yet the fine details of living space were rarely measured. The study homes all shared one trait: a past TB patient had lived there.

From August to December 2024, the team enrolled 105 confirmed cases and two control sets of about a hundred each. Home visits logged room air, house size, and building materials. Small bedroom volume and plaster ceilings went with case status in set comparisons. Outdoor work, frequent coffee shop visits, and more than a year since the prior patient also raised the odds. The authors suggest more bedroom space and screening that stays alert past the first year.
pmc-13574335:
Bittencourt and nine co-authors review how artificial intelligence is used in chronic kidney disease. Their 2026 review searched two large databases for studies from 2019 to 2025. Twenty-six studies made the cut. The team logged which tools were used and what they achieved.

Most studies used supervised or deep learning. Scores for spotting the disease and its stages were often high. Yet weak spots kept recurring across the set. Few models were tested on outside data, and data sets varied widely. The authors urge tighter methods before such tools guide care. The promise, they say, is real but not yet proven at scale.
pmc-13574435:
Chang Li, Xiang Yin, Menghan Jia, Jie Shao, and Li Cui describe a two thousand twenty-six case report on a rare brain inflammation disorder. Autoimmune diencephalitis makes the immune system attack the brain. Their patient, a middle-aged man, depended on immune therapy to stay well.

He had months of headache, fever, seizures, and clouded consciousness. Scans and lab tests confirmed the diagnosis. Standard drugs alone could not be reduced safely. Adding efgartigimod let doctors taper steroids while he steadily recovered. The case suggests a supporting role for the drug in hard-to-wean patients.
pmc-13574735:
Bina Tariq, with four colleagues, reports on a 2026 study of an AI tool that fixes messy labels on medical scans. Scan files carry DICOM tags for body part, side, and protocol, and sloppy tags block sharing and slow readers. The team tested a shop tool that standardises those tags and asked whether reading times fell after it went live.

Reviewers hand-checked tags on 422 X-ray images and 1,503 CT series, and accuracy ran from the low eighties to full marks by tag type. Reading times for near eleven thousand cases before and ten thousand after were compared. CT reading sped up for belly, whole body, head, and temple bone scans, worth about 270 hours a year. Chest and sinus scans showed no clear change. The authors credit tidier tags for the gains.
pmc-13574835:
Feras Qawasmi, Mustafa Yassin, and Adam C Watts describe a new surgical route to the inner elbow in a cadaver study. A certain elbow injury pattern tears the back band of the inner ligament and chips a key facet of the forearm bone. No standard approach let surgeons repair that back band directly.

Working on six donated upper limbs, the team used their posterior ulna medial approach, shortened to PUMA. The route reliably exposed the ligament's back band. It did so without detaching the main muscle origin, cutting the ligament's front band, or moving the ulnar nerve. Simulated repairs and facet fixation both proved feasible. Nearby vessels and nerves stayed safe throughout. Surgeon questionnaires backed the approach's usefulness.
pmc-13574935:
Yuan Li, writing alone in 2026, asks how a gene called DEK may drive Parkinson disease. The work links two themes: chemical marks on RNA and long-term swelling in the brain. Both have been tied to the illness, but their shared pattern was not clear. Li set out to find genes that sit at the join of the two.

The study blends blood data, gene data, and lab tests on cells. Three machine learning tools helped pick out key genes and group patients. DEK stood out as a hub found in nerve cells. The author then checked that role in cell tests. The result offers a fresh target for later work on cause and care, though it rests on data sets and cell work, not trials.
pmc-13575035:
Brian I Rini and Benjamin Garmezy discuss a new class of kidney cancer drugs in a 2026 podcast article. Advanced renal cell carcinoma is now treated mainly with immune therapy combinations or immune therapy plus a vessel-blocking drug. Progress has been slow for decades, so fresh options are still needed.

The pair explain bispecific antibodies, single drugs built to hit two targets at once: the PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint and VEGF, a signal that grows blood vessels. Lab work hints that joint targeting may bind more strongly and cut side effects. Several such drugs are in development, named here as PF-08634404, ivonescimab, and BNT327. Early results in other cancers and plans for kidney cancer trials are covered.
pmc-13575135:
A large team reports a platform study the catalog lists under 2026. The topic is a huge family of cell receptors that sense signals outside the cell. These receptors are the most common target for drugs. Yet many of the more than 800 human forms are still poorly known. The team built a way to test most of them side by side.

Their deep scanning platform covers 766 human receptors plus 174 splice variants. All were grown in one shared pool of lab cells. The team measured how much message each gene made, how well it was turned into protein, and how much reached the cell surface. Drug researchers get a fair side-by-side map of a whole receptor family. Such a map can point to neglected receptors worth a closer look. It also gives a base line for later studies of single receptors in depth.
pmc-13575235:
Lehu Bu and eight co-authors use a three-dimensional neural network to design composites that survive high-velocity impacts, in a two thousand twenty-six materials paper. Mixing stiff and soft phases can blunt impact stress, but the design space of arrangements is enormous.

Their model learns from split Hopkinson pressure bar experiments combined with finite element simulations, linking microstructure directly to dynamic response. Optimized designs improved dynamic stress uniformity from about twenty-two to ninety-seven percent and raised load capacity by roughly a quarter to a half versus random designs. A thermal module also evaluates heat spreading, revealing architectures that combine impact resistance with thermal conductivity for aerospace and automotive use.
pmc-13575435:
Alaa Gamal Ahmad and co-authors tested whether the time of day matters when melatonin protects the rat brain from a food additive in a 2026 paper. The additive, monosodium glutamate, damaged the cerebellum and caused clumsy movement in their model. Melatonin follows a daily rhythm, peaking in the middle of the night. Thirty two male rats were split into four groups: control, additive only, and additive plus melatonin given in the morning or at night.

The additive alone caused motor deficits, raised inflammatory genes and damage markers, and lowered antioxidant defenses and blood melatonin. Melatonin improved nearly all of those measures in both timing groups. Night dosing did better than morning dosing on movement, tissue appearance, and several gene measures. The authors tie that edge to matching the hormone's natural night peak.
pmc-13575835:
Adedokun Oluwasegun and seven co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-six on the fruit Xylopia aethiopica as a possible treatment for uterine fibroids. Fibroids are benign, hormone-driven tumors, and new multi-target options are wanted. The team combined animal experiments with computer docking studies.

Thirty rats were given monosodium glutamate to induce fibroid-like changes, then treated with three doses of the fruit extract. The extract brought raised progesterone and estradiol back toward normal, more so at higher doses. Docking suggested its compounds bind hormone, blood-vessel, and fibrosis receptors. Together the results portray the fruit as a natural agent acting on several fibroid pathways at once.
pmc-13575935:
Zexi Li and colleagues wrote a review in 2026 on mind and heart links. Strong evidence ties mental strain to heart and vessel disease. Depression, anxiety, and chronic stress raise disease risk. The link also runs the other way. Heart patients develop mental disorders at high rates. The authors propose a network frame for this two-way traffic. They call it the psycho-cardiovascular interaction network. It spans body systems, signaling paths, and daily behavior.

The review gathers population evidence for the link. It then maps the main pathways inside the network. Several named signaling routes carry messages between brain and heart. One route involves an inflammatory complex inside cells. The authors discuss combined care strategies. They include lifestyle and counseling routes plus targeted drugs. Future work should test these shared molecules as treatments or markers. Pairing mental profiles with blood markers may sharpen personal risk checks, they argue.
pmc-13576235:
Sema Taskin and co-authors test plain blood counts in children with eye swelling in a 2026 paper. The state, uveitis with no known cause, can threaten sight in children. Few cheap lab marks exist to track how active it runs.

Forty young patients and forty four healthy peers were matched in the study. Counts were read in flare, in calm, and against the healthy group. Patients with burns of other kinds were left out to keep the signal clean. Ratios drawn from white cells and platelets may serve as a low cost gauge of flare state for clinics.
pmc-13576435:
Delal Bektas, Giuseppe Lanzino, Stephen Graepel, and Kelly Flemming follow one patient whose brainstem growth slowly caused a rare kind of nerve decay on both sides. The growth, a cavernous malformation in the pons, can bleed and break a triangle of nerve paths. When that loop breaks, a relay station swells and decays, a change called hypertrophic olivary degeneration.

A 70-year-old woman was scanned over four years with no surgery. At first the decay sat on one side and she felt nothing. As the growth crossed the midline, the decay spread to both sides, and she developed an unsteady walk and a shaking palate. The case ties scan change to late symptoms.
pmc-13576935:
Pingping Liu and eight co-authors present a 2026 study on gut damage caused by iodine-125 seed treatment, a therapy that places tiny radioactive seeds near tumors. When seeds sit near the colon, some patients develop radiation colitis, a painful swelling of the bowel. The team asked how gut microbes and host gene activity together drive this harm.

In mice given the seeds, the bowel lining showed clear damage and weaker barrier proteins. Levels of several swelling signals rose. Gut microbe mixes shifted, with some helpful groups falling and others rising, while many host genes changed their activity. Combined analysis linked specific microbes to gene changes and to the damage seen. The authors caution that proof of cause still needs direct tests, but microbe-based care is a plausible next step.
pmc-13577035:
Bora Jin and co-authors compare sleep and autonomic function in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy, two disorders with overlapping faults in both areas. Published in 2026, the study reviews 136 patients with Parkinson's and 67 with multiple system atrophy, all drug naive and all with sleep complaints. Each had a sleep study, autonomic tests, and a heart scan.

The atrophy group had lighter deep sleep, more breathing pauses, lower oxygen lows, and bigger blood pressure drops on standing. The Parkinson's group showed lower uptake on the heart scan. A structural model in the atrophy group tied autonomic dysfunction to sleep disruption far more strongly than in Parkinson's. The authors draw out disease specific patterns.
pmc-13577435:
Saeko Ishibashi and Kazumi Kubota present a two thousand twenty-six viewpoint proposing guardrails for therapy chatbots used by young people with ADHD. Such tools can coach and check in between visits. Risks include bad content, overreliance, silent model changes, and missed crises.

Their framework is led by nurses and sorted by risk tier. Three layers cover policy levers, practical enablers, and measurable outcomes. Child-specific safeguards and human oversight run throughout. Nursing records, from triage to escalations, double as governance data. The proposal aims for access that stays safe and fair across clinic, school, and home.
pmc-13577535:
Liu and seven colleagues map the shared gene roots of psoriasis and metabolic syndrome in twenty twenty-six. The skin disease and the cluster of weight, sugar, and blood pressure risks often occur in the same people. The team merged large gene study data for both traits. They added gene activity maps from single cells placed back in tissue.

The two traits shared gene signals across the whole genome and in set regions. Shared risk spots passed cross checks by more than one method. Psoriasis genes lit up most in skin, fat, and liver tissue. The metabolic traits lit up in much the same tissues. The maps give testable leads on why the two go together.
pmc-13577735:
Five plant scientists test whether treating seeds with defense hormones protects the grown plant from pests. Seed priming wakes up stress readiness early, and earlier work showed it helped the model plant Arabidopsis without stunting growth. The team now asks if the benefit reaches a real crop, the Brassica rapa, and whether the machinery is the same in both species.

Both hormones, methyl jasmonate and salicylic acid, raised resistance to a generalist mite and a specialist caterpillar in both species, with no growth cost. Gene and chemistry profiling found shared defense networks but little overlap in the genes and compounds used. In the crop, priming raised salicylic acid under mite attack and switched on mustard-oil defenses under caterpillar feeding. The authors conclude the outward benefit is broad, but the molecular route is tuned by species and pest, so priming recipes should be tailored per crop.
pmc-13577935:
Tetsu Nakaichi and ten co-authors test a camera panel for checking radiation dose during whole-body treatment, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Whole-body irradiation readies patients for transplants, but dose checks usually rely on point sensors that say little about the wider field and add handling to a long session.

Their portable panel sits beyond the patient and reads the beam that passes through. In phantom tests the signal tracked dose and field size with near-perfect linearity, and the field was even across the panel. Calibrations tied the panel's summed signal to dose at the phantom's midline. Independent sensors at many points in a body-shaped phantom checked the estimates. The authors frame the work as groundwork for patient validation.
pmc-13578635:
Miguel Ángel Lammoglia-Villagómez and six co-authors track pregnancy loss in Mexican dairy cattle in this 2026 study. The herd of Holstein cows lives under intensive farming in a temperate semi-arid region. The team split losses into early, mid, and late windows and asked what raises the risk in each.

Records covered 772 pregnancies. Cows that had suffered uterine disease after calving, retained placenta or womb infection, lost pregnancies more often in every window. Cows that had calved before also lost more in the middle window than first time mothers. Survival style analysis agreed: the chance of staying pregnant ran lower for both groups across the whole span. The authors name uterine health and parity as the critical levers.
pmc-13578735:
Gloria Liou and Louis Tay hunt for visible signs of authenticity in recorded job interviews, in a 2026 study. Feeling genuine at work is praised often, yet what genuine looks like on camera was unclear, and self views may clash with viewer views. Mock interviews were run through automated video tools that count words, tense, and speech traits.

People who rated themselves as genuine used more I words and present tense, and spoke in a looser, less polished style. Raters judged others as genuine on quite different cues: more words overall, faster pace, and plainer speech with fewer adverbs. Short sentences linked to both views. No face or voice cues mattered in the recordings. The split warns firms that an interviewer's gut feel may miss how a candidate sees themselves.
pmc-13579035:
Amiyesh Sahay, Caitlin Sears, Mark Faulkner, and Rachael Fothergill ask how many London cardiac arrest patients can actually reach an advanced life-support pathway in time. The treatment, ECPR, puts the patient on a heart-lung machine during resuscitation. London's pathway aims to get eligible patients to a capable center within 45 minutes of the arrest.

From five years of ambulance records, the team found 776 eligible patients. Only three percent were estimated to arrive in time during the pathway's working hours. In many cases the clock ran out before the patient was even ready to move. Stretching the limit to sixty minutes would more than triple the number reached. Longer working hours and wider entry rules would also help, as would more receiving centers. The authors say small design changes could greatly widen access.
pmc-13579235:
Kamboh and seven co-authors pull the weed killer atrazine out of water with a cartridge packed with a zinc oxide and chitosan mix, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Atrazine, a herbicide, lingers in farm runoff and groundwater, so cheap ways to check for it are in demand. The mix is a biopolymer nanocomposite, made by a sol-gel route. Light-based and imaging tools probe what the mix is and how it looks.

At the best settings, the cartridge takes back ninety-eight percent of the atrazine from lab-made water. The cling to the surface fits a first-order rate law on a mixed surface. In real field water and groundwater, the take-back rate hits about seventy percent. A shop-bought cartridge took back just sixty percent from field water. Low cost, a green make, and a strong take all favor the new mix.
pmc-13579435:
Hyeong-taek Woo and Aesun Shin ask in 2026 whether starting a statin after bowel cancer care helps patients live longer. Past studies hinted at a gain, but flaws in how time was counted can fake such a gain.

Using health claims for a whole nation, the pair copy the shape of a fair trial. Patients were sorted by whether they began a statin within six months of first care. Death from the cancer and death from any cause were tracked for five years. Extra checks that plant known flaws on purpose help show whether the main result can be trusted.
pmc-13579835:
Jose Carlos Gasca-Aldama and co-authors write, in a 2026 letter, on a strain gauge for the heart's left pump in grave illness. A study they cite found the length-wise squeeze gauge more fit and more telling than the plain pump share in such patients. A second study cast a fast, over-strong pump as an ill sign in shock. A third found the strain gauge a strong death call in septic shock, where the plain share fails. Yet the letter warns of a big gap to bedside use, on three counts: how truth is gauged, drug effects, and the right pump's role.

One flaw is named first. The cited study smoothed two plain gauges over three to five beats, but read the strain gauge from one beat. In fast or wild hearts, that unbalance can skew the clash.
pmc-13580035:
Ana Fernandez-Agudo, Maria del Carmen Gonzalez-Caballero, and Jose Tarazona argue in 2026 for a new way to judge chemical risk. People meet complex mixes of chemicals in food, goods, and the world around them every day.

The old way of judging risk rests on fixed thresholds and animal tests, which miss real life spread, mix effects, and groups at high risk. The authors back a next generation method that turns lab evidence into chance based estimates of harm. Pathways link tiny cell changes to health at the scale of whole populations. The method also separates groups that are sensitive by life stage from groups left exposed by illness or high contact.
pmc-13580335:
Hannah Hart and co-authors present a 2026 study on hospital deaths in children with leukodystrophies. These genetic diseases attack the brain's white matter. Why some children die in hospital was poorly charted. The team mined a national children's hospital database for 2016 to 2024. It found 613 patients across 15 disease types.

Thirty-two children, about five percent, died as inpatients. Three diseases made up most deaths: Krabbe disease, adrenoleukodystrophy, and metachromatic leukodystrophy. Hospitals that saw more such patients had lower death rates. Girls died at higher rates than boys in raw counts. Black, Asian, and multiracial children also died more often than White children, though small numbers blur certainty. The authors call for work on those gaps.
pmc-13580535:
Dmitry Budker and three co-authors reflect on a century of spin in physics in a 2026 paper. Spin, a built-in twist of particles, has probed nature's deepest rules for one hundred years. The authors trace its role from early quantum theory to today's sharpest tests of the standard model.

Magnetic and electric dipole moments get close attention for what they reveal about symmetry rules. Searches for exotic spin-based forces may expose the nature of dark matter. The review also links spin studies to the geometry of spacetime itself. Short episodes throughout show spin still opening fresh views on basic questions. The piece serves as both history and research guide.
pmc-13580835:
Cancer care eats time: travel, waiting rooms, infusions, and chores at home that never appear on a bill. Gabrielle Rocque and co-authors measure that hidden workload objectively in a 2026 study of 110 patients.

For twenty-eight days, a phone app tracked location and motion while daily surveys logged care tasks at home. Patients recorded nearly six hundred trips for care. Lab-only visits were quick, but visits mixing labs with treatment ran a median of almost three hours door to door. Infusion patients carried heavier loads than pill-only patients, both at the facility and at home, where scheduling and symptom care took hours. The authors argue this time cost should shape how care is organized.
pmc-13581435:
Ioannis Adamopoulos and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how climate justice and the One Health framework appear in policies for adapting to climate change. One Health treats human, animal, and environmental health as one connected web. Following scoping review guidelines, the team searched databases and global health resources for work from 2005 to late October 2025.

From close to twenty thousand hits, just eight studies met the criteria. They span countries such as Pakistan, the United States, and Greece, plus worldwide analyses. The review finds that climate harms fall hardest on poor and marginalized groups, who have the least means to cope. Health voices remain weak in national adaptation plans, and plans tend to be fragmented or skewed toward cutting emissions over coping with effects. The authors call for shared measures of who is at risk, stronger joint work across fields, better early warnings, and more capacity building.
pmc-13581535:
Dan Li and co-authors trace, in a 2026 study, a possible chain from a lasting industrial chemical to an irregular heartbeat condition. The chemical, known as PFOA, lingers in the environment and has been linked to heart problems. What connects it to atrial fibrillation at the molecular level was unclear. The team combined gene databases, genetic analysis, computer modeling, and lab cell tests to hunt for a middleman.

One candidate stood out: complement factor B, part of the immune system's complement arm. Genetic evidence tied higher levels of this protein to greater fibrillation risk. In heart muscle cells grown in the lab, the chemical raised the protein's levels, and silencing its gene blunted the effect. The authors present the protein as a plausible link worth deeper testing.
pmc-13581735:
Gopal Nambi and six co-authors published a trial report in 2026 on treating painful shoulders in university volleyball players. Repeated overhead smashing often jams shoulder structures, a problem called subacromial impingement. Steroid injections calm pain quickly and hands-on mobilization restores mechanics, but whether the pair beats mobilization alone in young athletes was untested with imaging outcomes included.

Sixty male players aged eighteen to twenty-five were split evenly between the combined treatment and mobilization alone. Pain, movement range, and function were scored over six months. Scans tracked the space under the shoulder bone and the thickness of tendon and bursa. The design gives coaches and clinicians a fair test of whether adding one injection earns its cost.
pmc-13582435:
Neil Paprocki and Courtney Conway ask why bird species split by so wide a range in how far they migrate. Their 2026 study tests what seven mechanistic hypotheses say will take place. It uses data from tracking and traits of each species.

Four hundred forty-six migratory bird species, from across the world, were read with Bayesian phylogenetic methods that set species side by side. Breeding latitude was linked, in a positive way, with migration distance, as was thought in advance. Once that was held in check, body mass and the supply of food by season were linked, in a negative way, with distance. Wing elongation and soaring flight were linked, in a positive way. The link for body mass hung on how the birds flew and on the size of their winter group. It was most strong for species that flap, and that winter in small groups.
pmc-13582535:
Ying and co-authors study what drives secondary school students in China to learn English on their own. The team links four factors: beliefs about learning, confidence, classroom enjoyment, and self directed learning skill. Their 2026 survey drew 1,939 students from 11 provincial level regions.

Beliefs were strongly tied to self directed learning skill. Confidence carried part of that link, acting as a middle step between beliefs and skill. Classroom enjoyment strengthened the path from beliefs to confidence. As a result, the indirect link through confidence grew stronger when enjoyment was high. The authors say beliefs, confidence, and enjoyment all deserve attention in English teaching. The study used standard survey scales for each of the four factors.
pmc-13583035:
Qin and coauthors test a plant oil part that may ease liver scarring. Liver scarring grows when star-shaped liver cells switch on. A low-oxygen path drives self-cleaning in those cells. That cleaning flow may help scars form and persist.

The team used rats with chemical liver harm and lab liver cells. They gauged scar marks and cleaning flow in both models. The plant compound cut scar marks in the tests. It blocked the low-oxygen cleaning path in star cells. Those cells then died at a higher rate. Dead star cells mean less scar tissue can form.
pmc-13583235:
Menghan Li and co-authors build an at-home blood test around a smart gel coating in a 2026 paper. Electric sensors foul quickly in real blood and serum, which blurs their signals, and preparing them is fiddly. Their coating mixes seaweed gel, a slippery polymer, and graphene; a splash of calcium sets it on the electrode in about a minute, blocking stray sticking while letting current through.

A magnet-guided holder pulls target-bound magnetic beads onto the coated sensor, giving a reading within twenty-five minutes. Averaging the signal over a steady stretch cut its wobble to 3.4 percent. Three patient groups validated the platform, on a heart attack marker in serum, tiny cell vesicles in plasma, and an inflammation marker in fingertip blood, all matching reference results closely.
pmc-13583335:
Kelsey Clements and Leslie Griffith test whether a key learning protein must be freshly made at synapses for new growth to appear. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. In fruit fly larvae, spaced stimulation sprouts immature contact points called ghost boutons.

The protein, CaMKII, helps form those sprouts and can be built locally at the synapse. The team blocked only that local building, in nerve cells or in muscle, by trimming the gene's tail region. Sprouting stayed normal either way. Blocking the signals that trigger local building also changed nothing. Removing the protein from muscle did cut sprouting, while nerve removal did not. Steady supply, not fresh local supply, is what counts.
pmc-13583435:
Chaoqun Zhang and a large team of co-authors review fluopyram, a widely used farm fungicide, in a 2026 paper. The chemical blocks an energy enzyme in fungi and also kills some worms, which made it popular across cereals, fruits, and vegetables.

The review follows the chemical through soil and water and into living things. In non-target species it can cause death, energy failure, oxidative stress, and slow development. Fungal resistance has already appeared in several populations. The authors link older, scattered findings on power, fate, and toxicity into one account. They flag gaps on breakdown products and long-term exposure, and urge resistance monitoring.
pmc-13583835:
Music therapy eases chemotherapy's grind for many breast cancer patients, but each woman responds in her own way, and group averages erase that. Filippo Giordano and eleven co-authors lay out a 2026 pilot protocol in two Italian centers that tests the therapy one patient at a time.

Twenty-four women on adjuvant chemotherapy will alternate four-week blocks with and without music therapy, in random order, so each becomes her own control. Sessions mix listening, active music-making, and personal playlists, an hour a week. The pilot's real targets are feasibility: dropout, missing data, and whether the crossover rhythm works in clinic. If it does, the design offers a template for personal-effect trials.
pmc-13584135:
Dianqin Sun and co-authors model Helicobacter pylori trends and disease burden in China in a 2026 review and Bayesian study. This stomach germ is the top cause of stomach cancer and peptic ulcers, and China holds a huge share of infections.

Close to two hundred studies fed a model of age-specific infection from 1990 to 2023. Cohorts born after 1980 caught the germ far less in childhood. Yet total prevalence fell only modestly across the span. The model credits the germ with a large share of stomach cancer cases in 2023. Ulcer burden was also estimated. Health planners get a long view of slow progress and where prevention pays most.
pmc-13584235:
Qiumei Lu and twelve co-authors clone the gene behind Rht4, a dwarfing trait that could give wheat breeders an alternative to the famous Green Revolution genes. Those classic genes resist lodging but demand more water and fertilizer and weaken early vigor. Rht4 works through a different hormone pathway, making it attractive for leaner farming.

The causal gene encodes a membrane kinase in the brassinosteroid signaling pathway. Deleting it dampened that signaling, shortened stems by curbing cell expansion, and lowered active gibberellin levels. The same gene also helped plants tolerate drought, coordinating drought-related genes and physiology under water shortage. A natural variant tied to shorter plants was identified for breeders. The gene thus links height and resilience in one package.
pmc-13584935:
A dairy cow's hardest weeks are the dry period before calving and the first stretch of milking. Three authors profiled 360 healthy Brown Swiss cows across pregnancy and lactation stages and body conditions, measuring classic metabolic markers plus three newer fat-tissue signals and a cell-stress protein.

Stress markers peaked exactly in the danger window: the cell-stress protein, free fatty acids, and urea all topped out in the dry period or early lactation, while two blood proteins sagged. Two of the fat signals rose steadily as pregnancy and lactation advanced, marking successful adaptation once the hard weeks passed. Body condition interacted with stage for every measure. The authors propose reading the new markers together as an early-warning panel for metabolic trouble in the herd.
pmc-13585035:
Axel Kramer and Andreas Enz reply to a letter about a hand hygiene guideline in this 2026 response. The exchange centers on surgical gloves: standard double gloving versus indicator gloves, which show a color change when the outer glove is pierced. The writers argue the two systems protect in different ways and should not be judged by the same measure.

A plain double layer works as a stronger barrier, so counting piercings of the inner glove fits it well. Indicator gloves instead earn their keep by spotting a breach early, so the glove can be changed at once. Reviews found they detect holes two to six times more often than same-color pairs. Proof that they cut wound infections, though, is still limited, and the authors ask guideline writers to keep that split in view.
pmc-13585335:
Tomohiko Nakajima, Iwao Yamaguchi, and Yuki Kinoshita weigh rebuilding hydrogen gear in a 2026 study. Membrane water electrolysis makes low-carbon hydrogen, yet its stacks lean on scarce, heavy-impact parts like iridium and titanium. Stack swaps over a plant's life add up.

Using a benefit ratio that joins climate cost, saved cost, and value-weighted life factors, the team compare fresh builds against rebuilds across repeat cycles. Rebuilds won on balance each time, cut carbon burdens, and kept scarce stack stuff in play at like output. One electrode type ruled the circular value. Design for rebuild, the work argues, belongs in the first sketch.
pmc-13585435:
Attarbaschi and co-authors pool data in 2026 from nine trials to sort which children with a common leukemia type fare best. The type carries extra copies of many chromosomes and is the most frequent gene pattern in childhood blood cancer. It shows in a quarter to a third of cases and most often ends well, yet it still feeds a large share of relapses.

The team drew on more than eleven thousand patients aged 1 to 18, treated between 1998 and 2018. About three thousand held the extra-chromosome pattern. Past groups had each drawn the best subgroup in their own way, with no shared rule. The study tests each past rule in each trial to find which one flags the largest group with the best outcome. The team bills the work as a yardstick for new groups, not a call to ease care yet.
pmc-13585835:
Can Aydogdu and colleagues test a blood test meant to spot bladder cancer spread before surgery in this 2026 study. The test reads tumor DNA floating in the blood, matched to each patient's own tumor. At bladder removal surgery, doctors also take out nearby lymph nodes to check for spread. The step helps staging but adds risk, so a good forecast could spare low-risk patients from it.

Forty patients had the blood test before surgery, and node spread was later found in seven. The test caught most of those cases and, more striking, a negative result was right in the great bulk of cases. Pooling with a past group kept that negative accuracy high. A modeled plan that skipped node removal for negative patients would have missed one case, so the authors call for a larger trial first.
pmc-13586335:
Ulrike Lueken and co-authors ask mental health professionals who have themselves breathed their way into an altered state what the practice is worth. High ventilation breathwork can bring on experiences resembling moderate doses of psychedelic drugs, without any drug at all. That promises a scalable way to study, and maybe use, such states, but its risk-benefit shape was unmapped. Their 2026 study ran forty-eight professionals through a breathwork workshop and surveyed them.

Participants rated the states as strong as those in moderate-dose psychedelic studies. They pointed to internalizing disorders as the plausible targets, and named psychotic, dissociative, and bipolar conditions as reasons to stay away. Perceived promise significantly outweighed expected risk, and open, emotionally moved participants saw the most promise. The authors offer breathwork as a workable non-drug model of psychedelic-like states, with expert-drawn guardrails.
pmc-13586435:
Gonzalo Muñoz and eight co-authors used Chile's long shape, running from tropics to subantarctic, to test whether vitamin D levels track cancer deaths. Blood levels of the vitamin fall as one travels south and sunlight weakens, which the national health survey confirmed across forty-eight provinces. The team set those levels against every cancer death recorded from 2002 to 2020, over 446,000 in all.

Provinces with lower vitamin D had higher death rates for many cancers, most strongly breast, kidney, and liver. After adjusting for body weight and tobacco use, twenty-one of twenty-seven cancer types still showed the inverse link. Endometrial, thyroid, colorectal, liver, kidney, and larynx cancers stood out. Because the study compares places rather than people, the authors call it ecological evidence, consistent with earlier findings for colorectal and breast cancer.
pmc-13586535:
Mathilde Charbonnier and a large team of co-authors study how a dangerous bacterium handles zinc shortage in a 2026 paper. The bacterium is Staphylococcus aureus, a common cause of infection. Hosts starve germs of metals such as iron and zinc as a defense. Small RNA molecules help bacteria adapt to such stress. The team cataloged the small RNAs this bacterium makes when metals run low.

Two RNAs stood out, both controlled by zinc levels. One of them, called ZinS, binds to messages for enzymes that need zinc. It lowers the output of at least one such enzyme. Losing ZinS did not change how much metal the cells held, which points to a zinc saving role. ZinS also codes for a tiny peptide. Gene history shows the RNA grew out of that peptide's gene region in this species group.
pmc-13586635:
Shuman Wang and co-authors studied older adults with cancer in Melbourne in 2026, asking who gets referred for mental health care and why. Many older patients feel deep distress, yet few reach such services, and the reasons staff give are poorly recorded.

The team looked back at records for 557 adults referred to a cancer centre's psychology service and surveyed 18 health staff. Adults under 65 were more likely to be referred than those 65 or older, but both groups took up care at the same rate once referred. Staff said time, resources, and beliefs shaped their choices, while gaps in their own skills were the biggest block. Training for staff is the main fix proposed.
pmc-13587035:
Longji Li and Lifeng Zhang propose a closed-loop digital system for gaming disorder. Gaming disorder, where play escapes a person's control and harms school, work, or social life, is now a recognized diagnosis. Checks today rest on questionnaires and interviews, which freeze a moving problem into a single snapshot taken after the fact. Their review pulls together phone-based tracking, AI risk prediction, and digital therapy into one circle of care.

In the proposed loop, daily signals from behavior, body, mood, and social life feed a model that sorts risk and forecasts its path. When risk climbs, timed micro-interventions land on the person's phone, shaped to their current state. The authors say the loop moves care from one-off testing to constant watching, and from reacting to preventing. Privacy, clear reasoning from the models, and real clinic fit remain open work.
pmc-13587135:
Dan Liu and co-authors study how anxiety ties to poor sleep in people living with HIV, and what carries the link. Sleep trouble and anxiety feed each other, and three inner resources may sit on the path: social support, mental resilience, and a positive coping style. The team surveyed patients at clinics over one winter.

Their 2026 study runs standard scales for insomnia, anxiety, mood, support, coping, and resilience on hundreds of patients. Those with insomnia differed from the rest in age, schooling, work state, and immune counts. Better support, coping, and resilience each went with better sleep, while low mood went with worse. A mediation model tests all three carriers side by side.
pmc-13587235:
Charline Leclercq, Mylène Wespiser, Gaëlle Tachon, Adrien Buisson, Maurice Pérol, and Aurélie Swalduz review blood tests for leftover lung cancer after treatment. Their 2026 review covers non-small cell lung cancer that has not spread widely. Even with surgery and immune therapy, relapse rates stay high in this group.

Tumor DNA in blood, called ctDNA, can flag tiny leftover disease without a biopsy. Such flags could sort patients by risk soon after main treatment. High-risk patients might get stronger follow-up therapy, while low-risk patients skip needless side effects. The review lays out the biology and the two main test designs, with and without tumor data. It also weighs tech and clinic hurdles before routine use.
pmc-13587335:
Yiliminuer Abulajiang and Yumei Wu study an immune brake gene in ovarian cancer in a 2026 paper. The gene, BTLA, helps tumors hide from immune attack in some cancers, but its role in ovarian tumors was unclear. The team mined a large cancer atlas for its gene activity and patient outcomes. Lab assays then checked the gene's levels in real tissue.

The gene ran higher in tumors than in healthy tissue. Its level tied to survival in adjusted models, and to the mix of immune cells inside the tumor. Single-cell data showed which cells carry it and whom they talk to. Drug sensitivity screens and docking studies hint at treatments that could pair with it. The gene may serve as both marker and target.
pmc-13587435:
Morgan and three colleagues are the authors of a study that has now been retracted. The study, first published in two thousand nineteen, looked at two toxins, colibactin and Cnf-1, made by Escherichia coli bacteria. This notice from the journal's editor-in-chief explains why the work was withdrawn. The authors state that they disagree with the decision.

After publication, readers raised concerns about the study's figures. Several figure panels appear to overlap with each other, even though they were meant to show different test conditions. The authors could not give a clear account or the raw data to settle the doubts. The editor says the journal no longer trusts the results. Retractions like this one form part of the public record of how science corrects itself.
pmc-13587535:
Ying Ren and co-authors test pain control without opioids after keyhole surgery on the womb, in a 2026 trial. Opioid pain relief often brings dizziness, nausea, and poor sleep, so the team try a pair of non-opioid drugs, esketamine and dexmedetomidine, given through a patient-controlled pump. They compare it with a standard opioid pump in 132 women.

Pain scores over the first two days were just as good in the opioid-free group, meeting the trial's bar for equal performance. Recovery quality scores ran clearly higher in that group, by 8 points on the scale used, driven by comfort and mood. Pain scores alone were alike, and no serious side effects occurred in either group. The opioid-free mix looks like a sound option for this surgery, the team conclude.
pmc-13587835:
Katri Vainionpää and eleven colleagues present a 2026 study on a chemical imbalance inside eyes going blind from retinitis pigmentosa. The inherited disease kills light-sensing cells by many genetic routes, and no treatment exists. Dopamine, a signal chemical that tunes retinal circuits, had been hinted to misbehave during degeneration; two mouse models let the team measure it directly.

From infancy through adulthood, diseased retinas carried too much dopamine and too much of its raw material, and the gene for its main factory enzyme ran hot. The cleanup enzyme worked overtime as well, and a broader gene scan showed the whole dopamine system drifting. The authors say this early, persistent excess deserves study as a contributor to retinal decline.
pmc-13588135:
Xiaofei Wu and co-authors model how liver-targeted gene silencers act across species and targets over time. Their 2026 study deals with small RNA drugs tied to a sugar tag that homes to the liver. Such drugs act long, but how their action scales from mice to humans, and how the target gene sways it, stayed murky. The team pooled public time-course data for thirty such drugs across four species, from mice to humans, and fit one shared model.

Human action lasted longer in the body's active zone, while the dose needed ran lower than in test species. One model part, the turnover of the effect, held steadier within a target than the potency part. The frame should help forecast human action early.
pmc-13588235:
Sameer Kassem reviews how obesity treatments perform in daily practice, in a 2026 paper. Trials show these treatments work, yet real-world results are often weaker. Gaps in access, side effects, and weak long-term support all play a part. Kassem searched the medical literature through mid-2026 for studies of adults and teens with excess weight, and weighed how well people stick with each option.

Strict lifestyle plans yield about five percent weight loss, but drop-out and regain are common once a plan ends. New hormone-based drugs give large losses in trials, though real-world gains shrink when doses stall or gut side effects bite. Older drugs are cheap but often dropped for side effects. Surgery gives the largest, longest loss yet stays little used, with gaps by race and income. The review urges support that lasts as long as the treatment does.
pmc-13588635:
Borja Ibanez and Xavier Rossello reply in 2026 to comments on their analysis of the REBOOT trial, which tested beta-blockers after heart attack in patients whose heart pumping fraction was not reduced. Their reply argues that use of these drugs after myocardial infarction should follow indication, ejection fraction, and current evidence rather than habit.

The authors agree the trial's conclusions apply only to patients like those enrolled. The trials excluded anyone with another reason for beta-blockers. Such reasons include heart failure, reduced ejection fraction, or a need for rate control in atrial fibrillation. REBOOT therefore does not support stopping beta-blockers in all heart attack patients. It challenges only routine use when the recent heart attack is the sole reason, in stable, revascularised patients. The first step in any reduction, they argue, is reassessing why the drug was prescribed, with hypertension needing specific consideration.
pmc-13589335:
Maria Markus and co-authors ask whether a scan taken after treatment can foretell a cervical cancer's return, in a 2026 study. Women with locally advanced disease receive chemotherapy with radiation, and response is checked with PET-CT scans that light up sugar-hungry tissue. Doctors usually read the brightest spot's intensity. The team suspected volume measures, how much tissue glows in total, might predict better.

They re-analysed scans from 133 patients, before and after treatment, extracting intensity plus two volume-based measures across tumours, nodes, and spread sites. Responses were classed as complete, partial, or worse by each measure. Follow-up then showed which readings actually tracked recurrence and survival. The study aims to sharpen the post-treatment conversation: whose scan says cured, and whose says watch closely.
pmc-13589535:
Yuya Fukuda and four co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare stress fracture in a teen baseball pitcher. Overuse injuries of the chest part of the spine are uncommon in young athletes. A stress break at the growth zone of the first chest bone is rarer still.

The patient was a 13-year-old elite pitcher with pain at one spot in his upper back and no injury event. Scans showed an open growth zone with rough edges and swollen bone, which fit the diagnosis. He rested his upper body, then built back to throwing step by step. His pain cleared, and he pitched in games again about twelve weeks after the pain began.
pmc-13589735:
Four authors led by Dora Gjirlic study how a cell scaffold protein steers muscle cell growth and merging. Muscle fibres form when young cells exit their growth cycle, switch genes on, and fuse into tubes. A protein family that trims the cell inner scaffold, called cofilin, helps that shape change. Two forms of the protein trade places as growth runs, yet their split jobs were unclear.

Mouse muscle cells in dishes showed one form falling and the other rising as growth ran. Loss of the first form warped cell shape, stalled cycle exit, and cut tube growth sharply. Loss of the second form did far less harm early on. A mild cut of the first form helped cells fuse, while a deep cut harmed growth. Dose, not just presence, rules the protein role. A partner enzyme tunes it in waves.
pmc-13590135:
Hongxin Luo and co-authors designed new antifungal compounds from natural furan acids in a 2026 study. The targets are fungi that attack crops, and the compounds aim at an enzyme the fungi need to breathe, called succinate dehydrogenase. Blocking it is a proven fungicide strategy.

The team synthesized a series of furan amide variants and tested them against four plant-pathogenic fungi in dishes. Adding a trifluoromethyl group gave the strongest effects. One compound beat the standard agent against the rice pathogen Rhizoctonia solani, and another led against Fusarium oxysporum. Greenhouse-style tests confirmed both front-runners actually protect plants, not just petri dishes.
pmc-13590235:
Xianzhen Zhou and five co-authors published a 2026 study of how teens with ADHD carve a stream of experience into events. The brain constantly segments life into episodes to guide action, and ADHD involves trouble organizing behavior over time. Seventy-three teens with ADHD and 73 matched peers watched a movie and marked where they felt one event end and another begin, while brainwaves were recorded. The team tracked the background rhythm of the brain signals moment by moment.

Both groups found the real transitions, but the control teens reacted more keenly to social and spatial changes. Around boundaries, the ADHD group over-stabilized before the shift and re-engaged too weakly after it. In that group only, weaker re-engagement tied to poorer segmentation. The authors link everyday disorganization in ADHD to this imbalance in brain dynamics.
pmc-13590935:
Immune problems are suspected in Alzheimer's disease, but which parts of the antibody family matter has been unclear. Shihui Peng and co-authors combine human genetics with blood-marker data to test three antibody classes — IgG, IgA, and IgM — against Alzheimer's risk. Genetic methods that mimic a natural experiment pointed one way, and risk scores built in one large programme were checked in the UK Biobank and two Wisconsin cohorts against brain-related blood markers.

Higher IgM, as proxied by genes, was linked again and again to lower Alzheimer's risk. It also went with a healthier amyloid ratio and lower levels of a phosphorylated tau marker tied to disease. No steady pattern appeared for IgG or IgA. The authors suggest that IgM-based immunity may protect against Alzheimer's and deserves study for early prevention, while noting the evidence is genetic and indirect.
pmc-13591335:
Stomach tumours shed tiny sacs that carry notes to other cells, and those notes can help the tumour grow new blood paths and spread. Shaoxiong Bai and co-authors trace one such note in a 2026 study. The sacs from stomach tumour cells, but not from sound stomach cells, ran rich in a growth signal.

That signal woke mast cells, which drifted in, burst their stores, and freed a cutter enzyme. The enzyme switched on a growth path in blood path cells and raised a vessel growth factor. In mice, tumour sacs sped spread to the lungs and new vessel growth. A drug that blocks the signal's dock cut both. The team marks the sac to mast cell chain as a drug target.
pmc-13592035:
Tooth decay in small children runs high across Southeast Asia, and snacks are a prime suspect. Phue Han and five co-authors test which snack habits track with how bad the decay gets in Myanmar. Their 2026 study draws on a cohort of 815 children aged four and five at eight preschools in Yangon.

Each child's worst tooth was scored on a six-step scale of decay. Parents filled forms on the child's snack type, how often snacks come, when they come, and whether the child pockets food in the cheek. Home traits and wealth are in the mix as well. The team then weighs each habit's link to the decay score. Such detail can aim health advice at the habits that count, not at snacks in the abstract.
pmc-13592135:
Farhanah and co-authors describe a late diagnosis of Noonan syndrome in a woman with a severe heart infection. Noonan syndrome is a genetic condition often tied to heart defects present from birth. Such defects raise the risk of infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart lining. Late recognition, common in underserved areas, can let damage advance far.

The patient was a 29-year-old woman from a rural area with no past medical history. She arrived with severe breathlessness, weight loss, and a new heart murmur. Her facial traits, short stature, and broad chest pointed to Noonan syndrome. Scans showed severe leakage of the mitral valve with growths from infection. The case shows the strain late diagnosis places on care teams.
pmc-13592335:
Jianhua Zhao and co-authors review in 2026 how care for patients with many severe injuries at once can be improved in mid level hospitals. Such polytrauma cases strain any system, and smaller hospitals face them with fewer staff and tools. The review gathers world research on workflow, digital tools, and team based care tuned to that setting.

From a search of four databases for 2014 to 2024, 63 studies were kept and analyzed. The team names the main barriers: slow diagnosis, weak coordination between departments, and old emergency steps with needless repeats. They set out a whole process model that links those parts, with digital support at each stage. A clear model gives mid level hospitals a plan to speed care when minutes decide outcomes.
pmc-13593235:
Jing Tian leads a team grading, in 2026, how clearly studies report two stomach staging systems used to flag cancer risk. The OLGA and OLGIM schemes grade stomach lining damage from biopsies, yet papers describe their methods unevenly. Three databases plus citation chasing yielded 155 studies that applied at least one scheme. Two reviewers scored each report on biopsy sampling detail and on how grades turned into stages.

Just under half of the studies read as highly interpretable, a similar share landed in the middle, and a small slice scored low. Stage numbers were common, but the steps behind them often went missing. Tian and the team stress that weak reporting, not proven weak method, blocks comparison across studies, and they urge fuller method sections.
pmc-13593435:
Gabriella Cericola and co-authors evaluate a contrast ultrasound method for liver growths in infants in a 2026 study. The growths are benign blood vessel tumors that can strain the heart and thyroid when extensive. Magnetic resonance imaging is the usual deep look, but it often needs sedation in babies. Ultrasound with a contrast agent offers real-time images without that burden.

The multicenter review covered twenty-four infants seen between 2016 and 2024. In the six who had both scans, ultrasound matched the MRI on lesion size and count. Most treatment choices were in fact based on the ultrasound findings. Blood tests were mostly normal, though a heart stress marker rose in some infants with large disease. The authors support the method as a practical alternative or partner to MRI.
pmc-13594135:

pmc-13599635:

pmc-13601735:

pmc-13610435:

pmc-13612435:

pmc-13613135:

pmc-13614435:

pmc-13614735:

pmc-13619335:

pmc-13630835:

pmc-13630935:

pmc-13631235:

pmc-13631335:

pmc-13632735:

pmc-13633335:

pmc-13633735:
Erick Chamorro Segovia and co-authors study how families make sense of a traffic crash while a loved one lies in hospital, in a 2026 paper from Nicaragua. pmc-13635135:

pmc-13636335:

pmc-13638335:

pmc-13639735:

pmc-13640435:

Once transplanted, the primed cells settled in up to twenty-five times better than earlier cell preparations. pmc-13641535:
Ryosuke Chaya and co-authors join mouse kidney multi layer data with human gene wide scans to find molecules tied to oxalate kidney harm, in a study from 2026. Kidney stones are common, return often, and their roots stay tangled.

Two stood out in human kidney tissue with and without stones. Added gene tests backed the human weight of the set.
pmc-13642035:
A large team led by Johannes Hausharter checks whether Europe's mountain summit plants are shifting toward warmth loving species, and whether warming itself is the driver, in this 2026 study. Both trends are real: communities are thermophilizing, and temperatures are rising. Yet plot by plot the link is weak, especially against the microclimate a plant actually feels. What a plot gained depended more on its substrate and on whether warmth loving colonists lived nearby to move in. pmc-13645735:
Jiaxin Pu and fourteen colleagues map tiny deposits called hard drusen across the outer retina in a Chinese patient group, in a 2026 study from Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center. The authors suggest that checking the outer retina during these scans could help monitor patients at risk, once forward-looking studies confirm the link.
pmc-13646035:
Colin R Tang-Whitmore and eight colleagues follow thirty-six infants with critical congenital heart disease at one children's hospital, in a 2026 study, to see how feeding relates to growth. Meeting the protein goal alone showed no separate link with the growth scores. The authors stress that steady nutrition provision matters for these fragile infants, even when illness makes feeding hard to deliver.
pmc-13646135:

pmc-13646335:
Shao-Chia Chen and co-authors test diabetes drugs in leaner patients using a trial emulation in a study from 2026. pmc-13646835:

pmc-13647235:
Rajneesh Pathania and co-authors catch breast cancer in the act of spread, at a stage most labs miss, in a study from 2026. Loose cancer cells land in fresh organs, but most die or sleep; few grow into full spread. What tips the scale in that brief phase was a blank.

pmc-13648335:

pmc-13650335:

pmc-13650435:

pmc-13651335:

pmc-13651435:

pmc-13651535:

pmc-13651835:

pmc-13653335:

pmc-13653835:

pmc-13654035:

pmc-13654535:

pmc-13654635:

pmc-13655435:

pmc-13655935:

pmc-13657635:

pmc-13657835:

pmc-13661835:

pmc-13665135:

pmc-13668035:

pmc-13669635:

pmc-13670435:

pmc-13673335:

pmc-13675135:

pmc-13675435:

pmc-13675535:

pmc-13675635:
